name: dispatch-table
document:
dispatch-table
function table
jump table
method table
Keep the mapping from a discriminant (opcode, command name, message type, route, key) to the code that handles it in a lookup table, so that choosing the behaviour is a data lookup instead of a branching construct that must be edited for every new case.
Selection is written as a growing if/else or switch chain: each new operation edits the same function, the same case list is repeated wherever the operation is chosen, handling code is entangled with selection logic, and the set of supported operations cannot be enumerated, logged, generated, documented or extended at runtime.
Applies wherever one uniform operation is selected by a key that arrives as data - bytecode and instruction dispatch in interpreters, emulators and VMs, protocol message and RPC method tables, CLI subcommands, HTTP routes, state-machine transitions, file/MIME/payment-method plugin registries. It pays off when the key space is large or open (grown by configuration, by several modules or at runtime), when every handler can share one signature, and when the mapping itself must be introspectable; a small closed set of cases that a compiler can check exhaustively usually prefers pattern matching instead.
Bytecode and instruction dispatch in interpreters, VMs and CPU emulators, where the opcode is either an index into a dense array or a key into a sparse table.
Protocol and message dispatch: one handler per message/notification type or RPC method, keyed by a type tag or a method name.
Command routing in CLIs, shells and admin consoles, where the first argument names the command and the table names the handler.
HTTP routing tables (method and/or path key to controller) and gRPC service method registries.
Plugin and extension registries: modules register a key (file extension, MIME type, payment method, codec) and the core only ever looks it up.
State-machine and rule transitions keyed by (state, event) or by an event type, replacing a nested switch over transition cases.
System-level tables such as syscall tables and interrupt vector tables, where the key is the index of a privilege gateway.
Embedded systems with keypad/soft-key dispatch, where key meanings change per screen and a 2D function-pointer matrix maps (screen, key) to handlers.
Timed-task schedulers where an array of function pointers indexed by timer ID dispatches periodic work, allowing new tasks to be added by editing only the table.
Linux kernel syscall dispatch: the generated sys_call_table array binds syscall numbers to handler entry points, and the entry path bounds-checks and sanitizes the index (array_index_nospec) before the indirect call.
Git's builtin command table: a static cmd_struct commands[] array binds command names to cmd_foo handlers plus setup flags, looked up by get_builtin and executed by run_builtin; adding a builtin is a table entry per the api-builtin guide.
Redis command dispatch: the redisCommandTable binds command names to handler function pointers with arity and flags behind a case-insensitive dict lookup, and COMMAND dumps the live table so clients can discover server capabilities.

name: visitor
document:
visitor
visitor pattern
Represent an operation to be performed on the elements of an object structure, so that new operations can be defined and added over a stable element hierarchy without changing the classes of the elements on which they operate.
A heterogeneous structure (an AST, a document or widget tree, a shape or entity hierarchy) needs many independent operations, and they keep arriving: every new analysis, export format, validation or report adds another method to every element class, mixes unrelated concerns into the data model and forces the hierarchy to be recompiled. Moving the operation into a separate object does not solve it by itself either, because with single dispatch a call like visitor.visit(element) can only select on the visitor's type, never on the element's concrete class.
Applies when the element classes are stable or closed while operations over them are frequent, when the elements must not be edited (third-party, generated or shared model code), when the language offers single dispatch only, and when operations must stay open to other teams or modules. Typical settings: compiler and analyzer passes, document and tree exporters, tree-shaped domain models, and plugin-facing extension points over a class hierarchy.
Compiler and analyzer passes over an AST: type checking, constant folding, liveness analysis, code generation and pretty-printing are separate visitors over the same node classes.
Serializers and exporters over a document object model: HTML, PDF and Markdown renderers, accessibility audits and word counts all walk the same node hierarchy.
Public analysis APIs that let other people add rules without touching the model — the JDK's javax.lang.model.element.ElementVisitor and Roslyn's CSharpSyntaxVisitor are this pattern shipped as stable API.
Geometry, CAD and UI trees where area, bounding box, hit testing, transform and persistence are independent operations over a fixed shape or widget hierarchy.
Metrics, pricing and validation passes over domain models (billing rules, insurance rating, tax) where new report variants must ship without recompiling the entity classes.
Plugin systems where third parties implement operations over a host's object graph and the host enumerates available operations by their visitor type.
Linter and static-analysis rule engines (ESLint, typescript-eslint, clang-tidy): each rule is a visitor over the ESTree or Clang AST, keyed by node type; traversal is driven by the framework and rules are stateless functions with a context/report parameter.
Refactoring and code-rewrite tools (Roslyn CSharpSyntaxRewriter, OpenRewrite): a specialised visitor subclass returns modified nodes, enabling transformations across the tree in a single pass without mutable state.
Database query engines that build, optimise or execute query plans over typed AST nodes (e.g., JPA Criteria API, Hibernate's static metamodel, Apache Calcite's rel nodes): each physical operator or optimisation rule is a visitor over the plan tree.
Automated code transformation and migration frameworks (jscodeshift, codemod): one visitor per transformation script walks the AST and applies replace/edit operations; the same framework hosts hundreds of community-provided scripts.
Babel AST processing: @babel/types and @babel/traverse expose a Visitor object whose methods are keyed by AST node type (e.g., visitIdentifier, visitFunctionDeclaration); plugins return a Visitor that the traverse pipeline applies, supporting :exit suffixes for post-order traversal and selector strings for compound node matching.
OpenRewrite recipe framework: recipes are stateless visitor subclasses over typed AST nodes (Java, Python, YAML, Docker); the framework handles traversal, scope management and patch application, while recipe authors implement only the visit methods for the node types relevant to their transformation.
Abstract syntax tree traversal in program analysis tools: every time a new analysis is needed (security scan, code quality check, dependency finder), it can be implemented as a new visitor without modifying the AST node classes.
Serialization frameworks (XML/JSON marshalling): each serialization format (XML, JSON, YAML) is a separate visitor that walks the object graph and formats it accordingly.
Document conversion pipelines: converting between formats (Markdown to HTML, DOCX to PDF) where each format is a visitor that knows how to render each document element type.
CPython's ast module ships NodeVisitor in the standard library: subclass it with visit_<TypeName> methods, visit() dispatches on the node class name at runtime, generic_visit() descends into children, and the NodeTransformer subclass rewrites trees by returning replacement nodes — returning None deletes the node.
.NET ships System.Linq.Expressions.ExpressionVisitor in the BCL: Expression.Accept(ExpressionVisitor) is the accept() hook, Visit dispatches to VisitBinary/VisitLambda/VisitMethodCall per expression node type, and every LINQ provider subclasses it to inspect or rewrite query trees before translating them to SQL.
clang libTooling: RecursiveASTVisitor<Derived> (a CRTP template) walks the C++ AST via Traverse*/WalkUpFrom*/Visit* hooks dispatched on the node's dynamic type; clang-tidy checks and clang tools are ASTConsumer plus RecursiveASTVisitor pairs — the canonical C++ realisation, replacing the GoF virtual Visitor interface with templates.

name: row-data-gateway
document:
row-data-gateway
row data gateway
row gateway
Give each database row its own in-memory object that mirrors the row's columns and carries the row's own find, insert, update and delete operations, so all data-access code for a table lives in one place instead of being duplicated across the scripts that use it.
SQL text, parameter binding and result-set mapping are re-derived inside every transaction script that touches a table, while the in-memory objects those scripts work with know nothing about the database. No single place knows how one row is read, written and deleted, so a schema change ripples through every script and every new query is another chance to get parameterisation and type conversion wrong.
Applies when business logic is organised as transaction scripts or thin services over a relational schema whose columns map closely to the fields actually used: the gateway mirrors the table structure, no object/relational impedance mismatch is being managed, and identity maps, units of work and lazy loading are either unnecessary or added deliberately as separate patterns. It also fits generated persistence layers, where the gateway classes are produced from schema metadata during the build.
Transaction-script applications (order entry, billing runs, batch imports) where several scripts need the same handful of row-level reads and writes.
CRUD-heavy back-office and admin tooling where a screen edits one row at a time and columns map one-to-one onto form fields.
Legacy or externally owned schemas that must be mirrored rather than reshaped: one gateway per table gives an explicit, reviewable seam between the application and someone else's database.
Generated persistence layers: gateways produced from schema metadata on every build, so the tedious class-per-table work is automated and stays in sync with the schema.
Simple mappings inside an otherwise rich domain model, where a domain object keeps a gateway as its data holder instead of copying field values around.
Reporting and fixture utilities that need reusable, parameterised finders for one table without pulling in a full object/relational mapper.
Laminas\Db\RowGateway and RowGatewayFeature (the official laminas-db implementation) expose one row object with save/delete and can materialize table-query results as row gateways, fitting CRUD screens or transaction scripts that edit individual records.
Zend Framework 1's Zend_Db_Table_Row is a documented legacy row-gateway implementation: table queries return row objects with column access plus save/delete/createRow operations, useful when a simple schema is consumed by row-oriented scripts.
The Go dgw tool generates structs and lightweight Table/Row Data Gateway functions from PostgreSQL metadata, demonstrating the pattern as a code-generation choice when a project wants typed CRUD without a full ORM.

name: protected-system
document:
protected-system
protection proxy
Give a resource exactly one owning object whose published operations are the only way to touch it, so that every access is decided by an authorization check before the resource is used.
A resource - a credential store, a file tree, a socket, a connection pool, a device handle - is referenced from many places. When each use site performs its own permission check, the checks drift, new code paths forget them, and the resource remains reachable as a raw handle, so a missing check cannot even be detected. The recurring trigger: one object can own the resource and clients can be made to hold only that object, so ownership itself can carry the enforcement.
Applies where ownership is expressible in the language or runtime (private field, unexported type, opaque handle, module boundary) and an authorization policy - identity, role, permission, capability - can be evaluated at each public operation. The guard may sit in-process (object or module scope) or at a process/kernel boundary, where the same pattern becomes a real reference monitor; the assurance the implementation can claim depends on which side of that line it lives.
Credential and key stores: an in-process vault owns the keys and exposes only operations (sign, decrypt, rotate), so callers never receive the secret material.
Storage gateways: a library owns the directory handle or object-store client and applies path and tenant rules on every operation instead of handing out a raw client.
Pools: the pool owns its connections and leases checked-out views, so a caller cannot keep, share or resurrect a connection the pool must reclaim.
Multi-tenant data access: a tenant-scoped repository wrapper pins the tenant filter and refuses operations that would query outside it.
Device and driver access: a supervisor object owns the device handle and validates commands, or a privileged daemon owns the socket and checks each request from an unprivileged client.
Module-level boundaries: a package exports only the guard type and keeps the resource unexported, so code outside the package cannot even name the protected representation.
Linux Landlock: a kernel-enforced ruleset restricts a process and its future children to explicitly allowed filesystem or network rights, placing mediation below application code.
Kubernetes RBAC: the API server evaluates Roles and bindings for each API request, mediating verbs and resources instead of exposing the cluster's backing store to clients.
HashiCorp Vault policies: authenticated tokens are checked against path and capability rules before secret operations, while the storage backend remains behind the Vault service.

name: model-view-intent
document:
model-view-intent
mvi
Structure one UI feature as a single loop in which every user interaction becomes an intent value, a pure reduce step derives the next immutable state from the previous state and that intent, and the view renders only that state - so the screen's behaviour is determined by data instead of by scattered event handlers.
Presentation state is spread across the view, its presenter and several observable channels: every handler sets its own field or widget directly, a loading flag, a data field and an error field can contradict each other, the view keeps state of its own that a configuration change or process death destroys, and no state transition can be exercised without instantiating the UI.
Interactive applications with a declarative view layer and some reactive runtime - Android/Compose with coroutines and Flow, SwiftUI, React, Scala.js, or a hand-rolled event loop - where one screen or app-level feature can own a single immutable state object, user events can be represented as data values, and the view can re-render from a new state value. It is applied per feature, not per widget, and it is independent of any particular framework.
A search or feed screen where loading, empty, error and result states are concurrent flags in the old design and must become one state value the view can render without contradictions.
Complex screen flows - checkout, wizards, media players, editors - whose transitions must be explicit and reviewable rather than emerging from scattered handler code.
Screens that must survive configuration changes or process death by restoring one serializable state object instead of replaying a history of view commands.
Crash reports and support cases that carry the current state plus the last intent, making reproduction and replay possible without reproducing the exact tap sequence.
Cross-platform features that share the reducer between platforms and swap only the view layer (Android and iOS, web and desktop).
Large applications where each feature module exposes an intent/state contract and different teams own the loop for their screens.
A Cycle.js component whose DOM and HTTP driver streams become intents, whose model derives state, and whose view renders that state is a direct stream-based MVI implementation.
A Kotlin Multiplatform feature built with Orbit MVI can share an OrbitContainer's intent, reduce, state, and side-effect flow across Android, iOS, and desktop.
An Android Jetpack Compose feature following Android's official unidirectional-data-flow guidance can use a ViewModel-owned immutable UiState, upward events, and downward rendering as a framework-native MVI realization.

name: page-controller
document:
page-controller
model-1
Give each logical page or form its own input controller that handles the requests addressed to it — reading the request, invoking domain logic and choosing the view — instead of routing every request through one shared handler.
Dynamic pages repeat the same request handling: parse and validate the incoming request, call domain logic, pick a view, report errors. Without a per-page home for that logic it either spreads into templates or gets copied into every script; the recurring decision is whether one page or form owns its request handling, or whether a central controller multiplexes all of them.
Server-side web presentation where URLs map one-to-one onto logical pages, forms or actions: CGI programs, servlets and JSP pages, controller actions, Razor Pages, route handlers in micro-frameworks. It fits sites whose pages share little behaviour, page-focused areas of larger applications, and frameworks whose native unit is a page; it stops fitting as soon as most pages need the same authentication, internationalisation, layout or tracing.
Small to medium websites where each page has its own URL, its own data and its own template (CMS front ends, marketing pages with forms, internal tools).
Form-heavy areas where one page owns one interaction end to end: show the form, validate the submission, run one workflow, render the result.
Prototypes and scripting-era deployments where one program, servlet or route function per page is the natural deployment unit.
Page-focused corners of a larger application (account settings, an admin console) whose pages genuinely differ from one another.
Frameworks whose canonical unit is the page itself: Razor Pages (PageModel = Page Controller), ASP.NET Web Forms code-behind, Java Struts Actions, Django FBV (Function-Based Views) mapped one-per-URL, Flask route functions, PHP single-file-per-page.
Per-page Ajax callbacks that are tightly coupled to a specific page's data and logic, where extracting them into a shared controller would create artificial coupling.
Situations where page-specific code is large enough to warrant a dedicated class but small enough that a full command-object framework is overkill.
ASP.NET Core Razor Pages: each PageModel owns the handlers and view data for one page, with OnGet/OnPost methods providing a concrete page-controller unit for page-specific forms. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/razor-pages/?view=aspnetcore-10.0
Django function-based views: URLconf maps a URL pattern to one Python view function that receives HttpRequest and returns the page response, making small page-specific interactions explicit. https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/6.1/topics/http/views/
Flask route functions: the route decorator binds a URL and HTTP methods to one view function, a lightweight Page Controller shape for independent pages and forms. https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/quickstart/

name: attorney-client
document:
attorney-client
attorney pattern
attorney-client friendship idiom
Grant a named collaborator a deliberately narrow compile-time view of a class's private interface by making an attorney the client's sole friend; the attorney forwards selected operations or re-exports selected private nested types (often through controlled public typedefs), while unrelated private members and the public contract remain closed.
A C++ collaborator may need one private hook, constructor, iterator adapter or nested implementation type, but a friend class receives every private and protected member. Making the hook public leaks it to every caller; publishing a std::list<T>::iterator or the container type leaks representation and its invalidation contract; pImpl hides representation from everyone but does not grant one collaborator a typed privileged view. The missing mechanism is a small attorney contract that names exactly the operations or nested types this collaborator may use without turning the private interface into a second public API.
Object-oriented code whose encapsulation boundary is a class and whose language offers class- or scope-level access control but no per-collaborator grant - C++ with friend declarations, Java/C#/Kotlin with package, assembly or module access, and their test- and library-extension scenarios. It applies at object scope, where one type owns the implementation and one named collaborator needs a slice of it, and it is a source-level structuring device checked by the compiler, never a runtime protection mechanism.
White-box test access: a test harness reaches one private hook or state view through a named attorney instead of making the member public or redefining private with a test-only preprocessor switch.
Iterator adapters: Boost.Iterator's iterator_core_access is a canonical gateway class a user-defined iterator befriends, so iterator_facade and its operators reach private dereference/increment/advance core functions while those implementation hooks stay out of the iterator's public API.
Serialization: Boost.Serialization has serializable classes befriend boost::serialization::access, whose gateway reaches the private serialize() member so archives can reconstruct state without a public serialization method.
Private nested type exposure: LLVM's SchedulerInternalsAttorney publishes the selected nested Scheduler::BndlSchedState as a public type alias and supplies narrow static accessors for unit tests, without publishing every Scheduler private type.
A pImpl-backed adapter that must inspect one implementation-owned type: keep the public class opaque and put the attorney definition in the adapter or test header, so the privileged component gets a typed view without making the implementation part of the ordinary public contract.
Iterator facade over a hidden list-like representation: expose a stable nested iterator/view type through an attorney rather than publishing std::list<T>::iterator, so the owner can replace the container without promising its node and invalidation details to every caller.
Private virtual hooks: an attorney forwards one private virtual operation through a base reference, allowing the derived override to run even though friendship is not inherited.
Factory or construction control: a builder reaches one private constructor or initialization hook through an attorney, while unrelated callers still cannot construct an object through that path.
Spacecraft flight software (fsfw): LocalDpManagerAttorney keeps fetchPoolEntry and getMutexHandle as private static forwarders and befriends only LocalPoolVariable and LocalPoolVector, so the local data pool manager opens its internals to two named collaborators instead of every class that might befriend it.
Simulator tree traversal (Sandia Sparta Modeling Framework): sparta::TreeNodePrivateAttorney exposes TreeNode's private child vectors and subtrees through static accessors (getAllChildren, getChild, findChildren) for internal Reports and Pipeout processing, with a documented 'should NOT be used by simulation developers' restriction in place of an enforceable caller limit.

name: pipeline
document:
pipeline
assembly line
processing pipeline
Decompose a transformation into an ordered sequence of named stages that each consume the previous stage's output and produce the next stage's input, so the workflow reads top to bottom and every step can be tested, instrumented, reordered or replaced on its own.
A multi-step transformation is written as one long function or a tangle of nested calls: the steps are unnamed, their order is implicit in statement order, intermediate values need throwaway names, there is no seam at which a single step can be logged, tested or replaced, and the same sequence is retyped at every call site that needs it.
Processing that naturally decomposes into successive transformations of the same payload - request handling, ETL, compiler passes, message enrichment, image or byte-stream processing - whether the payload is a single value or a stream. It fits in-process, staged execution where one driver owns ordering, error handling and cancellation; distributing the stages across processes, transports and independently deployed filters is the architectural pipe-and-filter pattern instead.
Request handling: deserialise, authenticate, validate, enrich, persist and render a request, with each step named so a failing stage is attributable and testable in isolation.
ETL and data import: extract, clean, transform, validate and load large files as a stream, so no intermediate collection is materialised and memory stays bounded.
Compiler and interpreter passes: source, tokens, AST, resolution, optimisation and code emission, where each pass is an independent stage over the intermediate representation and the pass list is the pipeline.
Message enrichment in an integration flow: unwrap, translate, enrich and route a message, one stage per concern, with per-channel ordering; the cross-process version stays pipe-and-filter.
Image or byte-stream processing: decode, crop or resize, watermark and encode, lazily per frame or chunk, optionally overlapping stages across cores.
Configuration-driven data cleaning: the stage list is assembled from configuration or a plugin registry so different tenants get different ordered steps without changing the stages themselves.
TensorFlow tf.data input pipelines: tf.data.Dataset pipelines that chain map, prefetch, parallel_interleave and shuffle stages to feed a training loop efficiently, with each stage independently configurable and the whole pipeline testable in isolation.
LLM token streaming: HTTP server-sent event streams where an LLM produces tokens at inference speed while clients consume at variable network speed; stream.pipeline() prevents the inference server from buffering unbounded tokens in memory when a slow client disconnects (Node.js stream backpressure case study).
Observability telemetry pipelines: OpenTelemetry Collector chains receivers, processors (memory_limiter, batch, filter, transform, tail_sampling) and exporters for traces, metrics and logs, with connectors (e.g., spanmetrics) bridging signal types and memory_limiter placed first to prevent OOM before filtering.
Typed TypeScript pipeline with schema validation: Zod or io-ts schemas define the stage contract at each boundary, catching schema violations at the exact stage that produced bad data rather than at a distant consumer.
Async generator pipelines in Python: asyncio queues with bounded capacity connect async generator stages, propagating backpressure by pausing producers when the queue is full; the FinStream analytics case study showed 82% memory reduction and 99.7% latency reduction versus unbounded buffering.
Event-streaming pipelines with Kafka and Flink: producers, topic partitions, Flink consumers and checkpointing form a distributed pipeline where backpressure cascades across every boundary; the Kafka max.block.ms and Flink backpressure.sample.interval settings interact under partition saturation and must be tested together under load.
Dynamic pipeline parallelism: construct-and-run pipelines (MapReduce, Spark) fix stage count at construction, while on-the-fly pipelines (Cilk-P Piper algorithm) allow the structure to emerge at runtime, varying per iteration and supporting data-dependent branching; on-the-fly enables pipelines like x264 that cannot be expressed with a fixed static structure.
LLVM compiler pass pipelines: PassBuilder assembles ModulePassManager, CGSCCPassManager, FunctionPassManager and LoopPassManager across the IR hierarchy (Module → CGSCC → Function → Loop), with registered callbacks injecting passes at named extension points (pipeline-start, vectorizer-start, optimizer-last); incorrect PreservedAnalyses declarations invalidate all downstream analyses.
Continuous data pipelines at scale (Google model): periodic pipelines run on cron and suffer from depth growth and resource exhaustion as organic load increases; continuous pipelines (master-slave or event-triggered) replace idle-waiting with always-on processing, eliminating the 'pipeline vs cron' discontinuity at the cost of operational complexity.
ML pipeline orchestration (Airflow, Kubeflow, Prefect, Dagster): each orchestrator applies the pipeline pattern at the workflow level - Airflow's DAG-of-tasks, Kubeflow's per-container-step pipelines with GPU scheduling, Prefect's monoflow/subflow/orchestrator pattern, and Dagster's software-defined assets where asset dependencies imply the pipeline; the pipeline is the scheduler's unit of execution, not an implementation detail.
Apache Beam: PCollections flow through composable PTransforms (ParDo, Combine and GroupByKey) in a pipeline graph, making each transform boundary explicit while the runner handles execution.
Node.js stream.pipeline(): Readable, Transform and Writable stages compose with built-in backpressure, error propagation and AbortSignal cancellation; this is a concrete streaming realization, not a durable workflow engine.

name: watchman
document:
watchman
dead man's switch
heartbeat monitor
Detect that a message flow has gone silent - not that a message failed - and tell a responsible person or system within a bounded time by comparing each flow's arrivals against the cadence its business deadline implies.
Message systems fail silently in the one way no error handler observes: nothing arrives. A producer stops emitting, a consumer stops draining, a scheduled job never fires, a credential expires, a partition goes offline - and because no failing code path is ever entered, error dashboards stay green while downstream data quietly goes stale. The recurring trigger: a flow whose absence is business-visible (a nightly feed, an order stream, a partner interface) has no owner-facing signal for 'no messages', so the gap is discovered late - by a customer or a downstream job - instead of by the team that can fix it.
Applies wherever messages are expected on a knowable cadence (event streams, queues, batch hand-offs, partner interfaces, device check-ins) and their absence is a business-visible failure: the flow has an owner, the expected period and grace window can be derived from a downstream deadline, and either the transport can be observed passively (queue counters, a wire tap) or the producers can emit out-of-band heartbeats. The watchman sits at message-flow or boundary scope - an in-process watcher beside the consumer, a periodic sweep over persisted last-seen state, or a rule in the monitoring stack fed by metrics - and it must itself be watched, because a silent watchman is exactly the failure it exists to catch.
Nightly batch or ETL feed: page the integration owner when the 02:00 import has produced no messages by its deadline, instead of noticing an empty report at the morning stand-up.
Business-critical event stream (orders, payments, telemetry): alarm when the produce rate stays at zero through business hours, which separates a healthy quiet topic from a stopped producer.
External partner interface: notify when no messages have arrived from a B2B partner within the agreed window, turning a looming SLA breach into an early, actionable alert.
Long-running workflow stage: require a heartbeat from each process-manager step so a stuck instance is noticed before the surrounding batch closes or a compensation becomes necessary.
Retry or dead-letter pump: verify that the pump still drains failed messages - silence means the pump died, not that the backlog is empty.
Fleet check-ins (edge devices, agents, cron jobs on many hosts): raise a per-device or per-site alarm when scheduled check-ins stop arriving.
The alerting pipeline itself: an always-firing watchdog alert routed to an external service, so a broken alert path is discovered by its silence.
Cron and scheduled-job fleet via Healthchecks.io: each job pings a unique URL, the service holds the Period and Grace Time, flips the check Late then Down when no ping arrives by period + grace, and notifies integrations.
Dashboard alert rules in Grafana: an alert rule whose query returns no series enters the No Data state and can raise a DatasourceNoData alert - the platform form of deciding what silence means (No Data, Alerting, Normal or Keep last state).
Apache Burrow for Kafka (LinkedIn): committed offsets are evaluated per partition over a sliding window and a consumer is classified STALLED when its offset is frozen with non-zero lag, or STOPPED when no new commits arrive - consumer-silence detection without fixed lag thresholds.

name: metadata-mapping
document:
metadata-mapping
declarative mapping
orm mapping metadata
Holds the correspondence between object fields and database columns in metadata - annotations, mapping files, table objects, struct tags or a schema definition - so that one generic mapping engine performs the reads, inserts and updates instead of hand-written per-class mapper code.
Every class that is persisted needs the same tedious, repetitive code: which field maps to which column, which key is generated, how nulls and types convert, what the table is called. Written per class it is duplicated everywhere and drifts from the schema; the catalogue's trigger is that the mapping knowledge belongs in metadata or configuration, duplicated in no class.
Object-relational (or object-document) mapping layers where classes and tables do not line up mechanically - renamed columns, generated keys, relationships, inheritance strategies - and where many classes share the same mapping shape. It applies when the mapping can be declared once in a form a machine can read (code annotations or attributes, external XML, code-first table objects, struct tags, a schema DSL) and when the schema can either be generated from that metadata or validated against it at startup.
A system with dozens of similarly shaped tables where hand-written data mappers would be repetitive: one mapping engine plus one metadata declaration per class.
Schema-first projects where the database already exists and the mapping should be derived from it by introspection or a code generator (EF Core reverse engineering, Rails schema introspection, SeaORM entity generation).
Framework and library builders who must let users map their own classes without shipping per-class code - an ORM, an object-document mapper or a serialization library.
Multi-database products in which only the dialect and type map of the metadata changes between targets while the domain classes stay identical.
Teams that want one declaration to drive several artifacts: DDL or migrations, typed query APIs, validation rules and documentation.
Hibernate ORM/Jakarta Persistence applications declare @Entity, @Table and @Column metadata; the provider builds a persistent metamodel and generic Session or EntityManager operations perform CRUD, so one declaration replaces per-entity mapper code.
EF Core applications combine conventions, data annotations and Fluent API configuration to build an entity model that drives LINQ translation and updates; explicit configuration pins renamed columns and relationships.
SQLAlchemy declarative mappings turn class attributes and mapped_column() declarations into Table and Mapper metadata; that metadata feeds SQL compilation and unit-of-work persistence, while imperative mapping keeps existing classes annotation-free.

name: update-method
document:
update-method
per-frame update
tick method
Give every live object one self-contained per-frame step and let a single driver call each object's step every frame, so behaviour advances one frame at a time while input and rendering stay responsive.
A running world is full of objects that each have to keep doing their own thing - guards patrolling, statues charging, agents acting - and the recurring decision is where one object's per-frame behaviour lives and how all those behaviours get driven. Coding a behaviour as a loop that runs to completion blocks input and rendering (the skeleton walks, but nobody sees it); coding it inline in the game loop turns the loop into a switchboard over every kind of object, so every new behaviour edits central code; and there is no way for two actors to evolve independently and simultaneously.
Real-time software with many concurrent live objects whose behaviour is mostly independent and must be simulated over time: games, agent-based simulations, animation and particle systems, tick-based servers and live visualisations. It is the natural partner of a frame driver (Game Loop) - the loop supplies the cadence, Update Method supplies the per-object step - and it becomes the wrong shape in turn-based or purely event-driven domains where nothing changes between inputs.
Real-time games and simulations with many concurrent actors: patrolling guards, projectiles, particle effects and crowd agents each advance themselves once per frame while the driver walks the collection.
Component-based engines where the parts of one entity evolve independently - rendering, physics and AI components each implement their own step and the engine's registry dispatches per component (Unity, MonoGame, Bevy, GameplayKit, libGDX).
Per-frame animation and effect timelines outside games: tween/spring systems, sprite animation and UI transitions advanced from the browser's frame callback or a UI toolkit's animation timer.
Tick-based servers and headless simulations: game servers, digital twins and agent-based models where each agent's behaviour is a resumable step and the world advances in whole discrete frames.
Tools, editors and dashboards with continuously animating scenes, where many independent scene items (markers, live charts, gizmos) must advance on every repaint without a central per-item switch.
Porting straight-line behaviour into a frame loop: turning a scripted sequence (walk left, walk right) into a per-frame step, either by storing explicit state or by using coroutines/generators to keep the code linear.
Godot's SceneTree is the driver: a node opts into the walk with set_process(true) and its _process(delta) runs every render frame with the frame time passed in as an argument, while _physics_process(delta) is called at a fixed rate - so one object can implement two steps on two clocks and can leave the walk entirely (set_process(false)) instead of paying an enabled-flag check every frame.
Engines whose built-in driver leaves per-object order unspecified expose the order as configuration: Unity states you should not rely on the order of Update across GameObjects, so real projects fix dependencies through the Script Execution Order panel, a LateUpdate pass that runs after every Update, or the PlayerLoop API rather than through registration order.
Agent-based simulation models step whole populations in NetLogo: the go procedure runs ask turtles [ ... ] to give every agent its one turn and then tick advances the discrete clock - with documented semantics that agents take their turns in random order and only agents present when the ask began get to act.

name: durable-subscriber
document:
durable-subscriber
durable subscription
durable consumer
Keep a publish-subscribe consumer's place while it is offline: the broker binds a stable subscription identity to retained messages or a committed position, then resumes delivery after reconnect until retention, expiry, or quota says the backlog is no longer available.
A subscriber on a publish-subscribe channel can be unavailable during redeployment, maintenance, device disconnects, or scheduled batch work. A non-durable subscription drops messages published during that gap, so the design must choose a stable identity and broker-side state, then make finite retention, replay pressure, and at-least-once redelivery explicit; durable state prevents a gap only while that state remains available.
Broker-mediated publish-subscribe messaging where consumers are intermittently offline but individual messages matter: JMS topics, MQTT sessions, Kafka consumer groups, NATS JetStream durable consumers, cloud topic subscriptions. It presumes the messaging system can store messages (or positions) durably, so it is as much a broker-configuration decision as a client one, and it presumes at-least-once delivery is acceptable once the consumer is idempotent. It does not apply to in-process notification or to broadcast where only the newest value counts.
A Kafka-backed order-processing service that is redeployed or scaled to zero while events keep arriving: the consumer group resumes from its committed offsets and replays what it missed.
An IoT or mobile client on an intermittent link: an MQTT persistent session holds QoS 1/2 publications for its client id and delivers them when the client reconnects.
A partner integration that receives published documents while the partner's system is down: an unshared JMS durable subscription, or a cloud topic subscription, is registered on their behalf and holds the backlog until they acknowledge it.
A nightly audit or analytics consumer that must see every published change: the day's backlog is drained in bounded batches and acknowledged as it is persisted.
A ledger or compliance consumer that must never silently skip events: retention and lag alarms are configured so an offline subscriber is noticed before its backlog expires.
A cloud event-driven architecture (SNS FIFO → SQS FIFO): SNS preserves ordering and deduplication while SQS queues hold messages for durable fan-out to Lambda or EC2 consumers, with DLQs capturing failed deliveries for replay.
An industrial SCADA/IoT sensor fleet where devices connect sporadically over unstable networks: MQTT persistent sessions with a long session expiry interval preserve every telemetry reading until each device reconnects, even after multi-day outages.
A financial audit trail that must immutably record every state-changing event: events are durably retained in Kafka or JetStream and consumed by a compliance subscriber that must not skip or duplicate entries; idempotent deduplication and offset commits after durable persistence enforce this.
A supply-chain or logistics event-sourcing system where downstream services reconstruct state by replaying events after a crash or deliberate seek: the durable consumer starts from the committed position and replays the missing event window atomically with the state reconstruction.
A cross-region disaster-recovery subscriber that mirrors events to a secondary site: the durable subscription in the secondary region receives every event from the primary's topic, with a DLQ holding any events that fail cross-region delivery for manual retry.
A JMS topic consumer that must receive publications made while it is offline: the client reconnects with the same client identifier and durable subscription name, and the provider retains messages until acknowledgement, expiry, or unsubscribe.
An MQTT 3.1.1 device gateway that reconnects with the same client identifier and CleanSession=0: the broker resumes the stored session and queues matching QoS 1/2 publications for delivery after the link returns.
A NATS JetStream billing worker that restarts after an outage: it binds to the same durable consumer name and explicit-acks each message, so the server resumes its acknowledgement floor and redelivers unacknowledged work.
An Azure Service Bus fan-out topology: topic subscriptions are durable by default and each subscription stores its own copy of matching messages, so a receiver that reconnects later still drains its backlog; client-affine durable subscriptions bind the durable state to a stable client id.
A high-throughput replay consumer on RabbitMQ Streams: the consumer attaches with a stable tracking reference (name) and periodically stores its offset server-side, so a restart resumes from the last stored offset instead of re-reading the whole stream.
An event-sourced system on Google Cloud Pub/Sub that must reprocess history after a bug fix: the subscription enables acknowledged-message retention (default window 7 days, up to 31) and is seeked back to a past timestamp or snapshot to replay already-acked messages.

name: audit-interceptor
document:
audit-interceptor
audit trail interceptor
audit logging interceptor
Declare an audit policy at an invocation seam that records the actor, action, target, correlation id and both attempt and terminal outcome around a delegated operation, then sends the structured event to a dedicated integrity-protected sink, so security accountability is consistent without inline logging in every service.
Security-relevant operations (privileged actions, state changes and access to sensitive data) must be attributable, but inline logging misses denied and failed attempts, varies in schema, can leak raw arguments and disappears with a rolled-back transaction. Teams also need to cover components they cannot modify without pretending that a proxy sees calls that bypass it.
Business or service tiers whose sensitive operations pass through an interceptable seam: container-managed beans, proxied service objects, ORM entity lifecycles, message endpoints or an HTTP pipeline. Audit selection must be declarative and uniform, while the sink has its own integrity and retention requirements (Secure Logger); the design must make mediation gaps, redaction, transaction coupling, failure policy, clock source and correlation propagation explicit.
Business-tier auditing of money-moving or otherwise regulated operations (fund transfer, order placement, claim submission): who requested it, on which object, when, and whether it succeeded.
Privileged administration surfaces (role changes, key rotation, configuration changes) where every sensitive operation must leave a record naming the acting principal.
Authentication and authorization outcomes: successful and failed logins, access-denial decisions and lockouts routed into the same audit pipeline instead of ad-hoc log lines.
Access-to-sensitive-data events (who read which patient/customer record) recorded at the gateway or service boundary to satisfy data-protection obligations.
Retrofitting auditing onto legacy components whose code cannot be modified, by wrapping the service object or binding an interceptor to its interface.
Middleware-level auditing of message endpoints and database calls in a business tier, correlating the caller's subject with the operation performed.
Financial API request interception (Spring Boot global request interceptors) capturing who accessed which endpoint, with what payload, and what outcome — satisfying SOX financial reporting controls.
Entity-level change tracking via ORM subscribers (e.g., EF Core SaveChangesInterceptor, TypeORM subscribers): automatically diff old vs. new property values on create/update/delete and emit audit envelopes without manual logging calls.
API gateway-level audit logging: capture every external API call with timestamp, user identity, endpoint, method, and outcome, correlating across microservices via X-Request-ID / traceparent headers.
Compliance reporting automation: generate audit-ready reports for SOX (~7-year retention), HIPAA (~6-year retention), GDPR (data residency-aware), and PCI-DSS from structured interceptor events.
Zero-trust data access trails: record every read of sensitive fields (PHI, PII, financial data) so data-protection obligations (GDPR Article 5 data minimization, HIPAA access logging) are demonstrably met.
Hibernate Envers: @Audited entity lifecycle changes create per-entity _AUD revisions at transaction commit; a custom revision entity/listener can attach actor or request metadata.
Django admin: django.contrib.admin.models.LogEntry records action time, user, object, addition/change/deletion and change_message for ModelAdmin activity.
Rails Audited: the audited ActiveRecord extension creates audit rows for model create, update and destroy callbacks, including changed attributes and optional acting-user attribution.

name: assertion
document:
assertion
design by contract
Express a model object's preconditions, postconditions and class invariants as executable, side-effect-free predicates at the operations that must uphold them, so a broken contract fails at its boundary instead of remaining a comment or surfacing later as corrupt state. This pattern is for design-by-contract correctness checks, not routine validation of untrusted input or test-only assertions.
Model rules - a balance never below its floor, a period whose end follows its start, a status that cannot move backwards - are left in comments, documents and team memory while constructors and mutators check nothing. A caller can violate a precondition or an operation can break an invariant, allowing invalid state to propagate until an unrelated reader fails; if the assertion is elided by the build, the shipped program may enforce a different contract from the one tested.
Objects with genuine invariants - entities, value objects and aggregate roots - whose state changes through several operations or paths, in a language with an assertion facility, contract syntax or an exception mechanism. The invariant must be expressible as a deterministic, side-effect-free predicate over observable state. Use assertions for programmer/model defects; use always-on validation or typed errors for expected input failures, and decide explicitly whether a release build may elide the check.
Entities and value objects with cross-field rules: an amount that always carries its currency and scale, a date range whose end follows its start, an order whose total equals the sum of its lines.
Aggregate roots that enforce consistency across a cluster of objects: the root asserts its invariant before accepting a change and after applying it.
Domain services and application services checking the preconditions of a use-case operation, so a mis-wired caller fails on the spot instead of writing corrupt state.
Library and framework code that must state its contract: precondition checks on public constructors and methods that clients cannot legitimately violate.
Legacy models under refactoring: assertions turn implicit rules into explicit ones, and where the language strips assertions the same predicates are pasted into the test suite (Evans's fallback).
Reconstitution code that rebuilds objects from stored data, asserting that persisted state still satisfies the model's invariants before the object is used.
Event-sourced aggregates: each state-transition command asserts the preconditions before applying the event, and the event handler asserts the invariant after the state is reconstituted from the event stream.
CQRS write models: the command handler asserts that the incoming command is valid for the current aggregate state before persisting, catching mis-wired or concurrent commands at the write edge.
Microservice boundary contracts: the inbound adapter asserts the precondition of the domain operation before dispatching, preventing malformed commands from entering the domain core regardless of which transport delivered them (HTTP, queue, gRPC).
Money and quantity types: value objects that wrap a numeric amount and a currency/unit, asserting that amounts are non-negative and operations preserve currency matching, preventing silent unit-mixing bugs.
Workflow or saga state machines: assertions on transition preconditions (this status can only advance to that one) prevent illegal state progression from corrupted or out-of-order events.
Property-based test oracle: postconditions double as generative test properties - for all inputs satisfying preconditions, the postcondition holds - turning the same predicate into a specification that a property-based testing library (e.g. Eris for PHP, Hypothesis for Python, fast-check for TypeScript) can falsify.
EiffelBase container classes such as LINKED_LIST and HASH_TABLE: EiffelStudio contract monitoring checks exported-routine preconditions/postconditions and class invariants while the containers preserve their representation rules.
AutoProof-verified Eiffel classes: executable assertions also serve as formal specifications that the verifier can discharge or flag, pairing runtime diagnostics with static proof where available.

name: converter
document:
converter
translator
Give a pair of corresponding representations one owner that maps them into each other in both directions, so every caller converts through one place and neither representation has to import, know or be aware of the other.
The same information lives in two representations - domain object and DTO, in-memory value and wire or column format, internal model and third-party schema - and both directions are exercised in production. Hand-written field copying at each call site duplicates the mapping rules, drifts whenever either representation changes, and forces at least one side (or every caller) to import the other.
Component boundaries where an internal model meets an external representation: service or API layers exchanging DTOs, persistence layers mapping values to column formats, integration seams facing a third-party or legacy schema, and codec layers mapping typed values to a wire format. It applies whenever both directions are needed (read and write, decode and encode) and either side must stay independent of the other - different modules, teams, release cycles or libraries.
Domain object <-> DTO at a service or API boundary, where the transport shape must not leak into the model.
Value object <-> database column representation (JPA AttributeConverter, EF Core ValueConverter, Rails custom attribute type).
Third-party or legacy schema <-> internal model at an integration seam, including versioned wire formats.
Typed value <-> JSON, XML or protobuf payload with a custom codec when the default mapping is wrong (formats, units, enums).
Query rows or record sets <-> domain objects, where a full mapper framework would be oversized.
Single-value wrappers such as identifiers, money or unit-carrying quantities mapped to and from their primitive form.
Palindrome conversion chain (Entity -> DAO -> DTO -> Controller -> DTO -> DAO -> Entity) where each layer owns exactly one transformation direction, making the data flow explicit and each boundary independently testable.
Versioned API contracts: a DTO for API v1 and a separate DTO for API v2 coexist; a converter pair maps each version's DTO to the shared internal model, isolating API consumers from internal changes.
API gateway transformation: external third-party API payloads are normalized into an internal canonical format at the gateway, and outbound responses are converted back to the third-party schema; converters live at the seam.
Event-driven payload normalization: domain events carry one representation (e.g., enriched entity) while the event bus transports a flattened wire format (e.g., protobuf); converters at producer and consumer ends keep the two shapes in sync.
ORM entity vs. read-model DTO at the query boundary: a repository executes a query and the row-set converter maps each row to a read-model DTO, avoiding the entity in read-only paths entirely.
Anti-corruption layer at legacy integration seams: external system payloads are translated into the internal domain model at the boundary, and responses translated back; the converter owns the translation vocabulary, protecting the domain model from foreign concepts (Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design; Microsoft Azure Architecture Center; AWS Prescriptive Guidance).
Immutable value type <-> wire format for cryptographic or financial domains: the converter is a lawful isomorphism ensuring every wire value round-trips to an identical object (tested via property-based round-trip laws, as in the lawful-conversions Haskell library and Higher-Kinded-J Iso optics library).
Strangler-fig migration seam: new microservice functionality is accessed through an ACL that converts legacy system payloads to the new domain model and back, keeping the legacy interface unchanged while the new service evolves behind the seam.
Guava com.google.common.base.Converter<F, T>: an abstract bidirectional function with convert()/reverse(), automatic reverse() derivation for subclasses, mapAll() for whole iterables and Converter.normalize() to lift a converter into a function converter - the pattern as a shipped JDK-adjacent library type (Google Guava).
Go database/sql custom types: a type implementing both sql.Scanner (Scan(src any) error) and driver.Valuer (Value() (driver.Value, error)) owns the Go value <-> database column pair in both directions; the standard library's NullString, NullInt64 and NullTime are built-in pairs of exactly this shape.
Rails custom attribute types: subclass ActiveModel::Type::Value, override serialize (Ruby value -> database value) and deserialize (database value -> Ruby value) and bind with attribute :col, MyType.new - the converter pair at the ORM seam, with cast_value kept separate for user-input coercion.

name: passkey
document:
passkey
passkey idiom
constructor key
Restrict a constructor or method to chosen collaborators by requiring a token that only those collaborators can construct, so the operation stays in the public signature while remaining uncallable by everyone else - compile-time access control instead of blanket friendship.
A specific collaborator must call a constructor or method that must not become public API: a factory or helper that has to construct an object through a public constructor (make_unique, MakeGarbageCollected), a serialisation or framework layer that must reach one private hook, a subsystem that needs one internal operation, a test helper that must build a type in a state users cannot. The blunt mechanisms all miss: making the member public hands it to the world, friend (or its nearest equivalent) hands the collaborator the whole private surface, package/module/assembly access opens it to an entire scope, and a private constructor plus a factory just moves the gate into the factory. What is missing is a way to say 'this collaborator, and only this collaborator, may call exactly this operation'.
Statically checked code where the operation must stay visible in the type system (templates, frameworks and helper functions must be able to resolve the call) but must not be callable without a value that only the designated collaborators can create. The grant is a source-level construct checked by the compiler: the token is empty, disappears at run time and is never a defence against an adversary. Typical settings are factory-created types, library internals exposed to one subsystem, framework hooks, constructor or overload disambiguation, and test seams.
Factory-created objects with a public constructor: base::PassKey in Chromium exists for classes that a helper template (blink::MakeGarbageCollected) must construct while user code must not.
Serialisation and framework hooks: an archive, visitor or framework calls exactly one hook of a user type; the key names the framework instead of befriending it and exposing everything else.
Library-internal operations: one subsystem (allocator, persistence layer, test infrastructure) needs to construct or mutate a type users must not reach - the key names the subsystem where the language allows it, and module or assembly scope carries the rest.
Tests: a test helper constructs an otherwise unreachable state without '#define private public' builds, friend-everything test seams or reflection.
Constructor and overload disambiguation: a tag only the factory can produce selects the trusted overload and keeps the same argument list from being callable by everyone.
Deliberate delegation and revocation: the collaborator passes a key to another function that then performs the call, and a non-copyable key stops the ability from travelling further.
KDE Frameworks' KColorScheme (Frameworks 6.6.0) adopted a passkey specifically to avoid private-constructor issues, showing the idiom in a public Qt-based framework API.
Chromium's Mojo ProtoWrapperBytes uses base::PassKey to let named network, component and test classes access wrapped protobuf bytes while ordinary callers cannot supply the operation.
Abseil's C++ Tip of the Week #134 uses a passkey token with std::make_shared so a factory can keep single-allocation construction without making unconstrained construction the public API.

name: implicit-lock
document:
implicit-lock
framework-managed locking
automatic locking
Make the framework or layer-supertype code that every business operation must pass through acquire and release the locks, so no application method can forget an acquisition and silently invalidate the concurrency policy.
A locking scheme has no gaps only if every path that touches a lockable item acquires its lock: one forgotten acquisition, one lock released too early or too late, makes the whole offline concurrency strategy useless. Because the error shows up only under concurrent conflicting sessions, it survives unit tests, code review and single-user manual testing.
Multi-user enterprise applications whose business transactions outlive a single database transaction - a user reads a record, thinks for minutes, then saves - so locks live in a lock table or in version columns rather than in the database transaction. Typically a Unit of Work, a layer supertype, a session facade or a declarative transaction layer already exists, giving the application a place that can own the locking protocol centrally.
Request-as-business-transaction: a web application where an ORM Unit of Work or declarative transaction (Spring @Transactional, .NET TransactionScope, Django ATOMIC_REQUESTS) acquires the row locks or version checks for every record the request reads and writes.
Offline edit sessions: a user edits a record for minutes, and the session facade or layer supertype acquires a pessimistic lock when the record enters the business transaction and releases it on commit or abort, so no controller can forget it.
Batch and import jobs that modify aggregates: each chunk runs inside the framework's transactional scope, so locking follows the changed aggregates automatically.
In-process shared state in a service or worker: a scope construct (RAII guard, with block, defer, using declaration, withLock closure) binds release to the lexical block so exceptions and early returns cannot leak the lock.
Multi-tier clients with a session facade: the lock must follow the business transaction rather than the HTTP request, so the facade — not the UI — owns acquisition and release.
Optimistic concurrency: the mapper compares and increments the version column inside the framework's update path, so a hand-written UPDATE statement cannot skip the check.
Microservices saga orchestrator: the orchestrator drives each step inside an implicit transaction scope; each participant's framework layer acquires the lock or version check locally so the saga can compensate without distributed deadlocks.
Event-sourcing projections: a projection handler reads an event stream and writes to a read-model; the handler runs inside an implicit transaction so concurrent projection rebuilds do not corrupt the read-model — the framework decides whether to use optimistic or pessimistic locking based on the change set.
CQRS read-model updates: commands update the write model under an implicit write lock; the read-model update is published as an async event; the projection runs under its own implicit scope with conflict detection (optimistic) rather than blocking (pessimistic).
Database advisory locks for cross-connection coordination: an application holds a PostgreSQL advisory lock across a multi-statement business transaction that is not itself a DB transaction (e.g., involves an external HTTP call in the middle); the lock is acquired via a thin wrapper so callers do not call pg_advisory_lock directly.
Container-managed persistence (EJB CMT, Spring @Transactional): the container acquires and releases locks as part of the transaction lifecycle; developers write business methods without explicit lock calls, relying on the container's implicit concurrency control.
Retry and compensation with implicit lock release: when a business transaction fails after the lock is acquired but before commit, the framework's rollback path releases the lock automatically so the compensating transaction can retry without manual unlock calls.
Spring Framework proxy-managed services: a proxied @Transactional service method is the business entry point; Spring starts or joins the transaction for external calls, so persistence work and its configured optimistic or pessimistic checks stay inside one framework-owned boundary.
Hibernate ORM persistence contexts: an EntityManager or Session transaction can apply @Version optimistic checks or an explicit PESSIMISTIC_WRITE LockMode at the framework boundary, keeping lock acquisition and stale-version detection out of business methods.
EF Core Unit of Work: SaveChanges compares configured concurrency tokens, including SQL Server rowversion, and raises DbUpdateConcurrencyException on a stale update, making the version check implicit in the framework's commit path rather than a hand-written UPDATE predicate.

name: bulkhead
document:
bulkhead
bulkhead isolation
cell-based architecture
Partition finite shared capacity at the failure domain (dependency, tenant, priority class, or cell) into independently bounded pools or permits, with an explicit queue and saturation policy, so one slow, saturated, or failing participant cannot consume capacity reserved for others.
Several dependencies or tenants share thread, connection, worker, or permit pools. When one becomes slow, leaky, or overloaded, its calls hold shared slots and fill shared queues, so unrelated work queues and fails behind it; the design needs a boundary that contains resource exhaustion without pretending to isolate CPU, network, or server-side limits that remain shared.
Any component whose concurrency is a finite resource: a service calling multiple downstream APIs, a multi-tenant workload, a job runner mixing interactive and batch work, or an inference and gateway tier with per-deployment quotas. The failure mode to contain is degradation and overload (slow dependency, connection leak, traffic spike), not only hard failure, and the isolation boundary must be chosen at the failure domain - instance, dependency, tenant or priority class.
A service that calls several downstream APIs through one shared HTTP client: give each downstream its own connection and thread budget so one hanging endpoint cannot block the others.
Multi-tenant SaaS where one tenant's workload must not consume the concurrency available to other tenants (per-tenant pools).
Interactive request traffic sharing a database with batch or report jobs: separate pools per workload class keep the database from serialising everything behind the batch.
An API gateway or backend-for-frontend routing to many backends with per-route concurrency caps, so a slow backend does not consume the proxy's shared capacity.
Job workers that mix latency-critical and background queues: per-queue worker pools prevent a backlog of background jobs from starving urgent work.
Inference and AI serving where each model deployment has its own concurrency quota and a saturated model must not consume the shared request capacity.
Cell-based architectures: each cell (complete, independent service instance) is a bulkhead partition; load grows by adding cells, and a failure is contained to the single cell — used at AWS, Google, and Netflix scale.
Shuffle sharding: Amazon Route 53-style virtual shard assignment where each tenant is assigned to a random shard of two or more cells; with eight cells and two-per-shard there are 28 unique shards, so a problem affects only 1/28th of tenants — far better than regular per-cell partitioning.
AI and inference workloads: per-deployment or per-tenant Azure OpenAI or LLM deployment quotas prevent one saturated model from consuming the shared request capacity across the platform.
Database RU isolation: Azure Cosmos DB request-unit throughput assigned per container acts as a storage-layer bulkhead; one noisy container cannot exhaust the RU budget of others.
Resilience4j's SemaphoreBulkhead and FixedThreadPoolBulkhead give a JVM service per-dependency permits versus a bounded queue and worker pool; choose based on whether caller threads may be occupied.
Netflix Hystrix's per-command thread pools or semaphore isolation reject work and route it to fallback, containing a slow downstream to its command boundary (historical and deprecated).
.NET services use Polly's BulkheadPolicy/AsyncBulkheadPolicy (maxParallelization plus maxQueuingActions, rejecting with BulkheadRejectedException when both are full); Polly v8 replaced it with ConcurrencyLimiter over System.Threading.RateLimiting, whose partitioned per-key limiters give per-tenant bulkheads.
Service meshes enforce bulkheads at the platform layer: an Istio DestinationRule's trafficPolicy.connectionPool caps tcp.maxConnections, http.http1MaxPendingRequests and http.http2MaxRequests per upstream host, enforced by Envoy alongside its circuit-breaking limits.
Netflix's concurrency-limits library replaces hand-tuned static partitions with per-dependency adaptive limits (Vegas and Gradient algorithms modelled on TCP congestion control) that shrink the concurrency budget automatically as downstream latency rises, e.g. separating live from batch traffic on one gRPC server.
Envoy maintains per-upstream-cluster connection pools and circuit-breaking limits, while Kubernetes ResourceQuota caps aggregate namespace CPU, memory, or object use; both are platform-level capacity partitions rather than application call-site wrappers.

name: policy-based-design
document:
policy-based-design
policy-based class design
policy-based programming
Assemble a class's behaviour, structure and defaults from small interchangeable policy units bound when the host type is instantiated, so that each orthogonal design decision can be varied independently instead of being frozen in the class's code.
A reusable class hard-codes several independent design decisions - allocation, ownership, storage, threading, validation, error handling - inside its implementation, so a different combination is only reachable by editing or copying the class, while the runtime Strategy alternative costs a virtual call per use and gives up the guarantee that the choice is fixed, inlineable and checked before the program runs.
Generic library and framework code in languages whose type system can bind behaviour to types - C++ templates and concepts, Rust trait bounds, Scala contextual abstractions, and to a lesser degree C#, Kotlin, Swift and TypeScript generics: several orthogonal axes vary independently, the variant is known when the host type is instantiated, and the component is a widely reused primitive or a hot path where a virtual call, an allocation, or a per-instance configuration flag is undesirable.
Library primitives with several orthogonal decisions: smart pointers (ownership, checking, conversion, storage), object pools and allocators (allocation, threading), hash containers (hasher, equality, allocator) - a few policy classes covering an exponential family of types.
Numerical and algorithmic kernels that must run checked (assertions, bounds checks) in debug builds and unchecked in release builds without maintaining two parallel class hierarchies.
Object factories and registries whose creation method is the axis (new, clone/prototype, arena, pooled) while the lookup algorithm stays fixed - Alexandrescu's Creator/PrototypeCreator example.
Reusable components whose logging, locking or serialization strategy must be chosen per product configuration: no-op versus real logger, single-threaded versus thread-safe, compact versus verbose encoding.
Framework and standard-library style extension points: a component that must accept a user-written hash, comparison or allocation policy without being modified and without a class hierarchy.
Compile-time configuration of a data structure's shape (node layout, cache size, index arithmetic) where the decision is a type-level or constant policy rather than a value passed at run time.
Rust's std::collections::HashMap<K, V, S> makes hashing a type-bound policy: S implements BuildHasher and defaults to RandomState, while with_hasher selects a custom builder for specialized maps.
C++'s std::unordered_map<Key, T, Hash, KeyEqual, Allocator> exposes hashing, equality, and allocation as independent template policy parameters with standard defaults.
.NET 7 generic math uses C# static abstract interface members (for example INumber<TSelf>) so generic algorithms bind arithmetic behavior through a constrained type parameter instead of a runtime strategy.

name: traits
document:
traits
traits class
type traits
Attach behaviour, associated types and constants to a type from the outside, in a separate specialisable descriptor, so that generic code selects the right implementation from a type's properties instead of from an interface the type must inherit.
A generic algorithm has to adapt to the properties of the types it is instantiated with - is this type numeric, does it expose a nested value_type, how does it compare, what is its end-of-sequence value, is it trivially copyable? The types carrying those properties are built-in or third-party types that cannot be edited to declare them, and forcing them behind a common base class is intrusive, costs runtime dispatch and cannot be applied to fundamental types at all.
Generic (templated or compile-time-generic) libraries and algorithms that must work over types they do not own: containers and iterators, numeric and character utilities, serialisation, formatting, hashing and comparison frameworks, capability-dependent fast paths. Applies when the type's properties are knowable before the program runs and the design is free to describe the type from outside - and, with the same intent, wherever languages express ad-hoc polymorphism through type classes, implicit evidence, constraints or protocol conformance.
Iterator and range libraries that need value_type, reference, difference_type and an iterator category from every iterator - including raw pointers, for which no nested member can exist.
Numeric and character/string utilities that need per-type limits, precision and constants (numeric_limits) or a type's end-of-file value and comparison rules (char_traits).
Formatting, serialisation, hashing and comparison frameworks that must support types from other libraries by describing them from the outside (formatters, codecs, hash functions, ordering instances).
Capability-dependent implementations: detect whether a type has push_back/begin/serialize and pick the efficient or the safe implementation (memcpy fast path for trivially copyable types, buffered vs unbuffered readers).
Cross-language ad-hoc polymorphism: type classes, implicit evidence, generic constraints or protocol conformance give behaviour to types you do not own without subclassing them (Ordering, INumber<T>, Numeric, deserialiser registries).
Unit, quantity and domain-type libraries carrying per-type properties (dimension, epsilon, radix, zero/one identity) that the generic arithmetic code must consult.
{fmt} formatting of user-defined types: a formatter<T> specialization or a format_as conversion written beside the type joins it to fmt's formatting algorithm, which then handles types it was never compiled against.
serde (de)serialising structs from other crates through Serialize/Deserialize bindings written outside the data type - a remote-derive definition or newtype wrapper - because Rust's orphan rules forbid attaching the impl to a foreign type directly.
Haskell type classes binding operations (equality, show, arithmetic overloading) to types like Int or Maybe through instances declared apart from the type, and Swift protocol extensions retroactively conforming system types such as Date to Identifiable.
