name: crtp
document:
crtp
curiously recurring template pattern
static polymorphism
Give a base class template access to the concrete type that derives from it - passed as the base's own template argument - so that shared behaviour and interface methods are generated and resolved at compile time, with no virtual dispatch, no vtable and no runtime indirection.
A family of related types must share behaviour or an interface, but the shared code has to call members of the concrete type, and that type is already known at compile time. Virtual functions would answer the call, yet they add a per-object pointer, an indirect call that defeats inlining, and they force the participating types to become runtime-polymorphic - which costs size and speed for value types and is impossible where the operation itself is static (per-class counters, nested types) or must run in constexpr contexts.
Statically typed compiled languages with templates or compile-time generics, above all C++ (and, in weaker forms, languages with recursive generic bounds). It applies to header and library code and to value types where the set of participating types is closed at compile time, where the abstraction must stay inlinable and free of per-object state, and where the base must hand back the concrete type (fluent builders, clone, comparison suites, iterator facades). It does not apply where the concrete type is first known at runtime or where values of different participating types must be stored together behind one type.
Mixin operator suites for value types: define equality, ordering and arithmetic once in terms of a single primitive (the Barton-Nackman trick) so every participating type inherits the full operator set.
Fluent builders and self-typed APIs where each chained method must return the concrete builder type rather than a base type (the same need is served by recursive generic bounds in Java, C#, Kotlin and Scala).
Polymorphic cloning and copying: the base provides clone() returning a pointer to the derived type so each class only supplies its copy constructor.
Per-class static state such as instance counters, ID allocators and registries, where each derived type must own its own counter - impossible with a single non-templated base.
Facade and skeleton libraries that implement a large interface in terms of a few operations the derived type supplies (iterator facades, ranges::view_interface, visitor skeletons such as Clang's RecursiveASTVisitor).
Giving a type polymorphic-looking operations that need the exact derived type, e.g. enable_shared_from_this returning shared_ptr<Derived> / weak_from_this without a virtual function.
Chained CRTP inheritance: a CRTP base can itself derive from another CRTP base, enabling multi-axis mixin composition (e.g. Printable<Comparable<MyType>>) - each layer adds one behavioural dimension.
Compile-time interface contracts: use C++20 concepts to constrain what a CRTP-derived type must supply, turning the implicit CRTP hook contract into an explicit, checked, named concept.
Type-safe non-virtual visitors: a visitor base template receives the derived visitor type as its template argument, enabling static double dispatch without virtual inheritance.
Boost.Iterator's iterator_facade: a custom iterator passes itself as iterator_facade<Derived, Value, Category, Reference, Difference>'s first argument and supplies only dereference, increment, distance and equal; the facade synthesizes the whole standard iterator interface (operator->, [], arithmetic) and its associated types - chosen over policy objects precisely to allow custom constructors and descriptive types like indirect_iterator<T*>.
Clang's RecursiveASTVisitor as used in practice: class MyVisitor : public clang::RecursiveASTVisitor<MyVisitor> - the base's traversal code calls the user's Visit*/WalkUpFrom*/Traverse* hooks through the template parameter, so a full AST walker runs with no virtual call per node (and pays for it with a large instantiation per visitor).
Standard-library CRTP bases as precedent: std::enable_shared_from_this<T> (the shared_ptr constructor detects the base via a nested detector type and wires weak_this, so shared_from_this() returns shared_ptr<T> on the existing control block) and std::ranges::view_interface<D>.

name: tag-dispatching
document:
tag-dispatching
tag dispatch
tag-based dispatch
Select the implementation of an operation at compile time from the type of a tag argument, so that generic code can vary behaviour per type property with no virtual dispatch and no runtime branch.
Code that must behave differently for types sharing one signature but differing in a property the type system can express - an iterator's category, whether a type is trivially constructible, which numeric domain it belongs to. A dynamic decision (virtual call, type switch, enum field) costs a lookup, cannot be inlined, and demotes a static property to a runtime one.
Applies where the discriminating property is known at compile time and the set of implementations is either closed or deliberately extensible at compile time: standard-library algorithms selecting an O(1) or O(n) strategy from an iterator category, generic containers choosing trivial versus throwing construction, constructor disambiguation (range versus count, lock-adoption tags), and library extension points (serialization, hashing, formatting) that users must be able to extend for their own types without touching the dispatcher.
Standard-library style algorithm selection: advance/distance taking a constant-time path for random-access iterators and a linear path otherwise, with no runtime branch.
Generic containers distinguishing trivial, nothrow and throwing construction of element ranges.
Constructor and factory disambiguation: ranges versus (count, value), std::adopt_lock/defer_lock/try_to_lock for locks, nothrow allocation.
Extension points where users supply implementations for their own types - serialization, hashing, formatting, comparison, transport adapters - through one public API with per-type behaviour.
Compile-time policy refinement: choosing the most specific implementation a type provides and falling back to a generic one through a priority chain.
Numeric and generic programming that must avoid runtime type inspection in hot loops while still accepting many types.
Boost.Iterator generalizes the std iterator-tag ladder into an orthogonal traversal hierarchy (no/incrementable/single_pass/forward/bidirectional/random_access_traversal_tag): iterator_traversal and iterator_category_to_traversal map an iterator to its tag and algorithms dispatch on the tag's convertible-to ranking instead of a fixed category enum.
LLVM's ADT headers: filter_iterator_impl is specialized on std::forward_iterator_tag versus std::bidirectional_iterator_tag and detail::fwd_or_bidi_tag derives the tag from the wrapped iterator, so make_filter_range gives bidirectional ranges operator-- while forward-only ranges compile just the forward path.
Julia's standard-library Val{x}: an empty parametric struct carries a constant into the type domain so methods like firstlast(::Val{true})/firstlast(::Val{false}) select without a runtime test - the idiom ported to a dynamic language, documented as paying off only when the value is a compile-time constant.

name: envelope-letter
document:
envelope-letter
envelope and letter
delegated polymorphism
Give clients a stable, value-like facade (the envelope) that owns and forwards every operation to an interchangeable implementation object (the letter), so the implementation type stays hidden behind one interface and can be replaced, reconfigured or swapped while the program runs.
One interface must dispatch to several interchangeable implementations, but clients must not name them: the concrete type is chosen later (platform, configuration, plugin, test), and it may even change while the object lives. Hard-wiring the concrete class into the client re-couples the two, drags the implementation's header, module or library into every compile unit, and makes the choice global instead of per object.
Object-oriented code with a stable abstraction and several realizations - UI toolkits, protocol stacks, plugin hosts, numeric representations, test doubles - especially where the implementation type is a compile-time dependency that should not leak, where values must be copied, compared or stored in containers while still behaving polymorphically, or where the implementation is selected at run time rather than at construction.
UI and graphics toolkits where shapes, widgets or documents are handed around by value while drawing, layout and event handling live in replaceable backend objects (Coplien's widget-library example; the hush class library used exactly this handle/body split).
Numeric and domain value types whose arithmetic depends on the representation (real, complex, rational, interval, money with different rounding rules): the envelope is the number the program uses, the letter implements the operations for one representation.
Library APIs that must not expose the implementation type in a public header or module: the envelope declares the API, the letter is only visible in the source file — the compile-firewall use of the same mechanics.
Test seams: production code keeps using one envelope type while per-test fakes, spies or recorded letters are substituted, including for behaviour that is otherwise slow, remote or non-deterministic.
Plugin and driver dispatch: a loaded module supplies the letter, the host keeps only the envelope facade and the stable interface; swapping the loaded module swaps the letter for new objects (and, if the envelope allows it, for existing ones).
Adapting a legacy subsystem behind a modern interface: the envelope carries the new API and an adapter letter forwards into the old implementation, so callers migrate without the old code changing.
COM/OLE Automation and similar component frameworks: the public COM interface is an envelope, the hidden implementation object is the letter; IUnknown itself is a form of handle/body.
ORM and data-mapper proxies: an envelope represents an entity, a letter implements the persistence logic; the envelope can be passed around by value while the persistence backend is swapped between a test double and a live database connection.
Copy-on-write data structures: std::string and Qt's implicitly-shared classes use a handle/body split internally to defer the copy of large payloads until a mutation occurs.
Cross-language bridging (Python/C++, Java JNI, Node.js native addons): the native implementation is the letter, the language-bound wrapper is the envelope that hides the FFI boundary.
Java AWT widgets: java.awt.Component is the envelope the program manipulates, and each heavyweight component forwards painting, resizing and input to a native peer object behind the java.awt.peer.ComponentPeer interface — the letter is supplied by the platform toolkit, and the JDK deprecated direct peer manipulation (getPeer()) precisely so clients see only the envelope.
JDBC: Connection, Statement and ResultSet are the stable envelope the application compiles against, while each vendor driver supplies interchangeable letters implementing the same interfaces — application code never names a driver class and swaps databases by swapping the driver at deployment time.
Java NIO.2 filesystems: Path and Files act as envelopes whose operations dispatch to a provider-specific letter chosen per FileSystem through FileSystemProvider, so the same API drives both on-disk files and entries in a mounted ZIP filesystem.

name: either
document:
either
Either monad
disjoint union
Encode the two outcomes of a fallible operation - a value-carrying success (Right/Ok) and a reason-carrying failure (Left/Err) - in one sum-type value, so a caller must destructure both branches before going further and failures cannot escape as exceptions, sentinel values or undocumented convention.
An operation can fail in ways the caller must handle, but the failure channel is invisible in the signature: exceptions unwind past intermediate callers, where they get swallowed or merely logged, status codes and sentinels are silently ignored, and the reason for failure is flattened into a message string nobody can branch on.
Expected, recoverable failures in code that has to compose: parsing and validation at a boundary, persistence and I/O calls, service calls inside a pipeline, or any layer whose caller must render, translate, retry or count the failure. It pays off where the error type is part of an API contract between teams or modules, and where the language can express a two-case type (algebraic data type, sealed hierarchy, discriminated union) or a library supplies one.
Validating untrusted input at a boundary and returning the concrete reason (field, offset, rule violated) so the caller can render a precise message.
Domain operations that can fail for several business reasons (insufficient funds, account closed, limit exceeded) where callers must branch on the reason instead of guessing from a string.
Parsing and decoding (config, documents, wire formats) where the failure position or cause must travel back with the outcome.
Pipelines of fallible steps (authenticate -> load -> transform -> persist) that should stop at the first failure with the original reason intact instead of unwinding with a stack trace.
Translate-once boundaries: turn transport errors into domain errors in one adapter, so no layer above has to know about HTTP codes, IOExceptions or database error numbers.
Accumulating validation of independent fields, where every reason must be reported together rather than only the first one — use an Applicative validation instance with a Semigroup-based error accumulator.
Callbacks and async APIs whose failure cannot be thrown to the caller (completion handlers, event consumers) and therefore has to be delivered as a value.
Parallel fallible operations where you want to collect all successes and all failures separately before deciding, using partition or sequence operations on a List<Result>.
Domain-driven design aggregates where a root entity operation can fail for many reasons (invariant violations, business rule breaches) and the aggregate root returns Either to the application layer.
Service-to-service calls inside a pipeline where the downstream service returns a structured error response (not an exception), and the upstream must branch, translate, or propagate it.
Rust standard-library convention: fallible I/O, parsing and system calls return Result<T, E> and ? propagates the first Err up the call chain to a boundary (a main or entry point that returns Result) - the backbone of recoverable error handling in Rust.
Kotlin/Arrow typed-error pipelines: an either { } computation DSL where bind() short-circuits on Left and Either.catch turns a throwing interop call into a Left at the adapter boundary.
Java services using Vavr's right-biased Either: map/flatMap chains propagate Left without checked exceptions, keeping the failure type part of the signature in fluent pipelines.

name: version-number
document:
version-number
rowversion
entity versioning
Store a version token alongside each persistent record and make every write assert the token it read, so a write computed from stale data fails as a detectable conflict instead of silently overwriting a newer value.
Two sessions read the same record, both edit it, and the later write wins: the earlier update vanishes without any error (the lost update). Once the read-modify-write spans more than one system transaction the database cannot tell 'this is the record I read' from 'this record changed under me', so no code path can notice in time - unless the record itself carries a per-row token that changes on every write and the write tests that token before committing.
Applies to records that outlive the transaction that read them: edits spanning user think time, a web form round-trip, an offline client, a batch worker holding aggregates, or any read-modify-write over data other writers touch in between. It needs a store that can test the token and change the record in one atomic step (a conditional UPDATE, a compare-and-swap, a document revision check) and a caller willing to act on the conflict - re-read, merge, retry, or report. It assumes conflicts are the exception; when they are the rule a pessimistic lock prevents the wasted work instead.
Web forms and editors: a record is loaded into a page, edited for minutes or hours, then saved - the token makes the stale save fail instead of clobbering the other editor's change.
Distributed workers applying commands to the same entity: the second worker's write is rejected so it can refresh and re-apply, giving first-writer-wins with no held lock.
Data mappers and units of work: every dirty entity flushed at commit carries the version it was loaded with, so the whole transaction aborts on the first stale row.
Document stores and revision-based APIs: Mongoose's __v with optimisticConcurrency, CouchDB-style revisions, or a REST ETag/If-Match precondition all expose the same per-document token.
Leases, leader election and configuration records: one row represents ownership or a monotonic generation, and a write must prove it still holds the revision it acted on.
Offline or mobile sync: clients push edits made against a snapshot taken days earlier, and the version check decides which edits apply directly and which must go through a merge.
Hibernate ORM / JPA @Version: the mapper owns an integer (or timestamp) version property, appends it to every UPDATE's WHERE clause, bumps it on flush and raises StaleObjectStateException / OptimisticLockException when zero rows match, so the application code never writes the predicate by hand.
DynamoDB conditional writes: each item carries a Version attribute; UpdateItem sends ConditionExpression 'Version = :read_value' and increments Version in the same request, and ConditionalCheckFailedException is the conflict signal that triggers a bounded re-read-and-retry — the same contract exposed as @DynamoDBVersionAttribute in the enhanced client.
Cassandra lightweight transactions: UPDATE ... SET col = ? WHERE id = ? IF col = ? is a Paxos-backed compare-and-set, giving the token test linearizable semantics across replicas — at a documented cost (roughly four extra round-trips per conditional write), so it is reserved for rows that genuinely need the guard.

name: entity
document:
entity
reference object
domain entity
Give a domain concept a stable identity that survives attribute changes, representation changes and time, and define its equality, lifecycle and lookup in terms of that identity instead of in terms of its attributes.
A model that compares objects by their attributes cannot answer whether two instances are the same thing: a customer whose e-mail and plan changed looks like a different customer, while two distinct people who share a name look like one. References held by other objects, caches and audit records break silently, and every state change forces callers to re-identify the object.
Rich domain models in which some concepts must be tracked through time: the object is created, changes state, is stored and reloaded, and may exist in several representations (in-memory instance, database row, message payload, UI snapshot) that all have to denote the same thing. It is the modelling decision that pairs with Value Object: attribute clusters become values, while the things whose history matters keep an identity.
Master data tracked for years — customers, accounts, contracts, products, patients — where attributes change but the business entity stays the same (e.g., a Customer who moves house is still the same Customer).
Documents with a lifecycle: orders, invoices, bookings and shipments that move through states (pending → paid → shipped → delivered) while remaining the same document with a stable order number.
Shopping cart to order transition: a ShoppingCart is reconstituted as an Order with the same customer identity but a new order identity, preserving the correlation to the customer while starting a new business process.
Correlating representations across layers: an entity persisted as database rows, published as domain events, and displayed in a UI must be recognisable as the same thing in all three — identity is the correlation key across representations.
In-memory session consistency: a unit of work or identity map ensures the same Customer loaded twice in one request is one object reference, preventing edits from silently diverging into two copies.
Referencing across bounded contexts: one microservice holds a CustomerId reference to another service's aggregate root, allowing independent deployment and loading without a direct object pointer.
Healthcare records: a Patient entity persists across multiple visits, lab results and prescriptions — the patient identity is the anchor for the entire medical history regardless of demographic changes.
Versioned documents: an InsurancePolicy entity may be replaced by a new version while the original policy number (identity) remains the correlation handle for auditors and legacy systems.
Hibernate/JPA: an @Entity class with an @Id is managed by the persistence context, which guarantees one in-memory instance per identity per session — loading the same row twice in a session returns the same object reference, an Identity Map built into the framework.
Entity Framework Core: identity resolution makes the DbContext track a single entity instance per primary key, so duplicate instances arriving in a deserialized graph are merged into the already-tracked entity instead of diverging into two tracked copies.
Drupal Entity API: nodes, users and taxonomy terms (content entities) and roles or image styles (configuration entities) are identity-bearing objects with typed storage handlers, revisions and field bundles behind one CRUD and validation API.

name: newtype
document:
newtype
strong typedef
opaque type
Give a single primitive its own distinct type so that values with different meanings cannot be substituted for one another, and the raw representation is reachable only through the wrapper's own construction and accessors.
Several domain concepts share one representation - customer id, order id and tenant id are all strings or UUIDs, width/height/offset are all numbers, milliseconds and seconds are both integers - and the API therefore accepts them interchangeably. A swapped argument, a mixed unit or a mistyped literal compiles (or runs) silently, and the defect surfaces late, as a wrong lookup or a cross-tenant bug rather than a type error.
Code in which two or more values with the same underlying representation flow through the same functions, collections or persistence mapping, and in which a single value owns a rule (identifier syntax, non-emptiness, numeric range, unit). Applies at the value level of one field; clusters of attributes that change together belong to Value Object, and closed constant sets to Type-Safe Enum.
Identifier families in one codebase: CustomerId, OrderId, TenantId and SessionId all string- or UUID-shaped and passed to the same repository, logger and cache.
Unit-carrying measurements: Milliseconds vs Seconds, Meters vs Feet, Radians vs Degrees, Cents vs Dollars, where arithmetic must stay inside one unit and conversion is explicit.
Validated single values: EmailAddress, PhoneNumber, Iban, Slug, Percentage (0-100), PortNumber, NonEmptyString - parsed once at the edge, trusted everywhere afterwards.
Security-adjacent tokens: API token vs session id vs tenant id, where a swap becomes a cross-tenant or privilege defect rather than a wrong lookup.
Geometry and graphics APIs where Width, Height, X, Y, Offset and Length are all numbers and transposition should be a compile error.
Pagination and buffer arithmetic: PageSize vs PageIndex vs ByteOffset vs Count, integers that are trivially transposable in a long argument list.
Rust's official newtype examples use Millimeters(u32) and Meters(u32) to keep units distinct, and use Wrapper(Vec<T>) to give a local wrapper its own trait implementations.
Scala 3 opaque types model values such as Logarithm over Double as distinct outside their defining scope, with controlled extension methods and no runtime boxing.
Kotlin @JvmInline value classes wrap one property into a non-interchangeable domain type such as Password while allowing unboxed representations in many uses.

name: poison-pill
document:
poison-pill
sentinel message
end-of-stream marker
Terminate queue consumers cooperatively by sending a reserved sentinel message that each consumer recognises as "no more work", so consumers drain the backlog and exit without a separate control channel or forced cancellation.
A producer-consumer system must shut down, but its consumers block on an empty queue and the queue has no built-in "no more items" signal: callers either kill the workers mid-work and drop buffered items, or leave them blocked forever. Production has ended - how do the consumers learn that while still processing everything already queued?
In-process or broker-mediated producer-consumer systems with a FIFO work queue, a fixed set of long-lived consumers (threads, coroutines, actors) that block when the queue is empty, and a shutdown requirement that work already accepted by the queue be drained before the consumers exit - typically deployment, signal handling or test teardown.
Signal-driven shutdown of an in-process worker pool: the SIGTERM handler stops accepting work, then enqueues one pill per worker so the backlog is processed before the process exits.
Batch importers and ETL stages whose consumers block on a work queue and must finish the current batch before a run is considered complete.
Test harnesses and simulations: an explicit stop message makes thread-based systems deterministic to shut down, without sleeps or guessed timeouts.
Actor systems: a reserved stop message (for example Akka PoisonPill) terminates an actor after the messages already queued for it have been handled.
Log and event writers where the last records must reach the sink before consumers release their buffers and files.
Bounded-queue stages in a pipeline: pills travel the same backpressured channel as work, so upstream cannot keep producing after the stop decision.
Kubernetes pod shutdown: containers receive SIGTERM, workers stop pulling from the job queue, drain in-flight tasks, then exit within the terminationGracePeriodSeconds window.
Redis/Bull queue workers: a shutdown signal pushes a sentinel via BLPOP so workers exit cleanly without losing the right to process pending tasks.
Akka Streams and similar streaming frameworks: the GraphStage signals completion via onPull/downstream cancellation, which is the materialised equivalent of a poison pill.
Redis Streams consumer groups: XREADGROUP with block timeout naturally returns when the stream is empty; a special ID (e.g. ">") polling loop plus a shared shutdown flag replaces the in-process sentinel.
Broker-level poison message isolation: in Kafka, RabbitMQ, or Azure Service Bus, a permanently failing message (deserialisation error, validation failure) blocks a partition/consumer indefinitely; DLQ-based routing (publish to dead-letter topic after N retries, then commit offset and continue) is the broker-level analogue that prevents one poison message from halting the entire pipeline.
Kubernetes preStop hooks + pill drain: a container's lifecycle preStop hook can enqueue a sentinel into an in-process work queue while the orchestrator grants terminationGracePeriodSeconds for the drain to complete, ensuring zero work-drop during rolling updates.
Azure Service Bus competing-consumers workers: when a worker receives a shutdown notification it completes its current PeekLock message, then calls Abandon on any held locks before unregistering; Azure Service Bus dead-letter queues handle the poison-message variant when a message exceeds MaxDeliveryCount and cannot be delivered.
Akka hierarchical actor trees: sending PoisonPill to a parent actor stops it after all queued messages ahead of the pill are processed, and automatically sends stop messages to all children in bottom-up order; this is the idiomatic way to orchestrate ordered multi-actor shutdown.
Non-blocking retry architectures (RabbitMQ): rather than local Thread.sleep retries that block the consumer thread, use server-side TTL queues with Dead Letter Exchange routing to implement exponential backoff, keeping the consumer responsive to new messages and to shutdown pills.
Java's JDK BlockingQueue worker pools: because BlockingQueue has no built-in close, producers can enqueue a unique end-of-stream object after all work; each consumer takes until that sentinel and then the coordinator joins workers.
Python multiprocessing worker pools: multiprocessing.Queue/JoinableQueue supports FIFO task delivery with sentinel values and join-based drain tracking; send one sentinel per worker and join them after the queue is exhausted.
Akka Classic actors: PoisonPill is enqueued in the mailbox and processed after already queued messages, while Akka Typed requires an explicit Stop/Shutdown protocol; choose the API that matches the actor model.

name: dynamic-router
document:
dynamic-router
dynamic routing
rules-based routing
Route each message to a destination chosen from a rule base that can be changed while the system runs, so the router never depends on - or is redeployed for - the set of destinations it serves.
Routing logic hard-coded into the router (switch chains, static filter tables, deployment-time route configuration) couples it to every destination: adding, moving, throttling or retiring a destination needs a code change, a review and a restart, and each topology change forces the router back through the release process instead of being an operational edit.
Message-based integration where the destination set or the routing policy changes faster than the router's release cycle: rules are owned by operations, destinations announce themselves, scale out, or go down for maintenance, or one router instance serves several tenants or environments. Applies when the route can be expressed as rules over message content, headers or context evaluated per message, and the platform offers a usable control channel (config watch, control bus, admin endpoint, hot-reloadable table) to publish rule changes.
Multi-tenant integration hub: each tenant has its own routing table, loaded and swapped per tenant instead of one deployed router per tenant.
Event distribution where downstream teams add or retire consumers by publishing routing conditions rather than requesting a router release.
Canary and blue/green rollouts: send a slice of traffic to a new destination by editing a rule, and roll back by restoring the previous rule set.
Maintenance windows: reroute a destination's traffic to a standby, drain the destination, then restore the rule when it returns.
Regional or sharded routing where the region-to-destination mapping is maintained by operations and changes with capacity, not with code.
Rule-driven enterprise integration in the classic EIP sense, where a rule base is consulted per message and recipients announce themselves on a control channel.
Kubernetes Gateway API traffic splitting: use HTTPRoute weighted backends to shift a configurable percentage of traffic between versions without redeploying the router.
Service mesh canary deployments: an Istio VirtualService or Linkerd ServiceProfile acts as the rule base; routing rules are edited at runtime to steer canary traffic, then promoted or rolled back.
Multi-tenant SaaS routing: Spring Cloud Gateway or Envoy.DynamicRouter loads per-tenant routing rules from a registry, injecting tenant-specific headers or rewrites so one router instance serves hundreds of isolated tenants.
API version routing and A/B testing: route by Accept header, API version path prefix, or experimentCohort header to different backend versions, controlled by rules updated without a release.
Database or cache sharding: route a tenant or user ID hash to the correct shard's endpoint via a rule table that is repointed during resharding without touching application code.
BGP route-server testing: use a chaos-testing framework against a route server to validate that policy changes converge correctly and do not produce route leaks before production deployment.
Traefik dynamic configuration: Traefik builds its routing table at runtime from providers (Docker labels, Kubernetes IngressRoute, Consul/etcd KV stores), so services announce their own routes and rule changes hot-swap without restarting the proxy.
HAProxy Runtime API: add server and set server state/weight over the runtime socket repoint and drain backends without a reload; the Data Plane API layers persistence and validation on top of these runtime changes.
Kong Gateway admin API: Routes - including the expressions DSL when router_flavor is set to expressions - are created and updated at runtime via POST /routes and take effect on the next matching request, with priority-ordered rule evaluation replacing a redeployed config.

name: option-maybe
document:
option-maybe
Option
Maybe
Make the possible absence of a result part of the value and of the signature, so every caller has to decide what happens when nothing is there instead of meeting a null, a sentinel or a silently defaulted value at run time.
A function has something to return for some inputs and nothing for others, but the signature does not say so: it returns a null reference, a sentinel (-1, empty string, NULL), an out-parameter, or a value that quietly means 'not found'. Callers forget the check, dereference the null or treat the sentinel as data, and the 'this case does not exist' path is discovered in production rather than at the call site.
Lookups, parsing, searches, optional configuration, nullable database columns and any API whose result may legitimately not exist - wherever the language can express absence as a type (Option/Maybe/Optional, a nullable type, a union with undefined) or a convention can carry it. It pays off at module and service boundaries, in chains of partial steps, and wherever 'absent' must stay distinguishable from a legitimate empty, zero or falsey value.
Lookups that can miss: configuration keys, cache entries, registry entries, map/dictionary access - either through the language's two-value form or an Optional-returning accessor.
Parsing and conversion (integers, dates, URLs, decimal numbers, external identifiers) where 'no valid value' is a legitimate answer rather than an error.
Searches over collections and structures (find, first, min/max, binary search, regex match, tree traversal) where a miss is part of the contract.
Genuinely optional data: middle names, second addresses, unset feature flags, optional protocol fields - as opposed to missing state, which is a domain error.
Chains of partial steps (look up user, then their company, then its billing address) where any hop may be absent and the whole chain should collapse to 'nothing'.
Boundaries from nullable interfaces: a database column admits NULL, a legacy or interop API returns null or -1, a deserialized document lacks a field - converted once at the adapter.
Container and stream operations that can be empty (head, pop, next, dequeue, min) and should report emptiness instead of throwing or returning a sentinel.
Rust's standard library uses std::option::Option<T> with Some(T) and None for optional values; its map and pattern-matching APIs let lookup or parsing pipelines stop at absence without a null pointer.
Java SE's java.util.Optional<T> is a production API for method results that may be absent: ofNullable converts a nullable boundary value, map/flatMap compose follow-up work, and orElse/orElseThrow make the exit policy explicit.
Scala's standard-library scala.Option[A] models Some/None and documents map, flatMap, and for-comprehensions for chained partial steps; its API also demonstrates wrapping a Java HashMap lookup so a missing key becomes None.

name: pipeline
document:
pipeline
assembly line
processing pipeline
Decompose a transformation into an ordered sequence of named stages that each consume the previous stage's output and produce the next stage's input, so the workflow reads top to bottom and every step can be tested, instrumented, reordered or replaced on its own.
A multi-step transformation is written as one long function or a tangle of nested calls: the steps are unnamed, their order is implicit in statement order, intermediate values need throwaway names, there is no seam at which a single step can be logged, tested or replaced, and the same sequence is retyped at every call site that needs it.
Processing that naturally decomposes into successive transformations of the same payload - request handling, ETL, compiler passes, message enrichment, image or byte-stream processing - whether the payload is a single value or a stream. It fits in-process, staged execution where one driver owns ordering, error handling and cancellation; distributing the stages across processes, transports and independently deployed filters is the architectural pipe-and-filter pattern instead.
Request handling: deserialise, authenticate, validate, enrich, persist and render a request, with each step named so a failing stage is attributable and testable in isolation.
ETL and data import: extract, clean, transform, validate and load large files as a stream, so no intermediate collection is materialised and memory stays bounded.
Compiler and interpreter passes: source, tokens, AST, resolution, optimisation and code emission, where each pass is an independent stage over the intermediate representation and the pass list is the pipeline.
Message enrichment in an integration flow: unwrap, translate, enrich and route a message, one stage per concern, with per-channel ordering; the cross-process version stays pipe-and-filter.
Image or byte-stream processing: decode, crop or resize, watermark and encode, lazily per frame or chunk, optionally overlapping stages across cores.
Configuration-driven data cleaning: the stage list is assembled from configuration or a plugin registry so different tenants get different ordered steps without changing the stages themselves.
TensorFlow tf.data input pipelines: tf.data.Dataset pipelines that chain map, prefetch, parallel_interleave and shuffle stages to feed a training loop efficiently, with each stage independently configurable and the whole pipeline testable in isolation.
LLM token streaming: HTTP server-sent event streams where an LLM produces tokens at inference speed while clients consume at variable network speed; stream.pipeline() prevents the inference server from buffering unbounded tokens in memory when a slow client disconnects (Node.js stream backpressure case study).
Observability telemetry pipelines: OpenTelemetry Collector chains receivers, processors (memory_limiter, batch, filter, transform, tail_sampling) and exporters for traces, metrics and logs, with connectors (e.g., spanmetrics) bridging signal types and memory_limiter placed first to prevent OOM before filtering.
Typed TypeScript pipeline with schema validation: Zod or io-ts schemas define the stage contract at each boundary, catching schema violations at the exact stage that produced bad data rather than at a distant consumer.
Async generator pipelines in Python: asyncio queues with bounded capacity connect async generator stages, propagating backpressure by pausing producers when the queue is full; the FinStream analytics case study showed 82% memory reduction and 99.7% latency reduction versus unbounded buffering.
Event-streaming pipelines with Kafka and Flink: producers, topic partitions, Flink consumers and checkpointing form a distributed pipeline where backpressure cascades across every boundary; the Kafka max.block.ms and Flink backpressure.sample.interval settings interact under partition saturation and must be tested together under load.
Dynamic pipeline parallelism: construct-and-run pipelines (MapReduce, Spark) fix stage count at construction, while on-the-fly pipelines (Cilk-P Piper algorithm) allow the structure to emerge at runtime, varying per iteration and supporting data-dependent branching; on-the-fly enables pipelines like x264 that cannot be expressed with a fixed static structure.
LLVM compiler pass pipelines: PassBuilder assembles ModulePassManager, CGSCCPassManager, FunctionPassManager and LoopPassManager across the IR hierarchy (Module → CGSCC → Function → Loop), with registered callbacks injecting passes at named extension points (pipeline-start, vectorizer-start, optimizer-last); incorrect PreservedAnalyses declarations invalidate all downstream analyses.
Continuous data pipelines at scale (Google model): periodic pipelines run on cron and suffer from depth growth and resource exhaustion as organic load increases; continuous pipelines (master-slave or event-triggered) replace idle-waiting with always-on processing, eliminating the 'pipeline vs cron' discontinuity at the cost of operational complexity.
ML pipeline orchestration (Airflow, Kubeflow, Prefect, Dagster): each orchestrator applies the pipeline pattern at the workflow level - Airflow's DAG-of-tasks, Kubeflow's per-container-step pipelines with GPU scheduling, Prefect's monoflow/subflow/orchestrator pattern, and Dagster's software-defined assets where asset dependencies imply the pipeline; the pipeline is the scheduler's unit of execution, not an implementation detail.
Apache Beam: PCollections flow through composable PTransforms (ParDo, Combine and GroupByKey) in a pipeline graph, making each transform boundary explicit while the runner handles execution.
Node.js stream.pipeline(): Readable, Transform and Writable stages compose with built-in backpressure, error propagation and AbortSignal cancellation; this is a concrete streaming realization, not a durable workflow engine.

name: converter
document:
converter
translator
Give a pair of corresponding representations one owner that maps them into each other in both directions, so every caller converts through one place and neither representation has to import, know or be aware of the other.
The same information lives in two representations - domain object and DTO, in-memory value and wire or column format, internal model and third-party schema - and both directions are exercised in production. Hand-written field copying at each call site duplicates the mapping rules, drifts whenever either representation changes, and forces at least one side (or every caller) to import the other.
Component boundaries where an internal model meets an external representation: service or API layers exchanging DTOs, persistence layers mapping values to column formats, integration seams facing a third-party or legacy schema, and codec layers mapping typed values to a wire format. It applies whenever both directions are needed (read and write, decode and encode) and either side must stay independent of the other - different modules, teams, release cycles or libraries.
Domain object <-> DTO at a service or API boundary, where the transport shape must not leak into the model.
Value object <-> database column representation (JPA AttributeConverter, EF Core ValueConverter, Rails custom attribute type).
Third-party or legacy schema <-> internal model at an integration seam, including versioned wire formats.
Typed value <-> JSON, XML or protobuf payload with a custom codec when the default mapping is wrong (formats, units, enums).
Query rows or record sets <-> domain objects, where a full mapper framework would be oversized.
Single-value wrappers such as identifiers, money or unit-carrying quantities mapped to and from their primitive form.
Palindrome conversion chain (Entity -> DAO -> DTO -> Controller -> DTO -> DAO -> Entity) where each layer owns exactly one transformation direction, making the data flow explicit and each boundary independently testable.
Versioned API contracts: a DTO for API v1 and a separate DTO for API v2 coexist; a converter pair maps each version's DTO to the shared internal model, isolating API consumers from internal changes.
API gateway transformation: external third-party API payloads are normalized into an internal canonical format at the gateway, and outbound responses are converted back to the third-party schema; converters live at the seam.
Event-driven payload normalization: domain events carry one representation (e.g., enriched entity) while the event bus transports a flattened wire format (e.g., protobuf); converters at producer and consumer ends keep the two shapes in sync.
ORM entity vs. read-model DTO at the query boundary: a repository executes a query and the row-set converter maps each row to a read-model DTO, avoiding the entity in read-only paths entirely.
Anti-corruption layer at legacy integration seams: external system payloads are translated into the internal domain model at the boundary, and responses translated back; the converter owns the translation vocabulary, protecting the domain model from foreign concepts (Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design; Microsoft Azure Architecture Center; AWS Prescriptive Guidance).
Immutable value type <-> wire format for cryptographic or financial domains: the converter is a lawful isomorphism ensuring every wire value round-trips to an identical object (tested via property-based round-trip laws, as in the lawful-conversions Haskell library and Higher-Kinded-J Iso optics library).
Strangler-fig migration seam: new microservice functionality is accessed through an ACL that converts legacy system payloads to the new domain model and back, keeping the legacy interface unchanged while the new service evolves behind the seam.
Guava com.google.common.base.Converter<F, T>: an abstract bidirectional function with convert()/reverse(), automatic reverse() derivation for subclasses, mapAll() for whole iterables and Converter.normalize() to lift a converter into a function converter - the pattern as a shipped JDK-adjacent library type (Google Guava).
Go database/sql custom types: a type implementing both sql.Scanner (Scan(src any) error) and driver.Valuer (Value() (driver.Value, error)) owns the Go value <-> database column pair in both directions; the standard library's NullString, NullInt64 and NullTime are built-in pairs of exactly this shape.
Rails custom attribute types: subclass ActiveModel::Type::Value, override serialize (Ruby value -> database value) and deserialize (database value -> Ruby value) and bind with attribute :col, MyType.new - the converter pair at the ORM seam, with cast_value kept separate for user-input coercion.

name: durable-subscriber
document:
durable-subscriber
durable subscription
durable consumer
Keep a publish-subscribe consumer's place while it is offline: the broker binds a stable subscription identity to retained messages or a committed position, then resumes delivery after reconnect until retention, expiry, or quota says the backlog is no longer available.
A subscriber on a publish-subscribe channel can be unavailable during redeployment, maintenance, device disconnects, or scheduled batch work. A non-durable subscription drops messages published during that gap, so the design must choose a stable identity and broker-side state, then make finite retention, replay pressure, and at-least-once redelivery explicit; durable state prevents a gap only while that state remains available.
Broker-mediated publish-subscribe messaging where consumers are intermittently offline but individual messages matter: JMS topics, MQTT sessions, Kafka consumer groups, NATS JetStream durable consumers, cloud topic subscriptions. It presumes the messaging system can store messages (or positions) durably, so it is as much a broker-configuration decision as a client one, and it presumes at-least-once delivery is acceptable once the consumer is idempotent. It does not apply to in-process notification or to broadcast where only the newest value counts.
A Kafka-backed order-processing service that is redeployed or scaled to zero while events keep arriving: the consumer group resumes from its committed offsets and replays what it missed.
An IoT or mobile client on an intermittent link: an MQTT persistent session holds QoS 1/2 publications for its client id and delivers them when the client reconnects.
A partner integration that receives published documents while the partner's system is down: an unshared JMS durable subscription, or a cloud topic subscription, is registered on their behalf and holds the backlog until they acknowledge it.
A nightly audit or analytics consumer that must see every published change: the day's backlog is drained in bounded batches and acknowledged as it is persisted.
A ledger or compliance consumer that must never silently skip events: retention and lag alarms are configured so an offline subscriber is noticed before its backlog expires.
A cloud event-driven architecture (SNS FIFO → SQS FIFO): SNS preserves ordering and deduplication while SQS queues hold messages for durable fan-out to Lambda or EC2 consumers, with DLQs capturing failed deliveries for replay.
An industrial SCADA/IoT sensor fleet where devices connect sporadically over unstable networks: MQTT persistent sessions with a long session expiry interval preserve every telemetry reading until each device reconnects, even after multi-day outages.
A financial audit trail that must immutably record every state-changing event: events are durably retained in Kafka or JetStream and consumed by a compliance subscriber that must not skip or duplicate entries; idempotent deduplication and offset commits after durable persistence enforce this.
A supply-chain or logistics event-sourcing system where downstream services reconstruct state by replaying events after a crash or deliberate seek: the durable consumer starts from the committed position and replays the missing event window atomically with the state reconstruction.
A cross-region disaster-recovery subscriber that mirrors events to a secondary site: the durable subscription in the secondary region receives every event from the primary's topic, with a DLQ holding any events that fail cross-region delivery for manual retry.
A JMS topic consumer that must receive publications made while it is offline: the client reconnects with the same client identifier and durable subscription name, and the provider retains messages until acknowledgement, expiry, or unsubscribe.
An MQTT 3.1.1 device gateway that reconnects with the same client identifier and CleanSession=0: the broker resumes the stored session and queues matching QoS 1/2 publications for delivery after the link returns.
A NATS JetStream billing worker that restarts after an outage: it binds to the same durable consumer name and explicit-acks each message, so the server resumes its acknowledgement floor and redelivers unacknowledged work.
An Azure Service Bus fan-out topology: topic subscriptions are durable by default and each subscription stores its own copy of matching messages, so a receiver that reconnects later still drains its backlog; client-affine durable subscriptions bind the durable state to a stable client id.
A high-throughput replay consumer on RabbitMQ Streams: the consumer attaches with a stable tracking reference (name) and periodically stores its offset server-side, so a restart resumes from the last stored offset instead of re-reading the whole stream.
An event-sourced system on Google Cloud Pub/Sub that must reprocess history after a bug fix: the subscription enables acknowledged-message retention (default window 7 days, up to 31) and is seeked back to a past timestamp or snapshot to replay already-acked messages.

name: passkey
document:
passkey
passkey idiom
constructor key
Restrict a constructor or method to chosen collaborators by requiring a token that only those collaborators can construct, so the operation stays in the public signature while remaining uncallable by everyone else - compile-time access control instead of blanket friendship.
A specific collaborator must call a constructor or method that must not become public API: a factory or helper that has to construct an object through a public constructor (make_unique, MakeGarbageCollected), a serialisation or framework layer that must reach one private hook, a subsystem that needs one internal operation, a test helper that must build a type in a state users cannot. The blunt mechanisms all miss: making the member public hands it to the world, friend (or its nearest equivalent) hands the collaborator the whole private surface, package/module/assembly access opens it to an entire scope, and a private constructor plus a factory just moves the gate into the factory. What is missing is a way to say 'this collaborator, and only this collaborator, may call exactly this operation'.
Statically checked code where the operation must stay visible in the type system (templates, frameworks and helper functions must be able to resolve the call) but must not be callable without a value that only the designated collaborators can create. The grant is a source-level construct checked by the compiler: the token is empty, disappears at run time and is never a defence against an adversary. Typical settings are factory-created types, library internals exposed to one subsystem, framework hooks, constructor or overload disambiguation, and test seams.
Factory-created objects with a public constructor: base::PassKey in Chromium exists for classes that a helper template (blink::MakeGarbageCollected) must construct while user code must not.
Serialisation and framework hooks: an archive, visitor or framework calls exactly one hook of a user type; the key names the framework instead of befriending it and exposing everything else.
Library-internal operations: one subsystem (allocator, persistence layer, test infrastructure) needs to construct or mutate a type users must not reach - the key names the subsystem where the language allows it, and module or assembly scope carries the rest.
Tests: a test helper constructs an otherwise unreachable state without '#define private public' builds, friend-everything test seams or reflection.
Constructor and overload disambiguation: a tag only the factory can produce selects the trusted overload and keeps the same argument list from being callable by everyone.
Deliberate delegation and revocation: the collaborator passes a key to another function that then performs the call, and a non-copyable key stops the ability from travelling further.
KDE Frameworks' KColorScheme (Frameworks 6.6.0) adopted a passkey specifically to avoid private-constructor issues, showing the idiom in a public Qt-based framework API.
Chromium's Mojo ProtoWrapperBytes uses base::PassKey to let named network, component and test classes access wrapped protobuf bytes while ordinary callers cannot supply the operation.
Abseil's C++ Tip of the Week #134 uses a passkey token with std::make_shared so a factory can keep single-allocation construction without making unconstrained construction the public API.

name: stub
document:
stub
test stub
stub object
Replace a collaborator with a test-specific stand-in that returns canned answers, so the component under test can be driven down paths - success, empty, error, timeout - that the real collaborator cannot be made to produce on demand.
The component under test receives indirect inputs through a collaborator, and the branch that must be exercised is selected by what that collaborator returns. The real collaborator will not produce the needed value on request: it is slow, remote, licensed, non-deterministic, or simply never returns the rare case - the empty result, the declined payment, the timeout - that the test exists for. Without a controllable replacement the test either cannot reach the path at all or has to provoke it through the production system, which is exactly what unit testing was supposed to avoid.
Unit and component tests of a component whose collaborators are already, or can cheaply become, abstractions: the values and exceptions a collaborator returns are inputs to the component under test, and the test asserts what the component does with them rather than how the collaboration happened. Typical where the collaborator is remote or stateful (HTTP client, database, queue, clock, payment gateway) or where the branch under test is an edge case - empty page, declined payment, expired token, feature off. The pattern assumes a substitutable seam: a constructor parameter, an injected interface, a factory, a lookup, or a patchable module.
Exercising a rare branch of the component: an empty result set, a declined payment, a 429 from a gateway, a missing feature flag.
Testing error handling: programme the stub to raise the exception the real service would raise - timeout, connection reset, malformed payload - and assert that the SUT surfaces or recovers from it.
Unit-testing a component against a collaborator that is slow, paid, unavailable in CI or still being implemented; the stub encodes the agreed response while the real adapter is built.
Removing non-determinism from a path the real collaborator decides by clock, randomness or remote state (token expired, cache cold, retry budget exhausted), so one outcome can be asserted exactly.
View and presentation tests: a fixed dataset from the stub, so the assertion is about the rendering or the decision logic and nothing else.
Boundary values on contract edges - zero, maximum, empty string, unicode payloads - that the real system cannot be asked to return on demand.
Mockito (Java): when(warehouse.hasInventory(...)).thenReturn(false) programmes the declined-branch answer and thenThrow(SocketTimeoutException.class) injects the failure, and consecutive-value stubbing (thenReturn(v1, v2)) drives retry-then-succeed paths that the real warehouse would never produce on request.
Python unittest.mock (standard library): Mock(return_value=...) fixes the canned answer while side_effect set to an exception or an iterable raises or sequences answers per call - the library ships Responder and Saboteur behaviour as first-class configuration.
Moq (.NET): mock.Setup(x => x.HasInventory(...)).Returns(false) and .Throws<InvalidOperationException>() are the canned-answer primitives, so a C# test reaches the empty-inventory and fault branches of Order.Fill without touching a database.

name: typestate
document:
typestate
type state
typestate programming
Encode an object's state in its type - a type parameter or a distinct state type - so that only the operations legal in the current state exist and every transition is a checked, type-changing step.
An object's methods are valid only in certain states (a closed file cannot be read, a client that has not connected cannot send), but the state lives in a runtime field: callers must remember the protocol, illegal calls still compile and fail at run time, and the legal sequences are documented rather than enforced.
Statically typed languages with generics or usable distinct-type support, where a small, fixed set of states and legal transitions is known at compile time: protocol handshakes, resource lifecycles (files, sockets, peripherals), staged builders and configuration objects, and single-owner workflows. It pays where a wrong sequence is expensive - hardware, protocols, money - and the state machine is stable.
Staged builders where build() must not compile before every required property is supplied (typed request builders, configuration objects).
Resource lifecycles: files, sockets and streams whose read/write/close operations are meaningful only after open and before close.
Protocol handshakes - connect, authenticate, exchange, disconnect - including TLS or HTTP session setup and stateful client APIs.
Embedded peripheral configuration: a GPIO pin or timer whose mode (input, output, alternate function) is a type parameter, so wrong-mode register access is a compile error.
Transaction and workflow objects: begin, mutate, commit or roll back, where committing twice or mutating after commit must not be expressible.
Iterators and streams with an exhausted state, where next() consumes the iterator until it yields the end state.
Hardware or network state machines where a wrong sequence causes a fault rather than a catchable error (bus faults, half-open connections).
Embedded HALs in the Rust ecosystem (embedded-hal and device crates such as stm32f4xx-hal) model a pin as Pin<M> with its mode as the type parameter: set_high() compiles only for an output-mode pin and into_input()/into_output() consume the old pin, as prescribed by the Embedded Rust Book's GPIO design chapter.
The Checker Framework for Java runs typestate analysis over unmodified code: its Called Methods and Resource Leak checkers track @MustCall obligations so an InputStream cannot be read before its required initialization methods ran and must be closed on every path - the state is inferred by a checker rather than written into the type.
TypeScript builder libraries such as ts-fluent-builder thread a phantom state type through the builder's generics so build() only compiles once every required property is present, turning missing-field errors from runtime throws into compile errors.

name: higher-order-component
document:
higher-order-component
HOC
component enhancer
Add cross-cutting behaviour to many components at once by wrapping them in an enhancer function that takes a component and returns a new, enhanced component, so no wrapped component knows about the concern or has to be edited.
The same cross-cutting logic - subscribing to a data source, checking a permission, firing analytics, injecting a theme, a translation or a feature flag - is needed by many components, and copying it into each one couples every component to the concern, re-couples them to every change of it, and leaves the behaviour to be remembered at each new call site. React tried mixins and inheritance first and removed them (implicit dependencies between mixin and component, name clashes, snowballing coupling), so the recurring decision is how to apply one behaviour to many components without editing them, while the components stay reusable and unaware of the enhancement.
Component-model UI code where components are values the framework mounts with a stable identity (React and its ecosystem first; the same shape recurs with Compose composables, SwiftUI views, Blazor components, Scala.js layers and handler-based Go/Java web UIs), where the concern is genuinely cross-cutting rather than local to one screen, where the enhancement can be expressed as a pure function from component to component and applied once at the definition or export site, and where the wrapped component's inputs form a prop-like contract that can be extended by injection without touching its internals.
Subscribing many components to an external data source — React documentation's withSubscription example, or Redux's connect: store state arrives as injected props with no component knowing about the store.
Apollo Client data injection: graphql(Query, { options, props }) HOC maps query results and loading state to props; multiple graphql HOCs composed with @compose; historically the standard before useQuery.
Authorization and feature gating at the boundary: withAuthorization(Component, { requiredRole }) or withFeatureFlag(...) decides rendering without editing the component; useful for route-level guards applied across many pages.
Analytics, telemetry and instrumentation applied at export sites (withAnalytics): tracking calls stay out of presentation code and can be added or removed at one location per module.
Injecting ambient context into components that take it as props — translations via withTranslation (react-i18next), routing via withRouter (React Router v5 and below), theming via withTheme (Material-UI v4) — enabling third-party and vendored components to participate without modification.
Error and loading boundaries as an enhancer (withErrorBoundary): the boundary exists as a component in the tree anyway; an enhancer consolidates the concern into one reusable definition rather than repeating the try/catch at each call site.
Sharing logic into class components and older codebases where hooks cannot be used: the HOC reaches class components and library component-shaped APIs that hooks cannot wrap.
Material-UI v4 theming: withStyles and withTheme HOCs inject classes and theme as props; compose chains combine styling with data (connect + withStyles + graphql on the same export).
Internationalization testing: export both wrapped and unwrapped components; tests use the raw component with a mock t function while integration tests use the full I18nextProvider setup.
Conditional prop injection: a data-enhancer that only injects props when a condition is met (e.g. user is authenticated) lets the wrapped component remain agnostic about the absence of that data.
React Compiler (React Forget) compatibility: heavy HOC layering reduces the compiler's static analysis surface and may cause it to bailout — test compiler output when adding HOCs to a compiled codebase; prefer hooks for new logic the compiler should see.
React Server Components boundary: a HOC that calls hooks or reads client-only context (useAuth, useTheme, useRouter) cannot execute during a server render; the wrapped component may receive undefined injected props on the server and flash-change on hydration. Pass server-fetched data as props through the HOC boundary from a server parent instead.
Streaming SSR and Suspense integration: a HOC that wraps a component behind a Suspense boundary adds a node that may delay streaming; if the HOC itself is async it must be carefully placed to avoid blocking the fallback from showing.
Partial hydration patterns: on islands architectures (Next.js App Router, Astro), a HOC that subscribes to client-side state forces the entire island to be hydrated even if the wrapped component has no server payload; prefer passing hydrated state as props from a server parent.
Recompose (acdlite): a 'lodash for React' utility belt built entirely from composable HOCs (withState, mapProps, pure, branch) piped through enhance/compose - the pattern industrialised; its October 2018 deprecation in favour of Hooks (bug-fix maintenance only) is the canonical case study of the pattern's cost when a runtime offers a cheaper reuse primitive.
MobX React binding: observer from mobx-react / mobx-react-lite is an official HOC that subscribes the wrapped component to every observable read during render, re-rendering it automatically; MobX guidance is to apply observer first (innermost) when composing it with other HOCs, and to wrap every component that reads observables.

name: applicative
document:
applicative
applicative functor
applicative style
idiom (original McBride-Paterson name)
Apply one pure function to several independent effectful computations, letting the chosen context instance fix the semantics of absence, failure, ordering, and concurrency; the combining structure is fixed before execution - that static shape is what enables batching, parallel scheduling, and static analysis - and an accumulating error instance reports every independent failure instead of short-circuiting on the first.
You have several independent computations - parse this field, fetch that record, validate this quantity - and a pure function that combines their results, but each result lives inside a context such as Option, Either/Result, List, Promise/Task, or Validation. A bind/await chain can imply a dependency that does not exist, serialize work, or stop at the first failure; you need a fixed applicative structure that combines the values while leaving failure and scheduling policy to the chosen instance.
Value- or effect-level functional code where independent combination is the recurring decision: form and request validation that must report every field error at once, parallel-capable fetch coordination, configuration or tuple assembly from independent parses, and parser/stream composition. Applies when the language offers a context type (or validator abstraction) and the team accepts a small abstraction - a type class in Scala/Kotlin, a stdlib combinator such as Promise.all, or a hand-written lift2 - to express 'apply a pure function to several effectful arguments'. Applicative structure permits parallel execution but does not itself guarantee scheduling, cancellation, or error accumulation.
Form, request or configuration validation where every field is checked independently and the user must see all violations in one response.
Combining independent parses of a record (age, e-mail, quantity, date range) into one constructed value, reporting every malformed field.
Parallel IO combination: fetching several unrelated resources (Promise.all, CompletableFuture.thenCombine, parZipOrAccumulate, errgroup fan-out) and pairing the results positionally.
Parser and stream combinators where several parsers/subscribers consume the same input independently and their results are combined into a node.
Building a read model or report from several independent queries where a failure of one part should be reported without cancelling the others.
Statistics/diagnostics: computing several independent measurements of the same input and combining them with a pure summary function.
DSLs and embedded languages: building an abstract syntax tree of applicative operations (Free Applicative) that can be statically analyzed, optimized, or pretty-printed before interpretation - enabling query planning, dead code elimination, or validation of DSL constraints at construction time.
Traversable data structures: threading an Applicative effect through a container (tree, list, optional) so each element can be independently validated, transformed, or fetched without sequential coupling.
Collecting monoidal summaries: using Const as the Applicative to fold a Traversable structure into a single Monoid value (e.g., collecting all validation errors, or computing a checksum) without materializing a transformed structure.
API gateway aggregation: combining multiple downstream service calls where each call is independent and all results (or all errors) should be collected before returning a response to the caller.
Configuration loading at startup: validating all config fields independently and reporting every misconfiguration at once rather than failing on the first missing key.
CSV or batch row validation: validating each row independently and accumulating all row-level errors so the entire batch can be rejected with a full error report rather than failing on the first bad row.
Bidirectional codec composition: building parsers and serializers (e.g., with prismatic/schema, io-ts, or hkj's ValidatedPrism) where the parse direction is accumulating and fallible but the build direction is total, preserving the parse-don't-validate discipline applicatively.
GraphQL API input validation: validate independent arguments and return all field-level errors in one response instead of rejecting at the first failure.
Kubernetes or Helm configuration loading: validate independent keys and report the complete set of startup misconfigurations before deployment.
CI/CD pipeline policy checks: run independent static checks over a change and aggregate diagnostics before gating the build.
Haxl at Meta/Facebook: an applicative Fetch whose <*> explores both operands before blocking, so independent dataFetch calls to the same data source batch into one request and run concurrently without explicit forking ("There is no Fork", ICFP 2014).
Swift structured concurrency: async let starts each independent task as a child task immediately and a later await combines the results into a tuple or constructor call - applicative-shaped combination of a fixed set of independent effects in mainstream syntax, with cancellation and lifetime bounded by the enclosing scope.
Elm JSON decoders: Json.Decode map2..map8 (or elm-json-decode-pipeline's required/custom steps) assemble a record from independent per-field decoders - the production form of mapN in front-end code.

name: monad
document:
monad
io monad
programmable semicolon
Give a computation's effect (absence, failure, asynchrony, I/O, state) a type of its own with a unit and a bind operation, so that a sequence of steps in which each step depends on the previous value composes into one pipeline while bind propagates the effect automatically.
Sequencing computations where the next step needs the previous step's result and every step may additionally be absent, failing, asynchronous or effectful pushes the effect handling into the business logic: nested null checks, try/catch ladders, callback pyramids. Every call site repeats the same propagation decision (short-circuit? await? log?) and one forgotten check turns a controlled failure into a crash or a wrong value.
Applies wherever a value and the fact that it is absent, pending, failing or impure belong together: chained lookups, validation and error pipelines, asynchronous call chains, state threading, parser and interpreter pipelines, and effect-typed application cores. It matters most when the sequence is long, when the effect policy must be uniform and testable, and when the language already provides monadic types (Optional, Result, Promise, IO) or syntax that desugars to bind (do-notation, for-comprehensions, async/await).
Chained lookups where any link may be missing: user -> address -> city expressed with Maybe/Optional instead of nested null checks.
Validation and error pipelines in which each step can fail with a domain error and the first failure must short-circuit (Either/Result, railway-oriented programming).
Asynchronous workflows whose next call depends on the previous response (Promise/async-await, CompletableFuture.thenCompose, Kotlin suspend functions, Swift Task).
Effect description and interpretation: building an IO/program value that is pure data and running it through different interpreters in tests and production (IO monad, tagless-final).
State-threading computations such as compiler passes, random generators or incremental traversals written as a State monad pipeline.
Parser combinators and nondeterministic search, where each step consumes the previous parse result or explores every value produced by the previous step (parser monad, List monad).
Rust's std::result::Result composes fallible steps with and_then and the ? operator, returning early on Err while keeping the successful value available to the next dependent step.
Java's CompletableFuture.thenCompose chains dependent asynchronous stages: the function returns another CompletionStage and the outer stage adopts its completion or exceptional failure.
Scala for-comprehensions over Option, collections, or other types with map, flatMap, and withFilter desugar dependent bindings into the corresponding combinators, keeping the monadic sequence readable without hiding its operations.

name: contravariant-validators
document:
contravariant-validators
decidable validators
contravariant functor
divisible validators
predicate composition
Make a check on a value a reusable first-class validator that can be adapted to other input types and combined with other validators, so that rules are composed out of parts instead of being re-implemented for every type that carries the same value.
Reusable checks that narrow on a condition - 'is this a valid port', 'is this host name well formed', 'is this account allowed' - are needed for many representations of the same value (wire DTO, domain type, CLI string, database row). Written as a method or an inline if per site, the same rule is duplicated, cannot be combined with another rule without editing the check, and every new rule means editing the class that holds the data.
Value-level validation and parsing at a boundary: configuration and environment loading, request or message payload checking, domain-primitive construction, form validation, authorization predicates. It applies wherever checks are pure functions of one input, must be reused across several input shapes or composed into rule sets, and the language offers first-class functions or a typeclass layer for the composition. Rules that depend on I/O, transactions or clock state are outside the pattern.
Configuration and environment loading: parse an untyped map into a typed configuration record, with one reusable validator per field and all field errors reported in one pass.
Request and message payload checking: compose a schema/rule set from reusable field validators plus cross-field rules, then dispatch branch-specific rules after a case split (choose) on the payload type.
Domain primitives and refinement: define positive/Email/Iban-style checks once and apply them to every representation of that value through projections, or carry them in the type system as refinement/branded types.
Authorization and feature predicates: composable rules over a request or principal (admin OR owner, enabled AND within quota), each rule written against a small projection of the context.
Form and API error reporting: collect every failed rule with its field path instead of failing at the first problem, by combining verdicts with an accumulating monoid.
Archival or search predicates: build a rule tree once (conjunction of filters over properties) and hand it to a framework that evaluates it later (Foundation Predicate, SwiftData/query engines, filter DSLs).
gRPC and protobuf boundaries: validate oneof/discriminated union payloads by routing each variant through its own validator using choose, while shared fields are validated once via divide.
Event-sourced aggregate validation: validate command payloads at the aggregate root, collecting every domain invariant violation before rejecting the command rather than failing on the first broken rule.
Multi-tenant SaaS rule sets: compose tenant-specific validators from shared base rules via divide/conquer, so the same field rules are reused across tenants with tenant-specific constraint values injected via contramap.
gRPC/protobuf and wire format boundaries: validate at the deserialization boundary before the parsed message reaches business logic, using a composed validator that is reused for CLI, test fixtures, and service-to-service calls.
Typed FP standard libraries shipping the combinators as an API: Arrow Kotlin exposes Contravariant/Divisible/Decidable type classes (conquer, divide, choose, lose) for carriers like Predicate and Serializer, and the contravariant package in Haskell instances them for Predicate, Comparison, Equivalence and Op - the pattern realized as library infrastructure rather than application code.
Refinement-type libraries as validator stores: fthomas/refined attaches type-level predicates (Positive, MatchesRegex, Uri) composed with And/Or/Not to values, with custom checks arriving as a Validate instance built by Validate.fromPredicate - the same rule set read at compile time by macros and at runtime by refineV.
Accumulating verdict monoids in production effect systems: ZIO Prelude's Validation[E, A] carries a NonEmptyChunk of errors and composes per-field checks with validateWith, so a registration form built from independent field validators reports every violation in one pass instead of one per round trip.
