name: page-object
document:
page-object
page object model
window driver
Wrap each UI surface a test drives - a page or a significant component - in an object that exposes the services the surface offers and hides every locator, driver call and wait, so a UI change is absorbed by one class instead of by every test that touched the markup.
A UI test that drives the automation API directly - find an element, type, click, wait, read text - keeps the page's locators and interaction mechanics in the test body: the same selector is repeated across dozens of tests, a markup change breaks them all at once, and a reader must reconstruct the page's structure to understand what the test does. The catalog's trigger: a UI change should touch one class, not fifty assertions.
Automated tests that drive a user interface through a driver API - a browser (Selenium/WebDriver, Playwright, Cypress, WebdriverIO), a mobile app (Appium, Espresso, XCUITest) or a desktop window - where the same screens are exercised by many tests, where the UI changes independently of the tests, and where the suite is expected to survive redesigns. The pattern pays off when the interface can be named in the user's terms ('sign-in page', 'product row') and the driver offers stable element lookup; it is unnecessary for a single throwaway script or when the presentation logic has already been extracted behind a humble object.
A regression suite over a web application whose pages are exercised by dozens of tests: login, search, checkout and admin screens each get a class, and a redesign changes only those classes (the Selenium and Playwright POM guides' home scenario).
The same screens are driven by different kinds of test - functional, visual, accessibility, smoke - and the locator knowledge must live in one place that all of them import.
Mobile application suites (Appium, Espresso, XCUITest) where screens are widget hierarchies with platform-specific queries, and the page object is the only place that codifies the platform lookup.
BDD suites: Gherkin steps stay business-readable because step definitions delegate to page objects instead of calling the driver (Fowler's layering recommendation).
Suites migrating drivers or frameworks (Selenium to Playwright, a WebdriverIO restructure): the page API is kept while only its internals change.
A scripting interface over an application whose behaviour is stuck in the UI (Fowler's scripting use), or a legacy system that can only be exercised through its window.
Selenium's documented login flow: SignInPage.loginValidUser returns HomePage, so a regression suite can exercise authentication through services while locators and page-load checks stay in the page objects.
Playwright's official playwright.dev example: PlaywrightDevPage wraps a Page, owns locators for the getting-started flow and exposes goto, getStarted and pageObjectModel methods used by tests.
WebdriverIO's official The Internet login example: a getter-based LoginPage centralizes selectors and open/submit actions, letting login specs survive selector changes without duplicating driver calls.

name: page-controller
document:
page-controller
model-1
Give each logical page or form its own input controller that handles the requests addressed to it — reading the request, invoking domain logic and choosing the view — instead of routing every request through one shared handler.
Dynamic pages repeat the same request handling: parse and validate the incoming request, call domain logic, pick a view, report errors. Without a per-page home for that logic it either spreads into templates or gets copied into every script; the recurring decision is whether one page or form owns its request handling, or whether a central controller multiplexes all of them.
Server-side web presentation where URLs map one-to-one onto logical pages, forms or actions: CGI programs, servlets and JSP pages, controller actions, Razor Pages, route handlers in micro-frameworks. It fits sites whose pages share little behaviour, page-focused areas of larger applications, and frameworks whose native unit is a page; it stops fitting as soon as most pages need the same authentication, internationalisation, layout or tracing.
Small to medium websites where each page has its own URL, its own data and its own template (CMS front ends, marketing pages with forms, internal tools).
Form-heavy areas where one page owns one interaction end to end: show the form, validate the submission, run one workflow, render the result.
Prototypes and scripting-era deployments where one program, servlet or route function per page is the natural deployment unit.
Page-focused corners of a larger application (account settings, an admin console) whose pages genuinely differ from one another.
Frameworks whose canonical unit is the page itself: Razor Pages (PageModel = Page Controller), ASP.NET Web Forms code-behind, Java Struts Actions, Django FBV (Function-Based Views) mapped one-per-URL, Flask route functions, PHP single-file-per-page.
Per-page Ajax callbacks that are tightly coupled to a specific page's data and logic, where extracting them into a shared controller would create artificial coupling.
Situations where page-specific code is large enough to warrant a dedicated class but small enough that a full command-object framework is overkill.
ASP.NET Core Razor Pages: each PageModel owns the handlers and view data for one page, with OnGet/OnPost methods providing a concrete page-controller unit for page-specific forms. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/razor-pages/?view=aspnetcore-10.0
Django function-based views: URLconf maps a URL pattern to one Python view function that receives HttpRequest and returns the page response, making small page-specific interactions explicit. https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/6.1/topics/http/views/
Flask route functions: the route decorator binds a URL and HTTP methods to one view function, a lightweight Page Controller shape for independent pages and forms. https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/quickstart/

name: plugin
document:
plugin
plug-in
plugin architecture
Let a host application acquire behaviour from independently deployed modules that it discovers and links at configuration or start-up time, so new features, backends or device support can be added without recompiling or redeploying the host.
The behaviours a system must offer vary by deployment (customer, environment, backend, hardware) or grow after the host has shipped; hard-wiring every implementation behind a factory method or a configuration switch means each new variant edits core code and forces a rebuild and redeploy of the whole application.
Systems whose capability set is not fully known at build time: third-party or per-customer extensions, drivers and storage backends, editor and build tooling, test runners, media pipelines. It applies wherever a stable extension point can be published, the contract can be versioned, and the runtime can bind code after compilation (shared libraries, class or module loading, plugin packages).
IDEs, editors and build tools whose feature set grows through extensions (Eclipse, VS Code, webpack, ESLint, pytest, RuboCop).
Servers and frameworks that pick a codec, transport, storage or auth backend per deployment (JDBC drivers via ServiceLoader, .NET plugin hosts, Kafka connectors).
Infrastructure tooling that hosts independently released providers, such as Terraform providers over gRPC or Vault secret engines.
Media, imaging and device software that adds codecs, effects or drivers after the main program ships (Apache httpd modules, GStreamer, DAW and imaging plugins).
Document and data pipelines where per-customer transformation or validation steps are shipped as separate packages (Python entry points, Ruby gems).
Applications that must support tenant- or customer-specific behaviour without a private build per customer, composed at start-up from a plugin directory or a configuration list.
AI agent systems where tools, memory backends and LLMs are loaded as plugins (LangChain agents, semantic kernel plugins).
Cloud-native platforms that must support tenant-specific backends or third-party integrations without redeploying the control plane (Kubernetes operators, service mesh extensions).
DevOps and CI/CD pipelines where steps, reporters or cloud integrations are added as plugins (Jenkins plugins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI job templates).
Observability platforms where collectors, processors and exporters are pluginable (OpenTelemetry collectors, Grafana datasources and panels).
Editor ecosystems that declare contributions in manifests and run extension code behind a host boundary, as in Visual Studio Code's Extension Host and contribution points.
Infrastructure CLIs that launch provider binaries over a versioned RPC contract and negotiate compatibility, as in Terraform's Plugin Protocol and provider servers.
Web servers assembled from independently built dynamic modules loaded at startup or restart, as in Apache HTTP Server's DSO and mod_so module system.

name: single-table-inheritance
document:
single-table-inheritance
table per hierarchy
discriminator column mapping
Map an inheritance hierarchy of classes onto one shared table whose columns are the union of all classes' fields, using a type code (discriminator) column to decide which class each row instantiates, so polymorphic reads need no joins.
A class hierarchy must be persisted, the hierarchy is small and its classes share most fields, and cross-class queries or polymorphic loads are frequent: mapping each class to its own table would force a join per level on almost every read, while the subtypes differ by only a few columns.
Object-relational mapping of a small, shallow, stable class hierarchy whose subclasses are mostly variations on shared state - domain-model inheritance (Employee/Engineer/Manager), payment or content types - where the storage layer is chosen by the team and the persistence framework can be taught the type code (JPA/EF Core/ActiveRecord/SQLAlchemy/most ORMs make this their default strategy) or the mapping is written by hand over SQL.
Small stable hierarchies where subclasses share most state: Employee/Engineer/Manager, Payment/CardPayment/WirePayment, Notification/EmailNotification/PushNotification.
Content or asset models with a handful of similar types (Photo/Question/Post, Blog/RssBlog) distinguished by a type code, where cross-type queries and listings are the dominant read.
Legacy or third-party schemas that already hold a hierarchy in one table with a kind column and must be mapped onto domain classes without restructuring the database.
Reporting and analytics over a hierarchy where one wide table with a type column beats joining four tables for every subtype question.
ORM-default configurations: teams that pick the framework's default hierarchy mapping (JPA SINGLE_TABLE, EF Core TPH) because join avoidance and mapping simplicity outweigh column honesty for their hierarchy size.
Rails Active Record single-table inheritance: ActiveRecord::Inheritance stores the subclass name in the table's type column by default (Company/Firm/Client all live in companies with type = 'Firm'), so fetching via the base class returns correctly-typed objects - GitLab runs a production monolith on this mechanism and maintains a written policy on when STI must not be used.
EF Core's default table-per-hierarchy mapping: a Blog/RssBlog hierarchy shares one table, the discriminator's name, CLR type and per-class values are set with HasDiscriminator/HasValue, and EF Core automatically adds the discriminator predicate to derived-type queries (throwing on unmapped discriminator values).
SQLAlchemy declarative polymorphic mappers: the base class declares polymorphic_on = 'type' in __mapper_args__ and each subclass a unique polymorphic_identity, so one person table answers polymorphic queries for Person/Employee rows without joins.

name: converter
document:
converter
translator
Give a pair of corresponding representations one owner that maps them into each other in both directions, so every caller converts through one place and neither representation has to import, know or be aware of the other.
The same information lives in two representations - domain object and DTO, in-memory value and wire or column format, internal model and third-party schema - and both directions are exercised in production. Hand-written field copying at each call site duplicates the mapping rules, drifts whenever either representation changes, and forces at least one side (or every caller) to import the other.
Component boundaries where an internal model meets an external representation: service or API layers exchanging DTOs, persistence layers mapping values to column formats, integration seams facing a third-party or legacy schema, and codec layers mapping typed values to a wire format. It applies whenever both directions are needed (read and write, decode and encode) and either side must stay independent of the other - different modules, teams, release cycles or libraries.
Domain object <-> DTO at a service or API boundary, where the transport shape must not leak into the model.
Value object <-> database column representation (JPA AttributeConverter, EF Core ValueConverter, Rails custom attribute type).
Third-party or legacy schema <-> internal model at an integration seam, including versioned wire formats.
Typed value <-> JSON, XML or protobuf payload with a custom codec when the default mapping is wrong (formats, units, enums).
Query rows or record sets <-> domain objects, where a full mapper framework would be oversized.
Single-value wrappers such as identifiers, money or unit-carrying quantities mapped to and from their primitive form.
Palindrome conversion chain (Entity -> DAO -> DTO -> Controller -> DTO -> DAO -> Entity) where each layer owns exactly one transformation direction, making the data flow explicit and each boundary independently testable.
Versioned API contracts: a DTO for API v1 and a separate DTO for API v2 coexist; a converter pair maps each version's DTO to the shared internal model, isolating API consumers from internal changes.
API gateway transformation: external third-party API payloads are normalized into an internal canonical format at the gateway, and outbound responses are converted back to the third-party schema; converters live at the seam.
Event-driven payload normalization: domain events carry one representation (e.g., enriched entity) while the event bus transports a flattened wire format (e.g., protobuf); converters at producer and consumer ends keep the two shapes in sync.
ORM entity vs. read-model DTO at the query boundary: a repository executes a query and the row-set converter maps each row to a read-model DTO, avoiding the entity in read-only paths entirely.
Anti-corruption layer at legacy integration seams: external system payloads are translated into the internal domain model at the boundary, and responses translated back; the converter owns the translation vocabulary, protecting the domain model from foreign concepts (Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design; Microsoft Azure Architecture Center; AWS Prescriptive Guidance).
Immutable value type <-> wire format for cryptographic or financial domains: the converter is a lawful isomorphism ensuring every wire value round-trips to an identical object (tested via property-based round-trip laws, as in the lawful-conversions Haskell library and Higher-Kinded-J Iso optics library).
Strangler-fig migration seam: new microservice functionality is accessed through an ACL that converts legacy system payloads to the new domain model and back, keeping the legacy interface unchanged while the new service evolves behind the seam.
Guava com.google.common.base.Converter<F, T>: an abstract bidirectional function with convert()/reverse(), automatic reverse() derivation for subclasses, mapAll() for whole iterables and Converter.normalize() to lift a converter into a function converter - the pattern as a shipped JDK-adjacent library type (Google Guava).
Go database/sql custom types: a type implementing both sql.Scanner (Scan(src any) error) and driver.Valuer (Value() (driver.Value, error)) owns the Go value <-> database column pair in both directions; the standard library's NullString, NullInt64 and NullTime are built-in pairs of exactly this shape.
Rails custom attribute types: subclass ActiveModel::Type::Value, override serialize (Ruby value -> database value) and deserialize (database value -> Ruby value) and bind with attribute :col, MyType.new - the converter pair at the ORM seam, with cast_value kept separate for user-input coercion.

name: identity-map
document:
identity-map
first-level cache
session cache
Guarantee that within one session every database row is represented by exactly one in-memory object, by keeping a keyed registry of loaded objects that every load consults before hitting the database.
Two code paths in the same session load the same row into two different objects: updates through one are invisible to the other, the last flush silently wins, and every load pays the remote-call cost again. The catalog states the invariant as: the same row must never be two different in-memory objects in one session.
Object-oriented persistence (data mappers, repositories, unit of work) where entities carry a stable database identity (an Identity Field) and several parts of one business transaction or request refer to the same rows. Applies whenever duplicate in-memory instances would break graph consistency or lose updates - typically inside an ORM session or a hand-written persistence context whose lifetime bounds staleness.
ORM sessions in web request handling (JPA EntityManager, EF Core DbContext, SQLAlchemy Session, MikroORM EntityManager) where several services touch the same entities in one request.
Batch import and synchronisation jobs that re-read the same rows repeatedly inside one transaction and must not operate on divergent copies.
Object graph reconstruction in data mappers, where cycles and shared references need one in-memory instance per row.
Desktop and document applications with a context-scoped object space (Core Data contexts) where objects are edited, undone and saved as one unit.
Hand-written persistence layers over plain SQL where two repositories serve the same table and must agree on identity.
CQRS command handlers where the same aggregate is loaded multiple times within one command execution — the identity map prevents duplicate instances from forming across repository calls within the same session.
Event-sourced aggregate reconstruction: replaying events to rebuild aggregate state requires the same aggregate instance to accumulate state across multiple event applications; identity map guarantees a single instance per aggregate ID per reconstruction session.
Microservices saga and choreography: within one service's unit-of-work, multiple steps may load the same entity; identity map ensures all steps operate on the same instance even when the entity is referenced across different event handlers.
DDD bounded-context integration: when one bounded context holds a reference to an entity from another context (by ID), that entity is resolved through the local identity map — multiple resolution paths must all consult the same map to stay consistent.
Testing scenarios where the same entity is accessed via multiple repository paths: identity map guarantees test assertions see the same instance regardless of which repository method returned it, enabling meaningful state verification.
Multi-tenant applications where each tenant request gets its own session/identity-map scope, preventing cross-tenant data leakage by construction — a shared/global map would allow one tenant's rows to shadow another's.
SQLAlchemy Session.get in a unit of work: repeated primary-key loads return the same Python object from the Session identity map, while the Session is deliberately not a cross-session query cache.
EF Core tracked queries and AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution: the DbContext keeps one entity instance per key for tracked results, while no-tracking identity resolution is opt-in for read models.
Hibernate Session persistence contexts: repeated loads of the same entity type and identifier resolve to the one managed instance per Session, so entity graphs and dirty checking share state.

name: composed-method
document:
composed-method
compose method
Divide the work into methods that each perform one identifiable task, written as a short outline of invocations in which every operation sits at the same level of abstraction, so a reader grasps the task top-down and every change lands on one small, named step.
A method accumulates several concerns at once: high-level policy ('validate the order, then charge it') interleaved with low-level detail (a loop index, a string concatenation, a counter), so the method grows long, needs comments to mark its sections, and changes for more than one reason. Readers must simulate the whole body to learn what it does, duplication hides inside similar-looking blocks, and anyone who must change one decision - a subclass in particular - ends up copying the method and editing it.
Applies wherever code is decomposed into named routines and is read far more often than written: long-lived domain and application code, code review and onboarding, framework base classes that must expose override hooks, and code whose steps carry contracts worth testing separately. It is a source-level discipline rather than a runtime structure, so a language needs only routines and some notion of non-public helpers; it matters most exactly where methods have grown past the point a reader can hold them in mind.
Long methods built up over time whose sections are marked by comments: each comment becomes a step name and the method becomes an outline.
A method with several responsibilities (validate, compute, persist) that must change independently and be reviewed one concern at a time.
Framework or library base classes that must offer override points: each step becomes a documented extension point, usually combined with Template Method or NVI.
Top-down design of an algorithm: write the outline first, with steps as not-yet-implemented calls, and fill them in one at a time.
Bottom-up refactoring when the same block appears in several methods: extract it as a named step and call it from each outline.
Making behaviour testable in isolation: steps with their own contracts (parsing input, rounding money, validating rules) become separately testable units.
TDD workflow: write the test for the composed method outline first, asserting each step in sequence, then implement each step as a separate testable unit.
Complex business rules that combine multiple conditional branches: decompose each branch condition and its body into a clearly named step, making the rule engine visible and auditable.
Command or handler objects that orchestrate a multi-step process (validate request, authorize caller, execute operation, emit event, log outcome): each phase is a named step in the composed method.
Production Rails code: Basecamp's Event::Relaying#relay_now reads as an outline of named steps (relay_to_or_revoke_from_timeline, relay_to_webhooks_later), each descending into its own relayer class - the 'fractal' consistency of composed methods in a shipped product, documented by 37signals.
Acceptance and integration test suites: each scenario is written as a composed method at a single level of abstraction (sign_in, create_todo, mark_complete), delegating the mechanics to named helpers or page objects so the test tells the user-level story.
JUnit 4's refactored internals: Beck documents TestCase together with the RunAfter, ExpectException and FailedTest method objects as chained composed outlines, each invocation staying at one level of abstraction (his 'Nested Method Object' evolution of the pattern).

name: make-illegal-states-unrepresentable
document:
make-illegal-states-unrepresentable
make invalid states unrepresentable
Encode each domain rule in the shape of the data type so that values violating the rule cannot be constructed at all, replacing scattered run-time validation and defensive checks with a model in which only legal states exist.
Domain values are modelled as one record with independent fields - a status tag plus several nullable or optional attributes, or a handful of booleans - so the type admits every combination of those fields, including the ones the business rules forbid. Consumers cannot trust the type: each branch re-checks which fields are meaningful, the same guard is written in several places (and forgotten in one), and illegal states become runtime bugs that surface when a code path finally combines the wrong flags.
Applies when a value has a small, known set of mutually exclusive shapes whose payloads differ, when the same invalid combination keeps being defended against in several places, and when the language can close a set of variants (Rust/Swift enums, sealed hierarchies, discriminated unions) or at least hide constructors. It is equally a boundary discipline: untrusted input is parsed once into a type whose existence already proves it is valid, so no downstream code has to re-validate.
Lifecycle and state machines: orders, payments, subscriptions, bookings and connection states, one variant per state carrying exactly the data that exists in that state.
Client and API request state: a loading/success/error union instead of a data field, an error field and an isLoading flag that can contradict one another.
Message and protocol modelling: a closed set of commands, events or JSON payload shapes decoded once and dispatched with an exhaustive match (event sourcing, interpreters, RPC handlers).
Refined scalars that travel through the model: money with currency, email addresses, quantities with units and identifiers that are parsed once and never re-validated.
Configuration whose combinations are illegal: TLS settings that only apply when TLS is enabled, cursor-based versus offset pagination, mutually exclusive feature flags.
Import and deserialization boundaries: convert untrusted rows, CSV cells, query parameters or JSON into domain types with a failing factory, so invalid input cannot travel further.
Rust's standard `Option`/`Result` enums and exhaustive `match` make presence, absence, success and failure explicit cases that downstream code must handle at compile time (Rust Reference/Book).
Swift enums with associated values and exhaustive `switch` model state-specific payloads such as error cases without nullable companion fields (The Swift Programming Language).
Kotlin sealed classes and interfaces with exhaustive `when` expressions provide a closed hierarchy for finite state machines and error/result models, with the compiler checking that every known case is handled.

name: anti-corruption-layer
document:
anti-corruption-layer
acl
translation layer
Protect a downstream bounded context from a foreign model by making one explicitly owned boundary translate calls, data and failure semantics into the downstream language; unlike a mere wrapper, an anti-corruption layer prevents foreign concepts from becoming domain concepts.
A bounded context must use a legacy application, packaged product, partner API or another context whose model it cannot control, and the same words carry different meanings on each side. Reusing the foreign SDK types and status codes directly makes its names, optionality, units, errors and version churn load-bearing parts of the local domain; translation then drifts across callers and every upstream change becomes a core-model change. Without an explicit boundary, the contexts become accidental conformists and neither can evolve independently.
Use it at a durable integration seam where the models genuinely disagree and at least one side cannot be changed: a new core beside a legacy or packaged system, a core subdomain consuming a third-party service, two bounded contexts with different vocabularies, or a staged migration whose callers must survive a callee replacement. It is a boundary-scoped investment: a model worth protecting must exist on the downstream side, and the seam must be durable enough to own a component; a wire-level rename, a CRUD screen over a stable API or throwaway code does not justify it.
Staged migration (strangler style): a monolith keeps calling a capability that has been extracted into a service, and the layer converts the old call into the new semantics so existing callers are not modified while functionality moves out piece by piece.
Legacy or packaged systems: an ERP, mainframe, CRM or vendor database with convoluted schemas and obsolete protocols is consumed by a new core domain that refuses to adopt its concepts.
Third-party services inside a core subdomain: a payment, identity or logistics API whose model must not shape your domain — its statuses, optionality and error codes are mapped to your own types.
Two bounded contexts in one product: the upstream team publishes a model your context rejects (conformist would be too costly), so your side translates it and the context map records the relationship.
Event-driven integration: upstream events are translated, validated and re-emitted as downstream domain events before any handler in the core sees them.
Standardised external formats: EDI, ISO 20022, FHIR or partner schemas are parsed into a local model inside the layer, keeping the standard's vocabulary out of the domain.
Replacing an infrastructure dependency: swapping the persistence engine, message broker or identity provider behind a layer while the domain keeps exactly the same vocabulary.
Database-view ACL for analytics: a database view that maps another context's internal storage schema into an analytics-owned projection, used instead of direct cross-context SQL queries that couple the analytics context to the source's implementation details.
API-gateway-level ACL: an Azure Functions, AWS Lambda or similar serverless function deployed at the API gateway seam that performs domain-model translation before requests reach the downstream service, keeping protocol handling and semantic translation separate.
Dark launch / shadow traffic validation: an ACL running in parallel that receives mirrored traffic and logs translation discrepancies without affecting live callers, enabling validation of a new integration before any traffic is cut over.
Multi-system data aggregation: a domain that must compose data from multiple external systems with incompatible models (e.g., a customer dashboard pulling from Stripe, Salesforce and an on-premises ERP) translates each system's model separately before assembling a unified view.
Bidirectional payment provider integration: a payment gateway ACL that translates inbound webhooks (provider → local domain events) and outbound charge requests (local domain → provider format), with a stable provider-independent reference as the operation key on every call.
Legacy system read-through cache: an ACL that wraps a legacy system's slow query with asynchronous cache warming and model translation, so the domain sees a fast, semantically correct response without coupling to the legacy's latency profile.
AWS Migration Hub Refactor Spaces strangler migration: Amazon API Gateway routes a monolith's calls to legacy or Lambda services while an ACL converts the monolith's old interface to the migrated service and is removed after callers move.
Spring Boot customer integration: a Spring component with an external client, explicit mapper, retry policy and circuit breaker translates provider responses into local aggregates; keep the ACL inside the service unless several consumers need the same boundary.
Azure Strangler Fig migration: an Azure façade routes legacy and new services while a domain-owned ACL translates calls in both directions, letting clients keep the same interface until the legacy feature is retired.

name: copy-and-swap
document:
copy-and-swap
copy and swap idiom
create-temporary-and-swap
Implement assignment (and any in-place state replacement) so that a failure while producing the new state leaves the target untouched: build the complete replacement off to the side, commit it with operations that cannot fail, and let the temporary's destructor or the garbage collector release the old state.
A hand-written assignment has to tear down the old state and build a copy of the new one, but only the build can fail: destroying before allocating exposes a half-updated object when the allocation or the element copy throws, and the usual repair -- a self-assignment check plus manual rollback -- duplicates the per-member copying that already lives in the copy constructor. The trigger is an assignment (or, in a garbage-collected language, an in-place state replacement) that must satisfy the strong exception guarantee: either it completes, or the target still holds its previous value.
Types that own resources -- heap buffers, handles, file descriptors, trees, containers -- in a language where the programmer controls copy semantics: C++ special member functions, a C ADT with error codes, Rust with panic/abort failure modes. The same ordering also applies in garbage-collected languages whenever published state must never be mutated in place: building the complete replacement and publishing it once keeps readers consistent and moves the release of the old state to the collector. The precondition is a commit step that genuinely cannot fail -- a noexcept member swap, one reference or pointer store, or an atomic publish.
Container and buffer classes that own heap memory (dynamic array, string, matrix, tree) and must be assignable without leaking or leaving the target inconsistent when an allocation fails.
Handle/pimpl classes that keep their state behind a single pointer: the swap is a pointer exchange, so the commit is unconditionally non-throwing while the deep copy still happens in the copy constructor (Sutter's canonical Pimpl exception-safety transformation).
Pre-C++11 codebases where the same operator= must serve lvalues and rvalues and no move constructor exists, using the const-reference plus explicit-local-temporary form.
Value types stored inside standard containers: std::vector and friends need element assignment to be safe before they can offer their own strong guarantee on reallocation, and a noexcept swap participates in their internal move/swap dispatch.
Garbage-collected languages where shared state must be replaced rather than mutated: build a complete replacement value and publish it with one store (AtomicReference.updateAndGet, atomic.Pointer[T].Store, a record with-expression) so readers never observe a partially updated object.
In-place state replacement where identity must be preserved (a registry entry, a cached object with live references): copy into a scratch value, then commit with a member-wise exchange or a replace-style API instead of repointing the reference.
Concurrent programming with thread-safe local-then-publish: build the replacement in a local object (thread-private by definition), then publish atomically -- readers never see a partially updated state, and the previous value is released by the collector after the atomic write is visible.
Version-control-style update: check out a local copy, mutate freely, then commit or discard; copy-and-swap maps directly to this workflow and provides the same transactional semantics (Howard Hinnant's analogy from his C++ Con 2018 talk).
Compiler tooling treats the idiom as the canonical self-assignment-safe assignment: LLVM's clang-tidy bugprone-unhandled-self-assignment checker explicitly recognizes 'build a temporary in operator=, then swap it' as correct handling and matches extended (allocator-aware) constructors plus ADL swap forms so real copy-and-swap code is not flagged (llvm/llvm-project PR #147066).
Boost's move/assignment guidance converged on the single by-value form T operator=(T b) { swap(*this, b); return *this; } as the common way to get copy-, move-, and convertible-assignment from one operator, with dedicated macros (BOOST_COPYABLE_AND_MOVABLE_ALT) for classes that adopt it instead of separate overloads.
When a strong guarantee is needed on the standard containers, libc++ maintainers advise exactly this idiom at the call site -- 'construct a new vector and swap it with the one you want to assign to' (libc++ PR #117516 discussion) -- because the library's own copy assignment deliberately offers only the basic guarantee.

name: state-colocation
document:
state-colocation
colocated state
colocation
Keep each piece of presentation state in the component closest to where it is used — down to the single component that owns and reads it — instead of hoisting it to a common ancestor or a global store, so that a change touches only the smallest part of the view that can observe it.
State gets hoisted 'just in case': a value only one component reads is lifted to the screen or application root, or pushed into one global store, because someone may want it later. The consequences are components that receive props they never read, updates that invalidate far more of the UI than the value's actual consumers, an unclear owner for each value, and tests that must assemble the whole state container to exercise one field. The recurring decision is where a new piece of state should live: keep it at the smallest scope that actually needs it.
Declarative component UIs (React, Vue, Svelte, SwiftUI, Compose, Blazor, Qt Quick) and, in generalized form, any system where a mutable value is owned by one component-like unit: the consumers determine the state's scope, the framework invalidates only what the owner's subtree can observe, and components are composed, moved and deleted. Most compelling where over-lifted or global state has already become a performance and ownership problem.
A search or form input whose value is read only by the input, its own validation and its own preview: keep it in that component instead of the screen root (the canonical typing example where hoisting made every keystroke re-render the page).
Which panel of an accordion is open: leave it per panel while panels are independent, then lift exactly to the accordion once only one panel may be open at a time (the closest common parent).
Tooltip, hover, popover and dropdown state in a chart or table cell: own it in the cell component rather than in a global UI store.
Per-row edit or selection state in a data grid: the row component owns it; only cross-row operations need the grid to own it.
Dialog and modal open state in the button or list that opens it, until another surface must close or observe it.
Form draft state in the form component; lift it only when a sibling — summary panel, preview pane, wizard footer — genuinely must read it.
Extracting a self-contained widget for reuse or publication: keeping its state local makes the component portable and shrinks its API.
Per-cell expansion state in a tree view or file explorer: the tree node component owns whether it is expanded; the parent tree only coordinates multi-select or bulk-expand operations.
Media playback state for a single player (play/pause, current time, volume): colocate in the player component rather than a global audio store unless the same track plays in multiple places simultaneously.
Local filter/sort state for a data table or list: keep it in the list component until a URL parameter, shareable link, or sibling panel requires sharing it.
Vue: composable-local state (useSearch, useToggle) where each consumer needs its own independent instance of the same reactive logic pattern.
Angular Signals: feature-level signal stores scoped to a route or feature slice, not the entire application store, for UI state and feature-derived state.
SwiftUI: @State for view-local value types; @StateObject for view-owned reference types; keep @EnvironmentObject for genuinely cross-cutting state (auth session, theme) mounted as low in the hierarchy as consumers allow.
Svelte 5 runes: `let count = $state(0)` inside a component is per-component-instance reactive state — the component that declares it is its owner; Svelte's v5 migration explicitly replaced the pre-runes habit of reaching for a store whenever state sat at a component's top level, with $state plus $derived/$effect as the local cells, and module-level .svelte.js state only for deliberate sharing.
Jetpack Compose: the official hoisting guidance is this pattern's placement ladder — keep state as close as possible to where it is consumed, hoist only to the lowest common ancestor of all composables that read or write it, pass value down and onValueChange up, and make the ViewModel the owner only when business logic or lifecycle outlives the composition.
Blazor: component fields are the default owner for UI-local state; the official state-management guidance promotes to an in-memory state container service only when components must share non-persistent state, and to Protected Browser Storage only when the value must survive circuits or sessions — a three-rung ladder that mirrors local state, scoped provider, persistence.

name: messaging-gateway
document:
messaging-gateway
Encapsulate access to a messaging system behind an ordinary interface of domain methods, so calling application code makes method calls while a single component owns message construction, correlation, timeouts and error translation.
Application code that talks to a broker keeps importing messaging concepts: it builds the payload, picks the channel, attaches a reply address and a correlation id, parses the response and interprets broker errors. The trigger for this pattern is that callers should make a method call instead of writing messaging code - the messaging knowledge belongs in exactly one place that can change without touching business rules.
At the boundary between application logic and a messaging system (message broker, MQ, queue service or actor runtime): the other side is reached by messages, but the caller is ordinary domain code that should see typed parameters and typed results. Applies to one-way (fire and forget) and request-reply interactions alike, and to blocking as well as asynchronous call styles.
A domain service that must query another system (inventory, pricing, credit scoring) over a queue: the caller invokes checkStock(sku) and receives a typed answer.
An HTTP or API layer whose controller awaits a brokered round trip (Spring Integration gateway interface, NestJS ClientProxy, MassTransit request client).
Batch and background jobs that dispatch work through a typed job API instead of assembling payloads (ActiveJob perform_later, Celery delay).
Wrapping a legacy system's MQ interface once, so the rest of the codebase never learns its message format.
Test seams: unit tests substitute a fake gateway, integration tests run the same interface against a real broker.
Migration seam: keep the gateway contract stable while the transport moves from one broker to another.
Actor and streaming stacks where a facade wraps ask/request so callers never hold ActorRefs or inboxes.
Spring Integration's @MessagingGateway and GatewayProxyFactoryBean let application code inject a typed interface while the framework routes calls into channels and returns replies.
MassTransit's IRequestClient<T> and GetResponse<TResponse> provide a typed request-reply client over the bus, keeping request and response message contracts out of the calling service.
RabbitMQ's RPC tutorial demonstrates a gateway-like client that publishes to rpc_queue with reply_to and correlation_id, then resolves the matching callback response.

name: revocable-forwarder
document:
revocable-forwarder
caretaker
revocable proxy
Let a collaborator use an object through a forwarding wrapper that the grantor can switch off at any time through a separate control, so authority already handed out can be withdrawn without destroying the target and without the collaborator's cooperation.
A capability is just a reference, so once a collaborator has been given access to an object there is no built-in way to take it back: the grantor can destroy the object, ask the collaborator to stop, or leave the access standing. The recurring decision is how to grant access that is bounded in time - temporary use of a file, a service object, a session, an account - while keeping a control that only the grantor holds.
Object-capability settings, and any in-process design in which authority travels as references rather than as a global identity: plugin and extension hosts lending a service object to foreign code, multi-tenant object graphs giving a worker one tenant-scoped resource, session-scoped services, and capability-based workflow or financial systems in which a grant must be provably withdrawn. It applies when the grantor keeps its own reference to the target and can intercept every call through the reference it handed out; where the runtime lets references be forged, dereferenced around the wrapper or reached by reflection, marshalling or FFI, the same structure degrades from an enforcement mechanism to a discipline.
A plugin or extension host lends a file, network or service object to foreign code and revokes it when the plugin is unloaded or breaches policy.
A multi-tenant worker receives one tenant-scoped resource for the duration of a job and loses it at job end, without the tenant object being torn down.
Session teardown in a long-lived server: the handler works through the wrapper, and logout revokes future calls before the session's resources are freed.
Capability-based workflow and financial systems that give an agent temporary authority over an account or a document and revoke it when the task completes.
Temporary elevated access for maintenance or debugging, where the requirement is to show that the extra authority has provably ended (audit evidence).
Graceful decommissioning of a shared resource: revoke new work through the wrapper, drain the calls already in flight, then release the resource.
The Scala ocaps framework's Revocable/Caretaker API returns a proxied capability plus a private Revoker, so a session, logout, timeout or supervisor can make later calls fail without changing the target.
JavaScript's standard Proxy.revocable() and the Chrome Extensions chrome.permissions API provide browser/runtime counterparts: keep the revoke/remove control private, and do not mistake the platform wrapper or permission record for protection against an already leaked target reference.
AWS IAM role-session revocation for temporary STS credentials is a distributed analogue of withdrawing a forwarded grant: policy evaluation denies subsequent requests, but propagation and credential caching mean it is not the atomic in-process check-and-forward gate described here.

name: dependency-injection
document:
dependency-injection
di
constructor injection
setter injection
interface injection
ioc container
pure di
manual di
Supply an object with the collaborators it needs from the outside — through its constructor, its setters/properties, or a dedicated injection interface — so it never constructs or looks a dependency up itself and every wiring decision is made once, in a composition root or container.
An object that creates its own collaborators hard-wires a concrete class, a construction recipe and often a lifetime into itself: swapping the implementation for a test double, a second deployment or a new platform means editing the class, and the dependency graph stays invisible in the API. The recurring trigger is exactly the catalog's rule: an object should not create what it depends on — the caller, the framework or the composition root decides, and hands the dependency in.
Applies whenever a component's collaborators are chosen per deployment, per environment or per test, whenever constructing them is expensive or platform-specific, and whenever a framework owns object creation (request handlers, scheduled jobs, UI screens, message consumers). It matters most in large object graphs where one abstraction has several implementations and lifetimes must be managed (singleton, request-scoped, transient); it is unnecessary when the collaborators are pure values or when construction is a private detail nobody needs to vary.
Web and API backends whose handlers need repositories, clocks, mailers and caches that must be replaced by fakes in tests and by sandbox services in staging.
Hexagonal and clean architectures where the domain declares ports (interfaces) and the infrastructure layer supplies adapters at the composition root.
Frameworks that own object creation — request handlers, scheduled jobs, UI controllers, message consumers — where the framework's injector is the only practical wiring point.
Deployment variants (on-prem vs cloud, SQL vs in-memory, real vs stub payment gateway) selected per environment through binding configuration rather than conditional code.
Plugin and extension systems where the concrete implementation is chosen at start-up from a plugin registry, enabling third-party adapters without touching core code.
Expensive shared resources whose lifetime must be managed centrally (connection pools, HTTP clients, circuit breakers) while service classes stay stateless.
Unit tests that construct the class under test directly with test doubles, and integration tests that swap only the outer layer's bindings.
Microservices with sidecar containers: the sidecar provides logging, tracing and retry policies as injected collaborators, keeping the service logic untouched.
Cloud-native applications where the composition root is the only place that knows whether a dependency resolves locally, across a service mesh, or via a remote gRPC call.
Multi-tenant SaaS where tenant-specific adapters (tenant-scoped repositories, per-tenant feature flags) are bound at the composition root and switched by middleware.
Event-driven systems where message handlers receive their dependencies through injection, making the handler logic identical between in-process and distributed deployment.
AOT-compiled applications (Native AOT, Blazor WebAssembly, serverless) where runtime reflection is unavailable — dependencies are resolved via source generators or manually at the composition root.
Functional codebases using effect systems (ZIO, fp-ts, Reader monad) where the DI container is replaced by typed environments passed through function compositions.
Consumer-driven contract testing (Pact, OpenAPI pact) where DI swaps provider implementations with contract-mock stubs at the boundary, enabling parallel service development without shared integration environments.
Resilience and fault-injection testing: proxies or decorator-based fault injectors (e.g., Gremlin SDK, WireMock) are injected as collaborators to validate retry, timeout and circuit-breaker behaviour under simulated failure conditions.
Single-page application frameworks with DI built into the component tree: Angular resolves components, directives and services through hierarchical injectors, scoping providers to the application root, a component subtree or a route so features override implementations and lazy-load without global registration.
Android apps using Dagger (and Hilt over it) to build the object graph at compile time — generated, reflection-free code, bindings and cycles checked at build time, with field injection reserved for framework-created entry points like Activities and Fragments.
Python web APIs (FastAPI) where each path operation declares Depends(callable) parameters: the framework resolves nested dependency graphs with per-request caching and uses yield-based dependencies to open and close connections around each request.

name: row-data-gateway
document:
row-data-gateway
row data gateway
row gateway
Give each database row its own in-memory object that mirrors the row's columns and carries the row's own find, insert, update and delete operations, so all data-access code for a table lives in one place instead of being duplicated across the scripts that use it.
SQL text, parameter binding and result-set mapping are re-derived inside every transaction script that touches a table, while the in-memory objects those scripts work with know nothing about the database. No single place knows how one row is read, written and deleted, so a schema change ripples through every script and every new query is another chance to get parameterisation and type conversion wrong.
Applies when business logic is organised as transaction scripts or thin services over a relational schema whose columns map closely to the fields actually used: the gateway mirrors the table structure, no object/relational impedance mismatch is being managed, and identity maps, units of work and lazy loading are either unnecessary or added deliberately as separate patterns. It also fits generated persistence layers, where the gateway classes are produced from schema metadata during the build.
Transaction-script applications (order entry, billing runs, batch imports) where several scripts need the same handful of row-level reads and writes.
CRUD-heavy back-office and admin tooling where a screen edits one row at a time and columns map one-to-one onto form fields.
Legacy or externally owned schemas that must be mirrored rather than reshaped: one gateway per table gives an explicit, reviewable seam between the application and someone else's database.
Generated persistence layers: gateways produced from schema metadata on every build, so the tedious class-per-table work is automated and stays in sync with the schema.
Simple mappings inside an otherwise rich domain model, where a domain object keeps a gateway as its data holder instead of copying field values around.
Reporting and fixture utilities that need reusable, parameterised finders for one table without pulling in a full object/relational mapper.
Laminas\Db\RowGateway and RowGatewayFeature (the official laminas-db implementation) expose one row object with save/delete and can materialize table-query results as row gateways, fitting CRUD screens or transaction scripts that edit individual records.
Zend Framework 1's Zend_Db_Table_Row is a documented legacy row-gateway implementation: table queries return row objects with column access plus save/delete/createRow operations, useful when a simple schema is consumed by row-oriented scripts.
The Go dgw tool generates structs and lightweight Table/Row Data Gateway functions from PostgreSQL metadata, demonstrating the pattern as a code-generation choice when a project wants typed CRUD without a full ORM.

name: function-composition
document:
function-composition
compose
function pipeline
Combine a chain of small unary transformations into one reusable function by sequencing them with a composition combinator (compose/pipe), so the order of the steps is stated once, every step stays independently testable, and the chain itself becomes a value that can be named, passed and reassembled.
A transformation that is naturally a sequence of small pure steps gets written as nested calls or as repeated imperative assignment (`h(g(f(x)))`, or `y = f(x); y = g(y); ...; return y`) at every call site. The order is duplicated wherever the chain is used, the intermediate values need throwaway names, steps cannot be reused in a different order, and changing one stage means editing every copy.
Pure or nearly pure value transformations - parsing, normalisation, validation, formatting, pricing, AST rewriting - where each step is unary and the language treats functions as values. It pays off when the chain is reused or assembled from data (configuration, plugin lists, per-request policy), when steps must be unit-tested in isolation, and when the same steps must also run element-wise over a collection or lazily over a stream. It stops applying where steps need side effects or branching between stages: there the shell around the pure core owns control flow.
Input normalisation: trim, parse, canonicalise and validate a payload before it reaches domain logic, with the same chain reused by HTTP handlers and message consumers.
Pricing and rule chains: base price, discount, tax and rounding applied in a fixed, configurable order to an immutable value object.
Compiler and AST work: a pass list of rewrite functions composed once and applied over the tree, with passes added or reordered per optimisation level.
Serialisation and formatting: sanitise, format, encode and sign a document, where each step is tested separately and the composed chain is stored as a constant.
Data transformation over collections: the same pure steps composed into one function and passed to map/filter/stream operations, so element-wise processing reuses the chain.
Policy assembly at startup: the processing chain is built from configuration or plugin registrations and then applied per request without further branching.
Reactive stream processing: RxJS Observable.pipe chains the same logical steps across asynchronous event sequences, with operators composed once and reused across streams.
ETL and data pipeline transformation: extract-transform-load chains where each stage (parse, clean, enrich, aggregate, write) is a unary pure function composed into a reusable pipeline run over batches or streaming data.
HTTP request/response middleware: the middleware stack is a composed function chain where each layer (authenticate, authorise, rate-limit, deserialize, validate) is a unary handler; composition is resolved once at startup.
Matrix and vector transformations in numerical code: each linear algebra operation (scale, rotate, translate, project) is a unary function on a matrix type; composing them once builds the transformation pipeline that is applied to every vertex or pixel.
Ramda pipelines: R.pipe and R.compose assemble reusable data-last transformations from small functions, centralising the order while letting the same composed value run over many inputs.
Redux store setup: Redux's compose helper combines store enhancers right-to-left into one enhancer, so the enhancer order is defined once instead of reconstructed at each store boundary.
lodash/fp transformations: lodash/fp's auto-curried, data-last compose/flow helpers assemble immutable-friendly transformations from reusable steps that can be passed as values.

name: facade
document:
facade
façade
Provide one coarse-grained entry interface that hides a subsystem of many cooperating classes behind the few operations its clients actually need, so callers depend on a single stable API instead of orchestrating the subsystem themselves.
Every client of a complex subsystem must know which classes exist, in which order to call them, how to configure and dispose them and how to interpret their errors; that orchestration is then duplicated across the codebase, and any change inside the subsystem ripples through all callers.
Applies when a subsystem (a library, framework, legacy module, remote SDK, or a layer of your own system) is much broader than any single client needs, when its correct use is a recurring sequence of collaborations, and when client code should be insulated from its types and its evolution. Typical at module and system-boundary scope, where one entry point per layer or per external system is wanted.
Wrapping a third-party SDK, media framework or payment/HTTP client behind one class or module that exposes the application's own vocabulary (convert, charge, upload).
Application services that orchestrate repositories, gateways and domain services for one use case (checkout, report generation) and are the only seam controllers or jobs talk to.
Layered systems where every layer offers a facade as its entry point, so dependencies flow through coarse interfaces instead of reaching into a layer's internals.
Isolating a legacy subsystem while it is replaced incrementally: new code depends on the clean facade, and the migration swaps implementations behind it.
Remote and coarse-grained boundaries: a remote facade exposes a few chunky operations over a fine-grained object model to avoid chatty calls (see Remote Facade, Fowler's PEAA).
Startup/teardown sequences and device orchestration (the classic home-theatre example): clients need one 'watch movie' operation, not a dozen subsystem calls in the right order.
Service-container proxy facades (e.g. Laravel): a static-looking front-end that forwards calls to a resolved service instance, giving a terse API without sacrificing testability or DI flexibility.
JPA/service-layer facades: a single transactional entry point that receives DTOs, maps them to domain objects, orchestrates business logic, maps results back, and commits — one transaction per use case.
Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) in microservices: a thin per-client aggregation service (web, mobile, partner) that fans out to downstream microservices, reshapes responses for the client, and handles perimeter concerns. Each BFF is a specialized facade owned by the team that ships the corresponding client.
Anti-Corruption Layer (DDD): a facade placed between a bounded context and an external/legacy system to translate that system's model into domain concepts, preventing external concepts from polluting the internal domain model.
Event-driven/observable facades: a facade that exposes reactive streams (Observables, Promises, async generators) over the subsystem, buffering, batching or debouncing events for consumers that prefer push-based or streaming interfaces.
API gateway composition: an API gateway acts as a system-wide facade that unifies multiple backend services at the edge, handling auth, routing and cross-cutting concerns before delegating to more specific facades or services.
SDK wrapper facades: publishing a public-facing SDK over an internal microservice mesh; the facade shapes the external API surface, applies default configurations, and provides a stable consumer experience independent of internal service topology changes.
SLF4J (Simple Logging Facade for Java): slf4j-api is a minimal logging facade; applications code against Logger.debug()/info() once and bind the concrete framework (Logback, Log4j 2, java.util.logging) at deployment time by swapping the provider jar on the classpath — the textbook runtime-swappable facade.
Spring Framework JdbcClient / JdbcTemplate: a fluent facade over raw JDBC that owns connection and statement lifecycle, iterates ResultSets and translates SQLException into the DataAccessException hierarchy, so callers supply only SQL and result mapping instead of the full boilerplate workflow.
jQuery $.get/$.post/$.getJSON over $.ajax: a per-task facade layer that collapses cross-browser XMLHttpRequest differences, Deferred plumbing and HTTP defaults into one-line calls — the canonical JavaScript-library facade.

name: adapter
document:
adapter
wrapper
adaptor
Present an existing component through the exact target contract its client already consumes, translating calls, results and boundary semantics without adding responsibilities or pretending a missing capability exists.
An existing or foreign component has useful behaviour but speaks a different protocol: method names and signatures, data shapes, units, lifecycle, error model or sync/async contract do not satisfy the target. If every caller performs ad hoc conversion, semantics drift, vendor types leak and provider replacement becomes a cross-cutting rewrite; changing the adaptee or target may be impossible or too disruptive.
Integration work where one side is outside your control: legacy modules, vendor SDKs, generated clients, foreign data formats or units, and the ports-and-adapters boundary of a hexagonal architecture. Applies in statically typed languages - where an adapter class is also the compile-time proof that the required interface is satisfied - and in structurally or dynamically typed ones, where a thin wrapper usually replaces a declared target interface.
Wrapping a third-party or vendor SDK behind your own interface so business code never imports vendor types.
Modernising a legacy module incrementally: new code talks to the target interface while the old component is adapted in place.
Supporting several interchangeable providers (payments, storage, messaging, analytics) through one internal contract, with one adapter each.
Adapting a callback- or error-first API to promises/async or to an observer-style interface.
Ports-and-adapters boundaries where one domain port is realized over different transports (HTTP, message queue, in-process fake).
Unifying differently shaped data sources (row sets, DTOs, XML or JSON payloads) into one model before they reach domain logic.
Test doubles: an in-memory adapter satisfies the target interface without the real infrastructure.
API wrapper libraries: normalising third-party REST/gRPC APIs (Stripe, Twilio, payment providers) into a stable internal contract so business logic never imports vendor SDK types.
Legacy system integration: wrapping SOAP, CORBA, or mainframe APIs behind a modern interface, enabling incremental migration without rewriting existing clients.
Cloud provider abstraction: a single internal storage or queue interface implemented by AWS, GCP, or Azure adapters, letting the application swap providers via configuration.
ETL pipelines: adapting heterogeneous source record schemas (CSV, JSON, XML, database rows) into one canonical domain record, isolating format changes from downstream consumers.
Event-stream and streaming adapters: translating WebSocket frames or server-sent events into domain events in real time.
Multi-cloud and provider-agnostic interfaces: storage adapters (S3, GCS, Azure Blob), queue adapters (SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka), and notification adapters that abstract away provider-specific SDKs.
Backend for Frontend (BFF): each front-end client (web, mobile, third-party) gets its own lightweight adapter that shapes internal service responses into the exact payload that client needs.
Java's java.io.InputStreamReader is a byte-to-character bridge: it presents an InputStream through the Reader contract while decoding with an explicit charset.
SLF4J uses providers such as slf4j-reload4j to bind one Logger API to different backends, while log4j-over-slf4j and jul-to-slf4j redirect legacy APIs at a migration boundary; Spring MVC's HandlerAdapter similarly lets DispatcherServlet handle heterogeneous handler types through one SPI.
Go's net/http.HandlerFunc gives an ordinary func(ResponseWriter, *Request) the http.Handler contract by attaching ServeHTTP, so routing and middleware can consume functions and handlers uniformly.

name: pratt-parser
document:
pratt-parser
top-down operator precedence
tdop
Parse expressions with many prefix, infix and postfix operators by associating a binding power and a handler with each token type, so precedence and associativity live in one rule table instead of one parsing function per precedence level.
Operator precedence turns expression parsing into a ladder of near-identical functions - one per level - each of which must re-implement associativity, delegate to the next level for its operands, and be edited whenever an operator is added or moves. Grammars with prefix, infix, postfix and mixfix operators (ternary conditionals, assignment, calls, indexing, user-registered operators) make that ladder long, make associativity easy to get subtly wrong, and scatter the grammar across the parser so it cannot be read in one place.
Hand-written parsers for an expression-bearing language, DSL, query or configuration syntax: a token stream is already available (or is cheap to lex), the operator set is large or expected to grow, and the team wants the grammar visible as data. It is typically the expression layer under an ordinary recursive-descent parser for statements and declarations - interpreters, calculators, filter and rule engines, formula tools - and it is unnecessary when a parser generator already declares precedence for the grammar.
Expression evaluators and calculators whose operator set is expected to grow (arithmetic, units, comparisons, percentages, function calls, user-defined functions).
Query, filter and rule languages - search filters, feature-flag conditions, access-policy conditions, spreadsheet formulas - with many comparison, logical and string operators.
Front ends for small languages and DSLs that parse statements and declarations with recursive descent and need real precedence handling for the expression layer.
Single-pass compilers and interpreters that emit bytecode or IR while parsing, where each handler is also the point that emits the operator's instruction.
Template and configuration expression languages that must attach exact source positions and precise errors to every operator.
Host-language extension points that let plugins or users register additional operators at runtime, because registration is just a table entry.
Rust PEG grammars that use pest::pratt_parser::PrattParser to map prefix, postfix and infix operator pairs into calculator or DSL ASTs.
Rust parser-combinator expression grammars built with chumsky's pratt combinator, where atom parsers and prefix, postfix and infix operators declare precedence and associativity.
JavaScript expression-only tooling built on JSEP, where a compact Pratt-style parser produces ASTs and allows custom unary and binary operators with explicit precedence.

name: test-specific-subclass
document:
test-specific-subclass
test-specific extension
subclassed test double
Make an otherwise untestable class testable by defining a test-only subclass that overrides the method reaching the unusable dependency (or exposes the internal state the test needs), so the boundary can be substituted and observed without putting test hooks into production code.
A class that must be tested reaches its dependency through a call on itself - a self-call to a helper method, a field created inside the class, or a singleton/static lookup - so the test has no injection point: the collaborator cannot be replaced from outside, the indirect inputs cannot be controlled and the indirect outputs cannot be observed. Editing the production class to accept the dependency may be impossible (third-party or frozen code) or would introduce test logic into production.
Applies to legacy or third-party object-oriented code where the boundary call already sits behind an overridable (non-final, sufficiently visible) method, or can be extracted into one, and where test-only code may live next to the tests. It is a fallback for statically typed languages that need the double to stay type-compatible with a concrete class; where the code can be modified, dependency injection is the better seam.
A legacy class reads the wall clock inside a helper method (System.currentTimeMillis, DateTime.Now, Instant.now): override the helper so date/decision logic can be tested at a fixed instant.
A reporting or notification class sends mail or calls a remote API from a self-call: override that method with a canned or empty body so the unit test runs offline and deterministically.
A class reaches a database or the file system from inside its own method: override it to return an in-memory fixture instead of building the real object chain (entity-chain snipping).
Verifying the sequence and the set of steps of a template method: override the steps in a subclass and record which of them ran, in which order.
Exposing private state for state verification, or exposing a private algorithm step so it can be tested individually (state-exposing and behaviour-exposing subclasses).
Replacing a singleton or static accessor the SUT uses through a lookup with a controlled instance that is still type-compatible with the concrete class (substituted singleton).
Putting a legacy untested class under a characterization-test baseline before refactoring, while extracting the collaborator is not yet possible.
A Java class that cannot be modified (third-party or legacy jar) but has a non-final boundary method to stub: Mockito spy() / @Spy keeps the real methods and stubs only the overridden ones - the partial mocking Mockito's Javadoc documents for legacy code and third-party interfaces (final methods stay un-stubbable).
A PHP class whose constructor opens connections or performs other side effects: createPartialMock(Class::class, ['boundaryMethod']) or getMockBuilder()->onlyMethods([...])->disableOriginalConstructor() generates a double that overrides only the named methods and skips the real constructor - PHPUnit's documented form of the pattern (final, private and static methods and enums cannot be doubled).
A .NET class with virtual boundary members: NSubstitute Substitute.ForPartsOf<T>() creates a partial substitute that - as NSubstitute's own docs state - inherits the original type via Castle DynamicProxy and runs real code except for members configured with DoNotCallBase, i.e. a generated test-specific subclass with an official 'use with caution' caveat.

name: higher-order-component
document:
higher-order-component
HOC
component enhancer
Add cross-cutting behaviour to many components at once by wrapping them in an enhancer function that takes a component and returns a new, enhanced component, so no wrapped component knows about the concern or has to be edited.
The same cross-cutting logic - subscribing to a data source, checking a permission, firing analytics, injecting a theme, a translation or a feature flag - is needed by many components, and copying it into each one couples every component to the concern, re-couples them to every change of it, and leaves the behaviour to be remembered at each new call site. React tried mixins and inheritance first and removed them (implicit dependencies between mixin and component, name clashes, snowballing coupling), so the recurring decision is how to apply one behaviour to many components without editing them, while the components stay reusable and unaware of the enhancement.
Component-model UI code where components are values the framework mounts with a stable identity (React and its ecosystem first; the same shape recurs with Compose composables, SwiftUI views, Blazor components, Scala.js layers and handler-based Go/Java web UIs), where the concern is genuinely cross-cutting rather than local to one screen, where the enhancement can be expressed as a pure function from component to component and applied once at the definition or export site, and where the wrapped component's inputs form a prop-like contract that can be extended by injection without touching its internals.
Subscribing many components to an external data source — React documentation's withSubscription example, or Redux's connect: store state arrives as injected props with no component knowing about the store.
Apollo Client data injection: graphql(Query, { options, props }) HOC maps query results and loading state to props; multiple graphql HOCs composed with @compose; historically the standard before useQuery.
Authorization and feature gating at the boundary: withAuthorization(Component, { requiredRole }) or withFeatureFlag(...) decides rendering without editing the component; useful for route-level guards applied across many pages.
Analytics, telemetry and instrumentation applied at export sites (withAnalytics): tracking calls stay out of presentation code and can be added or removed at one location per module.
Injecting ambient context into components that take it as props — translations via withTranslation (react-i18next), routing via withRouter (React Router v5 and below), theming via withTheme (Material-UI v4) — enabling third-party and vendored components to participate without modification.
Error and loading boundaries as an enhancer (withErrorBoundary): the boundary exists as a component in the tree anyway; an enhancer consolidates the concern into one reusable definition rather than repeating the try/catch at each call site.
Sharing logic into class components and older codebases where hooks cannot be used: the HOC reaches class components and library component-shaped APIs that hooks cannot wrap.
Material-UI v4 theming: withStyles and withTheme HOCs inject classes and theme as props; compose chains combine styling with data (connect + withStyles + graphql on the same export).
Internationalization testing: export both wrapped and unwrapped components; tests use the raw component with a mock t function while integration tests use the full I18nextProvider setup.
Conditional prop injection: a data-enhancer that only injects props when a condition is met (e.g. user is authenticated) lets the wrapped component remain agnostic about the absence of that data.
React Compiler (React Forget) compatibility: heavy HOC layering reduces the compiler's static analysis surface and may cause it to bailout — test compiler output when adding HOCs to a compiled codebase; prefer hooks for new logic the compiler should see.
React Server Components boundary: a HOC that calls hooks or reads client-only context (useAuth, useTheme, useRouter) cannot execute during a server render; the wrapped component may receive undefined injected props on the server and flash-change on hydration. Pass server-fetched data as props through the HOC boundary from a server parent instead.
Streaming SSR and Suspense integration: a HOC that wraps a component behind a Suspense boundary adds a node that may delay streaming; if the HOC itself is async it must be carefully placed to avoid blocking the fallback from showing.
Partial hydration patterns: on islands architectures (Next.js App Router, Astro), a HOC that subscribes to client-side state forces the entire island to be hydrated even if the wrapped component has no server payload; prefer passing hydrated state as props from a server parent.
Recompose (acdlite): a 'lodash for React' utility belt built entirely from composable HOCs (withState, mapProps, pure, branch) piped through enhance/compose - the pattern industrialised; its October 2018 deprecation in favour of Hooks (bug-fix maintenance only) is the canonical case study of the pattern's cost when a runtime offers a cheaper reuse primitive.
MobX React binding: observer from mobx-react / mobx-react-lite is an official HOC that subscribes the wrapped component to every observable read during render, re-rendering it automatically; MobX guidance is to apply observer first (innermost) when composing it with other HOCs, and to wrap every component that reads observables.
