name: spatial-partition
document:
spatial-partition
spatial index
bucket grid
Store every object in a structure indexed by its position so that neighbourhood queries visit only the objects near a point or region instead of scanning the whole population.
Queries that ask 'what is near this position?' - collision checks, proximity and aggro radii, culling, spatial analytics - repeatedly scan every object: each query is linear in the population and a whole simulation step becomes quadratic, even though every object interacts only with the few objects next to it.
Per-object runtime systems and simulations - game worlds, crowd and particle solvers, location services, robotics - where objects are mobile, spread over space, and the queries are local (radius, region, k-nearest). The pattern applies once the population is large enough that a full scan dominates the frame or the request budget, and it requires a position-to-cell mapping and an update discipline that match how the objects move.
Game worlds: collision, proximity and aggro checks between many moving entities each tick (bullets versus enemies, pickups, area effects).
Physics broadphase: pruning candidate pairs before narrow-phase tests where colliders move constantly.
Map and GIS services: 'all points within radius' and viewport queries over millions of features.
Crowd, flocking and particle simulations: neighbours within a radius for boids or social forces instead of all-pairs tests.
Spatial analytics and robotics: k-nearest or region queries over vehicles, sensors and delivery points, and occupancy grids for pathfinding.
Physics engines: Box2D's broadphase is a dynamic AABB tree (b2DynamicTree) whose fattened leaf boxes absorb small moves before reinsertion, and whose region queries and ray casts prune candidates before narrow-phase tests.
Location services: Redis geospatial indexes store members as 52-bit geohash scores in a sorted set (GEOADD) so GEOSEARCH answers circle and bounding-box proximity queries server-side instead of scanning members.
GIS and analytics databases: PostGIS prunes radius queries through a GiST spatial index (the index-aware ST_DWithin predicate checks bounding boxes before computing exact distances), and scikit-learn backs radius and k-nearest neighbour queries with KDTree and BallTree instead of all-pairs distances.

name: authenticator
document:
authenticator
authentication provider
authentication service
Verify the identity a subject claims from mechanism-specific credentials and return one normalized principal or an explicit failure, so callers can select or replace password, certificate, token, Kerberos or passkey verification without coupling login, session, audit or authorization code to a credential format.
A request must decide whether presented evidence proves a subject's identity, but password, client-certificate, OIDC/JWT, Kerberos and passkey checks differ by deployment, tenant and channel. If one mechanism is hard-wired into the request path, every caller learns its credential format; adding OIDC, migrating from LDAP or accepting service tokens becomes a cross-cutting change, while comparison, retry/lockout and verifier-failure handling drift between endpoints.
Systems that verify identities at a trust boundary - HTTP APIs, message endpoints, CLIs or device onboarding - where more than one credential form is in use or expected, the mechanism is selectable per deployment, tenant or route, and downstream authorization, session and audit code needs a mechanism-independent principal. It is also the seam for composing MFA or step-up checks and for replacing an external identity provider in tests.
A web application that must accept password login, federated OIDC login and API bearer tokens, all producing the same session principal.
An enterprise service deployed at sites with different directories (LDAP/AD, Kerberos, local database) that selects its mechanism per deployment without a code fork.
A microservice that validates self-issued JWTs for normal traffic and falls back to token introspection at the corporate authorization server for opaque tokens.
A CLI or desktop agent with pluggable credential providers: OS keychain, smart card, TPM-backed passkey or an interactive password prompt.
Step-up authentication: a second authenticator (one-time code, WebAuthn assertion) chained behind the primary one for sensitive operations.
Test and simulation environments where a fake authenticator replaces the identity provider while the production authentication gate remains the exercised path.
A passkey Relying Party (RP) backend that implements WebAuthn registration and authentication ceremonies: generates session-bound challenges (CSPRNG, 16+ bytes, 60-120s TTL), verifies authenticator assertions (origin, challenge replay prevention via single-use challenge, UP/UV flags, signCount monotonicity, signature), and issues a normalized session principal.
Zero-trust microservice mesh: SPIFFE/SPIRE-issued short-lived X.509 SVIDs via mTLS, where each service presents a workload certificate encoded with its SPIFFE ID; the authenticator verifies the certificate chain and extracts the cryptographic workload identity as the principal.
Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) token storage: the BFF holds access/refresh tokens in server-side memory or encrypted httpOnly cookies, issuing scoped session cookies to the SPA; the authenticator seam is the BFF's token refresh logic, not the browser.
OAuth2 authorization code + PKCE public client: the authenticator validates the code, verifier and state on the backend, rotates refresh tokens on every use, and issues short-lived JWTs; the same interface normalizes this flow alongside password and passkey flows.
A Java service can keep application code independent of the mechanism by driving configured JAAS LoginModules through LoginContext, while Spring Security exposes the same seam through AuthenticationProvider and ProviderManager.
A Keycloak deployment can add a custom credential or challenge step by implementing the Authenticator and AuthenticatorFactory SPIs and placing that execution in an authentication flow.
A Node.js service can install Passport.js strategies such as passport-local or passport-openidconnect, register them with passport.use(), and normalize the verify callback's user into the application's principal.
A Django project extends authentication beyond its user database by listing custom backends in AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS; django.contrib.auth.authenticate() tries each backend's authenticate(request, **credentials) in order, first success wins, and the returned User is the normalized principal.
An ASP.NET Core app registers one named scheme per mechanism (AddJwtBearer, AddCookie, a custom AuthenticationHandler) and composes them with policy schemes (AddPolicyScheme, ForwardDefaultSelector) so one endpoint routes bearer and cookie requests to the right handler without branching in the controller.
The Kubernetes API server authenticates every request through a union of authenticators - front-proxy request-header (X-Remote-User / X-Remote-Group, trusted only after the proxy's client certificate validates against the configured CA), X.509 client certificates and TokenReview webhooks with cached decisions - and hands the resulting normalized user info to authorization.

name: identity-field
document:
identity-field
primary key field
identity column
Store the relational primary key inside the object so that an in-memory instance and its database row are recognised as the same entity across sessions, caches and process restarts, instead of relying on object identity.
Mappers, identity maps and unit-of-work bookkeeping need a stable handle on every object: without a key carried by the object there is no way to tell whether two instances are the same row, which row an UPDATE or DELETE must touch, or what value a referring row should store - and loading the same row twice silently produces two divergent objects.
Applies wherever objects outlive a single operation and are mapped to key-addressed rows: entities behind a Data Mapper or Row Data Gateway, aggregates in a Repository, session caches keyed by table plus id, and object graphs whose children must refer to a parent that is not inserted yet. The key has to survive serialisation and cross-process calls, and for application-generated keys it must exist before the row does.
ORM entities in a session: load a row into an object, mutate business fields, then flush an UPDATE or DELETE targeted at the same identity.
API resources addressed by key: /orders/{id} endpoints that fetch, mutate and delete by identity, with links stored as keys instead of object references.
Session-scoped identity maps and second-level caches keyed by (table, key), which need the key before they can return an existing instance.
Object graphs with parent-child references: the child's foreign key needs the parent's identity, generated before the insert (UUID/sequence) or read back after it (RETURNING/getGeneratedKeys).
Audit, versioning and optimistic locking: change logs and Version Number checks identify the affected row by its key.
Distributed or sharded writes: client-generated keys let a router place the row and let a retry overwrite the same identity idempotently.
Event-sourced aggregates: the aggregate root's identity is the correlation ID carried in every command and event, allowing the event log to reconstruct state by replaying events keyed to that identity.
GraphQL Relay node identification: globally unique node IDs are built from the entity's identity (base64 type-prefixed id), enabling the standardised node query and cache reching defined in the Relay specification.
Multi-tenant SaaS with tenant-scoped identity: a composite key of (tenant_id, id) ensures a tenant can never address another tenant's rows, even if the local id numbers happen to collide.
Idempotent message processing: a command's correlation ID (the entity's identity) lets a handler detect a duplicate and skip reprocessing without a distributed lock.
Hibernate ORM entities with an @Id and Session persistence context: loading by identifier reuses the session's first-level identity, while the chosen generated-id strategy determines when the key becomes available.
PostgreSQL tables with GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY and INSERT ... RETURNING id: the database owns key generation, then the mapper reads the assigned identity back onto the object in the same write.
Relay GraphQL servers implementing the Node interface: expose a globally unique opaque id and refetch the same object through node(id), carrying entity identity across a client cache and API boundary.

name: range
document:
range
interval
Represent a span of values as a single interval value whose bound inclusivity and open ends are explicit, so containment and interval-to-interval comparisons live in one place instead of repeated ad-hoc endpoint tests.
Start and end travel together through the code but every caller re-derives what they mean: containment is written as scattered <= / < comparisons that drift apart, "unbounded" is smuggled in as a sentinel value (Long.MAX_VALUE, 9999-12-31), and interval-to-interval questions - do these two overlap, does one enclose the other, what is the gap between them - have no home at all.
Applies wherever a domain concept is a span rather than a point: validity and effectivity periods, booking and availability windows, quantity or price tiers, measurement buckets, version and address ranges, pagination windows, and query parameters such as a date range. It pays off when the same interval is compared repeatedly or crosses a boundary (persistence, API payloads, UI widgets), because the bound convention then has to be written once instead of re-decided per call site. For a single comparison between two local variables the type is pure overhead.
Validity and effectivity windows: a contract, price or membership is valid over [effectiveFrom, effectiveTo), and every check is a membership test against one interval.
Booking and availability: a room, seat or resource is reserved during an interval; overlap (not adjacency) decides whether a new booking is possible, and back-to-back bookings must be allowed deliberately.
Quantity and price tiers: the unit price depends on the quantity interval ([1,10), [10,50), [50, +inf)), so a container of intervals with containment lookup replaces a cascade of if-statements.
Temporal queries and reporting: "last 7 days", "this quarter", "since the migration" are half-open or open-ended intervals passed to repositories and rendered by date-range pickers.
Version, port and address ranges: a compatibility claim covers [1.2, 2.0) of a library, a firewall rule covers a port interval - containment answers "is this covered?" and intersection answers "do these rules conflict?".
Pagination and slicing windows: a page is an interval over a sequence, and half-open semantics make adjacency exact ([0,20) followed by [20,40)),
PostgreSQL range and multirange columns: PostgreSQL's daterange, tsrange and numeric range types make lower-inclusive/upper-exclusive bounds, overlap and containment operators, and indexed range queries part of the persistence contract; choose the bound convention before mapping domain intervals.
Guava Range: Java's Guava Range models convex bounded or unbounded intervals with nine open/closed forms, isConnected and intersection; use ContiguousSet only when a discrete domain really requires enumeration rather than treating the interval itself as a sequence.
Standard-library and container choices: Rust's std::ops::RangeBounds covers included, excluded and unbounded bounds when its range forms fit; for many intervals requiring join/split policies, Boost ICL's interval_set and interval_map supply the container semantics instead of overloading one Range value.

name: guarded-suspension
document:
guarded-suspension
conditional block
suspended execution
Suspend a state-dependent method call inside the object that owns the state until another thread makes its guard predicate true, so callers neither poll nor get refused while the object is temporarily not ready.
A method may only proceed while a precondition over shared state holds - a buffer is non-empty, a pool still has a free lease, a session is authenticated, a worker has a task - and that state is produced by another thread at an unknown time. The recurring decision is what the caller should do while the guard is false: refusing the request would drop work the application still needs, forcing the transition would break the object's invariants, and polling wastes a core and still races. Guarded suspension answers it by waiting on a condition the object itself owns, and by making that wait atomic with respect to the state change that ends it.
Concurrent objects whose methods are state-dependent and whose state changes arrive from other threads: bounded buffers and handoff queues, resource pools, server request/response handoffs, readiness and shutdown gates, worker idle loops. Applicable where the runtime can efficiently park or suspend a caller (OS threads, coroutines) and where the object already owns a lock or monitor, so no notification can be lost between the predicate check and the wait. Ill-suited to single-threaded event loops, to callers that must never be delayed, and to waits whose eventual completion cannot be guaranteed.
Actor mailbox handoff: an Akka/Orleans/Swift-Actor mailbox is a lock-free guarded queue; the actor suspends on an empty mailbox and resumes when a message arrives, which is the same monitor-wait pattern expressed at the language level.
Swift async / Structured Concurrency: a Task.sleep or async let that suspends until a condition is a coroutine-level guarded suspension; the suspension point is backed by a condition variable or event channel inside the runtime.
CompletableFuture / async result: a future's blocking get() is a timed guarded suspension on the thread that submitted the asynchronous operation; the completion path (complete()) is the notifier.
Pipeline stage coordination: in a multi-stage streaming pipeline each stage blocks on input while the upstream stage processes, synchronising via a bounded channel whose put/get implement the guard.
Bounded buffers and handoff queues: a consumer's take waits while the buffer is empty and a producer's put waits while it is full (producer-consumer).
Resource pools: acquire blocks until a lease is returned to a connection, thread or object pool instead of failing or spinning when the pool is exhausted.
Server-side handoff: an acceptor or reader thread publishes a request and the worker waits for work to appear; a caller waits for the response slot to be filled.
Readiness and start-up gates: components wait until a dependency reports connected, initialised or ready, and callers wait until a session, device or circuit is open.
Shutdown and flush coordination: a terminator waits until in-flight work has drained, and a flusher waits while the buffer still holds entries (two-phase termination).
Platform queue and channel APIs: BlockingQueue.take/put, Queue#pop, Channel.receive/for-await, condition-variable waits - the same guard hidden behind a library type.
Project Loom virtual threads (JEP 444): a virtual thread calling Object.wait() parks its Continuation; the carrier thread is released for other virtual threads, so the program continues throughput while one virtual thread waits. The guarded action still re-checks the predicate on wake, and the pattern's semantics are preserved — only the threading model changes.
Akka typed actor mailbox: each actor has a single-threaded mailbox; receive() suspends the actor's continuation when the mailbox is empty, resuming when a message is dispatched. This is language-level guarded suspension where the wait set is the mailbox queue and the guard is 'mailbox non-empty'.
Kotlin coroutines rendezvous channel: Channel() (unbuffered/rendezvous) suspends the sender until a receiver is ready, and vice versa — the same lock-free handoff as an unbuffered Go channel. The suspension is a coroutine-level guarded wait on rendezvous.
Python asyncio.Condition: an async context manager that wraps an asyncio.Lock; await cond.wait() releases the lock and suspends the task until notify() is called, making it an async guarded suspension where the runtime schedules other tasks during the wait.
Go unbuffered channel send/receive: goroutine G1 executing ch <- x on an unbuffered channel sleeps (gopark) until goroutine G2 executes <-ch, at which point the runtime directly transfers the value and stack copy (rendezvous handoff). This is the language-level form of guarded suspension: the guard is 'receiver present', the wait set is the sudog queue in hchan.
Erlang/OTP process mailbox: a gen_server receiving messages from its mailbox blocks (receive...end) until a matching message arrives — the OTP process is a state machine whose transitions are guarded by message arrival, making each receive a suspension point in the actor's event loop.
.NET TaskCompletionSource<T>: GetAwaiter().GetResult() on a not-yet-completed TCS is a synchronous guarded suspension; the async continuation (ConfigureAwait, await) is an asynchronous one. SetResult() is the notifier. TCS is a one-shot asymmetric guarded suspension where one side never waits (the completor) and one side always waits (the synchronously blocked caller).
JDK ArrayBlockingQueue: the queue is one ReentrantLock plus two Condition objects, notEmpty and notFull - take() awaits notEmpty while count == 0, put() awaits notFull while the buffer is full, and each signals the other condition only after mutating count and the circular buffer inside the same critical section. It is the reference production realisation of a two-predicate guarded suspension, including the fairness switch and the timed offer/poll variants.
Go standard library: database/sql guards queries against a concurrent Close with closingMutex, which parks readers and the closing writer on two sync.Cond values (read/write), and net/http's Server.Shutdown waits until in-flight requests have drained. Both are the case Go's own guidance reserves sync.Cond for - a predicate that changes back and forth over time rather than a one-shot handoff.
HikariCP connection pool: DataSource.getConnection() suspends the caller until a lease is returned while the pool already holds maximumPoolSize connections, bounded by connectionTimeout (default 30000 ms, minimum 250 ms), after which it throws SQLException rather than waiting on - a guarded suspension in which the deadline is a documented, first-class outcome instead of an accident.

name: policy-guard
document:
policy-guard
policy pattern
policy decision point / policy enforcement point
Keep every authorisation decision out of the protected resource's code by moving the rules into a separate Policy component and letting a Guard - the enforcement point every access must pass through - obtain a decision from that policy before the operation is performed.
Access rules written inside the resource's own methods (checking roles or ownership inline) entangle business logic with security logic: the same rule is re-implemented at every call site, a forgotten check silently opens a bypass, and the rules cannot be reviewed, tested or changed without touching the resource's code.
Components that own protected resources or operations and must decide per access whether the authenticated subject - with its roles, attributes, tenant and request context - may perform the requested action. Typical at object, module or boundary scope: request handlers, domain services, document stores, message consumers and administrative tooling that all reach the same resources and should obey the same rules, especially when the rules change more often than the resource code.
HTTP and API request handling: authentication establishes the security context once, then every endpoint or method invocation is guarded by a policy decision (for example Spring Security's AuthorizationManager behind its AuthorizationFilter, or ASP.NET Core authorization middleware over registered policies).
Domain services that expose several operations on one aggregate: the guard checks the (subject, operation, resource) triple before each service method executes, instead of scattering role checks through the methods.
Multi-tenant backends where the decision must consider tenant, ownership and request attributes, not only roles; the guard resolves them from the security context and passes them to the policy.
Document or file stores: every read or write is wrapped by a guard that consults rules keyed by the document identifier and its classification.
Administrative and background code - CLI tools, batch jobs, message consumers - that must obey the same policy as the interactive API so that no side door exists.
Regulated environments where every access decision, including denials, must be logged consistently and the policy itself must be independently testable.
Spring Security request boundaries: AuthorizationFilter passes the current Authentication and HttpServletRequest to an AuthorizationManager and proceeds only after a grant; configure every protected route so an unlisted path cannot become a side door.
ASP.NET Core policy authorization: named policies combine requirements evaluated by IAuthorizationHandler implementations and attach with [Authorize(Policy = "...")] or RequireAuthorization; place UseAuthorization after authentication and before endpoints.
Open Policy Agent (OPA) deployments: AWS Prescriptive Guidance models a centralized or distributed Policy Decision Point with Policy Enforcement Points on APIs, allowing shared policy while using local sidecars when latency or availability requires it.

name: pratt-parser
document:
pratt-parser
top-down operator precedence
tdop
Parse expressions with many prefix, infix and postfix operators by associating a binding power and a handler with each token type, so precedence and associativity live in one rule table instead of one parsing function per precedence level.
Operator precedence turns expression parsing into a ladder of near-identical functions - one per level - each of which must re-implement associativity, delegate to the next level for its operands, and be edited whenever an operator is added or moves. Grammars with prefix, infix, postfix and mixfix operators (ternary conditionals, assignment, calls, indexing, user-registered operators) make that ladder long, make associativity easy to get subtly wrong, and scatter the grammar across the parser so it cannot be read in one place.
Hand-written parsers for an expression-bearing language, DSL, query or configuration syntax: a token stream is already available (or is cheap to lex), the operator set is large or expected to grow, and the team wants the grammar visible as data. It is typically the expression layer under an ordinary recursive-descent parser for statements and declarations - interpreters, calculators, filter and rule engines, formula tools - and it is unnecessary when a parser generator already declares precedence for the grammar.
Expression evaluators and calculators whose operator set is expected to grow (arithmetic, units, comparisons, percentages, function calls, user-defined functions).
Query, filter and rule languages - search filters, feature-flag conditions, access-policy conditions, spreadsheet formulas - with many comparison, logical and string operators.
Front ends for small languages and DSLs that parse statements and declarations with recursive descent and need real precedence handling for the expression layer.
Single-pass compilers and interpreters that emit bytecode or IR while parsing, where each handler is also the point that emits the operator's instruction.
Template and configuration expression languages that must attach exact source positions and precise errors to every operator.
Host-language extension points that let plugins or users register additional operators at runtime, because registration is just a table entry.
Rust PEG grammars that use pest::pratt_parser::PrattParser to map prefix, postfix and infix operator pairs into calculator or DSL ASTs.
Rust parser-combinator expression grammars built with chumsky's pratt combinator, where atom parsers and prefix, postfix and infix operators declare precedence and associativity.
JavaScript expression-only tooling built on JSEP, where a compact Pratt-style parser produces ASTs and allows custom unary and binary operators with explicit precedence.

name: request-reply
document:
request-reply
request-response
request-response messaging
Let a sender obtain a result or a domain error from an asynchronous or remote receiver by pairing each request with a correlated reply, and give the missing reply a defined outcome: timeout, cancellation and disposal of late replies.
Messaging is one-way, but the sender frequently needs a return value or a domain error from the receiver before it can continue. Without an agreed reply destination, a way to match replies to requests, and a rule for what happens when no reply arrives, the caller either blocks forever, mis-associates the next reply with the wrong request, or accumulates pending state it never cleans up.
Asynchronous interaction across a process, thread or network boundary where the caller cannot continue without the receiver's result: HTTP/gRPC-style RPC, broker-based RPC over a queue, actor or thread mailboxes, and browser-to-server exchanges over a socket. It applies when the interaction is naturally one request and one reply, and each exchange has a bounded deadline.
Service-to-service RPC where the caller needs the result to continue (HTTP, gRPC, or a broker-based RPC queue such as the RabbitMQ tutorial's rpc_queue).
Command dispatch that must return a domain error - a validation failure or business rejection - rather than only an acknowledgement of receipt.
In-process actor or thread mailboxes: ask a worker for state with a deadline so the caller can never block forever.
Front-end over a WebSocket asking the server for a value correlated by message id or acknowledgement callback.
Talking to devices, sensors or legacy systems over a socket whose protocol is inherently one request and one response.
Querying a cache or index cluster from a client library where each call is a key lookup with a per-call deadline.
NATS request-reply service calls: a client publishes with a unique inbox as the reply subject and waits for a response under a per-request timeout.
RabbitMQ RPC over an rpc_queue: the client sends reply_to and a unique correlation_id, then matches the worker's response on its callback queue.
gRPC unary RPC: a generated client stub sends one request and receives one response under a propagated deadline, with cancellation available for abandoned work.

name: recursive-descent-parser
document:
recursive-descent-parser
recursive descent
recursive descent parsing
Parse a small grammar by translating every rule directly into a function that consumes the tokens the rule matches and calls the functions of the rules it references, so the parser's control flow is the grammar itself and stays readable, debuggable and free of a code-generation step.
A hand-written parser is the only option - no generator in the toolchain, or the grammar is a small DSL - yet the grammar is not a flat token sequence: alternatives must be chosen from lookahead, repetition must become a loop, and the natural grammar for expressions is left-recursive, which a top-down parser cannot translate directly. Without a disciplined mapping from rules to functions the parser degenerates into ad-hoc index arithmetic and exception-driven backtracking, and errors end up without positions.
Front ends for small languages, DSLs, query/filter/rule grammars, configuration and protocol formats, and the parsing layer of compilers and interpreters that want no code-generation step. It applies when a lexer or token stream already exists (or is cheap to write), the grammar is small to medium and reasonably LL-friendly or rewritable into LL form, and the team values readable, step-debuggable, position-precise parsing over generated tables.
Front ends for small languages, DSLs and configuration formats (filter expressions, rule engines, policy languages, template syntaxes) where a generator and its build integration would be overkill.
Expression and statement parsing in single-pass compilers and interpreters that emit bytecode or IR while parsing, as in Crafting Interpreters' Lox.
Tooling for a grammar you own - formatters, linters, syntax highlighters, language servers - where error tolerance, multiple diagnostics and exact positions matter more than raw throughput.
Protocol and wire-format decoding with a small fixed grammar, where errors must carry byte offsets and malformed input must be rejected deterministically.
Context-dependent or indentation-sensitive syntaxes (templates with interpolation, layout-based blocks, configuration with embedded expressions) that a generated lexer handles poorly.
Codebases that must not carry generated code: security-reviewed, vendored or cross-compiled projects where an ordinary source file beats a build-time generator.
Clang's C-family front end uses a unified hand-built recursive-descent parser for C, C++, Objective-C and Objective-C++, pairing rule-oriented control flow with production-quality diagnostics.
The Go standard library's go/parser is a production recursive-descent parser for Go source, with explicit parser state, nesting-depth guards and error recovery.
rustc_parse is the Rust compiler's recursive-descent parser module, showing how a hand-written parser can scale to macros, recovery modes and detailed token/state handling.
Lua's reference implementation compiles with lparser.c, a single-pass recursive-descent parser that emits bytecode opcodes while reducing expressions instead of building a syntax tree, with precedence handled by parsing levels.

name: intercepting-validator
document:
intercepting-validator
validation interceptor
Insert one interception layer on the ingress path that validates every inbound message before any handler runs, so that input checking is uniform, central and impossible to forget per endpoint.
Inbound data - HTTP requests, RPC messages, queue events, protocol frames - is validated inside each handler: every new endpoint re-implements parsing, range and encoding checks, rules drift between handlers, and some paths end up with no validation at all. The recurring decision is where to put validation so that all inbound data passes through it exactly once, before application logic.
Request- or message-driven systems with a well-defined ingress - HTTP APIs, RPC services, queue consumers, protocol front ends - where several handlers accept external data, where shared constraints (schema, ranges, encodings, size limits) can be expressed without loading domain state, and where the ingress pipeline (filter chain, middleware stack, plugin pipeline, responder chain) can be owned and configured by the team.
A public REST or GraphQL API where every request body and query parameter must pass schema, range and size validation before any controller is invoked.
A message-queue consumer that validates every inbound event against its schema and version before dispatching it to a handler.
A file or protocol ingest pipeline (CSV, XML, binary frames) that validates frames in one front layer before domain processing begins.
A multi-tenant service that enforces tenant-scoped constraints uniformly - allowed fields, payload caps, encoding policy - on all inbound requests.
An RPC or WebSocket gateway that rejects non-conforming request messages with one error format before they reach service handlers.
A GraphQL API gateway that validates incoming query operations for schema conformance, depth limits and argument types at the boundary before query execution begins.
A gRPC service fronted by a protobuf interceptor that enforces proto-schema type and structural constraints on all inbound RPC requests before they reach the service implementation.
A FastAPI service that attaches a shared Depends() dependency to an APIRouter and uses Pydantic request models so invalid requests are rejected before the path operation.
An ASP.NET Core application that places request validation in the middleware pipeline or a Minimal API endpoint filter, short-circuiting with a problem response before the endpoint delegate.
An Express application that mounts schema-validation middleware on a router before its routes, returning a 4xx response without calling next() when the request is invalid.

name: protected-system
document:
protected-system
protection proxy
Give a resource exactly one owning object whose published operations are the only way to touch it, so that every access is decided by an authorization check before the resource is used.
A resource - a credential store, a file tree, a socket, a connection pool, a device handle - is referenced from many places. When each use site performs its own permission check, the checks drift, new code paths forget them, and the resource remains reachable as a raw handle, so a missing check cannot even be detected. The recurring trigger: one object can own the resource and clients can be made to hold only that object, so ownership itself can carry the enforcement.
Applies where ownership is expressible in the language or runtime (private field, unexported type, opaque handle, module boundary) and an authorization policy - identity, role, permission, capability - can be evaluated at each public operation. The guard may sit in-process (object or module scope) or at a process/kernel boundary, where the same pattern becomes a real reference monitor; the assurance the implementation can claim depends on which side of that line it lives.
Credential and key stores: an in-process vault owns the keys and exposes only operations (sign, decrypt, rotate), so callers never receive the secret material.
Storage gateways: a library owns the directory handle or object-store client and applies path and tenant rules on every operation instead of handing out a raw client.
Pools: the pool owns its connections and leases checked-out views, so a caller cannot keep, share or resurrect a connection the pool must reclaim.
Multi-tenant data access: a tenant-scoped repository wrapper pins the tenant filter and refuses operations that would query outside it.
Device and driver access: a supervisor object owns the device handle and validates commands, or a privileged daemon owns the socket and checks each request from an unprivileged client.
Module-level boundaries: a package exports only the guard type and keeps the resource unexported, so code outside the package cannot even name the protected representation.
Linux Landlock: a kernel-enforced ruleset restricts a process and its future children to explicitly allowed filesystem or network rights, placing mediation below application code.
Kubernetes RBAC: the API server evaluates Roles and bindings for each API request, mediating verbs and resources instead of exposing the cluster's backing store to clients.
HashiCorp Vault policies: authenticated tokens are checked against path and capability rules before secret operations, while the storage backend remains behind the Vault service.

statement: Choose how the Checkout API receives its repository, payment gateway, clock, and mailer so implementations are selected once and remain replaceable in tests.
name: dependency-injection
document:
dependency-injection
di
constructor injection
setter injection
interface injection
ioc container
pure di
manual di
Supply an object with the collaborators it needs from the outside — through its constructor, its setters/properties, or a dedicated injection interface — so it never constructs or looks a dependency up itself and every wiring decision is made once, in a composition root or container.
An object that creates its own collaborators hard-wires a concrete class, a construction recipe and often a lifetime into itself: swapping the implementation for a test double, a second deployment or a new platform means editing the class, and the dependency graph stays invisible in the API. The recurring trigger is exactly the catalog's rule: an object should not create what it depends on — the caller, the framework or the composition root decides, and hands the dependency in.
Applies whenever a component's collaborators are chosen per deployment, per environment or per test, whenever constructing them is expensive or platform-specific, and whenever a framework owns object creation (request handlers, scheduled jobs, UI screens, message consumers). It matters most in large object graphs where one abstraction has several implementations and lifetimes must be managed (singleton, request-scoped, transient); it is unnecessary when the collaborators are pure values or when construction is a private detail nobody needs to vary.
Web and API backends whose handlers need repositories, clocks, mailers and caches that must be replaced by fakes in tests and by sandbox services in staging.
Hexagonal and clean architectures where the domain declares ports (interfaces) and the infrastructure layer supplies adapters at the composition root.
Frameworks that own object creation — request handlers, scheduled jobs, UI controllers, message consumers — where the framework's injector is the only practical wiring point.
Deployment variants (on-prem vs cloud, SQL vs in-memory, real vs stub payment gateway) selected per environment through binding configuration rather than conditional code.
Plugin and extension systems where the concrete implementation is chosen at start-up from a plugin registry, enabling third-party adapters without touching core code.
Expensive shared resources whose lifetime must be managed centrally (connection pools, HTTP clients, circuit breakers) while service classes stay stateless.
Unit tests that construct the class under test directly with test doubles, and integration tests that swap only the outer layer's bindings.
Microservices with sidecar containers: the sidecar provides logging, tracing and retry policies as injected collaborators, keeping the service logic untouched.
Cloud-native applications where the composition root is the only place that knows whether a dependency resolves locally, across a service mesh, or via a remote gRPC call.
Multi-tenant SaaS where tenant-specific adapters (tenant-scoped repositories, per-tenant feature flags) are bound at the composition root and switched by middleware.
Event-driven systems where message handlers receive their dependencies through injection, making the handler logic identical between in-process and distributed deployment.
AOT-compiled applications (Native AOT, Blazor WebAssembly, serverless) where runtime reflection is unavailable — dependencies are resolved via source generators or manually at the composition root.
Functional codebases using effect systems (ZIO, fp-ts, Reader monad) where the DI container is replaced by typed environments passed through function compositions.
Consumer-driven contract testing (Pact, OpenAPI pact) where DI swaps provider implementations with contract-mock stubs at the boundary, enabling parallel service development without shared integration environments.
Resilience and fault-injection testing: proxies or decorator-based fault injectors (e.g., Gremlin SDK, WireMock) are injected as collaborators to validate retry, timeout and circuit-breaker behaviour under simulated failure conditions.
Single-page application frameworks with DI built into the component tree: Angular resolves components, directives and services through hierarchical injectors, scoping providers to the application root, a component subtree or a route so features override implementations and lazy-load without global registration.
Android apps using Dagger (and Hilt over it) to build the object graph at compile time — generated, reflection-free code, bindings and cycles checked at build time, with field injection reserved for framework-created entry points like Activities and Fragments.
Python web APIs (FastAPI) where each path operation declares Depends(callable) parameters: the framework resolves nested dependency graphs with per-request caching and uses yield-based dependencies to open and close connections around each request.

name: separated-interface
document:
separated-interface
Declare the contract in a deployment unit of its own so that clients depend only on the interface while the implementation lives - and can be deployed - somewhere else.
A dependency or deployment rule forbids the client package from depending on the package that holds the implementation, yet the client must call the implementation's operations. Keeping the interface next to the implementation drags the implementation's own dependencies into the client's dependency graph, and a client that cannot ship or load the implementation (embedded target, plugin host, published header set, ABI boundary) cannot use it at all.
Systems partitioned into packages, assemblies, modules, crates or shared libraries with enforced dependency direction: layered and hexagonal architectures, plugin and driver hosts, library ABI firewalls, multi-platform products, and test setups where a fake must stand in for the real component. Applies when contract and implementation can be carried by separate units, or when the contract must be usable where the implementation cannot go.
Hexagonal / ports-and-adapters architectures: the domain declares ports (repository, clock, notifier) in its own package and infrastructure supplies the adapters.
Plugin hosts, drivers and service provider interfaces: the host ships only the contract; providers are deployed later and discovered through module descriptors, service loader files, registries or configuration.
Library ABI boundaries: clients compile against a header or protocol definition while the implementation stays inside a shared library (C opaque handles, C++ pure abstract classes or pimpl, framework bundles).
Multi-platform products: one contract with per-platform implementations selected at build or run time.
Test doubles: fakes or in-memory implementations of the contract are injected in tests while production wiring binds the real component.
Remote or deferred work: the local interface is implemented by a stub, proxy or gateway that forwards across a process or network boundary (the plug point Fowler names for Gateway).
JDBC: applications compile only against java.sql (Driver, Connection) in the JDK's own contract module; the vendor driver JAR is deployed separately on the classpath or module path and DriverManager discovers implementations of java.sql.Driver through the ServiceLoader mechanism at initialization.
.NET plugin hosts (Microsoft's documented AppWithPlugin design): host and plugins compile against a shared contract assembly only; each implementation assembly is loaded later in a private AssemblyLoadContext via AssemblyDependencyResolver, so plugins ship and version independently of the host and may even carry conflicting dependencies.
Python plugin ecosystems (pytest and its hook plugins, flake8/black plugins): the host declares an entry-point group as the contract and discovers implementations installed as separate distributions through importlib.metadata.entry_points(), never importing a plugin package by name.

name: registry
document:
registry
service registry
plugin registry
Provide one well-known object through which otherwise unrelated objects register themselves and find one another by key, so callers can reach objects and services without holding a direct reference or knowing which concrete implementation is installed.
Collaborating objects have no association to navigate along: the caller holds only an identifier - a name, a symbol, a type, a token - while the reference to the implementation that provides the behaviour is not available at that point in the code. Hard-coding the implementation or its construction at each call site couples every caller to one choice and scatters wiring decisions across the codebase, and the set of available implementations is not known at compile time (plug-ins, drivers, per-deployment services).
Applies inside one process or a well-scoped subsystem when several modules, services or plug-ins coexist and the set varies with configuration, packaging or plug-in availability - registration happening at start-up, at import/link time or through discovery, and lookup happening later from code that could not be handed a reference. Typical settings: service discovery inside an application container, plug-in/extension registries resolved by name, keyed factories for runtime identifiers (formats, protocols, message types) and shared subsystems (loggers, codecs, connection factories) that many parts must reach. It matters most where a framework owns object creation but clients still need a way to reach what was created.
Plug-in and extension registries: a host resolves codecs, exporters, parsers, authentication mechanisms, world generators or rules by name, and third-party packages add their own registrations (Java SPI, Python entry points, Eclipse extension registry, database/sql drivers, mod loaders).
Service discovery inside an application container: framework and library services are registered under types or tokens at start-up and resolved by code that cannot receive them through constructors (framework callbacks, legacy helpers, static entry points).
Keyed factories: mapping an identifier that only arrives at runtime (protocol name, file format, message type, job kind) to the factory that builds the handler for it, keeping the dispatch table out of the caller.
Shared subsystems that must be reachable from many places without threading a reference through every layer: logger, metrics, configuration, connection factory, serializer.
Cross-package discovery where the provider must not be a compile-time dependency of the consumer: JARs on the class path, installed Python distributions, loadable modules or shared libraries.
Java's JDK ServiceLoader: a host discovers providers for a service interface from modules or META-INF/services and uses the common contract without compiling against each provider.
Python packaging entry points: installed distributions advertise named plug-in components in metadata, and consumers discover and load a selected group through importlib.metadata.
Eclipse Platform's extension registry: plug-ins declare extension points and contributions in plugin.xml, then the host queries Platform.getExtensionRegistry() to enumerate them.

name: newtype
document:
newtype
strong typedef
opaque type
Give a single primitive its own distinct type so that values with different meanings cannot be substituted for one another, and the raw representation is reachable only through the wrapper's own construction and accessors.
Several domain concepts share one representation - customer id, order id and tenant id are all strings or UUIDs, width/height/offset are all numbers, milliseconds and seconds are both integers - and the API therefore accepts them interchangeably. A swapped argument, a mixed unit or a mistyped literal compiles (or runs) silently, and the defect surfaces late, as a wrong lookup or a cross-tenant bug rather than a type error.
Code in which two or more values with the same underlying representation flow through the same functions, collections or persistence mapping, and in which a single value owns a rule (identifier syntax, non-emptiness, numeric range, unit). Applies at the value level of one field; clusters of attributes that change together belong to Value Object, and closed constant sets to Type-Safe Enum.
Identifier families in one codebase: CustomerId, OrderId, TenantId and SessionId all string- or UUID-shaped and passed to the same repository, logger and cache.
Unit-carrying measurements: Milliseconds vs Seconds, Meters vs Feet, Radians vs Degrees, Cents vs Dollars, where arithmetic must stay inside one unit and conversion is explicit.
Validated single values: EmailAddress, PhoneNumber, Iban, Slug, Percentage (0-100), PortNumber, NonEmptyString - parsed once at the edge, trusted everywhere afterwards.
Security-adjacent tokens: API token vs session id vs tenant id, where a swap becomes a cross-tenant or privilege defect rather than a wrong lookup.
Geometry and graphics APIs where Width, Height, X, Y, Offset and Length are all numbers and transposition should be a compile error.
Pagination and buffer arithmetic: PageSize vs PageIndex vs ByteOffset vs Count, integers that are trivially transposable in a long argument list.
Rust's official newtype examples use Millimeters(u32) and Meters(u32) to keep units distinct, and use Wrapper(Vec<T>) to give a local wrapper its own trait implementations.
Scala 3 opaque types model values such as Logarithm over Double as distinct outside their defining scope, with controlled extension methods and no runtime boxing.
Kotlin @JvmInline value classes wrap one property into a non-interchangeable domain type such as Password while allowing unboxed representations in many uses.

name: cursor-pagination
document:
cursor-pagination
keyset pagination
cursor-based pagination
Bound what a read boundary returns for a large or changing ordered collection by sending one page plus an opaque continuation token that pins the filter and ordering, so clients advance deterministically without offsets and without watching rows move under them.
A boundary must expose a collection that is too large to return at once and keeps changing while clients read it. Offset or page-number requests make the store count or scan everything up to the requested page, and concurrent inserts or deletes shift rows across page boundaries so consumers see duplicates or miss items; the server has no way to state where the sequence should resume.
Any read boundary - an HTTP or gRPC list operation, a GraphQL connection, a database-backed feed, a batch export job - over an ordered collection that is large, growing, or read under concurrent writes, where the server can identify a unique, immutable ordering key and wants to cap both response size and per-request query cost while letting clients iterate the whole sequence.
Public REST or gRPC list endpoints over unbounded, growing tables - messages, orders, audit events - where deep offsets are slow and responses must stay small.
Infinite-scroll or load-more feeds that keep returning newer items while a user scrolls, with the already-seen pages stable against inserts.
Whole-collection sync and export jobs (warehouse loads, backups, search reindexing) that must iterate every row exactly once while writers continue.
GraphQL Relay connections where first/after, edges and pageInfo carry the continuation contract in the schema instead of the URL.
Consumers of third-party list APIs (Stripe-style starting_after/has_more, Google page_token iterators) that keep parameters fixed across auto-paginated calls.
Administrative and operational tooling that streams very large tables for verification or cleanup with bounded memory and predictable server load.
Audit log and event stream retrieval where events are append-only and chronological, and clients stream continuously without needing to revisit earlier pages.
Real-time activity feeds (social media timelines, notification streams) where inserts at the head must not disturb pages the user has already loaded.
Database replication and change-data-capture (CDC) pipelines that must consume a changelog exactly once across restarts and failures.
Paginating over search results from a vector database or full-text index where OFFSET at depth is expensive and results may change between queries.
Bi-directional data synchronization (CDC pipelines, replica lag-catching) where a consumer must iterate forward and occasionally needs to resume from a previous position or re-sweep a window — requiring stable forward cursors plus a defined backward-resumption path.
Paginating a partitioned or sharded database table where each partition is queried independently and cursors carry both the partition hint and the per-partition keyset position.
Slack Web API collection methods (users.list, conversations.history) where response_metadata.next_cursor drives the loop, page limits are clamped per method, and expired or malformed tokens surface as invalid_cursor so the client restarts from the first page.
GitHub GraphQL-style cursor connections where first/last (bounded 1-100) and pageInfo.startCursor/endCursor carry the continuation position for after/before traversal.
Timeline-style feeds served by Django REST framework's CursorPagination, whose default -created ordering gives a consistent view that does not repeat items as new rows are inserted.

name: repository
document:
repository
collection-oriented repository
repository layer
Mediates between the domain model and the data mapping layer with a collection-like interface, so domain code adds, removes and finds persistent objects as if they lived in memory and never constructs queries or touches persistence APIs itself.
Persistence code spreads: every application service re-derives the same SQL or ORM queries, duplicate query logic drifts apart, table and column names leak into domain decisions, and testing domain rules without a database becomes impossible. Callers should be able to think in collections of domain objects instead of queries.
Applies to systems with a non-trivial domain model sitting on a data-mapping layer (Data Mapper, metadata mapping, or a hand-written mapper) where the same queries recur across application services; it becomes more valuable as domain classes and query volume grow. It is the standard persistence boundary of DDD aggregates (one repository per aggregate root) and presumes a unit of work or session that owns flush and commit. It is not a per-table data-access wrapper and not a replacement for transaction control.
DDD application services that must load an aggregate root, run domain logic on it and store it again without knowing the table layout.
Data-mapper backends where several application services and background jobs share recurring complex queries (overdue invoices, pending orders, open tickets).
Applications that must be unit-testable away from the database: repositories are the substitution point for in-memory doubles.
Systems that must support more than one store behind a stable domain interface — relational in production, in-memory in tests, a document store for a particular deployment.
Uniform cross-cutting access policy for an aggregate: caching, read-replica routing, audit logging or authorization applied as decorators around one interface.
Migration work where the persistence technology changes (ORM swap, schema split, service extraction) while the domain model and its tests stay untouched.
CQRS write-side aggregate loading where the aggregate must be reconstructed fully to apply business rules and enforce invariants.
Integration with heterogeneous data sources where one repository unifies access to a cache, primary database and a third-party API behind a domain interface.
Spring Data JPA applications can use Repository/CrudRepository for aggregate-typed CRUD, paging and derived queries, then add only domain-specific methods rather than wrapping every persistence operation.
The .NET eShopOnContainers ordering microservice uses an EF Core BuyerRepository over a shared scoped DbContext/unit of work, while CQRS/Dapper handles presentation reads.
Python applications using SQLAlchemy ORM can place an aggregate-facing repository over Session, whose identity map and unit-of-work flush semantics provide the mapper/session boundary.

name: characterization-test
document:
characterization-test
golden master
approval test
golden file test
snapshot test
golden session test
Pin the actual, currently deployed behaviour of existing code in committed reference artefacts (golden masters) so that a later edit can be distinguished from an accidental regression even when nobody can say what the code is supposed to do.
You must change code whose behaviour is undocumented, surprising or only known to production: there is no specification to test against, and tests written from intended behaviour would take too long and silently encode guesses as fact. The safety net therefore has to be built from observed behaviour: replay a corpus of real inputs through the untouched subject, capture everything observable, commit the result as the reference, and let every later run diff against it - pinning what the code does today before changing how it does it.
Applies whenever the subject already runs and can be exercised in a test process or from a test script: untested legacy modules, data transformations and report pipelines, serializers, parsers and code generators, CLI and protocol endpoints, rendering pipelines whose images can be diffed, and dependency or runtime upgrades where the old behaviour is the baseline. The precondition is determinism: volatile parts (timestamps, identifiers, paths, memory addresses, collection order, locale, floating-point formatting) must be normalized or redacted before capture, otherwise the comparison is noise. The pattern is a first move - build the net, then refactor under it - and pairs with a deliberate approval step, because a characterization test does not know which behaviour was intended.
Before refactoring an untested legacy module: capture outputs for a corpus of inputs, restructure the code, and require the reference artefacts to stay identical.
Data processing and batch jobs: pin how representative input files are transformed into output files or reports, so the nightly job can be changed safely.
Serializers, formatters and code generators: pin the emitted text or structured output for representative documents, with a redaction step for volatile values.
Rendering and UI pipelines: pin generated images (screenshot goldens) or rendered text output with an approval workflow and a visual diff tool.
CLI and protocol behaviour: pin stdout, stderr and exit codes, or request/response bytes, for a set of recorded invocations.
Dependency or runtime upgrades: pin behaviour before the upgrade and re-run afterwards, so only intended differences have to be reviewed.
Production defect triage: replay the failing production input into a new reference artefact, then fix the defect against that regression test.
AI/LLM output regression testing: pin model responses to a curated golden dataset; on model or prompt change, compare distributions, embedding similarity, or token-level diffs against the baseline rather than requiring exact matches (LLM eval pipelines, 2024-2026).
Generated code verification: pin the exact output of OpenAPI client generators, GraphQL type generators, SDK wrappers, or database migration previews so formatting and structural changes are caught.
Database schema migration testing: capture the before/after output of migration scripts for a set of schema variants, approving only intentional structural differences.
Computer vision pipeline regression: pin bounding-box distributions or classification confidence vectors from CV models across runs; statistical comparison prevents flaky failures from minor pixel noise.
Smart contract and blockchain output regression: pin deterministic contract outputs for a given input state; any divergence in on-chain behaviour is immediately visible (Nexlify case, 2025).
Database-engine regression suites: PostgreSQL's pg_regress replays each sql/*.sql script and diffs results/*.out against committed golden files in expected/*, with variant comparison files and a resultmap absorbing known platform differences (locale, float formatting, row ordering).
Compiler test corpora: LLVM's lit/FileCheck pins emitted IR and machine code by piping compiler output to FileCheck, which verifies CHECK directives committed inside each test file across the whole input corpus.
ORM query-change detection: ApprovalTests.Ruby's verify_sql approves the SQL an ActiveRecord call emits, so a gem or framework upgrade that silently rewrites generated queries fails the suite.

name: attorney-client
document:
attorney-client
attorney pattern
attorney-client friendship idiom
Grant a named collaborator a deliberately narrow compile-time view of a class's private interface by making an attorney the client's sole friend; the attorney forwards selected operations or re-exports selected private nested types (often through controlled public typedefs), while unrelated private members and the public contract remain closed.
A C++ collaborator may need one private hook, constructor, iterator adapter or nested implementation type, but a friend class receives every private and protected member. Making the hook public leaks it to every caller; publishing a std::list<T>::iterator or the container type leaks representation and its invalidation contract; pImpl hides representation from everyone but does not grant one collaborator a typed privileged view. The missing mechanism is a small attorney contract that names exactly the operations or nested types this collaborator may use without turning the private interface into a second public API.
Object-oriented code whose encapsulation boundary is a class and whose language offers class- or scope-level access control but no per-collaborator grant - C++ with friend declarations, Java/C#/Kotlin with package, assembly or module access, and their test- and library-extension scenarios. It applies at object scope, where one type owns the implementation and one named collaborator needs a slice of it, and it is a source-level structuring device checked by the compiler, never a runtime protection mechanism.
White-box test access: a test harness reaches one private hook or state view through a named attorney instead of making the member public or redefining private with a test-only preprocessor switch.
Iterator adapters: Boost.Iterator's iterator_core_access is a canonical gateway class a user-defined iterator befriends, so iterator_facade and its operators reach private dereference/increment/advance core functions while those implementation hooks stay out of the iterator's public API.
Serialization: Boost.Serialization has serializable classes befriend boost::serialization::access, whose gateway reaches the private serialize() member so archives can reconstruct state without a public serialization method.
Private nested type exposure: LLVM's SchedulerInternalsAttorney publishes the selected nested Scheduler::BndlSchedState as a public type alias and supplies narrow static accessors for unit tests, without publishing every Scheduler private type.
A pImpl-backed adapter that must inspect one implementation-owned type: keep the public class opaque and put the attorney definition in the adapter or test header, so the privileged component gets a typed view without making the implementation part of the ordinary public contract.
Iterator facade over a hidden list-like representation: expose a stable nested iterator/view type through an attorney rather than publishing std::list<T>::iterator, so the owner can replace the container without promising its node and invalidation details to every caller.
Private virtual hooks: an attorney forwards one private virtual operation through a base reference, allowing the derived override to run even though friendship is not inherited.
Factory or construction control: a builder reaches one private constructor or initialization hook through an attorney, while unrelated callers still cannot construct an object through that path.
Spacecraft flight software (fsfw): LocalDpManagerAttorney keeps fetchPoolEntry and getMutexHandle as private static forwarders and befriends only LocalPoolVariable and LocalPoolVector, so the local data pool manager opens its internals to two named collaborators instead of every class that might befriend it.
Simulator tree traversal (Sandia Sparta Modeling Framework): sparta::TreeNodePrivateAttorney exposes TreeNode's private child vectors and subtrees through static accessors (getAllChildren, getChild, findChildren) for internal Reports and Pipeout processing, with a documented 'should NOT be used by simulation developers' restriction in place of an enforceable caller limit.

name: active-record
document:
active-record
active record pattern
ActiveRecord
Make a domain object the record for one database row: keep the row's state, row-local behavior, and the methods that find and persist it together, so a small domain does not pay for a separate mapping layer.
A simple relational domain still needs a choice about where persistence lives. A Data Mapper or gateway separates table I/O from the object but adds mapping code and a second place to navigate, while direct SQL leaks schema knowledge into callers; the recurring question is whether one row object can own its data and CRUD without hiding transaction boundaries or pretending to model cross-row rules.
A relational store is the single system of record, the domain is small and its rules are mostly local to one row (validation, derivations, simple state transitions), and the team prefers a convention-driven persistence layer over a designed one. Typical homes are framework ecosystems where the ORM is the house style (Rails, Laravel Eloquent, Django, GORM, Vapor Fluent, TypeORM), CRUD-heavy applications, and thin layers over an already well-shaped legacy schema. Entity Framework Core can host behavior on entity classes, but its DbContext and mapping conventions are a Data Mapper-shaped boundary rather than pure Active Record. It stops applying as soon as invariants span several objects, several representations of one table are needed, or the store must be swappable.
CRUD-heavy applications where most screens and endpoints map onto a single table: forms, admin back offices, catalogs, content management.
Small-to-medium domains whose rules are mostly per-row - field validation, derived values, one-row state transitions - so a mapper layer would move data around without adding a model.
Prototypes and thin service layers over an existing, already normalised legacy schema where the table shape is stable and the domain is the schema.
Framework-default persistence: a Rails, Django, GORM, Vapor Fluent or TypeORM codebase where fighting the ORM for purity costs more than it returns.
Simple record-shaped bounded contexts inside a larger system - settings, audit entries, lookup tables - where a full domain model would be overhead.
JSON:API or REST backends for SPAs and mobile apps where the data model maps directly to a relational schema with minimal transformation.
Microservices with a single-responsibility data store: a service whose entire bounded context is one aggregate root table or a handful of tightly coupled tables.
Batch import pipelines where records are validated once and bulk-inserted (insert_all/upsert_all), and the domain logic has already been applied before the bulk operation.
Multi-tenant SaaS backends where row-level isolation is enforced at the database and the ORM connection handles tenant scoping automatically.
Real Rails systems such as GitLab and Discourse are good fits for row-shaped users, posts, permissions and settings backed by PostgreSQL; keep their reporting and cross-record workflows in query or service boundaries.
A Django or Laravel CRUD surface such as an admin or back-office module fits when each request mostly validates, loads, changes and saves one model; switch to a mapper or repository when the same data feeds materially different contracts.

name: spatial-partition
document:
spatial-partition
spatial index
bucket grid
Store every object in a structure indexed by its position so that neighbourhood queries visit only the objects near a point or region instead of scanning the whole population.
Queries that ask 'what is near this position?' - collision checks, proximity and aggro radii, culling, spatial analytics - repeatedly scan every object: each query is linear in the population and a whole simulation step becomes quadratic, even though every object interacts only with the few objects next to it.
Per-object runtime systems and simulations - game worlds, crowd and particle solvers, location services, robotics - where objects are mobile, spread over space, and the queries are local (radius, region, k-nearest). The pattern applies once the population is large enough that a full scan dominates the frame or the request budget, and it requires a position-to-cell mapping and an update discipline that match how the objects move.
Game worlds: collision, proximity and aggro checks between many moving entities each tick (bullets versus enemies, pickups, area effects).
Physics broadphase: pruning candidate pairs before narrow-phase tests where colliders move constantly.
Map and GIS services: 'all points within radius' and viewport queries over millions of features.
Crowd, flocking and particle simulations: neighbours within a radius for boids or social forces instead of all-pairs tests.
Spatial analytics and robotics: k-nearest or region queries over vehicles, sensors and delivery points, and occupancy grids for pathfinding.
Physics engines: Box2D's broadphase is a dynamic AABB tree (b2DynamicTree) whose fattened leaf boxes absorb small moves before reinsertion, and whose region queries and ray casts prune candidates before narrow-phase tests.
Location services: Redis geospatial indexes store members as 52-bit geohash scores in a sorted set (GEOADD) so GEOSEARCH answers circle and bounding-box proximity queries server-side instead of scanning members.
GIS and analytics databases: PostGIS prunes radius queries through a GiST spatial index (the index-aware ST_DWithin predicate checks bounding boxes before computing exact distances), and scikit-learn backs radius and k-nearest neighbour queries with KDTree and BallTree instead of all-pairs distances.

name: single-table-inheritance
document:
single-table-inheritance
table per hierarchy
discriminator column mapping
Map an inheritance hierarchy of classes onto one shared table whose columns are the union of all classes' fields, using a type code (discriminator) column to decide which class each row instantiates, so polymorphic reads need no joins.
A class hierarchy must be persisted, the hierarchy is small and its classes share most fields, and cross-class queries or polymorphic loads are frequent: mapping each class to its own table would force a join per level on almost every read, while the subtypes differ by only a few columns.
Object-relational mapping of a small, shallow, stable class hierarchy whose subclasses are mostly variations on shared state - domain-model inheritance (Employee/Engineer/Manager), payment or content types - where the storage layer is chosen by the team and the persistence framework can be taught the type code (JPA/EF Core/ActiveRecord/SQLAlchemy/most ORMs make this their default strategy) or the mapping is written by hand over SQL.
Small stable hierarchies where subclasses share most state: Employee/Engineer/Manager, Payment/CardPayment/WirePayment, Notification/EmailNotification/PushNotification.
Content or asset models with a handful of similar types (Photo/Question/Post, Blog/RssBlog) distinguished by a type code, where cross-type queries and listings are the dominant read.
Legacy or third-party schemas that already hold a hierarchy in one table with a kind column and must be mapped onto domain classes without restructuring the database.
Reporting and analytics over a hierarchy where one wide table with a type column beats joining four tables for every subtype question.
ORM-default configurations: teams that pick the framework's default hierarchy mapping (JPA SINGLE_TABLE, EF Core TPH) because join avoidance and mapping simplicity outweigh column honesty for their hierarchy size.
Rails Active Record single-table inheritance: ActiveRecord::Inheritance stores the subclass name in the table's type column by default (Company/Firm/Client all live in companies with type = 'Firm'), so fetching via the base class returns correctly-typed objects - GitLab runs a production monolith on this mechanism and maintains a written policy on when STI must not be used.
EF Core's default table-per-hierarchy mapping: a Blog/RssBlog hierarchy shares one table, the discriminator's name, CLR type and per-class values are set with HasDiscriminator/HasValue, and EF Core automatically adds the discriminator predicate to derived-type queries (throwing on unmapped discriminator values).
SQLAlchemy declarative polymorphic mappers: the base class declares polymorphic_on = 'type' in __mapper_args__ and each subclass a unique polymorphic_identity, so one person table answers polymorphic queries for Person/Employee rows without joins.

name: page-object
document:
page-object
page object model
window driver
Wrap each UI surface a test drives - a page or a significant component - in an object that exposes the services the surface offers and hides every locator, driver call and wait, so a UI change is absorbed by one class instead of by every test that touched the markup.
A UI test that drives the automation API directly - find an element, type, click, wait, read text - keeps the page's locators and interaction mechanics in the test body: the same selector is repeated across dozens of tests, a markup change breaks them all at once, and a reader must reconstruct the page's structure to understand what the test does. The catalog's trigger: a UI change should touch one class, not fifty assertions.
Automated tests that drive a user interface through a driver API - a browser (Selenium/WebDriver, Playwright, Cypress, WebdriverIO), a mobile app (Appium, Espresso, XCUITest) or a desktop window - where the same screens are exercised by many tests, where the UI changes independently of the tests, and where the suite is expected to survive redesigns. The pattern pays off when the interface can be named in the user's terms ('sign-in page', 'product row') and the driver offers stable element lookup; it is unnecessary for a single throwaway script or when the presentation logic has already been extracted behind a humble object.
A regression suite over a web application whose pages are exercised by dozens of tests: login, search, checkout and admin screens each get a class, and a redesign changes only those classes (the Selenium and Playwright POM guides' home scenario).
The same screens are driven by different kinds of test - functional, visual, accessibility, smoke - and the locator knowledge must live in one place that all of them import.
Mobile application suites (Appium, Espresso, XCUITest) where screens are widget hierarchies with platform-specific queries, and the page object is the only place that codifies the platform lookup.
BDD suites: Gherkin steps stay business-readable because step definitions delegate to page objects instead of calling the driver (Fowler's layering recommendation).
Suites migrating drivers or frameworks (Selenium to Playwright, a WebdriverIO restructure): the page API is kept while only its internals change.
A scripting interface over an application whose behaviour is stuck in the UI (Fowler's scripting use), or a legacy system that can only be exercised through its window.
Selenium's documented login flow: SignInPage.loginValidUser returns HomePage, so a regression suite can exercise authentication through services while locators and page-load checks stay in the page objects.
Playwright's official playwright.dev example: PlaywrightDevPage wraps a Page, owns locators for the getting-started flow and exposes goto, getStarted and pageObjectModel methods used by tests.
WebdriverIO's official The Internet login example: a getter-based LoginPage centralizes selectors and open/submit actions, letting login specs survive selector changes without duplicating driver calls.
