name: extensible-visitor
document:
extensible-visitor
extensible visitor pattern
extensible visitors with defaults
Keep the visitor open on both axes at once - new element kinds and new operations arrive without editing or recompiling any visitor that already exists - by giving every visitor a default method that catches element kinds it was not written for, introducing extended element kinds under an intermediate base whose accept hooks overload (not override) accept, and extending an operation by subclassing the existing concrete visitor so it inherits every case it already handled.
A classic Visitor is cheap in one direction only: a new operation is a new visitor, but a new element kind forces every visitor to grow one more method, so shipped visitors must be edited and redeployed. The trigger is an element hierarchy that is extended by parties who do not own the operations - language dialects, plugin node types, versioned grammars, third-party message formats - where the existing operations must keep working unchanged on the extended structure.
Recursively defined element hierarchies (abstract syntax trees, intermediate representations, document and message models) that grow over time, in a statically typed language whose visitors are concrete classes or interfaces with default bodies, and where the traversal logic itself lives inside the operations. It pays off when old operations must run against new element kinds and when element kinds are added by a different team than the operations; it assumes the visitor protocol can carry a default case and that a runtime type test is acceptable on the dispatch path.
A compiler front-end whose node kinds are extended by language dialects while every existing analysis pass keeps running unchanged (the extensible-compiler case the pattern was derived from).
An IDE or linter analysing a versioned language grammar: the version-1 analysis must not be recompiled when version 2 adds syntax nodes it does not understand.
Plugin systems where third-party modules contribute new node types (document formats, workflow elements, protocol messages) to a host that ships the operations.
Optimisation or lowering pipelines whose passes are shipped separately from the node hierarchy: the platform team adds representations, users add passes.
A published visitor API where other teams implement visitors and the element set grows every release, making 'which kinds does this visitor handle' an explicit, versioned contract.
Migration and validation tooling that must keep working on messages produced by newer producers than the tool itself.
Serialization and schema-generation frameworks such as Jackson's JsonFormatVisitor API, which uses a visitor to traverse Java type hierarchies for JSON/XML schema generation and allows third-party serializers to contribute handlers for new POJO shapes without modifying the core framework.
Query engines over tree-structured data (e.g. Apache Calcite's relational algebra, Rascal's AST analysis): new relational operators or AST node types are contributed by extension modules while existing optimisers and evaluators continue to function unchanged.
Static analysis and bug-finding tools (Coverity, CodeQL, ESLint plugin architectures): new checker plugins add new node-type coverage while the core traversal engine ships unchanged, and old checkers degrade gracefully over unknown node types.
Game engine entity-component systems: new component types are contributed at runtime while existing systems (physics, rendering, AI) continue to process entities; the visitor with default case handles component types added after a given system was written.
Python's ast.NodeVisitor: visit() dispatches to a visit_<Node> method and falls back to generic_visit as the built-in default case, so analysis tools written before newer node kinds existed (Match, TryStar, TypeAlias) keep traversing Python's evolving AST unchanged, exactly the degrade-don't-break contract of the pattern.
The JDK Compiler Tree API (com.sun.source.tree.TreeVisitor / SimpleTreeVisitor): every visit method defaults to visitOther/defaultAction as the catch-all, so javac-based tooling written against Java 8 trees keeps compiling and running as Java adds records, patterns and switch labels - old visitors land in visitOther instead of failing.
Roslyn's CSharpSyntaxVisitor / CSharpSyntaxWalker: the generated visitor carries one Visit method per syntax node kind plus DefaultVisit as the default case, and each C# language version extends the node hierarchy while existing analysers and the compiler's own passes keep working over the extended tree.

name: spatial-partition
document:
spatial-partition
spatial index
bucket grid
Store every object in a structure indexed by its position so that neighbourhood queries visit only the objects near a point or region instead of scanning the whole population.
Queries that ask 'what is near this position?' - collision checks, proximity and aggro radii, culling, spatial analytics - repeatedly scan every object: each query is linear in the population and a whole simulation step becomes quadratic, even though every object interacts only with the few objects next to it.
Per-object runtime systems and simulations - game worlds, crowd and particle solvers, location services, robotics - where objects are mobile, spread over space, and the queries are local (radius, region, k-nearest). The pattern applies once the population is large enough that a full scan dominates the frame or the request budget, and it requires a position-to-cell mapping and an update discipline that match how the objects move.
Game worlds: collision, proximity and aggro checks between many moving entities each tick (bullets versus enemies, pickups, area effects).
Physics broadphase: pruning candidate pairs before narrow-phase tests where colliders move constantly.
Map and GIS services: 'all points within radius' and viewport queries over millions of features.
Crowd, flocking and particle simulations: neighbours within a radius for boids or social forces instead of all-pairs tests.
Spatial analytics and robotics: k-nearest or region queries over vehicles, sensors and delivery points, and occupancy grids for pathfinding.
Physics engines: Box2D's broadphase is a dynamic AABB tree (b2DynamicTree) whose fattened leaf boxes absorb small moves before reinsertion, and whose region queries and ray casts prune candidates before narrow-phase tests.
Location services: Redis geospatial indexes store members as 52-bit geohash scores in a sorted set (GEOADD) so GEOSEARCH answers circle and bounding-box proximity queries server-side instead of scanning members.
GIS and analytics databases: PostGIS prunes radius queries through a GiST spatial index (the index-aware ST_DWithin predicate checks bounding boxes before computing exact distances), and scikit-learn backs radius and k-nearest neighbour queries with KDTree and BallTree instead of all-pairs distances.

name: row-data-gateway
document:
row-data-gateway
row data gateway
row gateway
Give each database row its own in-memory object that mirrors the row's columns and carries the row's own find, insert, update and delete operations, so all data-access code for a table lives in one place instead of being duplicated across the scripts that use it.
SQL text, parameter binding and result-set mapping are re-derived inside every transaction script that touches a table, while the in-memory objects those scripts work with know nothing about the database. No single place knows how one row is read, written and deleted, so a schema change ripples through every script and every new query is another chance to get parameterisation and type conversion wrong.
Applies when business logic is organised as transaction scripts or thin services over a relational schema whose columns map closely to the fields actually used: the gateway mirrors the table structure, no object/relational impedance mismatch is being managed, and identity maps, units of work and lazy loading are either unnecessary or added deliberately as separate patterns. It also fits generated persistence layers, where the gateway classes are produced from schema metadata during the build.
Transaction-script applications (order entry, billing runs, batch imports) where several scripts need the same handful of row-level reads and writes.
CRUD-heavy back-office and admin tooling where a screen edits one row at a time and columns map one-to-one onto form fields.
Legacy or externally owned schemas that must be mirrored rather than reshaped: one gateway per table gives an explicit, reviewable seam between the application and someone else's database.
Generated persistence layers: gateways produced from schema metadata on every build, so the tedious class-per-table work is automated and stays in sync with the schema.
Simple mappings inside an otherwise rich domain model, where a domain object keeps a gateway as its data holder instead of copying field values around.
Reporting and fixture utilities that need reusable, parameterised finders for one table without pulling in a full object/relational mapper.
Laminas\Db\RowGateway and RowGatewayFeature (the official laminas-db implementation) expose one row object with save/delete and can materialize table-query results as row gateways, fitting CRUD screens or transaction scripts that edit individual records.
Zend Framework 1's Zend_Db_Table_Row is a documented legacy row-gateway implementation: table queries return row objects with column access plus save/delete/createRow operations, useful when a simple schema is consumed by row-oriented scripts.
The Go dgw tool generates structs and lightweight Table/Row Data Gateway functions from PostgreSQL metadata, demonstrating the pattern as a code-generation choice when a project wants typed CRUD without a full ORM.

name: stub
document:
stub
test stub
stub object
Replace a collaborator with a test-specific stand-in that returns canned answers, so the component under test can be driven down paths - success, empty, error, timeout - that the real collaborator cannot be made to produce on demand.
The component under test receives indirect inputs through a collaborator, and the branch that must be exercised is selected by what that collaborator returns. The real collaborator will not produce the needed value on request: it is slow, remote, licensed, non-deterministic, or simply never returns the rare case - the empty result, the declined payment, the timeout - that the test exists for. Without a controllable replacement the test either cannot reach the path at all or has to provoke it through the production system, which is exactly what unit testing was supposed to avoid.
Unit and component tests of a component whose collaborators are already, or can cheaply become, abstractions: the values and exceptions a collaborator returns are inputs to the component under test, and the test asserts what the component does with them rather than how the collaboration happened. Typical where the collaborator is remote or stateful (HTTP client, database, queue, clock, payment gateway) or where the branch under test is an edge case - empty page, declined payment, expired token, feature off. The pattern assumes a substitutable seam: a constructor parameter, an injected interface, a factory, a lookup, or a patchable module.
Exercising a rare branch of the component: an empty result set, a declined payment, a 429 from a gateway, a missing feature flag.
Testing error handling: programme the stub to raise the exception the real service would raise - timeout, connection reset, malformed payload - and assert that the SUT surfaces or recovers from it.
Unit-testing a component against a collaborator that is slow, paid, unavailable in CI or still being implemented; the stub encodes the agreed response while the real adapter is built.
Removing non-determinism from a path the real collaborator decides by clock, randomness or remote state (token expired, cache cold, retry budget exhausted), so one outcome can be asserted exactly.
View and presentation tests: a fixed dataset from the stub, so the assertion is about the rendering or the decision logic and nothing else.
Boundary values on contract edges - zero, maximum, empty string, unicode payloads - that the real system cannot be asked to return on demand.
Mockito (Java): when(warehouse.hasInventory(...)).thenReturn(false) programmes the declined-branch answer and thenThrow(SocketTimeoutException.class) injects the failure, and consecutive-value stubbing (thenReturn(v1, v2)) drives retry-then-succeed paths that the real warehouse would never produce on request.
Python unittest.mock (standard library): Mock(return_value=...) fixes the canned answer while side_effect set to an exception or an iterable raises or sequences answers per call - the library ships Responder and Saboteur behaviour as first-class configuration.
Moq (.NET): mock.Setup(x => x.HasInventory(...)).Returns(false) and .Throws<InvalidOperationException>() are the canned-answer primitives, so a C# test reaches the empty-inventory and fault branches of Order.Fill without touching a database.

name: double-checked-locking
document:
double-checked-locking
double-checked locking optimization
DCL
DCLP
Initialise a shared resource exactly once and lazily while keeping the steady-state read path free of lock acquisition - by testing a cheaply published state first and taking the lock only for the one-time construction, where the platform can publish the built object safely to every reader.
An expensive object - configuration, a connection pool, a compiled plan, a cache - must be created once and only when it is first needed, but its accessor is called from many threads. The naive check-then-act form lets two threads build it at the same time, and guarding every read with a lock serialises a path that almost never needs synchronisation. The tempting fix - test a flag cheaply, lock only for the initialisation, test again inside the lock - is sound only if the write that publishes the object is ordered with respect to the readers' loads, which is exactly the part the classic formulation leaves implicit and the reason the idiom is famous for rare, unreproducible failures.
Concurrent, shared-memory software in which one object or cell must be built once and read many times: process-wide singletons and registries, per-object caches inside an object shared between threads, lazily built statics in languages whose runtime also provides the once semantics. The pattern presupposes a memory model with a defined publication ordering (volatile, acquire/release, an initialisation lock, or a runtime once primitive) and a read path hot enough that the lock it removes is measurable. On single-threaded runtimes there is nothing to synchronise, and where a single-threaded composition root can initialise eagerly the pattern is unnecessary.
Process-wide singletons whose construction is expensive or configuration-dependent: configuration snapshot, metrics registry, logger, connection pool, feature-flag view.
Per-object caches inside an object shared by several threads - compiled regular expression or query plan, parsed schema, symbol table - where the build is expensive and the read is hot.
Lazily built statics in languages where the runtime owns the once semantics: C++ function-local static, Swift static let or global let, Kotlin by lazy, Scala lazy val, Go sync.Once, Rust OnceLock/LazyLock.
Compensating for the static-initialisation-order problem: an accessor that builds the global on first use instead of relying on cross-translation-unit initialisation order.
Avoiding lock overhead on a read-mostly, write-once hot path (memo tables, symbol caches, thread-safe lazy proxies) where a contended lock would show up in a profile.
Small or freestanding runtimes without a once primitive, where the first caller must build the cell and an eager initialiser is not available.
RWMutex-protected maps in Go where readers check a fast path before the slower write-locked re-check, as a safer alternative to sync.Map for workloads with known access patterns.
Per-connection or per-session lazy fields in object-pooled servers where the pool itself is the shared cell and each borrowed object gets a lazy-computed field.
Cross-language plugin or extension registries where one language's runtime initialises a global handle that other language shards read without repeated synchronisation.
Rate-limiter or circuit-breaker state that must be lazily built from configuration: building eagerly would couple the policy to startup time, but the read path must be lock-free under high throughput.
Lazy compilation or query-plan warming in database connection pools where the pool is shared but individual plans are built on first use by the owning thread.
Spring Framework's DefaultSingletonBeanRegistry.getSingleton: check the singletonObjects map lock-free, take the singletonLock only when the bean is absent, re-check inside - a production evolution of the idiom whose correctness was formally challenged (SPR-13463) and upheld because the concurrent-map read already carries the needed memory barrier.
Chromium's base::LazyInstance / GetOrCreateLazyPointer: an atomic state word with a 'creating' bit, acquire-load fast path and release-store publication - since deprecated in favour of function-local statics with base::NoDestructor, a signal of how far hardened platforms have moved from hand-rolled DCL.
ACE toolkit's ACE_Singleton<TYPE, ACE_LOCK>: the pattern's original industrial home (the 1997 paper was written alongside ACE) - the template still guards instance() with a double-checked ACE_LOCK acquire and recommends ACE_Recursive_Thread_Mutex for multi-threaded access.
Swift runtime: every global/static let is lowered to swift_once (dispatch_once on Darwin), so the double-checked once structure is the default initialisation mechanism for lazily computed immutable globals rather than hand-written code.

name: copy-and-swap
document:
copy-and-swap
copy and swap idiom
create-temporary-and-swap
Implement assignment (and any in-place state replacement) so that a failure while producing the new state leaves the target untouched: build the complete replacement off to the side, commit it with operations that cannot fail, and let the temporary's destructor or the garbage collector release the old state.
A hand-written assignment has to tear down the old state and build a copy of the new one, but only the build can fail: destroying before allocating exposes a half-updated object when the allocation or the element copy throws, and the usual repair -- a self-assignment check plus manual rollback -- duplicates the per-member copying that already lives in the copy constructor. The trigger is an assignment (or, in a garbage-collected language, an in-place state replacement) that must satisfy the strong exception guarantee: either it completes, or the target still holds its previous value.
Types that own resources -- heap buffers, handles, file descriptors, trees, containers -- in a language where the programmer controls copy semantics: C++ special member functions, a C ADT with error codes, Rust with panic/abort failure modes. The same ordering also applies in garbage-collected languages whenever published state must never be mutated in place: building the complete replacement and publishing it once keeps readers consistent and moves the release of the old state to the collector. The precondition is a commit step that genuinely cannot fail -- a noexcept member swap, one reference or pointer store, or an atomic publish.
Container and buffer classes that own heap memory (dynamic array, string, matrix, tree) and must be assignable without leaking or leaving the target inconsistent when an allocation fails.
Handle/pimpl classes that keep their state behind a single pointer: the swap is a pointer exchange, so the commit is unconditionally non-throwing while the deep copy still happens in the copy constructor (Sutter's canonical Pimpl exception-safety transformation).
Pre-C++11 codebases where the same operator= must serve lvalues and rvalues and no move constructor exists, using the const-reference plus explicit-local-temporary form.
Value types stored inside standard containers: std::vector and friends need element assignment to be safe before they can offer their own strong guarantee on reallocation, and a noexcept swap participates in their internal move/swap dispatch.
Garbage-collected languages where shared state must be replaced rather than mutated: build a complete replacement value and publish it with one store (AtomicReference.updateAndGet, atomic.Pointer[T].Store, a record with-expression) so readers never observe a partially updated object.
In-place state replacement where identity must be preserved (a registry entry, a cached object with live references): copy into a scratch value, then commit with a member-wise exchange or a replace-style API instead of repointing the reference.
Concurrent programming with thread-safe local-then-publish: build the replacement in a local object (thread-private by definition), then publish atomically -- readers never see a partially updated state, and the previous value is released by the collector after the atomic write is visible.
Version-control-style update: check out a local copy, mutate freely, then commit or discard; copy-and-swap maps directly to this workflow and provides the same transactional semantics (Howard Hinnant's analogy from his C++ Con 2018 talk).
Compiler tooling treats the idiom as the canonical self-assignment-safe assignment: LLVM's clang-tidy bugprone-unhandled-self-assignment checker explicitly recognizes 'build a temporary in operator=, then swap it' as correct handling and matches extended (allocator-aware) constructors plus ADL swap forms so real copy-and-swap code is not flagged (llvm/llvm-project PR #147066).
Boost's move/assignment guidance converged on the single by-value form T operator=(T b) { swap(*this, b); return *this; } as the common way to get copy-, move-, and convertible-assignment from one operator, with dedicated macros (BOOST_COPYABLE_AND_MOVABLE_ALT) for classes that adopt it instead of separate overloads.
When a strong guarantee is needed on the standard containers, libc++ maintainers advise exactly this idiom at the call site -- 'construct a new vector and swap it with the one you want to assign to' (libc++ PR #117516 discussion) -- because the library's own copy assignment deliberately offers only the basic guarantee.

name: non-throwing-swap
document:
non-throwing-swap
exception safe swap
noexcept swap
Give a value-like type an exchange operation that moves only its ownership handles - no copies, no allocation, no fallible user code - and make the no-failure guarantee explicit, so commit and rollback paths such as copy-and-swap assignment can rely on it.
The catalog trigger is "swap must never throw, so rollback paths stay safe": the generic exchange (copy into a temporary, assign both ways) runs the copy constructor, so it can throw precisely where an infallible commit is needed. Whenever an update must be all-or-nothing, the fallible work has to happen before the commit, and the commit itself must be an exchange that cannot fail; a copy-based swap cannot be that step.
Types whose representation is (or can be made) a handle to a body - pimpl/handle-body classes, copy-on-write and reference-counted containers, smart pointers, and immutable state objects published behind one reference - plus the generic code that consumes them: standard containers and algorithms (sort, rotate, permutations), copy-and-swap assignment, transactional updates and reloads. The decision is sharp where user-defined copy/move code may throw (C++); elsewhere it collapses into ordinary reference assignment, leaving the discipline "build the new state first, exchange last".
Copy assignment implemented as copy-and-swap: build a temporary copy (the only fallible step), then exchange it with *this so the old state is released by the temporary's destructor.
Handle-body / pimpl classes whose swap exchanges one implementation pointer - the classic realization and the reason the idiom exists.
Copy-on-write and reference-counted containers: the commit step replaces the shared body with a freshly built one while readers of the old body stay valid.
Shrink-to-fit and clear-by-swap: Container(container).swap(container) releases capacity without disturbing the elements' storage semantics.
Rollback of an in-progress update: stage a modified copy (or a new state object) and exchange it into place only after every step succeeded; the previous state is still intact if anything failed.
Concurrent publication of an immutable snapshot: readers take the current state and the writer exchanges one reference (atomic exchange / AtomicReference / Interlocked.Exchange / atomic.Pointer) so no reader sees a half-installed state.
Standard algorithms and containers that require swappable elements: sort, rotate, permute and unique rely on the exchange being cheap and, in their strong-guarantee overloads, non-throwing.
Qt's QSharedDataPointer provides an explicit swap() documented as a fast, noexcept exchange for implicitly shared value classes, making the shared-data handle the commit unit.
C++ std::vector::swap exchanges contents and capacity in constant time without moving or copying elements; allocator propagation and equality conditions still govern its no-throw contract.
C++ std::shared_ptr::swap exchanges stored pointers and ownership in constant time without changing reference counts during the swap, providing a concrete smart-pointer handle exchange.

name: messaging-gateway
document:
messaging-gateway
Encapsulate access to a messaging system behind an ordinary interface of domain methods, so calling application code makes method calls while a single component owns message construction, correlation, timeouts and error translation.
Application code that talks to a broker keeps importing messaging concepts: it builds the payload, picks the channel, attaches a reply address and a correlation id, parses the response and interprets broker errors. The trigger for this pattern is that callers should make a method call instead of writing messaging code - the messaging knowledge belongs in exactly one place that can change without touching business rules.
At the boundary between application logic and a messaging system (message broker, MQ, queue service or actor runtime): the other side is reached by messages, but the caller is ordinary domain code that should see typed parameters and typed results. Applies to one-way (fire and forget) and request-reply interactions alike, and to blocking as well as asynchronous call styles.
A domain service that must query another system (inventory, pricing, credit scoring) over a queue: the caller invokes checkStock(sku) and receives a typed answer.
An HTTP or API layer whose controller awaits a brokered round trip (Spring Integration gateway interface, NestJS ClientProxy, MassTransit request client).
Batch and background jobs that dispatch work through a typed job API instead of assembling payloads (ActiveJob perform_later, Celery delay).
Wrapping a legacy system's MQ interface once, so the rest of the codebase never learns its message format.
Test seams: unit tests substitute a fake gateway, integration tests run the same interface against a real broker.
Migration seam: keep the gateway contract stable while the transport moves from one broker to another.
Actor and streaming stacks where a facade wraps ask/request so callers never hold ActorRefs or inboxes.
Spring Integration's @MessagingGateway and GatewayProxyFactoryBean let application code inject a typed interface while the framework routes calls into channels and returns replies.
MassTransit's IRequestClient<T> and GetResponse<TResponse> provide a typed request-reply client over the bus, keeping request and response message contracts out of the calling service.
RabbitMQ's RPC tutorial demonstrates a gateway-like client that publishes to rpc_queue with reply_to and correlation_id, then resolves the matching callback response.

name: transaction-script
document:
transaction-script
service object
Organizes the business logic of a single request as one procedure - read the data it needs, validate and calculate, write the results and complete in one database transaction - trading object-model structure for a straight-line implementation that can be read top to bottom.
A request-scoped use case (book a room, place an order, recognize revenue, import a file) has to be implemented, and its logic mixes input validation, calculation and persistence. Modelling the domain as objects may be premature, or the team may not be ready for it, yet the implementation still needs each request's steps to stay visible and its transaction boundary to be explicit.
Applies where business logic is simple to moderately complex, where the system is naturally described as a series of transactions each driven by one request (HTTP handler, CLI command, queue message, batch job), and where a thin data-source gateway or the database itself is the persistence seam. Also the right starting point under delivery pressure or for a team new to domain modelling - provided the growth path to a Domain Model is watched deliberately.
Booking a hotel room: check availability, calculate the rate, insert the booking and confirm - one request, one transaction.
Revenue recognition (Fowler's example): given a contract and an as-of date, calculate the recognitions and persist them, or report the revenue already recognized.
CRUD write endpoints in a simple admin or back-office application where each screen maps to one operation.
Batch and integration jobs: import a file, validate rows, write the accepted rows and report the rejects in one transaction per batch.
Queue or message handlers that carry out one command (place order, cancel subscription, refund payment) and acknowledge only after commit.
Reporting and ETL steps that read a slice of data, transform it and write results, where the logic is genuinely a straight line of steps.
Django request-atomicity: with ATOMIC_REQUESTS enabled (or @transaction.atomic on the view), the whole view function is the script - Django begins the transaction at request start, commits on a successful response and rolls back on exception, exactly the one-script-one-transaction shape.
Laravel request handlers that wrap the validate-calculate-persist sequence in a DB::transaction closure: the closure commits when it returns and rolls back automatically if it throws, so the closure body is the script and its extent is the boundary.
Spring @Transactional service methods: an AOP proxy begins the transaction before the method and commits after it returns, making each annotated method a Transaction Script whose signature is the request and whose boundary is declarative.

name: revocable-forwarder
document:
revocable-forwarder
caretaker
revocable proxy
Let a collaborator use an object through a forwarding wrapper that the grantor can switch off at any time through a separate control, so authority already handed out can be withdrawn without destroying the target and without the collaborator's cooperation.
A capability is just a reference, so once a collaborator has been given access to an object there is no built-in way to take it back: the grantor can destroy the object, ask the collaborator to stop, or leave the access standing. The recurring decision is how to grant access that is bounded in time - temporary use of a file, a service object, a session, an account - while keeping a control that only the grantor holds.
Object-capability settings, and any in-process design in which authority travels as references rather than as a global identity: plugin and extension hosts lending a service object to foreign code, multi-tenant object graphs giving a worker one tenant-scoped resource, session-scoped services, and capability-based workflow or financial systems in which a grant must be provably withdrawn. It applies when the grantor keeps its own reference to the target and can intercept every call through the reference it handed out; where the runtime lets references be forged, dereferenced around the wrapper or reached by reflection, marshalling or FFI, the same structure degrades from an enforcement mechanism to a discipline.
A plugin or extension host lends a file, network or service object to foreign code and revokes it when the plugin is unloaded or breaches policy.
A multi-tenant worker receives one tenant-scoped resource for the duration of a job and loses it at job end, without the tenant object being torn down.
Session teardown in a long-lived server: the handler works through the wrapper, and logout revokes future calls before the session's resources are freed.
Capability-based workflow and financial systems that give an agent temporary authority over an account or a document and revoke it when the task completes.
Temporary elevated access for maintenance or debugging, where the requirement is to show that the extra authority has provably ended (audit evidence).
Graceful decommissioning of a shared resource: revoke new work through the wrapper, drain the calls already in flight, then release the resource.
The Scala ocaps framework's Revocable/Caretaker API returns a proxied capability plus a private Revoker, so a session, logout, timeout or supervisor can make later calls fail without changing the target.
JavaScript's standard Proxy.revocable() and the Chrome Extensions chrome.permissions API provide browser/runtime counterparts: keep the revoke/remove control private, and do not mistake the platform wrapper or permission record for protection against an already leaked target reference.
AWS IAM role-session revocation for temporary STS credentials is a distributed analogue of withdrawing a forwarded grant: policy evaluation denies subsequent requests, but propagation and credential caching mean it is not the atomic in-process check-and-forward gate described here.

name: recursive-descent-parser
document:
recursive-descent-parser
recursive descent
recursive descent parsing
Parse a small grammar by translating every rule directly into a function that consumes the tokens the rule matches and calls the functions of the rules it references, so the parser's control flow is the grammar itself and stays readable, debuggable and free of a code-generation step.
A hand-written parser is the only option - no generator in the toolchain, or the grammar is a small DSL - yet the grammar is not a flat token sequence: alternatives must be chosen from lookahead, repetition must become a loop, and the natural grammar for expressions is left-recursive, which a top-down parser cannot translate directly. Without a disciplined mapping from rules to functions the parser degenerates into ad-hoc index arithmetic and exception-driven backtracking, and errors end up without positions.
Front ends for small languages, DSLs, query/filter/rule grammars, configuration and protocol formats, and the parsing layer of compilers and interpreters that want no code-generation step. It applies when a lexer or token stream already exists (or is cheap to write), the grammar is small to medium and reasonably LL-friendly or rewritable into LL form, and the team values readable, step-debuggable, position-precise parsing over generated tables.
Front ends for small languages, DSLs and configuration formats (filter expressions, rule engines, policy languages, template syntaxes) where a generator and its build integration would be overkill.
Expression and statement parsing in single-pass compilers and interpreters that emit bytecode or IR while parsing, as in Crafting Interpreters' Lox.
Tooling for a grammar you own - formatters, linters, syntax highlighters, language servers - where error tolerance, multiple diagnostics and exact positions matter more than raw throughput.
Protocol and wire-format decoding with a small fixed grammar, where errors must carry byte offsets and malformed input must be rejected deterministically.
Context-dependent or indentation-sensitive syntaxes (templates with interpolation, layout-based blocks, configuration with embedded expressions) that a generated lexer handles poorly.
Codebases that must not carry generated code: security-reviewed, vendored or cross-compiled projects where an ordinary source file beats a build-time generator.
Clang's C-family front end uses a unified hand-built recursive-descent parser for C, C++, Objective-C and Objective-C++, pairing rule-oriented control flow with production-quality diagnostics.
The Go standard library's go/parser is a production recursive-descent parser for Go source, with explicit parser state, nesting-depth guards and error recovery.
rustc_parse is the Rust compiler's recursive-descent parser module, showing how a hand-written parser can scale to macros, recovery modes and detailed token/state handling.
Lua's reference implementation compiles with lparser.c, a single-pass recursive-descent parser that emits bytecode opcodes while reducing expressions instead of building a syntax tree, with precedence handled by parsing levels.

name: remote-facade
document:
remote-facade
coarse-grained facade
Provide a single coarse-grained facade over a web of fine-grained objects so that a remote client can complete a unit of work in one round trip, while the fine-grained objects keep their local-only interfaces and the facade stays free of domain logic.
An object model tuned for in-process use has small objects with small methods and heavy interaction. Across a process boundary every one of those interactions becomes a marshalling, security and routing event, so one user action turns into dozens of remote calls; the decision is whether, and at which seam, to replace that chatty protocol with a few coarse operations.
Applies at any distribution boundary - a network hop, a service-mesh sidecar or merely a second process on the same host - where a fine-grained object model or service layer must be made remotely usable. It matters most when the interaction pattern is chatty (many small reads and writes per use case), when the model must not be exposed to remote clients, and when the transport is expensive relative to the work being done.
Enterprise application whose rich domain model is consumed by a thick client, another service or a batch job: the service layer gets a coarse remote interface instead of exposing entities and value objects.
Microservice boundary where a use case (place an order, update a shipment) must be a single call while the fine-grained aggregates stay internal to the service.
Legacy integration: a coarse adapter facade over an old object model so that new clients never see the legacy structure and the old model can be refactored behind it.
Mobile or high-latency clients, where every avoided round trip directly improves perceived latency and battery cost.
Batch and offline clients that need bulk operations (fetch a set, submit a set) instead of per-item calls.
Security boundary: one authenticated, authorised and audited entry point in front of the model.
Salesforce Composite API and Composite Graph API: a client submits related record operations, reference IDs and explicit all-or-none/graph boundaries in one request instead of making a remote call per sObject.
Microsoft Graph JSON batching: a `$batch` request groups up to 20 Graph operations behind one HTTP boundary while dependencies and per-request failures remain visible to the caller.
gRPC services such as the official RouteGuide example: generated stubs expose typed unary or streaming RPCs as the remote contract while the server's fine-grained implementation stays local.

name: double-dispatch
document:
double-dispatch
multiple dispatch
multiple polymorphism
two-level dispatch
Select the operation to execute from the runtime types of two collaborating objects, so behaviour can vary along two independent type axes instead of being resolved by hand-written type tests in the caller.
Behaviour depends on the runtime type of *two* objects - element and visitor, shape and surface, left operand and right operand - but an ordinary call resolves on the receiver only (or, in dynamic languages, on no argument at all). Every operation then grows its own type-test ladder, knowledge of the concrete classes leaks into callers, and adding a class silently breaks the cases nobody remembered to extend.
Object models in which two type hierarchies interact: shape x medium, AST node x operation, operand x operand, entity x entity in a collision matrix. It applies when the pair-specific behaviour is a real matrix rather than a single special case, when each hierarchy evolves on its own schedule, and when the language's own dispatch resolves only one of the two runtime types (classic single-dispatch OO) or none of them (method overloading is bound statically).
Collision and interaction rules in games and simulations: every pair of entity types (bullet × wall, ship × asteroid) has its own outcome. Double dispatch cleanly selects the correct collision algorithm at runtime. Used in Unity, Unreal, and custom game engines via visitor-like hierarchies or type-indexed collision matrices. Spatial partitioning (quad-trees, oct-trees) is used alongside to reduce O(n²) pair checks. Examples: Unity physics collision callbacks, Unreal collision/overlap event system, Box2D physics engine, custom engines with AABB/Sphere/OBB hierarchies.
Geometry predicates between two shape hierarchies: intersect, contains, distance and other predicates where each pair (circle-circle, circle-rectangle, rectangle-rectangle) uses a different algorithm and pairs are not symmetric. Used in game physics engines, computer graphics rendering pipelines, and GIS systems. Examples: Box2D, Chipmunk, computer graphics rendering engines.
Numeric promotion and operator semantics between unrelated numeric types: Rational × Integer, Money × Currency, BigInt × Float — operations that must consult both operands' concrete types. Ruby's Numeric#coerce is the canonical language mechanism enabling this pattern. Examples: Ruby Numeric#coerce, Java BigDecimal arithmetic, C# decimal/float/double mixed arithmetic.
Document rendering and media output: shapes or widgets × output targets (screen, printer, PDF, HTML), where each combination emits different code. The medium axis and the shape type axis independently determine the rendering path. Examples: Qt/wxWidgets painting systems, Java AWT/Swing paint(Graphics) dispatch, WebKit/Blink layout engines.
AST traversal and transformations: one node hierarchy × many analyses (type check, pretty-print, evaluate, optimise) — the primary use case the Visitor pattern was designed for. Each (Operation × NodeType) pair is a separate handler. Examples: Babel/TypeScript compiler, LLVM compiler infrastructure, Roslyn C# compiler API.
Plugin and extension architectures: a host application defines an element hierarchy and a plugin defines a visitor; new plugins add operations without modifying element classes. Examples: Eclipse IDE plugin system, Visual Studio Analyzer/extension APIs, static analysis tools (linters, formatters).
Serialization and deserialization frameworks: Format (JSON, XML, binary, protobuf) × type — each combination may need different encoding rules. Examples: Jackson/Gson in Java, Python dataclasses serialization, Protocol Buffers schema evolution.
Protocol handling in parsers and state machines: handler depends on both message kind and connection/session kind — a state × event matrix. Used in network protocol stacks, parsers, and finite state machine implementations. Examples: HTTP server request routing, game AI state machines, telecom protocol state tables.
Event handling in GUI frameworks: a widget hierarchy × an event hierarchy (mouse, keyboard, focus) — each (Widget × Event) pair may require different handling logic. The classic AWT/Swing processEvent double-dispatch was the motivating example for several academic multi-dispatch papers. Examples: Java AWT event delegation, Qt event handling, Swing ActionMap/InputMap.
Message routing in game architectures: entity × message type routing where the correct handler depends on both the receiver entity's type and the message's payload type. Common in Entity-Component-System (ECS) patterns where components process messages differently. Examples: Unity MessageSystem, Amazon Lumberyard (component × message routing).
Numeric and array operators as native multiple dispatch: Julia makes the pair axis first-class - arithmetic and promotion operators are generic functions whose methods select on the runtime types of all arguments, and the compiler emits a specialised version per concrete combination (Int,Int vs Float64,Float64) instead of a hand-rolled accept/visit round-trip; promote_type absorbs cross-type cells. The canonical modern realisation of the pattern. Examples: Julia Base arithmetic, Julia promote_type/coercion, heterogeneous-array dispatch costs documented in the Julia performance guide.
Generic functions in CLOS and Dylan-family languages: method selection keyed by the classes or identities of every required argument, with method combination (call-next-method) resolving ambiguity - double dispatch without the intrusive accept method, and the benchmark every manual encoding is measured against. Examples: ANSI Common Lisp CLOS defgeneric/defmethod, Dylan generic functions.
Runtime binder dispatch on the CLR: the C# dynamic keyword defers overload resolution to the Dynamic Language Runtime, binding the call on the runtime types of receiver and arguments with call-site caching; CallSiteBinder.Bind is documented as runtime binding (double-dispatch). A missing pair surfaces as a runtime binder exception rather than a compile error, so it suits dynamic-language and COM interop boundaries more than closed business matrices. Examples: DLR call-site caching, IronPython/IronRuby interop, COM interop via the runtime binder.

name: composite-entity
document:
composite-entity
coarse-grained-entity
Represent a cluster of related, dependent objects through one coarse-grained entity that owns them and persists and synchronises the whole graph as a single unit of work, so clients never reference, sequence, or save the parts themselves. Coined for coarse-grained EJB business objects; its modern form is the aggregate root with cascading or owned mappings.
A business concept clients treat as one thing (an order with its lines, a customer with addresses) is really a cluster of dependent objects, and persisting each part separately forces callers to know the parts, save them in the right order in the right transaction, delete the ones that left the relationship, and absorb a leaking physical schema. The catalog trigger: a cluster of related objects must persist and synchronise as one unit.
Relational or document stores where a coarse-grained business object is composed of finer-grained dependent objects whose lifecycle is bound to it. Applies when clients - especially remote ones - should exchange one coarse-grained structure instead of the parts, when the persist/synchronise boundary must coincide with one transaction, and when each dependent can still own its own mapping. Modern form: an aggregate root mapped with cascading associations or with components stored in the root's own row.
Order with line items, shipment addresses and payment allocations that must be written and deleted as one business unit.
Customer or account aggregate holding addresses, contact methods and preferences that are edited in one form and saved once.
Document-style clusters (invoice with revisions, article with embedded sections) where the parts only exist inside the root.
Legacy-style coarse-grained entity beans that wrap fine-grained POJOs so that clients exchange one composite transfer object instead of many fine-grained ones.
Mobile or remote clients that must send one coarse-grained payload per edit instead of a sequence of dependent calls.
Batch imports where a cluster is validated and written transactionally, so a partially imported entity never exists.
DDD Bounded Contexts where one aggregate encapsulates a complete business invariant enforced across multiple related entities — e.g., a Rental aggregate containing a rental agreement, reserved vehicle, and driver assignment that must all be created or fail together.
CQRS write models where the aggregate is the sole write target and all state changes flow through the root's command methods, ensuring every mutation is a coherent cluster-level operation.
Event sourcing snapshots where the aggregate root serialises its entire graph so that snapshot restore reconstructs the full composite in one operation rather than re-playing individual dependent events.
Legacy system facades that wrap a network of fine-grained remote beans behind a single coarse-grained composite interface, collapsing many remote calls into one round-trip for external clients.
SQLAlchemy parent-child clusters mapped with cascade='all, delete-orphan' on relationship(): disassociating a child deletes the row, so the Session flushes the cluster as one unit without per-child Session.delete() calls.
EF Core owned types: dependent types stored in the owner's table (or as owned navigations) share the aggregate root's identity and save with a single context.SaveChanges().
Mongoose subdocument arrays: embedded parts are saved, validated and removed through the top-level document, so the cluster's lifecycle is bound to the root document's save.

name: cancellation-token
document:
cancellation-token
cancellation signal
cooperative cancellation
Give a caller-owned operation tree a one-way request to stop: pass a read-only cancellation signal through every cancellable call, observe it at safe points, clean up what was acquired, and report a distinct cancelled outcome without pretending that cooperative cancellation is forced termination.
A request handler, background job or UI action starts work that fans out into nested calls, tasks or threads. When the caller disconnects, a deadline expires, the user presses stop or a sibling fails, merely abandoning the result leaves already-started work burning CPU, holding connections and calling dependencies. Force-killing a thread or process can interrupt a critical section and corrupt shared state, while a signal that is not propagated or observed cannot stop the call tree or make its cleanup visible to the joiner.
Use where work can outlive the caller's interest and the runtime exposes checkpoints, suspension points or interruptible waits: request-scoped servers, workers, UI tasks, stream pipelines and batch loops. The operation owns cleanup, cancellation may race any checkpoint, and the design must state what happens when a request arrives after an irreversible side effect or while a dependency ignores the signal.
Request-scoped server work: the handler gets a request signal that fires when the client disconnects or the deadline expires, cancelling in-flight database, queue and upstream calls instead of pinning worker threads and connections after the caller is gone.
UI and mobile tasks: navigating away, closing a window or pressing stop cancels the task tree that loads, renders or downloads for that view, and only that view's tokens are affected.
Graceful shutdown: a supervisor stops accepting work and cancels the token shared by worker loops; every worker stops at its next safe point, flushes and releases resources, and the process exits inside the shutdown budget.
Fan-out with short-circuit: as soon as one subtask fails, or as soon as any one result suffices (hedged or racing replicas), the scope cancels the siblings instead of waiting for all of them.
Batch and stream pipelines: a processor subscribes to the pipeline signal and stops consuming and producing when the pipeline is torn down, abandoning the current chunk when the job's deadline elapses.
Testing and tooling: inject an already-cancelled signal, or one cancelled after N iterations, to exercise the stop path without racing an actual shutdown.
HTTP client redirect and retry cancellation: when a request is redirected or a lower-level retry budget is exhausted, cancel the in-flight operation so the client can proceed with the next action without waiting for a result that is no longer relevant.
Health-check abortion: a liveness probe times out or a readiness check fails mid-flight; cancel the in-progress health metric collection so the pod can be restarted or pulled from service without waiting for a hung check.
GRPC deadline and cancellation propagation: a server receives a client deadline and cancellation token; both must be threaded through every async operation so that an expired deadline or a client disconnect promptly frees server resources.
LLM request fan-out: multiple model providers are queried in parallel; the first successful response wins and all pending requests are cancelled immediately, avoiding wasted compute on a result that will be discarded.
Database connection pool eviction: a query timeout or client disconnect cancels the in-flight query, releasing the connection back to the pool before the server's statement timeout fires; the pool's token is derived from the request context so pool eviction and request cancellation share the same stop signal.
Container orchestrator graceful shutdown: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM and waits the terminationGracePeriodSeconds; the application maps SIGTERM to a cancellation token that is shared by all in-flight request handlers, background workers and health-check loops, giving each the termination budget to drain cleanly.
Interactive search with typeahead: each keystroke cancels the previous search task and starts a new one; the token for the previous task is cancelled immediately on the next keystroke, preventing stale results from overwriting fresher ones.
File transfer with resume support: a large upload or download uses chunked transfers; cancelling the transfer sets a flag that causes the next resume attempt to verify which chunks were already received before retransmitting from scratch.
Event streaming with backpressure: a consumer reading from a message queue or Kafka partition uses the cancellation token to stop reading when the application is shutting down or the consumer group is rebalanced, committing its offset before exiting.
Machine learning inference pipeline: a batch inference job can be cancelled when a new model version is deployed or the job's priority drops; the cancellation token is checked between batches so that partial results are preserved and the job can resume without reprocessing completed chunks.
ASP.NET Core's HttpContext.RequestAborted token is passed into HttpClient, database and other long-running operations so a client disconnect or server abort releases work that can no longer contribute to the response.
Go net/http handlers propagate Request.Context through database/sql QueryContext and RPC calls; cancelling the request context closes the subtree's Done channel so backend goroutines can stop and return their resources.
Kotlin kotlinx.coroutines Job cancellation follows structured parent-child scopes, so a screen, request or worker scope can cancel its child coroutines while finally blocks release resources and CancellationException remains distinguishable from failure.
Node.js and browser fetch cancellation: AbortController.signal is passed as { signal } to fetch, EventTarget listeners and streams, so abort() tears down the socket and pending promises; AbortSignal.timeout and AbortSignal.any combine a deadline or several triggers into one signal without polling.
Database query abortion over a side channel: PostgreSQL's frontend/backend protocol sends a CancelRequest on a separate connection carrying the backend PID and secret key, letting a client that gave up - or an administrator via pg_cancel_backend - abort a running query without killing the session.
TPL/PLINQ cancellation acknowledgement: a delegate that throws OperationCanceledException carrying the supplied CancellationToken is treated by the Task Parallel Library as a cancellation acknowledgement rather than a fault, so joiners observe a cancelled task instead of an aggregated error.

name: producer-consumer
document:
producer-consumer
bounded buffer
consumer-producer
Insert a bounded buffer between producers and consumers of work items so the two sides run concurrently at their own rates, the buffer absorbs bursts and slack, and its bound turns overload into backpressure, queueing or an explicit drop policy instead of unbounded growth.
Production and consumption proceed at different rates: a fast producer outruns its consumer and either drops items or grows a backlog until memory runs out, a slow producer leaves consumers idle, and bursts arrive faster than they can be processed. Wiring the two sides together directly also couples their lifetimes and schedules - a synchronous hand-off makes the faster side wait for the slower - so neither side can be scaled, restarted or tested on its own.
Concurrent in-process software (threads, tasks, coroutines, event-loop callbacks) with one or more producers and one or more consumers that can run at the same time but not at the same average rate. The buffer is a component-level data structure owned by the application - a work queue for a thread pool, a pipeline hand-off, a logging or telemetry sink - not a durable broker, so the decisions are how to hand items over, how to bound the queue and how to end the arrangement cleanly.
Work queues behind thread or worker pools: request handlers enqueue tasks and a fixed set of workers consumes them, so pool size is independent of the arrival rate. Industry examples: Celery (Python), Sidekiq (Ruby), BullMQ (Node.js) all use this shape with Redis or a broker as the durable backing store.
Asynchronous logging and telemetry: hot paths enqueue records cheaply while a background writer drains, formats and writes them, keeping I/O latency off the request path. Structured log collectors (Fluent Bit, Vector) ingest from many sources into one consumer.
Multi-stage data pipelines (decode - transform - encode, extract - transform - load): bounded queues between stages give each stage its own workers and let a slow stage backpressure a fast one. Used in media transcoding, ETL workflows, and stream processors.
Ingestion buffers: a socket, file or broker reader produces records faster than the processing or indexing stage can absorb them, and the buffer smooths the mismatch without dropping data. Common in IoT telemetry ingestion, click-stream collection, and log aggregation.
UI/host integration: a background thread posts work or results to the main/event-loop thread's queue and vice versa, keeping the UI responsive without locks around application state. All major GUI frameworks (Qt, Swing, Flutter) use this internally.
Batch job scheduling: producers enqueue compute jobs (image resize, PDF generation, report creation) and a pool of consumers processes them. Systems like Celery, Hangfire, and AWS SQS follow this pattern, often with priority queues, delayed execution, and dead-letter routing.
Event streaming pre-processing: a Kafka, Pulsar, or NATS consumer-producer chain filters, transforms, and routes events through a series of bounded queues before landing in a data warehouse or search index.
Simulation and testing: a producer generates a deterministic stream of items while a consumer asserts on what it receives, with a sentinel marking the end of the stream. Property-based testing frameworks use this to drive scenario generation.
Print spooling and document processing: print jobs or document conversion tasks are queued and processed by a pool of workers, with bounded queues preventing runaway memory use even under burst load.
ML inference pipelines: a model-serving host receives requests via an API, enqueues them into a bounded queue, and a pool of worker coroutines or threads dequeues and runs inference. The queue decouples HTTP latency from inference latency and provides backpressure when the model GPU is saturated. Tools like Ray Serve, Triton Inference Server, and TorchServe use this shape.
Streaming audio/video processing: a media pipeline (capture - encode - mux - stream) uses bounded queues between stages; frames that arrive during a temporary encoding stall are buffered rather than dropped, and a full encoder output queue backpressures the camera capture stage to prevent unbounded memory growth from frame accumulation.
WebSocket connection management: a server's accept loop enqueues new connections into a bounded connection queue; a pool of handler coroutines or threads dequeues and upgrades them, preventing connection exhaustion under burst load while the handler pool limits concurrency independently of the arrival rate.
Financial order processing: high-frequency trading systems receive market data feeds (producer) and route orders through risk checks and execution engines (consumers), with bounded queues between stages preventing downstream latency from backpressuring the market data ingestion and applying backpressure to upstream feed handlers.
Go channel pipelines: a source goroutine produces values into a channel, transformation stages consume and emit through downstream channels, and a sink drains the final stage. Go's documented pipeline pattern makes channel closure and cancellation part of the producer-consumer lifecycle.
Python asyncio worker queues: an asyncio.Queue(maxsize=N) accepts work from coroutine producers while worker coroutines await get(), process items and call task_done(); finite maxsize suspends producers when consumers fall behind.
Java executor work queues: java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue coordinates multiple producer threads and consumer workers, with put()/take() waiting on full and empty capacity so an Executor-style worker pool can be bounded independently of arrival rate.

name: implicit-lock
document:
implicit-lock
framework-managed locking
automatic locking
Make the framework or layer-supertype code that every business operation must pass through acquire and release the locks, so no application method can forget an acquisition and silently invalidate the concurrency policy.
A locking scheme has no gaps only if every path that touches a lockable item acquires its lock: one forgotten acquisition, one lock released too early or too late, makes the whole offline concurrency strategy useless. Because the error shows up only under concurrent conflicting sessions, it survives unit tests, code review and single-user manual testing.
Multi-user enterprise applications whose business transactions outlive a single database transaction - a user reads a record, thinks for minutes, then saves - so locks live in a lock table or in version columns rather than in the database transaction. Typically a Unit of Work, a layer supertype, a session facade or a declarative transaction layer already exists, giving the application a place that can own the locking protocol centrally.
Request-as-business-transaction: a web application where an ORM Unit of Work or declarative transaction (Spring @Transactional, .NET TransactionScope, Django ATOMIC_REQUESTS) acquires the row locks or version checks for every record the request reads and writes.
Offline edit sessions: a user edits a record for minutes, and the session facade or layer supertype acquires a pessimistic lock when the record enters the business transaction and releases it on commit or abort, so no controller can forget it.
Batch and import jobs that modify aggregates: each chunk runs inside the framework's transactional scope, so locking follows the changed aggregates automatically.
In-process shared state in a service or worker: a scope construct (RAII guard, with block, defer, using declaration, withLock closure) binds release to the lexical block so exceptions and early returns cannot leak the lock.
Multi-tier clients with a session facade: the lock must follow the business transaction rather than the HTTP request, so the facade — not the UI — owns acquisition and release.
Optimistic concurrency: the mapper compares and increments the version column inside the framework's update path, so a hand-written UPDATE statement cannot skip the check.
Microservices saga orchestrator: the orchestrator drives each step inside an implicit transaction scope; each participant's framework layer acquires the lock or version check locally so the saga can compensate without distributed deadlocks.
Event-sourcing projections: a projection handler reads an event stream and writes to a read-model; the handler runs inside an implicit transaction so concurrent projection rebuilds do not corrupt the read-model — the framework decides whether to use optimistic or pessimistic locking based on the change set.
CQRS read-model updates: commands update the write model under an implicit write lock; the read-model update is published as an async event; the projection runs under its own implicit scope with conflict detection (optimistic) rather than blocking (pessimistic).
Database advisory locks for cross-connection coordination: an application holds a PostgreSQL advisory lock across a multi-statement business transaction that is not itself a DB transaction (e.g., involves an external HTTP call in the middle); the lock is acquired via a thin wrapper so callers do not call pg_advisory_lock directly.
Container-managed persistence (EJB CMT, Spring @Transactional): the container acquires and releases locks as part of the transaction lifecycle; developers write business methods without explicit lock calls, relying on the container's implicit concurrency control.
Retry and compensation with implicit lock release: when a business transaction fails after the lock is acquired but before commit, the framework's rollback path releases the lock automatically so the compensating transaction can retry without manual unlock calls.
Spring Framework proxy-managed services: a proxied @Transactional service method is the business entry point; Spring starts or joins the transaction for external calls, so persistence work and its configured optimistic or pessimistic checks stay inside one framework-owned boundary.
Hibernate ORM persistence contexts: an EntityManager or Session transaction can apply @Version optimistic checks or an explicit PESSIMISTIC_WRITE LockMode at the framework boundary, keeping lock acquisition and stale-version detection out of business methods.
EF Core Unit of Work: SaveChanges compares configured concurrency tokens, including SQL Server rowversion, and raises DbUpdateConcurrencyException on a stale update, making the version check implicit in the framework's commit path rather than a hand-written UPDATE predicate.

humble-object
humble dialog box
Move as much logic as possible out of a program element that the framework calls but tests cannot instantiate - a UI control, callback, entry point or active object - into a plain collaborator that unit tests drive synchronously, leaving the original element as a thin adapter without decisions.
The element the host invokes cannot be exercised in a test: constructing it needs the framework's environment (event loop, window, container, thread), so driving it means slow asynchronous tests with framework setup, or none at all. Because the decisions were written where the trigger arrives, business rules live inside the untestable element: they are verified only by expensive end-to-end runs, they cannot be test-first, and every framework upgrade threatens them.
Applies when an element is hard to test for environmental reasons rather than intrinsic ones: framework callbacks (widgets, dialogs, request handlers, message listeners), entry points (main, server bootstrap) and active objects (threads, processes, timer and interrupt handlers), plus container-managed components whose interfaces the server demands. The logic must be expressible as a computation over data, and the host must keep invoking the element through a stable callback or entry point.
A dialog or screen whose enablement, validation and navigation rules are hard to exercise: extract a presenter or view model, leave the widget showing fields and forwarding events (the Humble Dialog form).
Framework callbacks that mutate business state - HTTP handlers, message listeners, timer or interrupt callbacks - where a thin adapter reads the input and a service decides.
Active objects and executables: a thread or process whose per-request processing is extracted so tests run synchronously instead of sleeping and coordinating (the Humble Executable form).
Transaction boundaries: extract the business logic out of the transaction controller so a test can run the logic and roll the transaction back, leaving only commit/rollback behaviour in the controller (the Humble Transaction Controller form).
Container-managed components: implement the server's interface in a thin adapter and keep the logic in a container-independent class, so the edit-compile-test cycle stays fast (the Humble Container Adapter form).
Legacy code with an overridable or exposed dependency call but no injection point: expose or extract the method first (the Poor Man's form) and only then attempt a test harness.
Entry points: parse arguments, wire dependencies and map the exit code in main, and put the program's decisions in a library function that tests call.
Android Activities/Fragments and Unity MonoBehaviours: extract lifecycle-driven logic into a plain class, leaving the framework component as a thin shell that forwards lifecycle events — enables unit tests without an emulator or device.
React class components and Angular controllers: move state and business logic out of the component into a hook or service, keeping the component as a declarative renderer that delegates all decisions.
Embedded systems interrupt handlers: extract per-interrupt processing into a synchronous function tested with deterministic inputs; the ISR remains a thin vector that disables interrupts and calls the extracted logic.
Database transaction scripts: separate the SQL/transaction orchestration (humble controller) from the business logic (collaborator), so the logic is tested with a connection spy and the wiring is verified by a small number of integration tests.
Event-driven microservices: keep the event-listener adapter minimal (deserialize, delegate) and place all routing and business logic in a synchronous service that tests can drive directly with domain objects.
CLI entry points: extract argument parsing and environment setup from the main method into a plain runner class; the collaborator is tested with fake argv, and the shell only handles OS-level concerns.
Android Jetpack (AndroidX) ViewModel: Google's architecture guidance makes the ViewModel the testable collaborator - it MUST NOT reference Activity, Fragment, View or Context - so screen logic is unit-tested on the JVM with fakes, while the Activity/Fragment stays a humble shell exercised only by instrumentation tests.
WPF / .NET MVVM: Microsoft's guidance prescribes views with empty code-behind - controls bind to ViewModel properties and ICommand implementations (e.g. DelegateCommand) - so enablement, validation and action logic (CanExecute/Execute) are plain classes unit-tested without a window, and XAML binding is covered by a few integration checks.
Unity MonoBehaviour game code: teams extract game rules into plain C# classes unit-tested outside the engine's Play Mode, leaving the MonoBehaviour as a serialized-field shell that forwards Update/FixedUpdate - the Unity community reports this buys fast unit tests at the cost of harder in-engine integration tests, so the shell needs deliberate coverage.

name: authentication-enforcer
document:
authentication-enforcer
authentication interceptor
authentication gateway
auth middleware
Put one request-boundary checkpoint in front of protected actions that decides whether authentication is required, delegates credential verification to a replaceable mechanism, and attaches the resulting subject to request-scoped context before dispatch, so coverage is uniform without making handlers understand credentials.
When each handler decides whether and how to authenticate, protection is duplicated or omitted on exceptional paths, credential formats and user stores leak into business code, and a mechanism or policy change requires editing every handler instead of one auditable boundary.
Server-side request processing — web APIs, web applications and service endpoints — where many handlers share one protection policy, credentials arrive through a uniform convention (Authorization header, cookie, session id), verification technology must be replaceable or differ per route, and the runtime provides a request-pipeline hook (servlet filter, middleware chain, framework guard). Applies to session-based and token-based authentication alike; permissions and roles are out of scope. Three implementation strategies exist: (1) Container-Managed Authentication — the runtime container owns the checkpoint and realm configuration; (2) Authentication Provider Strategy — a custom provider behind a narrow interface, swapped without touching handlers; (3) JAAS Login Module Strategy — pluggable via standard JAAS configuration, supporting multifactor authentication via smart cards, biometrics, or third-party IdPs. The pattern is equally applicable at the edge level (API gateway, ingress proxy) and the service level (in-process middleware).
Web APIs where every route except health and login requires a bearer token, and the checkpoint is mounted in front of the whole router.
Multi-tenant applications with mixed protection levels: public marketing pages, session-protected tenant UI and token-protected integration endpoints behind one enforcement layer.
Services that must accept several credential types at once — browser sessions, mobile JWTs, mutual TLS for service-to-service traffic — while keeping one uniform enforcement point.
Credential-technology migration (basic auth to OIDC, on-premises LDAP to SSO) where enforcement stays put while the mechanism behind it is swapped.
Regulated environments where every rejected authentication attempt has to be logged centrally and identically across all endpoints.
Legacy applications with authentication checks scattered through servlets or handlers that must be consolidated behind one intercepting layer before an audit.
Zero Trust microservices where every internal service verifies JWTs independently (per-service verification) while an ingress gateway provides the first checkpoint — the enforcer exists at both layers.
OIDC/OAuth2 migration where an existing session-based app adds bearer-token support; the mechanism adapts to both while the enforcement point remains unchanged.
Multi-tenant SaaS platforms where tenant isolation depends on the enforcer resolving a tenant identifier from the token before the handler processes any data.
Platform-as-a-Service with mounted sub-applications where a parent ASGI middleware dispatches per-path authentication requirements from a config registry, injecting identity into ASGI scope for all sub-apps.
Spring Security servlet applications that use a SecurityFilterChain with anyRequest().authenticated() and an AuthenticationManager/AuthenticationProvider chain, so controllers consume the SecurityContext rather than parse credentials.
ASP.NET Core APIs that register JWT or cookie schemes, call UseAuthentication before dependent middleware, and use a fallback authorization policy to make authenticated access the default.
An nginx ingress location using auth_request to delegate identity verification to a central authentication service, forwarding only after a 2xx result and propagating 401/403 failures while services still verify their own trust boundary.
