name: thread-safe-copy-on-write
document:
thread-safe-copy-on-write
Share one body between many threads so that copying a value stays cheap and reading it never blocks, and protect the sharing state itself - the reference count or the published pointer - so that a writer clones the body and swaps in a new snapshot instead of mutating storage other threads can see.
A value is copied often and mutated rarely, so the copies should share storage until one of them diverges. That decision works single-threaded, but the moment several threads hold the value the sharing state becomes shared mutable state in its own right: a reference count incremented without atomics loses updates or frees a body another thread is still reading, a plain pointer dereferenced while another thread replaces it is a data race, and a 'copy' that still aliases its source turns a reader's snapshot into a moving target. The trigger is a read-mostly shared value - configuration, routing table, registry, cache snapshot - that must be read without locking and updated by cloning.
Applies where one object, or one immutable snapshot of an aggregate, is read by many threads and written rarely: configuration reloads, registries and symbol tables, caches with rare invalidation, listener registries, and large immutable values handed between threads. Manual memory management, non-atomic reference counts or a separate publication step make the problem sharpest (C, C++, hand-rolled counting); garbage-collected languages apply the same structure with the published reference replacing the count. It is an object/value-level data-sharing decision, not a lock strategy for write-heavy state.
Read-mostly configuration or routing tables that are reloaded occasionally and read on every request by every worker thread.
Registries, symbol tables and interning tables built once and consulted constantly, with rare additions or invalidations.
Caches and memo tables where invalidation is rare and readers must never wait behind a writer.
Listener and observer registries traversed on every event and modified rarely - the classic CopyOnWriteArrayList use.
Large immutable values - strings, byte buffers, message payloads, compiled artefacts - handed between threads, where a deep copy at each hand-off would dominate.
Language runtimes, interpreters and plugin hosts that keep configuration or environment objects read by many threads and updated by a single owner.
The Linux kernel's RCU (read-copy-update) mechanism in its purest form: readers enter an rcu_read_lock() critical section with no lock, atomic or shared-memory write, updaters publish a replacement with rcu_assign_pointer(), and the superseded body is freed only after a grace period proves no reader can still hold it - the dentry cache, routing tables and network-device lists.
Rust's std::sync::Arc as the atomically counted body of the standard library: cloning an Arc increments the count, and Arc::make_mut detaches - cloning the inner value only when other Arc handles exist - so the sharing state is protected by the type rather than by convention.
Go services publishing an immutable configuration or routing snapshot through sync/atomic's atomic.Pointer[T]: readers Load it once per request without locking, writers build a fresh snapshot under a writer lock and Store or Swap the pointer, and the collector reclaims each superseded snapshot when no reader references it.

statement: Choose one component that owns validation and promotion of the entire staged shipment batch as a set operation rather than distributing the rules across request procedures or row-level behaviors.
name: watchman
document:
watchman
dead man's switch
heartbeat monitor
Detect that a message flow has gone silent - not that a message failed - and tell a responsible person or system within a bounded time by comparing each flow's arrivals against the cadence its business deadline implies.
Message systems fail silently in the one way no error handler observes: nothing arrives. A producer stops emitting, a consumer stops draining, a scheduled job never fires, a credential expires, a partition goes offline - and because no failing code path is ever entered, error dashboards stay green while downstream data quietly goes stale. The recurring trigger: a flow whose absence is business-visible (a nightly feed, an order stream, a partner interface) has no owner-facing signal for 'no messages', so the gap is discovered late - by a customer or a downstream job - instead of by the team that can fix it.
Applies wherever messages are expected on a knowable cadence (event streams, queues, batch hand-offs, partner interfaces, device check-ins) and their absence is a business-visible failure: the flow has an owner, the expected period and grace window can be derived from a downstream deadline, and either the transport can be observed passively (queue counters, a wire tap) or the producers can emit out-of-band heartbeats. The watchman sits at message-flow or boundary scope - an in-process watcher beside the consumer, a periodic sweep over persisted last-seen state, or a rule in the monitoring stack fed by metrics - and it must itself be watched, because a silent watchman is exactly the failure it exists to catch.
Nightly batch or ETL feed: page the integration owner when the 02:00 import has produced no messages by its deadline, instead of noticing an empty report at the morning stand-up.
Business-critical event stream (orders, payments, telemetry): alarm when the produce rate stays at zero through business hours, which separates a healthy quiet topic from a stopped producer.
External partner interface: notify when no messages have arrived from a B2B partner within the agreed window, turning a looming SLA breach into an early, actionable alert.
Long-running workflow stage: require a heartbeat from each process-manager step so a stuck instance is noticed before the surrounding batch closes or a compensation becomes necessary.
Retry or dead-letter pump: verify that the pump still drains failed messages - silence means the pump died, not that the backlog is empty.
Fleet check-ins (edge devices, agents, cron jobs on many hosts): raise a per-device or per-site alarm when scheduled check-ins stop arriving.
The alerting pipeline itself: an always-firing watchdog alert routed to an external service, so a broken alert path is discovered by its silence.
Cron and scheduled-job fleet via Healthchecks.io: each job pings a unique URL, the service holds the Period and Grace Time, flips the check Late then Down when no ping arrives by period + grace, and notifies integrations.
Dashboard alert rules in Grafana: an alert rule whose query returns no series enters the No Data state and can raise a DatasourceNoData alert - the platform form of deciding what silence means (No Data, Alerting, Normal or Keep last state).
Apache Burrow for Kafka (LinkedIn): committed offsets are evaluated per partition over a sliding window and a consumer is classified STALLED when its offset is frozen with non-zero lag, or STOPPED when no new commits arrive - consumer-silence detection without fixed lag thresholds.

statement: Choose one component that owns validation and promotion of the entire staged shipment batch as a set operation rather than distributing the rules across request procedures or row-level behaviors.
name: update-method
document:
update-method
per-frame update
tick method
Give every live object one self-contained per-frame step and let a single driver call each object's step every frame, so behaviour advances one frame at a time while input and rendering stay responsive.
A running world is full of objects that each have to keep doing their own thing - guards patrolling, statues charging, agents acting - and the recurring decision is where one object's per-frame behaviour lives and how all those behaviours get driven. Coding a behaviour as a loop that runs to completion blocks input and rendering (the skeleton walks, but nobody sees it); coding it inline in the game loop turns the loop into a switchboard over every kind of object, so every new behaviour edits central code; and there is no way for two actors to evolve independently and simultaneously.
Real-time software with many concurrent live objects whose behaviour is mostly independent and must be simulated over time: games, agent-based simulations, animation and particle systems, tick-based servers and live visualisations. It is the natural partner of a frame driver (Game Loop) - the loop supplies the cadence, Update Method supplies the per-object step - and it becomes the wrong shape in turn-based or purely event-driven domains where nothing changes between inputs.
Real-time games and simulations with many concurrent actors: patrolling guards, projectiles, particle effects and crowd agents each advance themselves once per frame while the driver walks the collection.
Component-based engines where the parts of one entity evolve independently - rendering, physics and AI components each implement their own step and the engine's registry dispatches per component (Unity, MonoGame, Bevy, GameplayKit, libGDX).
Per-frame animation and effect timelines outside games: tween/spring systems, sprite animation and UI transitions advanced from the browser's frame callback or a UI toolkit's animation timer.
Tick-based servers and headless simulations: game servers, digital twins and agent-based models where each agent's behaviour is a resumable step and the world advances in whole discrete frames.
Tools, editors and dashboards with continuously animating scenes, where many independent scene items (markers, live charts, gizmos) must advance on every repaint without a central per-item switch.
Porting straight-line behaviour into a frame loop: turning a scripted sequence (walk left, walk right) into a per-frame step, either by storing explicit state or by using coroutines/generators to keep the code linear.
Godot's SceneTree is the driver: a node opts into the walk with set_process(true) and its _process(delta) runs every render frame with the frame time passed in as an argument, while _physics_process(delta) is called at a fixed rate - so one object can implement two steps on two clocks and can leave the walk entirely (set_process(false)) instead of paying an enabled-flag check every frame.
Engines whose built-in driver leaves per-object order unspecified expose the order as configuration: Unity states you should not rely on the order of Update across GameObjects, so real projects fix dependencies through the Script Execution Order panel, a LateUpdate pass that runs after every Update, or the PlayerLoop API rather than through registration order.
Agent-based simulation models step whole populations in NetLogo: the go procedure runs ask turtles [ ... ] to give every agent its one turn and then tick advances the discrete clock - with documented semantics that agents take their turns in random order and only agents present when the ask began get to act.

statement: Choose one component that owns validation and promotion of the entire staged shipment batch as a set operation rather than distributing the rules across request procedures or row-level behaviors.
name: extensible-visitor
document:
extensible-visitor
extensible visitor pattern
extensible visitors with defaults
Keep the visitor open on both axes at once - new element kinds and new operations arrive without editing or recompiling any visitor that already exists - by giving every visitor a default method that catches element kinds it was not written for, introducing extended element kinds under an intermediate base whose accept hooks overload (not override) accept, and extending an operation by subclassing the existing concrete visitor so it inherits every case it already handled.
A classic Visitor is cheap in one direction only: a new operation is a new visitor, but a new element kind forces every visitor to grow one more method, so shipped visitors must be edited and redeployed. The trigger is an element hierarchy that is extended by parties who do not own the operations - language dialects, plugin node types, versioned grammars, third-party message formats - where the existing operations must keep working unchanged on the extended structure.
Recursively defined element hierarchies (abstract syntax trees, intermediate representations, document and message models) that grow over time, in a statically typed language whose visitors are concrete classes or interfaces with default bodies, and where the traversal logic itself lives inside the operations. It pays off when old operations must run against new element kinds and when element kinds are added by a different team than the operations; it assumes the visitor protocol can carry a default case and that a runtime type test is acceptable on the dispatch path.
A compiler front-end whose node kinds are extended by language dialects while every existing analysis pass keeps running unchanged (the extensible-compiler case the pattern was derived from).
An IDE or linter analysing a versioned language grammar: the version-1 analysis must not be recompiled when version 2 adds syntax nodes it does not understand.
Plugin systems where third-party modules contribute new node types (document formats, workflow elements, protocol messages) to a host that ships the operations.
Optimisation or lowering pipelines whose passes are shipped separately from the node hierarchy: the platform team adds representations, users add passes.
A published visitor API where other teams implement visitors and the element set grows every release, making 'which kinds does this visitor handle' an explicit, versioned contract.
Migration and validation tooling that must keep working on messages produced by newer producers than the tool itself.
Serialization and schema-generation frameworks such as Jackson's JsonFormatVisitor API, which uses a visitor to traverse Java type hierarchies for JSON/XML schema generation and allows third-party serializers to contribute handlers for new POJO shapes without modifying the core framework.
Query engines over tree-structured data (e.g. Apache Calcite's relational algebra, Rascal's AST analysis): new relational operators or AST node types are contributed by extension modules while existing optimisers and evaluators continue to function unchanged.
Static analysis and bug-finding tools (Coverity, CodeQL, ESLint plugin architectures): new checker plugins add new node-type coverage while the core traversal engine ships unchanged, and old checkers degrade gracefully over unknown node types.
Game engine entity-component systems: new component types are contributed at runtime while existing systems (physics, rendering, AI) continue to process entities; the visitor with default case handles component types added after a given system was written.
Python's ast.NodeVisitor: visit() dispatches to a visit_<Node> method and falls back to generic_visit as the built-in default case, so analysis tools written before newer node kinds existed (Match, TryStar, TypeAlias) keep traversing Python's evolving AST unchanged, exactly the degrade-don't-break contract of the pattern.
The JDK Compiler Tree API (com.sun.source.tree.TreeVisitor / SimpleTreeVisitor): every visit method defaults to visitOther/defaultAction as the catch-all, so javac-based tooling written against Java 8 trees keeps compiling and running as Java adds records, patterns and switch labels - old visitors land in visitOther instead of failing.
Roslyn's CSharpSyntaxVisitor / CSharpSyntaxWalker: the generated visitor carries one Visit method per syntax node kind plus DefaultVisit as the default case, and each C# language version extends the node hierarchy while existing analysers and the compiler's own passes keep working over the extended tree.

name: pattern-matching
document:
pattern-matching
structural pattern matching
case analysis
Eliminate a value drawn from a closed set of variants by matching its structure and binding the payload, so the compiler proves that every variant is handled before the program runs.
Code that inspects which variant of a tagged value it received - a result type, a domain event, an AST node, a protocol frame, a state - drifts into chains of type tests, casts and accessor calls, and nothing guarantees that a variant added later is handled: the missing branch is found in production rather than by the compiler.
Applies when a value's type is a closed sum - an enum with payloads, a sealed hierarchy, a discriminated union, a tagged union - and behaviour depends on which variant arrived. It needs a match construct (language syntax, a variant type with visitation, or a type-level bottom-type check) plus a compiler or checker able to see the set as closed: same-unit sealing, private constructors, or explicit non_exhaustive / @unknown markers where a set is published to other teams.
Interpreter and compiler front ends: expression and statement types are evaluated with one total match per operation, and a new node kind cannot be forgotten.
Protocol and RPC dispatch: a frame or command is one of a fixed set of shapes, and each shape is deconstructed into its fields instead of being cast.
Result and error mapping at boundaries: translating domain failures into transport errors, where every failure variant must be given a mapping.
State machines and workflow states: states carry state-specific data, and transitions are written as a total match over (state, event) pairs.
Domain-event handling in reducers and event-sourced aggregates, where every event type must be applied to rebuild state.
Command-line and query parsing: token or request shapes are matched structurally, including literals and sequence patterns, before validation logic runs.
OpenJDK Java 21 sealed hierarchies: pattern switches over AST or domain-event variants can enumerate permitted types without a default, using the compiler's exhaustiveness analysis.
rustc and Rust enum APIs: match expressions destructure enum variants and the compiler rejects non-exhaustive arms, making protocol and compiler AST dispatch explicit.
CPython 3.10+ match/case: parsers and protocol adapters can select class, sequence, mapping and literal shapes with ordered guards before constructing domain values.
Scala 3 sealed ADTs and union types: the Scala compiler checks exhaustiveness while case-class patterns bind payloads for interpreters, reducers and protocol decoders.

statement: Choose a node representation and evaluation structure that binds case-specific fields and makes omissions of a supported expression kind a compile-time error.
name: algebraic-data-type
document:
algebraic-data-type
adt
sum type
product type
discriminated union
tagged union
Model a closed sum of product-shaped alternatives: each value is exactly one constructor or case, and each case carries only its own fields, so legal states are explicit and eliminators can be checked exhaustively.
Code often encodes mutually exclusive shapes as a tag beside optional or nullable fields, or as an open hierarchy. That representation admits tag/payload mismatches, forces callers to rediscover legal combinations, and lets a newly added case fall through silently; a sum-of-products type ties each case to its product payload and lets matchers be checked.
Applies where the variant set is known and small enough to close: domain values and state machines, ASTs and protocol payloads, command/message bodies, parser and interpreter results. It is most effective in languages with value semantics and pattern matching, where the compiler also proves match coverage; in languages without a closed-set type the same design is an emulation whose closure is enforced by convention, a linter or a type checker rather than by the language.
Domain state machines: an order is Draft, Placed, Shipped or Cancelled, and only Placed carries a payment reference and shipping address.
ASTs and interpreters: expression or statement nodes, or a parser result (Tree | Leaf | Error) consumed by recursive functions.
Command and message payloads: one discriminated command type routed by its tag, with one payload per command, serialised as tagged JSON.
Result and error modelling: success or failure with distinct payloads instead of exceptions or nullable fields (Option/Result/Either).
Protocols and event bodies that share a header but differ in content, where the tag selects the decoder.
UI and screen state: Loading | Ready(data) | Failed(error), so a screen can never be loading and failed at the same time.
Banking and financial workflows: modelling transaction lifecycle states (Pending, Settled, Failed, Reversed) with typed failure reasons per state, eliminating boolean explosion that allows 59 invalid combinations.
Multi-step business flows with typed error outcomes: login, order processing, or onboarding flows where each step can fail with a distinct domain error, and the flow short-circuits on the first failure.
Event sourcing: domain event unions where each event type carries only the fields relevant to that event, with a shared discriminant (type field) for routing handlers.
Parser and validator results: Success(value) | ValidationError(errors[]) | ServerError(details) with exhaustive handlers for each failure category.
Rust compiler (rustc) AST and MIR: compiler passes match enum variants carrying node-specific fields, so adding an IR case surfaces every stale pass.
TypeScript compiler API: SyntaxKind-discriminated AST nodes route transforms and printers, with runtime validation kept at parser boundaries because the union is erased.

statement: Choose a node representation and evaluation structure that binds case-specific fields and makes omissions of a supported expression kind a compile-time error.
name: sealed-case-class
document:
sealed-case-class
sealed class
case class
sealed trait
discriminated union
Fix the alternative shapes of a domain value in the type system: a sealed base type declares the complete, closed set of cases and one immutable data type carries each case's own fields, so invalid combinations cannot be built and every case analysis can be checked for completeness.
A domain value really comes in a small, fixed set of shapes - a payment is a card payment or a bank transfer, a request is pending, served or failed - but the code models it as an open class hierarchy with nullable fields, a tag plus a generic payload struct, or a bare enum with side tables. Nothing states that the set is complete, so a forgotten alternative surfaces as a runtime failure (a null dereference, an unhandled switch arm, a MatchError), and a new case silently changes behaviour instead of breaking the build. The pattern is the decision to close the variant set (`sealed`) and give every case its own immutable data type (`case class`).
Data-centric domain modelling where the alternatives are decided by the domain rather than by third-party extension: result and status types, domain events and commands, small state machines, ASTs, and payloads exchanged inside one service. It presupposes a declaration the compiler or an external checker can see in full (sealed/permits/enum/union alias) and a team that accepts the closure contract: adding a case becomes a deliberate, compiler-guided, source-breaking edit that must never cross a published extension boundary without an explicit unknown / `non_exhaustive` escape.
Outcome types such as `Ok`/`Err`, `Loading`/`Loaded`/`Failed` or `Parsed`/`Rejected` shared across a domain layer or driving UI state.
Domain events and commands with a vocabulary that is fixed for one bounded context (`PaymentCaptured`, `PaymentRefunded`, `PaymentDisputed`), where each event carries different fields.
Recursive structures - expression trees, document models, protocol frames - with one case per node kind eliminated by a single recursive match (using `indirect`/`Box`/sealed cases for the recursive case).
Payment instruments, shipping options or similar models where each alternative has its own fields and a nullable-field struct would permit nonsense combinations.
Option-like types (`Present[T]`/`Absent`, `Some`/`None`) that the compiler forces every consumer to handle.
State machines whose states carry their own data (connecting, open with a session, closing with a reason), so transitions become matches over closed sets.
Jetpack Compose's Android offline-first architecture models `AuthorUiState` as a sealed interface with `Loading`, `Success` and `Error`, so a UI can render every repository outcome explicitly.
The JDK's `java.lang.constant.ConstantDesc` sealed interface closes the family of nominal constant descriptors (`ClassDesc`, `MethodHandleDesc`, `MethodTypeDesc` and constant wrappers) used by bytecode tooling.
Rust's compiler AST (`rustc_ast::ast`) uses enums such as `ItemKind` and `VariantData` to represent syntax alternatives, keeping parser and compiler matches explicit.
Scala 3's `Option` ADT (`Some`/`None`) demonstrates the same closed, parameterized-versus-singleton case split using enum syntax.
Swift's standard library `Result` enum fixes the outcome vocabulary at exactly two cases, `.success(Success)` and `.failure(Failure)`, each with its own associated value, so every consumer `switch` must handle both arms.
Akka Typed persistent actors model an event-sourced entity's `Command`, `Event` and `State` as sealed traits with concrete case classes (`Add`/`Added`, `Clear`/`Cleared`, `EmptyAccount`/`OpenedAccount`/`ClosedAccount`), so command and event handlers are total matches over the persisted vocabulary.

statement: Choose a node representation and evaluation structure that binds case-specific fields and makes omissions of a supported expression kind a compile-time error.
name: make-illegal-states-unrepresentable
document:
make-illegal-states-unrepresentable
make invalid states unrepresentable
Encode each domain rule in the shape of the data type so that values violating the rule cannot be constructed at all, replacing scattered run-time validation and defensive checks with a model in which only legal states exist.
Domain values are modelled as one record with independent fields - a status tag plus several nullable or optional attributes, or a handful of booleans - so the type admits every combination of those fields, including the ones the business rules forbid. Consumers cannot trust the type: each branch re-checks which fields are meaningful, the same guard is written in several places (and forgotten in one), and illegal states become runtime bugs that surface when a code path finally combines the wrong flags.
Applies when a value has a small, known set of mutually exclusive shapes whose payloads differ, when the same invalid combination keeps being defended against in several places, and when the language can close a set of variants (Rust/Swift enums, sealed hierarchies, discriminated unions) or at least hide constructors. It is equally a boundary discipline: untrusted input is parsed once into a type whose existence already proves it is valid, so no downstream code has to re-validate.
Lifecycle and state machines: orders, payments, subscriptions, bookings and connection states, one variant per state carrying exactly the data that exists in that state.
Client and API request state: a loading/success/error union instead of a data field, an error field and an isLoading flag that can contradict one another.
Message and protocol modelling: a closed set of commands, events or JSON payload shapes decoded once and dispatched with an exhaustive match (event sourcing, interpreters, RPC handlers).
Refined scalars that travel through the model: money with currency, email addresses, quantities with units and identifiers that are parsed once and never re-validated.
Configuration whose combinations are illegal: TLS settings that only apply when TLS is enabled, cursor-based versus offset pagination, mutually exclusive feature flags.
Import and deserialization boundaries: convert untrusted rows, CSV cells, query parameters or JSON into domain types with a failing factory, so invalid input cannot travel further.
Rust's standard `Option`/`Result` enums and exhaustive `match` make presence, absence, success and failure explicit cases that downstream code must handle at compile time (Rust Reference/Book).
Swift enums with associated values and exhaustive `switch` model state-specific payloads such as error cases without nullable companion fields (The Swift Programming Language).
Kotlin sealed classes and interfaces with exhaustive `when` expressions provide a closed hierarchy for finite state machines and error/result models, with the compiler checking that every known case is handled.

name: thread-safe-copy-on-write
document:
thread-safe-copy-on-write
Share one body between many threads so that copying a value stays cheap and reading it never blocks, and protect the sharing state itself - the reference count or the published pointer - so that a writer clones the body and swaps in a new snapshot instead of mutating storage other threads can see.
A value is copied often and mutated rarely, so the copies should share storage until one of them diverges. That decision works single-threaded, but the moment several threads hold the value the sharing state becomes shared mutable state in its own right: a reference count incremented without atomics loses updates or frees a body another thread is still reading, a plain pointer dereferenced while another thread replaces it is a data race, and a 'copy' that still aliases its source turns a reader's snapshot into a moving target. The trigger is a read-mostly shared value - configuration, routing table, registry, cache snapshot - that must be read without locking and updated by cloning.
Applies where one object, or one immutable snapshot of an aggregate, is read by many threads and written rarely: configuration reloads, registries and symbol tables, caches with rare invalidation, listener registries, and large immutable values handed between threads. Manual memory management, non-atomic reference counts or a separate publication step make the problem sharpest (C, C++, hand-rolled counting); garbage-collected languages apply the same structure with the published reference replacing the count. It is an object/value-level data-sharing decision, not a lock strategy for write-heavy state.
Read-mostly configuration or routing tables that are reloaded occasionally and read on every request by every worker thread.
Registries, symbol tables and interning tables built once and consulted constantly, with rare additions or invalidations.
Caches and memo tables where invalidation is rare and readers must never wait behind a writer.
Listener and observer registries traversed on every event and modified rarely - the classic CopyOnWriteArrayList use.
Large immutable values - strings, byte buffers, message payloads, compiled artefacts - handed between threads, where a deep copy at each hand-off would dominate.
Language runtimes, interpreters and plugin hosts that keep configuration or environment objects read by many threads and updated by a single owner.
The Linux kernel's RCU (read-copy-update) mechanism in its purest form: readers enter an rcu_read_lock() critical section with no lock, atomic or shared-memory write, updaters publish a replacement with rcu_assign_pointer(), and the superseded body is freed only after a grace period proves no reader can still hold it - the dentry cache, routing tables and network-device lists.
Rust's std::sync::Arc as the atomically counted body of the standard library: cloning an Arc increments the count, and Arc::make_mut detaches - cloning the inner value only when other Arc handles exist - so the sharing state is protected by the type rather than by convention.
Go services publishing an immutable configuration or routing snapshot through sync/atomic's atomic.Pointer[T]: readers Load it once per request without locking, writers build a fresh snapshot under a writer lock and Store or Swap the pointer, and the collector reclaims each superseded snapshot when no reader references it.

name: deadline-propagation
document:
deadline-propagation
timeout propagation
Bound the total time and work of a logical request by carrying one deadline through its whole call tree: every hop forwards the remaining budget and the cancellation signal instead of inventing a fresh timeout, so work that can no longer succeed is abandoned at every level.
A request fans out into a chain or tree of downstream calls and each hop applies its own timeout: the end-to-end latency budget becomes the sum of N independent timeouts, servers keep working after the originating client has given up, and cancellation never reaches the deeper work - resources are consumed producing answers nobody will read.
Networked request handling with multi-hop calls: RPC and HTTP chains, service meshes, gateways, fan-out and hedged requests. It applies when one latency budget is meaningful for the whole logical request (an SLO or a user-facing timeout), when the hops are under your control and can carry request-scoped state (context, token, signal, call option or header), and when downstream work is cancellable or can be interrupted at checkpoints.
Microservice request chains (gateway -> frontend service -> several backends) under one user-facing latency SLO, where each hop converts the inbound deadline into its own outgoing calls.
gRPC services whose clients set a deadline and whose servers propagate it as a remaining timeout to downstream calls while cancelling server-side work once the deadline passes.
Fan-out and aggregation endpoints calling several backends in parallel: every sub-call shares the parent budget, and sub-calls still running when it expires are cancelled instead of awaited.
Hedged requests: the first replica to answer wins, and the duplicate requests are cancelled through the same carrier so their downstream work is stopped too.
Streaming and long-poll endpoints that must stop processing when the client disconnects or the connection times out, propagating that stop to services and storage.
Batch or pipeline steps with a per-request time budget that must check the remaining time before each stage and abandon a request that can no longer be finished in time.
ROS 2 / DDS-based robotics pipelines: autonomous vehicle perception pipelines where sensor data must traverse a chain of processing nodes (detect -> classify -> plan -> act) and missed deadlines invalidate downstream results entirely.
Distributed real-time databases with multi-hop queries (gateway -> shard router -> storage node -> index node) where each hop's latency budget is derived from a user-facing SLA.
Service mesh sidecar configurations (Istio/Linkerd/Envoy) where per-route timeout policies propagate deadline context to application code via headers like grpc-timeout or custom X-Request-Deadline headers.
Industrial IoT and edge computing pipelines (edge gateway -> fieldbus bridge -> PLC -> sensor) where end-to-end control loop deadlines must be enforced across heterogeneous network boundaries.
GraphQL federation: a federated query hitting multiple subgraphs in parallel must bound the total resolution time and cancel subgraph requests whose partial results can no longer affect the final response.
Go services on the standard library context package: context.WithDeadline and WithTimeout derive a child whose Done channel closes at the earliest of its own deadline, an explicit cancel, or the parent's cancellation, so cancelling the root request context tears down the whole goroutine tree, and WithDeadlineCause/WithTimeoutCause attach an explicit cause for attribution.
Envoy router filter in service meshes: Envoy sets x-envoy-expected-rq-timeout-ms on internal requests - derived from x-envoy-upstream-rq-timeout-ms or the route timeout - so upstream services can read the expected total completion time and exit early instead of finishing work the proxy has already timed out.
ASP.NET Core gRPC services map the inbound call's deadline onto the handler's CancellationToken; passing that token to database queries, HttpClient calls and Task.Delay stops server-side work the moment the client's deadline expires.

name: metadata-mapping
document:
metadata-mapping
declarative mapping
orm mapping metadata
Holds the correspondence between object fields and database columns in metadata - annotations, mapping files, table objects, struct tags or a schema definition - so that one generic mapping engine performs the reads, inserts and updates instead of hand-written per-class mapper code.
Every class that is persisted needs the same tedious, repetitive code: which field maps to which column, which key is generated, how nulls and types convert, what the table is called. Written per class it is duplicated everywhere and drifts from the schema; the catalogue's trigger is that the mapping knowledge belongs in metadata or configuration, duplicated in no class.
Object-relational (or object-document) mapping layers where classes and tables do not line up mechanically - renamed columns, generated keys, relationships, inheritance strategies - and where many classes share the same mapping shape. It applies when the mapping can be declared once in a form a machine can read (code annotations or attributes, external XML, code-first table objects, struct tags, a schema DSL) and when the schema can either be generated from that metadata or validated against it at startup.
A system with dozens of similarly shaped tables where hand-written data mappers would be repetitive: one mapping engine plus one metadata declaration per class.
Schema-first projects where the database already exists and the mapping should be derived from it by introspection or a code generator (EF Core reverse engineering, Rails schema introspection, SeaORM entity generation).
Framework and library builders who must let users map their own classes without shipping per-class code - an ORM, an object-document mapper or a serialization library.
Multi-database products in which only the dialect and type map of the metadata changes between targets while the domain classes stay identical.
Teams that want one declaration to drive several artifacts: DDL or migrations, typed query APIs, validation rules and documentation.
Hibernate ORM/Jakarta Persistence applications declare @Entity, @Table and @Column metadata; the provider builds a persistent metamodel and generic Session or EntityManager operations perform CRUD, so one declaration replaces per-entity mapper code.
EF Core applications combine conventions, data annotations and Fluent API configuration to build an entity model that drives LINQ translation and updates; explicit configuration pins renamed columns and relationships.
SQLAlchemy declarative mappings turn class attributes and mapped_column() declarations into Table and Mapper metadata; that metadata feeds SQL compilation and unit-of-work persistence, while imperative mapping keeps existing classes annotation-free.

name: inversion-of-control
document:
inversion-of-control
Hollywood Principle
IoC
Invert the direction of control between a reusable framework and application code: the framework owns the call flow and invokes the application's hooks at its extension points, so the generic sequence is reused while application code supplies only behaviour.
A reusable component - framework, container, UI toolkit, event loop, test runner - must own the sequence of calls (main loop, request dispatch, component lifecycle), while the behaviour at each step is application-specific; if application code had to call the framework's steps itself, the generic flow could neither be reused as a whole nor be extended without modifying it.
Applies wherever generic flow logic has to be specialised by application code: UI toolkits and event loops that decide when handlers fire, server containers and engines that own request dispatch and component lifecycle, test runners that own fixture and test sequencing, plugin hosts, and effect runtimes that own program entry. It is the defining characteristic of a framework as opposed to a library (a library is called by your code; a framework calls your code), and it usually arrives bundled with a container, dispatcher or engine - what remains to design is where the boundary sits and how much lifecycle you hand over.
GUI and event-driven applications: the windowing system or runtime owns the event loop and calls your event handlers, app delegate or declarative view body.
Server-side request handling: the container, engine or router owns listen-accept-dispatch and invokes the servlets, handlers, routes or middleware you registered.
Test frameworks: the runner owns discovery, fixture setup and teardown and calls your test methods and lifecycle hooks (JUnit, pytest, xUnit).
Container-managed components: EJB, Spring, Angular or Nest components whose construction, wiring and lifecycle callbacks are driven by the container that also owns the entry point.
Plugin and extension architectures: a host defines extension points and third-party plugins implement them, with the host deciding when each plugin is consulted (IDEs, browsers, build tools, game engines).
Inverted program entry: effect runtimes and app frameworks where the runtime's main calls the run value or app structure you provide instead of you orchestrating from main.
Callback-based C APIs: a library call such as qsort or a GLib main loop calls your function pointer per element or event - a small-scale realization of the same inversion.
Cloud Functions-as-a-Service: AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, and Google Cloud Functions own the request dispatch and cold-start lifecycle; your handler is a hook called by the platform, making serverless a live deployment of the Hollywood principle.
Reactive streams and event-driven pipelines: frameworks like Reactor, RxJava, or Node.js EventEmitter own the subscription and back-pressure loop; operators and subscribers are hooks that the runtime calls on data availability.
Microservices sidecar and service mesh: an Envoy or Linkerd proxy sidecar owns the connection lifecycle and calls application code through a defined protocol; the application registers health checks and request handlers as IoC hooks.
Orleans virtual actor model: the Orleans runtime owns the grain lifecycle, activation and deactivation, and calls grain methods as directed by the scheduler; grain code is a hook implementation invoked by the framework.
ASP.NET Core middleware: the host builds the request pipeline and invokes each registered RequestDelegate in order; middleware can run before and after the next delegate or short-circuit, so the application supplies components while the server owns request dispatch.
JUnit Jupiter extension model: the JUnit engine discovers tests and invokes registered Before*/After* lifecycle callbacks around user test methods; extensions customize execution without owning when tests run.
Kubernetes controllers: the controller manager owns reconciliation loops that watch API state and repeatedly invokes controller reconciliation logic to converge current state on desired state; controllers supply behavior while Kubernetes schedules dispatch.

name: fail-safe-defaults
document:
fail-safe-defaults
deny by default
default deny
Make denial the default outcome of every access decision, so that access exists only where it has been explicitly granted and no missing rule, missing identity or failed check can silently permit an operation.
Authorisation written as exclusion: code asks 'is this forbidden?' and everything the deny rules do not cover - a route added last sprint, a new operation, an unknown role, an object-level case, a request the parser cannot classify - is permitted by omission. The failure modes compound it: a missing principal, an unreachable policy source or an exception inside the check falls through to the permissive branch, so the code paths that look most careful are the ones that open the system.
Any boundary where access to a resource is decided: HTTP routes and APIs, message channels and queues, object-level data access, operating-system objects and descriptors, cloud and network policy, and the configuration a product ships with. It matters most where the space of possible requests grows faster than any list of forbidden cases can track, where the check itself can fail (policy store unreachable, identity missing, input unparseable), and where an unintended permission would not be visible in normal operation.
HTTP APIs and gateways: every route carries an explicit policy or permission and an endpoint whose handler was added without one is still decided (ASP.NET Core's fallback policy) or denied as unmatched (Spring Security's recommended final rule), so a forgotten decorator cannot expose it.
Message infrastructure: brokers grant publish/subscribe rights per topic, and a message whose type or destination matches no handler goes to an invalid-message or dead-letter channel instead of a catch-all consumer.
Operating-system and platform defaults: new files are created with restrictive modes (an explicit mode masked by umask, mkstemp's 0600 for temporary files, close-on-exec where descriptors cross exec), server processes run under a syscall allow-list and a least-privilege account, and firewall or network policy denies by default.
Multi-tenant data access: rows, schemas or objects are reachable only through a tenant-scoped grant, and a request with no resolvable tenant — or an unknown tenant id — is denied rather than defaulting to the shared or global dataset.
Cloud IAM and entitlement management: principals have implicit deny until a policy attaches an explicit allow, and service-to-service calls require a granted scope rather than being permitted because both ends are internal.
Product configuration and feature exposure: debug endpoints, sample data and experimental features ship disabled unless enabled, so a build cannot expose them by omission.
Kubernetes NetworkPolicy default-deny: a podSelector: {} NetworkPolicy with no allowed Ingress/Egress rules isolates every pod in the namespace; allow rules are added for only the traffic that is genuinely required, making lateral movement inside the cluster the exception rather than the default.
Service mesh and mTLS (Istio, Linkerd): every workload presents a client certificate; the mesh denies any packet between workloads that cannot present a matching allowed peer identity, so compromised containers cannot reach services outside their explicit allowlist.
Policy-as-Code with Open Policy Agent (OPA) or Cedar: authorization policies are written as declarative rules in a policy language, evaluated by a purpose-built engine, and applied to APIs, Kubernetes, CI/CD pipelines and cloud IAM — the grant set is code, diffed and reviewed like any other artefact.
Serverless function invocation: a function's invocation permission is an explicit resource-based policy; a caller with no matching permission is denied even when the function is invoked via an authenticated event source (SQS, SNS, EventBridge), preventing unintended cross-tenant or cross-function calls.
Database row-level and column-level security: a SELECT or DML operation must match an explicit row-level policy predicate for the caller's attributes (tenant_id, role, ownership), and a missing match returns no rows rather than all rows — preventing inadvertent data leakage across security boundaries.
CI/CD pipeline permissions: a pipeline step's ability to deploy, promote artefacts or access secrets is granted through a scoped, time-bounded, revokable token; any step that has not been explicitly granted a permission is denied access to the target environment, preventing lateral movement from a compromised pipeline.
Healthcare (HIPAA minimum necessary): a clinical application's access to patient records defaults to zero; a physician's identity is matched against a role-based record access policy and granted only the specific record types (e.g. active admissions, problem list, medication history) that the physician's specialty and current assignment require — a missing match returns zero records rather than a full dataset, preventing inadvertent PHI disclosure.
Financial services (PCI-DSS): cardholder data environment access is blocked by default for all accounts; a payment processing service is granted only the specific tokenisation and authorisation operations it requires, and only for the card ranges it actively manages. A network monitoring service that has no transaction role cannot reach the cardholder data database even if it shares a subnet.
IoT device posture and network isolation: a newly provisioned IoT device ships with all external communication channels closed; it may only reach the device management plane for firmware updates and telemetry, and only over a TLS channel with certificate pinning. Any application-layer attempt to reach an external IP address is denied by a local firewall policy that is immutable post-deployment.
Multi-cloud and hybrid IAM federation: a request arriving from a federated identity (SAML assertion, OIDC token) must carry a mapped grant in the local entitlement system before accessing a resource; the federation identity alone is insufficient. A missing local grant denies even when the upstream IdP has authenticated the user, preventing an IdP compromise from automatically granting access to all federated resources.
Supply chain and CI/CD artifact access: a CI/CD pipeline stage receives a scoped, time-limited, revokable token valid only for reading the specific artifact and writing to the specific deployment target it requires; it cannot read secrets store, cannot push to the artifact registry, and cannot promote artifacts to production without a separate approval gate — following the principle that pipeline permissions are the minimum for the job, not the union of all pipeline jobs.
Runtime application self-protection (RASP): a RASP agent embedded in an application enforces default-deny at the instrumentation layer — even if an attacker achieves code execution they cannot invoke system calls, network connections or database queries that the application's normal execution profile does not require, because those capabilities are absent from the process baseline by default.
Legal and compliance data environments: an e-discovery or legal hold system defaults to zero access to case documents; a paralegal's session is granted only the specific document set for an active matter and only for the duration of that matter; a revoked matter grant cannot be exercised even if the session token has not expired, because the grant itself is checked at each document access call.
Database engine shipped defaults: PostgreSQL 15 revoked CREATE on the public schema from PUBLIC by default, inverting a default that had permitted every role to create objects since the engine's early releases — evidence that the positive model must be re-asserted in the defaults a platform ships with, not only in the application's policy.

name: audit-interceptor
document:
audit-interceptor
audit trail interceptor
audit logging interceptor
Declare an audit policy at an invocation seam that records the actor, action, target, correlation id and both attempt and terminal outcome around a delegated operation, then sends the structured event to a dedicated integrity-protected sink, so security accountability is consistent without inline logging in every service.
Security-relevant operations (privileged actions, state changes and access to sensitive data) must be attributable, but inline logging misses denied and failed attempts, varies in schema, can leak raw arguments and disappears with a rolled-back transaction. Teams also need to cover components they cannot modify without pretending that a proxy sees calls that bypass it.
Business or service tiers whose sensitive operations pass through an interceptable seam: container-managed beans, proxied service objects, ORM entity lifecycles, message endpoints or an HTTP pipeline. Audit selection must be declarative and uniform, while the sink has its own integrity and retention requirements (Secure Logger); the design must make mediation gaps, redaction, transaction coupling, failure policy, clock source and correlation propagation explicit.
Business-tier auditing of money-moving or otherwise regulated operations (fund transfer, order placement, claim submission): who requested it, on which object, when, and whether it succeeded.
Privileged administration surfaces (role changes, key rotation, configuration changes) where every sensitive operation must leave a record naming the acting principal.
Authentication and authorization outcomes: successful and failed logins, access-denial decisions and lockouts routed into the same audit pipeline instead of ad-hoc log lines.
Access-to-sensitive-data events (who read which patient/customer record) recorded at the gateway or service boundary to satisfy data-protection obligations.
Retrofitting auditing onto legacy components whose code cannot be modified, by wrapping the service object or binding an interceptor to its interface.
Middleware-level auditing of message endpoints and database calls in a business tier, correlating the caller's subject with the operation performed.
Financial API request interception (Spring Boot global request interceptors) capturing who accessed which endpoint, with what payload, and what outcome — satisfying SOX financial reporting controls.
Entity-level change tracking via ORM subscribers (e.g., EF Core SaveChangesInterceptor, TypeORM subscribers): automatically diff old vs. new property values on create/update/delete and emit audit envelopes without manual logging calls.
API gateway-level audit logging: capture every external API call with timestamp, user identity, endpoint, method, and outcome, correlating across microservices via X-Request-ID / traceparent headers.
Compliance reporting automation: generate audit-ready reports for SOX (~7-year retention), HIPAA (~6-year retention), GDPR (data residency-aware), and PCI-DSS from structured interceptor events.
Zero-trust data access trails: record every read of sensitive fields (PHI, PII, financial data) so data-protection obligations (GDPR Article 5 data minimization, HIPAA access logging) are demonstrably met.
Hibernate Envers: @Audited entity lifecycle changes create per-entity _AUD revisions at transaction commit; a custom revision entity/listener can attach actor or request metadata.
Django admin: django.contrib.admin.models.LogEntry records action time, user, object, addition/change/deletion and change_message for ModelAdmin activity.
Rails Audited: the audited ActiveRecord extension creates audit rows for model create, update and destroy callbacks, including changed attributes and optional acting-user attribution.

name: function-composition
document:
function-composition
compose
function pipeline
Combine a chain of small unary transformations into one reusable function by sequencing them with a composition combinator (compose/pipe), so the order of the steps is stated once, every step stays independently testable, and the chain itself becomes a value that can be named, passed and reassembled.
A transformation that is naturally a sequence of small pure steps gets written as nested calls or as repeated imperative assignment (`h(g(f(x)))`, or `y = f(x); y = g(y); ...; return y`) at every call site. The order is duplicated wherever the chain is used, the intermediate values need throwaway names, steps cannot be reused in a different order, and changing one stage means editing every copy.
Pure or nearly pure value transformations - parsing, normalisation, validation, formatting, pricing, AST rewriting - where each step is unary and the language treats functions as values. It pays off when the chain is reused or assembled from data (configuration, plugin lists, per-request policy), when steps must be unit-tested in isolation, and when the same steps must also run element-wise over a collection or lazily over a stream. It stops applying where steps need side effects or branching between stages: there the shell around the pure core owns control flow.
Input normalisation: trim, parse, canonicalise and validate a payload before it reaches domain logic, with the same chain reused by HTTP handlers and message consumers.
Pricing and rule chains: base price, discount, tax and rounding applied in a fixed, configurable order to an immutable value object.
Compiler and AST work: a pass list of rewrite functions composed once and applied over the tree, with passes added or reordered per optimisation level.
Serialisation and formatting: sanitise, format, encode and sign a document, where each step is tested separately and the composed chain is stored as a constant.
Data transformation over collections: the same pure steps composed into one function and passed to map/filter/stream operations, so element-wise processing reuses the chain.
Policy assembly at startup: the processing chain is built from configuration or plugin registrations and then applied per request without further branching.
Reactive stream processing: RxJS Observable.pipe chains the same logical steps across asynchronous event sequences, with operators composed once and reused across streams.
ETL and data pipeline transformation: extract-transform-load chains where each stage (parse, clean, enrich, aggregate, write) is a unary pure function composed into a reusable pipeline run over batches or streaming data.
HTTP request/response middleware: the middleware stack is a composed function chain where each layer (authenticate, authorise, rate-limit, deserialize, validate) is a unary handler; composition is resolved once at startup.
Matrix and vector transformations in numerical code: each linear algebra operation (scale, rotate, translate, project) is a unary function on a matrix type; composing them once builds the transformation pipeline that is applied to every vertex or pixel.
Ramda pipelines: R.pipe and R.compose assemble reusable data-last transformations from small functions, centralising the order while letting the same composed value run over many inputs.
Redux store setup: Redux's compose helper combines store enhancers right-to-left into one enhancer, so the enhancer order is defined once instead of reconstructed at each store boundary.
lodash/fp transformations: lodash/fp's auto-curried, data-last compose/flow helpers assemble immutable-friendly transformations from reusable steps that can be passed as values.

name: test-specific-subclass
document:
test-specific-subclass
test-specific extension
subclassed test double
Make an otherwise untestable class testable by defining a test-only subclass that overrides the method reaching the unusable dependency (or exposes the internal state the test needs), so the boundary can be substituted and observed without putting test hooks into production code.
A class that must be tested reaches its dependency through a call on itself - a self-call to a helper method, a field created inside the class, or a singleton/static lookup - so the test has no injection point: the collaborator cannot be replaced from outside, the indirect inputs cannot be controlled and the indirect outputs cannot be observed. Editing the production class to accept the dependency may be impossible (third-party or frozen code) or would introduce test logic into production.
Applies to legacy or third-party object-oriented code where the boundary call already sits behind an overridable (non-final, sufficiently visible) method, or can be extracted into one, and where test-only code may live next to the tests. It is a fallback for statically typed languages that need the double to stay type-compatible with a concrete class; where the code can be modified, dependency injection is the better seam.
A legacy class reads the wall clock inside a helper method (System.currentTimeMillis, DateTime.Now, Instant.now): override the helper so date/decision logic can be tested at a fixed instant.
A reporting or notification class sends mail or calls a remote API from a self-call: override that method with a canned or empty body so the unit test runs offline and deterministically.
A class reaches a database or the file system from inside its own method: override it to return an in-memory fixture instead of building the real object chain (entity-chain snipping).
Verifying the sequence and the set of steps of a template method: override the steps in a subclass and record which of them ran, in which order.
Exposing private state for state verification, or exposing a private algorithm step so it can be tested individually (state-exposing and behaviour-exposing subclasses).
Replacing a singleton or static accessor the SUT uses through a lookup with a controlled instance that is still type-compatible with the concrete class (substituted singleton).
Putting a legacy untested class under a characterization-test baseline before refactoring, while extracting the collaborator is not yet possible.
A Java class that cannot be modified (third-party or legacy jar) but has a non-final boundary method to stub: Mockito spy() / @Spy keeps the real methods and stubs only the overridden ones - the partial mocking Mockito's Javadoc documents for legacy code and third-party interfaces (final methods stay un-stubbable).
A PHP class whose constructor opens connections or performs other side effects: createPartialMock(Class::class, ['boundaryMethod']) or getMockBuilder()->onlyMethods([...])->disableOriginalConstructor() generates a double that overrides only the named methods and skips the real constructor - PHPUnit's documented form of the pattern (final, private and static methods and enums cannot be doubled).
A .NET class with virtual boundary members: NSubstitute Substitute.ForPartsOf<T>() creates a partial substitute that - as NSubstitute's own docs state - inherits the original type via Castle DynamicProxy and runs real code except for members configured with DoNotCallBase, i.e. a generated test-specific subclass with an official 'use with caution' caveat.

name: update-method
document:
update-method
per-frame update
tick method
Give every live object one self-contained per-frame step and let a single driver call each object's step every frame, so behaviour advances one frame at a time while input and rendering stay responsive.
A running world is full of objects that each have to keep doing their own thing - guards patrolling, statues charging, agents acting - and the recurring decision is where one object's per-frame behaviour lives and how all those behaviours get driven. Coding a behaviour as a loop that runs to completion blocks input and rendering (the skeleton walks, but nobody sees it); coding it inline in the game loop turns the loop into a switchboard over every kind of object, so every new behaviour edits central code; and there is no way for two actors to evolve independently and simultaneously.
Real-time software with many concurrent live objects whose behaviour is mostly independent and must be simulated over time: games, agent-based simulations, animation and particle systems, tick-based servers and live visualisations. It is the natural partner of a frame driver (Game Loop) - the loop supplies the cadence, Update Method supplies the per-object step - and it becomes the wrong shape in turn-based or purely event-driven domains where nothing changes between inputs.
Real-time games and simulations with many concurrent actors: patrolling guards, projectiles, particle effects and crowd agents each advance themselves once per frame while the driver walks the collection.
Component-based engines where the parts of one entity evolve independently - rendering, physics and AI components each implement their own step and the engine's registry dispatches per component (Unity, MonoGame, Bevy, GameplayKit, libGDX).
Per-frame animation and effect timelines outside games: tween/spring systems, sprite animation and UI transitions advanced from the browser's frame callback or a UI toolkit's animation timer.
Tick-based servers and headless simulations: game servers, digital twins and agent-based models where each agent's behaviour is a resumable step and the world advances in whole discrete frames.
Tools, editors and dashboards with continuously animating scenes, where many independent scene items (markers, live charts, gizmos) must advance on every repaint without a central per-item switch.
Porting straight-line behaviour into a frame loop: turning a scripted sequence (walk left, walk right) into a per-frame step, either by storing explicit state or by using coroutines/generators to keep the code linear.
Godot's SceneTree is the driver: a node opts into the walk with set_process(true) and its _process(delta) runs every render frame with the frame time passed in as an argument, while _physics_process(delta) is called at a fixed rate - so one object can implement two steps on two clocks and can leave the walk entirely (set_process(false)) instead of paying an enabled-flag check every frame.
Engines whose built-in driver leaves per-object order unspecified expose the order as configuration: Unity states you should not rely on the order of Update across GameObjects, so real projects fix dependencies through the Script Execution Order panel, a LateUpdate pass that runs after every Update, or the PlayerLoop API rather than through registration order.
Agent-based simulation models step whole populations in NetLogo: the go procedure runs ask turtles [ ... ] to give every agent its one turn and then tick advances the discrete clock - with documented semantics that agents take their turns in random order and only agents present when the ask began get to act.

name: mock
document:
mock
mock object
Replace a collaborator of the system under test with a test-specific object that is programmed with the expected calls and verifies them as they happen, so the interaction itself - not the resulting state - is what the test asserts.
The expected interaction sequence is the behaviour under test: the outcome of the exercised method is not visible in the system under test's own state, and no observation point exposes the indirect outputs (the messages sent to collaborators) that the requirement is about. State-based assertions cannot reach them, so the test either reaches into the collaborator's internals - duplicating the collaboration logic - or asserts nothing at all.
Unit and component tests of an object whose collaboration protocol is the specification: exact calls, arguments, cardinality or order matter (handshakes, publish-once, audit logging, cache invalidation) and the collaborator is slow, unavailable, non-deterministic or side-effecting. It requires a substitutable dependency (dependency injection or lookup) and, for framework-based realizations, an interception mechanism - dynamic proxy, bytecode agent, generated code or macro. Typical in mockist, interaction-first TDD and in need-driven development.
Verifying that a component emits exactly the expected messages to a collaborator whose effects are otherwise invisible: an audit logger, notifier, event publisher or payment gateway.
Pinning an interaction protocol whose ordering and cardinality are the requirement - open before send, publish exactly once, flush before close - in tests of clients and adapters.
Simulating failure paths of a remote collaborator (timeout, exception, malformed response) to assert that the SUT surfaces or recovers from them deterministically.
Unit-testing a domain service against repository, clock, or gateway interfaces when the real implementations are slow, licensed or unavailable in the development environment.
Driving interface design from the outside in: write the expectation for the call the SUT should make, then let the implementation satisfy it (mockist TDD).
Verifying that a main operation triggers its side effects - cache invalidation, metrics emission, compensating call - with the required arguments.
In C++ tests built with GoogleTest gMock, using EXPECT_CALL matchers, Times cardinalities and InSequence ordering verifies an outbound collaborator protocol before the SUT runs.
In Java tests using Mockito, verify and InOrder assert required interactions with a dependency while keeping the interaction contract separate from the dependency's implementation.
In Python's unittest.mock, assert_called_once_with and assert_has_calls verify argument, cardinality and sequence requirements for calls made through a replaceable collaborator.

name: protected-system
document:
protected-system
protection proxy
Give a resource exactly one owning object whose published operations are the only way to touch it, so that every access is decided by an authorization check before the resource is used.
A resource - a credential store, a file tree, a socket, a connection pool, a device handle - is referenced from many places. When each use site performs its own permission check, the checks drift, new code paths forget them, and the resource remains reachable as a raw handle, so a missing check cannot even be detected. The recurring trigger: one object can own the resource and clients can be made to hold only that object, so ownership itself can carry the enforcement.
Applies where ownership is expressible in the language or runtime (private field, unexported type, opaque handle, module boundary) and an authorization policy - identity, role, permission, capability - can be evaluated at each public operation. The guard may sit in-process (object or module scope) or at a process/kernel boundary, where the same pattern becomes a real reference monitor; the assurance the implementation can claim depends on which side of that line it lives.
Credential and key stores: an in-process vault owns the keys and exposes only operations (sign, decrypt, rotate), so callers never receive the secret material.
Storage gateways: a library owns the directory handle or object-store client and applies path and tenant rules on every operation instead of handing out a raw client.
Pools: the pool owns its connections and leases checked-out views, so a caller cannot keep, share or resurrect a connection the pool must reclaim.
Multi-tenant data access: a tenant-scoped repository wrapper pins the tenant filter and refuses operations that would query outside it.
Device and driver access: a supervisor object owns the device handle and validates commands, or a privileged daemon owns the socket and checks each request from an unprivileged client.
Module-level boundaries: a package exports only the guard type and keeps the resource unexported, so code outside the package cannot even name the protected representation.
Linux Landlock: a kernel-enforced ruleset restricts a process and its future children to explicitly allowed filesystem or network rights, placing mediation below application code.
Kubernetes RBAC: the API server evaluates Roles and bindings for each API request, mediating verbs and resources instead of exposing the cluster's backing store to clients.
HashiCorp Vault policies: authenticated tokens are checked against path and capability rules before secret operations, while the storage backend remains behind the Vault service.

name: state-colocation
document:
state-colocation
colocated state
colocation
Keep each piece of presentation state in the component closest to where it is used — down to the single component that owns and reads it — instead of hoisting it to a common ancestor or a global store, so that a change touches only the smallest part of the view that can observe it.
State gets hoisted 'just in case': a value only one component reads is lifted to the screen or application root, or pushed into one global store, because someone may want it later. The consequences are components that receive props they never read, updates that invalidate far more of the UI than the value's actual consumers, an unclear owner for each value, and tests that must assemble the whole state container to exercise one field. The recurring decision is where a new piece of state should live: keep it at the smallest scope that actually needs it.
Declarative component UIs (React, Vue, Svelte, SwiftUI, Compose, Blazor, Qt Quick) and, in generalized form, any system where a mutable value is owned by one component-like unit: the consumers determine the state's scope, the framework invalidates only what the owner's subtree can observe, and components are composed, moved and deleted. Most compelling where over-lifted or global state has already become a performance and ownership problem.
A search or form input whose value is read only by the input, its own validation and its own preview: keep it in that component instead of the screen root (the canonical typing example where hoisting made every keystroke re-render the page).
Which panel of an accordion is open: leave it per panel while panels are independent, then lift exactly to the accordion once only one panel may be open at a time (the closest common parent).
Tooltip, hover, popover and dropdown state in a chart or table cell: own it in the cell component rather than in a global UI store.
Per-row edit or selection state in a data grid: the row component owns it; only cross-row operations need the grid to own it.
Dialog and modal open state in the button or list that opens it, until another surface must close or observe it.
Form draft state in the form component; lift it only when a sibling — summary panel, preview pane, wizard footer — genuinely must read it.
Extracting a self-contained widget for reuse or publication: keeping its state local makes the component portable and shrinks its API.
Per-cell expansion state in a tree view or file explorer: the tree node component owns whether it is expanded; the parent tree only coordinates multi-select or bulk-expand operations.
Media playback state for a single player (play/pause, current time, volume): colocate in the player component rather than a global audio store unless the same track plays in multiple places simultaneously.
Local filter/sort state for a data table or list: keep it in the list component until a URL parameter, shareable link, or sibling panel requires sharing it.
Vue: composable-local state (useSearch, useToggle) where each consumer needs its own independent instance of the same reactive logic pattern.
Angular Signals: feature-level signal stores scoped to a route or feature slice, not the entire application store, for UI state and feature-derived state.
SwiftUI: @State for view-local value types; @StateObject for view-owned reference types; keep @EnvironmentObject for genuinely cross-cutting state (auth session, theme) mounted as low in the hierarchy as consumers allow.
Svelte 5 runes: `let count = $state(0)` inside a component is per-component-instance reactive state — the component that declares it is its owner; Svelte's v5 migration explicitly replaced the pre-runes habit of reaching for a store whenever state sat at a component's top level, with $state plus $derived/$effect as the local cells, and module-level .svelte.js state only for deliberate sharing.
Jetpack Compose: the official hoisting guidance is this pattern's placement ladder — keep state as close as possible to where it is consumed, hoist only to the lowest common ancestor of all composables that read or write it, pass value down and onValueChange up, and make the ViewModel the owner only when business logic or lifecycle outlives the composition.
Blazor: component fields are the default owner for UI-local state; the official state-management guidance promotes to an in-memory state container service only when components must share non-persistent state, and to Protected Browser Storage only when the value must survive circuits or sessions — a three-rung ladder that mirrors local state, scoped provider, persistence.

name: cursor-pagination
document:
cursor-pagination
keyset pagination
cursor-based pagination
Bound what a read boundary returns for a large or changing ordered collection by sending one page plus an opaque continuation token that pins the filter and ordering, so clients advance deterministically without offsets and without watching rows move under them.
A boundary must expose a collection that is too large to return at once and keeps changing while clients read it. Offset or page-number requests make the store count or scan everything up to the requested page, and concurrent inserts or deletes shift rows across page boundaries so consumers see duplicates or miss items; the server has no way to state where the sequence should resume.
Any read boundary - an HTTP or gRPC list operation, a GraphQL connection, a database-backed feed, a batch export job - over an ordered collection that is large, growing, or read under concurrent writes, where the server can identify a unique, immutable ordering key and wants to cap both response size and per-request query cost while letting clients iterate the whole sequence.
Public REST or gRPC list endpoints over unbounded, growing tables - messages, orders, audit events - where deep offsets are slow and responses must stay small.
Infinite-scroll or load-more feeds that keep returning newer items while a user scrolls, with the already-seen pages stable against inserts.
Whole-collection sync and export jobs (warehouse loads, backups, search reindexing) that must iterate every row exactly once while writers continue.
GraphQL Relay connections where first/after, edges and pageInfo carry the continuation contract in the schema instead of the URL.
Consumers of third-party list APIs (Stripe-style starting_after/has_more, Google page_token iterators) that keep parameters fixed across auto-paginated calls.
Administrative and operational tooling that streams very large tables for verification or cleanup with bounded memory and predictable server load.
Audit log and event stream retrieval where events are append-only and chronological, and clients stream continuously without needing to revisit earlier pages.
Real-time activity feeds (social media timelines, notification streams) where inserts at the head must not disturb pages the user has already loaded.
Database replication and change-data-capture (CDC) pipelines that must consume a changelog exactly once across restarts and failures.
Paginating over search results from a vector database or full-text index where OFFSET at depth is expensive and results may change between queries.
Bi-directional data synchronization (CDC pipelines, replica lag-catching) where a consumer must iterate forward and occasionally needs to resume from a previous position or re-sweep a window — requiring stable forward cursors plus a defined backward-resumption path.
Paginating a partitioned or sharded database table where each partition is queried independently and cursors carry both the partition hint and the per-partition keyset position.
Slack Web API collection methods (users.list, conversations.history) where response_metadata.next_cursor drives the loop, page limits are clamped per method, and expired or malformed tokens surface as invalid_cursor so the client restarts from the first page.
GitHub GraphQL-style cursor connections where first/last (bounded 1-100) and pageInfo.startCursor/endCursor carry the continuation position for after/before traversal.
Timeline-style feeds served by Django REST framework's CursorPagination, whose default -created ordering gives a consistent view that does not repeat items as new rows are inserted.
