name: request-reply
document:
request-reply
request-response
request-response messaging
Let a sender obtain a result or a domain error from an asynchronous or remote receiver by pairing each request with a correlated reply, and give the missing reply a defined outcome: timeout, cancellation and disposal of late replies.
Messaging is one-way, but the sender frequently needs a return value or a domain error from the receiver before it can continue. Without an agreed reply destination, a way to match replies to requests, and a rule for what happens when no reply arrives, the caller either blocks forever, mis-associates the next reply with the wrong request, or accumulates pending state it never cleans up.
Asynchronous interaction across a process, thread or network boundary where the caller cannot continue without the receiver's result: HTTP/gRPC-style RPC, broker-based RPC over a queue, actor or thread mailboxes, and browser-to-server exchanges over a socket. It applies when the interaction is naturally one request and one reply, and each exchange has a bounded deadline.
Service-to-service RPC where the caller needs the result to continue (HTTP, gRPC, or a broker-based RPC queue such as the RabbitMQ tutorial's rpc_queue).
Command dispatch that must return a domain error - a validation failure or business rejection - rather than only an acknowledgement of receipt.
In-process actor or thread mailboxes: ask a worker for state with a deadline so the caller can never block forever.
Front-end over a WebSocket asking the server for a value correlated by message id or acknowledgement callback.
Talking to devices, sensors or legacy systems over a socket whose protocol is inherently one request and one response.
Querying a cache or index cluster from a client library where each call is a key lookup with a per-call deadline.
NATS request-reply service calls: a client publishes with a unique inbox as the reply subject and waits for a response under a per-request timeout.
RabbitMQ RPC over an rpc_queue: the client sends reply_to and a unique correlation_id, then matches the worker's response on its callback queue.
gRPC unary RPC: a generated client stub sends one request and receives one response under a propagated deadline, with cancellation available for abandoned work.

name: intercepting-validator
document:
intercepting-validator
validation interceptor
Insert one interception layer on the ingress path that validates every inbound message before any handler runs, so that input checking is uniform, central and impossible to forget per endpoint.
Inbound data - HTTP requests, RPC messages, queue events, protocol frames - is validated inside each handler: every new endpoint re-implements parsing, range and encoding checks, rules drift between handlers, and some paths end up with no validation at all. The recurring decision is where to put validation so that all inbound data passes through it exactly once, before application logic.
Request- or message-driven systems with a well-defined ingress - HTTP APIs, RPC services, queue consumers, protocol front ends - where several handlers accept external data, where shared constraints (schema, ranges, encodings, size limits) can be expressed without loading domain state, and where the ingress pipeline (filter chain, middleware stack, plugin pipeline, responder chain) can be owned and configured by the team.
A public REST or GraphQL API where every request body and query parameter must pass schema, range and size validation before any controller is invoked.
A message-queue consumer that validates every inbound event against its schema and version before dispatching it to a handler.
A file or protocol ingest pipeline (CSV, XML, binary frames) that validates frames in one front layer before domain processing begins.
A multi-tenant service that enforces tenant-scoped constraints uniformly - allowed fields, payload caps, encoding policy - on all inbound requests.
An RPC or WebSocket gateway that rejects non-conforming request messages with one error format before they reach service handlers.
A GraphQL API gateway that validates incoming query operations for schema conformance, depth limits and argument types at the boundary before query execution begins.
A gRPC service fronted by a protobuf interceptor that enforces proto-schema type and structural constraints on all inbound RPC requests before they reach the service implementation.
A FastAPI service that attaches a shared Depends() dependency to an APIRouter and uses Pydantic request models so invalid requests are rejected before the path operation.
An ASP.NET Core application that places request validation in the middleware pipeline or a Minimal API endpoint filter, short-circuiting with a problem response before the endpoint delegate.
An Express application that mounts schema-validation middleware on a router before its routes, returning a 4xx response without calling next() when the request is invalid.

name: assertion
document:
assertion
design by contract
Express a model object's preconditions, postconditions and class invariants as executable, side-effect-free predicates at the operations that must uphold them, so a broken contract fails at its boundary instead of remaining a comment or surfacing later as corrupt state. This pattern is for design-by-contract correctness checks, not routine validation of untrusted input or test-only assertions.
Model rules - a balance never below its floor, a period whose end follows its start, a status that cannot move backwards - are left in comments, documents and team memory while constructors and mutators check nothing. A caller can violate a precondition or an operation can break an invariant, allowing invalid state to propagate until an unrelated reader fails; if the assertion is elided by the build, the shipped program may enforce a different contract from the one tested.
Objects with genuine invariants - entities, value objects and aggregate roots - whose state changes through several operations or paths, in a language with an assertion facility, contract syntax or an exception mechanism. The invariant must be expressible as a deterministic, side-effect-free predicate over observable state. Use assertions for programmer/model defects; use always-on validation or typed errors for expected input failures, and decide explicitly whether a release build may elide the check.
Entities and value objects with cross-field rules: an amount that always carries its currency and scale, a date range whose end follows its start, an order whose total equals the sum of its lines.
Aggregate roots that enforce consistency across a cluster of objects: the root asserts its invariant before accepting a change and after applying it.
Domain services and application services checking the preconditions of a use-case operation, so a mis-wired caller fails on the spot instead of writing corrupt state.
Library and framework code that must state its contract: precondition checks on public constructors and methods that clients cannot legitimately violate.
Legacy models under refactoring: assertions turn implicit rules into explicit ones, and where the language strips assertions the same predicates are pasted into the test suite (Evans's fallback).
Reconstitution code that rebuilds objects from stored data, asserting that persisted state still satisfies the model's invariants before the object is used.
Event-sourced aggregates: each state-transition command asserts the preconditions before applying the event, and the event handler asserts the invariant after the state is reconstituted from the event stream.
CQRS write models: the command handler asserts that the incoming command is valid for the current aggregate state before persisting, catching mis-wired or concurrent commands at the write edge.
Microservice boundary contracts: the inbound adapter asserts the precondition of the domain operation before dispatching, preventing malformed commands from entering the domain core regardless of which transport delivered them (HTTP, queue, gRPC).
Money and quantity types: value objects that wrap a numeric amount and a currency/unit, asserting that amounts are non-negative and operations preserve currency matching, preventing silent unit-mixing bugs.
Workflow or saga state machines: assertions on transition preconditions (this status can only advance to that one) prevent illegal state progression from corrupted or out-of-order events.
Property-based test oracle: postconditions double as generative test properties - for all inputs satisfying preconditions, the postcondition holds - turning the same predicate into a specification that a property-based testing library (e.g. Eris for PHP, Hypothesis for Python, fast-check for TypeScript) can falsify.
EiffelBase container classes such as LINKED_LIST and HASH_TABLE: EiffelStudio contract monitoring checks exported-routine preconditions/postconditions and class invariants while the containers preserve their representation rules.
AutoProof-verified Eiffel classes: executable assertions also serve as formal specifications that the verifier can discharge or flag, pairing runtime diagnostics with static proof where available.

statement: Place executable preconditions, postconditions, and ledger invariants at the account and posting operations that must establish them, distinct from ordinary rejection of malformed external input.
name: side-effect-free-function
document:
side-effect-free-function
pure function
Put the model's logic into operations that compute a result from their inputs alone, so that a caller - and a test - can predict the result without knowing any state the operation might secretly touch.
Reasoning about a design becomes guesswork when operations do more than return a result: the caller must read the implementation and every delegation to know which state a call changes, and no result can be reproduced in a test without recreating the state around it. As rules compose, the number of hidden interactions grows faster than the behaviour being built, so the model stops being safely predictable.
Applies inside the model layer of any codebase whose rules are combined and composed - pricing, eligibility, allocation, validation - and where a computation must be exercised in tests without a database, clock or message broker in the loop. It matters most where several rules interact (composition multiplies hidden coupling) and in languages whose defaults are mutable objects, because there the discipline has to be stated rather than assumed.
Pricing and discount rules: unit prices, tax and rebates computed from immutable inputs, so the same basket always prices the same way.
Eligibility and specification checks: a rule expressed as a predicate over a value and reused in validation, selection and tests.
Money and quantity arithmetic: scaling, adding and rounding return new values instead of adjusting a running total in place.
Deriving test data and expected values from the same pure functions the model uses, instead of hand-copied golden values.
Query-side report assembly: projections, summaries and totals built by composing pure functions over already-loaded immutable data.
Memoizing an expensive domain computation, which is sound exactly because the function is referentially transparent.
Redux reducers: the store computes the next state by calling (previousState, action) => newState with no mutation, no clock, no randomness, so DevTools can replay a recorded action log and reproduce the exact state and useSelector can detect changes by reference comparison alone.
React function components: the official contract is that rendering must be a pure function of props, state and context, so React can cache components whose inputs are unchanged, abandon an outdated render mid-flight, and call each component twice in Strict Mode to expose impurity.
Haskell: ordinary functions are pure by default and effects are confined to IO-typed values, so the type signature itself states whether a computation touches the world and the compiler, not review, enforces the query half of the split.

statement: Place executable preconditions, postconditions, and ledger invariants at the account and posting operations that must establish them, distinct from ordinary rejection of malformed external input.
name: closure-of-operations
document:
closure-of-operations
closed operation
Define a value type's operations so that their arguments and their results are that same type, so that combinations compose freely and the type's interface depends on no other concept.
Callers that combine two model values fall back to primitives: an addition returns a raw amount, an interval intersection returns two dates, an append returns a bare collection - and every call site has to know how to rebuild a valid instance. Combination rules scatter across call sites, results are not guaranteed to satisfy the type's invariant, and the type's public interface leaks foreign concepts.
Rich value types - money, quantities, ranges, paths, sets with domain semantics - where the type is immutable, has a canonical representation and every result must satisfy its invariant. Most valuable when the type's operations have an arithmetic or algebraic flavour (sum, union, intersection, append, extend) and when callers chain or accumulate results; entities qualify only for the rare operations that genuinely yield another entity.
Money and quantity arithmetic in billing, pricing and accounting: Money + Money -> Money, with currency compatibility checked inside the operation.
Interval and period algebra in scheduling and effectivity modelling: intersect, union or hull of two ranges returns another range.
Geometry, physics and simulation values: vectors, matrices, complex numbers and colours whose combination law is genuinely part of the domain.
Logistics and navigation models: appending a leg to a route, extending a path, concatenating schedules - each returns the same concept.
Domain collections with set semantics: union and intersection of permission sets, tagging sets or mailing lists, keeping the collection's invariants (a Typed Collection).
Accumulation engines: folding a collection of values into a total with reduce/fold, where the closed operation plus an identity make the fold total.
Configuration and settings composition: merging configuration maps where each key's value has its own monoid (OR for booleans, MIN for timeouts, concatenation for strings), enabling layered defaults with precedence (Arolla PDF, 2018).
Event sourcing with monoidal aggregation: folding a stream of domain events into a single state object where the event type is a closed monoid over the state (Chassaing, referenced in Arolla PDF).
Supply chain impact aggregation: composing impact metrics (energy, carbon, supplier count) across a tree of suppliers where each metric forms its own closed operation, enabling parallel reduction (Arolla PDF, 2018).
Price plan and invoice composition: composing cash-flow sequences (monthly fees, annual fees, one-off options) as a monoid, eliminating combinatorial explosion of fee variants.
Interval algebra in production date-time libraries: Joda-Time's Interval.overlap(ReadableInterval) returns an Interval and NodaTime's DateInterval.Union and Intersection return a DateInterval - the same-type result re-establishes the start <= end invariant, and null (not a fabricated interval) signals an impossible combination.
Reduction APIs that codify closure as a contract: Java's Stream.reduce(T identity, BinaryOperator<T>) requires an accumulator whose arguments and result are all the element type, and its javadoc enforces associativity and a true identity - exactly the monoid recipe this pattern prescribes for domain values.
Set algebra in the Rust standard library: HashSet::union takes two sets and yields elements of the same element type, collected back into a HashSet - combination stays in the collection's own vocabulary without exposing its internals.

name: conceptual-contour
document:
conceptual-contour
conceptual contour
conceptual contours
Group the data, invariants and operations that belong to one domain concept into a single cohesive unit with a narrow domain interface, so the model's divisions follow the domain itself instead of technical convenience.
Conceptually related behaviour is scattered: one concept's rules live across *Service classes, helper modules and utility functions, while an unrelated monolithic class or module mixes meanings, duplicates functionality and exposes an interface that does not say what clients actually need.
Any non-trivial domain model (DDD entities, value objects, aggregates, domain services, modules) where the model is being built or refactored: cutting a god class, de-anemizing entities, or deciding which operations, types and functions share a file, package or namespace. It presupposes that the domain can be named - a ubiquitous language and access to domain knowledge - because the contour is taken from the domain, not from the code layout.
Refactoring an anemic domain model: moving validation, calculation and state-transition methods from *Service classes onto the entity or aggregate that owns the state.
Cutting a god class or god module (Manager, Core, System) into units that each mirror a term of the ubiquitous language.
Merging scattered helpers (OrderValidator, OrderCalculator, OrderUtils) back into the concept they serve, or justifying why they are genuinely separate.
Deciding the physical layout of a codebase - which types and functions share a file, namespace, package or module - as part of model refinement rather than code style.
Reviewing a model before it ossifies: testing candidate divisions against the axes of change and stability observed in recent refactorings.
Decomposing a microservice or bounded context: applying conceptual contours to decide which domain concepts belong together vs. should be separated into distinct services, using the principle that concepts changing together for the same reason should share a contour.
Designing aggregates: using conceptual contours to decide which entities and value objects travel together inside an aggregate boundary, keeping strongly coupled concepts with high co-change rates co-located.
Structuring an event-driven model: placing commands, events and their handlers inside the concept unit that owns the state they operate on, rather than in a separate event-handling layer.
Making the contour architecturally evident in Java: jMolecules annotates the concept units themselves (@AggregateRoot, @Entity, @ValueObject, @Identity on domain-typed ids like IBAN on BankAccount) so the model's divisions are visible in code, and jQAssistant plugins or ArchUnit rules verify that aggregate boundaries and identifier types are actually honoured.
Modelling event-sourced aggregates in Axon Framework: the aggregate root carries command-handling methods that validate commands against current state and apply events, so the consistency boundary is also the unit that owns behaviour and emits domain events (@AggregateIdentifier, @CommandHandler, @EventSourcingHandler).
Letting persistence follow the contour in Spring Data JDBC: the aggregate root is the unit of load and save and every entity reachable from it belongs to that aggregate, so a well-cut contour needs no manual object-graph management while a mis-cut one shows up immediately as mapping pain.

name: characterization-test
document:
characterization-test
golden master
approval test
golden file test
snapshot test
golden session test
Pin the actual, currently deployed behaviour of existing code in committed reference artefacts (golden masters) so that a later edit can be distinguished from an accidental regression even when nobody can say what the code is supposed to do.
You must change code whose behaviour is undocumented, surprising or only known to production: there is no specification to test against, and tests written from intended behaviour would take too long and silently encode guesses as fact. The safety net therefore has to be built from observed behaviour: replay a corpus of real inputs through the untouched subject, capture everything observable, commit the result as the reference, and let every later run diff against it - pinning what the code does today before changing how it does it.
Applies whenever the subject already runs and can be exercised in a test process or from a test script: untested legacy modules, data transformations and report pipelines, serializers, parsers and code generators, CLI and protocol endpoints, rendering pipelines whose images can be diffed, and dependency or runtime upgrades where the old behaviour is the baseline. The precondition is determinism: volatile parts (timestamps, identifiers, paths, memory addresses, collection order, locale, floating-point formatting) must be normalized or redacted before capture, otherwise the comparison is noise. The pattern is a first move - build the net, then refactor under it - and pairs with a deliberate approval step, because a characterization test does not know which behaviour was intended.
Before refactoring an untested legacy module: capture outputs for a corpus of inputs, restructure the code, and require the reference artefacts to stay identical.
Data processing and batch jobs: pin how representative input files are transformed into output files or reports, so the nightly job can be changed safely.
Serializers, formatters and code generators: pin the emitted text or structured output for representative documents, with a redaction step for volatile values.
Rendering and UI pipelines: pin generated images (screenshot goldens) or rendered text output with an approval workflow and a visual diff tool.
CLI and protocol behaviour: pin stdout, stderr and exit codes, or request/response bytes, for a set of recorded invocations.
Dependency or runtime upgrades: pin behaviour before the upgrade and re-run afterwards, so only intended differences have to be reviewed.
Production defect triage: replay the failing production input into a new reference artefact, then fix the defect against that regression test.
AI/LLM output regression testing: pin model responses to a curated golden dataset; on model or prompt change, compare distributions, embedding similarity, or token-level diffs against the baseline rather than requiring exact matches (LLM eval pipelines, 2024-2026).
Generated code verification: pin the exact output of OpenAPI client generators, GraphQL type generators, SDK wrappers, or database migration previews so formatting and structural changes are caught.
Database schema migration testing: capture the before/after output of migration scripts for a set of schema variants, approving only intentional structural differences.
Computer vision pipeline regression: pin bounding-box distributions or classification confidence vectors from CV models across runs; statistical comparison prevents flaky failures from minor pixel noise.
Smart contract and blockchain output regression: pin deterministic contract outputs for a given input state; any divergence in on-chain behaviour is immediately visible (Nexlify case, 2025).
Database-engine regression suites: PostgreSQL's pg_regress replays each sql/*.sql script and diffs results/*.out against committed golden files in expected/*, with variant comparison files and a resultmap absorbing known platform differences (locale, float formatting, row ordering).
Compiler test corpora: LLVM's lit/FileCheck pins emitted IR and machine code by piping compiler output to FileCheck, which verifies CHECK directives committed inside each test file across the whole input corpus.
ORM query-change detection: ApprovalTests.Ruby's verify_sql approves the SQL an ActiveRecord call emits, so a gem or framework upgrade that silently rewrites generated queries fails the suite.

name: watchman
document:
watchman
dead man's switch
heartbeat monitor
Detect that a message flow has gone silent - not that a message failed - and tell a responsible person or system within a bounded time by comparing each flow's arrivals against the cadence its business deadline implies.
Message systems fail silently in the one way no error handler observes: nothing arrives. A producer stops emitting, a consumer stops draining, a scheduled job never fires, a credential expires, a partition goes offline - and because no failing code path is ever entered, error dashboards stay green while downstream data quietly goes stale. The recurring trigger: a flow whose absence is business-visible (a nightly feed, an order stream, a partner interface) has no owner-facing signal for 'no messages', so the gap is discovered late - by a customer or a downstream job - instead of by the team that can fix it.
Applies wherever messages are expected on a knowable cadence (event streams, queues, batch hand-offs, partner interfaces, device check-ins) and their absence is a business-visible failure: the flow has an owner, the expected period and grace window can be derived from a downstream deadline, and either the transport can be observed passively (queue counters, a wire tap) or the producers can emit out-of-band heartbeats. The watchman sits at message-flow or boundary scope - an in-process watcher beside the consumer, a periodic sweep over persisted last-seen state, or a rule in the monitoring stack fed by metrics - and it must itself be watched, because a silent watchman is exactly the failure it exists to catch.
Nightly batch or ETL feed: page the integration owner when the 02:00 import has produced no messages by its deadline, instead of noticing an empty report at the morning stand-up.
Business-critical event stream (orders, payments, telemetry): alarm when the produce rate stays at zero through business hours, which separates a healthy quiet topic from a stopped producer.
External partner interface: notify when no messages have arrived from a B2B partner within the agreed window, turning a looming SLA breach into an early, actionable alert.
Long-running workflow stage: require a heartbeat from each process-manager step so a stuck instance is noticed before the surrounding batch closes or a compensation becomes necessary.
Retry or dead-letter pump: verify that the pump still drains failed messages - silence means the pump died, not that the backlog is empty.
Fleet check-ins (edge devices, agents, cron jobs on many hosts): raise a per-device or per-site alarm when scheduled check-ins stop arriving.
The alerting pipeline itself: an always-firing watchdog alert routed to an external service, so a broken alert path is discovered by its silence.
Cron and scheduled-job fleet via Healthchecks.io: each job pings a unique URL, the service holds the Period and Grace Time, flips the check Late then Down when no ping arrives by period + grace, and notifies integrations.
Dashboard alert rules in Grafana: an alert rule whose query returns no series enters the No Data state and can raise a DatasourceNoData alert - the platform form of deciding what silence means (No Data, Alerting, Normal or Keep last state).
Apache Burrow for Kafka (LinkedIn): committed offsets are evaluated per partition over a sliding window and a consumer is classified STALLED when its offset is frozen with non-zero lag, or STOPPED when no new commits arrive - consumer-silence detection without fixed lag thresholds.

name: audit-interceptor
document:
audit-interceptor
audit trail interceptor
audit logging interceptor
Declare an audit policy at an invocation seam that records the actor, action, target, correlation id and both attempt and terminal outcome around a delegated operation, then sends the structured event to a dedicated integrity-protected sink, so security accountability is consistent without inline logging in every service.
Security-relevant operations (privileged actions, state changes and access to sensitive data) must be attributable, but inline logging misses denied and failed attempts, varies in schema, can leak raw arguments and disappears with a rolled-back transaction. Teams also need to cover components they cannot modify without pretending that a proxy sees calls that bypass it.
Business or service tiers whose sensitive operations pass through an interceptable seam: container-managed beans, proxied service objects, ORM entity lifecycles, message endpoints or an HTTP pipeline. Audit selection must be declarative and uniform, while the sink has its own integrity and retention requirements (Secure Logger); the design must make mediation gaps, redaction, transaction coupling, failure policy, clock source and correlation propagation explicit.
Business-tier auditing of money-moving or otherwise regulated operations (fund transfer, order placement, claim submission): who requested it, on which object, when, and whether it succeeded.
Privileged administration surfaces (role changes, key rotation, configuration changes) where every sensitive operation must leave a record naming the acting principal.
Authentication and authorization outcomes: successful and failed logins, access-denial decisions and lockouts routed into the same audit pipeline instead of ad-hoc log lines.
Access-to-sensitive-data events (who read which patient/customer record) recorded at the gateway or service boundary to satisfy data-protection obligations.
Retrofitting auditing onto legacy components whose code cannot be modified, by wrapping the service object or binding an interceptor to its interface.
Middleware-level auditing of message endpoints and database calls in a business tier, correlating the caller's subject with the operation performed.
Financial API request interception (Spring Boot global request interceptors) capturing who accessed which endpoint, with what payload, and what outcome — satisfying SOX financial reporting controls.
Entity-level change tracking via ORM subscribers (e.g., EF Core SaveChangesInterceptor, TypeORM subscribers): automatically diff old vs. new property values on create/update/delete and emit audit envelopes without manual logging calls.
API gateway-level audit logging: capture every external API call with timestamp, user identity, endpoint, method, and outcome, correlating across microservices via X-Request-ID / traceparent headers.
Compliance reporting automation: generate audit-ready reports for SOX (~7-year retention), HIPAA (~6-year retention), GDPR (data residency-aware), and PCI-DSS from structured interceptor events.
Zero-trust data access trails: record every read of sensitive fields (PHI, PII, financial data) so data-protection obligations (GDPR Article 5 data minimization, HIPAA access logging) are demonstrably met.
Hibernate Envers: @Audited entity lifecycle changes create per-entity _AUD revisions at transaction commit; a custom revision entity/listener can attach actor or request metadata.
Django admin: django.contrib.admin.models.LogEntry records action time, user, object, addition/change/deletion and change_message for ModelAdmin activity.
Rails Audited: the audited ActiveRecord extension creates audit rows for model create, update and destroy callbacks, including changed attributes and optional acting-user attribution.

name: producer-consumer
document:
producer-consumer
bounded buffer
consumer-producer
Insert a bounded buffer between producers and consumers of work items so the two sides run concurrently at their own rates, the buffer absorbs bursts and slack, and its bound turns overload into backpressure, queueing or an explicit drop policy instead of unbounded growth.
Production and consumption proceed at different rates: a fast producer outruns its consumer and either drops items or grows a backlog until memory runs out, a slow producer leaves consumers idle, and bursts arrive faster than they can be processed. Wiring the two sides together directly also couples their lifetimes and schedules - a synchronous hand-off makes the faster side wait for the slower - so neither side can be scaled, restarted or tested on its own.
Concurrent in-process software (threads, tasks, coroutines, event-loop callbacks) with one or more producers and one or more consumers that can run at the same time but not at the same average rate. The buffer is a component-level data structure owned by the application - a work queue for a thread pool, a pipeline hand-off, a logging or telemetry sink - not a durable broker, so the decisions are how to hand items over, how to bound the queue and how to end the arrangement cleanly.
Work queues behind thread or worker pools: request handlers enqueue tasks and a fixed set of workers consumes them, so pool size is independent of the arrival rate. Industry examples: Celery (Python), Sidekiq (Ruby), BullMQ (Node.js) all use this shape with Redis or a broker as the durable backing store.
Asynchronous logging and telemetry: hot paths enqueue records cheaply while a background writer drains, formats and writes them, keeping I/O latency off the request path. Structured log collectors (Fluent Bit, Vector) ingest from many sources into one consumer.
Multi-stage data pipelines (decode - transform - encode, extract - transform - load): bounded queues between stages give each stage its own workers and let a slow stage backpressure a fast one. Used in media transcoding, ETL workflows, and stream processors.
Ingestion buffers: a socket, file or broker reader produces records faster than the processing or indexing stage can absorb them, and the buffer smooths the mismatch without dropping data. Common in IoT telemetry ingestion, click-stream collection, and log aggregation.
UI/host integration: a background thread posts work or results to the main/event-loop thread's queue and vice versa, keeping the UI responsive without locks around application state. All major GUI frameworks (Qt, Swing, Flutter) use this internally.
Batch job scheduling: producers enqueue compute jobs (image resize, PDF generation, report creation) and a pool of consumers processes them. Systems like Celery, Hangfire, and AWS SQS follow this pattern, often with priority queues, delayed execution, and dead-letter routing.
Event streaming pre-processing: a Kafka, Pulsar, or NATS consumer-producer chain filters, transforms, and routes events through a series of bounded queues before landing in a data warehouse or search index.
Simulation and testing: a producer generates a deterministic stream of items while a consumer asserts on what it receives, with a sentinel marking the end of the stream. Property-based testing frameworks use this to drive scenario generation.
Print spooling and document processing: print jobs or document conversion tasks are queued and processed by a pool of workers, with bounded queues preventing runaway memory use even under burst load.
ML inference pipelines: a model-serving host receives requests via an API, enqueues them into a bounded queue, and a pool of worker coroutines or threads dequeues and runs inference. The queue decouples HTTP latency from inference latency and provides backpressure when the model GPU is saturated. Tools like Ray Serve, Triton Inference Server, and TorchServe use this shape.
Streaming audio/video processing: a media pipeline (capture - encode - mux - stream) uses bounded queues between stages; frames that arrive during a temporary encoding stall are buffered rather than dropped, and a full encoder output queue backpressures the camera capture stage to prevent unbounded memory growth from frame accumulation.
WebSocket connection management: a server's accept loop enqueues new connections into a bounded connection queue; a pool of handler coroutines or threads dequeues and upgrades them, preventing connection exhaustion under burst load while the handler pool limits concurrency independently of the arrival rate.
Financial order processing: high-frequency trading systems receive market data feeds (producer) and route orders through risk checks and execution engines (consumers), with bounded queues between stages preventing downstream latency from backpressuring the market data ingestion and applying backpressure to upstream feed handlers.
Go channel pipelines: a source goroutine produces values into a channel, transformation stages consume and emit through downstream channels, and a sink drains the final stage. Go's documented pipeline pattern makes channel closure and cancellation part of the producer-consumer lifecycle.
Python asyncio worker queues: an asyncio.Queue(maxsize=N) accepts work from coroutine producers while worker coroutines await get(), process items and call task_done(); finite maxsize suspends producers when consumers fall behind.
Java executor work queues: java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue coordinates multiple producer threads and consumer workers, with put()/take() waiting on full and empty capacity so an Executor-style worker pool can be bounded independently of arrival rate.

name: table-data-gateway
document:
table-data-gateway
table gateway
Confine every SQL statement that touches one table or view inside a single gateway object whose methods take and return plain record structures, so that no other code contains SQL for that table and rows cross the boundary as data rather than as domain objects.
Access to one table is spread across the codebase: SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE fragments are copied into every caller, nobody can say which queries a schema change will break, DBAs cannot find the SQL that needs tuning, and each caller has to know the dialect, the placeholders and the column order. The desired boundary is a single object that mediates all access to the whole table while the individual rows remain records (tuples, structs, hashes, DataRows) instead of becoming mapped objects.
Relational persistence where the database is a stable, schema-first integration point and SQL-level control matters (indexes, hints, bulk loads, vendor features), where the team deliberately does not want O/R mapping machinery in the domain layer, and where the domain logic is simple enough that rows may travel as records - CRUD and query services, reporting/read models, ETL writers, local SQLite stores, or a legacy database mediated for several applications. It is also the packaging decision for 'the SQL has to live somewhere well known' before a DAO, repository or query object is justified.
A service or CRUD application over a handful of tables where every screen maps to a few statements per table and an ORM would add more machinery than it removes.
Reporting and read models: read-only gateways over views or wide tables that return records directly to a formatter, export or BI job.
Legacy databases mediated for several applications: one gateway library per database becomes the documented API and the place where vendor quirks are hidden.
Embedded/local storage (SQLite, SQLCipher) in a desktop or mobile app, where one gateway per table keeps SQL out of the UI and can be tested with an in-memory database.
Batch and ETL writers that need explicit control over statement batching, cursors and transaction size - control that generated mappers hide.
Gradual refactoring of SQL scattered through transaction scripts: the first step is to move each table's statements into a gateway, after which a Data Mapper or repository can be introduced deliberately.
Test fixtures and seeders that must write through the same statements as production code rather than through a second, divergent SQL path.
Generated gateways in Go: sqlc compiles a schema plus a file of named queries into one struct per table and one type-safe method per SQL statement, with the caller holding the database handle and opening transactions - the gateway's invariants are then enforced by the generator and compiler rather than by convention.
Local SQLite storage on Android: each Room @Dao is a gateway over one table - the SQL lives in @Query-annotated methods validated at compile time, rows travel as plain entity data classes, and @Transaction or database-level transactions keep atomic multi-DAO boundaries in the caller.
Java teams that want the gateway structure without hand-writing it: jOOQ's code generator emits one DAO class per table or view (findAll, findById, generated fetchByColumn methods) that reads and writes Record/POJO rows and borrows the caller's Configuration, so the per-table SQL surface is regenerated when the schema changes.

name: active-record
document:
active-record
active record pattern
ActiveRecord
Make a domain object the record for one database row: keep the row's state, row-local behavior, and the methods that find and persist it together, so a small domain does not pay for a separate mapping layer.
A simple relational domain still needs a choice about where persistence lives. A Data Mapper or gateway separates table I/O from the object but adds mapping code and a second place to navigate, while direct SQL leaks schema knowledge into callers; the recurring question is whether one row object can own its data and CRUD without hiding transaction boundaries or pretending to model cross-row rules.
A relational store is the single system of record, the domain is small and its rules are mostly local to one row (validation, derivations, simple state transitions), and the team prefers a convention-driven persistence layer over a designed one. Typical homes are framework ecosystems where the ORM is the house style (Rails, Laravel Eloquent, Django, GORM, Vapor Fluent, TypeORM), CRUD-heavy applications, and thin layers over an already well-shaped legacy schema. Entity Framework Core can host behavior on entity classes, but its DbContext and mapping conventions are a Data Mapper-shaped boundary rather than pure Active Record. It stops applying as soon as invariants span several objects, several representations of one table are needed, or the store must be swappable.
CRUD-heavy applications where most screens and endpoints map onto a single table: forms, admin back offices, catalogs, content management.
Small-to-medium domains whose rules are mostly per-row - field validation, derived values, one-row state transitions - so a mapper layer would move data around without adding a model.
Prototypes and thin service layers over an existing, already normalised legacy schema where the table shape is stable and the domain is the schema.
Framework-default persistence: a Rails, Django, GORM, Vapor Fluent or TypeORM codebase where fighting the ORM for purity costs more than it returns.
Simple record-shaped bounded contexts inside a larger system - settings, audit entries, lookup tables - where a full domain model would be overhead.
JSON:API or REST backends for SPAs and mobile apps where the data model maps directly to a relational schema with minimal transformation.
Microservices with a single-responsibility data store: a service whose entire bounded context is one aggregate root table or a handful of tightly coupled tables.
Batch import pipelines where records are validated once and bulk-inserted (insert_all/upsert_all), and the domain logic has already been applied before the bulk operation.
Multi-tenant SaaS backends where row-level isolation is enforced at the database and the ORM connection handles tenant scoping automatically.
Real Rails systems such as GitLab and Discourse are good fits for row-shaped users, posts, permissions and settings backed by PostgreSQL; keep their reporting and cross-record workflows in query or service boundaries.
A Django or Laravel CRUD surface such as an admin or back-office module fits when each request mostly validates, loads, changes and saves one model; switch to a mapper or repository when the same data feeds materially different contracts.

name: dynamic-router
document:
dynamic-router
dynamic routing
rules-based routing
Route each message to a destination chosen from a rule base that can be changed while the system runs, so the router never depends on - or is redeployed for - the set of destinations it serves.
Routing logic hard-coded into the router (switch chains, static filter tables, deployment-time route configuration) couples it to every destination: adding, moving, throttling or retiring a destination needs a code change, a review and a restart, and each topology change forces the router back through the release process instead of being an operational edit.
Message-based integration where the destination set or the routing policy changes faster than the router's release cycle: rules are owned by operations, destinations announce themselves, scale out, or go down for maintenance, or one router instance serves several tenants or environments. Applies when the route can be expressed as rules over message content, headers or context evaluated per message, and the platform offers a usable control channel (config watch, control bus, admin endpoint, hot-reloadable table) to publish rule changes.
Multi-tenant integration hub: each tenant has its own routing table, loaded and swapped per tenant instead of one deployed router per tenant.
Event distribution where downstream teams add or retire consumers by publishing routing conditions rather than requesting a router release.
Canary and blue/green rollouts: send a slice of traffic to a new destination by editing a rule, and roll back by restoring the previous rule set.
Maintenance windows: reroute a destination's traffic to a standby, drain the destination, then restore the rule when it returns.
Regional or sharded routing where the region-to-destination mapping is maintained by operations and changes with capacity, not with code.
Rule-driven enterprise integration in the classic EIP sense, where a rule base is consulted per message and recipients announce themselves on a control channel.
Kubernetes Gateway API traffic splitting: use HTTPRoute weighted backends to shift a configurable percentage of traffic between versions without redeploying the router.
Service mesh canary deployments: an Istio VirtualService or Linkerd ServiceProfile acts as the rule base; routing rules are edited at runtime to steer canary traffic, then promoted or rolled back.
Multi-tenant SaaS routing: Spring Cloud Gateway or Envoy.DynamicRouter loads per-tenant routing rules from a registry, injecting tenant-specific headers or rewrites so one router instance serves hundreds of isolated tenants.
API version routing and A/B testing: route by Accept header, API version path prefix, or experimentCohort header to different backend versions, controlled by rules updated without a release.
Database or cache sharding: route a tenant or user ID hash to the correct shard's endpoint via a rule table that is repointed during resharding without touching application code.
BGP route-server testing: use a chaos-testing framework against a route server to validate that policy changes converge correctly and do not produce route leaks before production deployment.
Traefik dynamic configuration: Traefik builds its routing table at runtime from providers (Docker labels, Kubernetes IngressRoute, Consul/etcd KV stores), so services announce their own routes and rule changes hot-swap without restarting the proxy.
HAProxy Runtime API: add server and set server state/weight over the runtime socket repoint and drain backends without a reload; the Data Plane API layers persistence and validation on top of these runtime changes.
Kong Gateway admin API: Routes - including the expressions DSL when router_flavor is set to expressions - are created and updated at runtime via POST /routes and take effect on the next matching request, with priority-ordered rule evaluation replacing a redeployed config.

name: extensible-visitor
document:
extensible-visitor
extensible visitor pattern
extensible visitors with defaults
Keep the visitor open on both axes at once - new element kinds and new operations arrive without editing or recompiling any visitor that already exists - by giving every visitor a default method that catches element kinds it was not written for, introducing extended element kinds under an intermediate base whose accept hooks overload (not override) accept, and extending an operation by subclassing the existing concrete visitor so it inherits every case it already handled.
A classic Visitor is cheap in one direction only: a new operation is a new visitor, but a new element kind forces every visitor to grow one more method, so shipped visitors must be edited and redeployed. The trigger is an element hierarchy that is extended by parties who do not own the operations - language dialects, plugin node types, versioned grammars, third-party message formats - where the existing operations must keep working unchanged on the extended structure.
Recursively defined element hierarchies (abstract syntax trees, intermediate representations, document and message models) that grow over time, in a statically typed language whose visitors are concrete classes or interfaces with default bodies, and where the traversal logic itself lives inside the operations. It pays off when old operations must run against new element kinds and when element kinds are added by a different team than the operations; it assumes the visitor protocol can carry a default case and that a runtime type test is acceptable on the dispatch path.
A compiler front-end whose node kinds are extended by language dialects while every existing analysis pass keeps running unchanged (the extensible-compiler case the pattern was derived from).
An IDE or linter analysing a versioned language grammar: the version-1 analysis must not be recompiled when version 2 adds syntax nodes it does not understand.
Plugin systems where third-party modules contribute new node types (document formats, workflow elements, protocol messages) to a host that ships the operations.
Optimisation or lowering pipelines whose passes are shipped separately from the node hierarchy: the platform team adds representations, users add passes.
A published visitor API where other teams implement visitors and the element set grows every release, making 'which kinds does this visitor handle' an explicit, versioned contract.
Migration and validation tooling that must keep working on messages produced by newer producers than the tool itself.
Serialization and schema-generation frameworks such as Jackson's JsonFormatVisitor API, which uses a visitor to traverse Java type hierarchies for JSON/XML schema generation and allows third-party serializers to contribute handlers for new POJO shapes without modifying the core framework.
Query engines over tree-structured data (e.g. Apache Calcite's relational algebra, Rascal's AST analysis): new relational operators or AST node types are contributed by extension modules while existing optimisers and evaluators continue to function unchanged.
Static analysis and bug-finding tools (Coverity, CodeQL, ESLint plugin architectures): new checker plugins add new node-type coverage while the core traversal engine ships unchanged, and old checkers degrade gracefully over unknown node types.
Game engine entity-component systems: new component types are contributed at runtime while existing systems (physics, rendering, AI) continue to process entities; the visitor with default case handles component types added after a given system was written.
Python's ast.NodeVisitor: visit() dispatches to a visit_<Node> method and falls back to generic_visit as the built-in default case, so analysis tools written before newer node kinds existed (Match, TryStar, TypeAlias) keep traversing Python's evolving AST unchanged, exactly the degrade-don't-break contract of the pattern.
The JDK Compiler Tree API (com.sun.source.tree.TreeVisitor / SimpleTreeVisitor): every visit method defaults to visitOther/defaultAction as the catch-all, so javac-based tooling written against Java 8 trees keeps compiling and running as Java adds records, patterns and switch labels - old visitors land in visitOther instead of failing.
Roslyn's CSharpSyntaxVisitor / CSharpSyntaxWalker: the generated visitor carries one Visit method per syntax node kind plus DefaultVisit as the default case, and each C# language version extends the node hierarchy while existing analysers and the compiler's own passes keep working over the extended tree.

name: guarded-suspension
document:
guarded-suspension
conditional block
suspended execution
Suspend a state-dependent method call inside the object that owns the state until another thread makes its guard predicate true, so callers neither poll nor get refused while the object is temporarily not ready.
A method may only proceed while a precondition over shared state holds - a buffer is non-empty, a pool still has a free lease, a session is authenticated, a worker has a task - and that state is produced by another thread at an unknown time. The recurring decision is what the caller should do while the guard is false: refusing the request would drop work the application still needs, forcing the transition would break the object's invariants, and polling wastes a core and still races. Guarded suspension answers it by waiting on a condition the object itself owns, and by making that wait atomic with respect to the state change that ends it.
Concurrent objects whose methods are state-dependent and whose state changes arrive from other threads: bounded buffers and handoff queues, resource pools, server request/response handoffs, readiness and shutdown gates, worker idle loops. Applicable where the runtime can efficiently park or suspend a caller (OS threads, coroutines) and where the object already owns a lock or monitor, so no notification can be lost between the predicate check and the wait. Ill-suited to single-threaded event loops, to callers that must never be delayed, and to waits whose eventual completion cannot be guaranteed.
Actor mailbox handoff: an Akka/Orleans/Swift-Actor mailbox is a lock-free guarded queue; the actor suspends on an empty mailbox and resumes when a message arrives, which is the same monitor-wait pattern expressed at the language level.
Swift async / Structured Concurrency: a Task.sleep or async let that suspends until a condition is a coroutine-level guarded suspension; the suspension point is backed by a condition variable or event channel inside the runtime.
CompletableFuture / async result: a future's blocking get() is a timed guarded suspension on the thread that submitted the asynchronous operation; the completion path (complete()) is the notifier.
Pipeline stage coordination: in a multi-stage streaming pipeline each stage blocks on input while the upstream stage processes, synchronising via a bounded channel whose put/get implement the guard.
Bounded buffers and handoff queues: a consumer's take waits while the buffer is empty and a producer's put waits while it is full (producer-consumer).
Resource pools: acquire blocks until a lease is returned to a connection, thread or object pool instead of failing or spinning when the pool is exhausted.
Server-side handoff: an acceptor or reader thread publishes a request and the worker waits for work to appear; a caller waits for the response slot to be filled.
Readiness and start-up gates: components wait until a dependency reports connected, initialised or ready, and callers wait until a session, device or circuit is open.
Shutdown and flush coordination: a terminator waits until in-flight work has drained, and a flusher waits while the buffer still holds entries (two-phase termination).
Platform queue and channel APIs: BlockingQueue.take/put, Queue#pop, Channel.receive/for-await, condition-variable waits - the same guard hidden behind a library type.
Project Loom virtual threads (JEP 444): a virtual thread calling Object.wait() parks its Continuation; the carrier thread is released for other virtual threads, so the program continues throughput while one virtual thread waits. The guarded action still re-checks the predicate on wake, and the pattern's semantics are preserved — only the threading model changes.
Akka typed actor mailbox: each actor has a single-threaded mailbox; receive() suspends the actor's continuation when the mailbox is empty, resuming when a message is dispatched. This is language-level guarded suspension where the wait set is the mailbox queue and the guard is 'mailbox non-empty'.
Kotlin coroutines rendezvous channel: Channel() (unbuffered/rendezvous) suspends the sender until a receiver is ready, and vice versa — the same lock-free handoff as an unbuffered Go channel. The suspension is a coroutine-level guarded wait on rendezvous.
Python asyncio.Condition: an async context manager that wraps an asyncio.Lock; await cond.wait() releases the lock and suspends the task until notify() is called, making it an async guarded suspension where the runtime schedules other tasks during the wait.
Go unbuffered channel send/receive: goroutine G1 executing ch <- x on an unbuffered channel sleeps (gopark) until goroutine G2 executes <-ch, at which point the runtime directly transfers the value and stack copy (rendezvous handoff). This is the language-level form of guarded suspension: the guard is 'receiver present', the wait set is the sudog queue in hchan.
Erlang/OTP process mailbox: a gen_server receiving messages from its mailbox blocks (receive...end) until a matching message arrives — the OTP process is a state machine whose transitions are guarded by message arrival, making each receive a suspension point in the actor's event loop.
.NET TaskCompletionSource<T>: GetAwaiter().GetResult() on a not-yet-completed TCS is a synchronous guarded suspension; the async continuation (ConfigureAwait, await) is an asynchronous one. SetResult() is the notifier. TCS is a one-shot asymmetric guarded suspension where one side never waits (the completor) and one side always waits (the synchronously blocked caller).
JDK ArrayBlockingQueue: the queue is one ReentrantLock plus two Condition objects, notEmpty and notFull - take() awaits notEmpty while count == 0, put() awaits notFull while the buffer is full, and each signals the other condition only after mutating count and the circular buffer inside the same critical section. It is the reference production realisation of a two-predicate guarded suspension, including the fairness switch and the timed offer/poll variants.
Go standard library: database/sql guards queries against a concurrent Close with closingMutex, which parks readers and the closing writer on two sync.Cond values (read/write), and net/http's Server.Shutdown waits until in-flight requests have drained. Both are the case Go's own guidance reserves sync.Cond for - a predicate that changes back and forth over time rather than a one-shot handoff.
HikariCP connection pool: DataSource.getConnection() suspends the caller until a lease is returned while the pool already holds maximumPoolSize connections, bounded by connectionTimeout (default 30000 ms, minimum 250 ms), after which it throws SQLException rather than waiting on - a guarded suspension in which the deadline is a documented, first-class outcome instead of an accident.

name: version-number
document:
version-number
rowversion
entity versioning
Store a version token alongside each persistent record and make every write assert the token it read, so a write computed from stale data fails as a detectable conflict instead of silently overwriting a newer value.
Two sessions read the same record, both edit it, and the later write wins: the earlier update vanishes without any error (the lost update). Once the read-modify-write spans more than one system transaction the database cannot tell 'this is the record I read' from 'this record changed under me', so no code path can notice in time - unless the record itself carries a per-row token that changes on every write and the write tests that token before committing.
Applies to records that outlive the transaction that read them: edits spanning user think time, a web form round-trip, an offline client, a batch worker holding aggregates, or any read-modify-write over data other writers touch in between. It needs a store that can test the token and change the record in one atomic step (a conditional UPDATE, a compare-and-swap, a document revision check) and a caller willing to act on the conflict - re-read, merge, retry, or report. It assumes conflicts are the exception; when they are the rule a pessimistic lock prevents the wasted work instead.
Web forms and editors: a record is loaded into a page, edited for minutes or hours, then saved - the token makes the stale save fail instead of clobbering the other editor's change.
Distributed workers applying commands to the same entity: the second worker's write is rejected so it can refresh and re-apply, giving first-writer-wins with no held lock.
Data mappers and units of work: every dirty entity flushed at commit carries the version it was loaded with, so the whole transaction aborts on the first stale row.
Document stores and revision-based APIs: Mongoose's __v with optimisticConcurrency, CouchDB-style revisions, or a REST ETag/If-Match precondition all expose the same per-document token.
Leases, leader election and configuration records: one row represents ownership or a monotonic generation, and a write must prove it still holds the revision it acted on.
Offline or mobile sync: clients push edits made against a snapshot taken days earlier, and the version check decides which edits apply directly and which must go through a merge.
Hibernate ORM / JPA @Version: the mapper owns an integer (or timestamp) version property, appends it to every UPDATE's WHERE clause, bumps it on flush and raises StaleObjectStateException / OptimisticLockException when zero rows match, so the application code never writes the predicate by hand.
DynamoDB conditional writes: each item carries a Version attribute; UpdateItem sends ConditionExpression 'Version = :read_value' and increments Version in the same request, and ConditionalCheckFailedException is the conflict signal that triggers a bounded re-read-and-retry — the same contract exposed as @DynamoDBVersionAttribute in the enhanced client.
Cassandra lightweight transactions: UPDATE ... SET col = ? WHERE id = ? IF col = ? is a Paxos-backed compare-and-set, giving the token test linearizable semantics across replicas — at a documented cost (roughly four extra round-trips per conditional write), so it is reserved for rows that genuinely need the guard.

name: implicit-lock
document:
implicit-lock
framework-managed locking
automatic locking
Make the framework or layer-supertype code that every business operation must pass through acquire and release the locks, so no application method can forget an acquisition and silently invalidate the concurrency policy.
A locking scheme has no gaps only if every path that touches a lockable item acquires its lock: one forgotten acquisition, one lock released too early or too late, makes the whole offline concurrency strategy useless. Because the error shows up only under concurrent conflicting sessions, it survives unit tests, code review and single-user manual testing.
Multi-user enterprise applications whose business transactions outlive a single database transaction - a user reads a record, thinks for minutes, then saves - so locks live in a lock table or in version columns rather than in the database transaction. Typically a Unit of Work, a layer supertype, a session facade or a declarative transaction layer already exists, giving the application a place that can own the locking protocol centrally.
Request-as-business-transaction: a web application where an ORM Unit of Work or declarative transaction (Spring @Transactional, .NET TransactionScope, Django ATOMIC_REQUESTS) acquires the row locks or version checks for every record the request reads and writes.
Offline edit sessions: a user edits a record for minutes, and the session facade or layer supertype acquires a pessimistic lock when the record enters the business transaction and releases it on commit or abort, so no controller can forget it.
Batch and import jobs that modify aggregates: each chunk runs inside the framework's transactional scope, so locking follows the changed aggregates automatically.
In-process shared state in a service or worker: a scope construct (RAII guard, with block, defer, using declaration, withLock closure) binds release to the lexical block so exceptions and early returns cannot leak the lock.
Multi-tier clients with a session facade: the lock must follow the business transaction rather than the HTTP request, so the facade — not the UI — owns acquisition and release.
Optimistic concurrency: the mapper compares and increments the version column inside the framework's update path, so a hand-written UPDATE statement cannot skip the check.
Microservices saga orchestrator: the orchestrator drives each step inside an implicit transaction scope; each participant's framework layer acquires the lock or version check locally so the saga can compensate without distributed deadlocks.
Event-sourcing projections: a projection handler reads an event stream and writes to a read-model; the handler runs inside an implicit transaction so concurrent projection rebuilds do not corrupt the read-model — the framework decides whether to use optimistic or pessimistic locking based on the change set.
CQRS read-model updates: commands update the write model under an implicit write lock; the read-model update is published as an async event; the projection runs under its own implicit scope with conflict detection (optimistic) rather than blocking (pessimistic).
Database advisory locks for cross-connection coordination: an application holds a PostgreSQL advisory lock across a multi-statement business transaction that is not itself a DB transaction (e.g., involves an external HTTP call in the middle); the lock is acquired via a thin wrapper so callers do not call pg_advisory_lock directly.
Container-managed persistence (EJB CMT, Spring @Transactional): the container acquires and releases locks as part of the transaction lifecycle; developers write business methods without explicit lock calls, relying on the container's implicit concurrency control.
Retry and compensation with implicit lock release: when a business transaction fails after the lock is acquired but before commit, the framework's rollback path releases the lock automatically so the compensating transaction can retry without manual unlock calls.
Spring Framework proxy-managed services: a proxied @Transactional service method is the business entry point; Spring starts or joins the transaction for external calls, so persistence work and its configured optimistic or pessimistic checks stay inside one framework-owned boundary.
Hibernate ORM persistence contexts: an EntityManager or Session transaction can apply @Version optimistic checks or an explicit PESSIMISTIC_WRITE LockMode at the framework boundary, keeping lock acquisition and stale-version detection out of business methods.
EF Core Unit of Work: SaveChanges compares configured concurrency tokens, including SQL Server rowversion, and raises DbUpdateConcurrencyException on a stale update, making the version check implicit in the framework's commit path rather than a hand-written UPDATE predicate.

name: composed-method
document:
composed-method
compose method
Divide the work into methods that each perform one identifiable task, written as a short outline of invocations in which every operation sits at the same level of abstraction, so a reader grasps the task top-down and every change lands on one small, named step.
A method accumulates several concerns at once: high-level policy ('validate the order, then charge it') interleaved with low-level detail (a loop index, a string concatenation, a counter), so the method grows long, needs comments to mark its sections, and changes for more than one reason. Readers must simulate the whole body to learn what it does, duplication hides inside similar-looking blocks, and anyone who must change one decision - a subclass in particular - ends up copying the method and editing it.
Applies wherever code is decomposed into named routines and is read far more often than written: long-lived domain and application code, code review and onboarding, framework base classes that must expose override hooks, and code whose steps carry contracts worth testing separately. It is a source-level discipline rather than a runtime structure, so a language needs only routines and some notion of non-public helpers; it matters most exactly where methods have grown past the point a reader can hold them in mind.
Long methods built up over time whose sections are marked by comments: each comment becomes a step name and the method becomes an outline.
A method with several responsibilities (validate, compute, persist) that must change independently and be reviewed one concern at a time.
Framework or library base classes that must offer override points: each step becomes a documented extension point, usually combined with Template Method or NVI.
Top-down design of an algorithm: write the outline first, with steps as not-yet-implemented calls, and fill them in one at a time.
Bottom-up refactoring when the same block appears in several methods: extract it as a named step and call it from each outline.
Making behaviour testable in isolation: steps with their own contracts (parsing input, rounding money, validating rules) become separately testable units.
TDD workflow: write the test for the composed method outline first, asserting each step in sequence, then implement each step as a separate testable unit.
Complex business rules that combine multiple conditional branches: decompose each branch condition and its body into a clearly named step, making the rule engine visible and auditable.
Command or handler objects that orchestrate a multi-step process (validate request, authorize caller, execute operation, emit event, log outcome): each phase is a named step in the composed method.
Production Rails code: Basecamp's Event::Relaying#relay_now reads as an outline of named steps (relay_to_or_revoke_from_timeline, relay_to_webhooks_later), each descending into its own relayer class - the 'fractal' consistency of composed methods in a shipped product, documented by 37signals.
Acceptance and integration test suites: each scenario is written as a composed method at a single level of abstraction (sign_in, create_todo, mark_complete), delegating the mechanics to named helpers or page objects so the test tells the user-level story.
JUnit 4's refactored internals: Beck documents TestCase together with the RunAfter, ExpectException and FailedTest method objects as chained composed outlines, each invocation staying at one level of abstraction (his 'Nested Method Object' evolution of the pattern).

name: pratt-parser
document:
pratt-parser
top-down operator precedence
tdop
Parse expressions with many prefix, infix and postfix operators by associating a binding power and a handler with each token type, so precedence and associativity live in one rule table instead of one parsing function per precedence level.
Operator precedence turns expression parsing into a ladder of near-identical functions - one per level - each of which must re-implement associativity, delegate to the next level for its operands, and be edited whenever an operator is added or moves. Grammars with prefix, infix, postfix and mixfix operators (ternary conditionals, assignment, calls, indexing, user-registered operators) make that ladder long, make associativity easy to get subtly wrong, and scatter the grammar across the parser so it cannot be read in one place.
Hand-written parsers for an expression-bearing language, DSL, query or configuration syntax: a token stream is already available (or is cheap to lex), the operator set is large or expected to grow, and the team wants the grammar visible as data. It is typically the expression layer under an ordinary recursive-descent parser for statements and declarations - interpreters, calculators, filter and rule engines, formula tools - and it is unnecessary when a parser generator already declares precedence for the grammar.
Expression evaluators and calculators whose operator set is expected to grow (arithmetic, units, comparisons, percentages, function calls, user-defined functions).
Query, filter and rule languages - search filters, feature-flag conditions, access-policy conditions, spreadsheet formulas - with many comparison, logical and string operators.
Front ends for small languages and DSLs that parse statements and declarations with recursive descent and need real precedence handling for the expression layer.
Single-pass compilers and interpreters that emit bytecode or IR while parsing, where each handler is also the point that emits the operator's instruction.
Template and configuration expression languages that must attach exact source positions and precise errors to every operator.
Host-language extension points that let plugins or users register additional operators at runtime, because registration is just a table entry.
Rust PEG grammars that use pest::pratt_parser::PrattParser to map prefix, postfix and infix operator pairs into calculator or DSL ASTs.
Rust parser-combinator expression grammars built with chumsky's pratt combinator, where atom parsers and prefix, postfix and infix operators declare precedence and associativity.
JavaScript expression-only tooling built on JSEP, where a compact Pratt-style parser produces ASTs and allows custom unary and binary operators with explicit precedence.
