name: guarded-suspension
document:
guarded-suspension
conditional block
suspended execution
Suspend a state-dependent method call inside the object that owns the state until another thread makes its guard predicate true, so callers neither poll nor get refused while the object is temporarily not ready.
A method may only proceed while a precondition over shared state holds - a buffer is non-empty, a pool still has a free lease, a session is authenticated, a worker has a task - and that state is produced by another thread at an unknown time. The recurring decision is what the caller should do while the guard is false: refusing the request would drop work the application still needs, forcing the transition would break the object's invariants, and polling wastes a core and still races. Guarded suspension answers it by waiting on a condition the object itself owns, and by making that wait atomic with respect to the state change that ends it.
Concurrent objects whose methods are state-dependent and whose state changes arrive from other threads: bounded buffers and handoff queues, resource pools, server request/response handoffs, readiness and shutdown gates, worker idle loops. Applicable where the runtime can efficiently park or suspend a caller (OS threads, coroutines) and where the object already owns a lock or monitor, so no notification can be lost between the predicate check and the wait. Ill-suited to single-threaded event loops, to callers that must never be delayed, and to waits whose eventual completion cannot be guaranteed.
Actor mailbox handoff: an Akka/Orleans/Swift-Actor mailbox is a lock-free guarded queue; the actor suspends on an empty mailbox and resumes when a message arrives, which is the same monitor-wait pattern expressed at the language level.
Swift async / Structured Concurrency: a Task.sleep or async let that suspends until a condition is a coroutine-level guarded suspension; the suspension point is backed by a condition variable or event channel inside the runtime.
CompletableFuture / async result: a future's blocking get() is a timed guarded suspension on the thread that submitted the asynchronous operation; the completion path (complete()) is the notifier.
Pipeline stage coordination: in a multi-stage streaming pipeline each stage blocks on input while the upstream stage processes, synchronising via a bounded channel whose put/get implement the guard.
Bounded buffers and handoff queues: a consumer's take waits while the buffer is empty and a producer's put waits while it is full (producer-consumer).
Resource pools: acquire blocks until a lease is returned to a connection, thread or object pool instead of failing or spinning when the pool is exhausted.
Server-side handoff: an acceptor or reader thread publishes a request and the worker waits for work to appear; a caller waits for the response slot to be filled.
Readiness and start-up gates: components wait until a dependency reports connected, initialised or ready, and callers wait until a session, device or circuit is open.
Shutdown and flush coordination: a terminator waits until in-flight work has drained, and a flusher waits while the buffer still holds entries (two-phase termination).
Platform queue and channel APIs: BlockingQueue.take/put, Queue#pop, Channel.receive/for-await, condition-variable waits - the same guard hidden behind a library type.
Project Loom virtual threads (JEP 444): a virtual thread calling Object.wait() parks its Continuation; the carrier thread is released for other virtual threads, so the program continues throughput while one virtual thread waits. The guarded action still re-checks the predicate on wake, and the pattern's semantics are preserved — only the threading model changes.
Akka typed actor mailbox: each actor has a single-threaded mailbox; receive() suspends the actor's continuation when the mailbox is empty, resuming when a message is dispatched. This is language-level guarded suspension where the wait set is the mailbox queue and the guard is 'mailbox non-empty'.
Kotlin coroutines rendezvous channel: Channel() (unbuffered/rendezvous) suspends the sender until a receiver is ready, and vice versa — the same lock-free handoff as an unbuffered Go channel. The suspension is a coroutine-level guarded wait on rendezvous.
Python asyncio.Condition: an async context manager that wraps an asyncio.Lock; await cond.wait() releases the lock and suspends the task until notify() is called, making it an async guarded suspension where the runtime schedules other tasks during the wait.
Go unbuffered channel send/receive: goroutine G1 executing ch <- x on an unbuffered channel sleeps (gopark) until goroutine G2 executes <-ch, at which point the runtime directly transfers the value and stack copy (rendezvous handoff). This is the language-level form of guarded suspension: the guard is 'receiver present', the wait set is the sudog queue in hchan.
Erlang/OTP process mailbox: a gen_server receiving messages from its mailbox blocks (receive...end) until a matching message arrives — the OTP process is a state machine whose transitions are guarded by message arrival, making each receive a suspension point in the actor's event loop.
.NET TaskCompletionSource<T>: GetAwaiter().GetResult() on a not-yet-completed TCS is a synchronous guarded suspension; the async continuation (ConfigureAwait, await) is an asynchronous one. SetResult() is the notifier. TCS is a one-shot asymmetric guarded suspension where one side never waits (the completor) and one side always waits (the synchronously blocked caller).
JDK ArrayBlockingQueue: the queue is one ReentrantLock plus two Condition objects, notEmpty and notFull - take() awaits notEmpty while count == 0, put() awaits notFull while the buffer is full, and each signals the other condition only after mutating count and the circular buffer inside the same critical section. It is the reference production realisation of a two-predicate guarded suspension, including the fairness switch and the timed offer/poll variants.
Go standard library: database/sql guards queries against a concurrent Close with closingMutex, which parks readers and the closing writer on two sync.Cond values (read/write), and net/http's Server.Shutdown waits until in-flight requests have drained. Both are the case Go's own guidance reserves sync.Cond for - a predicate that changes back and forth over time rather than a one-shot handoff.
HikariCP connection pool: DataSource.getConnection() suspends the caller until a lease is returned while the pool already holds maximumPoolSize connections, bounded by connectionTimeout (default 30000 ms, minimum 250 ms), after which it throws SQLException rather than waiting on - a guarded suspension in which the deadline is a documented, first-class outcome instead of an accident.

statement: Choose the value model that centralizes endpoint inclusion, unbounded ends, containment, overlap, and adjacency for reservation windows.
name: range
document:
range
interval
Represent a span of values as a single interval value whose bound inclusivity and open ends are explicit, so containment and interval-to-interval comparisons live in one place instead of repeated ad-hoc endpoint tests.
Start and end travel together through the code but every caller re-derives what they mean: containment is written as scattered <= / < comparisons that drift apart, "unbounded" is smuggled in as a sentinel value (Long.MAX_VALUE, 9999-12-31), and interval-to-interval questions - do these two overlap, does one enclose the other, what is the gap between them - have no home at all.
Applies wherever a domain concept is a span rather than a point: validity and effectivity periods, booking and availability windows, quantity or price tiers, measurement buckets, version and address ranges, pagination windows, and query parameters such as a date range. It pays off when the same interval is compared repeatedly or crosses a boundary (persistence, API payloads, UI widgets), because the bound convention then has to be written once instead of re-decided per call site. For a single comparison between two local variables the type is pure overhead.
Validity and effectivity windows: a contract, price or membership is valid over [effectiveFrom, effectiveTo), and every check is a membership test against one interval.
Booking and availability: a room, seat or resource is reserved during an interval; overlap (not adjacency) decides whether a new booking is possible, and back-to-back bookings must be allowed deliberately.
Quantity and price tiers: the unit price depends on the quantity interval ([1,10), [10,50), [50, +inf)), so a container of intervals with containment lookup replaces a cascade of if-statements.
Temporal queries and reporting: "last 7 days", "this quarter", "since the migration" are half-open or open-ended intervals passed to repositories and rendered by date-range pickers.
Version, port and address ranges: a compatibility claim covers [1.2, 2.0) of a library, a firewall rule covers a port interval - containment answers "is this covered?" and intersection answers "do these rules conflict?".
Pagination and slicing windows: a page is an interval over a sequence, and half-open semantics make adjacency exact ([0,20) followed by [20,40)),
PostgreSQL range and multirange columns: PostgreSQL's daterange, tsrange and numeric range types make lower-inclusive/upper-exclusive bounds, overlap and containment operators, and indexed range queries part of the persistence contract; choose the bound convention before mapping domain intervals.
Guava Range: Java's Guava Range models convex bounded or unbounded intervals with nine open/closed forms, isConnected and intersection; use ContiguousSet only when a discrete domain really requires enumeration rather than treating the interval itself as a sequence.
Standard-library and container choices: Rust's std::ops::RangeBounds covers included, excluded and unbounded bounds when its range forms fit; for many intervals requiring join/split policies, Boost ICL's interval_set and interval_map supply the container semantics instead of overloading one Range value.

statement: Choose the value model that centralizes endpoint inclusion, unbounded ends, containment, overlap, and adjacency for reservation windows.
name: effectivity
document:
effectivity
effective dating
validity period
Attach an explicit validity period - a Range of dates - to a fact or relationship, so every reader can ask "is this true on date D?" and get a defined answer instead of inferring history from insertion and modification timestamps.
Some facts hold only for a while: an employment, a price, a tariff, a regulation, an address, a role assignment, a permission. Without a validity period the model can only answer "what is in the database now": historical questions are unanswerable, future-dated changes need a job that edits rows on the day, and a late correction silently rewrites what was previously believed.
Domain models and stores where individual facts have a bounded lifetime and the as-of date is part of the question - pricing and tariffs, employment and contracts, regulatory or tax rules, organisational assignments, access grants, subscriptions. The pattern applies when only part of the data (not every attribute of an object) needs history, and when the domain itself understands that the fact has a period.
Employment and contract periods: one person holds two employments during a handover month, each with its own validity range, and "which company employed X on date D" is a containment query rather than a guess.
Price lists, tariffs and rate cards: an article has a sequence of prices, the price valid on the invoice date is the one that must be billed, and a price change is entered weeks before it takes effect.
Regulatory and tax rules: a threshold, rate or obligation is valid from a legislative date and replaced later, so a calculation for a historical period must use the rule set that was effective then.
Organisational and role assignments: who managed which unit, which cost centre belonged to which division, which supplier supplied which part with which share - effective-dated so reorganisations do not erase the previous structure.
Access grants and entitlements: a role, licence, subscription or territory grant is effective for a period, so "was this allowed at that moment" remains answerable after the grant is revoked.
Insurance, warranty and subscription terms: cover, excesses and renewal terms change on effective dates, and claims or invoices must be judged against the terms in force at the event date.
Contract and price validity in commerce and procurement: price lists, discount condition records, purchase agreements and carrier tariffs are valid only for a period, so an order, receipt, shipment or invoice must be priced against the agreement in force for the reference date, not the newest one on file (Oracle SCM pricing; SAP MM condition records; freight tariff resolution).
Manufacturing engineering changes: a BOM line, routing or revision is in effect from a date or serial number onward; production orders and field service resolve the structure effective at the order date or unit number, with overlap and gap rejected at change-draft time (SAP ECM parameter effectivity; PeopleSoft BOM revision maintenance).
Insurance cover and health-plan benefits: policy endorsements split the term, benefit versions and coverage spans decide what is payable for a loss date, a service date or a prescription, and retroactive changes force reprocessing or recalculation of closed periods (Salesforce endorsement versioning; Guidewire PolicyPeriod; Oracle HI policy versions; 834/271 eligibility).
Effective-dated rates, fees and market data in banking and asset management: interest rates, margins, promotional offers and reference prices carry an effective date and remain applicable until superseded, with back-dated corrections recalculating accruals and already-liquidated cycles (Oracle lending interest/fee modules; LUSID/IVP reference data).
HR master data as a platform primitive: Workday separates the effective date (when a change to a business object goes into effect - past, present, or future) from the entry date (when the change was actually recorded), so as-of reports over hires, salary changes and eligibility are a first-class capability rather than an application-layer convention; PeopleSoft makes the same structure a platform convention with EFFDT as a key field plus EFF_STATUS and EFFSEQ to disambiguate same-date rows; ServiceNow capacity and crew assignments carry Effective from/Effective to with validation rules that reject ranges conflicting with existing usage (Workday Administrator Guide; PeopleTools Application Designer; ServiceNow FSM documentation).

statement: Choose the value model that centralizes endpoint inclusion, unbounded ends, containment, overlap, and adjacency for reservation windows.
name: watchman
document:
watchman
dead man's switch
heartbeat monitor
Detect that a message flow has gone silent - not that a message failed - and tell a responsible person or system within a bounded time by comparing each flow's arrivals against the cadence its business deadline implies.
Message systems fail silently in the one way no error handler observes: nothing arrives. A producer stops emitting, a consumer stops draining, a scheduled job never fires, a credential expires, a partition goes offline - and because no failing code path is ever entered, error dashboards stay green while downstream data quietly goes stale. The recurring trigger: a flow whose absence is business-visible (a nightly feed, an order stream, a partner interface) has no owner-facing signal for 'no messages', so the gap is discovered late - by a customer or a downstream job - instead of by the team that can fix it.
Applies wherever messages are expected on a knowable cadence (event streams, queues, batch hand-offs, partner interfaces, device check-ins) and their absence is a business-visible failure: the flow has an owner, the expected period and grace window can be derived from a downstream deadline, and either the transport can be observed passively (queue counters, a wire tap) or the producers can emit out-of-band heartbeats. The watchman sits at message-flow or boundary scope - an in-process watcher beside the consumer, a periodic sweep over persisted last-seen state, or a rule in the monitoring stack fed by metrics - and it must itself be watched, because a silent watchman is exactly the failure it exists to catch.
Nightly batch or ETL feed: page the integration owner when the 02:00 import has produced no messages by its deadline, instead of noticing an empty report at the morning stand-up.
Business-critical event stream (orders, payments, telemetry): alarm when the produce rate stays at zero through business hours, which separates a healthy quiet topic from a stopped producer.
External partner interface: notify when no messages have arrived from a B2B partner within the agreed window, turning a looming SLA breach into an early, actionable alert.
Long-running workflow stage: require a heartbeat from each process-manager step so a stuck instance is noticed before the surrounding batch closes or a compensation becomes necessary.
Retry or dead-letter pump: verify that the pump still drains failed messages - silence means the pump died, not that the backlog is empty.
Fleet check-ins (edge devices, agents, cron jobs on many hosts): raise a per-device or per-site alarm when scheduled check-ins stop arriving.
The alerting pipeline itself: an always-firing watchdog alert routed to an external service, so a broken alert path is discovered by its silence.
Cron and scheduled-job fleet via Healthchecks.io: each job pings a unique URL, the service holds the Period and Grace Time, flips the check Late then Down when no ping arrives by period + grace, and notifies integrations.
Dashboard alert rules in Grafana: an alert rule whose query returns no series enters the No Data state and can raise a DatasourceNoData alert - the platform form of deciding what silence means (No Data, Alerting, Normal or Keep last state).
Apache Burrow for Kafka (LinkedIn): committed offsets are evaluated per partition over a sliding window and a consumer is classified STALLED when its offset is frozen with non-zero lag, or STOPPED when no new commits arrive - consumer-silence detection without fixed lag thresholds.

statement: Choose the value model that centralizes endpoint inclusion, unbounded ends, containment, overlap, and adjacency for reservation windows.
name: coarse-grained-lock
document:
coarse-grained-lock
aggregate lock
cluster lock
Give a cluster of objects that must change together one shared lock — held on the cluster's root object, on a lock entry keyed by that root, or on a version token the root carries — so a caller locks one thing instead of discovering and locking every member.
Changing one object really means changing a cluster: an edit that touches any member (a line item, an address, a child entity) has to be atomic with respect to the others, but a separate lock per member forces every caller to find and lock the whole set, makes the amount of locking grow with the object graph, and produces deadlocks whenever two callers acquire member locks in different orders.
Domain layers whose natural unit of change spans several related objects (an aggregate root plus its members) and whose edit sessions outlive a single statement — multi-user applications, rich clients, batch jobs — on stores that offer row locks, lock tables or version columns and where the team must pick one lock granularity that matches the unit of change.
Editing an order together with its lines and delivery addresses in one user session: the order is locked or versioned once and every line edit is covered.
A customer with its addresses and contacts that must stay consistent, where leaving one member stale breaks a business rule.
Pessimistic offline edit sessions in a rich client that hold a lock for minutes without locking dozens of rows across several tables.
Optimistic commit of a whole aggregate: the root's version token detects that any member changed since load, so members need no version columns of their own.
Batch jobs that rewrite every member of a cluster: one lock or one version check for the batch instead of thousands of row locks.
Sharded or multi-tenant stores where the cluster root is also the shard key, so locking the root pins the partitions that the edit will touch.
DDD aggregates where an invariant spans multiple child entities (e.g., total order quantity must not exceed 10) — the coarse-grained lock on the aggregate root prevents parallel transactions from breaking the invariant at the per-line level.
Saga state machines where concurrent messages may touch the same saga instance — NHibernate pessimistic locking combined with forced version increment on child updates ensures the saga instance stays consistent.
Multi-granularity lock hierarchies in database systems: coarse area/file locks for large scans paired with fine row locks for point updates, using intention-lock protocols (IS/IX/SIX) to prevent deadlocks.
Kubernetes control plane: kube-scheduler and kube-controller-manager contend for a single coordination.k8s.io Lease object — one coarse lock covering a whole controller, renewed at about half the lease duration, with resourceVersion optimistic concurrency so only one candidate can hold it.
CockroachDB epoch-based node leases: one lease per node covers every Raft range that node holds instead of one lease per range, cutting lease-renewal traffic; bumping the node's liveness epoch revokes all of its range leases at once.
JPA/Hibernate applications locking an aggregate with a single LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE on the root row (SELECT … FOR UPDATE) and relying on the root's @Version column as the version token for the whole cluster.

name: adapter
document:
adapter
wrapper
adaptor
Present an existing component through the exact target contract its client already consumes, translating calls, results and boundary semantics without adding responsibilities or pretending a missing capability exists.
An existing or foreign component has useful behaviour but speaks a different protocol: method names and signatures, data shapes, units, lifecycle, error model or sync/async contract do not satisfy the target. If every caller performs ad hoc conversion, semantics drift, vendor types leak and provider replacement becomes a cross-cutting rewrite; changing the adaptee or target may be impossible or too disruptive.
Integration work where one side is outside your control: legacy modules, vendor SDKs, generated clients, foreign data formats or units, and the ports-and-adapters boundary of a hexagonal architecture. Applies in statically typed languages - where an adapter class is also the compile-time proof that the required interface is satisfied - and in structurally or dynamically typed ones, where a thin wrapper usually replaces a declared target interface.
Wrapping a third-party or vendor SDK behind your own interface so business code never imports vendor types.
Modernising a legacy module incrementally: new code talks to the target interface while the old component is adapted in place.
Supporting several interchangeable providers (payments, storage, messaging, analytics) through one internal contract, with one adapter each.
Adapting a callback- or error-first API to promises/async or to an observer-style interface.
Ports-and-adapters boundaries where one domain port is realized over different transports (HTTP, message queue, in-process fake).
Unifying differently shaped data sources (row sets, DTOs, XML or JSON payloads) into one model before they reach domain logic.
Test doubles: an in-memory adapter satisfies the target interface without the real infrastructure.
API wrapper libraries: normalising third-party REST/gRPC APIs (Stripe, Twilio, payment providers) into a stable internal contract so business logic never imports vendor SDK types.
Legacy system integration: wrapping SOAP, CORBA, or mainframe APIs behind a modern interface, enabling incremental migration without rewriting existing clients.
Cloud provider abstraction: a single internal storage or queue interface implemented by AWS, GCP, or Azure adapters, letting the application swap providers via configuration.
ETL pipelines: adapting heterogeneous source record schemas (CSV, JSON, XML, database rows) into one canonical domain record, isolating format changes from downstream consumers.
Event-stream and streaming adapters: translating WebSocket frames or server-sent events into domain events in real time.
Multi-cloud and provider-agnostic interfaces: storage adapters (S3, GCS, Azure Blob), queue adapters (SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka), and notification adapters that abstract away provider-specific SDKs.
Backend for Frontend (BFF): each front-end client (web, mobile, third-party) gets its own lightweight adapter that shapes internal service responses into the exact payload that client needs.
Java's java.io.InputStreamReader is a byte-to-character bridge: it presents an InputStream through the Reader contract while decoding with an explicit charset.
SLF4J uses providers such as slf4j-reload4j to bind one Logger API to different backends, while log4j-over-slf4j and jul-to-slf4j redirect legacy APIs at a migration boundary; Spring MVC's HandlerAdapter similarly lets DispatcherServlet handle heterogeneous handler types through one SPI.
Go's net/http.HandlerFunc gives an ordinary func(ResponseWriter, *Request) the http.Handler contract by attaching ServeHTTP, so routing and middleware can consume functions and handlers uniformly.

name: separation-of-duties
document:
separation-of-duties
separation of privilege
four-eyes principle
Require two or more distinct principals or components to complete a sensitive operation, so that no single account, role or object can initiate and finish it alone.
A sensitive workflow is reachable end to end from one identity or one code path: the same operator creates and approves the payment, the same administrator changes the production configuration and signs it off, the same service account holds both the maker and the checker permission. The trigger is structural rather than accidental - all steps share one principal, one session, one process or one role, because splitting them costs a second pair of hands - and the failure surfaces only when an insider error or abuse is unremarkable in the audit trail: every step was authorized, because one principal held both halves of the duty.
Sensitive operations whose consequences must survive mistakes, coercion or misuse by authorized insiders: payments and disbursements, entitlement and permission changes, production configuration and deployment, key custody and signing, destructive data operations. It applies where identities can be kept distinct and authenticated (separate accounts, roles, services, processes), where the intermediate states of the operation can be persisted and observed, and where an enforcement point exists that can compare the acting principal with the recorded initiator - a policy engine, method security, an approval service, a separate process or account, a dual-control key ceremony. It is as much an organizational rule as a technical one: the split must follow the duties people actually hold, and recombination must be made awkward by design rather than merely discouraged.
Maker-checker payments: an operator above a threshold creates a disbursement and a second operator releases it; the ledger records both identities and refuses a release signed by the maker.
Change control and deployment: production IAM policy or infrastructure changes require a second administrator's approval, and the pipeline refuses to run a change approved by its own author (required reviewers / second signature).
Key custody and dual control: signing keys or root credentials are split so two authorized operators must each contribute a share (split knowledge, m-of-n threshold, dual-control key ceremony) and no single share can sign.
Access provisioning: the requester of an entitlement, its approver and the administrator who grants it are three distinct roles; the administrator cannot approve their own request, and access-control administrators do not administer the audit log.
Destructive data operations: schema migrations, production data edits and deletion jobs are prepared by one engineer and executed by a different operator account that cannot author the change.
Regulated back-office workflows: journal entries, refunds, credit adjustments and account closures are initiated by one clerk and posted by another, with the pairing recorded for audit.
GitHub protected branches: a pull request targeting a protected branch needs the configured number of approving reviews before it can merge, the platform refuses an approval from the PR author by design, and with dismiss-stale-review enabled a commit pushed after the review voids the approval - four-eyes enforced at the merge gate with the approval bound to the reviewed revision.
AWS Systems Manager Change Manager: a change request may run its Automation runbook only after approvals from named IAM users, groups or roles arrive across up to five approval levels, and a single rejection stops execution; because change templates list approvers separately from requesters, a request submitted under one IAM principal is released by another.
HashiCorp Vault key custody: vault operator init splits the root key with Shamir's Secret Sharing into key shares (default 5) under a threshold (default 3); unsealing or generating a root token needs a quorum of distinct share holders, and PGP-encrypting each share for a named operator makes dual control a property of the mechanism rather than of the procedure.

name: cancellation-token
document:
cancellation-token
cancellation signal
cooperative cancellation
Give a caller-owned operation tree a one-way request to stop: pass a read-only cancellation signal through every cancellable call, observe it at safe points, clean up what was acquired, and report a distinct cancelled outcome without pretending that cooperative cancellation is forced termination.
A request handler, background job or UI action starts work that fans out into nested calls, tasks or threads. When the caller disconnects, a deadline expires, the user presses stop or a sibling fails, merely abandoning the result leaves already-started work burning CPU, holding connections and calling dependencies. Force-killing a thread or process can interrupt a critical section and corrupt shared state, while a signal that is not propagated or observed cannot stop the call tree or make its cleanup visible to the joiner.
Use where work can outlive the caller's interest and the runtime exposes checkpoints, suspension points or interruptible waits: request-scoped servers, workers, UI tasks, stream pipelines and batch loops. The operation owns cleanup, cancellation may race any checkpoint, and the design must state what happens when a request arrives after an irreversible side effect or while a dependency ignores the signal.
Request-scoped server work: the handler gets a request signal that fires when the client disconnects or the deadline expires, cancelling in-flight database, queue and upstream calls instead of pinning worker threads and connections after the caller is gone.
UI and mobile tasks: navigating away, closing a window or pressing stop cancels the task tree that loads, renders or downloads for that view, and only that view's tokens are affected.
Graceful shutdown: a supervisor stops accepting work and cancels the token shared by worker loops; every worker stops at its next safe point, flushes and releases resources, and the process exits inside the shutdown budget.
Fan-out with short-circuit: as soon as one subtask fails, or as soon as any one result suffices (hedged or racing replicas), the scope cancels the siblings instead of waiting for all of them.
Batch and stream pipelines: a processor subscribes to the pipeline signal and stops consuming and producing when the pipeline is torn down, abandoning the current chunk when the job's deadline elapses.
Testing and tooling: inject an already-cancelled signal, or one cancelled after N iterations, to exercise the stop path without racing an actual shutdown.
HTTP client redirect and retry cancellation: when a request is redirected or a lower-level retry budget is exhausted, cancel the in-flight operation so the client can proceed with the next action without waiting for a result that is no longer relevant.
Health-check abortion: a liveness probe times out or a readiness check fails mid-flight; cancel the in-progress health metric collection so the pod can be restarted or pulled from service without waiting for a hung check.
GRPC deadline and cancellation propagation: a server receives a client deadline and cancellation token; both must be threaded through every async operation so that an expired deadline or a client disconnect promptly frees server resources.
LLM request fan-out: multiple model providers are queried in parallel; the first successful response wins and all pending requests are cancelled immediately, avoiding wasted compute on a result that will be discarded.
Database connection pool eviction: a query timeout or client disconnect cancels the in-flight query, releasing the connection back to the pool before the server's statement timeout fires; the pool's token is derived from the request context so pool eviction and request cancellation share the same stop signal.
Container orchestrator graceful shutdown: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM and waits the terminationGracePeriodSeconds; the application maps SIGTERM to a cancellation token that is shared by all in-flight request handlers, background workers and health-check loops, giving each the termination budget to drain cleanly.
Interactive search with typeahead: each keystroke cancels the previous search task and starts a new one; the token for the previous task is cancelled immediately on the next keystroke, preventing stale results from overwriting fresher ones.
File transfer with resume support: a large upload or download uses chunked transfers; cancelling the transfer sets a flag that causes the next resume attempt to verify which chunks were already received before retransmitting from scratch.
Event streaming with backpressure: a consumer reading from a message queue or Kafka partition uses the cancellation token to stop reading when the application is shutting down or the consumer group is rebalanced, committing its offset before exiting.
Machine learning inference pipeline: a batch inference job can be cancelled when a new model version is deployed or the job's priority drops; the cancellation token is checked between batches so that partial results are preserved and the job can resume without reprocessing completed chunks.
ASP.NET Core's HttpContext.RequestAborted token is passed into HttpClient, database and other long-running operations so a client disconnect or server abort releases work that can no longer contribute to the response.
Go net/http handlers propagate Request.Context through database/sql QueryContext and RPC calls; cancelling the request context closes the subtree's Done channel so backend goroutines can stop and return their resources.
Kotlin kotlinx.coroutines Job cancellation follows structured parent-child scopes, so a screen, request or worker scope can cancel its child coroutines while finally blocks release resources and CancellationException remains distinguishable from failure.
Node.js and browser fetch cancellation: AbortController.signal is passed as { signal } to fetch, EventTarget listeners and streams, so abort() tears down the socket and pending promises; AbortSignal.timeout and AbortSignal.any combine a deadline or several triggers into one signal without polling.
Database query abortion over a side channel: PostgreSQL's frontend/backend protocol sends a CancelRequest on a separate connection carrying the backend PID and secret key, letting a client that gave up - or an administrator via pg_cancel_backend - abort a running query without killing the session.
TPL/PLINQ cancellation acknowledgement: a delegate that throws OperationCanceledException carrying the supplied CancellationToken is treated by the Task Parallel Library as a cancellation acknowledgement rather than a fault, so joiners observe a cancelled task instead of an aggregated error.

name: policy-guard
document:
policy-guard
policy pattern
policy decision point / policy enforcement point
Keep every authorisation decision out of the protected resource's code by moving the rules into a separate Policy component and letting a Guard - the enforcement point every access must pass through - obtain a decision from that policy before the operation is performed.
Access rules written inside the resource's own methods (checking roles or ownership inline) entangle business logic with security logic: the same rule is re-implemented at every call site, a forgotten check silently opens a bypass, and the rules cannot be reviewed, tested or changed without touching the resource's code.
Components that own protected resources or operations and must decide per access whether the authenticated subject - with its roles, attributes, tenant and request context - may perform the requested action. Typical at object, module or boundary scope: request handlers, domain services, document stores, message consumers and administrative tooling that all reach the same resources and should obey the same rules, especially when the rules change more often than the resource code.
HTTP and API request handling: authentication establishes the security context once, then every endpoint or method invocation is guarded by a policy decision (for example Spring Security's AuthorizationManager behind its AuthorizationFilter, or ASP.NET Core authorization middleware over registered policies).
Domain services that expose several operations on one aggregate: the guard checks the (subject, operation, resource) triple before each service method executes, instead of scattering role checks through the methods.
Multi-tenant backends where the decision must consider tenant, ownership and request attributes, not only roles; the guard resolves them from the security context and passes them to the policy.
Document or file stores: every read or write is wrapped by a guard that consults rules keyed by the document identifier and its classification.
Administrative and background code - CLI tools, batch jobs, message consumers - that must obey the same policy as the interactive API so that no side door exists.
Regulated environments where every access decision, including denials, must be logged consistently and the policy itself must be independently testable.
Spring Security request boundaries: AuthorizationFilter passes the current Authentication and HttpServletRequest to an AuthorizationManager and proceeds only after a grant; configure every protected route so an unlisted path cannot become a side door.
ASP.NET Core policy authorization: named policies combine requirements evaluated by IAuthorizationHandler implementations and attach with [Authorize(Policy = "...")] or RequireAuthorization; place UseAuthorization after authentication and before endpoints.
Open Policy Agent (OPA) deployments: AWS Prescriptive Guidance models a centralized or distributed Policy Decision Point with Policy Enforcement Points on APIs, allowing shared policy while using local sidecars when latency or availability requires it.

statement: Choose the value model that centralizes endpoint inclusion, unbounded ends, containment, overlap, and adjacency for reservation windows.
name: humble-object
document:
humble-object
humble dialog box
Move as much logic as possible out of a program element that the framework calls but tests cannot instantiate - a UI control, callback, entry point or active object - into a plain collaborator that unit tests drive synchronously, leaving the original element as a thin adapter without decisions.
The element the host invokes cannot be exercised in a test: constructing it needs the framework's environment (event loop, window, container, thread), so driving it means slow asynchronous tests with framework setup, or none at all. Because the decisions were written where the trigger arrives, business rules live inside the untestable element: they are verified only by expensive end-to-end runs, they cannot be test-first, and every framework upgrade threatens them.
Applies when an element is hard to test for environmental reasons rather than intrinsic ones: framework callbacks (widgets, dialogs, request handlers, message listeners), entry points (main, server bootstrap) and active objects (threads, processes, timer and interrupt handlers), plus container-managed components whose interfaces the server demands. The logic must be expressible as a computation over data, and the host must keep invoking the element through a stable callback or entry point.
A dialog or screen whose enablement, validation and navigation rules are hard to exercise: extract a presenter or view model, leave the widget showing fields and forwarding events (the Humble Dialog form).
Framework callbacks that mutate business state - HTTP handlers, message listeners, timer or interrupt callbacks - where a thin adapter reads the input and a service decides.
Active objects and executables: a thread or process whose per-request processing is extracted so tests run synchronously instead of sleeping and coordinating (the Humble Executable form).
Transaction boundaries: extract the business logic out of the transaction controller so a test can run the logic and roll the transaction back, leaving only commit/rollback behaviour in the controller (the Humble Transaction Controller form).
Container-managed components: implement the server's interface in a thin adapter and keep the logic in a container-independent class, so the edit-compile-test cycle stays fast (the Humble Container Adapter form).
Legacy code with an overridable or exposed dependency call but no injection point: expose or extract the method first (the Poor Man's form) and only then attempt a test harness.
Entry points: parse arguments, wire dependencies and map the exit code in main, and put the program's decisions in a library function that tests call.
Android Activities/Fragments and Unity MonoBehaviours: extract lifecycle-driven logic into a plain class, leaving the framework component as a thin shell that forwards lifecycle events — enables unit tests without an emulator or device.
React class components and Angular controllers: move state and business logic out of the component into a hook or service, keeping the component as a declarative renderer that delegates all decisions.
Embedded systems interrupt handlers: extract per-interrupt processing into a synchronous function tested with deterministic inputs; the ISR remains a thin vector that disables interrupts and calls the extracted logic.
Database transaction scripts: separate the SQL/transaction orchestration (humble controller) from the business logic (collaborator), so the logic is tested with a connection spy and the wiring is verified by a small number of integration tests.
Event-driven microservices: keep the event-listener adapter minimal (deserialize, delegate) and place all routing and business logic in a synchronous service that tests can drive directly with domain objects.
CLI entry points: extract argument parsing and environment setup from the main method into a plain runner class; the collaborator is tested with fake argv, and the shell only handles OS-level concerns.
Android Jetpack (AndroidX) ViewModel: Google's architecture guidance makes the ViewModel the testable collaborator - it MUST NOT reference Activity, Fragment, View or Context - so screen logic is unit-tested on the JVM with fakes, while the Activity/Fragment stays a humble shell exercised only by instrumentation tests.
WPF / .NET MVVM: Microsoft's guidance prescribes views with empty code-behind - controls bind to ViewModel properties and ICommand implementations (e.g. DelegateCommand) - so enablement, validation and action logic (CanExecute/Execute) are plain classes unit-tested without a window, and XAML binding is covered by a few integration checks.
Unity MonoBehaviour game code: teams extract game rules into plain C# classes unit-tested outside the engine's Play Mode, leaving the MonoBehaviour as a serialized-field shell that forwards Update/FixedUpdate - the Unity community reports this buys fast unit tests at the cost of harder in-engine integration tests, so the shell needs deliberate coverage.

name: revocable-forwarder
document:
revocable-forwarder
caretaker
revocable proxy
Let a collaborator use an object through a forwarding wrapper that the grantor can switch off at any time through a separate control, so authority already handed out can be withdrawn without destroying the target and without the collaborator's cooperation.
A capability is just a reference, so once a collaborator has been given access to an object there is no built-in way to take it back: the grantor can destroy the object, ask the collaborator to stop, or leave the access standing. The recurring decision is how to grant access that is bounded in time - temporary use of a file, a service object, a session, an account - while keeping a control that only the grantor holds.
Object-capability settings, and any in-process design in which authority travels as references rather than as a global identity: plugin and extension hosts lending a service object to foreign code, multi-tenant object graphs giving a worker one tenant-scoped resource, session-scoped services, and capability-based workflow or financial systems in which a grant must be provably withdrawn. It applies when the grantor keeps its own reference to the target and can intercept every call through the reference it handed out; where the runtime lets references be forged, dereferenced around the wrapper or reached by reflection, marshalling or FFI, the same structure degrades from an enforcement mechanism to a discipline.
A plugin or extension host lends a file, network or service object to foreign code and revokes it when the plugin is unloaded or breaches policy.
A multi-tenant worker receives one tenant-scoped resource for the duration of a job and loses it at job end, without the tenant object being torn down.
Session teardown in a long-lived server: the handler works through the wrapper, and logout revokes future calls before the session's resources are freed.
Capability-based workflow and financial systems that give an agent temporary authority over an account or a document and revoke it when the task completes.
Temporary elevated access for maintenance or debugging, where the requirement is to show that the extra authority has provably ended (audit evidence).
Graceful decommissioning of a shared resource: revoke new work through the wrapper, drain the calls already in flight, then release the resource.
The Scala ocaps framework's Revocable/Caretaker API returns a proxied capability plus a private Revoker, so a session, logout, timeout or supervisor can make later calls fail without changing the target.
JavaScript's standard Proxy.revocable() and the Chrome Extensions chrome.permissions API provide browser/runtime counterparts: keep the revoke/remove control private, and do not mistake the platform wrapper or permission record for protection against an already leaked target reference.
AWS IAM role-session revocation for temporary STS credentials is a distributed analogue of withdrawing a forwarded grant: policy evaluation denies subsequent requests, but propagation and credential caching mean it is not the atomic in-process check-and-forward gate described here.

statement: Choose the value model that centralizes endpoint inclusion, unbounded ends, containment, overlap, and adjacency for reservation windows.
name: anti-corruption-layer
document:
anti-corruption-layer
acl
translation layer
Protect a downstream bounded context from a foreign model by making one explicitly owned boundary translate calls, data and failure semantics into the downstream language; unlike a mere wrapper, an anti-corruption layer prevents foreign concepts from becoming domain concepts.
A bounded context must use a legacy application, packaged product, partner API or another context whose model it cannot control, and the same words carry different meanings on each side. Reusing the foreign SDK types and status codes directly makes its names, optionality, units, errors and version churn load-bearing parts of the local domain; translation then drifts across callers and every upstream change becomes a core-model change. Without an explicit boundary, the contexts become accidental conformists and neither can evolve independently.
Use it at a durable integration seam where the models genuinely disagree and at least one side cannot be changed: a new core beside a legacy or packaged system, a core subdomain consuming a third-party service, two bounded contexts with different vocabularies, or a staged migration whose callers must survive a callee replacement. It is a boundary-scoped investment: a model worth protecting must exist on the downstream side, and the seam must be durable enough to own a component; a wire-level rename, a CRUD screen over a stable API or throwaway code does not justify it.
Staged migration (strangler style): a monolith keeps calling a capability that has been extracted into a service, and the layer converts the old call into the new semantics so existing callers are not modified while functionality moves out piece by piece.
Legacy or packaged systems: an ERP, mainframe, CRM or vendor database with convoluted schemas and obsolete protocols is consumed by a new core domain that refuses to adopt its concepts.
Third-party services inside a core subdomain: a payment, identity or logistics API whose model must not shape your domain — its statuses, optionality and error codes are mapped to your own types.
Two bounded contexts in one product: the upstream team publishes a model your context rejects (conformist would be too costly), so your side translates it and the context map records the relationship.
Event-driven integration: upstream events are translated, validated and re-emitted as downstream domain events before any handler in the core sees them.
Standardised external formats: EDI, ISO 20022, FHIR or partner schemas are parsed into a local model inside the layer, keeping the standard's vocabulary out of the domain.
Replacing an infrastructure dependency: swapping the persistence engine, message broker or identity provider behind a layer while the domain keeps exactly the same vocabulary.
Database-view ACL for analytics: a database view that maps another context's internal storage schema into an analytics-owned projection, used instead of direct cross-context SQL queries that couple the analytics context to the source's implementation details.
API-gateway-level ACL: an Azure Functions, AWS Lambda or similar serverless function deployed at the API gateway seam that performs domain-model translation before requests reach the downstream service, keeping protocol handling and semantic translation separate.
Dark launch / shadow traffic validation: an ACL running in parallel that receives mirrored traffic and logs translation discrepancies without affecting live callers, enabling validation of a new integration before any traffic is cut over.
Multi-system data aggregation: a domain that must compose data from multiple external systems with incompatible models (e.g., a customer dashboard pulling from Stripe, Salesforce and an on-premises ERP) translates each system's model separately before assembling a unified view.
Bidirectional payment provider integration: a payment gateway ACL that translates inbound webhooks (provider → local domain events) and outbound charge requests (local domain → provider format), with a stable provider-independent reference as the operation key on every call.
Legacy system read-through cache: an ACL that wraps a legacy system's slow query with asynchronous cache warming and model translation, so the domain sees a fast, semantically correct response without coupling to the legacy's latency profile.
AWS Migration Hub Refactor Spaces strangler migration: Amazon API Gateway routes a monolith's calls to legacy or Lambda services while an ACL converts the monolith's old interface to the migrated service and is removed after callers move.
Spring Boot customer integration: a Spring component with an external client, explicit mapper, retry policy and circuit breaker translates provider responses into local aggregates; keep the ACL inside the service unless several consumers need the same boundary.
Azure Strangler Fig migration: an Azure façade routes legacy and new services while a domain-owned ACL translates calls in both directions, letting clients keep the same interface until the legacy feature is retired.

name: producer-consumer
document:
producer-consumer
bounded buffer
consumer-producer
Insert a bounded buffer between producers and consumers of work items so the two sides run concurrently at their own rates, the buffer absorbs bursts and slack, and its bound turns overload into backpressure, queueing or an explicit drop policy instead of unbounded growth.
Production and consumption proceed at different rates: a fast producer outruns its consumer and either drops items or grows a backlog until memory runs out, a slow producer leaves consumers idle, and bursts arrive faster than they can be processed. Wiring the two sides together directly also couples their lifetimes and schedules - a synchronous hand-off makes the faster side wait for the slower - so neither side can be scaled, restarted or tested on its own.
Concurrent in-process software (threads, tasks, coroutines, event-loop callbacks) with one or more producers and one or more consumers that can run at the same time but not at the same average rate. The buffer is a component-level data structure owned by the application - a work queue for a thread pool, a pipeline hand-off, a logging or telemetry sink - not a durable broker, so the decisions are how to hand items over, how to bound the queue and how to end the arrangement cleanly.
Work queues behind thread or worker pools: request handlers enqueue tasks and a fixed set of workers consumes them, so pool size is independent of the arrival rate. Industry examples: Celery (Python), Sidekiq (Ruby), BullMQ (Node.js) all use this shape with Redis or a broker as the durable backing store.
Asynchronous logging and telemetry: hot paths enqueue records cheaply while a background writer drains, formats and writes them, keeping I/O latency off the request path. Structured log collectors (Fluent Bit, Vector) ingest from many sources into one consumer.
Multi-stage data pipelines (decode - transform - encode, extract - transform - load): bounded queues between stages give each stage its own workers and let a slow stage backpressure a fast one. Used in media transcoding, ETL workflows, and stream processors.
Ingestion buffers: a socket, file or broker reader produces records faster than the processing or indexing stage can absorb them, and the buffer smooths the mismatch without dropping data. Common in IoT telemetry ingestion, click-stream collection, and log aggregation.
UI/host integration: a background thread posts work or results to the main/event-loop thread's queue and vice versa, keeping the UI responsive without locks around application state. All major GUI frameworks (Qt, Swing, Flutter) use this internally.
Batch job scheduling: producers enqueue compute jobs (image resize, PDF generation, report creation) and a pool of consumers processes them. Systems like Celery, Hangfire, and AWS SQS follow this pattern, often with priority queues, delayed execution, and dead-letter routing.
Event streaming pre-processing: a Kafka, Pulsar, or NATS consumer-producer chain filters, transforms, and routes events through a series of bounded queues before landing in a data warehouse or search index.
Simulation and testing: a producer generates a deterministic stream of items while a consumer asserts on what it receives, with a sentinel marking the end of the stream. Property-based testing frameworks use this to drive scenario generation.
Print spooling and document processing: print jobs or document conversion tasks are queued and processed by a pool of workers, with bounded queues preventing runaway memory use even under burst load.
ML inference pipelines: a model-serving host receives requests via an API, enqueues them into a bounded queue, and a pool of worker coroutines or threads dequeues and runs inference. The queue decouples HTTP latency from inference latency and provides backpressure when the model GPU is saturated. Tools like Ray Serve, Triton Inference Server, and TorchServe use this shape.
Streaming audio/video processing: a media pipeline (capture - encode - mux - stream) uses bounded queues between stages; frames that arrive during a temporary encoding stall are buffered rather than dropped, and a full encoder output queue backpressures the camera capture stage to prevent unbounded memory growth from frame accumulation.
WebSocket connection management: a server's accept loop enqueues new connections into a bounded connection queue; a pool of handler coroutines or threads dequeues and upgrades them, preventing connection exhaustion under burst load while the handler pool limits concurrency independently of the arrival rate.
Financial order processing: high-frequency trading systems receive market data feeds (producer) and route orders through risk checks and execution engines (consumers), with bounded queues between stages preventing downstream latency from backpressuring the market data ingestion and applying backpressure to upstream feed handlers.
Go channel pipelines: a source goroutine produces values into a channel, transformation stages consume and emit through downstream channels, and a sink drains the final stage. Go's documented pipeline pattern makes channel closure and cancellation part of the producer-consumer lifecycle.
Python asyncio worker queues: an asyncio.Queue(maxsize=N) accepts work from coroutine producers while worker coroutines await get(), process items and call task_done(); finite maxsize suspends producers when consumers fall behind.
Java executor work queues: java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue coordinates multiple producer threads and consumer workers, with put()/take() waiting on full and empty capacity so an Executor-style worker pool can be bounded independently of arrival rate.

name: copy-and-swap
document:
copy-and-swap
copy and swap idiom
create-temporary-and-swap
Implement assignment (and any in-place state replacement) so that a failure while producing the new state leaves the target untouched: build the complete replacement off to the side, commit it with operations that cannot fail, and let the temporary's destructor or the garbage collector release the old state.
A hand-written assignment has to tear down the old state and build a copy of the new one, but only the build can fail: destroying before allocating exposes a half-updated object when the allocation or the element copy throws, and the usual repair -- a self-assignment check plus manual rollback -- duplicates the per-member copying that already lives in the copy constructor. The trigger is an assignment (or, in a garbage-collected language, an in-place state replacement) that must satisfy the strong exception guarantee: either it completes, or the target still holds its previous value.
Types that own resources -- heap buffers, handles, file descriptors, trees, containers -- in a language where the programmer controls copy semantics: C++ special member functions, a C ADT with error codes, Rust with panic/abort failure modes. The same ordering also applies in garbage-collected languages whenever published state must never be mutated in place: building the complete replacement and publishing it once keeps readers consistent and moves the release of the old state to the collector. The precondition is a commit step that genuinely cannot fail -- a noexcept member swap, one reference or pointer store, or an atomic publish.
Container and buffer classes that own heap memory (dynamic array, string, matrix, tree) and must be assignable without leaking or leaving the target inconsistent when an allocation fails.
Handle/pimpl classes that keep their state behind a single pointer: the swap is a pointer exchange, so the commit is unconditionally non-throwing while the deep copy still happens in the copy constructor (Sutter's canonical Pimpl exception-safety transformation).
Pre-C++11 codebases where the same operator= must serve lvalues and rvalues and no move constructor exists, using the const-reference plus explicit-local-temporary form.
Value types stored inside standard containers: std::vector and friends need element assignment to be safe before they can offer their own strong guarantee on reallocation, and a noexcept swap participates in their internal move/swap dispatch.
Garbage-collected languages where shared state must be replaced rather than mutated: build a complete replacement value and publish it with one store (AtomicReference.updateAndGet, atomic.Pointer[T].Store, a record with-expression) so readers never observe a partially updated object.
In-place state replacement where identity must be preserved (a registry entry, a cached object with live references): copy into a scratch value, then commit with a member-wise exchange or a replace-style API instead of repointing the reference.
Concurrent programming with thread-safe local-then-publish: build the replacement in a local object (thread-private by definition), then publish atomically -- readers never see a partially updated state, and the previous value is released by the collector after the atomic write is visible.
Version-control-style update: check out a local copy, mutate freely, then commit or discard; copy-and-swap maps directly to this workflow and provides the same transactional semantics (Howard Hinnant's analogy from his C++ Con 2018 talk).
Compiler tooling treats the idiom as the canonical self-assignment-safe assignment: LLVM's clang-tidy bugprone-unhandled-self-assignment checker explicitly recognizes 'build a temporary in operator=, then swap it' as correct handling and matches extended (allocator-aware) constructors plus ADL swap forms so real copy-and-swap code is not flagged (llvm/llvm-project PR #147066).
Boost's move/assignment guidance converged on the single by-value form T operator=(T b) { swap(*this, b); return *this; } as the common way to get copy-, move-, and convertible-assignment from one operator, with dedicated macros (BOOST_COPYABLE_AND_MOVABLE_ALT) for classes that adopt it instead of separate overloads.
When a strong guarantee is needed on the standard containers, libc++ maintainers advise exactly this idiom at the call site -- 'construct a new vector and swap it with the one you want to assign to' (libc++ PR #117516 discussion) -- because the library's own copy assignment deliberately offers only the basic guarantee.

name: protected-system
document:
protected-system
protection proxy
Give a resource exactly one owning object whose published operations are the only way to touch it, so that every access is decided by an authorization check before the resource is used.
A resource - a credential store, a file tree, a socket, a connection pool, a device handle - is referenced from many places. When each use site performs its own permission check, the checks drift, new code paths forget them, and the resource remains reachable as a raw handle, so a missing check cannot even be detected. The recurring trigger: one object can own the resource and clients can be made to hold only that object, so ownership itself can carry the enforcement.
Applies where ownership is expressible in the language or runtime (private field, unexported type, opaque handle, module boundary) and an authorization policy - identity, role, permission, capability - can be evaluated at each public operation. The guard may sit in-process (object or module scope) or at a process/kernel boundary, where the same pattern becomes a real reference monitor; the assurance the implementation can claim depends on which side of that line it lives.
Credential and key stores: an in-process vault owns the keys and exposes only operations (sign, decrypt, rotate), so callers never receive the secret material.
Storage gateways: a library owns the directory handle or object-store client and applies path and tenant rules on every operation instead of handing out a raw client.
Pools: the pool owns its connections and leases checked-out views, so a caller cannot keep, share or resurrect a connection the pool must reclaim.
Multi-tenant data access: a tenant-scoped repository wrapper pins the tenant filter and refuses operations that would query outside it.
Device and driver access: a supervisor object owns the device handle and validates commands, or a privileged daemon owns the socket and checks each request from an unprivileged client.
Module-level boundaries: a package exports only the guard type and keeps the resource unexported, so code outside the package cannot even name the protected representation.
Linux Landlock: a kernel-enforced ruleset restricts a process and its future children to explicitly allowed filesystem or network rights, placing mediation below application code.
Kubernetes RBAC: the API server evaluates Roles and bindings for each API request, mediating verbs and resources instead of exposing the cluster's backing store to clients.
HashiCorp Vault policies: authenticated tokens are checked against path and capability rules before secret operations, while the storage backend remains behind the Vault service.

name: pipeline
document:
pipeline
assembly line
processing pipeline
Decompose a transformation into an ordered sequence of named stages that each consume the previous stage's output and produce the next stage's input, so the workflow reads top to bottom and every step can be tested, instrumented, reordered or replaced on its own.
A multi-step transformation is written as one long function or a tangle of nested calls: the steps are unnamed, their order is implicit in statement order, intermediate values need throwaway names, there is no seam at which a single step can be logged, tested or replaced, and the same sequence is retyped at every call site that needs it.
Processing that naturally decomposes into successive transformations of the same payload - request handling, ETL, compiler passes, message enrichment, image or byte-stream processing - whether the payload is a single value or a stream. It fits in-process, staged execution where one driver owns ordering, error handling and cancellation; distributing the stages across processes, transports and independently deployed filters is the architectural pipe-and-filter pattern instead.
Request handling: deserialise, authenticate, validate, enrich, persist and render a request, with each step named so a failing stage is attributable and testable in isolation.
ETL and data import: extract, clean, transform, validate and load large files as a stream, so no intermediate collection is materialised and memory stays bounded.
Compiler and interpreter passes: source, tokens, AST, resolution, optimisation and code emission, where each pass is an independent stage over the intermediate representation and the pass list is the pipeline.
Message enrichment in an integration flow: unwrap, translate, enrich and route a message, one stage per concern, with per-channel ordering; the cross-process version stays pipe-and-filter.
Image or byte-stream processing: decode, crop or resize, watermark and encode, lazily per frame or chunk, optionally overlapping stages across cores.
Configuration-driven data cleaning: the stage list is assembled from configuration or a plugin registry so different tenants get different ordered steps without changing the stages themselves.
TensorFlow tf.data input pipelines: tf.data.Dataset pipelines that chain map, prefetch, parallel_interleave and shuffle stages to feed a training loop efficiently, with each stage independently configurable and the whole pipeline testable in isolation.
LLM token streaming: HTTP server-sent event streams where an LLM produces tokens at inference speed while clients consume at variable network speed; stream.pipeline() prevents the inference server from buffering unbounded tokens in memory when a slow client disconnects (Node.js stream backpressure case study).
Observability telemetry pipelines: OpenTelemetry Collector chains receivers, processors (memory_limiter, batch, filter, transform, tail_sampling) and exporters for traces, metrics and logs, with connectors (e.g., spanmetrics) bridging signal types and memory_limiter placed first to prevent OOM before filtering.
Typed TypeScript pipeline with schema validation: Zod or io-ts schemas define the stage contract at each boundary, catching schema violations at the exact stage that produced bad data rather than at a distant consumer.
Async generator pipelines in Python: asyncio queues with bounded capacity connect async generator stages, propagating backpressure by pausing producers when the queue is full; the FinStream analytics case study showed 82% memory reduction and 99.7% latency reduction versus unbounded buffering.
Event-streaming pipelines with Kafka and Flink: producers, topic partitions, Flink consumers and checkpointing form a distributed pipeline where backpressure cascades across every boundary; the Kafka max.block.ms and Flink backpressure.sample.interval settings interact under partition saturation and must be tested together under load.
Dynamic pipeline parallelism: construct-and-run pipelines (MapReduce, Spark) fix stage count at construction, while on-the-fly pipelines (Cilk-P Piper algorithm) allow the structure to emerge at runtime, varying per iteration and supporting data-dependent branching; on-the-fly enables pipelines like x264 that cannot be expressed with a fixed static structure.
LLVM compiler pass pipelines: PassBuilder assembles ModulePassManager, CGSCCPassManager, FunctionPassManager and LoopPassManager across the IR hierarchy (Module → CGSCC → Function → Loop), with registered callbacks injecting passes at named extension points (pipeline-start, vectorizer-start, optimizer-last); incorrect PreservedAnalyses declarations invalidate all downstream analyses.
Continuous data pipelines at scale (Google model): periodic pipelines run on cron and suffer from depth growth and resource exhaustion as organic load increases; continuous pipelines (master-slave or event-triggered) replace idle-waiting with always-on processing, eliminating the 'pipeline vs cron' discontinuity at the cost of operational complexity.
ML pipeline orchestration (Airflow, Kubeflow, Prefect, Dagster): each orchestrator applies the pipeline pattern at the workflow level - Airflow's DAG-of-tasks, Kubeflow's per-container-step pipelines with GPU scheduling, Prefect's monoflow/subflow/orchestrator pattern, and Dagster's software-defined assets where asset dependencies imply the pipeline; the pipeline is the scheduler's unit of execution, not an implementation detail.
Apache Beam: PCollections flow through composable PTransforms (ParDo, Combine and GroupByKey) in a pipeline graph, making each transform boundary explicit while the runner handles execution.
Node.js stream.pipeline(): Readable, Transform and Writable stages compose with built-in backpressure, error propagation and AbortSignal cancellation; this is a concrete streaming realization, not a durable workflow engine.

name: monitor-object
document:
monitor-object
thread-safe passive object
monitor
Serialise concurrent method invocations on a shared object by giving the object its own lock and condition variables, so that only one method executes inside it at a time and methods that cannot proceed wait cooperatively instead of polling.
Objects shared by several threads expose their state through ordinary methods, and nothing stops concurrent callers from interleaving inside those methods, corrupting the invariants they were written to maintain. The race is then papered over with ad-hoc locking, sleeps and busy-wait loops scattered through client code. The recurring decision is whether the object itself should own the serialisation (and the scheduling) of its methods instead of leaving that discipline to every caller.
Shared-memory concurrency, where the mutable state of an object is reached by more than one thread and its methods must be atomic with respect to one another. It matters most when some methods cannot run to completion until another method changes the state - a queue that is full or empty, a resource that is not yet available, a phase that has not been reached - because then a method must suspend and later resume, which requires releasing the lock while it waits.
Bounded buffers and work queues shared by producer and consumer threads, where producers wait while the queue is full and consumers wait while it is empty - the pattern's canonical example.
Session, connection or entity registries on a server, where lookups, insertion and eviction must be atomic and callers may have to wait for capacity or for an entry to reappear.
Caches with in-flight bookkeeping (single-flight computation), where a thread that requests an already-computed key waits for the first thread's result instead of recomputing it.
Shared configuration, counters or statistics objects read and updated by request threads, where each call must observe a consistent snapshot of the state.
State machines and simulators whose step methods block until another thread advances a transition, for example a test harness waiting for a worker to reach a known state.
In-process resource pools (connection, database or worker pools) where acquisition blocks until an entry is returned or a timeout expires.
Java's java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue is a fixed-capacity monitor-style bounded buffer: put blocks while full and take blocks while empty, making the producer-consumer coordination explicit.
.NET's System.Collections.Concurrent.BlockingCollection<T> supplies bounded Add/Take blocking, cancellation and completion semantics around a producer-consumer collection; use it instead of hand-rolling Monitor.Wait/Pulse.
Python's queue.Queue provides a thread-safe multi-producer/multi-consumer boundary with blocking put/get operations and optional timeouts, a standard monitor-style primitive for worker pools.

name: lazy-acquisition
document:
lazy-acquisition
lazy loading
deferred acquisition
Defer acquiring an expensive or scarce resource until it is first used, so the acquisition cost is paid only by the holders that actually use it, while clients keep seeing an ordinary interface.
A resource is costly to acquire, scarce, and on many execution paths never needed at all, yet the code that holds it acquires it during construction, at start-up or on a hot entry path: the process pays for resources it never dereferences, start-up time grows with every optional subsystem, and scarce capacity (descriptors, connections, licenses, memory) is consumed by holders that never use it.
Applies to long-lived holders - objects, modules, services, containers - that front an external resource such as a file, socket or database connection, license, thread pool, GPU context, translation catalog or large lookup table. It pays off when the acquisition cost is large relative to a use, when a significant fraction of holders never use the resource, and when the runtime offers a one-time guard (or the holder is provably single-threaded). It is the wrong tool when the resource must be validated at boot, when acquisition is cheap, or when first use sits on a latency-critical path.
A request-handling object that opens a file or blob stream only on the code paths that actually read it (report export, attachment download, audit sink).
A service holding connections to a rarely consulted downstream — archive store, fallback provider, secondary region — that most requests never call.
A large lookup table, model or translation catalog loaded on first use instead of at process start, keeping start-up and memory bounded for the sessions that never need it.
Optional subsystems in desktop and mobile apps (camera, location, payment SDK, plugins) initialized when the feature is opened rather than when the app launches.
Test fixtures and tooling: starting a container, browser or database only for the tests that need it, so the fast path stays fast.
Per-session state in a server — a scratch buffer, a decompressor, a TLS session or prepared statement — allocated on first use of the session rather than on accept.
Database connection pools: HikariCP and similar pools typically create connections lazily on the first checkout rather than at pool construction, to avoid pinninglicenses and consuming file descriptors before the application is fully started.
Dependency injection containers (Spring @Lazy, Dagger 2 Lazy<T>) defer the creation of bean instances until they are first injected, reducing start-up time and breaking circular dependency cycles during bootstrap.
Logging frameworks (SLF4J/Logback): Logger instances are static final but the actual appender (file, socket, console) is initialized when the first log event at that level is fired, so logging infrastructure does not block application start.
Configuration objects: large YAML or JSON config trees are parsed and validated lazily on first access rather than eagerly at start-up, keeping CLI tools fast for commands that do not need the full configuration.
GPU contexts in graphics applications (OpenGL, Vulkan, CUDA) are expensive to create and are deferred until the first draw call or compute kernel launch, allowing the application to start and display a window without claiming GPU memory.
HTTP/service clients (gRPC channels, REST clients): a channel is lazily opened on the first request, enabling the client to be instantiated at module load time while deferring the TCP handshake and TLS handshake to the first real call.
Spring Framework @Lazy bean definitions instantiate singleton beans when first requested rather than during ApplicationContext startup, making an optional integration genuinely demand-driven while retaining the container's proxy and lifecycle semantics.
Go's sync.Once lets a service wrap a one-time connection, parser or cache acquisition so concurrent first callers wait for one initializer and later callers reuse the published result.
.NET's System.Lazy<T> defers a factory until Value is first read and makes the thread-safety and exception-caching policy explicit through its constructors and LazyThreadSafetyMode.
