name: function-composition
document:
function-composition
compose
function pipeline
Combine a chain of small unary transformations into one reusable function by sequencing them with a composition combinator (compose/pipe), so the order of the steps is stated once, every step stays independently testable, and the chain itself becomes a value that can be named, passed and reassembled.
A transformation that is naturally a sequence of small pure steps gets written as nested calls or as repeated imperative assignment (`h(g(f(x)))`, or `y = f(x); y = g(y); ...; return y`) at every call site. The order is duplicated wherever the chain is used, the intermediate values need throwaway names, steps cannot be reused in a different order, and changing one stage means editing every copy.
Pure or nearly pure value transformations - parsing, normalisation, validation, formatting, pricing, AST rewriting - where each step is unary and the language treats functions as values. It pays off when the chain is reused or assembled from data (configuration, plugin lists, per-request policy), when steps must be unit-tested in isolation, and when the same steps must also run element-wise over a collection or lazily over a stream. It stops applying where steps need side effects or branching between stages: there the shell around the pure core owns control flow.
Input normalisation: trim, parse, canonicalise and validate a payload before it reaches domain logic, with the same chain reused by HTTP handlers and message consumers.
Pricing and rule chains: base price, discount, tax and rounding applied in a fixed, configurable order to an immutable value object.
Compiler and AST work: a pass list of rewrite functions composed once and applied over the tree, with passes added or reordered per optimisation level.
Serialisation and formatting: sanitise, format, encode and sign a document, where each step is tested separately and the composed chain is stored as a constant.
Data transformation over collections: the same pure steps composed into one function and passed to map/filter/stream operations, so element-wise processing reuses the chain.
Policy assembly at startup: the processing chain is built from configuration or plugin registrations and then applied per request without further branching.
Reactive stream processing: RxJS Observable.pipe chains the same logical steps across asynchronous event sequences, with operators composed once and reused across streams.
ETL and data pipeline transformation: extract-transform-load chains where each stage (parse, clean, enrich, aggregate, write) is a unary pure function composed into a reusable pipeline run over batches or streaming data.
HTTP request/response middleware: the middleware stack is a composed function chain where each layer (authenticate, authorise, rate-limit, deserialize, validate) is a unary handler; composition is resolved once at startup.
Matrix and vector transformations in numerical code: each linear algebra operation (scale, rotate, translate, project) is a unary function on a matrix type; composing them once builds the transformation pipeline that is applied to every vertex or pixel.
Ramda pipelines: R.pipe and R.compose assemble reusable data-last transformations from small functions, centralising the order while letting the same composed value run over many inputs.
Redux store setup: Redux's compose helper combines store enhancers right-to-left into one enhancer, so the enhancer order is defined once instead of reconstructed at each store boundary.
lodash/fp transformations: lodash/fp's auto-curried, data-last compose/flow helpers assemble immutable-friendly transformations from reusable steps that can be passed as values.

statement: Choose the value model that centralizes endpoint inclusion, unbounded ends, containment, overlap, and adjacency for reservation windows.
name: state-colocation
document:
state-colocation
colocated state
colocation
Keep each piece of presentation state in the component closest to where it is used — down to the single component that owns and reads it — instead of hoisting it to a common ancestor or a global store, so that a change touches only the smallest part of the view that can observe it.
State gets hoisted 'just in case': a value only one component reads is lifted to the screen or application root, or pushed into one global store, because someone may want it later. The consequences are components that receive props they never read, updates that invalidate far more of the UI than the value's actual consumers, an unclear owner for each value, and tests that must assemble the whole state container to exercise one field. The recurring decision is where a new piece of state should live: keep it at the smallest scope that actually needs it.
Declarative component UIs (React, Vue, Svelte, SwiftUI, Compose, Blazor, Qt Quick) and, in generalized form, any system where a mutable value is owned by one component-like unit: the consumers determine the state's scope, the framework invalidates only what the owner's subtree can observe, and components are composed, moved and deleted. Most compelling where over-lifted or global state has already become a performance and ownership problem.
A search or form input whose value is read only by the input, its own validation and its own preview: keep it in that component instead of the screen root (the canonical typing example where hoisting made every keystroke re-render the page).
Which panel of an accordion is open: leave it per panel while panels are independent, then lift exactly to the accordion once only one panel may be open at a time (the closest common parent).
Tooltip, hover, popover and dropdown state in a chart or table cell: own it in the cell component rather than in a global UI store.
Per-row edit or selection state in a data grid: the row component owns it; only cross-row operations need the grid to own it.
Dialog and modal open state in the button or list that opens it, until another surface must close or observe it.
Form draft state in the form component; lift it only when a sibling — summary panel, preview pane, wizard footer — genuinely must read it.
Extracting a self-contained widget for reuse or publication: keeping its state local makes the component portable and shrinks its API.
Per-cell expansion state in a tree view or file explorer: the tree node component owns whether it is expanded; the parent tree only coordinates multi-select or bulk-expand operations.
Media playback state for a single player (play/pause, current time, volume): colocate in the player component rather than a global audio store unless the same track plays in multiple places simultaneously.
Local filter/sort state for a data table or list: keep it in the list component until a URL parameter, shareable link, or sibling panel requires sharing it.
Vue: composable-local state (useSearch, useToggle) where each consumer needs its own independent instance of the same reactive logic pattern.
Angular Signals: feature-level signal stores scoped to a route or feature slice, not the entire application store, for UI state and feature-derived state.
SwiftUI: @State for view-local value types; @StateObject for view-owned reference types; keep @EnvironmentObject for genuinely cross-cutting state (auth session, theme) mounted as low in the hierarchy as consumers allow.
Svelte 5 runes: `let count = $state(0)` inside a component is per-component-instance reactive state — the component that declares it is its owner; Svelte's v5 migration explicitly replaced the pre-runes habit of reaching for a store whenever state sat at a component's top level, with $state plus $derived/$effect as the local cells, and module-level .svelte.js state only for deliberate sharing.
Jetpack Compose: the official hoisting guidance is this pattern's placement ladder — keep state as close as possible to where it is consumed, hoist only to the lowest common ancestor of all composables that read or write it, pass value down and onValueChange up, and make the ViewModel the owner only when business logic or lifecycle outlives the composition.
Blazor: component fields are the default owner for UI-local state; the official state-management guidance promotes to an in-memory state container service only when components must share non-persistent state, and to Protected Browser Storage only when the value must survive circuits or sessions — a three-rung ladder that mirrors local state, scoped provider, persistence.

statement: Should customer, order, shipment, tenant, and session identifiers be made statically distinct so their UUID representations cannot be accidentally interchanged?
name: newtype
document:
newtype
strong typedef
opaque type
Give a single primitive its own distinct type so that values with different meanings cannot be substituted for one another, and the raw representation is reachable only through the wrapper's own construction and accessors.
Several domain concepts share one representation - customer id, order id and tenant id are all strings or UUIDs, width/height/offset are all numbers, milliseconds and seconds are both integers - and the API therefore accepts them interchangeably. A swapped argument, a mixed unit or a mistyped literal compiles (or runs) silently, and the defect surfaces late, as a wrong lookup or a cross-tenant bug rather than a type error.
Code in which two or more values with the same underlying representation flow through the same functions, collections or persistence mapping, and in which a single value owns a rule (identifier syntax, non-emptiness, numeric range, unit). Applies at the value level of one field; clusters of attributes that change together belong to Value Object, and closed constant sets to Type-Safe Enum.
Identifier families in one codebase: CustomerId, OrderId, TenantId and SessionId all string- or UUID-shaped and passed to the same repository, logger and cache.
Unit-carrying measurements: Milliseconds vs Seconds, Meters vs Feet, Radians vs Degrees, Cents vs Dollars, where arithmetic must stay inside one unit and conversion is explicit.
Validated single values: EmailAddress, PhoneNumber, Iban, Slug, Percentage (0-100), PortNumber, NonEmptyString - parsed once at the edge, trusted everywhere afterwards.
Security-adjacent tokens: API token vs session id vs tenant id, where a swap becomes a cross-tenant or privilege defect rather than a wrong lookup.
Geometry and graphics APIs where Width, Height, X, Y, Offset and Length are all numbers and transposition should be a compile error.
Pagination and buffer arithmetic: PageSize vs PageIndex vs ByteOffset vs Count, integers that are trivially transposable in a long argument list.
Rust's official newtype examples use Millimeters(u32) and Meters(u32) to keep units distinct, and use Wrapper(Vec<T>) to give a local wrapper its own trait implementations.
Scala 3 opaque types model values such as Logarithm over Double as distinct outside their defining scope, with controlled extension methods and no runtime boxing.
Kotlin @JvmInline value classes wrap one property into a non-interchangeable domain type such as Password while allowing unboxed representations in many uses.

name: value-object
document:
value-object
whole value
value type
Model a descriptive concept that has no identity as an immutable object whose equality, hashing and validation are defined by its attributes, so a cluster of attributes that always changes together is created, compared and replaced as one unit.
A cluster of attributes that always changes as a whole is passed around as separate primitives or mutated field by field: validation is duplicated at every call site, partial updates leave inconsistent combinations behind, and equality or lookup by concept (which address, which money amount) has no owner.
Domain and application code where a concept is descriptive rather than identified (money, ranges, quantities, addresses, codes), where the same combination of attributes must stay consistent across creation, comparison, hashing and persistence mapping, and where instances are shared across call sites or threads so aliasing bugs and defensive copies have to be eliminated.
Money and quantities: amounts with currency or unit, rounding rules and unit-compatible arithmetic.
Validated identifiers and codes: email addresses, phone numbers, IBANs, tax ids or product codes with checksums.
Ranges and periods: date ranges, intervals and validity periods with their own containment, overlap and open-end semantics.
Geographic and postal values: coordinates, locations and addresses carried inside an Order, Shipment or Customer aggregate.
Measurements, rates and percentages in pricing, tariffs and rules that travel through several layers without drifting.
Composite keys for caches, dictionaries and deduplication (tenant + code + version) where equality by state is required.
Validated primitives for domain-specific strings: PersonName, PhoneNumber, Url, CountryCode that carry validation logic.
Complex numbers, vectors, matrices and geometric shapes in computational domains.
Temporal values beyond dates: TimeSlot, HolidaySchedule, BusinessHours with their own scheduling logic.
Financial instruments: exchange rates, interest rates, percentages and ratios with conversion rules.
Discriminated-union variants: modelling mutually exclusive states (open-ended intervals, recurring anniversaries, jurisdictional rules) where a single attribute determines which sub-type applies.
Composite identifiers across storage systems: a storage key combining partition, namespace and version that must be compared and serialised as one unit.
Audit/telemetry metadata: a timestamp plus user plus action cluster that always travels together and is replaced atomically.
Color values: RGB/HSL components with gamut validation and conversion methods.
Rust structs with #[derive(PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]: the language generates structural equality over all fields and a field-combining hash, which is what makes the value usable as a HashMap key; Eq is a marker trait that cannot be derived when a field is f64 (NaN breaks reflexivity), so float-carrying values stay only partially comparable.
Python @dataclass(frozen=True): the standard library generates __eq__ over the fields and, only when frozen is also true, a matching __hash__ — the documented recipe for read-only value objects with attribute equality (e.g., a frozen GeoPoint or Temperature passed around without defensive copies).
Java records (JEP 395): java.lang.Record carriers whose compiler-generated equals/hashCode are derived from exactly the record components — the mainstream Java vehicle for identity-less values such as Coordinates, DateRange or Money (amount + currency).

name: immutable-object
document:
immutable-object
Immutable
Immutable Value
Fix an object's state at construction and expose only queries, so references to it can be shared, cached and compared by content without defensive copying and without synchronising concurrent readers.
Sharing a mutable object by reference leaks control: any holder can change the state every other holder sees, so callers copy defensively in and out, objects used as map keys or cache entries change value silently, and concurrent access needs locking that mostly arbitrates reads. The recurring decision is whether this type is a value whose content is its identity or an entity with a lifecycle.
Applies where a type models a value rather than an entity: quantities, coordinates, date ranges, codes, snapshots, messages and events - small things that are compared by content and passed between components, threads or trust boundaries. It pays off most in languages with mutable reference semantics (Java, C#, JavaScript), where sharing an object is the default and copying is the exception, and where updates are naturally expressed as producing a new value instead of changing one in place.
Domain values with arithmetic or comparison - money and quantities, coordinates, date and time ranges, identifiers and codes - where operations return new values instead of editing their operands.
Configuration and policy snapshots handed to many components or threads, where nobody should be able to change the settings that others see.
Keys and cache entries: map keys, set members, memoisation keys and interned instances such as symbols, codes and canonical numbers.
Messages, events and DTOs crossing a boundary: a published fact or payload must not be edited in place by a receiver.
Read-mostly shared state in concurrent code: lookup tables, compiled rules and caches that many threads read without locking.
DDD value objects: EmailAddress, Money, Address, DateRange - where equality is by attribute content and mutation means replacement.
Functional pipeline stages in data processing frameworks: each stage receives an immutable record and emits a transformed copy.
React/Redux-style UI state management: actions produce new state objects rather than mutating in-place, enabling time-travel debugging and predictable rendering.
Event sourcing: events are immutable facts about what happened; replaying them must produce deterministic state.
Query objects and specification patterns: composable filter/sort/page objects used to parameterise repository queries without side effects.
High-performance message validation schemas: libraries such as msgspec or pydantic used at API entry points where deserialised payloads must not be mutated by downstream handlers.
Django REST framework serializer output and Celery task message payloads: immutable bodies prevent accidental mutation of shared task state across workers.
FastAPI dependency-injected shared state: immutable request-state objects prevent middleware from corrupting shared dependencies.
Swift value-type domain models: a User struct with let properties passed through a Coordinator/Router pipeline, where each navigation step can safely inspect the values without copying or locking.
Go functional-options configuration objects: a Server started via NewServer(timeout, tls, logger) where each option is a function applied after struct creation, producing a clearly-initialised instance without nil-pointer confusion.
Rust ownership-model data carriers: a Config struct with Copy fields (timeouts, ports) that can be cloned trivially and passed through async handlers without Arc<Mutex<...>> overhead.
Cross-language gRPC/Protobuf messages: generated immutable message types used as DTOs at service boundaries, where mutating a received payload corrupts the shared in-memory representation across all cores.
Immutable graph nodes in spatial/deductive databases: nodes as immutable records with child references by ID; historical snapshots are natural read-only views over the same node types.
Compliance and audit log records: append-only financial transaction records where regulatory requirements demand that historical entries never change, and current-state is derived by folding over the immutable event stream.
ML feature vectors: immutable feature maps passed through a preprocessing pipeline where each stage produces a new vector; traceability of which features were available at each stage is required for model debugging.
Kotlin Arrow Either-based domain results: an immutable Either<DomainError, OrderConfirmation> where the error branch carries a non-empty list of validation problems, enabling accumulate-and-report UX patterns.
OpenJDK record classes (JEP 395) for transparent data carriers: the generated value equality and final components fit immutable values, while compact constructors can copy mutable components.
.NET C# record class and readonly record struct models: compiler-generated value equality plus with-expressions provide non-destructive updates for DTOs and small domain values.
Python persistent mappings such as Pyrsistent PMap and MagicStack immutables.Map: structural sharing keeps immutable configuration or snapshot updates cheap without aliasing the prior value.

name: authentication-enforcer
document:
authentication-enforcer
authentication interceptor
authentication gateway
auth middleware
Put one request-boundary checkpoint in front of protected actions that decides whether authentication is required, delegates credential verification to a replaceable mechanism, and attaches the resulting subject to request-scoped context before dispatch, so coverage is uniform without making handlers understand credentials.
When each handler decides whether and how to authenticate, protection is duplicated or omitted on exceptional paths, credential formats and user stores leak into business code, and a mechanism or policy change requires editing every handler instead of one auditable boundary.
Server-side request processing — web APIs, web applications and service endpoints — where many handlers share one protection policy, credentials arrive through a uniform convention (Authorization header, cookie, session id), verification technology must be replaceable or differ per route, and the runtime provides a request-pipeline hook (servlet filter, middleware chain, framework guard). Applies to session-based and token-based authentication alike; permissions and roles are out of scope. Three implementation strategies exist: (1) Container-Managed Authentication — the runtime container owns the checkpoint and realm configuration; (2) Authentication Provider Strategy — a custom provider behind a narrow interface, swapped without touching handlers; (3) JAAS Login Module Strategy — pluggable via standard JAAS configuration, supporting multifactor authentication via smart cards, biometrics, or third-party IdPs. The pattern is equally applicable at the edge level (API gateway, ingress proxy) and the service level (in-process middleware).
Web APIs where every route except health and login requires a bearer token, and the checkpoint is mounted in front of the whole router.
Multi-tenant applications with mixed protection levels: public marketing pages, session-protected tenant UI and token-protected integration endpoints behind one enforcement layer.
Services that must accept several credential types at once — browser sessions, mobile JWTs, mutual TLS for service-to-service traffic — while keeping one uniform enforcement point.
Credential-technology migration (basic auth to OIDC, on-premises LDAP to SSO) where enforcement stays put while the mechanism behind it is swapped.
Regulated environments where every rejected authentication attempt has to be logged centrally and identically across all endpoints.
Legacy applications with authentication checks scattered through servlets or handlers that must be consolidated behind one intercepting layer before an audit.
Zero Trust microservices where every internal service verifies JWTs independently (per-service verification) while an ingress gateway provides the first checkpoint — the enforcer exists at both layers.
OIDC/OAuth2 migration where an existing session-based app adds bearer-token support; the mechanism adapts to both while the enforcement point remains unchanged.
Multi-tenant SaaS platforms where tenant isolation depends on the enforcer resolving a tenant identifier from the token before the handler processes any data.
Platform-as-a-Service with mounted sub-applications where a parent ASGI middleware dispatches per-path authentication requirements from a config registry, injecting identity into ASGI scope for all sub-apps.
Spring Security servlet applications that use a SecurityFilterChain with anyRequest().authenticated() and an AuthenticationManager/AuthenticationProvider chain, so controllers consume the SecurityContext rather than parse credentials.
ASP.NET Core APIs that register JWT or cookie schemes, call UseAuthentication before dependent middleware, and use a fallback authorization policy to make authenticated access the default.
An nginx ingress location using auth_request to delegate identity verification to a central authentication service, forwarding only after a 2xx result and propagating 401/403 failures while services still verify their own trust boundary.

name: event-aggregator
document:
event-aggregator
event bus
messenger
message bus
event hub
Funnel the events of many source objects into one hub that owns the subscription wiring, so that subscribers register once with the aggregator instead of tracking down and registering with every publisher.
Many components raise events and many components want to react: if every consumer registers directly with every producer, each consumer has to find the sources and subscribe to each event type separately, each producer accumulates knowledge of who listens, and both sides repeat the same registration and unsubscribe code at every pair. The trigger is a many-publisher / many-subscriber setting in which the wiring itself has become the maintenance problem.
In-process, event-driven software - a modular UI shell, a domain-event pipeline inside one bounded context, a plugin host, a simulation or instrumentation layer - where publishers and subscribers grow independently, both sides should stay unaware of each other, and registration plus lifetime management should live in one place. The aggregator is a component- or module-scope element of one process (one node); events that must cross a process boundary, survive a restart or be delivered reliably need a messaging channel instead.
Modular UI shells (WPF/MAUI, Android, SwiftUI) where view models living in separate modules must react to each other without holding references — the classic Prism and CommunityToolkit.Mvvm scenario.
Domain-event fan-out inside one bounded context: 'order placed' reaches billing, stock, notification and audit services that each subscribe to the hub instead of to the Order aggregate.
Plugin, extension or rule hosts where the listener set is only known at runtime and plugins are loaded and unloaded while the application runs.
Test and simulation harnesses: a test subscribes to the hub, drives one publisher and asserts on the published events without wiring up the real consumers.
Cross-cutting instrumentation and audit: metrics, tracing, logging and audit collectors receive events from many components through one hub rather than being called from each component.
Long-running services broadcasting rare state changes (configuration reload, presence change, feature-flag flip) to every interested subsystem exactly once per change.
Micro-frontend communication: independent web apps in one page communicating via a shared event bus with typed event maps and cross-tab synchronization (BroadcastChannel bridge).
IoT sensor aggregation: many sensor streams funnelled through one hub for filtering, transformation and fan-out to display or downstream processing services.
CQRS command/event pipeline: commands are dispatched to handlers that publish domain events through a bus; read-model projectors subscribe to build consistent query views.
Redux/Flux-style frontend state updates where UI components subscribe to dispatched actions rather than mutating shared state directly.
Event storm prevention harness: wrapping a batch save operation in a scoped subscriber-disable guard so that handlers triggered by the save do not re-publish events that would cascade back through the same handler.
Transactional outbox companion: publishing domain events through the hub after a transaction commits, ensuring that state changes and event emission are not separated by a process crash (in-process equivalent of the outbox pattern).
Java in-JVM decoupling with Guava EventBus: objects register via @Subscribe-annotated methods and publishers post typed events that the bus routes by parameter type (superclasses and interfaces included), with unmatched events wrapped as DeadEvent for a second-chance subscriber.
Spring application-context event pipeline: beans publish through ApplicationEventPublisher and react via @EventListener methods - in-process domain-event fan-out with the ApplicationEventMulticaster owning the registry, no message broker involved.
Vue 2 cross-component communication through a shared root instance used as a global bus ($on/$emit); Vue 3 removed that instance-emitter API, making external typed emitters like mitt, provide/inject, or a store (Pinia) the supported replacement - a cautionary real-world case for untyped global buses.

name: durable-subscriber
document:
durable-subscriber
durable subscription
durable consumer
Keep a publish-subscribe consumer's place while it is offline: the broker binds a stable subscription identity to retained messages or a committed position, then resumes delivery after reconnect until retention, expiry, or quota says the backlog is no longer available.
A subscriber on a publish-subscribe channel can be unavailable during redeployment, maintenance, device disconnects, or scheduled batch work. A non-durable subscription drops messages published during that gap, so the design must choose a stable identity and broker-side state, then make finite retention, replay pressure, and at-least-once redelivery explicit; durable state prevents a gap only while that state remains available.
Broker-mediated publish-subscribe messaging where consumers are intermittently offline but individual messages matter: JMS topics, MQTT sessions, Kafka consumer groups, NATS JetStream durable consumers, cloud topic subscriptions. It presumes the messaging system can store messages (or positions) durably, so it is as much a broker-configuration decision as a client one, and it presumes at-least-once delivery is acceptable once the consumer is idempotent. It does not apply to in-process notification or to broadcast where only the newest value counts.
A Kafka-backed order-processing service that is redeployed or scaled to zero while events keep arriving: the consumer group resumes from its committed offsets and replays what it missed.
An IoT or mobile client on an intermittent link: an MQTT persistent session holds QoS 1/2 publications for its client id and delivers them when the client reconnects.
A partner integration that receives published documents while the partner's system is down: an unshared JMS durable subscription, or a cloud topic subscription, is registered on their behalf and holds the backlog until they acknowledge it.
A nightly audit or analytics consumer that must see every published change: the day's backlog is drained in bounded batches and acknowledged as it is persisted.
A ledger or compliance consumer that must never silently skip events: retention and lag alarms are configured so an offline subscriber is noticed before its backlog expires.
A cloud event-driven architecture (SNS FIFO → SQS FIFO): SNS preserves ordering and deduplication while SQS queues hold messages for durable fan-out to Lambda or EC2 consumers, with DLQs capturing failed deliveries for replay.
An industrial SCADA/IoT sensor fleet where devices connect sporadically over unstable networks: MQTT persistent sessions with a long session expiry interval preserve every telemetry reading until each device reconnects, even after multi-day outages.
A financial audit trail that must immutably record every state-changing event: events are durably retained in Kafka or JetStream and consumed by a compliance subscriber that must not skip or duplicate entries; idempotent deduplication and offset commits after durable persistence enforce this.
A supply-chain or logistics event-sourcing system where downstream services reconstruct state by replaying events after a crash or deliberate seek: the durable consumer starts from the committed position and replays the missing event window atomically with the state reconstruction.
A cross-region disaster-recovery subscriber that mirrors events to a secondary site: the durable subscription in the secondary region receives every event from the primary's topic, with a DLQ holding any events that fail cross-region delivery for manual retry.
A JMS topic consumer that must receive publications made while it is offline: the client reconnects with the same client identifier and durable subscription name, and the provider retains messages until acknowledgement, expiry, or unsubscribe.
An MQTT 3.1.1 device gateway that reconnects with the same client identifier and CleanSession=0: the broker resumes the stored session and queues matching QoS 1/2 publications for delivery after the link returns.
A NATS JetStream billing worker that restarts after an outage: it binds to the same durable consumer name and explicit-acks each message, so the server resumes its acknowledgement floor and redelivers unacknowledged work.
An Azure Service Bus fan-out topology: topic subscriptions are durable by default and each subscription stores its own copy of matching messages, so a receiver that reconnects later still drains its backlog; client-affine durable subscriptions bind the durable state to a stable client id.
A high-throughput replay consumer on RabbitMQ Streams: the consumer attaches with a stable tracking reference (name) and periodically stores its offset server-side, so a restart resumes from the last stored offset instead of re-reading the whole stream.
An event-sourced system on Google Cloud Pub/Sub that must reprocess history after a bug fix: the subscription enables acknowledged-message retention (default window 7 days, up to 31) and is seeked back to a past timestamp or snapshot to replay already-acked messages.

name: revocable-forwarder
document:
revocable-forwarder
caretaker
revocable proxy
Let a collaborator use an object through a forwarding wrapper that the grantor can switch off at any time through a separate control, so authority already handed out can be withdrawn without destroying the target and without the collaborator's cooperation.
A capability is just a reference, so once a collaborator has been given access to an object there is no built-in way to take it back: the grantor can destroy the object, ask the collaborator to stop, or leave the access standing. The recurring decision is how to grant access that is bounded in time - temporary use of a file, a service object, a session, an account - while keeping a control that only the grantor holds.
Object-capability settings, and any in-process design in which authority travels as references rather than as a global identity: plugin and extension hosts lending a service object to foreign code, multi-tenant object graphs giving a worker one tenant-scoped resource, session-scoped services, and capability-based workflow or financial systems in which a grant must be provably withdrawn. It applies when the grantor keeps its own reference to the target and can intercept every call through the reference it handed out; where the runtime lets references be forged, dereferenced around the wrapper or reached by reflection, marshalling or FFI, the same structure degrades from an enforcement mechanism to a discipline.
A plugin or extension host lends a file, network or service object to foreign code and revokes it when the plugin is unloaded or breaches policy.
A multi-tenant worker receives one tenant-scoped resource for the duration of a job and loses it at job end, without the tenant object being torn down.
Session teardown in a long-lived server: the handler works through the wrapper, and logout revokes future calls before the session's resources are freed.
Capability-based workflow and financial systems that give an agent temporary authority over an account or a document and revoke it when the task completes.
Temporary elevated access for maintenance or debugging, where the requirement is to show that the extra authority has provably ended (audit evidence).
Graceful decommissioning of a shared resource: revoke new work through the wrapper, drain the calls already in flight, then release the resource.
The Scala ocaps framework's Revocable/Caretaker API returns a proxied capability plus a private Revoker, so a session, logout, timeout or supervisor can make later calls fail without changing the target.
JavaScript's standard Proxy.revocable() and the Chrome Extensions chrome.permissions API provide browser/runtime counterparts: keep the revoke/remove control private, and do not mistake the platform wrapper or permission record for protection against an already leaked target reference.
AWS IAM role-session revocation for temporary STS credentials is a distributed analogue of withdrawing a forwarded grant: policy evaluation denies subsequent requests, but propagation and credential caching mean it is not the atomic in-process check-and-forward gate described here.

name: anti-corruption-layer
document:
anti-corruption-layer
acl
translation layer
Protect a downstream bounded context from a foreign model by making one explicitly owned boundary translate calls, data and failure semantics into the downstream language; unlike a mere wrapper, an anti-corruption layer prevents foreign concepts from becoming domain concepts.
A bounded context must use a legacy application, packaged product, partner API or another context whose model it cannot control, and the same words carry different meanings on each side. Reusing the foreign SDK types and status codes directly makes its names, optionality, units, errors and version churn load-bearing parts of the local domain; translation then drifts across callers and every upstream change becomes a core-model change. Without an explicit boundary, the contexts become accidental conformists and neither can evolve independently.
Use it at a durable integration seam where the models genuinely disagree and at least one side cannot be changed: a new core beside a legacy or packaged system, a core subdomain consuming a third-party service, two bounded contexts with different vocabularies, or a staged migration whose callers must survive a callee replacement. It is a boundary-scoped investment: a model worth protecting must exist on the downstream side, and the seam must be durable enough to own a component; a wire-level rename, a CRUD screen over a stable API or throwaway code does not justify it.
Staged migration (strangler style): a monolith keeps calling a capability that has been extracted into a service, and the layer converts the old call into the new semantics so existing callers are not modified while functionality moves out piece by piece.
Legacy or packaged systems: an ERP, mainframe, CRM or vendor database with convoluted schemas and obsolete protocols is consumed by a new core domain that refuses to adopt its concepts.
Third-party services inside a core subdomain: a payment, identity or logistics API whose model must not shape your domain — its statuses, optionality and error codes are mapped to your own types.
Two bounded contexts in one product: the upstream team publishes a model your context rejects (conformist would be too costly), so your side translates it and the context map records the relationship.
Event-driven integration: upstream events are translated, validated and re-emitted as downstream domain events before any handler in the core sees them.
Standardised external formats: EDI, ISO 20022, FHIR or partner schemas are parsed into a local model inside the layer, keeping the standard's vocabulary out of the domain.
Replacing an infrastructure dependency: swapping the persistence engine, message broker or identity provider behind a layer while the domain keeps exactly the same vocabulary.
Database-view ACL for analytics: a database view that maps another context's internal storage schema into an analytics-owned projection, used instead of direct cross-context SQL queries that couple the analytics context to the source's implementation details.
API-gateway-level ACL: an Azure Functions, AWS Lambda or similar serverless function deployed at the API gateway seam that performs domain-model translation before requests reach the downstream service, keeping protocol handling and semantic translation separate.
Dark launch / shadow traffic validation: an ACL running in parallel that receives mirrored traffic and logs translation discrepancies without affecting live callers, enabling validation of a new integration before any traffic is cut over.
Multi-system data aggregation: a domain that must compose data from multiple external systems with incompatible models (e.g., a customer dashboard pulling from Stripe, Salesforce and an on-premises ERP) translates each system's model separately before assembling a unified view.
Bidirectional payment provider integration: a payment gateway ACL that translates inbound webhooks (provider → local domain events) and outbound charge requests (local domain → provider format), with a stable provider-independent reference as the operation key on every call.
Legacy system read-through cache: an ACL that wraps a legacy system's slow query with asynchronous cache warming and model translation, so the domain sees a fast, semantically correct response without coupling to the legacy's latency profile.
AWS Migration Hub Refactor Spaces strangler migration: Amazon API Gateway routes a monolith's calls to legacy or Lambda services while an ACL converts the monolith's old interface to the migrated service and is removed after callers move.
Spring Boot customer integration: a Spring component with an external client, explicit mapper, retry policy and circuit breaker translates provider responses into local aggregates; keep the ACL inside the service unless several consumers need the same boundary.
Azure Strangler Fig migration: an Azure façade routes legacy and new services while a domain-owned ACL translates calls in both directions, letting clients keep the same interface until the legacy feature is retired.

name: two-step-view
document:
two-step-view
two stage view
Split presentation into two transformations - first turn domain data into a channel-neutral logical page, then render that logical page into a concrete output format - so page structure is defined once while look-and-feel and output channel live entirely in the renderer.
Every page owns its own presentation decisions: with one template or one transform per page, a global look-and-feel change means editing every file, and serving a second channel (print/PDF, e-mail, plain text, a machine-readable feed) means duplicating the page's structure. Nothing in the codebase represents 'the page' independently of the markup it currently happens to be rendered as.
Server-side presentation or document-publishing boundaries where several output channels share one page structure, or where the house style changes often enough that it must change in exactly one place. It also fits where the rendering technology is expected to be replaced (XSLT today, a template engine or PDF formatter tomorrow) and where the page should be inspectable, testable or cacheable before it is rendered.
Multi-channel publishing: one invoice or statement rendered as HTML for a portal, XSL-FO/PDF for print and plain text for e-mail from a single logical page.
Site-wide restyling in a CMS or portal where the house style must be one artefact to change and review rather than one edit per page family.
API-plus-HTML endpoints: the same logical page is serialised as JSON for clients and rendered as HTML for the browsable interface.
Document and report pipelines in the DocBook tradition: the logical document is produced once and rendered to HTML, PDF and e-book formats by different stylesheets.
Constrained or legacy channels - plain text, WAP/XML, CSV - added next to HTML without touching the page assembly code.
Pages produced once and consumed by several renderers or locales: the logical page is cached and rendered per channel on demand.
Spring Web MVC XSLT views: an XsltController builds an XML DOM of the page content, puts it in the model, and XsltViewResolver applies a home.xslt stylesheet - stage one produces the logical document, stage two owns the HTML.
Aura.View (PHP) ships the pattern under the name TwoStepView: a content template renders first, then a separately registered layout wraps it via setLayout()/getContent(), keeping the site chrome in one artefact instead of every page.
Standards-based publishing toolchains: the DITA Open Toolkit transforms semantic DITA maps/topics through XSLT stages into HTML, PDF and other deliverables, and Apache Cocoon pipelines generator -> XSLT transformer -> serializer so one XML source serves HTML, PDF, SVG and text.

name: table-data-gateway
document:
table-data-gateway
table gateway
Confine every SQL statement that touches one table or view inside a single gateway object whose methods take and return plain record structures, so that no other code contains SQL for that table and rows cross the boundary as data rather than as domain objects.
Access to one table is spread across the codebase: SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE fragments are copied into every caller, nobody can say which queries a schema change will break, DBAs cannot find the SQL that needs tuning, and each caller has to know the dialect, the placeholders and the column order. The desired boundary is a single object that mediates all access to the whole table while the individual rows remain records (tuples, structs, hashes, DataRows) instead of becoming mapped objects.
Relational persistence where the database is a stable, schema-first integration point and SQL-level control matters (indexes, hints, bulk loads, vendor features), where the team deliberately does not want O/R mapping machinery in the domain layer, and where the domain logic is simple enough that rows may travel as records - CRUD and query services, reporting/read models, ETL writers, local SQLite stores, or a legacy database mediated for several applications. It is also the packaging decision for 'the SQL has to live somewhere well known' before a DAO, repository or query object is justified.
A service or CRUD application over a handful of tables where every screen maps to a few statements per table and an ORM would add more machinery than it removes.
Reporting and read models: read-only gateways over views or wide tables that return records directly to a formatter, export or BI job.
Legacy databases mediated for several applications: one gateway library per database becomes the documented API and the place where vendor quirks are hidden.
Embedded/local storage (SQLite, SQLCipher) in a desktop or mobile app, where one gateway per table keeps SQL out of the UI and can be tested with an in-memory database.
Batch and ETL writers that need explicit control over statement batching, cursors and transaction size - control that generated mappers hide.
Gradual refactoring of SQL scattered through transaction scripts: the first step is to move each table's statements into a gateway, after which a Data Mapper or repository can be introduced deliberately.
Test fixtures and seeders that must write through the same statements as production code rather than through a second, divergent SQL path.
Generated gateways in Go: sqlc compiles a schema plus a file of named queries into one struct per table and one type-safe method per SQL statement, with the caller holding the database handle and opening transactions - the gateway's invariants are then enforced by the generator and compiler rather than by convention.
Local SQLite storage on Android: each Room @Dao is a gateway over one table - the SQL lives in @Query-annotated methods validated at compile time, rows travel as plain entity data classes, and @Transaction or database-level transactions keep atomic multi-DAO boundaries in the caller.
Java teams that want the gateway structure without hand-writing it: jOOQ's code generator emits one DAO class per table or view (findAll, findById, generated fetchByColumn methods) that reads and writes Record/POJO rows and borrows the caller's Configuration, so the per-table SQL surface is regenerated when the schema changes.

name: inversion-of-control
document:
inversion-of-control
Hollywood Principle
IoC
Invert the direction of control between a reusable framework and application code: the framework owns the call flow and invokes the application's hooks at its extension points, so the generic sequence is reused while application code supplies only behaviour.
A reusable component - framework, container, UI toolkit, event loop, test runner - must own the sequence of calls (main loop, request dispatch, component lifecycle), while the behaviour at each step is application-specific; if application code had to call the framework's steps itself, the generic flow could neither be reused as a whole nor be extended without modifying it.
Applies wherever generic flow logic has to be specialised by application code: UI toolkits and event loops that decide when handlers fire, server containers and engines that own request dispatch and component lifecycle, test runners that own fixture and test sequencing, plugin hosts, and effect runtimes that own program entry. It is the defining characteristic of a framework as opposed to a library (a library is called by your code; a framework calls your code), and it usually arrives bundled with a container, dispatcher or engine - what remains to design is where the boundary sits and how much lifecycle you hand over.
GUI and event-driven applications: the windowing system or runtime owns the event loop and calls your event handlers, app delegate or declarative view body.
Server-side request handling: the container, engine or router owns listen-accept-dispatch and invokes the servlets, handlers, routes or middleware you registered.
Test frameworks: the runner owns discovery, fixture setup and teardown and calls your test methods and lifecycle hooks (JUnit, pytest, xUnit).
Container-managed components: EJB, Spring, Angular or Nest components whose construction, wiring and lifecycle callbacks are driven by the container that also owns the entry point.
Plugin and extension architectures: a host defines extension points and third-party plugins implement them, with the host deciding when each plugin is consulted (IDEs, browsers, build tools, game engines).
Inverted program entry: effect runtimes and app frameworks where the runtime's main calls the run value or app structure you provide instead of you orchestrating from main.
Callback-based C APIs: a library call such as qsort or a GLib main loop calls your function pointer per element or event - a small-scale realization of the same inversion.
Cloud Functions-as-a-Service: AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, and Google Cloud Functions own the request dispatch and cold-start lifecycle; your handler is a hook called by the platform, making serverless a live deployment of the Hollywood principle.
Reactive streams and event-driven pipelines: frameworks like Reactor, RxJava, or Node.js EventEmitter own the subscription and back-pressure loop; operators and subscribers are hooks that the runtime calls on data availability.
Microservices sidecar and service mesh: an Envoy or Linkerd proxy sidecar owns the connection lifecycle and calls application code through a defined protocol; the application registers health checks and request handlers as IoC hooks.
Orleans virtual actor model: the Orleans runtime owns the grain lifecycle, activation and deactivation, and calls grain methods as directed by the scheduler; grain code is a hook implementation invoked by the framework.
ASP.NET Core middleware: the host builds the request pipeline and invokes each registered RequestDelegate in order; middleware can run before and after the next delegate or short-circuit, so the application supplies components while the server owns request dispatch.
JUnit Jupiter extension model: the JUnit engine discovers tests and invokes registered Before*/After* lifecycle callbacks around user test methods; extensions customize execution without owning when tests run.
Kubernetes controllers: the controller manager owns reconciliation loops that watch API state and repeatedly invokes controller reconciliation logic to converge current state on desired state; controllers supply behavior while Kubernetes schedules dispatch.

name: identity-field
document:
identity-field
primary key field
identity column
Store the relational primary key inside the object so that an in-memory instance and its database row are recognised as the same entity across sessions, caches and process restarts, instead of relying on object identity.
Mappers, identity maps and unit-of-work bookkeeping need a stable handle on every object: without a key carried by the object there is no way to tell whether two instances are the same row, which row an UPDATE or DELETE must touch, or what value a referring row should store - and loading the same row twice silently produces two divergent objects.
Applies wherever objects outlive a single operation and are mapped to key-addressed rows: entities behind a Data Mapper or Row Data Gateway, aggregates in a Repository, session caches keyed by table plus id, and object graphs whose children must refer to a parent that is not inserted yet. The key has to survive serialisation and cross-process calls, and for application-generated keys it must exist before the row does.
ORM entities in a session: load a row into an object, mutate business fields, then flush an UPDATE or DELETE targeted at the same identity.
API resources addressed by key: /orders/{id} endpoints that fetch, mutate and delete by identity, with links stored as keys instead of object references.
Session-scoped identity maps and second-level caches keyed by (table, key), which need the key before they can return an existing instance.
Object graphs with parent-child references: the child's foreign key needs the parent's identity, generated before the insert (UUID/sequence) or read back after it (RETURNING/getGeneratedKeys).
Audit, versioning and optimistic locking: change logs and Version Number checks identify the affected row by its key.
Distributed or sharded writes: client-generated keys let a router place the row and let a retry overwrite the same identity idempotently.
Event-sourced aggregates: the aggregate root's identity is the correlation ID carried in every command and event, allowing the event log to reconstruct state by replaying events keyed to that identity.
GraphQL Relay node identification: globally unique node IDs are built from the entity's identity (base64 type-prefixed id), enabling the standardised node query and cache reching defined in the Relay specification.
Multi-tenant SaaS with tenant-scoped identity: a composite key of (tenant_id, id) ensures a tenant can never address another tenant's rows, even if the local id numbers happen to collide.
Idempotent message processing: a command's correlation ID (the entity's identity) lets a handler detect a duplicate and skip reprocessing without a distributed lock.
Hibernate ORM entities with an @Id and Session persistence context: loading by identifier reuses the session's first-level identity, while the chosen generated-id strategy determines when the key becomes available.
PostgreSQL tables with GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY and INSERT ... RETURNING id: the database owns key generation, then the mapper reads the assigned identity back onto the object in the same write.
Relay GraphQL servers implementing the Node interface: expose a globally unique opaque id and refetch the same object through node(id), carrying entity identity across a client cache and API boundary.

name: audit-interceptor
document:
audit-interceptor
audit trail interceptor
audit logging interceptor
Declare an audit policy at an invocation seam that records the actor, action, target, correlation id and both attempt and terminal outcome around a delegated operation, then sends the structured event to a dedicated integrity-protected sink, so security accountability is consistent without inline logging in every service.
Security-relevant operations (privileged actions, state changes and access to sensitive data) must be attributable, but inline logging misses denied and failed attempts, varies in schema, can leak raw arguments and disappears with a rolled-back transaction. Teams also need to cover components they cannot modify without pretending that a proxy sees calls that bypass it.
Business or service tiers whose sensitive operations pass through an interceptable seam: container-managed beans, proxied service objects, ORM entity lifecycles, message endpoints or an HTTP pipeline. Audit selection must be declarative and uniform, while the sink has its own integrity and retention requirements (Secure Logger); the design must make mediation gaps, redaction, transaction coupling, failure policy, clock source and correlation propagation explicit.
Business-tier auditing of money-moving or otherwise regulated operations (fund transfer, order placement, claim submission): who requested it, on which object, when, and whether it succeeded.
Privileged administration surfaces (role changes, key rotation, configuration changes) where every sensitive operation must leave a record naming the acting principal.
Authentication and authorization outcomes: successful and failed logins, access-denial decisions and lockouts routed into the same audit pipeline instead of ad-hoc log lines.
Access-to-sensitive-data events (who read which patient/customer record) recorded at the gateway or service boundary to satisfy data-protection obligations.
Retrofitting auditing onto legacy components whose code cannot be modified, by wrapping the service object or binding an interceptor to its interface.
Middleware-level auditing of message endpoints and database calls in a business tier, correlating the caller's subject with the operation performed.
Financial API request interception (Spring Boot global request interceptors) capturing who accessed which endpoint, with what payload, and what outcome — satisfying SOX financial reporting controls.
Entity-level change tracking via ORM subscribers (e.g., EF Core SaveChangesInterceptor, TypeORM subscribers): automatically diff old vs. new property values on create/update/delete and emit audit envelopes without manual logging calls.
API gateway-level audit logging: capture every external API call with timestamp, user identity, endpoint, method, and outcome, correlating across microservices via X-Request-ID / traceparent headers.
Compliance reporting automation: generate audit-ready reports for SOX (~7-year retention), HIPAA (~6-year retention), GDPR (data residency-aware), and PCI-DSS from structured interceptor events.
Zero-trust data access trails: record every read of sensitive fields (PHI, PII, financial data) so data-protection obligations (GDPR Article 5 data minimization, HIPAA access logging) are demonstrably met.
Hibernate Envers: @Audited entity lifecycle changes create per-entity _AUD revisions at transaction commit; a custom revision entity/listener can attach actor or request metadata.
Django admin: django.contrib.admin.models.LogEntry records action time, user, object, addition/change/deletion and change_message for ModelAdmin activity.
Rails Audited: the audited ActiveRecord extension creates audit rows for model create, update and destroy callbacks, including changed attributes and optional acting-user attribution.

name: active-record
document:
active-record
active record pattern
ActiveRecord
Make a domain object the record for one database row: keep the row's state, row-local behavior, and the methods that find and persist it together, so a small domain does not pay for a separate mapping layer.
A simple relational domain still needs a choice about where persistence lives. A Data Mapper or gateway separates table I/O from the object but adds mapping code and a second place to navigate, while direct SQL leaks schema knowledge into callers; the recurring question is whether one row object can own its data and CRUD without hiding transaction boundaries or pretending to model cross-row rules.
A relational store is the single system of record, the domain is small and its rules are mostly local to one row (validation, derivations, simple state transitions), and the team prefers a convention-driven persistence layer over a designed one. Typical homes are framework ecosystems where the ORM is the house style (Rails, Laravel Eloquent, Django, GORM, Vapor Fluent, TypeORM), CRUD-heavy applications, and thin layers over an already well-shaped legacy schema. Entity Framework Core can host behavior on entity classes, but its DbContext and mapping conventions are a Data Mapper-shaped boundary rather than pure Active Record. It stops applying as soon as invariants span several objects, several representations of one table are needed, or the store must be swappable.
CRUD-heavy applications where most screens and endpoints map onto a single table: forms, admin back offices, catalogs, content management.
Small-to-medium domains whose rules are mostly per-row - field validation, derived values, one-row state transitions - so a mapper layer would move data around without adding a model.
Prototypes and thin service layers over an existing, already normalised legacy schema where the table shape is stable and the domain is the schema.
Framework-default persistence: a Rails, Django, GORM, Vapor Fluent or TypeORM codebase where fighting the ORM for purity costs more than it returns.
Simple record-shaped bounded contexts inside a larger system - settings, audit entries, lookup tables - where a full domain model would be overhead.
JSON:API or REST backends for SPAs and mobile apps where the data model maps directly to a relational schema with minimal transformation.
Microservices with a single-responsibility data store: a service whose entire bounded context is one aggregate root table or a handful of tightly coupled tables.
Batch import pipelines where records are validated once and bulk-inserted (insert_all/upsert_all), and the domain logic has already been applied before the bulk operation.
Multi-tenant SaaS backends where row-level isolation is enforced at the database and the ORM connection handles tenant scoping automatically.
Real Rails systems such as GitLab and Discourse are good fits for row-shaped users, posts, permissions and settings backed by PostgreSQL; keep their reporting and cross-record workflows in query or service boundaries.
A Django or Laravel CRUD surface such as an admin or back-office module fits when each request mostly validates, loads, changes and saves one model; switch to a mapper or repository when the same data feeds materially different contracts.

name: cache-aside
document:
cache-aside
look-aside cache
lazy loading cache
Place the cache beside the authoritative store and make the application own the protocol: look up the cache first, load the entry from the store on a miss and populate it with a TTL, and invalidate the entry right after each write to the store - so repeated reads stay cheap while the store, never the cache, decides what is true.
A source of truth (relational database, downstream service, object store) is expensive or rate-limited for the read volume an application receives, while most reads repeat a small set of keys: without a cache every request pays the source-of-truth cost, and with an unmanaged cache the copies silently drift. The recurring decision is where the read path looks first, when a miss may populate the entry, and what a write must do so the cached copy stops lying.
Read-heavy paths in front of a slower or metered authoritative store, typically several application instances sharing a Redis or Memcached tier, or each holding an in-process cache, where a bounded amount of staleness is acceptable and every writer can be held to the same invalidation discipline. It applies when the read/write ratio is high, when the cache itself does not provide read-through or write-through, and when lost or evicted entries can always be recomputed from the store.
Read-heavy lookups by natural key (product catalogs, user profiles, article pages) in front of a relational database.
Several service instances sharing a Redis or Memcached tier where every instance must see the same cached copy and the same invalidation.
Reference data that changes slowly (currency rates, feature flags, configuration, price lists) refreshed by TTL with explicit invalidation when it is edited.
Expensive aggregate or derived results (dashboards, search pages, recommendations) recomputed into the cache per request key.
Per-instance in-process caches for hot, rarely changing values where a shared cache would add network latency without adding much.
Multi-level caching in Kubernetes: an in-process L1 (Caffeine) sidecar on each pod with an L2 Redis cluster, where the L1 is invalidated on each incoming request via a bloom filter or pub/sub.
CDN edge caching for static or semi-static API responses: the application server acts as the origin and issues cache-aside reads; CDN edges serve from their own look-aside cache with short TTLs and PURGE invalidation on writes.
RAG and vector cache in AI pipelines: embedding results cached by query hash so repeated semantically identical questions hit the vector store once and reuse cached results; TTL bounds staleness of the embedding index.
Django's low-level cache API (cache.get / cache.get_or_set with a per-key timeout, cache.delete on save) is cache-aside as a framework primitive; MediaWiki's WANObjectCache does the same at Wikipedia scale via getWithSet, invalidating page parses through cross-datacenter purges rather than direct writes.
Spring's cache abstraction applies the pattern declaratively: @Cacheable loads and populates on a miss, @CacheEvict removes the entry after the writer, with RedisCacheManager supplying the TTL - the application still owns both paths, the annotation only moves where.
Hibernate's second-level cache read-write concurrency strategy is a managed cache-aside: the updated entry is soft-locked around the transaction so concurrent readers miss to the database instead of repopulating the cache with the pre-commit value.

name: state-colocation
document:
state-colocation
colocated state
colocation
Keep each piece of presentation state in the component closest to where it is used — down to the single component that owns and reads it — instead of hoisting it to a common ancestor or a global store, so that a change touches only the smallest part of the view that can observe it.
State gets hoisted 'just in case': a value only one component reads is lifted to the screen or application root, or pushed into one global store, because someone may want it later. The consequences are components that receive props they never read, updates that invalidate far more of the UI than the value's actual consumers, an unclear owner for each value, and tests that must assemble the whole state container to exercise one field. The recurring decision is where a new piece of state should live: keep it at the smallest scope that actually needs it.
Declarative component UIs (React, Vue, Svelte, SwiftUI, Compose, Blazor, Qt Quick) and, in generalized form, any system where a mutable value is owned by one component-like unit: the consumers determine the state's scope, the framework invalidates only what the owner's subtree can observe, and components are composed, moved and deleted. Most compelling where over-lifted or global state has already become a performance and ownership problem.
A search or form input whose value is read only by the input, its own validation and its own preview: keep it in that component instead of the screen root (the canonical typing example where hoisting made every keystroke re-render the page).
Which panel of an accordion is open: leave it per panel while panels are independent, then lift exactly to the accordion once only one panel may be open at a time (the closest common parent).
Tooltip, hover, popover and dropdown state in a chart or table cell: own it in the cell component rather than in a global UI store.
Per-row edit or selection state in a data grid: the row component owns it; only cross-row operations need the grid to own it.
Dialog and modal open state in the button or list that opens it, until another surface must close or observe it.
Form draft state in the form component; lift it only when a sibling — summary panel, preview pane, wizard footer — genuinely must read it.
Extracting a self-contained widget for reuse or publication: keeping its state local makes the component portable and shrinks its API.
Per-cell expansion state in a tree view or file explorer: the tree node component owns whether it is expanded; the parent tree only coordinates multi-select or bulk-expand operations.
Media playback state for a single player (play/pause, current time, volume): colocate in the player component rather than a global audio store unless the same track plays in multiple places simultaneously.
Local filter/sort state for a data table or list: keep it in the list component until a URL parameter, shareable link, or sibling panel requires sharing it.
Vue: composable-local state (useSearch, useToggle) where each consumer needs its own independent instance of the same reactive logic pattern.
Angular Signals: feature-level signal stores scoped to a route or feature slice, not the entire application store, for UI state and feature-derived state.
SwiftUI: @State for view-local value types; @StateObject for view-owned reference types; keep @EnvironmentObject for genuinely cross-cutting state (auth session, theme) mounted as low in the hierarchy as consumers allow.
Svelte 5 runes: `let count = $state(0)` inside a component is per-component-instance reactive state — the component that declares it is its owner; Svelte's v5 migration explicitly replaced the pre-runes habit of reaching for a store whenever state sat at a component's top level, with $state plus $derived/$effect as the local cells, and module-level .svelte.js state only for deliberate sharing.
Jetpack Compose: the official hoisting guidance is this pattern's placement ladder — keep state as close as possible to where it is consumed, hoist only to the lowest common ancestor of all composables that read or write it, pass value down and onValueChange up, and make the ViewModel the owner only when business logic or lifecycle outlives the composition.
Blazor: component fields are the default owner for UI-local state; the official state-management guidance promotes to an in-memory state container service only when components must share non-persistent state, and to Protected Browser Storage only when the value must survive circuits or sessions — a three-rung ladder that mirrors local state, scoped provider, persistence.

name: dependency-injection
document:
dependency-injection
di
constructor injection
setter injection
interface injection
ioc container
pure di
manual di
Supply an object with the collaborators it needs from the outside — through its constructor, its setters/properties, or a dedicated injection interface — so it never constructs or looks a dependency up itself and every wiring decision is made once, in a composition root or container.
An object that creates its own collaborators hard-wires a concrete class, a construction recipe and often a lifetime into itself: swapping the implementation for a test double, a second deployment or a new platform means editing the class, and the dependency graph stays invisible in the API. The recurring trigger is exactly the catalog's rule: an object should not create what it depends on — the caller, the framework or the composition root decides, and hands the dependency in.
Applies whenever a component's collaborators are chosen per deployment, per environment or per test, whenever constructing them is expensive or platform-specific, and whenever a framework owns object creation (request handlers, scheduled jobs, UI screens, message consumers). It matters most in large object graphs where one abstraction has several implementations and lifetimes must be managed (singleton, request-scoped, transient); it is unnecessary when the collaborators are pure values or when construction is a private detail nobody needs to vary.
Web and API backends whose handlers need repositories, clocks, mailers and caches that must be replaced by fakes in tests and by sandbox services in staging.
Hexagonal and clean architectures where the domain declares ports (interfaces) and the infrastructure layer supplies adapters at the composition root.
Frameworks that own object creation — request handlers, scheduled jobs, UI controllers, message consumers — where the framework's injector is the only practical wiring point.
Deployment variants (on-prem vs cloud, SQL vs in-memory, real vs stub payment gateway) selected per environment through binding configuration rather than conditional code.
Plugin and extension systems where the concrete implementation is chosen at start-up from a plugin registry, enabling third-party adapters without touching core code.
Expensive shared resources whose lifetime must be managed centrally (connection pools, HTTP clients, circuit breakers) while service classes stay stateless.
Unit tests that construct the class under test directly with test doubles, and integration tests that swap only the outer layer's bindings.
Microservices with sidecar containers: the sidecar provides logging, tracing and retry policies as injected collaborators, keeping the service logic untouched.
Cloud-native applications where the composition root is the only place that knows whether a dependency resolves locally, across a service mesh, or via a remote gRPC call.
Multi-tenant SaaS where tenant-specific adapters (tenant-scoped repositories, per-tenant feature flags) are bound at the composition root and switched by middleware.
Event-driven systems where message handlers receive their dependencies through injection, making the handler logic identical between in-process and distributed deployment.
AOT-compiled applications (Native AOT, Blazor WebAssembly, serverless) where runtime reflection is unavailable — dependencies are resolved via source generators or manually at the composition root.
Functional codebases using effect systems (ZIO, fp-ts, Reader monad) where the DI container is replaced by typed environments passed through function compositions.
Consumer-driven contract testing (Pact, OpenAPI pact) where DI swaps provider implementations with contract-mock stubs at the boundary, enabling parallel service development without shared integration environments.
Resilience and fault-injection testing: proxies or decorator-based fault injectors (e.g., Gremlin SDK, WireMock) are injected as collaborators to validate retry, timeout and circuit-breaker behaviour under simulated failure conditions.
Single-page application frameworks with DI built into the component tree: Angular resolves components, directives and services through hierarchical injectors, scoping providers to the application root, a component subtree or a route so features override implementations and lazy-load without global registration.
Android apps using Dagger (and Hilt over it) to build the object graph at compile time — generated, reflection-free code, bindings and cycles checked at build time, with field injection reserved for framework-created entry points like Activities and Fragments.
Python web APIs (FastAPI) where each path operation declares Depends(callable) parameters: the framework resolves nested dependency graphs with per-request caching and uses yield-based dependencies to open and close connections around each request.
