name: pipeline
document:
pipeline
assembly line
processing pipeline
Decompose a transformation into an ordered sequence of named stages that each consume the previous stage's output and produce the next stage's input, so the workflow reads top to bottom and every step can be tested, instrumented, reordered or replaced on its own.
A multi-step transformation is written as one long function or a tangle of nested calls: the steps are unnamed, their order is implicit in statement order, intermediate values need throwaway names, there is no seam at which a single step can be logged, tested or replaced, and the same sequence is retyped at every call site that needs it.
Processing that naturally decomposes into successive transformations of the same payload - request handling, ETL, compiler passes, message enrichment, image or byte-stream processing - whether the payload is a single value or a stream. It fits in-process, staged execution where one driver owns ordering, error handling and cancellation; distributing the stages across processes, transports and independently deployed filters is the architectural pipe-and-filter pattern instead.
Request handling: deserialise, authenticate, validate, enrich, persist and render a request, with each step named so a failing stage is attributable and testable in isolation.
ETL and data import: extract, clean, transform, validate and load large files as a stream, so no intermediate collection is materialised and memory stays bounded.
Compiler and interpreter passes: source, tokens, AST, resolution, optimisation and code emission, where each pass is an independent stage over the intermediate representation and the pass list is the pipeline.
Message enrichment in an integration flow: unwrap, translate, enrich and route a message, one stage per concern, with per-channel ordering; the cross-process version stays pipe-and-filter.
Image or byte-stream processing: decode, crop or resize, watermark and encode, lazily per frame or chunk, optionally overlapping stages across cores.
Configuration-driven data cleaning: the stage list is assembled from configuration or a plugin registry so different tenants get different ordered steps without changing the stages themselves.
TensorFlow tf.data input pipelines: tf.data.Dataset pipelines that chain map, prefetch, parallel_interleave and shuffle stages to feed a training loop efficiently, with each stage independently configurable and the whole pipeline testable in isolation.
LLM token streaming: HTTP server-sent event streams where an LLM produces tokens at inference speed while clients consume at variable network speed; stream.pipeline() prevents the inference server from buffering unbounded tokens in memory when a slow client disconnects (Node.js stream backpressure case study).
Observability telemetry pipelines: OpenTelemetry Collector chains receivers, processors (memory_limiter, batch, filter, transform, tail_sampling) and exporters for traces, metrics and logs, with connectors (e.g., spanmetrics) bridging signal types and memory_limiter placed first to prevent OOM before filtering.
Typed TypeScript pipeline with schema validation: Zod or io-ts schemas define the stage contract at each boundary, catching schema violations at the exact stage that produced bad data rather than at a distant consumer.
Async generator pipelines in Python: asyncio queues with bounded capacity connect async generator stages, propagating backpressure by pausing producers when the queue is full; the FinStream analytics case study showed 82% memory reduction and 99.7% latency reduction versus unbounded buffering.
Event-streaming pipelines with Kafka and Flink: producers, topic partitions, Flink consumers and checkpointing form a distributed pipeline where backpressure cascades across every boundary; the Kafka max.block.ms and Flink backpressure.sample.interval settings interact under partition saturation and must be tested together under load.
Dynamic pipeline parallelism: construct-and-run pipelines (MapReduce, Spark) fix stage count at construction, while on-the-fly pipelines (Cilk-P Piper algorithm) allow the structure to emerge at runtime, varying per iteration and supporting data-dependent branching; on-the-fly enables pipelines like x264 that cannot be expressed with a fixed static structure.
LLVM compiler pass pipelines: PassBuilder assembles ModulePassManager, CGSCCPassManager, FunctionPassManager and LoopPassManager across the IR hierarchy (Module → CGSCC → Function → Loop), with registered callbacks injecting passes at named extension points (pipeline-start, vectorizer-start, optimizer-last); incorrect PreservedAnalyses declarations invalidate all downstream analyses.
Continuous data pipelines at scale (Google model): periodic pipelines run on cron and suffer from depth growth and resource exhaustion as organic load increases; continuous pipelines (master-slave or event-triggered) replace idle-waiting with always-on processing, eliminating the 'pipeline vs cron' discontinuity at the cost of operational complexity.
ML pipeline orchestration (Airflow, Kubeflow, Prefect, Dagster): each orchestrator applies the pipeline pattern at the workflow level - Airflow's DAG-of-tasks, Kubeflow's per-container-step pipelines with GPU scheduling, Prefect's monoflow/subflow/orchestrator pattern, and Dagster's software-defined assets where asset dependencies imply the pipeline; the pipeline is the scheduler's unit of execution, not an implementation detail.
Apache Beam: PCollections flow through composable PTransforms (ParDo, Combine and GroupByKey) in a pipeline graph, making each transform boundary explicit while the runner handles execution.
Node.js stream.pipeline(): Readable, Transform and Writable stages compose with built-in backpressure, error propagation and AbortSignal cancellation; this is a concrete streaming realization, not a durable workflow engine.

name: two-step-view
document:
two-step-view
two stage view
Split presentation into two transformations - first turn domain data into a channel-neutral logical page, then render that logical page into a concrete output format - so page structure is defined once while look-and-feel and output channel live entirely in the renderer.
Every page owns its own presentation decisions: with one template or one transform per page, a global look-and-feel change means editing every file, and serving a second channel (print/PDF, e-mail, plain text, a machine-readable feed) means duplicating the page's structure. Nothing in the codebase represents 'the page' independently of the markup it currently happens to be rendered as.
Server-side presentation or document-publishing boundaries where several output channels share one page structure, or where the house style changes often enough that it must change in exactly one place. It also fits where the rendering technology is expected to be replaced (XSLT today, a template engine or PDF formatter tomorrow) and where the page should be inspectable, testable or cacheable before it is rendered.
Multi-channel publishing: one invoice or statement rendered as HTML for a portal, XSL-FO/PDF for print and plain text for e-mail from a single logical page.
Site-wide restyling in a CMS or portal where the house style must be one artefact to change and review rather than one edit per page family.
API-plus-HTML endpoints: the same logical page is serialised as JSON for clients and rendered as HTML for the browsable interface.
Document and report pipelines in the DocBook tradition: the logical document is produced once and rendered to HTML, PDF and e-book formats by different stylesheets.
Constrained or legacy channels - plain text, WAP/XML, CSV - added next to HTML without touching the page assembly code.
Pages produced once and consumed by several renderers or locales: the logical page is cached and rendered per channel on demand.
Spring Web MVC XSLT views: an XsltController builds an XML DOM of the page content, puts it in the model, and XsltViewResolver applies a home.xslt stylesheet - stage one produces the logical document, stage two owns the HTML.
Aura.View (PHP) ships the pattern under the name TwoStepView: a content template renders first, then a separately registered layout wraps it via setLayout()/getContent(), keeping the site chrome in one artefact instead of every page.
Standards-based publishing toolchains: the DITA Open Toolkit transforms semantic DITA maps/topics through XSLT stages into HTML, PDF and other deliverables, and Apache Cocoon pipelines generator -> XSLT transformer -> serializer so one XML source serves HTML, PDF, SVG and text.

name: multiple-views
document:
multiple-views
multiple presentations
Keep one presentation-free model behind several independent view technologies, so each representation is produced by its own view while the domain data, its derivation rules and its consistency stay in one place.
A single body of data must be published through more than one presentation technology at the same time - an HTML page, a JSON or XML API, a CSV or PDF export, a mobile channel. Each technology is easy to satisfy with its own copy of the loading, filtering and formatting logic, so the representations drift apart and every model change has to be repeated per technology.
Server-side presentation layers of enterprise applications (and document/GUI tools) where one model is read by several rendering technologies, whether concurrently (a page and an API over the same resource; a table and a chart over the same document) or over time (channels added later), and where the model must stay unaware of any particular presentation technology.
A resource served both as an HTML page and as a JSON API from one model and one set of business rules (server-side rendering beside an API in the same application).
Exports beside the UI: the same dataset as HTML, CSV and PDF for reporting, with filtering and selection rules defined once.
Multi-channel delivery: web pages, mobile screens, feeds and partner XML from one model, with channel-specific markup over shared content.
A desktop or tool application with several simultaneous presentations of one document (table, chart, inspector) that must stay synchronized while editing.
Migration periods where an old and a new presentation technology (JSP beside Thymeleaf, XML beside JSON) are served from the same model until every consumer has moved.
An internal back-office view and a public storefront over the same catalogue model, where each side shows a different subset of the same data.
A Django REST Framework APIView that negotiates JSONRenderer and TemplateHTMLRenderer for the same resource, keeping content negotiation in one endpoint while each renderer owns its format.
A Qt Widgets application in which one QAbstractItemModel feeds table, list, or tree views so several presentations of the same document stay synchronized.
An ASP.NET Core Web API action whose JSON and XML output formatters select a response representation from the client's Accept header without changing the domain model.

name: view-helper
document:
view-helper
template helper
Keep a view free of processing logic by giving it dedicated helpers - objects or functions that adapt and format the model it displays - so markup and presentation logic can change independently.
A template needs more than plain property access (currency and date formatting, plurals, derived labels, repeated fragments) and there is no place to put that logic: written inline as scriptlets, template-language expressions or duplicated markup conditionals, it makes the view unreadable and untestable, cannot be reused by another page, and forces whoever edits markup to edit program logic.
Server-side presentation code whose views are authored in a template language (JSP, Razor, Thymeleaf, Django/Jinja, ERB, Handlebars, Twirl, Leaf) over dynamic business data. It applies with or without a Front Controller, and pays off most where markup is owned by a different role than the business objects and where several views need the same formatting or adaptation.
Product, invoice and account pages that must present money, dates, quantities and plurals consistently across many views.
The same data rendered for several channels - HTML, transactional mail, PDF, export - where formatting helpers are shared and only markup differs.
Legacy JSP/servlet views dominated by scriptlets, migrated to helper beans or custom tags one element at a time.
Design-team-owned templates where markup changes often and a markup change must not require touching application code.
Table and row rendering where a helper turns a domain object into cells, keeping loops and conditions out of the view language.
Dashboards that aggregate several services behind a delegate and hand the view a presentation-shaped value bean.
Rails Action View: helper modules mixed into the view context - built-in number, date, link, asset and capture helpers plus the application's own modules under app/helpers - are the View Helper realized as a framework default.
Django: custom template filters and tags implemented in Python, registered with a Library in an app's templatetags module and loaded with {% load %} - the sanctioned place for currency, date and derived-label formatting that the template language deliberately refuses to do.
ASP.NET Core Razor: tag helpers (ITagHelper classes targeting elements or attributes, scoped per view with @addTagHelper) and HTML helper extension methods generate markup so pages stay HTML-friendly instead of C#-heavy.

name: template-view
document:
template-view
template-based view
Render a mostly static markup document that contains markers, resolving each marker from a prepared view model at render time, so presentation lives in an editable artifact instead of in string-building code.
A response is fixed markup except for the few values that vary per request, but the page is produced by concatenating strings in program code: markup authors cannot touch it, indentation and quoting are lost in the concatenation, escaping is re-decided at every insertion point, and each layout change ripples through the code that emits it. The recurring decision is how the static text and the dynamic values are combined.
Server-side presentation where the output is a text document - HTML, XML, CSV, an email body, a report, the HTML behind a PDF - that is mostly static with holes to fill. It applies when presentation should be editable as a document (designers, translators, non-programmers), when the same chrome repeats across pages, and when escaping must be uniform; it assumes the model can be prepared before rendering and that no second presentation stage (a logical screen, a per-channel renderer) is needed.
Server-rendered HTML pages in a web application, where the route or controller prepares the model and the template owns the markup.
Transactional and marketing email bodies: HTML documents with per-recipient values and a shared layout fragment.
Document and report generation - invoices, statements, HTML rendered to PDF, configuration files, code and data exports - from the same template mechanism.
Static-site and documentation generators that merge content with a shared layout at build time.
Internationalised pages where the surrounding markup is stable and the localised strings and per-locale formatting are the values that change.
Admin and internal-tool screens whose markup is largely boilerplate with a few tables and fields filled from the model.
Go's html/template package: server-rendered HTML pages where {{.Field}} markers resolve against a supplied data structure and the engine escapes every value for the context it lands in - HTML, CSS, JavaScript or URL - instead of at the call site.
Play Framework's Twirl templates: .scala.html files compile to Scala functions at build time, so a marker naming a missing or renamed model field fails the build rather than rendering an empty region on the first request.
ASP.NET Core Razor Pages: each .cshtml page pairs with a PageModel class that handles the request and prepares the model while the Razor view places @-model values into mostly static markup - the handler/template split the pattern prescribes.

name: higher-order-component
document:
higher-order-component
HOC
component enhancer
Add cross-cutting behaviour to many components at once by wrapping them in an enhancer function that takes a component and returns a new, enhanced component, so no wrapped component knows about the concern or has to be edited.
The same cross-cutting logic - subscribing to a data source, checking a permission, firing analytics, injecting a theme, a translation or a feature flag - is needed by many components, and copying it into each one couples every component to the concern, re-couples them to every change of it, and leaves the behaviour to be remembered at each new call site. React tried mixins and inheritance first and removed them (implicit dependencies between mixin and component, name clashes, snowballing coupling), so the recurring decision is how to apply one behaviour to many components without editing them, while the components stay reusable and unaware of the enhancement.
Component-model UI code where components are values the framework mounts with a stable identity (React and its ecosystem first; the same shape recurs with Compose composables, SwiftUI views, Blazor components, Scala.js layers and handler-based Go/Java web UIs), where the concern is genuinely cross-cutting rather than local to one screen, where the enhancement can be expressed as a pure function from component to component and applied once at the definition or export site, and where the wrapped component's inputs form a prop-like contract that can be extended by injection without touching its internals.
Subscribing many components to an external data source — React documentation's withSubscription example, or Redux's connect: store state arrives as injected props with no component knowing about the store.
Apollo Client data injection: graphql(Query, { options, props }) HOC maps query results and loading state to props; multiple graphql HOCs composed with @compose; historically the standard before useQuery.
Authorization and feature gating at the boundary: withAuthorization(Component, { requiredRole }) or withFeatureFlag(...) decides rendering without editing the component; useful for route-level guards applied across many pages.
Analytics, telemetry and instrumentation applied at export sites (withAnalytics): tracking calls stay out of presentation code and can be added or removed at one location per module.
Injecting ambient context into components that take it as props — translations via withTranslation (react-i18next), routing via withRouter (React Router v5 and below), theming via withTheme (Material-UI v4) — enabling third-party and vendored components to participate without modification.
Error and loading boundaries as an enhancer (withErrorBoundary): the boundary exists as a component in the tree anyway; an enhancer consolidates the concern into one reusable definition rather than repeating the try/catch at each call site.
Sharing logic into class components and older codebases where hooks cannot be used: the HOC reaches class components and library component-shaped APIs that hooks cannot wrap.
Material-UI v4 theming: withStyles and withTheme HOCs inject classes and theme as props; compose chains combine styling with data (connect + withStyles + graphql on the same export).
Internationalization testing: export both wrapped and unwrapped components; tests use the raw component with a mock t function while integration tests use the full I18nextProvider setup.
Conditional prop injection: a data-enhancer that only injects props when a condition is met (e.g. user is authenticated) lets the wrapped component remain agnostic about the absence of that data.
React Compiler (React Forget) compatibility: heavy HOC layering reduces the compiler's static analysis surface and may cause it to bailout — test compiler output when adding HOCs to a compiled codebase; prefer hooks for new logic the compiler should see.
React Server Components boundary: a HOC that calls hooks or reads client-only context (useAuth, useTheme, useRouter) cannot execute during a server render; the wrapped component may receive undefined injected props on the server and flash-change on hydration. Pass server-fetched data as props through the HOC boundary from a server parent instead.
Streaming SSR and Suspense integration: a HOC that wraps a component behind a Suspense boundary adds a node that may delay streaming; if the HOC itself is async it must be carefully placed to avoid blocking the fallback from showing.
Partial hydration patterns: on islands architectures (Next.js App Router, Astro), a HOC that subscribes to client-side state forces the entire island to be hydrated even if the wrapped component has no server payload; prefer passing hydrated state as props from a server parent.
Recompose (acdlite): a 'lodash for React' utility belt built entirely from composable HOCs (withState, mapProps, pure, branch) piped through enhance/compose - the pattern industrialised; its October 2018 deprecation in favour of Hooks (bug-fix maintenance only) is the canonical case study of the pattern's cost when a runtime offers a cheaper reuse primitive.
MobX React binding: observer from mobx-react / mobx-react-lite is an official HOC that subscribes the wrapped component to every observable read during render, re-rendering it automatically; MobX guidance is to apply observer first (innermost) when composing it with other HOCs, and to wrap every component that reads observables.

name: attorney-client
document:
attorney-client
attorney pattern
attorney-client friendship idiom
Grant a named collaborator a deliberately narrow compile-time view of a class's private interface by making an attorney the client's sole friend; the attorney forwards selected operations or re-exports selected private nested types (often through controlled public typedefs), while unrelated private members and the public contract remain closed.
A C++ collaborator may need one private hook, constructor, iterator adapter or nested implementation type, but a friend class receives every private and protected member. Making the hook public leaks it to every caller; publishing a std::list<T>::iterator or the container type leaks representation and its invalidation contract; pImpl hides representation from everyone but does not grant one collaborator a typed privileged view. The missing mechanism is a small attorney contract that names exactly the operations or nested types this collaborator may use without turning the private interface into a second public API.
Object-oriented code whose encapsulation boundary is a class and whose language offers class- or scope-level access control but no per-collaborator grant - C++ with friend declarations, Java/C#/Kotlin with package, assembly or module access, and their test- and library-extension scenarios. It applies at object scope, where one type owns the implementation and one named collaborator needs a slice of it, and it is a source-level structuring device checked by the compiler, never a runtime protection mechanism.
White-box test access: a test harness reaches one private hook or state view through a named attorney instead of making the member public or redefining private with a test-only preprocessor switch.
Iterator adapters: Boost.Iterator's iterator_core_access is a canonical gateway class a user-defined iterator befriends, so iterator_facade and its operators reach private dereference/increment/advance core functions while those implementation hooks stay out of the iterator's public API.
Serialization: Boost.Serialization has serializable classes befriend boost::serialization::access, whose gateway reaches the private serialize() member so archives can reconstruct state without a public serialization method.
Private nested type exposure: LLVM's SchedulerInternalsAttorney publishes the selected nested Scheduler::BndlSchedState as a public type alias and supplies narrow static accessors for unit tests, without publishing every Scheduler private type.
A pImpl-backed adapter that must inspect one implementation-owned type: keep the public class opaque and put the attorney definition in the adapter or test header, so the privileged component gets a typed view without making the implementation part of the ordinary public contract.
Iterator facade over a hidden list-like representation: expose a stable nested iterator/view type through an attorney rather than publishing std::list<T>::iterator, so the owner can replace the container without promising its node and invalidation details to every caller.
Private virtual hooks: an attorney forwards one private virtual operation through a base reference, allowing the derived override to run even though friendship is not inherited.
Factory or construction control: a builder reaches one private constructor or initialization hook through an attorney, while unrelated callers still cannot construct an object through that path.
Spacecraft flight software (fsfw): LocalDpManagerAttorney keeps fetchPoolEntry and getMutexHandle as private static forwarders and befriends only LocalPoolVariable and LocalPoolVector, so the local data pool manager opens its internals to two named collaborators instead of every class that might befriend it.
Simulator tree traversal (Sandia Sparta Modeling Framework): sparta::TreeNodePrivateAttorney exposes TreeNode's private child vectors and subtrees through static accessors (getAllChildren, getChild, findChildren) for internal Reports and Pipeout processing, with a documented 'should NOT be used by simulation developers' restriction in place of an enforceable caller limit.

name: quantity
document:
quantity
units of measure
dimensioned value
Represent a dimensioned measurement as one value that carries its amount together with its unit, so that conversion, comparison, unit-compatible arithmetic and amount-plus-unit input/output all have a single owner and incompatible units cannot be combined by accident.
Measurements are stored as bare numbers whose unit lives only in a variable name, a column comment or the reader's memory: the same physical quantity appears in metres in one place and in feet in another, conversion factors are retyped at every call site, adding two numbers of different dimensions compiles (or runs) happily, and parsing and formatting '3 km' is reinvented per feature. The recurring trigger is that an amount and its unit always change together and are one conceptual whole, so leaving them as two unconnected things makes the unit rules impossible to own.
Value-scope code in domain, engineering or integration layers that handles physical quantities - length, mass, time, temperature, energy, data volume, concentration. It pays off when values arrive with heterogeneous units (sensors, imports, user input, third parties), when derived quantities such as speed or density are computed, when users select a unit system for display, and when values must survive persistence and transport. The language decides how much of the guarantee is compile-time (units as type parameters, phantom/branded types) and how much is a runtime value object backed by a conversion table or unit registry.
Sensor and telemetry pipelines where readings arrive tagged with a unit and must be normalised to a canonical unit before aggregation, alerting or storage.
Engineering and simulation code (CAD, robotics, structural, electrical) that computes derived quantities such as velocity, torque or energy and must keep the dimensions consistent.
Logistics and commerce where weight, dimensions and rate limits are expressed in different unit systems (kg/lb, cm/in, m^3/ft^3) and are displayed in the customer's chosen system.
Healthcare and laboratory systems that exchange doses and results between systems (mg/kg, mmol/L) with reference ranges in different units.
Energy and utility metering, where consumption (kWh, m^3) is billed through unit-price arithmetic and readings must be comparable across meter types.
UI-level unit-system switching: store and compute in one canonical unit, render and edit in metric or imperial according to a user preference.
Scientific Python applications built on Pint's UnitRegistry, such as sensor and laboratory pipelines, where quantities are parsed, converted and reduced dimensionally at integration boundaries.
.NET engineering and telemetry services using UnitsNet's strongly typed Length, Mass and related quantities, with parsing, conversion, serialization and display-unit selection centralized in the library.
Compile-time dimensional-analysis code using F# units of measure or C++ Boost.Units for simulation and control loops, where invalid unit arithmetic is rejected before runtime and derived units are expressed algebraically.

name: poison-pill
document:
poison-pill
sentinel message
end-of-stream marker
Terminate queue consumers cooperatively by sending a reserved sentinel message that each consumer recognises as "no more work", so consumers drain the backlog and exit without a separate control channel or forced cancellation.
A producer-consumer system must shut down, but its consumers block on an empty queue and the queue has no built-in "no more items" signal: callers either kill the workers mid-work and drop buffered items, or leave them blocked forever. Production has ended - how do the consumers learn that while still processing everything already queued?
In-process or broker-mediated producer-consumer systems with a FIFO work queue, a fixed set of long-lived consumers (threads, coroutines, actors) that block when the queue is empty, and a shutdown requirement that work already accepted by the queue be drained before the consumers exit - typically deployment, signal handling or test teardown.
Signal-driven shutdown of an in-process worker pool: the SIGTERM handler stops accepting work, then enqueues one pill per worker so the backlog is processed before the process exits.
Batch importers and ETL stages whose consumers block on a work queue and must finish the current batch before a run is considered complete.
Test harnesses and simulations: an explicit stop message makes thread-based systems deterministic to shut down, without sleeps or guessed timeouts.
Actor systems: a reserved stop message (for example Akka PoisonPill) terminates an actor after the messages already queued for it have been handled.
Log and event writers where the last records must reach the sink before consumers release their buffers and files.
Bounded-queue stages in a pipeline: pills travel the same backpressured channel as work, so upstream cannot keep producing after the stop decision.
Kubernetes pod shutdown: containers receive SIGTERM, workers stop pulling from the job queue, drain in-flight tasks, then exit within the terminationGracePeriodSeconds window.
Redis/Bull queue workers: a shutdown signal pushes a sentinel via BLPOP so workers exit cleanly without losing the right to process pending tasks.
Akka Streams and similar streaming frameworks: the GraphStage signals completion via onPull/downstream cancellation, which is the materialised equivalent of a poison pill.
Redis Streams consumer groups: XREADGROUP with block timeout naturally returns when the stream is empty; a special ID (e.g. ">") polling loop plus a shared shutdown flag replaces the in-process sentinel.
Broker-level poison message isolation: in Kafka, RabbitMQ, or Azure Service Bus, a permanently failing message (deserialisation error, validation failure) blocks a partition/consumer indefinitely; DLQ-based routing (publish to dead-letter topic after N retries, then commit offset and continue) is the broker-level analogue that prevents one poison message from halting the entire pipeline.
Kubernetes preStop hooks + pill drain: a container's lifecycle preStop hook can enqueue a sentinel into an in-process work queue while the orchestrator grants terminationGracePeriodSeconds for the drain to complete, ensuring zero work-drop during rolling updates.
Azure Service Bus competing-consumers workers: when a worker receives a shutdown notification it completes its current PeekLock message, then calls Abandon on any held locks before unregistering; Azure Service Bus dead-letter queues handle the poison-message variant when a message exceeds MaxDeliveryCount and cannot be delivered.
Akka hierarchical actor trees: sending PoisonPill to a parent actor stops it after all queued messages ahead of the pill are processed, and automatically sends stop messages to all children in bottom-up order; this is the idiomatic way to orchestrate ordered multi-actor shutdown.
Non-blocking retry architectures (RabbitMQ): rather than local Thread.sleep retries that block the consumer thread, use server-side TTL queues with Dead Letter Exchange routing to implement exponential backoff, keeping the consumer responsive to new messages and to shutdown pills.
Java's JDK BlockingQueue worker pools: because BlockingQueue has no built-in close, producers can enqueue a unique end-of-stream object after all work; each consumer takes until that sentinel and then the coordinator joins workers.
Python multiprocessing worker pools: multiprocessing.Queue/JoinableQueue supports FIFO task delivery with sentinel values and join-based drain tracking; send one sentinel per worker and join them after the queue is exhausted.
Akka Classic actors: PoisonPill is enqueued in the mailbox and processed after already queued messages, while Akka Typed requires an explicit Stop/Shutdown protocol; choose the API that matches the actor model.

name: copy-and-swap
document:
copy-and-swap
copy and swap idiom
create-temporary-and-swap
Implement assignment (and any in-place state replacement) so that a failure while producing the new state leaves the target untouched: build the complete replacement off to the side, commit it with operations that cannot fail, and let the temporary's destructor or the garbage collector release the old state.
A hand-written assignment has to tear down the old state and build a copy of the new one, but only the build can fail: destroying before allocating exposes a half-updated object when the allocation or the element copy throws, and the usual repair -- a self-assignment check plus manual rollback -- duplicates the per-member copying that already lives in the copy constructor. The trigger is an assignment (or, in a garbage-collected language, an in-place state replacement) that must satisfy the strong exception guarantee: either it completes, or the target still holds its previous value.
Types that own resources -- heap buffers, handles, file descriptors, trees, containers -- in a language where the programmer controls copy semantics: C++ special member functions, a C ADT with error codes, Rust with panic/abort failure modes. The same ordering also applies in garbage-collected languages whenever published state must never be mutated in place: building the complete replacement and publishing it once keeps readers consistent and moves the release of the old state to the collector. The precondition is a commit step that genuinely cannot fail -- a noexcept member swap, one reference or pointer store, or an atomic publish.
Container and buffer classes that own heap memory (dynamic array, string, matrix, tree) and must be assignable without leaking or leaving the target inconsistent when an allocation fails.
Handle/pimpl classes that keep their state behind a single pointer: the swap is a pointer exchange, so the commit is unconditionally non-throwing while the deep copy still happens in the copy constructor (Sutter's canonical Pimpl exception-safety transformation).
Pre-C++11 codebases where the same operator= must serve lvalues and rvalues and no move constructor exists, using the const-reference plus explicit-local-temporary form.
Value types stored inside standard containers: std::vector and friends need element assignment to be safe before they can offer their own strong guarantee on reallocation, and a noexcept swap participates in their internal move/swap dispatch.
Garbage-collected languages where shared state must be replaced rather than mutated: build a complete replacement value and publish it with one store (AtomicReference.updateAndGet, atomic.Pointer[T].Store, a record with-expression) so readers never observe a partially updated object.
In-place state replacement where identity must be preserved (a registry entry, a cached object with live references): copy into a scratch value, then commit with a member-wise exchange or a replace-style API instead of repointing the reference.
Concurrent programming with thread-safe local-then-publish: build the replacement in a local object (thread-private by definition), then publish atomically -- readers never see a partially updated state, and the previous value is released by the collector after the atomic write is visible.
Version-control-style update: check out a local copy, mutate freely, then commit or discard; copy-and-swap maps directly to this workflow and provides the same transactional semantics (Howard Hinnant's analogy from his C++ Con 2018 talk).
Compiler tooling treats the idiom as the canonical self-assignment-safe assignment: LLVM's clang-tidy bugprone-unhandled-self-assignment checker explicitly recognizes 'build a temporary in operator=, then swap it' as correct handling and matches extended (allocator-aware) constructors plus ADL swap forms so real copy-and-swap code is not flagged (llvm/llvm-project PR #147066).
Boost's move/assignment guidance converged on the single by-value form T operator=(T b) { swap(*this, b); return *this; } as the common way to get copy-, move-, and convertible-assignment from one operator, with dedicated macros (BOOST_COPYABLE_AND_MOVABLE_ALT) for classes that adopt it instead of separate overloads.
When a strong guarantee is needed on the standard containers, libc++ maintainers advise exactly this idiom at the call site -- 'construct a new vector and swap it with the one you want to assign to' (libc++ PR #117516 discussion) -- because the library's own copy assignment deliberately offers only the basic guarantee.

name: copy-on-write
document:
copy-on-write
lazy copy
clone-on-write
implicit sharing (Qt)
shadow paging
Let several handles of a value share one expensive body until the first write, which clones that body privately, so copying costs a pointer instead of a deep copy while every handle still behaves as an independent value.
A value with an expensive body (large buffer, collection, tree, document) is copied eagerly on assignment, argument passing and return even though most copies are never modified: time and memory are spent duplicating data that would have stayed identical. The naive fix - handing out one mutable object behind several handles - breaks the copy contract, and unrelated parts of the program then observe each other's writes.
Applies when copies of an expensive payload vastly outnumber modifications, when the payload is large enough that the copy dominates the cost of the handle (multi-kilobyte buffers, collection snapshots, editor or model state), and when the language offers a cheap way to know whether the body is still shared - a reference count, an explicit shared flag, or a uniqueness test. It is a single-threaded optimization first; sharing the count across threads turns it into the separate thread-safe copy-on-write concern.
Large buffers passed by value through API layers: strings, byte arrays and image/document payloads whose copies are usually read-only (Qt QString/QByteArray implicit sharing, ATL CString, pre-C++11 std::string).
Read-mostly collections whose traversals vastly outnumber mutations and must not block readers: listener and handler registries, routing tables, RuleEngine rule sets (CopyOnWriteArrayList/CopyOnWriteArraySet).
Configuration and state snapshots swapped atomically at the write boundary (feature flags, reloaded settings, event-sourced folds) so readers keep a consistent version without locking.
Persistent and functional data structures where an update returns a new version that structurally shares everything the change did not touch (Scala immutable collections, Immer drafts, persistent lists and maps).
Operating-system and memory-mapped sharing: fork and page-level copy-on-write share physical pages until a mapping is written, and file-backed buffers are shared until modified.
Columnar and data-frame workloads where slices are views and only the columns actually written are duplicated (pandas copy-on-write mode, Arrow buffers).
Fork-based process snapshots: Redis BGSAVE/BGREWRITEAOF forks a child to serialize memory to disk while the parent continues serving writes; only pages modified by the parent after fork are COW-copied, keeping the child's view consistent (vm.overcommit_memory=1 recommended).
COW filesystems for instant snapshots: ZFS and Btrfs never overwrite blocks in place; creating a snapshot is O(1) — save the root block pointer; reclaims O(1) more when the snapshot is deleted and no other reference remains. Enables self-healing via checksum propagation and efficient incremental replication via zfs send / btrfs send.
Database MVCC at row granularity: Postgres, LMDB, CockroachDB Pebble write new row versions on UPDATE/DELETE and reclaim old versions via VACUUM once no active transaction can see them; readers see consistent snapshots without read locks.
Container image layering: Docker/OCI images use layered COW where lower layers are read-only and the upper layer copies on write; base images are shared across many containers until a layer is actually modified.
APFS reflinks and XFS/ref ext4 ioctl(FICLONE): file-level COW that shares extents until either fork writes, enabling instant file clones (e.g., `cp --reflink=auto`) at near-zero cost.
LMDB's single-level store: a CoW B+tree using two fixed root pages (double buffering) where readers are fully latch-free and writers never block readers; no WAL needed because old trees remain intact until the new root is durably synced.
Swift standard library collections (Array, Dictionary, Set, String, Data) where isKnownUniquelyReferenced() checks the heap object's strong reference count at runtime to decide whether to mutate in-place or clone.
Qt QSharedData/QSharedDataPointer: implicit sharing for pimpl'd d-pointer classes where non-const operator-> triggers detach() automatically before any write access; QExplicitlySharedDataPointer suppresses automatic detach.
Rust std::borrow::Cow: a generic enum (Borrowed | Owned) that defers the clone until to_mut() is called, especially useful in APIs that accept both borrowed and owned data without multiple signatures.
PHP arrays and strings: reference-counted value types where assignment and argument passing share the zval and the first write 'separates' it (copy-on-write) when refcount > 1; taking a reference with & turns the sharing into an explicit alias set (php.net reference counting, php-src core docs).
pandas 3.0, where copy-on-write is the default and only mode: any DataFrame or Series derived by indexing behaves as an independent copy, chained assignment (df["foo"][mask] = v) silently doing nothing is eliminated - it raises ChainedAssignmentError - and every update must be a single .loc step (PDEP-7).
Linux kernel OverlayFS copy_up: a container write to a lowerdir file (open for write or metadata change) copies the file up into upperdir first; the metacopy feature delays the data copy until the first data write, and an fsync before the finalizing rename guards against zero-filled files after a crash (kernel overlayfs docs, Docker overlay2 driver).

name: iterator
document:
iterator
cursor
enumerator
Provide a way to access the elements of an aggregate object sequentially without exposing its underlying representation, by moving traversal state and the traversal algorithm out of the aggregate into a separate iterator object.
Traversal leaks into every client: code that walks a collection has to know its storage layout (array indices, node links, hash buckets), the same loop is rewritten once per aggregate and once per client, and adding a new traversal order means changing the aggregate's interface — which is exactly what prevents algorithms from being written once and applied to any collection.
Applies wherever a collection with a non-trivial or changeable representation must be traversed by outsiders: collection libraries, trees and graphs with several traversal orders, lazy or unbounded sources, and streaming pipelines. It matters most when more than one traversal may be pending at the same time, when the storage must stay hidden for encapsulation or safety, or when traversal algorithms must be added without touching the aggregate; the toolchain only decides which realization is available (a language iteration protocol, generators, lazy sequences, or a hand-written cursor).
Collection libraries that must serve arrays, linked lists, trees, and hash tables through one protocol — e.g. std::begin/end in C++, java.util.Iterator, IEnumerable<T> in C#, Symbol.iterator in JavaScript, IntoIterator in Rust.
Tree and graph APIs exposing depth-first, breadth-first, in-order, or post-order traversal without publishing node links or parent pointers, enabling clients to walk composite structures without coupling to the storage representation.
Lazy or unbounded sources consumed one element at a time: file lines (BufferedReader.lines()), network socket streams, paginated API responses, sensor data, event streams, and generated sequences (random numbers, Fibonacci, permutations).
Streaming data pipelines (map/filter/reduce over any iterable) that stay O(1) in memory regardless of input size, implemented via itertools, Java Stream API, Kotlin Sequence, C++ ranges, Rust iterator adapters, or Go iter package.
Legacy or third-party aggregates whose internal layout must stay private behind a stable traversal interface, allowing the aggregate to refactor its storage without breaking existing clients.
Custom containers that must participate in the language's own for/foreach/for-in/for-await loop, spread operators, destructuring assignment, or list comprehensions.
Database result sets and ORM cursors where the full result set is never materialised in memory; the iterator fetches pages on demand.
Parser and lexer token streams where the input is consumed incrementally and the full source may not fit in memory.
Async I/O pipelines where the iteration protocol yields Promises (JavaScript async generators, C# IAsyncEnumerable<T>, Python async generators) enabling for-await iteration over network responses or file reads.
Multidimensional collection traversal (matrices, nested lists, spatial grids) via flattened iterators that expose a flat index space while hiding the multi-dimensional layout.
Paginated REST or GraphQL API clients where a client-side iterator transparently fetches successive pages as the consumer pulls elements, keeping memory constant regardless of result set size.
Kafka, log-processor, or ETL pipelines where each stage is a transforming iterator: parse → filter → enrich → validate → sink, with each stage evaluated lazily.
Event-driven systems using async iterators to consume WebSocket messages, SSE streams, or queue consumers through a uniform for-await-of interface.
Batch-processing jobs over large file sets (CSV, Parquet, NDJSON) where an iterator wraps a file reader and yields one record per next() call without loading the file into memory.
Cursor-based (keyset) pagination over large, live datasets where offset/limit pagination causes duplicates or missed rows when data is inserted or deleted mid-traversal; the iterator stores the last-seen key rather than a page offset, making traversal stable across concurrent modifications.
Iterator fusion in compilers and runtimes: adjacent map/filter/map chains fused into a single pass with zero intermediate allocation (Rust iterator adapters, Java Spliterators, Haskell stream fusion, C++ range views), giving lazy pipelines near-handwritten performance.
Parallel iterators for data-parallel workloads: Rust Rayon, Java parallel streams, and Kotlin asFlow().buffer() split the iterator across worker threads — identical interface to serial iteration, transparent parallel execution.
Reactive streams bridging pull and push: RxJava, RxJS, and Project Reactor implement backpressure (consumer signals demand, producer emits at requested rate), combining iterator's pull semantics with observer's push delivery.
LLM and streaming AI responses where the model yields tokens incrementally; an async iterator wraps the SSE/stream endpoint and the client consumes tokens one at a time via for-await-of, keeping first-token latency low and enabling progressive rendering.
Cursor-based database driver iterators (Node.js pg cursor, Python asyncpg, Go database/sql rows) where the driver streams rows from the server without loading the full result set, with configurable fetch size controlling server-side memory usage.
Java's Spliterator API exposes a cursor that can be advanced one element at a time or split into subranges for parallel streams; it demonstrates that an iterator contract can include explicit partitioning and size/order characteristics rather than only next().
.NET's IAsyncEnumerable<T> and IAsyncEnumerator<T> expose asynchronous pull iteration through await foreach; GetAsyncEnumerator(CancellationToken) makes cancellation part of the iterator boundary for network, file, and database streams.
WHATWG ReadableStream async iteration lets browser and server consumers use for-await-of over streamed chunks while the iterator locks a reader and defines whether early return() cancels or merely releases it.

name: repository
document:
repository
collection-oriented repository
repository layer
Mediates between the domain model and the data mapping layer with a collection-like interface, so domain code adds, removes and finds persistent objects as if they lived in memory and never constructs queries or touches persistence APIs itself.
Persistence code spreads: every application service re-derives the same SQL or ORM queries, duplicate query logic drifts apart, table and column names leak into domain decisions, and testing domain rules without a database becomes impossible. Callers should be able to think in collections of domain objects instead of queries.
Applies to systems with a non-trivial domain model sitting on a data-mapping layer (Data Mapper, metadata mapping, or a hand-written mapper) where the same queries recur across application services; it becomes more valuable as domain classes and query volume grow. It is the standard persistence boundary of DDD aggregates (one repository per aggregate root) and presumes a unit of work or session that owns flush and commit. It is not a per-table data-access wrapper and not a replacement for transaction control.
DDD application services that must load an aggregate root, run domain logic on it and store it again without knowing the table layout.
Data-mapper backends where several application services and background jobs share recurring complex queries (overdue invoices, pending orders, open tickets).
Applications that must be unit-testable away from the database: repositories are the substitution point for in-memory doubles.
Systems that must support more than one store behind a stable domain interface — relational in production, in-memory in tests, a document store for a particular deployment.
Uniform cross-cutting access policy for an aggregate: caching, read-replica routing, audit logging or authorization applied as decorators around one interface.
Migration work where the persistence technology changes (ORM swap, schema split, service extraction) while the domain model and its tests stay untouched.
CQRS write-side aggregate loading where the aggregate must be reconstructed fully to apply business rules and enforce invariants.
Integration with heterogeneous data sources where one repository unifies access to a cache, primary database and a third-party API behind a domain interface.
Spring Data JPA applications can use Repository/CrudRepository for aggregate-typed CRUD, paging and derived queries, then add only domain-specific methods rather than wrapping every persistence operation.
The .NET eShopOnContainers ordering microservice uses an EF Core BuyerRepository over a shared scoped DbContext/unit of work, while CQRS/Dapper handles presentation reads.
Python applications using SQLAlchemy ORM can place an aggregate-facing repository over Session, whose identity map and unit-of-work flush semantics provide the mapper/session boundary.

name: watchman
document:
watchman
dead man's switch
heartbeat monitor
Detect that a message flow has gone silent - not that a message failed - and tell a responsible person or system within a bounded time by comparing each flow's arrivals against the cadence its business deadline implies.
Message systems fail silently in the one way no error handler observes: nothing arrives. A producer stops emitting, a consumer stops draining, a scheduled job never fires, a credential expires, a partition goes offline - and because no failing code path is ever entered, error dashboards stay green while downstream data quietly goes stale. The recurring trigger: a flow whose absence is business-visible (a nightly feed, an order stream, a partner interface) has no owner-facing signal for 'no messages', so the gap is discovered late - by a customer or a downstream job - instead of by the team that can fix it.
Applies wherever messages are expected on a knowable cadence (event streams, queues, batch hand-offs, partner interfaces, device check-ins) and their absence is a business-visible failure: the flow has an owner, the expected period and grace window can be derived from a downstream deadline, and either the transport can be observed passively (queue counters, a wire tap) or the producers can emit out-of-band heartbeats. The watchman sits at message-flow or boundary scope - an in-process watcher beside the consumer, a periodic sweep over persisted last-seen state, or a rule in the monitoring stack fed by metrics - and it must itself be watched, because a silent watchman is exactly the failure it exists to catch.
Nightly batch or ETL feed: page the integration owner when the 02:00 import has produced no messages by its deadline, instead of noticing an empty report at the morning stand-up.
Business-critical event stream (orders, payments, telemetry): alarm when the produce rate stays at zero through business hours, which separates a healthy quiet topic from a stopped producer.
External partner interface: notify when no messages have arrived from a B2B partner within the agreed window, turning a looming SLA breach into an early, actionable alert.
Long-running workflow stage: require a heartbeat from each process-manager step so a stuck instance is noticed before the surrounding batch closes or a compensation becomes necessary.
Retry or dead-letter pump: verify that the pump still drains failed messages - silence means the pump died, not that the backlog is empty.
Fleet check-ins (edge devices, agents, cron jobs on many hosts): raise a per-device or per-site alarm when scheduled check-ins stop arriving.
The alerting pipeline itself: an always-firing watchdog alert routed to an external service, so a broken alert path is discovered by its silence.
Cron and scheduled-job fleet via Healthchecks.io: each job pings a unique URL, the service holds the Period and Grace Time, flips the check Late then Down when no ping arrives by period + grace, and notifies integrations.
Dashboard alert rules in Grafana: an alert rule whose query returns no series enters the No Data state and can raise a DatasourceNoData alert - the platform form of deciding what silence means (No Data, Alerting, Normal or Keep last state).
Apache Burrow for Kafka (LinkedIn): committed offsets are evaluated per partition over a sliding window and a consumer is classified STALLED when its offset is frozen with non-zero lag, or STOPPED when no new commits arrive - consumer-silence detection without fixed lag thresholds.

name: identity-field
document:
identity-field
primary key field
identity column
Store the relational primary key inside the object so that an in-memory instance and its database row are recognised as the same entity across sessions, caches and process restarts, instead of relying on object identity.
Mappers, identity maps and unit-of-work bookkeeping need a stable handle on every object: without a key carried by the object there is no way to tell whether two instances are the same row, which row an UPDATE or DELETE must touch, or what value a referring row should store - and loading the same row twice silently produces two divergent objects.
Applies wherever objects outlive a single operation and are mapped to key-addressed rows: entities behind a Data Mapper or Row Data Gateway, aggregates in a Repository, session caches keyed by table plus id, and object graphs whose children must refer to a parent that is not inserted yet. The key has to survive serialisation and cross-process calls, and for application-generated keys it must exist before the row does.
ORM entities in a session: load a row into an object, mutate business fields, then flush an UPDATE or DELETE targeted at the same identity.
API resources addressed by key: /orders/{id} endpoints that fetch, mutate and delete by identity, with links stored as keys instead of object references.
Session-scoped identity maps and second-level caches keyed by (table, key), which need the key before they can return an existing instance.
Object graphs with parent-child references: the child's foreign key needs the parent's identity, generated before the insert (UUID/sequence) or read back after it (RETURNING/getGeneratedKeys).
Audit, versioning and optimistic locking: change logs and Version Number checks identify the affected row by its key.
Distributed or sharded writes: client-generated keys let a router place the row and let a retry overwrite the same identity idempotently.
Event-sourced aggregates: the aggregate root's identity is the correlation ID carried in every command and event, allowing the event log to reconstruct state by replaying events keyed to that identity.
GraphQL Relay node identification: globally unique node IDs are built from the entity's identity (base64 type-prefixed id), enabling the standardised node query and cache reching defined in the Relay specification.
Multi-tenant SaaS with tenant-scoped identity: a composite key of (tenant_id, id) ensures a tenant can never address another tenant's rows, even if the local id numbers happen to collide.
Idempotent message processing: a command's correlation ID (the entity's identity) lets a handler detect a duplicate and skip reprocessing without a distributed lock.
Hibernate ORM entities with an @Id and Session persistence context: loading by identifier reuses the session's first-level identity, while the chosen generated-id strategy determines when the key becomes available.
PostgreSQL tables with GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY and INSERT ... RETURNING id: the database owns key generation, then the mapper reads the assigned identity back onto the object in the same write.
Relay GraphQL servers implementing the Node interface: expose a globally unique opaque id and refetch the same object through node(id), carrying entity identity across a client cache and API boundary.

name: make-illegal-states-unrepresentable
document:
make-illegal-states-unrepresentable
make invalid states unrepresentable
Encode each domain rule in the shape of the data type so that values violating the rule cannot be constructed at all, replacing scattered run-time validation and defensive checks with a model in which only legal states exist.
Domain values are modelled as one record with independent fields - a status tag plus several nullable or optional attributes, or a handful of booleans - so the type admits every combination of those fields, including the ones the business rules forbid. Consumers cannot trust the type: each branch re-checks which fields are meaningful, the same guard is written in several places (and forgotten in one), and illegal states become runtime bugs that surface when a code path finally combines the wrong flags.
Applies when a value has a small, known set of mutually exclusive shapes whose payloads differ, when the same invalid combination keeps being defended against in several places, and when the language can close a set of variants (Rust/Swift enums, sealed hierarchies, discriminated unions) or at least hide constructors. It is equally a boundary discipline: untrusted input is parsed once into a type whose existence already proves it is valid, so no downstream code has to re-validate.
Lifecycle and state machines: orders, payments, subscriptions, bookings and connection states, one variant per state carrying exactly the data that exists in that state.
Client and API request state: a loading/success/error union instead of a data field, an error field and an isLoading flag that can contradict one another.
Message and protocol modelling: a closed set of commands, events or JSON payload shapes decoded once and dispatched with an exhaustive match (event sourcing, interpreters, RPC handlers).
Refined scalars that travel through the model: money with currency, email addresses, quantities with units and identifiers that are parsed once and never re-validated.
Configuration whose combinations are illegal: TLS settings that only apply when TLS is enabled, cursor-based versus offset pagination, mutually exclusive feature flags.
Import and deserialization boundaries: convert untrusted rows, CSV cells, query parameters or JSON into domain types with a failing factory, so invalid input cannot travel further.
Rust's standard `Option`/`Result` enums and exhaustive `match` make presence, absence, success and failure explicit cases that downstream code must handle at compile time (Rust Reference/Book).
Swift enums with associated values and exhaustive `switch` model state-specific payloads such as error cases without nullable companion fields (The Swift Programming Language).
Kotlin sealed classes and interfaces with exhaustive `when` expressions provide a closed hierarchy for finite state machines and error/result models, with the compiler checking that every known case is handled.

name: humble-object
document:
humble-object
humble dialog box
Move as much logic as possible out of a program element that the framework calls but tests cannot instantiate - a UI control, callback, entry point or active object - into a plain collaborator that unit tests drive synchronously, leaving the original element as a thin adapter without decisions.
The element the host invokes cannot be exercised in a test: constructing it needs the framework's environment (event loop, window, container, thread), so driving it means slow asynchronous tests with framework setup, or none at all. Because the decisions were written where the trigger arrives, business rules live inside the untestable element: they are verified only by expensive end-to-end runs, they cannot be test-first, and every framework upgrade threatens them.
Applies when an element is hard to test for environmental reasons rather than intrinsic ones: framework callbacks (widgets, dialogs, request handlers, message listeners), entry points (main, server bootstrap) and active objects (threads, processes, timer and interrupt handlers), plus container-managed components whose interfaces the server demands. The logic must be expressible as a computation over data, and the host must keep invoking the element through a stable callback or entry point.
A dialog or screen whose enablement, validation and navigation rules are hard to exercise: extract a presenter or view model, leave the widget showing fields and forwarding events (the Humble Dialog form).
Framework callbacks that mutate business state - HTTP handlers, message listeners, timer or interrupt callbacks - where a thin adapter reads the input and a service decides.
Active objects and executables: a thread or process whose per-request processing is extracted so tests run synchronously instead of sleeping and coordinating (the Humble Executable form).
Transaction boundaries: extract the business logic out of the transaction controller so a test can run the logic and roll the transaction back, leaving only commit/rollback behaviour in the controller (the Humble Transaction Controller form).
Container-managed components: implement the server's interface in a thin adapter and keep the logic in a container-independent class, so the edit-compile-test cycle stays fast (the Humble Container Adapter form).
Legacy code with an overridable or exposed dependency call but no injection point: expose or extract the method first (the Poor Man's form) and only then attempt a test harness.
Entry points: parse arguments, wire dependencies and map the exit code in main, and put the program's decisions in a library function that tests call.
Android Activities/Fragments and Unity MonoBehaviours: extract lifecycle-driven logic into a plain class, leaving the framework component as a thin shell that forwards lifecycle events — enables unit tests without an emulator or device.
React class components and Angular controllers: move state and business logic out of the component into a hook or service, keeping the component as a declarative renderer that delegates all decisions.
Embedded systems interrupt handlers: extract per-interrupt processing into a synchronous function tested with deterministic inputs; the ISR remains a thin vector that disables interrupts and calls the extracted logic.
Database transaction scripts: separate the SQL/transaction orchestration (humble controller) from the business logic (collaborator), so the logic is tested with a connection spy and the wiring is verified by a small number of integration tests.
Event-driven microservices: keep the event-listener adapter minimal (deserialize, delegate) and place all routing and business logic in a synchronous service that tests can drive directly with domain objects.
CLI entry points: extract argument parsing and environment setup from the main method into a plain runner class; the collaborator is tested with fake argv, and the shell only handles OS-level concerns.
Android Jetpack (AndroidX) ViewModel: Google's architecture guidance makes the ViewModel the testable collaborator - it MUST NOT reference Activity, Fragment, View or Context - so screen logic is unit-tested on the JVM with fakes, while the Activity/Fragment stays a humble shell exercised only by instrumentation tests.
WPF / .NET MVVM: Microsoft's guidance prescribes views with empty code-behind - controls bind to ViewModel properties and ICommand implementations (e.g. DelegateCommand) - so enablement, validation and action logic (CanExecute/Execute) are plain classes unit-tested without a window, and XAML binding is covered by a few integration checks.
Unity MonoBehaviour game code: teams extract game rules into plain C# classes unit-tested outside the engine's Play Mode, leaving the MonoBehaviour as a serialized-field shell that forwards Update/FixedUpdate - the Unity community reports this buys fast unit tests at the cost of harder in-engine integration tests, so the shell needs deliberate coverage.

name: passkey
document:
passkey
passkey idiom
constructor key
Restrict a constructor or method to chosen collaborators by requiring a token that only those collaborators can construct, so the operation stays in the public signature while remaining uncallable by everyone else - compile-time access control instead of blanket friendship.
A specific collaborator must call a constructor or method that must not become public API: a factory or helper that has to construct an object through a public constructor (make_unique, MakeGarbageCollected), a serialisation or framework layer that must reach one private hook, a subsystem that needs one internal operation, a test helper that must build a type in a state users cannot. The blunt mechanisms all miss: making the member public hands it to the world, friend (or its nearest equivalent) hands the collaborator the whole private surface, package/module/assembly access opens it to an entire scope, and a private constructor plus a factory just moves the gate into the factory. What is missing is a way to say 'this collaborator, and only this collaborator, may call exactly this operation'.
Statically checked code where the operation must stay visible in the type system (templates, frameworks and helper functions must be able to resolve the call) but must not be callable without a value that only the designated collaborators can create. The grant is a source-level construct checked by the compiler: the token is empty, disappears at run time and is never a defence against an adversary. Typical settings are factory-created types, library internals exposed to one subsystem, framework hooks, constructor or overload disambiguation, and test seams.
Factory-created objects with a public constructor: base::PassKey in Chromium exists for classes that a helper template (blink::MakeGarbageCollected) must construct while user code must not.
Serialisation and framework hooks: an archive, visitor or framework calls exactly one hook of a user type; the key names the framework instead of befriending it and exposing everything else.
Library-internal operations: one subsystem (allocator, persistence layer, test infrastructure) needs to construct or mutate a type users must not reach - the key names the subsystem where the language allows it, and module or assembly scope carries the rest.
Tests: a test helper constructs an otherwise unreachable state without '#define private public' builds, friend-everything test seams or reflection.
Constructor and overload disambiguation: a tag only the factory can produce selects the trusted overload and keeps the same argument list from being callable by everyone.
Deliberate delegation and revocation: the collaborator passes a key to another function that then performs the call, and a non-copyable key stops the ability from travelling further.
KDE Frameworks' KColorScheme (Frameworks 6.6.0) adopted a passkey specifically to avoid private-constructor issues, showing the idiom in a public Qt-based framework API.
Chromium's Mojo ProtoWrapperBytes uses base::PassKey to let named network, component and test classes access wrapped protobuf bytes while ordinary callers cannot supply the operation.
Abseil's C++ Tip of the Week #134 uses a passkey token with std::make_shared so a factory can keep single-allocation construction without making unconstrained construction the public API.

name: guarded-suspension
document:
guarded-suspension
conditional block
suspended execution
Suspend a state-dependent method call inside the object that owns the state until another thread makes its guard predicate true, so callers neither poll nor get refused while the object is temporarily not ready.
A method may only proceed while a precondition over shared state holds - a buffer is non-empty, a pool still has a free lease, a session is authenticated, a worker has a task - and that state is produced by another thread at an unknown time. The recurring decision is what the caller should do while the guard is false: refusing the request would drop work the application still needs, forcing the transition would break the object's invariants, and polling wastes a core and still races. Guarded suspension answers it by waiting on a condition the object itself owns, and by making that wait atomic with respect to the state change that ends it.
Concurrent objects whose methods are state-dependent and whose state changes arrive from other threads: bounded buffers and handoff queues, resource pools, server request/response handoffs, readiness and shutdown gates, worker idle loops. Applicable where the runtime can efficiently park or suspend a caller (OS threads, coroutines) and where the object already owns a lock or monitor, so no notification can be lost between the predicate check and the wait. Ill-suited to single-threaded event loops, to callers that must never be delayed, and to waits whose eventual completion cannot be guaranteed.
Actor mailbox handoff: an Akka/Orleans/Swift-Actor mailbox is a lock-free guarded queue; the actor suspends on an empty mailbox and resumes when a message arrives, which is the same monitor-wait pattern expressed at the language level.
Swift async / Structured Concurrency: a Task.sleep or async let that suspends until a condition is a coroutine-level guarded suspension; the suspension point is backed by a condition variable or event channel inside the runtime.
CompletableFuture / async result: a future's blocking get() is a timed guarded suspension on the thread that submitted the asynchronous operation; the completion path (complete()) is the notifier.
Pipeline stage coordination: in a multi-stage streaming pipeline each stage blocks on input while the upstream stage processes, synchronising via a bounded channel whose put/get implement the guard.
Bounded buffers and handoff queues: a consumer's take waits while the buffer is empty and a producer's put waits while it is full (producer-consumer).
Resource pools: acquire blocks until a lease is returned to a connection, thread or object pool instead of failing or spinning when the pool is exhausted.
Server-side handoff: an acceptor or reader thread publishes a request and the worker waits for work to appear; a caller waits for the response slot to be filled.
Readiness and start-up gates: components wait until a dependency reports connected, initialised or ready, and callers wait until a session, device or circuit is open.
Shutdown and flush coordination: a terminator waits until in-flight work has drained, and a flusher waits while the buffer still holds entries (two-phase termination).
Platform queue and channel APIs: BlockingQueue.take/put, Queue#pop, Channel.receive/for-await, condition-variable waits - the same guard hidden behind a library type.
Project Loom virtual threads (JEP 444): a virtual thread calling Object.wait() parks its Continuation; the carrier thread is released for other virtual threads, so the program continues throughput while one virtual thread waits. The guarded action still re-checks the predicate on wake, and the pattern's semantics are preserved — only the threading model changes.
Akka typed actor mailbox: each actor has a single-threaded mailbox; receive() suspends the actor's continuation when the mailbox is empty, resuming when a message is dispatched. This is language-level guarded suspension where the wait set is the mailbox queue and the guard is 'mailbox non-empty'.
Kotlin coroutines rendezvous channel: Channel() (unbuffered/rendezvous) suspends the sender until a receiver is ready, and vice versa — the same lock-free handoff as an unbuffered Go channel. The suspension is a coroutine-level guarded wait on rendezvous.
Python asyncio.Condition: an async context manager that wraps an asyncio.Lock; await cond.wait() releases the lock and suspends the task until notify() is called, making it an async guarded suspension where the runtime schedules other tasks during the wait.
Go unbuffered channel send/receive: goroutine G1 executing ch <- x on an unbuffered channel sleeps (gopark) until goroutine G2 executes <-ch, at which point the runtime directly transfers the value and stack copy (rendezvous handoff). This is the language-level form of guarded suspension: the guard is 'receiver present', the wait set is the sudog queue in hchan.
Erlang/OTP process mailbox: a gen_server receiving messages from its mailbox blocks (receive...end) until a matching message arrives — the OTP process is a state machine whose transitions are guarded by message arrival, making each receive a suspension point in the actor's event loop.
.NET TaskCompletionSource<T>: GetAwaiter().GetResult() on a not-yet-completed TCS is a synchronous guarded suspension; the async continuation (ConfigureAwait, await) is an asynchronous one. SetResult() is the notifier. TCS is a one-shot asymmetric guarded suspension where one side never waits (the completor) and one side always waits (the synchronously blocked caller).
JDK ArrayBlockingQueue: the queue is one ReentrantLock plus two Condition objects, notEmpty and notFull - take() awaits notEmpty while count == 0, put() awaits notFull while the buffer is full, and each signals the other condition only after mutating count and the circular buffer inside the same critical section. It is the reference production realisation of a two-predicate guarded suspension, including the fairness switch and the timed offer/poll variants.
Go standard library: database/sql guards queries against a concurrent Close with closingMutex, which parks readers and the closing writer on two sync.Cond values (read/write), and net/http's Server.Shutdown waits until in-flight requests have drained. Both are the case Go's own guidance reserves sync.Cond for - a predicate that changes back and forth over time rather than a one-shot handoff.
HikariCP connection pool: DataSource.getConnection() suspends the caller until a lease is returned while the pool already holds maximumPoolSize connections, bounded by connectionTimeout (default 30000 ms, minimum 250 ms), after which it throws SQLException rather than waiting on - a guarded suspension in which the deadline is a documented, first-class outcome instead of an accident.
