name: identity-map
document:
identity-map
first-level cache
session cache
Guarantee that within one session every database row is represented by exactly one in-memory object, by keeping a keyed registry of loaded objects that every load consults before hitting the database.
Two code paths in the same session load the same row into two different objects: updates through one are invisible to the other, the last flush silently wins, and every load pays the remote-call cost again. The catalog states the invariant as: the same row must never be two different in-memory objects in one session.
Object-oriented persistence (data mappers, repositories, unit of work) where entities carry a stable database identity (an Identity Field) and several parts of one business transaction or request refer to the same rows. Applies whenever duplicate in-memory instances would break graph consistency or lose updates - typically inside an ORM session or a hand-written persistence context whose lifetime bounds staleness.
ORM sessions in web request handling (JPA EntityManager, EF Core DbContext, SQLAlchemy Session, MikroORM EntityManager) where several services touch the same entities in one request.
Batch import and synchronisation jobs that re-read the same rows repeatedly inside one transaction and must not operate on divergent copies.
Object graph reconstruction in data mappers, where cycles and shared references need one in-memory instance per row.
Desktop and document applications with a context-scoped object space (Core Data contexts) where objects are edited, undone and saved as one unit.
Hand-written persistence layers over plain SQL where two repositories serve the same table and must agree on identity.
CQRS command handlers where the same aggregate is loaded multiple times within one command execution — the identity map prevents duplicate instances from forming across repository calls within the same session.
Event-sourced aggregate reconstruction: replaying events to rebuild aggregate state requires the same aggregate instance to accumulate state across multiple event applications; identity map guarantees a single instance per aggregate ID per reconstruction session.
Microservices saga and choreography: within one service's unit-of-work, multiple steps may load the same entity; identity map ensures all steps operate on the same instance even when the entity is referenced across different event handlers.
DDD bounded-context integration: when one bounded context holds a reference to an entity from another context (by ID), that entity is resolved through the local identity map — multiple resolution paths must all consult the same map to stay consistent.
Testing scenarios where the same entity is accessed via multiple repository paths: identity map guarantees test assertions see the same instance regardless of which repository method returned it, enabling meaningful state verification.
Multi-tenant applications where each tenant request gets its own session/identity-map scope, preventing cross-tenant data leakage by construction — a shared/global map would allow one tenant's rows to shadow another's.
SQLAlchemy Session.get in a unit of work: repeated primary-key loads return the same Python object from the Session identity map, while the Session is deliberately not a cross-session query cache.
EF Core tracked queries and AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution: the DbContext keeps one entity instance per key for tracked results, while no-tracking identity resolution is opt-in for read models.
Hibernate Session persistence contexts: repeated loads of the same entity type and identifier resolve to the one managed instance per Session, so entity graphs and dirty checking share state.

name: thread-safe-copy-on-write
document:
thread-safe-copy-on-write
Share one body between many threads so that copying a value stays cheap and reading it never blocks, and protect the sharing state itself - the reference count or the published pointer - so that a writer clones the body and swaps in a new snapshot instead of mutating storage other threads can see.
A value is copied often and mutated rarely, so the copies should share storage until one of them diverges. That decision works single-threaded, but the moment several threads hold the value the sharing state becomes shared mutable state in its own right: a reference count incremented without atomics loses updates or frees a body another thread is still reading, a plain pointer dereferenced while another thread replaces it is a data race, and a 'copy' that still aliases its source turns a reader's snapshot into a moving target. The trigger is a read-mostly shared value - configuration, routing table, registry, cache snapshot - that must be read without locking and updated by cloning.
Applies where one object, or one immutable snapshot of an aggregate, is read by many threads and written rarely: configuration reloads, registries and symbol tables, caches with rare invalidation, listener registries, and large immutable values handed between threads. Manual memory management, non-atomic reference counts or a separate publication step make the problem sharpest (C, C++, hand-rolled counting); garbage-collected languages apply the same structure with the published reference replacing the count. It is an object/value-level data-sharing decision, not a lock strategy for write-heavy state.
Read-mostly configuration or routing tables that are reloaded occasionally and read on every request by every worker thread.
Registries, symbol tables and interning tables built once and consulted constantly, with rare additions or invalidations.
Caches and memo tables where invalidation is rare and readers must never wait behind a writer.
Listener and observer registries traversed on every event and modified rarely - the classic CopyOnWriteArrayList use.
Large immutable values - strings, byte buffers, message payloads, compiled artefacts - handed between threads, where a deep copy at each hand-off would dominate.
Language runtimes, interpreters and plugin hosts that keep configuration or environment objects read by many threads and updated by a single owner.
The Linux kernel's RCU (read-copy-update) mechanism in its purest form: readers enter an rcu_read_lock() critical section with no lock, atomic or shared-memory write, updaters publish a replacement with rcu_assign_pointer(), and the superseded body is freed only after a grace period proves no reader can still hold it - the dentry cache, routing tables and network-device lists.
Rust's std::sync::Arc as the atomically counted body of the standard library: cloning an Arc increments the count, and Arc::make_mut detaches - cloning the inner value only when other Arc handles exist - so the sharing state is protected by the type rather than by convention.
Go services publishing an immutable configuration or routing snapshot through sync/atomic's atomic.Pointer[T]: readers Load it once per request without locking, writers build a fresh snapshot under a writer lock and Store or Swap the pointer, and the collector reclaims each superseded snapshot when no reader references it.

name: deadline-propagation
document:
deadline-propagation
timeout propagation
Bound the total time and work of a logical request by carrying one deadline through its whole call tree: every hop forwards the remaining budget and the cancellation signal instead of inventing a fresh timeout, so work that can no longer succeed is abandoned at every level.
A request fans out into a chain or tree of downstream calls and each hop applies its own timeout: the end-to-end latency budget becomes the sum of N independent timeouts, servers keep working after the originating client has given up, and cancellation never reaches the deeper work - resources are consumed producing answers nobody will read.
Networked request handling with multi-hop calls: RPC and HTTP chains, service meshes, gateways, fan-out and hedged requests. It applies when one latency budget is meaningful for the whole logical request (an SLO or a user-facing timeout), when the hops are under your control and can carry request-scoped state (context, token, signal, call option or header), and when downstream work is cancellable or can be interrupted at checkpoints.
Microservice request chains (gateway -> frontend service -> several backends) under one user-facing latency SLO, where each hop converts the inbound deadline into its own outgoing calls.
gRPC services whose clients set a deadline and whose servers propagate it as a remaining timeout to downstream calls while cancelling server-side work once the deadline passes.
Fan-out and aggregation endpoints calling several backends in parallel: every sub-call shares the parent budget, and sub-calls still running when it expires are cancelled instead of awaited.
Hedged requests: the first replica to answer wins, and the duplicate requests are cancelled through the same carrier so their downstream work is stopped too.
Streaming and long-poll endpoints that must stop processing when the client disconnects or the connection times out, propagating that stop to services and storage.
Batch or pipeline steps with a per-request time budget that must check the remaining time before each stage and abandon a request that can no longer be finished in time.
ROS 2 / DDS-based robotics pipelines: autonomous vehicle perception pipelines where sensor data must traverse a chain of processing nodes (detect -> classify -> plan -> act) and missed deadlines invalidate downstream results entirely.
Distributed real-time databases with multi-hop queries (gateway -> shard router -> storage node -> index node) where each hop's latency budget is derived from a user-facing SLA.
Service mesh sidecar configurations (Istio/Linkerd/Envoy) where per-route timeout policies propagate deadline context to application code via headers like grpc-timeout or custom X-Request-Deadline headers.
Industrial IoT and edge computing pipelines (edge gateway -> fieldbus bridge -> PLC -> sensor) where end-to-end control loop deadlines must be enforced across heterogeneous network boundaries.
GraphQL federation: a federated query hitting multiple subgraphs in parallel must bound the total resolution time and cancel subgraph requests whose partial results can no longer affect the final response.
Go services on the standard library context package: context.WithDeadline and WithTimeout derive a child whose Done channel closes at the earliest of its own deadline, an explicit cancel, or the parent's cancellation, so cancelling the root request context tears down the whole goroutine tree, and WithDeadlineCause/WithTimeoutCause attach an explicit cause for attribution.
Envoy router filter in service meshes: Envoy sets x-envoy-expected-rq-timeout-ms on internal requests - derived from x-envoy-upstream-rq-timeout-ms or the route timeout - so upstream services can read the expected total completion time and exit early instead of finishing work the proxy has already timed out.
ASP.NET Core gRPC services map the inbound call's deadline onto the handler's CancellationToken; passing that token to database queries, HttpClient calls and Task.Delay stops server-side work the moment the client's deadline expires.

name: table-module
document:
table-module
Organise the domain logic of a table or view as one module with a single instance whose operations act on whole sets of rows, so table-shaped rules are written once against tabular record sets instead of being scattered over per-row objects or per-request procedures.
The rules for a table are set-shaped - recalculating a column across all rows, validating an import batch, posting a period, aggregating or exporting a whole table - and the platform already speaks in tables and record sets (result sets, DataTables, grids, reports). A Domain Model would build one object per row and pay for identity, hydration and per-object behaviour the rules never use, while a Transaction Script repeats the same table-shaped logic in every use case that touches the table.
Data-centric enterprise applications with moderate, table-shaped logic: batch jobs, imports and reconciliation, reporting and export modules, and applications whose UI and data tooling is table-based (typed DataSets, data grids, report engines). It assumes that data access is already provided by a Table Data Gateway or equivalent, and that callers - typically a Service Layer - own the transaction boundary around the module's calls.
Periodic batch posting: recompute balances or fees for every row in a period in one set-oriented pass.
Import and reconciliation: validate, normalise and promote a staging table before its rows become live data, reporting row-level errors as a batch.
Reporting and export modules that fetch a record set for a grid, report engine or CSV/Excel export, where tabular output is the goal.
Bulk recalculation after a rule change: apply a corrected formula to all existing rows of a table without loading them into a model.
Small-to-medium applications where each table has a handful of well-defined operations and no rich invariants spanning rows or tables.
Cleansing and reconciliation jobs over an operational table where the database should do the heavy lifting (aggregate, update ... where) and the application only orchestrates.
.NET ADO.NET typed DataSet / typed DataTable modules: the generated table is the record set, business methods operate over all its rows and it binds directly to grids and report controls.
Ruby on Rails set-oriented surface: an ActiveRecord::Relation scoped to one table applies table-wide rules via update_all/delete_all as a single SQL statement without instantiating row models, whose official documentation warns that validations and callbacks are skipped so the statement must carry the rule.
Django set-wide recalculation: QuerySet.update() and bulk_update() write whole filtered sets with direct SQL that bypasses per-row save(), used exactly where per-object persistence would mean one round trip per row.

name: converter
document:
converter
translator
Give a pair of corresponding representations one owner that maps them into each other in both directions, so every caller converts through one place and neither representation has to import, know or be aware of the other.
The same information lives in two representations - domain object and DTO, in-memory value and wire or column format, internal model and third-party schema - and both directions are exercised in production. Hand-written field copying at each call site duplicates the mapping rules, drifts whenever either representation changes, and forces at least one side (or every caller) to import the other.
Component boundaries where an internal model meets an external representation: service or API layers exchanging DTOs, persistence layers mapping values to column formats, integration seams facing a third-party or legacy schema, and codec layers mapping typed values to a wire format. It applies whenever both directions are needed (read and write, decode and encode) and either side must stay independent of the other - different modules, teams, release cycles or libraries.
Domain object <-> DTO at a service or API boundary, where the transport shape must not leak into the model.
Value object <-> database column representation (JPA AttributeConverter, EF Core ValueConverter, Rails custom attribute type).
Third-party or legacy schema <-> internal model at an integration seam, including versioned wire formats.
Typed value <-> JSON, XML or protobuf payload with a custom codec when the default mapping is wrong (formats, units, enums).
Query rows or record sets <-> domain objects, where a full mapper framework would be oversized.
Single-value wrappers such as identifiers, money or unit-carrying quantities mapped to and from their primitive form.
Palindrome conversion chain (Entity -> DAO -> DTO -> Controller -> DTO -> DAO -> Entity) where each layer owns exactly one transformation direction, making the data flow explicit and each boundary independently testable.
Versioned API contracts: a DTO for API v1 and a separate DTO for API v2 coexist; a converter pair maps each version's DTO to the shared internal model, isolating API consumers from internal changes.
API gateway transformation: external third-party API payloads are normalized into an internal canonical format at the gateway, and outbound responses are converted back to the third-party schema; converters live at the seam.
Event-driven payload normalization: domain events carry one representation (e.g., enriched entity) while the event bus transports a flattened wire format (e.g., protobuf); converters at producer and consumer ends keep the two shapes in sync.
ORM entity vs. read-model DTO at the query boundary: a repository executes a query and the row-set converter maps each row to a read-model DTO, avoiding the entity in read-only paths entirely.
Anti-corruption layer at legacy integration seams: external system payloads are translated into the internal domain model at the boundary, and responses translated back; the converter owns the translation vocabulary, protecting the domain model from foreign concepts (Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design; Microsoft Azure Architecture Center; AWS Prescriptive Guidance).
Immutable value type <-> wire format for cryptographic or financial domains: the converter is a lawful isomorphism ensuring every wire value round-trips to an identical object (tested via property-based round-trip laws, as in the lawful-conversions Haskell library and Higher-Kinded-J Iso optics library).
Strangler-fig migration seam: new microservice functionality is accessed through an ACL that converts legacy system payloads to the new domain model and back, keeping the legacy interface unchanged while the new service evolves behind the seam.
Guava com.google.common.base.Converter<F, T>: an abstract bidirectional function with convert()/reverse(), automatic reverse() derivation for subclasses, mapAll() for whole iterables and Converter.normalize() to lift a converter into a function converter - the pattern as a shipped JDK-adjacent library type (Google Guava).
Go database/sql custom types: a type implementing both sql.Scanner (Scan(src any) error) and driver.Valuer (Value() (driver.Value, error)) owns the Go value <-> database column pair in both directions; the standard library's NullString, NullInt64 and NullTime are built-in pairs of exactly this shape.
Rails custom attribute types: subclass ActiveModel::Type::Value, override serialize (Ruby value -> database value) and deserialize (database value -> Ruby value) and bind with attribute :col, MyType.new - the converter pair at the ORM seam, with cast_value kept separate for user-input coercion.

name: test-specific-subclass
document:
test-specific-subclass
test-specific extension
subclassed test double
Make an otherwise untestable class testable by defining a test-only subclass that overrides the method reaching the unusable dependency (or exposes the internal state the test needs), so the boundary can be substituted and observed without putting test hooks into production code.
A class that must be tested reaches its dependency through a call on itself - a self-call to a helper method, a field created inside the class, or a singleton/static lookup - so the test has no injection point: the collaborator cannot be replaced from outside, the indirect inputs cannot be controlled and the indirect outputs cannot be observed. Editing the production class to accept the dependency may be impossible (third-party or frozen code) or would introduce test logic into production.
Applies to legacy or third-party object-oriented code where the boundary call already sits behind an overridable (non-final, sufficiently visible) method, or can be extracted into one, and where test-only code may live next to the tests. It is a fallback for statically typed languages that need the double to stay type-compatible with a concrete class; where the code can be modified, dependency injection is the better seam.
A legacy class reads the wall clock inside a helper method (System.currentTimeMillis, DateTime.Now, Instant.now): override the helper so date/decision logic can be tested at a fixed instant.
A reporting or notification class sends mail or calls a remote API from a self-call: override that method with a canned or empty body so the unit test runs offline and deterministically.
A class reaches a database or the file system from inside its own method: override it to return an in-memory fixture instead of building the real object chain (entity-chain snipping).
Verifying the sequence and the set of steps of a template method: override the steps in a subclass and record which of them ran, in which order.
Exposing private state for state verification, or exposing a private algorithm step so it can be tested individually (state-exposing and behaviour-exposing subclasses).
Replacing a singleton or static accessor the SUT uses through a lookup with a controlled instance that is still type-compatible with the concrete class (substituted singleton).
Putting a legacy untested class under a characterization-test baseline before refactoring, while extracting the collaborator is not yet possible.
A Java class that cannot be modified (third-party or legacy jar) but has a non-final boundary method to stub: Mockito spy() / @Spy keeps the real methods and stubs only the overridden ones - the partial mocking Mockito's Javadoc documents for legacy code and third-party interfaces (final methods stay un-stubbable).
A PHP class whose constructor opens connections or performs other side effects: createPartialMock(Class::class, ['boundaryMethod']) or getMockBuilder()->onlyMethods([...])->disableOriginalConstructor() generates a double that overrides only the named methods and skips the real constructor - PHPUnit's documented form of the pattern (final, private and static methods and enums cannot be doubled).
A .NET class with virtual boundary members: NSubstitute Substitute.ForPartsOf<T>() creates a partial substitute that - as NSubstitute's own docs state - inherits the original type via Castle DynamicProxy and runs real code except for members configured with DoNotCallBase, i.e. a generated test-specific subclass with an official 'use with caution' caveat.

name: model-view-intent
document:
model-view-intent
mvi
Structure one UI feature as a single loop in which every user interaction becomes an intent value, a pure reduce step derives the next immutable state from the previous state and that intent, and the view renders only that state - so the screen's behaviour is determined by data instead of by scattered event handlers.
Presentation state is spread across the view, its presenter and several observable channels: every handler sets its own field or widget directly, a loading flag, a data field and an error field can contradict each other, the view keeps state of its own that a configuration change or process death destroys, and no state transition can be exercised without instantiating the UI.
Interactive applications with a declarative view layer and some reactive runtime - Android/Compose with coroutines and Flow, SwiftUI, React, Scala.js, or a hand-rolled event loop - where one screen or app-level feature can own a single immutable state object, user events can be represented as data values, and the view can re-render from a new state value. It is applied per feature, not per widget, and it is independent of any particular framework.
A search or feed screen where loading, empty, error and result states are concurrent flags in the old design and must become one state value the view can render without contradictions.
Complex screen flows - checkout, wizards, media players, editors - whose transitions must be explicit and reviewable rather than emerging from scattered handler code.
Screens that must survive configuration changes or process death by restoring one serializable state object instead of replaying a history of view commands.
Crash reports and support cases that carry the current state plus the last intent, making reproduction and replay possible without reproducing the exact tap sequence.
Cross-platform features that share the reducer between platforms and swap only the view layer (Android and iOS, web and desktop).
Large applications where each feature module exposes an intent/state contract and different teams own the loop for their screens.
A Cycle.js component whose DOM and HTTP driver streams become intents, whose model derives state, and whose view renders that state is a direct stream-based MVI implementation.
A Kotlin Multiplatform feature built with Orbit MVI can share an OrbitContainer's intent, reduce, state, and side-effect flow across Android, iOS, and desktop.
An Android Jetpack Compose feature following Android's official unidirectional-data-flow guidance can use a ViewModel-owned immutable UiState, upward events, and downward rendering as a framework-native MVI realization.

name: policy-guard
document:
policy-guard
policy pattern
policy decision point / policy enforcement point
Keep every authorisation decision out of the protected resource's code by moving the rules into a separate Policy component and letting a Guard - the enforcement point every access must pass through - obtain a decision from that policy before the operation is performed.
Access rules written inside the resource's own methods (checking roles or ownership inline) entangle business logic with security logic: the same rule is re-implemented at every call site, a forgotten check silently opens a bypass, and the rules cannot be reviewed, tested or changed without touching the resource's code.
Components that own protected resources or operations and must decide per access whether the authenticated subject - with its roles, attributes, tenant and request context - may perform the requested action. Typical at object, module or boundary scope: request handlers, domain services, document stores, message consumers and administrative tooling that all reach the same resources and should obey the same rules, especially when the rules change more often than the resource code.
HTTP and API request handling: authentication establishes the security context once, then every endpoint or method invocation is guarded by a policy decision (for example Spring Security's AuthorizationManager behind its AuthorizationFilter, or ASP.NET Core authorization middleware over registered policies).
Domain services that expose several operations on one aggregate: the guard checks the (subject, operation, resource) triple before each service method executes, instead of scattering role checks through the methods.
Multi-tenant backends where the decision must consider tenant, ownership and request attributes, not only roles; the guard resolves them from the security context and passes them to the policy.
Document or file stores: every read or write is wrapped by a guard that consults rules keyed by the document identifier and its classification.
Administrative and background code - CLI tools, batch jobs, message consumers - that must obey the same policy as the interactive API so that no side door exists.
Regulated environments where every access decision, including denials, must be logged consistently and the policy itself must be independently testable.
Spring Security request boundaries: AuthorizationFilter passes the current Authentication and HttpServletRequest to an AuthorizationManager and proceeds only after a grant; configure every protected route so an unlisted path cannot become a side door.
ASP.NET Core policy authorization: named policies combine requirements evaluated by IAuthorizationHandler implementations and attach with [Authorize(Policy = "...")] or RequireAuthorization; place UseAuthorization after authentication and before endpoints.
Open Policy Agent (OPA) deployments: AWS Prescriptive Guidance models a centralized or distributed Policy Decision Point with Policy Enforcement Points on APIs, allowing shared policy while using local sidecars when latency or availability requires it.

name: double-dispatch
document:
double-dispatch
multiple dispatch
multiple polymorphism
two-level dispatch
Select the operation to execute from the runtime types of two collaborating objects, so behaviour can vary along two independent type axes instead of being resolved by hand-written type tests in the caller.
Behaviour depends on the runtime type of *two* objects - element and visitor, shape and surface, left operand and right operand - but an ordinary call resolves on the receiver only (or, in dynamic languages, on no argument at all). Every operation then grows its own type-test ladder, knowledge of the concrete classes leaks into callers, and adding a class silently breaks the cases nobody remembered to extend.
Object models in which two type hierarchies interact: shape x medium, AST node x operation, operand x operand, entity x entity in a collision matrix. It applies when the pair-specific behaviour is a real matrix rather than a single special case, when each hierarchy evolves on its own schedule, and when the language's own dispatch resolves only one of the two runtime types (classic single-dispatch OO) or none of them (method overloading is bound statically).
Collision and interaction rules in games and simulations: every pair of entity types (bullet × wall, ship × asteroid) has its own outcome. Double dispatch cleanly selects the correct collision algorithm at runtime. Used in Unity, Unreal, and custom game engines via visitor-like hierarchies or type-indexed collision matrices. Spatial partitioning (quad-trees, oct-trees) is used alongside to reduce O(n²) pair checks. Examples: Unity physics collision callbacks, Unreal collision/overlap event system, Box2D physics engine, custom engines with AABB/Sphere/OBB hierarchies.
Geometry predicates between two shape hierarchies: intersect, contains, distance and other predicates where each pair (circle-circle, circle-rectangle, rectangle-rectangle) uses a different algorithm and pairs are not symmetric. Used in game physics engines, computer graphics rendering pipelines, and GIS systems. Examples: Box2D, Chipmunk, computer graphics rendering engines.
Numeric promotion and operator semantics between unrelated numeric types: Rational × Integer, Money × Currency, BigInt × Float — operations that must consult both operands' concrete types. Ruby's Numeric#coerce is the canonical language mechanism enabling this pattern. Examples: Ruby Numeric#coerce, Java BigDecimal arithmetic, C# decimal/float/double mixed arithmetic.
Document rendering and media output: shapes or widgets × output targets (screen, printer, PDF, HTML), where each combination emits different code. The medium axis and the shape type axis independently determine the rendering path. Examples: Qt/wxWidgets painting systems, Java AWT/Swing paint(Graphics) dispatch, WebKit/Blink layout engines.
AST traversal and transformations: one node hierarchy × many analyses (type check, pretty-print, evaluate, optimise) — the primary use case the Visitor pattern was designed for. Each (Operation × NodeType) pair is a separate handler. Examples: Babel/TypeScript compiler, LLVM compiler infrastructure, Roslyn C# compiler API.
Plugin and extension architectures: a host application defines an element hierarchy and a plugin defines a visitor; new plugins add operations without modifying element classes. Examples: Eclipse IDE plugin system, Visual Studio Analyzer/extension APIs, static analysis tools (linters, formatters).
Serialization and deserialization frameworks: Format (JSON, XML, binary, protobuf) × type — each combination may need different encoding rules. Examples: Jackson/Gson in Java, Python dataclasses serialization, Protocol Buffers schema evolution.
Protocol handling in parsers and state machines: handler depends on both message kind and connection/session kind — a state × event matrix. Used in network protocol stacks, parsers, and finite state machine implementations. Examples: HTTP server request routing, game AI state machines, telecom protocol state tables.
Event handling in GUI frameworks: a widget hierarchy × an event hierarchy (mouse, keyboard, focus) — each (Widget × Event) pair may require different handling logic. The classic AWT/Swing processEvent double-dispatch was the motivating example for several academic multi-dispatch papers. Examples: Java AWT event delegation, Qt event handling, Swing ActionMap/InputMap.
Message routing in game architectures: entity × message type routing where the correct handler depends on both the receiver entity's type and the message's payload type. Common in Entity-Component-System (ECS) patterns where components process messages differently. Examples: Unity MessageSystem, Amazon Lumberyard (component × message routing).
Numeric and array operators as native multiple dispatch: Julia makes the pair axis first-class - arithmetic and promotion operators are generic functions whose methods select on the runtime types of all arguments, and the compiler emits a specialised version per concrete combination (Int,Int vs Float64,Float64) instead of a hand-rolled accept/visit round-trip; promote_type absorbs cross-type cells. The canonical modern realisation of the pattern. Examples: Julia Base arithmetic, Julia promote_type/coercion, heterogeneous-array dispatch costs documented in the Julia performance guide.
Generic functions in CLOS and Dylan-family languages: method selection keyed by the classes or identities of every required argument, with method combination (call-next-method) resolving ambiguity - double dispatch without the intrusive accept method, and the benchmark every manual encoding is measured against. Examples: ANSI Common Lisp CLOS defgeneric/defmethod, Dylan generic functions.
Runtime binder dispatch on the CLR: the C# dynamic keyword defers overload resolution to the Dynamic Language Runtime, binding the call on the runtime types of receiver and arguments with call-site caching; CallSiteBinder.Bind is documented as runtime binding (double-dispatch). A missing pair surfaces as a runtime binder exception rather than a compile error, so it suits dynamic-language and COM interop boundaries more than closed business matrices. Examples: DLR call-site caching, IronPython/IronRuby interop, COM interop via the runtime binder.

name: watchman
document:
watchman
dead man's switch
heartbeat monitor
Detect that a message flow has gone silent - not that a message failed - and tell a responsible person or system within a bounded time by comparing each flow's arrivals against the cadence its business deadline implies.
Message systems fail silently in the one way no error handler observes: nothing arrives. A producer stops emitting, a consumer stops draining, a scheduled job never fires, a credential expires, a partition goes offline - and because no failing code path is ever entered, error dashboards stay green while downstream data quietly goes stale. The recurring trigger: a flow whose absence is business-visible (a nightly feed, an order stream, a partner interface) has no owner-facing signal for 'no messages', so the gap is discovered late - by a customer or a downstream job - instead of by the team that can fix it.
Applies wherever messages are expected on a knowable cadence (event streams, queues, batch hand-offs, partner interfaces, device check-ins) and their absence is a business-visible failure: the flow has an owner, the expected period and grace window can be derived from a downstream deadline, and either the transport can be observed passively (queue counters, a wire tap) or the producers can emit out-of-band heartbeats. The watchman sits at message-flow or boundary scope - an in-process watcher beside the consumer, a periodic sweep over persisted last-seen state, or a rule in the monitoring stack fed by metrics - and it must itself be watched, because a silent watchman is exactly the failure it exists to catch.
Nightly batch or ETL feed: page the integration owner when the 02:00 import has produced no messages by its deadline, instead of noticing an empty report at the morning stand-up.
Business-critical event stream (orders, payments, telemetry): alarm when the produce rate stays at zero through business hours, which separates a healthy quiet topic from a stopped producer.
External partner interface: notify when no messages have arrived from a B2B partner within the agreed window, turning a looming SLA breach into an early, actionable alert.
Long-running workflow stage: require a heartbeat from each process-manager step so a stuck instance is noticed before the surrounding batch closes or a compensation becomes necessary.
Retry or dead-letter pump: verify that the pump still drains failed messages - silence means the pump died, not that the backlog is empty.
Fleet check-ins (edge devices, agents, cron jobs on many hosts): raise a per-device or per-site alarm when scheduled check-ins stop arriving.
The alerting pipeline itself: an always-firing watchdog alert routed to an external service, so a broken alert path is discovered by its silence.
Cron and scheduled-job fleet via Healthchecks.io: each job pings a unique URL, the service holds the Period and Grace Time, flips the check Late then Down when no ping arrives by period + grace, and notifies integrations.
Dashboard alert rules in Grafana: an alert rule whose query returns no series enters the No Data state and can raise a DatasourceNoData alert - the platform form of deciding what silence means (No Data, Alerting, Normal or Keep last state).
Apache Burrow for Kafka (LinkedIn): committed offsets are evaluated per partition over a sliding window and a consumer is classified STALLED when its offset is frozen with non-zero lag, or STOPPED when no new commits arrive - consumer-silence detection without fixed lag thresholds.

name: point-to-point-channel
document:
point-to-point-channel
point-to-point queue
p2p channel
Deliver each message on a channel to exactly one consumer, so senders never have to coordinate with receivers and no unit of work is handled twice.
A producer must hand work to exactly one handler while several receivers are running (or the intended handler is temporarily unavailable): broadcasting the message makes every receiver deduplicate, and addressing a specific consumer instance couples the sender to its identity, location and liveness.
Asynchronous messaging inside one process, between processes or across services, where each message is a unit of work (command, job, document, RPC request) and duplicate handling is as unacceptable as loss. Applies to in-process worker queues and to brokered channels (JMS queue, AMQP queue, Kafka partition, cloud queue) alike; the channel - not the consumer and not the sender - owns the routing decision.
Work queues: a web tier enqueues jobs and a pool of workers consumes them, with each job running exactly once.
Request-reply over messaging: the request goes to a queue, exactly one service instance answers it, and the reply returns on a reply queue identified by a correlation identifier.
Command dispatch in a service-oriented system: an order service appends commands that exactly one instance of the command processor executes.
Media or log processing pipelines where every stage pulls its input from a queue and each item is handled by one of the stage's replicas.
Legacy and batch integration: jobs handed to a single consumer daemon through a queue, with the channel providing the transactional hand-off.
Scaling an existing single-consumer endpoint by attaching additional instances (Competing Consumers) without changing producers or the message contract.
Apache Kafka consumer groups: records in each topic partition are assigned to one group member at a time, so a group scales work while separate group IDs retain independent pub-sub copies.
RabbitMQ Work Queues: a task queue distributes jobs among competing workers with round-robin or fair dispatch; manual acknowledgements allow unacknowledged work to be redelivered after a worker failure.
Amazon SQS Standard queues: distribute background jobs among consumers with visibility timeouts, while at-least-once delivery requires idempotent handlers because duplicate deliveries remain possible.

name: range
document:
range
interval
Represent a span of values as a single interval value whose bound inclusivity and open ends are explicit, so containment and interval-to-interval comparisons live in one place instead of repeated ad-hoc endpoint tests.
Start and end travel together through the code but every caller re-derives what they mean: containment is written as scattered <= / < comparisons that drift apart, "unbounded" is smuggled in as a sentinel value (Long.MAX_VALUE, 9999-12-31), and interval-to-interval questions - do these two overlap, does one enclose the other, what is the gap between them - have no home at all.
Applies wherever a domain concept is a span rather than a point: validity and effectivity periods, booking and availability windows, quantity or price tiers, measurement buckets, version and address ranges, pagination windows, and query parameters such as a date range. It pays off when the same interval is compared repeatedly or crosses a boundary (persistence, API payloads, UI widgets), because the bound convention then has to be written once instead of re-decided per call site. For a single comparison between two local variables the type is pure overhead.
Validity and effectivity windows: a contract, price or membership is valid over [effectiveFrom, effectiveTo), and every check is a membership test against one interval.
Booking and availability: a room, seat or resource is reserved during an interval; overlap (not adjacency) decides whether a new booking is possible, and back-to-back bookings must be allowed deliberately.
Quantity and price tiers: the unit price depends on the quantity interval ([1,10), [10,50), [50, +inf)), so a container of intervals with containment lookup replaces a cascade of if-statements.
Temporal queries and reporting: "last 7 days", "this quarter", "since the migration" are half-open or open-ended intervals passed to repositories and rendered by date-range pickers.
Version, port and address ranges: a compatibility claim covers [1.2, 2.0) of a library, a firewall rule covers a port interval - containment answers "is this covered?" and intersection answers "do these rules conflict?".
Pagination and slicing windows: a page is an interval over a sequence, and half-open semantics make adjacency exact ([0,20) followed by [20,40)),
PostgreSQL range and multirange columns: PostgreSQL's daterange, tsrange and numeric range types make lower-inclusive/upper-exclusive bounds, overlap and containment operators, and indexed range queries part of the persistence contract; choose the bound convention before mapping domain intervals.
Guava Range: Java's Guava Range models convex bounded or unbounded intervals with nine open/closed forms, isConnected and intersection; use ContiguousSet only when a discrete domain really requires enumeration rather than treating the interval itself as a sequence.
Standard-library and container choices: Rust's std::ops::RangeBounds covers included, excluded and unbounded bounds when its range forms fit; for many intervals requiring join/split policies, Boost ICL's interval_set and interval_map supply the container semantics instead of overloading one Range value.

name: recursive-descent-parser
document:
recursive-descent-parser
recursive descent
recursive descent parsing
Parse a small grammar by translating every rule directly into a function that consumes the tokens the rule matches and calls the functions of the rules it references, so the parser's control flow is the grammar itself and stays readable, debuggable and free of a code-generation step.
A hand-written parser is the only option - no generator in the toolchain, or the grammar is a small DSL - yet the grammar is not a flat token sequence: alternatives must be chosen from lookahead, repetition must become a loop, and the natural grammar for expressions is left-recursive, which a top-down parser cannot translate directly. Without a disciplined mapping from rules to functions the parser degenerates into ad-hoc index arithmetic and exception-driven backtracking, and errors end up without positions.
Front ends for small languages, DSLs, query/filter/rule grammars, configuration and protocol formats, and the parsing layer of compilers and interpreters that want no code-generation step. It applies when a lexer or token stream already exists (or is cheap to write), the grammar is small to medium and reasonably LL-friendly or rewritable into LL form, and the team values readable, step-debuggable, position-precise parsing over generated tables.
Front ends for small languages, DSLs and configuration formats (filter expressions, rule engines, policy languages, template syntaxes) where a generator and its build integration would be overkill.
Expression and statement parsing in single-pass compilers and interpreters that emit bytecode or IR while parsing, as in Crafting Interpreters' Lox.
Tooling for a grammar you own - formatters, linters, syntax highlighters, language servers - where error tolerance, multiple diagnostics and exact positions matter more than raw throughput.
Protocol and wire-format decoding with a small fixed grammar, where errors must carry byte offsets and malformed input must be rejected deterministically.
Context-dependent or indentation-sensitive syntaxes (templates with interpolation, layout-based blocks, configuration with embedded expressions) that a generated lexer handles poorly.
Codebases that must not carry generated code: security-reviewed, vendored or cross-compiled projects where an ordinary source file beats a build-time generator.
Clang's C-family front end uses a unified hand-built recursive-descent parser for C, C++, Objective-C and Objective-C++, pairing rule-oriented control flow with production-quality diagnostics.
The Go standard library's go/parser is a production recursive-descent parser for Go source, with explicit parser state, nesting-depth guards and error recovery.
rustc_parse is the Rust compiler's recursive-descent parser module, showing how a hand-written parser can scale to macros, recovery modes and detailed token/state handling.
Lua's reference implementation compiles with lparser.c, a single-pass recursive-descent parser that emits bytecode opcodes while reducing expressions instead of building a syntax tree, with precedence handled by parsing levels.

name: side-effect-free-function
document:
side-effect-free-function
pure function
Put the model's logic into operations that compute a result from their inputs alone, so that a caller - and a test - can predict the result without knowing any state the operation might secretly touch.
Reasoning about a design becomes guesswork when operations do more than return a result: the caller must read the implementation and every delegation to know which state a call changes, and no result can be reproduced in a test without recreating the state around it. As rules compose, the number of hidden interactions grows faster than the behaviour being built, so the model stops being safely predictable.
Applies inside the model layer of any codebase whose rules are combined and composed - pricing, eligibility, allocation, validation - and where a computation must be exercised in tests without a database, clock or message broker in the loop. It matters most where several rules interact (composition multiplies hidden coupling) and in languages whose defaults are mutable objects, because there the discipline has to be stated rather than assumed.
Pricing and discount rules: unit prices, tax and rebates computed from immutable inputs, so the same basket always prices the same way.
Eligibility and specification checks: a rule expressed as a predicate over a value and reused in validation, selection and tests.
Money and quantity arithmetic: scaling, adding and rounding return new values instead of adjusting a running total in place.
Deriving test data and expected values from the same pure functions the model uses, instead of hand-copied golden values.
Query-side report assembly: projections, summaries and totals built by composing pure functions over already-loaded immutable data.
Memoizing an expensive domain computation, which is sound exactly because the function is referentially transparent.
Redux reducers: the store computes the next state by calling (previousState, action) => newState with no mutation, no clock, no randomness, so DevTools can replay a recorded action log and reproduce the exact state and useSelector can detect changes by reference comparison alone.
React function components: the official contract is that rendering must be a pure function of props, state and context, so React can cache components whose inputs are unchanged, abandon an outdated render mid-flight, and call each component twice in Strict Mode to expose impurity.
Haskell: ordinary functions are pure by default and effects are confined to IO-typed values, so the type signature itself states whether a computation touches the world and the compiler, not review, enforces the query half of the split.

name: dynamic-router
document:
dynamic-router
dynamic routing
rules-based routing
Route each message to a destination chosen from a rule base that can be changed while the system runs, so the router never depends on - or is redeployed for - the set of destinations it serves.
Routing logic hard-coded into the router (switch chains, static filter tables, deployment-time route configuration) couples it to every destination: adding, moving, throttling or retiring a destination needs a code change, a review and a restart, and each topology change forces the router back through the release process instead of being an operational edit.
Message-based integration where the destination set or the routing policy changes faster than the router's release cycle: rules are owned by operations, destinations announce themselves, scale out, or go down for maintenance, or one router instance serves several tenants or environments. Applies when the route can be expressed as rules over message content, headers or context evaluated per message, and the platform offers a usable control channel (config watch, control bus, admin endpoint, hot-reloadable table) to publish rule changes.
Multi-tenant integration hub: each tenant has its own routing table, loaded and swapped per tenant instead of one deployed router per tenant.
Event distribution where downstream teams add or retire consumers by publishing routing conditions rather than requesting a router release.
Canary and blue/green rollouts: send a slice of traffic to a new destination by editing a rule, and roll back by restoring the previous rule set.
Maintenance windows: reroute a destination's traffic to a standby, drain the destination, then restore the rule when it returns.
Regional or sharded routing where the region-to-destination mapping is maintained by operations and changes with capacity, not with code.
Rule-driven enterprise integration in the classic EIP sense, where a rule base is consulted per message and recipients announce themselves on a control channel.
Kubernetes Gateway API traffic splitting: use HTTPRoute weighted backends to shift a configurable percentage of traffic between versions without redeploying the router.
Service mesh canary deployments: an Istio VirtualService or Linkerd ServiceProfile acts as the rule base; routing rules are edited at runtime to steer canary traffic, then promoted or rolled back.
Multi-tenant SaaS routing: Spring Cloud Gateway or Envoy.DynamicRouter loads per-tenant routing rules from a registry, injecting tenant-specific headers or rewrites so one router instance serves hundreds of isolated tenants.
API version routing and A/B testing: route by Accept header, API version path prefix, or experimentCohort header to different backend versions, controlled by rules updated without a release.
Database or cache sharding: route a tenant or user ID hash to the correct shard's endpoint via a rule table that is repointed during resharding without touching application code.
BGP route-server testing: use a chaos-testing framework against a route server to validate that policy changes converge correctly and do not produce route leaks before production deployment.
Traefik dynamic configuration: Traefik builds its routing table at runtime from providers (Docker labels, Kubernetes IngressRoute, Consul/etcd KV stores), so services announce their own routes and rule changes hot-swap without restarting the proxy.
HAProxy Runtime API: add server and set server state/weight over the runtime socket repoint and drain backends without a reload; the Data Plane API layers persistence and validation on top of these runtime changes.
Kong Gateway admin API: Routes - including the expressions DSL when router_flavor is set to expressions - are created and updated at runtime via POST /routes and take effect on the next matching request, with priority-ordered rule evaluation replacing a redeployed config.

name: option-maybe
document:
option-maybe
Option
Maybe
Make the possible absence of a result part of the value and of the signature, so every caller has to decide what happens when nothing is there instead of meeting a null, a sentinel or a silently defaulted value at run time.
A function has something to return for some inputs and nothing for others, but the signature does not say so: it returns a null reference, a sentinel (-1, empty string, NULL), an out-parameter, or a value that quietly means 'not found'. Callers forget the check, dereference the null or treat the sentinel as data, and the 'this case does not exist' path is discovered in production rather than at the call site.
Lookups, parsing, searches, optional configuration, nullable database columns and any API whose result may legitimately not exist - wherever the language can express absence as a type (Option/Maybe/Optional, a nullable type, a union with undefined) or a convention can carry it. It pays off at module and service boundaries, in chains of partial steps, and wherever 'absent' must stay distinguishable from a legitimate empty, zero or falsey value.
Lookups that can miss: configuration keys, cache entries, registry entries, map/dictionary access - either through the language's two-value form or an Optional-returning accessor.
Parsing and conversion (integers, dates, URLs, decimal numbers, external identifiers) where 'no valid value' is a legitimate answer rather than an error.
Searches over collections and structures (find, first, min/max, binary search, regex match, tree traversal) where a miss is part of the contract.
Genuinely optional data: middle names, second addresses, unset feature flags, optional protocol fields - as opposed to missing state, which is a domain error.
Chains of partial steps (look up user, then their company, then its billing address) where any hop may be absent and the whole chain should collapse to 'nothing'.
Boundaries from nullable interfaces: a database column admits NULL, a legacy or interop API returns null or -1, a deserialized document lacks a field - converted once at the adapter.
Container and stream operations that can be empty (head, pop, next, dequeue, min) and should report emptiness instead of throwing or returning a sentinel.
Rust's standard library uses std::option::Option<T> with Some(T) and None for optional values; its map and pattern-matching APIs let lookup or parsing pipelines stop at absence without a null pointer.
Java SE's java.util.Optional<T> is a production API for method results that may be absent: ofNullable converts a nullable boundary value, map/flatMap compose follow-up work, and orElse/orElseThrow make the exit policy explicit.
Scala's standard-library scala.Option[A] models Some/None and documents map, flatMap, and for-comprehensions for chained partial steps; its API also demonstrates wrapping a Java HashMap lookup so a missing key becomes None.

name: quantity
document:
quantity
units of measure
dimensioned value
Represent a dimensioned measurement as one value that carries its amount together with its unit, so that conversion, comparison, unit-compatible arithmetic and amount-plus-unit input/output all have a single owner and incompatible units cannot be combined by accident.
Measurements are stored as bare numbers whose unit lives only in a variable name, a column comment or the reader's memory: the same physical quantity appears in metres in one place and in feet in another, conversion factors are retyped at every call site, adding two numbers of different dimensions compiles (or runs) happily, and parsing and formatting '3 km' is reinvented per feature. The recurring trigger is that an amount and its unit always change together and are one conceptual whole, so leaving them as two unconnected things makes the unit rules impossible to own.
Value-scope code in domain, engineering or integration layers that handles physical quantities - length, mass, time, temperature, energy, data volume, concentration. It pays off when values arrive with heterogeneous units (sensors, imports, user input, third parties), when derived quantities such as speed or density are computed, when users select a unit system for display, and when values must survive persistence and transport. The language decides how much of the guarantee is compile-time (units as type parameters, phantom/branded types) and how much is a runtime value object backed by a conversion table or unit registry.
Sensor and telemetry pipelines where readings arrive tagged with a unit and must be normalised to a canonical unit before aggregation, alerting or storage.
Engineering and simulation code (CAD, robotics, structural, electrical) that computes derived quantities such as velocity, torque or energy and must keep the dimensions consistent.
Logistics and commerce where weight, dimensions and rate limits are expressed in different unit systems (kg/lb, cm/in, m^3/ft^3) and are displayed in the customer's chosen system.
Healthcare and laboratory systems that exchange doses and results between systems (mg/kg, mmol/L) with reference ranges in different units.
Energy and utility metering, where consumption (kWh, m^3) is billed through unit-price arithmetic and readings must be comparable across meter types.
UI-level unit-system switching: store and compute in one canonical unit, render and edit in metric or imperial according to a user preference.
Scientific Python applications built on Pint's UnitRegistry, such as sensor and laboratory pipelines, where quantities are parsed, converted and reduced dimensionally at integration boundaries.
.NET engineering and telemetry services using UnitsNet's strongly typed Length, Mass and related quantities, with parsing, conversion, serialization and display-unit selection centralized in the library.
Compile-time dimensional-analysis code using F# units of measure or C++ Boost.Units for simulation and control loops, where invalid unit arithmetic is rejected before runtime and derived units are expressed algebraically.

statement: Should each database row be represented by an object that owns its own read and write operations, rather than repeating row mapping and SQL in transaction scripts?
name: row-data-gateway
document:
row-data-gateway
row data gateway
row gateway
Give each database row its own in-memory object that mirrors the row's columns and carries the row's own find, insert, update and delete operations, so all data-access code for a table lives in one place instead of being duplicated across the scripts that use it.
SQL text, parameter binding and result-set mapping are re-derived inside every transaction script that touches a table, while the in-memory objects those scripts work with know nothing about the database. No single place knows how one row is read, written and deleted, so a schema change ripples through every script and every new query is another chance to get parameterisation and type conversion wrong.
Applies when business logic is organised as transaction scripts or thin services over a relational schema whose columns map closely to the fields actually used: the gateway mirrors the table structure, no object/relational impedance mismatch is being managed, and identity maps, units of work and lazy loading are either unnecessary or added deliberately as separate patterns. It also fits generated persistence layers, where the gateway classes are produced from schema metadata during the build.
Transaction-script applications (order entry, billing runs, batch imports) where several scripts need the same handful of row-level reads and writes.
CRUD-heavy back-office and admin tooling where a screen edits one row at a time and columns map one-to-one onto form fields.
Legacy or externally owned schemas that must be mirrored rather than reshaped: one gateway per table gives an explicit, reviewable seam between the application and someone else's database.
Generated persistence layers: gateways produced from schema metadata on every build, so the tedious class-per-table work is automated and stays in sync with the schema.
Simple mappings inside an otherwise rich domain model, where a domain object keeps a gateway as its data holder instead of copying field values around.
Reporting and fixture utilities that need reusable, parameterised finders for one table without pulling in a full object/relational mapper.
Laminas\Db\RowGateway and RowGatewayFeature (the official laminas-db implementation) expose one row object with save/delete and can materialize table-query results as row gateways, fitting CRUD screens or transaction scripts that edit individual records.
Zend Framework 1's Zend_Db_Table_Row is a documented legacy row-gateway implementation: table queries return row objects with column access plus save/delete/createRow operations, useful when a simple schema is consumed by row-oriented scripts.
The Go dgw tool generates structs and lightweight Table/Row Data Gateway functions from PostgreSQL metadata, demonstrating the pattern as a code-generation choice when a project wants typed CRUD without a full ORM.

statement: Should each database row be represented by an object that owns its own read and write operations, rather than repeating row mapping and SQL in transaction scripts?
name: table-data-gateway
document:
table-data-gateway
table gateway
Confine every SQL statement that touches one table or view inside a single gateway object whose methods take and return plain record structures, so that no other code contains SQL for that table and rows cross the boundary as data rather than as domain objects.
Access to one table is spread across the codebase: SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE fragments are copied into every caller, nobody can say which queries a schema change will break, DBAs cannot find the SQL that needs tuning, and each caller has to know the dialect, the placeholders and the column order. The desired boundary is a single object that mediates all access to the whole table while the individual rows remain records (tuples, structs, hashes, DataRows) instead of becoming mapped objects.
Relational persistence where the database is a stable, schema-first integration point and SQL-level control matters (indexes, hints, bulk loads, vendor features), where the team deliberately does not want O/R mapping machinery in the domain layer, and where the domain logic is simple enough that rows may travel as records - CRUD and query services, reporting/read models, ETL writers, local SQLite stores, or a legacy database mediated for several applications. It is also the packaging decision for 'the SQL has to live somewhere well known' before a DAO, repository or query object is justified.
A service or CRUD application over a handful of tables where every screen maps to a few statements per table and an ORM would add more machinery than it removes.
Reporting and read models: read-only gateways over views or wide tables that return records directly to a formatter, export or BI job.
Legacy databases mediated for several applications: one gateway library per database becomes the documented API and the place where vendor quirks are hidden.
Embedded/local storage (SQLite, SQLCipher) in a desktop or mobile app, where one gateway per table keeps SQL out of the UI and can be tested with an in-memory database.
Batch and ETL writers that need explicit control over statement batching, cursors and transaction size - control that generated mappers hide.
Gradual refactoring of SQL scattered through transaction scripts: the first step is to move each table's statements into a gateway, after which a Data Mapper or repository can be introduced deliberately.
Test fixtures and seeders that must write through the same statements as production code rather than through a second, divergent SQL path.
Generated gateways in Go: sqlc compiles a schema plus a file of named queries into one struct per table and one type-safe method per SQL statement, with the caller holding the database handle and opening transactions - the gateway's invariants are then enforced by the generator and compiler rather than by convention.
Local SQLite storage on Android: each Room @Dao is a gateway over one table - the SQL lives in @Query-annotated methods validated at compile time, rows travel as plain entity data classes, and @Transaction or database-level transactions keep atomic multi-DAO boundaries in the caller.
Java teams that want the gateway structure without hand-writing it: jOOQ's code generator emits one DAO class per table or view (findAll, findById, generated fetchByColumn methods) that reads and writes Record/POJO rows and borrows the caller's Configuration, so the per-table SQL surface is regenerated when the schema changes.

name: data-access-object
document:
data-access-object
DAO
Abstract and encapsulate all access to one particular data store behind a store-specific interface whose methods speak in domain terms, so business code never sees the store's API, dialect, connection handling or vendor error codes and the quirks of that store stay in one place.
Business objects talk to the store directly, embedding SQL, driver calls, connection handling and vendor error codes in ordinary application code: the application is coupled to one vendor's dialect and API, the same persistence details are duplicated across components, the store cannot be substituted (for a test, a second vendor or a replica) without editing business logic, and no single place can enforce access rules.
Applications that must reach a persistent store whose API is proprietary or vendor-specific - a relational database, a directory, a flat file, a legacy or remote service - especially when that store may later be swapped, reached through a second path (batch job, replica, cache) or faked in tests. It presupposes a language with interfaces, protocols or duck typing, and it is a decision about the access boundary only: the pattern says nothing about how domain objects are mapped, which is the separate concern of Data Mapper, Active Record or Table/Row Data Gateway.
An application that must run against more than one relational vendor, or against an embedded database in tests, keeps one DAO interface per aggregate and one implementation per vendor.
A legacy or third-party data source - mainframe, LDAP directory, SOAP/HTTP service, flat file - whose nonstandard API must not spread into business code.
A component that reaches the same store through a second path (bulk loader, nightly job, read replica) and needs the same domain-level operations as the online path.
Persistence code that stores domain objects as rows while business code must stay free of SQL and result sets, including hand-written mapping on top of a driver.
Test suites that need a fast in-memory or stub implementation behind the same interface so business logic can be exercised without a database.
Access layers that must enforce a policy (audit logging, tenant filtering, statement limits) at one place for every caller.
Microservices that own their own data store and expose it only through a typed interface, keeping service boundaries strict and enabling independent schema evolution.
CQRS read-model projections where the read side needs a denormalised view; a dedicated DAO isolates the projection logic from the command-side persistence.
Applications using async/await frameworks (FastAPI, asyncio) where data-access calls must be non-blocking and the DAO interface is naturally async.
Android apps using Room persistence: interfaces annotated @Dao declare insert/update/delete and @Query methods, and Room generates the implementation at compile time with SQL validated against the schema, so raw SQLite access never reaches view models.
Spring applications on JDBC, Hibernate or JPA use Spring's DAO support: DAO classes annotated @Repository get technology-specific exceptions (SQLException, HibernateException) translated into Spring's unified DataAccessException hierarchy, so one error-handling style works across persistence technologies.
Java services generated with jOOQ enable DAO generation to obtain a typed org.jooq.DAO per table (findById, exists, deleteById, per-column fetch methods) used as a base class underneath hand-written queries.

name: dao-factory
document:
dao-factory
DAOFactory
Factory for DataAccessObjects
Hand out a coherent family of data access objects bound to the store this deployment actually runs on: one factory object per store (the Factory Method form when there is a single store, the Abstract Factory form when stores vary) owns driver, dialect, connection and pooling policy, so the store choice is made once at the composition root and business components never name a vendor.
The persistence technology is not fixed: development runs on SQLite or H2, production on PostgreSQL or Oracle, one customer keeps a legacy system behind a service, tests want an in-memory store. Yet every business component constructs its own DAOs, so each one hard-codes a driver, a dialect, a connection policy and often a store key. Changing or adding a store then means editing business code in many places, and nothing prevents two components from silently talking to two different stores.
Persistence layers where the store implementation varies per deployment, per customer or per environment (relational vendors, embedded databases, files, remote services) and where clients must stay independent of the vendor API. It applies when DAO interfaces exist or can be defined cleanly, when the store choice can be made once per application, tenant or session at a composition root or onboarding step, and - in the Factory Method form - when a single store merely needs one place to construct its DAOs. Where a dependency-injection container, an ORM dialect layer or a provider factory already resolves implementations from configuration, that mechanism is the factory and a hand-written hierarchy only adds a second composition root.
Multi-database deployments: one application runs on SQLite or H2 in development and PostgreSQL or Oracle in production, and the factory reads the active store from configuration.
Vendor-portable products: an ISV hands the same DAO interfaces to customers running SQL Server, PostgreSQL or Oracle, with one concrete factory family per supported store.
Test infrastructure: a fake or in-memory factory family is bound in tests while the real factory is bound in production, so application flows run without a database.
Multi-tenant SaaS: the factory resolves the tenant's store (its schema, database or shard) and hands out DAOs bound to that tenant's connection. Tenant-scoped factory families prevent cross-tenant data leakage by ensuring every DAO query carries the tenant context from the factory's connection or session state.
Legacy and cloud coexistence during migration: two factory families stand behind one DAO interface set, letting reads and writes move store by store instead of in one big-bang cutover.
Pluggable backends: DAOs contributed by plugins or optional modules (a JDBC driver JAR, a ServiceLoader provider, a Python entry-point package) are resolved at startup by store key without recompiling the application.
Runtime data source selection: the factory selects the active data source at startup or request time based on environment variables, feature flags or feature flags, enabling blue-green deployments where different store families are active for different traffic shares.
ORM-backed persistence with portable interfaces: when using JPA/Hibernate, wrap EntityManagerFactory or SessionFactory behind a DAO factory interface so that the domain layer stays independent of the ORM provider and unit tests can substitute a lightweight in-memory implementation.
Microservices with per-service data stores: each microservice owns its data store; the service's DAO factory hides whether that store is PostgreSQL, MongoDB or a proprietary external service, and the factory interface becomes the integration contract for that service's data domain.
A/B testing with different storage backends: a feature flag routes traffic to one of several concrete factory families (e.g., legacy v2 vs. new v3 store), enabling gradual rollout and canary testing of a new database technology without changing any DAO interface.
ADO.NET provider factory: System.Data.Common's DbProviderFactory is the framework's own Abstract Factory - DbProviderFactories.GetFactory(invariantName) returns the registered SqlClientFactory or Npgsql factory and creates provider-specific Connection, Command and DataAdapter objects from a config-supplied provider name, which is exactly the store-selection machinery a hand-written DAO factory duplicates.
JDBC DataSource: javax.sql.DataSource is a vendor-implemented factory for connections; bound to a JNDI logical name (jdbc/sampledb) the application asks for a logical resource instead of naming a driver class or URL, and swapping the database vendor becomes a deployment change - the Java platform's built-in version of the DAO factory seam.
Spring Boot DataSourceBuilder: Boot reads spring.datasource.url, infers the driver and pooling implementation from the classpath and builds a HikariDataSource or vendor DataSource; here the framework is the factory, so the DAO layer consumes the built DataSource rather than re-deciding the store in a parallel hand-written hierarchy.
