name: cancellation-token
document:
cancellation-token
cancellation signal
cooperative cancellation
Give a caller-owned operation tree a one-way request to stop: pass a read-only cancellation signal through every cancellable call, observe it at safe points, clean up what was acquired, and report a distinct cancelled outcome without pretending that cooperative cancellation is forced termination.
A request handler, background job or UI action starts work that fans out into nested calls, tasks or threads. When the caller disconnects, a deadline expires, the user presses stop or a sibling fails, merely abandoning the result leaves already-started work burning CPU, holding connections and calling dependencies. Force-killing a thread or process can interrupt a critical section and corrupt shared state, while a signal that is not propagated or observed cannot stop the call tree or make its cleanup visible to the joiner.
Use where work can outlive the caller's interest and the runtime exposes checkpoints, suspension points or interruptible waits: request-scoped servers, workers, UI tasks, stream pipelines and batch loops. The operation owns cleanup, cancellation may race any checkpoint, and the design must state what happens when a request arrives after an irreversible side effect or while a dependency ignores the signal.
Request-scoped server work: the handler gets a request signal that fires when the client disconnects or the deadline expires, cancelling in-flight database, queue and upstream calls instead of pinning worker threads and connections after the caller is gone.
UI and mobile tasks: navigating away, closing a window or pressing stop cancels the task tree that loads, renders or downloads for that view, and only that view's tokens are affected.
Graceful shutdown: a supervisor stops accepting work and cancels the token shared by worker loops; every worker stops at its next safe point, flushes and releases resources, and the process exits inside the shutdown budget.
Fan-out with short-circuit: as soon as one subtask fails, or as soon as any one result suffices (hedged or racing replicas), the scope cancels the siblings instead of waiting for all of them.
Batch and stream pipelines: a processor subscribes to the pipeline signal and stops consuming and producing when the pipeline is torn down, abandoning the current chunk when the job's deadline elapses.
Testing and tooling: inject an already-cancelled signal, or one cancelled after N iterations, to exercise the stop path without racing an actual shutdown.
HTTP client redirect and retry cancellation: when a request is redirected or a lower-level retry budget is exhausted, cancel the in-flight operation so the client can proceed with the next action without waiting for a result that is no longer relevant.
Health-check abortion: a liveness probe times out or a readiness check fails mid-flight; cancel the in-progress health metric collection so the pod can be restarted or pulled from service without waiting for a hung check.
GRPC deadline and cancellation propagation: a server receives a client deadline and cancellation token; both must be threaded through every async operation so that an expired deadline or a client disconnect promptly frees server resources.
LLM request fan-out: multiple model providers are queried in parallel; the first successful response wins and all pending requests are cancelled immediately, avoiding wasted compute on a result that will be discarded.
Database connection pool eviction: a query timeout or client disconnect cancels the in-flight query, releasing the connection back to the pool before the server's statement timeout fires; the pool's token is derived from the request context so pool eviction and request cancellation share the same stop signal.
Container orchestrator graceful shutdown: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM and waits the terminationGracePeriodSeconds; the application maps SIGTERM to a cancellation token that is shared by all in-flight request handlers, background workers and health-check loops, giving each the termination budget to drain cleanly.
Interactive search with typeahead: each keystroke cancels the previous search task and starts a new one; the token for the previous task is cancelled immediately on the next keystroke, preventing stale results from overwriting fresher ones.
File transfer with resume support: a large upload or download uses chunked transfers; cancelling the transfer sets a flag that causes the next resume attempt to verify which chunks were already received before retransmitting from scratch.
Event streaming with backpressure: a consumer reading from a message queue or Kafka partition uses the cancellation token to stop reading when the application is shutting down or the consumer group is rebalanced, committing its offset before exiting.
Machine learning inference pipeline: a batch inference job can be cancelled when a new model version is deployed or the job's priority drops; the cancellation token is checked between batches so that partial results are preserved and the job can resume without reprocessing completed chunks.
ASP.NET Core's HttpContext.RequestAborted token is passed into HttpClient, database and other long-running operations so a client disconnect or server abort releases work that can no longer contribute to the response.
Go net/http handlers propagate Request.Context through database/sql QueryContext and RPC calls; cancelling the request context closes the subtree's Done channel so backend goroutines can stop and return their resources.
Kotlin kotlinx.coroutines Job cancellation follows structured parent-child scopes, so a screen, request or worker scope can cancel its child coroutines while finally blocks release resources and CancellationException remains distinguishable from failure.
Node.js and browser fetch cancellation: AbortController.signal is passed as { signal } to fetch, EventTarget listeners and streams, so abort() tears down the socket and pending promises; AbortSignal.timeout and AbortSignal.any combine a deadline or several triggers into one signal without polling.
Database query abortion over a side channel: PostgreSQL's frontend/backend protocol sends a CancelRequest on a separate connection carrying the backend PID and secret key, letting a client that gave up - or an administrator via pg_cancel_backend - abort a running query without killing the session.
TPL/PLINQ cancellation acknowledgement: a delegate that throws OperationCanceledException carrying the supplied CancellationToken is treated by the Task Parallel Library as a cancellation acknowledgement rather than a fault, so joiners observe a cancelled task instead of an aggregated error.

name: messaging-gateway
document:
messaging-gateway
Encapsulate access to a messaging system behind an ordinary interface of domain methods, so calling application code makes method calls while a single component owns message construction, correlation, timeouts and error translation.
Application code that talks to a broker keeps importing messaging concepts: it builds the payload, picks the channel, attaches a reply address and a correlation id, parses the response and interprets broker errors. The trigger for this pattern is that callers should make a method call instead of writing messaging code - the messaging knowledge belongs in exactly one place that can change without touching business rules.
At the boundary between application logic and a messaging system (message broker, MQ, queue service or actor runtime): the other side is reached by messages, but the caller is ordinary domain code that should see typed parameters and typed results. Applies to one-way (fire and forget) and request-reply interactions alike, and to blocking as well as asynchronous call styles.
A domain service that must query another system (inventory, pricing, credit scoring) over a queue: the caller invokes checkStock(sku) and receives a typed answer.
An HTTP or API layer whose controller awaits a brokered round trip (Spring Integration gateway interface, NestJS ClientProxy, MassTransit request client).
Batch and background jobs that dispatch work through a typed job API instead of assembling payloads (ActiveJob perform_later, Celery delay).
Wrapping a legacy system's MQ interface once, so the rest of the codebase never learns its message format.
Test seams: unit tests substitute a fake gateway, integration tests run the same interface against a real broker.
Migration seam: keep the gateway contract stable while the transport moves from one broker to another.
Actor and streaming stacks where a facade wraps ask/request so callers never hold ActorRefs or inboxes.
Spring Integration's @MessagingGateway and GatewayProxyFactoryBean let application code inject a typed interface while the framework routes calls into channels and returns replies.
MassTransit's IRequestClient<T> and GetResponse<TResponse> provide a typed request-reply client over the bus, keeping request and response message contracts out of the calling service.
RabbitMQ's RPC tutorial demonstrates a gateway-like client that publishes to rpc_queue with reply_to and correlation_id, then resolves the matching callback response.

name: adapter
document:
adapter
wrapper
adaptor
Present an existing component through the exact target contract its client already consumes, translating calls, results and boundary semantics without adding responsibilities or pretending a missing capability exists.
An existing or foreign component has useful behaviour but speaks a different protocol: method names and signatures, data shapes, units, lifecycle, error model or sync/async contract do not satisfy the target. If every caller performs ad hoc conversion, semantics drift, vendor types leak and provider replacement becomes a cross-cutting rewrite; changing the adaptee or target may be impossible or too disruptive.
Integration work where one side is outside your control: legacy modules, vendor SDKs, generated clients, foreign data formats or units, and the ports-and-adapters boundary of a hexagonal architecture. Applies in statically typed languages - where an adapter class is also the compile-time proof that the required interface is satisfied - and in structurally or dynamically typed ones, where a thin wrapper usually replaces a declared target interface.
Wrapping a third-party or vendor SDK behind your own interface so business code never imports vendor types.
Modernising a legacy module incrementally: new code talks to the target interface while the old component is adapted in place.
Supporting several interchangeable providers (payments, storage, messaging, analytics) through one internal contract, with one adapter each.
Adapting a callback- or error-first API to promises/async or to an observer-style interface.
Ports-and-adapters boundaries where one domain port is realized over different transports (HTTP, message queue, in-process fake).
Unifying differently shaped data sources (row sets, DTOs, XML or JSON payloads) into one model before they reach domain logic.
Test doubles: an in-memory adapter satisfies the target interface without the real infrastructure.
API wrapper libraries: normalising third-party REST/gRPC APIs (Stripe, Twilio, payment providers) into a stable internal contract so business logic never imports vendor SDK types.
Legacy system integration: wrapping SOAP, CORBA, or mainframe APIs behind a modern interface, enabling incremental migration without rewriting existing clients.
Cloud provider abstraction: a single internal storage or queue interface implemented by AWS, GCP, or Azure adapters, letting the application swap providers via configuration.
ETL pipelines: adapting heterogeneous source record schemas (CSV, JSON, XML, database rows) into one canonical domain record, isolating format changes from downstream consumers.
Event-stream and streaming adapters: translating WebSocket frames or server-sent events into domain events in real time.
Multi-cloud and provider-agnostic interfaces: storage adapters (S3, GCS, Azure Blob), queue adapters (SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka), and notification adapters that abstract away provider-specific SDKs.
Backend for Frontend (BFF): each front-end client (web, mobile, third-party) gets its own lightweight adapter that shapes internal service responses into the exact payload that client needs.
Java's java.io.InputStreamReader is a byte-to-character bridge: it presents an InputStream through the Reader contract while decoding with an explicit charset.
SLF4J uses providers such as slf4j-reload4j to bind one Logger API to different backends, while log4j-over-slf4j and jul-to-slf4j redirect legacy APIs at a migration boundary; Spring MVC's HandlerAdapter similarly lets DispatcherServlet handle heterogeneous handler types through one SPI.
Go's net/http.HandlerFunc gives an ordinary func(ResponseWriter, *Request) the http.Handler contract by attaching ServeHTTP, so routing and middleware can consume functions and handlers uniformly.

name: either
document:
either
Either monad
disjoint union
Encode the two outcomes of a fallible operation - a value-carrying success (Right/Ok) and a reason-carrying failure (Left/Err) - in one sum-type value, so a caller must destructure both branches before going further and failures cannot escape as exceptions, sentinel values or undocumented convention.
An operation can fail in ways the caller must handle, but the failure channel is invisible in the signature: exceptions unwind past intermediate callers, where they get swallowed or merely logged, status codes and sentinels are silently ignored, and the reason for failure is flattened into a message string nobody can branch on.
Expected, recoverable failures in code that has to compose: parsing and validation at a boundary, persistence and I/O calls, service calls inside a pipeline, or any layer whose caller must render, translate, retry or count the failure. It pays off where the error type is part of an API contract between teams or modules, and where the language can express a two-case type (algebraic data type, sealed hierarchy, discriminated union) or a library supplies one.
Validating untrusted input at a boundary and returning the concrete reason (field, offset, rule violated) so the caller can render a precise message.
Domain operations that can fail for several business reasons (insufficient funds, account closed, limit exceeded) where callers must branch on the reason instead of guessing from a string.
Parsing and decoding (config, documents, wire formats) where the failure position or cause must travel back with the outcome.
Pipelines of fallible steps (authenticate -> load -> transform -> persist) that should stop at the first failure with the original reason intact instead of unwinding with a stack trace.
Translate-once boundaries: turn transport errors into domain errors in one adapter, so no layer above has to know about HTTP codes, IOExceptions or database error numbers.
Accumulating validation of independent fields, where every reason must be reported together rather than only the first one — use an Applicative validation instance with a Semigroup-based error accumulator.
Callbacks and async APIs whose failure cannot be thrown to the caller (completion handlers, event consumers) and therefore has to be delivered as a value.
Parallel fallible operations where you want to collect all successes and all failures separately before deciding, using partition or sequence operations on a List<Result>.
Domain-driven design aggregates where a root entity operation can fail for many reasons (invariant violations, business rule breaches) and the aggregate root returns Either to the application layer.
Service-to-service calls inside a pipeline where the downstream service returns a structured error response (not an exception), and the upstream must branch, translate, or propagate it.
Rust standard-library convention: fallible I/O, parsing and system calls return Result<T, E> and ? propagates the first Err up the call chain to a boundary (a main or entry point that returns Result) - the backbone of recoverable error handling in Rust.
Kotlin/Arrow typed-error pipelines: an either { } computation DSL where bind() short-circuits on Left and Either.catch turns a throwing interop call into a Left at the adapter boundary.
Java services using Vavr's right-biased Either: map/flatMap chains propagate Left without checked exceptions, keeping the failure type part of the signature in fluent pipelines.

name: compound-components
document:
compound-components
compound component
compound component pattern
Give a family of cooperating components one owner — the parent — that holds the shared state and publishes it implicitly to every child, so consumers compose the family declaratively while the parent alone enforces its invariants and behaviour.
A widget only works when a parent and its children agree on one piece of state (which option is selected, which panel is open, whether a field is invalid), but the call site is the only place that knows the children. Holding the state at the call site means threading the value and its update callbacks into every child (prop drilling), and holding it in the children means the parent cannot enforce the family's invariants — exclusivity, ordering, keyboard behaviour — nor react to a child's change in one place. The recurring decision is where the shared state lives and how children participate in it without the call site wiring them.
Component-tree UI code: design-system and widget libraries (select/option, tabs, menus, field groups) in frameworks that can inject state into descendants without passing it through props — React context or child cloning, Angular content projection plus DI, Vue provide/inject, Compose CompositionLocal and slot scopes, SwiftUI environment and preference keys, Blazor cascading values, WPF attached properties over the logical tree — and in widget toolkits whose group objects (Swing ButtonGroup, JavaFX ToggleGroup, Qt QButtonGroup, tkinter control variables) play the same role. It pays off where the public API must stay small and the children must stay replaceable; it does not apply in languages without a component tree or without an implicit-injection channel.
Custom select, combobox or autocomplete families built from Option children — the canonical example: the parent owns the selection, the highlight and the keyboard interaction while options only declare their value and label.
Tabs, accordions and menus where Tab/TabPanel/MenuItem children register their identity and the parent owns the active item, the ordering and the ARIA wiring.
Form-field families (Field + Label + Input + Error) that share one validation/invalid state and generated ids without the call site passing them around.
Data-group widgets: tables with Column definitions, list widgets with Item children, tree views with Node children, chart legends with Series children.
Design-system libraries that export one namespaced symbol whose parts must be used together — the context in which the pattern is most often documented and most valuable.
Collapsible panel families (Disclosure pattern) where a parent owns the open/closed state and Trigger/Content children read it — also known as the Disclosure pattern in ARIA authoring practices.
Stepper/wizard widgets where a parent owns current-step state and Step/StepIndicator children read it without the consumer threading step indices.
Popover/tooltip families where a trigger button and a content panel share open/close state through the parent without prop drilling.
Radix UI Primitives — Dialog.Root owns the open/close context and Trigger/Portal/Content/Title/Description consume it, while asChild (Slot) merges each part's props, refs and keyboard behaviour into the consumer's own button or link.
Ark UI headless components (built on Zag.js state machines) — Popover.Root/Trigger/Positioner/Content share state through the root, ids props compose aria bindings across two families, and the same compound anatomy works in React, Solid, Vue and Svelte.
Headless UI's Dialog family (Dialog, DialogBackdrop, DialogPanel, DialogTitle, Description) — the root enforces the dismiss contract (open prop, onClose callback, focus trap, aria-labelledby) and every part reads the shared open/closed state, exposed for styling as data-open/data-closed attributes.

statement: Place acquisition and release of required data protection in a mandatory framework or shared supertype boundary so every business operation follows the same policy.
name: watchman
document:
watchman
dead man's switch
heartbeat monitor
Detect that a message flow has gone silent - not that a message failed - and tell a responsible person or system within a bounded time by comparing each flow's arrivals against the cadence its business deadline implies.
Message systems fail silently in the one way no error handler observes: nothing arrives. A producer stops emitting, a consumer stops draining, a scheduled job never fires, a credential expires, a partition goes offline - and because no failing code path is ever entered, error dashboards stay green while downstream data quietly goes stale. The recurring trigger: a flow whose absence is business-visible (a nightly feed, an order stream, a partner interface) has no owner-facing signal for 'no messages', so the gap is discovered late - by a customer or a downstream job - instead of by the team that can fix it.
Applies wherever messages are expected on a knowable cadence (event streams, queues, batch hand-offs, partner interfaces, device check-ins) and their absence is a business-visible failure: the flow has an owner, the expected period and grace window can be derived from a downstream deadline, and either the transport can be observed passively (queue counters, a wire tap) or the producers can emit out-of-band heartbeats. The watchman sits at message-flow or boundary scope - an in-process watcher beside the consumer, a periodic sweep over persisted last-seen state, or a rule in the monitoring stack fed by metrics - and it must itself be watched, because a silent watchman is exactly the failure it exists to catch.
Nightly batch or ETL feed: page the integration owner when the 02:00 import has produced no messages by its deadline, instead of noticing an empty report at the morning stand-up.
Business-critical event stream (orders, payments, telemetry): alarm when the produce rate stays at zero through business hours, which separates a healthy quiet topic from a stopped producer.
External partner interface: notify when no messages have arrived from a B2B partner within the agreed window, turning a looming SLA breach into an early, actionable alert.
Long-running workflow stage: require a heartbeat from each process-manager step so a stuck instance is noticed before the surrounding batch closes or a compensation becomes necessary.
Retry or dead-letter pump: verify that the pump still drains failed messages - silence means the pump died, not that the backlog is empty.
Fleet check-ins (edge devices, agents, cron jobs on many hosts): raise a per-device or per-site alarm when scheduled check-ins stop arriving.
The alerting pipeline itself: an always-firing watchdog alert routed to an external service, so a broken alert path is discovered by its silence.
Cron and scheduled-job fleet via Healthchecks.io: each job pings a unique URL, the service holds the Period and Grace Time, flips the check Late then Down when no ping arrives by period + grace, and notifies integrations.
Dashboard alert rules in Grafana: an alert rule whose query returns no series enters the No Data state and can raise a DatasourceNoData alert - the platform form of deciding what silence means (No Data, Alerting, Normal or Keep last state).
Apache Burrow for Kafka (LinkedIn): committed offsets are evaluated per partition over a sliding window and a consumer is classified STALLED when its offset is frozen with non-zero lag, or STOPPED when no new commits arrive - consumer-silence detection without fixed lag thresholds.

statement: Place acquisition and release of required data protection in a mandatory framework or shared supertype boundary so every business operation follows the same policy.
name: intercepting-validator
document:
intercepting-validator
validation interceptor
Insert one interception layer on the ingress path that validates every inbound message before any handler runs, so that input checking is uniform, central and impossible to forget per endpoint.
Inbound data - HTTP requests, RPC messages, queue events, protocol frames - is validated inside each handler: every new endpoint re-implements parsing, range and encoding checks, rules drift between handlers, and some paths end up with no validation at all. The recurring decision is where to put validation so that all inbound data passes through it exactly once, before application logic.
Request- or message-driven systems with a well-defined ingress - HTTP APIs, RPC services, queue consumers, protocol front ends - where several handlers accept external data, where shared constraints (schema, ranges, encodings, size limits) can be expressed without loading domain state, and where the ingress pipeline (filter chain, middleware stack, plugin pipeline, responder chain) can be owned and configured by the team.
A public REST or GraphQL API where every request body and query parameter must pass schema, range and size validation before any controller is invoked.
A message-queue consumer that validates every inbound event against its schema and version before dispatching it to a handler.
A file or protocol ingest pipeline (CSV, XML, binary frames) that validates frames in one front layer before domain processing begins.
A multi-tenant service that enforces tenant-scoped constraints uniformly - allowed fields, payload caps, encoding policy - on all inbound requests.
An RPC or WebSocket gateway that rejects non-conforming request messages with one error format before they reach service handlers.
A GraphQL API gateway that validates incoming query operations for schema conformance, depth limits and argument types at the boundary before query execution begins.
A gRPC service fronted by a protobuf interceptor that enforces proto-schema type and structural constraints on all inbound RPC requests before they reach the service implementation.
A FastAPI service that attaches a shared Depends() dependency to an APIRouter and uses Pydantic request models so invalid requests are rejected before the path operation.
An ASP.NET Core application that places request validation in the middleware pipeline or a Minimal API endpoint filter, short-circuiting with a problem response before the endpoint delegate.
An Express application that mounts schema-validation middleware on a router before its routes, returning a 4xx response without calling next() when the request is invalid.

statement: Place acquisition and release of required data protection in a mandatory framework or shared supertype boundary so every business operation follows the same policy.
name: separation-of-duties
document:
separation-of-duties
separation of privilege
four-eyes principle
Require two or more distinct principals or components to complete a sensitive operation, so that no single account, role or object can initiate and finish it alone.
A sensitive workflow is reachable end to end from one identity or one code path: the same operator creates and approves the payment, the same administrator changes the production configuration and signs it off, the same service account holds both the maker and the checker permission. The trigger is structural rather than accidental - all steps share one principal, one session, one process or one role, because splitting them costs a second pair of hands - and the failure surfaces only when an insider error or abuse is unremarkable in the audit trail: every step was authorized, because one principal held both halves of the duty.
Sensitive operations whose consequences must survive mistakes, coercion or misuse by authorized insiders: payments and disbursements, entitlement and permission changes, production configuration and deployment, key custody and signing, destructive data operations. It applies where identities can be kept distinct and authenticated (separate accounts, roles, services, processes), where the intermediate states of the operation can be persisted and observed, and where an enforcement point exists that can compare the acting principal with the recorded initiator - a policy engine, method security, an approval service, a separate process or account, a dual-control key ceremony. It is as much an organizational rule as a technical one: the split must follow the duties people actually hold, and recombination must be made awkward by design rather than merely discouraged.
Maker-checker payments: an operator above a threshold creates a disbursement and a second operator releases it; the ledger records both identities and refuses a release signed by the maker.
Change control and deployment: production IAM policy or infrastructure changes require a second administrator's approval, and the pipeline refuses to run a change approved by its own author (required reviewers / second signature).
Key custody and dual control: signing keys or root credentials are split so two authorized operators must each contribute a share (split knowledge, m-of-n threshold, dual-control key ceremony) and no single share can sign.
Access provisioning: the requester of an entitlement, its approver and the administrator who grants it are three distinct roles; the administrator cannot approve their own request, and access-control administrators do not administer the audit log.
Destructive data operations: schema migrations, production data edits and deletion jobs are prepared by one engineer and executed by a different operator account that cannot author the change.
Regulated back-office workflows: journal entries, refunds, credit adjustments and account closures are initiated by one clerk and posted by another, with the pairing recorded for audit.
GitHub protected branches: a pull request targeting a protected branch needs the configured number of approving reviews before it can merge, the platform refuses an approval from the PR author by design, and with dismiss-stale-review enabled a commit pushed after the review voids the approval - four-eyes enforced at the merge gate with the approval bound to the reviewed revision.
AWS Systems Manager Change Manager: a change request may run its Automation runbook only after approvals from named IAM users, groups or roles arrive across up to five approval levels, and a single rejection stops execution; because change templates list approvers separately from requesters, a request submitted under one IAM principal is released by another.
HashiCorp Vault key custody: vault operator init splits the root key with Shamir's Secret Sharing into key shares (default 5) under a threshold (default 3); unsealing or generating a root token needs a quorum of distinct share holders, and PGP-encrypting each share for a named operator makes dual control a property of the mechanism rather than of the procedure.

name: double-checked-locking
document:
double-checked-locking
double-checked locking optimization
DCL
DCLP
Initialise a shared resource exactly once and lazily while keeping the steady-state read path free of lock acquisition - by testing a cheaply published state first and taking the lock only for the one-time construction, where the platform can publish the built object safely to every reader.
An expensive object - configuration, a connection pool, a compiled plan, a cache - must be created once and only when it is first needed, but its accessor is called from many threads. The naive check-then-act form lets two threads build it at the same time, and guarding every read with a lock serialises a path that almost never needs synchronisation. The tempting fix - test a flag cheaply, lock only for the initialisation, test again inside the lock - is sound only if the write that publishes the object is ordered with respect to the readers' loads, which is exactly the part the classic formulation leaves implicit and the reason the idiom is famous for rare, unreproducible failures.
Concurrent, shared-memory software in which one object or cell must be built once and read many times: process-wide singletons and registries, per-object caches inside an object shared between threads, lazily built statics in languages whose runtime also provides the once semantics. The pattern presupposes a memory model with a defined publication ordering (volatile, acquire/release, an initialisation lock, or a runtime once primitive) and a read path hot enough that the lock it removes is measurable. On single-threaded runtimes there is nothing to synchronise, and where a single-threaded composition root can initialise eagerly the pattern is unnecessary.
Process-wide singletons whose construction is expensive or configuration-dependent: configuration snapshot, metrics registry, logger, connection pool, feature-flag view.
Per-object caches inside an object shared by several threads - compiled regular expression or query plan, parsed schema, symbol table - where the build is expensive and the read is hot.
Lazily built statics in languages where the runtime owns the once semantics: C++ function-local static, Swift static let or global let, Kotlin by lazy, Scala lazy val, Go sync.Once, Rust OnceLock/LazyLock.
Compensating for the static-initialisation-order problem: an accessor that builds the global on first use instead of relying on cross-translation-unit initialisation order.
Avoiding lock overhead on a read-mostly, write-once hot path (memo tables, symbol caches, thread-safe lazy proxies) where a contended lock would show up in a profile.
Small or freestanding runtimes without a once primitive, where the first caller must build the cell and an eager initialiser is not available.
RWMutex-protected maps in Go where readers check a fast path before the slower write-locked re-check, as a safer alternative to sync.Map for workloads with known access patterns.
Per-connection or per-session lazy fields in object-pooled servers where the pool itself is the shared cell and each borrowed object gets a lazy-computed field.
Cross-language plugin or extension registries where one language's runtime initialises a global handle that other language shards read without repeated synchronisation.
Rate-limiter or circuit-breaker state that must be lazily built from configuration: building eagerly would couple the policy to startup time, but the read path must be lock-free under high throughput.
Lazy compilation or query-plan warming in database connection pools where the pool is shared but individual plans are built on first use by the owning thread.
Spring Framework's DefaultSingletonBeanRegistry.getSingleton: check the singletonObjects map lock-free, take the singletonLock only when the bean is absent, re-check inside - a production evolution of the idiom whose correctness was formally challenged (SPR-13463) and upheld because the concurrent-map read already carries the needed memory barrier.
Chromium's base::LazyInstance / GetOrCreateLazyPointer: an atomic state word with a 'creating' bit, acquire-load fast path and release-store publication - since deprecated in favour of function-local statics with base::NoDestructor, a signal of how far hardened platforms have moved from hand-rolled DCL.
ACE toolkit's ACE_Singleton<TYPE, ACE_LOCK>: the pattern's original industrial home (the 1997 paper was written alongside ACE) - the template still guards instance() with a double-checked ACE_LOCK acquire and recommends ACE_Recursive_Thread_Mutex for multi-threaded access.
Swift runtime: every global/static let is lowered to swift_once (dispatch_once on Darwin), so the double-checked once structure is the default initialisation mechanism for lazily computed immutable globals rather than hand-written code.

statement: Place acquisition and release of required data protection in a mandatory framework or shared supertype boundary so every business operation follows the same policy.
name: table-module
document:
table-module
Organise the domain logic of a table or view as one module with a single instance whose operations act on whole sets of rows, so table-shaped rules are written once against tabular record sets instead of being scattered over per-row objects or per-request procedures.
The rules for a table are set-shaped - recalculating a column across all rows, validating an import batch, posting a period, aggregating or exporting a whole table - and the platform already speaks in tables and record sets (result sets, DataTables, grids, reports). A Domain Model would build one object per row and pay for identity, hydration and per-object behaviour the rules never use, while a Transaction Script repeats the same table-shaped logic in every use case that touches the table.
Data-centric enterprise applications with moderate, table-shaped logic: batch jobs, imports and reconciliation, reporting and export modules, and applications whose UI and data tooling is table-based (typed DataSets, data grids, report engines). It assumes that data access is already provided by a Table Data Gateway or equivalent, and that callers - typically a Service Layer - own the transaction boundary around the module's calls.
Periodic batch posting: recompute balances or fees for every row in a period in one set-oriented pass.
Import and reconciliation: validate, normalise and promote a staging table before its rows become live data, reporting row-level errors as a batch.
Reporting and export modules that fetch a record set for a grid, report engine or CSV/Excel export, where tabular output is the goal.
Bulk recalculation after a rule change: apply a corrected formula to all existing rows of a table without loading them into a model.
Small-to-medium applications where each table has a handful of well-defined operations and no rich invariants spanning rows or tables.
Cleansing and reconciliation jobs over an operational table where the database should do the heavy lifting (aggregate, update ... where) and the application only orchestrates.
.NET ADO.NET typed DataSet / typed DataTable modules: the generated table is the record set, business methods operate over all its rows and it binds directly to grids and report controls.
Ruby on Rails set-oriented surface: an ActiveRecord::Relation scoped to one table applies table-wide rules via update_all/delete_all as a single SQL statement without instantiating row models, whose official documentation warns that validations and callbacks are skipped so the statement must carry the rule.
Django set-wide recalculation: QuerySet.update() and bulk_update() write whole filtered sets with direct SQL that bypasses per-row save(), used exactly where per-object persistence would mean one round trip per row.

statement: Place acquisition and release of required data protection in a mandatory framework or shared supertype boundary so every business operation follows the same policy.
name: composed-method
document:
composed-method
compose method
Divide the work into methods that each perform one identifiable task, written as a short outline of invocations in which every operation sits at the same level of abstraction, so a reader grasps the task top-down and every change lands on one small, named step.
A method accumulates several concerns at once: high-level policy ('validate the order, then charge it') interleaved with low-level detail (a loop index, a string concatenation, a counter), so the method grows long, needs comments to mark its sections, and changes for more than one reason. Readers must simulate the whole body to learn what it does, duplication hides inside similar-looking blocks, and anyone who must change one decision - a subclass in particular - ends up copying the method and editing it.
Applies wherever code is decomposed into named routines and is read far more often than written: long-lived domain and application code, code review and onboarding, framework base classes that must expose override hooks, and code whose steps carry contracts worth testing separately. It is a source-level discipline rather than a runtime structure, so a language needs only routines and some notion of non-public helpers; it matters most exactly where methods have grown past the point a reader can hold them in mind.
Long methods built up over time whose sections are marked by comments: each comment becomes a step name and the method becomes an outline.
A method with several responsibilities (validate, compute, persist) that must change independently and be reviewed one concern at a time.
Framework or library base classes that must offer override points: each step becomes a documented extension point, usually combined with Template Method or NVI.
Top-down design of an algorithm: write the outline first, with steps as not-yet-implemented calls, and fill them in one at a time.
Bottom-up refactoring when the same block appears in several methods: extract it as a named step and call it from each outline.
Making behaviour testable in isolation: steps with their own contracts (parsing input, rounding money, validating rules) become separately testable units.
TDD workflow: write the test for the composed method outline first, asserting each step in sequence, then implement each step as a separate testable unit.
Complex business rules that combine multiple conditional branches: decompose each branch condition and its body into a clearly named step, making the rule engine visible and auditable.
Command or handler objects that orchestrate a multi-step process (validate request, authorize caller, execute operation, emit event, log outcome): each phase is a named step in the composed method.
Production Rails code: Basecamp's Event::Relaying#relay_now reads as an outline of named steps (relay_to_or_revoke_from_timeline, relay_to_webhooks_later), each descending into its own relayer class - the 'fractal' consistency of composed methods in a shipped product, documented by 37signals.
Acceptance and integration test suites: each scenario is written as a composed method at a single level of abstraction (sign_in, create_todo, mark_complete), delegating the mechanics to named helpers or page objects so the test tells the user-level story.
JUnit 4's refactored internals: Beck documents TestCase together with the RunAfter, ExpectException and FailedTest method objects as chained composed outlines, each invocation staying at one level of abstraction (his 'Nested Method Object' evolution of the pattern).

statement: Place acquisition and release of required data protection in a mandatory framework or shared supertype boundary so every business operation follows the same policy.
name: state-colocation
document:
state-colocation
colocated state
colocation
Keep each piece of presentation state in the component closest to where it is used — down to the single component that owns and reads it — instead of hoisting it to a common ancestor or a global store, so that a change touches only the smallest part of the view that can observe it.
State gets hoisted 'just in case': a value only one component reads is lifted to the screen or application root, or pushed into one global store, because someone may want it later. The consequences are components that receive props they never read, updates that invalidate far more of the UI than the value's actual consumers, an unclear owner for each value, and tests that must assemble the whole state container to exercise one field. The recurring decision is where a new piece of state should live: keep it at the smallest scope that actually needs it.
Declarative component UIs (React, Vue, Svelte, SwiftUI, Compose, Blazor, Qt Quick) and, in generalized form, any system where a mutable value is owned by one component-like unit: the consumers determine the state's scope, the framework invalidates only what the owner's subtree can observe, and components are composed, moved and deleted. Most compelling where over-lifted or global state has already become a performance and ownership problem.
A search or form input whose value is read only by the input, its own validation and its own preview: keep it in that component instead of the screen root (the canonical typing example where hoisting made every keystroke re-render the page).
Which panel of an accordion is open: leave it per panel while panels are independent, then lift exactly to the accordion once only one panel may be open at a time (the closest common parent).
Tooltip, hover, popover and dropdown state in a chart or table cell: own it in the cell component rather than in a global UI store.
Per-row edit or selection state in a data grid: the row component owns it; only cross-row operations need the grid to own it.
Dialog and modal open state in the button or list that opens it, until another surface must close or observe it.
Form draft state in the form component; lift it only when a sibling — summary panel, preview pane, wizard footer — genuinely must read it.
Extracting a self-contained widget for reuse or publication: keeping its state local makes the component portable and shrinks its API.
Per-cell expansion state in a tree view or file explorer: the tree node component owns whether it is expanded; the parent tree only coordinates multi-select or bulk-expand operations.
Media playback state for a single player (play/pause, current time, volume): colocate in the player component rather than a global audio store unless the same track plays in multiple places simultaneously.
Local filter/sort state for a data table or list: keep it in the list component until a URL parameter, shareable link, or sibling panel requires sharing it.
Vue: composable-local state (useSearch, useToggle) where each consumer needs its own independent instance of the same reactive logic pattern.
Angular Signals: feature-level signal stores scoped to a route or feature slice, not the entire application store, for UI state and feature-derived state.
SwiftUI: @State for view-local value types; @StateObject for view-owned reference types; keep @EnvironmentObject for genuinely cross-cutting state (auth session, theme) mounted as low in the hierarchy as consumers allow.
Svelte 5 runes: `let count = $state(0)` inside a component is per-component-instance reactive state — the component that declares it is its owner; Svelte's v5 migration explicitly replaced the pre-runes habit of reaching for a store whenever state sat at a component's top level, with $state plus $derived/$effect as the local cells, and module-level .svelte.js state only for deliberate sharing.
Jetpack Compose: the official hoisting guidance is this pattern's placement ladder — keep state as close as possible to where it is consumed, hoist only to the lowest common ancestor of all composables that read or write it, pass value down and onValueChange up, and make the ViewModel the owner only when business logic or lifecycle outlives the composition.
Blazor: component fields are the default owner for UI-local state; the official state-management guidance promotes to an in-memory state container service only when components must share non-persistent state, and to Protected Browser Storage only when the value must survive circuits or sessions — a three-rung ladder that mirrors local state, scoped provider, persistence.

statement: Should field-to-column correspondence and conversion rules be held in external declarations consumed by one generic engine, keeping persistence details out of the domain classes?
name: metadata-mapping
document:
metadata-mapping
declarative mapping
orm mapping metadata
Holds the correspondence between object fields and database columns in metadata - annotations, mapping files, table objects, struct tags or a schema definition - so that one generic mapping engine performs the reads, inserts and updates instead of hand-written per-class mapper code.
Every class that is persisted needs the same tedious, repetitive code: which field maps to which column, which key is generated, how nulls and types convert, what the table is called. Written per class it is duplicated everywhere and drifts from the schema; the catalogue's trigger is that the mapping knowledge belongs in metadata or configuration, duplicated in no class.
Object-relational (or object-document) mapping layers where classes and tables do not line up mechanically - renamed columns, generated keys, relationships, inheritance strategies - and where many classes share the same mapping shape. It applies when the mapping can be declared once in a form a machine can read (code annotations or attributes, external XML, code-first table objects, struct tags, a schema DSL) and when the schema can either be generated from that metadata or validated against it at startup.
A system with dozens of similarly shaped tables where hand-written data mappers would be repetitive: one mapping engine plus one metadata declaration per class.
Schema-first projects where the database already exists and the mapping should be derived from it by introspection or a code generator (EF Core reverse engineering, Rails schema introspection, SeaORM entity generation).
Framework and library builders who must let users map their own classes without shipping per-class code - an ORM, an object-document mapper or a serialization library.
Multi-database products in which only the dialect and type map of the metadata changes between targets while the domain classes stay identical.
Teams that want one declaration to drive several artifacts: DDL or migrations, typed query APIs, validation rules and documentation.
Hibernate ORM/Jakarta Persistence applications declare @Entity, @Table and @Column metadata; the provider builds a persistent metamodel and generic Session or EntityManager operations perform CRUD, so one declaration replaces per-entity mapper code.
EF Core applications combine conventions, data annotations and Fluent API configuration to build an entity model that drives LINQ translation and updates; explicit configuration pins renamed columns and relationships.
SQLAlchemy declarative mappings turn class attributes and mapped_column() declarations into Table and Mapper metadata; that metadata feeds SQL compilation and unit-of-work persistence, while imperative mapping keeps existing classes annotation-free.

statement: Should field-to-column correspondence and conversion rules be held in external declarations consumed by one generic engine, keeping persistence details out of the domain classes?
name: lightweight-entity
document:
lightweight-entity
persistence-ignorant entity
pojo entity
Keep domain entity classes free of persistence logic - no queries, no save/delete, no table knowledge - so that all knowledge of how the object maps to the store lives in metadata (annotations, mapping files, tags, descriptor tables) that a generic mapper consumes.
When each entity class carries its own mapping code (table name, column list, SQL, load/save methods) the same schema knowledge is duplicated in every class, the domain model is welded to the store, and a schema change becomes an edit inside the model. Moving the mapping out then raises the reverse problem: the entities must be dumb enough for a generic mapper to drive them, i.e. they may carry state and domain behaviour but no persistence behaviour.
The persistence-state layer of an application whose domain objects outlive a single operation: entities are stored relationally or document-wise, their schema evolves independently of the model, and a mapper (Data Mapper/ORM/session) - not the object itself - must own reads, writes, identity and lazy loading. It applies where the language can carry mapping metadata outside the entity (annotations, XML/DSL mapping files, struct tags, descriptor tables, external schema files) and something can read that metadata generically.
Layered applications whose domain model is persisted through an ORM: JPA/Hibernate annotations or orm.xml, EF Core configuration, SQLAlchemy mappings, Diesel/SeaORM derives.
Products that map one domain model onto different schemas per customer or deployment through interchangeable metadata sets, without recompiling the model.
Legacy schemas with hostile column names and shapes that must not leak into the domain model: the mapping layer is the translation seam.
Systems that need entities testable in isolation without a database, while the mapping layer is exercised separately against a real database.
Schema-as-code workflows where the mapping metadata also drives migrations or DDL and generated query clients (Prisma, EF Core migrations, SQLAlchemy metadata.create_all).
CQRS read-side projections: lightweight entities serve as denormalized read models populated from the write side, with no behaviour beyond data access.
Event-sourcing snapshots: entities are rebuilt from an event stream and must carry state without invoking the event store.
API boundary DTOs that translate between the internal domain model and external representations, decoupling schema evolution from API contracts.
Distributed system message payloads: serialized lightweight entities travel across process boundaries (queues, event buses) where no persistence context exists.
Hibernate/JPA applications can keep POJO entities focused on domain state while annotations or XML mapping descriptors tell the ORM how to persist them through an EntityManager or Session.
EF Core applications can configure CLR entity-to-table and property-to-column metadata in OnModelCreating/Fluent API or data annotations, leaving persistence orchestration in the DbContext rather than entity methods.
SQLAlchemy applications can use registry-based declarative or imperative mappings to bind Python classes to tables while sessions, not entities, own database operations.

statement: Should field-to-column correspondence and conversion rules be held in external declarations consumed by one generic engine, keeping persistence details out of the domain classes?
name: repository
document:
repository
collection-oriented repository
repository layer
Mediates between the domain model and the data mapping layer with a collection-like interface, so domain code adds, removes and finds persistent objects as if they lived in memory and never constructs queries or touches persistence APIs itself.
Persistence code spreads: every application service re-derives the same SQL or ORM queries, duplicate query logic drifts apart, table and column names leak into domain decisions, and testing domain rules without a database becomes impossible. Callers should be able to think in collections of domain objects instead of queries.
Applies to systems with a non-trivial domain model sitting on a data-mapping layer (Data Mapper, metadata mapping, or a hand-written mapper) where the same queries recur across application services; it becomes more valuable as domain classes and query volume grow. It is the standard persistence boundary of DDD aggregates (one repository per aggregate root) and presumes a unit of work or session that owns flush and commit. It is not a per-table data-access wrapper and not a replacement for transaction control.
DDD application services that must load an aggregate root, run domain logic on it and store it again without knowing the table layout.
Data-mapper backends where several application services and background jobs share recurring complex queries (overdue invoices, pending orders, open tickets).
Applications that must be unit-testable away from the database: repositories are the substitution point for in-memory doubles.
Systems that must support more than one store behind a stable domain interface — relational in production, in-memory in tests, a document store for a particular deployment.
Uniform cross-cutting access policy for an aggregate: caching, read-replica routing, audit logging or authorization applied as decorators around one interface.
Migration work where the persistence technology changes (ORM swap, schema split, service extraction) while the domain model and its tests stay untouched.
CQRS write-side aggregate loading where the aggregate must be reconstructed fully to apply business rules and enforce invariants.
Integration with heterogeneous data sources where one repository unifies access to a cache, primary database and a third-party API behind a domain interface.
Spring Data JPA applications can use Repository/CrudRepository for aggregate-typed CRUD, paging and derived queries, then add only domain-specific methods rather than wrapping every persistence operation.
The .NET eShopOnContainers ordering microservice uses an EF Core BuyerRepository over a shared scoped DbContext/unit of work, while CQRS/Dapper handles presentation reads.
Python applications using SQLAlchemy ORM can place an aggregate-facing repository over Session, whose identity map and unit-of-work flush semantics provide the mapper/session boundary.

name: extensible-visitor
document:
extensible-visitor
extensible visitor pattern
extensible visitors with defaults
Keep the visitor open on both axes at once - new element kinds and new operations arrive without editing or recompiling any visitor that already exists - by giving every visitor a default method that catches element kinds it was not written for, introducing extended element kinds under an intermediate base whose accept hooks overload (not override) accept, and extending an operation by subclassing the existing concrete visitor so it inherits every case it already handled.
A classic Visitor is cheap in one direction only: a new operation is a new visitor, but a new element kind forces every visitor to grow one more method, so shipped visitors must be edited and redeployed. The trigger is an element hierarchy that is extended by parties who do not own the operations - language dialects, plugin node types, versioned grammars, third-party message formats - where the existing operations must keep working unchanged on the extended structure.
Recursively defined element hierarchies (abstract syntax trees, intermediate representations, document and message models) that grow over time, in a statically typed language whose visitors are concrete classes or interfaces with default bodies, and where the traversal logic itself lives inside the operations. It pays off when old operations must run against new element kinds and when element kinds are added by a different team than the operations; it assumes the visitor protocol can carry a default case and that a runtime type test is acceptable on the dispatch path.
A compiler front-end whose node kinds are extended by language dialects while every existing analysis pass keeps running unchanged (the extensible-compiler case the pattern was derived from).
An IDE or linter analysing a versioned language grammar: the version-1 analysis must not be recompiled when version 2 adds syntax nodes it does not understand.
Plugin systems where third-party modules contribute new node types (document formats, workflow elements, protocol messages) to a host that ships the operations.
Optimisation or lowering pipelines whose passes are shipped separately from the node hierarchy: the platform team adds representations, users add passes.
A published visitor API where other teams implement visitors and the element set grows every release, making 'which kinds does this visitor handle' an explicit, versioned contract.
Migration and validation tooling that must keep working on messages produced by newer producers than the tool itself.
Serialization and schema-generation frameworks such as Jackson's JsonFormatVisitor API, which uses a visitor to traverse Java type hierarchies for JSON/XML schema generation and allows third-party serializers to contribute handlers for new POJO shapes without modifying the core framework.
Query engines over tree-structured data (e.g. Apache Calcite's relational algebra, Rascal's AST analysis): new relational operators or AST node types are contributed by extension modules while existing optimisers and evaluators continue to function unchanged.
Static analysis and bug-finding tools (Coverity, CodeQL, ESLint plugin architectures): new checker plugins add new node-type coverage while the core traversal engine ships unchanged, and old checkers degrade gracefully over unknown node types.
Game engine entity-component systems: new component types are contributed at runtime while existing systems (physics, rendering, AI) continue to process entities; the visitor with default case handles component types added after a given system was written.
Python's ast.NodeVisitor: visit() dispatches to a visit_<Node> method and falls back to generic_visit as the built-in default case, so analysis tools written before newer node kinds existed (Match, TryStar, TypeAlias) keep traversing Python's evolving AST unchanged, exactly the degrade-don't-break contract of the pattern.
The JDK Compiler Tree API (com.sun.source.tree.TreeVisitor / SimpleTreeVisitor): every visit method defaults to visitOther/defaultAction as the catch-all, so javac-based tooling written against Java 8 trees keeps compiling and running as Java adds records, patterns and switch labels - old visitors land in visitOther instead of failing.
Roslyn's CSharpSyntaxVisitor / CSharpSyntaxWalker: the generated visitor carries one Visit method per syntax node kind plus DefaultVisit as the default case, and each C# language version extends the node hierarchy while existing analysers and the compiler's own passes keep working over the extended tree.

name: characterization-test
document:
characterization-test
golden master
approval test
golden file test
snapshot test
golden session test
Pin the actual, currently deployed behaviour of existing code in committed reference artefacts (golden masters) so that a later edit can be distinguished from an accidental regression even when nobody can say what the code is supposed to do.
You must change code whose behaviour is undocumented, surprising or only known to production: there is no specification to test against, and tests written from intended behaviour would take too long and silently encode guesses as fact. The safety net therefore has to be built from observed behaviour: replay a corpus of real inputs through the untouched subject, capture everything observable, commit the result as the reference, and let every later run diff against it - pinning what the code does today before changing how it does it.
Applies whenever the subject already runs and can be exercised in a test process or from a test script: untested legacy modules, data transformations and report pipelines, serializers, parsers and code generators, CLI and protocol endpoints, rendering pipelines whose images can be diffed, and dependency or runtime upgrades where the old behaviour is the baseline. The precondition is determinism: volatile parts (timestamps, identifiers, paths, memory addresses, collection order, locale, floating-point formatting) must be normalized or redacted before capture, otherwise the comparison is noise. The pattern is a first move - build the net, then refactor under it - and pairs with a deliberate approval step, because a characterization test does not know which behaviour was intended.
Before refactoring an untested legacy module: capture outputs for a corpus of inputs, restructure the code, and require the reference artefacts to stay identical.
Data processing and batch jobs: pin how representative input files are transformed into output files or reports, so the nightly job can be changed safely.
Serializers, formatters and code generators: pin the emitted text or structured output for representative documents, with a redaction step for volatile values.
Rendering and UI pipelines: pin generated images (screenshot goldens) or rendered text output with an approval workflow and a visual diff tool.
CLI and protocol behaviour: pin stdout, stderr and exit codes, or request/response bytes, for a set of recorded invocations.
Dependency or runtime upgrades: pin behaviour before the upgrade and re-run afterwards, so only intended differences have to be reviewed.
Production defect triage: replay the failing production input into a new reference artefact, then fix the defect against that regression test.
AI/LLM output regression testing: pin model responses to a curated golden dataset; on model or prompt change, compare distributions, embedding similarity, or token-level diffs against the baseline rather than requiring exact matches (LLM eval pipelines, 2024-2026).
Generated code verification: pin the exact output of OpenAPI client generators, GraphQL type generators, SDK wrappers, or database migration previews so formatting and structural changes are caught.
Database schema migration testing: capture the before/after output of migration scripts for a set of schema variants, approving only intentional structural differences.
Computer vision pipeline regression: pin bounding-box distributions or classification confidence vectors from CV models across runs; statistical comparison prevents flaky failures from minor pixel noise.
Smart contract and blockchain output regression: pin deterministic contract outputs for a given input state; any divergence in on-chain behaviour is immediately visible (Nexlify case, 2025).
Database-engine regression suites: PostgreSQL's pg_regress replays each sql/*.sql script and diffs results/*.out against committed golden files in expected/*, with variant comparison files and a resultmap absorbing known platform differences (locale, float formatting, row ordering).
Compiler test corpora: LLVM's lit/FileCheck pins emitted IR and machine code by piping compiler output to FileCheck, which verifies CHECK directives committed inside each test file across the whole input corpus.
ORM query-change detection: ApprovalTests.Ruby's verify_sql approves the SQL an ActiveRecord call emits, so a gem or framework upgrade that silently rewrites generated queries fails the suite.

name: model-view-intent
document:
model-view-intent
mvi
Structure one UI feature as a single loop in which every user interaction becomes an intent value, a pure reduce step derives the next immutable state from the previous state and that intent, and the view renders only that state - so the screen's behaviour is determined by data instead of by scattered event handlers.
Presentation state is spread across the view, its presenter and several observable channels: every handler sets its own field or widget directly, a loading flag, a data field and an error field can contradict each other, the view keeps state of its own that a configuration change or process death destroys, and no state transition can be exercised without instantiating the UI.
Interactive applications with a declarative view layer and some reactive runtime - Android/Compose with coroutines and Flow, SwiftUI, React, Scala.js, or a hand-rolled event loop - where one screen or app-level feature can own a single immutable state object, user events can be represented as data values, and the view can re-render from a new state value. It is applied per feature, not per widget, and it is independent of any particular framework.
A search or feed screen where loading, empty, error and result states are concurrent flags in the old design and must become one state value the view can render without contradictions.
Complex screen flows - checkout, wizards, media players, editors - whose transitions must be explicit and reviewable rather than emerging from scattered handler code.
Screens that must survive configuration changes or process death by restoring one serializable state object instead of replaying a history of view commands.
Crash reports and support cases that carry the current state plus the last intent, making reproduction and replay possible without reproducing the exact tap sequence.
Cross-platform features that share the reducer between platforms and swap only the view layer (Android and iOS, web and desktop).
Large applications where each feature module exposes an intent/state contract and different teams own the loop for their screens.
A Cycle.js component whose DOM and HTTP driver streams become intents, whose model derives state, and whose view renders that state is a direct stream-based MVI implementation.
A Kotlin Multiplatform feature built with Orbit MVI can share an OrbitContainer's intent, reduce, state, and side-effect flow across Android, iOS, and desktop.
An Android Jetpack Compose feature following Android's official unidirectional-data-flow guidance can use a ViewModel-owned immutable UiState, upward events, and downward rendering as a framework-native MVI realization.

name: event-message
document:
event-message
event notification
Announce that something has happened by publishing an immutable, self-describing event message - a past fact that expects no reply - on a channel, so that any number of interested receivers can react without the producer knowing who they are or what they do.
A component has completed a state change that other parts of the system care about, but it must not - and usually cannot - know which ones care. Calling each interested party directly couples the producer to every consumer, to their availability and to their processing order, and every new consumer (search index, audit, notification, analytics) forces a change and a redeploy in the producer. The trigger is open-ended interest: something changed, and the set of parties wanting to know is neither closed nor known at compile time.
Applies wherever a system reports occurrences instead of requesting work: integration between services over a broker or a log (Kafka, RabbitMQ, NATS, SNS/SQS/EventBridge), module boundaries inside one process (domain publishing to notification, search or reporting modules), and state propagation towards caches, read models or clients. It fits when the announcement matters more than any single response - audit trails, cache invalidation, read-model updates, downstream reactions - when consumers may be slow or temporarily offline, and when the producer's transaction boundary is the natural publication point.
Order placement in a service landscape: after the order transaction commits, OrderPlaced is published once and consumed independently by billing, warehouse, loyalty, search-index and notification services.
Cache and replica invalidation: CustomerAddressChanged tells every service holding a copy of the customer data to refresh or drop it, without the producing service knowing the replicas.
Audit and compliance: every state transition is emitted as an event to an append-only log, giving an ordered record of facts that a separate consumer turns into the audit trail.
Read-model / projection maintenance in CQRS: events from the write model update materialized views and search indexes asynchronously.
In-process module decoupling: a domain model publishes InvoiceIssued on an internal channel; e-mail, reporting and webhook modules subscribe without the domain importing them, keeping the dependency direction inward.
Platform-wide notifications: user lifecycle events (AccountCreated, PasswordResetRequested) fanned out to analytics, anti-fraud and e-mail consumers, each with its own retention and retry policy.
Financial trade confirmation: a matching engine emits TradeExecuted to a topic; clearing, risk management, position keeping and regulatory reporting services each consume the same event independently without the exchange knowing their identities or processing logic.
IoT telemetry ingestion: sensors publish DeviceReading events to a broker; stream-processing consumers compute rolling aggregates, rule engines evaluate thresholds, and archival systems persist the raw history — all decoupled from the sensor firmware.
Healthcare resource-change events: a FHIR-compliant system emits ObservationCreated, PatientUpdated and EncounterClosed events; downstream systems (clinical decision support, population health, billing) subscribe to precisely the event types they need without tight coupling to the EMR.
Apache Kafka event streams: producers append events (OrderPlaced, PaymentSettled) to a retained topic; consumer groups for billing, analytics and search indexing each read the same log at their own offsets, and a new consumer can replay from any point without the producer changing a line of code.
RabbitMQ fan-out notification: a producer publishes to a fanout exchange and the broker copies every event message to each bound queue - the official 'logs' tutorial has ephemeral subscribers joining and leaving while every bound consumer still receives every message.
GitHub webhooks: GitHub posts past-tense event messages (push, pull_request, release) with an event-type header, delivery GUID and HMAC signature to subscribed endpoints; integrations declare which event types they care about without ever modifying the producer.

name: authentication-enforcer
document:
authentication-enforcer
authentication interceptor
authentication gateway
auth middleware
Put one request-boundary checkpoint in front of protected actions that decides whether authentication is required, delegates credential verification to a replaceable mechanism, and attaches the resulting subject to request-scoped context before dispatch, so coverage is uniform without making handlers understand credentials.
When each handler decides whether and how to authenticate, protection is duplicated or omitted on exceptional paths, credential formats and user stores leak into business code, and a mechanism or policy change requires editing every handler instead of one auditable boundary.
Server-side request processing — web APIs, web applications and service endpoints — where many handlers share one protection policy, credentials arrive through a uniform convention (Authorization header, cookie, session id), verification technology must be replaceable or differ per route, and the runtime provides a request-pipeline hook (servlet filter, middleware chain, framework guard). Applies to session-based and token-based authentication alike; permissions and roles are out of scope. Three implementation strategies exist: (1) Container-Managed Authentication — the runtime container owns the checkpoint and realm configuration; (2) Authentication Provider Strategy — a custom provider behind a narrow interface, swapped without touching handlers; (3) JAAS Login Module Strategy — pluggable via standard JAAS configuration, supporting multifactor authentication via smart cards, biometrics, or third-party IdPs. The pattern is equally applicable at the edge level (API gateway, ingress proxy) and the service level (in-process middleware).
Web APIs where every route except health and login requires a bearer token, and the checkpoint is mounted in front of the whole router.
Multi-tenant applications with mixed protection levels: public marketing pages, session-protected tenant UI and token-protected integration endpoints behind one enforcement layer.
Services that must accept several credential types at once — browser sessions, mobile JWTs, mutual TLS for service-to-service traffic — while keeping one uniform enforcement point.
Credential-technology migration (basic auth to OIDC, on-premises LDAP to SSO) where enforcement stays put while the mechanism behind it is swapped.
Regulated environments where every rejected authentication attempt has to be logged centrally and identically across all endpoints.
Legacy applications with authentication checks scattered through servlets or handlers that must be consolidated behind one intercepting layer before an audit.
Zero Trust microservices where every internal service verifies JWTs independently (per-service verification) while an ingress gateway provides the first checkpoint — the enforcer exists at both layers.
OIDC/OAuth2 migration where an existing session-based app adds bearer-token support; the mechanism adapts to both while the enforcement point remains unchanged.
Multi-tenant SaaS platforms where tenant isolation depends on the enforcer resolving a tenant identifier from the token before the handler processes any data.
Platform-as-a-Service with mounted sub-applications where a parent ASGI middleware dispatches per-path authentication requirements from a config registry, injecting identity into ASGI scope for all sub-apps.
Spring Security servlet applications that use a SecurityFilterChain with anyRequest().authenticated() and an AuthenticationManager/AuthenticationProvider chain, so controllers consume the SecurityContext rather than parse credentials.
ASP.NET Core APIs that register JWT or cookie schemes, call UseAuthentication before dependent middleware, and use a fallback authorization policy to make authenticated access the default.
An nginx ingress location using auth_request to delegate identity verification to a central authentication service, forwarding only after a 2xx result and propagating 401/403 failures while services still verify their own trust boundary.
