name: facade
document:
facade
façade
Provide one coarse-grained entry interface that hides a subsystem of many cooperating classes behind the few operations its clients actually need, so callers depend on a single stable API instead of orchestrating the subsystem themselves.
Every client of a complex subsystem must know which classes exist, in which order to call them, how to configure and dispose them and how to interpret their errors; that orchestration is then duplicated across the codebase, and any change inside the subsystem ripples through all callers.
Applies when a subsystem (a library, framework, legacy module, remote SDK, or a layer of your own system) is much broader than any single client needs, when its correct use is a recurring sequence of collaborations, and when client code should be insulated from its types and its evolution. Typical at module and system-boundary scope, where one entry point per layer or per external system is wanted.
Wrapping a third-party SDK, media framework or payment/HTTP client behind one class or module that exposes the application's own vocabulary (convert, charge, upload).
Application services that orchestrate repositories, gateways and domain services for one use case (checkout, report generation) and are the only seam controllers or jobs talk to.
Layered systems where every layer offers a facade as its entry point, so dependencies flow through coarse interfaces instead of reaching into a layer's internals.
Isolating a legacy subsystem while it is replaced incrementally: new code depends on the clean facade, and the migration swaps implementations behind it.
Remote and coarse-grained boundaries: a remote facade exposes a few chunky operations over a fine-grained object model to avoid chatty calls (see Remote Facade, Fowler's PEAA).
Startup/teardown sequences and device orchestration (the classic home-theatre example): clients need one 'watch movie' operation, not a dozen subsystem calls in the right order.
Service-container proxy facades (e.g. Laravel): a static-looking front-end that forwards calls to a resolved service instance, giving a terse API without sacrificing testability or DI flexibility.
JPA/service-layer facades: a single transactional entry point that receives DTOs, maps them to domain objects, orchestrates business logic, maps results back, and commits — one transaction per use case.
Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) in microservices: a thin per-client aggregation service (web, mobile, partner) that fans out to downstream microservices, reshapes responses for the client, and handles perimeter concerns. Each BFF is a specialized facade owned by the team that ships the corresponding client.
Anti-Corruption Layer (DDD): a facade placed between a bounded context and an external/legacy system to translate that system's model into domain concepts, preventing external concepts from polluting the internal domain model.
Event-driven/observable facades: a facade that exposes reactive streams (Observables, Promises, async generators) over the subsystem, buffering, batching or debouncing events for consumers that prefer push-based or streaming interfaces.
API gateway composition: an API gateway acts as a system-wide facade that unifies multiple backend services at the edge, handling auth, routing and cross-cutting concerns before delegating to more specific facades or services.
SDK wrapper facades: publishing a public-facing SDK over an internal microservice mesh; the facade shapes the external API surface, applies default configurations, and provides a stable consumer experience independent of internal service topology changes.
SLF4J (Simple Logging Facade for Java): slf4j-api is a minimal logging facade; applications code against Logger.debug()/info() once and bind the concrete framework (Logback, Log4j 2, java.util.logging) at deployment time by swapping the provider jar on the classpath — the textbook runtime-swappable facade.
Spring Framework JdbcClient / JdbcTemplate: a fluent facade over raw JDBC that owns connection and statement lifecycle, iterates ResultSets and translates SQLException into the DataAccessException hierarchy, so callers supply only SQL and result mapping instead of the full boilerplate workflow.
jQuery $.get/$.post/$.getJSON over $.ajax: a per-task facade layer that collapses cross-browser XMLHttpRequest differences, Deferred plumbing and HTTP defaults into one-line calls — the canonical JavaScript-library facade.

name: double-dispatch
document:
double-dispatch
multiple dispatch
multiple polymorphism
two-level dispatch
Select the operation to execute from the runtime types of two collaborating objects, so behaviour can vary along two independent type axes instead of being resolved by hand-written type tests in the caller.
Behaviour depends on the runtime type of *two* objects - element and visitor, shape and surface, left operand and right operand - but an ordinary call resolves on the receiver only (or, in dynamic languages, on no argument at all). Every operation then grows its own type-test ladder, knowledge of the concrete classes leaks into callers, and adding a class silently breaks the cases nobody remembered to extend.
Object models in which two type hierarchies interact: shape x medium, AST node x operation, operand x operand, entity x entity in a collision matrix. It applies when the pair-specific behaviour is a real matrix rather than a single special case, when each hierarchy evolves on its own schedule, and when the language's own dispatch resolves only one of the two runtime types (classic single-dispatch OO) or none of them (method overloading is bound statically).
Collision and interaction rules in games and simulations: every pair of entity types (bullet × wall, ship × asteroid) has its own outcome. Double dispatch cleanly selects the correct collision algorithm at runtime. Used in Unity, Unreal, and custom game engines via visitor-like hierarchies or type-indexed collision matrices. Spatial partitioning (quad-trees, oct-trees) is used alongside to reduce O(n²) pair checks. Examples: Unity physics collision callbacks, Unreal collision/overlap event system, Box2D physics engine, custom engines with AABB/Sphere/OBB hierarchies.
Geometry predicates between two shape hierarchies: intersect, contains, distance and other predicates where each pair (circle-circle, circle-rectangle, rectangle-rectangle) uses a different algorithm and pairs are not symmetric. Used in game physics engines, computer graphics rendering pipelines, and GIS systems. Examples: Box2D, Chipmunk, computer graphics rendering engines.
Numeric promotion and operator semantics between unrelated numeric types: Rational × Integer, Money × Currency, BigInt × Float — operations that must consult both operands' concrete types. Ruby's Numeric#coerce is the canonical language mechanism enabling this pattern. Examples: Ruby Numeric#coerce, Java BigDecimal arithmetic, C# decimal/float/double mixed arithmetic.
Document rendering and media output: shapes or widgets × output targets (screen, printer, PDF, HTML), where each combination emits different code. The medium axis and the shape type axis independently determine the rendering path. Examples: Qt/wxWidgets painting systems, Java AWT/Swing paint(Graphics) dispatch, WebKit/Blink layout engines.
AST traversal and transformations: one node hierarchy × many analyses (type check, pretty-print, evaluate, optimise) — the primary use case the Visitor pattern was designed for. Each (Operation × NodeType) pair is a separate handler. Examples: Babel/TypeScript compiler, LLVM compiler infrastructure, Roslyn C# compiler API.
Plugin and extension architectures: a host application defines an element hierarchy and a plugin defines a visitor; new plugins add operations without modifying element classes. Examples: Eclipse IDE plugin system, Visual Studio Analyzer/extension APIs, static analysis tools (linters, formatters).
Serialization and deserialization frameworks: Format (JSON, XML, binary, protobuf) × type — each combination may need different encoding rules. Examples: Jackson/Gson in Java, Python dataclasses serialization, Protocol Buffers schema evolution.
Protocol handling in parsers and state machines: handler depends on both message kind and connection/session kind — a state × event matrix. Used in network protocol stacks, parsers, and finite state machine implementations. Examples: HTTP server request routing, game AI state machines, telecom protocol state tables.
Event handling in GUI frameworks: a widget hierarchy × an event hierarchy (mouse, keyboard, focus) — each (Widget × Event) pair may require different handling logic. The classic AWT/Swing processEvent double-dispatch was the motivating example for several academic multi-dispatch papers. Examples: Java AWT event delegation, Qt event handling, Swing ActionMap/InputMap.
Message routing in game architectures: entity × message type routing where the correct handler depends on both the receiver entity's type and the message's payload type. Common in Entity-Component-System (ECS) patterns where components process messages differently. Examples: Unity MessageSystem, Amazon Lumberyard (component × message routing).
Numeric and array operators as native multiple dispatch: Julia makes the pair axis first-class - arithmetic and promotion operators are generic functions whose methods select on the runtime types of all arguments, and the compiler emits a specialised version per concrete combination (Int,Int vs Float64,Float64) instead of a hand-rolled accept/visit round-trip; promote_type absorbs cross-type cells. The canonical modern realisation of the pattern. Examples: Julia Base arithmetic, Julia promote_type/coercion, heterogeneous-array dispatch costs documented in the Julia performance guide.
Generic functions in CLOS and Dylan-family languages: method selection keyed by the classes or identities of every required argument, with method combination (call-next-method) resolving ambiguity - double dispatch without the intrusive accept method, and the benchmark every manual encoding is measured against. Examples: ANSI Common Lisp CLOS defgeneric/defmethod, Dylan generic functions.
Runtime binder dispatch on the CLR: the C# dynamic keyword defers overload resolution to the Dynamic Language Runtime, binding the call on the runtime types of receiver and arguments with call-site caching; CallSiteBinder.Bind is documented as runtime binding (double-dispatch). A missing pair surfaces as a runtime binder exception rather than a compile error, so it suits dynamic-language and COM interop boundaries more than closed business matrices. Examples: DLR call-site caching, IronPython/IronRuby interop, COM interop via the runtime binder.

name: mock
document:
mock
mock object
Replace a collaborator of the system under test with a test-specific object that is programmed with the expected calls and verifies them as they happen, so the interaction itself - not the resulting state - is what the test asserts.
The expected interaction sequence is the behaviour under test: the outcome of the exercised method is not visible in the system under test's own state, and no observation point exposes the indirect outputs (the messages sent to collaborators) that the requirement is about. State-based assertions cannot reach them, so the test either reaches into the collaborator's internals - duplicating the collaboration logic - or asserts nothing at all.
Unit and component tests of an object whose collaboration protocol is the specification: exact calls, arguments, cardinality or order matter (handshakes, publish-once, audit logging, cache invalidation) and the collaborator is slow, unavailable, non-deterministic or side-effecting. It requires a substitutable dependency (dependency injection or lookup) and, for framework-based realizations, an interception mechanism - dynamic proxy, bytecode agent, generated code or macro. Typical in mockist, interaction-first TDD and in need-driven development.
Verifying that a component emits exactly the expected messages to a collaborator whose effects are otherwise invisible: an audit logger, notifier, event publisher or payment gateway.
Pinning an interaction protocol whose ordering and cardinality are the requirement - open before send, publish exactly once, flush before close - in tests of clients and adapters.
Simulating failure paths of a remote collaborator (timeout, exception, malformed response) to assert that the SUT surfaces or recovers from them deterministically.
Unit-testing a domain service against repository, clock, or gateway interfaces when the real implementations are slow, licensed or unavailable in the development environment.
Driving interface design from the outside in: write the expectation for the call the SUT should make, then let the implementation satisfy it (mockist TDD).
Verifying that a main operation triggers its side effects - cache invalidation, metrics emission, compensating call - with the required arguments.
In C++ tests built with GoogleTest gMock, using EXPECT_CALL matchers, Times cardinalities and InSequence ordering verifies an outbound collaborator protocol before the SUT runs.
In Java tests using Mockito, verify and InOrder assert required interactions with a dependency while keeping the interaction contract separate from the dependency's implementation.
In Python's unittest.mock, assert_called_once_with and assert_has_calls verify argument, cardinality and sequence requirements for calls made through a replaceable collaborator.

name: plugin
document:
plugin
plug-in
plugin architecture
Let a host application acquire behaviour from independently deployed modules that it discovers and links at configuration or start-up time, so new features, backends or device support can be added without recompiling or redeploying the host.
The behaviours a system must offer vary by deployment (customer, environment, backend, hardware) or grow after the host has shipped; hard-wiring every implementation behind a factory method or a configuration switch means each new variant edits core code and forces a rebuild and redeploy of the whole application.
Systems whose capability set is not fully known at build time: third-party or per-customer extensions, drivers and storage backends, editor and build tooling, test runners, media pipelines. It applies wherever a stable extension point can be published, the contract can be versioned, and the runtime can bind code after compilation (shared libraries, class or module loading, plugin packages).
IDEs, editors and build tools whose feature set grows through extensions (Eclipse, VS Code, webpack, ESLint, pytest, RuboCop).
Servers and frameworks that pick a codec, transport, storage or auth backend per deployment (JDBC drivers via ServiceLoader, .NET plugin hosts, Kafka connectors).
Infrastructure tooling that hosts independently released providers, such as Terraform providers over gRPC or Vault secret engines.
Media, imaging and device software that adds codecs, effects or drivers after the main program ships (Apache httpd modules, GStreamer, DAW and imaging plugins).
Document and data pipelines where per-customer transformation or validation steps are shipped as separate packages (Python entry points, Ruby gems).
Applications that must support tenant- or customer-specific behaviour without a private build per customer, composed at start-up from a plugin directory or a configuration list.
AI agent systems where tools, memory backends and LLMs are loaded as plugins (LangChain agents, semantic kernel plugins).
Cloud-native platforms that must support tenant-specific backends or third-party integrations without redeploying the control plane (Kubernetes operators, service mesh extensions).
DevOps and CI/CD pipelines where steps, reporters or cloud integrations are added as plugins (Jenkins plugins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI job templates).
Observability platforms where collectors, processors and exporters are pluginable (OpenTelemetry collectors, Grafana datasources and panels).
Editor ecosystems that declare contributions in manifests and run extension code behind a host boundary, as in Visual Studio Code's Extension Host and contribution points.
Infrastructure CLIs that launch provider binaries over a versioned RPC contract and negotiate compatibility, as in Terraform's Plugin Protocol and provider servers.
Web servers assembled from independently built dynamic modules loaded at startup or restart, as in Apache HTTP Server's DSO and mod_so module system.

name: test-data-builder
document:
test-data-builder
test builder
Give each domain type used in tests a builder that starts from valid, commonly used defaults, so a test states only the data its assertion depends on and everything else is supplied correctly without being mentioned.
Strict constructors and immutable value objects make test setup a chore: every test that needs an object must supply all constructor arguments, so tests fill up with values that have nothing to do with the behaviour under test, break whenever a constructor argument or the object's structure changes, and copy the same construction code from test to test. The ready-made fixtures of an object mother remove the repetition but not the variation - every slightly different case adds another factory method, and the mother degenerates into duplicated code or a swarm of methods holding a single new statement.
Applies to test suites over a domain model whose objects have many required fields or cross-field invariants, where each test varies only a small part of the data and a valid instance can be constructed without external systems. It is language-neutral but pays off most where the language lacks named/default arguments or copy-with-modification, and it belongs to the test sources: production code keeps its own constructors and must not depend on a builder whose defaults are chosen for tests.
Unit tests over domain types with many constructor parameters and cross-field invariants (invoices, users, policies) where each test cares about one or two values.
Mock-based interaction tests that must hand a valid collaborator object to the system under test with e.g. only its id varied to observe request routing.
Bug-reproduction tests: the builder encodes the standard valid case and the test states only the faulty value from the report.
Suites with many test classes over the same domain fixtures (payroll, insurance, orders) that need per-test variation rather than a handful of canned objects.
Table-driven or property-style tests over one dimension: build the valid base once and override that dimension for each case.
Integration tests that need a complete, plausible object graph (nested entities, collections, ids) deviating in a single field.
factory_bot (thoughtbot) for Ruby/Rails: one factory per class holding a minimal valid set of default attributes, with tests overriding only the fields under test at call time (build(:user, email: "bad@example.com")) - the builder shape generalized into a library.
factory_boy for Python: class-based factories declare the default keyword arguments for the target class' __init__ (Meta.model), and each test overrides just what it asserts (UserFactory.build(first_name="Joe")), with factory inheritance standing in for object-mother variants.
Instancio for Java implements the same contract generically: create(Person.class) populates every field, and .set(field(Person::getName), "Homer") overrides only the fields the test names - its user guide states the goal as populating everything you are not interested in.

name: page-object
document:
page-object
page object model
window driver
Wrap each UI surface a test drives - a page or a significant component - in an object that exposes the services the surface offers and hides every locator, driver call and wait, so a UI change is absorbed by one class instead of by every test that touched the markup.
A UI test that drives the automation API directly - find an element, type, click, wait, read text - keeps the page's locators and interaction mechanics in the test body: the same selector is repeated across dozens of tests, a markup change breaks them all at once, and a reader must reconstruct the page's structure to understand what the test does. The catalog's trigger: a UI change should touch one class, not fifty assertions.
Automated tests that drive a user interface through a driver API - a browser (Selenium/WebDriver, Playwright, Cypress, WebdriverIO), a mobile app (Appium, Espresso, XCUITest) or a desktop window - where the same screens are exercised by many tests, where the UI changes independently of the tests, and where the suite is expected to survive redesigns. The pattern pays off when the interface can be named in the user's terms ('sign-in page', 'product row') and the driver offers stable element lookup; it is unnecessary for a single throwaway script or when the presentation logic has already been extracted behind a humble object.
A regression suite over a web application whose pages are exercised by dozens of tests: login, search, checkout and admin screens each get a class, and a redesign changes only those classes (the Selenium and Playwright POM guides' home scenario).
The same screens are driven by different kinds of test - functional, visual, accessibility, smoke - and the locator knowledge must live in one place that all of them import.
Mobile application suites (Appium, Espresso, XCUITest) where screens are widget hierarchies with platform-specific queries, and the page object is the only place that codifies the platform lookup.
BDD suites: Gherkin steps stay business-readable because step definitions delegate to page objects instead of calling the driver (Fowler's layering recommendation).
Suites migrating drivers or frameworks (Selenium to Playwright, a WebdriverIO restructure): the page API is kept while only its internals change.
A scripting interface over an application whose behaviour is stuck in the UI (Fowler's scripting use), or a legacy system that can only be exercised through its window.
Selenium's documented login flow: SignInPage.loginValidUser returns HomePage, so a regression suite can exercise authentication through services while locators and page-load checks stay in the page objects.
Playwright's official playwright.dev example: PlaywrightDevPage wraps a Page, owns locators for the getting-started flow and exposes goto, getStarted and pageObjectModel methods used by tests.
WebdriverIO's official The Internet login example: a getter-based LoginPage centralizes selectors and open/submit actions, letting login specs survive selector changes without duplicating driver calls.

name: two-step-view
document:
two-step-view
two stage view
Split presentation into two transformations - first turn domain data into a channel-neutral logical page, then render that logical page into a concrete output format - so page structure is defined once while look-and-feel and output channel live entirely in the renderer.
Every page owns its own presentation decisions: with one template or one transform per page, a global look-and-feel change means editing every file, and serving a second channel (print/PDF, e-mail, plain text, a machine-readable feed) means duplicating the page's structure. Nothing in the codebase represents 'the page' independently of the markup it currently happens to be rendered as.
Server-side presentation or document-publishing boundaries where several output channels share one page structure, or where the house style changes often enough that it must change in exactly one place. It also fits where the rendering technology is expected to be replaced (XSLT today, a template engine or PDF formatter tomorrow) and where the page should be inspectable, testable or cacheable before it is rendered.
Multi-channel publishing: one invoice or statement rendered as HTML for a portal, XSL-FO/PDF for print and plain text for e-mail from a single logical page.
Site-wide restyling in a CMS or portal where the house style must be one artefact to change and review rather than one edit per page family.
API-plus-HTML endpoints: the same logical page is serialised as JSON for clients and rendered as HTML for the browsable interface.
Document and report pipelines in the DocBook tradition: the logical document is produced once and rendered to HTML, PDF and e-book formats by different stylesheets.
Constrained or legacy channels - plain text, WAP/XML, CSV - added next to HTML without touching the page assembly code.
Pages produced once and consumed by several renderers or locales: the logical page is cached and rendered per channel on demand.
Spring Web MVC XSLT views: an XsltController builds an XML DOM of the page content, puts it in the model, and XsltViewResolver applies a home.xslt stylesheet - stage one produces the logical document, stage two owns the HTML.
Aura.View (PHP) ships the pattern under the name TwoStepView: a content template renders first, then a separately registered layout wraps it via setLayout()/getContent(), keeping the site chrome in one artefact instead of every page.
Standards-based publishing toolchains: the DITA Open Toolkit transforms semantic DITA maps/topics through XSLT stages into HTML, PDF and other deliverables, and Apache Cocoon pipelines generator -> XSLT transformer -> serializer so one XML source serves HTML, PDF, SVG and text.

name: cancellation-token
document:
cancellation-token
cancellation signal
cooperative cancellation
Give a caller-owned operation tree a one-way request to stop: pass a read-only cancellation signal through every cancellable call, observe it at safe points, clean up what was acquired, and report a distinct cancelled outcome without pretending that cooperative cancellation is forced termination.
A request handler, background job or UI action starts work that fans out into nested calls, tasks or threads. When the caller disconnects, a deadline expires, the user presses stop or a sibling fails, merely abandoning the result leaves already-started work burning CPU, holding connections and calling dependencies. Force-killing a thread or process can interrupt a critical section and corrupt shared state, while a signal that is not propagated or observed cannot stop the call tree or make its cleanup visible to the joiner.
Use where work can outlive the caller's interest and the runtime exposes checkpoints, suspension points or interruptible waits: request-scoped servers, workers, UI tasks, stream pipelines and batch loops. The operation owns cleanup, cancellation may race any checkpoint, and the design must state what happens when a request arrives after an irreversible side effect or while a dependency ignores the signal.
Request-scoped server work: the handler gets a request signal that fires when the client disconnects or the deadline expires, cancelling in-flight database, queue and upstream calls instead of pinning worker threads and connections after the caller is gone.
UI and mobile tasks: navigating away, closing a window or pressing stop cancels the task tree that loads, renders or downloads for that view, and only that view's tokens are affected.
Graceful shutdown: a supervisor stops accepting work and cancels the token shared by worker loops; every worker stops at its next safe point, flushes and releases resources, and the process exits inside the shutdown budget.
Fan-out with short-circuit: as soon as one subtask fails, or as soon as any one result suffices (hedged or racing replicas), the scope cancels the siblings instead of waiting for all of them.
Batch and stream pipelines: a processor subscribes to the pipeline signal and stops consuming and producing when the pipeline is torn down, abandoning the current chunk when the job's deadline elapses.
Testing and tooling: inject an already-cancelled signal, or one cancelled after N iterations, to exercise the stop path without racing an actual shutdown.
HTTP client redirect and retry cancellation: when a request is redirected or a lower-level retry budget is exhausted, cancel the in-flight operation so the client can proceed with the next action without waiting for a result that is no longer relevant.
Health-check abortion: a liveness probe times out or a readiness check fails mid-flight; cancel the in-progress health metric collection so the pod can be restarted or pulled from service without waiting for a hung check.
GRPC deadline and cancellation propagation: a server receives a client deadline and cancellation token; both must be threaded through every async operation so that an expired deadline or a client disconnect promptly frees server resources.
LLM request fan-out: multiple model providers are queried in parallel; the first successful response wins and all pending requests are cancelled immediately, avoiding wasted compute on a result that will be discarded.
Database connection pool eviction: a query timeout or client disconnect cancels the in-flight query, releasing the connection back to the pool before the server's statement timeout fires; the pool's token is derived from the request context so pool eviction and request cancellation share the same stop signal.
Container orchestrator graceful shutdown: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM and waits the terminationGracePeriodSeconds; the application maps SIGTERM to a cancellation token that is shared by all in-flight request handlers, background workers and health-check loops, giving each the termination budget to drain cleanly.
Interactive search with typeahead: each keystroke cancels the previous search task and starts a new one; the token for the previous task is cancelled immediately on the next keystroke, preventing stale results from overwriting fresher ones.
File transfer with resume support: a large upload or download uses chunked transfers; cancelling the transfer sets a flag that causes the next resume attempt to verify which chunks were already received before retransmitting from scratch.
Event streaming with backpressure: a consumer reading from a message queue or Kafka partition uses the cancellation token to stop reading when the application is shutting down or the consumer group is rebalanced, committing its offset before exiting.
Machine learning inference pipeline: a batch inference job can be cancelled when a new model version is deployed or the job's priority drops; the cancellation token is checked between batches so that partial results are preserved and the job can resume without reprocessing completed chunks.
ASP.NET Core's HttpContext.RequestAborted token is passed into HttpClient, database and other long-running operations so a client disconnect or server abort releases work that can no longer contribute to the response.
Go net/http handlers propagate Request.Context through database/sql QueryContext and RPC calls; cancelling the request context closes the subtree's Done channel so backend goroutines can stop and return their resources.
Kotlin kotlinx.coroutines Job cancellation follows structured parent-child scopes, so a screen, request or worker scope can cancel its child coroutines while finally blocks release resources and CancellationException remains distinguishable from failure.
Node.js and browser fetch cancellation: AbortController.signal is passed as { signal } to fetch, EventTarget listeners and streams, so abort() tears down the socket and pending promises; AbortSignal.timeout and AbortSignal.any combine a deadline or several triggers into one signal without polling.
Database query abortion over a side channel: PostgreSQL's frontend/backend protocol sends a CancelRequest on a separate connection carrying the backend PID and secret key, letting a client that gave up - or an administrator via pg_cancel_backend - abort a running query without killing the session.
TPL/PLINQ cancellation acknowledgement: a delegate that throws OperationCanceledException carrying the supplied CancellationToken is treated by the Task Parallel Library as a cancellation acknowledgement rather than a fault, so joiners observe a cancelled task instead of an aggregated error.

name: side-effect-free-function
document:
side-effect-free-function
pure function
Put the model's logic into operations that compute a result from their inputs alone, so that a caller - and a test - can predict the result without knowing any state the operation might secretly touch.
Reasoning about a design becomes guesswork when operations do more than return a result: the caller must read the implementation and every delegation to know which state a call changes, and no result can be reproduced in a test without recreating the state around it. As rules compose, the number of hidden interactions grows faster than the behaviour being built, so the model stops being safely predictable.
Applies inside the model layer of any codebase whose rules are combined and composed - pricing, eligibility, allocation, validation - and where a computation must be exercised in tests without a database, clock or message broker in the loop. It matters most where several rules interact (composition multiplies hidden coupling) and in languages whose defaults are mutable objects, because there the discipline has to be stated rather than assumed.
Pricing and discount rules: unit prices, tax and rebates computed from immutable inputs, so the same basket always prices the same way.
Eligibility and specification checks: a rule expressed as a predicate over a value and reused in validation, selection and tests.
Money and quantity arithmetic: scaling, adding and rounding return new values instead of adjusting a running total in place.
Deriving test data and expected values from the same pure functions the model uses, instead of hand-copied golden values.
Query-side report assembly: projections, summaries and totals built by composing pure functions over already-loaded immutable data.
Memoizing an expensive domain computation, which is sound exactly because the function is referentially transparent.
Redux reducers: the store computes the next state by calling (previousState, action) => newState with no mutation, no clock, no randomness, so DevTools can replay a recorded action log and reproduce the exact state and useSelector can detect changes by reference comparison alone.
React function components: the official contract is that rendering must be a pure function of props, state and context, so React can cache components whose inputs are unchanged, abandon an outdated render mid-flight, and call each component twice in Strict Mode to expose impurity.
Haskell: ordinary functions are pure by default and effects are confined to IO-typed values, so the type signature itself states whether a computation touches the world and the compiler, not review, enforces the query half of the split.

name: fail-safe-defaults
document:
fail-safe-defaults
deny by default
default deny
Make denial the default outcome of every access decision, so that access exists only where it has been explicitly granted and no missing rule, missing identity or failed check can silently permit an operation.
Authorisation written as exclusion: code asks 'is this forbidden?' and everything the deny rules do not cover - a route added last sprint, a new operation, an unknown role, an object-level case, a request the parser cannot classify - is permitted by omission. The failure modes compound it: a missing principal, an unreachable policy source or an exception inside the check falls through to the permissive branch, so the code paths that look most careful are the ones that open the system.
Any boundary where access to a resource is decided: HTTP routes and APIs, message channels and queues, object-level data access, operating-system objects and descriptors, cloud and network policy, and the configuration a product ships with. It matters most where the space of possible requests grows faster than any list of forbidden cases can track, where the check itself can fail (policy store unreachable, identity missing, input unparseable), and where an unintended permission would not be visible in normal operation.
HTTP APIs and gateways: every route carries an explicit policy or permission and an endpoint whose handler was added without one is still decided (ASP.NET Core's fallback policy) or denied as unmatched (Spring Security's recommended final rule), so a forgotten decorator cannot expose it.
Message infrastructure: brokers grant publish/subscribe rights per topic, and a message whose type or destination matches no handler goes to an invalid-message or dead-letter channel instead of a catch-all consumer.
Operating-system and platform defaults: new files are created with restrictive modes (an explicit mode masked by umask, mkstemp's 0600 for temporary files, close-on-exec where descriptors cross exec), server processes run under a syscall allow-list and a least-privilege account, and firewall or network policy denies by default.
Multi-tenant data access: rows, schemas or objects are reachable only through a tenant-scoped grant, and a request with no resolvable tenant — or an unknown tenant id — is denied rather than defaulting to the shared or global dataset.
Cloud IAM and entitlement management: principals have implicit deny until a policy attaches an explicit allow, and service-to-service calls require a granted scope rather than being permitted because both ends are internal.
Product configuration and feature exposure: debug endpoints, sample data and experimental features ship disabled unless enabled, so a build cannot expose them by omission.
Kubernetes NetworkPolicy default-deny: a podSelector: {} NetworkPolicy with no allowed Ingress/Egress rules isolates every pod in the namespace; allow rules are added for only the traffic that is genuinely required, making lateral movement inside the cluster the exception rather than the default.
Service mesh and mTLS (Istio, Linkerd): every workload presents a client certificate; the mesh denies any packet between workloads that cannot present a matching allowed peer identity, so compromised containers cannot reach services outside their explicit allowlist.
Policy-as-Code with Open Policy Agent (OPA) or Cedar: authorization policies are written as declarative rules in a policy language, evaluated by a purpose-built engine, and applied to APIs, Kubernetes, CI/CD pipelines and cloud IAM — the grant set is code, diffed and reviewed like any other artefact.
Serverless function invocation: a function's invocation permission is an explicit resource-based policy; a caller with no matching permission is denied even when the function is invoked via an authenticated event source (SQS, SNS, EventBridge), preventing unintended cross-tenant or cross-function calls.
Database row-level and column-level security: a SELECT or DML operation must match an explicit row-level policy predicate for the caller's attributes (tenant_id, role, ownership), and a missing match returns no rows rather than all rows — preventing inadvertent data leakage across security boundaries.
CI/CD pipeline permissions: a pipeline step's ability to deploy, promote artefacts or access secrets is granted through a scoped, time-bounded, revokable token; any step that has not been explicitly granted a permission is denied access to the target environment, preventing lateral movement from a compromised pipeline.
Healthcare (HIPAA minimum necessary): a clinical application's access to patient records defaults to zero; a physician's identity is matched against a role-based record access policy and granted only the specific record types (e.g. active admissions, problem list, medication history) that the physician's specialty and current assignment require — a missing match returns zero records rather than a full dataset, preventing inadvertent PHI disclosure.
Financial services (PCI-DSS): cardholder data environment access is blocked by default for all accounts; a payment processing service is granted only the specific tokenisation and authorisation operations it requires, and only for the card ranges it actively manages. A network monitoring service that has no transaction role cannot reach the cardholder data database even if it shares a subnet.
IoT device posture and network isolation: a newly provisioned IoT device ships with all external communication channels closed; it may only reach the device management plane for firmware updates and telemetry, and only over a TLS channel with certificate pinning. Any application-layer attempt to reach an external IP address is denied by a local firewall policy that is immutable post-deployment.
Multi-cloud and hybrid IAM federation: a request arriving from a federated identity (SAML assertion, OIDC token) must carry a mapped grant in the local entitlement system before accessing a resource; the federation identity alone is insufficient. A missing local grant denies even when the upstream IdP has authenticated the user, preventing an IdP compromise from automatically granting access to all federated resources.
Supply chain and CI/CD artifact access: a CI/CD pipeline stage receives a scoped, time-limited, revokable token valid only for reading the specific artifact and writing to the specific deployment target it requires; it cannot read secrets store, cannot push to the artifact registry, and cannot promote artifacts to production without a separate approval gate — following the principle that pipeline permissions are the minimum for the job, not the union of all pipeline jobs.
Runtime application self-protection (RASP): a RASP agent embedded in an application enforces default-deny at the instrumentation layer — even if an attacker achieves code execution they cannot invoke system calls, network connections or database queries that the application's normal execution profile does not require, because those capabilities are absent from the process baseline by default.
Legal and compliance data environments: an e-discovery or legal hold system defaults to zero access to case documents; a paralegal's session is granted only the specific document set for an active matter and only for the duration of that matter; a revoked matter grant cannot be exercised even if the session token has not expired, because the grant itself is checked at each document access call.
Database engine shipped defaults: PostgreSQL 15 revoked CREATE on the public schema from PUBLIC by default, inverting a default that had permitted every role to create objects since the engine's early releases — evidence that the positive model must be re-asserted in the defaults a platform ships with, not only in the application's policy.

name: pipeline
document:
pipeline
assembly line
processing pipeline
Decompose a transformation into an ordered sequence of named stages that each consume the previous stage's output and produce the next stage's input, so the workflow reads top to bottom and every step can be tested, instrumented, reordered or replaced on its own.
A multi-step transformation is written as one long function or a tangle of nested calls: the steps are unnamed, their order is implicit in statement order, intermediate values need throwaway names, there is no seam at which a single step can be logged, tested or replaced, and the same sequence is retyped at every call site that needs it.
Processing that naturally decomposes into successive transformations of the same payload - request handling, ETL, compiler passes, message enrichment, image or byte-stream processing - whether the payload is a single value or a stream. It fits in-process, staged execution where one driver owns ordering, error handling and cancellation; distributing the stages across processes, transports and independently deployed filters is the architectural pipe-and-filter pattern instead.
Request handling: deserialise, authenticate, validate, enrich, persist and render a request, with each step named so a failing stage is attributable and testable in isolation.
ETL and data import: extract, clean, transform, validate and load large files as a stream, so no intermediate collection is materialised and memory stays bounded.
Compiler and interpreter passes: source, tokens, AST, resolution, optimisation and code emission, where each pass is an independent stage over the intermediate representation and the pass list is the pipeline.
Message enrichment in an integration flow: unwrap, translate, enrich and route a message, one stage per concern, with per-channel ordering; the cross-process version stays pipe-and-filter.
Image or byte-stream processing: decode, crop or resize, watermark and encode, lazily per frame or chunk, optionally overlapping stages across cores.
Configuration-driven data cleaning: the stage list is assembled from configuration or a plugin registry so different tenants get different ordered steps without changing the stages themselves.
TensorFlow tf.data input pipelines: tf.data.Dataset pipelines that chain map, prefetch, parallel_interleave and shuffle stages to feed a training loop efficiently, with each stage independently configurable and the whole pipeline testable in isolation.
LLM token streaming: HTTP server-sent event streams where an LLM produces tokens at inference speed while clients consume at variable network speed; stream.pipeline() prevents the inference server from buffering unbounded tokens in memory when a slow client disconnects (Node.js stream backpressure case study).
Observability telemetry pipelines: OpenTelemetry Collector chains receivers, processors (memory_limiter, batch, filter, transform, tail_sampling) and exporters for traces, metrics and logs, with connectors (e.g., spanmetrics) bridging signal types and memory_limiter placed first to prevent OOM before filtering.
Typed TypeScript pipeline with schema validation: Zod or io-ts schemas define the stage contract at each boundary, catching schema violations at the exact stage that produced bad data rather than at a distant consumer.
Async generator pipelines in Python: asyncio queues with bounded capacity connect async generator stages, propagating backpressure by pausing producers when the queue is full; the FinStream analytics case study showed 82% memory reduction and 99.7% latency reduction versus unbounded buffering.
Event-streaming pipelines with Kafka and Flink: producers, topic partitions, Flink consumers and checkpointing form a distributed pipeline where backpressure cascades across every boundary; the Kafka max.block.ms and Flink backpressure.sample.interval settings interact under partition saturation and must be tested together under load.
Dynamic pipeline parallelism: construct-and-run pipelines (MapReduce, Spark) fix stage count at construction, while on-the-fly pipelines (Cilk-P Piper algorithm) allow the structure to emerge at runtime, varying per iteration and supporting data-dependent branching; on-the-fly enables pipelines like x264 that cannot be expressed with a fixed static structure.
LLVM compiler pass pipelines: PassBuilder assembles ModulePassManager, CGSCCPassManager, FunctionPassManager and LoopPassManager across the IR hierarchy (Module → CGSCC → Function → Loop), with registered callbacks injecting passes at named extension points (pipeline-start, vectorizer-start, optimizer-last); incorrect PreservedAnalyses declarations invalidate all downstream analyses.
Continuous data pipelines at scale (Google model): periodic pipelines run on cron and suffer from depth growth and resource exhaustion as organic load increases; continuous pipelines (master-slave or event-triggered) replace idle-waiting with always-on processing, eliminating the 'pipeline vs cron' discontinuity at the cost of operational complexity.
ML pipeline orchestration (Airflow, Kubeflow, Prefect, Dagster): each orchestrator applies the pipeline pattern at the workflow level - Airflow's DAG-of-tasks, Kubeflow's per-container-step pipelines with GPU scheduling, Prefect's monoflow/subflow/orchestrator pattern, and Dagster's software-defined assets where asset dependencies imply the pipeline; the pipeline is the scheduler's unit of execution, not an implementation detail.
Apache Beam: PCollections flow through composable PTransforms (ParDo, Combine and GroupByKey) in a pipeline graph, making each transform boundary explicit while the runner handles execution.
Node.js stream.pipeline(): Readable, Transform and Writable stages compose with built-in backpressure, error propagation and AbortSignal cancellation; this is a concrete streaming realization, not a durable workflow engine.

statement: Decide whether the archive gateway session should be acquired during service construction or only when an attachment is first requested, while preventing duplicate concurrent acquisitions and preserving shutdown behavior.
name: lazy-acquisition
document:
lazy-acquisition
lazy loading
deferred acquisition
Defer acquiring an expensive or scarce resource until it is first used, so the acquisition cost is paid only by the holders that actually use it, while clients keep seeing an ordinary interface.
A resource is costly to acquire, scarce, and on many execution paths never needed at all, yet the code that holds it acquires it during construction, at start-up or on a hot entry path: the process pays for resources it never dereferences, start-up time grows with every optional subsystem, and scarce capacity (descriptors, connections, licenses, memory) is consumed by holders that never use it.
Applies to long-lived holders - objects, modules, services, containers - that front an external resource such as a file, socket or database connection, license, thread pool, GPU context, translation catalog or large lookup table. It pays off when the acquisition cost is large relative to a use, when a significant fraction of holders never use the resource, and when the runtime offers a one-time guard (or the holder is provably single-threaded). It is the wrong tool when the resource must be validated at boot, when acquisition is cheap, or when first use sits on a latency-critical path.
A request-handling object that opens a file or blob stream only on the code paths that actually read it (report export, attachment download, audit sink).
A service holding connections to a rarely consulted downstream — archive store, fallback provider, secondary region — that most requests never call.
A large lookup table, model or translation catalog loaded on first use instead of at process start, keeping start-up and memory bounded for the sessions that never need it.
Optional subsystems in desktop and mobile apps (camera, location, payment SDK, plugins) initialized when the feature is opened rather than when the app launches.
Test fixtures and tooling: starting a container, browser or database only for the tests that need it, so the fast path stays fast.
Per-session state in a server — a scratch buffer, a decompressor, a TLS session or prepared statement — allocated on first use of the session rather than on accept.
Database connection pools: HikariCP and similar pools typically create connections lazily on the first checkout rather than at pool construction, to avoid pinninglicenses and consuming file descriptors before the application is fully started.
Dependency injection containers (Spring @Lazy, Dagger 2 Lazy<T>) defer the creation of bean instances until they are first injected, reducing start-up time and breaking circular dependency cycles during bootstrap.
Logging frameworks (SLF4J/Logback): Logger instances are static final but the actual appender (file, socket, console) is initialized when the first log event at that level is fired, so logging infrastructure does not block application start.
Configuration objects: large YAML or JSON config trees are parsed and validated lazily on first access rather than eagerly at start-up, keeping CLI tools fast for commands that do not need the full configuration.
GPU contexts in graphics applications (OpenGL, Vulkan, CUDA) are expensive to create and are deferred until the first draw call or compute kernel launch, allowing the application to start and display a window without claiming GPU memory.
HTTP/service clients (gRPC channels, REST clients): a channel is lazily opened on the first request, enabling the client to be instantiated at module load time while deferring the TCP handshake and TLS handshake to the first real call.
Spring Framework @Lazy bean definitions instantiate singleton beans when first requested rather than during ApplicationContext startup, making an optional integration genuinely demand-driven while retaining the container's proxy and lifecycle semantics.
Go's sync.Once lets a service wrap a one-time connection, parser or cache acquisition so concurrent first callers wait for one initializer and later callers reuse the published result.
.NET's System.Lazy<T> defers a factory until Value is first read and makes the thread-safety and exception-caching policy explicit through its constructors and LazyThreadSafetyMode.

name: lazy-initialization
document:
lazy-initialization
lazy instantiation
on-demand initialization
Defer building an expensive or frequently unused value until the moment it is first needed, so an object, module or process pays for a resource only if some code path actually uses it.
A field is expensive to build - a query result, a decoded blob, a connection, an index - and most instances never read it: building it eagerly makes every construction slow, allocates memory nobody uses and can fail for objects that would have worked without it, while rebuilding it on each access repeats the cost.
Applies inside an object, a module or a process-global facility whose members have uneven and hard-to-predict access patterns, where construction cost dominates and where the resource may legitimately never be needed. In single-threaded code the decision is only about cost and error locality; once several threads can arrive at the value at the same time the decision also covers publication (a marker check, a once-primitive or a language-level lazy binding), and that is where the pattern's real risks live.
ORM entities whose large column or related collection is materialised only when business logic touches it (the classic Lazy Load field).
Configuration/application objects holding optional expensive subsystems - database pool, TLS context, model, decoder - that most code paths never reach.
Caches and indexes built on first query, such as an in-process lookup table, a compiled regular expression or a parsed schema.
Module or package initialisation: a heavyweight submodule imported on first attribute access (Python module __getattr__, JavaScript dynamic import, Java holder class).
Process-wide infrastructure (loggers, clients, thread pools) that must not be constructed during static initialisation, including construct-on-first-use accessors for shared objects.
View models and UI objects that materialise expensive child graphics or detail data only when first displayed.
Python module-level lazy imports (PEP 0793, Python 3.15+): heavy submodules such as parsers, regex engines, or ML libraries imported only when first referenced, reducing startup time and baseline memory for code paths that never touch them.
Rust process-global OnceLock singletons: database clients, HTTP connectors, or telemetry exporters initialised at first use but shared across the entire program, avoiding static init order bugs and the static-lifetime constraint that plague raw statics.
Python's importlib.util.LazyLoader wraps an import loader so module code executes only when an attribute is first accessed, a concrete module-level implementation for optional imports.
.NET's System.Lazy<T> wraps an initializer and creates the value only when Value is first accessed; LazyThreadSafetyMode makes publication and exception-caching policy explicit.
Entity Framework Core's UseLazyLoadingProxies and ILazyLoader materialise navigation properties on access, a framework-owned object-level implementation whose query cost must be measured.

name: eager-acquisition
document:
eager-acquisition
eager initialization
pre-warming
Acquire and initialise a resource before anything needs it - at construction, at process start-up or at task activation - so every use pays a small, predictable cost and any acquisition failure surfaces before the deadline instead of inside it.
A resource whose acquisition is slow, blocking or failure-prone - a connection, a decoded model, a thread pool, a buffer, a warm cache - is first touched on a path that has a deadline: the first call pays the whole cost, the latency curve shows unexplained spikes after every cold start, and a misconfigured dependency is discovered inside a user request rather than during deployment. The recurring decision is whether to acquire the resource up front and hold it, or to keep deferring its cost to first use.
Applies wherever the use-time budget is tight or contractual (real-time and control loops, latency-SLO services, media and trading paths, batch windows) and start-up is a controlled phase that may perform I/O while the hot path may not. It is a resource-lifecycle policy of the resource's owner rather than of a call site: it also applies inside an object that pre-warms its own dependencies during construction, and inside a worker that provisions everything before entering its loop.
Service bootstrap: open and pre-fill the database pool, load configuration and secrets, build TLS contexts and pre-touch hot caches before the readiness probe starts routing traffic.
Latency-critical first call: trading, telecom and media paths where a lazy model load or cache warm-up would blow the deadline - decode the model and build the lookup tables at boot.
Worker capacity: pre-start executor threads (prestartAllCoreThreads, a pre-spawned goroutine pool) so the first burst does not pay thread-creation and scheduler latency.
Real-time and embedded loops: pre-allocate buffers, DMA-capable memory and fixed-size queues during initialisation so the control loop contains no allocation or blocking call.
Batch and ETL windows: open every shard, file and index before the processing window starts, so the whole window is productive instead of paying setup.
Cold-start-sensitive deployments: provisioned concurrency, warmed container pools or an explicit warm-up endpoint after a deploy, moving JIT and first-call cost out of user traffic.
Cache warm-up in front of a hot read path: populate the entries the next minutes of traffic will ask for, so the source of truth never sees a miss storm at start-up.
HTTP client pool hardening: configure pool_max_idle_per_host and pool_idle_timeout with tcp_keepalive on long-running services to prevent silent connection rot after hours of idle time.
Database connection pool validation: validate connections on checkout (e.g., Hibernate's validate() or HikariCP's connectionTestQuery) rather than trusting the pool to be healthy after idle periods.
Microservice dependency pre-warming: eagerly resolve service mesh certificates, feature flag values and remote configuration before accepting traffic, so a cold dependency does not cascade into a request failure.
ML model serving: load and compile the inference model during the initialization phase of the serving process, keeping the handler path pure computation.
Serverless function initialization: move heavy library imports, JIT compilation and one-time setup into the init phase (Lambda's init handler, Provisioned Concurrency environments) so the handler stays lean.
Spring container boot: ApplicationContext pre-instantiates all non-lazy singleton beans at context refresh by default, so misconfiguration, missing dependencies and bad credentials fail the boot instead of the first request; @Lazy exists precisely to opt rarely used beans out of the eager set.
PostgreSQL pg_prewarm: preload relation blocks into the OS or shared buffer cache at server start; the autoprewarm worker records the cached block set and reloads it after a restart so the first queries post-restart skip cold disk reads.
Kubernetes pod bootstrap: init containers run setup work - waiting for dependencies, preloading data, fetching configuration - sequentially to completion before any app container starts, so the app container's first action already finds its resources in place.

name: dispose
document:
dispose
deterministic release
dispose pattern
context manager protocol
Give a garbage-collected object an explicit, idempotent release operation behind a named protocol (IDisposable, AutoCloseable, Disposable / [Symbol.dispose], __exit__) so that the scarce external resources it owns - and the resources those own, transitively - are freed at a caller-chosen moment instead of whenever the collector happens to run.
The collector reclaims only heap memory, so an object holding file and socket handles, native buffers, locks, subscriptions or pooled connections releases them late, in arbitrary order and at most once when it relies on finalization; and without an explicit release contract callers cannot tell whether closing an object cascades to the resources layered on top of it, stops at its own fields, or silently closes a handle borrowed from the caller.
Applies to garbage-collected runtimes whenever an object's lifetime outlives a single lexical scope while its resources have an external lifetime: sessions and connections held across operations, wrappers around native memory, locks expressed as objects, and cached open resources. The pattern is the runtime-boundary answer for languages without destructors (JVM, .NET, JavaScript), whereas scope-bound languages realize the same contract through destructors or scope-exit constructs. Python's `with` statement (PEP 343), Java's `try-with-resources` (Java 7+), and C#'s `using`/`using` declaration are the canonical syntactic forms that guarantee the release call on every exit path.
Session or connection objects held across several operations in a server (database session, message-channel session, SSH session) that must be closed at a known point.
Wrappers around native or unmanaged memory (interop buffers, mapped files, GPU handles) whose release cannot wait for a collection.
Locks expressed as objects, where closing releases the lock and the cascade guarantees nested acquisitions unwind in order.
Pools and lifecycle managers that reclaim instances - release hands the resource back rather than destroying it, and each instance must be returned exactly once.
Long-lived caches of open resources (one open socket or file per backend) where disposing a cache entry must cascade to the connection it owns.
Libraries exposing streams over other streams (buffered/compressing/encrypting decorators) that must document whether disposal cascades to the wrapped stream.
Database transaction scopes where a transaction is committed on success and rolled back on failure - the scope's Dispose chooses the path based on whether an exception is pending.
Async I/O with IAsyncDisposable/DisposeAsync where flush or network-shutdown is asynchronous and must be awaited (e.g., StreamWriter, network sockets).
Python ExitStack for dynamically registered cleanup callbacks and heterogeneous context managers combined in one scope.
Reentrant lock objects (RLock in Python, ReentrantLock in Java) where the dispose must track acquisition count and only release on the outermost exit.
VS Code extension API: every registration (commands, providers, event listeners) returns a Disposable that the extension pushes onto ExtensionContext.subscriptions, and the host calls dispose() on deactivation to unregister everything at a known point.
JavaScript Explicit Resource Management (TC39 Stage 3): handles, streams and Wasm resources implement [Symbol.dispose] so `using` declarations and DisposableStack release them deterministically at block exit.
Java's java.lang.ref.Cleaner as the finalizer replacement: direct byte buffers and MemorySegment arenas register a cleaning action that runs at most once when the owner becomes phantom-reachable, with close() as the deterministic path.

name: range
document:
range
interval
Represent a span of values as a single interval value whose bound inclusivity and open ends are explicit, so containment and interval-to-interval comparisons live in one place instead of repeated ad-hoc endpoint tests.
Start and end travel together through the code but every caller re-derives what they mean: containment is written as scattered <= / < comparisons that drift apart, "unbounded" is smuggled in as a sentinel value (Long.MAX_VALUE, 9999-12-31), and interval-to-interval questions - do these two overlap, does one enclose the other, what is the gap between them - have no home at all.
Applies wherever a domain concept is a span rather than a point: validity and effectivity periods, booking and availability windows, quantity or price tiers, measurement buckets, version and address ranges, pagination windows, and query parameters such as a date range. It pays off when the same interval is compared repeatedly or crosses a boundary (persistence, API payloads, UI widgets), because the bound convention then has to be written once instead of re-decided per call site. For a single comparison between two local variables the type is pure overhead.
Validity and effectivity windows: a contract, price or membership is valid over [effectiveFrom, effectiveTo), and every check is a membership test against one interval.
Booking and availability: a room, seat or resource is reserved during an interval; overlap (not adjacency) decides whether a new booking is possible, and back-to-back bookings must be allowed deliberately.
Quantity and price tiers: the unit price depends on the quantity interval ([1,10), [10,50), [50, +inf)), so a container of intervals with containment lookup replaces a cascade of if-statements.
Temporal queries and reporting: "last 7 days", "this quarter", "since the migration" are half-open or open-ended intervals passed to repositories and rendered by date-range pickers.
Version, port and address ranges: a compatibility claim covers [1.2, 2.0) of a library, a firewall rule covers a port interval - containment answers "is this covered?" and intersection answers "do these rules conflict?".
Pagination and slicing windows: a page is an interval over a sequence, and half-open semantics make adjacency exact ([0,20) followed by [20,40)),
PostgreSQL range and multirange columns: PostgreSQL's daterange, tsrange and numeric range types make lower-inclusive/upper-exclusive bounds, overlap and containment operators, and indexed range queries part of the persistence contract; choose the bound convention before mapping domain intervals.
Guava Range: Java's Guava Range models convex bounded or unbounded intervals with nine open/closed forms, isConnected and intersection; use ContiguousSet only when a discrete domain really requires enumeration rather than treating the interval itself as a sequence.
Standard-library and container choices: Rust's std::ops::RangeBounds covers included, excluded and unbounded bounds when its range forms fit; for many intervals requiring join/split policies, Boost ICL's interval_set and interval_map supply the container semantics instead of overloading one Range value.

name: characterization-test
document:
characterization-test
golden master
approval test
golden file test
snapshot test
golden session test
Pin the actual, currently deployed behaviour of existing code in committed reference artefacts (golden masters) so that a later edit can be distinguished from an accidental regression even when nobody can say what the code is supposed to do.
You must change code whose behaviour is undocumented, surprising or only known to production: there is no specification to test against, and tests written from intended behaviour would take too long and silently encode guesses as fact. The safety net therefore has to be built from observed behaviour: replay a corpus of real inputs through the untouched subject, capture everything observable, commit the result as the reference, and let every later run diff against it - pinning what the code does today before changing how it does it.
Applies whenever the subject already runs and can be exercised in a test process or from a test script: untested legacy modules, data transformations and report pipelines, serializers, parsers and code generators, CLI and protocol endpoints, rendering pipelines whose images can be diffed, and dependency or runtime upgrades where the old behaviour is the baseline. The precondition is determinism: volatile parts (timestamps, identifiers, paths, memory addresses, collection order, locale, floating-point formatting) must be normalized or redacted before capture, otherwise the comparison is noise. The pattern is a first move - build the net, then refactor under it - and pairs with a deliberate approval step, because a characterization test does not know which behaviour was intended.
Before refactoring an untested legacy module: capture outputs for a corpus of inputs, restructure the code, and require the reference artefacts to stay identical.
Data processing and batch jobs: pin how representative input files are transformed into output files or reports, so the nightly job can be changed safely.
Serializers, formatters and code generators: pin the emitted text or structured output for representative documents, with a redaction step for volatile values.
Rendering and UI pipelines: pin generated images (screenshot goldens) or rendered text output with an approval workflow and a visual diff tool.
CLI and protocol behaviour: pin stdout, stderr and exit codes, or request/response bytes, for a set of recorded invocations.
Dependency or runtime upgrades: pin behaviour before the upgrade and re-run afterwards, so only intended differences have to be reviewed.
Production defect triage: replay the failing production input into a new reference artefact, then fix the defect against that regression test.
AI/LLM output regression testing: pin model responses to a curated golden dataset; on model or prompt change, compare distributions, embedding similarity, or token-level diffs against the baseline rather than requiring exact matches (LLM eval pipelines, 2024-2026).
Generated code verification: pin the exact output of OpenAPI client generators, GraphQL type generators, SDK wrappers, or database migration previews so formatting and structural changes are caught.
Database schema migration testing: capture the before/after output of migration scripts for a set of schema variants, approving only intentional structural differences.
Computer vision pipeline regression: pin bounding-box distributions or classification confidence vectors from CV models across runs; statistical comparison prevents flaky failures from minor pixel noise.
Smart contract and blockchain output regression: pin deterministic contract outputs for a given input state; any divergence in on-chain behaviour is immediately visible (Nexlify case, 2025).
Database-engine regression suites: PostgreSQL's pg_regress replays each sql/*.sql script and diffs results/*.out against committed golden files in expected/*, with variant comparison files and a resultmap absorbing known platform differences (locale, float formatting, row ordering).
Compiler test corpora: LLVM's lit/FileCheck pins emitted IR and machine code by piping compiler output to FileCheck, which verifies CHECK directives committed inside each test file across the whole input corpus.
ORM query-change detection: ApprovalTests.Ruby's verify_sql approves the SQL an ActiveRecord call emits, so a gem or framework upgrade that silently rewrites generated queries fails the suite.

name: request-reply
document:
request-reply
request-response
request-response messaging
Let a sender obtain a result or a domain error from an asynchronous or remote receiver by pairing each request with a correlated reply, and give the missing reply a defined outcome: timeout, cancellation and disposal of late replies.
Messaging is one-way, but the sender frequently needs a return value or a domain error from the receiver before it can continue. Without an agreed reply destination, a way to match replies to requests, and a rule for what happens when no reply arrives, the caller either blocks forever, mis-associates the next reply with the wrong request, or accumulates pending state it never cleans up.
Asynchronous interaction across a process, thread or network boundary where the caller cannot continue without the receiver's result: HTTP/gRPC-style RPC, broker-based RPC over a queue, actor or thread mailboxes, and browser-to-server exchanges over a socket. It applies when the interaction is naturally one request and one reply, and each exchange has a bounded deadline.
Service-to-service RPC where the caller needs the result to continue (HTTP, gRPC, or a broker-based RPC queue such as the RabbitMQ tutorial's rpc_queue).
Command dispatch that must return a domain error - a validation failure or business rejection - rather than only an acknowledgement of receipt.
In-process actor or thread mailboxes: ask a worker for state with a deadline so the caller can never block forever.
Front-end over a WebSocket asking the server for a value correlated by message id or acknowledgement callback.
Talking to devices, sensors or legacy systems over a socket whose protocol is inherently one request and one response.
Querying a cache or index cluster from a client library where each call is a key lookup with a per-call deadline.
NATS request-reply service calls: a client publishes with a unique inbox as the reply subject and waits for a response under a per-request timeout.
RabbitMQ RPC over an rpc_queue: the client sends reply_to and a unique correlation_id, then matches the worker's response on its callback queue.
gRPC unary RPC: a generated client stub sends one request and receives one response under a propagated deadline, with cancellation available for abandoned work.

name: consumer-driven-contract-test
document:
consumer-driven-contract-test
consumer-driven contract
contract test
Capture, from each consumer's own tests, the concrete provider interactions that consumer depends on, and verify the provider against that contract inside the provider's own build, so consumer and provider can be released independently without a shared end-to-end environment.
Independently released consumers and providers must keep working together, yet the only reliable check is a shared end-to-end environment per pair - slow, brittle and usually out of date; at the same time the provider cannot see which parts of its API each consumer actually exercises, so every refactoring is a guess about who will break.
HTTP/request-reply, messaging and gRPC integrations where consumer and provider are owned by different teams on different release cadences and each consumer uses only a narrow slice of the provider's surface. It assumes the provider team is willing to run verification of consumer contracts in its own build; without that half, the consumer test is only a better mock.
Microservice landscapes where a front end, a mobile app or another service consumes an API released by a different team on its own schedule.
A provider team that must refactor or replace internals and needs to know, before merging, which consumer expectations it is about to break.
Mobile or desktop clients that cannot be deployed in lockstep with the backend, so each client's expectations must hold against every backend version.
Event- and message-based integrations (Kafka, SQS, SNS, RabbitMQ) where the consumer processes messages produced by another team; contracts pin the message body shape and metadata (topic, headers, content-type) while abstracting the transport.
Migration or strangler-fig work, where a replacement provider must be proven compatible with the existing consumers before traffic is moved.
Using the contract as the source of stubs for development and integration environments, so those environments no longer need the real provider.
BFF (Backend for Frontend) patterns where each frontend channel (web, mobile, third-party) has its own contract with a shared backend, allowing independent evolution of each BFF without cross-channel breakage.
Multi-team Kafka event streaming where consumers (downstream services) define which topics, partitions and message schemas they depend on, so producers can evolve events without silently breaking subscribers; Pact message pacts handle both JSON and Schema Registry messages (with magic bytes for Avro/Protobuf over Schema Registry).
gRPC service integrations where protocol buffer message shapes are exercised by the actual consumer client code, pinning the wire format, service method signatures and metadata the consumer actually calls; synchronous message pacts cover the request-response pairing.
Breaking up a monolith: individual microservices are extracted and their CDC contracts verify that the new service boundaries behave identically to the original module interfaces before traffic is migrated.
Schema Registry integrations (Confluent, AWS Glue) where consumers pin compatible message schemas and producers must not publish breaking schemas without migrating all dependent consumers first.
Third-party or vendor API integrations where the consumer team cannot rely on the provider to run verification: the consumer-side mock-only workflow with published contracts documents expectations even without provider participation.
Webhook and callback integrations where a provider calls a consumer-defined endpoint; CDC captures the consumer's expected payload shape, headers and authentication, and the provider verifies it can deliver to that shape.
Contract migration at scale: when a provider must migrate from v1 to v2 of an API, CDC with pending/wip pacts allows the provider to signal new expectations to consumers without blocking either side's pipeline while migration is in progress.
Spring Cloud Contract in JVM/Spring landscapes: the consumer's contract change lands in the producer's repository (or an external contract repo), the producer build generates verification tests from the contract DSL, and the consumer develops against StubRunner-served WireMock stubs pulled from an artifact repository (Nexus/Artifactory) - the contract is the single artifact both sides build from.
Nubank replaced its flaky shared-environment end-to-end suite with consumer-driven contract tests to regain deploy velocity - the public account of the pattern paying off as an e2e-substitute at a single organisation rather than as an addition to it.
Large polyglot estates such as JSTOR/ITHAKA (300+ microservices, 12+ teams, Pact) and M1 Finance (Pact plus PactFlow rolled out to 17 teams in under six months): the broker's compatibility matrix replaces per-pair end-to-end environments as the release gate.
