name: durable-subscriber
document:
durable-subscriber
durable subscription
durable consumer
Keep a publish-subscribe consumer's place while it is offline: the broker binds a stable subscription identity to retained messages or a committed position, then resumes delivery after reconnect until retention, expiry, or quota says the backlog is no longer available.
A subscriber on a publish-subscribe channel can be unavailable during redeployment, maintenance, device disconnects, or scheduled batch work. A non-durable subscription drops messages published during that gap, so the design must choose a stable identity and broker-side state, then make finite retention, replay pressure, and at-least-once redelivery explicit; durable state prevents a gap only while that state remains available.
Broker-mediated publish-subscribe messaging where consumers are intermittently offline but individual messages matter: JMS topics, MQTT sessions, Kafka consumer groups, NATS JetStream durable consumers, cloud topic subscriptions. It presumes the messaging system can store messages (or positions) durably, so it is as much a broker-configuration decision as a client one, and it presumes at-least-once delivery is acceptable once the consumer is idempotent. It does not apply to in-process notification or to broadcast where only the newest value counts.
A Kafka-backed order-processing service that is redeployed or scaled to zero while events keep arriving: the consumer group resumes from its committed offsets and replays what it missed.
An IoT or mobile client on an intermittent link: an MQTT persistent session holds QoS 1/2 publications for its client id and delivers them when the client reconnects.
A partner integration that receives published documents while the partner's system is down: an unshared JMS durable subscription, or a cloud topic subscription, is registered on their behalf and holds the backlog until they acknowledge it.
A nightly audit or analytics consumer that must see every published change: the day's backlog is drained in bounded batches and acknowledged as it is persisted.
A ledger or compliance consumer that must never silently skip events: retention and lag alarms are configured so an offline subscriber is noticed before its backlog expires.
A cloud event-driven architecture (SNS FIFO → SQS FIFO): SNS preserves ordering and deduplication while SQS queues hold messages for durable fan-out to Lambda or EC2 consumers, with DLQs capturing failed deliveries for replay.
An industrial SCADA/IoT sensor fleet where devices connect sporadically over unstable networks: MQTT persistent sessions with a long session expiry interval preserve every telemetry reading until each device reconnects, even after multi-day outages.
A financial audit trail that must immutably record every state-changing event: events are durably retained in Kafka or JetStream and consumed by a compliance subscriber that must not skip or duplicate entries; idempotent deduplication and offset commits after durable persistence enforce this.
A supply-chain or logistics event-sourcing system where downstream services reconstruct state by replaying events after a crash or deliberate seek: the durable consumer starts from the committed position and replays the missing event window atomically with the state reconstruction.
A cross-region disaster-recovery subscriber that mirrors events to a secondary site: the durable subscription in the secondary region receives every event from the primary's topic, with a DLQ holding any events that fail cross-region delivery for manual retry.
A JMS topic consumer that must receive publications made while it is offline: the client reconnects with the same client identifier and durable subscription name, and the provider retains messages until acknowledgement, expiry, or unsubscribe.
An MQTT 3.1.1 device gateway that reconnects with the same client identifier and CleanSession=0: the broker resumes the stored session and queues matching QoS 1/2 publications for delivery after the link returns.
A NATS JetStream billing worker that restarts after an outage: it binds to the same durable consumer name and explicit-acks each message, so the server resumes its acknowledgement floor and redelivers unacknowledged work.
An Azure Service Bus fan-out topology: topic subscriptions are durable by default and each subscription stores its own copy of matching messages, so a receiver that reconnects later still drains its backlog; client-affine durable subscriptions bind the durable state to a stable client id.
A high-throughput replay consumer on RabbitMQ Streams: the consumer attaches with a stable tracking reference (name) and periodically stores its offset server-side, so a restart resumes from the last stored offset instead of re-reading the whole stream.
An event-sourced system on Google Cloud Pub/Sub that must reprocess history after a bug fix: the subscription enables acknowledged-message retention (default window 7 days, up to 31) and is seeked back to a past timestamp or snapshot to replay already-acked messages.

name: copy-and-swap
document:
copy-and-swap
copy and swap idiom
create-temporary-and-swap
Implement assignment (and any in-place state replacement) so that a failure while producing the new state leaves the target untouched: build the complete replacement off to the side, commit it with operations that cannot fail, and let the temporary's destructor or the garbage collector release the old state.
A hand-written assignment has to tear down the old state and build a copy of the new one, but only the build can fail: destroying before allocating exposes a half-updated object when the allocation or the element copy throws, and the usual repair -- a self-assignment check plus manual rollback -- duplicates the per-member copying that already lives in the copy constructor. The trigger is an assignment (or, in a garbage-collected language, an in-place state replacement) that must satisfy the strong exception guarantee: either it completes, or the target still holds its previous value.
Types that own resources -- heap buffers, handles, file descriptors, trees, containers -- in a language where the programmer controls copy semantics: C++ special member functions, a C ADT with error codes, Rust with panic/abort failure modes. The same ordering also applies in garbage-collected languages whenever published state must never be mutated in place: building the complete replacement and publishing it once keeps readers consistent and moves the release of the old state to the collector. The precondition is a commit step that genuinely cannot fail -- a noexcept member swap, one reference or pointer store, or an atomic publish.
Container and buffer classes that own heap memory (dynamic array, string, matrix, tree) and must be assignable without leaking or leaving the target inconsistent when an allocation fails.
Handle/pimpl classes that keep their state behind a single pointer: the swap is a pointer exchange, so the commit is unconditionally non-throwing while the deep copy still happens in the copy constructor (Sutter's canonical Pimpl exception-safety transformation).
Pre-C++11 codebases where the same operator= must serve lvalues and rvalues and no move constructor exists, using the const-reference plus explicit-local-temporary form.
Value types stored inside standard containers: std::vector and friends need element assignment to be safe before they can offer their own strong guarantee on reallocation, and a noexcept swap participates in their internal move/swap dispatch.
Garbage-collected languages where shared state must be replaced rather than mutated: build a complete replacement value and publish it with one store (AtomicReference.updateAndGet, atomic.Pointer[T].Store, a record with-expression) so readers never observe a partially updated object.
In-place state replacement where identity must be preserved (a registry entry, a cached object with live references): copy into a scratch value, then commit with a member-wise exchange or a replace-style API instead of repointing the reference.
Concurrent programming with thread-safe local-then-publish: build the replacement in a local object (thread-private by definition), then publish atomically -- readers never see a partially updated state, and the previous value is released by the collector after the atomic write is visible.
Version-control-style update: check out a local copy, mutate freely, then commit or discard; copy-and-swap maps directly to this workflow and provides the same transactional semantics (Howard Hinnant's analogy from his C++ Con 2018 talk).
Compiler tooling treats the idiom as the canonical self-assignment-safe assignment: LLVM's clang-tidy bugprone-unhandled-self-assignment checker explicitly recognizes 'build a temporary in operator=, then swap it' as correct handling and matches extended (allocator-aware) constructors plus ADL swap forms so real copy-and-swap code is not flagged (llvm/llvm-project PR #147066).
Boost's move/assignment guidance converged on the single by-value form T operator=(T b) { swap(*this, b); return *this; } as the common way to get copy-, move-, and convertible-assignment from one operator, with dedicated macros (BOOST_COPYABLE_AND_MOVABLE_ALT) for classes that adopt it instead of separate overloads.
When a strong guarantee is needed on the standard containers, libc++ maintainers advise exactly this idiom at the call site -- 'construct a new vector and swap it with the one you want to assign to' (libc++ PR #117516 discussion) -- because the library's own copy assignment deliberately offers only the basic guarantee.

name: composite-entity
document:
composite-entity
coarse-grained-entity
Represent a cluster of related, dependent objects through one coarse-grained entity that owns them and persists and synchronises the whole graph as a single unit of work, so clients never reference, sequence, or save the parts themselves. Coined for coarse-grained EJB business objects; its modern form is the aggregate root with cascading or owned mappings.
A business concept clients treat as one thing (an order with its lines, a customer with addresses) is really a cluster of dependent objects, and persisting each part separately forces callers to know the parts, save them in the right order in the right transaction, delete the ones that left the relationship, and absorb a leaking physical schema. The catalog trigger: a cluster of related objects must persist and synchronise as one unit.
Relational or document stores where a coarse-grained business object is composed of finer-grained dependent objects whose lifecycle is bound to it. Applies when clients - especially remote ones - should exchange one coarse-grained structure instead of the parts, when the persist/synchronise boundary must coincide with one transaction, and when each dependent can still own its own mapping. Modern form: an aggregate root mapped with cascading associations or with components stored in the root's own row.
Order with line items, shipment addresses and payment allocations that must be written and deleted as one business unit.
Customer or account aggregate holding addresses, contact methods and preferences that are edited in one form and saved once.
Document-style clusters (invoice with revisions, article with embedded sections) where the parts only exist inside the root.
Legacy-style coarse-grained entity beans that wrap fine-grained POJOs so that clients exchange one composite transfer object instead of many fine-grained ones.
Mobile or remote clients that must send one coarse-grained payload per edit instead of a sequence of dependent calls.
Batch imports where a cluster is validated and written transactionally, so a partially imported entity never exists.
DDD Bounded Contexts where one aggregate encapsulates a complete business invariant enforced across multiple related entities — e.g., a Rental aggregate containing a rental agreement, reserved vehicle, and driver assignment that must all be created or fail together.
CQRS write models where the aggregate is the sole write target and all state changes flow through the root's command methods, ensuring every mutation is a coherent cluster-level operation.
Event sourcing snapshots where the aggregate root serialises its entire graph so that snapshot restore reconstructs the full composite in one operation rather than re-playing individual dependent events.
Legacy system facades that wrap a network of fine-grained remote beans behind a single coarse-grained composite interface, collapsing many remote calls into one round-trip for external clients.
SQLAlchemy parent-child clusters mapped with cascade='all, delete-orphan' on relationship(): disassociating a child deletes the row, so the Session flushes the cluster as one unit without per-child Session.delete() calls.
EF Core owned types: dependent types stored in the owner's table (or as owned navigations) share the aggregate root's identity and save with a single context.SaveChanges().
Mongoose subdocument arrays: embedded parts are saved, validated and removed through the top-level document, so the cluster's lifecycle is bound to the root document's save.

name: poison-pill
document:
poison-pill
sentinel message
end-of-stream marker
Terminate queue consumers cooperatively by sending a reserved sentinel message that each consumer recognises as "no more work", so consumers drain the backlog and exit without a separate control channel or forced cancellation.
A producer-consumer system must shut down, but its consumers block on an empty queue and the queue has no built-in "no more items" signal: callers either kill the workers mid-work and drop buffered items, or leave them blocked forever. Production has ended - how do the consumers learn that while still processing everything already queued?
In-process or broker-mediated producer-consumer systems with a FIFO work queue, a fixed set of long-lived consumers (threads, coroutines, actors) that block when the queue is empty, and a shutdown requirement that work already accepted by the queue be drained before the consumers exit - typically deployment, signal handling or test teardown.
Signal-driven shutdown of an in-process worker pool: the SIGTERM handler stops accepting work, then enqueues one pill per worker so the backlog is processed before the process exits.
Batch importers and ETL stages whose consumers block on a work queue and must finish the current batch before a run is considered complete.
Test harnesses and simulations: an explicit stop message makes thread-based systems deterministic to shut down, without sleeps or guessed timeouts.
Actor systems: a reserved stop message (for example Akka PoisonPill) terminates an actor after the messages already queued for it have been handled.
Log and event writers where the last records must reach the sink before consumers release their buffers and files.
Bounded-queue stages in a pipeline: pills travel the same backpressured channel as work, so upstream cannot keep producing after the stop decision.
Kubernetes pod shutdown: containers receive SIGTERM, workers stop pulling from the job queue, drain in-flight tasks, then exit within the terminationGracePeriodSeconds window.
Redis/Bull queue workers: a shutdown signal pushes a sentinel via BLPOP so workers exit cleanly without losing the right to process pending tasks.
Akka Streams and similar streaming frameworks: the GraphStage signals completion via onPull/downstream cancellation, which is the materialised equivalent of a poison pill.
Redis Streams consumer groups: XREADGROUP with block timeout naturally returns when the stream is empty; a special ID (e.g. ">") polling loop plus a shared shutdown flag replaces the in-process sentinel.
Broker-level poison message isolation: in Kafka, RabbitMQ, or Azure Service Bus, a permanently failing message (deserialisation error, validation failure) blocks a partition/consumer indefinitely; DLQ-based routing (publish to dead-letter topic after N retries, then commit offset and continue) is the broker-level analogue that prevents one poison message from halting the entire pipeline.
Kubernetes preStop hooks + pill drain: a container's lifecycle preStop hook can enqueue a sentinel into an in-process work queue while the orchestrator grants terminationGracePeriodSeconds for the drain to complete, ensuring zero work-drop during rolling updates.
Azure Service Bus competing-consumers workers: when a worker receives a shutdown notification it completes its current PeekLock message, then calls Abandon on any held locks before unregistering; Azure Service Bus dead-letter queues handle the poison-message variant when a message exceeds MaxDeliveryCount and cannot be delivered.
Akka hierarchical actor trees: sending PoisonPill to a parent actor stops it after all queued messages ahead of the pill are processed, and automatically sends stop messages to all children in bottom-up order; this is the idiomatic way to orchestrate ordered multi-actor shutdown.
Non-blocking retry architectures (RabbitMQ): rather than local Thread.sleep retries that block the consumer thread, use server-side TTL queues with Dead Letter Exchange routing to implement exponential backoff, keeping the consumer responsive to new messages and to shutdown pills.
Java's JDK BlockingQueue worker pools: because BlockingQueue has no built-in close, producers can enqueue a unique end-of-stream object after all work; each consumer takes until that sentinel and then the coordinator joins workers.
Python multiprocessing worker pools: multiprocessing.Queue/JoinableQueue supports FIFO task delivery with sentinel values and join-based drain tracking; send one sentinel per worker and join them after the queue is exhausted.
Akka Classic actors: PoisonPill is enqueued in the mailbox and processed after already queued messages, while Akka Typed requires an explicit Stop/Shutdown protocol; choose the API that matches the actor model.

name: applicative
document:
applicative
applicative functor
applicative style
idiom (original McBride-Paterson name)
Apply one pure function to several independent effectful computations, letting the chosen context instance fix the semantics of absence, failure, ordering, and concurrency; the combining structure is fixed before execution - that static shape is what enables batching, parallel scheduling, and static analysis - and an accumulating error instance reports every independent failure instead of short-circuiting on the first.
You have several independent computations - parse this field, fetch that record, validate this quantity - and a pure function that combines their results, but each result lives inside a context such as Option, Either/Result, List, Promise/Task, or Validation. A bind/await chain can imply a dependency that does not exist, serialize work, or stop at the first failure; you need a fixed applicative structure that combines the values while leaving failure and scheduling policy to the chosen instance.
Value- or effect-level functional code where independent combination is the recurring decision: form and request validation that must report every field error at once, parallel-capable fetch coordination, configuration or tuple assembly from independent parses, and parser/stream composition. Applies when the language offers a context type (or validator abstraction) and the team accepts a small abstraction - a type class in Scala/Kotlin, a stdlib combinator such as Promise.all, or a hand-written lift2 - to express 'apply a pure function to several effectful arguments'. Applicative structure permits parallel execution but does not itself guarantee scheduling, cancellation, or error accumulation.
Form, request or configuration validation where every field is checked independently and the user must see all violations in one response.
Combining independent parses of a record (age, e-mail, quantity, date range) into one constructed value, reporting every malformed field.
Parallel IO combination: fetching several unrelated resources (Promise.all, CompletableFuture.thenCombine, parZipOrAccumulate, errgroup fan-out) and pairing the results positionally.
Parser and stream combinators where several parsers/subscribers consume the same input independently and their results are combined into a node.
Building a read model or report from several independent queries where a failure of one part should be reported without cancelling the others.
Statistics/diagnostics: computing several independent measurements of the same input and combining them with a pure summary function.
DSLs and embedded languages: building an abstract syntax tree of applicative operations (Free Applicative) that can be statically analyzed, optimized, or pretty-printed before interpretation - enabling query planning, dead code elimination, or validation of DSL constraints at construction time.
Traversable data structures: threading an Applicative effect through a container (tree, list, optional) so each element can be independently validated, transformed, or fetched without sequential coupling.
Collecting monoidal summaries: using Const as the Applicative to fold a Traversable structure into a single Monoid value (e.g., collecting all validation errors, or computing a checksum) without materializing a transformed structure.
API gateway aggregation: combining multiple downstream service calls where each call is independent and all results (or all errors) should be collected before returning a response to the caller.
Configuration loading at startup: validating all config fields independently and reporting every misconfiguration at once rather than failing on the first missing key.
CSV or batch row validation: validating each row independently and accumulating all row-level errors so the entire batch can be rejected with a full error report rather than failing on the first bad row.
Bidirectional codec composition: building parsers and serializers (e.g., with prismatic/schema, io-ts, or hkj's ValidatedPrism) where the parse direction is accumulating and fallible but the build direction is total, preserving the parse-don't-validate discipline applicatively.
GraphQL API input validation: validate independent arguments and return all field-level errors in one response instead of rejecting at the first failure.
Kubernetes or Helm configuration loading: validate independent keys and report the complete set of startup misconfigurations before deployment.
CI/CD pipeline policy checks: run independent static checks over a change and aggregate diagnostics before gating the build.
Haxl at Meta/Facebook: an applicative Fetch whose <*> explores both operands before blocking, so independent dataFetch calls to the same data source batch into one request and run concurrently without explicit forking ("There is no Fork", ICFP 2014).
Swift structured concurrency: async let starts each independent task as a child task immediately and a later await combines the results into a tuple or constructor call - applicative-shaped combination of a fixed set of independent effects in mainstream syntax, with cancellation and lifetime bounded by the enclosing scope.
Elm JSON decoders: Json.Decode map2..map8 (or elm-json-decode-pipeline's required/custom steps) assemble a record from independent per-field decoders - the production form of mapN in front-end code.

name: repository
document:
repository
collection-oriented repository
repository layer
Mediates between the domain model and the data mapping layer with a collection-like interface, so domain code adds, removes and finds persistent objects as if they lived in memory and never constructs queries or touches persistence APIs itself.
Persistence code spreads: every application service re-derives the same SQL or ORM queries, duplicate query logic drifts apart, table and column names leak into domain decisions, and testing domain rules without a database becomes impossible. Callers should be able to think in collections of domain objects instead of queries.
Applies to systems with a non-trivial domain model sitting on a data-mapping layer (Data Mapper, metadata mapping, or a hand-written mapper) where the same queries recur across application services; it becomes more valuable as domain classes and query volume grow. It is the standard persistence boundary of DDD aggregates (one repository per aggregate root) and presumes a unit of work or session that owns flush and commit. It is not a per-table data-access wrapper and not a replacement for transaction control.
DDD application services that must load an aggregate root, run domain logic on it and store it again without knowing the table layout.
Data-mapper backends where several application services and background jobs share recurring complex queries (overdue invoices, pending orders, open tickets).
Applications that must be unit-testable away from the database: repositories are the substitution point for in-memory doubles.
Systems that must support more than one store behind a stable domain interface — relational in production, in-memory in tests, a document store for a particular deployment.
Uniform cross-cutting access policy for an aggregate: caching, read-replica routing, audit logging or authorization applied as decorators around one interface.
Migration work where the persistence technology changes (ORM swap, schema split, service extraction) while the domain model and its tests stay untouched.
CQRS write-side aggregate loading where the aggregate must be reconstructed fully to apply business rules and enforce invariants.
Integration with heterogeneous data sources where one repository unifies access to a cache, primary database and a third-party API behind a domain interface.
Spring Data JPA applications can use Repository/CrudRepository for aggregate-typed CRUD, paging and derived queries, then add only domain-specific methods rather than wrapping every persistence operation.
The .NET eShopOnContainers ordering microservice uses an EF Core BuyerRepository over a shared scoped DbContext/unit of work, while CQRS/Dapper handles presentation reads.
Python applications using SQLAlchemy ORM can place an aggregate-facing repository over Session, whose identity map and unit-of-work flush semantics provide the mapper/session boundary.

name: guarded-suspension
document:
guarded-suspension
conditional block
suspended execution
Suspend a state-dependent method call inside the object that owns the state until another thread makes its guard predicate true, so callers neither poll nor get refused while the object is temporarily not ready.
A method may only proceed while a precondition over shared state holds - a buffer is non-empty, a pool still has a free lease, a session is authenticated, a worker has a task - and that state is produced by another thread at an unknown time. The recurring decision is what the caller should do while the guard is false: refusing the request would drop work the application still needs, forcing the transition would break the object's invariants, and polling wastes a core and still races. Guarded suspension answers it by waiting on a condition the object itself owns, and by making that wait atomic with respect to the state change that ends it.
Concurrent objects whose methods are state-dependent and whose state changes arrive from other threads: bounded buffers and handoff queues, resource pools, server request/response handoffs, readiness and shutdown gates, worker idle loops. Applicable where the runtime can efficiently park or suspend a caller (OS threads, coroutines) and where the object already owns a lock or monitor, so no notification can be lost between the predicate check and the wait. Ill-suited to single-threaded event loops, to callers that must never be delayed, and to waits whose eventual completion cannot be guaranteed.
Actor mailbox handoff: an Akka/Orleans/Swift-Actor mailbox is a lock-free guarded queue; the actor suspends on an empty mailbox and resumes when a message arrives, which is the same monitor-wait pattern expressed at the language level.
Swift async / Structured Concurrency: a Task.sleep or async let that suspends until a condition is a coroutine-level guarded suspension; the suspension point is backed by a condition variable or event channel inside the runtime.
CompletableFuture / async result: a future's blocking get() is a timed guarded suspension on the thread that submitted the asynchronous operation; the completion path (complete()) is the notifier.
Pipeline stage coordination: in a multi-stage streaming pipeline each stage blocks on input while the upstream stage processes, synchronising via a bounded channel whose put/get implement the guard.
Bounded buffers and handoff queues: a consumer's take waits while the buffer is empty and a producer's put waits while it is full (producer-consumer).
Resource pools: acquire blocks until a lease is returned to a connection, thread or object pool instead of failing or spinning when the pool is exhausted.
Server-side handoff: an acceptor or reader thread publishes a request and the worker waits for work to appear; a caller waits for the response slot to be filled.
Readiness and start-up gates: components wait until a dependency reports connected, initialised or ready, and callers wait until a session, device or circuit is open.
Shutdown and flush coordination: a terminator waits until in-flight work has drained, and a flusher waits while the buffer still holds entries (two-phase termination).
Platform queue and channel APIs: BlockingQueue.take/put, Queue#pop, Channel.receive/for-await, condition-variable waits - the same guard hidden behind a library type.
Project Loom virtual threads (JEP 444): a virtual thread calling Object.wait() parks its Continuation; the carrier thread is released for other virtual threads, so the program continues throughput while one virtual thread waits. The guarded action still re-checks the predicate on wake, and the pattern's semantics are preserved — only the threading model changes.
Akka typed actor mailbox: each actor has a single-threaded mailbox; receive() suspends the actor's continuation when the mailbox is empty, resuming when a message is dispatched. This is language-level guarded suspension where the wait set is the mailbox queue and the guard is 'mailbox non-empty'.
Kotlin coroutines rendezvous channel: Channel() (unbuffered/rendezvous) suspends the sender until a receiver is ready, and vice versa — the same lock-free handoff as an unbuffered Go channel. The suspension is a coroutine-level guarded wait on rendezvous.
Python asyncio.Condition: an async context manager that wraps an asyncio.Lock; await cond.wait() releases the lock and suspends the task until notify() is called, making it an async guarded suspension where the runtime schedules other tasks during the wait.
Go unbuffered channel send/receive: goroutine G1 executing ch <- x on an unbuffered channel sleeps (gopark) until goroutine G2 executes <-ch, at which point the runtime directly transfers the value and stack copy (rendezvous handoff). This is the language-level form of guarded suspension: the guard is 'receiver present', the wait set is the sudog queue in hchan.
Erlang/OTP process mailbox: a gen_server receiving messages from its mailbox blocks (receive...end) until a matching message arrives — the OTP process is a state machine whose transitions are guarded by message arrival, making each receive a suspension point in the actor's event loop.
.NET TaskCompletionSource<T>: GetAwaiter().GetResult() on a not-yet-completed TCS is a synchronous guarded suspension; the async continuation (ConfigureAwait, await) is an asynchronous one. SetResult() is the notifier. TCS is a one-shot asymmetric guarded suspension where one side never waits (the completor) and one side always waits (the synchronously blocked caller).
JDK ArrayBlockingQueue: the queue is one ReentrantLock plus two Condition objects, notEmpty and notFull - take() awaits notEmpty while count == 0, put() awaits notFull while the buffer is full, and each signals the other condition only after mutating count and the circular buffer inside the same critical section. It is the reference production realisation of a two-predicate guarded suspension, including the fairness switch and the timed offer/poll variants.
Go standard library: database/sql guards queries against a concurrent Close with closingMutex, which parks readers and the closing writer on two sync.Cond values (read/write), and net/http's Server.Shutdown waits until in-flight requests have drained. Both are the case Go's own guidance reserves sync.Cond for - a predicate that changes back and forth over time rather than a one-shot handoff.
HikariCP connection pool: DataSource.getConnection() suspends the caller until a lease is returned while the pool already holds maximumPoolSize connections, bounded by connectionTimeout (default 30000 ms, minimum 250 ms), after which it throws SQLException rather than waiting on - a guarded suspension in which the deadline is a documented, first-class outcome instead of an accident.

name: newtype
document:
newtype
strong typedef
opaque type
Give a single primitive its own distinct type so that values with different meanings cannot be substituted for one another, and the raw representation is reachable only through the wrapper's own construction and accessors.
Several domain concepts share one representation - customer id, order id and tenant id are all strings or UUIDs, width/height/offset are all numbers, milliseconds and seconds are both integers - and the API therefore accepts them interchangeably. A swapped argument, a mixed unit or a mistyped literal compiles (or runs) silently, and the defect surfaces late, as a wrong lookup or a cross-tenant bug rather than a type error.
Code in which two or more values with the same underlying representation flow through the same functions, collections or persistence mapping, and in which a single value owns a rule (identifier syntax, non-emptiness, numeric range, unit). Applies at the value level of one field; clusters of attributes that change together belong to Value Object, and closed constant sets to Type-Safe Enum.
Identifier families in one codebase: CustomerId, OrderId, TenantId and SessionId all string- or UUID-shaped and passed to the same repository, logger and cache.
Unit-carrying measurements: Milliseconds vs Seconds, Meters vs Feet, Radians vs Degrees, Cents vs Dollars, where arithmetic must stay inside one unit and conversion is explicit.
Validated single values: EmailAddress, PhoneNumber, Iban, Slug, Percentage (0-100), PortNumber, NonEmptyString - parsed once at the edge, trusted everywhere afterwards.
Security-adjacent tokens: API token vs session id vs tenant id, where a swap becomes a cross-tenant or privilege defect rather than a wrong lookup.
Geometry and graphics APIs where Width, Height, X, Y, Offset and Length are all numbers and transposition should be a compile error.
Pagination and buffer arithmetic: PageSize vs PageIndex vs ByteOffset vs Count, integers that are trivially transposable in a long argument list.
Rust's official newtype examples use Millimeters(u32) and Meters(u32) to keep units distinct, and use Wrapper(Vec<T>) to give a local wrapper its own trait implementations.
Scala 3 opaque types model values such as Logarithm over Double as distinct outside their defining scope, with controlled extension methods and no runtime boxing.
Kotlin @JvmInline value classes wrap one property into a non-interchangeable domain type such as Password while allowing unboxed representations in many uses.

name: point-to-point-channel
document:
point-to-point-channel
point-to-point queue
p2p channel
Deliver each message on a channel to exactly one consumer, so senders never have to coordinate with receivers and no unit of work is handled twice.
A producer must hand work to exactly one handler while several receivers are running (or the intended handler is temporarily unavailable): broadcasting the message makes every receiver deduplicate, and addressing a specific consumer instance couples the sender to its identity, location and liveness.
Asynchronous messaging inside one process, between processes or across services, where each message is a unit of work (command, job, document, RPC request) and duplicate handling is as unacceptable as loss. Applies to in-process worker queues and to brokered channels (JMS queue, AMQP queue, Kafka partition, cloud queue) alike; the channel - not the consumer and not the sender - owns the routing decision.
Work queues: a web tier enqueues jobs and a pool of workers consumes them, with each job running exactly once.
Request-reply over messaging: the request goes to a queue, exactly one service instance answers it, and the reply returns on a reply queue identified by a correlation identifier.
Command dispatch in a service-oriented system: an order service appends commands that exactly one instance of the command processor executes.
Media or log processing pipelines where every stage pulls its input from a queue and each item is handled by one of the stage's replicas.
Legacy and batch integration: jobs handed to a single consumer daemon through a queue, with the channel providing the transactional hand-off.
Scaling an existing single-consumer endpoint by attaching additional instances (Competing Consumers) without changing producers or the message contract.
Apache Kafka consumer groups: records in each topic partition are assigned to one group member at a time, so a group scales work while separate group IDs retain independent pub-sub copies.
RabbitMQ Work Queues: a task queue distributes jobs among competing workers with round-robin or fair dispatch; manual acknowledgements allow unacknowledged work to be redelivered after a worker failure.
Amazon SQS Standard queues: distribute background jobs among consumers with visibility timeouts, while at-least-once delivery requires idempotent handlers because duplicate deliveries remain possible.

name: remote-facade
document:
remote-facade
coarse-grained facade
Provide a single coarse-grained facade over a web of fine-grained objects so that a remote client can complete a unit of work in one round trip, while the fine-grained objects keep their local-only interfaces and the facade stays free of domain logic.
An object model tuned for in-process use has small objects with small methods and heavy interaction. Across a process boundary every one of those interactions becomes a marshalling, security and routing event, so one user action turns into dozens of remote calls; the decision is whether, and at which seam, to replace that chatty protocol with a few coarse operations.
Applies at any distribution boundary - a network hop, a service-mesh sidecar or merely a second process on the same host - where a fine-grained object model or service layer must be made remotely usable. It matters most when the interaction pattern is chatty (many small reads and writes per use case), when the model must not be exposed to remote clients, and when the transport is expensive relative to the work being done.
Enterprise application whose rich domain model is consumed by a thick client, another service or a batch job: the service layer gets a coarse remote interface instead of exposing entities and value objects.
Microservice boundary where a use case (place an order, update a shipment) must be a single call while the fine-grained aggregates stay internal to the service.
Legacy integration: a coarse adapter facade over an old object model so that new clients never see the legacy structure and the old model can be refactored behind it.
Mobile or high-latency clients, where every avoided round trip directly improves perceived latency and battery cost.
Batch and offline clients that need bulk operations (fetch a set, submit a set) instead of per-item calls.
Security boundary: one authenticated, authorised and audited entry point in front of the model.
Salesforce Composite API and Composite Graph API: a client submits related record operations, reference IDs and explicit all-or-none/graph boundaries in one request instead of making a remote call per sObject.
Microsoft Graph JSON batching: a `$batch` request groups up to 20 Graph operations behind one HTTP boundary while dependencies and per-request failures remain visible to the caller.
gRPC services such as the official RouteGuide example: generated stubs expose typed unary or streaming RPCs as the remote contract while the server's fine-grained implementation stays local.

name: table-module
document:
table-module
Organise the domain logic of a table or view as one module with a single instance whose operations act on whole sets of rows, so table-shaped rules are written once against tabular record sets instead of being scattered over per-row objects or per-request procedures.
The rules for a table are set-shaped - recalculating a column across all rows, validating an import batch, posting a period, aggregating or exporting a whole table - and the platform already speaks in tables and record sets (result sets, DataTables, grids, reports). A Domain Model would build one object per row and pay for identity, hydration and per-object behaviour the rules never use, while a Transaction Script repeats the same table-shaped logic in every use case that touches the table.
Data-centric enterprise applications with moderate, table-shaped logic: batch jobs, imports and reconciliation, reporting and export modules, and applications whose UI and data tooling is table-based (typed DataSets, data grids, report engines). It assumes that data access is already provided by a Table Data Gateway or equivalent, and that callers - typically a Service Layer - own the transaction boundary around the module's calls.
Periodic batch posting: recompute balances or fees for every row in a period in one set-oriented pass.
Import and reconciliation: validate, normalise and promote a staging table before its rows become live data, reporting row-level errors as a batch.
Reporting and export modules that fetch a record set for a grid, report engine or CSV/Excel export, where tabular output is the goal.
Bulk recalculation after a rule change: apply a corrected formula to all existing rows of a table without loading them into a model.
Small-to-medium applications where each table has a handful of well-defined operations and no rich invariants spanning rows or tables.
Cleansing and reconciliation jobs over an operational table where the database should do the heavy lifting (aggregate, update ... where) and the application only orchestrates.
.NET ADO.NET typed DataSet / typed DataTable modules: the generated table is the record set, business methods operate over all its rows and it binds directly to grids and report controls.
Ruby on Rails set-oriented surface: an ActiveRecord::Relation scoped to one table applies table-wide rules via update_all/delete_all as a single SQL statement without instantiating row models, whose official documentation warns that validations and callbacks are skipped so the statement must carry the rule.
Django set-wide recalculation: QuerySet.update() and bulk_update() write whole filtered sets with direct SQL that bypasses per-row save(), used exactly where per-object persistence would mean one round trip per row.

name: higher-order-component
document:
higher-order-component
HOC
component enhancer
Add cross-cutting behaviour to many components at once by wrapping them in an enhancer function that takes a component and returns a new, enhanced component, so no wrapped component knows about the concern or has to be edited.
The same cross-cutting logic - subscribing to a data source, checking a permission, firing analytics, injecting a theme, a translation or a feature flag - is needed by many components, and copying it into each one couples every component to the concern, re-couples them to every change of it, and leaves the behaviour to be remembered at each new call site. React tried mixins and inheritance first and removed them (implicit dependencies between mixin and component, name clashes, snowballing coupling), so the recurring decision is how to apply one behaviour to many components without editing them, while the components stay reusable and unaware of the enhancement.
Component-model UI code where components are values the framework mounts with a stable identity (React and its ecosystem first; the same shape recurs with Compose composables, SwiftUI views, Blazor components, Scala.js layers and handler-based Go/Java web UIs), where the concern is genuinely cross-cutting rather than local to one screen, where the enhancement can be expressed as a pure function from component to component and applied once at the definition or export site, and where the wrapped component's inputs form a prop-like contract that can be extended by injection without touching its internals.
Subscribing many components to an external data source — React documentation's withSubscription example, or Redux's connect: store state arrives as injected props with no component knowing about the store.
Apollo Client data injection: graphql(Query, { options, props }) HOC maps query results and loading state to props; multiple graphql HOCs composed with @compose; historically the standard before useQuery.
Authorization and feature gating at the boundary: withAuthorization(Component, { requiredRole }) or withFeatureFlag(...) decides rendering without editing the component; useful for route-level guards applied across many pages.
Analytics, telemetry and instrumentation applied at export sites (withAnalytics): tracking calls stay out of presentation code and can be added or removed at one location per module.
Injecting ambient context into components that take it as props — translations via withTranslation (react-i18next), routing via withRouter (React Router v5 and below), theming via withTheme (Material-UI v4) — enabling third-party and vendored components to participate without modification.
Error and loading boundaries as an enhancer (withErrorBoundary): the boundary exists as a component in the tree anyway; an enhancer consolidates the concern into one reusable definition rather than repeating the try/catch at each call site.
Sharing logic into class components and older codebases where hooks cannot be used: the HOC reaches class components and library component-shaped APIs that hooks cannot wrap.
Material-UI v4 theming: withStyles and withTheme HOCs inject classes and theme as props; compose chains combine styling with data (connect + withStyles + graphql on the same export).
Internationalization testing: export both wrapped and unwrapped components; tests use the raw component with a mock t function while integration tests use the full I18nextProvider setup.
Conditional prop injection: a data-enhancer that only injects props when a condition is met (e.g. user is authenticated) lets the wrapped component remain agnostic about the absence of that data.
React Compiler (React Forget) compatibility: heavy HOC layering reduces the compiler's static analysis surface and may cause it to bailout — test compiler output when adding HOCs to a compiled codebase; prefer hooks for new logic the compiler should see.
React Server Components boundary: a HOC that calls hooks or reads client-only context (useAuth, useTheme, useRouter) cannot execute during a server render; the wrapped component may receive undefined injected props on the server and flash-change on hydration. Pass server-fetched data as props through the HOC boundary from a server parent instead.
Streaming SSR and Suspense integration: a HOC that wraps a component behind a Suspense boundary adds a node that may delay streaming; if the HOC itself is async it must be carefully placed to avoid blocking the fallback from showing.
Partial hydration patterns: on islands architectures (Next.js App Router, Astro), a HOC that subscribes to client-side state forces the entire island to be hydrated even if the wrapped component has no server payload; prefer passing hydrated state as props from a server parent.
Recompose (acdlite): a 'lodash for React' utility belt built entirely from composable HOCs (withState, mapProps, pure, branch) piped through enhance/compose - the pattern industrialised; its October 2018 deprecation in favour of Hooks (bug-fix maintenance only) is the canonical case study of the pattern's cost when a runtime offers a cheaper reuse primitive.
MobX React binding: observer from mobx-react / mobx-react-lite is an official HOC that subscribes the wrapped component to every observable read during render, re-rendering it automatically; MobX guidance is to apply observer first (innermost) when composing it with other HOCs, and to wrap every component that reads observables.

name: inversion-of-control
document:
inversion-of-control
Hollywood Principle
IoC
Invert the direction of control between a reusable framework and application code: the framework owns the call flow and invokes the application's hooks at its extension points, so the generic sequence is reused while application code supplies only behaviour.
A reusable component - framework, container, UI toolkit, event loop, test runner - must own the sequence of calls (main loop, request dispatch, component lifecycle), while the behaviour at each step is application-specific; if application code had to call the framework's steps itself, the generic flow could neither be reused as a whole nor be extended without modifying it.
Applies wherever generic flow logic has to be specialised by application code: UI toolkits and event loops that decide when handlers fire, server containers and engines that own request dispatch and component lifecycle, test runners that own fixture and test sequencing, plugin hosts, and effect runtimes that own program entry. It is the defining characteristic of a framework as opposed to a library (a library is called by your code; a framework calls your code), and it usually arrives bundled with a container, dispatcher or engine - what remains to design is where the boundary sits and how much lifecycle you hand over.
GUI and event-driven applications: the windowing system or runtime owns the event loop and calls your event handlers, app delegate or declarative view body.
Server-side request handling: the container, engine or router owns listen-accept-dispatch and invokes the servlets, handlers, routes or middleware you registered.
Test frameworks: the runner owns discovery, fixture setup and teardown and calls your test methods and lifecycle hooks (JUnit, pytest, xUnit).
Container-managed components: EJB, Spring, Angular or Nest components whose construction, wiring and lifecycle callbacks are driven by the container that also owns the entry point.
Plugin and extension architectures: a host defines extension points and third-party plugins implement them, with the host deciding when each plugin is consulted (IDEs, browsers, build tools, game engines).
Inverted program entry: effect runtimes and app frameworks where the runtime's main calls the run value or app structure you provide instead of you orchestrating from main.
Callback-based C APIs: a library call such as qsort or a GLib main loop calls your function pointer per element or event - a small-scale realization of the same inversion.
Cloud Functions-as-a-Service: AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, and Google Cloud Functions own the request dispatch and cold-start lifecycle; your handler is a hook called by the platform, making serverless a live deployment of the Hollywood principle.
Reactive streams and event-driven pipelines: frameworks like Reactor, RxJava, or Node.js EventEmitter own the subscription and back-pressure loop; operators and subscribers are hooks that the runtime calls on data availability.
Microservices sidecar and service mesh: an Envoy or Linkerd proxy sidecar owns the connection lifecycle and calls application code through a defined protocol; the application registers health checks and request handlers as IoC hooks.
Orleans virtual actor model: the Orleans runtime owns the grain lifecycle, activation and deactivation, and calls grain methods as directed by the scheduler; grain code is a hook implementation invoked by the framework.
ASP.NET Core middleware: the host builds the request pipeline and invokes each registered RequestDelegate in order; middleware can run before and after the next delegate or short-circuit, so the application supplies components while the server owns request dispatch.
JUnit Jupiter extension model: the JUnit engine discovers tests and invokes registered Before*/After* lifecycle callbacks around user test methods; extensions customize execution without owning when tests run.
Kubernetes controllers: the controller manager owns reconciliation loops that watch API state and repeatedly invokes controller reconciliation logic to converge current state on desired state; controllers supply behavior while Kubernetes schedules dispatch.

name: compound-components
document:
compound-components
compound component
compound component pattern
Give a family of cooperating components one owner — the parent — that holds the shared state and publishes it implicitly to every child, so consumers compose the family declaratively while the parent alone enforces its invariants and behaviour.
A widget only works when a parent and its children agree on one piece of state (which option is selected, which panel is open, whether a field is invalid), but the call site is the only place that knows the children. Holding the state at the call site means threading the value and its update callbacks into every child (prop drilling), and holding it in the children means the parent cannot enforce the family's invariants — exclusivity, ordering, keyboard behaviour — nor react to a child's change in one place. The recurring decision is where the shared state lives and how children participate in it without the call site wiring them.
Component-tree UI code: design-system and widget libraries (select/option, tabs, menus, field groups) in frameworks that can inject state into descendants without passing it through props — React context or child cloning, Angular content projection plus DI, Vue provide/inject, Compose CompositionLocal and slot scopes, SwiftUI environment and preference keys, Blazor cascading values, WPF attached properties over the logical tree — and in widget toolkits whose group objects (Swing ButtonGroup, JavaFX ToggleGroup, Qt QButtonGroup, tkinter control variables) play the same role. It pays off where the public API must stay small and the children must stay replaceable; it does not apply in languages without a component tree or without an implicit-injection channel.
Custom select, combobox or autocomplete families built from Option children — the canonical example: the parent owns the selection, the highlight and the keyboard interaction while options only declare their value and label.
Tabs, accordions and menus where Tab/TabPanel/MenuItem children register their identity and the parent owns the active item, the ordering and the ARIA wiring.
Form-field families (Field + Label + Input + Error) that share one validation/invalid state and generated ids without the call site passing them around.
Data-group widgets: tables with Column definitions, list widgets with Item children, tree views with Node children, chart legends with Series children.
Design-system libraries that export one namespaced symbol whose parts must be used together — the context in which the pattern is most often documented and most valuable.
Collapsible panel families (Disclosure pattern) where a parent owns the open/closed state and Trigger/Content children read it — also known as the Disclosure pattern in ARIA authoring practices.
Stepper/wizard widgets where a parent owns current-step state and Step/StepIndicator children read it without the consumer threading step indices.
Popover/tooltip families where a trigger button and a content panel share open/close state through the parent without prop drilling.
Radix UI Primitives — Dialog.Root owns the open/close context and Trigger/Portal/Content/Title/Description consume it, while asChild (Slot) merges each part's props, refs and keyboard behaviour into the consumer's own button or link.
Ark UI headless components (built on Zag.js state machines) — Popover.Root/Trigger/Positioner/Content share state through the root, ids props compose aria bindings across two families, and the same compound anatomy works in React, Solid, Vue and Svelte.
Headless UI's Dialog family (Dialog, DialogBackdrop, DialogPanel, DialogTitle, Description) — the root enforces the dismiss contract (open prop, onClose callback, focus trap, aria-labelledby) and every part reads the shared open/closed state, exposed for styling as data-open/data-closed attributes.

name: custom-hook
document:
custom-hook
custom hooks
composable logic
composable
use hook
Extract reusable stateful behaviour — state plus the effects that keep it synchronized — into a plain function that a component invokes, so unrelated components share the logic without a mixin, a wrapper component or a base class.
Several unrelated components need the same stateful logic (subscribe to a browser or platform API, fetch with loading and error states, validate a form, debounce a value), but the state and its effect wiring are entangled with one component's markup. Copying the logic duplicates the cleanup path, and the classic reuse mechanisms force the consumer into a wrapper (higher-order component), a render-prop callback or an inheritance/mixin structure — all of which distort the component tree and hide the logic just as much as the duplication did.
Component-based UI codebases whose runtime owns state slots and drives re-rendering from state changes (React and Vue Composition API on the web, Jetpack Compose on Android, SwiftUI on Apple platforms), where behaviour must be shared between components that have no other relationship. It applies whenever state plus lifecycle effects form a unit of reuse that is independent of any particular visual output; it does not apply to stateless helpers, which should remain ordinary functions.
Exposing a browser or platform capability as reactive state: online status, window size, media-query match, geolocation, app foreground state, dark mode, reduced-motion preference.
Data fetching with loading, error and refresh semantics (a useQuery-style unit) reused by list, detail and search components; including cancellation via AbortController.
Form state and validation shared by unrelated forms, including touched/dirty tracking, field-level errors, submit handling and reset.
Debounced or throttled derived values (search boxes, resize handlers) with correct timer cleanup and leading/trailing edge options.
Subscribing to an external reactive store (Redux-style store, WebSocket, EventSource, SSE, platform service) and mapping snapshots into component state; using useSyncExternalStore for tear-free reads.
Timers, polling and animations whose start and stop must be tied to the component lifetime; including pause/resume semantics.
Cross-cutting checks such as permissions, feature flags or entitlement checks that combine context values with local state.
Animation and transition state derived from scroll position, pointer proximity or layout metrics.
Encapsulating a specific third-party library or browser API behind a declarative interface (e.g., Web Audio API, Battery Status, Vibration API).
Abstracting away SSR guards and window/document checks so consumers receive a client-only reactive value without needing to know the platform detail.
Capturing and persisting UI state across sessions: localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB-backed state with hydration.
Library APIs delivered as hook calls instead of injected props or wrapper components: TanStack Query exposes fetching, caching and synchronising server state as useQuery; React Router exposes routing as useParams, useNavigate and useLocation.
Curated composable ecosystems shipped as versioned packages: VueUse's 200+ Vue composables (useMouse, useLocalStorage, createSharedComposable) built tree-shakeable, TypeScript-first and SSR-friendly.

name: headless-component
document:
headless-component
headless ui
unstyled component
Publish a widget's behaviour - state, event handling, keyboard and ARIA wiring - as a headless primitive that the consumer renders with its own markup, so one interaction implementation serves many visual designs instead of being forked or restyled around.
A widget's behaviour is worth reusing, but it ships tangled with one component's markup: consumers that need a different element structure, different class names or a different styling solution must copy the logic or bend their design around the shipped DOM, and every copy re-implements the keyboard, focus and ARIA behaviour. The recurring decision is how an interaction primitive hands its state and event wiring to an unknown call site without dictating what that call site renders.
Component-based UI codebases - web (React, Vue, Angular) and native (Compose, SwiftUI, Blazor, WPF, Qt, Swing/JavaFX) - where a design system or widget library must ship one interaction (combobox, menu, dialog, tabs, tooltip, disclosure) across several visual variants, or where an application must integrate an interaction into markup it already owns. It applies where the reuse mechanism can carry a caller-supplied render value: hooks, render props, scoped slots, slot APIs, content templates or headless directives. It does not apply when the look is the product, when a single call site owns both halves, or when the platform control already has the semantics the consumer wants.
Design systems shipping one interaction (combobox, select, menu, dialog, tabs, tooltip, disclosure) in several visual variants for different brands, densities or element structures.
A component library that must work with the consumer's styling solution and DOM instead of shipping its own wrapper elements and class names.
Application code that needs the same interaction behaviour in unrelated places - a typeahead, a focus trap, roving keyboard navigation, outside-click dismissal - without adopting the library's visuals.
Data-heavy widgets (tables, trees, command palettes) whose rows, cells and items must be rendered by the consuming application from its own data types.
Porting an interaction to another framework: one framework-agnostic state machine with per-framework adapters keeps the behaviour identical while the markup changes.
Testing interaction logic in isolation: state and getter contracts exercised without mounting a UI, leaving integration to the consumers' own tests.
Cross-framework component libraries: one framework-agnostic state machine (xstate or equivalent) with per-framework headless adapters keeps the behaviour bit-identical across React, Vue, Angular, Svelte, and native platforms, eliminating the need to re-implement interaction logic for each ecosystem.
RTL (right-to-left) and internationalisation testing: because the accessibility contract lives in the primitive, testing keyboard interaction, focus order, and ARIA semantics in an RTL layout is isolated from visual styling, making it practical to validate in CI.
Multi-brand and white-label design systems: the same headless primitives (tabs, combobox, dialog) serve multiple brands that each bring their own design tokens, class names and element structures, avoiding the fork of behaviour per brand that a styled-component approach would require.
CMS-driven content sites: headless CMS content (Sanity, Contentful) rendered into headless primitives (Disclosure, Accordion, Tabs) where the CMS supplies the panel content and the site supplies the visual design — the CMS never touches markup or styles, only structured content.
Design token integration: a brand system with token-driven spacing, colour, and typography passes those tokens to headless primitives via a Theme context; the primitives consume tokens but emit no styles, so the same behaviour works across light/dark/high-contrast themes without any code change.
Animation library integration: headless primitives emit state changes (open/close, activeIndex) that animation libraries (Framer Motion, Motion One) consume to drive transitions; the primitive remains the single source of truth for interaction state while the animation library owns the visual transition, keeping concerns cleanly separated.
A/B testing and feature flags: a headless Dialog primitive can be composed with a feature-flag wrapper that conditionally mounts either a rich visual variant or a minimal fallback, without the primitive knowing about the flag — enabling a/b testing of interaction UX independently of visual design.
Micro-frontend / module federation: shared headless primitives (published as a federated module) provide interaction consistency across independently-deployed micro-frontends; each team brings its own visual design but the keyboard, focus, and ARIA behaviour is guaranteed identical across all federated pieces.
Storybook-driven documentation: ship headless primitives with stories that demonstrate every getter applied to the right element, using Storybook's Controls and Actions addons to let documentation readers exercise every state transition and inspect the getter output — turning the accessibility contract into an interactive reference rather than a static doc.
White-label product lines: a SaaS product serving multiple vertical markets (healthcare, finance, retail) uses the same headless primitive set with per-vertical Tailwind config overrides; each market gets a visually distinct product that behaves identically at the interaction level, and regulatory accessibility testing covers all markets simultaneously.
Cross-framework product lines: Ark UI ships the same headless components (dialog, tabs, select, date picker) with an identical API for React, Vue, Solid and Svelte because a shared Zag.js finite state machine drives every adapter - the interaction is written once and behaves identically across ecosystems while each app supplies its own markup.
Adobe React Spectrum: React Aria hooks return the accessibility props (roles, aria-* attributes, event handlers) for buttons, dialogs, listboxes and pickers, and the application - or the React Aria Components layer on top - supplies the markup, so the behaviour is audited once against the ARIA contract and reused across the product family.
shadcn/ui distribution: applications copy Radix headless primitives together with their Tailwind markup into their own repository, so the composition of each primitive becomes consumer-owned source - a distribution form of the pattern in which the headless behaviour stays a dependency while the markup half is edited in place.

name: render-props
document:
render-props
render prop
children as a function
Let a component hand its own state to a caller-supplied function-valued prop and render whatever that function returns, so one piece of behaviour serves many appearances while every call site keeps control of the markup.
A component owns reusable state or behaviour - a subscription, form state, list data, animation values - but its output is hard-wired to one markup structure, so consumers that need different markup must copy the logic, wrap and patch the component, or bend their design around the shipped DOM. The recurring decision is how a stateful component can expose its state to an unknown call site without dictating what that call site renders.
Component-based UI codebases where the reuse mechanism can pass a function into a component and the framework re-renders the call site when the owner's state changes: React/Vue props and scoped slots, Blazor templated components, Compose and SwiftUI composable closures, WPF data templates, and toolkit cell/renderer factories. It applies when the owner must keep the behaviour - lifecycle, subscriptions, context, refs, portals - while the consumer owns structure and styling; it is largely superseded by hooks and composables when only logic or state is shared.
Headless component libraries that ship behaviour with consumer markup (Downshift's render-prop form, React Aria builders, TanStack Table).
Drag-and-drop and other wrappers that must own a subtree boundary - context, refs or portals - while the consumer authors the children (react-beautiful-dnd's provided/snapshot arguments).
Animation primitives that thread interpolated values into consumer markup every frame (Framer Motion, React Spring).
List and table renderers with per-slot functions such as renderItem, renderEmpty and ListHeaderComponent - the shape React Native's FlatList popularised.
Cross-cutting state such as mouse position, geolocation or form validation shared by screens that each display it differently.
Pre-hooks data fetching components (Apollo Query/Mutation) retained for consumers that cannot use hooks.
Downshift's <Downshift> children function exposes combobox state and prop getters while rendering no UI, so consumers can build custom accessible autocomplete markup.
react-beautiful-dnd's <Droppable> and <Draggable> function children pass refs, required props and drag snapshots while the consumer controls each draggable element's structure and styling.
React Motion's <Motion> children function receives interpolated style values on each animation frame, allowing those values to drive arbitrary consumer markup.

name: request-reply
document:
request-reply
request-response
request-response messaging
Let a sender obtain a result or a domain error from an asynchronous or remote receiver by pairing each request with a correlated reply, and give the missing reply a defined outcome: timeout, cancellation and disposal of late replies.
Messaging is one-way, but the sender frequently needs a return value or a domain error from the receiver before it can continue. Without an agreed reply destination, a way to match replies to requests, and a rule for what happens when no reply arrives, the caller either blocks forever, mis-associates the next reply with the wrong request, or accumulates pending state it never cleans up.
Asynchronous interaction across a process, thread or network boundary where the caller cannot continue without the receiver's result: HTTP/gRPC-style RPC, broker-based RPC over a queue, actor or thread mailboxes, and browser-to-server exchanges over a socket. It applies when the interaction is naturally one request and one reply, and each exchange has a bounded deadline.
Service-to-service RPC where the caller needs the result to continue (HTTP, gRPC, or a broker-based RPC queue such as the RabbitMQ tutorial's rpc_queue).
Command dispatch that must return a domain error - a validation failure or business rejection - rather than only an acknowledgement of receipt.
In-process actor or thread mailboxes: ask a worker for state with a deadline so the caller can never block forever.
Front-end over a WebSocket asking the server for a value correlated by message id or acknowledgement callback.
Talking to devices, sensors or legacy systems over a socket whose protocol is inherently one request and one response.
Querying a cache or index cluster from a client library where each call is a key lookup with a per-call deadline.
NATS request-reply service calls: a client publishes with a unique inbox as the reply subject and waits for a response under a per-request timeout.
RabbitMQ RPC over an rpc_queue: the client sends reply_to and a unique correlation_id, then matches the worker's response on its callback queue.
gRPC unary RPC: a generated client stub sends one request and receives one response under a propagated deadline, with cancellation available for abandoned work.

name: producer-consumer
document:
producer-consumer
bounded buffer
consumer-producer
Insert a bounded buffer between producers and consumers of work items so the two sides run concurrently at their own rates, the buffer absorbs bursts and slack, and its bound turns overload into backpressure, queueing or an explicit drop policy instead of unbounded growth.
Production and consumption proceed at different rates: a fast producer outruns its consumer and either drops items or grows a backlog until memory runs out, a slow producer leaves consumers idle, and bursts arrive faster than they can be processed. Wiring the two sides together directly also couples their lifetimes and schedules - a synchronous hand-off makes the faster side wait for the slower - so neither side can be scaled, restarted or tested on its own.
Concurrent in-process software (threads, tasks, coroutines, event-loop callbacks) with one or more producers and one or more consumers that can run at the same time but not at the same average rate. The buffer is a component-level data structure owned by the application - a work queue for a thread pool, a pipeline hand-off, a logging or telemetry sink - not a durable broker, so the decisions are how to hand items over, how to bound the queue and how to end the arrangement cleanly.
Work queues behind thread or worker pools: request handlers enqueue tasks and a fixed set of workers consumes them, so pool size is independent of the arrival rate. Industry examples: Celery (Python), Sidekiq (Ruby), BullMQ (Node.js) all use this shape with Redis or a broker as the durable backing store.
Asynchronous logging and telemetry: hot paths enqueue records cheaply while a background writer drains, formats and writes them, keeping I/O latency off the request path. Structured log collectors (Fluent Bit, Vector) ingest from many sources into one consumer.
Multi-stage data pipelines (decode - transform - encode, extract - transform - load): bounded queues between stages give each stage its own workers and let a slow stage backpressure a fast one. Used in media transcoding, ETL workflows, and stream processors.
Ingestion buffers: a socket, file or broker reader produces records faster than the processing or indexing stage can absorb them, and the buffer smooths the mismatch without dropping data. Common in IoT telemetry ingestion, click-stream collection, and log aggregation.
UI/host integration: a background thread posts work or results to the main/event-loop thread's queue and vice versa, keeping the UI responsive without locks around application state. All major GUI frameworks (Qt, Swing, Flutter) use this internally.
Batch job scheduling: producers enqueue compute jobs (image resize, PDF generation, report creation) and a pool of consumers processes them. Systems like Celery, Hangfire, and AWS SQS follow this pattern, often with priority queues, delayed execution, and dead-letter routing.
Event streaming pre-processing: a Kafka, Pulsar, or NATS consumer-producer chain filters, transforms, and routes events through a series of bounded queues before landing in a data warehouse or search index.
Simulation and testing: a producer generates a deterministic stream of items while a consumer asserts on what it receives, with a sentinel marking the end of the stream. Property-based testing frameworks use this to drive scenario generation.
Print spooling and document processing: print jobs or document conversion tasks are queued and processed by a pool of workers, with bounded queues preventing runaway memory use even under burst load.
ML inference pipelines: a model-serving host receives requests via an API, enqueues them into a bounded queue, and a pool of worker coroutines or threads dequeues and runs inference. The queue decouples HTTP latency from inference latency and provides backpressure when the model GPU is saturated. Tools like Ray Serve, Triton Inference Server, and TorchServe use this shape.
Streaming audio/video processing: a media pipeline (capture - encode - mux - stream) uses bounded queues between stages; frames that arrive during a temporary encoding stall are buffered rather than dropped, and a full encoder output queue backpressures the camera capture stage to prevent unbounded memory growth from frame accumulation.
WebSocket connection management: a server's accept loop enqueues new connections into a bounded connection queue; a pool of handler coroutines or threads dequeues and upgrades them, preventing connection exhaustion under burst load while the handler pool limits concurrency independently of the arrival rate.
Financial order processing: high-frequency trading systems receive market data feeds (producer) and route orders through risk checks and execution engines (consumers), with bounded queues between stages preventing downstream latency from backpressuring the market data ingestion and applying backpressure to upstream feed handlers.
Go channel pipelines: a source goroutine produces values into a channel, transformation stages consume and emit through downstream channels, and a sink drains the final stage. Go's documented pipeline pattern makes channel closure and cancellation part of the producer-consumer lifecycle.
Python asyncio worker queues: an asyncio.Queue(maxsize=N) accepts work from coroutine producers while worker coroutines await get(), process items and call task_done(); finite maxsize suspends producers when consumers fall behind.
Java executor work queues: java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue coordinates multiple producer threads and consumer workers, with put()/take() waiting on full and empty capacity so an Executor-style worker pool can be bounded independently of arrival rate.
