name: policy-guard
document:
policy-guard
policy pattern
policy decision point / policy enforcement point
Keep every authorisation decision out of the protected resource's code by moving the rules into a separate Policy component and letting a Guard - the enforcement point every access must pass through - obtain a decision from that policy before the operation is performed.
Access rules written inside the resource's own methods (checking roles or ownership inline) entangle business logic with security logic: the same rule is re-implemented at every call site, a forgotten check silently opens a bypass, and the rules cannot be reviewed, tested or changed without touching the resource's code.
Components that own protected resources or operations and must decide per access whether the authenticated subject - with its roles, attributes, tenant and request context - may perform the requested action. Typical at object, module or boundary scope: request handlers, domain services, document stores, message consumers and administrative tooling that all reach the same resources and should obey the same rules, especially when the rules change more often than the resource code.
HTTP and API request handling: authentication establishes the security context once, then every endpoint or method invocation is guarded by a policy decision (for example Spring Security's AuthorizationManager behind its AuthorizationFilter, or ASP.NET Core authorization middleware over registered policies).
Domain services that expose several operations on one aggregate: the guard checks the (subject, operation, resource) triple before each service method executes, instead of scattering role checks through the methods.
Multi-tenant backends where the decision must consider tenant, ownership and request attributes, not only roles; the guard resolves them from the security context and passes them to the policy.
Document or file stores: every read or write is wrapped by a guard that consults rules keyed by the document identifier and its classification.
Administrative and background code - CLI tools, batch jobs, message consumers - that must obey the same policy as the interactive API so that no side door exists.
Regulated environments where every access decision, including denials, must be logged consistently and the policy itself must be independently testable.
Spring Security request boundaries: AuthorizationFilter passes the current Authentication and HttpServletRequest to an AuthorizationManager and proceeds only after a grant; configure every protected route so an unlisted path cannot become a side door.
ASP.NET Core policy authorization: named policies combine requirements evaluated by IAuthorizationHandler implementations and attach with [Authorize(Policy = "...")] or RequireAuthorization; place UseAuthorization after authentication and before endpoints.
Open Policy Agent (OPA) deployments: AWS Prescriptive Guidance models a centralized or distributed Policy Decision Point with Policy Enforcement Points on APIs, allowing shared policy while using local sidecars when latency or availability requires it.

name: entity
document:
entity
reference object
domain entity
Give a domain concept a stable identity that survives attribute changes, representation changes and time, and define its equality, lifecycle and lookup in terms of that identity instead of in terms of its attributes.
A model that compares objects by their attributes cannot answer whether two instances are the same thing: a customer whose e-mail and plan changed looks like a different customer, while two distinct people who share a name look like one. References held by other objects, caches and audit records break silently, and every state change forces callers to re-identify the object.
Rich domain models in which some concepts must be tracked through time: the object is created, changes state, is stored and reloaded, and may exist in several representations (in-memory instance, database row, message payload, UI snapshot) that all have to denote the same thing. It is the modelling decision that pairs with Value Object: attribute clusters become values, while the things whose history matters keep an identity.
Master data tracked for years — customers, accounts, contracts, products, patients — where attributes change but the business entity stays the same (e.g., a Customer who moves house is still the same Customer).
Documents with a lifecycle: orders, invoices, bookings and shipments that move through states (pending → paid → shipped → delivered) while remaining the same document with a stable order number.
Shopping cart to order transition: a ShoppingCart is reconstituted as an Order with the same customer identity but a new order identity, preserving the correlation to the customer while starting a new business process.
Correlating representations across layers: an entity persisted as database rows, published as domain events, and displayed in a UI must be recognisable as the same thing in all three — identity is the correlation key across representations.
In-memory session consistency: a unit of work or identity map ensures the same Customer loaded twice in one request is one object reference, preventing edits from silently diverging into two copies.
Referencing across bounded contexts: one microservice holds a CustomerId reference to another service's aggregate root, allowing independent deployment and loading without a direct object pointer.
Healthcare records: a Patient entity persists across multiple visits, lab results and prescriptions — the patient identity is the anchor for the entire medical history regardless of demographic changes.
Versioned documents: an InsurancePolicy entity may be replaced by a new version while the original policy number (identity) remains the correlation handle for auditors and legacy systems.
Hibernate/JPA: an @Entity class with an @Id is managed by the persistence context, which guarantees one in-memory instance per identity per session — loading the same row twice in a session returns the same object reference, an Identity Map built into the framework.
Entity Framework Core: identity resolution makes the DbContext track a single entity instance per primary key, so duplicate instances arriving in a deserialized graph are merged into the already-tracked entity instead of diverging into two tracked copies.
Drupal Entity API: nodes, users and taxonomy terms (content entities) and roles or image styles (configuration entities) are identity-bearing objects with typed storage handlers, revisions and field bundles behind one CRUD and validation API.

name: range
document:
range
interval
Represent a span of values as a single interval value whose bound inclusivity and open ends are explicit, so containment and interval-to-interval comparisons live in one place instead of repeated ad-hoc endpoint tests.
Start and end travel together through the code but every caller re-derives what they mean: containment is written as scattered <= / < comparisons that drift apart, "unbounded" is smuggled in as a sentinel value (Long.MAX_VALUE, 9999-12-31), and interval-to-interval questions - do these two overlap, does one enclose the other, what is the gap between them - have no home at all.
Applies wherever a domain concept is a span rather than a point: validity and effectivity periods, booking and availability windows, quantity or price tiers, measurement buckets, version and address ranges, pagination windows, and query parameters such as a date range. It pays off when the same interval is compared repeatedly or crosses a boundary (persistence, API payloads, UI widgets), because the bound convention then has to be written once instead of re-decided per call site. For a single comparison between two local variables the type is pure overhead.
Validity and effectivity windows: a contract, price or membership is valid over [effectiveFrom, effectiveTo), and every check is a membership test against one interval.
Booking and availability: a room, seat or resource is reserved during an interval; overlap (not adjacency) decides whether a new booking is possible, and back-to-back bookings must be allowed deliberately.
Quantity and price tiers: the unit price depends on the quantity interval ([1,10), [10,50), [50, +inf)), so a container of intervals with containment lookup replaces a cascade of if-statements.
Temporal queries and reporting: "last 7 days", "this quarter", "since the migration" are half-open or open-ended intervals passed to repositories and rendered by date-range pickers.
Version, port and address ranges: a compatibility claim covers [1.2, 2.0) of a library, a firewall rule covers a port interval - containment answers "is this covered?" and intersection answers "do these rules conflict?".
Pagination and slicing windows: a page is an interval over a sequence, and half-open semantics make adjacency exact ([0,20) followed by [20,40)),
PostgreSQL range and multirange columns: PostgreSQL's daterange, tsrange and numeric range types make lower-inclusive/upper-exclusive bounds, overlap and containment operators, and indexed range queries part of the persistence contract; choose the bound convention before mapping domain intervals.
Guava Range: Java's Guava Range models convex bounded or unbounded intervals with nine open/closed forms, isConnected and intersection; use ContiguousSet only when a discrete domain really requires enumeration rather than treating the interval itself as a sequence.
Standard-library and container choices: Rust's std::ops::RangeBounds covers included, excluded and unbounded bounds when its range forms fit; for many intervals requiring join/split policies, Boost ICL's interval_set and interval_map supply the container semantics instead of overloading one Range value.

name: fail-safe-defaults
document:
fail-safe-defaults
deny by default
default deny
Make denial the default outcome of every access decision, so that access exists only where it has been explicitly granted and no missing rule, missing identity or failed check can silently permit an operation.
Authorisation written as exclusion: code asks 'is this forbidden?' and everything the deny rules do not cover - a route added last sprint, a new operation, an unknown role, an object-level case, a request the parser cannot classify - is permitted by omission. The failure modes compound it: a missing principal, an unreachable policy source or an exception inside the check falls through to the permissive branch, so the code paths that look most careful are the ones that open the system.
Any boundary where access to a resource is decided: HTTP routes and APIs, message channels and queues, object-level data access, operating-system objects and descriptors, cloud and network policy, and the configuration a product ships with. It matters most where the space of possible requests grows faster than any list of forbidden cases can track, where the check itself can fail (policy store unreachable, identity missing, input unparseable), and where an unintended permission would not be visible in normal operation.
HTTP APIs and gateways: every route carries an explicit policy or permission and an endpoint whose handler was added without one is still decided (ASP.NET Core's fallback policy) or denied as unmatched (Spring Security's recommended final rule), so a forgotten decorator cannot expose it.
Message infrastructure: brokers grant publish/subscribe rights per topic, and a message whose type or destination matches no handler goes to an invalid-message or dead-letter channel instead of a catch-all consumer.
Operating-system and platform defaults: new files are created with restrictive modes (an explicit mode masked by umask, mkstemp's 0600 for temporary files, close-on-exec where descriptors cross exec), server processes run under a syscall allow-list and a least-privilege account, and firewall or network policy denies by default.
Multi-tenant data access: rows, schemas or objects are reachable only through a tenant-scoped grant, and a request with no resolvable tenant — or an unknown tenant id — is denied rather than defaulting to the shared or global dataset.
Cloud IAM and entitlement management: principals have implicit deny until a policy attaches an explicit allow, and service-to-service calls require a granted scope rather than being permitted because both ends are internal.
Product configuration and feature exposure: debug endpoints, sample data and experimental features ship disabled unless enabled, so a build cannot expose them by omission.
Kubernetes NetworkPolicy default-deny: a podSelector: {} NetworkPolicy with no allowed Ingress/Egress rules isolates every pod in the namespace; allow rules are added for only the traffic that is genuinely required, making lateral movement inside the cluster the exception rather than the default.
Service mesh and mTLS (Istio, Linkerd): every workload presents a client certificate; the mesh denies any packet between workloads that cannot present a matching allowed peer identity, so compromised containers cannot reach services outside their explicit allowlist.
Policy-as-Code with Open Policy Agent (OPA) or Cedar: authorization policies are written as declarative rules in a policy language, evaluated by a purpose-built engine, and applied to APIs, Kubernetes, CI/CD pipelines and cloud IAM — the grant set is code, diffed and reviewed like any other artefact.
Serverless function invocation: a function's invocation permission is an explicit resource-based policy; a caller with no matching permission is denied even when the function is invoked via an authenticated event source (SQS, SNS, EventBridge), preventing unintended cross-tenant or cross-function calls.
Database row-level and column-level security: a SELECT or DML operation must match an explicit row-level policy predicate for the caller's attributes (tenant_id, role, ownership), and a missing match returns no rows rather than all rows — preventing inadvertent data leakage across security boundaries.
CI/CD pipeline permissions: a pipeline step's ability to deploy, promote artefacts or access secrets is granted through a scoped, time-bounded, revokable token; any step that has not been explicitly granted a permission is denied access to the target environment, preventing lateral movement from a compromised pipeline.
Healthcare (HIPAA minimum necessary): a clinical application's access to patient records defaults to zero; a physician's identity is matched against a role-based record access policy and granted only the specific record types (e.g. active admissions, problem list, medication history) that the physician's specialty and current assignment require — a missing match returns zero records rather than a full dataset, preventing inadvertent PHI disclosure.
Financial services (PCI-DSS): cardholder data environment access is blocked by default for all accounts; a payment processing service is granted only the specific tokenisation and authorisation operations it requires, and only for the card ranges it actively manages. A network monitoring service that has no transaction role cannot reach the cardholder data database even if it shares a subnet.
IoT device posture and network isolation: a newly provisioned IoT device ships with all external communication channels closed; it may only reach the device management plane for firmware updates and telemetry, and only over a TLS channel with certificate pinning. Any application-layer attempt to reach an external IP address is denied by a local firewall policy that is immutable post-deployment.
Multi-cloud and hybrid IAM federation: a request arriving from a federated identity (SAML assertion, OIDC token) must carry a mapped grant in the local entitlement system before accessing a resource; the federation identity alone is insufficient. A missing local grant denies even when the upstream IdP has authenticated the user, preventing an IdP compromise from automatically granting access to all federated resources.
Supply chain and CI/CD artifact access: a CI/CD pipeline stage receives a scoped, time-limited, revokable token valid only for reading the specific artifact and writing to the specific deployment target it requires; it cannot read secrets store, cannot push to the artifact registry, and cannot promote artifacts to production without a separate approval gate — following the principle that pipeline permissions are the minimum for the job, not the union of all pipeline jobs.
Runtime application self-protection (RASP): a RASP agent embedded in an application enforces default-deny at the instrumentation layer — even if an attacker achieves code execution they cannot invoke system calls, network connections or database queries that the application's normal execution profile does not require, because those capabilities are absent from the process baseline by default.
Legal and compliance data environments: an e-discovery or legal hold system defaults to zero access to case documents; a paralegal's session is granted only the specific document set for an active matter and only for the duration of that matter; a revoked matter grant cannot be exercised even if the session token has not expired, because the grant itself is checked at each document access call.
Database engine shipped defaults: PostgreSQL 15 revoked CREATE on the public schema from PUBLIC by default, inverting a default that had permitted every role to create objects since the engine's early releases — evidence that the positive model must be re-asserted in the defaults a platform ships with, not only in the application's policy.

statement: Choose how to encode precedence, association, and operand handling for a growing set of prefix, infix, postfix, and mixfix expression operators.
name: passkey
document:
passkey
passkey idiom
constructor key
Restrict a constructor or method to chosen collaborators by requiring a token that only those collaborators can construct, so the operation stays in the public signature while remaining uncallable by everyone else - compile-time access control instead of blanket friendship.
A specific collaborator must call a constructor or method that must not become public API: a factory or helper that has to construct an object through a public constructor (make_unique, MakeGarbageCollected), a serialisation or framework layer that must reach one private hook, a subsystem that needs one internal operation, a test helper that must build a type in a state users cannot. The blunt mechanisms all miss: making the member public hands it to the world, friend (or its nearest equivalent) hands the collaborator the whole private surface, package/module/assembly access opens it to an entire scope, and a private constructor plus a factory just moves the gate into the factory. What is missing is a way to say 'this collaborator, and only this collaborator, may call exactly this operation'.
Statically checked code where the operation must stay visible in the type system (templates, frameworks and helper functions must be able to resolve the call) but must not be callable without a value that only the designated collaborators can create. The grant is a source-level construct checked by the compiler: the token is empty, disappears at run time and is never a defence against an adversary. Typical settings are factory-created types, library internals exposed to one subsystem, framework hooks, constructor or overload disambiguation, and test seams.
Factory-created objects with a public constructor: base::PassKey in Chromium exists for classes that a helper template (blink::MakeGarbageCollected) must construct while user code must not.
Serialisation and framework hooks: an archive, visitor or framework calls exactly one hook of a user type; the key names the framework instead of befriending it and exposing everything else.
Library-internal operations: one subsystem (allocator, persistence layer, test infrastructure) needs to construct or mutate a type users must not reach - the key names the subsystem where the language allows it, and module or assembly scope carries the rest.
Tests: a test helper constructs an otherwise unreachable state without '#define private public' builds, friend-everything test seams or reflection.
Constructor and overload disambiguation: a tag only the factory can produce selects the trusted overload and keeps the same argument list from being callable by everyone.
Deliberate delegation and revocation: the collaborator passes a key to another function that then performs the call, and a non-copyable key stops the ability from travelling further.
KDE Frameworks' KColorScheme (Frameworks 6.6.0) adopted a passkey specifically to avoid private-constructor issues, showing the idiom in a public Qt-based framework API.
Chromium's Mojo ProtoWrapperBytes uses base::PassKey to let named network, component and test classes access wrapped protobuf bytes while ordinary callers cannot supply the operation.
Abseil's C++ Tip of the Week #134 uses a passkey token with std::make_shared so a factory can keep single-allocation construction without making unconstrained construction the public API.

statement: Choose how to encode precedence, association, and operand handling for a growing set of prefix, infix, postfix, and mixfix expression operators.
name: test-specific-subclass
document:
test-specific-subclass
test-specific extension
subclassed test double
Make an otherwise untestable class testable by defining a test-only subclass that overrides the method reaching the unusable dependency (or exposes the internal state the test needs), so the boundary can be substituted and observed without putting test hooks into production code.
A class that must be tested reaches its dependency through a call on itself - a self-call to a helper method, a field created inside the class, or a singleton/static lookup - so the test has no injection point: the collaborator cannot be replaced from outside, the indirect inputs cannot be controlled and the indirect outputs cannot be observed. Editing the production class to accept the dependency may be impossible (third-party or frozen code) or would introduce test logic into production.
Applies to legacy or third-party object-oriented code where the boundary call already sits behind an overridable (non-final, sufficiently visible) method, or can be extracted into one, and where test-only code may live next to the tests. It is a fallback for statically typed languages that need the double to stay type-compatible with a concrete class; where the code can be modified, dependency injection is the better seam.
A legacy class reads the wall clock inside a helper method (System.currentTimeMillis, DateTime.Now, Instant.now): override the helper so date/decision logic can be tested at a fixed instant.
A reporting or notification class sends mail or calls a remote API from a self-call: override that method with a canned or empty body so the unit test runs offline and deterministically.
A class reaches a database or the file system from inside its own method: override it to return an in-memory fixture instead of building the real object chain (entity-chain snipping).
Verifying the sequence and the set of steps of a template method: override the steps in a subclass and record which of them ran, in which order.
Exposing private state for state verification, or exposing a private algorithm step so it can be tested individually (state-exposing and behaviour-exposing subclasses).
Replacing a singleton or static accessor the SUT uses through a lookup with a controlled instance that is still type-compatible with the concrete class (substituted singleton).
Putting a legacy untested class under a characterization-test baseline before refactoring, while extracting the collaborator is not yet possible.
A Java class that cannot be modified (third-party or legacy jar) but has a non-final boundary method to stub: Mockito spy() / @Spy keeps the real methods and stubs only the overridden ones - the partial mocking Mockito's Javadoc documents for legacy code and third-party interfaces (final methods stay un-stubbable).
A PHP class whose constructor opens connections or performs other side effects: createPartialMock(Class::class, ['boundaryMethod']) or getMockBuilder()->onlyMethods([...])->disableOriginalConstructor() generates a double that overrides only the named methods and skips the real constructor - PHPUnit's documented form of the pattern (final, private and static methods and enums cannot be doubled).
A .NET class with virtual boundary members: NSubstitute Substitute.ForPartsOf<T>() creates a partial substitute that - as NSubstitute's own docs state - inherits the original type via Castle DynamicProxy and runs real code except for members configured with DoNotCallBase, i.e. a generated test-specific subclass with an official 'use with caution' caveat.

statement: Choose how to encode precedence, association, and operand handling for a growing set of prefix, infix, postfix, and mixfix expression operators.
name: lazy-acquisition
document:
lazy-acquisition
lazy loading
deferred acquisition
Defer acquiring an expensive or scarce resource until it is first used, so the acquisition cost is paid only by the holders that actually use it, while clients keep seeing an ordinary interface.
A resource is costly to acquire, scarce, and on many execution paths never needed at all, yet the code that holds it acquires it during construction, at start-up or on a hot entry path: the process pays for resources it never dereferences, start-up time grows with every optional subsystem, and scarce capacity (descriptors, connections, licenses, memory) is consumed by holders that never use it.
Applies to long-lived holders - objects, modules, services, containers - that front an external resource such as a file, socket or database connection, license, thread pool, GPU context, translation catalog or large lookup table. It pays off when the acquisition cost is large relative to a use, when a significant fraction of holders never use the resource, and when the runtime offers a one-time guard (or the holder is provably single-threaded). It is the wrong tool when the resource must be validated at boot, when acquisition is cheap, or when first use sits on a latency-critical path.
A request-handling object that opens a file or blob stream only on the code paths that actually read it (report export, attachment download, audit sink).
A service holding connections to a rarely consulted downstream — archive store, fallback provider, secondary region — that most requests never call.
A large lookup table, model or translation catalog loaded on first use instead of at process start, keeping start-up and memory bounded for the sessions that never need it.
Optional subsystems in desktop and mobile apps (camera, location, payment SDK, plugins) initialized when the feature is opened rather than when the app launches.
Test fixtures and tooling: starting a container, browser or database only for the tests that need it, so the fast path stays fast.
Per-session state in a server — a scratch buffer, a decompressor, a TLS session or prepared statement — allocated on first use of the session rather than on accept.
Database connection pools: HikariCP and similar pools typically create connections lazily on the first checkout rather than at pool construction, to avoid pinninglicenses and consuming file descriptors before the application is fully started.
Dependency injection containers (Spring @Lazy, Dagger 2 Lazy<T>) defer the creation of bean instances until they are first injected, reducing start-up time and breaking circular dependency cycles during bootstrap.
Logging frameworks (SLF4J/Logback): Logger instances are static final but the actual appender (file, socket, console) is initialized when the first log event at that level is fired, so logging infrastructure does not block application start.
Configuration objects: large YAML or JSON config trees are parsed and validated lazily on first access rather than eagerly at start-up, keeping CLI tools fast for commands that do not need the full configuration.
GPU contexts in graphics applications (OpenGL, Vulkan, CUDA) are expensive to create and are deferred until the first draw call or compute kernel launch, allowing the application to start and display a window without claiming GPU memory.
HTTP/service clients (gRPC channels, REST clients): a channel is lazily opened on the first request, enabling the client to be instantiated at module load time while deferring the TCP handshake and TLS handshake to the first real call.
Spring Framework @Lazy bean definitions instantiate singleton beans when first requested rather than during ApplicationContext startup, making an optional integration genuinely demand-driven while retaining the container's proxy and lifecycle semantics.
Go's sync.Once lets a service wrap a one-time connection, parser or cache acquisition so concurrent first callers wait for one initializer and later callers reuse the published result.
.NET's System.Lazy<T> defers a factory until Value is first read and makes the thread-safety and exception-caching policy explicit through its constructors and LazyThreadSafetyMode.

name: two-step-view
document:
two-step-view
two stage view
Split presentation into two transformations - first turn domain data into a channel-neutral logical page, then render that logical page into a concrete output format - so page structure is defined once while look-and-feel and output channel live entirely in the renderer.
Every page owns its own presentation decisions: with one template or one transform per page, a global look-and-feel change means editing every file, and serving a second channel (print/PDF, e-mail, plain text, a machine-readable feed) means duplicating the page's structure. Nothing in the codebase represents 'the page' independently of the markup it currently happens to be rendered as.
Server-side presentation or document-publishing boundaries where several output channels share one page structure, or where the house style changes often enough that it must change in exactly one place. It also fits where the rendering technology is expected to be replaced (XSLT today, a template engine or PDF formatter tomorrow) and where the page should be inspectable, testable or cacheable before it is rendered.
Multi-channel publishing: one invoice or statement rendered as HTML for a portal, XSL-FO/PDF for print and plain text for e-mail from a single logical page.
Site-wide restyling in a CMS or portal where the house style must be one artefact to change and review rather than one edit per page family.
API-plus-HTML endpoints: the same logical page is serialised as JSON for clients and rendered as HTML for the browsable interface.
Document and report pipelines in the DocBook tradition: the logical document is produced once and rendered to HTML, PDF and e-book formats by different stylesheets.
Constrained or legacy channels - plain text, WAP/XML, CSV - added next to HTML without touching the page assembly code.
Pages produced once and consumed by several renderers or locales: the logical page is cached and rendered per channel on demand.
Spring Web MVC XSLT views: an XsltController builds an XML DOM of the page content, puts it in the model, and XsltViewResolver applies a home.xslt stylesheet - stage one produces the logical document, stage two owns the HTML.
Aura.View (PHP) ships the pattern under the name TwoStepView: a content template renders first, then a separately registered layout wraps it via setLayout()/getContent(), keeping the site chrome in one artefact instead of every page.
Standards-based publishing toolchains: the DITA Open Toolkit transforms semantic DITA maps/topics through XSLT stages into HTML, PDF and other deliverables, and Apache Cocoon pipelines generator -> XSLT transformer -> serializer so one XML source serves HTML, PDF, SVG and text.

name: revocable-forwarder
document:
revocable-forwarder
caretaker
revocable proxy
Let a collaborator use an object through a forwarding wrapper that the grantor can switch off at any time through a separate control, so authority already handed out can be withdrawn without destroying the target and without the collaborator's cooperation.
A capability is just a reference, so once a collaborator has been given access to an object there is no built-in way to take it back: the grantor can destroy the object, ask the collaborator to stop, or leave the access standing. The recurring decision is how to grant access that is bounded in time - temporary use of a file, a service object, a session, an account - while keeping a control that only the grantor holds.
Object-capability settings, and any in-process design in which authority travels as references rather than as a global identity: plugin and extension hosts lending a service object to foreign code, multi-tenant object graphs giving a worker one tenant-scoped resource, session-scoped services, and capability-based workflow or financial systems in which a grant must be provably withdrawn. It applies when the grantor keeps its own reference to the target and can intercept every call through the reference it handed out; where the runtime lets references be forged, dereferenced around the wrapper or reached by reflection, marshalling or FFI, the same structure degrades from an enforcement mechanism to a discipline.
A plugin or extension host lends a file, network or service object to foreign code and revokes it when the plugin is unloaded or breaches policy.
A multi-tenant worker receives one tenant-scoped resource for the duration of a job and loses it at job end, without the tenant object being torn down.
Session teardown in a long-lived server: the handler works through the wrapper, and logout revokes future calls before the session's resources are freed.
Capability-based workflow and financial systems that give an agent temporary authority over an account or a document and revoke it when the task completes.
Temporary elevated access for maintenance or debugging, where the requirement is to show that the extra authority has provably ended (audit evidence).
Graceful decommissioning of a shared resource: revoke new work through the wrapper, drain the calls already in flight, then release the resource.
The Scala ocaps framework's Revocable/Caretaker API returns a proxied capability plus a private Revoker, so a session, logout, timeout or supervisor can make later calls fail without changing the target.
JavaScript's standard Proxy.revocable() and the Chrome Extensions chrome.permissions API provide browser/runtime counterparts: keep the revoke/remove control private, and do not mistake the platform wrapper or permission record for protection against an already leaked target reference.
AWS IAM role-session revocation for temporary STS credentials is a distributed analogue of withdrawing a forwarded grant: policy evaluation denies subsequent requests, but propagation and credential caching mean it is not the atomic in-process check-and-forward gate described here.

name: spatial-partition
document:
spatial-partition
spatial index
bucket grid
Store every object in a structure indexed by its position so that neighbourhood queries visit only the objects near a point or region instead of scanning the whole population.
Queries that ask 'what is near this position?' - collision checks, proximity and aggro radii, culling, spatial analytics - repeatedly scan every object: each query is linear in the population and a whole simulation step becomes quadratic, even though every object interacts only with the few objects next to it.
Per-object runtime systems and simulations - game worlds, crowd and particle solvers, location services, robotics - where objects are mobile, spread over space, and the queries are local (radius, region, k-nearest). The pattern applies once the population is large enough that a full scan dominates the frame or the request budget, and it requires a position-to-cell mapping and an update discipline that match how the objects move.
Game worlds: collision, proximity and aggro checks between many moving entities each tick (bullets versus enemies, pickups, area effects).
Physics broadphase: pruning candidate pairs before narrow-phase tests where colliders move constantly.
Map and GIS services: 'all points within radius' and viewport queries over millions of features.
Crowd, flocking and particle simulations: neighbours within a radius for boids or social forces instead of all-pairs tests.
Spatial analytics and robotics: k-nearest or region queries over vehicles, sensors and delivery points, and occupancy grids for pathfinding.
Physics engines: Box2D's broadphase is a dynamic AABB tree (b2DynamicTree) whose fattened leaf boxes absorb small moves before reinsertion, and whose region queries and ray casts prune candidates before narrow-phase tests.
Location services: Redis geospatial indexes store members as 52-bit geohash scores in a sorted set (GEOADD) so GEOSEARCH answers circle and bounding-box proximity queries server-side instead of scanning members.
GIS and analytics databases: PostGIS prunes radius queries through a GiST spatial index (the index-aware ST_DWithin predicate checks bounding boxes before computing exact distances), and scikit-learn backs radius and k-nearest neighbour queries with KDTree and BallTree instead of all-pairs distances.

name: data-locality
document:
data-locality
data-oriented design
cache-friendly layout
structure of arrays
SoA
AoS to SoA transformation
Arrange data so the values a loop will process next are already in the cache lines it has fetched - contiguous arrays of values in processing order instead of pointer-linked objects, handles instead of references, hot fields separated from cold - so a hot loop streams through CPU cache instead of stalling on a fresh main-memory access per element.
A performance-critical loop is bound by memory latency rather than its own instructions: the data it touches is scattered across the heap - the container holds pointers, each object points at its own separately allocated fields or components, and every dereference lands on a cache line that must first be fetched from RAM, so the CPU idles while the prefetcher chases an unpredictable path. The recurring decision is whether the physical layout follows the class hierarchy (objects owning references) or the order and frequency in which the code processes the data (packed arrays addressed by index).
Applies when a hot loop processes many similar items and profiling shows that cache misses, not the algorithm, dominate its time - entity/component updates in games and simulations, particle and physics systems, bulk numeric processing, and data pipelines in C, C++, Rust, Go, and managed runtimes where the object model (headers, boxing, GC movement) has to be bypassed deliberately. It is a measured trade of abstraction for throughput, not a default style.
Entity/component systems (ECS): one packed array per component type with entity ids as handles, so each update system sweeps one contiguous array per domain. Archetype-based ECS (Unity DOTS, Flecs, Bevy) further groups entities sharing the same component set into columnar tables, enabling O(1) component lookup and streaming traversal — empirically measured to yield higher frame rates and better frame stability than object-oriented layouts for large entity counts.
Particle systems and physics: a fixed pool of particle records with active elements kept in the front of the array, so the integration loop has no branch and no gaps. GPU physics kernels follow the same principle: threads in a warp access adjacent particle data, maximizing memory coalescing on the device.
Frame-critical rendering and UI lists: transform, visibility and bounding-volume data in parallel arrays so culling walks contiguous spans instead of a tree of objects. This is the layout underlying tiled rendering, frustum culling, and LOD selection in modern game engines.
Numeric kernels and analytics: columnar/struct-of-arrays layouts that scan a field at a time and vectorize (SIMD) without padding waste. Database column stores (Apache Arrow, Parquet) are the canonical production instance: analytical queries that aggregate one column across millions of rows get maximum cache reuse and SIMD throughput.
Interop and I/O paths: packed record arrays or typed-array views over one buffer shared with native code, a file mapping, or the GPU, avoiding per-object marshalling. Memory-mapped files, GPU upload buffers, and zero-copy network rings (DPDK, io_uring) all require flat, cache-aligned record layouts.
Real-time audio DSP: sample buffers processed in fixed-size blocks with hot sample values in contiguous arrays; vectorizable EQ, compression and reverb kernels that process thousands of samples per loop iteration without pointer chasing.
Network packet processing: flow tables and ring buffers in network stacks (Linux kernel AF_XDP, DPDK) store per-flow state in contiguous arrays indexed by packet header fields, turning flow classification into an array lookup rather than a hash-map traversal.
Sparse-set ECS in C++ (EnTT): each component pool keeps its entities and components in paged packed arrays, so a view iterates a compact contiguous span, groups can additionally own their columns for raw-pointer iteration, and page size is a tuning knob that trades pointer stability against strict contiguity.
Columnar analytics formats (Apache Arrow): the Arrow columnar specification prescribes 8- or 64-byte aligned buffers - 64-byte padding preferred to match wide SIMD registers - and a pointer/offset layout that is relocatable without pointer swizzling, so record batches can be scanned zero-copy in shared memory.
Unity Entities (DOTS): entities sharing the same component set are stored together in 16KB archetype chunks with one dense column per component type, and Burst-compiled systems iterate those columns - a commercial production form of the packed-array-per-component design.

name: update-method
document:
update-method
per-frame update
tick method
Give every live object one self-contained per-frame step and let a single driver call each object's step every frame, so behaviour advances one frame at a time while input and rendering stay responsive.
A running world is full of objects that each have to keep doing their own thing - guards patrolling, statues charging, agents acting - and the recurring decision is where one object's per-frame behaviour lives and how all those behaviours get driven. Coding a behaviour as a loop that runs to completion blocks input and rendering (the skeleton walks, but nobody sees it); coding it inline in the game loop turns the loop into a switchboard over every kind of object, so every new behaviour edits central code; and there is no way for two actors to evolve independently and simultaneously.
Real-time software with many concurrent live objects whose behaviour is mostly independent and must be simulated over time: games, agent-based simulations, animation and particle systems, tick-based servers and live visualisations. It is the natural partner of a frame driver (Game Loop) - the loop supplies the cadence, Update Method supplies the per-object step - and it becomes the wrong shape in turn-based or purely event-driven domains where nothing changes between inputs.
Real-time games and simulations with many concurrent actors: patrolling guards, projectiles, particle effects and crowd agents each advance themselves once per frame while the driver walks the collection.
Component-based engines where the parts of one entity evolve independently - rendering, physics and AI components each implement their own step and the engine's registry dispatches per component (Unity, MonoGame, Bevy, GameplayKit, libGDX).
Per-frame animation and effect timelines outside games: tween/spring systems, sprite animation and UI transitions advanced from the browser's frame callback or a UI toolkit's animation timer.
Tick-based servers and headless simulations: game servers, digital twins and agent-based models where each agent's behaviour is a resumable step and the world advances in whole discrete frames.
Tools, editors and dashboards with continuously animating scenes, where many independent scene items (markers, live charts, gizmos) must advance on every repaint without a central per-item switch.
Porting straight-line behaviour into a frame loop: turning a scripted sequence (walk left, walk right) into a per-frame step, either by storing explicit state or by using coroutines/generators to keep the code linear.
Godot's SceneTree is the driver: a node opts into the walk with set_process(true) and its _process(delta) runs every render frame with the frame time passed in as an argument, while _physics_process(delta) is called at a fixed rate - so one object can implement two steps on two clocks and can leave the walk entirely (set_process(false)) instead of paying an enabled-flag check every frame.
Engines whose built-in driver leaves per-object order unspecified expose the order as configuration: Unity states you should not rely on the order of Update across GameObjects, so real projects fix dependencies through the Script Execution Order panel, a LateUpdate pass that runs after every Update, or the PlayerLoop API rather than through registration order.
Agent-based simulation models step whole populations in NetLogo: the go procedure runs ask turtles [ ... ] to give every agent its one turn and then tick advances the discrete clock - with documented semantics that agents take their turns in random order and only agents present when the ask began get to act.

name: strategy
document:
strategy
policy
Define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one behind a common operation, and make them interchangeable, so the algorithm a context executes can vary independently of the context and its clients - including at run time.
One class supports several variants of the same computation - sort orders, pricing or tax rules, routing and backoff policies, compression codecs - and the variant has to be selected at run time. Hard-wiring the variants into the class (or into one subclass per variant) mixes algorithm detail with the class's own logic, forces recompilation for every new variant, and turns selection into a growing conditional that runs on every call.
Applies when one context object owns the data but delegates one algorithm (or a small set of related algorithms) to a pluggable implementation, when the implementations share a stable operation signature, and when the choice is made at run time - from user input, configuration, request data or deployment - or from a closed family of variants that already differ in space/time or accuracy trade-offs. Typical homes: pricing, discount and tax calculation; sorting and comparison orders; routing, load-balancing, retry/backoff and rate-limiting policies; compression, serialization and encoding codecs; validation and normalization rules; numerical solvers chosen per problem.
Pricing, discount and tax calculation where the rule set is selected per customer, region or campaign and changes independently of the checkout or invoicing flow.
Sorting and comparison orders chosen by context - a UI column, a request parameter, a locale - which is how the JDK uses the pattern for Comparator in Collections.sort/List.sort and how C uses it for qsort's comparison function.
Routing and policy selection: path finding, load balancing, retry/backoff and rate-limiting algorithms chosen from configuration without editing the caller.
Compression, serialization and encoding codecs (gzip/deflate/zstd, JSON/Protobuf, character encodings) selected per stream, per record or per request.
Validation and normalization rule sets for pluggable document or form types, where each variant knows its own schema quirks and error format.
Numerical and scientific kernels: integration, interpolation or solver algorithms chosen per problem with different accuracy/performance trade-offs.
Pluggable authentication/authorization or hashing policies chosen per tenant, where the same code path must run different algorithms behind one signature.
E-commerce shipping provider selection (UPS, FedEx, DHL) where each carrier implements a different rate-calculation algorithm, and the shipping calculator is decoupled from the carrier specifics.
Payment processing gateways (credit card, virtual account, wallet) where each method has distinct validation, fee calculation and settlement rules, but the checkout flow is uniform.
Data retrieval at runtime: selecting between an API client, a web scraper, a database query or a cache-first lookup depending on availability, cost or latency requirements.
ML inference: choosing between ONNX, TensorRT, CPU or GPU backends for model execution, each with different latency/throughput trade-offs, selected per request or per deployment environment.
Travel and navigation: routing algorithms (walking, cycling, driving, public transit) with distinct distance/time/transfer calculations, chosen by user preference or real-time conditions.
Hybrid AI systems: combining symbolic decision logic with sub-symbolic ML model inference behind a uniform interface, enabling runtime selection of the reasoning strategy.
Log routing: dispatching log events to different backends (file, console, cloud observability platforms) selected by deployment environment or tenant configuration.
Encryption and cipher suites: selecting TLS cipher suites, password hashing algorithms (bcrypt, argon2), or encoding schemes based on security policy and compliance requirements.
File format processing: parsing and rendering strategies for documents, images, or data files where each format requires different handling but the pipeline remains uniform.
Game AI: selecting enemy behavior algorithms (aggressive, defensive, evasive, patrol) per entity type or difficulty level, enabling runtime personality changes.
Apache Kafka producers select or replace the partition-selection algorithm through the org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.Partitioner interface (default sticky/key-hash, RoundRobinPartitioner for even distribution), configured per producer via partitioner.class.
Envoy proxy chooses one load balancing algorithm per upstream cluster from the envoy.load_balancing_policies extension category (ROUND_ROBIN, LEAST_REQUEST and third-party policies), each implementing one host-selection operation behind the cluster's router call path.
scikit-learn estimators expose interchangeable optimization algorithms behind one fit/predict API via the solver parameter (LogisticRegression: lbfgs, liblinear, saga, newton-cg, newton-cholesky), documented as a choice driven by dataset size and penalty rather than by a different client interface.

name: deadline-propagation
document:
deadline-propagation
timeout propagation
Bound the total time and work of a logical request by carrying one deadline through its whole call tree: every hop forwards the remaining budget and the cancellation signal instead of inventing a fresh timeout, so work that can no longer succeed is abandoned at every level.
A request fans out into a chain or tree of downstream calls and each hop applies its own timeout: the end-to-end latency budget becomes the sum of N independent timeouts, servers keep working after the originating client has given up, and cancellation never reaches the deeper work - resources are consumed producing answers nobody will read.
Networked request handling with multi-hop calls: RPC and HTTP chains, service meshes, gateways, fan-out and hedged requests. It applies when one latency budget is meaningful for the whole logical request (an SLO or a user-facing timeout), when the hops are under your control and can carry request-scoped state (context, token, signal, call option or header), and when downstream work is cancellable or can be interrupted at checkpoints.
Microservice request chains (gateway -> frontend service -> several backends) under one user-facing latency SLO, where each hop converts the inbound deadline into its own outgoing calls.
gRPC services whose clients set a deadline and whose servers propagate it as a remaining timeout to downstream calls while cancelling server-side work once the deadline passes.
Fan-out and aggregation endpoints calling several backends in parallel: every sub-call shares the parent budget, and sub-calls still running when it expires are cancelled instead of awaited.
Hedged requests: the first replica to answer wins, and the duplicate requests are cancelled through the same carrier so their downstream work is stopped too.
Streaming and long-poll endpoints that must stop processing when the client disconnects or the connection times out, propagating that stop to services and storage.
Batch or pipeline steps with a per-request time budget that must check the remaining time before each stage and abandon a request that can no longer be finished in time.
ROS 2 / DDS-based robotics pipelines: autonomous vehicle perception pipelines where sensor data must traverse a chain of processing nodes (detect -> classify -> plan -> act) and missed deadlines invalidate downstream results entirely.
Distributed real-time databases with multi-hop queries (gateway -> shard router -> storage node -> index node) where each hop's latency budget is derived from a user-facing SLA.
Service mesh sidecar configurations (Istio/Linkerd/Envoy) where per-route timeout policies propagate deadline context to application code via headers like grpc-timeout or custom X-Request-Deadline headers.
Industrial IoT and edge computing pipelines (edge gateway -> fieldbus bridge -> PLC -> sensor) where end-to-end control loop deadlines must be enforced across heterogeneous network boundaries.
GraphQL federation: a federated query hitting multiple subgraphs in parallel must bound the total resolution time and cancel subgraph requests whose partial results can no longer affect the final response.
Go services on the standard library context package: context.WithDeadline and WithTimeout derive a child whose Done channel closes at the earliest of its own deadline, an explicit cancel, or the parent's cancellation, so cancelling the root request context tears down the whole goroutine tree, and WithDeadlineCause/WithTimeoutCause attach an explicit cause for attribution.
Envoy router filter in service meshes: Envoy sets x-envoy-expected-rq-timeout-ms on internal requests - derived from x-envoy-upstream-rq-timeout-ms or the route timeout - so upstream services can read the expected total completion time and exit early instead of finishing work the proxy has already timed out.
ASP.NET Core gRPC services map the inbound call's deadline onto the handler's CancellationToken; passing that token to database queries, HttpClient calls and Task.Delay stops server-side work the moment the client's deadline expires.

name: typestate
document:
typestate
type state
typestate programming
Encode an object's state in its type - a type parameter or a distinct state type - so that only the operations legal in the current state exist and every transition is a checked, type-changing step.
An object's methods are valid only in certain states (a closed file cannot be read, a client that has not connected cannot send), but the state lives in a runtime field: callers must remember the protocol, illegal calls still compile and fail at run time, and the legal sequences are documented rather than enforced.
Statically typed languages with generics or usable distinct-type support, where a small, fixed set of states and legal transitions is known at compile time: protocol handshakes, resource lifecycles (files, sockets, peripherals), staged builders and configuration objects, and single-owner workflows. It pays where a wrong sequence is expensive - hardware, protocols, money - and the state machine is stable.
Staged builders where build() must not compile before every required property is supplied (typed request builders, configuration objects).
Resource lifecycles: files, sockets and streams whose read/write/close operations are meaningful only after open and before close.
Protocol handshakes - connect, authenticate, exchange, disconnect - including TLS or HTTP session setup and stateful client APIs.
Embedded peripheral configuration: a GPIO pin or timer whose mode (input, output, alternate function) is a type parameter, so wrong-mode register access is a compile error.
Transaction and workflow objects: begin, mutate, commit or roll back, where committing twice or mutating after commit must not be expressible.
Iterators and streams with an exhausted state, where next() consumes the iterator until it yields the end state.
Hardware or network state machines where a wrong sequence causes a fault rather than a catchable error (bus faults, half-open connections).
Embedded HALs in the Rust ecosystem (embedded-hal and device crates such as stm32f4xx-hal) model a pin as Pin<M> with its mode as the type parameter: set_high() compiles only for an output-mode pin and into_input()/into_output() consume the old pin, as prescribed by the Embedded Rust Book's GPIO design chapter.
The Checker Framework for Java runs typestate analysis over unmodified code: its Called Methods and Resource Leak checkers track @MustCall obligations so an InputStream cannot be read before its required initialization methods ran and must be closed on every path - the state is inferred by a checker rather than written into the type.
TypeScript builder libraries such as ts-fluent-builder thread a phantom state type through the builder's generics so build() only compiles once every required property is present, turning missing-field errors from runtime throws into compile errors.

name: option-maybe
document:
option-maybe
Option
Maybe
Make the possible absence of a result part of the value and of the signature, so every caller has to decide what happens when nothing is there instead of meeting a null, a sentinel or a silently defaulted value at run time.
A function has something to return for some inputs and nothing for others, but the signature does not say so: it returns a null reference, a sentinel (-1, empty string, NULL), an out-parameter, or a value that quietly means 'not found'. Callers forget the check, dereference the null or treat the sentinel as data, and the 'this case does not exist' path is discovered in production rather than at the call site.
Lookups, parsing, searches, optional configuration, nullable database columns and any API whose result may legitimately not exist - wherever the language can express absence as a type (Option/Maybe/Optional, a nullable type, a union with undefined) or a convention can carry it. It pays off at module and service boundaries, in chains of partial steps, and wherever 'absent' must stay distinguishable from a legitimate empty, zero or falsey value.
Lookups that can miss: configuration keys, cache entries, registry entries, map/dictionary access - either through the language's two-value form or an Optional-returning accessor.
Parsing and conversion (integers, dates, URLs, decimal numbers, external identifiers) where 'no valid value' is a legitimate answer rather than an error.
Searches over collections and structures (find, first, min/max, binary search, regex match, tree traversal) where a miss is part of the contract.
Genuinely optional data: middle names, second addresses, unset feature flags, optional protocol fields - as opposed to missing state, which is a domain error.
Chains of partial steps (look up user, then their company, then its billing address) where any hop may be absent and the whole chain should collapse to 'nothing'.
Boundaries from nullable interfaces: a database column admits NULL, a legacy or interop API returns null or -1, a deserialized document lacks a field - converted once at the adapter.
Container and stream operations that can be empty (head, pop, next, dequeue, min) and should report emptiness instead of throwing or returning a sentinel.
Rust's standard library uses std::option::Option<T> with Some(T) and None for optional values; its map and pattern-matching APIs let lookup or parsing pipelines stop at absence without a null pointer.
Java SE's java.util.Optional<T> is a production API for method results that may be absent: ofNullable converts a nullable boundary value, map/flatMap compose follow-up work, and orElse/orElseThrow make the exit policy explicit.
Scala's standard-library scala.Option[A] models Some/None and documents map, flatMap, and for-comprehensions for chained partial steps; its API also demonstrates wrapping a Java HashMap lookup so a missing key becomes None.

name: extensible-visitor
document:
extensible-visitor
extensible visitor pattern
extensible visitors with defaults
Keep the visitor open on both axes at once - new element kinds and new operations arrive without editing or recompiling any visitor that already exists - by giving every visitor a default method that catches element kinds it was not written for, introducing extended element kinds under an intermediate base whose accept hooks overload (not override) accept, and extending an operation by subclassing the existing concrete visitor so it inherits every case it already handled.
A classic Visitor is cheap in one direction only: a new operation is a new visitor, but a new element kind forces every visitor to grow one more method, so shipped visitors must be edited and redeployed. The trigger is an element hierarchy that is extended by parties who do not own the operations - language dialects, plugin node types, versioned grammars, third-party message formats - where the existing operations must keep working unchanged on the extended structure.
Recursively defined element hierarchies (abstract syntax trees, intermediate representations, document and message models) that grow over time, in a statically typed language whose visitors are concrete classes or interfaces with default bodies, and where the traversal logic itself lives inside the operations. It pays off when old operations must run against new element kinds and when element kinds are added by a different team than the operations; it assumes the visitor protocol can carry a default case and that a runtime type test is acceptable on the dispatch path.
A compiler front-end whose node kinds are extended by language dialects while every existing analysis pass keeps running unchanged (the extensible-compiler case the pattern was derived from).
An IDE or linter analysing a versioned language grammar: the version-1 analysis must not be recompiled when version 2 adds syntax nodes it does not understand.
Plugin systems where third-party modules contribute new node types (document formats, workflow elements, protocol messages) to a host that ships the operations.
Optimisation or lowering pipelines whose passes are shipped separately from the node hierarchy: the platform team adds representations, users add passes.
A published visitor API where other teams implement visitors and the element set grows every release, making 'which kinds does this visitor handle' an explicit, versioned contract.
Migration and validation tooling that must keep working on messages produced by newer producers than the tool itself.
Serialization and schema-generation frameworks such as Jackson's JsonFormatVisitor API, which uses a visitor to traverse Java type hierarchies for JSON/XML schema generation and allows third-party serializers to contribute handlers for new POJO shapes without modifying the core framework.
Query engines over tree-structured data (e.g. Apache Calcite's relational algebra, Rascal's AST analysis): new relational operators or AST node types are contributed by extension modules while existing optimisers and evaluators continue to function unchanged.
Static analysis and bug-finding tools (Coverity, CodeQL, ESLint plugin architectures): new checker plugins add new node-type coverage while the core traversal engine ships unchanged, and old checkers degrade gracefully over unknown node types.
Game engine entity-component systems: new component types are contributed at runtime while existing systems (physics, rendering, AI) continue to process entities; the visitor with default case handles component types added after a given system was written.
Python's ast.NodeVisitor: visit() dispatches to a visit_<Node> method and falls back to generic_visit as the built-in default case, so analysis tools written before newer node kinds existed (Match, TryStar, TypeAlias) keep traversing Python's evolving AST unchanged, exactly the degrade-don't-break contract of the pattern.
The JDK Compiler Tree API (com.sun.source.tree.TreeVisitor / SimpleTreeVisitor): every visit method defaults to visitOther/defaultAction as the catch-all, so javac-based tooling written against Java 8 trees keeps compiling and running as Java adds records, patterns and switch labels - old visitors land in visitOther instead of failing.
Roslyn's CSharpSyntaxVisitor / CSharpSyntaxWalker: the generated visitor carries one Visit method per syntax node kind plus DefaultVisit as the default case, and each C# language version extends the node hierarchy while existing analysers and the compiler's own passes keep working over the extended tree.

name: stub
document:
stub
test stub
stub object
Replace a collaborator with a test-specific stand-in that returns canned answers, so the component under test can be driven down paths - success, empty, error, timeout - that the real collaborator cannot be made to produce on demand.
The component under test receives indirect inputs through a collaborator, and the branch that must be exercised is selected by what that collaborator returns. The real collaborator will not produce the needed value on request: it is slow, remote, licensed, non-deterministic, or simply never returns the rare case - the empty result, the declined payment, the timeout - that the test exists for. Without a controllable replacement the test either cannot reach the path at all or has to provoke it through the production system, which is exactly what unit testing was supposed to avoid.
Unit and component tests of a component whose collaborators are already, or can cheaply become, abstractions: the values and exceptions a collaborator returns are inputs to the component under test, and the test asserts what the component does with them rather than how the collaboration happened. Typical where the collaborator is remote or stateful (HTTP client, database, queue, clock, payment gateway) or where the branch under test is an edge case - empty page, declined payment, expired token, feature off. The pattern assumes a substitutable seam: a constructor parameter, an injected interface, a factory, a lookup, or a patchable module.
Exercising a rare branch of the component: an empty result set, a declined payment, a 429 from a gateway, a missing feature flag.
Testing error handling: programme the stub to raise the exception the real service would raise - timeout, connection reset, malformed payload - and assert that the SUT surfaces or recovers from it.
Unit-testing a component against a collaborator that is slow, paid, unavailable in CI or still being implemented; the stub encodes the agreed response while the real adapter is built.
Removing non-determinism from a path the real collaborator decides by clock, randomness or remote state (token expired, cache cold, retry budget exhausted), so one outcome can be asserted exactly.
View and presentation tests: a fixed dataset from the stub, so the assertion is about the rendering or the decision logic and nothing else.
Boundary values on contract edges - zero, maximum, empty string, unicode payloads - that the real system cannot be asked to return on demand.
Mockito (Java): when(warehouse.hasInventory(...)).thenReturn(false) programmes the declined-branch answer and thenThrow(SocketTimeoutException.class) injects the failure, and consecutive-value stubbing (thenReturn(v1, v2)) drives retry-then-succeed paths that the real warehouse would never produce on request.
Python unittest.mock (standard library): Mock(return_value=...) fixes the canned answer while side_effect set to an exception or an iterable raises or sequences answers per call - the library ships Responder and Saboteur behaviour as first-class configuration.
Moq (.NET): mock.Setup(x => x.HasInventory(...)).Returns(false) and .Throws<InvalidOperationException>() are the canned-answer primitives, so a C# test reaches the empty-inventory and fault branches of Order.Fill without touching a database.

name: audit-interceptor
document:
audit-interceptor
audit trail interceptor
audit logging interceptor
Declare an audit policy at an invocation seam that records the actor, action, target, correlation id and both attempt and terminal outcome around a delegated operation, then sends the structured event to a dedicated integrity-protected sink, so security accountability is consistent without inline logging in every service.
Security-relevant operations (privileged actions, state changes and access to sensitive data) must be attributable, but inline logging misses denied and failed attempts, varies in schema, can leak raw arguments and disappears with a rolled-back transaction. Teams also need to cover components they cannot modify without pretending that a proxy sees calls that bypass it.
Business or service tiers whose sensitive operations pass through an interceptable seam: container-managed beans, proxied service objects, ORM entity lifecycles, message endpoints or an HTTP pipeline. Audit selection must be declarative and uniform, while the sink has its own integrity and retention requirements (Secure Logger); the design must make mediation gaps, redaction, transaction coupling, failure policy, clock source and correlation propagation explicit.
Business-tier auditing of money-moving or otherwise regulated operations (fund transfer, order placement, claim submission): who requested it, on which object, when, and whether it succeeded.
Privileged administration surfaces (role changes, key rotation, configuration changes) where every sensitive operation must leave a record naming the acting principal.
Authentication and authorization outcomes: successful and failed logins, access-denial decisions and lockouts routed into the same audit pipeline instead of ad-hoc log lines.
Access-to-sensitive-data events (who read which patient/customer record) recorded at the gateway or service boundary to satisfy data-protection obligations.
Retrofitting auditing onto legacy components whose code cannot be modified, by wrapping the service object or binding an interceptor to its interface.
Middleware-level auditing of message endpoints and database calls in a business tier, correlating the caller's subject with the operation performed.
Financial API request interception (Spring Boot global request interceptors) capturing who accessed which endpoint, with what payload, and what outcome — satisfying SOX financial reporting controls.
Entity-level change tracking via ORM subscribers (e.g., EF Core SaveChangesInterceptor, TypeORM subscribers): automatically diff old vs. new property values on create/update/delete and emit audit envelopes without manual logging calls.
API gateway-level audit logging: capture every external API call with timestamp, user identity, endpoint, method, and outcome, correlating across microservices via X-Request-ID / traceparent headers.
Compliance reporting automation: generate audit-ready reports for SOX (~7-year retention), HIPAA (~6-year retention), GDPR (data residency-aware), and PCI-DSS from structured interceptor events.
Zero-trust data access trails: record every read of sensitive fields (PHI, PII, financial data) so data-protection obligations (GDPR Article 5 data minimization, HIPAA access logging) are demonstrably met.
Hibernate Envers: @Audited entity lifecycle changes create per-entity _AUD revisions at transaction commit; a custom revision entity/listener can attach actor or request metadata.
Django admin: django.contrib.admin.models.LogEntry records action time, user, object, addition/change/deletion and change_message for ModelAdmin activity.
Rails Audited: the audited ActiveRecord extension creates audit rows for model create, update and destroy callbacks, including changed attributes and optional acting-user attribution.

name: monitor-object
document:
monitor-object
thread-safe passive object
monitor
Serialise concurrent method invocations on a shared object by giving the object its own lock and condition variables, so that only one method executes inside it at a time and methods that cannot proceed wait cooperatively instead of polling.
Objects shared by several threads expose their state through ordinary methods, and nothing stops concurrent callers from interleaving inside those methods, corrupting the invariants they were written to maintain. The race is then papered over with ad-hoc locking, sleeps and busy-wait loops scattered through client code. The recurring decision is whether the object itself should own the serialisation (and the scheduling) of its methods instead of leaving that discipline to every caller.
Shared-memory concurrency, where the mutable state of an object is reached by more than one thread and its methods must be atomic with respect to one another. It matters most when some methods cannot run to completion until another method changes the state - a queue that is full or empty, a resource that is not yet available, a phase that has not been reached - because then a method must suspend and later resume, which requires releasing the lock while it waits.
Bounded buffers and work queues shared by producer and consumer threads, where producers wait while the queue is full and consumers wait while it is empty - the pattern's canonical example.
Session, connection or entity registries on a server, where lookups, insertion and eviction must be atomic and callers may have to wait for capacity or for an entry to reappear.
Caches with in-flight bookkeeping (single-flight computation), where a thread that requests an already-computed key waits for the first thread's result instead of recomputing it.
Shared configuration, counters or statistics objects read and updated by request threads, where each call must observe a consistent snapshot of the state.
State machines and simulators whose step methods block until another thread advances a transition, for example a test harness waiting for a worker to reach a known state.
In-process resource pools (connection, database or worker pools) where acquisition blocks until an entry is returned or a timeout expires.
Java's java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue is a fixed-capacity monitor-style bounded buffer: put blocks while full and take blocks while empty, making the producer-consumer coordination explicit.
.NET's System.Collections.Concurrent.BlockingCollection<T> supplies bounded Add/Take blocking, cancellation and completion semantics around a producer-consumer collection; use it instead of hand-rolling Monitor.Wait/Pulse.
Python's queue.Queue provides a thread-safe multi-producer/multi-consumer boundary with blocking put/get operations and optional timeouts, a standard monitor-style primitive for worker pools.

name: event-aggregator
document:
event-aggregator
event bus
messenger
message bus
event hub
Funnel the events of many source objects into one hub that owns the subscription wiring, so that subscribers register once with the aggregator instead of tracking down and registering with every publisher.
Many components raise events and many components want to react: if every consumer registers directly with every producer, each consumer has to find the sources and subscribe to each event type separately, each producer accumulates knowledge of who listens, and both sides repeat the same registration and unsubscribe code at every pair. The trigger is a many-publisher / many-subscriber setting in which the wiring itself has become the maintenance problem.
In-process, event-driven software - a modular UI shell, a domain-event pipeline inside one bounded context, a plugin host, a simulation or instrumentation layer - where publishers and subscribers grow independently, both sides should stay unaware of each other, and registration plus lifetime management should live in one place. The aggregator is a component- or module-scope element of one process (one node); events that must cross a process boundary, survive a restart or be delivered reliably need a messaging channel instead.
Modular UI shells (WPF/MAUI, Android, SwiftUI) where view models living in separate modules must react to each other without holding references — the classic Prism and CommunityToolkit.Mvvm scenario.
Domain-event fan-out inside one bounded context: 'order placed' reaches billing, stock, notification and audit services that each subscribe to the hub instead of to the Order aggregate.
Plugin, extension or rule hosts where the listener set is only known at runtime and plugins are loaded and unloaded while the application runs.
Test and simulation harnesses: a test subscribes to the hub, drives one publisher and asserts on the published events without wiring up the real consumers.
Cross-cutting instrumentation and audit: metrics, tracing, logging and audit collectors receive events from many components through one hub rather than being called from each component.
Long-running services broadcasting rare state changes (configuration reload, presence change, feature-flag flip) to every interested subsystem exactly once per change.
Micro-frontend communication: independent web apps in one page communicating via a shared event bus with typed event maps and cross-tab synchronization (BroadcastChannel bridge).
IoT sensor aggregation: many sensor streams funnelled through one hub for filtering, transformation and fan-out to display or downstream processing services.
CQRS command/event pipeline: commands are dispatched to handlers that publish domain events through a bus; read-model projectors subscribe to build consistent query views.
Redux/Flux-style frontend state updates where UI components subscribe to dispatched actions rather than mutating shared state directly.
Event storm prevention harness: wrapping a batch save operation in a scoped subscriber-disable guard so that handlers triggered by the save do not re-publish events that would cascade back through the same handler.
Transactional outbox companion: publishing domain events through the hub after a transaction commits, ensuring that state changes and event emission are not separated by a process crash (in-process equivalent of the outbox pattern).
Java in-JVM decoupling with Guava EventBus: objects register via @Subscribe-annotated methods and publishers post typed events that the bus routes by parameter type (superclasses and interfaces included), with unmatched events wrapped as DeadEvent for a second-chance subscriber.
Spring application-context event pipeline: beans publish through ApplicationEventPublisher and react via @EventListener methods - in-process domain-event fan-out with the ApplicationEventMulticaster owning the registry, no message broker involved.
Vue 2 cross-component communication through a shared root instance used as a global bus ($on/$emit); Vue 3 removed that instance-emitter API, making external typed emitters like mitt, provide/inject, or a store (Pinia) the supported replacement - a cautionary real-world case for untyped global buses.
