name: composite-entity
document:
composite-entity
coarse-grained-entity
Represent a cluster of related, dependent objects through one coarse-grained entity that owns them and persists and synchronises the whole graph as a single unit of work, so clients never reference, sequence, or save the parts themselves. Coined for coarse-grained EJB business objects; its modern form is the aggregate root with cascading or owned mappings.
A business concept clients treat as one thing (an order with its lines, a customer with addresses) is really a cluster of dependent objects, and persisting each part separately forces callers to know the parts, save them in the right order in the right transaction, delete the ones that left the relationship, and absorb a leaking physical schema. The catalog trigger: a cluster of related objects must persist and synchronise as one unit.
Relational or document stores where a coarse-grained business object is composed of finer-grained dependent objects whose lifecycle is bound to it. Applies when clients - especially remote ones - should exchange one coarse-grained structure instead of the parts, when the persist/synchronise boundary must coincide with one transaction, and when each dependent can still own its own mapping. Modern form: an aggregate root mapped with cascading associations or with components stored in the root's own row.
Order with line items, shipment addresses and payment allocations that must be written and deleted as one business unit.
Customer or account aggregate holding addresses, contact methods and preferences that are edited in one form and saved once.
Document-style clusters (invoice with revisions, article with embedded sections) where the parts only exist inside the root.
Legacy-style coarse-grained entity beans that wrap fine-grained POJOs so that clients exchange one composite transfer object instead of many fine-grained ones.
Mobile or remote clients that must send one coarse-grained payload per edit instead of a sequence of dependent calls.
Batch imports where a cluster is validated and written transactionally, so a partially imported entity never exists.
DDD Bounded Contexts where one aggregate encapsulates a complete business invariant enforced across multiple related entities — e.g., a Rental aggregate containing a rental agreement, reserved vehicle, and driver assignment that must all be created or fail together.
CQRS write models where the aggregate is the sole write target and all state changes flow through the root's command methods, ensuring every mutation is a coherent cluster-level operation.
Event sourcing snapshots where the aggregate root serialises its entire graph so that snapshot restore reconstructs the full composite in one operation rather than re-playing individual dependent events.
Legacy system facades that wrap a network of fine-grained remote beans behind a single coarse-grained composite interface, collapsing many remote calls into one round-trip for external clients.
SQLAlchemy parent-child clusters mapped with cascade='all, delete-orphan' on relationship(): disassociating a child deletes the row, so the Session flushes the cluster as one unit without per-child Session.delete() calls.
EF Core owned types: dependent types stored in the owner's table (or as owned navigations) share the aggregate root's identity and save with a single context.SaveChanges().
Mongoose subdocument arrays: embedded parts are saved, validated and removed through the top-level document, so the cluster's lifecycle is bound to the root document's save.

statement: Maintain routing rules in reloadable configuration so destinations and traffic allocations can change while the running gateway continues processing messages.
name: dynamic-router
document:
dynamic-router
dynamic routing
rules-based routing
Route each message to a destination chosen from a rule base that can be changed while the system runs, so the router never depends on - or is redeployed for - the set of destinations it serves.
Routing logic hard-coded into the router (switch chains, static filter tables, deployment-time route configuration) couples it to every destination: adding, moving, throttling or retiring a destination needs a code change, a review and a restart, and each topology change forces the router back through the release process instead of being an operational edit.
Message-based integration where the destination set or the routing policy changes faster than the router's release cycle: rules are owned by operations, destinations announce themselves, scale out, or go down for maintenance, or one router instance serves several tenants or environments. Applies when the route can be expressed as rules over message content, headers or context evaluated per message, and the platform offers a usable control channel (config watch, control bus, admin endpoint, hot-reloadable table) to publish rule changes.
Multi-tenant integration hub: each tenant has its own routing table, loaded and swapped per tenant instead of one deployed router per tenant.
Event distribution where downstream teams add or retire consumers by publishing routing conditions rather than requesting a router release.
Canary and blue/green rollouts: send a slice of traffic to a new destination by editing a rule, and roll back by restoring the previous rule set.
Maintenance windows: reroute a destination's traffic to a standby, drain the destination, then restore the rule when it returns.
Regional or sharded routing where the region-to-destination mapping is maintained by operations and changes with capacity, not with code.
Rule-driven enterprise integration in the classic EIP sense, where a rule base is consulted per message and recipients announce themselves on a control channel.
Kubernetes Gateway API traffic splitting: use HTTPRoute weighted backends to shift a configurable percentage of traffic between versions without redeploying the router.
Service mesh canary deployments: an Istio VirtualService or Linkerd ServiceProfile acts as the rule base; routing rules are edited at runtime to steer canary traffic, then promoted or rolled back.
Multi-tenant SaaS routing: Spring Cloud Gateway or Envoy.DynamicRouter loads per-tenant routing rules from a registry, injecting tenant-specific headers or rewrites so one router instance serves hundreds of isolated tenants.
API version routing and A/B testing: route by Accept header, API version path prefix, or experimentCohort header to different backend versions, controlled by rules updated without a release.
Database or cache sharding: route a tenant or user ID hash to the correct shard's endpoint via a rule table that is repointed during resharding without touching application code.
BGP route-server testing: use a chaos-testing framework against a route server to validate that policy changes converge correctly and do not produce route leaks before production deployment.
Traefik dynamic configuration: Traefik builds its routing table at runtime from providers (Docker labels, Kubernetes IngressRoute, Consul/etcd KV stores), so services announce their own routes and rule changes hot-swap without restarting the proxy.
HAProxy Runtime API: add server and set server state/weight over the runtime socket repoint and drain backends without a reload; the Data Plane API layers persistence and validation on top of these runtime changes.
Kong Gateway admin API: Routes - including the expressions DSL when router_flavor is set to expressions - are created and updated at runtime via POST /routes and take effect on the next matching request, with priority-ordered rule evaluation replacing a redeployed config.

statement: Maintain routing rules in reloadable configuration so destinations and traffic allocations can change while the running gateway continues processing messages.
name: content-based-router
document:
content-based-router
content router
content-based routing
CBR
Route each message to the one destination whose consumer can handle it, by evaluating the message's own content against explicit routing rules, so the decision lives in a single maintained routing component instead of being re-derived by every receiver.
One logical input stream carries work belonging to several different back-ends - orders per region, events per type, requests per priority - and destination and content are merely correlated, not addressable from each other. The producer would have to know the whole topology and pre-sort its output, every new destination makes that pre-sorting more wrong, and each receiver ends up re-inspecting the payload to decide whether the message is even for it.
Message-based integration - in-process pipelines, broker topologies, API edges - where several destinations exist for one logical message type and the choice depends on data the message itself carries (a discriminator field, a region code, an amount threshold, a priority header), while the rules themselves are fixed at build or configuration time. If the rules must change per message or at runtime without a redeployment, the pattern to reach for is the Dynamic Router, not this one.
Regional or tenant routing: one order stream split per region or tenant because each back-end owns its own data and must not see the others'.
Classification in a canonical pipeline: invoices to finance, cancellations to a reversal service, high-value orders to manual review, everything else to standard fulfilment.
Partner or protocol edge: each partner dialect or payload version is dispatched to a version-specific handler, so a legacy handler keeps receiving exactly its shape.
Priority routing: messages whose content indicates an SLA breach or a premium customer bypass the bulk queue and go to the expedited channel.
Broker-level dispatch: AMQP headers exchanges, JMS message selectors and Service Bus subscription rules implement the pattern inside the broker so the application never sees the irrelevant traffic.
Event fan-in in an in-process pipeline: one stream of heterogeneous commands is dispatched to the branch that handles each kind, keeping every branch's contract narrow.
Unroutable-message handling: content no rule recognises is sent to an inspection channel instead of being retried forever against a destination that cannot process it.
Multi-cloud or multi-region routing: based on message attributes (e.g., data residency requirements, x-region header), messages are routed to region-specific processing endpoints or cloud-specific backends.
Regulatory routing: messages containing specific data categories (PII, financial, health) are routed to compliance-mandated processing or audit destinations; for example, PCI-DSS scoped messages to a secure lane, HIPAA-scoped messages to a PHI-compliant processor.
API Gateway tenant routing: SaaS or multi-tenant APIs route incoming requests to tenant-specific backends based on API keys, tenant IDs in JWTs, or header values (e.g., x-tenant-id → tenant-specific upstream).
Event mesh distribution: in a distributed event mesh, events of different schemas or domain origins are routed to appropriate consumer groups based on event type or source system; for example, domain events routed to domain-specificSaga State Machines.
Log and telemetry fan-out: observability pipelines route logs or traces to different destinations (SIEM, data lake, real-time analytics) based on severity, service name, or environment.
GraphQL operation routing: requests are routed to different backend services based on the GraphQL operation type or name in the request body (e.g., mutations to a write service, queries to a read service) - useful when the gateway cannot determine the target from the URL alone.
gRPC method routing: in microservices using gRPC, the router inspects the :path or :method headers to route to the appropriate backend service when a single gRPC gateway fronts multiple backend packages.
Istio/Envoy service mesh traffic shaping: VirtualService HTTP match rules route requests to specific service subsets (v1 vs v2) based on custom headers, enabling canary deployments and progressive traffic shifts without application-level routing logic.
AWS API Gateway routing: regional REST APIs route requests to different Lambda functions or ECS services based on the request body, headers, or HTTP method, enabling a single API endpoint to serve multiple backend implementations.
Kafka Streams substream split by event field — one input topic split into per-genre output topics using split().branch(pred, Branched.withConsumer(ks -> ks.to(...))), with a literal true catch-all branch as the explicit default (Confluent vendor tutorial).
Dynamic branches generated from a closed enum in Kafka Streams — one branch per RecordType value built in a loop, so the routing table is derived from the enum rather than hand-written string comparisons.
Enrich-then-route pattern with Kafka Streams — orders joined with a GlobalKTable of customer data, then routed to platinum/gold/silver/bronze topics by loyalty level, so the decision uses external data without putting a lookup inside the router.
Ballerina healthcare appointment routing — a single REST resource receives a reservation payload and routes on hospital_id to three hospital back-ends, keeping each backend unaware of the front door (official WSO2 integration tutorial).
Ballerina partner/county tracking routing — a tracking request routed by a typed union (UK/DE) to two different carrier APIs with different response shapes, the wildcard case returning an error rather than silently mapping to a default destination (official Ballerina EIP page).
NServiceBus command routing by assembly/namespace/type — RouteToEndpoint at the type level selects the destination endpoint from the message's declared identity, with per-type routes overriding namespace routes overriding assembly routes.
NServiceBus periodically refreshed route table as data — a FeatureStartupTask timer calls UnicastRoutingTable.AddOrReplaceRoutes so centralized or DB-driven route information updates without redeploying the endpoint.
MassTransit per-message destination resolution — AddMessageRoute<T>((provider, message) => new Uri(...)) computes the queue from the message instance at send time, enabling a slow-lane queue under load.
MassTransit routing slip for per-transaction itineraries — a routing slip built per transaction with payment method, billing address and customer preferences as the routing data, combined with saga state machines for monitoring and compensation.
Camel route-template + precondition deploy-time branch — one parameterized route family where the branch is selected from property placeholders at route initialization, contrasted with content-based when() predicates evaluated per message.
AWS SNS payload-based routing with FilterPolicyScope: MessageBody — a single REST endpoint dispatches to Lambda functions or SQS queues based on nested JSON payload fields, with separate metrics for unmatched versus malformed payloads.
Azure Event Grid advanced data-field filters on detail.* fields — routing Blob storage events by container name or numeric operators (NumberIn, NumberLessThan) without parsing the full event body.
Amazon EventBridge event-bus pattern matching on event metadata and detail body fields — one event bus receives events from multiple sources, with rules dispatching to different targets based on source, detail-type and detail.state, with the Sandbox for pre-deployment testing.
Azure Service Bus autoforwarding chain for subscription scale-out — a first-level topic with subscriptions forwarding to second-level topics to stay within the 2,000-subscription cap while maintaining per-region routing graphs (4-hop chain limit applies).
Google Cloud Pub/Sub multiple subscription filters on one topic — each subscription carries a different filter expression so different consumer groups receive only relevant events, with non-matching messages auto-acknowledged.
AWS IoT SQL rules over MQTT message streams — messages evaluated via SQL SELECT/WHERE and republished to S3, DynamoDB, SQS, Lambda or Step Functions based on payload content, with Basic Ingest bypassing the broker for cost-sensitive paths.
FHIR R4 subscription-based routing with id-only payloads — routing notifications to clinical systems using only resource IDs rather than full resources, limiting disclosure surface (recommended in FHIR security considerations).
PHI routing to HIPAA-eligible AWS services — SNS, SQS, EventBridge, MSK and Lambda marked as HIPAA-eligible are the only valid destinations for ePHI-bearing messages; the router's destination set encodes compliance eligibility.
Smart order router under best-execution duty — FIX protocol ExDestination field carries the routing decision as an auditable artifact, with the router required to document venue selection rationale per FINRA Rule 5310 and SEC Rule 606 disclosures.
PCI DSS scope reduction via routing into a segmented cardholder data environment — the CBR is the enforcement point that keeps PAN-bearing flows inside the CDE boundary and must avoid writing PANs into rule conditions, logs or routing attributes.
LLM request routing as an economic CBR — RouteLLM-style routers decide per request between a strong and a weak model to cut cost (>2x reported) without degrading quality; routing decisions become statistical and failure modes are quality regressions.
Semantic router for vLLM — a model classifies queries by reasoning requirements and selectively applies reasoning only when beneficial; the discriminator is a learned embedding rather than a header or discriminator field.
Istio fragmented VirtualService with a single catch-all — when a VirtualService is split across resources, only one catch-all rule should exist as all catch-alls are moved to the end of the merged list and whichever is applied first disables the others.
Envoy scoped routing by tenant-derived scope key — a scope key computed from a request header selects an independent route table per tenant, enabling tenant-shaped routing without one growing rule list.
Apache ActiveMQ message selectors — JMS subscriptions filter with SQL-92 expressions over headers and properties (JMSType = 'car' AND color = 'blue' AND weight > 2500), implementing broker-side content-based routing so consumers never see irrelevant traffic; XPath selectors additionally evaluate XML message bodies (official ActiveMQ selectors documentation).
Mule EIP mapping — MuleSoft's official EIP documentation maps Content-Based Router to the Mule Choice router, which evaluates expressions against the message payload and attributes to dispatch each event down exactly one route.

statement: Maintain routing rules in reloadable configuration so destinations and traffic allocations can change while the running gateway continues processing messages.
name: control-bus
document:
control-bus
management bus
control channel
Administer a running message flow through a control bus: a second set of channels that reuses the same messaging mechanism as the application flow but is reserved for management traffic, over which every component receives commands (start, stop, suspend, resume, reconfigure, fail, status) and reports its own state - so a distributed flow gets a single point of control that can be secured, prioritised and audited apart from payload traffic.
Operating a message-based integration system means changing routing rules, throttling or stopping adapters, draining queues, resizing worker pools and collecting status from components spread across processes, hosts and platforms. If every component invents its own management interface, the operator is left with a patchwork of bespoke APIs, credentials and consoles; if management commands are pushed through the application channels, they compete with payload traffic, inherit the same backlog and delivery semantics, and cannot be authorised or audited separately from business messages.
Distributed integration and messaging systems whose components run in separate processes and must be managed at runtime: brokers and channel adapters, routers and pipelines, worker pools and job runners, and cross-platform deployments where the console sits somewhere else entirely. It applies whenever operations need to change behaviour without redeploying (switch steps on and off, adjust limits, drain or stop a component for a deployment) or need status from components that would otherwise be black boxes.
Central console for an integration platform: operators start, stop and suspend routes, adapters and channel connections, and read statistics from every node of the flow.
Deployment and maintenance windows: quiet a worker pool (stop fetching, finish in-flight work), drain channels, run a controlled restart and resume - instead of killing processes.
Dynamic reconfiguration: change routing rules or thresholds, switch a detour (validation, logging, extra transformation) on when needed and off again when latency matters, without a redeploy.
Fleet-wide health and metrics collection: each component publishes liveness, queue depth and throughput over the control bus, and the console or alerting consumes them.
Injecting a test message into the running system to verify that the deployed paths still work end to end, rather than trusting staging alone.
Incident response: quarantine a failing component (stop consuming from a queue), purge a channel, throttle a sender or deliberately fail a route over to a standby path.
Kubernetes operator reconciliation: a custom controller watches CRD spec, compares to actual cluster state, and issues control bus commands (start, stop, scale, configure) to reconcile the gap - the control bus is the operator's API surface.
Service mesh control plane: Istio's istiod or Linkerd's destination service acts as a control bus, pushing proxy configuration (routes, certificates, authorization policies) to sidecar proxies via xDS gRPC streams.
GitOps-driven state propagation: a GitOps operator (Flux, Argo CD) watches a Git repository and issues control bus commands to reconcile the declared desired state with actual running state.
Multi-cluster federated management: a central management plane issues commands to integration components distributed across clusters, regions or cloud boundaries.
Canary deployments and traffic shifting: route specific percentages of traffic through new versions by dynamically updating routing rules across the fleet without redeployment.
Feature flag toggles at the routing layer: enable or disable processing steps across distributed components by sending configuration commands over the control bus.
Batch job orchestration: submit, monitor, pause, and cancel long-running batch workloads across a grid of worker nodes through a centralized control interface.
Secrets rotation at runtime: push updated credentials (certificates, API keys, database passwords) to managed components over the control bus without a restart, enabling zero-downtime credential rotation.
On-demand feature flag activation: enable or disable feature flags at specific routing nodes across the fleet by sending targeted configuration commands, bypassing redeployment.
A/B testing traffic splitting: dynamically update routing weights across endpoints to shift a percentage of traffic to a new version, then roll back if error rates spike.
RabbitMQ Management plugin: the broker's own control bus - an HTTP API, browser UI and rabbitmqadmin CLI that declare, inspect and delete queues, exchanges, bindings, users and vhosts and scrape per-queue and per-node statistics at a configurable interval.
NATS system account: servers publish heartbeats, advisories and connection/metrics events on the reserved $SYS subject hierarchy, isolated in a dedicated system account with its own system-user authorization, giving operators an out-of-band observability and control surface over the cluster.
Envoy xDS: managed proxies keep a bidirectional gRPC stream to a management server (Aggregated Discovery Service), receive versioned Listener/Cluster/Route/Endpoint updates and answer with ACK/NACK - a per-proxy control bus with correlated acknowledgement for the data plane.

statement: Maintain routing rules in reloadable configuration so destinations and traffic allocations can change while the running gateway continues processing messages.
name: pipeline
document:
pipeline
assembly line
processing pipeline
Decompose a transformation into an ordered sequence of named stages that each consume the previous stage's output and produce the next stage's input, so the workflow reads top to bottom and every step can be tested, instrumented, reordered or replaced on its own.
A multi-step transformation is written as one long function or a tangle of nested calls: the steps are unnamed, their order is implicit in statement order, intermediate values need throwaway names, there is no seam at which a single step can be logged, tested or replaced, and the same sequence is retyped at every call site that needs it.
Processing that naturally decomposes into successive transformations of the same payload - request handling, ETL, compiler passes, message enrichment, image or byte-stream processing - whether the payload is a single value or a stream. It fits in-process, staged execution where one driver owns ordering, error handling and cancellation; distributing the stages across processes, transports and independently deployed filters is the architectural pipe-and-filter pattern instead.
Request handling: deserialise, authenticate, validate, enrich, persist and render a request, with each step named so a failing stage is attributable and testable in isolation.
ETL and data import: extract, clean, transform, validate and load large files as a stream, so no intermediate collection is materialised and memory stays bounded.
Compiler and interpreter passes: source, tokens, AST, resolution, optimisation and code emission, where each pass is an independent stage over the intermediate representation and the pass list is the pipeline.
Message enrichment in an integration flow: unwrap, translate, enrich and route a message, one stage per concern, with per-channel ordering; the cross-process version stays pipe-and-filter.
Image or byte-stream processing: decode, crop or resize, watermark and encode, lazily per frame or chunk, optionally overlapping stages across cores.
Configuration-driven data cleaning: the stage list is assembled from configuration or a plugin registry so different tenants get different ordered steps without changing the stages themselves.
TensorFlow tf.data input pipelines: tf.data.Dataset pipelines that chain map, prefetch, parallel_interleave and shuffle stages to feed a training loop efficiently, with each stage independently configurable and the whole pipeline testable in isolation.
LLM token streaming: HTTP server-sent event streams where an LLM produces tokens at inference speed while clients consume at variable network speed; stream.pipeline() prevents the inference server from buffering unbounded tokens in memory when a slow client disconnects (Node.js stream backpressure case study).
Observability telemetry pipelines: OpenTelemetry Collector chains receivers, processors (memory_limiter, batch, filter, transform, tail_sampling) and exporters for traces, metrics and logs, with connectors (e.g., spanmetrics) bridging signal types and memory_limiter placed first to prevent OOM before filtering.
Typed TypeScript pipeline with schema validation: Zod or io-ts schemas define the stage contract at each boundary, catching schema violations at the exact stage that produced bad data rather than at a distant consumer.
Async generator pipelines in Python: asyncio queues with bounded capacity connect async generator stages, propagating backpressure by pausing producers when the queue is full; the FinStream analytics case study showed 82% memory reduction and 99.7% latency reduction versus unbounded buffering.
Event-streaming pipelines with Kafka and Flink: producers, topic partitions, Flink consumers and checkpointing form a distributed pipeline where backpressure cascades across every boundary; the Kafka max.block.ms and Flink backpressure.sample.interval settings interact under partition saturation and must be tested together under load.
Dynamic pipeline parallelism: construct-and-run pipelines (MapReduce, Spark) fix stage count at construction, while on-the-fly pipelines (Cilk-P Piper algorithm) allow the structure to emerge at runtime, varying per iteration and supporting data-dependent branching; on-the-fly enables pipelines like x264 that cannot be expressed with a fixed static structure.
LLVM compiler pass pipelines: PassBuilder assembles ModulePassManager, CGSCCPassManager, FunctionPassManager and LoopPassManager across the IR hierarchy (Module → CGSCC → Function → Loop), with registered callbacks injecting passes at named extension points (pipeline-start, vectorizer-start, optimizer-last); incorrect PreservedAnalyses declarations invalidate all downstream analyses.
Continuous data pipelines at scale (Google model): periodic pipelines run on cron and suffer from depth growth and resource exhaustion as organic load increases; continuous pipelines (master-slave or event-triggered) replace idle-waiting with always-on processing, eliminating the 'pipeline vs cron' discontinuity at the cost of operational complexity.
ML pipeline orchestration (Airflow, Kubeflow, Prefect, Dagster): each orchestrator applies the pipeline pattern at the workflow level - Airflow's DAG-of-tasks, Kubeflow's per-container-step pipelines with GPU scheduling, Prefect's monoflow/subflow/orchestrator pattern, and Dagster's software-defined assets where asset dependencies imply the pipeline; the pipeline is the scheduler's unit of execution, not an implementation detail.
Apache Beam: PCollections flow through composable PTransforms (ParDo, Combine and GroupByKey) in a pipeline graph, making each transform boundary explicit while the runner handles execution.
Node.js stream.pipeline(): Readable, Transform and Writable stages compose with built-in backpressure, error propagation and AbortSignal cancellation; this is a concrete streaming realization, not a durable workflow engine.

name: anti-corruption-layer
document:
anti-corruption-layer
acl
translation layer
Protect a downstream bounded context from a foreign model by making one explicitly owned boundary translate calls, data and failure semantics into the downstream language; unlike a mere wrapper, an anti-corruption layer prevents foreign concepts from becoming domain concepts.
A bounded context must use a legacy application, packaged product, partner API or another context whose model it cannot control, and the same words carry different meanings on each side. Reusing the foreign SDK types and status codes directly makes its names, optionality, units, errors and version churn load-bearing parts of the local domain; translation then drifts across callers and every upstream change becomes a core-model change. Without an explicit boundary, the contexts become accidental conformists and neither can evolve independently.
Use it at a durable integration seam where the models genuinely disagree and at least one side cannot be changed: a new core beside a legacy or packaged system, a core subdomain consuming a third-party service, two bounded contexts with different vocabularies, or a staged migration whose callers must survive a callee replacement. It is a boundary-scoped investment: a model worth protecting must exist on the downstream side, and the seam must be durable enough to own a component; a wire-level rename, a CRUD screen over a stable API or throwaway code does not justify it.
Staged migration (strangler style): a monolith keeps calling a capability that has been extracted into a service, and the layer converts the old call into the new semantics so existing callers are not modified while functionality moves out piece by piece.
Legacy or packaged systems: an ERP, mainframe, CRM or vendor database with convoluted schemas and obsolete protocols is consumed by a new core domain that refuses to adopt its concepts.
Third-party services inside a core subdomain: a payment, identity or logistics API whose model must not shape your domain — its statuses, optionality and error codes are mapped to your own types.
Two bounded contexts in one product: the upstream team publishes a model your context rejects (conformist would be too costly), so your side translates it and the context map records the relationship.
Event-driven integration: upstream events are translated, validated and re-emitted as downstream domain events before any handler in the core sees them.
Standardised external formats: EDI, ISO 20022, FHIR or partner schemas are parsed into a local model inside the layer, keeping the standard's vocabulary out of the domain.
Replacing an infrastructure dependency: swapping the persistence engine, message broker or identity provider behind a layer while the domain keeps exactly the same vocabulary.
Database-view ACL for analytics: a database view that maps another context's internal storage schema into an analytics-owned projection, used instead of direct cross-context SQL queries that couple the analytics context to the source's implementation details.
API-gateway-level ACL: an Azure Functions, AWS Lambda or similar serverless function deployed at the API gateway seam that performs domain-model translation before requests reach the downstream service, keeping protocol handling and semantic translation separate.
Dark launch / shadow traffic validation: an ACL running in parallel that receives mirrored traffic and logs translation discrepancies without affecting live callers, enabling validation of a new integration before any traffic is cut over.
Multi-system data aggregation: a domain that must compose data from multiple external systems with incompatible models (e.g., a customer dashboard pulling from Stripe, Salesforce and an on-premises ERP) translates each system's model separately before assembling a unified view.
Bidirectional payment provider integration: a payment gateway ACL that translates inbound webhooks (provider → local domain events) and outbound charge requests (local domain → provider format), with a stable provider-independent reference as the operation key on every call.
Legacy system read-through cache: an ACL that wraps a legacy system's slow query with asynchronous cache warming and model translation, so the domain sees a fast, semantically correct response without coupling to the legacy's latency profile.
AWS Migration Hub Refactor Spaces strangler migration: Amazon API Gateway routes a monolith's calls to legacy or Lambda services while an ACL converts the monolith's old interface to the migrated service and is removed after callers move.
Spring Boot customer integration: a Spring component with an external client, explicit mapper, retry policy and circuit breaker translates provider responses into local aggregates; keep the ACL inside the service unless several consumers need the same boundary.
Azure Strangler Fig migration: an Azure façade routes legacy and new services while a domain-owned ACL translates calls in both directions, letting clients keep the same interface until the legacy feature is retired.

name: make-illegal-states-unrepresentable
document:
make-illegal-states-unrepresentable
make invalid states unrepresentable
Encode each domain rule in the shape of the data type so that values violating the rule cannot be constructed at all, replacing scattered run-time validation and defensive checks with a model in which only legal states exist.
Domain values are modelled as one record with independent fields - a status tag plus several nullable or optional attributes, or a handful of booleans - so the type admits every combination of those fields, including the ones the business rules forbid. Consumers cannot trust the type: each branch re-checks which fields are meaningful, the same guard is written in several places (and forgotten in one), and illegal states become runtime bugs that surface when a code path finally combines the wrong flags.
Applies when a value has a small, known set of mutually exclusive shapes whose payloads differ, when the same invalid combination keeps being defended against in several places, and when the language can close a set of variants (Rust/Swift enums, sealed hierarchies, discriminated unions) or at least hide constructors. It is equally a boundary discipline: untrusted input is parsed once into a type whose existence already proves it is valid, so no downstream code has to re-validate.
Lifecycle and state machines: orders, payments, subscriptions, bookings and connection states, one variant per state carrying exactly the data that exists in that state.
Client and API request state: a loading/success/error union instead of a data field, an error field and an isLoading flag that can contradict one another.
Message and protocol modelling: a closed set of commands, events or JSON payload shapes decoded once and dispatched with an exhaustive match (event sourcing, interpreters, RPC handlers).
Refined scalars that travel through the model: money with currency, email addresses, quantities with units and identifiers that are parsed once and never re-validated.
Configuration whose combinations are illegal: TLS settings that only apply when TLS is enabled, cursor-based versus offset pagination, mutually exclusive feature flags.
Import and deserialization boundaries: convert untrusted rows, CSV cells, query parameters or JSON into domain types with a failing factory, so invalid input cannot travel further.
Rust's standard `Option`/`Result` enums and exhaustive `match` make presence, absence, success and failure explicit cases that downstream code must handle at compile time (Rust Reference/Book).
Swift enums with associated values and exhaustive `switch` model state-specific payloads such as error cases without nullable companion fields (The Swift Programming Language).
Kotlin sealed classes and interfaces with exhaustive `when` expressions provide a closed hierarchy for finite state machines and error/result models, with the compiler checking that every known case is handled.

name: deadline-propagation
document:
deadline-propagation
timeout propagation
Bound the total time and work of a logical request by carrying one deadline through its whole call tree: every hop forwards the remaining budget and the cancellation signal instead of inventing a fresh timeout, so work that can no longer succeed is abandoned at every level.
A request fans out into a chain or tree of downstream calls and each hop applies its own timeout: the end-to-end latency budget becomes the sum of N independent timeouts, servers keep working after the originating client has given up, and cancellation never reaches the deeper work - resources are consumed producing answers nobody will read.
Networked request handling with multi-hop calls: RPC and HTTP chains, service meshes, gateways, fan-out and hedged requests. It applies when one latency budget is meaningful for the whole logical request (an SLO or a user-facing timeout), when the hops are under your control and can carry request-scoped state (context, token, signal, call option or header), and when downstream work is cancellable or can be interrupted at checkpoints.
Microservice request chains (gateway -> frontend service -> several backends) under one user-facing latency SLO, where each hop converts the inbound deadline into its own outgoing calls.
gRPC services whose clients set a deadline and whose servers propagate it as a remaining timeout to downstream calls while cancelling server-side work once the deadline passes.
Fan-out and aggregation endpoints calling several backends in parallel: every sub-call shares the parent budget, and sub-calls still running when it expires are cancelled instead of awaited.
Hedged requests: the first replica to answer wins, and the duplicate requests are cancelled through the same carrier so their downstream work is stopped too.
Streaming and long-poll endpoints that must stop processing when the client disconnects or the connection times out, propagating that stop to services and storage.
Batch or pipeline steps with a per-request time budget that must check the remaining time before each stage and abandon a request that can no longer be finished in time.
ROS 2 / DDS-based robotics pipelines: autonomous vehicle perception pipelines where sensor data must traverse a chain of processing nodes (detect -> classify -> plan -> act) and missed deadlines invalidate downstream results entirely.
Distributed real-time databases with multi-hop queries (gateway -> shard router -> storage node -> index node) where each hop's latency budget is derived from a user-facing SLA.
Service mesh sidecar configurations (Istio/Linkerd/Envoy) where per-route timeout policies propagate deadline context to application code via headers like grpc-timeout or custom X-Request-Deadline headers.
Industrial IoT and edge computing pipelines (edge gateway -> fieldbus bridge -> PLC -> sensor) where end-to-end control loop deadlines must be enforced across heterogeneous network boundaries.
GraphQL federation: a federated query hitting multiple subgraphs in parallel must bound the total resolution time and cancel subgraph requests whose partial results can no longer affect the final response.
Go services on the standard library context package: context.WithDeadline and WithTimeout derive a child whose Done channel closes at the earliest of its own deadline, an explicit cancel, or the parent's cancellation, so cancelling the root request context tears down the whole goroutine tree, and WithDeadlineCause/WithTimeoutCause attach an explicit cause for attribution.
Envoy router filter in service meshes: Envoy sets x-envoy-expected-rq-timeout-ms on internal requests - derived from x-envoy-upstream-rq-timeout-ms or the route timeout - so upstream services can read the expected total completion time and exit early instead of finishing work the proxy has already timed out.
ASP.NET Core gRPC services map the inbound call's deadline onto the handler's CancellationToken; passing that token to database queries, HttpClient calls and Task.Delay stops server-side work the moment the client's deadline expires.

name: function-composition
document:
function-composition
compose
function pipeline
Combine a chain of small unary transformations into one reusable function by sequencing them with a composition combinator (compose/pipe), so the order of the steps is stated once, every step stays independently testable, and the chain itself becomes a value that can be named, passed and reassembled.
A transformation that is naturally a sequence of small pure steps gets written as nested calls or as repeated imperative assignment (`h(g(f(x)))`, or `y = f(x); y = g(y); ...; return y`) at every call site. The order is duplicated wherever the chain is used, the intermediate values need throwaway names, steps cannot be reused in a different order, and changing one stage means editing every copy.
Pure or nearly pure value transformations - parsing, normalisation, validation, formatting, pricing, AST rewriting - where each step is unary and the language treats functions as values. It pays off when the chain is reused or assembled from data (configuration, plugin lists, per-request policy), when steps must be unit-tested in isolation, and when the same steps must also run element-wise over a collection or lazily over a stream. It stops applying where steps need side effects or branching between stages: there the shell around the pure core owns control flow.
Input normalisation: trim, parse, canonicalise and validate a payload before it reaches domain logic, with the same chain reused by HTTP handlers and message consumers.
Pricing and rule chains: base price, discount, tax and rounding applied in a fixed, configurable order to an immutable value object.
Compiler and AST work: a pass list of rewrite functions composed once and applied over the tree, with passes added or reordered per optimisation level.
Serialisation and formatting: sanitise, format, encode and sign a document, where each step is tested separately and the composed chain is stored as a constant.
Data transformation over collections: the same pure steps composed into one function and passed to map/filter/stream operations, so element-wise processing reuses the chain.
Policy assembly at startup: the processing chain is built from configuration or plugin registrations and then applied per request without further branching.
Reactive stream processing: RxJS Observable.pipe chains the same logical steps across asynchronous event sequences, with operators composed once and reused across streams.
ETL and data pipeline transformation: extract-transform-load chains where each stage (parse, clean, enrich, aggregate, write) is a unary pure function composed into a reusable pipeline run over batches or streaming data.
HTTP request/response middleware: the middleware stack is a composed function chain where each layer (authenticate, authorise, rate-limit, deserialize, validate) is a unary handler; composition is resolved once at startup.
Matrix and vector transformations in numerical code: each linear algebra operation (scale, rotate, translate, project) is a unary function on a matrix type; composing them once builds the transformation pipeline that is applied to every vertex or pixel.
Ramda pipelines: R.pipe and R.compose assemble reusable data-last transformations from small functions, centralising the order while letting the same composed value run over many inputs.
Redux store setup: Redux's compose helper combines store enhancers right-to-left into one enhancer, so the enhancer order is defined once instead of reconstructed at each store boundary.
lodash/fp transformations: lodash/fp's auto-curried, data-last compose/flow helpers assemble immutable-friendly transformations from reusable steps that can be passed as values.

name: test-specific-subclass
document:
test-specific-subclass
test-specific extension
subclassed test double
Make an otherwise untestable class testable by defining a test-only subclass that overrides the method reaching the unusable dependency (or exposes the internal state the test needs), so the boundary can be substituted and observed without putting test hooks into production code.
A class that must be tested reaches its dependency through a call on itself - a self-call to a helper method, a field created inside the class, or a singleton/static lookup - so the test has no injection point: the collaborator cannot be replaced from outside, the indirect inputs cannot be controlled and the indirect outputs cannot be observed. Editing the production class to accept the dependency may be impossible (third-party or frozen code) or would introduce test logic into production.
Applies to legacy or third-party object-oriented code where the boundary call already sits behind an overridable (non-final, sufficiently visible) method, or can be extracted into one, and where test-only code may live next to the tests. It is a fallback for statically typed languages that need the double to stay type-compatible with a concrete class; where the code can be modified, dependency injection is the better seam.
A legacy class reads the wall clock inside a helper method (System.currentTimeMillis, DateTime.Now, Instant.now): override the helper so date/decision logic can be tested at a fixed instant.
A reporting or notification class sends mail or calls a remote API from a self-call: override that method with a canned or empty body so the unit test runs offline and deterministically.
A class reaches a database or the file system from inside its own method: override it to return an in-memory fixture instead of building the real object chain (entity-chain snipping).
Verifying the sequence and the set of steps of a template method: override the steps in a subclass and record which of them ran, in which order.
Exposing private state for state verification, or exposing a private algorithm step so it can be tested individually (state-exposing and behaviour-exposing subclasses).
Replacing a singleton or static accessor the SUT uses through a lookup with a controlled instance that is still type-compatible with the concrete class (substituted singleton).
Putting a legacy untested class under a characterization-test baseline before refactoring, while extracting the collaborator is not yet possible.
A Java class that cannot be modified (third-party or legacy jar) but has a non-final boundary method to stub: Mockito spy() / @Spy keeps the real methods and stubs only the overridden ones - the partial mocking Mockito's Javadoc documents for legacy code and third-party interfaces (final methods stay un-stubbable).
A PHP class whose constructor opens connections or performs other side effects: createPartialMock(Class::class, ['boundaryMethod']) or getMockBuilder()->onlyMethods([...])->disableOriginalConstructor() generates a double that overrides only the named methods and skips the real constructor - PHPUnit's documented form of the pattern (final, private and static methods and enums cannot be doubled).
A .NET class with virtual boundary members: NSubstitute Substitute.ForPartsOf<T>() creates a partial substitute that - as NSubstitute's own docs state - inherits the original type via Castle DynamicProxy and runs real code except for members configured with DoNotCallBase, i.e. a generated test-specific subclass with an official 'use with caution' caveat.

name: composed-method
document:
composed-method
compose method
Divide the work into methods that each perform one identifiable task, written as a short outline of invocations in which every operation sits at the same level of abstraction, so a reader grasps the task top-down and every change lands on one small, named step.
A method accumulates several concerns at once: high-level policy ('validate the order, then charge it') interleaved with low-level detail (a loop index, a string concatenation, a counter), so the method grows long, needs comments to mark its sections, and changes for more than one reason. Readers must simulate the whole body to learn what it does, duplication hides inside similar-looking blocks, and anyone who must change one decision - a subclass in particular - ends up copying the method and editing it.
Applies wherever code is decomposed into named routines and is read far more often than written: long-lived domain and application code, code review and onboarding, framework base classes that must expose override hooks, and code whose steps carry contracts worth testing separately. It is a source-level discipline rather than a runtime structure, so a language needs only routines and some notion of non-public helpers; it matters most exactly where methods have grown past the point a reader can hold them in mind.
Long methods built up over time whose sections are marked by comments: each comment becomes a step name and the method becomes an outline.
A method with several responsibilities (validate, compute, persist) that must change independently and be reviewed one concern at a time.
Framework or library base classes that must offer override points: each step becomes a documented extension point, usually combined with Template Method or NVI.
Top-down design of an algorithm: write the outline first, with steps as not-yet-implemented calls, and fill them in one at a time.
Bottom-up refactoring when the same block appears in several methods: extract it as a named step and call it from each outline.
Making behaviour testable in isolation: steps with their own contracts (parsing input, rounding money, validating rules) become separately testable units.
TDD workflow: write the test for the composed method outline first, asserting each step in sequence, then implement each step as a separate testable unit.
Complex business rules that combine multiple conditional branches: decompose each branch condition and its body into a clearly named step, making the rule engine visible and auditable.
Command or handler objects that orchestrate a multi-step process (validate request, authorize caller, execute operation, emit event, log outcome): each phase is a named step in the composed method.
Production Rails code: Basecamp's Event::Relaying#relay_now reads as an outline of named steps (relay_to_or_revoke_from_timeline, relay_to_webhooks_later), each descending into its own relayer class - the 'fractal' consistency of composed methods in a shipped product, documented by 37signals.
Acceptance and integration test suites: each scenario is written as a composed method at a single level of abstraction (sign_in, create_todo, mark_complete), delegating the mechanics to named helpers or page objects so the test tells the user-level story.
JUnit 4's refactored internals: Beck documents TestCase together with the RunAfter, ExpectException and FailedTest method objects as chained composed outlines, each invocation staying at one level of abstraction (his 'Nested Method Object' evolution of the pattern).

name: copy-on-write
document:
copy-on-write
lazy copy
clone-on-write
implicit sharing (Qt)
shadow paging
Let several handles of a value share one expensive body until the first write, which clones that body privately, so copying costs a pointer instead of a deep copy while every handle still behaves as an independent value.
A value with an expensive body (large buffer, collection, tree, document) is copied eagerly on assignment, argument passing and return even though most copies are never modified: time and memory are spent duplicating data that would have stayed identical. The naive fix - handing out one mutable object behind several handles - breaks the copy contract, and unrelated parts of the program then observe each other's writes.
Applies when copies of an expensive payload vastly outnumber modifications, when the payload is large enough that the copy dominates the cost of the handle (multi-kilobyte buffers, collection snapshots, editor or model state), and when the language offers a cheap way to know whether the body is still shared - a reference count, an explicit shared flag, or a uniqueness test. It is a single-threaded optimization first; sharing the count across threads turns it into the separate thread-safe copy-on-write concern.
Large buffers passed by value through API layers: strings, byte arrays and image/document payloads whose copies are usually read-only (Qt QString/QByteArray implicit sharing, ATL CString, pre-C++11 std::string).
Read-mostly collections whose traversals vastly outnumber mutations and must not block readers: listener and handler registries, routing tables, RuleEngine rule sets (CopyOnWriteArrayList/CopyOnWriteArraySet).
Configuration and state snapshots swapped atomically at the write boundary (feature flags, reloaded settings, event-sourced folds) so readers keep a consistent version without locking.
Persistent and functional data structures where an update returns a new version that structurally shares everything the change did not touch (Scala immutable collections, Immer drafts, persistent lists and maps).
Operating-system and memory-mapped sharing: fork and page-level copy-on-write share physical pages until a mapping is written, and file-backed buffers are shared until modified.
Columnar and data-frame workloads where slices are views and only the columns actually written are duplicated (pandas copy-on-write mode, Arrow buffers).
Fork-based process snapshots: Redis BGSAVE/BGREWRITEAOF forks a child to serialize memory to disk while the parent continues serving writes; only pages modified by the parent after fork are COW-copied, keeping the child's view consistent (vm.overcommit_memory=1 recommended).
COW filesystems for instant snapshots: ZFS and Btrfs never overwrite blocks in place; creating a snapshot is O(1) — save the root block pointer; reclaims O(1) more when the snapshot is deleted and no other reference remains. Enables self-healing via checksum propagation and efficient incremental replication via zfs send / btrfs send.
Database MVCC at row granularity: Postgres, LMDB, CockroachDB Pebble write new row versions on UPDATE/DELETE and reclaim old versions via VACUUM once no active transaction can see them; readers see consistent snapshots without read locks.
Container image layering: Docker/OCI images use layered COW where lower layers are read-only and the upper layer copies on write; base images are shared across many containers until a layer is actually modified.
APFS reflinks and XFS/ref ext4 ioctl(FICLONE): file-level COW that shares extents until either fork writes, enabling instant file clones (e.g., `cp --reflink=auto`) at near-zero cost.
LMDB's single-level store: a CoW B+tree using two fixed root pages (double buffering) where readers are fully latch-free and writers never block readers; no WAL needed because old trees remain intact until the new root is durably synced.
Swift standard library collections (Array, Dictionary, Set, String, Data) where isKnownUniquelyReferenced() checks the heap object's strong reference count at runtime to decide whether to mutate in-place or clone.
Qt QSharedData/QSharedDataPointer: implicit sharing for pimpl'd d-pointer classes where non-const operator-> triggers detach() automatically before any write access; QExplicitlySharedDataPointer suppresses automatic detach.
Rust std::borrow::Cow: a generic enum (Borrowed | Owned) that defers the clone until to_mut() is called, especially useful in APIs that accept both borrowed and owned data without multiple signatures.
PHP arrays and strings: reference-counted value types where assignment and argument passing share the zval and the first write 'separates' it (copy-on-write) when refcount > 1; taking a reference with & turns the sharing into an explicit alias set (php.net reference counting, php-src core docs).
pandas 3.0, where copy-on-write is the default and only mode: any DataFrame or Series derived by indexing behaves as an independent copy, chained assignment (df["foo"][mask] = v) silently doing nothing is eliminated - it raises ChainedAssignmentError - and every update must be a single .loc step (PDEP-7).
Linux kernel OverlayFS copy_up: a container write to a lowerdir file (open for write or metadata change) copies the file up into upperdir first; the metacopy feature delays the data copy until the first data write, and an fsync before the finalizing rename guards against zero-filled files after a crash (kernel overlayfs docs, Docker overlay2 driver).

name: separation-of-duties
document:
separation-of-duties
separation of privilege
four-eyes principle
Require two or more distinct principals or components to complete a sensitive operation, so that no single account, role or object can initiate and finish it alone.
A sensitive workflow is reachable end to end from one identity or one code path: the same operator creates and approves the payment, the same administrator changes the production configuration and signs it off, the same service account holds both the maker and the checker permission. The trigger is structural rather than accidental - all steps share one principal, one session, one process or one role, because splitting them costs a second pair of hands - and the failure surfaces only when an insider error or abuse is unremarkable in the audit trail: every step was authorized, because one principal held both halves of the duty.
Sensitive operations whose consequences must survive mistakes, coercion or misuse by authorized insiders: payments and disbursements, entitlement and permission changes, production configuration and deployment, key custody and signing, destructive data operations. It applies where identities can be kept distinct and authenticated (separate accounts, roles, services, processes), where the intermediate states of the operation can be persisted and observed, and where an enforcement point exists that can compare the acting principal with the recorded initiator - a policy engine, method security, an approval service, a separate process or account, a dual-control key ceremony. It is as much an organizational rule as a technical one: the split must follow the duties people actually hold, and recombination must be made awkward by design rather than merely discouraged.
Maker-checker payments: an operator above a threshold creates a disbursement and a second operator releases it; the ledger records both identities and refuses a release signed by the maker.
Change control and deployment: production IAM policy or infrastructure changes require a second administrator's approval, and the pipeline refuses to run a change approved by its own author (required reviewers / second signature).
Key custody and dual control: signing keys or root credentials are split so two authorized operators must each contribute a share (split knowledge, m-of-n threshold, dual-control key ceremony) and no single share can sign.
Access provisioning: the requester of an entitlement, its approver and the administrator who grants it are three distinct roles; the administrator cannot approve their own request, and access-control administrators do not administer the audit log.
Destructive data operations: schema migrations, production data edits and deletion jobs are prepared by one engineer and executed by a different operator account that cannot author the change.
Regulated back-office workflows: journal entries, refunds, credit adjustments and account closures are initiated by one clerk and posted by another, with the pairing recorded for audit.
GitHub protected branches: a pull request targeting a protected branch needs the configured number of approving reviews before it can merge, the platform refuses an approval from the PR author by design, and with dismiss-stale-review enabled a commit pushed after the review voids the approval - four-eyes enforced at the merge gate with the approval bound to the reviewed revision.
AWS Systems Manager Change Manager: a change request may run its Automation runbook only after approvals from named IAM users, groups or roles arrive across up to five approval levels, and a single rejection stops execution; because change templates list approvers separately from requesters, a request submitted under one IAM principal is released by another.
HashiCorp Vault key custody: vault operator init splits the root key with Shamir's Secret Sharing into key shares (default 5) under a threshold (default 3); unsealing or generating a root token needs a quorum of distinct share holders, and PGP-encrypting each share for a named operator makes dual control a property of the mechanism rather than of the procedure.

name: stub
document:
stub
test stub
stub object
Replace a collaborator with a test-specific stand-in that returns canned answers, so the component under test can be driven down paths - success, empty, error, timeout - that the real collaborator cannot be made to produce on demand.
The component under test receives indirect inputs through a collaborator, and the branch that must be exercised is selected by what that collaborator returns. The real collaborator will not produce the needed value on request: it is slow, remote, licensed, non-deterministic, or simply never returns the rare case - the empty result, the declined payment, the timeout - that the test exists for. Without a controllable replacement the test either cannot reach the path at all or has to provoke it through the production system, which is exactly what unit testing was supposed to avoid.
Unit and component tests of a component whose collaborators are already, or can cheaply become, abstractions: the values and exceptions a collaborator returns are inputs to the component under test, and the test asserts what the component does with them rather than how the collaboration happened. Typical where the collaborator is remote or stateful (HTTP client, database, queue, clock, payment gateway) or where the branch under test is an edge case - empty page, declined payment, expired token, feature off. The pattern assumes a substitutable seam: a constructor parameter, an injected interface, a factory, a lookup, or a patchable module.
Exercising a rare branch of the component: an empty result set, a declined payment, a 429 from a gateway, a missing feature flag.
Testing error handling: programme the stub to raise the exception the real service would raise - timeout, connection reset, malformed payload - and assert that the SUT surfaces or recovers from it.
Unit-testing a component against a collaborator that is slow, paid, unavailable in CI or still being implemented; the stub encodes the agreed response while the real adapter is built.
Removing non-determinism from a path the real collaborator decides by clock, randomness or remote state (token expired, cache cold, retry budget exhausted), so one outcome can be asserted exactly.
View and presentation tests: a fixed dataset from the stub, so the assertion is about the rendering or the decision logic and nothing else.
Boundary values on contract edges - zero, maximum, empty string, unicode payloads - that the real system cannot be asked to return on demand.
Mockito (Java): when(warehouse.hasInventory(...)).thenReturn(false) programmes the declined-branch answer and thenThrow(SocketTimeoutException.class) injects the failure, and consecutive-value stubbing (thenReturn(v1, v2)) drives retry-then-succeed paths that the real warehouse would never produce on request.
Python unittest.mock (standard library): Mock(return_value=...) fixes the canned answer while side_effect set to an exception or an iterable raises or sequences answers per call - the library ships Responder and Saboteur behaviour as first-class configuration.
Moq (.NET): mock.Setup(x => x.HasInventory(...)).Returns(false) and .Throws<InvalidOperationException>() are the canned-answer primitives, so a C# test reaches the empty-inventory and fault branches of Order.Fill without touching a database.

name: cursor-pagination
document:
cursor-pagination
keyset pagination
cursor-based pagination
Bound what a read boundary returns for a large or changing ordered collection by sending one page plus an opaque continuation token that pins the filter and ordering, so clients advance deterministically without offsets and without watching rows move under them.
A boundary must expose a collection that is too large to return at once and keeps changing while clients read it. Offset or page-number requests make the store count or scan everything up to the requested page, and concurrent inserts or deletes shift rows across page boundaries so consumers see duplicates or miss items; the server has no way to state where the sequence should resume.
Any read boundary - an HTTP or gRPC list operation, a GraphQL connection, a database-backed feed, a batch export job - over an ordered collection that is large, growing, or read under concurrent writes, where the server can identify a unique, immutable ordering key and wants to cap both response size and per-request query cost while letting clients iterate the whole sequence.
Public REST or gRPC list endpoints over unbounded, growing tables - messages, orders, audit events - where deep offsets are slow and responses must stay small.
Infinite-scroll or load-more feeds that keep returning newer items while a user scrolls, with the already-seen pages stable against inserts.
Whole-collection sync and export jobs (warehouse loads, backups, search reindexing) that must iterate every row exactly once while writers continue.
GraphQL Relay connections where first/after, edges and pageInfo carry the continuation contract in the schema instead of the URL.
Consumers of third-party list APIs (Stripe-style starting_after/has_more, Google page_token iterators) that keep parameters fixed across auto-paginated calls.
Administrative and operational tooling that streams very large tables for verification or cleanup with bounded memory and predictable server load.
Audit log and event stream retrieval where events are append-only and chronological, and clients stream continuously without needing to revisit earlier pages.
Real-time activity feeds (social media timelines, notification streams) where inserts at the head must not disturb pages the user has already loaded.
Database replication and change-data-capture (CDC) pipelines that must consume a changelog exactly once across restarts and failures.
Paginating over search results from a vector database or full-text index where OFFSET at depth is expensive and results may change between queries.
Bi-directional data synchronization (CDC pipelines, replica lag-catching) where a consumer must iterate forward and occasionally needs to resume from a previous position or re-sweep a window — requiring stable forward cursors plus a defined backward-resumption path.
Paginating a partitioned or sharded database table where each partition is queried independently and cursors carry both the partition hint and the per-partition keyset position.
Slack Web API collection methods (users.list, conversations.history) where response_metadata.next_cursor drives the loop, page limits are clamped per method, and expired or malformed tokens surface as invalid_cursor so the client restarts from the first page.
GitHub GraphQL-style cursor connections where first/last (bounded 1-100) and pageInfo.startCursor/endCursor carry the continuation position for after/before traversal.
Timeline-style feeds served by Django REST framework's CursorPagination, whose default -created ordering gives a consistent view that does not repeat items as new rows are inserted.

name: secure-logger
document:
secure-logger
tamper-evident logging
secure audit log
Record security-relevant events through a single logging chokepoint and chain every record's authenticator to its predecessor, so that altering, deleting, reordering or truncating the log is detectable by an independent verifier rather than merely inconvenient for the party being recorded.
The audit trail exists, but the party it records - a privileged operator, a compromised service, the application itself - can also rewrite it: files are appendable and rotatable by the same process that writes them, there is no gap detection when a record or a whole file disappears, and nobody can prove after the fact that a log line is the line that was written. The log answers questions only as long as everyone trusts the host that produced it.
Systems where a security-relevant event stream has evidentiary or compliance weight - privileged action and break-glass accounts, authentication and authorisation decisions, regulated transaction trails - and where an adversary on the recording host (or the recorded subject itself) is inside the threat model. It applies to a component boundary: the application writes through one logger, the store is append-only for that application, and verification happens elsewhere, so key custody and the trust anchor are part of the design rather than an afterthought.
Privileged and administrative activity: break-glass accounts, role and policy changes, configuration and key operations that must remain provable after the fact.
Regulated transaction audit trails (PCI DSS 10.x, HIPAA, SOX) where an independently verifiable sequence of attributable events is the compliance artefact.
Authentication and authorisation decision records: who was denied, by which rule, in which service - the evidence security operations triages incidents from.
Cloud and API activity logging built the CloudTrail way: per-file digests plus signed digest files that chain the previous digest, so a customer can verify what the provider delivered.
Edge and IoT devices that can be physically captured: the device keeps chaining into a remote anchor, so records written before an attack stay trustworthy after it.
systemd-journald Forward Secure Sealing: journalctl --setup-keys keeps a sealing key on the host that derives forward-securely per epoch while the verification key is stored externally; per-epoch SHA-256 HMAC tags seal the journal file, and journalctl --verify with the external key detects alteration, removal or reordering of records.
Certificate Transparency (RFC 6962) generalises the chain into an append-only Merkle tree: the log signs each tree head within the Maximum Merge Delay, and auditors verify with Merkle consistency proofs that newer heads preserve every earlier entry - the anchor is published and independently checked rather than merely kept.
Google Pixel Binary Transparency: factory images are leaves of a tile-based Merkle tree whose signed checkpoint roots are published, and witness monitors routinely verify consistency between checkpoints so a rolled-back or rewritten log is detected by third parties, not just the log operator.

name: update-method
document:
update-method
per-frame update
tick method
Give every live object one self-contained per-frame step and let a single driver call each object's step every frame, so behaviour advances one frame at a time while input and rendering stay responsive.
A running world is full of objects that each have to keep doing their own thing - guards patrolling, statues charging, agents acting - and the recurring decision is where one object's per-frame behaviour lives and how all those behaviours get driven. Coding a behaviour as a loop that runs to completion blocks input and rendering (the skeleton walks, but nobody sees it); coding it inline in the game loop turns the loop into a switchboard over every kind of object, so every new behaviour edits central code; and there is no way for two actors to evolve independently and simultaneously.
Real-time software with many concurrent live objects whose behaviour is mostly independent and must be simulated over time: games, agent-based simulations, animation and particle systems, tick-based servers and live visualisations. It is the natural partner of a frame driver (Game Loop) - the loop supplies the cadence, Update Method supplies the per-object step - and it becomes the wrong shape in turn-based or purely event-driven domains where nothing changes between inputs.
Real-time games and simulations with many concurrent actors: patrolling guards, projectiles, particle effects and crowd agents each advance themselves once per frame while the driver walks the collection.
Component-based engines where the parts of one entity evolve independently - rendering, physics and AI components each implement their own step and the engine's registry dispatches per component (Unity, MonoGame, Bevy, GameplayKit, libGDX).
Per-frame animation and effect timelines outside games: tween/spring systems, sprite animation and UI transitions advanced from the browser's frame callback or a UI toolkit's animation timer.
Tick-based servers and headless simulations: game servers, digital twins and agent-based models where each agent's behaviour is a resumable step and the world advances in whole discrete frames.
Tools, editors and dashboards with continuously animating scenes, where many independent scene items (markers, live charts, gizmos) must advance on every repaint without a central per-item switch.
Porting straight-line behaviour into a frame loop: turning a scripted sequence (walk left, walk right) into a per-frame step, either by storing explicit state or by using coroutines/generators to keep the code linear.
Godot's SceneTree is the driver: a node opts into the walk with set_process(true) and its _process(delta) runs every render frame with the frame time passed in as an argument, while _physics_process(delta) is called at a fixed rate - so one object can implement two steps on two clocks and can leave the walk entirely (set_process(false)) instead of paying an enabled-flag check every frame.
Engines whose built-in driver leaves per-object order unspecified expose the order as configuration: Unity states you should not rely on the order of Update across GameObjects, so real projects fix dependencies through the Script Execution Order panel, a LateUpdate pass that runs after every Update, or the PlayerLoop API rather than through registration order.
Agent-based simulation models step whole populations in NetLogo: the go procedure runs ask turtles [ ... ] to give every agent its one turn and then tick advances the discrete clock - with documented semantics that agents take their turns in random order and only agents present when the ask began get to act.

name: two-step-view
document:
two-step-view
two stage view
Split presentation into two transformations - first turn domain data into a channel-neutral logical page, then render that logical page into a concrete output format - so page structure is defined once while look-and-feel and output channel live entirely in the renderer.
Every page owns its own presentation decisions: with one template or one transform per page, a global look-and-feel change means editing every file, and serving a second channel (print/PDF, e-mail, plain text, a machine-readable feed) means duplicating the page's structure. Nothing in the codebase represents 'the page' independently of the markup it currently happens to be rendered as.
Server-side presentation or document-publishing boundaries where several output channels share one page structure, or where the house style changes often enough that it must change in exactly one place. It also fits where the rendering technology is expected to be replaced (XSLT today, a template engine or PDF formatter tomorrow) and where the page should be inspectable, testable or cacheable before it is rendered.
Multi-channel publishing: one invoice or statement rendered as HTML for a portal, XSL-FO/PDF for print and plain text for e-mail from a single logical page.
Site-wide restyling in a CMS or portal where the house style must be one artefact to change and review rather than one edit per page family.
API-plus-HTML endpoints: the same logical page is serialised as JSON for clients and rendered as HTML for the browsable interface.
Document and report pipelines in the DocBook tradition: the logical document is produced once and rendered to HTML, PDF and e-book formats by different stylesheets.
Constrained or legacy channels - plain text, WAP/XML, CSV - added next to HTML without touching the page assembly code.
Pages produced once and consumed by several renderers or locales: the logical page is cached and rendered per channel on demand.
Spring Web MVC XSLT views: an XsltController builds an XML DOM of the page content, puts it in the model, and XsltViewResolver applies a home.xslt stylesheet - stage one produces the logical document, stage two owns the HTML.
Aura.View (PHP) ships the pattern under the name TwoStepView: a content template renders first, then a separately registered layout wraps it via setLayout()/getContent(), keeping the site chrome in one artefact instead of every page.
Standards-based publishing toolchains: the DITA Open Toolkit transforms semantic DITA maps/topics through XSLT stages into HTML, PDF and other deliverables, and Apache Cocoon pipelines generator -> XSLT transformer -> serializer so one XML source serves HTML, PDF, SVG and text.
