name: repository
document:
repository
collection-oriented repository
repository layer
Mediates between the domain model and the data mapping layer with a collection-like interface, so domain code adds, removes and finds persistent objects as if they lived in memory and never constructs queries or touches persistence APIs itself.
Persistence code spreads: every application service re-derives the same SQL or ORM queries, duplicate query logic drifts apart, table and column names leak into domain decisions, and testing domain rules without a database becomes impossible. Callers should be able to think in collections of domain objects instead of queries.
Applies to systems with a non-trivial domain model sitting on a data-mapping layer (Data Mapper, metadata mapping, or a hand-written mapper) where the same queries recur across application services; it becomes more valuable as domain classes and query volume grow. It is the standard persistence boundary of DDD aggregates (one repository per aggregate root) and presumes a unit of work or session that owns flush and commit. It is not a per-table data-access wrapper and not a replacement for transaction control.
DDD application services that must load an aggregate root, run domain logic on it and store it again without knowing the table layout.
Data-mapper backends where several application services and background jobs share recurring complex queries (overdue invoices, pending orders, open tickets).
Applications that must be unit-testable away from the database: repositories are the substitution point for in-memory doubles.
Systems that must support more than one store behind a stable domain interface — relational in production, in-memory in tests, a document store for a particular deployment.
Uniform cross-cutting access policy for an aggregate: caching, read-replica routing, audit logging or authorization applied as decorators around one interface.
Migration work where the persistence technology changes (ORM swap, schema split, service extraction) while the domain model and its tests stay untouched.
CQRS write-side aggregate loading where the aggregate must be reconstructed fully to apply business rules and enforce invariants.
Integration with heterogeneous data sources where one repository unifies access to a cache, primary database and a third-party API behind a domain interface.
Spring Data JPA applications can use Repository/CrudRepository for aggregate-typed CRUD, paging and derived queries, then add only domain-specific methods rather than wrapping every persistence operation.
The .NET eShopOnContainers ordering microservice uses an EF Core BuyerRepository over a shared scoped DbContext/unit of work, while CQRS/Dapper handles presentation reads.
Python applications using SQLAlchemy ORM can place an aggregate-facing repository over Session, whose identity map and unit-of-work flush semantics provide the mapper/session boundary.

statement: Decide how to compose a sequence whose next action depends on the prior result while absence, failure, and asynchronous completion are propagated uniformly.
name: entity
document:
entity
reference object
domain entity
Give a domain concept a stable identity that survives attribute changes, representation changes and time, and define its equality, lifecycle and lookup in terms of that identity instead of in terms of its attributes.
A model that compares objects by their attributes cannot answer whether two instances are the same thing: a customer whose e-mail and plan changed looks like a different customer, while two distinct people who share a name look like one. References held by other objects, caches and audit records break silently, and every state change forces callers to re-identify the object.
Rich domain models in which some concepts must be tracked through time: the object is created, changes state, is stored and reloaded, and may exist in several representations (in-memory instance, database row, message payload, UI snapshot) that all have to denote the same thing. It is the modelling decision that pairs with Value Object: attribute clusters become values, while the things whose history matters keep an identity.
Master data tracked for years — customers, accounts, contracts, products, patients — where attributes change but the business entity stays the same (e.g., a Customer who moves house is still the same Customer).
Documents with a lifecycle: orders, invoices, bookings and shipments that move through states (pending → paid → shipped → delivered) while remaining the same document with a stable order number.
Shopping cart to order transition: a ShoppingCart is reconstituted as an Order with the same customer identity but a new order identity, preserving the correlation to the customer while starting a new business process.
Correlating representations across layers: an entity persisted as database rows, published as domain events, and displayed in a UI must be recognisable as the same thing in all three — identity is the correlation key across representations.
In-memory session consistency: a unit of work or identity map ensures the same Customer loaded twice in one request is one object reference, preventing edits from silently diverging into two copies.
Referencing across bounded contexts: one microservice holds a CustomerId reference to another service's aggregate root, allowing independent deployment and loading without a direct object pointer.
Healthcare records: a Patient entity persists across multiple visits, lab results and prescriptions — the patient identity is the anchor for the entire medical history regardless of demographic changes.
Versioned documents: an InsurancePolicy entity may be replaced by a new version while the original policy number (identity) remains the correlation handle for auditors and legacy systems.
Hibernate/JPA: an @Entity class with an @Id is managed by the persistence context, which guarantees one in-memory instance per identity per session — loading the same row twice in a session returns the same object reference, an Identity Map built into the framework.
Entity Framework Core: identity resolution makes the DbContext track a single entity instance per primary key, so duplicate instances arriving in a deserialized graph are merged into the already-tracked entity instead of diverging into two tracked copies.
Drupal Entity API: nodes, users and taxonomy terms (content entities) and roles or image styles (configuration entities) are identity-bearing objects with typed storage handlers, revisions and field bundles behind one CRUD and validation API.

statement: Decide how to compose a sequence whose next action depends on the prior result while absence, failure, and asynchronous completion are propagated uniformly.
name: humble-object
document:
humble-object
humble dialog box
Move as much logic as possible out of a program element that the framework calls but tests cannot instantiate - a UI control, callback, entry point or active object - into a plain collaborator that unit tests drive synchronously, leaving the original element as a thin adapter without decisions.
The element the host invokes cannot be exercised in a test: constructing it needs the framework's environment (event loop, window, container, thread), so driving it means slow asynchronous tests with framework setup, or none at all. Because the decisions were written where the trigger arrives, business rules live inside the untestable element: they are verified only by expensive end-to-end runs, they cannot be test-first, and every framework upgrade threatens them.
Applies when an element is hard to test for environmental reasons rather than intrinsic ones: framework callbacks (widgets, dialogs, request handlers, message listeners), entry points (main, server bootstrap) and active objects (threads, processes, timer and interrupt handlers), plus container-managed components whose interfaces the server demands. The logic must be expressible as a computation over data, and the host must keep invoking the element through a stable callback or entry point.
A dialog or screen whose enablement, validation and navigation rules are hard to exercise: extract a presenter or view model, leave the widget showing fields and forwarding events (the Humble Dialog form).
Framework callbacks that mutate business state - HTTP handlers, message listeners, timer or interrupt callbacks - where a thin adapter reads the input and a service decides.
Active objects and executables: a thread or process whose per-request processing is extracted so tests run synchronously instead of sleeping and coordinating (the Humble Executable form).
Transaction boundaries: extract the business logic out of the transaction controller so a test can run the logic and roll the transaction back, leaving only commit/rollback behaviour in the controller (the Humble Transaction Controller form).
Container-managed components: implement the server's interface in a thin adapter and keep the logic in a container-independent class, so the edit-compile-test cycle stays fast (the Humble Container Adapter form).
Legacy code with an overridable or exposed dependency call but no injection point: expose or extract the method first (the Poor Man's form) and only then attempt a test harness.
Entry points: parse arguments, wire dependencies and map the exit code in main, and put the program's decisions in a library function that tests call.
Android Activities/Fragments and Unity MonoBehaviours: extract lifecycle-driven logic into a plain class, leaving the framework component as a thin shell that forwards lifecycle events — enables unit tests without an emulator or device.
React class components and Angular controllers: move state and business logic out of the component into a hook or service, keeping the component as a declarative renderer that delegates all decisions.
Embedded systems interrupt handlers: extract per-interrupt processing into a synchronous function tested with deterministic inputs; the ISR remains a thin vector that disables interrupts and calls the extracted logic.
Database transaction scripts: separate the SQL/transaction orchestration (humble controller) from the business logic (collaborator), so the logic is tested with a connection spy and the wiring is verified by a small number of integration tests.
Event-driven microservices: keep the event-listener adapter minimal (deserialize, delegate) and place all routing and business logic in a synchronous service that tests can drive directly with domain objects.
CLI entry points: extract argument parsing and environment setup from the main method into a plain runner class; the collaborator is tested with fake argv, and the shell only handles OS-level concerns.
Android Jetpack (AndroidX) ViewModel: Google's architecture guidance makes the ViewModel the testable collaborator - it MUST NOT reference Activity, Fragment, View or Context - so screen logic is unit-tested on the JVM with fakes, while the Activity/Fragment stays a humble shell exercised only by instrumentation tests.
WPF / .NET MVVM: Microsoft's guidance prescribes views with empty code-behind - controls bind to ViewModel properties and ICommand implementations (e.g. DelegateCommand) - so enablement, validation and action logic (CanExecute/Execute) are plain classes unit-tested without a window, and XAML binding is covered by a few integration checks.
Unity MonoBehaviour game code: teams extract game rules into plain C# classes unit-tested outside the engine's Play Mode, leaving the MonoBehaviour as a serialized-field shell that forwards Update/FixedUpdate - the Unity community reports this buys fast unit tests at the cost of harder in-engine integration tests, so the shell needs deliberate coverage.

statement: Decide how to compose a sequence whose next action depends on the prior result while absence, failure, and asynchronous completion are propagated uniformly.
name: secure-logger
document:
secure-logger
tamper-evident logging
secure audit log
Record security-relevant events through a single logging chokepoint and chain every record's authenticator to its predecessor, so that altering, deleting, reordering or truncating the log is detectable by an independent verifier rather than merely inconvenient for the party being recorded.
The audit trail exists, but the party it records - a privileged operator, a compromised service, the application itself - can also rewrite it: files are appendable and rotatable by the same process that writes them, there is no gap detection when a record or a whole file disappears, and nobody can prove after the fact that a log line is the line that was written. The log answers questions only as long as everyone trusts the host that produced it.
Systems where a security-relevant event stream has evidentiary or compliance weight - privileged action and break-glass accounts, authentication and authorisation decisions, regulated transaction trails - and where an adversary on the recording host (or the recorded subject itself) is inside the threat model. It applies to a component boundary: the application writes through one logger, the store is append-only for that application, and verification happens elsewhere, so key custody and the trust anchor are part of the design rather than an afterthought.
Privileged and administrative activity: break-glass accounts, role and policy changes, configuration and key operations that must remain provable after the fact.
Regulated transaction audit trails (PCI DSS 10.x, HIPAA, SOX) where an independently verifiable sequence of attributable events is the compliance artefact.
Authentication and authorisation decision records: who was denied, by which rule, in which service - the evidence security operations triages incidents from.
Cloud and API activity logging built the CloudTrail way: per-file digests plus signed digest files that chain the previous digest, so a customer can verify what the provider delivered.
Edge and IoT devices that can be physically captured: the device keeps chaining into a remote anchor, so records written before an attack stay trustworthy after it.
systemd-journald Forward Secure Sealing: journalctl --setup-keys keeps a sealing key on the host that derives forward-securely per epoch while the verification key is stored externally; per-epoch SHA-256 HMAC tags seal the journal file, and journalctl --verify with the external key detects alteration, removal or reordering of records.
Certificate Transparency (RFC 6962) generalises the chain into an append-only Merkle tree: the log signs each tree head within the Maximum Merge Delay, and auditors verify with Merkle consistency proofs that newer heads preserve every earlier entry - the anchor is published and independently checked rather than merely kept.
Google Pixel Binary Transparency: factory images are leaves of a tile-based Merkle tree whose signed checkpoint roots are published, and witness monitors routinely verify consistency between checkpoints so a rolled-back or rewritten log is detected by third parties, not just the log operator.

statement: Decide how to compose a sequence whose next action depends on the prior result while absence, failure, and asynchronous completion are propagated uniformly.
name: durable-subscriber
document:
durable-subscriber
durable subscription
durable consumer
Keep a publish-subscribe consumer's place while it is offline: the broker binds a stable subscription identity to retained messages or a committed position, then resumes delivery after reconnect until retention, expiry, or quota says the backlog is no longer available.
A subscriber on a publish-subscribe channel can be unavailable during redeployment, maintenance, device disconnects, or scheduled batch work. A non-durable subscription drops messages published during that gap, so the design must choose a stable identity and broker-side state, then make finite retention, replay pressure, and at-least-once redelivery explicit; durable state prevents a gap only while that state remains available.
Broker-mediated publish-subscribe messaging where consumers are intermittently offline but individual messages matter: JMS topics, MQTT sessions, Kafka consumer groups, NATS JetStream durable consumers, cloud topic subscriptions. It presumes the messaging system can store messages (or positions) durably, so it is as much a broker-configuration decision as a client one, and it presumes at-least-once delivery is acceptable once the consumer is idempotent. It does not apply to in-process notification or to broadcast where only the newest value counts.
A Kafka-backed order-processing service that is redeployed or scaled to zero while events keep arriving: the consumer group resumes from its committed offsets and replays what it missed.
An IoT or mobile client on an intermittent link: an MQTT persistent session holds QoS 1/2 publications for its client id and delivers them when the client reconnects.
A partner integration that receives published documents while the partner's system is down: an unshared JMS durable subscription, or a cloud topic subscription, is registered on their behalf and holds the backlog until they acknowledge it.
A nightly audit or analytics consumer that must see every published change: the day's backlog is drained in bounded batches and acknowledged as it is persisted.
A ledger or compliance consumer that must never silently skip events: retention and lag alarms are configured so an offline subscriber is noticed before its backlog expires.
A cloud event-driven architecture (SNS FIFO → SQS FIFO): SNS preserves ordering and deduplication while SQS queues hold messages for durable fan-out to Lambda or EC2 consumers, with DLQs capturing failed deliveries for replay.
An industrial SCADA/IoT sensor fleet where devices connect sporadically over unstable networks: MQTT persistent sessions with a long session expiry interval preserve every telemetry reading until each device reconnects, even after multi-day outages.
A financial audit trail that must immutably record every state-changing event: events are durably retained in Kafka or JetStream and consumed by a compliance subscriber that must not skip or duplicate entries; idempotent deduplication and offset commits after durable persistence enforce this.
A supply-chain or logistics event-sourcing system where downstream services reconstruct state by replaying events after a crash or deliberate seek: the durable consumer starts from the committed position and replays the missing event window atomically with the state reconstruction.
A cross-region disaster-recovery subscriber that mirrors events to a secondary site: the durable subscription in the secondary region receives every event from the primary's topic, with a DLQ holding any events that fail cross-region delivery for manual retry.
A JMS topic consumer that must receive publications made while it is offline: the client reconnects with the same client identifier and durable subscription name, and the provider retains messages until acknowledgement, expiry, or unsubscribe.
An MQTT 3.1.1 device gateway that reconnects with the same client identifier and CleanSession=0: the broker resumes the stored session and queues matching QoS 1/2 publications for delivery after the link returns.
A NATS JetStream billing worker that restarts after an outage: it binds to the same durable consumer name and explicit-acks each message, so the server resumes its acknowledgement floor and redelivers unacknowledged work.
An Azure Service Bus fan-out topology: topic subscriptions are durable by default and each subscription stores its own copy of matching messages, so a receiver that reconnects later still drains its backlog; client-affine durable subscriptions bind the durable state to a stable client id.
A high-throughput replay consumer on RabbitMQ Streams: the consumer attaches with a stable tracking reference (name) and periodically stores its offset server-side, so a restart resumes from the last stored offset instead of re-reading the whole stream.
An event-sourced system on Google Cloud Pub/Sub that must reprocess history after a bug fix: the subscription enables acknowledged-message retention (default window 7 days, up to 31) and is seeked back to a past timestamp or snapshot to replay already-acked messages.

statement: Should each inventory record own the synchronization and waiting mechanism that enforces exact reservations and lets callers wait for replenishment?
name: monitor-object
document:
monitor-object
thread-safe passive object
monitor
Serialise concurrent method invocations on a shared object by giving the object its own lock and condition variables, so that only one method executes inside it at a time and methods that cannot proceed wait cooperatively instead of polling.
Objects shared by several threads expose their state through ordinary methods, and nothing stops concurrent callers from interleaving inside those methods, corrupting the invariants they were written to maintain. The race is then papered over with ad-hoc locking, sleeps and busy-wait loops scattered through client code. The recurring decision is whether the object itself should own the serialisation (and the scheduling) of its methods instead of leaving that discipline to every caller.
Shared-memory concurrency, where the mutable state of an object is reached by more than one thread and its methods must be atomic with respect to one another. It matters most when some methods cannot run to completion until another method changes the state - a queue that is full or empty, a resource that is not yet available, a phase that has not been reached - because then a method must suspend and later resume, which requires releasing the lock while it waits.
Bounded buffers and work queues shared by producer and consumer threads, where producers wait while the queue is full and consumers wait while it is empty - the pattern's canonical example.
Session, connection or entity registries on a server, where lookups, insertion and eviction must be atomic and callers may have to wait for capacity or for an entry to reappear.
Caches with in-flight bookkeeping (single-flight computation), where a thread that requests an already-computed key waits for the first thread's result instead of recomputing it.
Shared configuration, counters or statistics objects read and updated by request threads, where each call must observe a consistent snapshot of the state.
State machines and simulators whose step methods block until another thread advances a transition, for example a test harness waiting for a worker to reach a known state.
In-process resource pools (connection, database or worker pools) where acquisition blocks until an entry is returned or a timeout expires.
Java's java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue is a fixed-capacity monitor-style bounded buffer: put blocks while full and take blocks while empty, making the producer-consumer coordination explicit.
.NET's System.Collections.Concurrent.BlockingCollection<T> supplies bounded Add/Take blocking, cancellation and completion semantics around a producer-consumer collection; use it instead of hand-rolling Monitor.Wait/Pulse.
Python's queue.Queue provides a thread-safe multi-producer/multi-consumer boundary with blocking put/get operations and optional timeouts, a standard monitor-style primitive for worker pools.

statement: Should each inventory record own the synchronization and waiting mechanism that enforces exact reservations and lets callers wait for replenishment?
name: guarded-suspension
document:
guarded-suspension
conditional block
suspended execution
Suspend a state-dependent method call inside the object that owns the state until another thread makes its guard predicate true, so callers neither poll nor get refused while the object is temporarily not ready.
A method may only proceed while a precondition over shared state holds - a buffer is non-empty, a pool still has a free lease, a session is authenticated, a worker has a task - and that state is produced by another thread at an unknown time. The recurring decision is what the caller should do while the guard is false: refusing the request would drop work the application still needs, forcing the transition would break the object's invariants, and polling wastes a core and still races. Guarded suspension answers it by waiting on a condition the object itself owns, and by making that wait atomic with respect to the state change that ends it.
Concurrent objects whose methods are state-dependent and whose state changes arrive from other threads: bounded buffers and handoff queues, resource pools, server request/response handoffs, readiness and shutdown gates, worker idle loops. Applicable where the runtime can efficiently park or suspend a caller (OS threads, coroutines) and where the object already owns a lock or monitor, so no notification can be lost between the predicate check and the wait. Ill-suited to single-threaded event loops, to callers that must never be delayed, and to waits whose eventual completion cannot be guaranteed.
Actor mailbox handoff: an Akka/Orleans/Swift-Actor mailbox is a lock-free guarded queue; the actor suspends on an empty mailbox and resumes when a message arrives, which is the same monitor-wait pattern expressed at the language level.
Swift async / Structured Concurrency: a Task.sleep or async let that suspends until a condition is a coroutine-level guarded suspension; the suspension point is backed by a condition variable or event channel inside the runtime.
CompletableFuture / async result: a future's blocking get() is a timed guarded suspension on the thread that submitted the asynchronous operation; the completion path (complete()) is the notifier.
Pipeline stage coordination: in a multi-stage streaming pipeline each stage blocks on input while the upstream stage processes, synchronising via a bounded channel whose put/get implement the guard.
Bounded buffers and handoff queues: a consumer's take waits while the buffer is empty and a producer's put waits while it is full (producer-consumer).
Resource pools: acquire blocks until a lease is returned to a connection, thread or object pool instead of failing or spinning when the pool is exhausted.
Server-side handoff: an acceptor or reader thread publishes a request and the worker waits for work to appear; a caller waits for the response slot to be filled.
Readiness and start-up gates: components wait until a dependency reports connected, initialised or ready, and callers wait until a session, device or circuit is open.
Shutdown and flush coordination: a terminator waits until in-flight work has drained, and a flusher waits while the buffer still holds entries (two-phase termination).
Platform queue and channel APIs: BlockingQueue.take/put, Queue#pop, Channel.receive/for-await, condition-variable waits - the same guard hidden behind a library type.
Project Loom virtual threads (JEP 444): a virtual thread calling Object.wait() parks its Continuation; the carrier thread is released for other virtual threads, so the program continues throughput while one virtual thread waits. The guarded action still re-checks the predicate on wake, and the pattern's semantics are preserved — only the threading model changes.
Akka typed actor mailbox: each actor has a single-threaded mailbox; receive() suspends the actor's continuation when the mailbox is empty, resuming when a message is dispatched. This is language-level guarded suspension where the wait set is the mailbox queue and the guard is 'mailbox non-empty'.
Kotlin coroutines rendezvous channel: Channel() (unbuffered/rendezvous) suspends the sender until a receiver is ready, and vice versa — the same lock-free handoff as an unbuffered Go channel. The suspension is a coroutine-level guarded wait on rendezvous.
Python asyncio.Condition: an async context manager that wraps an asyncio.Lock; await cond.wait() releases the lock and suspends the task until notify() is called, making it an async guarded suspension where the runtime schedules other tasks during the wait.
Go unbuffered channel send/receive: goroutine G1 executing ch <- x on an unbuffered channel sleeps (gopark) until goroutine G2 executes <-ch, at which point the runtime directly transfers the value and stack copy (rendezvous handoff). This is the language-level form of guarded suspension: the guard is 'receiver present', the wait set is the sudog queue in hchan.
Erlang/OTP process mailbox: a gen_server receiving messages from its mailbox blocks (receive...end) until a matching message arrives — the OTP process is a state machine whose transitions are guarded by message arrival, making each receive a suspension point in the actor's event loop.
.NET TaskCompletionSource<T>: GetAwaiter().GetResult() on a not-yet-completed TCS is a synchronous guarded suspension; the async continuation (ConfigureAwait, await) is an asynchronous one. SetResult() is the notifier. TCS is a one-shot asymmetric guarded suspension where one side never waits (the completor) and one side always waits (the synchronously blocked caller).
JDK ArrayBlockingQueue: the queue is one ReentrantLock plus two Condition objects, notEmpty and notFull - take() awaits notEmpty while count == 0, put() awaits notFull while the buffer is full, and each signals the other condition only after mutating count and the circular buffer inside the same critical section. It is the reference production realisation of a two-predicate guarded suspension, including the fairness switch and the timed offer/poll variants.
Go standard library: database/sql guards queries against a concurrent Close with closingMutex, which parks readers and the closing writer on two sync.Cond values (read/write), and net/http's Server.Shutdown waits until in-flight requests have drained. Both are the case Go's own guidance reserves sync.Cond for - a predicate that changes back and forth over time rather than a one-shot handoff.
HikariCP connection pool: DataSource.getConnection() suspends the caller until a lease is returned while the pool already holds maximumPoolSize connections, bounded by connectionTimeout (default 30000 ms, minimum 250 ms), after which it throws SQLException rather than waiting on - a guarded suspension in which the deadline is a documented, first-class outcome instead of an accident.

name: lockable-object
document:
lockable-object
Resource Lock
Mutual Exclusion Object
Let an object own the lock that guards its state and publish that lock, so collaborators can satisfy multi-call invariants and condition waits explicitly instead of relying on synchronisation hidden inside individual methods.
Collaborators must keep a shared object stable across a sequence of calls - read, decide and write; transfer between two objects; wait until a predicate holds - but the object's synchronisation is private and per-method, so no client can make the sequence atomic, wait on the same lock, or substitute a different locking policy.
Several threads or tasks share mutable objects inside one process and the unit of exclusion is the object (or a small set of objects): clients need compound atomic operations, condition waits on the same lock, pluggable locking policies, or visibility into contention.
Registries and caches with get-or-create semantics: the caller reads, decides and inserts under one lock instead of racing between separate synchronised calls.
Transfers between two objects: both publish their lock, so the client acquires them in one documented global order and updates both atomically.
Deployments where the same class needs different synchronisation: mutex under contention, read-write lock for read-mostly state, no-op lock in single-threaded builds (strategized locking).
Predicate-driven workers: a consumer holds the object's published lock, waits on its condition and re-checks the predicate before proceeding (guarded suspension).
Contention-aware front doors: the lock object exposes queue length and hold time for metrics, and try-lock acquisition implements admission control under overload.
Deterministic concurrency tests: a test acquires the published lock to hold a worker at a chosen point and asserts the invariant that must hold there.
Connection-pool management: a pool publishes its lock so callers can acquire and release connections atomically within a transaction, avoiding connection-leak races and get-or-create thundering-herds.
Entity-component systems with shared mutable state: components that cross system boundaries are guarded by their owner's published lock so systems can read, validate and update a component atomically without holding the entire world lock.
Read-mostly caches with periodic invalidation: a read-write lock variant lets readers proceed concurrently while a single writer holds exclusive access during cache refresh; the lockable object's published lock is the read-write lock itself.
Deterministic simulation and testing: a simulated process or game loop uses a lockable object's published lock to pause a worker at an injection point (yield) and assert invariants, then resumes — the same pattern used in time-travel debuggers.
Java resource owners can publish a dedicated java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock to trusted collaborators; reentrancy, timed tryLock, newCondition and queue/hold diagnostics support compound operations and guarded waits while callers still bracket unlock in finally.
Portable in-process resource adapters can use Python's threading.Condition with an existing Lock or RLock, while .NET's System.Threading.Lock provides the analogous dedicated lock member with scoped EnterScope and timed TryEnter acquisition.
Rust's std::sync::Mutex<T> binds protected data to its lock and exposes access through MutexGuard RAII; sharing an Arc<Mutex<T>> gives collaborators shared ownership without separating the state from its exclusion guard.

name: thread-safe-interface
document:
thread-safe-interface
Keep a component's locking discipline out of its internal call graph: public interface methods acquire the component's lock once at the border and delegate to implementation methods that never re-acquire it, so intra-component calls cannot self-deadlock and never pay for a second acquisition.
A multi-threaded component guards its state with one lock, and every method that touches that state takes the lock. When such a method calls another method of the same component, the lock is re-acquired: a non-recursive mutex deadlocks the component against itself, and a recursive mutex makes the nested calls legal but pays lock-count bookkeeping for every one of them while hiding the design problem.
Concurrent components that own mutable state, guard it with a single lock and contain intra-component method calls - caches, registries, buffers, pools. It matters most where the lock must stay non-recursive (default POSIX, Go, Rust, Kotlin, Python and Swift mutexes) or where lock traffic must stay minimal, and it applies whenever the synchronization mechanism is chosen independently of the component logic (Strategized Locking), including a Null Mutex for single-threaded deployments.
Cache components where a public lookup inserts on a miss through internal bind/check helpers (the POSA2 file-cache example).
Bounded buffers and queues whose public put/get share bookkeeping helpers and condition signalling.
Registry and metrics objects whose update methods fan out into several internal mutations that must be atomic with the update.
Connection and object pools whose acquire operation validates and replaces dead entries through internal helpers.
In-memory indexes (inverted index, LRU, session table) where lookups trigger maintenance work.
Components instantiated with a pluggable lock strategy, including a Null Mutex for single-threaded deployments.
CPython's free-threaded runtime splits its internal object APIs into locking entry points and *_LockHeld helpers (_PyDict_SetItem_LockHeld, _PyDict_Clear_LockHeld) that the caller may invoke only while holding the per-object or global lock.
Linux kernel subsystems: public functions acquire the lock and call internal helpers whose documentation states the caller must already hold it, the calling convention described in the kernel-hacking locking guide.
Go components built on sync.Mutex: the package documents the mutex as non-reentrant - a goroutine holding it that calls Lock again blocks forever - so exported methods lock at the border and delegate to unexported helpers that assume the lock is held.

name: scoped-locking
document:
scoped-locking
guard
synchronized block
Bind a lock's lifetime to the lifetime of a scope so that the lock is acquired when control enters the scope and released automatically on every exit path, not merely on the path the programmer remembered.
Critical sections that acquire and release a lock explicitly are correct only as long as every exit path releases it. A later early return, a newly thrown exception, a cancellation or a routine maintenance edit adds an exit path without an unlock, and the leaked lock blocks every subsequent thread forever.
Concurrent code that serializes shared mutable state with a mutex or similar synchronizer and whose guarded region has more than one exit path (early returns, exceptions, cancellation, callbacks). It applies wherever the language provides a reliable scope-exit hook - a destructor (RAII), try/finally, using, with, defer or a block-scoped synchronizer - or where one can be emulated without losing the guarantee.
Incrementing a shared hit counter or metrics table from request threads (POSA2's canonical hit-count example), where the method has several bail-out paths.
Guarding an in-memory cache or registry around find-or-create, where the lookup may insert, miss, fail or throw.
Updating session or connection state under a per-object lock in a server that processes many concurrent connections (ACE's ACE_Guard on ACE_Thread_Mutex).
Multi-mutex operations such as a bank transfer, where std::scoped_lock or std::lock acquires both guards deadlock-free and releases them at scope exit.
Suspending critical sections in coroutine code (kotlinx.coroutines Mutex.withLock, tokio::sync::Mutex) where the guard must survive suspension points.
Logging and serialization subsystems that must not keep the lock if a formatter or sink throws.
Java synchronized blocks, C# lock statements, Python with statements and Ruby synchronize blocks around read-modify-write on shared collections.
Go's idiomatic scoped lock: mu.Lock() immediately followed by defer mu.Unlock() at the top of the function, so every return path and panic releases the mutex (Go sync.Mutex); note a Go mutex is not bound to the locking goroutine, so any goroutine may unlock it.
Rust std::sync::Mutex: Mutex::lock returns a MutexGuard whose Deref/DerefMut expose the data and whose Drop unlocks at end of scope; the guard is deliberately !Send so the release always happens on the acquiring thread.
Chromium's base::AutoLock family (AutoLock, AutoTryLock, AutoUnlock, ReleasableAutoLock) guarding members annotated for Clang thread-safety analysis, with copy operations deleted so the guard cannot be duplicated or escaped.

name: identity-map
document:
identity-map
first-level cache
session cache
Guarantee that within one session every database row is represented by exactly one in-memory object, by keeping a keyed registry of loaded objects that every load consults before hitting the database.
Two code paths in the same session load the same row into two different objects: updates through one are invisible to the other, the last flush silently wins, and every load pays the remote-call cost again. The catalog states the invariant as: the same row must never be two different in-memory objects in one session.
Object-oriented persistence (data mappers, repositories, unit of work) where entities carry a stable database identity (an Identity Field) and several parts of one business transaction or request refer to the same rows. Applies whenever duplicate in-memory instances would break graph consistency or lose updates - typically inside an ORM session or a hand-written persistence context whose lifetime bounds staleness.
ORM sessions in web request handling (JPA EntityManager, EF Core DbContext, SQLAlchemy Session, MikroORM EntityManager) where several services touch the same entities in one request.
Batch import and synchronisation jobs that re-read the same rows repeatedly inside one transaction and must not operate on divergent copies.
Object graph reconstruction in data mappers, where cycles and shared references need one in-memory instance per row.
Desktop and document applications with a context-scoped object space (Core Data contexts) where objects are edited, undone and saved as one unit.
Hand-written persistence layers over plain SQL where two repositories serve the same table and must agree on identity.
CQRS command handlers where the same aggregate is loaded multiple times within one command execution — the identity map prevents duplicate instances from forming across repository calls within the same session.
Event-sourced aggregate reconstruction: replaying events to rebuild aggregate state requires the same aggregate instance to accumulate state across multiple event applications; identity map guarantees a single instance per aggregate ID per reconstruction session.
Microservices saga and choreography: within one service's unit-of-work, multiple steps may load the same entity; identity map ensures all steps operate on the same instance even when the entity is referenced across different event handlers.
DDD bounded-context integration: when one bounded context holds a reference to an entity from another context (by ID), that entity is resolved through the local identity map — multiple resolution paths must all consult the same map to stay consistent.
Testing scenarios where the same entity is accessed via multiple repository paths: identity map guarantees test assertions see the same instance regardless of which repository method returned it, enabling meaningful state verification.
Multi-tenant applications where each tenant request gets its own session/identity-map scope, preventing cross-tenant data leakage by construction — a shared/global map would allow one tenant's rows to shadow another's.
SQLAlchemy Session.get in a unit of work: repeated primary-key loads return the same Python object from the Session identity map, while the Session is deliberately not a cross-session query cache.
EF Core tracked queries and AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution: the DbContext keeps one entity instance per key for tracked results, while no-tracking identity resolution is opt-in for read models.
Hibernate Session persistence contexts: repeated loads of the same entity type and identifier resolve to the one managed instance per Session, so entity graphs and dirty checking share state.

name: mock
document:
mock
mock object
Replace a collaborator of the system under test with a test-specific object that is programmed with the expected calls and verifies them as they happen, so the interaction itself - not the resulting state - is what the test asserts.
The expected interaction sequence is the behaviour under test: the outcome of the exercised method is not visible in the system under test's own state, and no observation point exposes the indirect outputs (the messages sent to collaborators) that the requirement is about. State-based assertions cannot reach them, so the test either reaches into the collaborator's internals - duplicating the collaboration logic - or asserts nothing at all.
Unit and component tests of an object whose collaboration protocol is the specification: exact calls, arguments, cardinality or order matter (handshakes, publish-once, audit logging, cache invalidation) and the collaborator is slow, unavailable, non-deterministic or side-effecting. It requires a substitutable dependency (dependency injection or lookup) and, for framework-based realizations, an interception mechanism - dynamic proxy, bytecode agent, generated code or macro. Typical in mockist, interaction-first TDD and in need-driven development.
Verifying that a component emits exactly the expected messages to a collaborator whose effects are otherwise invisible: an audit logger, notifier, event publisher or payment gateway.
Pinning an interaction protocol whose ordering and cardinality are the requirement - open before send, publish exactly once, flush before close - in tests of clients and adapters.
Simulating failure paths of a remote collaborator (timeout, exception, malformed response) to assert that the SUT surfaces or recovers from them deterministically.
Unit-testing a domain service against repository, clock, or gateway interfaces when the real implementations are slow, licensed or unavailable in the development environment.
Driving interface design from the outside in: write the expectation for the call the SUT should make, then let the implementation satisfy it (mockist TDD).
Verifying that a main operation triggers its side effects - cache invalidation, metrics emission, compensating call - with the required arguments.
In C++ tests built with GoogleTest gMock, using EXPECT_CALL matchers, Times cardinalities and InSequence ordering verifies an outbound collaborator protocol before the SUT runs.
In Java tests using Mockito, verify and InOrder assert required interactions with a dependency while keeping the interaction contract separate from the dependency's implementation.
In Python's unittest.mock, assert_called_once_with and assert_has_calls verify argument, cardinality and sequence requirements for calls made through a replaceable collaborator.

name: cache-aside
document:
cache-aside
look-aside cache
lazy loading cache
Place the cache beside the authoritative store and make the application own the protocol: look up the cache first, load the entry from the store on a miss and populate it with a TTL, and invalidate the entry right after each write to the store - so repeated reads stay cheap while the store, never the cache, decides what is true.
A source of truth (relational database, downstream service, object store) is expensive or rate-limited for the read volume an application receives, while most reads repeat a small set of keys: without a cache every request pays the source-of-truth cost, and with an unmanaged cache the copies silently drift. The recurring decision is where the read path looks first, when a miss may populate the entry, and what a write must do so the cached copy stops lying.
Read-heavy paths in front of a slower or metered authoritative store, typically several application instances sharing a Redis or Memcached tier, or each holding an in-process cache, where a bounded amount of staleness is acceptable and every writer can be held to the same invalidation discipline. It applies when the read/write ratio is high, when the cache itself does not provide read-through or write-through, and when lost or evicted entries can always be recomputed from the store.
Read-heavy lookups by natural key (product catalogs, user profiles, article pages) in front of a relational database.
Several service instances sharing a Redis or Memcached tier where every instance must see the same cached copy and the same invalidation.
Reference data that changes slowly (currency rates, feature flags, configuration, price lists) refreshed by TTL with explicit invalidation when it is edited.
Expensive aggregate or derived results (dashboards, search pages, recommendations) recomputed into the cache per request key.
Per-instance in-process caches for hot, rarely changing values where a shared cache would add network latency without adding much.
Multi-level caching in Kubernetes: an in-process L1 (Caffeine) sidecar on each pod with an L2 Redis cluster, where the L1 is invalidated on each incoming request via a bloom filter or pub/sub.
CDN edge caching for static or semi-static API responses: the application server acts as the origin and issues cache-aside reads; CDN edges serve from their own look-aside cache with short TTLs and PURGE invalidation on writes.
RAG and vector cache in AI pipelines: embedding results cached by query hash so repeated semantically identical questions hit the vector store once and reuse cached results; TTL bounds staleness of the embedding index.
Django's low-level cache API (cache.get / cache.get_or_set with a per-key timeout, cache.delete on save) is cache-aside as a framework primitive; MediaWiki's WANObjectCache does the same at Wikipedia scale via getWithSet, invalidating page parses through cross-datacenter purges rather than direct writes.
Spring's cache abstraction applies the pattern declaratively: @Cacheable loads and populates on a miss, @CacheEvict removes the entry after the writer, with RedisCacheManager supplying the TTL - the application still owns both paths, the annotation only moves where.
Hibernate's second-level cache read-write concurrency strategy is a managed cache-aside: the updated entry is soft-locked around the transaction so concurrent readers miss to the database instead of repopulating the cache with the pre-commit value.

name: copy-and-swap
document:
copy-and-swap
copy and swap idiom
create-temporary-and-swap
Implement assignment (and any in-place state replacement) so that a failure while producing the new state leaves the target untouched: build the complete replacement off to the side, commit it with operations that cannot fail, and let the temporary's destructor or the garbage collector release the old state.
A hand-written assignment has to tear down the old state and build a copy of the new one, but only the build can fail: destroying before allocating exposes a half-updated object when the allocation or the element copy throws, and the usual repair -- a self-assignment check plus manual rollback -- duplicates the per-member copying that already lives in the copy constructor. The trigger is an assignment (or, in a garbage-collected language, an in-place state replacement) that must satisfy the strong exception guarantee: either it completes, or the target still holds its previous value.
Types that own resources -- heap buffers, handles, file descriptors, trees, containers -- in a language where the programmer controls copy semantics: C++ special member functions, a C ADT with error codes, Rust with panic/abort failure modes. The same ordering also applies in garbage-collected languages whenever published state must never be mutated in place: building the complete replacement and publishing it once keeps readers consistent and moves the release of the old state to the collector. The precondition is a commit step that genuinely cannot fail -- a noexcept member swap, one reference or pointer store, or an atomic publish.
Container and buffer classes that own heap memory (dynamic array, string, matrix, tree) and must be assignable without leaking or leaving the target inconsistent when an allocation fails.
Handle/pimpl classes that keep their state behind a single pointer: the swap is a pointer exchange, so the commit is unconditionally non-throwing while the deep copy still happens in the copy constructor (Sutter's canonical Pimpl exception-safety transformation).
Pre-C++11 codebases where the same operator= must serve lvalues and rvalues and no move constructor exists, using the const-reference plus explicit-local-temporary form.
Value types stored inside standard containers: std::vector and friends need element assignment to be safe before they can offer their own strong guarantee on reallocation, and a noexcept swap participates in their internal move/swap dispatch.
Garbage-collected languages where shared state must be replaced rather than mutated: build a complete replacement value and publish it with one store (AtomicReference.updateAndGet, atomic.Pointer[T].Store, a record with-expression) so readers never observe a partially updated object.
In-place state replacement where identity must be preserved (a registry entry, a cached object with live references): copy into a scratch value, then commit with a member-wise exchange or a replace-style API instead of repointing the reference.
Concurrent programming with thread-safe local-then-publish: build the replacement in a local object (thread-private by definition), then publish atomically -- readers never see a partially updated state, and the previous value is released by the collector after the atomic write is visible.
Version-control-style update: check out a local copy, mutate freely, then commit or discard; copy-and-swap maps directly to this workflow and provides the same transactional semantics (Howard Hinnant's analogy from his C++ Con 2018 talk).
Compiler tooling treats the idiom as the canonical self-assignment-safe assignment: LLVM's clang-tidy bugprone-unhandled-self-assignment checker explicitly recognizes 'build a temporary in operator=, then swap it' as correct handling and matches extended (allocator-aware) constructors plus ADL swap forms so real copy-and-swap code is not flagged (llvm/llvm-project PR #147066).
Boost's move/assignment guidance converged on the single by-value form T operator=(T b) { swap(*this, b); return *this; } as the common way to get copy-, move-, and convertible-assignment from one operator, with dedicated macros (BOOST_COPYABLE_AND_MOVABLE_ALT) for classes that adopt it instead of separate overloads.
When a strong guarantee is needed on the standard containers, libc++ maintainers advise exactly this idiom at the call site -- 'construct a new vector and swap it with the one you want to assign to' (libc++ PR #117516 discussion) -- because the library's own copy assignment deliberately offers only the basic guarantee.

name: audit-interceptor
document:
audit-interceptor
audit trail interceptor
audit logging interceptor
Declare an audit policy at an invocation seam that records the actor, action, target, correlation id and both attempt and terminal outcome around a delegated operation, then sends the structured event to a dedicated integrity-protected sink, so security accountability is consistent without inline logging in every service.
Security-relevant operations (privileged actions, state changes and access to sensitive data) must be attributable, but inline logging misses denied and failed attempts, varies in schema, can leak raw arguments and disappears with a rolled-back transaction. Teams also need to cover components they cannot modify without pretending that a proxy sees calls that bypass it.
Business or service tiers whose sensitive operations pass through an interceptable seam: container-managed beans, proxied service objects, ORM entity lifecycles, message endpoints or an HTTP pipeline. Audit selection must be declarative and uniform, while the sink has its own integrity and retention requirements (Secure Logger); the design must make mediation gaps, redaction, transaction coupling, failure policy, clock source and correlation propagation explicit.
Business-tier auditing of money-moving or otherwise regulated operations (fund transfer, order placement, claim submission): who requested it, on which object, when, and whether it succeeded.
Privileged administration surfaces (role changes, key rotation, configuration changes) where every sensitive operation must leave a record naming the acting principal.
Authentication and authorization outcomes: successful and failed logins, access-denial decisions and lockouts routed into the same audit pipeline instead of ad-hoc log lines.
Access-to-sensitive-data events (who read which patient/customer record) recorded at the gateway or service boundary to satisfy data-protection obligations.
Retrofitting auditing onto legacy components whose code cannot be modified, by wrapping the service object or binding an interceptor to its interface.
Middleware-level auditing of message endpoints and database calls in a business tier, correlating the caller's subject with the operation performed.
Financial API request interception (Spring Boot global request interceptors) capturing who accessed which endpoint, with what payload, and what outcome — satisfying SOX financial reporting controls.
Entity-level change tracking via ORM subscribers (e.g., EF Core SaveChangesInterceptor, TypeORM subscribers): automatically diff old vs. new property values on create/update/delete and emit audit envelopes without manual logging calls.
API gateway-level audit logging: capture every external API call with timestamp, user identity, endpoint, method, and outcome, correlating across microservices via X-Request-ID / traceparent headers.
Compliance reporting automation: generate audit-ready reports for SOX (~7-year retention), HIPAA (~6-year retention), GDPR (data residency-aware), and PCI-DSS from structured interceptor events.
Zero-trust data access trails: record every read of sensitive fields (PHI, PII, financial data) so data-protection obligations (GDPR Article 5 data minimization, HIPAA access logging) are demonstrably met.
Hibernate Envers: @Audited entity lifecycle changes create per-entity _AUD revisions at transaction commit; a custom revision entity/listener can attach actor or request metadata.
Django admin: django.contrib.admin.models.LogEntry records action time, user, object, addition/change/deletion and change_message for ModelAdmin activity.
Rails Audited: the audited ActiveRecord extension creates audit rows for model create, update and destroy callbacks, including changed attributes and optional acting-user attribution.

name: monad
document:
monad
io monad
programmable semicolon
Give a computation's effect (absence, failure, asynchrony, I/O, state) a type of its own with a unit and a bind operation, so that a sequence of steps in which each step depends on the previous value composes into one pipeline while bind propagates the effect automatically.
Sequencing computations where the next step needs the previous step's result and every step may additionally be absent, failing, asynchronous or effectful pushes the effect handling into the business logic: nested null checks, try/catch ladders, callback pyramids. Every call site repeats the same propagation decision (short-circuit? await? log?) and one forgotten check turns a controlled failure into a crash or a wrong value.
Applies wherever a value and the fact that it is absent, pending, failing or impure belong together: chained lookups, validation and error pipelines, asynchronous call chains, state threading, parser and interpreter pipelines, and effect-typed application cores. It matters most when the sequence is long, when the effect policy must be uniform and testable, and when the language already provides monadic types (Optional, Result, Promise, IO) or syntax that desugars to bind (do-notation, for-comprehensions, async/await).
Chained lookups where any link may be missing: user -> address -> city expressed with Maybe/Optional instead of nested null checks.
Validation and error pipelines in which each step can fail with a domain error and the first failure must short-circuit (Either/Result, railway-oriented programming).
Asynchronous workflows whose next call depends on the previous response (Promise/async-await, CompletableFuture.thenCompose, Kotlin suspend functions, Swift Task).
Effect description and interpretation: building an IO/program value that is pure data and running it through different interpreters in tests and production (IO monad, tagless-final).
State-threading computations such as compiler passes, random generators or incremental traversals written as a State monad pipeline.
Parser combinators and nondeterministic search, where each step consumes the previous parse result or explores every value produced by the previous step (parser monad, List monad).
Rust's std::result::Result composes fallible steps with and_then and the ? operator, returning early on Err while keeping the successful value available to the next dependent step.
Java's CompletableFuture.thenCompose chains dependent asynchronous stages: the function returns another CompletionStage and the outer stage adopts its completion or exceptional failure.
Scala for-comprehensions over Option, collections, or other types with map, flatMap, and withFilter desugar dependent bindings into the corresponding combinators, keeping the monadic sequence readable without hiding its operations.

name: compound-components
document:
compound-components
compound component
compound component pattern
Give a family of cooperating components one owner — the parent — that holds the shared state and publishes it implicitly to every child, so consumers compose the family declaratively while the parent alone enforces its invariants and behaviour.
A widget only works when a parent and its children agree on one piece of state (which option is selected, which panel is open, whether a field is invalid), but the call site is the only place that knows the children. Holding the state at the call site means threading the value and its update callbacks into every child (prop drilling), and holding it in the children means the parent cannot enforce the family's invariants — exclusivity, ordering, keyboard behaviour — nor react to a child's change in one place. The recurring decision is where the shared state lives and how children participate in it without the call site wiring them.
Component-tree UI code: design-system and widget libraries (select/option, tabs, menus, field groups) in frameworks that can inject state into descendants without passing it through props — React context or child cloning, Angular content projection plus DI, Vue provide/inject, Compose CompositionLocal and slot scopes, SwiftUI environment and preference keys, Blazor cascading values, WPF attached properties over the logical tree — and in widget toolkits whose group objects (Swing ButtonGroup, JavaFX ToggleGroup, Qt QButtonGroup, tkinter control variables) play the same role. It pays off where the public API must stay small and the children must stay replaceable; it does not apply in languages without a component tree or without an implicit-injection channel.
Custom select, combobox or autocomplete families built from Option children — the canonical example: the parent owns the selection, the highlight and the keyboard interaction while options only declare their value and label.
Tabs, accordions and menus where Tab/TabPanel/MenuItem children register their identity and the parent owns the active item, the ordering and the ARIA wiring.
Form-field families (Field + Label + Input + Error) that share one validation/invalid state and generated ids without the call site passing them around.
Data-group widgets: tables with Column definitions, list widgets with Item children, tree views with Node children, chart legends with Series children.
Design-system libraries that export one namespaced symbol whose parts must be used together — the context in which the pattern is most often documented and most valuable.
Collapsible panel families (Disclosure pattern) where a parent owns the open/closed state and Trigger/Content children read it — also known as the Disclosure pattern in ARIA authoring practices.
Stepper/wizard widgets where a parent owns current-step state and Step/StepIndicator children read it without the consumer threading step indices.
Popover/tooltip families where a trigger button and a content panel share open/close state through the parent without prop drilling.
Radix UI Primitives — Dialog.Root owns the open/close context and Trigger/Portal/Content/Title/Description consume it, while asChild (Slot) merges each part's props, refs and keyboard behaviour into the consumer's own button or link.
Ark UI headless components (built on Zag.js state machines) — Popover.Root/Trigger/Positioner/Content share state through the root, ids props compose aria bindings across two families, and the same compound anatomy works in React, Solid, Vue and Svelte.
Headless UI's Dialog family (Dialog, DialogBackdrop, DialogPanel, DialogTitle, Description) — the root enforces the dismiss contract (open prop, onClose callback, focus trap, aria-labelledby) and every part reads the shared open/closed state, exposed for styling as data-open/data-closed attributes.

caretaker
revocable proxy
Let a collaborator use an object through a forwarding wrapper that the grantor can switch off at any time through a separate control, so authority already handed out can be withdrawn without destroying the target and without the collaborator's cooperation.
A capability is just a reference, so once a collaborator has been given access to an object there is no built-in way to take it back: the grantor can destroy the object, ask the collaborator to stop, or leave the access standing. The recurring decision is how to grant access that is bounded in time - temporary use of a file, a service object, a session, an account - while keeping a control that only the grantor holds.
Object-capability settings, and any in-process design in which authority travels as references rather than as a global identity: plugin and extension hosts lending a service object to foreign code, multi-tenant object graphs giving a worker one tenant-scoped resource, session-scoped services, and capability-based workflow or financial systems in which a grant must be provably withdrawn. It applies when the grantor keeps its own reference to the target and can intercept every call through the reference it handed out; where the runtime lets references be forged, dereferenced around the wrapper or reached by reflection, marshalling or FFI, the same structure degrades from an enforcement mechanism to a discipline.
A plugin or extension host lends a file, network or service object to foreign code and revokes it when the plugin is unloaded or breaches policy.
A multi-tenant worker receives one tenant-scoped resource for the duration of a job and loses it at job end, without the tenant object being torn down.
Session teardown in a long-lived server: the handler works through the wrapper, and logout revokes future calls before the session's resources are freed.
Capability-based workflow and financial systems that give an agent temporary authority over an account or a document and revoke it when the task completes.
Temporary elevated access for maintenance or debugging, where the requirement is to show that the extra authority has provably ended (audit evidence).
Graceful decommissioning of a shared resource: revoke new work through the wrapper, drain the calls already in flight, then release the resource.
The Scala ocaps framework's Revocable/Caretaker API returns a proxied capability plus a private Revoker, so a session, logout, timeout or supervisor can make later calls fail without changing the target.
JavaScript's standard Proxy.revocable() and the Chrome Extensions chrome.permissions API provide browser/runtime counterparts: keep the revoke/remove control private, and do not mistake the platform wrapper or permission record for protection against an already leaked target reference.
AWS IAM role-session revocation for temporary STS credentials is a distributed analogue of withdrawing a forwarded grant: policy evaluation denies subsequent requests, but propagation and credential caching mean it is not the atomic in-process check-and-forward gate described here.

name: pattern-matching
document:
pattern-matching
structural pattern matching
case analysis
Eliminate a value drawn from a closed set of variants by matching its structure and binding the payload, so the compiler proves that every variant is handled before the program runs.
Code that inspects which variant of a tagged value it received - a result type, a domain event, an AST node, a protocol frame, a state - drifts into chains of type tests, casts and accessor calls, and nothing guarantees that a variant added later is handled: the missing branch is found in production rather than by the compiler.
Applies when a value's type is a closed sum - an enum with payloads, a sealed hierarchy, a discriminated union, a tagged union - and behaviour depends on which variant arrived. It needs a match construct (language syntax, a variant type with visitation, or a type-level bottom-type check) plus a compiler or checker able to see the set as closed: same-unit sealing, private constructors, or explicit non_exhaustive / @unknown markers where a set is published to other teams.
Interpreter and compiler front ends: expression and statement types are evaluated with one total match per operation, and a new node kind cannot be forgotten.
Protocol and RPC dispatch: a frame or command is one of a fixed set of shapes, and each shape is deconstructed into its fields instead of being cast.
Result and error mapping at boundaries: translating domain failures into transport errors, where every failure variant must be given a mapping.
State machines and workflow states: states carry state-specific data, and transitions are written as a total match over (state, event) pairs.
Domain-event handling in reducers and event-sourced aggregates, where every event type must be applied to rebuild state.
Command-line and query parsing: token or request shapes are matched structurally, including literals and sequence patterns, before validation logic runs.
OpenJDK Java 21 sealed hierarchies: pattern switches over AST or domain-event variants can enumerate permitted types without a default, using the compiler's exhaustiveness analysis.
rustc and Rust enum APIs: match expressions destructure enum variants and the compiler rejects non-exhaustive arms, making protocol and compiler AST dispatch explicit.
CPython 3.10+ match/case: parsers and protocol adapters can select class, sequence, mapping and literal shapes with ordered guards before constructing domain values.
Scala 3 sealed ADTs and union types: the Scala compiler checks exhaustiveness while case-class patterns bind payloads for interpreters, reducers and protocol decoders.

name: consumer-driven-contract-test
document:
consumer-driven-contract-test
consumer-driven contract
contract test
Capture, from each consumer's own tests, the concrete provider interactions that consumer depends on, and verify the provider against that contract inside the provider's own build, so consumer and provider can be released independently without a shared end-to-end environment.
Independently released consumers and providers must keep working together, yet the only reliable check is a shared end-to-end environment per pair - slow, brittle and usually out of date; at the same time the provider cannot see which parts of its API each consumer actually exercises, so every refactoring is a guess about who will break.
HTTP/request-reply, messaging and gRPC integrations where consumer and provider are owned by different teams on different release cadences and each consumer uses only a narrow slice of the provider's surface. It assumes the provider team is willing to run verification of consumer contracts in its own build; without that half, the consumer test is only a better mock.
Microservice landscapes where a front end, a mobile app or another service consumes an API released by a different team on its own schedule.
A provider team that must refactor or replace internals and needs to know, before merging, which consumer expectations it is about to break.
Mobile or desktop clients that cannot be deployed in lockstep with the backend, so each client's expectations must hold against every backend version.
Event- and message-based integrations (Kafka, SQS, SNS, RabbitMQ) where the consumer processes messages produced by another team; contracts pin the message body shape and metadata (topic, headers, content-type) while abstracting the transport.
Migration or strangler-fig work, where a replacement provider must be proven compatible with the existing consumers before traffic is moved.
Using the contract as the source of stubs for development and integration environments, so those environments no longer need the real provider.
BFF (Backend for Frontend) patterns where each frontend channel (web, mobile, third-party) has its own contract with a shared backend, allowing independent evolution of each BFF without cross-channel breakage.
Multi-team Kafka event streaming where consumers (downstream services) define which topics, partitions and message schemas they depend on, so producers can evolve events without silently breaking subscribers; Pact message pacts handle both JSON and Schema Registry messages (with magic bytes for Avro/Protobuf over Schema Registry).
gRPC service integrations where protocol buffer message shapes are exercised by the actual consumer client code, pinning the wire format, service method signatures and metadata the consumer actually calls; synchronous message pacts cover the request-response pairing.
Breaking up a monolith: individual microservices are extracted and their CDC contracts verify that the new service boundaries behave identically to the original module interfaces before traffic is migrated.
Schema Registry integrations (Confluent, AWS Glue) where consumers pin compatible message schemas and producers must not publish breaking schemas without migrating all dependent consumers first.
Third-party or vendor API integrations where the consumer team cannot rely on the provider to run verification: the consumer-side mock-only workflow with published contracts documents expectations even without provider participation.
Webhook and callback integrations where a provider calls a consumer-defined endpoint; CDC captures the consumer's expected payload shape, headers and authentication, and the provider verifies it can deliver to that shape.
Contract migration at scale: when a provider must migrate from v1 to v2 of an API, CDC with pending/wip pacts allows the provider to signal new expectations to consumers without blocking either side's pipeline while migration is in progress.
Spring Cloud Contract in JVM/Spring landscapes: the consumer's contract change lands in the producer's repository (or an external contract repo), the producer build generates verification tests from the contract DSL, and the consumer develops against StubRunner-served WireMock stubs pulled from an artifact repository (Nexus/Artifactory) - the contract is the single artifact both sides build from.
Nubank replaced its flaky shared-environment end-to-end suite with consumer-driven contract tests to regain deploy velocity - the public account of the pattern paying off as an e2e-substitute at a single organisation rather than as an addition to it.
Large polyglot estates such as JSTOR/ITHAKA (300+ microservices, 12+ teams, Pact) and M1 Finance (Pact plus PactFlow rolled out to 17 teams in under six months): the broker's compatibility matrix replaces per-pair end-to-end environments as the release gate.

name: authentication-enforcer
document:
authentication-enforcer
authentication interceptor
authentication gateway
auth middleware
Put one request-boundary checkpoint in front of protected actions that decides whether authentication is required, delegates credential verification to a replaceable mechanism, and attaches the resulting subject to request-scoped context before dispatch, so coverage is uniform without making handlers understand credentials.
When each handler decides whether and how to authenticate, protection is duplicated or omitted on exceptional paths, credential formats and user stores leak into business code, and a mechanism or policy change requires editing every handler instead of one auditable boundary.
Server-side request processing — web APIs, web applications and service endpoints — where many handlers share one protection policy, credentials arrive through a uniform convention (Authorization header, cookie, session id), verification technology must be replaceable or differ per route, and the runtime provides a request-pipeline hook (servlet filter, middleware chain, framework guard). Applies to session-based and token-based authentication alike; permissions and roles are out of scope. Three implementation strategies exist: (1) Container-Managed Authentication — the runtime container owns the checkpoint and realm configuration; (2) Authentication Provider Strategy — a custom provider behind a narrow interface, swapped without touching handlers; (3) JAAS Login Module Strategy — pluggable via standard JAAS configuration, supporting multifactor authentication via smart cards, biometrics, or third-party IdPs. The pattern is equally applicable at the edge level (API gateway, ingress proxy) and the service level (in-process middleware).
Web APIs where every route except health and login requires a bearer token, and the checkpoint is mounted in front of the whole router.
Multi-tenant applications with mixed protection levels: public marketing pages, session-protected tenant UI and token-protected integration endpoints behind one enforcement layer.
Services that must accept several credential types at once — browser sessions, mobile JWTs, mutual TLS for service-to-service traffic — while keeping one uniform enforcement point.
Credential-technology migration (basic auth to OIDC, on-premises LDAP to SSO) where enforcement stays put while the mechanism behind it is swapped.
Regulated environments where every rejected authentication attempt has to be logged centrally and identically across all endpoints.
Legacy applications with authentication checks scattered through servlets or handlers that must be consolidated behind one intercepting layer before an audit.
Zero Trust microservices where every internal service verifies JWTs independently (per-service verification) while an ingress gateway provides the first checkpoint — the enforcer exists at both layers.
OIDC/OAuth2 migration where an existing session-based app adds bearer-token support; the mechanism adapts to both while the enforcement point remains unchanged.
Multi-tenant SaaS platforms where tenant isolation depends on the enforcer resolving a tenant identifier from the token before the handler processes any data.
Platform-as-a-Service with mounted sub-applications where a parent ASGI middleware dispatches per-path authentication requirements from a config registry, injecting identity into ASGI scope for all sub-apps.
Spring Security servlet applications that use a SecurityFilterChain with anyRequest().authenticated() and an AuthenticationManager/AuthenticationProvider chain, so controllers consume the SecurityContext rather than parse credentials.
ASP.NET Core APIs that register JWT or cookie schemes, call UseAuthentication before dependent middleware, and use a fallback authorization policy to make authenticated access the default.
An nginx ingress location using auth_request to delegate identity verification to a central authentication service, forwarding only after a 2xx result and propagating 401/403 failures while services still verify their own trust boundary.
