name: option-maybe
document:
option-maybe
Option
Maybe
Make the possible absence of a result part of the value and of the signature, so every caller has to decide what happens when nothing is there instead of meeting a null, a sentinel or a silently defaulted value at run time.
A function has something to return for some inputs and nothing for others, but the signature does not say so: it returns a null reference, a sentinel (-1, empty string, NULL), an out-parameter, or a value that quietly means 'not found'. Callers forget the check, dereference the null or treat the sentinel as data, and the 'this case does not exist' path is discovered in production rather than at the call site.
Lookups, parsing, searches, optional configuration, nullable database columns and any API whose result may legitimately not exist - wherever the language can express absence as a type (Option/Maybe/Optional, a nullable type, a union with undefined) or a convention can carry it. It pays off at module and service boundaries, in chains of partial steps, and wherever 'absent' must stay distinguishable from a legitimate empty, zero or falsey value.
Lookups that can miss: configuration keys, cache entries, registry entries, map/dictionary access - either through the language's two-value form or an Optional-returning accessor.
Parsing and conversion (integers, dates, URLs, decimal numbers, external identifiers) where 'no valid value' is a legitimate answer rather than an error.
Searches over collections and structures (find, first, min/max, binary search, regex match, tree traversal) where a miss is part of the contract.
Genuinely optional data: middle names, second addresses, unset feature flags, optional protocol fields - as opposed to missing state, which is a domain error.
Chains of partial steps (look up user, then their company, then its billing address) where any hop may be absent and the whole chain should collapse to 'nothing'.
Boundaries from nullable interfaces: a database column admits NULL, a legacy or interop API returns null or -1, a deserialized document lacks a field - converted once at the adapter.
Container and stream operations that can be empty (head, pop, next, dequeue, min) and should report emptiness instead of throwing or returning a sentinel.
Rust's standard library uses std::option::Option<T> with Some(T) and None for optional values; its map and pattern-matching APIs let lookup or parsing pipelines stop at absence without a null pointer.
Java SE's java.util.Optional<T> is a production API for method results that may be absent: ofNullable converts a nullable boundary value, map/flatMap compose follow-up work, and orElse/orElseThrow make the exit policy explicit.
Scala's standard-library scala.Option[A] models Some/None and documents map, flatMap, and for-comprehensions for chained partial steps; its API also demonstrates wrapping a Java HashMap lookup so a missing key becomes None.

statement: How should the handler propagate one cooperative stop request through its dependent calls, clean up safely, and report cancellation separately from failure?
name: cursor-pagination
document:
cursor-pagination
keyset pagination
cursor-based pagination
Bound what a read boundary returns for a large or changing ordered collection by sending one page plus an opaque continuation token that pins the filter and ordering, so clients advance deterministically without offsets and without watching rows move under them.
A boundary must expose a collection that is too large to return at once and keeps changing while clients read it. Offset or page-number requests make the store count or scan everything up to the requested page, and concurrent inserts or deletes shift rows across page boundaries so consumers see duplicates or miss items; the server has no way to state where the sequence should resume.
Any read boundary - an HTTP or gRPC list operation, a GraphQL connection, a database-backed feed, a batch export job - over an ordered collection that is large, growing, or read under concurrent writes, where the server can identify a unique, immutable ordering key and wants to cap both response size and per-request query cost while letting clients iterate the whole sequence.
Public REST or gRPC list endpoints over unbounded, growing tables - messages, orders, audit events - where deep offsets are slow and responses must stay small.
Infinite-scroll or load-more feeds that keep returning newer items while a user scrolls, with the already-seen pages stable against inserts.
Whole-collection sync and export jobs (warehouse loads, backups, search reindexing) that must iterate every row exactly once while writers continue.
GraphQL Relay connections where first/after, edges and pageInfo carry the continuation contract in the schema instead of the URL.
Consumers of third-party list APIs (Stripe-style starting_after/has_more, Google page_token iterators) that keep parameters fixed across auto-paginated calls.
Administrative and operational tooling that streams very large tables for verification or cleanup with bounded memory and predictable server load.
Audit log and event stream retrieval where events are append-only and chronological, and clients stream continuously without needing to revisit earlier pages.
Real-time activity feeds (social media timelines, notification streams) where inserts at the head must not disturb pages the user has already loaded.
Database replication and change-data-capture (CDC) pipelines that must consume a changelog exactly once across restarts and failures.
Paginating over search results from a vector database or full-text index where OFFSET at depth is expensive and results may change between queries.
Bi-directional data synchronization (CDC pipelines, replica lag-catching) where a consumer must iterate forward and occasionally needs to resume from a previous position or re-sweep a window — requiring stable forward cursors plus a defined backward-resumption path.
Paginating a partitioned or sharded database table where each partition is queried independently and cursors carry both the partition hint and the per-partition keyset position.
Slack Web API collection methods (users.list, conversations.history) where response_metadata.next_cursor drives the loop, page limits are clamped per method, and expired or malformed tokens surface as invalid_cursor so the client restarts from the first page.
GitHub GraphQL-style cursor connections where first/last (bounded 1-100) and pageInfo.startCursor/endCursor carry the continuation position for after/before traversal.
Timeline-style feeds served by Django REST framework's CursorPagination, whose default -created ordering gives a consistent view that does not repeat items as new rows are inserted.

statement: How should the handler propagate one cooperative stop request through its dependent calls, clean up safely, and report cancellation separately from failure?
name: newtype
document:
newtype
strong typedef
opaque type
Give a single primitive its own distinct type so that values with different meanings cannot be substituted for one another, and the raw representation is reachable only through the wrapper's own construction and accessors.
Several domain concepts share one representation - customer id, order id and tenant id are all strings or UUIDs, width/height/offset are all numbers, milliseconds and seconds are both integers - and the API therefore accepts them interchangeably. A swapped argument, a mixed unit or a mistyped literal compiles (or runs) silently, and the defect surfaces late, as a wrong lookup or a cross-tenant bug rather than a type error.
Code in which two or more values with the same underlying representation flow through the same functions, collections or persistence mapping, and in which a single value owns a rule (identifier syntax, non-emptiness, numeric range, unit). Applies at the value level of one field; clusters of attributes that change together belong to Value Object, and closed constant sets to Type-Safe Enum.
Identifier families in one codebase: CustomerId, OrderId, TenantId and SessionId all string- or UUID-shaped and passed to the same repository, logger and cache.
Unit-carrying measurements: Milliseconds vs Seconds, Meters vs Feet, Radians vs Degrees, Cents vs Dollars, where arithmetic must stay inside one unit and conversion is explicit.
Validated single values: EmailAddress, PhoneNumber, Iban, Slug, Percentage (0-100), PortNumber, NonEmptyString - parsed once at the edge, trusted everywhere afterwards.
Security-adjacent tokens: API token vs session id vs tenant id, where a swap becomes a cross-tenant or privilege defect rather than a wrong lookup.
Geometry and graphics APIs where Width, Height, X, Y, Offset and Length are all numbers and transposition should be a compile error.
Pagination and buffer arithmetic: PageSize vs PageIndex vs ByteOffset vs Count, integers that are trivially transposable in a long argument list.
Rust's official newtype examples use Millimeters(u32) and Meters(u32) to keep units distinct, and use Wrapper(Vec<T>) to give a local wrapper its own trait implementations.
Scala 3 opaque types model values such as Logarithm over Double as distinct outside their defining scope, with controlled extension methods and no runtime boxing.
Kotlin @JvmInline value classes wrap one property into a non-interchangeable domain type such as Password while allowing unboxed representations in many uses.

statement: How should the handler propagate one cooperative stop request through its dependent calls, clean up safely, and report cancellation separately from failure?
name: identity-field
document:
identity-field
primary key field
identity column
Store the relational primary key inside the object so that an in-memory instance and its database row are recognised as the same entity across sessions, caches and process restarts, instead of relying on object identity.
Mappers, identity maps and unit-of-work bookkeeping need a stable handle on every object: without a key carried by the object there is no way to tell whether two instances are the same row, which row an UPDATE or DELETE must touch, or what value a referring row should store - and loading the same row twice silently produces two divergent objects.
Applies wherever objects outlive a single operation and are mapped to key-addressed rows: entities behind a Data Mapper or Row Data Gateway, aggregates in a Repository, session caches keyed by table plus id, and object graphs whose children must refer to a parent that is not inserted yet. The key has to survive serialisation and cross-process calls, and for application-generated keys it must exist before the row does.
ORM entities in a session: load a row into an object, mutate business fields, then flush an UPDATE or DELETE targeted at the same identity.
API resources addressed by key: /orders/{id} endpoints that fetch, mutate and delete by identity, with links stored as keys instead of object references.
Session-scoped identity maps and second-level caches keyed by (table, key), which need the key before they can return an existing instance.
Object graphs with parent-child references: the child's foreign key needs the parent's identity, generated before the insert (UUID/sequence) or read back after it (RETURNING/getGeneratedKeys).
Audit, versioning and optimistic locking: change logs and Version Number checks identify the affected row by its key.
Distributed or sharded writes: client-generated keys let a router place the row and let a retry overwrite the same identity idempotently.
Event-sourced aggregates: the aggregate root's identity is the correlation ID carried in every command and event, allowing the event log to reconstruct state by replaying events keyed to that identity.
GraphQL Relay node identification: globally unique node IDs are built from the entity's identity (base64 type-prefixed id), enabling the standardised node query and cache reching defined in the Relay specification.
Multi-tenant SaaS with tenant-scoped identity: a composite key of (tenant_id, id) ensures a tenant can never address another tenant's rows, even if the local id numbers happen to collide.
Idempotent message processing: a command's correlation ID (the entity's identity) lets a handler detect a duplicate and skip reprocessing without a distributed lock.
Hibernate ORM entities with an @Id and Session persistence context: loading by identifier reuses the session's first-level identity, while the chosen generated-id strategy determines when the key becomes available.
PostgreSQL tables with GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY and INSERT ... RETURNING id: the database owns key generation, then the mapper reads the assigned identity back onto the object in the same write.
Relay GraphQL servers implementing the Node interface: expose a globally unique opaque id and refetch the same object through node(id), carrying entity identity across a client cache and API boundary.

statement: How should the handler propagate one cooperative stop request through its dependent calls, clean up safely, and report cancellation separately from failure?
name: state-colocation
document:
state-colocation
colocated state
colocation
Keep each piece of presentation state in the component closest to where it is used — down to the single component that owns and reads it — instead of hoisting it to a common ancestor or a global store, so that a change touches only the smallest part of the view that can observe it.
State gets hoisted 'just in case': a value only one component reads is lifted to the screen or application root, or pushed into one global store, because someone may want it later. The consequences are components that receive props they never read, updates that invalidate far more of the UI than the value's actual consumers, an unclear owner for each value, and tests that must assemble the whole state container to exercise one field. The recurring decision is where a new piece of state should live: keep it at the smallest scope that actually needs it.
Declarative component UIs (React, Vue, Svelte, SwiftUI, Compose, Blazor, Qt Quick) and, in generalized form, any system where a mutable value is owned by one component-like unit: the consumers determine the state's scope, the framework invalidates only what the owner's subtree can observe, and components are composed, moved and deleted. Most compelling where over-lifted or global state has already become a performance and ownership problem.
A search or form input whose value is read only by the input, its own validation and its own preview: keep it in that component instead of the screen root (the canonical typing example where hoisting made every keystroke re-render the page).
Which panel of an accordion is open: leave it per panel while panels are independent, then lift exactly to the accordion once only one panel may be open at a time (the closest common parent).
Tooltip, hover, popover and dropdown state in a chart or table cell: own it in the cell component rather than in a global UI store.
Per-row edit or selection state in a data grid: the row component owns it; only cross-row operations need the grid to own it.
Dialog and modal open state in the button or list that opens it, until another surface must close or observe it.
Form draft state in the form component; lift it only when a sibling — summary panel, preview pane, wizard footer — genuinely must read it.
Extracting a self-contained widget for reuse or publication: keeping its state local makes the component portable and shrinks its API.
Per-cell expansion state in a tree view or file explorer: the tree node component owns whether it is expanded; the parent tree only coordinates multi-select or bulk-expand operations.
Media playback state for a single player (play/pause, current time, volume): colocate in the player component rather than a global audio store unless the same track plays in multiple places simultaneously.
Local filter/sort state for a data table or list: keep it in the list component until a URL parameter, shareable link, or sibling panel requires sharing it.
Vue: composable-local state (useSearch, useToggle) where each consumer needs its own independent instance of the same reactive logic pattern.
Angular Signals: feature-level signal stores scoped to a route or feature slice, not the entire application store, for UI state and feature-derived state.
SwiftUI: @State for view-local value types; @StateObject for view-owned reference types; keep @EnvironmentObject for genuinely cross-cutting state (auth session, theme) mounted as low in the hierarchy as consumers allow.
Svelte 5 runes: `let count = $state(0)` inside a component is per-component-instance reactive state — the component that declares it is its owner; Svelte's v5 migration explicitly replaced the pre-runes habit of reaching for a store whenever state sat at a component's top level, with $state plus $derived/$effect as the local cells, and module-level .svelte.js state only for deliberate sharing.
Jetpack Compose: the official hoisting guidance is this pattern's placement ladder — keep state as close as possible to where it is consumed, hoist only to the lowest common ancestor of all composables that read or write it, pass value down and onValueChange up, and make the ViewModel the owner only when business logic or lifecycle outlives the composition.
Blazor: component fields are the default owner for UI-local state; the official state-management guidance promotes to an in-memory state container service only when components must share non-persistent state, and to Protected Browser Storage only when the value must survive circuits or sessions — a three-rung ladder that mirrors local state, scoped provider, persistence.

statement: How should the handler propagate one cooperative stop request through its dependent calls, clean up safely, and report cancellation separately from failure?
name: revocable-forwarder
document:
revocable-forwarder
caretaker
revocable proxy
Let a collaborator use an object through a forwarding wrapper that the grantor can switch off at any time through a separate control, so authority already handed out can be withdrawn without destroying the target and without the collaborator's cooperation.
A capability is just a reference, so once a collaborator has been given access to an object there is no built-in way to take it back: the grantor can destroy the object, ask the collaborator to stop, or leave the access standing. The recurring decision is how to grant access that is bounded in time - temporary use of a file, a service object, a session, an account - while keeping a control that only the grantor holds.
Object-capability settings, and any in-process design in which authority travels as references rather than as a global identity: plugin and extension hosts lending a service object to foreign code, multi-tenant object graphs giving a worker one tenant-scoped resource, session-scoped services, and capability-based workflow or financial systems in which a grant must be provably withdrawn. It applies when the grantor keeps its own reference to the target and can intercept every call through the reference it handed out; where the runtime lets references be forged, dereferenced around the wrapper or reached by reflection, marshalling or FFI, the same structure degrades from an enforcement mechanism to a discipline.
A plugin or extension host lends a file, network or service object to foreign code and revokes it when the plugin is unloaded or breaches policy.
A multi-tenant worker receives one tenant-scoped resource for the duration of a job and loses it at job end, without the tenant object being torn down.
Session teardown in a long-lived server: the handler works through the wrapper, and logout revokes future calls before the session's resources are freed.
Capability-based workflow and financial systems that give an agent temporary authority over an account or a document and revoke it when the task completes.
Temporary elevated access for maintenance or debugging, where the requirement is to show that the extra authority has provably ended (audit evidence).
Graceful decommissioning of a shared resource: revoke new work through the wrapper, drain the calls already in flight, then release the resource.
The Scala ocaps framework's Revocable/Caretaker API returns a proxied capability plus a private Revoker, so a session, logout, timeout or supervisor can make later calls fail without changing the target.
JavaScript's standard Proxy.revocable() and the Chrome Extensions chrome.permissions API provide browser/runtime counterparts: keep the revoke/remove control private, and do not mistake the platform wrapper or permission record for protection against an already leaked target reference.
AWS IAM role-session revocation for temporary STS credentials is a distributed analogue of withdrawing a forwarded grant: policy evaluation denies subsequent requests, but propagation and credential caching mean it is not the atomic in-process check-and-forward gate described here.

statement: How should the handler propagate one cooperative stop request through its dependent calls, clean up safely, and report cancellation separately from failure?
name: consumer-driven-contract-test
document:
consumer-driven-contract-test
consumer-driven contract
contract test
Capture, from each consumer's own tests, the concrete provider interactions that consumer depends on, and verify the provider against that contract inside the provider's own build, so consumer and provider can be released independently without a shared end-to-end environment.
Independently released consumers and providers must keep working together, yet the only reliable check is a shared end-to-end environment per pair - slow, brittle and usually out of date; at the same time the provider cannot see which parts of its API each consumer actually exercises, so every refactoring is a guess about who will break.
HTTP/request-reply, messaging and gRPC integrations where consumer and provider are owned by different teams on different release cadences and each consumer uses only a narrow slice of the provider's surface. It assumes the provider team is willing to run verification of consumer contracts in its own build; without that half, the consumer test is only a better mock.
Microservice landscapes where a front end, a mobile app or another service consumes an API released by a different team on its own schedule.
A provider team that must refactor or replace internals and needs to know, before merging, which consumer expectations it is about to break.
Mobile or desktop clients that cannot be deployed in lockstep with the backend, so each client's expectations must hold against every backend version.
Event- and message-based integrations (Kafka, SQS, SNS, RabbitMQ) where the consumer processes messages produced by another team; contracts pin the message body shape and metadata (topic, headers, content-type) while abstracting the transport.
Migration or strangler-fig work, where a replacement provider must be proven compatible with the existing consumers before traffic is moved.
Using the contract as the source of stubs for development and integration environments, so those environments no longer need the real provider.
BFF (Backend for Frontend) patterns where each frontend channel (web, mobile, third-party) has its own contract with a shared backend, allowing independent evolution of each BFF without cross-channel breakage.
Multi-team Kafka event streaming where consumers (downstream services) define which topics, partitions and message schemas they depend on, so producers can evolve events without silently breaking subscribers; Pact message pacts handle both JSON and Schema Registry messages (with magic bytes for Avro/Protobuf over Schema Registry).
gRPC service integrations where protocol buffer message shapes are exercised by the actual consumer client code, pinning the wire format, service method signatures and metadata the consumer actually calls; synchronous message pacts cover the request-response pairing.
Breaking up a monolith: individual microservices are extracted and their CDC contracts verify that the new service boundaries behave identically to the original module interfaces before traffic is migrated.
Schema Registry integrations (Confluent, AWS Glue) where consumers pin compatible message schemas and producers must not publish breaking schemas without migrating all dependent consumers first.
Third-party or vendor API integrations where the consumer team cannot rely on the provider to run verification: the consumer-side mock-only workflow with published contracts documents expectations even without provider participation.
Webhook and callback integrations where a provider calls a consumer-defined endpoint; CDC captures the consumer's expected payload shape, headers and authentication, and the provider verifies it can deliver to that shape.
Contract migration at scale: when a provider must migrate from v1 to v2 of an API, CDC with pending/wip pacts allows the provider to signal new expectations to consumers without blocking either side's pipeline while migration is in progress.
Spring Cloud Contract in JVM/Spring landscapes: the consumer's contract change lands in the producer's repository (or an external contract repo), the producer build generates verification tests from the contract DSL, and the consumer develops against StubRunner-served WireMock stubs pulled from an artifact repository (Nexus/Artifactory) - the contract is the single artifact both sides build from.
Nubank replaced its flaky shared-environment end-to-end suite with consumer-driven contract tests to regain deploy velocity - the public account of the pattern paying off as an e2e-substitute at a single organisation rather than as an addition to it.
Large polyglot estates such as JSTOR/ITHAKA (300+ microservices, 12+ teams, Pact) and M1 Finance (Pact plus PactFlow rolled out to 17 teams in under six months): the broker's compatibility matrix replaces per-pair end-to-end environments as the release gate.

statement: Choose where to preserve the billing application's existing synchronous charge contract while translating the vendor SDK's major-unit, callback-based protocol without leaking vendor types or adding unrelated behavior.
name: adapter
document:
adapter
wrapper
adaptor
Present an existing component through the exact target contract its client already consumes, translating calls, results and boundary semantics without adding responsibilities or pretending a missing capability exists.
An existing or foreign component has useful behaviour but speaks a different protocol: method names and signatures, data shapes, units, lifecycle, error model or sync/async contract do not satisfy the target. If every caller performs ad hoc conversion, semantics drift, vendor types leak and provider replacement becomes a cross-cutting rewrite; changing the adaptee or target may be impossible or too disruptive.
Integration work where one side is outside your control: legacy modules, vendor SDKs, generated clients, foreign data formats or units, and the ports-and-adapters boundary of a hexagonal architecture. Applies in statically typed languages - where an adapter class is also the compile-time proof that the required interface is satisfied - and in structurally or dynamically typed ones, where a thin wrapper usually replaces a declared target interface.
Wrapping a third-party or vendor SDK behind your own interface so business code never imports vendor types.
Modernising a legacy module incrementally: new code talks to the target interface while the old component is adapted in place.
Supporting several interchangeable providers (payments, storage, messaging, analytics) through one internal contract, with one adapter each.
Adapting a callback- or error-first API to promises/async or to an observer-style interface.
Ports-and-adapters boundaries where one domain port is realized over different transports (HTTP, message queue, in-process fake).
Unifying differently shaped data sources (row sets, DTOs, XML or JSON payloads) into one model before they reach domain logic.
Test doubles: an in-memory adapter satisfies the target interface without the real infrastructure.
API wrapper libraries: normalising third-party REST/gRPC APIs (Stripe, Twilio, payment providers) into a stable internal contract so business logic never imports vendor SDK types.
Legacy system integration: wrapping SOAP, CORBA, or mainframe APIs behind a modern interface, enabling incremental migration without rewriting existing clients.
Cloud provider abstraction: a single internal storage or queue interface implemented by AWS, GCP, or Azure adapters, letting the application swap providers via configuration.
ETL pipelines: adapting heterogeneous source record schemas (CSV, JSON, XML, database rows) into one canonical domain record, isolating format changes from downstream consumers.
Event-stream and streaming adapters: translating WebSocket frames or server-sent events into domain events in real time.
Multi-cloud and provider-agnostic interfaces: storage adapters (S3, GCS, Azure Blob), queue adapters (SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka), and notification adapters that abstract away provider-specific SDKs.
Backend for Frontend (BFF): each front-end client (web, mobile, third-party) gets its own lightweight adapter that shapes internal service responses into the exact payload that client needs.
Java's java.io.InputStreamReader is a byte-to-character bridge: it presents an InputStream through the Reader contract while decoding with an explicit charset.
SLF4J uses providers such as slf4j-reload4j to bind one Logger API to different backends, while log4j-over-slf4j and jul-to-slf4j redirect legacy APIs at a migration boundary; Spring MVC's HandlerAdapter similarly lets DispatcherServlet handle heterogeneous handler types through one SPI.
Go's net/http.HandlerFunc gives an ordinary func(ResponseWriter, *Request) the http.Handler contract by attaching ServeHTTP, so routing and middleware can consume functions and handlers uniformly.

statement: Choose where to preserve the billing application's existing synchronous charge contract while translating the vendor SDK's major-unit, callback-based protocol without leaking vendor types or adding unrelated behavior.
name: wrapper-facade
document:
wrapper-facade
wrapper
api wrapper
Encapsulate a non-object-oriented API - C functions, raw syscalls or the byte-level routines of a wire protocol - behind one cohesive class (or handle type plus function cluster) that owns the underlying resource, coalesces calls that must happen in order, and presents a safe, portable interface to application code.
The interface the application needs is a cohesive object with a lifetime, but the API it must call is a loose set of functions and raw data structures: a file descriptor plus open/read/write/close, a mutex variable plus init/lock/unlock/destroy, a device handle plus create/query/release, a protocol plus frame-encode/decode steps. Calling that API from everywhere scatters resource ownership, call ordering, error checking and platform differences across the codebase, so every new call site can leak a handle, skip a check or hard-code one operating system.
Systems software - portable daemons and services, device or FFI integrations, protocol implementations, libraries that must build on several platforms - where the boundary to the non-OO API is crossed from many call sites, where the underlying resources need deterministic release, and where the same application code has to run over different operating systems, library revisions or protocol versions. The facade is written once per cohesive abstraction (thread, mutex, socket, file, codec, protocol session) and becomes the portability layer the rest of the system is built on.
A portable daemon or service that must build on several operating systems: wrap the OS threading, synchronization and socket APIs once and keep everything above it platform-neutral.
Integrating a third-party C library (codec, database driver, device SDK) that hands out opaque handles and expects create/use/destroy ordering: wrap each handle in a type that owns it.
Implementing one side of a wire protocol: encapsulate framing, encoding and decoding behind a session object so application code sends messages instead of managing byte buffers and partial reads.
Giving the layers above a seam: define the facade as an interface and provide a fake or recording implementation so dispatchers, handlers and business logic can be tested without the OS, the network or the device.
Keeping a binary interface stable across library versions: publish an opaque-handle (pimpl-style) wrapper so the implementation can change without recompiling or breaking clients.
Encapsulating a legacy in-house C API (globals, callback tables, errno conventions) while new code is written in a higher-level style, migrating call sites incrementally.
ACE (Adaptive Communication Environment): the ACE_OS namespace and the C++ Wrapper Facade layer over it wrap POSIX, Win32 and RTOS calls - threads, locks, sockets, IPC, timers, memory - so the framework's higher layers (Reactor, Proactor, Acceptor-Connector) compile unchanged across dozens of operating systems from a single source tree.
.NET's System.Runtime.InteropServices.SafeHandle and the Microsoft.Win32.SafeHandles family (SafeFileHandle, SafeWaitHandle, SafeRegistryHandle, SafeProcessHandle): each derives a facade per OS handle type, overriding IsInvalid and ReleaseHandle so CloseHandle-style teardown, ownership (ownsHandle) and double-close protection live in the wrapper instead of every P/Invoke call site.
Rust's standard library as the canonical modern instance: per RFC 3128 (I/O Safety), std::fs::File, TcpStream and UdpSocket own a raw file descriptor and close it exactly once on Drop, while std::os::fd splits RawFd, BorrowedFd<'a> and OwnedFd so the wrapper's ownership contract is enforced by the type system rather than convention.

name: facade
document:
facade
façade
Provide one coarse-grained entry interface that hides a subsystem of many cooperating classes behind the few operations its clients actually need, so callers depend on a single stable API instead of orchestrating the subsystem themselves.
Every client of a complex subsystem must know which classes exist, in which order to call them, how to configure and dispose them and how to interpret their errors; that orchestration is then duplicated across the codebase, and any change inside the subsystem ripples through all callers.
Applies when a subsystem (a library, framework, legacy module, remote SDK, or a layer of your own system) is much broader than any single client needs, when its correct use is a recurring sequence of collaborations, and when client code should be insulated from its types and its evolution. Typical at module and system-boundary scope, where one entry point per layer or per external system is wanted.
Wrapping a third-party SDK, media framework or payment/HTTP client behind one class or module that exposes the application's own vocabulary (convert, charge, upload).
Application services that orchestrate repositories, gateways and domain services for one use case (checkout, report generation) and are the only seam controllers or jobs talk to.
Layered systems where every layer offers a facade as its entry point, so dependencies flow through coarse interfaces instead of reaching into a layer's internals.
Isolating a legacy subsystem while it is replaced incrementally: new code depends on the clean facade, and the migration swaps implementations behind it.
Remote and coarse-grained boundaries: a remote facade exposes a few chunky operations over a fine-grained object model to avoid chatty calls (see Remote Facade, Fowler's PEAA).
Startup/teardown sequences and device orchestration (the classic home-theatre example): clients need one 'watch movie' operation, not a dozen subsystem calls in the right order.
Service-container proxy facades (e.g. Laravel): a static-looking front-end that forwards calls to a resolved service instance, giving a terse API without sacrificing testability or DI flexibility.
JPA/service-layer facades: a single transactional entry point that receives DTOs, maps them to domain objects, orchestrates business logic, maps results back, and commits — one transaction per use case.
Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) in microservices: a thin per-client aggregation service (web, mobile, partner) that fans out to downstream microservices, reshapes responses for the client, and handles perimeter concerns. Each BFF is a specialized facade owned by the team that ships the corresponding client.
Anti-Corruption Layer (DDD): a facade placed between a bounded context and an external/legacy system to translate that system's model into domain concepts, preventing external concepts from polluting the internal domain model.
Event-driven/observable facades: a facade that exposes reactive streams (Observables, Promises, async generators) over the subsystem, buffering, batching or debouncing events for consumers that prefer push-based or streaming interfaces.
API gateway composition: an API gateway acts as a system-wide facade that unifies multiple backend services at the edge, handling auth, routing and cross-cutting concerns before delegating to more specific facades or services.
SDK wrapper facades: publishing a public-facing SDK over an internal microservice mesh; the facade shapes the external API surface, applies default configurations, and provides a stable consumer experience independent of internal service topology changes.
SLF4J (Simple Logging Facade for Java): slf4j-api is a minimal logging facade; applications code against Logger.debug()/info() once and bind the concrete framework (Logback, Log4j 2, java.util.logging) at deployment time by swapping the provider jar on the classpath — the textbook runtime-swappable facade.
Spring Framework JdbcClient / JdbcTemplate: a fluent facade over raw JDBC that owns connection and statement lifecycle, iterates ResultSets and translates SQLException into the DataAccessException hierarchy, so callers supply only SQL and result mapping instead of the full boilerplate workflow.
jQuery $.get/$.post/$.getJSON over $.ajax: a per-task facade layer that collapses cross-browser XMLHttpRequest differences, Deferred plumbing and HTTP defaults into one-line calls — the canonical JavaScript-library facade.

name: interface-class
document:
interface-class
pure abstract class
abstract interface
Declare a role as a type that carries only operations and no state, so clients depend on what an object promises to do rather than on the class that happens to supply it.
The type that names a role also carries representation: once clients type their variables to the supplier's class they inherit its fields, its constructor and its implementation choices, and a class that already extends something else or lives in another module cannot join the role at all. Asking two unrelated classes to answer the same protocol - or replacing the supplier with a fake, a decorator or a second implementation - then means editing every client, which is the recurring trigger for a contract that has no separate existence from its first implementation.
Applies at the seam between a caller and a replaceable supplier: layered subsystems, ports in a hexagonal architecture, plug-in and extension points, test seams and published libraries. It pays off wherever more than one implementation is expected, wherever implementations arrive from another team or are chosen at run time, or wherever the caller must not depend on the supplier's representation. It assumes the language offers some way to name an operation set (a keyword, a pure abstract class, a protocol or trait) or accepts a documented structural convention where it has none.
Ports in a layered or hexagonal design: the domain declares what it needs from storage, messaging, clock or payment, and the infrastructure module implements that contract.
Plug-in and extension points: a driver or service-provider contract (JDBC, SAX, logging, storage or payment providers) that third parties implement without touching the host.
Test seams: a fast in-memory fake and the slow real service implement the same contract, so business rules run with no infrastructure at all.
Interchangeable algorithms and wrappers at a call site: pricing rules, serializers or caching decorators that the client selects without naming the concrete type.
Cross-module decoupling: the contract lives where both sides may depend on it, so neither side imports the other and the implementations are compiled and deployed separately.
Roles over existing classes: a class that already inherits from a framework base still promises the contract, which a common state-carrying base class could not express.
Event-driven systems and message brokers: event consumers declare a typed handler contract (message type plus acknowledgement semantics), and the runtime dispatches to any implementation — Kafka consumer, in-process handler, or test fake — without the producer knowing the consumer's representation.
Plugin architectures and service-provider interfaces (Java ServiceLoader, OSGi, Eclipse adapter, VS Code extension host): a host defines a contract that third parties implement, loaded and instantiated at run time, so the host never links against the implementing module.
Middleware and pipeline chains: each stage declares a handler contract (request, response, next-chain reference) and the chain hands an opaque context typed only through the contract — ASP.NET Core, Express/Koa, Django middleware, or gRPC interceptors all follow this pattern.
Interchangeable algorithmic strategies selected at a call site without naming the concrete type: pricing rules, sorting strategies, compression codecs or caching decorators where the policy is injected but the algorithm can be swapped without touching the caller.
Cross-module or cross-team decoupling: the contract lives in a shared package that both sides may depend on, so neither side imports the other's implementation assembly and each team can ship, test and deploy independently.
Cloud SDK client abstractions: the SDK surface is a set of contracts (operation request/response types, configuration, retry policy) so users can swap the wire protocol (REST, gRPC) or inject a test double without recompiling against the cloud's own libraries.
Service interfaces in microservices: each service publishes a typed API contract that other services call, and API gateways or service meshes route to the implementation — consumer-driven contract testing (Pact, Spring Cloud Contract) validates the contract against both sides.
Java's ServiceLoader: a service interface is loaded with provider implementations discovered at run time, so application code selects providers through the contract instead of naming provider classes.
ASP.NET Core's IMiddleware pipeline: middleware implementations satisfy InvokeAsync(HttpContext, RequestDelegate), and the host composes or replaces stages without clients depending on each middleware class.
Go's implicit interfaces: a consuming package can accept any concrete type with the required method set, so implementations from unrelated packages satisfy the role without a shared base class or registration.

name: monad
document:
monad
io monad
programmable semicolon
Give a computation's effect (absence, failure, asynchrony, I/O, state) a type of its own with a unit and a bind operation, so that a sequence of steps in which each step depends on the previous value composes into one pipeline while bind propagates the effect automatically.
Sequencing computations where the next step needs the previous step's result and every step may additionally be absent, failing, asynchronous or effectful pushes the effect handling into the business logic: nested null checks, try/catch ladders, callback pyramids. Every call site repeats the same propagation decision (short-circuit? await? log?) and one forgotten check turns a controlled failure into a crash or a wrong value.
Applies wherever a value and the fact that it is absent, pending, failing or impure belong together: chained lookups, validation and error pipelines, asynchronous call chains, state threading, parser and interpreter pipelines, and effect-typed application cores. It matters most when the sequence is long, when the effect policy must be uniform and testable, and when the language already provides monadic types (Optional, Result, Promise, IO) or syntax that desugars to bind (do-notation, for-comprehensions, async/await).
Chained lookups where any link may be missing: user -> address -> city expressed with Maybe/Optional instead of nested null checks.
Validation and error pipelines in which each step can fail with a domain error and the first failure must short-circuit (Either/Result, railway-oriented programming).
Asynchronous workflows whose next call depends on the previous response (Promise/async-await, CompletableFuture.thenCompose, Kotlin suspend functions, Swift Task).
Effect description and interpretation: building an IO/program value that is pure data and running it through different interpreters in tests and production (IO monad, tagless-final).
State-threading computations such as compiler passes, random generators or incremental traversals written as a State monad pipeline.
Parser combinators and nondeterministic search, where each step consumes the previous parse result or explores every value produced by the previous step (parser monad, List monad).
Rust's std::result::Result composes fallible steps with and_then and the ? operator, returning early on Err while keeping the successful value available to the next dependent step.
Java's CompletableFuture.thenCompose chains dependent asynchronous stages: the function returns another CompletionStage and the outer stage adopts its completion or exceptional failure.
Scala for-comprehensions over Option, collections, or other types with map, flatMap, and withFilter desugar dependent bindings into the corresponding combinators, keeping the monadic sequence readable without hiding its operations.

name: version-number
document:
version-number
rowversion
entity versioning
Store a version token alongside each persistent record and make every write assert the token it read, so a write computed from stale data fails as a detectable conflict instead of silently overwriting a newer value.
Two sessions read the same record, both edit it, and the later write wins: the earlier update vanishes without any error (the lost update). Once the read-modify-write spans more than one system transaction the database cannot tell 'this is the record I read' from 'this record changed under me', so no code path can notice in time - unless the record itself carries a per-row token that changes on every write and the write tests that token before committing.
Applies to records that outlive the transaction that read them: edits spanning user think time, a web form round-trip, an offline client, a batch worker holding aggregates, or any read-modify-write over data other writers touch in between. It needs a store that can test the token and change the record in one atomic step (a conditional UPDATE, a compare-and-swap, a document revision check) and a caller willing to act on the conflict - re-read, merge, retry, or report. It assumes conflicts are the exception; when they are the rule a pessimistic lock prevents the wasted work instead.
Web forms and editors: a record is loaded into a page, edited for minutes or hours, then saved - the token makes the stale save fail instead of clobbering the other editor's change.
Distributed workers applying commands to the same entity: the second worker's write is rejected so it can refresh and re-apply, giving first-writer-wins with no held lock.
Data mappers and units of work: every dirty entity flushed at commit carries the version it was loaded with, so the whole transaction aborts on the first stale row.
Document stores and revision-based APIs: Mongoose's __v with optimisticConcurrency, CouchDB-style revisions, or a REST ETag/If-Match precondition all expose the same per-document token.
Leases, leader election and configuration records: one row represents ownership or a monotonic generation, and a write must prove it still holds the revision it acted on.
Offline or mobile sync: clients push edits made against a snapshot taken days earlier, and the version check decides which edits apply directly and which must go through a merge.
Hibernate ORM / JPA @Version: the mapper owns an integer (or timestamp) version property, appends it to every UPDATE's WHERE clause, bumps it on flush and raises StaleObjectStateException / OptimisticLockException when zero rows match, so the application code never writes the predicate by hand.
DynamoDB conditional writes: each item carries a Version attribute; UpdateItem sends ConditionExpression 'Version = :read_value' and increments Version in the same request, and ConditionalCheckFailedException is the conflict signal that triggers a bounded re-read-and-retry — the same contract exposed as @DynamoDBVersionAttribute in the enhanced client.
Cassandra lightweight transactions: UPDATE ... SET col = ? WHERE id = ? IF col = ? is a Paxos-backed compare-and-set, giving the token test linearizable semantics across replicas — at a documented cost (roughly four extra round-trips per conditional write), so it is reserved for rows that genuinely need the guard.

name: iterator
document:
iterator
cursor
enumerator
Provide a way to access the elements of an aggregate object sequentially without exposing its underlying representation, by moving traversal state and the traversal algorithm out of the aggregate into a separate iterator object.
Traversal leaks into every client: code that walks a collection has to know its storage layout (array indices, node links, hash buckets), the same loop is rewritten once per aggregate and once per client, and adding a new traversal order means changing the aggregate's interface — which is exactly what prevents algorithms from being written once and applied to any collection.
Applies wherever a collection with a non-trivial or changeable representation must be traversed by outsiders: collection libraries, trees and graphs with several traversal orders, lazy or unbounded sources, and streaming pipelines. It matters most when more than one traversal may be pending at the same time, when the storage must stay hidden for encapsulation or safety, or when traversal algorithms must be added without touching the aggregate; the toolchain only decides which realization is available (a language iteration protocol, generators, lazy sequences, or a hand-written cursor).
Collection libraries that must serve arrays, linked lists, trees, and hash tables through one protocol — e.g. std::begin/end in C++, java.util.Iterator, IEnumerable<T> in C#, Symbol.iterator in JavaScript, IntoIterator in Rust.
Tree and graph APIs exposing depth-first, breadth-first, in-order, or post-order traversal without publishing node links or parent pointers, enabling clients to walk composite structures without coupling to the storage representation.
Lazy or unbounded sources consumed one element at a time: file lines (BufferedReader.lines()), network socket streams, paginated API responses, sensor data, event streams, and generated sequences (random numbers, Fibonacci, permutations).
Streaming data pipelines (map/filter/reduce over any iterable) that stay O(1) in memory regardless of input size, implemented via itertools, Java Stream API, Kotlin Sequence, C++ ranges, Rust iterator adapters, or Go iter package.
Legacy or third-party aggregates whose internal layout must stay private behind a stable traversal interface, allowing the aggregate to refactor its storage without breaking existing clients.
Custom containers that must participate in the language's own for/foreach/for-in/for-await loop, spread operators, destructuring assignment, or list comprehensions.
Database result sets and ORM cursors where the full result set is never materialised in memory; the iterator fetches pages on demand.
Parser and lexer token streams where the input is consumed incrementally and the full source may not fit in memory.
Async I/O pipelines where the iteration protocol yields Promises (JavaScript async generators, C# IAsyncEnumerable<T>, Python async generators) enabling for-await iteration over network responses or file reads.
Multidimensional collection traversal (matrices, nested lists, spatial grids) via flattened iterators that expose a flat index space while hiding the multi-dimensional layout.
Paginated REST or GraphQL API clients where a client-side iterator transparently fetches successive pages as the consumer pulls elements, keeping memory constant regardless of result set size.
Kafka, log-processor, or ETL pipelines where each stage is a transforming iterator: parse → filter → enrich → validate → sink, with each stage evaluated lazily.
Event-driven systems using async iterators to consume WebSocket messages, SSE streams, or queue consumers through a uniform for-await-of interface.
Batch-processing jobs over large file sets (CSV, Parquet, NDJSON) where an iterator wraps a file reader and yields one record per next() call without loading the file into memory.
Cursor-based (keyset) pagination over large, live datasets where offset/limit pagination causes duplicates or missed rows when data is inserted or deleted mid-traversal; the iterator stores the last-seen key rather than a page offset, making traversal stable across concurrent modifications.
Iterator fusion in compilers and runtimes: adjacent map/filter/map chains fused into a single pass with zero intermediate allocation (Rust iterator adapters, Java Spliterators, Haskell stream fusion, C++ range views), giving lazy pipelines near-handwritten performance.
Parallel iterators for data-parallel workloads: Rust Rayon, Java parallel streams, and Kotlin asFlow().buffer() split the iterator across worker threads — identical interface to serial iteration, transparent parallel execution.
Reactive streams bridging pull and push: RxJava, RxJS, and Project Reactor implement backpressure (consumer signals demand, producer emits at requested rate), combining iterator's pull semantics with observer's push delivery.
LLM and streaming AI responses where the model yields tokens incrementally; an async iterator wraps the SSE/stream endpoint and the client consumes tokens one at a time via for-await-of, keeping first-token latency low and enabling progressive rendering.
Cursor-based database driver iterators (Node.js pg cursor, Python asyncpg, Go database/sql rows) where the driver streams rows from the server without loading the full result set, with configurable fetch size controlling server-side memory usage.
Java's Spliterator API exposes a cursor that can be advanced one element at a time or split into subranges for parallel streams; it demonstrates that an iterator contract can include explicit partitioning and size/order characteristics rather than only next().
.NET's IAsyncEnumerable<T> and IAsyncEnumerator<T> expose asynchronous pull iteration through await foreach; GetAsyncEnumerator(CancellationToken) makes cancellation part of the iterator boundary for network, file, and database streams.
WHATWG ReadableStream async iteration lets browser and server consumers use for-await-of over streamed chunks while the iterator locks a reader and defines whether early return() cancels or merely releases it.

name: transaction-script
document:
transaction-script
service object
Organizes the business logic of a single request as one procedure - read the data it needs, validate and calculate, write the results and complete in one database transaction - trading object-model structure for a straight-line implementation that can be read top to bottom.
A request-scoped use case (book a room, place an order, recognize revenue, import a file) has to be implemented, and its logic mixes input validation, calculation and persistence. Modelling the domain as objects may be premature, or the team may not be ready for it, yet the implementation still needs each request's steps to stay visible and its transaction boundary to be explicit.
Applies where business logic is simple to moderately complex, where the system is naturally described as a series of transactions each driven by one request (HTTP handler, CLI command, queue message, batch job), and where a thin data-source gateway or the database itself is the persistence seam. Also the right starting point under delivery pressure or for a team new to domain modelling - provided the growth path to a Domain Model is watched deliberately.
Booking a hotel room: check availability, calculate the rate, insert the booking and confirm - one request, one transaction.
Revenue recognition (Fowler's example): given a contract and an as-of date, calculate the recognitions and persist them, or report the revenue already recognized.
CRUD write endpoints in a simple admin or back-office application where each screen maps to one operation.
Batch and integration jobs: import a file, validate rows, write the accepted rows and report the rejects in one transaction per batch.
Queue or message handlers that carry out one command (place order, cancel subscription, refund payment) and acknowledge only after commit.
Reporting and ETL steps that read a slice of data, transform it and write results, where the logic is genuinely a straight line of steps.
Django request-atomicity: with ATOMIC_REQUESTS enabled (or @transaction.atomic on the view), the whole view function is the script - Django begins the transaction at request start, commits on a successful response and rolls back on exception, exactly the one-script-one-transaction shape.
Laravel request handlers that wrap the validate-calculate-persist sequence in a DB::transaction closure: the closure commits when it returns and rolls back automatically if it throws, so the closure body is the script and its extent is the boundary.
Spring @Transactional service methods: an AOP proxy begins the transaction before the method and commits after it returns, making each annotated method a Transaction Script whose signature is the request and whose boundary is declarative.

name: extensible-visitor
document:
extensible-visitor
extensible visitor pattern
extensible visitors with defaults
Keep the visitor open on both axes at once - new element kinds and new operations arrive without editing or recompiling any visitor that already exists - by giving every visitor a default method that catches element kinds it was not written for, introducing extended element kinds under an intermediate base whose accept hooks overload (not override) accept, and extending an operation by subclassing the existing concrete visitor so it inherits every case it already handled.
A classic Visitor is cheap in one direction only: a new operation is a new visitor, but a new element kind forces every visitor to grow one more method, so shipped visitors must be edited and redeployed. The trigger is an element hierarchy that is extended by parties who do not own the operations - language dialects, plugin node types, versioned grammars, third-party message formats - where the existing operations must keep working unchanged on the extended structure.
Recursively defined element hierarchies (abstract syntax trees, intermediate representations, document and message models) that grow over time, in a statically typed language whose visitors are concrete classes or interfaces with default bodies, and where the traversal logic itself lives inside the operations. It pays off when old operations must run against new element kinds and when element kinds are added by a different team than the operations; it assumes the visitor protocol can carry a default case and that a runtime type test is acceptable on the dispatch path.
A compiler front-end whose node kinds are extended by language dialects while every existing analysis pass keeps running unchanged (the extensible-compiler case the pattern was derived from).
An IDE or linter analysing a versioned language grammar: the version-1 analysis must not be recompiled when version 2 adds syntax nodes it does not understand.
Plugin systems where third-party modules contribute new node types (document formats, workflow elements, protocol messages) to a host that ships the operations.
Optimisation or lowering pipelines whose passes are shipped separately from the node hierarchy: the platform team adds representations, users add passes.
A published visitor API where other teams implement visitors and the element set grows every release, making 'which kinds does this visitor handle' an explicit, versioned contract.
Migration and validation tooling that must keep working on messages produced by newer producers than the tool itself.
Serialization and schema-generation frameworks such as Jackson's JsonFormatVisitor API, which uses a visitor to traverse Java type hierarchies for JSON/XML schema generation and allows third-party serializers to contribute handlers for new POJO shapes without modifying the core framework.
Query engines over tree-structured data (e.g. Apache Calcite's relational algebra, Rascal's AST analysis): new relational operators or AST node types are contributed by extension modules while existing optimisers and evaluators continue to function unchanged.
Static analysis and bug-finding tools (Coverity, CodeQL, ESLint plugin architectures): new checker plugins add new node-type coverage while the core traversal engine ships unchanged, and old checkers degrade gracefully over unknown node types.
Game engine entity-component systems: new component types are contributed at runtime while existing systems (physics, rendering, AI) continue to process entities; the visitor with default case handles component types added after a given system was written.
Python's ast.NodeVisitor: visit() dispatches to a visit_<Node> method and falls back to generic_visit as the built-in default case, so analysis tools written before newer node kinds existed (Match, TryStar, TypeAlias) keep traversing Python's evolving AST unchanged, exactly the degrade-don't-break contract of the pattern.
The JDK Compiler Tree API (com.sun.source.tree.TreeVisitor / SimpleTreeVisitor): every visit method defaults to visitOther/defaultAction as the catch-all, so javac-based tooling written against Java 8 trees keeps compiling and running as Java adds records, patterns and switch labels - old visitors land in visitOther instead of failing.
Roslyn's CSharpSyntaxVisitor / CSharpSyntaxWalker: the generated visitor carries one Visit method per syntax node kind plus DefaultVisit as the default case, and each C# language version extends the node hierarchy while existing analysers and the compiler's own passes keep working over the extended tree.

name: remote-facade
document:
remote-facade
coarse-grained facade
Provide a single coarse-grained facade over a web of fine-grained objects so that a remote client can complete a unit of work in one round trip, while the fine-grained objects keep their local-only interfaces and the facade stays free of domain logic.
An object model tuned for in-process use has small objects with small methods and heavy interaction. Across a process boundary every one of those interactions becomes a marshalling, security and routing event, so one user action turns into dozens of remote calls; the decision is whether, and at which seam, to replace that chatty protocol with a few coarse operations.
Applies at any distribution boundary - a network hop, a service-mesh sidecar or merely a second process on the same host - where a fine-grained object model or service layer must be made remotely usable. It matters most when the interaction pattern is chatty (many small reads and writes per use case), when the model must not be exposed to remote clients, and when the transport is expensive relative to the work being done.
Enterprise application whose rich domain model is consumed by a thick client, another service or a batch job: the service layer gets a coarse remote interface instead of exposing entities and value objects.
Microservice boundary where a use case (place an order, update a shipment) must be a single call while the fine-grained aggregates stay internal to the service.
Legacy integration: a coarse adapter facade over an old object model so that new clients never see the legacy structure and the old model can be refactored behind it.
Mobile or high-latency clients, where every avoided round trip directly improves perceived latency and battery cost.
Batch and offline clients that need bulk operations (fetch a set, submit a set) instead of per-item calls.
Security boundary: one authenticated, authorised and audited entry point in front of the model.
Salesforce Composite API and Composite Graph API: a client submits related record operations, reference IDs and explicit all-or-none/graph boundaries in one request instead of making a remote call per sObject.
Microsoft Graph JSON batching: a `$batch` request groups up to 20 Graph operations behind one HTTP boundary while dependencies and per-request failures remain visible to the caller.
gRPC services such as the official RouteGuide example: generated stubs expose typed unary or streaming RPCs as the remote contract while the server's fine-grained implementation stays local.

name: page-object
document:
page-object
page object model
window driver
Wrap each UI surface a test drives - a page or a significant component - in an object that exposes the services the surface offers and hides every locator, driver call and wait, so a UI change is absorbed by one class instead of by every test that touched the markup.
A UI test that drives the automation API directly - find an element, type, click, wait, read text - keeps the page's locators and interaction mechanics in the test body: the same selector is repeated across dozens of tests, a markup change breaks them all at once, and a reader must reconstruct the page's structure to understand what the test does. The catalog's trigger: a UI change should touch one class, not fifty assertions.
Automated tests that drive a user interface through a driver API - a browser (Selenium/WebDriver, Playwright, Cypress, WebdriverIO), a mobile app (Appium, Espresso, XCUITest) or a desktop window - where the same screens are exercised by many tests, where the UI changes independently of the tests, and where the suite is expected to survive redesigns. The pattern pays off when the interface can be named in the user's terms ('sign-in page', 'product row') and the driver offers stable element lookup; it is unnecessary for a single throwaway script or when the presentation logic has already been extracted behind a humble object.
A regression suite over a web application whose pages are exercised by dozens of tests: login, search, checkout and admin screens each get a class, and a redesign changes only those classes (the Selenium and Playwright POM guides' home scenario).
The same screens are driven by different kinds of test - functional, visual, accessibility, smoke - and the locator knowledge must live in one place that all of them import.
Mobile application suites (Appium, Espresso, XCUITest) where screens are widget hierarchies with platform-specific queries, and the page object is the only place that codifies the platform lookup.
BDD suites: Gherkin steps stay business-readable because step definitions delegate to page objects instead of calling the driver (Fowler's layering recommendation).
Suites migrating drivers or frameworks (Selenium to Playwright, a WebdriverIO restructure): the page API is kept while only its internals change.
A scripting interface over an application whose behaviour is stuck in the UI (Fowler's scripting use), or a legacy system that can only be exercised through its window.
Selenium's documented login flow: SignInPage.loginValidUser returns HomePage, so a regression suite can exercise authentication through services while locators and page-load checks stay in the page objects.
Playwright's official playwright.dev example: PlaywrightDevPage wraps a Page, owns locators for the getting-started flow and exposes goto, getStarted and pageObjectModel methods used by tests.
WebdriverIO's official The Internet login example: a getter-based LoginPage centralizes selectors and open/submit actions, letting login specs survive selector changes without duplicating driver calls.

name: single-table-inheritance
document:
single-table-inheritance
table per hierarchy
discriminator column mapping
Map an inheritance hierarchy of classes onto one shared table whose columns are the union of all classes' fields, using a type code (discriminator) column to decide which class each row instantiates, so polymorphic reads need no joins.
A class hierarchy must be persisted, the hierarchy is small and its classes share most fields, and cross-class queries or polymorphic loads are frequent: mapping each class to its own table would force a join per level on almost every read, while the subtypes differ by only a few columns.
Object-relational mapping of a small, shallow, stable class hierarchy whose subclasses are mostly variations on shared state - domain-model inheritance (Employee/Engineer/Manager), payment or content types - where the storage layer is chosen by the team and the persistence framework can be taught the type code (JPA/EF Core/ActiveRecord/SQLAlchemy/most ORMs make this their default strategy) or the mapping is written by hand over SQL.
Small stable hierarchies where subclasses share most state: Employee/Engineer/Manager, Payment/CardPayment/WirePayment, Notification/EmailNotification/PushNotification.
Content or asset models with a handful of similar types (Photo/Question/Post, Blog/RssBlog) distinguished by a type code, where cross-type queries and listings are the dominant read.
Legacy or third-party schemas that already hold a hierarchy in one table with a kind column and must be mapped onto domain classes without restructuring the database.
Reporting and analytics over a hierarchy where one wide table with a type column beats joining four tables for every subtype question.
ORM-default configurations: teams that pick the framework's default hierarchy mapping (JPA SINGLE_TABLE, EF Core TPH) because join avoidance and mapping simplicity outweigh column honesty for their hierarchy size.
Rails Active Record single-table inheritance: ActiveRecord::Inheritance stores the subclass name in the table's type column by default (Company/Firm/Client all live in companies with type = 'Firm'), so fetching via the base class returns correctly-typed objects - GitLab runs a production monolith on this mechanism and maintains a written policy on when STI must not be used.
EF Core's default table-per-hierarchy mapping: a Blog/RssBlog hierarchy shares one table, the discriminator's name, CLR type and per-class values are set with HasDiscriminator/HasValue, and EF Core automatically adds the discriminator predicate to derived-type queries (throwing on unmapped discriminator values).
SQLAlchemy declarative polymorphic mappers: the base class declares polymorphic_on = 'type' in __mapper_args__ and each subclass a unique polymorphic_identity, so one person table answers polymorphic queries for Person/Employee rows without joins.

name: double-checked-locking
document:
double-checked-locking
double-checked locking optimization
DCL
DCLP
Initialise a shared resource exactly once and lazily while keeping the steady-state read path free of lock acquisition - by testing a cheaply published state first and taking the lock only for the one-time construction, where the platform can publish the built object safely to every reader.
An expensive object - configuration, a connection pool, a compiled plan, a cache - must be created once and only when it is first needed, but its accessor is called from many threads. The naive check-then-act form lets two threads build it at the same time, and guarding every read with a lock serialises a path that almost never needs synchronisation. The tempting fix - test a flag cheaply, lock only for the initialisation, test again inside the lock - is sound only if the write that publishes the object is ordered with respect to the readers' loads, which is exactly the part the classic formulation leaves implicit and the reason the idiom is famous for rare, unreproducible failures.
Concurrent, shared-memory software in which one object or cell must be built once and read many times: process-wide singletons and registries, per-object caches inside an object shared between threads, lazily built statics in languages whose runtime also provides the once semantics. The pattern presupposes a memory model with a defined publication ordering (volatile, acquire/release, an initialisation lock, or a runtime once primitive) and a read path hot enough that the lock it removes is measurable. On single-threaded runtimes there is nothing to synchronise, and where a single-threaded composition root can initialise eagerly the pattern is unnecessary.
Process-wide singletons whose construction is expensive or configuration-dependent: configuration snapshot, metrics registry, logger, connection pool, feature-flag view.
Per-object caches inside an object shared by several threads - compiled regular expression or query plan, parsed schema, symbol table - where the build is expensive and the read is hot.
Lazily built statics in languages where the runtime owns the once semantics: C++ function-local static, Swift static let or global let, Kotlin by lazy, Scala lazy val, Go sync.Once, Rust OnceLock/LazyLock.
Compensating for the static-initialisation-order problem: an accessor that builds the global on first use instead of relying on cross-translation-unit initialisation order.
Avoiding lock overhead on a read-mostly, write-once hot path (memo tables, symbol caches, thread-safe lazy proxies) where a contended lock would show up in a profile.
Small or freestanding runtimes without a once primitive, where the first caller must build the cell and an eager initialiser is not available.
RWMutex-protected maps in Go where readers check a fast path before the slower write-locked re-check, as a safer alternative to sync.Map for workloads with known access patterns.
Per-connection or per-session lazy fields in object-pooled servers where the pool itself is the shared cell and each borrowed object gets a lazy-computed field.
Cross-language plugin or extension registries where one language's runtime initialises a global handle that other language shards read without repeated synchronisation.
Rate-limiter or circuit-breaker state that must be lazily built from configuration: building eagerly would couple the policy to startup time, but the read path must be lock-free under high throughput.
Lazy compilation or query-plan warming in database connection pools where the pool is shared but individual plans are built on first use by the owning thread.
Spring Framework's DefaultSingletonBeanRegistry.getSingleton: check the singletonObjects map lock-free, take the singletonLock only when the bean is absent, re-check inside - a production evolution of the idiom whose correctness was formally challenged (SPR-13463) and upheld because the concurrent-map read already carries the needed memory barrier.
Chromium's base::LazyInstance / GetOrCreateLazyPointer: an atomic state word with a 'creating' bit, acquire-load fast path and release-store publication - since deprecated in favour of function-local statics with base::NoDestructor, a signal of how far hardened platforms have moved from hand-rolled DCL.
ACE toolkit's ACE_Singleton<TYPE, ACE_LOCK>: the pattern's original industrial home (the 1997 paper was written alongside ACE) - the template still guards instance() with a double-checked ACE_LOCK acquire and recommends ACE_Recursive_Thread_Mutex for multi-threaded access.
Swift runtime: every global/static let is lowered to swift_once (dispatch_once on Darwin), so the double-checked once structure is the default initialisation mechanism for lazily computed immutable globals rather than hand-written code.

name: revocable-forwarder
document:
revocable-forwarder
caretaker
revocable proxy
Let a collaborator use an object through a forwarding wrapper that the grantor can switch off at any time through a separate control, so authority already handed out can be withdrawn without destroying the target and without the collaborator's cooperation.
A capability is just a reference, so once a collaborator has been given access to an object there is no built-in way to take it back: the grantor can destroy the object, ask the collaborator to stop, or leave the access standing. The recurring decision is how to grant access that is bounded in time - temporary use of a file, a service object, a session, an account - while keeping a control that only the grantor holds.
Object-capability settings, and any in-process design in which authority travels as references rather than as a global identity: plugin and extension hosts lending a service object to foreign code, multi-tenant object graphs giving a worker one tenant-scoped resource, session-scoped services, and capability-based workflow or financial systems in which a grant must be provably withdrawn. It applies when the grantor keeps its own reference to the target and can intercept every call through the reference it handed out; where the runtime lets references be forged, dereferenced around the wrapper or reached by reflection, marshalling or FFI, the same structure degrades from an enforcement mechanism to a discipline.
A plugin or extension host lends a file, network or service object to foreign code and revokes it when the plugin is unloaded or breaches policy.
A multi-tenant worker receives one tenant-scoped resource for the duration of a job and loses it at job end, without the tenant object being torn down.
Session teardown in a long-lived server: the handler works through the wrapper, and logout revokes future calls before the session's resources are freed.
Capability-based workflow and financial systems that give an agent temporary authority over an account or a document and revoke it when the task completes.
Temporary elevated access for maintenance or debugging, where the requirement is to show that the extra authority has provably ended (audit evidence).
Graceful decommissioning of a shared resource: revoke new work through the wrapper, drain the calls already in flight, then release the resource.
The Scala ocaps framework's Revocable/Caretaker API returns a proxied capability plus a private Revoker, so a session, logout, timeout or supervisor can make later calls fail without changing the target.
JavaScript's standard Proxy.revocable() and the Chrome Extensions chrome.permissions API provide browser/runtime counterparts: keep the revoke/remove control private, and do not mistake the platform wrapper or permission record for protection against an already leaked target reference.
AWS IAM role-session revocation for temporary STS credentials is a distributed analogue of withdrawing a forwarded grant: policy evaluation denies subsequent requests, but propagation and credential caching mean it is not the atomic in-process check-and-forward gate described here.
