name: plugin
document:
plugin
plug-in
plugin architecture
Let a host application acquire behaviour from independently deployed modules that it discovers and links at configuration or start-up time, so new features, backends or device support can be added without recompiling or redeploying the host.
The behaviours a system must offer vary by deployment (customer, environment, backend, hardware) or grow after the host has shipped; hard-wiring every implementation behind a factory method or a configuration switch means each new variant edits core code and forces a rebuild and redeploy of the whole application.
Systems whose capability set is not fully known at build time: third-party or per-customer extensions, drivers and storage backends, editor and build tooling, test runners, media pipelines. It applies wherever a stable extension point can be published, the contract can be versioned, and the runtime can bind code after compilation (shared libraries, class or module loading, plugin packages).
IDEs, editors and build tools whose feature set grows through extensions (Eclipse, VS Code, webpack, ESLint, pytest, RuboCop).
Servers and frameworks that pick a codec, transport, storage or auth backend per deployment (JDBC drivers via ServiceLoader, .NET plugin hosts, Kafka connectors).
Infrastructure tooling that hosts independently released providers, such as Terraform providers over gRPC or Vault secret engines.
Media, imaging and device software that adds codecs, effects or drivers after the main program ships (Apache httpd modules, GStreamer, DAW and imaging plugins).
Document and data pipelines where per-customer transformation or validation steps are shipped as separate packages (Python entry points, Ruby gems).
Applications that must support tenant- or customer-specific behaviour without a private build per customer, composed at start-up from a plugin directory or a configuration list.
AI agent systems where tools, memory backends and LLMs are loaded as plugins (LangChain agents, semantic kernel plugins).
Cloud-native platforms that must support tenant-specific backends or third-party integrations without redeploying the control plane (Kubernetes operators, service mesh extensions).
DevOps and CI/CD pipelines where steps, reporters or cloud integrations are added as plugins (Jenkins plugins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI job templates).
Observability platforms where collectors, processors and exporters are pluginable (OpenTelemetry collectors, Grafana datasources and panels).
Editor ecosystems that declare contributions in manifests and run extension code behind a host boundary, as in Visual Studio Code's Extension Host and contribution points.
Infrastructure CLIs that launch provider binaries over a versioned RPC contract and negotiate compatibility, as in Terraform's Plugin Protocol and provider servers.
Web servers assembled from independently built dynamic modules loaded at startup or restart, as in Apache HTTP Server's DSO and mod_so module system.

statement: Choose whether the reporting engine or each customer job controls the run lifecycle, including setup, invocation, result recording, and retries.
name: point-to-point-channel
document:
point-to-point-channel
point-to-point queue
p2p channel
Deliver each message on a channel to exactly one consumer, so senders never have to coordinate with receivers and no unit of work is handled twice.
A producer must hand work to exactly one handler while several receivers are running (or the intended handler is temporarily unavailable): broadcasting the message makes every receiver deduplicate, and addressing a specific consumer instance couples the sender to its identity, location and liveness.
Asynchronous messaging inside one process, between processes or across services, where each message is a unit of work (command, job, document, RPC request) and duplicate handling is as unacceptable as loss. Applies to in-process worker queues and to brokered channels (JMS queue, AMQP queue, Kafka partition, cloud queue) alike; the channel - not the consumer and not the sender - owns the routing decision.
Work queues: a web tier enqueues jobs and a pool of workers consumes them, with each job running exactly once.
Request-reply over messaging: the request goes to a queue, exactly one service instance answers it, and the reply returns on a reply queue identified by a correlation identifier.
Command dispatch in a service-oriented system: an order service appends commands that exactly one instance of the command processor executes.
Media or log processing pipelines where every stage pulls its input from a queue and each item is handled by one of the stage's replicas.
Legacy and batch integration: jobs handed to a single consumer daemon through a queue, with the channel providing the transactional hand-off.
Scaling an existing single-consumer endpoint by attaching additional instances (Competing Consumers) without changing producers or the message contract.
Apache Kafka consumer groups: records in each topic partition are assigned to one group member at a time, so a group scales work while separate group IDs retain independent pub-sub copies.
RabbitMQ Work Queues: a task queue distributes jobs among competing workers with round-robin or fair dispatch; manual acknowledgements allow unacknowledged work to be redelivered after a worker failure.
Amazon SQS Standard queues: distribute background jobs among consumers with visibility timeouts, while at-least-once delivery requires idempotent handlers because duplicate deliveries remain possible.

statement: Choose whether the reporting engine or each customer job controls the run lifecycle, including setup, invocation, result recording, and retries.
name: implicit-lock
document:
implicit-lock
framework-managed locking
automatic locking
Make the framework or layer-supertype code that every business operation must pass through acquire and release the locks, so no application method can forget an acquisition and silently invalidate the concurrency policy.
A locking scheme has no gaps only if every path that touches a lockable item acquires its lock: one forgotten acquisition, one lock released too early or too late, makes the whole offline concurrency strategy useless. Because the error shows up only under concurrent conflicting sessions, it survives unit tests, code review and single-user manual testing.
Multi-user enterprise applications whose business transactions outlive a single database transaction - a user reads a record, thinks for minutes, then saves - so locks live in a lock table or in version columns rather than in the database transaction. Typically a Unit of Work, a layer supertype, a session facade or a declarative transaction layer already exists, giving the application a place that can own the locking protocol centrally.
Request-as-business-transaction: a web application where an ORM Unit of Work or declarative transaction (Spring @Transactional, .NET TransactionScope, Django ATOMIC_REQUESTS) acquires the row locks or version checks for every record the request reads and writes.
Offline edit sessions: a user edits a record for minutes, and the session facade or layer supertype acquires a pessimistic lock when the record enters the business transaction and releases it on commit or abort, so no controller can forget it.
Batch and import jobs that modify aggregates: each chunk runs inside the framework's transactional scope, so locking follows the changed aggregates automatically.
In-process shared state in a service or worker: a scope construct (RAII guard, with block, defer, using declaration, withLock closure) binds release to the lexical block so exceptions and early returns cannot leak the lock.
Multi-tier clients with a session facade: the lock must follow the business transaction rather than the HTTP request, so the facade — not the UI — owns acquisition and release.
Optimistic concurrency: the mapper compares and increments the version column inside the framework's update path, so a hand-written UPDATE statement cannot skip the check.
Microservices saga orchestrator: the orchestrator drives each step inside an implicit transaction scope; each participant's framework layer acquires the lock or version check locally so the saga can compensate without distributed deadlocks.
Event-sourcing projections: a projection handler reads an event stream and writes to a read-model; the handler runs inside an implicit transaction so concurrent projection rebuilds do not corrupt the read-model — the framework decides whether to use optimistic or pessimistic locking based on the change set.
CQRS read-model updates: commands update the write model under an implicit write lock; the read-model update is published as an async event; the projection runs under its own implicit scope with conflict detection (optimistic) rather than blocking (pessimistic).
Database advisory locks for cross-connection coordination: an application holds a PostgreSQL advisory lock across a multi-statement business transaction that is not itself a DB transaction (e.g., involves an external HTTP call in the middle); the lock is acquired via a thin wrapper so callers do not call pg_advisory_lock directly.
Container-managed persistence (EJB CMT, Spring @Transactional): the container acquires and releases locks as part of the transaction lifecycle; developers write business methods without explicit lock calls, relying on the container's implicit concurrency control.
Retry and compensation with implicit lock release: when a business transaction fails after the lock is acquired but before commit, the framework's rollback path releases the lock automatically so the compensating transaction can retry without manual unlock calls.
Spring Framework proxy-managed services: a proxied @Transactional service method is the business entry point; Spring starts or joins the transaction for external calls, so persistence work and its configured optimistic or pessimistic checks stay inside one framework-owned boundary.
Hibernate ORM persistence contexts: an EntityManager or Session transaction can apply @Version optimistic checks or an explicit PESSIMISTIC_WRITE LockMode at the framework boundary, keeping lock acquisition and stale-version detection out of business methods.
EF Core Unit of Work: SaveChanges compares configured concurrency tokens, including SQL Server rowversion, and raises DbUpdateConcurrencyException on a stale update, making the version check implicit in the framework's commit path rather than a hand-written UPDATE predicate.

statement: Choose whether the reporting engine or each customer job controls the run lifecycle, including setup, invocation, result recording, and retries.
name: side-effect-free-function
document:
side-effect-free-function
pure function
Put the model's logic into operations that compute a result from their inputs alone, so that a caller - and a test - can predict the result without knowing any state the operation might secretly touch.
Reasoning about a design becomes guesswork when operations do more than return a result: the caller must read the implementation and every delegation to know which state a call changes, and no result can be reproduced in a test without recreating the state around it. As rules compose, the number of hidden interactions grows faster than the behaviour being built, so the model stops being safely predictable.
Applies inside the model layer of any codebase whose rules are combined and composed - pricing, eligibility, allocation, validation - and where a computation must be exercised in tests without a database, clock or message broker in the loop. It matters most where several rules interact (composition multiplies hidden coupling) and in languages whose defaults are mutable objects, because there the discipline has to be stated rather than assumed.
Pricing and discount rules: unit prices, tax and rebates computed from immutable inputs, so the same basket always prices the same way.
Eligibility and specification checks: a rule expressed as a predicate over a value and reused in validation, selection and tests.
Money and quantity arithmetic: scaling, adding and rounding return new values instead of adjusting a running total in place.
Deriving test data and expected values from the same pure functions the model uses, instead of hand-copied golden values.
Query-side report assembly: projections, summaries and totals built by composing pure functions over already-loaded immutable data.
Memoizing an expensive domain computation, which is sound exactly because the function is referentially transparent.
Redux reducers: the store computes the next state by calling (previousState, action) => newState with no mutation, no clock, no randomness, so DevTools can replay a recorded action log and reproduce the exact state and useSelector can detect changes by reference comparison alone.
React function components: the official contract is that rendering must be a pure function of props, state and context, so React can cache components whose inputs are unchanged, abandon an outdated render mid-flight, and call each component twice in Strict Mode to expose impurity.
Haskell: ordinary functions are pure by default and effects are confined to IO-typed values, so the type signature itself states whether a computation touches the world and the compiler, not review, enforces the query half of the split.

statement: Choose whether the reporting engine or each customer job controls the run lifecycle, including setup, invocation, result recording, and retries.
name: messaging-gateway
document:
messaging-gateway
Encapsulate access to a messaging system behind an ordinary interface of domain methods, so calling application code makes method calls while a single component owns message construction, correlation, timeouts and error translation.
Application code that talks to a broker keeps importing messaging concepts: it builds the payload, picks the channel, attaches a reply address and a correlation id, parses the response and interprets broker errors. The trigger for this pattern is that callers should make a method call instead of writing messaging code - the messaging knowledge belongs in exactly one place that can change without touching business rules.
At the boundary between application logic and a messaging system (message broker, MQ, queue service or actor runtime): the other side is reached by messages, but the caller is ordinary domain code that should see typed parameters and typed results. Applies to one-way (fire and forget) and request-reply interactions alike, and to blocking as well as asynchronous call styles.
A domain service that must query another system (inventory, pricing, credit scoring) over a queue: the caller invokes checkStock(sku) and receives a typed answer.
An HTTP or API layer whose controller awaits a brokered round trip (Spring Integration gateway interface, NestJS ClientProxy, MassTransit request client).
Batch and background jobs that dispatch work through a typed job API instead of assembling payloads (ActiveJob perform_later, Celery delay).
Wrapping a legacy system's MQ interface once, so the rest of the codebase never learns its message format.
Test seams: unit tests substitute a fake gateway, integration tests run the same interface against a real broker.
Migration seam: keep the gateway contract stable while the transport moves from one broker to another.
Actor and streaming stacks where a facade wraps ask/request so callers never hold ActorRefs or inboxes.
Spring Integration's @MessagingGateway and GatewayProxyFactoryBean let application code inject a typed interface while the framework routes calls into channels and returns replies.
MassTransit's IRequestClient<T> and GetResponse<TResponse> provide a typed request-reply client over the bus, keeping request and response message contracts out of the calling service.
RabbitMQ's RPC tutorial demonstrates a gateway-like client that publishes to rpc_queue with reply_to and correlation_id, then resolves the matching callback response.

statement: Choose whether the reporting engine or each customer job controls the run lifecycle, including setup, invocation, result recording, and retries.
name: guarded-suspension
document:
guarded-suspension
conditional block
suspended execution
Suspend a state-dependent method call inside the object that owns the state until another thread makes its guard predicate true, so callers neither poll nor get refused while the object is temporarily not ready.
A method may only proceed while a precondition over shared state holds - a buffer is non-empty, a pool still has a free lease, a session is authenticated, a worker has a task - and that state is produced by another thread at an unknown time. The recurring decision is what the caller should do while the guard is false: refusing the request would drop work the application still needs, forcing the transition would break the object's invariants, and polling wastes a core and still races. Guarded suspension answers it by waiting on a condition the object itself owns, and by making that wait atomic with respect to the state change that ends it.
Concurrent objects whose methods are state-dependent and whose state changes arrive from other threads: bounded buffers and handoff queues, resource pools, server request/response handoffs, readiness and shutdown gates, worker idle loops. Applicable where the runtime can efficiently park or suspend a caller (OS threads, coroutines) and where the object already owns a lock or monitor, so no notification can be lost between the predicate check and the wait. Ill-suited to single-threaded event loops, to callers that must never be delayed, and to waits whose eventual completion cannot be guaranteed.
Actor mailbox handoff: an Akka/Orleans/Swift-Actor mailbox is a lock-free guarded queue; the actor suspends on an empty mailbox and resumes when a message arrives, which is the same monitor-wait pattern expressed at the language level.
Swift async / Structured Concurrency: a Task.sleep or async let that suspends until a condition is a coroutine-level guarded suspension; the suspension point is backed by a condition variable or event channel inside the runtime.
CompletableFuture / async result: a future's blocking get() is a timed guarded suspension on the thread that submitted the asynchronous operation; the completion path (complete()) is the notifier.
Pipeline stage coordination: in a multi-stage streaming pipeline each stage blocks on input while the upstream stage processes, synchronising via a bounded channel whose put/get implement the guard.
Bounded buffers and handoff queues: a consumer's take waits while the buffer is empty and a producer's put waits while it is full (producer-consumer).
Resource pools: acquire blocks until a lease is returned to a connection, thread or object pool instead of failing or spinning when the pool is exhausted.
Server-side handoff: an acceptor or reader thread publishes a request and the worker waits for work to appear; a caller waits for the response slot to be filled.
Readiness and start-up gates: components wait until a dependency reports connected, initialised or ready, and callers wait until a session, device or circuit is open.
Shutdown and flush coordination: a terminator waits until in-flight work has drained, and a flusher waits while the buffer still holds entries (two-phase termination).
Platform queue and channel APIs: BlockingQueue.take/put, Queue#pop, Channel.receive/for-await, condition-variable waits - the same guard hidden behind a library type.
Project Loom virtual threads (JEP 444): a virtual thread calling Object.wait() parks its Continuation; the carrier thread is released for other virtual threads, so the program continues throughput while one virtual thread waits. The guarded action still re-checks the predicate on wake, and the pattern's semantics are preserved — only the threading model changes.
Akka typed actor mailbox: each actor has a single-threaded mailbox; receive() suspends the actor's continuation when the mailbox is empty, resuming when a message is dispatched. This is language-level guarded suspension where the wait set is the mailbox queue and the guard is 'mailbox non-empty'.
Kotlin coroutines rendezvous channel: Channel() (unbuffered/rendezvous) suspends the sender until a receiver is ready, and vice versa — the same lock-free handoff as an unbuffered Go channel. The suspension is a coroutine-level guarded wait on rendezvous.
Python asyncio.Condition: an async context manager that wraps an asyncio.Lock; await cond.wait() releases the lock and suspends the task until notify() is called, making it an async guarded suspension where the runtime schedules other tasks during the wait.
Go unbuffered channel send/receive: goroutine G1 executing ch <- x on an unbuffered channel sleeps (gopark) until goroutine G2 executes <-ch, at which point the runtime directly transfers the value and stack copy (rendezvous handoff). This is the language-level form of guarded suspension: the guard is 'receiver present', the wait set is the sudog queue in hchan.
Erlang/OTP process mailbox: a gen_server receiving messages from its mailbox blocks (receive...end) until a matching message arrives — the OTP process is a state machine whose transitions are guarded by message arrival, making each receive a suspension point in the actor's event loop.
.NET TaskCompletionSource<T>: GetAwaiter().GetResult() on a not-yet-completed TCS is a synchronous guarded suspension; the async continuation (ConfigureAwait, await) is an asynchronous one. SetResult() is the notifier. TCS is a one-shot asymmetric guarded suspension where one side never waits (the completor) and one side always waits (the synchronously blocked caller).
JDK ArrayBlockingQueue: the queue is one ReentrantLock plus two Condition objects, notEmpty and notFull - take() awaits notEmpty while count == 0, put() awaits notFull while the buffer is full, and each signals the other condition only after mutating count and the circular buffer inside the same critical section. It is the reference production realisation of a two-predicate guarded suspension, including the fairness switch and the timed offer/poll variants.
Go standard library: database/sql guards queries against a concurrent Close with closingMutex, which parks readers and the closing writer on two sync.Cond values (read/write), and net/http's Server.Shutdown waits until in-flight requests have drained. Both are the case Go's own guidance reserves sync.Cond for - a predicate that changes back and forth over time rather than a one-shot handoff.
HikariCP connection pool: DataSource.getConnection() suspends the caller until a lease is returned while the pool already holds maximumPoolSize connections, bounded by connectionTimeout (default 30000 ms, minimum 250 ms), after which it throws SQLException rather than waiting on - a guarded suspension in which the deadline is a documented, first-class outcome instead of an accident.

statement: Should the handler be decomposed into independently replaceable named stages with an explicit order, or retained as one method with local intermediate variables?
name: pipeline
document:
pipeline
assembly line
processing pipeline
Decompose a transformation into an ordered sequence of named stages that each consume the previous stage's output and produce the next stage's input, so the workflow reads top to bottom and every step can be tested, instrumented, reordered or replaced on its own.
A multi-step transformation is written as one long function or a tangle of nested calls: the steps are unnamed, their order is implicit in statement order, intermediate values need throwaway names, there is no seam at which a single step can be logged, tested or replaced, and the same sequence is retyped at every call site that needs it.
Processing that naturally decomposes into successive transformations of the same payload - request handling, ETL, compiler passes, message enrichment, image or byte-stream processing - whether the payload is a single value or a stream. It fits in-process, staged execution where one driver owns ordering, error handling and cancellation; distributing the stages across processes, transports and independently deployed filters is the architectural pipe-and-filter pattern instead.
Request handling: deserialise, authenticate, validate, enrich, persist and render a request, with each step named so a failing stage is attributable and testable in isolation.
ETL and data import: extract, clean, transform, validate and load large files as a stream, so no intermediate collection is materialised and memory stays bounded.
Compiler and interpreter passes: source, tokens, AST, resolution, optimisation and code emission, where each pass is an independent stage over the intermediate representation and the pass list is the pipeline.
Message enrichment in an integration flow: unwrap, translate, enrich and route a message, one stage per concern, with per-channel ordering; the cross-process version stays pipe-and-filter.
Image or byte-stream processing: decode, crop or resize, watermark and encode, lazily per frame or chunk, optionally overlapping stages across cores.
Configuration-driven data cleaning: the stage list is assembled from configuration or a plugin registry so different tenants get different ordered steps without changing the stages themselves.
TensorFlow tf.data input pipelines: tf.data.Dataset pipelines that chain map, prefetch, parallel_interleave and shuffle stages to feed a training loop efficiently, with each stage independently configurable and the whole pipeline testable in isolation.
LLM token streaming: HTTP server-sent event streams where an LLM produces tokens at inference speed while clients consume at variable network speed; stream.pipeline() prevents the inference server from buffering unbounded tokens in memory when a slow client disconnects (Node.js stream backpressure case study).
Observability telemetry pipelines: OpenTelemetry Collector chains receivers, processors (memory_limiter, batch, filter, transform, tail_sampling) and exporters for traces, metrics and logs, with connectors (e.g., spanmetrics) bridging signal types and memory_limiter placed first to prevent OOM before filtering.
Typed TypeScript pipeline with schema validation: Zod or io-ts schemas define the stage contract at each boundary, catching schema violations at the exact stage that produced bad data rather than at a distant consumer.
Async generator pipelines in Python: asyncio queues with bounded capacity connect async generator stages, propagating backpressure by pausing producers when the queue is full; the FinStream analytics case study showed 82% memory reduction and 99.7% latency reduction versus unbounded buffering.
Event-streaming pipelines with Kafka and Flink: producers, topic partitions, Flink consumers and checkpointing form a distributed pipeline where backpressure cascades across every boundary; the Kafka max.block.ms and Flink backpressure.sample.interval settings interact under partition saturation and must be tested together under load.
Dynamic pipeline parallelism: construct-and-run pipelines (MapReduce, Spark) fix stage count at construction, while on-the-fly pipelines (Cilk-P Piper algorithm) allow the structure to emerge at runtime, varying per iteration and supporting data-dependent branching; on-the-fly enables pipelines like x264 that cannot be expressed with a fixed static structure.
LLVM compiler pass pipelines: PassBuilder assembles ModulePassManager, CGSCCPassManager, FunctionPassManager and LoopPassManager across the IR hierarchy (Module → CGSCC → Function → Loop), with registered callbacks injecting passes at named extension points (pipeline-start, vectorizer-start, optimizer-last); incorrect PreservedAnalyses declarations invalidate all downstream analyses.
Continuous data pipelines at scale (Google model): periodic pipelines run on cron and suffer from depth growth and resource exhaustion as organic load increases; continuous pipelines (master-slave or event-triggered) replace idle-waiting with always-on processing, eliminating the 'pipeline vs cron' discontinuity at the cost of operational complexity.
ML pipeline orchestration (Airflow, Kubeflow, Prefect, Dagster): each orchestrator applies the pipeline pattern at the workflow level - Airflow's DAG-of-tasks, Kubeflow's per-container-step pipelines with GPU scheduling, Prefect's monoflow/subflow/orchestrator pattern, and Dagster's software-defined assets where asset dependencies imply the pipeline; the pipeline is the scheduler's unit of execution, not an implementation detail.
Apache Beam: PCollections flow through composable PTransforms (ParDo, Combine and GroupByKey) in a pipeline graph, making each transform boundary explicit while the runner handles execution.
Node.js stream.pipeline(): Readable, Transform and Writable stages compose with built-in backpressure, error propagation and AbortSignal cancellation; this is a concrete streaming realization, not a durable workflow engine.

statement: Should the handler be decomposed into independently replaceable named stages with an explicit order, or retained as one method with local intermediate variables?
name: function-composition
document:
function-composition
compose
function pipeline
Combine a chain of small unary transformations into one reusable function by sequencing them with a composition combinator (compose/pipe), so the order of the steps is stated once, every step stays independently testable, and the chain itself becomes a value that can be named, passed and reassembled.
A transformation that is naturally a sequence of small pure steps gets written as nested calls or as repeated imperative assignment (`h(g(f(x)))`, or `y = f(x); y = g(y); ...; return y`) at every call site. The order is duplicated wherever the chain is used, the intermediate values need throwaway names, steps cannot be reused in a different order, and changing one stage means editing every copy.
Pure or nearly pure value transformations - parsing, normalisation, validation, formatting, pricing, AST rewriting - where each step is unary and the language treats functions as values. It pays off when the chain is reused or assembled from data (configuration, plugin lists, per-request policy), when steps must be unit-tested in isolation, and when the same steps must also run element-wise over a collection or lazily over a stream. It stops applying where steps need side effects or branching between stages: there the shell around the pure core owns control flow.
Input normalisation: trim, parse, canonicalise and validate a payload before it reaches domain logic, with the same chain reused by HTTP handlers and message consumers.
Pricing and rule chains: base price, discount, tax and rounding applied in a fixed, configurable order to an immutable value object.
Compiler and AST work: a pass list of rewrite functions composed once and applied over the tree, with passes added or reordered per optimisation level.
Serialisation and formatting: sanitise, format, encode and sign a document, where each step is tested separately and the composed chain is stored as a constant.
Data transformation over collections: the same pure steps composed into one function and passed to map/filter/stream operations, so element-wise processing reuses the chain.
Policy assembly at startup: the processing chain is built from configuration or plugin registrations and then applied per request without further branching.
Reactive stream processing: RxJS Observable.pipe chains the same logical steps across asynchronous event sequences, with operators composed once and reused across streams.
ETL and data pipeline transformation: extract-transform-load chains where each stage (parse, clean, enrich, aggregate, write) is a unary pure function composed into a reusable pipeline run over batches or streaming data.
HTTP request/response middleware: the middleware stack is a composed function chain where each layer (authenticate, authorise, rate-limit, deserialize, validate) is a unary handler; composition is resolved once at startup.
Matrix and vector transformations in numerical code: each linear algebra operation (scale, rotate, translate, project) is a unary function on a matrix type; composing them once builds the transformation pipeline that is applied to every vertex or pixel.
Ramda pipelines: R.pipe and R.compose assemble reusable data-last transformations from small functions, centralising the order while letting the same composed value run over many inputs.
Redux store setup: Redux's compose helper combines store enhancers right-to-left into one enhancer, so the enhancer order is defined once instead of reconstructed at each store boundary.
lodash/fp transformations: lodash/fp's auto-curried, data-last compose/flow helpers assemble immutable-friendly transformations from reusable steps that can be passed as values.

statement: Should the handler be decomposed into independently replaceable named stages with an explicit order, or retained as one method with local intermediate variables?
name: functional-core-imperative-shell
document:
functional-core-imperative-shell
impureim sandwich
pure core, imperative shell
Split a unit of code into a pure functional core that turns values into decisions and a thin imperative shell that gathers the world, calls the core and carries out its decision, so the business rules can be reasoned about and tested without I/O or test doubles.
A module mixes decision logic with I/O: the rules for what should happen are interleaved with reading the database, reading the clock, logging, and writing back - so every branch is reachable only through a live environment, the behaviour is verifiable only with mocks or an end-to-end test, and the same rule gets re-implemented in each entry point that needs it.
Applies wherever a unit both decides and does: request handlers, CLI commands, batch jobs, protocol and reconciliation loops, UI stores, domain services that already know about a repository. It needs a place where inputs can be gathered before the decision and effects applied after it (an entry point, a handler, a composition root), and it pays off most where the decision space is large relative to the I/O - combinatorially rich rules over a small set of already-loaded values - while I/O-dominated code should be left alone.
Request handlers: gather (load entities, resolve the caller, take the current time), call one pure decision function, then write back and publish events - the handler keeps no rules of its own.
Pricing, billing and entitlement decisions: a pure function over a cart or subscription plus a date returns the charge, discount and proration, so money rules are verified in table tests instead of through a service and a database.
Validation and normalisation at the edges: parsing untrusted input into domain values through smart constructors is pure, while the shell decides where the bytes came from and what to do with the failures.
Schedulers, controllers and reconcilers: the loop computes the desired effects from a snapshot of current state (Kubernetes-style reconcile, sync jobs, sagas, outbox flushes) and an executor applies them, which makes the controller testable without the cluster or the queue.
UI and application state: a reducer (state + action -> new state) is the functional core, while the store/object layer holds the state, talks to the network and performs the effects in unidirectional flow.
Domain services in an existing layered application: keep the aggregate and its rules pure and let the application service become the shell that loads, decides and saves, without introducing a new architecture.
CQRS command handlers and Event Sourcing projections: the command handler is a shell that loads the aggregate, calls a pure transition function, and persists events; the projection is a pure fold over an event stream.
DDD aggregates and domain events: the aggregate's state transitions are pure functions, serialised by the shell; the same aggregate logic is reused in synchronous REST handlers and asynchronous message consumers.
FaaS and serverless functions: each invocation is a shell that fetches its inputs from a queue or KV store, calls the pure core, and writes the result back - cold-start time is spent on I/O, not on test setup.
Microservices adopting strangler-fig migration: new behaviour is added as a pure core behind a feature flag or router; the shell handles the old and new code paths side-by-side until the old path is retired.
Event-driven systems and outbox patterns: the shell reads a message, calls a pure handler that returns a list of effects (persist, publish, email), and the shell executes them inside a transaction or outbox relay.
Redux applications: reducers are a pure state-transition core (state plus action to new state), while middleware performs asynchronous work and other side effects around dispatch; the official Redux guidance makes the reducer/middleware boundary explicit.
Kubernetes controllers: the reconciliation loop reads observed and desired resource state, computes the next change as a decision, and uses the API server to apply effects; the controller documentation is a production example of separating state-based decisions from cluster I/O.

statement: Should the handler be decomposed into independently replaceable named stages with an explicit order, or retained as one method with local intermediate variables?
name: table-data-gateway
document:
table-data-gateway
table gateway
Confine every SQL statement that touches one table or view inside a single gateway object whose methods take and return plain record structures, so that no other code contains SQL for that table and rows cross the boundary as data rather than as domain objects.
Access to one table is spread across the codebase: SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE fragments are copied into every caller, nobody can say which queries a schema change will break, DBAs cannot find the SQL that needs tuning, and each caller has to know the dialect, the placeholders and the column order. The desired boundary is a single object that mediates all access to the whole table while the individual rows remain records (tuples, structs, hashes, DataRows) instead of becoming mapped objects.
Relational persistence where the database is a stable, schema-first integration point and SQL-level control matters (indexes, hints, bulk loads, vendor features), where the team deliberately does not want O/R mapping machinery in the domain layer, and where the domain logic is simple enough that rows may travel as records - CRUD and query services, reporting/read models, ETL writers, local SQLite stores, or a legacy database mediated for several applications. It is also the packaging decision for 'the SQL has to live somewhere well known' before a DAO, repository or query object is justified.
A service or CRUD application over a handful of tables where every screen maps to a few statements per table and an ORM would add more machinery than it removes.
Reporting and read models: read-only gateways over views or wide tables that return records directly to a formatter, export or BI job.
Legacy databases mediated for several applications: one gateway library per database becomes the documented API and the place where vendor quirks are hidden.
Embedded/local storage (SQLite, SQLCipher) in a desktop or mobile app, where one gateway per table keeps SQL out of the UI and can be tested with an in-memory database.
Batch and ETL writers that need explicit control over statement batching, cursors and transaction size - control that generated mappers hide.
Gradual refactoring of SQL scattered through transaction scripts: the first step is to move each table's statements into a gateway, after which a Data Mapper or repository can be introduced deliberately.
Test fixtures and seeders that must write through the same statements as production code rather than through a second, divergent SQL path.
Generated gateways in Go: sqlc compiles a schema plus a file of named queries into one struct per table and one type-safe method per SQL statement, with the caller holding the database handle and opening transactions - the gateway's invariants are then enforced by the generator and compiler rather than by convention.
Local SQLite storage on Android: each Room @Dao is a gateway over one table - the SQL lives in @Query-annotated methods validated at compile time, rows travel as plain entity data classes, and @Transaction or database-level transactions keep atomic multi-DAO boundaries in the caller.
Java teams that want the gateway structure without hand-writing it: jOOQ's code generator emits one DAO class per table or view (findAll, findById, generated fetchByColumn methods) that reads and writes Record/POJO rows and borrows the caller's Configuration, so the per-table SQL surface is regenerated when the schema changes.

name: quantity
document:
quantity
units of measure
dimensioned value
Represent a dimensioned measurement as one value that carries its amount together with its unit, so that conversion, comparison, unit-compatible arithmetic and amount-plus-unit input/output all have a single owner and incompatible units cannot be combined by accident.
Measurements are stored as bare numbers whose unit lives only in a variable name, a column comment or the reader's memory: the same physical quantity appears in metres in one place and in feet in another, conversion factors are retyped at every call site, adding two numbers of different dimensions compiles (or runs) happily, and parsing and formatting '3 km' is reinvented per feature. The recurring trigger is that an amount and its unit always change together and are one conceptual whole, so leaving them as two unconnected things makes the unit rules impossible to own.
Value-scope code in domain, engineering or integration layers that handles physical quantities - length, mass, time, temperature, energy, data volume, concentration. It pays off when values arrive with heterogeneous units (sensors, imports, user input, third parties), when derived quantities such as speed or density are computed, when users select a unit system for display, and when values must survive persistence and transport. The language decides how much of the guarantee is compile-time (units as type parameters, phantom/branded types) and how much is a runtime value object backed by a conversion table or unit registry.
Sensor and telemetry pipelines where readings arrive tagged with a unit and must be normalised to a canonical unit before aggregation, alerting or storage.
Engineering and simulation code (CAD, robotics, structural, electrical) that computes derived quantities such as velocity, torque or energy and must keep the dimensions consistent.
Logistics and commerce where weight, dimensions and rate limits are expressed in different unit systems (kg/lb, cm/in, m^3/ft^3) and are displayed in the customer's chosen system.
Healthcare and laboratory systems that exchange doses and results between systems (mg/kg, mmol/L) with reference ranges in different units.
Energy and utility metering, where consumption (kWh, m^3) is billed through unit-price arithmetic and readings must be comparable across meter types.
UI-level unit-system switching: store and compute in one canonical unit, render and edit in metric or imperial according to a user preference.
Scientific Python applications built on Pint's UnitRegistry, such as sensor and laboratory pipelines, where quantities are parsed, converted and reduced dimensionally at integration boundaries.
.NET engineering and telemetry services using UnitsNet's strongly typed Length, Mass and related quantities, with parsing, conversion, serialization and display-unit selection centralized in the library.
Compile-time dimensional-analysis code using F# units of measure or C++ Boost.Units for simulation and control loops, where invalid unit arithmetic is rejected before runtime and derived units are expressed algebraically.

name: active-record
document:
active-record
active record pattern
ActiveRecord
Make a domain object the record for one database row: keep the row's state, row-local behavior, and the methods that find and persist it together, so a small domain does not pay for a separate mapping layer.
A simple relational domain still needs a choice about where persistence lives. A Data Mapper or gateway separates table I/O from the object but adds mapping code and a second place to navigate, while direct SQL leaks schema knowledge into callers; the recurring question is whether one row object can own its data and CRUD without hiding transaction boundaries or pretending to model cross-row rules.
A relational store is the single system of record, the domain is small and its rules are mostly local to one row (validation, derivations, simple state transitions), and the team prefers a convention-driven persistence layer over a designed one. Typical homes are framework ecosystems where the ORM is the house style (Rails, Laravel Eloquent, Django, GORM, Vapor Fluent, TypeORM), CRUD-heavy applications, and thin layers over an already well-shaped legacy schema. Entity Framework Core can host behavior on entity classes, but its DbContext and mapping conventions are a Data Mapper-shaped boundary rather than pure Active Record. It stops applying as soon as invariants span several objects, several representations of one table are needed, or the store must be swappable.
CRUD-heavy applications where most screens and endpoints map onto a single table: forms, admin back offices, catalogs, content management.
Small-to-medium domains whose rules are mostly per-row - field validation, derived values, one-row state transitions - so a mapper layer would move data around without adding a model.
Prototypes and thin service layers over an existing, already normalised legacy schema where the table shape is stable and the domain is the schema.
Framework-default persistence: a Rails, Django, GORM, Vapor Fluent or TypeORM codebase where fighting the ORM for purity costs more than it returns.
Simple record-shaped bounded contexts inside a larger system - settings, audit entries, lookup tables - where a full domain model would be overhead.
JSON:API or REST backends for SPAs and mobile apps where the data model maps directly to a relational schema with minimal transformation.
Microservices with a single-responsibility data store: a service whose entire bounded context is one aggregate root table or a handful of tightly coupled tables.
Batch import pipelines where records are validated once and bulk-inserted (insert_all/upsert_all), and the domain logic has already been applied before the bulk operation.
Multi-tenant SaaS backends where row-level isolation is enforced at the database and the ORM connection handles tenant scoping automatically.
Real Rails systems such as GitLab and Discourse are good fits for row-shaped users, posts, permissions and settings backed by PostgreSQL; keep their reporting and cross-record workflows in query or service boundaries.
A Django or Laravel CRUD surface such as an admin or back-office module fits when each request mostly validates, loads, changes and saves one model; switch to a mapper or repository when the same data feeds materially different contracts.

name: watchman
document:
watchman
dead man's switch
heartbeat monitor
Detect that a message flow has gone silent - not that a message failed - and tell a responsible person or system within a bounded time by comparing each flow's arrivals against the cadence its business deadline implies.
Message systems fail silently in the one way no error handler observes: nothing arrives. A producer stops emitting, a consumer stops draining, a scheduled job never fires, a credential expires, a partition goes offline - and because no failing code path is ever entered, error dashboards stay green while downstream data quietly goes stale. The recurring trigger: a flow whose absence is business-visible (a nightly feed, an order stream, a partner interface) has no owner-facing signal for 'no messages', so the gap is discovered late - by a customer or a downstream job - instead of by the team that can fix it.
Applies wherever messages are expected on a knowable cadence (event streams, queues, batch hand-offs, partner interfaces, device check-ins) and their absence is a business-visible failure: the flow has an owner, the expected period and grace window can be derived from a downstream deadline, and either the transport can be observed passively (queue counters, a wire tap) or the producers can emit out-of-band heartbeats. The watchman sits at message-flow or boundary scope - an in-process watcher beside the consumer, a periodic sweep over persisted last-seen state, or a rule in the monitoring stack fed by metrics - and it must itself be watched, because a silent watchman is exactly the failure it exists to catch.
Nightly batch or ETL feed: page the integration owner when the 02:00 import has produced no messages by its deadline, instead of noticing an empty report at the morning stand-up.
Business-critical event stream (orders, payments, telemetry): alarm when the produce rate stays at zero through business hours, which separates a healthy quiet topic from a stopped producer.
External partner interface: notify when no messages have arrived from a B2B partner within the agreed window, turning a looming SLA breach into an early, actionable alert.
Long-running workflow stage: require a heartbeat from each process-manager step so a stuck instance is noticed before the surrounding batch closes or a compensation becomes necessary.
Retry or dead-letter pump: verify that the pump still drains failed messages - silence means the pump died, not that the backlog is empty.
Fleet check-ins (edge devices, agents, cron jobs on many hosts): raise a per-device or per-site alarm when scheduled check-ins stop arriving.
The alerting pipeline itself: an always-firing watchdog alert routed to an external service, so a broken alert path is discovered by its silence.
Cron and scheduled-job fleet via Healthchecks.io: each job pings a unique URL, the service holds the Period and Grace Time, flips the check Late then Down when no ping arrives by period + grace, and notifies integrations.
Dashboard alert rules in Grafana: an alert rule whose query returns no series enters the No Data state and can raise a DatasourceNoData alert - the platform form of deciding what silence means (No Data, Alerting, Normal or Keep last state).
Apache Burrow for Kafka (LinkedIn): committed offsets are evaluated per partition over a sliding window and a consumer is classified STALLED when its offset is frozen with non-zero lag, or STOPPED when no new commits arrive - consumer-silence detection without fixed lag thresholds.

name: option-maybe
document:
option-maybe
Option
Maybe
Make the possible absence of a result part of the value and of the signature, so every caller has to decide what happens when nothing is there instead of meeting a null, a sentinel or a silently defaulted value at run time.
A function has something to return for some inputs and nothing for others, but the signature does not say so: it returns a null reference, a sentinel (-1, empty string, NULL), an out-parameter, or a value that quietly means 'not found'. Callers forget the check, dereference the null or treat the sentinel as data, and the 'this case does not exist' path is discovered in production rather than at the call site.
Lookups, parsing, searches, optional configuration, nullable database columns and any API whose result may legitimately not exist - wherever the language can express absence as a type (Option/Maybe/Optional, a nullable type, a union with undefined) or a convention can carry it. It pays off at module and service boundaries, in chains of partial steps, and wherever 'absent' must stay distinguishable from a legitimate empty, zero or falsey value.
Lookups that can miss: configuration keys, cache entries, registry entries, map/dictionary access - either through the language's two-value form or an Optional-returning accessor.
Parsing and conversion (integers, dates, URLs, decimal numbers, external identifiers) where 'no valid value' is a legitimate answer rather than an error.
Searches over collections and structures (find, first, min/max, binary search, regex match, tree traversal) where a miss is part of the contract.
Genuinely optional data: middle names, second addresses, unset feature flags, optional protocol fields - as opposed to missing state, which is a domain error.
Chains of partial steps (look up user, then their company, then its billing address) where any hop may be absent and the whole chain should collapse to 'nothing'.
Boundaries from nullable interfaces: a database column admits NULL, a legacy or interop API returns null or -1, a deserialized document lacks a field - converted once at the adapter.
Container and stream operations that can be empty (head, pop, next, dequeue, min) and should report emptiness instead of throwing or returning a sentinel.
Rust's standard library uses std::option::Option<T> with Some(T) and None for optional values; its map and pattern-matching APIs let lookup or parsing pipelines stop at absence without a null pointer.
Java SE's java.util.Optional<T> is a production API for method results that may be absent: ofNullable converts a nullable boundary value, map/flatMap compose follow-up work, and orElse/orElseThrow make the exit policy explicit.
Scala's standard-library scala.Option[A] models Some/None and documents map, flatMap, and for-comprehensions for chained partial steps; its API also demonstrates wrapping a Java HashMap lookup so a missing key becomes None.

name: thread-safe-copy-on-write
document:
thread-safe-copy-on-write
Share one body between many threads so that copying a value stays cheap and reading it never blocks, and protect the sharing state itself - the reference count or the published pointer - so that a writer clones the body and swaps in a new snapshot instead of mutating storage other threads can see.
A value is copied often and mutated rarely, so the copies should share storage until one of them diverges. That decision works single-threaded, but the moment several threads hold the value the sharing state becomes shared mutable state in its own right: a reference count incremented without atomics loses updates or frees a body another thread is still reading, a plain pointer dereferenced while another thread replaces it is a data race, and a 'copy' that still aliases its source turns a reader's snapshot into a moving target. The trigger is a read-mostly shared value - configuration, routing table, registry, cache snapshot - that must be read without locking and updated by cloning.
Applies where one object, or one immutable snapshot of an aggregate, is read by many threads and written rarely: configuration reloads, registries and symbol tables, caches with rare invalidation, listener registries, and large immutable values handed between threads. Manual memory management, non-atomic reference counts or a separate publication step make the problem sharpest (C, C++, hand-rolled counting); garbage-collected languages apply the same structure with the published reference replacing the count. It is an object/value-level data-sharing decision, not a lock strategy for write-heavy state.
Read-mostly configuration or routing tables that are reloaded occasionally and read on every request by every worker thread.
Registries, symbol tables and interning tables built once and consulted constantly, with rare additions or invalidations.
Caches and memo tables where invalidation is rare and readers must never wait behind a writer.
Listener and observer registries traversed on every event and modified rarely - the classic CopyOnWriteArrayList use.
Large immutable values - strings, byte buffers, message payloads, compiled artefacts - handed between threads, where a deep copy at each hand-off would dominate.
Language runtimes, interpreters and plugin hosts that keep configuration or environment objects read by many threads and updated by a single owner.
The Linux kernel's RCU (read-copy-update) mechanism in its purest form: readers enter an rcu_read_lock() critical section with no lock, atomic or shared-memory write, updaters publish a replacement with rcu_assign_pointer(), and the superseded body is freed only after a grace period proves no reader can still hold it - the dentry cache, routing tables and network-device lists.
Rust's std::sync::Arc as the atomically counted body of the standard library: cloning an Arc increments the count, and Arc::make_mut detaches - cloning the inner value only when other Arc handles exist - so the sharing state is protected by the type rather than by convention.
Go services publishing an immutable configuration or routing snapshot through sync/atomic's atomic.Pointer[T]: readers Load it once per request without locking, writers build a fresh snapshot under a writer lock and Store or Swap the pointer, and the collector reclaims each superseded snapshot when no reader references it.

name: update-method
document:
update-method
per-frame update
tick method
Give every live object one self-contained per-frame step and let a single driver call each object's step every frame, so behaviour advances one frame at a time while input and rendering stay responsive.
A running world is full of objects that each have to keep doing their own thing - guards patrolling, statues charging, agents acting - and the recurring decision is where one object's per-frame behaviour lives and how all those behaviours get driven. Coding a behaviour as a loop that runs to completion blocks input and rendering (the skeleton walks, but nobody sees it); coding it inline in the game loop turns the loop into a switchboard over every kind of object, so every new behaviour edits central code; and there is no way for two actors to evolve independently and simultaneously.
Real-time software with many concurrent live objects whose behaviour is mostly independent and must be simulated over time: games, agent-based simulations, animation and particle systems, tick-based servers and live visualisations. It is the natural partner of a frame driver (Game Loop) - the loop supplies the cadence, Update Method supplies the per-object step - and it becomes the wrong shape in turn-based or purely event-driven domains where nothing changes between inputs.
Real-time games and simulations with many concurrent actors: patrolling guards, projectiles, particle effects and crowd agents each advance themselves once per frame while the driver walks the collection.
Component-based engines where the parts of one entity evolve independently - rendering, physics and AI components each implement their own step and the engine's registry dispatches per component (Unity, MonoGame, Bevy, GameplayKit, libGDX).
Per-frame animation and effect timelines outside games: tween/spring systems, sprite animation and UI transitions advanced from the browser's frame callback or a UI toolkit's animation timer.
Tick-based servers and headless simulations: game servers, digital twins and agent-based models where each agent's behaviour is a resumable step and the world advances in whole discrete frames.
Tools, editors and dashboards with continuously animating scenes, where many independent scene items (markers, live charts, gizmos) must advance on every repaint without a central per-item switch.
Porting straight-line behaviour into a frame loop: turning a scripted sequence (walk left, walk right) into a per-frame step, either by storing explicit state or by using coroutines/generators to keep the code linear.
Godot's SceneTree is the driver: a node opts into the walk with set_process(true) and its _process(delta) runs every render frame with the frame time passed in as an argument, while _physics_process(delta) is called at a fixed rate - so one object can implement two steps on two clocks and can leave the walk entirely (set_process(false)) instead of paying an enabled-flag check every frame.
Engines whose built-in driver leaves per-object order unspecified expose the order as configuration: Unity states you should not rely on the order of Update across GameObjects, so real projects fix dependencies through the Script Execution Order panel, a LateUpdate pass that runs after every Update, or the PlayerLoop API rather than through registration order.
Agent-based simulation models step whole populations in NetLogo: the go procedure runs ask turtles [ ... ] to give every agent its one turn and then tick advances the discrete clock - with documented semantics that agents take their turns in random order and only agents present when the ask began get to act.

statement: Should the handler be decomposed into independently replaceable named stages with an explicit order, or retained as one method with local intermediate variables?
name: humble-object
document:
humble-object
humble dialog box
Move as much logic as possible out of a program element that the framework calls but tests cannot instantiate - a UI control, callback, entry point or active object - into a plain collaborator that unit tests drive synchronously, leaving the original element as a thin adapter without decisions.
The element the host invokes cannot be exercised in a test: constructing it needs the framework's environment (event loop, window, container, thread), so driving it means slow asynchronous tests with framework setup, or none at all. Because the decisions were written where the trigger arrives, business rules live inside the untestable element: they are verified only by expensive end-to-end runs, they cannot be test-first, and every framework upgrade threatens them.
Applies when an element is hard to test for environmental reasons rather than intrinsic ones: framework callbacks (widgets, dialogs, request handlers, message listeners), entry points (main, server bootstrap) and active objects (threads, processes, timer and interrupt handlers), plus container-managed components whose interfaces the server demands. The logic must be expressible as a computation over data, and the host must keep invoking the element through a stable callback or entry point.
A dialog or screen whose enablement, validation and navigation rules are hard to exercise: extract a presenter or view model, leave the widget showing fields and forwarding events (the Humble Dialog form).
Framework callbacks that mutate business state - HTTP handlers, message listeners, timer or interrupt callbacks - where a thin adapter reads the input and a service decides.
Active objects and executables: a thread or process whose per-request processing is extracted so tests run synchronously instead of sleeping and coordinating (the Humble Executable form).
Transaction boundaries: extract the business logic out of the transaction controller so a test can run the logic and roll the transaction back, leaving only commit/rollback behaviour in the controller (the Humble Transaction Controller form).
Container-managed components: implement the server's interface in a thin adapter and keep the logic in a container-independent class, so the edit-compile-test cycle stays fast (the Humble Container Adapter form).
Legacy code with an overridable or exposed dependency call but no injection point: expose or extract the method first (the Poor Man's form) and only then attempt a test harness.
Entry points: parse arguments, wire dependencies and map the exit code in main, and put the program's decisions in a library function that tests call.
Android Activities/Fragments and Unity MonoBehaviours: extract lifecycle-driven logic into a plain class, leaving the framework component as a thin shell that forwards lifecycle events — enables unit tests without an emulator or device.
React class components and Angular controllers: move state and business logic out of the component into a hook or service, keeping the component as a declarative renderer that delegates all decisions.
Embedded systems interrupt handlers: extract per-interrupt processing into a synchronous function tested with deterministic inputs; the ISR remains a thin vector that disables interrupts and calls the extracted logic.
Database transaction scripts: separate the SQL/transaction orchestration (humble controller) from the business logic (collaborator), so the logic is tested with a connection spy and the wiring is verified by a small number of integration tests.
Event-driven microservices: keep the event-listener adapter minimal (deserialize, delegate) and place all routing and business logic in a synchronous service that tests can drive directly with domain objects.
CLI entry points: extract argument parsing and environment setup from the main method into a plain runner class; the collaborator is tested with fake argv, and the shell only handles OS-level concerns.
Android Jetpack (AndroidX) ViewModel: Google's architecture guidance makes the ViewModel the testable collaborator - it MUST NOT reference Activity, Fragment, View or Context - so screen logic is unit-tested on the JVM with fakes, while the Activity/Fragment stays a humble shell exercised only by instrumentation tests.
WPF / .NET MVVM: Microsoft's guidance prescribes views with empty code-behind - controls bind to ViewModel properties and ICommand implementations (e.g. DelegateCommand) - so enablement, validation and action logic (CanExecute/Execute) are plain classes unit-tested without a window, and XAML binding is covered by a few integration checks.
Unity MonoBehaviour game code: teams extract game rules into plain C# classes unit-tested outside the engine's Play Mode, leaving the MonoBehaviour as a serialized-field shell that forwards Update/FixedUpdate - the Unity community reports this buys fast unit tests at the cost of harder in-engine integration tests, so the shell needs deliberate coverage.

name: stub
document:
stub
test stub
stub object
Replace a collaborator with a test-specific stand-in that returns canned answers, so the component under test can be driven down paths - success, empty, error, timeout - that the real collaborator cannot be made to produce on demand.
The component under test receives indirect inputs through a collaborator, and the branch that must be exercised is selected by what that collaborator returns. The real collaborator will not produce the needed value on request: it is slow, remote, licensed, non-deterministic, or simply never returns the rare case - the empty result, the declined payment, the timeout - that the test exists for. Without a controllable replacement the test either cannot reach the path at all or has to provoke it through the production system, which is exactly what unit testing was supposed to avoid.
Unit and component tests of a component whose collaborators are already, or can cheaply become, abstractions: the values and exceptions a collaborator returns are inputs to the component under test, and the test asserts what the component does with them rather than how the collaboration happened. Typical where the collaborator is remote or stateful (HTTP client, database, queue, clock, payment gateway) or where the branch under test is an edge case - empty page, declined payment, expired token, feature off. The pattern assumes a substitutable seam: a constructor parameter, an injected interface, a factory, a lookup, or a patchable module.
Exercising a rare branch of the component: an empty result set, a declined payment, a 429 from a gateway, a missing feature flag.
Testing error handling: programme the stub to raise the exception the real service would raise - timeout, connection reset, malformed payload - and assert that the SUT surfaces or recovers from it.
Unit-testing a component against a collaborator that is slow, paid, unavailable in CI or still being implemented; the stub encodes the agreed response while the real adapter is built.
Removing non-determinism from a path the real collaborator decides by clock, randomness or remote state (token expired, cache cold, retry budget exhausted), so one outcome can be asserted exactly.
View and presentation tests: a fixed dataset from the stub, so the assertion is about the rendering or the decision logic and nothing else.
Boundary values on contract edges - zero, maximum, empty string, unicode payloads - that the real system cannot be asked to return on demand.
Mockito (Java): when(warehouse.hasInventory(...)).thenReturn(false) programmes the declined-branch answer and thenThrow(SocketTimeoutException.class) injects the failure, and consecutive-value stubbing (thenReturn(v1, v2)) drives retry-then-succeed paths that the real warehouse would never produce on request.
Python unittest.mock (standard library): Mock(return_value=...) fixes the canned answer while side_effect set to an exception or an iterable raises or sequences answers per call - the library ships Responder and Saboteur behaviour as first-class configuration.
Moq (.NET): mock.Setup(x => x.HasInventory(...)).Returns(false) and .Throws<InvalidOperationException>() are the canned-answer primitives, so a C# test reaches the empty-inventory and fault branches of Order.Fill without touching a database.

statement: Should the handler be decomposed into independently replaceable named stages with an explicit order, or retained as one method with local intermediate variables?
name: deadline-propagation
document:
deadline-propagation
timeout propagation
Bound the total time and work of a logical request by carrying one deadline through its whole call tree: every hop forwards the remaining budget and the cancellation signal instead of inventing a fresh timeout, so work that can no longer succeed is abandoned at every level.
A request fans out into a chain or tree of downstream calls and each hop applies its own timeout: the end-to-end latency budget becomes the sum of N independent timeouts, servers keep working after the originating client has given up, and cancellation never reaches the deeper work - resources are consumed producing answers nobody will read.
Networked request handling with multi-hop calls: RPC and HTTP chains, service meshes, gateways, fan-out and hedged requests. It applies when one latency budget is meaningful for the whole logical request (an SLO or a user-facing timeout), when the hops are under your control and can carry request-scoped state (context, token, signal, call option or header), and when downstream work is cancellable or can be interrupted at checkpoints.
Microservice request chains (gateway -> frontend service -> several backends) under one user-facing latency SLO, where each hop converts the inbound deadline into its own outgoing calls.
gRPC services whose clients set a deadline and whose servers propagate it as a remaining timeout to downstream calls while cancelling server-side work once the deadline passes.
Fan-out and aggregation endpoints calling several backends in parallel: every sub-call shares the parent budget, and sub-calls still running when it expires are cancelled instead of awaited.
Hedged requests: the first replica to answer wins, and the duplicate requests are cancelled through the same carrier so their downstream work is stopped too.
Streaming and long-poll endpoints that must stop processing when the client disconnects or the connection times out, propagating that stop to services and storage.
Batch or pipeline steps with a per-request time budget that must check the remaining time before each stage and abandon a request that can no longer be finished in time.
ROS 2 / DDS-based robotics pipelines: autonomous vehicle perception pipelines where sensor data must traverse a chain of processing nodes (detect -> classify -> plan -> act) and missed deadlines invalidate downstream results entirely.
Distributed real-time databases with multi-hop queries (gateway -> shard router -> storage node -> index node) where each hop's latency budget is derived from a user-facing SLA.
Service mesh sidecar configurations (Istio/Linkerd/Envoy) where per-route timeout policies propagate deadline context to application code via headers like grpc-timeout or custom X-Request-Deadline headers.
Industrial IoT and edge computing pipelines (edge gateway -> fieldbus bridge -> PLC -> sensor) where end-to-end control loop deadlines must be enforced across heterogeneous network boundaries.
GraphQL federation: a federated query hitting multiple subgraphs in parallel must bound the total resolution time and cancel subgraph requests whose partial results can no longer affect the final response.
Go services on the standard library context package: context.WithDeadline and WithTimeout derive a child whose Done channel closes at the earliest of its own deadline, an explicit cancel, or the parent's cancellation, so cancelling the root request context tears down the whole goroutine tree, and WithDeadlineCause/WithTimeoutCause attach an explicit cause for attribution.
Envoy router filter in service meshes: Envoy sets x-envoy-expected-rq-timeout-ms on internal requests - derived from x-envoy-upstream-rq-timeout-ms or the route timeout - so upstream services can read the expected total completion time and exit early instead of finishing work the proxy has already timed out.
ASP.NET Core gRPC services map the inbound call's deadline onto the handler's CancellationToken; passing that token to database queries, HttpClient calls and Task.Delay stops server-side work the moment the client's deadline expires.

statement: Should the handler be decomposed into independently replaceable named stages with an explicit order, or retained as one method with local intermediate variables?
name: attorney-client
document:
attorney-client
attorney pattern
attorney-client friendship idiom
Grant a named collaborator a deliberately narrow compile-time view of a class's private interface by making an attorney the client's sole friend; the attorney forwards selected operations or re-exports selected private nested types (often through controlled public typedefs), while unrelated private members and the public contract remain closed.
A C++ collaborator may need one private hook, constructor, iterator adapter or nested implementation type, but a friend class receives every private and protected member. Making the hook public leaks it to every caller; publishing a std::list<T>::iterator or the container type leaks representation and its invalidation contract; pImpl hides representation from everyone but does not grant one collaborator a typed privileged view. The missing mechanism is a small attorney contract that names exactly the operations or nested types this collaborator may use without turning the private interface into a second public API.
Object-oriented code whose encapsulation boundary is a class and whose language offers class- or scope-level access control but no per-collaborator grant - C++ with friend declarations, Java/C#/Kotlin with package, assembly or module access, and their test- and library-extension scenarios. It applies at object scope, where one type owns the implementation and one named collaborator needs a slice of it, and it is a source-level structuring device checked by the compiler, never a runtime protection mechanism.
White-box test access: a test harness reaches one private hook or state view through a named attorney instead of making the member public or redefining private with a test-only preprocessor switch.
Iterator adapters: Boost.Iterator's iterator_core_access is a canonical gateway class a user-defined iterator befriends, so iterator_facade and its operators reach private dereference/increment/advance core functions while those implementation hooks stay out of the iterator's public API.
Serialization: Boost.Serialization has serializable classes befriend boost::serialization::access, whose gateway reaches the private serialize() member so archives can reconstruct state without a public serialization method.
Private nested type exposure: LLVM's SchedulerInternalsAttorney publishes the selected nested Scheduler::BndlSchedState as a public type alias and supplies narrow static accessors for unit tests, without publishing every Scheduler private type.
A pImpl-backed adapter that must inspect one implementation-owned type: keep the public class opaque and put the attorney definition in the adapter or test header, so the privileged component gets a typed view without making the implementation part of the ordinary public contract.
Iterator facade over a hidden list-like representation: expose a stable nested iterator/view type through an attorney rather than publishing std::list<T>::iterator, so the owner can replace the container without promising its node and invalidation details to every caller.
Private virtual hooks: an attorney forwards one private virtual operation through a base reference, allowing the derived override to run even though friendship is not inherited.
Factory or construction control: a builder reaches one private constructor or initialization hook through an attorney, while unrelated callers still cannot construct an object through that path.
Spacecraft flight software (fsfw): LocalDpManagerAttorney keeps fetchPoolEntry and getMutexHandle as private static forwarders and befriends only LocalPoolVariable and LocalPoolVector, so the local data pool manager opens its internals to two named collaborators instead of every class that might befriend it.
Simulator tree traversal (Sandia Sparta Modeling Framework): sparta::TreeNodePrivateAttorney exposes TreeNode's private child vectors and subtrees through static accessors (getAllChildren, getChild, findChildren) for internal Reports and Pipeout processing, with a documented 'should NOT be used by simulation developers' restriction in place of an enforceable caller limit.
