name: aggregate
document:
aggregate
aggregate root
consistency boundary
Define a transactional consistency boundary around domain objects: one root entity is the sole externally reachable entry point, owns internal entities and value objects, and is the only object application code modifies directly; each command loads and commits one root instance, while other roots are referenced by identity and coordinated separately.
Business rules relate several objects at once - an order total that must stay within a credit limit, allocations that must never exceed stock - but if every object is writable on its own, no single place can enforce the rule at commit time. Concurrent callers interleave, persistence updates parts separately, and the invariant survives only while every caller remembers to check it; the model needs one owner and one atomic persistence boundary.
Tactical domain modelling inside a bounded context with genuine transaction-wide invariants: an object graph whose parts must agree at every commit, a store that can persist one root and its cluster as one unit (one transaction, a cascade or an explicit unit of work), and domain experts who can state which rules must hold immediately. It matters most where concurrency, distribution or graph size make 'everything is consistent with everything' unaffordable.
Order capture with line items where the order total must not exceed a credit limit - the purchase-order invariant Evans uses to motivate the pattern.
Inventory allocation where allocated quantity must never exceed on-hand stock for one stock item (Vernon's StockItem example).
Booking and reservation models where a seat, room or slot must not be double-booked inside one boundary.
Invoicing: an invoice with its lines and a tax total that must equal the sum of the lines, loaded and committed as one unit.
A shopping cart or basket with a maximum line count or quantity per item enforced per cart.
Write models under CQRS whose command handlers must modify exactly one consistency boundary and let the rest of the system catch up from events.
Banking account transfers: a debit and credit of the same amount must be atomic within one account aggregate.
Subscription lifecycle management: a plan change must atomically update status, record the new plan, and create a proration record.
Patient treatment records: a treatment episode where diagnosis, prescriptions, and progress notes must remain consistent.
Axon Framework's event-sourced GiftCard aggregate: an IssueCard command targets the root identifier, replays that aggregate's stream, and applies events to rebuild state.
EventStoreDB event-sourced orders: one order stream is replayed to rebuild the aggregate and appended with an expected stream version for optimistic concurrency.
SQLAlchemy's Order.items relationship with cascade='all, delete-orphan': a Session flushes owned line items with their root while the application transaction remains scoped to that aggregate.
EF Core owned entity types ([Owned] / OwnsOne / OwnsMany): owned parts cannot exist or be persisted independently, are loaded with their owner by default, and map the aggregate's ownership boundary onto the ORM's change tracker.
Protean's BaseAggregate: invariants are validated before and after every state change, the aggregate is the unit of persistence and optimistic concurrency, and a stale version raises ExpectedVersionError for retry.
Axon Framework 5 event-sourced entities: commands target the @EventSourcedEntity root's identifier and @EntityMember child entities receive only their routed events, so the consistency boundary survives under the entity-based model.

name: domain-service
document:
domain-service
stateless service
service object
Model a significant domain operation - transfer, allocation, conversion - that is not a natural part of any single Entity or Value Object as a standalone, stateless service: declare its interface in the language of the model, make the operation name part of the ubiquitous language, and use it judiciously so services never strip entities and value objects of their behaviour.
Some operations of the ubiquitous language - transferring funds, allocating cargo, pricing a basket, converting money - span several model elements and fit none of them: attaching the operation to an arbitrary entity turns that object into a script for someone else's job, and scattering it across callers leaves the rule unnamed and unowned. The recurring decision is whether to force the operation onto an object that does not really own it, or to model it explicitly as a service.
Model-driven design (Domain Model, Aggregate, Entity and Value Object) where behaviour is expected to live with the data it works on: the operation is a verb of the ubiquitous language, combines several entities or value objects (or a policy none of them owns), has no per-client state, and is invoked from a use case or from another model element. Typical in the domain layer of a layered or hexagonal architecture, with its collaborators declared as domain-owned abstractions.
Funds transfer between two accounts, including the interbank and clearing steps that are no single Account's responsibility (Evans' canonical example).
Cargo allocation: assigning shipments to voyages with a routing and capacity algorithm that walks the whole cargo/voyage graph.
Currency conversion or fee and interest calculation driven by rates and policies shared across many accounts and products (Vernon's calculation-process service).
Generating a unique, human-meaningful identifier - invoice number, order number, policy number - whose format spans several aggregates.
Evaluating a basket-level discount or eligibility rule that combines products, customer history and promotions before any aggregate is mutated.
Answering a domain question that needs several aggregates in one consistent decision, such as whether a customer may reserve this cargo.
Inventory reservation: checking availability across multiple warehouse locations and reserving stock before order confirmation — spans Product, Warehouse, and Reservation aggregates.
Credit limit evaluation: determining whether a customer can place an order based on their outstanding balance, credit terms, and current order value — crosses Customer, Order, and Pricing aggregates.
Route optimisation: calculating the best delivery route given constraints on vehicle capacity, time windows, and driver availability (Microsoft Azure drone-delivery Scheduler example).
Tax calculation for cross-border transactions: computing applicable taxes given the seller's jurisdiction, buyer's jurisdiction, product category, and current treaty rates — involves multiple fiscal policy value objects.
Fraud scoring: evaluating a transaction against patterns stored across Account, Session, and History aggregates to assign a risk score before authorisation.
Merging duplicate customer records: identifying and consolidating two Customer aggregates into one, transferring all associated Order and Contact references atomically.
Commission calculation for a multi-tier sales representative hierarchy: traversing the rep tree, applying different rates at each level, and producing a Commission value object.
Assigning an issue to a user with a per-assignee open-limit check that needs a repository count and mutates the Issue aggregate - ABP Framework's canonical IssueManager domain service, registered stateless with a transient DI lifetime.
Annotating service-layer classes with Spring Framework's @Service stereotype, whose Javadoc defines the role verbatim in Evans' terms - 'an operation offered as an interface that stands alone in the model, with no encapsulated state'.
Funds transfer as a banking domain service that interacts with Account and Ledger objects, making debits and credits and confirming whether the transfer was allowed (Evans' worked example in Chapter 5)

name: entity
document:
entity
reference object
domain entity
Give a domain concept a stable identity that survives attribute changes, representation changes and time, and define its equality, lifecycle and lookup in terms of that identity instead of in terms of its attributes.
A model that compares objects by their attributes cannot answer whether two instances are the same thing: a customer whose e-mail and plan changed looks like a different customer, while two distinct people who share a name look like one. References held by other objects, caches and audit records break silently, and every state change forces callers to re-identify the object.
Rich domain models in which some concepts must be tracked through time: the object is created, changes state, is stored and reloaded, and may exist in several representations (in-memory instance, database row, message payload, UI snapshot) that all have to denote the same thing. It is the modelling decision that pairs with Value Object: attribute clusters become values, while the things whose history matters keep an identity.
Master data tracked for years — customers, accounts, contracts, products, patients — where attributes change but the business entity stays the same (e.g., a Customer who moves house is still the same Customer).
Documents with a lifecycle: orders, invoices, bookings and shipments that move through states (pending → paid → shipped → delivered) while remaining the same document with a stable order number.
Shopping cart to order transition: a ShoppingCart is reconstituted as an Order with the same customer identity but a new order identity, preserving the correlation to the customer while starting a new business process.
Correlating representations across layers: an entity persisted as database rows, published as domain events, and displayed in a UI must be recognisable as the same thing in all three — identity is the correlation key across representations.
In-memory session consistency: a unit of work or identity map ensures the same Customer loaded twice in one request is one object reference, preventing edits from silently diverging into two copies.
Referencing across bounded contexts: one microservice holds a CustomerId reference to another service's aggregate root, allowing independent deployment and loading without a direct object pointer.
Healthcare records: a Patient entity persists across multiple visits, lab results and prescriptions — the patient identity is the anchor for the entire medical history regardless of demographic changes.
Versioned documents: an InsurancePolicy entity may be replaced by a new version while the original policy number (identity) remains the correlation handle for auditors and legacy systems.
Hibernate/JPA: an @Entity class with an @Id is managed by the persistence context, which guarantees one in-memory instance per identity per session — loading the same row twice in a session returns the same object reference, an Identity Map built into the framework.
Entity Framework Core: identity resolution makes the DbContext track a single entity instance per primary key, so duplicate instances arriving in a deserialized graph are merged into the already-tracked entity instead of diverging into two tracked copies.
Drupal Entity API: nodes, users and taxonomy terms (content entities) and roles or image styles (configuration entities) are identity-bearing objects with typed storage handlers, revisions and field bundles behind one CRUD and validation API.

name: application-service
document:
application-service
use case
interactor
command handler
Give each externally callable business use case a thin, stateless application boundary that translates a request, loads the required aggregates, delegates every invariant to the domain model, commits one local unit of work, and returns a stable result without exposing domain objects.
A business operation may need to load several aggregates, ask a domain service for a decision, persist the result, record an event and commit atomically. If an HTTP controller, CLI command, queue handler and scheduler each assemble that sequence, transaction scope, authorization, idempotency, error mapping and event handling drift. The application service gives that use case one explicit owner, while the domain model remains the owner of business truth.
A deliberately rich domain model (Entity, Aggregate, Value Object, Domain Service and Repository) with one or more use cases that cross object or repository boundaries, multiple inbound clients, and a local transaction boundary that must be consistent for all of them. The model stays persistence-ignorant, so the application layer supplies the unit of work and the boundary concerns the model should not carry: authorization, tenant and user resolution, idempotency, input and DTO translation, audit, and durable domain-event dispatch.
A web API, a CLI command and a queue consumer must execute the same 'place an order' operation: all three call one service method, so validation, authorization, transaction and event publication cannot drift.
A use case spanning several aggregates: a domain service decides whether a transfer is permitted, the application service loads both accounts, invokes the decision, saves the outcome and publishes the event inside one transaction (Vernon's transactional application service).
CQRS systems: commands are executed by application services or command handlers, while queries bypass the domain model through a dedicated read model. The application service loads the aggregate, calls its behaviour, persists, and publishes domain events - all inside one transaction.
Background and batch processing where the same use case must run without an HTTP request, with its own transaction, logging and retry policy.
Greenfield domain modelling where per-aggregate CRUD services are the first cut and are then refined into one operation per use case as dependencies and rules grow.
Multi-tenant or heavily audited applications where the boundary is the single place to resolve the current user/tenant, check permission and record the audit entry for a business operation.
Saga / process manager orchestration: an application service drives a multi-step workflow across bounded contexts, loading a process-manager aggregate, advancing its state, persisting it, and dispatching commands to participant services; each step is its own transaction with compensating transactions for failure.
Event-driven workflows where a domain event triggers a use case that must atomically update business state and schedule or publish follow-on events (outbox pattern) so that downstream consumers receive every event exactly once.
Cross-bounded context integration: one bounded context's application service subscribes to published events from another, translates them into commands or queries, and coordinates the local response with its own transaction.
Vaughn Vernon's SaaSOvation identity/access and project-management examples: a ProductBacklogItem application service loads a Product aggregate, invokes its behavior and persists the new item under one transaction.
An NServiceBus endpoint handles a PlaceOrder command through a message handler: the handler coordinates the local repositories and outbox, while the endpoint's unit of work and recoverability policy make retries safe only when the use case is idempotent.
A FastAPI router injects a request-scoped application service and repository with Depends; the endpoint translates HTTP input, the service executes the domain command, and the response mapper returns a DTO rather than an aggregate.

name: copy-on-write
document:
copy-on-write
lazy copy
clone-on-write
implicit sharing (Qt)
shadow paging
Let several handles of a value share one expensive body until the first write, which clones that body privately, so copying costs a pointer instead of a deep copy while every handle still behaves as an independent value.
A value with an expensive body (large buffer, collection, tree, document) is copied eagerly on assignment, argument passing and return even though most copies are never modified: time and memory are spent duplicating data that would have stayed identical. The naive fix - handing out one mutable object behind several handles - breaks the copy contract, and unrelated parts of the program then observe each other's writes.
Applies when copies of an expensive payload vastly outnumber modifications, when the payload is large enough that the copy dominates the cost of the handle (multi-kilobyte buffers, collection snapshots, editor or model state), and when the language offers a cheap way to know whether the body is still shared - a reference count, an explicit shared flag, or a uniqueness test. It is a single-threaded optimization first; sharing the count across threads turns it into the separate thread-safe copy-on-write concern.
Large buffers passed by value through API layers: strings, byte arrays and image/document payloads whose copies are usually read-only (Qt QString/QByteArray implicit sharing, ATL CString, pre-C++11 std::string).
Read-mostly collections whose traversals vastly outnumber mutations and must not block readers: listener and handler registries, routing tables, RuleEngine rule sets (CopyOnWriteArrayList/CopyOnWriteArraySet).
Configuration and state snapshots swapped atomically at the write boundary (feature flags, reloaded settings, event-sourced folds) so readers keep a consistent version without locking.
Persistent and functional data structures where an update returns a new version that structurally shares everything the change did not touch (Scala immutable collections, Immer drafts, persistent lists and maps).
Operating-system and memory-mapped sharing: fork and page-level copy-on-write share physical pages until a mapping is written, and file-backed buffers are shared until modified.
Columnar and data-frame workloads where slices are views and only the columns actually written are duplicated (pandas copy-on-write mode, Arrow buffers).
Fork-based process snapshots: Redis BGSAVE/BGREWRITEAOF forks a child to serialize memory to disk while the parent continues serving writes; only pages modified by the parent after fork are COW-copied, keeping the child's view consistent (vm.overcommit_memory=1 recommended).
COW filesystems for instant snapshots: ZFS and Btrfs never overwrite blocks in place; creating a snapshot is O(1) — save the root block pointer; reclaims O(1) more when the snapshot is deleted and no other reference remains. Enables self-healing via checksum propagation and efficient incremental replication via zfs send / btrfs send.
Database MVCC at row granularity: Postgres, LMDB, CockroachDB Pebble write new row versions on UPDATE/DELETE and reclaim old versions via VACUUM once no active transaction can see them; readers see consistent snapshots without read locks.
Container image layering: Docker/OCI images use layered COW where lower layers are read-only and the upper layer copies on write; base images are shared across many containers until a layer is actually modified.
APFS reflinks and XFS/ref ext4 ioctl(FICLONE): file-level COW that shares extents until either fork writes, enabling instant file clones (e.g., `cp --reflink=auto`) at near-zero cost.
LMDB's single-level store: a CoW B+tree using two fixed root pages (double buffering) where readers are fully latch-free and writers never block readers; no WAL needed because old trees remain intact until the new root is durably synced.
Swift standard library collections (Array, Dictionary, Set, String, Data) where isKnownUniquelyReferenced() checks the heap object's strong reference count at runtime to decide whether to mutate in-place or clone.
Qt QSharedData/QSharedDataPointer: implicit sharing for pimpl'd d-pointer classes where non-const operator-> triggers detach() automatically before any write access; QExplicitlySharedDataPointer suppresses automatic detach.
Rust std::borrow::Cow: a generic enum (Borrowed | Owned) that defers the clone until to_mut() is called, especially useful in APIs that accept both borrowed and owned data without multiple signatures.
PHP arrays and strings: reference-counted value types where assignment and argument passing share the zval and the first write 'separates' it (copy-on-write) when refcount > 1; taking a reference with & turns the sharing into an explicit alias set (php.net reference counting, php-src core docs).
pandas 3.0, where copy-on-write is the default and only mode: any DataFrame or Series derived by indexing behaves as an independent copy, chained assignment (df["foo"][mask] = v) silently doing nothing is eliminated - it raises ChainedAssignmentError - and every update must be a single .loc step (PDEP-7).
Linux kernel OverlayFS copy_up: a container write to a lowerdir file (open for write or metadata change) copies the file up into upperdir first; the metacopy feature delays the data copy until the first data write, and an fsync before the finalizing rename guards against zero-filled files after a crash (kernel overlayfs docs, Docker overlay2 driver).

name: event-aggregator
document:
event-aggregator
event bus
messenger
message bus
event hub
Funnel the events of many source objects into one hub that owns the subscription wiring, so that subscribers register once with the aggregator instead of tracking down and registering with every publisher.
Many components raise events and many components want to react: if every consumer registers directly with every producer, each consumer has to find the sources and subscribe to each event type separately, each producer accumulates knowledge of who listens, and both sides repeat the same registration and unsubscribe code at every pair. The trigger is a many-publisher / many-subscriber setting in which the wiring itself has become the maintenance problem.
In-process, event-driven software - a modular UI shell, a domain-event pipeline inside one bounded context, a plugin host, a simulation or instrumentation layer - where publishers and subscribers grow independently, both sides should stay unaware of each other, and registration plus lifetime management should live in one place. The aggregator is a component- or module-scope element of one process (one node); events that must cross a process boundary, survive a restart or be delivered reliably need a messaging channel instead.
Modular UI shells (WPF/MAUI, Android, SwiftUI) where view models living in separate modules must react to each other without holding references — the classic Prism and CommunityToolkit.Mvvm scenario.
Domain-event fan-out inside one bounded context: 'order placed' reaches billing, stock, notification and audit services that each subscribe to the hub instead of to the Order aggregate.
Plugin, extension or rule hosts where the listener set is only known at runtime and plugins are loaded and unloaded while the application runs.
Test and simulation harnesses: a test subscribes to the hub, drives one publisher and asserts on the published events without wiring up the real consumers.
Cross-cutting instrumentation and audit: metrics, tracing, logging and audit collectors receive events from many components through one hub rather than being called from each component.
Long-running services broadcasting rare state changes (configuration reload, presence change, feature-flag flip) to every interested subsystem exactly once per change.
Micro-frontend communication: independent web apps in one page communicating via a shared event bus with typed event maps and cross-tab synchronization (BroadcastChannel bridge).
IoT sensor aggregation: many sensor streams funnelled through one hub for filtering, transformation and fan-out to display or downstream processing services.
CQRS command/event pipeline: commands are dispatched to handlers that publish domain events through a bus; read-model projectors subscribe to build consistent query views.
Redux/Flux-style frontend state updates where UI components subscribe to dispatched actions rather than mutating shared state directly.
Event storm prevention harness: wrapping a batch save operation in a scoped subscriber-disable guard so that handlers triggered by the save do not re-publish events that would cascade back through the same handler.
Transactional outbox companion: publishing domain events through the hub after a transaction commits, ensuring that state changes and event emission are not separated by a process crash (in-process equivalent of the outbox pattern).
Java in-JVM decoupling with Guava EventBus: objects register via @Subscribe-annotated methods and publishers post typed events that the bus routes by parameter type (superclasses and interfaces included), with unmatched events wrapped as DeadEvent for a second-chance subscriber.
Spring application-context event pipeline: beans publish through ApplicationEventPublisher and react via @EventListener methods - in-process domain-event fan-out with the ApplicationEventMulticaster owning the registry, no message broker involved.
Vue 2 cross-component communication through a shared root instance used as a global bus ($on/$emit); Vue 3 removed that instance-emitter API, making external typed emitters like mitt, provide/inject, or a store (Pinia) the supported replacement - a cautionary real-world case for untyped global buses.

name: table-data-gateway
document:
table-data-gateway
table gateway
Confine every SQL statement that touches one table or view inside a single gateway object whose methods take and return plain record structures, so that no other code contains SQL for that table and rows cross the boundary as data rather than as domain objects.
Access to one table is spread across the codebase: SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE fragments are copied into every caller, nobody can say which queries a schema change will break, DBAs cannot find the SQL that needs tuning, and each caller has to know the dialect, the placeholders and the column order. The desired boundary is a single object that mediates all access to the whole table while the individual rows remain records (tuples, structs, hashes, DataRows) instead of becoming mapped objects.
Relational persistence where the database is a stable, schema-first integration point and SQL-level control matters (indexes, hints, bulk loads, vendor features), where the team deliberately does not want O/R mapping machinery in the domain layer, and where the domain logic is simple enough that rows may travel as records - CRUD and query services, reporting/read models, ETL writers, local SQLite stores, or a legacy database mediated for several applications. It is also the packaging decision for 'the SQL has to live somewhere well known' before a DAO, repository or query object is justified.
A service or CRUD application over a handful of tables where every screen maps to a few statements per table and an ORM would add more machinery than it removes.
Reporting and read models: read-only gateways over views or wide tables that return records directly to a formatter, export or BI job.
Legacy databases mediated for several applications: one gateway library per database becomes the documented API and the place where vendor quirks are hidden.
Embedded/local storage (SQLite, SQLCipher) in a desktop or mobile app, where one gateway per table keeps SQL out of the UI and can be tested with an in-memory database.
Batch and ETL writers that need explicit control over statement batching, cursors and transaction size - control that generated mappers hide.
Gradual refactoring of SQL scattered through transaction scripts: the first step is to move each table's statements into a gateway, after which a Data Mapper or repository can be introduced deliberately.
Test fixtures and seeders that must write through the same statements as production code rather than through a second, divergent SQL path.
Generated gateways in Go: sqlc compiles a schema plus a file of named queries into one struct per table and one type-safe method per SQL statement, with the caller holding the database handle and opening transactions - the gateway's invariants are then enforced by the generator and compiler rather than by convention.
Local SQLite storage on Android: each Room @Dao is a gateway over one table - the SQL lives in @Query-annotated methods validated at compile time, rows travel as plain entity data classes, and @Transaction or database-level transactions keep atomic multi-DAO boundaries in the caller.
Java teams that want the gateway structure without hand-writing it: jOOQ's code generator emits one DAO class per table or view (findAll, findById, generated fetchByColumn methods) that reads and writes Record/POJO rows and borrows the caller's Configuration, so the per-table SQL surface is regenerated when the schema changes.

name: dependency-injection
document:
dependency-injection
di
constructor injection
setter injection
interface injection
ioc container
pure di
manual di
Supply an object with the collaborators it needs from the outside — through its constructor, its setters/properties, or a dedicated injection interface — so it never constructs or looks a dependency up itself and every wiring decision is made once, in a composition root or container.
An object that creates its own collaborators hard-wires a concrete class, a construction recipe and often a lifetime into itself: swapping the implementation for a test double, a second deployment or a new platform means editing the class, and the dependency graph stays invisible in the API. The recurring trigger is exactly the catalog's rule: an object should not create what it depends on — the caller, the framework or the composition root decides, and hands the dependency in.
Applies whenever a component's collaborators are chosen per deployment, per environment or per test, whenever constructing them is expensive or platform-specific, and whenever a framework owns object creation (request handlers, scheduled jobs, UI screens, message consumers). It matters most in large object graphs where one abstraction has several implementations and lifetimes must be managed (singleton, request-scoped, transient); it is unnecessary when the collaborators are pure values or when construction is a private detail nobody needs to vary.
Web and API backends whose handlers need repositories, clocks, mailers and caches that must be replaced by fakes in tests and by sandbox services in staging.
Hexagonal and clean architectures where the domain declares ports (interfaces) and the infrastructure layer supplies adapters at the composition root.
Frameworks that own object creation — request handlers, scheduled jobs, UI controllers, message consumers — where the framework's injector is the only practical wiring point.
Deployment variants (on-prem vs cloud, SQL vs in-memory, real vs stub payment gateway) selected per environment through binding configuration rather than conditional code.
Plugin and extension systems where the concrete implementation is chosen at start-up from a plugin registry, enabling third-party adapters without touching core code.
Expensive shared resources whose lifetime must be managed centrally (connection pools, HTTP clients, circuit breakers) while service classes stay stateless.
Unit tests that construct the class under test directly with test doubles, and integration tests that swap only the outer layer's bindings.
Microservices with sidecar containers: the sidecar provides logging, tracing and retry policies as injected collaborators, keeping the service logic untouched.
Cloud-native applications where the composition root is the only place that knows whether a dependency resolves locally, across a service mesh, or via a remote gRPC call.
Multi-tenant SaaS where tenant-specific adapters (tenant-scoped repositories, per-tenant feature flags) are bound at the composition root and switched by middleware.
Event-driven systems where message handlers receive their dependencies through injection, making the handler logic identical between in-process and distributed deployment.
AOT-compiled applications (Native AOT, Blazor WebAssembly, serverless) where runtime reflection is unavailable — dependencies are resolved via source generators or manually at the composition root.
Functional codebases using effect systems (ZIO, fp-ts, Reader monad) where the DI container is replaced by typed environments passed through function compositions.
Consumer-driven contract testing (Pact, OpenAPI pact) where DI swaps provider implementations with contract-mock stubs at the boundary, enabling parallel service development without shared integration environments.
Resilience and fault-injection testing: proxies or decorator-based fault injectors (e.g., Gremlin SDK, WireMock) are injected as collaborators to validate retry, timeout and circuit-breaker behaviour under simulated failure conditions.
Single-page application frameworks with DI built into the component tree: Angular resolves components, directives and services through hierarchical injectors, scoping providers to the application root, a component subtree or a route so features override implementations and lazy-load without global registration.
Android apps using Dagger (and Hilt over it) to build the object graph at compile time — generated, reflection-free code, bindings and cycles checked at build time, with field injection reserved for framework-created entry points like Activities and Fragments.
Python web APIs (FastAPI) where each path operation declares Depends(callable) parameters: the framework resolves nested dependency graphs with per-request caching and uses yield-based dependencies to open and close connections around each request.

name: composed-method
document:
composed-method
compose method
Divide the work into methods that each perform one identifiable task, written as a short outline of invocations in which every operation sits at the same level of abstraction, so a reader grasps the task top-down and every change lands on one small, named step.
A method accumulates several concerns at once: high-level policy ('validate the order, then charge it') interleaved with low-level detail (a loop index, a string concatenation, a counter), so the method grows long, needs comments to mark its sections, and changes for more than one reason. Readers must simulate the whole body to learn what it does, duplication hides inside similar-looking blocks, and anyone who must change one decision - a subclass in particular - ends up copying the method and editing it.
Applies wherever code is decomposed into named routines and is read far more often than written: long-lived domain and application code, code review and onboarding, framework base classes that must expose override hooks, and code whose steps carry contracts worth testing separately. It is a source-level discipline rather than a runtime structure, so a language needs only routines and some notion of non-public helpers; it matters most exactly where methods have grown past the point a reader can hold them in mind.
Long methods built up over time whose sections are marked by comments: each comment becomes a step name and the method becomes an outline.
A method with several responsibilities (validate, compute, persist) that must change independently and be reviewed one concern at a time.
Framework or library base classes that must offer override points: each step becomes a documented extension point, usually combined with Template Method or NVI.
Top-down design of an algorithm: write the outline first, with steps as not-yet-implemented calls, and fill them in one at a time.
Bottom-up refactoring when the same block appears in several methods: extract it as a named step and call it from each outline.
Making behaviour testable in isolation: steps with their own contracts (parsing input, rounding money, validating rules) become separately testable units.
TDD workflow: write the test for the composed method outline first, asserting each step in sequence, then implement each step as a separate testable unit.
Complex business rules that combine multiple conditional branches: decompose each branch condition and its body into a clearly named step, making the rule engine visible and auditable.
Command or handler objects that orchestrate a multi-step process (validate request, authorize caller, execute operation, emit event, log outcome): each phase is a named step in the composed method.
Production Rails code: Basecamp's Event::Relaying#relay_now reads as an outline of named steps (relay_to_or_revoke_from_timeline, relay_to_webhooks_later), each descending into its own relayer class - the 'fractal' consistency of composed methods in a shipped product, documented by 37signals.
Acceptance and integration test suites: each scenario is written as a composed method at a single level of abstraction (sign_in, create_todo, mark_complete), delegating the mechanics to named helpers or page objects so the test tells the user-level story.
JUnit 4's refactored internals: Beck documents TestCase together with the RunAfter, ExpectException and FailedTest method objects as chained composed outlines, each invocation staying at one level of abstraction (his 'Nested Method Object' evolution of the pattern).

name: single-table-inheritance
document:
single-table-inheritance
table per hierarchy
discriminator column mapping
Map an inheritance hierarchy of classes onto one shared table whose columns are the union of all classes' fields, using a type code (discriminator) column to decide which class each row instantiates, so polymorphic reads need no joins.
A class hierarchy must be persisted, the hierarchy is small and its classes share most fields, and cross-class queries or polymorphic loads are frequent: mapping each class to its own table would force a join per level on almost every read, while the subtypes differ by only a few columns.
Object-relational mapping of a small, shallow, stable class hierarchy whose subclasses are mostly variations on shared state - domain-model inheritance (Employee/Engineer/Manager), payment or content types - where the storage layer is chosen by the team and the persistence framework can be taught the type code (JPA/EF Core/ActiveRecord/SQLAlchemy/most ORMs make this their default strategy) or the mapping is written by hand over SQL.
Small stable hierarchies where subclasses share most state: Employee/Engineer/Manager, Payment/CardPayment/WirePayment, Notification/EmailNotification/PushNotification.
Content or asset models with a handful of similar types (Photo/Question/Post, Blog/RssBlog) distinguished by a type code, where cross-type queries and listings are the dominant read.
Legacy or third-party schemas that already hold a hierarchy in one table with a kind column and must be mapped onto domain classes without restructuring the database.
Reporting and analytics over a hierarchy where one wide table with a type column beats joining four tables for every subtype question.
ORM-default configurations: teams that pick the framework's default hierarchy mapping (JPA SINGLE_TABLE, EF Core TPH) because join avoidance and mapping simplicity outweigh column honesty for their hierarchy size.
Rails Active Record single-table inheritance: ActiveRecord::Inheritance stores the subclass name in the table's type column by default (Company/Firm/Client all live in companies with type = 'Firm'), so fetching via the base class returns correctly-typed objects - GitLab runs a production monolith on this mechanism and maintains a written policy on when STI must not be used.
EF Core's default table-per-hierarchy mapping: a Blog/RssBlog hierarchy shares one table, the discriminator's name, CLR type and per-class values are set with HasDiscriminator/HasValue, and EF Core automatically adds the discriminator predicate to derived-type queries (throwing on unmapped discriminator values).
SQLAlchemy declarative polymorphic mappers: the base class declares polymorphic_on = 'type' in __mapper_args__ and each subclass a unique polymorphic_identity, so one person table answers polymorphic queries for Person/Employee rows without joins.

name: adapter
document:
adapter
wrapper
adaptor
Present an existing component through the exact target contract its client already consumes, translating calls, results and boundary semantics without adding responsibilities or pretending a missing capability exists.
An existing or foreign component has useful behaviour but speaks a different protocol: method names and signatures, data shapes, units, lifecycle, error model or sync/async contract do not satisfy the target. If every caller performs ad hoc conversion, semantics drift, vendor types leak and provider replacement becomes a cross-cutting rewrite; changing the adaptee or target may be impossible or too disruptive.
Integration work where one side is outside your control: legacy modules, vendor SDKs, generated clients, foreign data formats or units, and the ports-and-adapters boundary of a hexagonal architecture. Applies in statically typed languages - where an adapter class is also the compile-time proof that the required interface is satisfied - and in structurally or dynamically typed ones, where a thin wrapper usually replaces a declared target interface.
Wrapping a third-party or vendor SDK behind your own interface so business code never imports vendor types.
Modernising a legacy module incrementally: new code talks to the target interface while the old component is adapted in place.
Supporting several interchangeable providers (payments, storage, messaging, analytics) through one internal contract, with one adapter each.
Adapting a callback- or error-first API to promises/async or to an observer-style interface.
Ports-and-adapters boundaries where one domain port is realized over different transports (HTTP, message queue, in-process fake).
Unifying differently shaped data sources (row sets, DTOs, XML or JSON payloads) into one model before they reach domain logic.
Test doubles: an in-memory adapter satisfies the target interface without the real infrastructure.
API wrapper libraries: normalising third-party REST/gRPC APIs (Stripe, Twilio, payment providers) into a stable internal contract so business logic never imports vendor SDK types.
Legacy system integration: wrapping SOAP, CORBA, or mainframe APIs behind a modern interface, enabling incremental migration without rewriting existing clients.
Cloud provider abstraction: a single internal storage or queue interface implemented by AWS, GCP, or Azure adapters, letting the application swap providers via configuration.
ETL pipelines: adapting heterogeneous source record schemas (CSV, JSON, XML, database rows) into one canonical domain record, isolating format changes from downstream consumers.
Event-stream and streaming adapters: translating WebSocket frames or server-sent events into domain events in real time.
Multi-cloud and provider-agnostic interfaces: storage adapters (S3, GCS, Azure Blob), queue adapters (SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka), and notification adapters that abstract away provider-specific SDKs.
Backend for Frontend (BFF): each front-end client (web, mobile, third-party) gets its own lightweight adapter that shapes internal service responses into the exact payload that client needs.
Java's java.io.InputStreamReader is a byte-to-character bridge: it presents an InputStream through the Reader contract while decoding with an explicit charset.
SLF4J uses providers such as slf4j-reload4j to bind one Logger API to different backends, while log4j-over-slf4j and jul-to-slf4j redirect legacy APIs at a migration boundary; Spring MVC's HandlerAdapter similarly lets DispatcherServlet handle heterogeneous handler types through one SPI.
Go's net/http.HandlerFunc gives an ordinary func(ResponseWriter, *Request) the http.Handler contract by attaching ServeHTTP, so routing and middleware can consume functions and handlers uniformly.

name: separation-of-duties
document:
separation-of-duties
separation of privilege
four-eyes principle
Require two or more distinct principals or components to complete a sensitive operation, so that no single account, role or object can initiate and finish it alone.
A sensitive workflow is reachable end to end from one identity or one code path: the same operator creates and approves the payment, the same administrator changes the production configuration and signs it off, the same service account holds both the maker and the checker permission. The trigger is structural rather than accidental - all steps share one principal, one session, one process or one role, because splitting them costs a second pair of hands - and the failure surfaces only when an insider error or abuse is unremarkable in the audit trail: every step was authorized, because one principal held both halves of the duty.
Sensitive operations whose consequences must survive mistakes, coercion or misuse by authorized insiders: payments and disbursements, entitlement and permission changes, production configuration and deployment, key custody and signing, destructive data operations. It applies where identities can be kept distinct and authenticated (separate accounts, roles, services, processes), where the intermediate states of the operation can be persisted and observed, and where an enforcement point exists that can compare the acting principal with the recorded initiator - a policy engine, method security, an approval service, a separate process or account, a dual-control key ceremony. It is as much an organizational rule as a technical one: the split must follow the duties people actually hold, and recombination must be made awkward by design rather than merely discouraged.
Maker-checker payments: an operator above a threshold creates a disbursement and a second operator releases it; the ledger records both identities and refuses a release signed by the maker.
Change control and deployment: production IAM policy or infrastructure changes require a second administrator's approval, and the pipeline refuses to run a change approved by its own author (required reviewers / second signature).
Key custody and dual control: signing keys or root credentials are split so two authorized operators must each contribute a share (split knowledge, m-of-n threshold, dual-control key ceremony) and no single share can sign.
Access provisioning: the requester of an entitlement, its approver and the administrator who grants it are three distinct roles; the administrator cannot approve their own request, and access-control administrators do not administer the audit log.
Destructive data operations: schema migrations, production data edits and deletion jobs are prepared by one engineer and executed by a different operator account that cannot author the change.
Regulated back-office workflows: journal entries, refunds, credit adjustments and account closures are initiated by one clerk and posted by another, with the pairing recorded for audit.
GitHub protected branches: a pull request targeting a protected branch needs the configured number of approving reviews before it can merge, the platform refuses an approval from the PR author by design, and with dismiss-stale-review enabled a commit pushed after the review voids the approval - four-eyes enforced at the merge gate with the approval bound to the reviewed revision.
AWS Systems Manager Change Manager: a change request may run its Automation runbook only after approvals from named IAM users, groups or roles arrive across up to five approval levels, and a single rejection stops execution; because change templates list approvers separately from requesters, a request submitted under one IAM principal is released by another.
HashiCorp Vault key custody: vault operator init splits the root key with Shamir's Secret Sharing into key shares (default 5) under a threshold (default 3); unsealing or generating a root token needs a quorum of distinct share holders, and PGP-encrypting each share for a named operator makes dual control a property of the mechanism rather than of the procedure.

name: poison-pill
document:
poison-pill
sentinel message
end-of-stream marker
Terminate queue consumers cooperatively by sending a reserved sentinel message that each consumer recognises as "no more work", so consumers drain the backlog and exit without a separate control channel or forced cancellation.
A producer-consumer system must shut down, but its consumers block on an empty queue and the queue has no built-in "no more items" signal: callers either kill the workers mid-work and drop buffered items, or leave them blocked forever. Production has ended - how do the consumers learn that while still processing everything already queued?
In-process or broker-mediated producer-consumer systems with a FIFO work queue, a fixed set of long-lived consumers (threads, coroutines, actors) that block when the queue is empty, and a shutdown requirement that work already accepted by the queue be drained before the consumers exit - typically deployment, signal handling or test teardown.
Signal-driven shutdown of an in-process worker pool: the SIGTERM handler stops accepting work, then enqueues one pill per worker so the backlog is processed before the process exits.
Batch importers and ETL stages whose consumers block on a work queue and must finish the current batch before a run is considered complete.
Test harnesses and simulations: an explicit stop message makes thread-based systems deterministic to shut down, without sleeps or guessed timeouts.
Actor systems: a reserved stop message (for example Akka PoisonPill) terminates an actor after the messages already queued for it have been handled.
Log and event writers where the last records must reach the sink before consumers release their buffers and files.
Bounded-queue stages in a pipeline: pills travel the same backpressured channel as work, so upstream cannot keep producing after the stop decision.
Kubernetes pod shutdown: containers receive SIGTERM, workers stop pulling from the job queue, drain in-flight tasks, then exit within the terminationGracePeriodSeconds window.
Redis/Bull queue workers: a shutdown signal pushes a sentinel via BLPOP so workers exit cleanly without losing the right to process pending tasks.
Akka Streams and similar streaming frameworks: the GraphStage signals completion via onPull/downstream cancellation, which is the materialised equivalent of a poison pill.
Redis Streams consumer groups: XREADGROUP with block timeout naturally returns when the stream is empty; a special ID (e.g. ">") polling loop plus a shared shutdown flag replaces the in-process sentinel.
Broker-level poison message isolation: in Kafka, RabbitMQ, or Azure Service Bus, a permanently failing message (deserialisation error, validation failure) blocks a partition/consumer indefinitely; DLQ-based routing (publish to dead-letter topic after N retries, then commit offset and continue) is the broker-level analogue that prevents one poison message from halting the entire pipeline.
Kubernetes preStop hooks + pill drain: a container's lifecycle preStop hook can enqueue a sentinel into an in-process work queue while the orchestrator grants terminationGracePeriodSeconds for the drain to complete, ensuring zero work-drop during rolling updates.
Azure Service Bus competing-consumers workers: when a worker receives a shutdown notification it completes its current PeekLock message, then calls Abandon on any held locks before unregistering; Azure Service Bus dead-letter queues handle the poison-message variant when a message exceeds MaxDeliveryCount and cannot be delivered.
Akka hierarchical actor trees: sending PoisonPill to a parent actor stops it after all queued messages ahead of the pill are processed, and automatically sends stop messages to all children in bottom-up order; this is the idiomatic way to orchestrate ordered multi-actor shutdown.
Non-blocking retry architectures (RabbitMQ): rather than local Thread.sleep retries that block the consumer thread, use server-side TTL queues with Dead Letter Exchange routing to implement exponential backoff, keeping the consumer responsive to new messages and to shutdown pills.
Java's JDK BlockingQueue worker pools: because BlockingQueue has no built-in close, producers can enqueue a unique end-of-stream object after all work; each consumer takes until that sentinel and then the coordinator joins workers.
Python multiprocessing worker pools: multiprocessing.Queue/JoinableQueue supports FIFO task delivery with sentinel values and join-based drain tracking; send one sentinel per worker and join them after the queue is exhausted.
Akka Classic actors: PoisonPill is enqueued in the mailbox and processed after already queued messages, while Akka Typed requires an explicit Stop/Shutdown protocol; choose the API that matches the actor model.

name: either
document:
either
Either monad
disjoint union
Encode the two outcomes of a fallible operation - a value-carrying success (Right/Ok) and a reason-carrying failure (Left/Err) - in one sum-type value, so a caller must destructure both branches before going further and failures cannot escape as exceptions, sentinel values or undocumented convention.
An operation can fail in ways the caller must handle, but the failure channel is invisible in the signature: exceptions unwind past intermediate callers, where they get swallowed or merely logged, status codes and sentinels are silently ignored, and the reason for failure is flattened into a message string nobody can branch on.
Expected, recoverable failures in code that has to compose: parsing and validation at a boundary, persistence and I/O calls, service calls inside a pipeline, or any layer whose caller must render, translate, retry or count the failure. It pays off where the error type is part of an API contract between teams or modules, and where the language can express a two-case type (algebraic data type, sealed hierarchy, discriminated union) or a library supplies one.
Validating untrusted input at a boundary and returning the concrete reason (field, offset, rule violated) so the caller can render a precise message.
Domain operations that can fail for several business reasons (insufficient funds, account closed, limit exceeded) where callers must branch on the reason instead of guessing from a string.
Parsing and decoding (config, documents, wire formats) where the failure position or cause must travel back with the outcome.
Pipelines of fallible steps (authenticate -> load -> transform -> persist) that should stop at the first failure with the original reason intact instead of unwinding with a stack trace.
Translate-once boundaries: turn transport errors into domain errors in one adapter, so no layer above has to know about HTTP codes, IOExceptions or database error numbers.
Accumulating validation of independent fields, where every reason must be reported together rather than only the first one — use an Applicative validation instance with a Semigroup-based error accumulator.
Callbacks and async APIs whose failure cannot be thrown to the caller (completion handlers, event consumers) and therefore has to be delivered as a value.
Parallel fallible operations where you want to collect all successes and all failures separately before deciding, using partition or sequence operations on a List<Result>.
Domain-driven design aggregates where a root entity operation can fail for many reasons (invariant violations, business rule breaches) and the aggregate root returns Either to the application layer.
Service-to-service calls inside a pipeline where the downstream service returns a structured error response (not an exception), and the upstream must branch, translate, or propagate it.
Rust standard-library convention: fallible I/O, parsing and system calls return Result<T, E> and ? propagates the first Err up the call chain to a boundary (a main or entry point that returns Result) - the backbone of recoverable error handling in Rust.
Kotlin/Arrow typed-error pipelines: an either { } computation DSL where bind() short-circuits on Left and Either.catch turns a throwing interop call into a Left at the adapter boundary.
Java services using Vavr's right-biased Either: map/flatMap chains propagate Left without checked exceptions, keeping the failure type part of the signature in fluent pipelines.

name: consumer-driven-contract-test
document:
consumer-driven-contract-test
consumer-driven contract
contract test
Capture, from each consumer's own tests, the concrete provider interactions that consumer depends on, and verify the provider against that contract inside the provider's own build, so consumer and provider can be released independently without a shared end-to-end environment.
Independently released consumers and providers must keep working together, yet the only reliable check is a shared end-to-end environment per pair - slow, brittle and usually out of date; at the same time the provider cannot see which parts of its API each consumer actually exercises, so every refactoring is a guess about who will break.
HTTP/request-reply, messaging and gRPC integrations where consumer and provider are owned by different teams on different release cadences and each consumer uses only a narrow slice of the provider's surface. It assumes the provider team is willing to run verification of consumer contracts in its own build; without that half, the consumer test is only a better mock.
Microservice landscapes where a front end, a mobile app or another service consumes an API released by a different team on its own schedule.
A provider team that must refactor or replace internals and needs to know, before merging, which consumer expectations it is about to break.
Mobile or desktop clients that cannot be deployed in lockstep with the backend, so each client's expectations must hold against every backend version.
Event- and message-based integrations (Kafka, SQS, SNS, RabbitMQ) where the consumer processes messages produced by another team; contracts pin the message body shape and metadata (topic, headers, content-type) while abstracting the transport.
Migration or strangler-fig work, where a replacement provider must be proven compatible with the existing consumers before traffic is moved.
Using the contract as the source of stubs for development and integration environments, so those environments no longer need the real provider.
BFF (Backend for Frontend) patterns where each frontend channel (web, mobile, third-party) has its own contract with a shared backend, allowing independent evolution of each BFF without cross-channel breakage.
Multi-team Kafka event streaming where consumers (downstream services) define which topics, partitions and message schemas they depend on, so producers can evolve events without silently breaking subscribers; Pact message pacts handle both JSON and Schema Registry messages (with magic bytes for Avro/Protobuf over Schema Registry).
gRPC service integrations where protocol buffer message shapes are exercised by the actual consumer client code, pinning the wire format, service method signatures and metadata the consumer actually calls; synchronous message pacts cover the request-response pairing.
Breaking up a monolith: individual microservices are extracted and their CDC contracts verify that the new service boundaries behave identically to the original module interfaces before traffic is migrated.
Schema Registry integrations (Confluent, AWS Glue) where consumers pin compatible message schemas and producers must not publish breaking schemas without migrating all dependent consumers first.
Third-party or vendor API integrations where the consumer team cannot rely on the provider to run verification: the consumer-side mock-only workflow with published contracts documents expectations even without provider participation.
Webhook and callback integrations where a provider calls a consumer-defined endpoint; CDC captures the consumer's expected payload shape, headers and authentication, and the provider verifies it can deliver to that shape.
Contract migration at scale: when a provider must migrate from v1 to v2 of an API, CDC with pending/wip pacts allows the provider to signal new expectations to consumers without blocking either side's pipeline while migration is in progress.
Spring Cloud Contract in JVM/Spring landscapes: the consumer's contract change lands in the producer's repository (or an external contract repo), the producer build generates verification tests from the contract DSL, and the consumer develops against StubRunner-served WireMock stubs pulled from an artifact repository (Nexus/Artifactory) - the contract is the single artifact both sides build from.
Nubank replaced its flaky shared-environment end-to-end suite with consumer-driven contract tests to regain deploy velocity - the public account of the pattern paying off as an e2e-substitute at a single organisation rather than as an addition to it.
Large polyglot estates such as JSTOR/ITHAKA (300+ microservices, 12+ teams, Pact) and M1 Finance (Pact plus PactFlow rolled out to 17 teams in under six months): the broker's compatibility matrix replaces per-pair end-to-end environments as the release gate.

name: deadline-propagation
document:
deadline-propagation
timeout propagation
Bound the total time and work of a logical request by carrying one deadline through its whole call tree: every hop forwards the remaining budget and the cancellation signal instead of inventing a fresh timeout, so work that can no longer succeed is abandoned at every level.
A request fans out into a chain or tree of downstream calls and each hop applies its own timeout: the end-to-end latency budget becomes the sum of N independent timeouts, servers keep working after the originating client has given up, and cancellation never reaches the deeper work - resources are consumed producing answers nobody will read.
Networked request handling with multi-hop calls: RPC and HTTP chains, service meshes, gateways, fan-out and hedged requests. It applies when one latency budget is meaningful for the whole logical request (an SLO or a user-facing timeout), when the hops are under your control and can carry request-scoped state (context, token, signal, call option or header), and when downstream work is cancellable or can be interrupted at checkpoints.
Microservice request chains (gateway -> frontend service -> several backends) under one user-facing latency SLO, where each hop converts the inbound deadline into its own outgoing calls.
gRPC services whose clients set a deadline and whose servers propagate it as a remaining timeout to downstream calls while cancelling server-side work once the deadline passes.
Fan-out and aggregation endpoints calling several backends in parallel: every sub-call shares the parent budget, and sub-calls still running when it expires are cancelled instead of awaited.
Hedged requests: the first replica to answer wins, and the duplicate requests are cancelled through the same carrier so their downstream work is stopped too.
Streaming and long-poll endpoints that must stop processing when the client disconnects or the connection times out, propagating that stop to services and storage.
Batch or pipeline steps with a per-request time budget that must check the remaining time before each stage and abandon a request that can no longer be finished in time.
ROS 2 / DDS-based robotics pipelines: autonomous vehicle perception pipelines where sensor data must traverse a chain of processing nodes (detect -> classify -> plan -> act) and missed deadlines invalidate downstream results entirely.
Distributed real-time databases with multi-hop queries (gateway -> shard router -> storage node -> index node) where each hop's latency budget is derived from a user-facing SLA.
Service mesh sidecar configurations (Istio/Linkerd/Envoy) where per-route timeout policies propagate deadline context to application code via headers like grpc-timeout or custom X-Request-Deadline headers.
Industrial IoT and edge computing pipelines (edge gateway -> fieldbus bridge -> PLC -> sensor) where end-to-end control loop deadlines must be enforced across heterogeneous network boundaries.
GraphQL federation: a federated query hitting multiple subgraphs in parallel must bound the total resolution time and cancel subgraph requests whose partial results can no longer affect the final response.
Go services on the standard library context package: context.WithDeadline and WithTimeout derive a child whose Done channel closes at the earliest of its own deadline, an explicit cancel, or the parent's cancellation, so cancelling the root request context tears down the whole goroutine tree, and WithDeadlineCause/WithTimeoutCause attach an explicit cause for attribution.
Envoy router filter in service meshes: Envoy sets x-envoy-expected-rq-timeout-ms on internal requests - derived from x-envoy-upstream-rq-timeout-ms or the route timeout - so upstream services can read the expected total completion time and exit early instead of finishing work the proxy has already timed out.
ASP.NET Core gRPC services map the inbound call's deadline onto the handler's CancellationToken; passing that token to database queries, HttpClient calls and Task.Delay stops server-side work the moment the client's deadline expires.

name: abstract-factory
document:
abstract-factory
kit
factory of factories
Expose one creation contract for each product kind in a coherent family, letting clients switch the selected family at the composition root without naming concrete products or mixing incompatible variants.
A client must construct several related products that collaborate as a matched set, but direct construction spreads family keys and concrete class names through the code. Adding a family then becomes configuration branches plus constructor edits, while mixing products from different families can fail only after incompatible objects interact.
Use in object- or interface-based subsystems with two independent axes of change: product kinds (button, slider, connection, command) and product families or variants (dark/light, PostgreSQL/Oracle, AWS/GCP). The family is normally selected once at a composition root, products from one family are intended to collaborate, and clients must compile, test and ship without knowing concrete product types; if products are intentionally mixed or only one kind is created, use a smaller creator instead.
Cross-platform or themable UI toolkits: Qt's QStyleFactory resolves keys such as "windows" and "fusion" to built-in or plugin QStyle implementations that govern a coherent widget look-and-feel; a fuller abstract factory applies the same family key across several product interfaces.
Provider-independent database code: ADO.NET's DbProviderFactory/DbProviderFactories create a matched DbConnection, DbCommand, DbParameter and DbDataAdapter set for a selected provider such as SQL Server or OLE DB.
Parser-provider plugins: JAXP's DocumentBuilderFactory and SAXParserFactory hide implementation classes behind standard factory APIs, allowing the composition root to select a provider while client code uses parser abstractions.
Java's ServiceLoader documentation uses a CodecFactory service with getEncoder and getDecoder operations; the selected provider supplies a coherent codec family while clients depend only on the service interface.
Test infrastructure: an in-memory factory family whose products are fakes, injected in place of the production family so integration tests need no network.
Game and simulation engines: per-biome object families (terrain, props, audio) that must stay aesthetically consistent when a level is loaded.
SaaS multi-tenant applications: per-tenant theme factories so every rendered page uses the tenant's brand colours, fonts and spacing without per-request conditionals.
Document-format parsers: factory per format (PDF, HTML, EPUB) producing matched tokenizer, layout engine and renderer so a viewer can switch formats from a single configuration key.

name: repository
document:
repository
collection-oriented repository
repository layer
Mediates between the domain model and the data mapping layer with a collection-like interface, so domain code adds, removes and finds persistent objects as if they lived in memory and never constructs queries or touches persistence APIs itself.
Persistence code spreads: every application service re-derives the same SQL or ORM queries, duplicate query logic drifts apart, table and column names leak into domain decisions, and testing domain rules without a database becomes impossible. Callers should be able to think in collections of domain objects instead of queries.
Applies to systems with a non-trivial domain model sitting on a data-mapping layer (Data Mapper, metadata mapping, or a hand-written mapper) where the same queries recur across application services; it becomes more valuable as domain classes and query volume grow. It is the standard persistence boundary of DDD aggregates (one repository per aggregate root) and presumes a unit of work or session that owns flush and commit. It is not a per-table data-access wrapper and not a replacement for transaction control.
DDD application services that must load an aggregate root, run domain logic on it and store it again without knowing the table layout.
Data-mapper backends where several application services and background jobs share recurring complex queries (overdue invoices, pending orders, open tickets).
Applications that must be unit-testable away from the database: repositories are the substitution point for in-memory doubles.
Systems that must support more than one store behind a stable domain interface — relational in production, in-memory in tests, a document store for a particular deployment.
Uniform cross-cutting access policy for an aggregate: caching, read-replica routing, audit logging or authorization applied as decorators around one interface.
Migration work where the persistence technology changes (ORM swap, schema split, service extraction) while the domain model and its tests stay untouched.
CQRS write-side aggregate loading where the aggregate must be reconstructed fully to apply business rules and enforce invariants.
Integration with heterogeneous data sources where one repository unifies access to a cache, primary database and a third-party API behind a domain interface.
Spring Data JPA applications can use Repository/CrudRepository for aggregate-typed CRUD, paging and derived queries, then add only domain-specific methods rather than wrapping every persistence operation.
The .NET eShopOnContainers ordering microservice uses an EF Core BuyerRepository over a shared scoped DbContext/unit of work, while CQRS/Dapper handles presentation reads.
Python applications using SQLAlchemy ORM can place an aggregate-facing repository over Session, whose identity map and unit-of-work flush semantics provide the mapper/session boundary.

name: audit-interceptor
document:
audit-interceptor
audit trail interceptor
audit logging interceptor
Declare an audit policy at an invocation seam that records the actor, action, target, correlation id and both attempt and terminal outcome around a delegated operation, then sends the structured event to a dedicated integrity-protected sink, so security accountability is consistent without inline logging in every service.
Security-relevant operations (privileged actions, state changes and access to sensitive data) must be attributable, but inline logging misses denied and failed attempts, varies in schema, can leak raw arguments and disappears with a rolled-back transaction. Teams also need to cover components they cannot modify without pretending that a proxy sees calls that bypass it.
Business or service tiers whose sensitive operations pass through an interceptable seam: container-managed beans, proxied service objects, ORM entity lifecycles, message endpoints or an HTTP pipeline. Audit selection must be declarative and uniform, while the sink has its own integrity and retention requirements (Secure Logger); the design must make mediation gaps, redaction, transaction coupling, failure policy, clock source and correlation propagation explicit.
Business-tier auditing of money-moving or otherwise regulated operations (fund transfer, order placement, claim submission): who requested it, on which object, when, and whether it succeeded.
Privileged administration surfaces (role changes, key rotation, configuration changes) where every sensitive operation must leave a record naming the acting principal.
Authentication and authorization outcomes: successful and failed logins, access-denial decisions and lockouts routed into the same audit pipeline instead of ad-hoc log lines.
Access-to-sensitive-data events (who read which patient/customer record) recorded at the gateway or service boundary to satisfy data-protection obligations.
Retrofitting auditing onto legacy components whose code cannot be modified, by wrapping the service object or binding an interceptor to its interface.
Middleware-level auditing of message endpoints and database calls in a business tier, correlating the caller's subject with the operation performed.
Financial API request interception (Spring Boot global request interceptors) capturing who accessed which endpoint, with what payload, and what outcome — satisfying SOX financial reporting controls.
Entity-level change tracking via ORM subscribers (e.g., EF Core SaveChangesInterceptor, TypeORM subscribers): automatically diff old vs. new property values on create/update/delete and emit audit envelopes without manual logging calls.
API gateway-level audit logging: capture every external API call with timestamp, user identity, endpoint, method, and outcome, correlating across microservices via X-Request-ID / traceparent headers.
Compliance reporting automation: generate audit-ready reports for SOX (~7-year retention), HIPAA (~6-year retention), GDPR (data residency-aware), and PCI-DSS from structured interceptor events.
Zero-trust data access trails: record every read of sensitive fields (PHI, PII, financial data) so data-protection obligations (GDPR Article 5 data minimization, HIPAA access logging) are demonstrably met.
Hibernate Envers: @Audited entity lifecycle changes create per-entity _AUD revisions at transaction commit; a custom revision entity/listener can attach actor or request metadata.
Django admin: django.contrib.admin.models.LogEntry records action time, user, object, addition/change/deletion and change_message for ModelAdmin activity.
Rails Audited: the audited ActiveRecord extension creates audit rows for model create, update and destroy callbacks, including changed attributes and optional acting-user attribution.

name: quantity
document:
quantity
units of measure
dimensioned value
Represent a dimensioned measurement as one value that carries its amount together with its unit, so that conversion, comparison, unit-compatible arithmetic and amount-plus-unit input/output all have a single owner and incompatible units cannot be combined by accident.
Measurements are stored as bare numbers whose unit lives only in a variable name, a column comment or the reader's memory: the same physical quantity appears in metres in one place and in feet in another, conversion factors are retyped at every call site, adding two numbers of different dimensions compiles (or runs) happily, and parsing and formatting '3 km' is reinvented per feature. The recurring trigger is that an amount and its unit always change together and are one conceptual whole, so leaving them as two unconnected things makes the unit rules impossible to own.
Value-scope code in domain, engineering or integration layers that handles physical quantities - length, mass, time, temperature, energy, data volume, concentration. It pays off when values arrive with heterogeneous units (sensors, imports, user input, third parties), when derived quantities such as speed or density are computed, when users select a unit system for display, and when values must survive persistence and transport. The language decides how much of the guarantee is compile-time (units as type parameters, phantom/branded types) and how much is a runtime value object backed by a conversion table or unit registry.
Sensor and telemetry pipelines where readings arrive tagged with a unit and must be normalised to a canonical unit before aggregation, alerting or storage.
Engineering and simulation code (CAD, robotics, structural, electrical) that computes derived quantities such as velocity, torque or energy and must keep the dimensions consistent.
Logistics and commerce where weight, dimensions and rate limits are expressed in different unit systems (kg/lb, cm/in, m^3/ft^3) and are displayed in the customer's chosen system.
Healthcare and laboratory systems that exchange doses and results between systems (mg/kg, mmol/L) with reference ranges in different units.
Energy and utility metering, where consumption (kWh, m^3) is billed through unit-price arithmetic and readings must be comparable across meter types.
UI-level unit-system switching: store and compute in one canonical unit, render and edit in metric or imperial according to a user preference.
Scientific Python applications built on Pint's UnitRegistry, such as sensor and laboratory pipelines, where quantities are parsed, converted and reduced dimensionally at integration boundaries.
.NET engineering and telemetry services using UnitsNet's strongly typed Length, Mass and related quantities, with parsing, conversion, serialization and display-unit selection centralized in the library.
Compile-time dimensional-analysis code using F# units of measure or C++ Boost.Units for simulation and control loops, where invalid unit arithmetic is rejected before runtime and derived units are expressed algebraically.
