name: range
document:
range
interval
Represent a span of values as a single interval value whose bound inclusivity and open ends are explicit, so containment and interval-to-interval comparisons live in one place instead of repeated ad-hoc endpoint tests.
Start and end travel together through the code but every caller re-derives what they mean: containment is written as scattered <= / < comparisons that drift apart, "unbounded" is smuggled in as a sentinel value (Long.MAX_VALUE, 9999-12-31), and interval-to-interval questions - do these two overlap, does one enclose the other, what is the gap between them - have no home at all.
Applies wherever a domain concept is a span rather than a point: validity and effectivity periods, booking and availability windows, quantity or price tiers, measurement buckets, version and address ranges, pagination windows, and query parameters such as a date range. It pays off when the same interval is compared repeatedly or crosses a boundary (persistence, API payloads, UI widgets), because the bound convention then has to be written once instead of re-decided per call site. For a single comparison between two local variables the type is pure overhead.
Validity and effectivity windows: a contract, price or membership is valid over [effectiveFrom, effectiveTo), and every check is a membership test against one interval.
Booking and availability: a room, seat or resource is reserved during an interval; overlap (not adjacency) decides whether a new booking is possible, and back-to-back bookings must be allowed deliberately.
Quantity and price tiers: the unit price depends on the quantity interval ([1,10), [10,50), [50, +inf)), so a container of intervals with containment lookup replaces a cascade of if-statements.
Temporal queries and reporting: "last 7 days", "this quarter", "since the migration" are half-open or open-ended intervals passed to repositories and rendered by date-range pickers.
Version, port and address ranges: a compatibility claim covers [1.2, 2.0) of a library, a firewall rule covers a port interval - containment answers "is this covered?" and intersection answers "do these rules conflict?".
Pagination and slicing windows: a page is an interval over a sequence, and half-open semantics make adjacency exact ([0,20) followed by [20,40)),
PostgreSQL range and multirange columns: PostgreSQL's daterange, tsrange and numeric range types make lower-inclusive/upper-exclusive bounds, overlap and containment operators, and indexed range queries part of the persistence contract; choose the bound convention before mapping domain intervals.
Guava Range: Java's Guava Range models convex bounded or unbounded intervals with nine open/closed forms, isConnected and intersection; use ContiguousSet only when a discrete domain really requires enumeration rather than treating the interval itself as a sequence.
Standard-library and container choices: Rust's std::ops::RangeBounds covers included, excluded and unbounded bounds when its range forms fit; for many intervals requiring join/split policies, Boost ICL's interval_set and interval_map supply the container semantics instead of overloading one Range value.

name: composite-entity
document:
composite-entity
coarse-grained-entity
Represent a cluster of related, dependent objects through one coarse-grained entity that owns them and persists and synchronises the whole graph as a single unit of work, so clients never reference, sequence, or save the parts themselves. Coined for coarse-grained EJB business objects; its modern form is the aggregate root with cascading or owned mappings.
A business concept clients treat as one thing (an order with its lines, a customer with addresses) is really a cluster of dependent objects, and persisting each part separately forces callers to know the parts, save them in the right order in the right transaction, delete the ones that left the relationship, and absorb a leaking physical schema. The catalog trigger: a cluster of related objects must persist and synchronise as one unit.
Relational or document stores where a coarse-grained business object is composed of finer-grained dependent objects whose lifecycle is bound to it. Applies when clients - especially remote ones - should exchange one coarse-grained structure instead of the parts, when the persist/synchronise boundary must coincide with one transaction, and when each dependent can still own its own mapping. Modern form: an aggregate root mapped with cascading associations or with components stored in the root's own row.
Order with line items, shipment addresses and payment allocations that must be written and deleted as one business unit.
Customer or account aggregate holding addresses, contact methods and preferences that are edited in one form and saved once.
Document-style clusters (invoice with revisions, article with embedded sections) where the parts only exist inside the root.
Legacy-style coarse-grained entity beans that wrap fine-grained POJOs so that clients exchange one composite transfer object instead of many fine-grained ones.
Mobile or remote clients that must send one coarse-grained payload per edit instead of a sequence of dependent calls.
Batch imports where a cluster is validated and written transactionally, so a partially imported entity never exists.
DDD Bounded Contexts where one aggregate encapsulates a complete business invariant enforced across multiple related entities — e.g., a Rental aggregate containing a rental agreement, reserved vehicle, and driver assignment that must all be created or fail together.
CQRS write models where the aggregate is the sole write target and all state changes flow through the root's command methods, ensuring every mutation is a coherent cluster-level operation.
Event sourcing snapshots where the aggregate root serialises its entire graph so that snapshot restore reconstructs the full composite in one operation rather than re-playing individual dependent events.
Legacy system facades that wrap a network of fine-grained remote beans behind a single coarse-grained composite interface, collapsing many remote calls into one round-trip for external clients.
SQLAlchemy parent-child clusters mapped with cascade='all, delete-orphan' on relationship(): disassociating a child deletes the row, so the Session flushes the cluster as one unit without per-child Session.delete() calls.
EF Core owned types: dependent types stored in the owner's table (or as owned navigations) share the aggregate root's identity and save with a single context.SaveChanges().
Mongoose subdocument arrays: embedded parts are saved, validated and removed through the top-level document, so the cluster's lifecycle is bound to the root document's save.

name: mock
document:
mock
mock object
Replace a collaborator of the system under test with a test-specific object that is programmed with the expected calls and verifies them as they happen, so the interaction itself - not the resulting state - is what the test asserts.
The expected interaction sequence is the behaviour under test: the outcome of the exercised method is not visible in the system under test's own state, and no observation point exposes the indirect outputs (the messages sent to collaborators) that the requirement is about. State-based assertions cannot reach them, so the test either reaches into the collaborator's internals - duplicating the collaboration logic - or asserts nothing at all.
Unit and component tests of an object whose collaboration protocol is the specification: exact calls, arguments, cardinality or order matter (handshakes, publish-once, audit logging, cache invalidation) and the collaborator is slow, unavailable, non-deterministic or side-effecting. It requires a substitutable dependency (dependency injection or lookup) and, for framework-based realizations, an interception mechanism - dynamic proxy, bytecode agent, generated code or macro. Typical in mockist, interaction-first TDD and in need-driven development.
Verifying that a component emits exactly the expected messages to a collaborator whose effects are otherwise invisible: an audit logger, notifier, event publisher or payment gateway.
Pinning an interaction protocol whose ordering and cardinality are the requirement - open before send, publish exactly once, flush before close - in tests of clients and adapters.
Simulating failure paths of a remote collaborator (timeout, exception, malformed response) to assert that the SUT surfaces or recovers from them deterministically.
Unit-testing a domain service against repository, clock, or gateway interfaces when the real implementations are slow, licensed or unavailable in the development environment.
Driving interface design from the outside in: write the expectation for the call the SUT should make, then let the implementation satisfy it (mockist TDD).
Verifying that a main operation triggers its side effects - cache invalidation, metrics emission, compensating call - with the required arguments.
In C++ tests built with GoogleTest gMock, using EXPECT_CALL matchers, Times cardinalities and InSequence ordering verifies an outbound collaborator protocol before the SUT runs.
In Java tests using Mockito, verify and InOrder assert required interactions with a dependency while keeping the interaction contract separate from the dependency's implementation.
In Python's unittest.mock, assert_called_once_with and assert_has_calls verify argument, cardinality and sequence requirements for calls made through a replaceable collaborator.

name: recursive-descent-parser
document:
recursive-descent-parser
recursive descent
recursive descent parsing
Parse a small grammar by translating every rule directly into a function that consumes the tokens the rule matches and calls the functions of the rules it references, so the parser's control flow is the grammar itself and stays readable, debuggable and free of a code-generation step.
A hand-written parser is the only option - no generator in the toolchain, or the grammar is a small DSL - yet the grammar is not a flat token sequence: alternatives must be chosen from lookahead, repetition must become a loop, and the natural grammar for expressions is left-recursive, which a top-down parser cannot translate directly. Without a disciplined mapping from rules to functions the parser degenerates into ad-hoc index arithmetic and exception-driven backtracking, and errors end up without positions.
Front ends for small languages, DSLs, query/filter/rule grammars, configuration and protocol formats, and the parsing layer of compilers and interpreters that want no code-generation step. It applies when a lexer or token stream already exists (or is cheap to write), the grammar is small to medium and reasonably LL-friendly or rewritable into LL form, and the team values readable, step-debuggable, position-precise parsing over generated tables.
Front ends for small languages, DSLs and configuration formats (filter expressions, rule engines, policy languages, template syntaxes) where a generator and its build integration would be overkill.
Expression and statement parsing in single-pass compilers and interpreters that emit bytecode or IR while parsing, as in Crafting Interpreters' Lox.
Tooling for a grammar you own - formatters, linters, syntax highlighters, language servers - where error tolerance, multiple diagnostics and exact positions matter more than raw throughput.
Protocol and wire-format decoding with a small fixed grammar, where errors must carry byte offsets and malformed input must be rejected deterministically.
Context-dependent or indentation-sensitive syntaxes (templates with interpolation, layout-based blocks, configuration with embedded expressions) that a generated lexer handles poorly.
Codebases that must not carry generated code: security-reviewed, vendored or cross-compiled projects where an ordinary source file beats a build-time generator.
Clang's C-family front end uses a unified hand-built recursive-descent parser for C, C++, Objective-C and Objective-C++, pairing rule-oriented control flow with production-quality diagnostics.
The Go standard library's go/parser is a production recursive-descent parser for Go source, with explicit parser state, nesting-depth guards and error recovery.
rustc_parse is the Rust compiler's recursive-descent parser module, showing how a hand-written parser can scale to macros, recovery modes and detailed token/state handling.
Lua's reference implementation compiles with lparser.c, a single-pass recursive-descent parser that emits bytecode opcodes while reducing expressions instead of building a syntax tree, with precedence handled by parsing levels.

name: bulkhead
document:
bulkhead
bulkhead isolation
cell-based architecture
Partition finite shared capacity at the failure domain (dependency, tenant, priority class, or cell) into independently bounded pools or permits, with an explicit queue and saturation policy, so one slow, saturated, or failing participant cannot consume capacity reserved for others.
Several dependencies or tenants share thread, connection, worker, or permit pools. When one becomes slow, leaky, or overloaded, its calls hold shared slots and fill shared queues, so unrelated work queues and fails behind it; the design needs a boundary that contains resource exhaustion without pretending to isolate CPU, network, or server-side limits that remain shared.
Any component whose concurrency is a finite resource: a service calling multiple downstream APIs, a multi-tenant workload, a job runner mixing interactive and batch work, or an inference and gateway tier with per-deployment quotas. The failure mode to contain is degradation and overload (slow dependency, connection leak, traffic spike), not only hard failure, and the isolation boundary must be chosen at the failure domain - instance, dependency, tenant or priority class.
A service that calls several downstream APIs through one shared HTTP client: give each downstream its own connection and thread budget so one hanging endpoint cannot block the others.
Multi-tenant SaaS where one tenant's workload must not consume the concurrency available to other tenants (per-tenant pools).
Interactive request traffic sharing a database with batch or report jobs: separate pools per workload class keep the database from serialising everything behind the batch.
An API gateway or backend-for-frontend routing to many backends with per-route concurrency caps, so a slow backend does not consume the proxy's shared capacity.
Job workers that mix latency-critical and background queues: per-queue worker pools prevent a backlog of background jobs from starving urgent work.
Inference and AI serving where each model deployment has its own concurrency quota and a saturated model must not consume the shared request capacity.
Cell-based architectures: each cell (complete, independent service instance) is a bulkhead partition; load grows by adding cells, and a failure is contained to the single cell — used at AWS, Google, and Netflix scale.
Shuffle sharding: Amazon Route 53-style virtual shard assignment where each tenant is assigned to a random shard of two or more cells; with eight cells and two-per-shard there are 28 unique shards, so a problem affects only 1/28th of tenants — far better than regular per-cell partitioning.
AI and inference workloads: per-deployment or per-tenant Azure OpenAI or LLM deployment quotas prevent one saturated model from consuming the shared request capacity across the platform.
Database RU isolation: Azure Cosmos DB request-unit throughput assigned per container acts as a storage-layer bulkhead; one noisy container cannot exhaust the RU budget of others.
Resilience4j's SemaphoreBulkhead and FixedThreadPoolBulkhead give a JVM service per-dependency permits versus a bounded queue and worker pool; choose based on whether caller threads may be occupied.
Netflix Hystrix's per-command thread pools or semaphore isolation reject work and route it to fallback, containing a slow downstream to its command boundary (historical and deprecated).
.NET services use Polly's BulkheadPolicy/AsyncBulkheadPolicy (maxParallelization plus maxQueuingActions, rejecting with BulkheadRejectedException when both are full); Polly v8 replaced it with ConcurrencyLimiter over System.Threading.RateLimiting, whose partitioned per-key limiters give per-tenant bulkheads.
Service meshes enforce bulkheads at the platform layer: an Istio DestinationRule's trafficPolicy.connectionPool caps tcp.maxConnections, http.http1MaxPendingRequests and http.http2MaxRequests per upstream host, enforced by Envoy alongside its circuit-breaking limits.
Netflix's concurrency-limits library replaces hand-tuned static partitions with per-dependency adaptive limits (Vegas and Gradient algorithms modelled on TCP congestion control) that shrink the concurrency budget automatically as downstream latency rises, e.g. separating live from batch traffic on one gRPC server.
Envoy maintains per-upstream-cluster connection pools and circuit-breaking limits, while Kubernetes ResourceQuota caps aggregate namespace CPU, memory, or object use; both are platform-level capacity partitions rather than application call-site wrappers.

name: spatial-partition
document:
spatial-partition
spatial index
bucket grid
Store every object in a structure indexed by its position so that neighbourhood queries visit only the objects near a point or region instead of scanning the whole population.
Queries that ask 'what is near this position?' - collision checks, proximity and aggro radii, culling, spatial analytics - repeatedly scan every object: each query is linear in the population and a whole simulation step becomes quadratic, even though every object interacts only with the few objects next to it.
Per-object runtime systems and simulations - game worlds, crowd and particle solvers, location services, robotics - where objects are mobile, spread over space, and the queries are local (radius, region, k-nearest). The pattern applies once the population is large enough that a full scan dominates the frame or the request budget, and it requires a position-to-cell mapping and an update discipline that match how the objects move.
Game worlds: collision, proximity and aggro checks between many moving entities each tick (bullets versus enemies, pickups, area effects).
Physics broadphase: pruning candidate pairs before narrow-phase tests where colliders move constantly.
Map and GIS services: 'all points within radius' and viewport queries over millions of features.
Crowd, flocking and particle simulations: neighbours within a radius for boids or social forces instead of all-pairs tests.
Spatial analytics and robotics: k-nearest or region queries over vehicles, sensors and delivery points, and occupancy grids for pathfinding.
Physics engines: Box2D's broadphase is a dynamic AABB tree (b2DynamicTree) whose fattened leaf boxes absorb small moves before reinsertion, and whose region queries and ray casts prune candidates before narrow-phase tests.
Location services: Redis geospatial indexes store members as 52-bit geohash scores in a sorted set (GEOADD) so GEOSEARCH answers circle and bounding-box proximity queries server-side instead of scanning members.
GIS and analytics databases: PostGIS prunes radius queries through a GiST spatial index (the index-aware ST_DWithin predicate checks bounding boxes before computing exact distances), and scikit-learn backs radius and k-nearest neighbour queries with KDTree and BallTree instead of all-pairs distances.

name: applicative
document:
applicative
applicative functor
applicative style
idiom (original McBride-Paterson name)
Apply one pure function to several independent effectful computations, letting the chosen context instance fix the semantics of absence, failure, ordering, and concurrency; the combining structure is fixed before execution - that static shape is what enables batching, parallel scheduling, and static analysis - and an accumulating error instance reports every independent failure instead of short-circuiting on the first.
You have several independent computations - parse this field, fetch that record, validate this quantity - and a pure function that combines their results, but each result lives inside a context such as Option, Either/Result, List, Promise/Task, or Validation. A bind/await chain can imply a dependency that does not exist, serialize work, or stop at the first failure; you need a fixed applicative structure that combines the values while leaving failure and scheduling policy to the chosen instance.
Value- or effect-level functional code where independent combination is the recurring decision: form and request validation that must report every field error at once, parallel-capable fetch coordination, configuration or tuple assembly from independent parses, and parser/stream composition. Applies when the language offers a context type (or validator abstraction) and the team accepts a small abstraction - a type class in Scala/Kotlin, a stdlib combinator such as Promise.all, or a hand-written lift2 - to express 'apply a pure function to several effectful arguments'. Applicative structure permits parallel execution but does not itself guarantee scheduling, cancellation, or error accumulation.
Form, request or configuration validation where every field is checked independently and the user must see all violations in one response.
Combining independent parses of a record (age, e-mail, quantity, date range) into one constructed value, reporting every malformed field.
Parallel IO combination: fetching several unrelated resources (Promise.all, CompletableFuture.thenCombine, parZipOrAccumulate, errgroup fan-out) and pairing the results positionally.
Parser and stream combinators where several parsers/subscribers consume the same input independently and their results are combined into a node.
Building a read model or report from several independent queries where a failure of one part should be reported without cancelling the others.
Statistics/diagnostics: computing several independent measurements of the same input and combining them with a pure summary function.
DSLs and embedded languages: building an abstract syntax tree of applicative operations (Free Applicative) that can be statically analyzed, optimized, or pretty-printed before interpretation - enabling query planning, dead code elimination, or validation of DSL constraints at construction time.
Traversable data structures: threading an Applicative effect through a container (tree, list, optional) so each element can be independently validated, transformed, or fetched without sequential coupling.
Collecting monoidal summaries: using Const as the Applicative to fold a Traversable structure into a single Monoid value (e.g., collecting all validation errors, or computing a checksum) without materializing a transformed structure.
API gateway aggregation: combining multiple downstream service calls where each call is independent and all results (or all errors) should be collected before returning a response to the caller.
Configuration loading at startup: validating all config fields independently and reporting every misconfiguration at once rather than failing on the first missing key.
CSV or batch row validation: validating each row independently and accumulating all row-level errors so the entire batch can be rejected with a full error report rather than failing on the first bad row.
Bidirectional codec composition: building parsers and serializers (e.g., with prismatic/schema, io-ts, or hkj's ValidatedPrism) where the parse direction is accumulating and fallible but the build direction is total, preserving the parse-don't-validate discipline applicatively.
GraphQL API input validation: validate independent arguments and return all field-level errors in one response instead of rejecting at the first failure.
Kubernetes or Helm configuration loading: validate independent keys and report the complete set of startup misconfigurations before deployment.
CI/CD pipeline policy checks: run independent static checks over a change and aggregate diagnostics before gating the build.
Haxl at Meta/Facebook: an applicative Fetch whose <*> explores both operands before blocking, so independent dataFetch calls to the same data source batch into one request and run concurrently without explicit forking ("There is no Fork", ICFP 2014).
Swift structured concurrency: async let starts each independent task as a child task immediately and a later await combines the results into a tuple or constructor call - applicative-shaped combination of a fixed set of independent effects in mainstream syntax, with cancellation and lifetime bounded by the enclosing scope.
Elm JSON decoders: Json.Decode map2..map8 (or elm-json-decode-pipeline's required/custom steps) assemble a record from independent per-field decoders - the production form of mapN in front-end code.

name: thread-safe-copy-on-write
document:
thread-safe-copy-on-write
Share one body between many threads so that copying a value stays cheap and reading it never blocks, and protect the sharing state itself - the reference count or the published pointer - so that a writer clones the body and swaps in a new snapshot instead of mutating storage other threads can see.
A value is copied often and mutated rarely, so the copies should share storage until one of them diverges. That decision works single-threaded, but the moment several threads hold the value the sharing state becomes shared mutable state in its own right: a reference count incremented without atomics loses updates or frees a body another thread is still reading, a plain pointer dereferenced while another thread replaces it is a data race, and a 'copy' that still aliases its source turns a reader's snapshot into a moving target. The trigger is a read-mostly shared value - configuration, routing table, registry, cache snapshot - that must be read without locking and updated by cloning.
Applies where one object, or one immutable snapshot of an aggregate, is read by many threads and written rarely: configuration reloads, registries and symbol tables, caches with rare invalidation, listener registries, and large immutable values handed between threads. Manual memory management, non-atomic reference counts or a separate publication step make the problem sharpest (C, C++, hand-rolled counting); garbage-collected languages apply the same structure with the published reference replacing the count. It is an object/value-level data-sharing decision, not a lock strategy for write-heavy state.
Read-mostly configuration or routing tables that are reloaded occasionally and read on every request by every worker thread.
Registries, symbol tables and interning tables built once and consulted constantly, with rare additions or invalidations.
Caches and memo tables where invalidation is rare and readers must never wait behind a writer.
Listener and observer registries traversed on every event and modified rarely - the classic CopyOnWriteArrayList use.
Large immutable values - strings, byte buffers, message payloads, compiled artefacts - handed between threads, where a deep copy at each hand-off would dominate.
Language runtimes, interpreters and plugin hosts that keep configuration or environment objects read by many threads and updated by a single owner.
The Linux kernel's RCU (read-copy-update) mechanism in its purest form: readers enter an rcu_read_lock() critical section with no lock, atomic or shared-memory write, updaters publish a replacement with rcu_assign_pointer(), and the superseded body is freed only after a grace period proves no reader can still hold it - the dentry cache, routing tables and network-device lists.
Rust's std::sync::Arc as the atomically counted body of the standard library: cloning an Arc increments the count, and Arc::make_mut detaches - cloning the inner value only when other Arc handles exist - so the sharing state is protected by the type rather than by convention.
Go services publishing an immutable configuration or routing snapshot through sync/atomic's atomic.Pointer[T]: readers Load it once per request without locking, writers build a fresh snapshot under a writer lock and Store or Swap the pointer, and the collector reclaims each superseded snapshot when no reader references it.

name: row-data-gateway
document:
row-data-gateway
row data gateway
row gateway
Give each database row its own in-memory object that mirrors the row's columns and carries the row's own find, insert, update and delete operations, so all data-access code for a table lives in one place instead of being duplicated across the scripts that use it.
SQL text, parameter binding and result-set mapping are re-derived inside every transaction script that touches a table, while the in-memory objects those scripts work with know nothing about the database. No single place knows how one row is read, written and deleted, so a schema change ripples through every script and every new query is another chance to get parameterisation and type conversion wrong.
Applies when business logic is organised as transaction scripts or thin services over a relational schema whose columns map closely to the fields actually used: the gateway mirrors the table structure, no object/relational impedance mismatch is being managed, and identity maps, units of work and lazy loading are either unnecessary or added deliberately as separate patterns. It also fits generated persistence layers, where the gateway classes are produced from schema metadata during the build.
Transaction-script applications (order entry, billing runs, batch imports) where several scripts need the same handful of row-level reads and writes.
CRUD-heavy back-office and admin tooling where a screen edits one row at a time and columns map one-to-one onto form fields.
Legacy or externally owned schemas that must be mirrored rather than reshaped: one gateway per table gives an explicit, reviewable seam between the application and someone else's database.
Generated persistence layers: gateways produced from schema metadata on every build, so the tedious class-per-table work is automated and stays in sync with the schema.
Simple mappings inside an otherwise rich domain model, where a domain object keeps a gateway as its data holder instead of copying field values around.
Reporting and fixture utilities that need reusable, parameterised finders for one table without pulling in a full object/relational mapper.
Laminas\Db\RowGateway and RowGatewayFeature (the official laminas-db implementation) expose one row object with save/delete and can materialize table-query results as row gateways, fitting CRUD screens or transaction scripts that edit individual records.
Zend Framework 1's Zend_Db_Table_Row is a documented legacy row-gateway implementation: table queries return row objects with column access plus save/delete/createRow operations, useful when a simple schema is consumed by row-oriented scripts.
The Go dgw tool generates structs and lightweight Table/Row Data Gateway functions from PostgreSQL metadata, demonstrating the pattern as a code-generation choice when a project wants typed CRUD without a full ORM.

name: attorney-client
document:
attorney-client
attorney pattern
attorney-client friendship idiom
Grant a named collaborator a deliberately narrow compile-time view of a class's private interface by making an attorney the client's sole friend; the attorney forwards selected operations or re-exports selected private nested types (often through controlled public typedefs), while unrelated private members and the public contract remain closed.
A C++ collaborator may need one private hook, constructor, iterator adapter or nested implementation type, but a friend class receives every private and protected member. Making the hook public leaks it to every caller; publishing a std::list<T>::iterator or the container type leaks representation and its invalidation contract; pImpl hides representation from everyone but does not grant one collaborator a typed privileged view. The missing mechanism is a small attorney contract that names exactly the operations or nested types this collaborator may use without turning the private interface into a second public API.
Object-oriented code whose encapsulation boundary is a class and whose language offers class- or scope-level access control but no per-collaborator grant - C++ with friend declarations, Java/C#/Kotlin with package, assembly or module access, and their test- and library-extension scenarios. It applies at object scope, where one type owns the implementation and one named collaborator needs a slice of it, and it is a source-level structuring device checked by the compiler, never a runtime protection mechanism.
White-box test access: a test harness reaches one private hook or state view through a named attorney instead of making the member public or redefining private with a test-only preprocessor switch.
Iterator adapters: Boost.Iterator's iterator_core_access is a canonical gateway class a user-defined iterator befriends, so iterator_facade and its operators reach private dereference/increment/advance core functions while those implementation hooks stay out of the iterator's public API.
Serialization: Boost.Serialization has serializable classes befriend boost::serialization::access, whose gateway reaches the private serialize() member so archives can reconstruct state without a public serialization method.
Private nested type exposure: LLVM's SchedulerInternalsAttorney publishes the selected nested Scheduler::BndlSchedState as a public type alias and supplies narrow static accessors for unit tests, without publishing every Scheduler private type.
A pImpl-backed adapter that must inspect one implementation-owned type: keep the public class opaque and put the attorney definition in the adapter or test header, so the privileged component gets a typed view without making the implementation part of the ordinary public contract.
Iterator facade over a hidden list-like representation: expose a stable nested iterator/view type through an attorney rather than publishing std::list<T>::iterator, so the owner can replace the container without promising its node and invalidation details to every caller.
Private virtual hooks: an attorney forwards one private virtual operation through a base reference, allowing the derived override to run even though friendship is not inherited.
Factory or construction control: a builder reaches one private constructor or initialization hook through an attorney, while unrelated callers still cannot construct an object through that path.
Spacecraft flight software (fsfw): LocalDpManagerAttorney keeps fetchPoolEntry and getMutexHandle as private static forwarders and befriends only LocalPoolVariable and LocalPoolVector, so the local data pool manager opens its internals to two named collaborators instead of every class that might befriend it.
Simulator tree traversal (Sandia Sparta Modeling Framework): sparta::TreeNodePrivateAttorney exposes TreeNode's private child vectors and subtrees through static accessors (getAllChildren, getChild, findChildren) for internal Reports and Pipeout processing, with a documented 'should NOT be used by simulation developers' restriction in place of an enforceable caller limit.

name: remote-facade
document:
remote-facade
coarse-grained facade
Provide a single coarse-grained facade over a web of fine-grained objects so that a remote client can complete a unit of work in one round trip, while the fine-grained objects keep their local-only interfaces and the facade stays free of domain logic.
An object model tuned for in-process use has small objects with small methods and heavy interaction. Across a process boundary every one of those interactions becomes a marshalling, security and routing event, so one user action turns into dozens of remote calls; the decision is whether, and at which seam, to replace that chatty protocol with a few coarse operations.
Applies at any distribution boundary - a network hop, a service-mesh sidecar or merely a second process on the same host - where a fine-grained object model or service layer must be made remotely usable. It matters most when the interaction pattern is chatty (many small reads and writes per use case), when the model must not be exposed to remote clients, and when the transport is expensive relative to the work being done.
Enterprise application whose rich domain model is consumed by a thick client, another service or a batch job: the service layer gets a coarse remote interface instead of exposing entities and value objects.
Microservice boundary where a use case (place an order, update a shipment) must be a single call while the fine-grained aggregates stay internal to the service.
Legacy integration: a coarse adapter facade over an old object model so that new clients never see the legacy structure and the old model can be refactored behind it.
Mobile or high-latency clients, where every avoided round trip directly improves perceived latency and battery cost.
Batch and offline clients that need bulk operations (fetch a set, submit a set) instead of per-item calls.
Security boundary: one authenticated, authorised and audited entry point in front of the model.
Salesforce Composite API and Composite Graph API: a client submits related record operations, reference IDs and explicit all-or-none/graph boundaries in one request instead of making a remote call per sObject.
Microsoft Graph JSON batching: a `$batch` request groups up to 20 Graph operations behind one HTTP boundary while dependencies and per-request failures remain visible to the caller.
gRPC services such as the official RouteGuide example: generated stubs expose typed unary or streaming RPCs as the remote contract while the server's fine-grained implementation stays local.

name: table-data-gateway
document:
table-data-gateway
table gateway
Confine every SQL statement that touches one table or view inside a single gateway object whose methods take and return plain record structures, so that no other code contains SQL for that table and rows cross the boundary as data rather than as domain objects.
Access to one table is spread across the codebase: SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE fragments are copied into every caller, nobody can say which queries a schema change will break, DBAs cannot find the SQL that needs tuning, and each caller has to know the dialect, the placeholders and the column order. The desired boundary is a single object that mediates all access to the whole table while the individual rows remain records (tuples, structs, hashes, DataRows) instead of becoming mapped objects.
Relational persistence where the database is a stable, schema-first integration point and SQL-level control matters (indexes, hints, bulk loads, vendor features), where the team deliberately does not want O/R mapping machinery in the domain layer, and where the domain logic is simple enough that rows may travel as records - CRUD and query services, reporting/read models, ETL writers, local SQLite stores, or a legacy database mediated for several applications. It is also the packaging decision for 'the SQL has to live somewhere well known' before a DAO, repository or query object is justified.
A service or CRUD application over a handful of tables where every screen maps to a few statements per table and an ORM would add more machinery than it removes.
Reporting and read models: read-only gateways over views or wide tables that return records directly to a formatter, export or BI job.
Legacy databases mediated for several applications: one gateway library per database becomes the documented API and the place where vendor quirks are hidden.
Embedded/local storage (SQLite, SQLCipher) in a desktop or mobile app, where one gateway per table keeps SQL out of the UI and can be tested with an in-memory database.
Batch and ETL writers that need explicit control over statement batching, cursors and transaction size - control that generated mappers hide.
Gradual refactoring of SQL scattered through transaction scripts: the first step is to move each table's statements into a gateway, after which a Data Mapper or repository can be introduced deliberately.
Test fixtures and seeders that must write through the same statements as production code rather than through a second, divergent SQL path.
Generated gateways in Go: sqlc compiles a schema plus a file of named queries into one struct per table and one type-safe method per SQL statement, with the caller holding the database handle and opening transactions - the gateway's invariants are then enforced by the generator and compiler rather than by convention.
Local SQLite storage on Android: each Room @Dao is a gateway over one table - the SQL lives in @Query-annotated methods validated at compile time, rows travel as plain entity data classes, and @Transaction or database-level transactions keep atomic multi-DAO boundaries in the caller.
Java teams that want the gateway structure without hand-writing it: jOOQ's code generator emits one DAO class per table or view (findAll, findById, generated fetchByColumn methods) that reads and writes Record/POJO rows and borrows the caller's Configuration, so the per-table SQL surface is regenerated when the schema changes.

name: identity-map
document:
identity-map
first-level cache
session cache
Guarantee that within one session every database row is represented by exactly one in-memory object, by keeping a keyed registry of loaded objects that every load consults before hitting the database.
Two code paths in the same session load the same row into two different objects: updates through one are invisible to the other, the last flush silently wins, and every load pays the remote-call cost again. The catalog states the invariant as: the same row must never be two different in-memory objects in one session.
Object-oriented persistence (data mappers, repositories, unit of work) where entities carry a stable database identity (an Identity Field) and several parts of one business transaction or request refer to the same rows. Applies whenever duplicate in-memory instances would break graph consistency or lose updates - typically inside an ORM session or a hand-written persistence context whose lifetime bounds staleness.
ORM sessions in web request handling (JPA EntityManager, EF Core DbContext, SQLAlchemy Session, MikroORM EntityManager) where several services touch the same entities in one request.
Batch import and synchronisation jobs that re-read the same rows repeatedly inside one transaction and must not operate on divergent copies.
Object graph reconstruction in data mappers, where cycles and shared references need one in-memory instance per row.
Desktop and document applications with a context-scoped object space (Core Data contexts) where objects are edited, undone and saved as one unit.
Hand-written persistence layers over plain SQL where two repositories serve the same table and must agree on identity.
CQRS command handlers where the same aggregate is loaded multiple times within one command execution — the identity map prevents duplicate instances from forming across repository calls within the same session.
Event-sourced aggregate reconstruction: replaying events to rebuild aggregate state requires the same aggregate instance to accumulate state across multiple event applications; identity map guarantees a single instance per aggregate ID per reconstruction session.
Microservices saga and choreography: within one service's unit-of-work, multiple steps may load the same entity; identity map ensures all steps operate on the same instance even when the entity is referenced across different event handlers.
DDD bounded-context integration: when one bounded context holds a reference to an entity from another context (by ID), that entity is resolved through the local identity map — multiple resolution paths must all consult the same map to stay consistent.
Testing scenarios where the same entity is accessed via multiple repository paths: identity map guarantees test assertions see the same instance regardless of which repository method returned it, enabling meaningful state verification.
Multi-tenant applications where each tenant request gets its own session/identity-map scope, preventing cross-tenant data leakage by construction — a shared/global map would allow one tenant's rows to shadow another's.
SQLAlchemy Session.get in a unit of work: repeated primary-key loads return the same Python object from the Session identity map, while the Session is deliberately not a cross-session query cache.
EF Core tracked queries and AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution: the DbContext keeps one entity instance per key for tracked results, while no-tracking identity resolution is opt-in for read models.
Hibernate Session persistence contexts: repeated loads of the same entity type and identifier resolve to the one managed instance per Session, so entity graphs and dirty checking share state.

name: guarded-suspension
document:
guarded-suspension
conditional block
suspended execution
Suspend a state-dependent method call inside the object that owns the state until another thread makes its guard predicate true, so callers neither poll nor get refused while the object is temporarily not ready.
A method may only proceed while a precondition over shared state holds - a buffer is non-empty, a pool still has a free lease, a session is authenticated, a worker has a task - and that state is produced by another thread at an unknown time. The recurring decision is what the caller should do while the guard is false: refusing the request would drop work the application still needs, forcing the transition would break the object's invariants, and polling wastes a core and still races. Guarded suspension answers it by waiting on a condition the object itself owns, and by making that wait atomic with respect to the state change that ends it.
Concurrent objects whose methods are state-dependent and whose state changes arrive from other threads: bounded buffers and handoff queues, resource pools, server request/response handoffs, readiness and shutdown gates, worker idle loops. Applicable where the runtime can efficiently park or suspend a caller (OS threads, coroutines) and where the object already owns a lock or monitor, so no notification can be lost between the predicate check and the wait. Ill-suited to single-threaded event loops, to callers that must never be delayed, and to waits whose eventual completion cannot be guaranteed.
Actor mailbox handoff: an Akka/Orleans/Swift-Actor mailbox is a lock-free guarded queue; the actor suspends on an empty mailbox and resumes when a message arrives, which is the same monitor-wait pattern expressed at the language level.
Swift async / Structured Concurrency: a Task.sleep or async let that suspends until a condition is a coroutine-level guarded suspension; the suspension point is backed by a condition variable or event channel inside the runtime.
CompletableFuture / async result: a future's blocking get() is a timed guarded suspension on the thread that submitted the asynchronous operation; the completion path (complete()) is the notifier.
Pipeline stage coordination: in a multi-stage streaming pipeline each stage blocks on input while the upstream stage processes, synchronising via a bounded channel whose put/get implement the guard.
Bounded buffers and handoff queues: a consumer's take waits while the buffer is empty and a producer's put waits while it is full (producer-consumer).
Resource pools: acquire blocks until a lease is returned to a connection, thread or object pool instead of failing or spinning when the pool is exhausted.
Server-side handoff: an acceptor or reader thread publishes a request and the worker waits for work to appear; a caller waits for the response slot to be filled.
Readiness and start-up gates: components wait until a dependency reports connected, initialised or ready, and callers wait until a session, device or circuit is open.
Shutdown and flush coordination: a terminator waits until in-flight work has drained, and a flusher waits while the buffer still holds entries (two-phase termination).
Platform queue and channel APIs: BlockingQueue.take/put, Queue#pop, Channel.receive/for-await, condition-variable waits - the same guard hidden behind a library type.
Project Loom virtual threads (JEP 444): a virtual thread calling Object.wait() parks its Continuation; the carrier thread is released for other virtual threads, so the program continues throughput while one virtual thread waits. The guarded action still re-checks the predicate on wake, and the pattern's semantics are preserved — only the threading model changes.
Akka typed actor mailbox: each actor has a single-threaded mailbox; receive() suspends the actor's continuation when the mailbox is empty, resuming when a message is dispatched. This is language-level guarded suspension where the wait set is the mailbox queue and the guard is 'mailbox non-empty'.
Kotlin coroutines rendezvous channel: Channel() (unbuffered/rendezvous) suspends the sender until a receiver is ready, and vice versa — the same lock-free handoff as an unbuffered Go channel. The suspension is a coroutine-level guarded wait on rendezvous.
Python asyncio.Condition: an async context manager that wraps an asyncio.Lock; await cond.wait() releases the lock and suspends the task until notify() is called, making it an async guarded suspension where the runtime schedules other tasks during the wait.
Go unbuffered channel send/receive: goroutine G1 executing ch <- x on an unbuffered channel sleeps (gopark) until goroutine G2 executes <-ch, at which point the runtime directly transfers the value and stack copy (rendezvous handoff). This is the language-level form of guarded suspension: the guard is 'receiver present', the wait set is the sudog queue in hchan.
Erlang/OTP process mailbox: a gen_server receiving messages from its mailbox blocks (receive...end) until a matching message arrives — the OTP process is a state machine whose transitions are guarded by message arrival, making each receive a suspension point in the actor's event loop.
.NET TaskCompletionSource<T>: GetAwaiter().GetResult() on a not-yet-completed TCS is a synchronous guarded suspension; the async continuation (ConfigureAwait, await) is an asynchronous one. SetResult() is the notifier. TCS is a one-shot asymmetric guarded suspension where one side never waits (the completor) and one side always waits (the synchronously blocked caller).
JDK ArrayBlockingQueue: the queue is one ReentrantLock plus two Condition objects, notEmpty and notFull - take() awaits notEmpty while count == 0, put() awaits notFull while the buffer is full, and each signals the other condition only after mutating count and the circular buffer inside the same critical section. It is the reference production realisation of a two-predicate guarded suspension, including the fairness switch and the timed offer/poll variants.
Go standard library: database/sql guards queries against a concurrent Close with closingMutex, which parks readers and the closing writer on two sync.Cond values (read/write), and net/http's Server.Shutdown waits until in-flight requests have drained. Both are the case Go's own guidance reserves sync.Cond for - a predicate that changes back and forth over time rather than a one-shot handoff.
HikariCP connection pool: DataSource.getConnection() suspends the caller until a lease is returned while the pool already holds maximumPoolSize connections, bounded by connectionTimeout (default 30000 ms, minimum 250 ms), after which it throws SQLException rather than waiting on - a guarded suspension in which the deadline is a documented, first-class outcome instead of an accident.

name: cancellation-token
document:
cancellation-token
cancellation signal
cooperative cancellation
Give a caller-owned operation tree a one-way request to stop: pass a read-only cancellation signal through every cancellable call, observe it at safe points, clean up what was acquired, and report a distinct cancelled outcome without pretending that cooperative cancellation is forced termination.
A request handler, background job or UI action starts work that fans out into nested calls, tasks or threads. When the caller disconnects, a deadline expires, the user presses stop or a sibling fails, merely abandoning the result leaves already-started work burning CPU, holding connections and calling dependencies. Force-killing a thread or process can interrupt a critical section and corrupt shared state, while a signal that is not propagated or observed cannot stop the call tree or make its cleanup visible to the joiner.
Use where work can outlive the caller's interest and the runtime exposes checkpoints, suspension points or interruptible waits: request-scoped servers, workers, UI tasks, stream pipelines and batch loops. The operation owns cleanup, cancellation may race any checkpoint, and the design must state what happens when a request arrives after an irreversible side effect or while a dependency ignores the signal.
Request-scoped server work: the handler gets a request signal that fires when the client disconnects or the deadline expires, cancelling in-flight database, queue and upstream calls instead of pinning worker threads and connections after the caller is gone.
UI and mobile tasks: navigating away, closing a window or pressing stop cancels the task tree that loads, renders or downloads for that view, and only that view's tokens are affected.
Graceful shutdown: a supervisor stops accepting work and cancels the token shared by worker loops; every worker stops at its next safe point, flushes and releases resources, and the process exits inside the shutdown budget.
Fan-out with short-circuit: as soon as one subtask fails, or as soon as any one result suffices (hedged or racing replicas), the scope cancels the siblings instead of waiting for all of them.
Batch and stream pipelines: a processor subscribes to the pipeline signal and stops consuming and producing when the pipeline is torn down, abandoning the current chunk when the job's deadline elapses.
Testing and tooling: inject an already-cancelled signal, or one cancelled after N iterations, to exercise the stop path without racing an actual shutdown.
HTTP client redirect and retry cancellation: when a request is redirected or a lower-level retry budget is exhausted, cancel the in-flight operation so the client can proceed with the next action without waiting for a result that is no longer relevant.
Health-check abortion: a liveness probe times out or a readiness check fails mid-flight; cancel the in-progress health metric collection so the pod can be restarted or pulled from service without waiting for a hung check.
GRPC deadline and cancellation propagation: a server receives a client deadline and cancellation token; both must be threaded through every async operation so that an expired deadline or a client disconnect promptly frees server resources.
LLM request fan-out: multiple model providers are queried in parallel; the first successful response wins and all pending requests are cancelled immediately, avoiding wasted compute on a result that will be discarded.
Database connection pool eviction: a query timeout or client disconnect cancels the in-flight query, releasing the connection back to the pool before the server's statement timeout fires; the pool's token is derived from the request context so pool eviction and request cancellation share the same stop signal.
Container orchestrator graceful shutdown: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM and waits the terminationGracePeriodSeconds; the application maps SIGTERM to a cancellation token that is shared by all in-flight request handlers, background workers and health-check loops, giving each the termination budget to drain cleanly.
Interactive search with typeahead: each keystroke cancels the previous search task and starts a new one; the token for the previous task is cancelled immediately on the next keystroke, preventing stale results from overwriting fresher ones.
File transfer with resume support: a large upload or download uses chunked transfers; cancelling the transfer sets a flag that causes the next resume attempt to verify which chunks were already received before retransmitting from scratch.
Event streaming with backpressure: a consumer reading from a message queue or Kafka partition uses the cancellation token to stop reading when the application is shutting down or the consumer group is rebalanced, committing its offset before exiting.
Machine learning inference pipeline: a batch inference job can be cancelled when a new model version is deployed or the job's priority drops; the cancellation token is checked between batches so that partial results are preserved and the job can resume without reprocessing completed chunks.
ASP.NET Core's HttpContext.RequestAborted token is passed into HttpClient, database and other long-running operations so a client disconnect or server abort releases work that can no longer contribute to the response.
Go net/http handlers propagate Request.Context through database/sql QueryContext and RPC calls; cancelling the request context closes the subtree's Done channel so backend goroutines can stop and return their resources.
Kotlin kotlinx.coroutines Job cancellation follows structured parent-child scopes, so a screen, request or worker scope can cancel its child coroutines while finally blocks release resources and CancellationException remains distinguishable from failure.
Node.js and browser fetch cancellation: AbortController.signal is passed as { signal } to fetch, EventTarget listeners and streams, so abort() tears down the socket and pending promises; AbortSignal.timeout and AbortSignal.any combine a deadline or several triggers into one signal without polling.
Database query abortion over a side channel: PostgreSQL's frontend/backend protocol sends a CancelRequest on a separate connection carrying the backend PID and secret key, letting a client that gave up - or an administrator via pg_cancel_backend - abort a running query without killing the session.
TPL/PLINQ cancellation acknowledgement: a delegate that throws OperationCanceledException carrying the supplied CancellationToken is treated by the Task Parallel Library as a cancellation acknowledgement rather than a fault, so joiners observe a cancelled task instead of an aggregated error.

name: cursor-pagination
document:
cursor-pagination
keyset pagination
cursor-based pagination
Bound what a read boundary returns for a large or changing ordered collection by sending one page plus an opaque continuation token that pins the filter and ordering, so clients advance deterministically without offsets and without watching rows move under them.
A boundary must expose a collection that is too large to return at once and keeps changing while clients read it. Offset or page-number requests make the store count or scan everything up to the requested page, and concurrent inserts or deletes shift rows across page boundaries so consumers see duplicates or miss items; the server has no way to state where the sequence should resume.
Any read boundary - an HTTP or gRPC list operation, a GraphQL connection, a database-backed feed, a batch export job - over an ordered collection that is large, growing, or read under concurrent writes, where the server can identify a unique, immutable ordering key and wants to cap both response size and per-request query cost while letting clients iterate the whole sequence.
Public REST or gRPC list endpoints over unbounded, growing tables - messages, orders, audit events - where deep offsets are slow and responses must stay small.
Infinite-scroll or load-more feeds that keep returning newer items while a user scrolls, with the already-seen pages stable against inserts.
Whole-collection sync and export jobs (warehouse loads, backups, search reindexing) that must iterate every row exactly once while writers continue.
GraphQL Relay connections where first/after, edges and pageInfo carry the continuation contract in the schema instead of the URL.
Consumers of third-party list APIs (Stripe-style starting_after/has_more, Google page_token iterators) that keep parameters fixed across auto-paginated calls.
Administrative and operational tooling that streams very large tables for verification or cleanup with bounded memory and predictable server load.
Audit log and event stream retrieval where events are append-only and chronological, and clients stream continuously without needing to revisit earlier pages.
Real-time activity feeds (social media timelines, notification streams) where inserts at the head must not disturb pages the user has already loaded.
Database replication and change-data-capture (CDC) pipelines that must consume a changelog exactly once across restarts and failures.
Paginating over search results from a vector database or full-text index where OFFSET at depth is expensive and results may change between queries.
Bi-directional data synchronization (CDC pipelines, replica lag-catching) where a consumer must iterate forward and occasionally needs to resume from a previous position or re-sweep a window — requiring stable forward cursors plus a defined backward-resumption path.
Paginating a partitioned or sharded database table where each partition is queried independently and cursors carry both the partition hint and the per-partition keyset position.
Slack Web API collection methods (users.list, conversations.history) where response_metadata.next_cursor drives the loop, page limits are clamped per method, and expired or malformed tokens surface as invalid_cursor so the client restarts from the first page.
GitHub GraphQL-style cursor connections where first/last (bounded 1-100) and pageInfo.startCursor/endCursor carry the continuation position for after/before traversal.
Timeline-style feeds served by Django REST framework's CursorPagination, whose default -created ordering gives a consistent view that does not repeat items as new rows are inserted.

name: event-aggregator
document:
event-aggregator
event bus
messenger
message bus
event hub
Funnel the events of many source objects into one hub that owns the subscription wiring, so that subscribers register once with the aggregator instead of tracking down and registering with every publisher.
Many components raise events and many components want to react: if every consumer registers directly with every producer, each consumer has to find the sources and subscribe to each event type separately, each producer accumulates knowledge of who listens, and both sides repeat the same registration and unsubscribe code at every pair. The trigger is a many-publisher / many-subscriber setting in which the wiring itself has become the maintenance problem.
In-process, event-driven software - a modular UI shell, a domain-event pipeline inside one bounded context, a plugin host, a simulation or instrumentation layer - where publishers and subscribers grow independently, both sides should stay unaware of each other, and registration plus lifetime management should live in one place. The aggregator is a component- or module-scope element of one process (one node); events that must cross a process boundary, survive a restart or be delivered reliably need a messaging channel instead.
Modular UI shells (WPF/MAUI, Android, SwiftUI) where view models living in separate modules must react to each other without holding references — the classic Prism and CommunityToolkit.Mvvm scenario.
Domain-event fan-out inside one bounded context: 'order placed' reaches billing, stock, notification and audit services that each subscribe to the hub instead of to the Order aggregate.
Plugin, extension or rule hosts where the listener set is only known at runtime and plugins are loaded and unloaded while the application runs.
Test and simulation harnesses: a test subscribes to the hub, drives one publisher and asserts on the published events without wiring up the real consumers.
Cross-cutting instrumentation and audit: metrics, tracing, logging and audit collectors receive events from many components through one hub rather than being called from each component.
Long-running services broadcasting rare state changes (configuration reload, presence change, feature-flag flip) to every interested subsystem exactly once per change.
Micro-frontend communication: independent web apps in one page communicating via a shared event bus with typed event maps and cross-tab synchronization (BroadcastChannel bridge).
IoT sensor aggregation: many sensor streams funnelled through one hub for filtering, transformation and fan-out to display or downstream processing services.
CQRS command/event pipeline: commands are dispatched to handlers that publish domain events through a bus; read-model projectors subscribe to build consistent query views.
Redux/Flux-style frontend state updates where UI components subscribe to dispatched actions rather than mutating shared state directly.
Event storm prevention harness: wrapping a batch save operation in a scoped subscriber-disable guard so that handlers triggered by the save do not re-publish events that would cascade back through the same handler.
Transactional outbox companion: publishing domain events through the hub after a transaction commits, ensuring that state changes and event emission are not separated by a process crash (in-process equivalent of the outbox pattern).
Java in-JVM decoupling with Guava EventBus: objects register via @Subscribe-annotated methods and publishers post typed events that the bus routes by parameter type (superclasses and interfaces included), with unmatched events wrapped as DeadEvent for a second-chance subscriber.
Spring application-context event pipeline: beans publish through ApplicationEventPublisher and react via @EventListener methods - in-process domain-event fan-out with the ApplicationEventMulticaster owning the registry, no message broker involved.
Vue 2 cross-component communication through a shared root instance used as a global bus ($on/$emit); Vue 3 removed that instance-emitter API, making external typed emitters like mitt, provide/inject, or a store (Pinia) the supported replacement - a cautionary real-world case for untyped global buses.

name: test-specific-subclass
document:
test-specific-subclass
test-specific extension
subclassed test double
Make an otherwise untestable class testable by defining a test-only subclass that overrides the method reaching the unusable dependency (or exposes the internal state the test needs), so the boundary can be substituted and observed without putting test hooks into production code.
A class that must be tested reaches its dependency through a call on itself - a self-call to a helper method, a field created inside the class, or a singleton/static lookup - so the test has no injection point: the collaborator cannot be replaced from outside, the indirect inputs cannot be controlled and the indirect outputs cannot be observed. Editing the production class to accept the dependency may be impossible (third-party or frozen code) or would introduce test logic into production.
Applies to legacy or third-party object-oriented code where the boundary call already sits behind an overridable (non-final, sufficiently visible) method, or can be extracted into one, and where test-only code may live next to the tests. It is a fallback for statically typed languages that need the double to stay type-compatible with a concrete class; where the code can be modified, dependency injection is the better seam.
A legacy class reads the wall clock inside a helper method (System.currentTimeMillis, DateTime.Now, Instant.now): override the helper so date/decision logic can be tested at a fixed instant.
A reporting or notification class sends mail or calls a remote API from a self-call: override that method with a canned or empty body so the unit test runs offline and deterministically.
A class reaches a database or the file system from inside its own method: override it to return an in-memory fixture instead of building the real object chain (entity-chain snipping).
Verifying the sequence and the set of steps of a template method: override the steps in a subclass and record which of them ran, in which order.
Exposing private state for state verification, or exposing a private algorithm step so it can be tested individually (state-exposing and behaviour-exposing subclasses).
Replacing a singleton or static accessor the SUT uses through a lookup with a controlled instance that is still type-compatible with the concrete class (substituted singleton).
Putting a legacy untested class under a characterization-test baseline before refactoring, while extracting the collaborator is not yet possible.
A Java class that cannot be modified (third-party or legacy jar) but has a non-final boundary method to stub: Mockito spy() / @Spy keeps the real methods and stubs only the overridden ones - the partial mocking Mockito's Javadoc documents for legacy code and third-party interfaces (final methods stay un-stubbable).
A PHP class whose constructor opens connections or performs other side effects: createPartialMock(Class::class, ['boundaryMethod']) or getMockBuilder()->onlyMethods([...])->disableOriginalConstructor() generates a double that overrides only the named methods and skips the real constructor - PHPUnit's documented form of the pattern (final, private and static methods and enums cannot be doubled).
A .NET class with virtual boundary members: NSubstitute Substitute.ForPartsOf<T>() creates a partial substitute that - as NSubstitute's own docs state - inherits the original type via Castle DynamicProxy and runs real code except for members configured with DoNotCallBase, i.e. a generated test-specific subclass with an official 'use with caution' caveat.

name: typestate
document:
typestate
type state
typestate programming
Encode an object's state in its type - a type parameter or a distinct state type - so that only the operations legal in the current state exist and every transition is a checked, type-changing step.
An object's methods are valid only in certain states (a closed file cannot be read, a client that has not connected cannot send), but the state lives in a runtime field: callers must remember the protocol, illegal calls still compile and fail at run time, and the legal sequences are documented rather than enforced.
Statically typed languages with generics or usable distinct-type support, where a small, fixed set of states and legal transitions is known at compile time: protocol handshakes, resource lifecycles (files, sockets, peripherals), staged builders and configuration objects, and single-owner workflows. It pays where a wrong sequence is expensive - hardware, protocols, money - and the state machine is stable.
Staged builders where build() must not compile before every required property is supplied (typed request builders, configuration objects).
Resource lifecycles: files, sockets and streams whose read/write/close operations are meaningful only after open and before close.
Protocol handshakes - connect, authenticate, exchange, disconnect - including TLS or HTTP session setup and stateful client APIs.
Embedded peripheral configuration: a GPIO pin or timer whose mode (input, output, alternate function) is a type parameter, so wrong-mode register access is a compile error.
Transaction and workflow objects: begin, mutate, commit or roll back, where committing twice or mutating after commit must not be expressible.
Iterators and streams with an exhausted state, where next() consumes the iterator until it yields the end state.
Hardware or network state machines where a wrong sequence causes a fault rather than a catchable error (bus faults, half-open connections).
Embedded HALs in the Rust ecosystem (embedded-hal and device crates such as stm32f4xx-hal) model a pin as Pin<M> with its mode as the type parameter: set_high() compiles only for an output-mode pin and into_input()/into_output() consume the old pin, as prescribed by the Embedded Rust Book's GPIO design chapter.
The Checker Framework for Java runs typestate analysis over unmodified code: its Called Methods and Resource Leak checkers track @MustCall obligations so an InputStream cannot be read before its required initialization methods ran and must be closed on every path - the state is inferred by a checker rather than written into the type.
TypeScript builder libraries such as ts-fluent-builder thread a phantom state type through the builder's generics so build() only compiles once every required property is present, turning missing-field errors from runtime throws into compile errors.

name: type-safe-enum
document:
type-safe-enum
typesafe enum
enumeration class
Give a fixed set of constants its own nominal type whose legal values are exactly the declared members, so values cannot be mixed with - or silently converted from - unrelated integers and strings.
A fixed set of related constants is represented as bare integers or strings (`public static final int APPLE_FUJI = 0`, `#define SEASON_SPRING "spring"`): nothing stops a caller from passing an unrelated number, adding two members, comparing across two different sets, or mistyping a string; the compiler cannot distinguish a typo from a valid value and the mistake surfaces at run time.
Whenever a domain concept is a mutually exclusive, compile-time-known set of alternatives - order states, card suits, log levels, protocol codes - and those values travel through method signatures, persistence and wire formats where the underlying primitive (int, ordinal, string) is also used for unrelated purposes. It matters most where an invalid value must fail compilation rather than corrupt data, and where the set is declared once and used by many callers.
Domain vocabularies with a fixed set of alternatives: order and payment states, card suits, log levels, HTTP methods, units of measure.
Replacing legacy int or string constants (int enum pattern, #define groups, static final String) so that invalid or mistyped values stop compiling.
Values that cross a persistence or transport boundary, where one conversion and validation point is wanted for parsing and formatting.
Enum-keyed collections and configuration (EnumSet/EnumMap, entries, allCases, switch exhaustiveness) instead of parallel arrays and count constants.
A small closed family of algorithms or policies whose members carry their own data and behaviour (constant-specific methods, strategy enums).
State machines and protocols in which a value must be one of a fixed, compiler-known set and illegal states must be unrepresentable.
The JDK's java.time API models month-of-year and day-of-week as the enum types Month and DayOfWeek, which carry explicit getValue() integers aligned with ISO-8601 and behavior like plus()/maxLength(), so calendar APIs (LocalDate.of(year, Month, dayOfMonth)) accept members, never bare ints; the Javadoc tells callers to prefer getValue() over ordinal().
Protocol Buffers compiles each .proto enum into a closed enum type in the generated target-language code (Java, C++, C#, Python EnumDescriptor), and the wire boundary converts via forNumber() with proto3's UNRECOGNIZED member or integer retention, exemplifying the single validated conversion point for a cross-language vocabulary.
Django ships models.TextChoices and models.IntegerChoices (built on Python's enum.Enum) as the typed way to declare model field choices: the field takes the enum class, members carry value plus human-readable label, and .choices/.labels/.values drive validation and form rendering.

name: protected-system
document:
protected-system
protection proxy
Give a resource exactly one owning object whose published operations are the only way to touch it, so that every access is decided by an authorization check before the resource is used.
A resource - a credential store, a file tree, a socket, a connection pool, a device handle - is referenced from many places. When each use site performs its own permission check, the checks drift, new code paths forget them, and the resource remains reachable as a raw handle, so a missing check cannot even be detected. The recurring trigger: one object can own the resource and clients can be made to hold only that object, so ownership itself can carry the enforcement.
Applies where ownership is expressible in the language or runtime (private field, unexported type, opaque handle, module boundary) and an authorization policy - identity, role, permission, capability - can be evaluated at each public operation. The guard may sit in-process (object or module scope) or at a process/kernel boundary, where the same pattern becomes a real reference monitor; the assurance the implementation can claim depends on which side of that line it lives.
Credential and key stores: an in-process vault owns the keys and exposes only operations (sign, decrypt, rotate), so callers never receive the secret material.
Storage gateways: a library owns the directory handle or object-store client and applies path and tenant rules on every operation instead of handing out a raw client.
Pools: the pool owns its connections and leases checked-out views, so a caller cannot keep, share or resurrect a connection the pool must reclaim.
Multi-tenant data access: a tenant-scoped repository wrapper pins the tenant filter and refuses operations that would query outside it.
Device and driver access: a supervisor object owns the device handle and validates commands, or a privileged daemon owns the socket and checks each request from an unprivileged client.
Module-level boundaries: a package exports only the guard type and keeps the resource unexported, so code outside the package cannot even name the protected representation.
Linux Landlock: a kernel-enforced ruleset restricts a process and its future children to explicitly allowed filesystem or network rights, placing mediation below application code.
Kubernetes RBAC: the API server evaluates Roles and bindings for each API request, mediating verbs and resources instead of exposing the cluster's backing store to clients.
HashiCorp Vault policies: authenticated tokens are checked against path and capability rules before secret operations, while the storage backend remains behind the Vault service.
