name: applicative
document:
applicative
applicative functor
applicative style
idiom (original McBride-Paterson name)
Apply one pure function to several independent effectful computations, letting the chosen context instance fix the semantics of absence, failure, ordering, and concurrency; the combining structure is fixed before execution - that static shape is what enables batching, parallel scheduling, and static analysis - and an accumulating error instance reports every independent failure instead of short-circuiting on the first.
You have several independent computations - parse this field, fetch that record, validate this quantity - and a pure function that combines their results, but each result lives inside a context such as Option, Either/Result, List, Promise/Task, or Validation. A bind/await chain can imply a dependency that does not exist, serialize work, or stop at the first failure; you need a fixed applicative structure that combines the values while leaving failure and scheduling policy to the chosen instance.
Value- or effect-level functional code where independent combination is the recurring decision: form and request validation that must report every field error at once, parallel-capable fetch coordination, configuration or tuple assembly from independent parses, and parser/stream composition. Applies when the language offers a context type (or validator abstraction) and the team accepts a small abstraction - a type class in Scala/Kotlin, a stdlib combinator such as Promise.all, or a hand-written lift2 - to express 'apply a pure function to several effectful arguments'. Applicative structure permits parallel execution but does not itself guarantee scheduling, cancellation, or error accumulation.
Form, request or configuration validation where every field is checked independently and the user must see all violations in one response.
Combining independent parses of a record (age, e-mail, quantity, date range) into one constructed value, reporting every malformed field.
Parallel IO combination: fetching several unrelated resources (Promise.all, CompletableFuture.thenCombine, parZipOrAccumulate, errgroup fan-out) and pairing the results positionally.
Parser and stream combinators where several parsers/subscribers consume the same input independently and their results are combined into a node.
Building a read model or report from several independent queries where a failure of one part should be reported without cancelling the others.
Statistics/diagnostics: computing several independent measurements of the same input and combining them with a pure summary function.
DSLs and embedded languages: building an abstract syntax tree of applicative operations (Free Applicative) that can be statically analyzed, optimized, or pretty-printed before interpretation - enabling query planning, dead code elimination, or validation of DSL constraints at construction time.
Traversable data structures: threading an Applicative effect through a container (tree, list, optional) so each element can be independently validated, transformed, or fetched without sequential coupling.
Collecting monoidal summaries: using Const as the Applicative to fold a Traversable structure into a single Monoid value (e.g., collecting all validation errors, or computing a checksum) without materializing a transformed structure.
API gateway aggregation: combining multiple downstream service calls where each call is independent and all results (or all errors) should be collected before returning a response to the caller.
Configuration loading at startup: validating all config fields independently and reporting every misconfiguration at once rather than failing on the first missing key.
CSV or batch row validation: validating each row independently and accumulating all row-level errors so the entire batch can be rejected with a full error report rather than failing on the first bad row.
Bidirectional codec composition: building parsers and serializers (e.g., with prismatic/schema, io-ts, or hkj's ValidatedPrism) where the parse direction is accumulating and fallible but the build direction is total, preserving the parse-don't-validate discipline applicatively.
GraphQL API input validation: validate independent arguments and return all field-level errors in one response instead of rejecting at the first failure.
Kubernetes or Helm configuration loading: validate independent keys and report the complete set of startup misconfigurations before deployment.
CI/CD pipeline policy checks: run independent static checks over a change and aggregate diagnostics before gating the build.
Haxl at Meta/Facebook: an applicative Fetch whose <*> explores both operands before blocking, so independent dataFetch calls to the same data source batch into one request and run concurrently without explicit forking ("There is no Fork", ICFP 2014).
Swift structured concurrency: async let starts each independent task as a child task immediately and a later await combines the results into a tuple or constructor call - applicative-shaped combination of a fixed set of independent effects in mainstream syntax, with cancellation and lifetime bounded by the enclosing scope.
Elm JSON decoders: Json.Decode map2..map8 (or elm-json-decode-pipeline's required/custom steps) assemble a record from independent per-field decoders - the production form of mapN in front-end code.

name: attorney-client
document:
attorney-client
attorney pattern
attorney-client friendship idiom
Grant a named collaborator a deliberately narrow compile-time view of a class's private interface by making an attorney the client's sole friend; the attorney forwards selected operations or re-exports selected private nested types (often through controlled public typedefs), while unrelated private members and the public contract remain closed.
A C++ collaborator may need one private hook, constructor, iterator adapter or nested implementation type, but a friend class receives every private and protected member. Making the hook public leaks it to every caller; publishing a std::list<T>::iterator or the container type leaks representation and its invalidation contract; pImpl hides representation from everyone but does not grant one collaborator a typed privileged view. The missing mechanism is a small attorney contract that names exactly the operations or nested types this collaborator may use without turning the private interface into a second public API.
Object-oriented code whose encapsulation boundary is a class and whose language offers class- or scope-level access control but no per-collaborator grant - C++ with friend declarations, Java/C#/Kotlin with package, assembly or module access, and their test- and library-extension scenarios. It applies at object scope, where one type owns the implementation and one named collaborator needs a slice of it, and it is a source-level structuring device checked by the compiler, never a runtime protection mechanism.
White-box test access: a test harness reaches one private hook or state view through a named attorney instead of making the member public or redefining private with a test-only preprocessor switch.
Iterator adapters: Boost.Iterator's iterator_core_access is a canonical gateway class a user-defined iterator befriends, so iterator_facade and its operators reach private dereference/increment/advance core functions while those implementation hooks stay out of the iterator's public API.
Serialization: Boost.Serialization has serializable classes befriend boost::serialization::access, whose gateway reaches the private serialize() member so archives can reconstruct state without a public serialization method.
Private nested type exposure: LLVM's SchedulerInternalsAttorney publishes the selected nested Scheduler::BndlSchedState as a public type alias and supplies narrow static accessors for unit tests, without publishing every Scheduler private type.
A pImpl-backed adapter that must inspect one implementation-owned type: keep the public class opaque and put the attorney definition in the adapter or test header, so the privileged component gets a typed view without making the implementation part of the ordinary public contract.
Iterator facade over a hidden list-like representation: expose a stable nested iterator/view type through an attorney rather than publishing std::list<T>::iterator, so the owner can replace the container without promising its node and invalidation details to every caller.
Private virtual hooks: an attorney forwards one private virtual operation through a base reference, allowing the derived override to run even though friendship is not inherited.
Factory or construction control: a builder reaches one private constructor or initialization hook through an attorney, while unrelated callers still cannot construct an object through that path.
Spacecraft flight software (fsfw): LocalDpManagerAttorney keeps fetchPoolEntry and getMutexHandle as private static forwarders and befriends only LocalPoolVariable and LocalPoolVector, so the local data pool manager opens its internals to two named collaborators instead of every class that might befriend it.
Simulator tree traversal (Sandia Sparta Modeling Framework): sparta::TreeNodePrivateAttorney exposes TreeNode's private child vectors and subtrees through static accessors (getAllChildren, getChild, findChildren) for internal Reports and Pipeout processing, with a documented 'should NOT be used by simulation developers' restriction in place of an enforceable caller limit.

name: audit-interceptor
document:
audit-interceptor
audit trail interceptor
audit logging interceptor
Declare an audit policy at an invocation seam that records the actor, action, target, correlation id and both attempt and terminal outcome around a delegated operation, then sends the structured event to a dedicated integrity-protected sink, so security accountability is consistent without inline logging in every service.
Security-relevant operations (privileged actions, state changes and access to sensitive data) must be attributable, but inline logging misses denied and failed attempts, varies in schema, can leak raw arguments and disappears with a rolled-back transaction. Teams also need to cover components they cannot modify without pretending that a proxy sees calls that bypass it.
Business or service tiers whose sensitive operations pass through an interceptable seam: container-managed beans, proxied service objects, ORM entity lifecycles, message endpoints or an HTTP pipeline. Audit selection must be declarative and uniform, while the sink has its own integrity and retention requirements (Secure Logger); the design must make mediation gaps, redaction, transaction coupling, failure policy, clock source and correlation propagation explicit.
Business-tier auditing of money-moving or otherwise regulated operations (fund transfer, order placement, claim submission): who requested it, on which object, when, and whether it succeeded.
Privileged administration surfaces (role changes, key rotation, configuration changes) where every sensitive operation must leave a record naming the acting principal.
Authentication and authorization outcomes: successful and failed logins, access-denial decisions and lockouts routed into the same audit pipeline instead of ad-hoc log lines.
Access-to-sensitive-data events (who read which patient/customer record) recorded at the gateway or service boundary to satisfy data-protection obligations.
Retrofitting auditing onto legacy components whose code cannot be modified, by wrapping the service object or binding an interceptor to its interface.
Middleware-level auditing of message endpoints and database calls in a business tier, correlating the caller's subject with the operation performed.
Financial API request interception (Spring Boot global request interceptors) capturing who accessed which endpoint, with what payload, and what outcome — satisfying SOX financial reporting controls.
Entity-level change tracking via ORM subscribers (e.g., EF Core SaveChangesInterceptor, TypeORM subscribers): automatically diff old vs. new property values on create/update/delete and emit audit envelopes without manual logging calls.
API gateway-level audit logging: capture every external API call with timestamp, user identity, endpoint, method, and outcome, correlating across microservices via X-Request-ID / traceparent headers.
Compliance reporting automation: generate audit-ready reports for SOX (~7-year retention), HIPAA (~6-year retention), GDPR (data residency-aware), and PCI-DSS from structured interceptor events.
Zero-trust data access trails: record every read of sensitive fields (PHI, PII, financial data) so data-protection obligations (GDPR Article 5 data minimization, HIPAA access logging) are demonstrably met.
Hibernate Envers: @Audited entity lifecycle changes create per-entity _AUD revisions at transaction commit; a custom revision entity/listener can attach actor or request metadata.
Django admin: django.contrib.admin.models.LogEntry records action time, user, object, addition/change/deletion and change_message for ModelAdmin activity.
Rails Audited: the audited ActiveRecord extension creates audit rows for model create, update and destroy callbacks, including changed attributes and optional acting-user attribution.

name: higher-order-component
document:
higher-order-component
HOC
component enhancer
Add cross-cutting behaviour to many components at once by wrapping them in an enhancer function that takes a component and returns a new, enhanced component, so no wrapped component knows about the concern or has to be edited.
The same cross-cutting logic - subscribing to a data source, checking a permission, firing analytics, injecting a theme, a translation or a feature flag - is needed by many components, and copying it into each one couples every component to the concern, re-couples them to every change of it, and leaves the behaviour to be remembered at each new call site. React tried mixins and inheritance first and removed them (implicit dependencies between mixin and component, name clashes, snowballing coupling), so the recurring decision is how to apply one behaviour to many components without editing them, while the components stay reusable and unaware of the enhancement.
Component-model UI code where components are values the framework mounts with a stable identity (React and its ecosystem first; the same shape recurs with Compose composables, SwiftUI views, Blazor components, Scala.js layers and handler-based Go/Java web UIs), where the concern is genuinely cross-cutting rather than local to one screen, where the enhancement can be expressed as a pure function from component to component and applied once at the definition or export site, and where the wrapped component's inputs form a prop-like contract that can be extended by injection without touching its internals.
Subscribing many components to an external data source — React documentation's withSubscription example, or Redux's connect: store state arrives as injected props with no component knowing about the store.
Apollo Client data injection: graphql(Query, { options, props }) HOC maps query results and loading state to props; multiple graphql HOCs composed with @compose; historically the standard before useQuery.
Authorization and feature gating at the boundary: withAuthorization(Component, { requiredRole }) or withFeatureFlag(...) decides rendering without editing the component; useful for route-level guards applied across many pages.
Analytics, telemetry and instrumentation applied at export sites (withAnalytics): tracking calls stay out of presentation code and can be added or removed at one location per module.
Injecting ambient context into components that take it as props — translations via withTranslation (react-i18next), routing via withRouter (React Router v5 and below), theming via withTheme (Material-UI v4) — enabling third-party and vendored components to participate without modification.
Error and loading boundaries as an enhancer (withErrorBoundary): the boundary exists as a component in the tree anyway; an enhancer consolidates the concern into one reusable definition rather than repeating the try/catch at each call site.
Sharing logic into class components and older codebases where hooks cannot be used: the HOC reaches class components and library component-shaped APIs that hooks cannot wrap.
Material-UI v4 theming: withStyles and withTheme HOCs inject classes and theme as props; compose chains combine styling with data (connect + withStyles + graphql on the same export).
Internationalization testing: export both wrapped and unwrapped components; tests use the raw component with a mock t function while integration tests use the full I18nextProvider setup.
Conditional prop injection: a data-enhancer that only injects props when a condition is met (e.g. user is authenticated) lets the wrapped component remain agnostic about the absence of that data.
React Compiler (React Forget) compatibility: heavy HOC layering reduces the compiler's static analysis surface and may cause it to bailout — test compiler output when adding HOCs to a compiled codebase; prefer hooks for new logic the compiler should see.
React Server Components boundary: a HOC that calls hooks or reads client-only context (useAuth, useTheme, useRouter) cannot execute during a server render; the wrapped component may receive undefined injected props on the server and flash-change on hydration. Pass server-fetched data as props through the HOC boundary from a server parent instead.
Streaming SSR and Suspense integration: a HOC that wraps a component behind a Suspense boundary adds a node that may delay streaming; if the HOC itself is async it must be carefully placed to avoid blocking the fallback from showing.
Partial hydration patterns: on islands architectures (Next.js App Router, Astro), a HOC that subscribes to client-side state forces the entire island to be hydrated even if the wrapped component has no server payload; prefer passing hydrated state as props from a server parent.
Recompose (acdlite): a 'lodash for React' utility belt built entirely from composable HOCs (withState, mapProps, pure, branch) piped through enhance/compose - the pattern industrialised; its October 2018 deprecation in favour of Hooks (bug-fix maintenance only) is the canonical case study of the pattern's cost when a runtime offers a cheaper reuse primitive.
MobX React binding: observer from mobx-react / mobx-react-lite is an official HOC that subscribes the wrapped component to every observable read during render, re-rendering it automatically; MobX guidance is to apply observer first (innermost) when composing it with other HOCs, and to wrap every component that reads observables.

name: poison-pill
document:
poison-pill
sentinel message
end-of-stream marker
Terminate queue consumers cooperatively by sending a reserved sentinel message that each consumer recognises as "no more work", so consumers drain the backlog and exit without a separate control channel or forced cancellation.
A producer-consumer system must shut down, but its consumers block on an empty queue and the queue has no built-in "no more items" signal: callers either kill the workers mid-work and drop buffered items, or leave them blocked forever. Production has ended - how do the consumers learn that while still processing everything already queued?
In-process or broker-mediated producer-consumer systems with a FIFO work queue, a fixed set of long-lived consumers (threads, coroutines, actors) that block when the queue is empty, and a shutdown requirement that work already accepted by the queue be drained before the consumers exit - typically deployment, signal handling or test teardown.
Signal-driven shutdown of an in-process worker pool: the SIGTERM handler stops accepting work, then enqueues one pill per worker so the backlog is processed before the process exits.
Batch importers and ETL stages whose consumers block on a work queue and must finish the current batch before a run is considered complete.
Test harnesses and simulations: an explicit stop message makes thread-based systems deterministic to shut down, without sleeps or guessed timeouts.
Actor systems: a reserved stop message (for example Akka PoisonPill) terminates an actor after the messages already queued for it have been handled.
Log and event writers where the last records must reach the sink before consumers release their buffers and files.
Bounded-queue stages in a pipeline: pills travel the same backpressured channel as work, so upstream cannot keep producing after the stop decision.
Kubernetes pod shutdown: containers receive SIGTERM, workers stop pulling from the job queue, drain in-flight tasks, then exit within the terminationGracePeriodSeconds window.
Redis/Bull queue workers: a shutdown signal pushes a sentinel via BLPOP so workers exit cleanly without losing the right to process pending tasks.
Akka Streams and similar streaming frameworks: the GraphStage signals completion via onPull/downstream cancellation, which is the materialised equivalent of a poison pill.
Redis Streams consumer groups: XREADGROUP with block timeout naturally returns when the stream is empty; a special ID (e.g. ">") polling loop plus a shared shutdown flag replaces the in-process sentinel.
Broker-level poison message isolation: in Kafka, RabbitMQ, or Azure Service Bus, a permanently failing message (deserialisation error, validation failure) blocks a partition/consumer indefinitely; DLQ-based routing (publish to dead-letter topic after N retries, then commit offset and continue) is the broker-level analogue that prevents one poison message from halting the entire pipeline.
Kubernetes preStop hooks + pill drain: a container's lifecycle preStop hook can enqueue a sentinel into an in-process work queue while the orchestrator grants terminationGracePeriodSeconds for the drain to complete, ensuring zero work-drop during rolling updates.
Azure Service Bus competing-consumers workers: when a worker receives a shutdown notification it completes its current PeekLock message, then calls Abandon on any held locks before unregistering; Azure Service Bus dead-letter queues handle the poison-message variant when a message exceeds MaxDeliveryCount and cannot be delivered.
Akka hierarchical actor trees: sending PoisonPill to a parent actor stops it after all queued messages ahead of the pill are processed, and automatically sends stop messages to all children in bottom-up order; this is the idiomatic way to orchestrate ordered multi-actor shutdown.
Non-blocking retry architectures (RabbitMQ): rather than local Thread.sleep retries that block the consumer thread, use server-side TTL queues with Dead Letter Exchange routing to implement exponential backoff, keeping the consumer responsive to new messages and to shutdown pills.
Java's JDK BlockingQueue worker pools: because BlockingQueue has no built-in close, producers can enqueue a unique end-of-stream object after all work; each consumer takes until that sentinel and then the coordinator joins workers.
Python multiprocessing worker pools: multiprocessing.Queue/JoinableQueue supports FIFO task delivery with sentinel values and join-based drain tracking; send one sentinel per worker and join them after the queue is exhausted.
Akka Classic actors: PoisonPill is enqueued in the mailbox and processed after already queued messages, while Akka Typed requires an explicit Stop/Shutdown protocol; choose the API that matches the actor model.

name: pipeline
document:
pipeline
assembly line
processing pipeline
Decompose a transformation into an ordered sequence of named stages that each consume the previous stage's output and produce the next stage's input, so the workflow reads top to bottom and every step can be tested, instrumented, reordered or replaced on its own.
A multi-step transformation is written as one long function or a tangle of nested calls: the steps are unnamed, their order is implicit in statement order, intermediate values need throwaway names, there is no seam at which a single step can be logged, tested or replaced, and the same sequence is retyped at every call site that needs it.
Processing that naturally decomposes into successive transformations of the same payload - request handling, ETL, compiler passes, message enrichment, image or byte-stream processing - whether the payload is a single value or a stream. It fits in-process, staged execution where one driver owns ordering, error handling and cancellation; distributing the stages across processes, transports and independently deployed filters is the architectural pipe-and-filter pattern instead.
Request handling: deserialise, authenticate, validate, enrich, persist and render a request, with each step named so a failing stage is attributable and testable in isolation.
ETL and data import: extract, clean, transform, validate and load large files as a stream, so no intermediate collection is materialised and memory stays bounded.
Compiler and interpreter passes: source, tokens, AST, resolution, optimisation and code emission, where each pass is an independent stage over the intermediate representation and the pass list is the pipeline.
Message enrichment in an integration flow: unwrap, translate, enrich and route a message, one stage per concern, with per-channel ordering; the cross-process version stays pipe-and-filter.
Image or byte-stream processing: decode, crop or resize, watermark and encode, lazily per frame or chunk, optionally overlapping stages across cores.
Configuration-driven data cleaning: the stage list is assembled from configuration or a plugin registry so different tenants get different ordered steps without changing the stages themselves.
TensorFlow tf.data input pipelines: tf.data.Dataset pipelines that chain map, prefetch, parallel_interleave and shuffle stages to feed a training loop efficiently, with each stage independently configurable and the whole pipeline testable in isolation.
LLM token streaming: HTTP server-sent event streams where an LLM produces tokens at inference speed while clients consume at variable network speed; stream.pipeline() prevents the inference server from buffering unbounded tokens in memory when a slow client disconnects (Node.js stream backpressure case study).
Observability telemetry pipelines: OpenTelemetry Collector chains receivers, processors (memory_limiter, batch, filter, transform, tail_sampling) and exporters for traces, metrics and logs, with connectors (e.g., spanmetrics) bridging signal types and memory_limiter placed first to prevent OOM before filtering.
Typed TypeScript pipeline with schema validation: Zod or io-ts schemas define the stage contract at each boundary, catching schema violations at the exact stage that produced bad data rather than at a distant consumer.
Async generator pipelines in Python: asyncio queues with bounded capacity connect async generator stages, propagating backpressure by pausing producers when the queue is full; the FinStream analytics case study showed 82% memory reduction and 99.7% latency reduction versus unbounded buffering.
Event-streaming pipelines with Kafka and Flink: producers, topic partitions, Flink consumers and checkpointing form a distributed pipeline where backpressure cascades across every boundary; the Kafka max.block.ms and Flink backpressure.sample.interval settings interact under partition saturation and must be tested together under load.
Dynamic pipeline parallelism: construct-and-run pipelines (MapReduce, Spark) fix stage count at construction, while on-the-fly pipelines (Cilk-P Piper algorithm) allow the structure to emerge at runtime, varying per iteration and supporting data-dependent branching; on-the-fly enables pipelines like x264 that cannot be expressed with a fixed static structure.
LLVM compiler pass pipelines: PassBuilder assembles ModulePassManager, CGSCCPassManager, FunctionPassManager and LoopPassManager across the IR hierarchy (Module → CGSCC → Function → Loop), with registered callbacks injecting passes at named extension points (pipeline-start, vectorizer-start, optimizer-last); incorrect PreservedAnalyses declarations invalidate all downstream analyses.
Continuous data pipelines at scale (Google model): periodic pipelines run on cron and suffer from depth growth and resource exhaustion as organic load increases; continuous pipelines (master-slave or event-triggered) replace idle-waiting with always-on processing, eliminating the 'pipeline vs cron' discontinuity at the cost of operational complexity.
ML pipeline orchestration (Airflow, Kubeflow, Prefect, Dagster): each orchestrator applies the pipeline pattern at the workflow level - Airflow's DAG-of-tasks, Kubeflow's per-container-step pipelines with GPU scheduling, Prefect's monoflow/subflow/orchestrator pattern, and Dagster's software-defined assets where asset dependencies imply the pipeline; the pipeline is the scheduler's unit of execution, not an implementation detail.
Apache Beam: PCollections flow through composable PTransforms (ParDo, Combine and GroupByKey) in a pipeline graph, making each transform boundary explicit while the runner handles execution.
Node.js stream.pipeline(): Readable, Transform and Writable stages compose with built-in backpressure, error propagation and AbortSignal cancellation; this is a concrete streaming realization, not a durable workflow engine.

name: single-table-inheritance
document:
single-table-inheritance
table per hierarchy
discriminator column mapping
Map an inheritance hierarchy of classes onto one shared table whose columns are the union of all classes' fields, using a type code (discriminator) column to decide which class each row instantiates, so polymorphic reads need no joins.
A class hierarchy must be persisted, the hierarchy is small and its classes share most fields, and cross-class queries or polymorphic loads are frequent: mapping each class to its own table would force a join per level on almost every read, while the subtypes differ by only a few columns.
Object-relational mapping of a small, shallow, stable class hierarchy whose subclasses are mostly variations on shared state - domain-model inheritance (Employee/Engineer/Manager), payment or content types - where the storage layer is chosen by the team and the persistence framework can be taught the type code (JPA/EF Core/ActiveRecord/SQLAlchemy/most ORMs make this their default strategy) or the mapping is written by hand over SQL.
Small stable hierarchies where subclasses share most state: Employee/Engineer/Manager, Payment/CardPayment/WirePayment, Notification/EmailNotification/PushNotification.
Content or asset models with a handful of similar types (Photo/Question/Post, Blog/RssBlog) distinguished by a type code, where cross-type queries and listings are the dominant read.
Legacy or third-party schemas that already hold a hierarchy in one table with a kind column and must be mapped onto domain classes without restructuring the database.
Reporting and analytics over a hierarchy where one wide table with a type column beats joining four tables for every subtype question.
ORM-default configurations: teams that pick the framework's default hierarchy mapping (JPA SINGLE_TABLE, EF Core TPH) because join avoidance and mapping simplicity outweigh column honesty for their hierarchy size.
Rails Active Record single-table inheritance: ActiveRecord::Inheritance stores the subclass name in the table's type column by default (Company/Firm/Client all live in companies with type = 'Firm'), so fetching via the base class returns correctly-typed objects - GitLab runs a production monolith on this mechanism and maintains a written policy on when STI must not be used.
EF Core's default table-per-hierarchy mapping: a Blog/RssBlog hierarchy shares one table, the discriminator's name, CLR type and per-class values are set with HasDiscriminator/HasValue, and EF Core automatically adds the discriminator predicate to derived-type queries (throwing on unmapped discriminator values).
SQLAlchemy declarative polymorphic mappers: the base class declares polymorphic_on = 'type' in __mapper_args__ and each subclass a unique polymorphic_identity, so one person table answers polymorphic queries for Person/Employee rows without joins.

name: test-data-builder
document:
test-data-builder
test builder
Give each domain type used in tests a builder that starts from valid, commonly used defaults, so a test states only the data its assertion depends on and everything else is supplied correctly without being mentioned.
Strict constructors and immutable value objects make test setup a chore: every test that needs an object must supply all constructor arguments, so tests fill up with values that have nothing to do with the behaviour under test, break whenever a constructor argument or the object's structure changes, and copy the same construction code from test to test. The ready-made fixtures of an object mother remove the repetition but not the variation - every slightly different case adds another factory method, and the mother degenerates into duplicated code or a swarm of methods holding a single new statement.
Applies to test suites over a domain model whose objects have many required fields or cross-field invariants, where each test varies only a small part of the data and a valid instance can be constructed without external systems. It is language-neutral but pays off most where the language lacks named/default arguments or copy-with-modification, and it belongs to the test sources: production code keeps its own constructors and must not depend on a builder whose defaults are chosen for tests.
Unit tests over domain types with many constructor parameters and cross-field invariants (invoices, users, policies) where each test cares about one or two values.
Mock-based interaction tests that must hand a valid collaborator object to the system under test with e.g. only its id varied to observe request routing.
Bug-reproduction tests: the builder encodes the standard valid case and the test states only the faulty value from the report.
Suites with many test classes over the same domain fixtures (payroll, insurance, orders) that need per-test variation rather than a handful of canned objects.
Table-driven or property-style tests over one dimension: build the valid base once and override that dimension for each case.
Integration tests that need a complete, plausible object graph (nested entities, collections, ids) deviating in a single field.
factory_bot (thoughtbot) for Ruby/Rails: one factory per class holding a minimal valid set of default attributes, with tests overriding only the fields under test at call time (build(:user, email: "bad@example.com")) - the builder shape generalized into a library.
factory_boy for Python: class-based factories declare the default keyword arguments for the target class' __init__ (Meta.model), and each test overrides just what it asserts (UserFactory.build(first_name="Joe")), with factory inheritance standing in for object-mother variants.
Instancio for Java implements the same contract generically: create(Person.class) populates every field, and .set(field(Person::getName), "Homer") overrides only the fields the test names - its user guide states the goal as populating everything you are not interested in.

name: active-record
document:
active-record
active record pattern
ActiveRecord
Make a domain object the record for one database row: keep the row's state, row-local behavior, and the methods that find and persist it together, so a small domain does not pay for a separate mapping layer.
A simple relational domain still needs a choice about where persistence lives. A Data Mapper or gateway separates table I/O from the object but adds mapping code and a second place to navigate, while direct SQL leaks schema knowledge into callers; the recurring question is whether one row object can own its data and CRUD without hiding transaction boundaries or pretending to model cross-row rules.
A relational store is the single system of record, the domain is small and its rules are mostly local to one row (validation, derivations, simple state transitions), and the team prefers a convention-driven persistence layer over a designed one. Typical homes are framework ecosystems where the ORM is the house style (Rails, Laravel Eloquent, Django, GORM, Vapor Fluent, TypeORM), CRUD-heavy applications, and thin layers over an already well-shaped legacy schema. Entity Framework Core can host behavior on entity classes, but its DbContext and mapping conventions are a Data Mapper-shaped boundary rather than pure Active Record. It stops applying as soon as invariants span several objects, several representations of one table are needed, or the store must be swappable.
CRUD-heavy applications where most screens and endpoints map onto a single table: forms, admin back offices, catalogs, content management.
Small-to-medium domains whose rules are mostly per-row - field validation, derived values, one-row state transitions - so a mapper layer would move data around without adding a model.
Prototypes and thin service layers over an existing, already normalised legacy schema where the table shape is stable and the domain is the schema.
Framework-default persistence: a Rails, Django, GORM, Vapor Fluent or TypeORM codebase where fighting the ORM for purity costs more than it returns.
Simple record-shaped bounded contexts inside a larger system - settings, audit entries, lookup tables - where a full domain model would be overhead.
JSON:API or REST backends for SPAs and mobile apps where the data model maps directly to a relational schema with minimal transformation.
Microservices with a single-responsibility data store: a service whose entire bounded context is one aggregate root table or a handful of tightly coupled tables.
Batch import pipelines where records are validated once and bulk-inserted (insert_all/upsert_all), and the domain logic has already been applied before the bulk operation.
Multi-tenant SaaS backends where row-level isolation is enforced at the database and the ORM connection handles tenant scoping automatically.
Real Rails systems such as GitLab and Discourse are good fits for row-shaped users, posts, permissions and settings backed by PostgreSQL; keep their reporting and cross-record workflows in query or service boundaries.
A Django or Laravel CRUD surface such as an admin or back-office module fits when each request mostly validates, loads, changes and saves one model; switch to a mapper or repository when the same data feeds materially different contracts.

name: dependency-injection
document:
dependency-injection
di
constructor injection
setter injection
interface injection
ioc container
pure di
manual di
Supply an object with the collaborators it needs from the outside — through its constructor, its setters/properties, or a dedicated injection interface — so it never constructs or looks a dependency up itself and every wiring decision is made once, in a composition root or container.
An object that creates its own collaborators hard-wires a concrete class, a construction recipe and often a lifetime into itself: swapping the implementation for a test double, a second deployment or a new platform means editing the class, and the dependency graph stays invisible in the API. The recurring trigger is exactly the catalog's rule: an object should not create what it depends on — the caller, the framework or the composition root decides, and hands the dependency in.
Applies whenever a component's collaborators are chosen per deployment, per environment or per test, whenever constructing them is expensive or platform-specific, and whenever a framework owns object creation (request handlers, scheduled jobs, UI screens, message consumers). It matters most in large object graphs where one abstraction has several implementations and lifetimes must be managed (singleton, request-scoped, transient); it is unnecessary when the collaborators are pure values or when construction is a private detail nobody needs to vary.
Web and API backends whose handlers need repositories, clocks, mailers and caches that must be replaced by fakes in tests and by sandbox services in staging.
Hexagonal and clean architectures where the domain declares ports (interfaces) and the infrastructure layer supplies adapters at the composition root.
Frameworks that own object creation — request handlers, scheduled jobs, UI controllers, message consumers — where the framework's injector is the only practical wiring point.
Deployment variants (on-prem vs cloud, SQL vs in-memory, real vs stub payment gateway) selected per environment through binding configuration rather than conditional code.
Plugin and extension systems where the concrete implementation is chosen at start-up from a plugin registry, enabling third-party adapters without touching core code.
Expensive shared resources whose lifetime must be managed centrally (connection pools, HTTP clients, circuit breakers) while service classes stay stateless.
Unit tests that construct the class under test directly with test doubles, and integration tests that swap only the outer layer's bindings.
Microservices with sidecar containers: the sidecar provides logging, tracing and retry policies as injected collaborators, keeping the service logic untouched.
Cloud-native applications where the composition root is the only place that knows whether a dependency resolves locally, across a service mesh, or via a remote gRPC call.
Multi-tenant SaaS where tenant-specific adapters (tenant-scoped repositories, per-tenant feature flags) are bound at the composition root and switched by middleware.
Event-driven systems where message handlers receive their dependencies through injection, making the handler logic identical between in-process and distributed deployment.
AOT-compiled applications (Native AOT, Blazor WebAssembly, serverless) where runtime reflection is unavailable — dependencies are resolved via source generators or manually at the composition root.
Functional codebases using effect systems (ZIO, fp-ts, Reader monad) where the DI container is replaced by typed environments passed through function compositions.
Consumer-driven contract testing (Pact, OpenAPI pact) where DI swaps provider implementations with contract-mock stubs at the boundary, enabling parallel service development without shared integration environments.
Resilience and fault-injection testing: proxies or decorator-based fault injectors (e.g., Gremlin SDK, WireMock) are injected as collaborators to validate retry, timeout and circuit-breaker behaviour under simulated failure conditions.
Single-page application frameworks with DI built into the component tree: Angular resolves components, directives and services through hierarchical injectors, scoping providers to the application root, a component subtree or a route so features override implementations and lazy-load without global registration.
Android apps using Dagger (and Hilt over it) to build the object graph at compile time — generated, reflection-free code, bindings and cycles checked at build time, with field injection reserved for framework-created entry points like Activities and Fragments.
Python web APIs (FastAPI) where each path operation declares Depends(callable) parameters: the framework resolves nested dependency graphs with per-request caching and uses yield-based dependencies to open and close connections around each request.

name: intercepting-validator
document:
intercepting-validator
validation interceptor
Insert one interception layer on the ingress path that validates every inbound message before any handler runs, so that input checking is uniform, central and impossible to forget per endpoint.
Inbound data - HTTP requests, RPC messages, queue events, protocol frames - is validated inside each handler: every new endpoint re-implements parsing, range and encoding checks, rules drift between handlers, and some paths end up with no validation at all. The recurring decision is where to put validation so that all inbound data passes through it exactly once, before application logic.
Request- or message-driven systems with a well-defined ingress - HTTP APIs, RPC services, queue consumers, protocol front ends - where several handlers accept external data, where shared constraints (schema, ranges, encodings, size limits) can be expressed without loading domain state, and where the ingress pipeline (filter chain, middleware stack, plugin pipeline, responder chain) can be owned and configured by the team.
A public REST or GraphQL API where every request body and query parameter must pass schema, range and size validation before any controller is invoked.
A message-queue consumer that validates every inbound event against its schema and version before dispatching it to a handler.
A file or protocol ingest pipeline (CSV, XML, binary frames) that validates frames in one front layer before domain processing begins.
A multi-tenant service that enforces tenant-scoped constraints uniformly - allowed fields, payload caps, encoding policy - on all inbound requests.
An RPC or WebSocket gateway that rejects non-conforming request messages with one error format before they reach service handlers.
A GraphQL API gateway that validates incoming query operations for schema conformance, depth limits and argument types at the boundary before query execution begins.
A gRPC service fronted by a protobuf interceptor that enforces proto-schema type and structural constraints on all inbound RPC requests before they reach the service implementation.
A FastAPI service that attaches a shared Depends() dependency to an APIRouter and uses Pydantic request models so invalid requests are rejected before the path operation.
An ASP.NET Core application that places request validation in the middleware pipeline or a Minimal API endpoint filter, short-circuiting with a problem response before the endpoint delegate.
An Express application that mounts schema-validation middleware on a router before its routes, returning a 4xx response without calling next() when the request is invalid.

name: lazy-acquisition
document:
lazy-acquisition
lazy loading
deferred acquisition
Defer acquiring an expensive or scarce resource until it is first used, so the acquisition cost is paid only by the holders that actually use it, while clients keep seeing an ordinary interface.
A resource is costly to acquire, scarce, and on many execution paths never needed at all, yet the code that holds it acquires it during construction, at start-up or on a hot entry path: the process pays for resources it never dereferences, start-up time grows with every optional subsystem, and scarce capacity (descriptors, connections, licenses, memory) is consumed by holders that never use it.
Applies to long-lived holders - objects, modules, services, containers - that front an external resource such as a file, socket or database connection, license, thread pool, GPU context, translation catalog or large lookup table. It pays off when the acquisition cost is large relative to a use, when a significant fraction of holders never use the resource, and when the runtime offers a one-time guard (or the holder is provably single-threaded). It is the wrong tool when the resource must be validated at boot, when acquisition is cheap, or when first use sits on a latency-critical path.
A request-handling object that opens a file or blob stream only on the code paths that actually read it (report export, attachment download, audit sink).
A service holding connections to a rarely consulted downstream — archive store, fallback provider, secondary region — that most requests never call.
A large lookup table, model or translation catalog loaded on first use instead of at process start, keeping start-up and memory bounded for the sessions that never need it.
Optional subsystems in desktop and mobile apps (camera, location, payment SDK, plugins) initialized when the feature is opened rather than when the app launches.
Test fixtures and tooling: starting a container, browser or database only for the tests that need it, so the fast path stays fast.
Per-session state in a server — a scratch buffer, a decompressor, a TLS session or prepared statement — allocated on first use of the session rather than on accept.
Database connection pools: HikariCP and similar pools typically create connections lazily on the first checkout rather than at pool construction, to avoid pinninglicenses and consuming file descriptors before the application is fully started.
Dependency injection containers (Spring @Lazy, Dagger 2 Lazy<T>) defer the creation of bean instances until they are first injected, reducing start-up time and breaking circular dependency cycles during bootstrap.
Logging frameworks (SLF4J/Logback): Logger instances are static final but the actual appender (file, socket, console) is initialized when the first log event at that level is fired, so logging infrastructure does not block application start.
Configuration objects: large YAML or JSON config trees are parsed and validated lazily on first access rather than eagerly at start-up, keeping CLI tools fast for commands that do not need the full configuration.
GPU contexts in graphics applications (OpenGL, Vulkan, CUDA) are expensive to create and are deferred until the first draw call or compute kernel launch, allowing the application to start and display a window without claiming GPU memory.
HTTP/service clients (gRPC channels, REST clients): a channel is lazily opened on the first request, enabling the client to be instantiated at module load time while deferring the TCP handshake and TLS handshake to the first real call.
Spring Framework @Lazy bean definitions instantiate singleton beans when first requested rather than during ApplicationContext startup, making an optional integration genuinely demand-driven while retaining the container's proxy and lifecycle semantics.
Go's sync.Once lets a service wrap a one-time connection, parser or cache acquisition so concurrent first callers wait for one initializer and later callers reuse the published result.
.NET's System.Lazy<T> defers a factory until Value is first read and makes the thread-safety and exception-caching policy explicit through its constructors and LazyThreadSafetyMode.

name: cursor-pagination
document:
cursor-pagination
keyset pagination
cursor-based pagination
Bound what a read boundary returns for a large or changing ordered collection by sending one page plus an opaque continuation token that pins the filter and ordering, so clients advance deterministically without offsets and without watching rows move under them.
A boundary must expose a collection that is too large to return at once and keeps changing while clients read it. Offset or page-number requests make the store count or scan everything up to the requested page, and concurrent inserts or deletes shift rows across page boundaries so consumers see duplicates or miss items; the server has no way to state where the sequence should resume.
Any read boundary - an HTTP or gRPC list operation, a GraphQL connection, a database-backed feed, a batch export job - over an ordered collection that is large, growing, or read under concurrent writes, where the server can identify a unique, immutable ordering key and wants to cap both response size and per-request query cost while letting clients iterate the whole sequence.
Public REST or gRPC list endpoints over unbounded, growing tables - messages, orders, audit events - where deep offsets are slow and responses must stay small.
Infinite-scroll or load-more feeds that keep returning newer items while a user scrolls, with the already-seen pages stable against inserts.
Whole-collection sync and export jobs (warehouse loads, backups, search reindexing) that must iterate every row exactly once while writers continue.
GraphQL Relay connections where first/after, edges and pageInfo carry the continuation contract in the schema instead of the URL.
Consumers of third-party list APIs (Stripe-style starting_after/has_more, Google page_token iterators) that keep parameters fixed across auto-paginated calls.
Administrative and operational tooling that streams very large tables for verification or cleanup with bounded memory and predictable server load.
Audit log and event stream retrieval where events are append-only and chronological, and clients stream continuously without needing to revisit earlier pages.
Real-time activity feeds (social media timelines, notification streams) where inserts at the head must not disturb pages the user has already loaded.
Database replication and change-data-capture (CDC) pipelines that must consume a changelog exactly once across restarts and failures.
Paginating over search results from a vector database or full-text index where OFFSET at depth is expensive and results may change between queries.
Bi-directional data synchronization (CDC pipelines, replica lag-catching) where a consumer must iterate forward and occasionally needs to resume from a previous position or re-sweep a window — requiring stable forward cursors plus a defined backward-resumption path.
Paginating a partitioned or sharded database table where each partition is queried independently and cursors carry both the partition hint and the per-partition keyset position.
Slack Web API collection methods (users.list, conversations.history) where response_metadata.next_cursor drives the loop, page limits are clamped per method, and expired or malformed tokens surface as invalid_cursor so the client restarts from the first page.
GitHub GraphQL-style cursor connections where first/last (bounded 1-100) and pageInfo.startCursor/endCursor carry the continuation position for after/before traversal.
Timeline-style feeds served by Django REST framework's CursorPagination, whose default -created ordering gives a consistent view that does not repeat items as new rows are inserted.

name: compound-components
document:
compound-components
compound component
compound component pattern
Give a family of cooperating components one owner — the parent — that holds the shared state and publishes it implicitly to every child, so consumers compose the family declaratively while the parent alone enforces its invariants and behaviour.
A widget only works when a parent and its children agree on one piece of state (which option is selected, which panel is open, whether a field is invalid), but the call site is the only place that knows the children. Holding the state at the call site means threading the value and its update callbacks into every child (prop drilling), and holding it in the children means the parent cannot enforce the family's invariants — exclusivity, ordering, keyboard behaviour — nor react to a child's change in one place. The recurring decision is where the shared state lives and how children participate in it without the call site wiring them.
Component-tree UI code: design-system and widget libraries (select/option, tabs, menus, field groups) in frameworks that can inject state into descendants without passing it through props — React context or child cloning, Angular content projection plus DI, Vue provide/inject, Compose CompositionLocal and slot scopes, SwiftUI environment and preference keys, Blazor cascading values, WPF attached properties over the logical tree — and in widget toolkits whose group objects (Swing ButtonGroup, JavaFX ToggleGroup, Qt QButtonGroup, tkinter control variables) play the same role. It pays off where the public API must stay small and the children must stay replaceable; it does not apply in languages without a component tree or without an implicit-injection channel.
Custom select, combobox or autocomplete families built from Option children — the canonical example: the parent owns the selection, the highlight and the keyboard interaction while options only declare their value and label.
Tabs, accordions and menus where Tab/TabPanel/MenuItem children register their identity and the parent owns the active item, the ordering and the ARIA wiring.
Form-field families (Field + Label + Input + Error) that share one validation/invalid state and generated ids without the call site passing them around.
Data-group widgets: tables with Column definitions, list widgets with Item children, tree views with Node children, chart legends with Series children.
Design-system libraries that export one namespaced symbol whose parts must be used together — the context in which the pattern is most often documented and most valuable.
Collapsible panel families (Disclosure pattern) where a parent owns the open/closed state and Trigger/Content children read it — also known as the Disclosure pattern in ARIA authoring practices.
Stepper/wizard widgets where a parent owns current-step state and Step/StepIndicator children read it without the consumer threading step indices.
Popover/tooltip families where a trigger button and a content panel share open/close state through the parent without prop drilling.
Radix UI Primitives — Dialog.Root owns the open/close context and Trigger/Portal/Content/Title/Description consume it, while asChild (Slot) merges each part's props, refs and keyboard behaviour into the consumer's own button or link.
Ark UI headless components (built on Zag.js state machines) — Popover.Root/Trigger/Positioner/Content share state through the root, ids props compose aria bindings across two families, and the same compound anatomy works in React, Solid, Vue and Svelte.
Headless UI's Dialog family (Dialog, DialogBackdrop, DialogPanel, DialogTitle, Description) — the root enforces the dismiss contract (open prop, onClose callback, focus trap, aria-labelledby) and every part reads the shared open/closed state, exposed for styling as data-open/data-closed attributes.

name: event-message
document:
event-message
event notification
Announce that something has happened by publishing an immutable, self-describing event message - a past fact that expects no reply - on a channel, so that any number of interested receivers can react without the producer knowing who they are or what they do.
A component has completed a state change that other parts of the system care about, but it must not - and usually cannot - know which ones care. Calling each interested party directly couples the producer to every consumer, to their availability and to their processing order, and every new consumer (search index, audit, notification, analytics) forces a change and a redeploy in the producer. The trigger is open-ended interest: something changed, and the set of parties wanting to know is neither closed nor known at compile time.
Applies wherever a system reports occurrences instead of requesting work: integration between services over a broker or a log (Kafka, RabbitMQ, NATS, SNS/SQS/EventBridge), module boundaries inside one process (domain publishing to notification, search or reporting modules), and state propagation towards caches, read models or clients. It fits when the announcement matters more than any single response - audit trails, cache invalidation, read-model updates, downstream reactions - when consumers may be slow or temporarily offline, and when the producer's transaction boundary is the natural publication point.
Order placement in a service landscape: after the order transaction commits, OrderPlaced is published once and consumed independently by billing, warehouse, loyalty, search-index and notification services.
Cache and replica invalidation: CustomerAddressChanged tells every service holding a copy of the customer data to refresh or drop it, without the producing service knowing the replicas.
Audit and compliance: every state transition is emitted as an event to an append-only log, giving an ordered record of facts that a separate consumer turns into the audit trail.
Read-model / projection maintenance in CQRS: events from the write model update materialized views and search indexes asynchronously.
In-process module decoupling: a domain model publishes InvoiceIssued on an internal channel; e-mail, reporting and webhook modules subscribe without the domain importing them, keeping the dependency direction inward.
Platform-wide notifications: user lifecycle events (AccountCreated, PasswordResetRequested) fanned out to analytics, anti-fraud and e-mail consumers, each with its own retention and retry policy.
Financial trade confirmation: a matching engine emits TradeExecuted to a topic; clearing, risk management, position keeping and regulatory reporting services each consume the same event independently without the exchange knowing their identities or processing logic.
IoT telemetry ingestion: sensors publish DeviceReading events to a broker; stream-processing consumers compute rolling aggregates, rule engines evaluate thresholds, and archival systems persist the raw history — all decoupled from the sensor firmware.
Healthcare resource-change events: a FHIR-compliant system emits ObservationCreated, PatientUpdated and EncounterClosed events; downstream systems (clinical decision support, population health, billing) subscribe to precisely the event types they need without tight coupling to the EMR.
Apache Kafka event streams: producers append events (OrderPlaced, PaymentSettled) to a retained topic; consumer groups for billing, analytics and search indexing each read the same log at their own offsets, and a new consumer can replay from any point without the producer changing a line of code.
RabbitMQ fan-out notification: a producer publishes to a fanout exchange and the broker copies every event message to each bound queue - the official 'logs' tutorial has ephemeral subscribers joining and leaving while every bound consumer still receives every message.
GitHub webhooks: GitHub posts past-tense event messages (push, pull_request, release) with an event-type header, delivery GUID and HMAC signature to subscribed endpoints; integrations declare which event types they care about without ever modifying the producer.

name: subject-descriptor
document:
subject-descriptor
principal
subject
Give every part of a system one credential-independent representation of the entity on whose behalf an operation is performed, so authorization, audit and domain code can ask who is acting and read that subject's security-relevant attributes without knowing which credential format proved it.
Authentication arrives in many formats - password plus session cookie, OIDC/JWT, mTLS certificate, API key, Kerberos ticket, signed assertion - while every decision downstream only needs the same few facts: a stable identifier for the acting subject and its roles or attributes. Without a common representation each consumer parses the credential itself, or a raw token or user-record type is threaded through the layers: consumers are coupled to one mechanism, two layers can disagree about who the caller is, attributes are re-derived per component, and values that were never verified get treated as authenticated.
Systems that establish identity once at a trust boundary and consume it in many places afterwards, and that have (or expect to have) more than one authentication mechanism feeding the same authorization and domain logic: server-side request processing (filters, middleware, interceptors, handlers), enterprise applications in front of JAAS, an STS or an identity provider, and service meshes where mTLS, bearer tokens and session cookies meet.
A web API reached by several mechanisms at once - session cookie for the browser app, bearer token for mobile clients, mTLS for service-to-service calls - where every path ends in the same descriptor and controllers and policies are written once.
An enterprise application behind a JAAS login module, an STS or an identity provider: the validated authentication result is converted into the descriptor, which carries subject id, roles and tenant for downstream authorization and audit.
A multi-tenant SaaS where tenant membership and subject identity travel together, so repository-level guards enforce isolation by reading one attribute instead of trusting a request parameter.
Support and impersonation workflows: the descriptor records acting subject and impersonated subject separately, so audit names both while authorization evaluates the acting one.
An authorization engine or policy decision point that expects subject attributes as input: the descriptor is serialized into the policy request instead of the raw token.
Migrating off a legacy identity stack (JAAS, Windows identities, a homegrown user table) to OIDC: consumers are switched to the descriptor first, and the mechanism behind it is replaced second.
Java SE with JAAS: login modules of any type assemble one javax.security.auth.Subject holding the caller's Principals plus public/private credential sets, and application code running inside Subject.doAs authorizes from the principals without ever touching the ticket that logged the subject in.
An ASP.NET Core app with cookie, JWT-bearer and certificate handlers registered as separate authentication schemes: each handler turns its verified credential into the same ClaimsPrincipal on HttpContext.User, so [Authorize] and authorization policies inspect claims whichever scheme authenticated the request.
A Spring Security application combining form login, OAuth2/OIDC login and mTLS: every AuthenticationProvider emits the same authenticated Authentication object inside a SecurityContext held by the SecurityContextHolder, so @PreAuthorize rules and domain services read one subject shape for all mechanisms.

statement: Define a correlated asynchronous question-and-answer exchange with a temporary reply destination, a bounded wait, cancellation, and explicit late-reply disposal.
name: request-reply
document:
request-reply
request-response
request-response messaging
Let a sender obtain a result or a domain error from an asynchronous or remote receiver by pairing each request with a correlated reply, and give the missing reply a defined outcome: timeout, cancellation and disposal of late replies.
Messaging is one-way, but the sender frequently needs a return value or a domain error from the receiver before it can continue. Without an agreed reply destination, a way to match replies to requests, and a rule for what happens when no reply arrives, the caller either blocks forever, mis-associates the next reply with the wrong request, or accumulates pending state it never cleans up.
Asynchronous interaction across a process, thread or network boundary where the caller cannot continue without the receiver's result: HTTP/gRPC-style RPC, broker-based RPC over a queue, actor or thread mailboxes, and browser-to-server exchanges over a socket. It applies when the interaction is naturally one request and one reply, and each exchange has a bounded deadline.
Service-to-service RPC where the caller needs the result to continue (HTTP, gRPC, or a broker-based RPC queue such as the RabbitMQ tutorial's rpc_queue).
Command dispatch that must return a domain error - a validation failure or business rejection - rather than only an acknowledgement of receipt.
In-process actor or thread mailboxes: ask a worker for state with a deadline so the caller can never block forever.
Front-end over a WebSocket asking the server for a value correlated by message id or acknowledgement callback.
Talking to devices, sensors or legacy systems over a socket whose protocol is inherently one request and one response.
Querying a cache or index cluster from a client library where each call is a key lookup with a per-call deadline.
NATS request-reply service calls: a client publishes with a unique inbox as the reply subject and waits for a response under a per-request timeout.
RabbitMQ RPC over an rpc_queue: the client sends reply_to and a unique correlation_id, then matches the worker's response on its callback queue.
gRPC unary RPC: a generated client stub sends one request and receives one response under a propagated deadline, with cancellation available for abandoned work.

statement: Define a correlated asynchronous question-and-answer exchange with a temporary reply destination, a bounded wait, cancellation, and explicit late-reply disposal.
name: return-address
document:
return-address
reply-to
callback queue
Let a requester embed the address of the channel where the answer should be delivered in the request itself, so a replier can respond to any caller without knowing who they are, where they are, or which of many clients is waiting.
In request-reply messaging the replier must send its answer somewhere, yet it usually cannot know where: requesters are anonymous, ephemeral, behind NAT or a firewall, or simply one of many clients. Hard-coding a reply destination per caller couples the service to its callers and breaks as soon as a reply has to go somewhere else than the sender's usual inbound channel.
Request-reply over a message broker or message-capable transport (AMQP, JMS, NATS, MQTT 5, ZeroMQ, socket and callback protocols), where requests and replies travel on different channels and the requester's inbound address is either dynamic (temporary or exclusive queue, inbox subject, socket id, ack slot) or private and therefore not derivable by the replier. The same decision appears inside a process whenever an asynchronous request value must carry its own reply handle.
RPC over RabbitMQ, NATS or JMS: the client declares an exclusive callback queue (or uses a direct reply-to pseudo queue) and workers answer to the address carried by the request.
Scatter-gather: every sub-request carries the aggregator's reply channel so partial results converge on the component that joined the fan-out.
A messaging gateway in front of a synchronous client (HTTP, WebSocket): the gateway puts its inbound connection's reply slot into the request so the far side can answer asynchronously.
Mobile and IoT devices behind NAT with short-lived connections: the request names a response topic, inbox or device shadow address instead of the device's unreachable socket address.
Serverless and edge functions that must answer into a still-open callback URL, WebSocket or ack slot rather than to a fixed queue.
Per-tenant or per-request isolation where each request gets its own reply channel that can be firewalled, metered and expired independently.
NATS Core request-reply: the client subscribes to a unique inbox subject, carries that subject as the request's reply address, and the service publishes its response there; request() adds timeout and no-responders handling.
MQTT 5 request/response as documented by RabbitMQ: the requester subscribes to a Response Topic and sends it with the request, while the responder publishes the reply there and echoes Correlation Data.

statement: Define a correlated asynchronous question-and-answer exchange with a temporary reply destination, a bounded wait, cancellation, and explicit late-reply disposal.
name: correlation-identifier
document:
correlation-identifier
correlation id
correlation-id
request id
trace id
Give every request a unique request id and have the replier echo it as the correlation id of the reply, so a requestor with many requests in flight can match each reply to the request that caused it without per-request channels, sessions or shared state.
A requestor multiplexes several requests over one shared channel or connection — or one reply queue serves many clients — so replies can arrive out of order, on an arbitrary thread and with nothing in the transport that says which request they answer. Without an identifier the requestor cannot tell which waiting caller should receive a reply, or silently mis-delivers it, and a late reply to an abandoned request corrupts the next one.
Message-based request-reply over a shared reply path: one callback queue per client (AMQP/JMS), one duplex connection carrying many concurrent exchanges (JSON-RPC over WebSocket, a custom TCP or binary protocol), an actor mailbox, or an in-process dispatch loop with many outstanding calls. It also applies when replies traverse intermediaries that do not preserve ordering, and to distributed tracing, where the identifier travels in a header so spans in different services can be stitched into one trace. In event-driven systems the same pattern stitches commands to their resulting events across service boundaries.
RPC over a shared queue: one callback queue per client and the AMQP correlation_id (or JMS JMSCorrelationID) property selecting the pending call — the mechanism the RabbitMQ RPC tutorial is built around.
Multiplexing thousands of request/response exchanges over one duplex connection — JSON-RPC over WebSocket, a binary protocol, or a database driver pipelining statements — where a request id in each frame is the only association available.
Actor ask: a temporary actor (Akka ask, Erlang-style reply ref) or a request id echoed in the protocol ties the response back to the sender's future when the protocol has no reply correlation of its own.
Batched or long-polling transports that pack several requests into one round trip and dispatch the responses by identifier.
Distributed tracing: the W3C trace-context header carries trace-id and parent-id across service hops so spans produced by different processes can be stitched into a single trace.
In-process hand-off between callers and a shared dispatch loop: a promise/future/continuation table keyed by the id (tokio oneshot senders in a map, TaskCompletionSource in a dictionary, CompletableDeferred in a coroutine map) when one reader serves many waiters.
Event-driven choreography: a command event carries a correlation_id (constant across the entire operation) and a causation_id (pointing to the immediate parent). The responding service echoes the correlation_id in the reply event, preserving the chain across Kafka topics or message buses.
Saga orchestration: each step of a saga carries the saga's correlation id so compensating transactions can be identified and correlated to the original saga instance even across service restarts.
Webhook and callback integrations: an external service calls back with a correlation id that the original sender minted, so the callback can be routed to the right pending handler without a registered endpoint.
Database driver request pipelining: multiple SQL statements are sent in one network round-trip and responses are dispatched back to the correct awaiter by the server-supplied request id.
Azure Service Bus makes the pattern a broker feature: the sender sets MessageId and ReplyTo, the consumer replies to the ReplyTo destination and copies the request's MessageId into the reply's CorrelationId (correlation-id header) — the documented simple request/reply mechanic.
Envoy mints a UUID x-request-id for every external request, preserves it on internal hops (governed by generate_request_id, use_remote_address and preserve_external_request_id) and binds it to access logs and trace sampling — the request id generated once at the edge and propagated by every host.
