name: message
document:
message
message envelope
Package the information a boundary must carry into one self-describing unit - a header section the messaging infrastructure can read, route and mediate on, plus a body that travels unchanged - so that senders, mediators and receivers share a uniform unit of communication without sharing a payload schema.
A boundary must carry data between parties that do not share a domain model. Without one agreed unit of communication every endpoint invents its own record shape: the transport cannot route, filter, enrich, trace or selectively log without parsing payloads, each mediator becomes coupled to every payload schema, and adding a consumer, a transport or a policy means renegotiating the framing with every producer.
Message-oriented and request/response boundaries between processes, services or systems - brokers and queues, RPC, HTTP, mail, event buses - where more than two parties (or middleware the endpoints do not own) inspect the traffic, where the payload format must evolve independently of routing metadata, and where the transport should stay replaceable. The decision is a data-shape one, taken together with the channel (Message Channel) and the message type (Command/Document/Event Message).
Events and commands across services on a broker, where record/message headers carry the routing and idempotency metadata and the key/value or body carries the payload.
HTTP and gRPC APIs: request and response types pair a header block with a content-typed body, and gateways, sidecars and proxies route on the metadata alone.
Integration middleware that must route, filter, enrich or translate traffic for schemas it does not own — the mediators work entirely in the header section.
Store-and-forward packages such as mail (MIME headers plus body) and file transfer, where disposition, content type and origin live in headers and the payload stays opaque.
Long-running asynchronous workflows: correlation id, causation id, trace context, timestamp and expiry ride in the headers while payloads stay domain-specific and versioned independently.
Dead-lettering and message store scenarios where a message must be captured, inspected and replayed later; the header/body split makes both metadata queries and payload replay possible.
Kafka and event-streaming platforms: messages carry partition keys, offset metadata, schema version and trace context in headers while the body carries the domain event, enabling platform tooling to operate without payload parsing.
Cross-bounded-context integration with DDD: each bounded context owns its payload semantics; the envelope carries only technical metadata (type, version, source, tenant) so an anti-corruption layer can translate at context boundaries.
CDC (Change Data Capture) feeds from databases, where the envelope carries operation type, change sequence, source system and capture timestamp while the body carries the changed record.
Multi-region and multi-tenant platforms: envelope metadata carries tenant markers, region indicators and security classifications so routing, isolation and compliance auditing operate at the infrastructure layer.
Spring Integration's Message<T> abstraction: MessageHeaders carries correlation, content type and routing metadata while getPayload() remains the application payload, letting channels and endpoints mediate without owning its schema.
RabbitMQ AMQP publishers: Basic properties and headers (content type, message ID, correlation ID, reply-to, expiration and delivery mode) travel separately from the message body, so exchanges and consumers can use delivery metadata while payload codecs remain endpoint-owned.
Apache Camel routes: org.apache.camel.Message keeps a body, headers, message ID and timestamp inside an Exchange, so processors can enrich or route metadata while leaving payload handling to endpoints.

statement: Define a correlated asynchronous question-and-answer exchange with a temporary reply destination, a bounded wait, cancellation, and explicit late-reply disposal.
name: message-expiration
document:
message-expiration
message TTL
expiring message
Attach a time limit to a message so that the messaging system and the receiver can discard it once it is no longer viable, instead of delivering work whose result has stopped being meaningful.
A message that arrived too late is worse than no message: its data or request no longer describes reality, yet the receiver cannot tell 'late' from 'still valid' unless the sender said so. Queues, retry cycles and durable subscriptions therefore keep carrying work nobody wants, and request-reply partners wait for answers that no longer matter.
Asynchronous messaging where delivery is not real-time: brokers with backlog and dead-letter paths, retry pipelines, durable subscriptions, off-peak batching, and any request-reply exchange with a bounded waiting period. Applying it requires a sender that can state the freshness requirement, an enforcement point (broker TTL or consumer check), and - to stay observable - a destination for expired messages.
Request-reply over messaging: quotes, confirmations or RPC-style answers that must not be applied after the waiting period has ended.
Market data, telemetry and sensor readings where a late value is not merely old but wrong (price ticks, positions, bidding rounds).
Time-boxed workflow steps: approvals, SLA escalations and reservations whose window closes at a known instant.
Cache or read-model update messages that must not overwrite newer state once superseded.
Poison-message and retry handling that bounds the total age of a message so it cannot be requeued past its usefulness.
Publish-subscribe retention for durable subscribers, where a backlog is kept only as long as replaying it is legitimate (Google Pub/Sub message_retention_duration).
In-process work queues (thread pools, actor mailboxes, async mailboxes) where an item produced by a request that has already timed out must not be executed.
RabbitMQ queues with x-message-ttl or per-message expiration plus a dead-letter exchange, where queue-head evaluation and per-queue copies make the expiry enforcement boundary explicit.
Azure Service Bus queues and topics with per-message TimeToLive bounded by DefaultTimeToLive and TTLExpiredException dead-lettering, for commands or replies whose usefulness ends at an enqueue-time deadline.
Google Cloud Pub/Sub subscriptions with message-retention-duration (and optional acknowledged-message retention), for bounded replay of durable-subscription backlogs; pair retention with consumer-side freshness checks when old events must not be applied.

statement: Define a correlated asynchronous question-and-answer exchange with a temporary reply destination, a bounded wait, cancellation, and explicit late-reply disposal.
name: transaction-script
document:
transaction-script
service object
Organizes the business logic of a single request as one procedure - read the data it needs, validate and calculate, write the results and complete in one database transaction - trading object-model structure for a straight-line implementation that can be read top to bottom.
A request-scoped use case (book a room, place an order, recognize revenue, import a file) has to be implemented, and its logic mixes input validation, calculation and persistence. Modelling the domain as objects may be premature, or the team may not be ready for it, yet the implementation still needs each request's steps to stay visible and its transaction boundary to be explicit.
Applies where business logic is simple to moderately complex, where the system is naturally described as a series of transactions each driven by one request (HTTP handler, CLI command, queue message, batch job), and where a thin data-source gateway or the database itself is the persistence seam. Also the right starting point under delivery pressure or for a team new to domain modelling - provided the growth path to a Domain Model is watched deliberately.
Booking a hotel room: check availability, calculate the rate, insert the booking and confirm - one request, one transaction.
Revenue recognition (Fowler's example): given a contract and an as-of date, calculate the recognitions and persist them, or report the revenue already recognized.
CRUD write endpoints in a simple admin or back-office application where each screen maps to one operation.
Batch and integration jobs: import a file, validate rows, write the accepted rows and report the rejects in one transaction per batch.
Queue or message handlers that carry out one command (place order, cancel subscription, refund payment) and acknowledge only after commit.
Reporting and ETL steps that read a slice of data, transform it and write results, where the logic is genuinely a straight line of steps.
Django request-atomicity: with ATOMIC_REQUESTS enabled (or @transaction.atomic on the view), the whole view function is the script - Django begins the transaction at request start, commits on a successful response and rolls back on exception, exactly the one-script-one-transaction shape.
Laravel request handlers that wrap the validate-calculate-persist sequence in a DB::transaction closure: the closure commits when it returns and rolls back automatically if it throws, so the closure body is the script and its extent is the boundary.
Spring @Transactional service methods: an AOP proxy begins the transaction before the method and commits after it returns, making each annotated method a Transaction Script whose signature is the request and whose boundary is declarative.

name: bulkhead
document:
bulkhead
bulkhead isolation
cell-based architecture
Partition finite shared capacity at the failure domain (dependency, tenant, priority class, or cell) into independently bounded pools or permits, with an explicit queue and saturation policy, so one slow, saturated, or failing participant cannot consume capacity reserved for others.
Several dependencies or tenants share thread, connection, worker, or permit pools. When one becomes slow, leaky, or overloaded, its calls hold shared slots and fill shared queues, so unrelated work queues and fails behind it; the design needs a boundary that contains resource exhaustion without pretending to isolate CPU, network, or server-side limits that remain shared.
Any component whose concurrency is a finite resource: a service calling multiple downstream APIs, a multi-tenant workload, a job runner mixing interactive and batch work, or an inference and gateway tier with per-deployment quotas. The failure mode to contain is degradation and overload (slow dependency, connection leak, traffic spike), not only hard failure, and the isolation boundary must be chosen at the failure domain - instance, dependency, tenant or priority class.
A service that calls several downstream APIs through one shared HTTP client: give each downstream its own connection and thread budget so one hanging endpoint cannot block the others.
Multi-tenant SaaS where one tenant's workload must not consume the concurrency available to other tenants (per-tenant pools).
Interactive request traffic sharing a database with batch or report jobs: separate pools per workload class keep the database from serialising everything behind the batch.
An API gateway or backend-for-frontend routing to many backends with per-route concurrency caps, so a slow backend does not consume the proxy's shared capacity.
Job workers that mix latency-critical and background queues: per-queue worker pools prevent a backlog of background jobs from starving urgent work.
Inference and AI serving where each model deployment has its own concurrency quota and a saturated model must not consume the shared request capacity.
Cell-based architectures: each cell (complete, independent service instance) is a bulkhead partition; load grows by adding cells, and a failure is contained to the single cell — used at AWS, Google, and Netflix scale.
Shuffle sharding: Amazon Route 53-style virtual shard assignment where each tenant is assigned to a random shard of two or more cells; with eight cells and two-per-shard there are 28 unique shards, so a problem affects only 1/28th of tenants — far better than regular per-cell partitioning.
AI and inference workloads: per-deployment or per-tenant Azure OpenAI or LLM deployment quotas prevent one saturated model from consuming the shared request capacity across the platform.
Database RU isolation: Azure Cosmos DB request-unit throughput assigned per container acts as a storage-layer bulkhead; one noisy container cannot exhaust the RU budget of others.
Resilience4j's SemaphoreBulkhead and FixedThreadPoolBulkhead give a JVM service per-dependency permits versus a bounded queue and worker pool; choose based on whether caller threads may be occupied.
Netflix Hystrix's per-command thread pools or semaphore isolation reject work and route it to fallback, containing a slow downstream to its command boundary (historical and deprecated).
.NET services use Polly's BulkheadPolicy/AsyncBulkheadPolicy (maxParallelization plus maxQueuingActions, rejecting with BulkheadRejectedException when both are full); Polly v8 replaced it with ConcurrencyLimiter over System.Threading.RateLimiting, whose partitioned per-key limiters give per-tenant bulkheads.
Service meshes enforce bulkheads at the platform layer: an Istio DestinationRule's trafficPolicy.connectionPool caps tcp.maxConnections, http.http1MaxPendingRequests and http.http2MaxRequests per upstream host, enforced by Envoy alongside its circuit-breaking limits.
Netflix's concurrency-limits library replaces hand-tuned static partitions with per-dependency adaptive limits (Vegas and Gradient algorithms modelled on TCP congestion control) that shrink the concurrency budget automatically as downstream latency rises, e.g. separating live from batch traffic on one gRPC server.
Envoy maintains per-upstream-cluster connection pools and circuit-breaking limits, while Kubernetes ResourceQuota caps aggregate namespace CPU, memory, or object use; both are platform-level capacity partitions rather than application call-site wrappers.

name: version-number
document:
version-number
rowversion
entity versioning
Store a version token alongside each persistent record and make every write assert the token it read, so a write computed from stale data fails as a detectable conflict instead of silently overwriting a newer value.
Two sessions read the same record, both edit it, and the later write wins: the earlier update vanishes without any error (the lost update). Once the read-modify-write spans more than one system transaction the database cannot tell 'this is the record I read' from 'this record changed under me', so no code path can notice in time - unless the record itself carries a per-row token that changes on every write and the write tests that token before committing.
Applies to records that outlive the transaction that read them: edits spanning user think time, a web form round-trip, an offline client, a batch worker holding aggregates, or any read-modify-write over data other writers touch in between. It needs a store that can test the token and change the record in one atomic step (a conditional UPDATE, a compare-and-swap, a document revision check) and a caller willing to act on the conflict - re-read, merge, retry, or report. It assumes conflicts are the exception; when they are the rule a pessimistic lock prevents the wasted work instead.
Web forms and editors: a record is loaded into a page, edited for minutes or hours, then saved - the token makes the stale save fail instead of clobbering the other editor's change.
Distributed workers applying commands to the same entity: the second worker's write is rejected so it can refresh and re-apply, giving first-writer-wins with no held lock.
Data mappers and units of work: every dirty entity flushed at commit carries the version it was loaded with, so the whole transaction aborts on the first stale row.
Document stores and revision-based APIs: Mongoose's __v with optimisticConcurrency, CouchDB-style revisions, or a REST ETag/If-Match precondition all expose the same per-document token.
Leases, leader election and configuration records: one row represents ownership or a monotonic generation, and a write must prove it still holds the revision it acted on.
Offline or mobile sync: clients push edits made against a snapshot taken days earlier, and the version check decides which edits apply directly and which must go through a merge.
Hibernate ORM / JPA @Version: the mapper owns an integer (or timestamp) version property, appends it to every UPDATE's WHERE clause, bumps it on flush and raises StaleObjectStateException / OptimisticLockException when zero rows match, so the application code never writes the predicate by hand.
DynamoDB conditional writes: each item carries a Version attribute; UpdateItem sends ConditionExpression 'Version = :read_value' and increments Version in the same request, and ConditionalCheckFailedException is the conflict signal that triggers a bounded re-read-and-retry — the same contract exposed as @DynamoDBVersionAttribute in the enhanced client.
Cassandra lightweight transactions: UPDATE ... SET col = ? WHERE id = ? IF col = ? is a Paxos-backed compare-and-set, giving the token test linearizable semantics across replicas — at a documented cost (roughly four extra round-trips per conditional write), so it is reserved for rows that genuinely need the guard.

name: make-illegal-states-unrepresentable
document:
make-illegal-states-unrepresentable
make invalid states unrepresentable
Encode each domain rule in the shape of the data type so that values violating the rule cannot be constructed at all, replacing scattered run-time validation and defensive checks with a model in which only legal states exist.
Domain values are modelled as one record with independent fields - a status tag plus several nullable or optional attributes, or a handful of booleans - so the type admits every combination of those fields, including the ones the business rules forbid. Consumers cannot trust the type: each branch re-checks which fields are meaningful, the same guard is written in several places (and forgotten in one), and illegal states become runtime bugs that surface when a code path finally combines the wrong flags.
Applies when a value has a small, known set of mutually exclusive shapes whose payloads differ, when the same invalid combination keeps being defended against in several places, and when the language can close a set of variants (Rust/Swift enums, sealed hierarchies, discriminated unions) or at least hide constructors. It is equally a boundary discipline: untrusted input is parsed once into a type whose existence already proves it is valid, so no downstream code has to re-validate.
Lifecycle and state machines: orders, payments, subscriptions, bookings and connection states, one variant per state carrying exactly the data that exists in that state.
Client and API request state: a loading/success/error union instead of a data field, an error field and an isLoading flag that can contradict one another.
Message and protocol modelling: a closed set of commands, events or JSON payload shapes decoded once and dispatched with an exhaustive match (event sourcing, interpreters, RPC handlers).
Refined scalars that travel through the model: money with currency, email addresses, quantities with units and identifiers that are parsed once and never re-validated.
Configuration whose combinations are illegal: TLS settings that only apply when TLS is enabled, cursor-based versus offset pagination, mutually exclusive feature flags.
Import and deserialization boundaries: convert untrusted rows, CSV cells, query parameters or JSON into domain types with a failing factory, so invalid input cannot travel further.
Rust's standard `Option`/`Result` enums and exhaustive `match` make presence, absence, success and failure explicit cases that downstream code must handle at compile time (Rust Reference/Book).
Swift enums with associated values and exhaustive `switch` model state-specific payloads such as error cases without nullable companion fields (The Swift Programming Language).
Kotlin sealed classes and interfaces with exhaustive `when` expressions provide a closed hierarchy for finite state machines and error/result models, with the compiler checking that every known case is handled.

name: table-module
document:
table-module
Organise the domain logic of a table or view as one module with a single instance whose operations act on whole sets of rows, so table-shaped rules are written once against tabular record sets instead of being scattered over per-row objects or per-request procedures.
The rules for a table are set-shaped - recalculating a column across all rows, validating an import batch, posting a period, aggregating or exporting a whole table - and the platform already speaks in tables and record sets (result sets, DataTables, grids, reports). A Domain Model would build one object per row and pay for identity, hydration and per-object behaviour the rules never use, while a Transaction Script repeats the same table-shaped logic in every use case that touches the table.
Data-centric enterprise applications with moderate, table-shaped logic: batch jobs, imports and reconciliation, reporting and export modules, and applications whose UI and data tooling is table-based (typed DataSets, data grids, report engines). It assumes that data access is already provided by a Table Data Gateway or equivalent, and that callers - typically a Service Layer - own the transaction boundary around the module's calls.
Periodic batch posting: recompute balances or fees for every row in a period in one set-oriented pass.
Import and reconciliation: validate, normalise and promote a staging table before its rows become live data, reporting row-level errors as a batch.
Reporting and export modules that fetch a record set for a grid, report engine or CSV/Excel export, where tabular output is the goal.
Bulk recalculation after a rule change: apply a corrected formula to all existing rows of a table without loading them into a model.
Small-to-medium applications where each table has a handful of well-defined operations and no rich invariants spanning rows or tables.
Cleansing and reconciliation jobs over an operational table where the database should do the heavy lifting (aggregate, update ... where) and the application only orchestrates.
.NET ADO.NET typed DataSet / typed DataTable modules: the generated table is the record set, business methods operate over all its rows and it binds directly to grids and report controls.
Ruby on Rails set-oriented surface: an ActiveRecord::Relation scoped to one table applies table-wide rules via update_all/delete_all as a single SQL statement without instantiating row models, whose official documentation warns that validations and callbacks are skipped so the statement must carry the rule.
Django set-wide recalculation: QuerySet.update() and bulk_update() write whole filtered sets with direct SQL that bypasses per-row save(), used exactly where per-object persistence would mean one round trip per row.

name: compound-components
document:
compound-components
compound component
compound component pattern
Give a family of cooperating components one owner — the parent — that holds the shared state and publishes it implicitly to every child, so consumers compose the family declaratively while the parent alone enforces its invariants and behaviour.
A widget only works when a parent and its children agree on one piece of state (which option is selected, which panel is open, whether a field is invalid), but the call site is the only place that knows the children. Holding the state at the call site means threading the value and its update callbacks into every child (prop drilling), and holding it in the children means the parent cannot enforce the family's invariants — exclusivity, ordering, keyboard behaviour — nor react to a child's change in one place. The recurring decision is where the shared state lives and how children participate in it without the call site wiring them.
Component-tree UI code: design-system and widget libraries (select/option, tabs, menus, field groups) in frameworks that can inject state into descendants without passing it through props — React context or child cloning, Angular content projection plus DI, Vue provide/inject, Compose CompositionLocal and slot scopes, SwiftUI environment and preference keys, Blazor cascading values, WPF attached properties over the logical tree — and in widget toolkits whose group objects (Swing ButtonGroup, JavaFX ToggleGroup, Qt QButtonGroup, tkinter control variables) play the same role. It pays off where the public API must stay small and the children must stay replaceable; it does not apply in languages without a component tree or without an implicit-injection channel.
Custom select, combobox or autocomplete families built from Option children — the canonical example: the parent owns the selection, the highlight and the keyboard interaction while options only declare their value and label.
Tabs, accordions and menus where Tab/TabPanel/MenuItem children register their identity and the parent owns the active item, the ordering and the ARIA wiring.
Form-field families (Field + Label + Input + Error) that share one validation/invalid state and generated ids without the call site passing them around.
Data-group widgets: tables with Column definitions, list widgets with Item children, tree views with Node children, chart legends with Series children.
Design-system libraries that export one namespaced symbol whose parts must be used together — the context in which the pattern is most often documented and most valuable.
Collapsible panel families (Disclosure pattern) where a parent owns the open/closed state and Trigger/Content children read it — also known as the Disclosure pattern in ARIA authoring practices.
Stepper/wizard widgets where a parent owns current-step state and Step/StepIndicator children read it without the consumer threading step indices.
Popover/tooltip families where a trigger button and a content panel share open/close state through the parent without prop drilling.
Radix UI Primitives — Dialog.Root owns the open/close context and Trigger/Portal/Content/Title/Description consume it, while asChild (Slot) merges each part's props, refs and keyboard behaviour into the consumer's own button or link.
Ark UI headless components (built on Zag.js state machines) — Popover.Root/Trigger/Positioner/Content share state through the root, ids props compose aria bindings across two families, and the same compound anatomy works in React, Solid, Vue and Svelte.
Headless UI's Dialog family (Dialog, DialogBackdrop, DialogPanel, DialogTitle, Description) — the root enforces the dismiss contract (open prop, onClose callback, focus trap, aria-labelledby) and every part reads the shared open/closed state, exposed for styling as data-open/data-closed attributes.

name: applicative
document:
applicative
applicative functor
applicative style
idiom (original McBride-Paterson name)
Apply one pure function to several independent effectful computations, letting the chosen context instance fix the semantics of absence, failure, ordering, and concurrency; the combining structure is fixed before execution - that static shape is what enables batching, parallel scheduling, and static analysis - and an accumulating error instance reports every independent failure instead of short-circuiting on the first.
You have several independent computations - parse this field, fetch that record, validate this quantity - and a pure function that combines their results, but each result lives inside a context such as Option, Either/Result, List, Promise/Task, or Validation. A bind/await chain can imply a dependency that does not exist, serialize work, or stop at the first failure; you need a fixed applicative structure that combines the values while leaving failure and scheduling policy to the chosen instance.
Value- or effect-level functional code where independent combination is the recurring decision: form and request validation that must report every field error at once, parallel-capable fetch coordination, configuration or tuple assembly from independent parses, and parser/stream composition. Applies when the language offers a context type (or validator abstraction) and the team accepts a small abstraction - a type class in Scala/Kotlin, a stdlib combinator such as Promise.all, or a hand-written lift2 - to express 'apply a pure function to several effectful arguments'. Applicative structure permits parallel execution but does not itself guarantee scheduling, cancellation, or error accumulation.
Form, request or configuration validation where every field is checked independently and the user must see all violations in one response.
Combining independent parses of a record (age, e-mail, quantity, date range) into one constructed value, reporting every malformed field.
Parallel IO combination: fetching several unrelated resources (Promise.all, CompletableFuture.thenCombine, parZipOrAccumulate, errgroup fan-out) and pairing the results positionally.
Parser and stream combinators where several parsers/subscribers consume the same input independently and their results are combined into a node.
Building a read model or report from several independent queries where a failure of one part should be reported without cancelling the others.
Statistics/diagnostics: computing several independent measurements of the same input and combining them with a pure summary function.
DSLs and embedded languages: building an abstract syntax tree of applicative operations (Free Applicative) that can be statically analyzed, optimized, or pretty-printed before interpretation - enabling query planning, dead code elimination, or validation of DSL constraints at construction time.
Traversable data structures: threading an Applicative effect through a container (tree, list, optional) so each element can be independently validated, transformed, or fetched without sequential coupling.
Collecting monoidal summaries: using Const as the Applicative to fold a Traversable structure into a single Monoid value (e.g., collecting all validation errors, or computing a checksum) without materializing a transformed structure.
API gateway aggregation: combining multiple downstream service calls where each call is independent and all results (or all errors) should be collected before returning a response to the caller.
Configuration loading at startup: validating all config fields independently and reporting every misconfiguration at once rather than failing on the first missing key.
CSV or batch row validation: validating each row independently and accumulating all row-level errors so the entire batch can be rejected with a full error report rather than failing on the first bad row.
Bidirectional codec composition: building parsers and serializers (e.g., with prismatic/schema, io-ts, or hkj's ValidatedPrism) where the parse direction is accumulating and fallible but the build direction is total, preserving the parse-don't-validate discipline applicatively.
GraphQL API input validation: validate independent arguments and return all field-level errors in one response instead of rejecting at the first failure.
Kubernetes or Helm configuration loading: validate independent keys and report the complete set of startup misconfigurations before deployment.
CI/CD pipeline policy checks: run independent static checks over a change and aggregate diagnostics before gating the build.
Haxl at Meta/Facebook: an applicative Fetch whose <*> explores both operands before blocking, so independent dataFetch calls to the same data source batch into one request and run concurrently without explicit forking ("There is no Fork", ICFP 2014).
Swift structured concurrency: async let starts each independent task as a child task immediately and a later await combines the results into a tuple or constructor call - applicative-shaped combination of a fixed set of independent effects in mainstream syntax, with cancellation and lifetime bounded by the enclosing scope.
Elm JSON decoders: Json.Decode map2..map8 (or elm-json-decode-pipeline's required/custom steps) assemble a record from independent per-field decoders - the production form of mapN in front-end code.

name: iterator
document:
iterator
cursor
enumerator
Provide a way to access the elements of an aggregate object sequentially without exposing its underlying representation, by moving traversal state and the traversal algorithm out of the aggregate into a separate iterator object.
Traversal leaks into every client: code that walks a collection has to know its storage layout (array indices, node links, hash buckets), the same loop is rewritten once per aggregate and once per client, and adding a new traversal order means changing the aggregate's interface — which is exactly what prevents algorithms from being written once and applied to any collection.
Applies wherever a collection with a non-trivial or changeable representation must be traversed by outsiders: collection libraries, trees and graphs with several traversal orders, lazy or unbounded sources, and streaming pipelines. It matters most when more than one traversal may be pending at the same time, when the storage must stay hidden for encapsulation or safety, or when traversal algorithms must be added without touching the aggregate; the toolchain only decides which realization is available (a language iteration protocol, generators, lazy sequences, or a hand-written cursor).
Collection libraries that must serve arrays, linked lists, trees, and hash tables through one protocol — e.g. std::begin/end in C++, java.util.Iterator, IEnumerable<T> in C#, Symbol.iterator in JavaScript, IntoIterator in Rust.
Tree and graph APIs exposing depth-first, breadth-first, in-order, or post-order traversal without publishing node links or parent pointers, enabling clients to walk composite structures without coupling to the storage representation.
Lazy or unbounded sources consumed one element at a time: file lines (BufferedReader.lines()), network socket streams, paginated API responses, sensor data, event streams, and generated sequences (random numbers, Fibonacci, permutations).
Streaming data pipelines (map/filter/reduce over any iterable) that stay O(1) in memory regardless of input size, implemented via itertools, Java Stream API, Kotlin Sequence, C++ ranges, Rust iterator adapters, or Go iter package.
Legacy or third-party aggregates whose internal layout must stay private behind a stable traversal interface, allowing the aggregate to refactor its storage without breaking existing clients.
Custom containers that must participate in the language's own for/foreach/for-in/for-await loop, spread operators, destructuring assignment, or list comprehensions.
Database result sets and ORM cursors where the full result set is never materialised in memory; the iterator fetches pages on demand.
Parser and lexer token streams where the input is consumed incrementally and the full source may not fit in memory.
Async I/O pipelines where the iteration protocol yields Promises (JavaScript async generators, C# IAsyncEnumerable<T>, Python async generators) enabling for-await iteration over network responses or file reads.
Multidimensional collection traversal (matrices, nested lists, spatial grids) via flattened iterators that expose a flat index space while hiding the multi-dimensional layout.
Paginated REST or GraphQL API clients where a client-side iterator transparently fetches successive pages as the consumer pulls elements, keeping memory constant regardless of result set size.
Kafka, log-processor, or ETL pipelines where each stage is a transforming iterator: parse → filter → enrich → validate → sink, with each stage evaluated lazily.
Event-driven systems using async iterators to consume WebSocket messages, SSE streams, or queue consumers through a uniform for-await-of interface.
Batch-processing jobs over large file sets (CSV, Parquet, NDJSON) where an iterator wraps a file reader and yields one record per next() call without loading the file into memory.
Cursor-based (keyset) pagination over large, live datasets where offset/limit pagination causes duplicates or missed rows when data is inserted or deleted mid-traversal; the iterator stores the last-seen key rather than a page offset, making traversal stable across concurrent modifications.
Iterator fusion in compilers and runtimes: adjacent map/filter/map chains fused into a single pass with zero intermediate allocation (Rust iterator adapters, Java Spliterators, Haskell stream fusion, C++ range views), giving lazy pipelines near-handwritten performance.
Parallel iterators for data-parallel workloads: Rust Rayon, Java parallel streams, and Kotlin asFlow().buffer() split the iterator across worker threads — identical interface to serial iteration, transparent parallel execution.
Reactive streams bridging pull and push: RxJava, RxJS, and Project Reactor implement backpressure (consumer signals demand, producer emits at requested rate), combining iterator's pull semantics with observer's push delivery.
LLM and streaming AI responses where the model yields tokens incrementally; an async iterator wraps the SSE/stream endpoint and the client consumes tokens one at a time via for-await-of, keeping first-token latency low and enabling progressive rendering.
Cursor-based database driver iterators (Node.js pg cursor, Python asyncpg, Go database/sql rows) where the driver streams rows from the server without loading the full result set, with configurable fetch size controlling server-side memory usage.
Java's Spliterator API exposes a cursor that can be advanced one element at a time or split into subranges for parallel streams; it demonstrates that an iterator contract can include explicit partitioning and size/order characteristics rather than only next().
.NET's IAsyncEnumerable<T> and IAsyncEnumerator<T> expose asynchronous pull iteration through await foreach; GetAsyncEnumerator(CancellationToken) makes cancellation part of the iterator boundary for network, file, and database streams.
WHATWG ReadableStream async iteration lets browser and server consumers use for-await-of over streamed chunks while the iterator locks a reader and defines whether early return() cancels or merely releases it.

name: update-method
document:
update-method
per-frame update
tick method
Give every live object one self-contained per-frame step and let a single driver call each object's step every frame, so behaviour advances one frame at a time while input and rendering stay responsive.
A running world is full of objects that each have to keep doing their own thing - guards patrolling, statues charging, agents acting - and the recurring decision is where one object's per-frame behaviour lives and how all those behaviours get driven. Coding a behaviour as a loop that runs to completion blocks input and rendering (the skeleton walks, but nobody sees it); coding it inline in the game loop turns the loop into a switchboard over every kind of object, so every new behaviour edits central code; and there is no way for two actors to evolve independently and simultaneously.
Real-time software with many concurrent live objects whose behaviour is mostly independent and must be simulated over time: games, agent-based simulations, animation and particle systems, tick-based servers and live visualisations. It is the natural partner of a frame driver (Game Loop) - the loop supplies the cadence, Update Method supplies the per-object step - and it becomes the wrong shape in turn-based or purely event-driven domains where nothing changes between inputs.
Real-time games and simulations with many concurrent actors: patrolling guards, projectiles, particle effects and crowd agents each advance themselves once per frame while the driver walks the collection.
Component-based engines where the parts of one entity evolve independently - rendering, physics and AI components each implement their own step and the engine's registry dispatches per component (Unity, MonoGame, Bevy, GameplayKit, libGDX).
Per-frame animation and effect timelines outside games: tween/spring systems, sprite animation and UI transitions advanced from the browser's frame callback or a UI toolkit's animation timer.
Tick-based servers and headless simulations: game servers, digital twins and agent-based models where each agent's behaviour is a resumable step and the world advances in whole discrete frames.
Tools, editors and dashboards with continuously animating scenes, where many independent scene items (markers, live charts, gizmos) must advance on every repaint without a central per-item switch.
Porting straight-line behaviour into a frame loop: turning a scripted sequence (walk left, walk right) into a per-frame step, either by storing explicit state or by using coroutines/generators to keep the code linear.
Godot's SceneTree is the driver: a node opts into the walk with set_process(true) and its _process(delta) runs every render frame with the frame time passed in as an argument, while _physics_process(delta) is called at a fixed rate - so one object can implement two steps on two clocks and can leave the walk entirely (set_process(false)) instead of paying an enabled-flag check every frame.
Engines whose built-in driver leaves per-object order unspecified expose the order as configuration: Unity states you should not rely on the order of Update across GameObjects, so real projects fix dependencies through the Script Execution Order panel, a LateUpdate pass that runs after every Update, or the PlayerLoop API rather than through registration order.
Agent-based simulation models step whole populations in NetLogo: the go procedure runs ask turtles [ ... ] to give every agent its one turn and then tick advances the discrete clock - with documented semantics that agents take their turns in random order and only agents present when the ask began get to act.

name: side-effect-free-function
document:
side-effect-free-function
pure function
Put the model's logic into operations that compute a result from their inputs alone, so that a caller - and a test - can predict the result without knowing any state the operation might secretly touch.
Reasoning about a design becomes guesswork when operations do more than return a result: the caller must read the implementation and every delegation to know which state a call changes, and no result can be reproduced in a test without recreating the state around it. As rules compose, the number of hidden interactions grows faster than the behaviour being built, so the model stops being safely predictable.
Applies inside the model layer of any codebase whose rules are combined and composed - pricing, eligibility, allocation, validation - and where a computation must be exercised in tests without a database, clock or message broker in the loop. It matters most where several rules interact (composition multiplies hidden coupling) and in languages whose defaults are mutable objects, because there the discipline has to be stated rather than assumed.
Pricing and discount rules: unit prices, tax and rebates computed from immutable inputs, so the same basket always prices the same way.
Eligibility and specification checks: a rule expressed as a predicate over a value and reused in validation, selection and tests.
Money and quantity arithmetic: scaling, adding and rounding return new values instead of adjusting a running total in place.
Deriving test data and expected values from the same pure functions the model uses, instead of hand-copied golden values.
Query-side report assembly: projections, summaries and totals built by composing pure functions over already-loaded immutable data.
Memoizing an expensive domain computation, which is sound exactly because the function is referentially transparent.
Redux reducers: the store computes the next state by calling (previousState, action) => newState with no mutation, no clock, no randomness, so DevTools can replay a recorded action log and reproduce the exact state and useSelector can detect changes by reference comparison alone.
React function components: the official contract is that rendering must be a pure function of props, state and context, so React can cache components whose inputs are unchanged, abandon an outdated render mid-flight, and call each component twice in Strict Mode to expose impurity.
Haskell: ordinary functions are pure by default and effects are confined to IO-typed values, so the type signature itself states whether a computation touches the world and the compiler, not review, enforces the query half of the split.

name: monad
document:
monad
io monad
programmable semicolon
Give a computation's effect (absence, failure, asynchrony, I/O, state) a type of its own with a unit and a bind operation, so that a sequence of steps in which each step depends on the previous value composes into one pipeline while bind propagates the effect automatically.
Sequencing computations where the next step needs the previous step's result and every step may additionally be absent, failing, asynchronous or effectful pushes the effect handling into the business logic: nested null checks, try/catch ladders, callback pyramids. Every call site repeats the same propagation decision (short-circuit? await? log?) and one forgotten check turns a controlled failure into a crash or a wrong value.
Applies wherever a value and the fact that it is absent, pending, failing or impure belong together: chained lookups, validation and error pipelines, asynchronous call chains, state threading, parser and interpreter pipelines, and effect-typed application cores. It matters most when the sequence is long, when the effect policy must be uniform and testable, and when the language already provides monadic types (Optional, Result, Promise, IO) or syntax that desugars to bind (do-notation, for-comprehensions, async/await).
Chained lookups where any link may be missing: user -> address -> city expressed with Maybe/Optional instead of nested null checks.
Validation and error pipelines in which each step can fail with a domain error and the first failure must short-circuit (Either/Result, railway-oriented programming).
Asynchronous workflows whose next call depends on the previous response (Promise/async-await, CompletableFuture.thenCompose, Kotlin suspend functions, Swift Task).
Effect description and interpretation: building an IO/program value that is pure data and running it through different interpreters in tests and production (IO monad, tagless-final).
State-threading computations such as compiler passes, random generators or incremental traversals written as a State monad pipeline.
Parser combinators and nondeterministic search, where each step consumes the previous parse result or explores every value produced by the previous step (parser monad, List monad).
Rust's std::result::Result composes fallible steps with and_then and the ? operator, returning early on Err while keeping the successful value available to the next dependent step.
Java's CompletableFuture.thenCompose chains dependent asynchronous stages: the function returns another CompletionStage and the outer stage adopts its completion or exceptional failure.
Scala for-comprehensions over Option, collections, or other types with map, flatMap, and withFilter desugar dependent bindings into the corresponding combinators, keeping the monadic sequence readable without hiding its operations.

name: watchman
document:
watchman
dead man's switch
heartbeat monitor
Detect that a message flow has gone silent - not that a message failed - and tell a responsible person or system within a bounded time by comparing each flow's arrivals against the cadence its business deadline implies.
Message systems fail silently in the one way no error handler observes: nothing arrives. A producer stops emitting, a consumer stops draining, a scheduled job never fires, a credential expires, a partition goes offline - and because no failing code path is ever entered, error dashboards stay green while downstream data quietly goes stale. The recurring trigger: a flow whose absence is business-visible (a nightly feed, an order stream, a partner interface) has no owner-facing signal for 'no messages', so the gap is discovered late - by a customer or a downstream job - instead of by the team that can fix it.
Applies wherever messages are expected on a knowable cadence (event streams, queues, batch hand-offs, partner interfaces, device check-ins) and their absence is a business-visible failure: the flow has an owner, the expected period and grace window can be derived from a downstream deadline, and either the transport can be observed passively (queue counters, a wire tap) or the producers can emit out-of-band heartbeats. The watchman sits at message-flow or boundary scope - an in-process watcher beside the consumer, a periodic sweep over persisted last-seen state, or a rule in the monitoring stack fed by metrics - and it must itself be watched, because a silent watchman is exactly the failure it exists to catch.
Nightly batch or ETL feed: page the integration owner when the 02:00 import has produced no messages by its deadline, instead of noticing an empty report at the morning stand-up.
Business-critical event stream (orders, payments, telemetry): alarm when the produce rate stays at zero through business hours, which separates a healthy quiet topic from a stopped producer.
External partner interface: notify when no messages have arrived from a B2B partner within the agreed window, turning a looming SLA breach into an early, actionable alert.
Long-running workflow stage: require a heartbeat from each process-manager step so a stuck instance is noticed before the surrounding batch closes or a compensation becomes necessary.
Retry or dead-letter pump: verify that the pump still drains failed messages - silence means the pump died, not that the backlog is empty.
Fleet check-ins (edge devices, agents, cron jobs on many hosts): raise a per-device or per-site alarm when scheduled check-ins stop arriving.
The alerting pipeline itself: an always-firing watchdog alert routed to an external service, so a broken alert path is discovered by its silence.
Cron and scheduled-job fleet via Healthchecks.io: each job pings a unique URL, the service holds the Period and Grace Time, flips the check Late then Down when no ping arrives by period + grace, and notifies integrations.
Dashboard alert rules in Grafana: an alert rule whose query returns no series enters the No Data state and can raise a DatasourceNoData alert - the platform form of deciding what silence means (No Data, Alerting, Normal or Keep last state).
Apache Burrow for Kafka (LinkedIn): committed offsets are evaluated per partition over a sliding window and a consumer is classified STALLED when its offset is frozen with non-zero lag, or STOPPED when no new commits arrive - consumer-silence detection without fixed lag thresholds.

name: policy-guard
document:
policy-guard
policy pattern
policy decision point / policy enforcement point
Keep every authorisation decision out of the protected resource's code by moving the rules into a separate Policy component and letting a Guard - the enforcement point every access must pass through - obtain a decision from that policy before the operation is performed.
Access rules written inside the resource's own methods (checking roles or ownership inline) entangle business logic with security logic: the same rule is re-implemented at every call site, a forgotten check silently opens a bypass, and the rules cannot be reviewed, tested or changed without touching the resource's code.
Components that own protected resources or operations and must decide per access whether the authenticated subject - with its roles, attributes, tenant and request context - may perform the requested action. Typical at object, module or boundary scope: request handlers, domain services, document stores, message consumers and administrative tooling that all reach the same resources and should obey the same rules, especially when the rules change more often than the resource code.
HTTP and API request handling: authentication establishes the security context once, then every endpoint or method invocation is guarded by a policy decision (for example Spring Security's AuthorizationManager behind its AuthorizationFilter, or ASP.NET Core authorization middleware over registered policies).
Domain services that expose several operations on one aggregate: the guard checks the (subject, operation, resource) triple before each service method executes, instead of scattering role checks through the methods.
Multi-tenant backends where the decision must consider tenant, ownership and request attributes, not only roles; the guard resolves them from the security context and passes them to the policy.
Document or file stores: every read or write is wrapped by a guard that consults rules keyed by the document identifier and its classification.
Administrative and background code - CLI tools, batch jobs, message consumers - that must obey the same policy as the interactive API so that no side door exists.
Regulated environments where every access decision, including denials, must be logged consistently and the policy itself must be independently testable.
Spring Security request boundaries: AuthorizationFilter passes the current Authentication and HttpServletRequest to an AuthorizationManager and proceeds only after a grant; configure every protected route so an unlisted path cannot become a side door.
ASP.NET Core policy authorization: named policies combine requirements evaluated by IAuthorizationHandler implementations and attach with [Authorize(Policy = "...")] or RequireAuthorization; place UseAuthorization after authentication and before endpoints.
Open Policy Agent (OPA) deployments: AWS Prescriptive Guidance models a centralized or distributed Policy Decision Point with Policy Enforcement Points on APIs, allowing shared policy while using local sidecars when latency or availability requires it.

name: coarse-grained-lock
document:
coarse-grained-lock
aggregate lock
cluster lock
Give a cluster of objects that must change together one shared lock — held on the cluster's root object, on a lock entry keyed by that root, or on a version token the root carries — so a caller locks one thing instead of discovering and locking every member.
Changing one object really means changing a cluster: an edit that touches any member (a line item, an address, a child entity) has to be atomic with respect to the others, but a separate lock per member forces every caller to find and lock the whole set, makes the amount of locking grow with the object graph, and produces deadlocks whenever two callers acquire member locks in different orders.
Domain layers whose natural unit of change spans several related objects (an aggregate root plus its members) and whose edit sessions outlive a single statement — multi-user applications, rich clients, batch jobs — on stores that offer row locks, lock tables or version columns and where the team must pick one lock granularity that matches the unit of change.
Editing an order together with its lines and delivery addresses in one user session: the order is locked or versioned once and every line edit is covered.
A customer with its addresses and contacts that must stay consistent, where leaving one member stale breaks a business rule.
Pessimistic offline edit sessions in a rich client that hold a lock for minutes without locking dozens of rows across several tables.
Optimistic commit of a whole aggregate: the root's version token detects that any member changed since load, so members need no version columns of their own.
Batch jobs that rewrite every member of a cluster: one lock or one version check for the batch instead of thousands of row locks.
Sharded or multi-tenant stores where the cluster root is also the shard key, so locking the root pins the partitions that the edit will touch.
DDD aggregates where an invariant spans multiple child entities (e.g., total order quantity must not exceed 10) — the coarse-grained lock on the aggregate root prevents parallel transactions from breaking the invariant at the per-line level.
Saga state machines where concurrent messages may touch the same saga instance — NHibernate pessimistic locking combined with forced version increment on child updates ensures the saga instance stays consistent.
Multi-granularity lock hierarchies in database systems: coarse area/file locks for large scans paired with fine row locks for point updates, using intention-lock protocols (IS/IX/SIX) to prevent deadlocks.
Kubernetes control plane: kube-scheduler and kube-controller-manager contend for a single coordination.k8s.io Lease object — one coarse lock covering a whole controller, renewed at about half the lease duration, with resourceVersion optimistic concurrency so only one candidate can hold it.
CockroachDB epoch-based node leases: one lease per node covers every Raft range that node holds instead of one lease per range, cutting lease-renewal traffic; bumping the node's liveness epoch revokes all of its range leases at once.
JPA/Hibernate applications locking an aggregate with a single LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE on the root row (SELECT … FOR UPDATE) and relying on the root's @Version column as the version token for the whole cluster.

name: messaging-gateway
document:
messaging-gateway
Encapsulate access to a messaging system behind an ordinary interface of domain methods, so calling application code makes method calls while a single component owns message construction, correlation, timeouts and error translation.
Application code that talks to a broker keeps importing messaging concepts: it builds the payload, picks the channel, attaches a reply address and a correlation id, parses the response and interprets broker errors. The trigger for this pattern is that callers should make a method call instead of writing messaging code - the messaging knowledge belongs in exactly one place that can change without touching business rules.
At the boundary between application logic and a messaging system (message broker, MQ, queue service or actor runtime): the other side is reached by messages, but the caller is ordinary domain code that should see typed parameters and typed results. Applies to one-way (fire and forget) and request-reply interactions alike, and to blocking as well as asynchronous call styles.
A domain service that must query another system (inventory, pricing, credit scoring) over a queue: the caller invokes checkStock(sku) and receives a typed answer.
An HTTP or API layer whose controller awaits a brokered round trip (Spring Integration gateway interface, NestJS ClientProxy, MassTransit request client).
Batch and background jobs that dispatch work through a typed job API instead of assembling payloads (ActiveJob perform_later, Celery delay).
Wrapping a legacy system's MQ interface once, so the rest of the codebase never learns its message format.
Test seams: unit tests substitute a fake gateway, integration tests run the same interface against a real broker.
Migration seam: keep the gateway contract stable while the transport moves from one broker to another.
Actor and streaming stacks where a facade wraps ask/request so callers never hold ActorRefs or inboxes.
Spring Integration's @MessagingGateway and GatewayProxyFactoryBean let application code inject a typed interface while the framework routes calls into channels and returns replies.
MassTransit's IRequestClient<T> and GetResponse<TResponse> provide a typed request-reply client over the bus, keeping request and response message contracts out of the calling service.
RabbitMQ's RPC tutorial demonstrates a gateway-like client that publishes to rpc_queue with reply_to and correlation_id, then resolves the matching callback response.

name: service-activator
document:
service-activator
Connect an incoming message channel to an ordinary service so that the service is invoked like a local method call and its result or exception is carried back into the messaging flow.
An application owns a service that other parts of the system must reach through messaging, but the service code must not depend on the messaging API: the message has to be translated into a method invocation, the return value into a reply message, and a failure into an error path, without the service ever knowing that a channel was involved.
Integrators that own both a channel and a piece of application logic: a broker consumer, an in-process work queue or a request-reply channel in an enterprise integration flow, where the invoked code is ordinary local (often service-layer) code and the channel may be pushed, polled or driven by a dispatcher.
Expose an existing service-layer method to a queue or topic without adding a broker dependency to the domain code (order received -> OrderService.place).
Request-reply over messaging: a command message carries a return address and correlation id; the activator invokes the service and sends the reply so the caller continues as if it had made a remote call.
In-process worker: a work queue (asyncio.Queue, Channel<T>, tokio mpsc, Go channel, Thread::Queue) drained by a background loop that calls an application service - the same pattern without a broker.
Event-driven microservice endpoints: a command or event message is matched by pattern to a handler method that performs the business action and returns the acknowledgement.
Terminal stage of a batch or streaming pipeline, where a domain service is invoked per record instead of business rules being embedded in the stage.
Multi-transport exposure of one service during a migration: the same business method attached to a JMS queue, an HTTP adapter and a file poller by declaring three activators.
Spring Integration makes the endpoint declarative: @ServiceActivator(inputChannel = "orders") turns a method on a Spring-managed POJO into a consumer - the framework injects the payload (or @Header values), picks the method by payload type, and sends a non-null return to the configured output-channel or the inbound replyChannel header.
Apache Camel implements the EIP directly as bean integration: a route's .to("bean:myService") binds the message Exchange to an ordinary Java bean method, so the same service stays callable both from routes and by local callers.
NestJS microservices: a controller method decorated with @MessagePattern receives only the message payload over the transport (TCP, Redis, NATS, RabbitMQ) and its return value is sent back automatically as the reply; @EventPattern is the fire-and-forget variant of the same endpoint.

name: message-endpoint
document:
message-endpoint
messaging endpoint
Connect an application to a messaging channel through a named, isolated component that turns application data into messages and back again, so the rest of the application stays unaware of message formats, channels and the messaging client API.
An application must send or receive messages over a messaging channel, but its domain code must not be littered with connection, session, serialization and acknowledgement calls: without a dedicated place for the send/receive code, messaging API details and their failure modes spread through the codebase, and every additional channel, queue or broker client multiplies the duplication.
Enterprise integration and distributed systems where applications exchange messages through a messaging system (queues, topics, brokers, event streams) instead of calling each other directly. It applies at the seam between an application and the messaging infrastructure, on both the sending and the receiving side, and it is the entry point for the further endpoint decisions - event-driven vs. polling consumption, selective consumption, durable subscriptions, transactional clients - that only matter once such a component exists.
A service that publishes domain events to a topic and subscribes to the commands it must handle, keeping its domain layer free of broker client types.
A legacy application that must be integrated with several other applications over a message broker; the endpoint is the seam on which the adapter and gateway arrangements are then built.
A worker process whose only job is consuming tasks from a queue, executing them and acknowledging the outcome with explicit retry and dead-letter behaviour.
Replacing a synchronous remote call between two services with asynchronous messaging: the caller keeps its method call and the callee keeps its service method, while endpoints on both sides absorb the messaging.
A polyglot ecosystem where each application is written in a different language but all must speak the same messaging infrastructure; each language's endpoint realisation hides its own client library.
A Spring AMQP service exposes @RabbitListener methods backed by listener containers and uses RabbitTemplate for outbound messages, keeping RabbitMQ client details at the endpoint.
A Java worker wraps the AWS SDK for Java SqsClient sendMessage, receiveMessage and deleteMessage operations in producer and consumer endpoints, deleting only after processing succeeds.
A Kafka service puts Apache Kafka Producer and Consumer APIs behind separate topic endpoints, keeping serializers, consumer offsets and broker-specific records out of domain code.

name: facade
document:
facade
façade
Provide one coarse-grained entry interface that hides a subsystem of many cooperating classes behind the few operations its clients actually need, so callers depend on a single stable API instead of orchestrating the subsystem themselves.
Every client of a complex subsystem must know which classes exist, in which order to call them, how to configure and dispose them and how to interpret their errors; that orchestration is then duplicated across the codebase, and any change inside the subsystem ripples through all callers.
Applies when a subsystem (a library, framework, legacy module, remote SDK, or a layer of your own system) is much broader than any single client needs, when its correct use is a recurring sequence of collaborations, and when client code should be insulated from its types and its evolution. Typical at module and system-boundary scope, where one entry point per layer or per external system is wanted.
Wrapping a third-party SDK, media framework or payment/HTTP client behind one class or module that exposes the application's own vocabulary (convert, charge, upload).
Application services that orchestrate repositories, gateways and domain services for one use case (checkout, report generation) and are the only seam controllers or jobs talk to.
Layered systems where every layer offers a facade as its entry point, so dependencies flow through coarse interfaces instead of reaching into a layer's internals.
Isolating a legacy subsystem while it is replaced incrementally: new code depends on the clean facade, and the migration swaps implementations behind it.
Remote and coarse-grained boundaries: a remote facade exposes a few chunky operations over a fine-grained object model to avoid chatty calls (see Remote Facade, Fowler's PEAA).
Startup/teardown sequences and device orchestration (the classic home-theatre example): clients need one 'watch movie' operation, not a dozen subsystem calls in the right order.
Service-container proxy facades (e.g. Laravel): a static-looking front-end that forwards calls to a resolved service instance, giving a terse API without sacrificing testability or DI flexibility.
JPA/service-layer facades: a single transactional entry point that receives DTOs, maps them to domain objects, orchestrates business logic, maps results back, and commits — one transaction per use case.
Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) in microservices: a thin per-client aggregation service (web, mobile, partner) that fans out to downstream microservices, reshapes responses for the client, and handles perimeter concerns. Each BFF is a specialized facade owned by the team that ships the corresponding client.
Anti-Corruption Layer (DDD): a facade placed between a bounded context and an external/legacy system to translate that system's model into domain concepts, preventing external concepts from polluting the internal domain model.
Event-driven/observable facades: a facade that exposes reactive streams (Observables, Promises, async generators) over the subsystem, buffering, batching or debouncing events for consumers that prefer push-based or streaming interfaces.
API gateway composition: an API gateway acts as a system-wide facade that unifies multiple backend services at the edge, handling auth, routing and cross-cutting concerns before delegating to more specific facades or services.
SDK wrapper facades: publishing a public-facing SDK over an internal microservice mesh; the facade shapes the external API surface, applies default configurations, and provides a stable consumer experience independent of internal service topology changes.
SLF4J (Simple Logging Facade for Java): slf4j-api is a minimal logging facade; applications code against Logger.debug()/info() once and bind the concrete framework (Logback, Log4j 2, java.util.logging) at deployment time by swapping the provider jar on the classpath — the textbook runtime-swappable facade.
Spring Framework JdbcClient / JdbcTemplate: a fluent facade over raw JDBC that owns connection and statement lifecycle, iterates ResultSets and translates SQLException into the DataAccessException hierarchy, so callers supply only SQL and result mapping instead of the full boilerplate workflow.
jQuery $.get/$.post/$.getJSON over $.ajax: a per-task facade layer that collapses cross-browser XMLHttpRequest differences, Deferred plumbing and HTTP defaults into one-line calls — the canonical JavaScript-library facade.

name: authentication-enforcer
document:
authentication-enforcer
authentication interceptor
authentication gateway
auth middleware
Put one request-boundary checkpoint in front of protected actions that decides whether authentication is required, delegates credential verification to a replaceable mechanism, and attaches the resulting subject to request-scoped context before dispatch, so coverage is uniform without making handlers understand credentials.
When each handler decides whether and how to authenticate, protection is duplicated or omitted on exceptional paths, credential formats and user stores leak into business code, and a mechanism or policy change requires editing every handler instead of one auditable boundary.
Server-side request processing — web APIs, web applications and service endpoints — where many handlers share one protection policy, credentials arrive through a uniform convention (Authorization header, cookie, session id), verification technology must be replaceable or differ per route, and the runtime provides a request-pipeline hook (servlet filter, middleware chain, framework guard). Applies to session-based and token-based authentication alike; permissions and roles are out of scope. Three implementation strategies exist: (1) Container-Managed Authentication — the runtime container owns the checkpoint and realm configuration; (2) Authentication Provider Strategy — a custom provider behind a narrow interface, swapped without touching handlers; (3) JAAS Login Module Strategy — pluggable via standard JAAS configuration, supporting multifactor authentication via smart cards, biometrics, or third-party IdPs. The pattern is equally applicable at the edge level (API gateway, ingress proxy) and the service level (in-process middleware).
Web APIs where every route except health and login requires a bearer token, and the checkpoint is mounted in front of the whole router.
Multi-tenant applications with mixed protection levels: public marketing pages, session-protected tenant UI and token-protected integration endpoints behind one enforcement layer.
Services that must accept several credential types at once — browser sessions, mobile JWTs, mutual TLS for service-to-service traffic — while keeping one uniform enforcement point.
Credential-technology migration (basic auth to OIDC, on-premises LDAP to SSO) where enforcement stays put while the mechanism behind it is swapped.
Regulated environments where every rejected authentication attempt has to be logged centrally and identically across all endpoints.
Legacy applications with authentication checks scattered through servlets or handlers that must be consolidated behind one intercepting layer before an audit.
Zero Trust microservices where every internal service verifies JWTs independently (per-service verification) while an ingress gateway provides the first checkpoint — the enforcer exists at both layers.
OIDC/OAuth2 migration where an existing session-based app adds bearer-token support; the mechanism adapts to both while the enforcement point remains unchanged.
Multi-tenant SaaS platforms where tenant isolation depends on the enforcer resolving a tenant identifier from the token before the handler processes any data.
Platform-as-a-Service with mounted sub-applications where a parent ASGI middleware dispatches per-path authentication requirements from a config registry, injecting identity into ASGI scope for all sub-apps.
Spring Security servlet applications that use a SecurityFilterChain with anyRequest().authenticated() and an AuthenticationManager/AuthenticationProvider chain, so controllers consume the SecurityContext rather than parse credentials.
ASP.NET Core APIs that register JWT or cookie schemes, call UseAuthentication before dependent middleware, and use a fallback authorization policy to make authenticated access the default.
An nginx ingress location using auth_request to delegate identity verification to a central authentication service, forwarding only after a 2xx result and propagating 401/403 failures while services still verify their own trust boundary.

name: test-specific-subclass
document:
test-specific-subclass
test-specific extension
subclassed test double
Make an otherwise untestable class testable by defining a test-only subclass that overrides the method reaching the unusable dependency (or exposes the internal state the test needs), so the boundary can be substituted and observed without putting test hooks into production code.
A class that must be tested reaches its dependency through a call on itself - a self-call to a helper method, a field created inside the class, or a singleton/static lookup - so the test has no injection point: the collaborator cannot be replaced from outside, the indirect inputs cannot be controlled and the indirect outputs cannot be observed. Editing the production class to accept the dependency may be impossible (third-party or frozen code) or would introduce test logic into production.
Applies to legacy or third-party object-oriented code where the boundary call already sits behind an overridable (non-final, sufficiently visible) method, or can be extracted into one, and where test-only code may live next to the tests. It is a fallback for statically typed languages that need the double to stay type-compatible with a concrete class; where the code can be modified, dependency injection is the better seam.
A legacy class reads the wall clock inside a helper method (System.currentTimeMillis, DateTime.Now, Instant.now): override the helper so date/decision logic can be tested at a fixed instant.
A reporting or notification class sends mail or calls a remote API from a self-call: override that method with a canned or empty body so the unit test runs offline and deterministically.
A class reaches a database or the file system from inside its own method: override it to return an in-memory fixture instead of building the real object chain (entity-chain snipping).
Verifying the sequence and the set of steps of a template method: override the steps in a subclass and record which of them ran, in which order.
Exposing private state for state verification, or exposing a private algorithm step so it can be tested individually (state-exposing and behaviour-exposing subclasses).
Replacing a singleton or static accessor the SUT uses through a lookup with a controlled instance that is still type-compatible with the concrete class (substituted singleton).
Putting a legacy untested class under a characterization-test baseline before refactoring, while extracting the collaborator is not yet possible.
A Java class that cannot be modified (third-party or legacy jar) but has a non-final boundary method to stub: Mockito spy() / @Spy keeps the real methods and stubs only the overridden ones - the partial mocking Mockito's Javadoc documents for legacy code and third-party interfaces (final methods stay un-stubbable).
A PHP class whose constructor opens connections or performs other side effects: createPartialMock(Class::class, ['boundaryMethod']) or getMockBuilder()->onlyMethods([...])->disableOriginalConstructor() generates a double that overrides only the named methods and skips the real constructor - PHPUnit's documented form of the pattern (final, private and static methods and enums cannot be doubled).
A .NET class with virtual boundary members: NSubstitute Substitute.ForPartsOf<T>() creates a partial substitute that - as NSubstitute's own docs state - inherits the original type via Castle DynamicProxy and runs real code except for members configured with DoNotCallBase, i.e. a generated test-specific subclass with an official 'use with caution' caveat.
