Session teardown in a long-lived server: the handler works through the wrapper, and logout revokes future calls before the session's resources are freed.
Capability-based workflow and financial systems that give an agent temporary authority over an account or a document and revoke it when the task completes.
Temporary elevated access for maintenance or debugging, where the requirement is to show that the extra authority has provably ended (audit evidence).
Graceful decommissioning of a shared resource: revoke new work through the wrapper, drain the calls already in flight, then release the resource.
The Scala ocaps framework's Revocable/Caretaker API returns a proxied capability plus a private Revoker, so a session, logout, timeout or supervisor can make later calls fail without changing the target.
JavaScript's standard Proxy.revocable() and the Chrome Extensions chrome.permissions API provide browser/runtime counterparts: keep the revoke/remove control private, and do not mistake the platform wrapper or permission record for protection against an already leaked target reference.
AWS IAM role-session revocation for temporary STS credentials is a distributed analogue of withdrawing a forwarded grant: policy evaluation denies subsequent requests, but propagation and credential caching mean it is not the atomic in-process check-and-forward gate described here.

statement: Should each page or form have a dedicated component that owns input parsing, validation, domain invocation, and response selection, or should one shared component multiplex all of these behaviors?
name: pipeline
document:
pipeline
assembly line
processing pipeline
Decompose a transformation into an ordered sequence of named stages that each consume the previous stage's output and produce the next stage's input, so the workflow reads top to bottom and every step can be tested, instrumented, reordered or replaced on its own.
A multi-step transformation is written as one long function or a tangle of nested calls: the steps are unnamed, their order is implicit in statement order, intermediate values need throwaway names, there is no seam at which a single step can be logged, tested or replaced, and the same sequence is retyped at every call site that needs it.
Processing that naturally decomposes into successive transformations of the same payload - request handling, ETL, compiler passes, message enrichment, image or byte-stream processing - whether the payload is a single value or a stream. It fits in-process, staged execution where one driver owns ordering, error handling and cancellation; distributing the stages across processes, transports and independently deployed filters is the architectural pipe-and-filter pattern instead.
Request handling: deserialise, authenticate, validate, enrich, persist and render a request, with each step named so a failing stage is attributable and testable in isolation.
ETL and data import: extract, clean, transform, validate and load large files as a stream, so no intermediate collection is materialised and memory stays bounded.
Compiler and interpreter passes: source, tokens, AST, resolution, optimisation and code emission, where each pass is an independent stage over the intermediate representation and the pass list is the pipeline.
Message enrichment in an integration flow: unwrap, translate, enrich and route a message, one stage per concern, with per-channel ordering; the cross-process version stays pipe-and-filter.
Image or byte-stream processing: decode, crop or resize, watermark and encode, lazily per frame or chunk, optionally overlapping stages across cores.
Configuration-driven data cleaning: the stage list is assembled from configuration or a plugin registry so different tenants get different ordered steps without changing the stages themselves.
TensorFlow tf.data input pipelines: tf.data.Dataset pipelines that chain map, prefetch, parallel_interleave and shuffle stages to feed a training loop efficiently, with each stage independently configurable and the whole pipeline testable in isolation.
LLM token streaming: HTTP server-sent event streams where an LLM produces tokens at inference speed while clients consume at variable network speed; stream.pipeline() prevents the inference server from buffering unbounded tokens in memory when a slow client disconnects (Node.js stream backpressure case study).
Observability telemetry pipelines: OpenTelemetry Collector chains receivers, processors (memory_limiter, batch, filter, transform, tail_sampling) and exporters for traces, metrics and logs, with connectors (e.g., spanmetrics) bridging signal types and memory_limiter placed first to prevent OOM before filtering.
Typed TypeScript pipeline with schema validation: Zod or io-ts schemas define the stage contract at each boundary, catching schema violations at the exact stage that produced bad data rather than at a distant consumer.
Async generator pipelines in Python: asyncio queues with bounded capacity connect async generator stages, propagating backpressure by pausing producers when the queue is full; the FinStream analytics case study showed 82% memory reduction and 99.7% latency reduction versus unbounded buffering.
Event-streaming pipelines with Kafka and Flink: producers, topic partitions, Flink consumers and checkpointing form a distributed pipeline where backpressure cascades across every boundary; the Kafka max.block.ms and Flink backpressure.sample.interval settings interact under partition saturation and must be tested together under load.
Dynamic pipeline parallelism: construct-and-run pipelines (MapReduce, Spark) fix stage count at construction, while on-the-fly pipelines (Cilk-P Piper algorithm) allow the structure to emerge at runtime, varying per iteration and supporting data-dependent branching; on-the-fly enables pipelines like x264 that cannot be expressed with a fixed static structure.
LLVM compiler pass pipelines: PassBuilder assembles ModulePassManager, CGSCCPassManager, FunctionPassManager and LoopPassManager across the IR hierarchy (Module → CGSCC → Function → Loop), with registered callbacks injecting passes at named extension points (pipeline-start, vectorizer-start, optimizer-last); incorrect PreservedAnalyses declarations invalidate all downstream analyses.
Continuous data pipelines at scale (Google model): periodic pipelines run on cron and suffer from depth growth and resource exhaustion as organic load increases; continuous pipelines (master-slave or event-triggered) replace idle-waiting with always-on processing, eliminating the 'pipeline vs cron' discontinuity at the cost of operational complexity.
ML pipeline orchestration (Airflow, Kubeflow, Prefect, Dagster): each orchestrator applies the pipeline pattern at the workflow level - Airflow's DAG-of-tasks, Kubeflow's per-container-step pipelines with GPU scheduling, Prefect's monoflow/subflow/orchestrator pattern, and Dagster's software-defined assets where asset dependencies imply the pipeline; the pipeline is the scheduler's unit of execution, not an implementation detail.
Apache Beam: PCollections flow through composable PTransforms (ParDo, Combine and GroupByKey) in a pipeline graph, making each transform boundary explicit while the runner handles execution.
Node.js stream.pipeline(): Readable, Transform and Writable stages compose with built-in backpressure, error propagation and AbortSignal cancellation; this is a concrete streaming realization, not a durable workflow engine.

statement: Should each page or form have a dedicated component that owns input parsing, validation, domain invocation, and response selection, or should one shared component multiplex all of these behaviors?
name: abstract-factory
document:
abstract-factory
kit
factory of factories
Expose one creation contract for each product kind in a coherent family, letting clients switch the selected family at the composition root without naming concrete products or mixing incompatible variants.
A client must construct several related products that collaborate as a matched set, but direct construction spreads family keys and concrete class names through the code. Adding a family then becomes configuration branches plus constructor edits, while mixing products from different families can fail only after incompatible objects interact.
Use in object- or interface-based subsystems with two independent axes of change: product kinds (button, slider, connection, command) and product families or variants (dark/light, PostgreSQL/Oracle, AWS/GCP). The family is normally selected once at a composition root, products from one family are intended to collaborate, and clients must compile, test and ship without knowing concrete product types; if products are intentionally mixed or only one kind is created, use a smaller creator instead.
Cross-platform or themable UI toolkits: Qt's QStyleFactory resolves keys such as "windows" and "fusion" to built-in or plugin QStyle implementations that govern a coherent widget look-and-feel; a fuller abstract factory applies the same family key across several product interfaces.
Provider-independent database code: ADO.NET's DbProviderFactory/DbProviderFactories create a matched DbConnection, DbCommand, DbParameter and DbDataAdapter set for a selected provider such as SQL Server or OLE DB.
Parser-provider plugins: JAXP's DocumentBuilderFactory and SAXParserFactory hide implementation classes behind standard factory APIs, allowing the composition root to select a provider while client code uses parser abstractions.
Java's ServiceLoader documentation uses a CodecFactory service with getEncoder and getDecoder operations; the selected provider supplies a coherent codec family while clients depend only on the service interface.
Test infrastructure: an in-memory factory family whose products are fakes, injected in place of the production family so integration tests need no network.
Game and simulation engines: per-biome object families (terrain, props, audio) that must stay aesthetically consistent when a level is loaded.
SaaS multi-tenant applications: per-tenant theme factories so every rendered page uses the tenant's brand colours, fonts and spacing without per-request conditionals.
Document-format parsers: factory per format (PDF, HTML, EPUB) producing matched tokenizer, layout engine and renderer so a viewer can switch formats from a single configuration key.

statement: Should each page or form have a dedicated component that owns input parsing, validation, domain invocation, and response selection, or should one shared component multiplex all of these behaviors?
name: coarse-grained-lock
document:
coarse-grained-lock
aggregate lock
cluster lock
Give a cluster of objects that must change together one shared lock — held on the cluster's root object, on a lock entry keyed by that root, or on a version token the root carries — so a caller locks one thing instead of discovering and locking every member.
Changing one object really means changing a cluster: an edit that touches any member (a line item, an address, a child entity) has to be atomic with respect to the others, but a separate lock per member forces every caller to find and lock the whole set, makes the amount of locking grow with the object graph, and produces deadlocks whenever two callers acquire member locks in different orders.
Domain layers whose natural unit of change spans several related objects (an aggregate root plus its members) and whose edit sessions outlive a single statement — multi-user applications, rich clients, batch jobs — on stores that offer row locks, lock tables or version columns and where the team must pick one lock granularity that matches the unit of change.
Editing an order together with its lines and delivery addresses in one user session: the order is locked or versioned once and every line edit is covered.
A customer with its addresses and contacts that must stay consistent, where leaving one member stale breaks a business rule.
Pessimistic offline edit sessions in a rich client that hold a lock for minutes without locking dozens of rows across several tables.
Optimistic commit of a whole aggregate: the root's version token detects that any member changed since load, so members need no version columns of their own.
Batch jobs that rewrite every member of a cluster: one lock or one version check for the batch instead of thousands of row locks.
Sharded or multi-tenant stores where the cluster root is also the shard key, so locking the root pins the partitions that the edit will touch.
DDD aggregates where an invariant spans multiple child entities (e.g., total order quantity must not exceed 10) — the coarse-grained lock on the aggregate root prevents parallel transactions from breaking the invariant at the per-line level.
Saga state machines where concurrent messages may touch the same saga instance — NHibernate pessimistic locking combined with forced version increment on child updates ensures the saga instance stays consistent.
Multi-granularity lock hierarchies in database systems: coarse area/file locks for large scans paired with fine row locks for point updates, using intention-lock protocols (IS/IX/SIX) to prevent deadlocks.
Kubernetes control plane: kube-scheduler and kube-controller-manager contend for a single coordination.k8s.io Lease object — one coarse lock covering a whole controller, renewed at about half the lease duration, with resourceVersion optimistic concurrency so only one candidate can hold it.
CockroachDB epoch-based node leases: one lease per node covers every Raft range that node holds instead of one lease per range, cutting lease-renewal traffic; bumping the node's liveness epoch revokes all of its range leases at once.
JPA/Hibernate applications locking an aggregate with a single LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE on the root row (SELECT … FOR UPDATE) and relying on the root's @Version column as the version token for the whole cluster.

statement: Should each page or form have a dedicated component that owns input parsing, validation, domain invocation, and response selection, or should one shared component multiplex all of these behaviors?
name: characterization-test
document:
characterization-test
golden master
approval test
golden file test
snapshot test
golden session test
Pin the actual, currently deployed behaviour of existing code in committed reference artefacts (golden masters) so that a later edit can be distinguished from an accidental regression even when nobody can say what the code is supposed to do.
You must change code whose behaviour is undocumented, surprising or only known to production: there is no specification to test against, and tests written from intended behaviour would take too long and silently encode guesses as fact. The safety net therefore has to be built from observed behaviour: replay a corpus of real inputs through the untouched subject, capture everything observable, commit the result as the reference, and let every later run diff against it - pinning what the code does today before changing how it does it.
Applies whenever the subject already runs and can be exercised in a test process or from a test script: untested legacy modules, data transformations and report pipelines, serializers, parsers and code generators, CLI and protocol endpoints, rendering pipelines whose images can be diffed, and dependency or runtime upgrades where the old behaviour is the baseline. The precondition is determinism: volatile parts (timestamps, identifiers, paths, memory addresses, collection order, locale, floating-point formatting) must be normalized or redacted before capture, otherwise the comparison is noise. The pattern is a first move - build the net, then refactor under it - and pairs with a deliberate approval step, because a characterization test does not know which behaviour was intended.
Before refactoring an untested legacy module: capture outputs for a corpus of inputs, restructure the code, and require the reference artefacts to stay identical.
Data processing and batch jobs: pin how representative input files are transformed into output files or reports, so the nightly job can be changed safely.
Serializers, formatters and code generators: pin the emitted text or structured output for representative documents, with a redaction step for volatile values.
Rendering and UI pipelines: pin generated images (screenshot goldens) or rendered text output with an approval workflow and a visual diff tool.
CLI and protocol behaviour: pin stdout, stderr and exit codes, or request/response bytes, for a set of recorded invocations.
Dependency or runtime upgrades: pin behaviour before the upgrade and re-run afterwards, so only intended differences have to be reviewed.
Production defect triage: replay the failing production input into a new reference artefact, then fix the defect against that regression test.
AI/LLM output regression testing: pin model responses to a curated golden dataset; on model or prompt change, compare distributions, embedding similarity, or token-level diffs against the baseline rather than requiring exact matches (LLM eval pipelines, 2024-2026).
Generated code verification: pin the exact output of OpenAPI client generators, GraphQL type generators, SDK wrappers, or database migration previews so formatting and structural changes are caught.
Database schema migration testing: capture the before/after output of migration scripts for a set of schema variants, approving only intentional structural differences.
Computer vision pipeline regression: pin bounding-box distributions or classification confidence vectors from CV models across runs; statistical comparison prevents flaky failures from minor pixel noise.
Smart contract and blockchain output regression: pin deterministic contract outputs for a given input state; any divergence in on-chain behaviour is immediately visible (Nexlify case, 2025).
Database-engine regression suites: PostgreSQL's pg_regress replays each sql/*.sql script and diffs results/*.out against committed golden files in expected/*, with variant comparison files and a resultmap absorbing known platform differences (locale, float formatting, row ordering).
Compiler test corpora: LLVM's lit/FileCheck pins emitted IR and machine code by piping compiler output to FileCheck, which verifies CHECK directives committed inside each test file across the whole input corpus.
ORM query-change detection: ApprovalTests.Ruby's verify_sql approves the SQL an ActiveRecord call emits, so a gem or framework upgrade that silently rewrites generated queries fails the suite.

statement: Should each page or form have a dedicated component that owns input parsing, validation, domain invocation, and response selection, or should one shared component multiplex all of these behaviors?
name: entity
document:
entity
reference object
domain entity
Give a domain concept a stable identity that survives attribute changes, representation changes and time, and define its equality, lifecycle and lookup in terms of that identity instead of in terms of its attributes.
A model that compares objects by their attributes cannot answer whether two instances are the same thing: a customer whose e-mail and plan changed looks like a different customer, while two distinct people who share a name look like one. References held by other objects, caches and audit records break silently, and every state change forces callers to re-identify the object.
Rich domain models in which some concepts must be tracked through time: the object is created, changes state, is stored and reloaded, and may exist in several representations (in-memory instance, database row, message payload, UI snapshot) that all have to denote the same thing. It is the modelling decision that pairs with Value Object: attribute clusters become values, while the things whose history matters keep an identity.
Master data tracked for years — customers, accounts, contracts, products, patients — where attributes change but the business entity stays the same (e.g., a Customer who moves house is still the same Customer).
Documents with a lifecycle: orders, invoices, bookings and shipments that move through states (pending → paid → shipped → delivered) while remaining the same document with a stable order number.
Shopping cart to order transition: a ShoppingCart is reconstituted as an Order with the same customer identity but a new order identity, preserving the correlation to the customer while starting a new business process.
Correlating representations across layers: an entity persisted as database rows, published as domain events, and displayed in a UI must be recognisable as the same thing in all three — identity is the correlation key across representations.
In-memory session consistency: a unit of work or identity map ensures the same Customer loaded twice in one request is one object reference, preventing edits from silently diverging into two copies.
Referencing across bounded contexts: one microservice holds a CustomerId reference to another service's aggregate root, allowing independent deployment and loading without a direct object pointer.
Healthcare records: a Patient entity persists across multiple visits, lab results and prescriptions — the patient identity is the anchor for the entire medical history regardless of demographic changes.
Versioned documents: an InsurancePolicy entity may be replaced by a new version while the original policy number (identity) remains the correlation handle for auditors and legacy systems.
Hibernate/JPA: an @Entity class with an @Id is managed by the persistence context, which guarantees one in-memory instance per identity per session — loading the same row twice in a session returns the same object reference, an Identity Map built into the framework.
Entity Framework Core: identity resolution makes the DbContext track a single entity instance per primary key, so duplicate instances arriving in a deserialized graph are merged into the already-tracked entity instead of diverging into two tracked copies.
Drupal Entity API: nodes, users and taxonomy terms (content entities) and roles or image styles (configuration entities) are identity-bearing objects with typed storage handlers, revisions and field bundles behind one CRUD and validation API.

statement: Should each page or form have a dedicated component that owns input parsing, validation, domain invocation, and response selection, or should one shared component multiplex all of these behaviors?
name: transaction-script
document:
transaction-script
service object
Organizes the business logic of a single request as one procedure - read the data it needs, validate and calculate, write the results and complete in one database transaction - trading object-model structure for a straight-line implementation that can be read top to bottom.
A request-scoped use case (book a room, place an order, recognize revenue, import a file) has to be implemented, and its logic mixes input validation, calculation and persistence. Modelling the domain as objects may be premature, or the team may not be ready for it, yet the implementation still needs each request's steps to stay visible and its transaction boundary to be explicit.
Applies where business logic is simple to moderately complex, where the system is naturally described as a series of transactions each driven by one request (HTTP handler, CLI command, queue message, batch job), and where a thin data-source gateway or the database itself is the persistence seam. Also the right starting point under delivery pressure or for a team new to domain modelling - provided the growth path to a Domain Model is watched deliberately.
Booking a hotel room: check availability, calculate the rate, insert the booking and confirm - one request, one transaction.
Revenue recognition (Fowler's example): given a contract and an as-of date, calculate the recognitions and persist them, or report the revenue already recognized.
CRUD write endpoints in a simple admin or back-office application where each screen maps to one operation.
Batch and integration jobs: import a file, validate rows, write the accepted rows and report the rejects in one transaction per batch.
Queue or message handlers that carry out one command (place order, cancel subscription, refund payment) and acknowledge only after commit.
Reporting and ETL steps that read a slice of data, transform it and write results, where the logic is genuinely a straight line of steps.
Django request-atomicity: with ATOMIC_REQUESTS enabled (or @transaction.atomic on the view), the whole view function is the script - Django begins the transaction at request start, commits on a successful response and rolls back on exception, exactly the one-script-one-transaction shape.
Laravel request handlers that wrap the validate-calculate-persist sequence in a DB::transaction closure: the closure commits when it returns and rolls back automatically if it throws, so the closure body is the script and its extent is the boundary.
Spring @Transactional service methods: an AOP proxy begins the transaction before the method and commits after it returns, making each annotated method a Transaction Script whose signature is the request and whose boundary is declarative.

statement: Should each page or form have a dedicated component that owns input parsing, validation, domain invocation, and response selection, or should one shared component multiplex all of these behaviors?
name: point-to-point-channel
document:
point-to-point-channel
point-to-point queue
p2p channel
Deliver each message on a channel to exactly one consumer, so senders never have to coordinate with receivers and no unit of work is handled twice.
A producer must hand work to exactly one handler while several receivers are running (or the intended handler is temporarily unavailable): broadcasting the message makes every receiver deduplicate, and addressing a specific consumer instance couples the sender to its identity, location and liveness.
Asynchronous messaging inside one process, between processes or across services, where each message is a unit of work (command, job, document, RPC request) and duplicate handling is as unacceptable as loss. Applies to in-process worker queues and to brokered channels (JMS queue, AMQP queue, Kafka partition, cloud queue) alike; the channel - not the consumer and not the sender - owns the routing decision.
Work queues: a web tier enqueues jobs and a pool of workers consumes them, with each job running exactly once.
Request-reply over messaging: the request goes to a queue, exactly one service instance answers it, and the reply returns on a reply queue identified by a correlation identifier.
Command dispatch in a service-oriented system: an order service appends commands that exactly one instance of the command processor executes.
Media or log processing pipelines where every stage pulls its input from a queue and each item is handled by one of the stage's replicas.
Legacy and batch integration: jobs handed to a single consumer daemon through a queue, with the channel providing the transactional hand-off.
Scaling an existing single-consumer endpoint by attaching additional instances (Competing Consumers) without changing producers or the message contract.
Apache Kafka consumer groups: records in each topic partition are assigned to one group member at a time, so a group scales work while separate group IDs retain independent pub-sub copies.
RabbitMQ Work Queues: a task queue distributes jobs among competing workers with round-robin or fair dispatch; manual acknowledgements allow unacknowledged work to be redelivered after a worker failure.
Amazon SQS Standard queues: distribute background jobs among consumers with visibility timeouts, while at-least-once delivery requires idempotent handlers because duplicate deliveries remain possible.

statement: Should each page or form have a dedicated component that owns input parsing, validation, domain invocation, and response selection, or should one shared component multiplex all of these behaviors?
name: option-maybe
document:
option-maybe
Option
Maybe
Make the possible absence of a result part of the value and of the signature, so every caller has to decide what happens when nothing is there instead of meeting a null, a sentinel or a silently defaulted value at run time.
A function has something to return for some inputs and nothing for others, but the signature does not say so: it returns a null reference, a sentinel (-1, empty string, NULL), an out-parameter, or a value that quietly means 'not found'. Callers forget the check, dereference the null or treat the sentinel as data, and the 'this case does not exist' path is discovered in production rather than at the call site.
Lookups, parsing, searches, optional configuration, nullable database columns and any API whose result may legitimately not exist - wherever the language can express absence as a type (Option/Maybe/Optional, a nullable type, a union with undefined) or a convention can carry it. It pays off at module and service boundaries, in chains of partial steps, and wherever 'absent' must stay distinguishable from a legitimate empty, zero or falsey value.
Lookups that can miss: configuration keys, cache entries, registry entries, map/dictionary access - either through the language's two-value form or an Optional-returning accessor.
Parsing and conversion (integers, dates, URLs, decimal numbers, external identifiers) where 'no valid value' is a legitimate answer rather than an error.
Searches over collections and structures (find, first, min/max, binary search, regex match, tree traversal) where a miss is part of the contract.
Genuinely optional data: middle names, second addresses, unset feature flags, optional protocol fields - as opposed to missing state, which is a domain error.
Chains of partial steps (look up user, then their company, then its billing address) where any hop may be absent and the whole chain should collapse to 'nothing'.
Boundaries from nullable interfaces: a database column admits NULL, a legacy or interop API returns null or -1, a deserialized document lacks a field - converted once at the adapter.
Container and stream operations that can be empty (head, pop, next, dequeue, min) and should report emptiness instead of throwing or returning a sentinel.
Rust's standard library uses std::option::Option<T> with Some(T) and None for optional values; its map and pattern-matching APIs let lookup or parsing pipelines stop at absence without a null pointer.
Java SE's java.util.Optional<T> is a production API for method results that may be absent: ofNullable converts a nullable boundary value, map/flatMap compose follow-up work, and orElse/orElseThrow make the exit policy explicit.
Scala's standard-library scala.Option[A] models Some/None and documents map, flatMap, and for-comprehensions for chained partial steps; its API also demonstrates wrapping a Java HashMap lookup so a missing key becomes None.

statement: Should each page or form have a dedicated component that owns input parsing, validation, domain invocation, and response selection, or should one shared component multiplex all of these behaviors?
name: extensible-visitor
document:
extensible-visitor
extensible visitor pattern
extensible visitors with defaults
Keep the visitor open on both axes at once - new element kinds and new operations arrive without editing or recompiling any visitor that already exists - by giving every visitor a default method that catches element kinds it was not written for, introducing extended element kinds under an intermediate base whose accept hooks overload (not override) accept, and extending an operation by subclassing the existing concrete visitor so it inherits every case it already handled.
A classic Visitor is cheap in one direction only: a new operation is a new visitor, but a new element kind forces every visitor to grow one more method, so shipped visitors must be edited and redeployed. The trigger is an element hierarchy that is extended by parties who do not own the operations - language dialects, plugin node types, versioned grammars, third-party message formats - where the existing operations must keep working unchanged on the extended structure.
Recursively defined element hierarchies (abstract syntax trees, intermediate representations, document and message models) that grow over time, in a statically typed language whose visitors are concrete classes or interfaces with default bodies, and where the traversal logic itself lives inside the operations. It pays off when old operations must run against new element kinds and when element kinds are added by a different team than the operations; it assumes the visitor protocol can carry a default case and that a runtime type test is acceptable on the dispatch path.
A compiler front-end whose node kinds are extended by language dialects while every existing analysis pass keeps running unchanged (the extensible-compiler case the pattern was derived from).
An IDE or linter analysing a versioned language grammar: the version-1 analysis must not be recompiled when version 2 adds syntax nodes it does not understand.
Plugin systems where third-party modules contribute new node types (document formats, workflow elements, protocol messages) to a host that ships the operations.
Optimisation or lowering pipelines whose passes are shipped separately from the node hierarchy: the platform team adds representations, users add passes.
A published visitor API where other teams implement visitors and the element set grows every release, making 'which kinds does this visitor handle' an explicit, versioned contract.
Migration and validation tooling that must keep working on messages produced by newer producers than the tool itself.
Serialization and schema-generation frameworks such as Jackson's JsonFormatVisitor API, which uses a visitor to traverse Java type hierarchies for JSON/XML schema generation and allows third-party serializers to contribute handlers for new POJO shapes without modifying the core framework.
Query engines over tree-structured data (e.g. Apache Calcite's relational algebra, Rascal's AST analysis): new relational operators or AST node types are contributed by extension modules while existing optimisers and evaluators continue to function unchanged.
Static analysis and bug-finding tools (Coverity, CodeQL, ESLint plugin architectures): new checker plugins add new node-type coverage while the core traversal engine ships unchanged, and old checkers degrade gracefully over unknown node types.
Game engine entity-component systems: new component types are contributed at runtime while existing systems (physics, rendering, AI) continue to process entities; the visitor with default case handles component types added after a given system was written.
Python's ast.NodeVisitor: visit() dispatches to a visit_<Node> method and falls back to generic_visit as the built-in default case, so analysis tools written before newer node kinds existed (Match, TryStar, TypeAlias) keep traversing Python's evolving AST unchanged, exactly the degrade-don't-break contract of the pattern.
The JDK Compiler Tree API (com.sun.source.tree.TreeVisitor / SimpleTreeVisitor): every visit method defaults to visitOther/defaultAction as the catch-all, so javac-based tooling written against Java 8 trees keeps compiling and running as Java adds records, patterns and switch labels - old visitors land in visitOther instead of failing.
Roslyn's CSharpSyntaxVisitor / CSharpSyntaxWalker: the generated visitor carries one Visit method per syntax node kind plus DefaultVisit as the default case, and each C# language version extends the node hierarchy while existing analysers and the compiler's own passes keep working over the extended tree.

statement: Should each page or form have a dedicated component that owns input parsing, validation, domain invocation, and response selection, or should one shared component multiplex all of these behaviors?
name: either
document:
either
Either monad
disjoint union
Encode the two outcomes of a fallible operation - a value-carrying success (Right/Ok) and a reason-carrying failure (Left/Err) - in one sum-type value, so a caller must destructure both branches before going further and failures cannot escape as exceptions, sentinel values or undocumented convention.
An operation can fail in ways the caller must handle, but the failure channel is invisible in the signature: exceptions unwind past intermediate callers, where they get swallowed or merely logged, status codes and sentinels are silently ignored, and the reason for failure is flattened into a message string nobody can branch on.
Expected, recoverable failures in code that has to compose: parsing and validation at a boundary, persistence and I/O calls, service calls inside a pipeline, or any layer whose caller must render, translate, retry or count the failure. It pays off where the error type is part of an API contract between teams or modules, and where the language can express a two-case type (algebraic data type, sealed hierarchy, discriminated union) or a library supplies one.
Validating untrusted input at a boundary and returning the concrete reason (field, offset, rule violated) so the caller can render a precise message.
Domain operations that can fail for several business reasons (insufficient funds, account closed, limit exceeded) where callers must branch on the reason instead of guessing from a string.
Parsing and decoding (config, documents, wire formats) where the failure position or cause must travel back with the outcome.
Pipelines of fallible steps (authenticate -> load -> transform -> persist) that should stop at the first failure with the original reason intact instead of unwinding with a stack trace.
Translate-once boundaries: turn transport errors into domain errors in one adapter, so no layer above has to know about HTTP codes, IOExceptions or database error numbers.
Accumulating validation of independent fields, where every reason must be reported together rather than only the first one — use an Applicative validation instance with a Semigroup-based error accumulator.
Callbacks and async APIs whose failure cannot be thrown to the caller (completion handlers, event consumers) and therefore has to be delivered as a value.
Parallel fallible operations where you want to collect all successes and all failures separately before deciding, using partition or sequence operations on a List<Result>.
Domain-driven design aggregates where a root entity operation can fail for many reasons (invariant violations, business rule breaches) and the aggregate root returns Either to the application layer.
Service-to-service calls inside a pipeline where the downstream service returns a structured error response (not an exception), and the upstream must branch, translate, or propagate it.
Rust standard-library convention: fallible I/O, parsing and system calls return Result<T, E> and ? propagates the first Err up the call chain to a boundary (a main or entry point that returns Result) - the backbone of recoverable error handling in Rust.
Kotlin/Arrow typed-error pipelines: an either { } computation DSL where bind() short-circuits on Left and Either.catch turns a throwing interop call into a Left at the adapter boundary.
Java services using Vavr's right-biased Either: map/flatMap chains propagate Left without checked exceptions, keeping the failure type part of the signature in fluent pipelines.

statement: Should ProcurementCore place Acme-specific calls, data, and failure semantics behind its own translation boundary?
name: anti-corruption-layer
document:
anti-corruption-layer
acl
translation layer
Protect a downstream bounded context from a foreign model by making one explicitly owned boundary translate calls, data and failure semantics into the downstream language; unlike a mere wrapper, an anti-corruption layer prevents foreign concepts from becoming domain concepts.
A bounded context must use a legacy application, packaged product, partner API or another context whose model it cannot control, and the same words carry different meanings on each side. Reusing the foreign SDK types and status codes directly makes its names, optionality, units, errors and version churn load-bearing parts of the local domain; translation then drifts across callers and every upstream change becomes a core-model change. Without an explicit boundary, the contexts become accidental conformists and neither can evolve independently.
Use it at a durable integration seam where the models genuinely disagree and at least one side cannot be changed: a new core beside a legacy or packaged system, a core subdomain consuming a third-party service, two bounded contexts with different vocabularies, or a staged migration whose callers must survive a callee replacement. It is a boundary-scoped investment: a model worth protecting must exist on the downstream side, and the seam must be durable enough to own a component; a wire-level rename, a CRUD screen over a stable API or throwaway code does not justify it.
Staged migration (strangler style): a monolith keeps calling a capability that has been extracted into a service, and the layer converts the old call into the new semantics so existing callers are not modified while functionality moves out piece by piece.
Legacy or packaged systems: an ERP, mainframe, CRM or vendor database with convoluted schemas and obsolete protocols is consumed by a new core domain that refuses to adopt its concepts.
Third-party services inside a core subdomain: a payment, identity or logistics API whose model must not shape your domain — its statuses, optionality and error codes are mapped to your own types.
Two bounded contexts in one product: the upstream team publishes a model your context rejects (conformist would be too costly), so your side translates it and the context map records the relationship.
Event-driven integration: upstream events are translated, validated and re-emitted as downstream domain events before any handler in the core sees them.
Standardised external formats: EDI, ISO 20022, FHIR or partner schemas are parsed into a local model inside the layer, keeping the standard's vocabulary out of the domain.
Replacing an infrastructure dependency: swapping the persistence engine, message broker or identity provider behind a layer while the domain keeps exactly the same vocabulary.
Database-view ACL for analytics: a database view that maps another context's internal storage schema into an analytics-owned projection, used instead of direct cross-context SQL queries that couple the analytics context to the source's implementation details.
API-gateway-level ACL: an Azure Functions, AWS Lambda or similar serverless function deployed at the API gateway seam that performs domain-model translation before requests reach the downstream service, keeping protocol handling and semantic translation separate.
Dark launch / shadow traffic validation: an ACL running in parallel that receives mirrored traffic and logs translation discrepancies without affecting live callers, enabling validation of a new integration before any traffic is cut over.
Multi-system data aggregation: a domain that must compose data from multiple external systems with incompatible models (e.g., a customer dashboard pulling from Stripe, Salesforce and an on-premises ERP) translates each system's model separately before assembling a unified view.
Bidirectional payment provider integration: a payment gateway ACL that translates inbound webhooks (provider → local domain events) and outbound charge requests (local domain → provider format), with a stable provider-independent reference as the operation key on every call.
Legacy system read-through cache: an ACL that wraps a legacy system's slow query with asynchronous cache warming and model translation, so the domain sees a fast, semantically correct response without coupling to the legacy's latency profile.
AWS Migration Hub Refactor Spaces strangler migration: Amazon API Gateway routes a monolith's calls to legacy or Lambda services while an ACL converts the monolith's old interface to the migrated service and is removed after callers move.
Spring Boot customer integration: a Spring component with an external client, explicit mapper, retry policy and circuit breaker translates provider responses into local aggregates; keep the ACL inside the service unless several consumers need the same boundary.
Azure Strangler Fig migration: an Azure façade routes legacy and new services while a domain-owned ACL translates calls in both directions, letting clients keep the same interface until the legacy feature is retired.

name: converter
document:
converter
translator
Give a pair of corresponding representations one owner that maps them into each other in both directions, so every caller converts through one place and neither representation has to import, know or be aware of the other.
The same information lives in two representations - domain object and DTO, in-memory value and wire or column format, internal model and third-party schema - and both directions are exercised in production. Hand-written field copying at each call site duplicates the mapping rules, drifts whenever either representation changes, and forces at least one side (or every caller) to import the other.
Component boundaries where an internal model meets an external representation: service or API layers exchanging DTOs, persistence layers mapping values to column formats, integration seams facing a third-party or legacy schema, and codec layers mapping typed values to a wire format. It applies whenever both directions are needed (read and write, decode and encode) and either side must stay independent of the other - different modules, teams, release cycles or libraries.
Domain object <-> DTO at a service or API boundary, where the transport shape must not leak into the model.
Value object <-> database column representation (JPA AttributeConverter, EF Core ValueConverter, Rails custom attribute type).
Third-party or legacy schema <-> internal model at an integration seam, including versioned wire formats.
Typed value <-> JSON, XML or protobuf payload with a custom codec when the default mapping is wrong (formats, units, enums).
Query rows or record sets <-> domain objects, where a full mapper framework would be oversized.
Single-value wrappers such as identifiers, money or unit-carrying quantities mapped to and from their primitive form.
Palindrome conversion chain (Entity -> DAO -> DTO -> Controller -> DTO -> DAO -> Entity) where each layer owns exactly one transformation direction, making the data flow explicit and each boundary independently testable.
Versioned API contracts: a DTO for API v1 and a separate DTO for API v2 coexist; a converter pair maps each version's DTO to the shared internal model, isolating API consumers from internal changes.
API gateway transformation: external third-party API payloads are normalized into an internal canonical format at the gateway, and outbound responses are converted back to the third-party schema; converters live at the seam.
Event-driven payload normalization: domain events carry one representation (e.g., enriched entity) while the event bus transports a flattened wire format (e.g., protobuf); converters at producer and consumer ends keep the two shapes in sync.
ORM entity vs. read-model DTO at the query boundary: a repository executes a query and the row-set converter maps each row to a read-model DTO, avoiding the entity in read-only paths entirely.
Anti-corruption layer at legacy integration seams: external system payloads are translated into the internal domain model at the boundary, and responses translated back; the converter owns the translation vocabulary, protecting the domain model from foreign concepts (Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design; Microsoft Azure Architecture Center; AWS Prescriptive Guidance).
Immutable value type <-> wire format for cryptographic or financial domains: the converter is a lawful isomorphism ensuring every wire value round-trips to an identical object (tested via property-based round-trip laws, as in the lawful-conversions Haskell library and Higher-Kinded-J Iso optics library).
Strangler-fig migration seam: new microservice functionality is accessed through an ACL that converts legacy system payloads to the new domain model and back, keeping the legacy interface unchanged while the new service evolves behind the seam.
Guava com.google.common.base.Converter<F, T>: an abstract bidirectional function with convert()/reverse(), automatic reverse() derivation for subclasses, mapAll() for whole iterables and Converter.normalize() to lift a converter into a function converter - the pattern as a shipped JDK-adjacent library type (Google Guava).
Go database/sql custom types: a type implementing both sql.Scanner (Scan(src any) error) and driver.Valuer (Value() (driver.Value, error)) owns the Go value <-> database column pair in both directions; the standard library's NullString, NullInt64 and NullTime are built-in pairs of exactly this shape.
Rails custom attribute types: subclass ActiveModel::Type::Value, override serialize (Ruby value -> database value) and deserialize (database value -> Ruby value) and bind with attribute :col, MyType.new - the converter pair at the ORM seam, with cast_value kept separate for user-input coercion.

name: message-translator
document:
message-translator
translator
Convert a message from one data format into another at the integration seam, so that systems with different data models or wire contracts can exchange messages without either side having to learn the other's representation.
Two systems that must exchange messages disagree on format - field names, structure, units, encodings, what is optional - and neither can be changed (legacy systems, packaged applications, external partners). Without an explicit translation step every consumer parses and reinterprets the producer's format, both models leak across the boundary, and each new pair of systems multiplies the parsing code.
Integration boundaries between applications that each own a proprietary data model, or between an internal model and a standardised external format (EDIFACT, RosettaNet, a partner API). It applies wherever messages cross a seam that neither side can move - legacy adapters, EDI gateways, protocol bridges, published partner interfaces - and the source-to-target mapping therefore has to live in a component of its own, wired between the two channels.
Legacy integration: a fixed-width mainframe record or COBOL copybook file is translated into the JSON contract of a modern service.
B2B/EDI: an internal order model is translated into EDIFACT/X12 (or a partner-specific XML dialect) and the inbound acknowledgements back.
Versioned public API: v1 requests and responses are translated to v2 so existing clients keep working during a migration.
Protocol bridging: a JSON message consumed from a queue is translated into an Avro or Protobuf record for a different broker or stream processor.
Anti-corruption layer: data arriving from a SaaS/CRM model is translated into the internal domain model so vendor field names never reach the core.
Normalisation at the edge: dates, units, currency and character encodings are converted to the internal conventions before domain logic runs.
Format migration with coexistence: old and new formats run side by side during a staged rollout, one translator per direction and a deprecation date.
Apache Camel route: Camel's Message Translator EIP uses a transform or setBody step, a bean or processor, a template, or marshal/unmarshal data formats to adapt a payload between endpoints.
Spring Integration flow: a transformer endpoint converts payloads between producers and consumers, using an @Transformer method or the IntegrationFlow transform() DSL operator.
WSO2 Integrator: Micro Integrator's Message Translator/Data Mapper converts a client payload to the backend service's schema before invoking the backend endpoint.

statement: Should ProcurementCore place Acme-specific calls, data, and failure semantics behind its own translation boundary?
name: compound-components
document:
compound-components
compound component
compound component pattern
Give a family of cooperating components one owner — the parent — that holds the shared state and publishes it implicitly to every child, so consumers compose the family declaratively while the parent alone enforces its invariants and behaviour.
A widget only works when a parent and its children agree on one piece of state (which option is selected, which panel is open, whether a field is invalid), but the call site is the only place that knows the children. Holding the state at the call site means threading the value and its update callbacks into every child (prop drilling), and holding it in the children means the parent cannot enforce the family's invariants — exclusivity, ordering, keyboard behaviour — nor react to a child's change in one place. The recurring decision is where the shared state lives and how children participate in it without the call site wiring them.
Component-tree UI code: design-system and widget libraries (select/option, tabs, menus, field groups) in frameworks that can inject state into descendants without passing it through props — React context or child cloning, Angular content projection plus DI, Vue provide/inject, Compose CompositionLocal and slot scopes, SwiftUI environment and preference keys, Blazor cascading values, WPF attached properties over the logical tree — and in widget toolkits whose group objects (Swing ButtonGroup, JavaFX ToggleGroup, Qt QButtonGroup, tkinter control variables) play the same role. It pays off where the public API must stay small and the children must stay replaceable; it does not apply in languages without a component tree or without an implicit-injection channel.
Custom select, combobox or autocomplete families built from Option children — the canonical example: the parent owns the selection, the highlight and the keyboard interaction while options only declare their value and label.
Tabs, accordions and menus where Tab/TabPanel/MenuItem children register their identity and the parent owns the active item, the ordering and the ARIA wiring.
Form-field families (Field + Label + Input + Error) that share one validation/invalid state and generated ids without the call site passing them around.
Data-group widgets: tables with Column definitions, list widgets with Item children, tree views with Node children, chart legends with Series children.
Design-system libraries that export one namespaced symbol whose parts must be used together — the context in which the pattern is most often documented and most valuable.
Collapsible panel families (Disclosure pattern) where a parent owns the open/closed state and Trigger/Content children read it — also known as the Disclosure pattern in ARIA authoring practices.
Stepper/wizard widgets where a parent owns current-step state and Step/StepIndicator children read it without the consumer threading step indices.
Popover/tooltip families where a trigger button and a content panel share open/close state through the parent without prop drilling.
Radix UI Primitives — Dialog.Root owns the open/close context and Trigger/Portal/Content/Title/Description consume it, while asChild (Slot) merges each part's props, refs and keyboard behaviour into the consumer's own button or link.
Ark UI headless components (built on Zag.js state machines) — Popover.Root/Trigger/Positioner/Content share state through the root, ids props compose aria bindings across two families, and the same compound anatomy works in React, Solid, Vue and Svelte.
Headless UI's Dialog family (Dialog, DialogBackdrop, DialogPanel, DialogTitle, Description) — the root enforces the dismiss contract (open prop, onClose callback, focus trap, aria-labelledby) and every part reads the shared open/closed state, exposed for styling as data-open/data-closed attributes.

statement: Should ProcurementCore place Acme-specific calls, data, and failure semantics behind its own translation boundary?
name: row-data-gateway
document:
row-data-gateway
row data gateway
row gateway
Give each database row its own in-memory object that mirrors the row's columns and carries the row's own find, insert, update and delete operations, so all data-access code for a table lives in one place instead of being duplicated across the scripts that use it.
SQL text, parameter binding and result-set mapping are re-derived inside every transaction script that touches a table, while the in-memory objects those scripts work with know nothing about the database. No single place knows how one row is read, written and deleted, so a schema change ripples through every script and every new query is another chance to get parameterisation and type conversion wrong.
Applies when business logic is organised as transaction scripts or thin services over a relational schema whose columns map closely to the fields actually used: the gateway mirrors the table structure, no object/relational impedance mismatch is being managed, and identity maps, units of work and lazy loading are either unnecessary or added deliberately as separate patterns. It also fits generated persistence layers, where the gateway classes are produced from schema metadata during the build.
Transaction-script applications (order entry, billing runs, batch imports) where several scripts need the same handful of row-level reads and writes.
CRUD-heavy back-office and admin tooling where a screen edits one row at a time and columns map one-to-one onto form fields.
Legacy or externally owned schemas that must be mirrored rather than reshaped: one gateway per table gives an explicit, reviewable seam between the application and someone else's database.
Generated persistence layers: gateways produced from schema metadata on every build, so the tedious class-per-table work is automated and stays in sync with the schema.
Simple mappings inside an otherwise rich domain model, where a domain object keeps a gateway as its data holder instead of copying field values around.
Reporting and fixture utilities that need reusable, parameterised finders for one table without pulling in a full object/relational mapper.
Laminas\Db\RowGateway and RowGatewayFeature (the official laminas-db implementation) expose one row object with save/delete and can materialize table-query results as row gateways, fitting CRUD screens or transaction scripts that edit individual records.
Zend Framework 1's Zend_Db_Table_Row is a documented legacy row-gateway implementation: table queries return row objects with column access plus save/delete/createRow operations, useful when a simple schema is consumed by row-oriented scripts.
The Go dgw tool generates structs and lightweight Table/Row Data Gateway functions from PostgreSQL metadata, demonstrating the pattern as a code-generation choice when a project wants typed CRUD without a full ORM.

statement: Should ProcurementCore place Acme-specific calls, data, and failure semantics behind its own translation boundary?
name: double-checked-locking
document:
double-checked-locking
double-checked locking optimization
DCL
DCLP
Initialise a shared resource exactly once and lazily while keeping the steady-state read path free of lock acquisition - by testing a cheaply published state first and taking the lock only for the one-time construction, where the platform can publish the built object safely to every reader.
An expensive object - configuration, a connection pool, a compiled plan, a cache - must be created once and only when it is first needed, but its accessor is called from many threads. The naive check-then-act form lets two threads build it at the same time, and guarding every read with a lock serialises a path that almost never needs synchronisation. The tempting fix - test a flag cheaply, lock only for the initialisation, test again inside the lock - is sound only if the write that publishes the object is ordered with respect to the readers' loads, which is exactly the part the classic formulation leaves implicit and the reason the idiom is famous for rare, unreproducible failures.
Concurrent, shared-memory software in which one object or cell must be built once and read many times: process-wide singletons and registries, per-object caches inside an object shared between threads, lazily built statics in languages whose runtime also provides the once semantics. The pattern presupposes a memory model with a defined publication ordering (volatile, acquire/release, an initialisation lock, or a runtime once primitive) and a read path hot enough that the lock it removes is measurable. On single-threaded runtimes there is nothing to synchronise, and where a single-threaded composition root can initialise eagerly the pattern is unnecessary.
Process-wide singletons whose construction is expensive or configuration-dependent: configuration snapshot, metrics registry, logger, connection pool, feature-flag view.
Per-object caches inside an object shared by several threads - compiled regular expression or query plan, parsed schema, symbol table - where the build is expensive and the read is hot.
Lazily built statics in languages where the runtime owns the once semantics: C++ function-local static, Swift static let or global let, Kotlin by lazy, Scala lazy val, Go sync.Once, Rust OnceLock/LazyLock.
Compensating for the static-initialisation-order problem: an accessor that builds the global on first use instead of relying on cross-translation-unit initialisation order.
Avoiding lock overhead on a read-mostly, write-once hot path (memo tables, symbol caches, thread-safe lazy proxies) where a contended lock would show up in a profile.
Small or freestanding runtimes without a once primitive, where the first caller must build the cell and an eager initialiser is not available.
RWMutex-protected maps in Go where readers check a fast path before the slower write-locked re-check, as a safer alternative to sync.Map for workloads with known access patterns.
Per-connection or per-session lazy fields in object-pooled servers where the pool itself is the shared cell and each borrowed object gets a lazy-computed field.
Cross-language plugin or extension registries where one language's runtime initialises a global handle that other language shards read without repeated synchronisation.
Rate-limiter or circuit-breaker state that must be lazily built from configuration: building eagerly would couple the policy to startup time, but the read path must be lock-free under high throughput.
Lazy compilation or query-plan warming in database connection pools where the pool is shared but individual plans are built on first use by the owning thread.
Spring Framework's DefaultSingletonBeanRegistry.getSingleton: check the singletonObjects map lock-free, take the singletonLock only when the bean is absent, re-check inside - a production evolution of the idiom whose correctness was formally challenged (SPR-13463) and upheld because the concurrent-map read already carries the needed memory barrier.
Chromium's base::LazyInstance / GetOrCreateLazyPointer: an atomic state word with a 'creating' bit, acquire-load fast path and release-store publication - since deprecated in favour of function-local statics with base::NoDestructor, a signal of how far hardened platforms have moved from hand-rolled DCL.
ACE toolkit's ACE_Singleton<TYPE, ACE_LOCK>: the pattern's original industrial home (the 1997 paper was written alongside ACE) - the template still guards instance() with a double-checked ACE_LOCK acquire and recommends ACE_Recursive_Thread_Mutex for multi-threaded access.
Swift runtime: every global/static let is lowered to swift_once (dispatch_once on Darwin), so the double-checked once structure is the default initialisation mechanism for lazily computed immutable globals rather than hand-written code.

statement: Should ProcurementCore place Acme-specific calls, data, and failure semantics behind its own translation boundary?
name: page-object
document:
page-object
page object model
window driver
Wrap each UI surface a test drives - a page or a significant component - in an object that exposes the services the surface offers and hides every locator, driver call and wait, so a UI change is absorbed by one class instead of by every test that touched the markup.
A UI test that drives the automation API directly - find an element, type, click, wait, read text - keeps the page's locators and interaction mechanics in the test body: the same selector is repeated across dozens of tests, a markup change breaks them all at once, and a reader must reconstruct the page's structure to understand what the test does. The catalog's trigger: a UI change should touch one class, not fifty assertions.
Automated tests that drive a user interface through a driver API - a browser (Selenium/WebDriver, Playwright, Cypress, WebdriverIO), a mobile app (Appium, Espresso, XCUITest) or a desktop window - where the same screens are exercised by many tests, where the UI changes independently of the tests, and where the suite is expected to survive redesigns. The pattern pays off when the interface can be named in the user's terms ('sign-in page', 'product row') and the driver offers stable element lookup; it is unnecessary for a single throwaway script or when the presentation logic has already been extracted behind a humble object.
A regression suite over a web application whose pages are exercised by dozens of tests: login, search, checkout and admin screens each get a class, and a redesign changes only those classes (the Selenium and Playwright POM guides' home scenario).
The same screens are driven by different kinds of test - functional, visual, accessibility, smoke - and the locator knowledge must live in one place that all of them import.
Mobile application suites (Appium, Espresso, XCUITest) where screens are widget hierarchies with platform-specific queries, and the page object is the only place that codifies the platform lookup.
BDD suites: Gherkin steps stay business-readable because step definitions delegate to page objects instead of calling the driver (Fowler's layering recommendation).
Suites migrating drivers or frameworks (Selenium to Playwright, a WebdriverIO restructure): the page API is kept while only its internals change.
A scripting interface over an application whose behaviour is stuck in the UI (Fowler's scripting use), or a legacy system that can only be exercised through its window.
Selenium's documented login flow: SignInPage.loginValidUser returns HomePage, so a regression suite can exercise authentication through services while locators and page-load checks stay in the page objects.
Playwright's official playwright.dev example: PlaywrightDevPage wraps a Page, owns locators for the getting-started flow and exposes goto, getStarted and pageObjectModel methods used by tests.
WebdriverIO's official The Internet login example: a getter-based LoginPage centralizes selectors and open/submit actions, letting login specs survive selector changes without duplicating driver calls.

statement: Should ProcurementCore place Acme-specific calls, data, and failure semantics behind its own translation boundary?
name: characterization-test
document:
characterization-test
golden master
approval test
golden file test
snapshot test
golden session test
Pin the actual, currently deployed behaviour of existing code in committed reference artefacts (golden masters) so that a later edit can be distinguished from an accidental regression even when nobody can say what the code is supposed to do.
You must change code whose behaviour is undocumented, surprising or only known to production: there is no specification to test against, and tests written from intended behaviour would take too long and silently encode guesses as fact. The safety net therefore has to be built from observed behaviour: replay a corpus of real inputs through the untouched subject, capture everything observable, commit the result as the reference, and let every later run diff against it - pinning what the code does today before changing how it does it.
Applies whenever the subject already runs and can be exercised in a test process or from a test script: untested legacy modules, data transformations and report pipelines, serializers, parsers and code generators, CLI and protocol endpoints, rendering pipelines whose images can be diffed, and dependency or runtime upgrades where the old behaviour is the baseline. The precondition is determinism: volatile parts (timestamps, identifiers, paths, memory addresses, collection order, locale, floating-point formatting) must be normalized or redacted before capture, otherwise the comparison is noise. The pattern is a first move - build the net, then refactor under it - and pairs with a deliberate approval step, because a characterization test does not know which behaviour was intended.
Before refactoring an untested legacy module: capture outputs for a corpus of inputs, restructure the code, and require the reference artefacts to stay identical.
Data processing and batch jobs: pin how representative input files are transformed into output files or reports, so the nightly job can be changed safely.
Serializers, formatters and code generators: pin the emitted text or structured output for representative documents, with a redaction step for volatile values.
Rendering and UI pipelines: pin generated images (screenshot goldens) or rendered text output with an approval workflow and a visual diff tool.
CLI and protocol behaviour: pin stdout, stderr and exit codes, or request/response bytes, for a set of recorded invocations.
Dependency or runtime upgrades: pin behaviour before the upgrade and re-run afterwards, so only intended differences have to be reviewed.
Production defect triage: replay the failing production input into a new reference artefact, then fix the defect against that regression test.
AI/LLM output regression testing: pin model responses to a curated golden dataset; on model or prompt change, compare distributions, embedding similarity, or token-level diffs against the baseline rather than requiring exact matches (LLM eval pipelines, 2024-2026).
Generated code verification: pin the exact output of OpenAPI client generators, GraphQL type generators, SDK wrappers, or database migration previews so formatting and structural changes are caught.
Database schema migration testing: capture the before/after output of migration scripts for a set of schema variants, approving only intentional structural differences.
Computer vision pipeline regression: pin bounding-box distributions or classification confidence vectors from CV models across runs; statistical comparison prevents flaky failures from minor pixel noise.
Smart contract and blockchain output regression: pin deterministic contract outputs for a given input state; any divergence in on-chain behaviour is immediately visible (Nexlify case, 2025).
Database-engine regression suites: PostgreSQL's pg_regress replays each sql/*.sql script and diffs results/*.out against committed golden files in expected/*, with variant comparison files and a resultmap absorbing known platform differences (locale, float formatting, row ordering).
Compiler test corpora: LLVM's lit/FileCheck pins emitted IR and machine code by piping compiler output to FileCheck, which verifies CHECK directives committed inside each test file across the whole input corpus.
ORM query-change detection: ApprovalTests.Ruby's verify_sql approves the SQL an ActiveRecord call emits, so a gem or framework upgrade that silently rewrites generated queries fails the suite.

name: repository
document:
repository
collection-oriented repository
repository layer
Mediates between the domain model and the data mapping layer with a collection-like interface, so domain code adds, removes and finds persistent objects as if they lived in memory and never constructs queries or touches persistence APIs itself.
Persistence code spreads: every application service re-derives the same SQL or ORM queries, duplicate query logic drifts apart, table and column names leak into domain decisions, and testing domain rules without a database becomes impossible. Callers should be able to think in collections of domain objects instead of queries.
Applies to systems with a non-trivial domain model sitting on a data-mapping layer (Data Mapper, metadata mapping, or a hand-written mapper) where the same queries recur across application services; it becomes more valuable as domain classes and query volume grow. It is the standard persistence boundary of DDD aggregates (one repository per aggregate root) and presumes a unit of work or session that owns flush and commit. It is not a per-table data-access wrapper and not a replacement for transaction control.
DDD application services that must load an aggregate root, run domain logic on it and store it again without knowing the table layout.
Data-mapper backends where several application services and background jobs share recurring complex queries (overdue invoices, pending orders, open tickets).
Applications that must be unit-testable away from the database: repositories are the substitution point for in-memory doubles.
Systems that must support more than one store behind a stable domain interface — relational in production, in-memory in tests, a document store for a particular deployment.
Uniform cross-cutting access policy for an aggregate: caching, read-replica routing, audit logging or authorization applied as decorators around one interface.
Migration work where the persistence technology changes (ORM swap, schema split, service extraction) while the domain model and its tests stay untouched.
CQRS write-side aggregate loading where the aggregate must be reconstructed fully to apply business rules and enforce invariants.
Integration with heterogeneous data sources where one repository unifies access to a cache, primary database and a third-party API behind a domain interface.
Spring Data JPA applications can use Repository/CrudRepository for aggregate-typed CRUD, paging and derived queries, then add only domain-specific methods rather than wrapping every persistence operation.
The .NET eShopOnContainers ordering microservice uses an EF Core BuyerRepository over a shared scoped DbContext/unit of work, while CQRS/Dapper handles presentation reads.
Python applications using SQLAlchemy ORM can place an aggregate-facing repository over Session, whose identity map and unit-of-work flush semantics provide the mapper/session boundary.

name: functional-options
document:
functional-options
option functions
self-referential functions
Keep a constructor's required parameter list fixed while optional settings arrive as named configuration functions that are applied in order over built-in defaults, so the API can grow without breaking callers and without exposing a mutable configuration object.
A constructor accumulates optional settings: every new setting changes the signature for all callers, zero values and booleans cannot be distinguished from 'not supplied', and a configuration struct has to be handed out (often by pointer, with nil meaning 'default') so callers can retain and mutate the very state the library depends on. The recurring decision is how to let an option set grow across the life of a public API while keeping meaningful defaults, source compatibility and a documented resolution rule for conflicting options.
Public constructors and factories of libraries, clients, servers and loggers whose option set grows across releases; languages without named or default arguments, or APIs that must stay source-compatible while options multiply; settings whose defaults are meaningful and whose combinations need a stated precedence (last wins) or explicit conflict handling.
Client and server constructors that must keep a stable signature while gaining credentials, timeouts, retries, interceptors and keep-alive settings across releases (gRPC-Go dialoptions, GCP Go SDK, Uber's internal service clients).
Loggers and instrumentation: severity, sampling, sinks and caller-annotation settings composed per component or per test.
Test fixtures: a production default plus a handful of overrides per scenario, without a builder class or a configuration file.
Reusable option groups baked into exported helpers for common deployments (insecure/local mode, tracing on, hardened defaults) that expand to several settings in one call.
Environment- or flag-driven construction where the option list is assembled at runtime from parsed input and applied to a single target.
OpenTelemetry SDK initialization: service name, endpoint, sampling ratio, resource attributes and exporter configuration composed via functional options with environment-variable fallback (otel-libs, OpenTelemetry Go resource construction).
SDK and library configuration for public APIs where the library must evolve without breaking caller code: adding a new tracing exporter or timeout setting does not change existing call sites.
Kubernetes operator and controller configuration where resources need environment-driven defaults but also explicit per-deployment overrides (o11y.Init, otelhelper.Setup patterns).
Database and message-broker client pools: connection limits, timeouts, TLS and credentials wired at construction time; per-query options (context, routing keys) stay out of the constructor.
HTTP middleware chain composition where each middleware is an option that wraps the next handler, enabling selective instrumentation without a fixed middleware list.
Feature-flag-driven service construction where the enabled feature set determines which options are applied, allowing a single NewService constructor to produce different service variants.
gRPC and Protobuf code generation integration where generated builder types expose functional options for fields that were not known at the time the proto was compiled.
gRPC-Go connection setup uses typed DialOption values such as WithUnaryInterceptor, WithChainStreamInterceptor and WithDefaultCallOptions to grow Dial/NewClient configuration without changing the constructor signature (grpc-go).
OpenTelemetry Go's TracerProvider is assembled with options such as sdktrace.WithBatcher, WithResource and WithSampler, composing exporter, resource and sampling choices at initialization (OpenTelemetry Go).
Kubernetes controller-runtime exposes typed per-operation options such as MatchingLabels, FieldOwner, DryRun and FieldValidation for client CRUD calls, keeping method signatures stable while extending request behavior (controller-runtime).
