name: either
document:
either
Either monad
disjoint union
Encode the two outcomes of a fallible operation - a value-carrying success (Right/Ok) and a reason-carrying failure (Left/Err) - in one sum-type value, so a caller must destructure both branches before going further and failures cannot escape as exceptions, sentinel values or undocumented convention.
An operation can fail in ways the caller must handle, but the failure channel is invisible in the signature: exceptions unwind past intermediate callers, where they get swallowed or merely logged, status codes and sentinels are silently ignored, and the reason for failure is flattened into a message string nobody can branch on.
Expected, recoverable failures in code that has to compose: parsing and validation at a boundary, persistence and I/O calls, service calls inside a pipeline, or any layer whose caller must render, translate, retry or count the failure. It pays off where the error type is part of an API contract between teams or modules, and where the language can express a two-case type (algebraic data type, sealed hierarchy, discriminated union) or a library supplies one.
Validating untrusted input at a boundary and returning the concrete reason (field, offset, rule violated) so the caller can render a precise message.
Domain operations that can fail for several business reasons (insufficient funds, account closed, limit exceeded) where callers must branch on the reason instead of guessing from a string.
Parsing and decoding (config, documents, wire formats) where the failure position or cause must travel back with the outcome.
Pipelines of fallible steps (authenticate -> load -> transform -> persist) that should stop at the first failure with the original reason intact instead of unwinding with a stack trace.
Translate-once boundaries: turn transport errors into domain errors in one adapter, so no layer above has to know about HTTP codes, IOExceptions or database error numbers.
Accumulating validation of independent fields, where every reason must be reported together rather than only the first one — use an Applicative validation instance with a Semigroup-based error accumulator.
Callbacks and async APIs whose failure cannot be thrown to the caller (completion handlers, event consumers) and therefore has to be delivered as a value.
Parallel fallible operations where you want to collect all successes and all failures separately before deciding, using partition or sequence operations on a List<Result>.
Domain-driven design aggregates where a root entity operation can fail for many reasons (invariant violations, business rule breaches) and the aggregate root returns Either to the application layer.
Service-to-service calls inside a pipeline where the downstream service returns a structured error response (not an exception), and the upstream must branch, translate, or propagate it.
Rust standard-library convention: fallible I/O, parsing and system calls return Result<T, E> and ? propagates the first Err up the call chain to a boundary (a main or entry point that returns Result) - the backbone of recoverable error handling in Rust.
Kotlin/Arrow typed-error pipelines: an either { } computation DSL where bind() short-circuits on Left and Either.catch turns a throwing interop call into a Left at the adapter boundary.
Java services using Vavr's right-biased Either: map/flatMap chains propagate Left without checked exceptions, keeping the failure type part of the signature in fluent pipelines.

name: point-to-point-channel
document:
point-to-point-channel
point-to-point queue
p2p channel
Deliver each message on a channel to exactly one consumer, so senders never have to coordinate with receivers and no unit of work is handled twice.
A producer must hand work to exactly one handler while several receivers are running (or the intended handler is temporarily unavailable): broadcasting the message makes every receiver deduplicate, and addressing a specific consumer instance couples the sender to its identity, location and liveness.
Asynchronous messaging inside one process, between processes or across services, where each message is a unit of work (command, job, document, RPC request) and duplicate handling is as unacceptable as loss. Applies to in-process worker queues and to brokered channels (JMS queue, AMQP queue, Kafka partition, cloud queue) alike; the channel - not the consumer and not the sender - owns the routing decision.
Work queues: a web tier enqueues jobs and a pool of workers consumes them, with each job running exactly once.
Request-reply over messaging: the request goes to a queue, exactly one service instance answers it, and the reply returns on a reply queue identified by a correlation identifier.
Command dispatch in a service-oriented system: an order service appends commands that exactly one instance of the command processor executes.
Media or log processing pipelines where every stage pulls its input from a queue and each item is handled by one of the stage's replicas.
Legacy and batch integration: jobs handed to a single consumer daemon through a queue, with the channel providing the transactional hand-off.
Scaling an existing single-consumer endpoint by attaching additional instances (Competing Consumers) without changing producers or the message contract.
Apache Kafka consumer groups: records in each topic partition are assigned to one group member at a time, so a group scales work while separate group IDs retain independent pub-sub copies.
RabbitMQ Work Queues: a task queue distributes jobs among competing workers with round-robin or fair dispatch; manual acknowledgements allow unacknowledged work to be redelivered after a worker failure.
Amazon SQS Standard queues: distribute background jobs among consumers with visibility timeouts, while at-least-once delivery requires idempotent handlers because duplicate deliveries remain possible.

name: pratt-parser
document:
pratt-parser
top-down operator precedence
tdop
Parse expressions with many prefix, infix and postfix operators by associating a binding power and a handler with each token type, so precedence and associativity live in one rule table instead of one parsing function per precedence level.
Operator precedence turns expression parsing into a ladder of near-identical functions - one per level - each of which must re-implement associativity, delegate to the next level for its operands, and be edited whenever an operator is added or moves. Grammars with prefix, infix, postfix and mixfix operators (ternary conditionals, assignment, calls, indexing, user-registered operators) make that ladder long, make associativity easy to get subtly wrong, and scatter the grammar across the parser so it cannot be read in one place.
Hand-written parsers for an expression-bearing language, DSL, query or configuration syntax: a token stream is already available (or is cheap to lex), the operator set is large or expected to grow, and the team wants the grammar visible as data. It is typically the expression layer under an ordinary recursive-descent parser for statements and declarations - interpreters, calculators, filter and rule engines, formula tools - and it is unnecessary when a parser generator already declares precedence for the grammar.
Expression evaluators and calculators whose operator set is expected to grow (arithmetic, units, comparisons, percentages, function calls, user-defined functions).
Query, filter and rule languages - search filters, feature-flag conditions, access-policy conditions, spreadsheet formulas - with many comparison, logical and string operators.
Front ends for small languages and DSLs that parse statements and declarations with recursive descent and need real precedence handling for the expression layer.
Single-pass compilers and interpreters that emit bytecode or IR while parsing, where each handler is also the point that emits the operator's instruction.
Template and configuration expression languages that must attach exact source positions and precise errors to every operator.
Host-language extension points that let plugins or users register additional operators at runtime, because registration is just a table entry.
Rust PEG grammars that use pest::pratt_parser::PrattParser to map prefix, postfix and infix operator pairs into calculator or DSL ASTs.
Rust parser-combinator expression grammars built with chumsky's pratt combinator, where atom parsers and prefix, postfix and infix operators declare precedence and associativity.
JavaScript expression-only tooling built on JSEP, where a compact Pratt-style parser produces ASTs and allows custom unary and binary operators with explicit precedence.

name: authentication-enforcer
document:
authentication-enforcer
authentication interceptor
authentication gateway
auth middleware
Put one request-boundary checkpoint in front of protected actions that decides whether authentication is required, delegates credential verification to a replaceable mechanism, and attaches the resulting subject to request-scoped context before dispatch, so coverage is uniform without making handlers understand credentials.
When each handler decides whether and how to authenticate, protection is duplicated or omitted on exceptional paths, credential formats and user stores leak into business code, and a mechanism or policy change requires editing every handler instead of one auditable boundary.
Server-side request processing — web APIs, web applications and service endpoints — where many handlers share one protection policy, credentials arrive through a uniform convention (Authorization header, cookie, session id), verification technology must be replaceable or differ per route, and the runtime provides a request-pipeline hook (servlet filter, middleware chain, framework guard). Applies to session-based and token-based authentication alike; permissions and roles are out of scope. Three implementation strategies exist: (1) Container-Managed Authentication — the runtime container owns the checkpoint and realm configuration; (2) Authentication Provider Strategy — a custom provider behind a narrow interface, swapped without touching handlers; (3) JAAS Login Module Strategy — pluggable via standard JAAS configuration, supporting multifactor authentication via smart cards, biometrics, or third-party IdPs. The pattern is equally applicable at the edge level (API gateway, ingress proxy) and the service level (in-process middleware).
Web APIs where every route except health and login requires a bearer token, and the checkpoint is mounted in front of the whole router.
Multi-tenant applications with mixed protection levels: public marketing pages, session-protected tenant UI and token-protected integration endpoints behind one enforcement layer.
Services that must accept several credential types at once — browser sessions, mobile JWTs, mutual TLS for service-to-service traffic — while keeping one uniform enforcement point.
Credential-technology migration (basic auth to OIDC, on-premises LDAP to SSO) where enforcement stays put while the mechanism behind it is swapped.
Regulated environments where every rejected authentication attempt has to be logged centrally and identically across all endpoints.
Legacy applications with authentication checks scattered through servlets or handlers that must be consolidated behind one intercepting layer before an audit.
Zero Trust microservices where every internal service verifies JWTs independently (per-service verification) while an ingress gateway provides the first checkpoint — the enforcer exists at both layers.
OIDC/OAuth2 migration where an existing session-based app adds bearer-token support; the mechanism adapts to both while the enforcement point remains unchanged.
Multi-tenant SaaS platforms where tenant isolation depends on the enforcer resolving a tenant identifier from the token before the handler processes any data.
Platform-as-a-Service with mounted sub-applications where a parent ASGI middleware dispatches per-path authentication requirements from a config registry, injecting identity into ASGI scope for all sub-apps.
Spring Security servlet applications that use a SecurityFilterChain with anyRequest().authenticated() and an AuthenticationManager/AuthenticationProvider chain, so controllers consume the SecurityContext rather than parse credentials.
ASP.NET Core APIs that register JWT or cookie schemes, call UseAuthentication before dependent middleware, and use a fallback authorization policy to make authenticated access the default.
An nginx ingress location using auth_request to delegate identity verification to a central authentication service, forwarding only after a 2xx result and propagating 401/403 failures while services still verify their own trust boundary.

name: facade
document:
facade
façade
Provide one coarse-grained entry interface that hides a subsystem of many cooperating classes behind the few operations its clients actually need, so callers depend on a single stable API instead of orchestrating the subsystem themselves.
Every client of a complex subsystem must know which classes exist, in which order to call them, how to configure and dispose them and how to interpret their errors; that orchestration is then duplicated across the codebase, and any change inside the subsystem ripples through all callers.
Applies when a subsystem (a library, framework, legacy module, remote SDK, or a layer of your own system) is much broader than any single client needs, when its correct use is a recurring sequence of collaborations, and when client code should be insulated from its types and its evolution. Typical at module and system-boundary scope, where one entry point per layer or per external system is wanted.
Wrapping a third-party SDK, media framework or payment/HTTP client behind one class or module that exposes the application's own vocabulary (convert, charge, upload).
Application services that orchestrate repositories, gateways and domain services for one use case (checkout, report generation) and are the only seam controllers or jobs talk to.
Layered systems where every layer offers a facade as its entry point, so dependencies flow through coarse interfaces instead of reaching into a layer's internals.
Isolating a legacy subsystem while it is replaced incrementally: new code depends on the clean facade, and the migration swaps implementations behind it.
Remote and coarse-grained boundaries: a remote facade exposes a few chunky operations over a fine-grained object model to avoid chatty calls (see Remote Facade, Fowler's PEAA).
Startup/teardown sequences and device orchestration (the classic home-theatre example): clients need one 'watch movie' operation, not a dozen subsystem calls in the right order.
Service-container proxy facades (e.g. Laravel): a static-looking front-end that forwards calls to a resolved service instance, giving a terse API without sacrificing testability or DI flexibility.
JPA/service-layer facades: a single transactional entry point that receives DTOs, maps them to domain objects, orchestrates business logic, maps results back, and commits — one transaction per use case.
Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) in microservices: a thin per-client aggregation service (web, mobile, partner) that fans out to downstream microservices, reshapes responses for the client, and handles perimeter concerns. Each BFF is a specialized facade owned by the team that ships the corresponding client.
Anti-Corruption Layer (DDD): a facade placed between a bounded context and an external/legacy system to translate that system's model into domain concepts, preventing external concepts from polluting the internal domain model.
Event-driven/observable facades: a facade that exposes reactive streams (Observables, Promises, async generators) over the subsystem, buffering, batching or debouncing events for consumers that prefer push-based or streaming interfaces.
API gateway composition: an API gateway acts as a system-wide facade that unifies multiple backend services at the edge, handling auth, routing and cross-cutting concerns before delegating to more specific facades or services.
SDK wrapper facades: publishing a public-facing SDK over an internal microservice mesh; the facade shapes the external API surface, applies default configurations, and provides a stable consumer experience independent of internal service topology changes.
SLF4J (Simple Logging Facade for Java): slf4j-api is a minimal logging facade; applications code against Logger.debug()/info() once and bind the concrete framework (Logback, Log4j 2, java.util.logging) at deployment time by swapping the provider jar on the classpath — the textbook runtime-swappable facade.
Spring Framework JdbcClient / JdbcTemplate: a fluent facade over raw JDBC that owns connection and statement lifecycle, iterates ResultSets and translates SQLException into the DataAccessException hierarchy, so callers supply only SQL and result mapping instead of the full boilerplate workflow.
jQuery $.get/$.post/$.getJSON over $.ajax: a per-task facade layer that collapses cross-browser XMLHttpRequest differences, Deferred plumbing and HTTP defaults into one-line calls — the canonical JavaScript-library facade.

name: abstract-factory
document:
abstract-factory
kit
factory of factories
Expose one creation contract for each product kind in a coherent family, letting clients switch the selected family at the composition root without naming concrete products or mixing incompatible variants.
A client must construct several related products that collaborate as a matched set, but direct construction spreads family keys and concrete class names through the code. Adding a family then becomes configuration branches plus constructor edits, while mixing products from different families can fail only after incompatible objects interact.
Use in object- or interface-based subsystems with two independent axes of change: product kinds (button, slider, connection, command) and product families or variants (dark/light, PostgreSQL/Oracle, AWS/GCP). The family is normally selected once at a composition root, products from one family are intended to collaborate, and clients must compile, test and ship without knowing concrete product types; if products are intentionally mixed or only one kind is created, use a smaller creator instead.
Cross-platform or themable UI toolkits: Qt's QStyleFactory resolves keys such as "windows" and "fusion" to built-in or plugin QStyle implementations that govern a coherent widget look-and-feel; a fuller abstract factory applies the same family key across several product interfaces.
Provider-independent database code: ADO.NET's DbProviderFactory/DbProviderFactories create a matched DbConnection, DbCommand, DbParameter and DbDataAdapter set for a selected provider such as SQL Server or OLE DB.
Parser-provider plugins: JAXP's DocumentBuilderFactory and SAXParserFactory hide implementation classes behind standard factory APIs, allowing the composition root to select a provider while client code uses parser abstractions.
Java's ServiceLoader documentation uses a CodecFactory service with getEncoder and getDecoder operations; the selected provider supplies a coherent codec family while clients depend only on the service interface.
Test infrastructure: an in-memory factory family whose products are fakes, injected in place of the production family so integration tests need no network.
Game and simulation engines: per-biome object families (terrain, props, audio) that must stay aesthetically consistent when a level is loaded.
SaaS multi-tenant applications: per-tenant theme factories so every rendered page uses the tenant's brand colours, fonts and spacing without per-request conditionals.
Document-format parsers: factory per format (PDF, HTML, EPUB) producing matched tokenizer, layout engine and renderer so a viewer can switch formats from a single configuration key.

statement: Should all SQL for each database table be confined to one component whose methods exchange plain record structures, rather than leaving statements in transaction scripts?
name: table-data-gateway
document:
table-data-gateway
table gateway
Confine every SQL statement that touches one table or view inside a single gateway object whose methods take and return plain record structures, so that no other code contains SQL for that table and rows cross the boundary as data rather than as domain objects.
Access to one table is spread across the codebase: SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE fragments are copied into every caller, nobody can say which queries a schema change will break, DBAs cannot find the SQL that needs tuning, and each caller has to know the dialect, the placeholders and the column order. The desired boundary is a single object that mediates all access to the whole table while the individual rows remain records (tuples, structs, hashes, DataRows) instead of becoming mapped objects.
Relational persistence where the database is a stable, schema-first integration point and SQL-level control matters (indexes, hints, bulk loads, vendor features), where the team deliberately does not want O/R mapping machinery in the domain layer, and where the domain logic is simple enough that rows may travel as records - CRUD and query services, reporting/read models, ETL writers, local SQLite stores, or a legacy database mediated for several applications. It is also the packaging decision for 'the SQL has to live somewhere well known' before a DAO, repository or query object is justified.
A service or CRUD application over a handful of tables where every screen maps to a few statements per table and an ORM would add more machinery than it removes.
Reporting and read models: read-only gateways over views or wide tables that return records directly to a formatter, export or BI job.
Legacy databases mediated for several applications: one gateway library per database becomes the documented API and the place where vendor quirks are hidden.
Embedded/local storage (SQLite, SQLCipher) in a desktop or mobile app, where one gateway per table keeps SQL out of the UI and can be tested with an in-memory database.
Batch and ETL writers that need explicit control over statement batching, cursors and transaction size - control that generated mappers hide.
Gradual refactoring of SQL scattered through transaction scripts: the first step is to move each table's statements into a gateway, after which a Data Mapper or repository can be introduced deliberately.
Test fixtures and seeders that must write through the same statements as production code rather than through a second, divergent SQL path.
Generated gateways in Go: sqlc compiles a schema plus a file of named queries into one struct per table and one type-safe method per SQL statement, with the caller holding the database handle and opening transactions - the gateway's invariants are then enforced by the generator and compiler rather than by convention.
Local SQLite storage on Android: each Room @Dao is a gateway over one table - the SQL lives in @Query-annotated methods validated at compile time, rows travel as plain entity data classes, and @Transaction or database-level transactions keep atomic multi-DAO boundaries in the caller.
Java teams that want the gateway structure without hand-writing it: jOOQ's code generator emits one DAO class per table or view (findAll, findById, generated fetchByColumn methods) that reads and writes Record/POJO rows and borrows the caller's Configuration, so the per-table SQL surface is regenerated when the schema changes.

name: row-data-gateway
document:
row-data-gateway
row data gateway
row gateway
Give each database row its own in-memory object that mirrors the row's columns and carries the row's own find, insert, update and delete operations, so all data-access code for a table lives in one place instead of being duplicated across the scripts that use it.
SQL text, parameter binding and result-set mapping are re-derived inside every transaction script that touches a table, while the in-memory objects those scripts work with know nothing about the database. No single place knows how one row is read, written and deleted, so a schema change ripples through every script and every new query is another chance to get parameterisation and type conversion wrong.
Applies when business logic is organised as transaction scripts or thin services over a relational schema whose columns map closely to the fields actually used: the gateway mirrors the table structure, no object/relational impedance mismatch is being managed, and identity maps, units of work and lazy loading are either unnecessary or added deliberately as separate patterns. It also fits generated persistence layers, where the gateway classes are produced from schema metadata during the build.
Transaction-script applications (order entry, billing runs, batch imports) where several scripts need the same handful of row-level reads and writes.
CRUD-heavy back-office and admin tooling where a screen edits one row at a time and columns map one-to-one onto form fields.
Legacy or externally owned schemas that must be mirrored rather than reshaped: one gateway per table gives an explicit, reviewable seam between the application and someone else's database.
Generated persistence layers: gateways produced from schema metadata on every build, so the tedious class-per-table work is automated and stays in sync with the schema.
Simple mappings inside an otherwise rich domain model, where a domain object keeps a gateway as its data holder instead of copying field values around.
Reporting and fixture utilities that need reusable, parameterised finders for one table without pulling in a full object/relational mapper.
Laminas\Db\RowGateway and RowGatewayFeature (the official laminas-db implementation) expose one row object with save/delete and can materialize table-query results as row gateways, fitting CRUD screens or transaction scripts that edit individual records.
Zend Framework 1's Zend_Db_Table_Row is a documented legacy row-gateway implementation: table queries return row objects with column access plus save/delete/createRow operations, useful when a simple schema is consumed by row-oriented scripts.
The Go dgw tool generates structs and lightweight Table/Row Data Gateway functions from PostgreSQL metadata, demonstrating the pattern as a code-generation choice when a project wants typed CRUD without a full ORM.

name: data-access-object
document:
data-access-object
DAO
Abstract and encapsulate all access to one particular data store behind a store-specific interface whose methods speak in domain terms, so business code never sees the store's API, dialect, connection handling or vendor error codes and the quirks of that store stay in one place.
Business objects talk to the store directly, embedding SQL, driver calls, connection handling and vendor error codes in ordinary application code: the application is coupled to one vendor's dialect and API, the same persistence details are duplicated across components, the store cannot be substituted (for a test, a second vendor or a replica) without editing business logic, and no single place can enforce access rules.
Applications that must reach a persistent store whose API is proprietary or vendor-specific - a relational database, a directory, a flat file, a legacy or remote service - especially when that store may later be swapped, reached through a second path (batch job, replica, cache) or faked in tests. It presupposes a language with interfaces, protocols or duck typing, and it is a decision about the access boundary only: the pattern says nothing about how domain objects are mapped, which is the separate concern of Data Mapper, Active Record or Table/Row Data Gateway.
An application that must run against more than one relational vendor, or against an embedded database in tests, keeps one DAO interface per aggregate and one implementation per vendor.
A legacy or third-party data source - mainframe, LDAP directory, SOAP/HTTP service, flat file - whose nonstandard API must not spread into business code.
A component that reaches the same store through a second path (bulk loader, nightly job, read replica) and needs the same domain-level operations as the online path.
Persistence code that stores domain objects as rows while business code must stay free of SQL and result sets, including hand-written mapping on top of a driver.
Test suites that need a fast in-memory or stub implementation behind the same interface so business logic can be exercised without a database.
Access layers that must enforce a policy (audit logging, tenant filtering, statement limits) at one place for every caller.
Microservices that own their own data store and expose it only through a typed interface, keeping service boundaries strict and enabling independent schema evolution.
CQRS read-model projections where the read side needs a denormalised view; a dedicated DAO isolates the projection logic from the command-side persistence.
Applications using async/await frameworks (FastAPI, asyncio) where data-access calls must be non-blocking and the DAO interface is naturally async.
Android apps using Room persistence: interfaces annotated @Dao declare insert/update/delete and @Query methods, and Room generates the implementation at compile time with SQL validated against the schema, so raw SQLite access never reaches view models.
Spring applications on JDBC, Hibernate or JPA use Spring's DAO support: DAO classes annotated @Repository get technology-specific exceptions (SQLException, HibernateException) translated into Spring's unified DataAccessException hierarchy, so one error-handling style works across persistence technologies.
Java services generated with jOOQ enable DAO generation to obtain a typed org.jooq.DAO per table (findById, exists, deleteById, per-column fetch methods) used as a base class underneath hand-written queries.

name: dao-factory
document:
dao-factory
DAOFactory
Factory for DataAccessObjects
Hand out a coherent family of data access objects bound to the store this deployment actually runs on: one factory object per store (the Factory Method form when there is a single store, the Abstract Factory form when stores vary) owns driver, dialect, connection and pooling policy, so the store choice is made once at the composition root and business components never name a vendor.
The persistence technology is not fixed: development runs on SQLite or H2, production on PostgreSQL or Oracle, one customer keeps a legacy system behind a service, tests want an in-memory store. Yet every business component constructs its own DAOs, so each one hard-codes a driver, a dialect, a connection policy and often a store key. Changing or adding a store then means editing business code in many places, and nothing prevents two components from silently talking to two different stores.
Persistence layers where the store implementation varies per deployment, per customer or per environment (relational vendors, embedded databases, files, remote services) and where clients must stay independent of the vendor API. It applies when DAO interfaces exist or can be defined cleanly, when the store choice can be made once per application, tenant or session at a composition root or onboarding step, and - in the Factory Method form - when a single store merely needs one place to construct its DAOs. Where a dependency-injection container, an ORM dialect layer or a provider factory already resolves implementations from configuration, that mechanism is the factory and a hand-written hierarchy only adds a second composition root.
Multi-database deployments: one application runs on SQLite or H2 in development and PostgreSQL or Oracle in production, and the factory reads the active store from configuration.
Vendor-portable products: an ISV hands the same DAO interfaces to customers running SQL Server, PostgreSQL or Oracle, with one concrete factory family per supported store.
Test infrastructure: a fake or in-memory factory family is bound in tests while the real factory is bound in production, so application flows run without a database.
Multi-tenant SaaS: the factory resolves the tenant's store (its schema, database or shard) and hands out DAOs bound to that tenant's connection. Tenant-scoped factory families prevent cross-tenant data leakage by ensuring every DAO query carries the tenant context from the factory's connection or session state.
Legacy and cloud coexistence during migration: two factory families stand behind one DAO interface set, letting reads and writes move store by store instead of in one big-bang cutover.
Pluggable backends: DAOs contributed by plugins or optional modules (a JDBC driver JAR, a ServiceLoader provider, a Python entry-point package) are resolved at startup by store key without recompiling the application.
Runtime data source selection: the factory selects the active data source at startup or request time based on environment variables, feature flags or feature flags, enabling blue-green deployments where different store families are active for different traffic shares.
ORM-backed persistence with portable interfaces: when using JPA/Hibernate, wrap EntityManagerFactory or SessionFactory behind a DAO factory interface so that the domain layer stays independent of the ORM provider and unit tests can substitute a lightweight in-memory implementation.
Microservices with per-service data stores: each microservice owns its data store; the service's DAO factory hides whether that store is PostgreSQL, MongoDB or a proprietary external service, and the factory interface becomes the integration contract for that service's data domain.
A/B testing with different storage backends: a feature flag routes traffic to one of several concrete factory families (e.g., legacy v2 vs. new v3 store), enabling gradual rollout and canary testing of a new database technology without changing any DAO interface.
ADO.NET provider factory: System.Data.Common's DbProviderFactory is the framework's own Abstract Factory - DbProviderFactories.GetFactory(invariantName) returns the registered SqlClientFactory or Npgsql factory and creates provider-specific Connection, Command and DataAdapter objects from a config-supplied provider name, which is exactly the store-selection machinery a hand-written DAO factory duplicates.
JDBC DataSource: javax.sql.DataSource is a vendor-implemented factory for connections; bound to a JNDI logical name (jdbc/sampledb) the application asks for a logical resource instead of naming a driver class or URL, and swapping the database vendor becomes a deployment change - the Java platform's built-in version of the DAO factory seam.
Spring Boot DataSourceBuilder: Boot reads spring.datasource.url, infers the driver and pooling implementation from the classpath and builds a HikariDataSource or vendor DataSource; here the framework is the factory, so the DAO layer consumes the built DataSource rather than re-deciding the store in a parallel hand-written hierarchy.

name: converter
document:
converter
translator
Give a pair of corresponding representations one owner that maps them into each other in both directions, so every caller converts through one place and neither representation has to import, know or be aware of the other.
The same information lives in two representations - domain object and DTO, in-memory value and wire or column format, internal model and third-party schema - and both directions are exercised in production. Hand-written field copying at each call site duplicates the mapping rules, drifts whenever either representation changes, and forces at least one side (or every caller) to import the other.
Component boundaries where an internal model meets an external representation: service or API layers exchanging DTOs, persistence layers mapping values to column formats, integration seams facing a third-party or legacy schema, and codec layers mapping typed values to a wire format. It applies whenever both directions are needed (read and write, decode and encode) and either side must stay independent of the other - different modules, teams, release cycles or libraries.
Domain object <-> DTO at a service or API boundary, where the transport shape must not leak into the model.
Value object <-> database column representation (JPA AttributeConverter, EF Core ValueConverter, Rails custom attribute type).
Third-party or legacy schema <-> internal model at an integration seam, including versioned wire formats.
Typed value <-> JSON, XML or protobuf payload with a custom codec when the default mapping is wrong (formats, units, enums).
Query rows or record sets <-> domain objects, where a full mapper framework would be oversized.
Single-value wrappers such as identifiers, money or unit-carrying quantities mapped to and from their primitive form.
Palindrome conversion chain (Entity -> DAO -> DTO -> Controller -> DTO -> DAO -> Entity) where each layer owns exactly one transformation direction, making the data flow explicit and each boundary independently testable.
Versioned API contracts: a DTO for API v1 and a separate DTO for API v2 coexist; a converter pair maps each version's DTO to the shared internal model, isolating API consumers from internal changes.
API gateway transformation: external third-party API payloads are normalized into an internal canonical format at the gateway, and outbound responses are converted back to the third-party schema; converters live at the seam.
Event-driven payload normalization: domain events carry one representation (e.g., enriched entity) while the event bus transports a flattened wire format (e.g., protobuf); converters at producer and consumer ends keep the two shapes in sync.
ORM entity vs. read-model DTO at the query boundary: a repository executes a query and the row-set converter maps each row to a read-model DTO, avoiding the entity in read-only paths entirely.
Anti-corruption layer at legacy integration seams: external system payloads are translated into the internal domain model at the boundary, and responses translated back; the converter owns the translation vocabulary, protecting the domain model from foreign concepts (Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design; Microsoft Azure Architecture Center; AWS Prescriptive Guidance).
Immutable value type <-> wire format for cryptographic or financial domains: the converter is a lawful isomorphism ensuring every wire value round-trips to an identical object (tested via property-based round-trip laws, as in the lawful-conversions Haskell library and Higher-Kinded-J Iso optics library).
Strangler-fig migration seam: new microservice functionality is accessed through an ACL that converts legacy system payloads to the new domain model and back, keeping the legacy interface unchanged while the new service evolves behind the seam.
Guava com.google.common.base.Converter<F, T>: an abstract bidirectional function with convert()/reverse(), automatic reverse() derivation for subclasses, mapAll() for whole iterables and Converter.normalize() to lift a converter into a function converter - the pattern as a shipped JDK-adjacent library type (Google Guava).
Go database/sql custom types: a type implementing both sql.Scanner (Scan(src any) error) and driver.Valuer (Value() (driver.Value, error)) owns the Go value <-> database column pair in both directions; the standard library's NullString, NullInt64 and NullTime are built-in pairs of exactly this shape.
Rails custom attribute types: subclass ActiveModel::Type::Value, override serialize (Ruby value -> database value) and deserialize (database value -> Ruby value) and bind with attribute :col, MyType.new - the converter pair at the ORM seam, with cast_value kept separate for user-input coercion.

name: passkey
document:
passkey
passkey idiom
constructor key
Restrict a constructor or method to chosen collaborators by requiring a token that only those collaborators can construct, so the operation stays in the public signature while remaining uncallable by everyone else - compile-time access control instead of blanket friendship.
A specific collaborator must call a constructor or method that must not become public API: a factory or helper that has to construct an object through a public constructor (make_unique, MakeGarbageCollected), a serialisation or framework layer that must reach one private hook, a subsystem that needs one internal operation, a test helper that must build a type in a state users cannot. The blunt mechanisms all miss: making the member public hands it to the world, friend (or its nearest equivalent) hands the collaborator the whole private surface, package/module/assembly access opens it to an entire scope, and a private constructor plus a factory just moves the gate into the factory. What is missing is a way to say 'this collaborator, and only this collaborator, may call exactly this operation'.
Statically checked code where the operation must stay visible in the type system (templates, frameworks and helper functions must be able to resolve the call) but must not be callable without a value that only the designated collaborators can create. The grant is a source-level construct checked by the compiler: the token is empty, disappears at run time and is never a defence against an adversary. Typical settings are factory-created types, library internals exposed to one subsystem, framework hooks, constructor or overload disambiguation, and test seams.
Factory-created objects with a public constructor: base::PassKey in Chromium exists for classes that a helper template (blink::MakeGarbageCollected) must construct while user code must not.
Serialisation and framework hooks: an archive, visitor or framework calls exactly one hook of a user type; the key names the framework instead of befriending it and exposing everything else.
Library-internal operations: one subsystem (allocator, persistence layer, test infrastructure) needs to construct or mutate a type users must not reach - the key names the subsystem where the language allows it, and module or assembly scope carries the rest.
Tests: a test helper constructs an otherwise unreachable state without '#define private public' builds, friend-everything test seams or reflection.
Constructor and overload disambiguation: a tag only the factory can produce selects the trusted overload and keeps the same argument list from being callable by everyone.
Deliberate delegation and revocation: the collaborator passes a key to another function that then performs the call, and a non-copyable key stops the ability from travelling further.
KDE Frameworks' KColorScheme (Frameworks 6.6.0) adopted a passkey specifically to avoid private-constructor issues, showing the idiom in a public Qt-based framework API.
Chromium's Mojo ProtoWrapperBytes uses base::PassKey to let named network, component and test classes access wrapped protobuf bytes while ordinary callers cannot supply the operation.
Abseil's C++ Tip of the Week #134 uses a passkey token with std::make_shared so a factory can keep single-allocation construction without making unconstrained construction the public API.

name: state-colocation
document:
state-colocation
colocated state
colocation
Keep each piece of presentation state in the component closest to where it is used — down to the single component that owns and reads it — instead of hoisting it to a common ancestor or a global store, so that a change touches only the smallest part of the view that can observe it.
State gets hoisted 'just in case': a value only one component reads is lifted to the screen or application root, or pushed into one global store, because someone may want it later. The consequences are components that receive props they never read, updates that invalidate far more of the UI than the value's actual consumers, an unclear owner for each value, and tests that must assemble the whole state container to exercise one field. The recurring decision is where a new piece of state should live: keep it at the smallest scope that actually needs it.
Declarative component UIs (React, Vue, Svelte, SwiftUI, Compose, Blazor, Qt Quick) and, in generalized form, any system where a mutable value is owned by one component-like unit: the consumers determine the state's scope, the framework invalidates only what the owner's subtree can observe, and components are composed, moved and deleted. Most compelling where over-lifted or global state has already become a performance and ownership problem.
A search or form input whose value is read only by the input, its own validation and its own preview: keep it in that component instead of the screen root (the canonical typing example where hoisting made every keystroke re-render the page).
Which panel of an accordion is open: leave it per panel while panels are independent, then lift exactly to the accordion once only one panel may be open at a time (the closest common parent).
Tooltip, hover, popover and dropdown state in a chart or table cell: own it in the cell component rather than in a global UI store.
Per-row edit or selection state in a data grid: the row component owns it; only cross-row operations need the grid to own it.
Dialog and modal open state in the button or list that opens it, until another surface must close or observe it.
Form draft state in the form component; lift it only when a sibling — summary panel, preview pane, wizard footer — genuinely must read it.
Extracting a self-contained widget for reuse or publication: keeping its state local makes the component portable and shrinks its API.
Per-cell expansion state in a tree view or file explorer: the tree node component owns whether it is expanded; the parent tree only coordinates multi-select or bulk-expand operations.
Media playback state for a single player (play/pause, current time, volume): colocate in the player component rather than a global audio store unless the same track plays in multiple places simultaneously.
Local filter/sort state for a data table or list: keep it in the list component until a URL parameter, shareable link, or sibling panel requires sharing it.
Vue: composable-local state (useSearch, useToggle) where each consumer needs its own independent instance of the same reactive logic pattern.
Angular Signals: feature-level signal stores scoped to a route or feature slice, not the entire application store, for UI state and feature-derived state.
SwiftUI: @State for view-local value types; @StateObject for view-owned reference types; keep @EnvironmentObject for genuinely cross-cutting state (auth session, theme) mounted as low in the hierarchy as consumers allow.
Svelte 5 runes: `let count = $state(0)` inside a component is per-component-instance reactive state — the component that declares it is its owner; Svelte's v5 migration explicitly replaced the pre-runes habit of reaching for a store whenever state sat at a component's top level, with $state plus $derived/$effect as the local cells, and module-level .svelte.js state only for deliberate sharing.
Jetpack Compose: the official hoisting guidance is this pattern's placement ladder — keep state as close as possible to where it is consumed, hoist only to the lowest common ancestor of all composables that read or write it, pass value down and onValueChange up, and make the ViewModel the owner only when business logic or lifecycle outlives the composition.
Blazor: component fields are the default owner for UI-local state; the official state-management guidance promotes to an in-memory state container service only when components must share non-persistent state, and to Protected Browser Storage only when the value must survive circuits or sessions — a three-rung ladder that mirrors local state, scoped provider, persistence.

name: assertion
document:
assertion
design by contract
Express a model object's preconditions, postconditions and class invariants as executable, side-effect-free predicates at the operations that must uphold them, so a broken contract fails at its boundary instead of remaining a comment or surfacing later as corrupt state. This pattern is for design-by-contract correctness checks, not routine validation of untrusted input or test-only assertions.
Model rules - a balance never below its floor, a period whose end follows its start, a status that cannot move backwards - are left in comments, documents and team memory while constructors and mutators check nothing. A caller can violate a precondition or an operation can break an invariant, allowing invalid state to propagate until an unrelated reader fails; if the assertion is elided by the build, the shipped program may enforce a different contract from the one tested.
Objects with genuine invariants - entities, value objects and aggregate roots - whose state changes through several operations or paths, in a language with an assertion facility, contract syntax or an exception mechanism. The invariant must be expressible as a deterministic, side-effect-free predicate over observable state. Use assertions for programmer/model defects; use always-on validation or typed errors for expected input failures, and decide explicitly whether a release build may elide the check.
Entities and value objects with cross-field rules: an amount that always carries its currency and scale, a date range whose end follows its start, an order whose total equals the sum of its lines.
Aggregate roots that enforce consistency across a cluster of objects: the root asserts its invariant before accepting a change and after applying it.
Domain services and application services checking the preconditions of a use-case operation, so a mis-wired caller fails on the spot instead of writing corrupt state.
Library and framework code that must state its contract: precondition checks on public constructors and methods that clients cannot legitimately violate.
Legacy models under refactoring: assertions turn implicit rules into explicit ones, and where the language strips assertions the same predicates are pasted into the test suite (Evans's fallback).
Reconstitution code that rebuilds objects from stored data, asserting that persisted state still satisfies the model's invariants before the object is used.
Event-sourced aggregates: each state-transition command asserts the preconditions before applying the event, and the event handler asserts the invariant after the state is reconstituted from the event stream.
CQRS write models: the command handler asserts that the incoming command is valid for the current aggregate state before persisting, catching mis-wired or concurrent commands at the write edge.
Microservice boundary contracts: the inbound adapter asserts the precondition of the domain operation before dispatching, preventing malformed commands from entering the domain core regardless of which transport delivered them (HTTP, queue, gRPC).
Money and quantity types: value objects that wrap a numeric amount and a currency/unit, asserting that amounts are non-negative and operations preserve currency matching, preventing silent unit-mixing bugs.
Workflow or saga state machines: assertions on transition preconditions (this status can only advance to that one) prevent illegal state progression from corrupted or out-of-order events.
Property-based test oracle: postconditions double as generative test properties - for all inputs satisfying preconditions, the postcondition holds - turning the same predicate into a specification that a property-based testing library (e.g. Eris for PHP, Hypothesis for Python, fast-check for TypeScript) can falsify.
EiffelBase container classes such as LINKED_LIST and HASH_TABLE: EiffelStudio contract monitoring checks exported-routine preconditions/postconditions and class invariants while the containers preserve their representation rules.
AutoProof-verified Eiffel classes: executable assertions also serve as formal specifications that the verifier can discharge or flag, pairing runtime diagnostics with static proof where available.

name: cursor-pagination
document:
cursor-pagination
keyset pagination
cursor-based pagination
Bound what a read boundary returns for a large or changing ordered collection by sending one page plus an opaque continuation token that pins the filter and ordering, so clients advance deterministically without offsets and without watching rows move under them.
A boundary must expose a collection that is too large to return at once and keeps changing while clients read it. Offset or page-number requests make the store count or scan everything up to the requested page, and concurrent inserts or deletes shift rows across page boundaries so consumers see duplicates or miss items; the server has no way to state where the sequence should resume.
Any read boundary - an HTTP or gRPC list operation, a GraphQL connection, a database-backed feed, a batch export job - over an ordered collection that is large, growing, or read under concurrent writes, where the server can identify a unique, immutable ordering key and wants to cap both response size and per-request query cost while letting clients iterate the whole sequence.
Public REST or gRPC list endpoints over unbounded, growing tables - messages, orders, audit events - where deep offsets are slow and responses must stay small.
Infinite-scroll or load-more feeds that keep returning newer items while a user scrolls, with the already-seen pages stable against inserts.
Whole-collection sync and export jobs (warehouse loads, backups, search reindexing) that must iterate every row exactly once while writers continue.
GraphQL Relay connections where first/after, edges and pageInfo carry the continuation contract in the schema instead of the URL.
Consumers of third-party list APIs (Stripe-style starting_after/has_more, Google page_token iterators) that keep parameters fixed across auto-paginated calls.
Administrative and operational tooling that streams very large tables for verification or cleanup with bounded memory and predictable server load.
Audit log and event stream retrieval where events are append-only and chronological, and clients stream continuously without needing to revisit earlier pages.
Real-time activity feeds (social media timelines, notification streams) where inserts at the head must not disturb pages the user has already loaded.
Database replication and change-data-capture (CDC) pipelines that must consume a changelog exactly once across restarts and failures.
Paginating over search results from a vector database or full-text index where OFFSET at depth is expensive and results may change between queries.
Bi-directional data synchronization (CDC pipelines, replica lag-catching) where a consumer must iterate forward and occasionally needs to resume from a previous position or re-sweep a window — requiring stable forward cursors plus a defined backward-resumption path.
Paginating a partitioned or sharded database table where each partition is queried independently and cursors carry both the partition hint and the per-partition keyset position.
Slack Web API collection methods (users.list, conversations.history) where response_metadata.next_cursor drives the loop, page limits are clamped per method, and expired or malformed tokens surface as invalid_cursor so the client restarts from the first page.
GitHub GraphQL-style cursor connections where first/last (bounded 1-100) and pageInfo.startCursor/endCursor carry the continuation position for after/before traversal.
Timeline-style feeds served by Django REST framework's CursorPagination, whose default -created ordering gives a consistent view that does not repeat items as new rows are inserted.

name: inversion-of-control
document:
inversion-of-control
Hollywood Principle
IoC
Invert the direction of control between a reusable framework and application code: the framework owns the call flow and invokes the application's hooks at its extension points, so the generic sequence is reused while application code supplies only behaviour.
A reusable component - framework, container, UI toolkit, event loop, test runner - must own the sequence of calls (main loop, request dispatch, component lifecycle), while the behaviour at each step is application-specific; if application code had to call the framework's steps itself, the generic flow could neither be reused as a whole nor be extended without modifying it.
Applies wherever generic flow logic has to be specialised by application code: UI toolkits and event loops that decide when handlers fire, server containers and engines that own request dispatch and component lifecycle, test runners that own fixture and test sequencing, plugin hosts, and effect runtimes that own program entry. It is the defining characteristic of a framework as opposed to a library (a library is called by your code; a framework calls your code), and it usually arrives bundled with a container, dispatcher or engine - what remains to design is where the boundary sits and how much lifecycle you hand over.
GUI and event-driven applications: the windowing system or runtime owns the event loop and calls your event handlers, app delegate or declarative view body.
Server-side request handling: the container, engine or router owns listen-accept-dispatch and invokes the servlets, handlers, routes or middleware you registered.
Test frameworks: the runner owns discovery, fixture setup and teardown and calls your test methods and lifecycle hooks (JUnit, pytest, xUnit).
Container-managed components: EJB, Spring, Angular or Nest components whose construction, wiring and lifecycle callbacks are driven by the container that also owns the entry point.
Plugin and extension architectures: a host defines extension points and third-party plugins implement them, with the host deciding when each plugin is consulted (IDEs, browsers, build tools, game engines).
Inverted program entry: effect runtimes and app frameworks where the runtime's main calls the run value or app structure you provide instead of you orchestrating from main.
Callback-based C APIs: a library call such as qsort or a GLib main loop calls your function pointer per element or event - a small-scale realization of the same inversion.
Cloud Functions-as-a-Service: AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, and Google Cloud Functions own the request dispatch and cold-start lifecycle; your handler is a hook called by the platform, making serverless a live deployment of the Hollywood principle.
Reactive streams and event-driven pipelines: frameworks like Reactor, RxJava, or Node.js EventEmitter own the subscription and back-pressure loop; operators and subscribers are hooks that the runtime calls on data availability.
Microservices sidecar and service mesh: an Envoy or Linkerd proxy sidecar owns the connection lifecycle and calls application code through a defined protocol; the application registers health checks and request handlers as IoC hooks.
Orleans virtual actor model: the Orleans runtime owns the grain lifecycle, activation and deactivation, and calls grain methods as directed by the scheduler; grain code is a hook implementation invoked by the framework.
ASP.NET Core middleware: the host builds the request pipeline and invokes each registered RequestDelegate in order; middleware can run before and after the next delegate or short-circuit, so the application supplies components while the server owns request dispatch.
JUnit Jupiter extension model: the JUnit engine discovers tests and invokes registered Before*/After* lifecycle callbacks around user test methods; extensions customize execution without owning when tests run.
Kubernetes controllers: the controller manager owns reconciliation loops that watch API state and repeatedly invokes controller reconciliation logic to converge current state on desired state; controllers supply behavior while Kubernetes schedules dispatch.

name: aggregate
document:
aggregate
aggregate root
consistency boundary
Define a transactional consistency boundary around domain objects: one root entity is the sole externally reachable entry point, owns internal entities and value objects, and is the only object application code modifies directly; each command loads and commits one root instance, while other roots are referenced by identity and coordinated separately.
Business rules relate several objects at once - an order total that must stay within a credit limit, allocations that must never exceed stock - but if every object is writable on its own, no single place can enforce the rule at commit time. Concurrent callers interleave, persistence updates parts separately, and the invariant survives only while every caller remembers to check it; the model needs one owner and one atomic persistence boundary.
Tactical domain modelling inside a bounded context with genuine transaction-wide invariants: an object graph whose parts must agree at every commit, a store that can persist one root and its cluster as one unit (one transaction, a cascade or an explicit unit of work), and domain experts who can state which rules must hold immediately. It matters most where concurrency, distribution or graph size make 'everything is consistent with everything' unaffordable.
Order capture with line items where the order total must not exceed a credit limit - the purchase-order invariant Evans uses to motivate the pattern.
Inventory allocation where allocated quantity must never exceed on-hand stock for one stock item (Vernon's StockItem example).
Booking and reservation models where a seat, room or slot must not be double-booked inside one boundary.
Invoicing: an invoice with its lines and a tax total that must equal the sum of the lines, loaded and committed as one unit.
A shopping cart or basket with a maximum line count or quantity per item enforced per cart.
Write models under CQRS whose command handlers must modify exactly one consistency boundary and let the rest of the system catch up from events.
Banking account transfers: a debit and credit of the same amount must be atomic within one account aggregate.
Subscription lifecycle management: a plan change must atomically update status, record the new plan, and create a proration record.
Patient treatment records: a treatment episode where diagnosis, prescriptions, and progress notes must remain consistent.
Axon Framework's event-sourced GiftCard aggregate: an IssueCard command targets the root identifier, replays that aggregate's stream, and applies events to rebuild state.
EventStoreDB event-sourced orders: one order stream is replayed to rebuild the aggregate and appended with an expected stream version for optimistic concurrency.
SQLAlchemy's Order.items relationship with cascade='all, delete-orphan': a Session flushes owned line items with their root while the application transaction remains scoped to that aggregate.
EF Core owned entity types ([Owned] / OwnsOne / OwnsMany): owned parts cannot exist or be persisted independently, are loaded with their owner by default, and map the aggregate's ownership boundary onto the ORM's change tracker.
Protean's BaseAggregate: invariants are validated before and after every state change, the aggregate is the unit of persistence and optimistic concurrency, and a stale version raises ExpectedVersionError for retry.
Axon Framework 5 event-sourced entities: commands target the @EventSourcedEntity root's identifier and @EntityMember child entities receive only their routed events, so the consistency boundary survives under the entity-based model.

name: monitor-object
document:
monitor-object
thread-safe passive object
monitor
Serialise concurrent method invocations on a shared object by giving the object its own lock and condition variables, so that only one method executes inside it at a time and methods that cannot proceed wait cooperatively instead of polling.
Objects shared by several threads expose their state through ordinary methods, and nothing stops concurrent callers from interleaving inside those methods, corrupting the invariants they were written to maintain. The race is then papered over with ad-hoc locking, sleeps and busy-wait loops scattered through client code. The recurring decision is whether the object itself should own the serialisation (and the scheduling) of its methods instead of leaving that discipline to every caller.
Shared-memory concurrency, where the mutable state of an object is reached by more than one thread and its methods must be atomic with respect to one another. It matters most when some methods cannot run to completion until another method changes the state - a queue that is full or empty, a resource that is not yet available, a phase that has not been reached - because then a method must suspend and later resume, which requires releasing the lock while it waits.
Bounded buffers and work queues shared by producer and consumer threads, where producers wait while the queue is full and consumers wait while it is empty - the pattern's canonical example.
Session, connection or entity registries on a server, where lookups, insertion and eviction must be atomic and callers may have to wait for capacity or for an entry to reappear.
Caches with in-flight bookkeeping (single-flight computation), where a thread that requests an already-computed key waits for the first thread's result instead of recomputing it.
Shared configuration, counters or statistics objects read and updated by request threads, where each call must observe a consistent snapshot of the state.
State machines and simulators whose step methods block until another thread advances a transition, for example a test harness waiting for a worker to reach a known state.
In-process resource pools (connection, database or worker pools) where acquisition blocks until an entry is returned or a timeout expires.
Java's java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue is a fixed-capacity monitor-style bounded buffer: put blocks while full and take blocks while empty, making the producer-consumer coordination explicit.
.NET's System.Collections.Concurrent.BlockingCollection<T> supplies bounded Add/Take blocking, cancellation and completion semantics around a producer-consumer collection; use it instead of hand-rolling Monitor.Wait/Pulse.
Python's queue.Queue provides a thread-safe multi-producer/multi-consumer boundary with blocking put/get operations and optional timeouts, a standard monitor-style primitive for worker pools.

name: separation-of-duties
document:
separation-of-duties
separation of privilege
four-eyes principle
Require two or more distinct principals or components to complete a sensitive operation, so that no single account, role or object can initiate and finish it alone.
A sensitive workflow is reachable end to end from one identity or one code path: the same operator creates and approves the payment, the same administrator changes the production configuration and signs it off, the same service account holds both the maker and the checker permission. The trigger is structural rather than accidental - all steps share one principal, one session, one process or one role, because splitting them costs a second pair of hands - and the failure surfaces only when an insider error or abuse is unremarkable in the audit trail: every step was authorized, because one principal held both halves of the duty.
Sensitive operations whose consequences must survive mistakes, coercion or misuse by authorized insiders: payments and disbursements, entitlement and permission changes, production configuration and deployment, key custody and signing, destructive data operations. It applies where identities can be kept distinct and authenticated (separate accounts, roles, services, processes), where the intermediate states of the operation can be persisted and observed, and where an enforcement point exists that can compare the acting principal with the recorded initiator - a policy engine, method security, an approval service, a separate process or account, a dual-control key ceremony. It is as much an organizational rule as a technical one: the split must follow the duties people actually hold, and recombination must be made awkward by design rather than merely discouraged.
Maker-checker payments: an operator above a threshold creates a disbursement and a second operator releases it; the ledger records both identities and refuses a release signed by the maker.
Change control and deployment: production IAM policy or infrastructure changes require a second administrator's approval, and the pipeline refuses to run a change approved by its own author (required reviewers / second signature).
Key custody and dual control: signing keys or root credentials are split so two authorized operators must each contribute a share (split knowledge, m-of-n threshold, dual-control key ceremony) and no single share can sign.
Access provisioning: the requester of an entitlement, its approver and the administrator who grants it are three distinct roles; the administrator cannot approve their own request, and access-control administrators do not administer the audit log.
Destructive data operations: schema migrations, production data edits and deletion jobs are prepared by one engineer and executed by a different operator account that cannot author the change.
Regulated back-office workflows: journal entries, refunds, credit adjustments and account closures are initiated by one clerk and posted by another, with the pairing recorded for audit.
GitHub protected branches: a pull request targeting a protected branch needs the configured number of approving reviews before it can merge, the platform refuses an approval from the PR author by design, and with dismiss-stale-review enabled a commit pushed after the review voids the approval - four-eyes enforced at the merge gate with the approval bound to the reviewed revision.
AWS Systems Manager Change Manager: a change request may run its Automation runbook only after approvals from named IAM users, groups or roles arrive across up to five approval levels, and a single rejection stops execution; because change templates list approvers separately from requesters, a request submitted under one IAM principal is released by another.
HashiCorp Vault key custody: vault operator init splits the root key with Shamir's Secret Sharing into key shares (default 5) under a threshold (default 3); unsealing or generating a root token needs a quorum of distinct share holders, and PGP-encrypting each share for a named operator makes dual control a property of the mechanism rather than of the procedure.

name: pratt-parser
document:
pratt-parser
top-down operator precedence
tdop
Parse expressions with many prefix, infix and postfix operators by associating a binding power and a handler with each token type, so precedence and associativity live in one rule table instead of one parsing function per precedence level.
Operator precedence turns expression parsing into a ladder of near-identical functions - one per level - each of which must re-implement associativity, delegate to the next level for its operands, and be edited whenever an operator is added or moves. Grammars with prefix, infix, postfix and mixfix operators (ternary conditionals, assignment, calls, indexing, user-registered operators) make that ladder long, make associativity easy to get subtly wrong, and scatter the grammar across the parser so it cannot be read in one place.
Hand-written parsers for an expression-bearing language, DSL, query or configuration syntax: a token stream is already available (or is cheap to lex), the operator set is large or expected to grow, and the team wants the grammar visible as data. It is typically the expression layer under an ordinary recursive-descent parser for statements and declarations - interpreters, calculators, filter and rule engines, formula tools - and it is unnecessary when a parser generator already declares precedence for the grammar.
Expression evaluators and calculators whose operator set is expected to grow (arithmetic, units, comparisons, percentages, function calls, user-defined functions).
Query, filter and rule languages - search filters, feature-flag conditions, access-policy conditions, spreadsheet formulas - with many comparison, logical and string operators.
Front ends for small languages and DSLs that parse statements and declarations with recursive descent and need real precedence handling for the expression layer.
Single-pass compilers and interpreters that emit bytecode or IR while parsing, where each handler is also the point that emits the operator's instruction.
Template and configuration expression languages that must attach exact source positions and precise errors to every operator.
Host-language extension points that let plugins or users register additional operators at runtime, because registration is just a table entry.
Rust PEG grammars that use pest::pratt_parser::PrattParser to map prefix, postfix and infix operator pairs into calculator or DSL ASTs.
Rust parser-combinator expression grammars built with chumsky's pratt combinator, where atom parsers and prefix, postfix and infix operators declare precedence and associativity.
JavaScript expression-only tooling built on JSEP, where a compact Pratt-style parser produces ASTs and allows custom unary and binary operators with explicit precedence.

name: authentication-enforcer
document:
authentication-enforcer
authentication interceptor
authentication gateway
auth middleware
Put one request-boundary checkpoint in front of protected actions that decides whether authentication is required, delegates credential verification to a replaceable mechanism, and attaches the resulting subject to request-scoped context before dispatch, so coverage is uniform without making handlers understand credentials.
When each handler decides whether and how to authenticate, protection is duplicated or omitted on exceptional paths, credential formats and user stores leak into business code, and a mechanism or policy change requires editing every handler instead of one auditable boundary.
Server-side request processing — web APIs, web applications and service endpoints — where many handlers share one protection policy, credentials arrive through a uniform convention (Authorization header, cookie, session id), verification technology must be replaceable or differ per route, and the runtime provides a request-pipeline hook (servlet filter, middleware chain, framework guard). Applies to session-based and token-based authentication alike; permissions and roles are out of scope. Three implementation strategies exist: (1) Container-Managed Authentication — the runtime container owns the checkpoint and realm configuration; (2) Authentication Provider Strategy — a custom provider behind a narrow interface, swapped without touching handlers; (3) JAAS Login Module Strategy — pluggable via standard JAAS configuration, supporting multifactor authentication via smart cards, biometrics, or third-party IdPs. The pattern is equally applicable at the edge level (API gateway, ingress proxy) and the service level (in-process middleware).
Web APIs where every route except health and login requires a bearer token, and the checkpoint is mounted in front of the whole router.
Multi-tenant applications with mixed protection levels: public marketing pages, session-protected tenant UI and token-protected integration endpoints behind one enforcement layer.
Services that must accept several credential types at once — browser sessions, mobile JWTs, mutual TLS for service-to-service traffic — while keeping one uniform enforcement point.
Credential-technology migration (basic auth to OIDC, on-premises LDAP to SSO) where enforcement stays put while the mechanism behind it is swapped.
Regulated environments where every rejected authentication attempt has to be logged centrally and identically across all endpoints.
Legacy applications with authentication checks scattered through servlets or handlers that must be consolidated behind one intercepting layer before an audit.
Zero Trust microservices where every internal service verifies JWTs independently (per-service verification) while an ingress gateway provides the first checkpoint — the enforcer exists at both layers.
OIDC/OAuth2 migration where an existing session-based app adds bearer-token support; the mechanism adapts to both while the enforcement point remains unchanged.
Multi-tenant SaaS platforms where tenant isolation depends on the enforcer resolving a tenant identifier from the token before the handler processes any data.
Platform-as-a-Service with mounted sub-applications where a parent ASGI middleware dispatches per-path authentication requirements from a config registry, injecting identity into ASGI scope for all sub-apps.
Spring Security servlet applications that use a SecurityFilterChain with anyRequest().authenticated() and an AuthenticationManager/AuthenticationProvider chain, so controllers consume the SecurityContext rather than parse credentials.
ASP.NET Core APIs that register JWT or cookie schemes, call UseAuthentication before dependent middleware, and use a fallback authorization policy to make authenticated access the default.
An nginx ingress location using auth_request to delegate identity verification to a central authentication service, forwarding only after a 2xx result and propagating 401/403 failures while services still verify their own trust boundary.
