name: entity
document:
entity
reference object
domain entity
Give a domain concept a stable identity that survives attribute changes, representation changes and time, and define its equality, lifecycle and lookup in terms of that identity instead of in terms of its attributes.
A model that compares objects by their attributes cannot answer whether two instances are the same thing: a customer whose e-mail and plan changed looks like a different customer, while two distinct people who share a name look like one. References held by other objects, caches and audit records break silently, and every state change forces callers to re-identify the object.
Rich domain models in which some concepts must be tracked through time: the object is created, changes state, is stored and reloaded, and may exist in several representations (in-memory instance, database row, message payload, UI snapshot) that all have to denote the same thing. It is the modelling decision that pairs with Value Object: attribute clusters become values, while the things whose history matters keep an identity.
Master data tracked for years — customers, accounts, contracts, products, patients — where attributes change but the business entity stays the same (e.g., a Customer who moves house is still the same Customer).
Documents with a lifecycle: orders, invoices, bookings and shipments that move through states (pending → paid → shipped → delivered) while remaining the same document with a stable order number.
Shopping cart to order transition: a ShoppingCart is reconstituted as an Order with the same customer identity but a new order identity, preserving the correlation to the customer while starting a new business process.
Correlating representations across layers: an entity persisted as database rows, published as domain events, and displayed in a UI must be recognisable as the same thing in all three — identity is the correlation key across representations.
In-memory session consistency: a unit of work or identity map ensures the same Customer loaded twice in one request is one object reference, preventing edits from silently diverging into two copies.
Referencing across bounded contexts: one microservice holds a CustomerId reference to another service's aggregate root, allowing independent deployment and loading without a direct object pointer.
Healthcare records: a Patient entity persists across multiple visits, lab results and prescriptions — the patient identity is the anchor for the entire medical history regardless of demographic changes.
Versioned documents: an InsurancePolicy entity may be replaced by a new version while the original policy number (identity) remains the correlation handle for auditors and legacy systems.
Hibernate/JPA: an @Entity class with an @Id is managed by the persistence context, which guarantees one in-memory instance per identity per session — loading the same row twice in a session returns the same object reference, an Identity Map built into the framework.
Entity Framework Core: identity resolution makes the DbContext track a single entity instance per primary key, so duplicate instances arriving in a deserialized graph are merged into the already-tracked entity instead of diverging into two tracked copies.
Drupal Entity API: nodes, users and taxonomy terms (content entities) and roles or image styles (configuration entities) are identity-bearing objects with typed storage handlers, revisions and field bundles behind one CRUD and validation API.

name: messaging-gateway
document:
messaging-gateway
Encapsulate access to a messaging system behind an ordinary interface of domain methods, so calling application code makes method calls while a single component owns message construction, correlation, timeouts and error translation.
Application code that talks to a broker keeps importing messaging concepts: it builds the payload, picks the channel, attaches a reply address and a correlation id, parses the response and interprets broker errors. The trigger for this pattern is that callers should make a method call instead of writing messaging code - the messaging knowledge belongs in exactly one place that can change without touching business rules.
At the boundary between application logic and a messaging system (message broker, MQ, queue service or actor runtime): the other side is reached by messages, but the caller is ordinary domain code that should see typed parameters and typed results. Applies to one-way (fire and forget) and request-reply interactions alike, and to blocking as well as asynchronous call styles.
A domain service that must query another system (inventory, pricing, credit scoring) over a queue: the caller invokes checkStock(sku) and receives a typed answer.
An HTTP or API layer whose controller awaits a brokered round trip (Spring Integration gateway interface, NestJS ClientProxy, MassTransit request client).
Batch and background jobs that dispatch work through a typed job API instead of assembling payloads (ActiveJob perform_later, Celery delay).
Wrapping a legacy system's MQ interface once, so the rest of the codebase never learns its message format.
Test seams: unit tests substitute a fake gateway, integration tests run the same interface against a real broker.
Migration seam: keep the gateway contract stable while the transport moves from one broker to another.
Actor and streaming stacks where a facade wraps ask/request so callers never hold ActorRefs or inboxes.
Spring Integration's @MessagingGateway and GatewayProxyFactoryBean let application code inject a typed interface while the framework routes calls into channels and returns replies.
MassTransit's IRequestClient<T> and GetResponse<TResponse> provide a typed request-reply client over the bus, keeping request and response message contracts out of the calling service.
RabbitMQ's RPC tutorial demonstrates a gateway-like client that publishes to rpc_queue with reply_to and correlation_id, then resolves the matching callback response.

name: plugin
document:
plugin
plug-in
plugin architecture
Let a host application acquire behaviour from independently deployed modules that it discovers and links at configuration or start-up time, so new features, backends or device support can be added without recompiling or redeploying the host.
The behaviours a system must offer vary by deployment (customer, environment, backend, hardware) or grow after the host has shipped; hard-wiring every implementation behind a factory method or a configuration switch means each new variant edits core code and forces a rebuild and redeploy of the whole application.
Systems whose capability set is not fully known at build time: third-party or per-customer extensions, drivers and storage backends, editor and build tooling, test runners, media pipelines. It applies wherever a stable extension point can be published, the contract can be versioned, and the runtime can bind code after compilation (shared libraries, class or module loading, plugin packages).
IDEs, editors and build tools whose feature set grows through extensions (Eclipse, VS Code, webpack, ESLint, pytest, RuboCop).
Servers and frameworks that pick a codec, transport, storage or auth backend per deployment (JDBC drivers via ServiceLoader, .NET plugin hosts, Kafka connectors).
Infrastructure tooling that hosts independently released providers, such as Terraform providers over gRPC or Vault secret engines.
Media, imaging and device software that adds codecs, effects or drivers after the main program ships (Apache httpd modules, GStreamer, DAW and imaging plugins).
Document and data pipelines where per-customer transformation or validation steps are shipped as separate packages (Python entry points, Ruby gems).
Applications that must support tenant- or customer-specific behaviour without a private build per customer, composed at start-up from a plugin directory or a configuration list.
AI agent systems where tools, memory backends and LLMs are loaded as plugins (LangChain agents, semantic kernel plugins).
Cloud-native platforms that must support tenant-specific backends or third-party integrations without redeploying the control plane (Kubernetes operators, service mesh extensions).
DevOps and CI/CD pipelines where steps, reporters or cloud integrations are added as plugins (Jenkins plugins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI job templates).
Observability platforms where collectors, processors and exporters are pluginable (OpenTelemetry collectors, Grafana datasources and panels).
Editor ecosystems that declare contributions in manifests and run extension code behind a host boundary, as in Visual Studio Code's Extension Host and contribution points.
Infrastructure CLIs that launch provider binaries over a versioned RPC contract and negotiate compatibility, as in Terraform's Plugin Protocol and provider servers.
Web servers assembled from independently built dynamic modules loaded at startup or restart, as in Apache HTTP Server's DSO and mod_so module system.

name: poison-pill
document:
poison-pill
sentinel message
end-of-stream marker
Terminate queue consumers cooperatively by sending a reserved sentinel message that each consumer recognises as "no more work", so consumers drain the backlog and exit without a separate control channel or forced cancellation.
A producer-consumer system must shut down, but its consumers block on an empty queue and the queue has no built-in "no more items" signal: callers either kill the workers mid-work and drop buffered items, or leave them blocked forever. Production has ended - how do the consumers learn that while still processing everything already queued?
In-process or broker-mediated producer-consumer systems with a FIFO work queue, a fixed set of long-lived consumers (threads, coroutines, actors) that block when the queue is empty, and a shutdown requirement that work already accepted by the queue be drained before the consumers exit - typically deployment, signal handling or test teardown.
Signal-driven shutdown of an in-process worker pool: the SIGTERM handler stops accepting work, then enqueues one pill per worker so the backlog is processed before the process exits.
Batch importers and ETL stages whose consumers block on a work queue and must finish the current batch before a run is considered complete.
Test harnesses and simulations: an explicit stop message makes thread-based systems deterministic to shut down, without sleeps or guessed timeouts.
Actor systems: a reserved stop message (for example Akka PoisonPill) terminates an actor after the messages already queued for it have been handled.
Log and event writers where the last records must reach the sink before consumers release their buffers and files.
Bounded-queue stages in a pipeline: pills travel the same backpressured channel as work, so upstream cannot keep producing after the stop decision.
Kubernetes pod shutdown: containers receive SIGTERM, workers stop pulling from the job queue, drain in-flight tasks, then exit within the terminationGracePeriodSeconds window.
Redis/Bull queue workers: a shutdown signal pushes a sentinel via BLPOP so workers exit cleanly without losing the right to process pending tasks.
Akka Streams and similar streaming frameworks: the GraphStage signals completion via onPull/downstream cancellation, which is the materialised equivalent of a poison pill.
Redis Streams consumer groups: XREADGROUP with block timeout naturally returns when the stream is empty; a special ID (e.g. ">") polling loop plus a shared shutdown flag replaces the in-process sentinel.
Broker-level poison message isolation: in Kafka, RabbitMQ, or Azure Service Bus, a permanently failing message (deserialisation error, validation failure) blocks a partition/consumer indefinitely; DLQ-based routing (publish to dead-letter topic after N retries, then commit offset and continue) is the broker-level analogue that prevents one poison message from halting the entire pipeline.
Kubernetes preStop hooks + pill drain: a container's lifecycle preStop hook can enqueue a sentinel into an in-process work queue while the orchestrator grants terminationGracePeriodSeconds for the drain to complete, ensuring zero work-drop during rolling updates.
Azure Service Bus competing-consumers workers: when a worker receives a shutdown notification it completes its current PeekLock message, then calls Abandon on any held locks before unregistering; Azure Service Bus dead-letter queues handle the poison-message variant when a message exceeds MaxDeliveryCount and cannot be delivered.
Akka hierarchical actor trees: sending PoisonPill to a parent actor stops it after all queued messages ahead of the pill are processed, and automatically sends stop messages to all children in bottom-up order; this is the idiomatic way to orchestrate ordered multi-actor shutdown.
Non-blocking retry architectures (RabbitMQ): rather than local Thread.sleep retries that block the consumer thread, use server-side TTL queues with Dead Letter Exchange routing to implement exponential backoff, keeping the consumer responsive to new messages and to shutdown pills.
Java's JDK BlockingQueue worker pools: because BlockingQueue has no built-in close, producers can enqueue a unique end-of-stream object after all work; each consumer takes until that sentinel and then the coordinator joins workers.
Python multiprocessing worker pools: multiprocessing.Queue/JoinableQueue supports FIFO task delivery with sentinel values and join-based drain tracking; send one sentinel per worker and join them after the queue is exhausted.
Akka Classic actors: PoisonPill is enqueued in the mailbox and processed after already queued messages, while Akka Typed requires an explicit Stop/Shutdown protocol; choose the API that matches the actor model.

statement: Choose the ownership boundary for persisting an order and all of its dependent parts as one synchronized unit of work.
name: composite-entity
document:
composite-entity
coarse-grained-entity
Represent a cluster of related, dependent objects through one coarse-grained entity that owns them and persists and synchronises the whole graph as a single unit of work, so clients never reference, sequence, or save the parts themselves. Coined for coarse-grained EJB business objects; its modern form is the aggregate root with cascading or owned mappings.
A business concept clients treat as one thing (an order with its lines, a customer with addresses) is really a cluster of dependent objects, and persisting each part separately forces callers to know the parts, save them in the right order in the right transaction, delete the ones that left the relationship, and absorb a leaking physical schema. The catalog trigger: a cluster of related objects must persist and synchronise as one unit.
Relational or document stores where a coarse-grained business object is composed of finer-grained dependent objects whose lifecycle is bound to it. Applies when clients - especially remote ones - should exchange one coarse-grained structure instead of the parts, when the persist/synchronise boundary must coincide with one transaction, and when each dependent can still own its own mapping. Modern form: an aggregate root mapped with cascading associations or with components stored in the root's own row.
Order with line items, shipment addresses and payment allocations that must be written and deleted as one business unit.
Customer or account aggregate holding addresses, contact methods and preferences that are edited in one form and saved once.
Document-style clusters (invoice with revisions, article with embedded sections) where the parts only exist inside the root.
Legacy-style coarse-grained entity beans that wrap fine-grained POJOs so that clients exchange one composite transfer object instead of many fine-grained ones.
Mobile or remote clients that must send one coarse-grained payload per edit instead of a sequence of dependent calls.
Batch imports where a cluster is validated and written transactionally, so a partially imported entity never exists.
DDD Bounded Contexts where one aggregate encapsulates a complete business invariant enforced across multiple related entities — e.g., a Rental aggregate containing a rental agreement, reserved vehicle, and driver assignment that must all be created or fail together.
CQRS write models where the aggregate is the sole write target and all state changes flow through the root's command methods, ensuring every mutation is a coherent cluster-level operation.
Event sourcing snapshots where the aggregate root serialises its entire graph so that snapshot restore reconstructs the full composite in one operation rather than re-playing individual dependent events.
Legacy system facades that wrap a network of fine-grained remote beans behind a single coarse-grained composite interface, collapsing many remote calls into one round-trip for external clients.
SQLAlchemy parent-child clusters mapped with cascade='all, delete-orphan' on relationship(): disassociating a child deletes the row, so the Session flushes the cluster as one unit without per-child Session.delete() calls.
EF Core owned types: dependent types stored in the owner's table (or as owned navigations) share the aggregate root's identity and save with a single context.SaveChanges().
Mongoose subdocument arrays: embedded parts are saved, validated and removed through the top-level document, so the cluster's lifecycle is bound to the root document's save.

statement: Choose the ownership boundary for persisting an order and all of its dependent parts as one synchronized unit of work.
name: dependent-mapping
document:
dependent-mapping
Let the parent object's mapper perform the mapping for a dependent child object, so the child needs no identity, no finder and no mapper of its own while its rows are still loaded, saved and deleted with the parent.
A child object exists only in the context of its parent - order lines, tracks on an album, invoice positions - and no other table references it, yet the ordinary one-mapper-per-class approach gives it its own identity, its own finders and its own mapper: API surface and code that suggest an independent lifecycle the domain does not have, and that invite loads and saves out of context. The decision trigger is the child's mapping strategy: map it like any other class, or let the parent's mapper map it as part of the parent?
Object-relational or document mapping where a parent owns a collection (or a single child) whose lifecycle never outlives the parent, and the store is reached only through the parent. Applies when no other table holds a foreign key to the child, when the child has no meaningful identity of its own (or only a key that is unique within the parent), and when a Data Mapper or an ORM session can drive the child's rows from the parent. It stops applying as soon as another aggregate references the child or the child must be queried on its own.
Order lines, invoice positions or shipment items: rows that exist only inside one parent and are edited through it (Fowler's album/tracks example).
Value-like children of an aggregate root — address entries, contact methods, tags owned by one aggregate — which are never looked up on their own.
Legacy schemas where the child table has no natural key of its own and is identified only by the parent's key plus a position column.
Offline or mobile sync payloads that ship a parent graph as one unit, so the child is written only as part of the parent's message.
Import or reporting pipelines that rebuild a parent and its details in one transaction and must never leave orphan rows behind.
Coarse-grained clusters already persisted as one unit (Composite Entity) where the children must be given exactly one write path.
Owned collections of value objects — e.g. a product's size variants, a customer's historical addresses — where the collection is always loaded as a whole and mutated only through the parent.
Post/comment hierarchies in a blogging aggregate where comments have no global identity and are only reachable through their parent post.
Playlist tracks, album tracks, or setlist items: each track belongs to exactly one parent playlist/album and is never referenced by another aggregate.
Configuration sections or preference rows that are scoped to a single user or tenant and are replaced wholesale on update.
EF Core owned types (OwnsOne/OwnsMany): the owned type cannot have its own DbSet, is keyed as (owner key, per-item key) or a shadow key, and is loaded, saved and deleted only through the owner — dependent mapping as a first-class modeling concept in Microsoft's ORM.
JPA @ElementCollection of @Embeddable elements (e.g. Person.nickNames in the Jakarta Persistence spec example): the elements get a collection table keyed by the owner and no entity identity, finder or lifecycle of their own.
SQLAlchemy's cascade='all, delete-orphan' relationships: a child de-associated from its parent is deleted by the Session, making the parent's Session the single write path for child rows.

name: dependency-injection
document:
dependency-injection
di
constructor injection
setter injection
interface injection
ioc container
pure di
manual di
Supply an object with the collaborators it needs from the outside — through its constructor, its setters/properties, or a dedicated injection interface — so it never constructs or looks a dependency up itself and every wiring decision is made once, in a composition root or container.
An object that creates its own collaborators hard-wires a concrete class, a construction recipe and often a lifetime into itself: swapping the implementation for a test double, a second deployment or a new platform means editing the class, and the dependency graph stays invisible in the API. The recurring trigger is exactly the catalog's rule: an object should not create what it depends on — the caller, the framework or the composition root decides, and hands the dependency in.
Applies whenever a component's collaborators are chosen per deployment, per environment or per test, whenever constructing them is expensive or platform-specific, and whenever a framework owns object creation (request handlers, scheduled jobs, UI screens, message consumers). It matters most in large object graphs where one abstraction has several implementations and lifetimes must be managed (singleton, request-scoped, transient); it is unnecessary when the collaborators are pure values or when construction is a private detail nobody needs to vary.
Web and API backends whose handlers need repositories, clocks, mailers and caches that must be replaced by fakes in tests and by sandbox services in staging.
Hexagonal and clean architectures where the domain declares ports (interfaces) and the infrastructure layer supplies adapters at the composition root.
Frameworks that own object creation — request handlers, scheduled jobs, UI controllers, message consumers — where the framework's injector is the only practical wiring point.
Deployment variants (on-prem vs cloud, SQL vs in-memory, real vs stub payment gateway) selected per environment through binding configuration rather than conditional code.
Plugin and extension systems where the concrete implementation is chosen at start-up from a plugin registry, enabling third-party adapters without touching core code.
Expensive shared resources whose lifetime must be managed centrally (connection pools, HTTP clients, circuit breakers) while service classes stay stateless.
Unit tests that construct the class under test directly with test doubles, and integration tests that swap only the outer layer's bindings.
Microservices with sidecar containers: the sidecar provides logging, tracing and retry policies as injected collaborators, keeping the service logic untouched.
Cloud-native applications where the composition root is the only place that knows whether a dependency resolves locally, across a service mesh, or via a remote gRPC call.
Multi-tenant SaaS where tenant-specific adapters (tenant-scoped repositories, per-tenant feature flags) are bound at the composition root and switched by middleware.
Event-driven systems where message handlers receive their dependencies through injection, making the handler logic identical between in-process and distributed deployment.
AOT-compiled applications (Native AOT, Blazor WebAssembly, serverless) where runtime reflection is unavailable — dependencies are resolved via source generators or manually at the composition root.
Functional codebases using effect systems (ZIO, fp-ts, Reader monad) where the DI container is replaced by typed environments passed through function compositions.
Consumer-driven contract testing (Pact, OpenAPI pact) where DI swaps provider implementations with contract-mock stubs at the boundary, enabling parallel service development without shared integration environments.
Resilience and fault-injection testing: proxies or decorator-based fault injectors (e.g., Gremlin SDK, WireMock) are injected as collaborators to validate retry, timeout and circuit-breaker behaviour under simulated failure conditions.
Single-page application frameworks with DI built into the component tree: Angular resolves components, directives and services through hierarchical injectors, scoping providers to the application root, a component subtree or a route so features override implementations and lazy-load without global registration.
Android apps using Dagger (and Hilt over it) to build the object graph at compile time — generated, reflection-free code, bindings and cycles checked at build time, with field injection reserved for framework-created entry points like Activities and Fragments.
Python web APIs (FastAPI) where each path operation declares Depends(callable) parameters: the framework resolves nested dependency graphs with per-request caching and uses yield-based dependencies to open and close connections around each request.

name: producer-consumer
document:
producer-consumer
bounded buffer
consumer-producer
Insert a bounded buffer between producers and consumers of work items so the two sides run concurrently at their own rates, the buffer absorbs bursts and slack, and its bound turns overload into backpressure, queueing or an explicit drop policy instead of unbounded growth.
Production and consumption proceed at different rates: a fast producer outruns its consumer and either drops items or grows a backlog until memory runs out, a slow producer leaves consumers idle, and bursts arrive faster than they can be processed. Wiring the two sides together directly also couples their lifetimes and schedules - a synchronous hand-off makes the faster side wait for the slower - so neither side can be scaled, restarted or tested on its own.
Concurrent in-process software (threads, tasks, coroutines, event-loop callbacks) with one or more producers and one or more consumers that can run at the same time but not at the same average rate. The buffer is a component-level data structure owned by the application - a work queue for a thread pool, a pipeline hand-off, a logging or telemetry sink - not a durable broker, so the decisions are how to hand items over, how to bound the queue and how to end the arrangement cleanly.
Work queues behind thread or worker pools: request handlers enqueue tasks and a fixed set of workers consumes them, so pool size is independent of the arrival rate. Industry examples: Celery (Python), Sidekiq (Ruby), BullMQ (Node.js) all use this shape with Redis or a broker as the durable backing store.
Asynchronous logging and telemetry: hot paths enqueue records cheaply while a background writer drains, formats and writes them, keeping I/O latency off the request path. Structured log collectors (Fluent Bit, Vector) ingest from many sources into one consumer.
Multi-stage data pipelines (decode - transform - encode, extract - transform - load): bounded queues between stages give each stage its own workers and let a slow stage backpressure a fast one. Used in media transcoding, ETL workflows, and stream processors.
Ingestion buffers: a socket, file or broker reader produces records faster than the processing or indexing stage can absorb them, and the buffer smooths the mismatch without dropping data. Common in IoT telemetry ingestion, click-stream collection, and log aggregation.
UI/host integration: a background thread posts work or results to the main/event-loop thread's queue and vice versa, keeping the UI responsive without locks around application state. All major GUI frameworks (Qt, Swing, Flutter) use this internally.
Batch job scheduling: producers enqueue compute jobs (image resize, PDF generation, report creation) and a pool of consumers processes them. Systems like Celery, Hangfire, and AWS SQS follow this pattern, often with priority queues, delayed execution, and dead-letter routing.
Event streaming pre-processing: a Kafka, Pulsar, or NATS consumer-producer chain filters, transforms, and routes events through a series of bounded queues before landing in a data warehouse or search index.
Simulation and testing: a producer generates a deterministic stream of items while a consumer asserts on what it receives, with a sentinel marking the end of the stream. Property-based testing frameworks use this to drive scenario generation.
Print spooling and document processing: print jobs or document conversion tasks are queued and processed by a pool of workers, with bounded queues preventing runaway memory use even under burst load.
ML inference pipelines: a model-serving host receives requests via an API, enqueues them into a bounded queue, and a pool of worker coroutines or threads dequeues and runs inference. The queue decouples HTTP latency from inference latency and provides backpressure when the model GPU is saturated. Tools like Ray Serve, Triton Inference Server, and TorchServe use this shape.
Streaming audio/video processing: a media pipeline (capture - encode - mux - stream) uses bounded queues between stages; frames that arrive during a temporary encoding stall are buffered rather than dropped, and a full encoder output queue backpressures the camera capture stage to prevent unbounded memory growth from frame accumulation.
WebSocket connection management: a server's accept loop enqueues new connections into a bounded connection queue; a pool of handler coroutines or threads dequeues and upgrades them, preventing connection exhaustion under burst load while the handler pool limits concurrency independently of the arrival rate.
Financial order processing: high-frequency trading systems receive market data feeds (producer) and route orders through risk checks and execution engines (consumers), with bounded queues between stages preventing downstream latency from backpressuring the market data ingestion and applying backpressure to upstream feed handlers.
Go channel pipelines: a source goroutine produces values into a channel, transformation stages consume and emit through downstream channels, and a sink drains the final stage. Go's documented pipeline pattern makes channel closure and cancellation part of the producer-consumer lifecycle.
Python asyncio worker queues: an asyncio.Queue(maxsize=N) accepts work from coroutine producers while worker coroutines await get(), process items and call task_done(); finite maxsize suspends producers when consumers fall behind.
Java executor work queues: java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue coordinates multiple producer threads and consumer workers, with put()/take() waiting on full and empty capacity so an Executor-style worker pool can be bounded independently of arrival rate.

name: revocable-forwarder
document:
revocable-forwarder
caretaker
revocable proxy
Let a collaborator use an object through a forwarding wrapper that the grantor can switch off at any time through a separate control, so authority already handed out can be withdrawn without destroying the target and without the collaborator's cooperation.
A capability is just a reference, so once a collaborator has been given access to an object there is no built-in way to take it back: the grantor can destroy the object, ask the collaborator to stop, or leave the access standing. The recurring decision is how to grant access that is bounded in time - temporary use of a file, a service object, a session, an account - while keeping a control that only the grantor holds.
Object-capability settings, and any in-process design in which authority travels as references rather than as a global identity: plugin and extension hosts lending a service object to foreign code, multi-tenant object graphs giving a worker one tenant-scoped resource, session-scoped services, and capability-based workflow or financial systems in which a grant must be provably withdrawn. It applies when the grantor keeps its own reference to the target and can intercept every call through the reference it handed out; where the runtime lets references be forged, dereferenced around the wrapper or reached by reflection, marshalling or FFI, the same structure degrades from an enforcement mechanism to a discipline.
A plugin or extension host lends a file, network or service object to foreign code and revokes it when the plugin is unloaded or breaches policy.
A multi-tenant worker receives one tenant-scoped resource for the duration of a job and loses it at job end, without the tenant object being torn down.
Session teardown in a long-lived server: the handler works through the wrapper, and logout revokes future calls before the session's resources are freed.
Capability-based workflow and financial systems that give an agent temporary authority over an account or a document and revoke it when the task completes.
Temporary elevated access for maintenance or debugging, where the requirement is to show that the extra authority has provably ended (audit evidence).
Graceful decommissioning of a shared resource: revoke new work through the wrapper, drain the calls already in flight, then release the resource.
The Scala ocaps framework's Revocable/Caretaker API returns a proxied capability plus a private Revoker, so a session, logout, timeout or supervisor can make later calls fail without changing the target.
JavaScript's standard Proxy.revocable() and the Chrome Extensions chrome.permissions API provide browser/runtime counterparts: keep the revoke/remove control private, and do not mistake the platform wrapper or permission record for protection against an already leaked target reference.
AWS IAM role-session revocation for temporary STS credentials is a distributed analogue of withdrawing a forwarded grant: policy evaluation denies subsequent requests, but propagation and credential caching mean it is not the atomic in-process check-and-forward gate described here.

name: deadline-propagation
document:
deadline-propagation
timeout propagation
Bound the total time and work of a logical request by carrying one deadline through its whole call tree: every hop forwards the remaining budget and the cancellation signal instead of inventing a fresh timeout, so work that can no longer succeed is abandoned at every level.
A request fans out into a chain or tree of downstream calls and each hop applies its own timeout: the end-to-end latency budget becomes the sum of N independent timeouts, servers keep working after the originating client has given up, and cancellation never reaches the deeper work - resources are consumed producing answers nobody will read.
Networked request handling with multi-hop calls: RPC and HTTP chains, service meshes, gateways, fan-out and hedged requests. It applies when one latency budget is meaningful for the whole logical request (an SLO or a user-facing timeout), when the hops are under your control and can carry request-scoped state (context, token, signal, call option or header), and when downstream work is cancellable or can be interrupted at checkpoints.
Microservice request chains (gateway -> frontend service -> several backends) under one user-facing latency SLO, where each hop converts the inbound deadline into its own outgoing calls.
gRPC services whose clients set a deadline and whose servers propagate it as a remaining timeout to downstream calls while cancelling server-side work once the deadline passes.
Fan-out and aggregation endpoints calling several backends in parallel: every sub-call shares the parent budget, and sub-calls still running when it expires are cancelled instead of awaited.
Hedged requests: the first replica to answer wins, and the duplicate requests are cancelled through the same carrier so their downstream work is stopped too.
Streaming and long-poll endpoints that must stop processing when the client disconnects or the connection times out, propagating that stop to services and storage.
Batch or pipeline steps with a per-request time budget that must check the remaining time before each stage and abandon a request that can no longer be finished in time.
ROS 2 / DDS-based robotics pipelines: autonomous vehicle perception pipelines where sensor data must traverse a chain of processing nodes (detect -> classify -> plan -> act) and missed deadlines invalidate downstream results entirely.
Distributed real-time databases with multi-hop queries (gateway -> shard router -> storage node -> index node) where each hop's latency budget is derived from a user-facing SLA.
Service mesh sidecar configurations (Istio/Linkerd/Envoy) where per-route timeout policies propagate deadline context to application code via headers like grpc-timeout or custom X-Request-Deadline headers.
Industrial IoT and edge computing pipelines (edge gateway -> fieldbus bridge -> PLC -> sensor) where end-to-end control loop deadlines must be enforced across heterogeneous network boundaries.
GraphQL federation: a federated query hitting multiple subgraphs in parallel must bound the total resolution time and cancel subgraph requests whose partial results can no longer affect the final response.
Go services on the standard library context package: context.WithDeadline and WithTimeout derive a child whose Done channel closes at the earliest of its own deadline, an explicit cancel, or the parent's cancellation, so cancelling the root request context tears down the whole goroutine tree, and WithDeadlineCause/WithTimeoutCause attach an explicit cause for attribution.
Envoy router filter in service meshes: Envoy sets x-envoy-expected-rq-timeout-ms on internal requests - derived from x-envoy-upstream-rq-timeout-ms or the route timeout - so upstream services can read the expected total completion time and exit early instead of finishing work the proxy has already timed out.
ASP.NET Core gRPC services map the inbound call's deadline onto the handler's CancellationToken; passing that token to database queries, HttpClient calls and Task.Delay stops server-side work the moment the client's deadline expires.

name: watchman
document:
watchman
dead man's switch
heartbeat monitor
Detect that a message flow has gone silent - not that a message failed - and tell a responsible person or system within a bounded time by comparing each flow's arrivals against the cadence its business deadline implies.
Message systems fail silently in the one way no error handler observes: nothing arrives. A producer stops emitting, a consumer stops draining, a scheduled job never fires, a credential expires, a partition goes offline - and because no failing code path is ever entered, error dashboards stay green while downstream data quietly goes stale. The recurring trigger: a flow whose absence is business-visible (a nightly feed, an order stream, a partner interface) has no owner-facing signal for 'no messages', so the gap is discovered late - by a customer or a downstream job - instead of by the team that can fix it.
Applies wherever messages are expected on a knowable cadence (event streams, queues, batch hand-offs, partner interfaces, device check-ins) and their absence is a business-visible failure: the flow has an owner, the expected period and grace window can be derived from a downstream deadline, and either the transport can be observed passively (queue counters, a wire tap) or the producers can emit out-of-band heartbeats. The watchman sits at message-flow or boundary scope - an in-process watcher beside the consumer, a periodic sweep over persisted last-seen state, or a rule in the monitoring stack fed by metrics - and it must itself be watched, because a silent watchman is exactly the failure it exists to catch.
Nightly batch or ETL feed: page the integration owner when the 02:00 import has produced no messages by its deadline, instead of noticing an empty report at the morning stand-up.
Business-critical event stream (orders, payments, telemetry): alarm when the produce rate stays at zero through business hours, which separates a healthy quiet topic from a stopped producer.
External partner interface: notify when no messages have arrived from a B2B partner within the agreed window, turning a looming SLA breach into an early, actionable alert.
Long-running workflow stage: require a heartbeat from each process-manager step so a stuck instance is noticed before the surrounding batch closes or a compensation becomes necessary.
Retry or dead-letter pump: verify that the pump still drains failed messages - silence means the pump died, not that the backlog is empty.
Fleet check-ins (edge devices, agents, cron jobs on many hosts): raise a per-device or per-site alarm when scheduled check-ins stop arriving.
The alerting pipeline itself: an always-firing watchdog alert routed to an external service, so a broken alert path is discovered by its silence.
Cron and scheduled-job fleet via Healthchecks.io: each job pings a unique URL, the service holds the Period and Grace Time, flips the check Late then Down when no ping arrives by period + grace, and notifies integrations.
Dashboard alert rules in Grafana: an alert rule whose query returns no series enters the No Data state and can raise a DatasourceNoData alert - the platform form of deciding what silence means (No Data, Alerting, Normal or Keep last state).
Apache Burrow for Kafka (LinkedIn): committed offsets are evaluated per partition over a sliding window and a consumer is classified STALLED when its offset is frozen with non-zero lag, or STOPPED when no new commits arrive - consumer-silence detection without fixed lag thresholds.

name: authentication-enforcer
document:
authentication-enforcer
authentication interceptor
authentication gateway
auth middleware
Put one request-boundary checkpoint in front of protected actions that decides whether authentication is required, delegates credential verification to a replaceable mechanism, and attaches the resulting subject to request-scoped context before dispatch, so coverage is uniform without making handlers understand credentials.
When each handler decides whether and how to authenticate, protection is duplicated or omitted on exceptional paths, credential formats and user stores leak into business code, and a mechanism or policy change requires editing every handler instead of one auditable boundary.
Server-side request processing — web APIs, web applications and service endpoints — where many handlers share one protection policy, credentials arrive through a uniform convention (Authorization header, cookie, session id), verification technology must be replaceable or differ per route, and the runtime provides a request-pipeline hook (servlet filter, middleware chain, framework guard). Applies to session-based and token-based authentication alike; permissions and roles are out of scope. Three implementation strategies exist: (1) Container-Managed Authentication — the runtime container owns the checkpoint and realm configuration; (2) Authentication Provider Strategy — a custom provider behind a narrow interface, swapped without touching handlers; (3) JAAS Login Module Strategy — pluggable via standard JAAS configuration, supporting multifactor authentication via smart cards, biometrics, or third-party IdPs. The pattern is equally applicable at the edge level (API gateway, ingress proxy) and the service level (in-process middleware).
Web APIs where every route except health and login requires a bearer token, and the checkpoint is mounted in front of the whole router.
Multi-tenant applications with mixed protection levels: public marketing pages, session-protected tenant UI and token-protected integration endpoints behind one enforcement layer.
Services that must accept several credential types at once — browser sessions, mobile JWTs, mutual TLS for service-to-service traffic — while keeping one uniform enforcement point.
Credential-technology migration (basic auth to OIDC, on-premises LDAP to SSO) where enforcement stays put while the mechanism behind it is swapped.
Regulated environments where every rejected authentication attempt has to be logged centrally and identically across all endpoints.
Legacy applications with authentication checks scattered through servlets or handlers that must be consolidated behind one intercepting layer before an audit.
Zero Trust microservices where every internal service verifies JWTs independently (per-service verification) while an ingress gateway provides the first checkpoint — the enforcer exists at both layers.
OIDC/OAuth2 migration where an existing session-based app adds bearer-token support; the mechanism adapts to both while the enforcement point remains unchanged.
Multi-tenant SaaS platforms where tenant isolation depends on the enforcer resolving a tenant identifier from the token before the handler processes any data.
Platform-as-a-Service with mounted sub-applications where a parent ASGI middleware dispatches per-path authentication requirements from a config registry, injecting identity into ASGI scope for all sub-apps.
Spring Security servlet applications that use a SecurityFilterChain with anyRequest().authenticated() and an AuthenticationManager/AuthenticationProvider chain, so controllers consume the SecurityContext rather than parse credentials.
ASP.NET Core APIs that register JWT or cookie schemes, call UseAuthentication before dependent middleware, and use a fallback authorization policy to make authenticated access the default.
An nginx ingress location using auth_request to delegate identity verification to a central authentication service, forwarding only after a 2xx result and propagating 401/403 failures while services still verify their own trust boundary.

name: attorney-client
document:
attorney-client
attorney pattern
attorney-client friendship idiom
Grant a named collaborator a deliberately narrow compile-time view of a class's private interface by making an attorney the client's sole friend; the attorney forwards selected operations or re-exports selected private nested types (often through controlled public typedefs), while unrelated private members and the public contract remain closed.
A C++ collaborator may need one private hook, constructor, iterator adapter or nested implementation type, but a friend class receives every private and protected member. Making the hook public leaks it to every caller; publishing a std::list<T>::iterator or the container type leaks representation and its invalidation contract; pImpl hides representation from everyone but does not grant one collaborator a typed privileged view. The missing mechanism is a small attorney contract that names exactly the operations or nested types this collaborator may use without turning the private interface into a second public API.
Object-oriented code whose encapsulation boundary is a class and whose language offers class- or scope-level access control but no per-collaborator grant - C++ with friend declarations, Java/C#/Kotlin with package, assembly or module access, and their test- and library-extension scenarios. It applies at object scope, where one type owns the implementation and one named collaborator needs a slice of it, and it is a source-level structuring device checked by the compiler, never a runtime protection mechanism.
White-box test access: a test harness reaches one private hook or state view through a named attorney instead of making the member public or redefining private with a test-only preprocessor switch.
Iterator adapters: Boost.Iterator's iterator_core_access is a canonical gateway class a user-defined iterator befriends, so iterator_facade and its operators reach private dereference/increment/advance core functions while those implementation hooks stay out of the iterator's public API.
Serialization: Boost.Serialization has serializable classes befriend boost::serialization::access, whose gateway reaches the private serialize() member so archives can reconstruct state without a public serialization method.
Private nested type exposure: LLVM's SchedulerInternalsAttorney publishes the selected nested Scheduler::BndlSchedState as a public type alias and supplies narrow static accessors for unit tests, without publishing every Scheduler private type.
A pImpl-backed adapter that must inspect one implementation-owned type: keep the public class opaque and put the attorney definition in the adapter or test header, so the privileged component gets a typed view without making the implementation part of the ordinary public contract.
Iterator facade over a hidden list-like representation: expose a stable nested iterator/view type through an attorney rather than publishing std::list<T>::iterator, so the owner can replace the container without promising its node and invalidation details to every caller.
Private virtual hooks: an attorney forwards one private virtual operation through a base reference, allowing the derived override to run even though friendship is not inherited.
Factory or construction control: a builder reaches one private constructor or initialization hook through an attorney, while unrelated callers still cannot construct an object through that path.
Spacecraft flight software (fsfw): LocalDpManagerAttorney keeps fetchPoolEntry and getMutexHandle as private static forwarders and befriends only LocalPoolVariable and LocalPoolVector, so the local data pool manager opens its internals to two named collaborators instead of every class that might befriend it.
Simulator tree traversal (Sandia Sparta Modeling Framework): sparta::TreeNodePrivateAttorney exposes TreeNode's private child vectors and subtrees through static accessors (getAllChildren, getChild, findChildren) for internal Reports and Pipeout processing, with a documented 'should NOT be used by simulation developers' restriction in place of an enforceable caller limit.

name: plugin
document:
plugin
plug-in
plugin architecture
Let a host application acquire behaviour from independently deployed modules that it discovers and links at configuration or start-up time, so new features, backends or device support can be added without recompiling or redeploying the host.
The behaviours a system must offer vary by deployment (customer, environment, backend, hardware) or grow after the host has shipped; hard-wiring every implementation behind a factory method or a configuration switch means each new variant edits core code and forces a rebuild and redeploy of the whole application.
Systems whose capability set is not fully known at build time: third-party or per-customer extensions, drivers and storage backends, editor and build tooling, test runners, media pipelines. It applies wherever a stable extension point can be published, the contract can be versioned, and the runtime can bind code after compilation (shared libraries, class or module loading, plugin packages).
IDEs, editors and build tools whose feature set grows through extensions (Eclipse, VS Code, webpack, ESLint, pytest, RuboCop).
Servers and frameworks that pick a codec, transport, storage or auth backend per deployment (JDBC drivers via ServiceLoader, .NET plugin hosts, Kafka connectors).
Infrastructure tooling that hosts independently released providers, such as Terraform providers over gRPC or Vault secret engines.
Media, imaging and device software that adds codecs, effects or drivers after the main program ships (Apache httpd modules, GStreamer, DAW and imaging plugins).
Document and data pipelines where per-customer transformation or validation steps are shipped as separate packages (Python entry points, Ruby gems).
Applications that must support tenant- or customer-specific behaviour without a private build per customer, composed at start-up from a plugin directory or a configuration list.
AI agent systems where tools, memory backends and LLMs are loaded as plugins (LangChain agents, semantic kernel plugins).
Cloud-native platforms that must support tenant-specific backends or third-party integrations without redeploying the control plane (Kubernetes operators, service mesh extensions).
DevOps and CI/CD pipelines where steps, reporters or cloud integrations are added as plugins (Jenkins plugins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI job templates).
Observability platforms where collectors, processors and exporters are pluginable (OpenTelemetry collectors, Grafana datasources and panels).
Editor ecosystems that declare contributions in manifests and run extension code behind a host boundary, as in Visual Studio Code's Extension Host and contribution points.
Infrastructure CLIs that launch provider binaries over a versioned RPC contract and negotiate compatibility, as in Terraform's Plugin Protocol and provider servers.
Web servers assembled from independently built dynamic modules loaded at startup or restart, as in Apache HTTP Server's DSO and mod_so module system.

name: newtype
document:
newtype
strong typedef
opaque type
Give a single primitive its own distinct type so that values with different meanings cannot be substituted for one another, and the raw representation is reachable only through the wrapper's own construction and accessors.
Several domain concepts share one representation - customer id, order id and tenant id are all strings or UUIDs, width/height/offset are all numbers, milliseconds and seconds are both integers - and the API therefore accepts them interchangeably. A swapped argument, a mixed unit or a mistyped literal compiles (or runs) silently, and the defect surfaces late, as a wrong lookup or a cross-tenant bug rather than a type error.
Code in which two or more values with the same underlying representation flow through the same functions, collections or persistence mapping, and in which a single value owns a rule (identifier syntax, non-emptiness, numeric range, unit). Applies at the value level of one field; clusters of attributes that change together belong to Value Object, and closed constant sets to Type-Safe Enum.
Identifier families in one codebase: CustomerId, OrderId, TenantId and SessionId all string- or UUID-shaped and passed to the same repository, logger and cache.
Unit-carrying measurements: Milliseconds vs Seconds, Meters vs Feet, Radians vs Degrees, Cents vs Dollars, where arithmetic must stay inside one unit and conversion is explicit.
Validated single values: EmailAddress, PhoneNumber, Iban, Slug, Percentage (0-100), PortNumber, NonEmptyString - parsed once at the edge, trusted everywhere afterwards.
Security-adjacent tokens: API token vs session id vs tenant id, where a swap becomes a cross-tenant or privilege defect rather than a wrong lookup.
Geometry and graphics APIs where Width, Height, X, Y, Offset and Length are all numbers and transposition should be a compile error.
Pagination and buffer arithmetic: PageSize vs PageIndex vs ByteOffset vs Count, integers that are trivially transposable in a long argument list.
Rust's official newtype examples use Millimeters(u32) and Meters(u32) to keep units distinct, and use Wrapper(Vec<T>) to give a local wrapper its own trait implementations.
Scala 3 opaque types model values such as Logarithm over Double as distinct outside their defining scope, with controlled extension methods and no runtime boxing.
Kotlin @JvmInline value classes wrap one property into a non-interchangeable domain type such as Password while allowing unboxed representations in many uses.

DCL
DCLP
Initialise a shared resource exactly once and lazily while keeping the steady-state read path free of lock acquisition - by testing a cheaply published state first and taking the lock only for the one-time construction, where the platform can publish the built object safely to every reader.
An expensive object - configuration, a connection pool, a compiled plan, a cache - must be created once and only when it is first needed, but its accessor is called from many threads. The naive check-then-act form lets two threads build it at the same time, and guarding every read with a lock serialises a path that almost never needs synchronisation. The tempting fix - test a flag cheaply, lock only for the initialisation, test again inside the lock - is sound only if the write that publishes the object is ordered with respect to the readers' loads, which is exactly the part the classic formulation leaves implicit and the reason the idiom is famous for rare, unreproducible failures.
Concurrent, shared-memory software in which one object or cell must be built once and read many times: process-wide singletons and registries, per-object caches inside an object shared between threads, lazily built statics in languages whose runtime also provides the once semantics. The pattern presupposes a memory model with a defined publication ordering (volatile, acquire/release, an initialisation lock, or a runtime once primitive) and a read path hot enough that the lock it removes is measurable. On single-threaded runtimes there is nothing to synchronise, and where a single-threaded composition root can initialise eagerly the pattern is unnecessary.
Process-wide singletons whose construction is expensive or configuration-dependent: configuration snapshot, metrics registry, logger, connection pool, feature-flag view.
Per-object caches inside an object shared by several threads - compiled regular expression or query plan, parsed schema, symbol table - where the build is expensive and the read is hot.
Lazily built statics in languages where the runtime owns the once semantics: C++ function-local static, Swift static let or global let, Kotlin by lazy, Scala lazy val, Go sync.Once, Rust OnceLock/LazyLock.
Compensating for the static-initialisation-order problem: an accessor that builds the global on first use instead of relying on cross-translation-unit initialisation order.
Avoiding lock overhead on a read-mostly, write-once hot path (memo tables, symbol caches, thread-safe lazy proxies) where a contended lock would show up in a profile.
Small or freestanding runtimes without a once primitive, where the first caller must build the cell and an eager initialiser is not available.
RWMutex-protected maps in Go where readers check a fast path before the slower write-locked re-check, as a safer alternative to sync.Map for workloads with known access patterns.
Per-connection or per-session lazy fields in object-pooled servers where the pool itself is the shared cell and each borrowed object gets a lazy-computed field.
Cross-language plugin or extension registries where one language's runtime initialises a global handle that other language shards read without repeated synchronisation.
Rate-limiter or circuit-breaker state that must be lazily built from configuration: building eagerly would couple the policy to startup time, but the read path must be lock-free under high throughput.
Lazy compilation or query-plan warming in database connection pools where the pool is shared but individual plans are built on first use by the owning thread.
Spring Framework's DefaultSingletonBeanRegistry.getSingleton: check the singletonObjects map lock-free, take the singletonLock only when the bean is absent, re-check inside - a production evolution of the idiom whose correctness was formally challenged (SPR-13463) and upheld because the concurrent-map read already carries the needed memory barrier.
Chromium's base::LazyInstance / GetOrCreateLazyPointer: an atomic state word with a 'creating' bit, acquire-load fast path and release-store publication - since deprecated in favour of function-local statics with base::NoDestructor, a signal of how far hardened platforms have moved from hand-rolled DCL.
ACE toolkit's ACE_Singleton<TYPE, ACE_LOCK>: the pattern's original industrial home (the 1997 paper was written alongside ACE) - the template still guards instance() with a double-checked ACE_LOCK acquire and recommends ACE_Recursive_Thread_Mutex for multi-threaded access.
Swift runtime: every global/static let is lowered to swift_once (dispatch_once on Darwin), so the double-checked once structure is the default initialisation mechanism for lazily computed immutable globals rather than hand-written code.

name: secure-logger
document:
secure-logger
tamper-evident logging
secure audit log
Record security-relevant events through a single logging chokepoint and chain every record's authenticator to its predecessor, so that altering, deleting, reordering or truncating the log is detectable by an independent verifier rather than merely inconvenient for the party being recorded.
The audit trail exists, but the party it records - a privileged operator, a compromised service, the application itself - can also rewrite it: files are appendable and rotatable by the same process that writes them, there is no gap detection when a record or a whole file disappears, and nobody can prove after the fact that a log line is the line that was written. The log answers questions only as long as everyone trusts the host that produced it.
Systems where a security-relevant event stream has evidentiary or compliance weight - privileged action and break-glass accounts, authentication and authorisation decisions, regulated transaction trails - and where an adversary on the recording host (or the recorded subject itself) is inside the threat model. It applies to a component boundary: the application writes through one logger, the store is append-only for that application, and verification happens elsewhere, so key custody and the trust anchor are part of the design rather than an afterthought.
Privileged and administrative activity: break-glass accounts, role and policy changes, configuration and key operations that must remain provable after the fact.
Regulated transaction audit trails (PCI DSS 10.x, HIPAA, SOX) where an independently verifiable sequence of attributable events is the compliance artefact.
Authentication and authorisation decision records: who was denied, by which rule, in which service - the evidence security operations triages incidents from.
Cloud and API activity logging built the CloudTrail way: per-file digests plus signed digest files that chain the previous digest, so a customer can verify what the provider delivered.
Edge and IoT devices that can be physically captured: the device keeps chaining into a remote anchor, so records written before an attack stay trustworthy after it.
systemd-journald Forward Secure Sealing: journalctl --setup-keys keeps a sealing key on the host that derives forward-securely per epoch while the verification key is stored externally; per-epoch SHA-256 HMAC tags seal the journal file, and journalctl --verify with the external key detects alteration, removal or reordering of records.
Certificate Transparency (RFC 6962) generalises the chain into an append-only Merkle tree: the log signs each tree head within the Maximum Merge Delay, and auditors verify with Merkle consistency proofs that newer heads preserve every earlier entry - the anchor is published and independently checked rather than merely kept.
Google Pixel Binary Transparency: factory images are leaves of a tile-based Merkle tree whose signed checkpoint roots are published, and witness monitors routinely verify consistency between checkpoints so a rolled-back or rewritten log is detected by third parties, not just the log operator.

name: page-controller
document:
page-controller
model-1
Give each logical page or form its own input controller that handles the requests addressed to it — reading the request, invoking domain logic and choosing the view — instead of routing every request through one shared handler.
Dynamic pages repeat the same request handling: parse and validate the incoming request, call domain logic, pick a view, report errors. Without a per-page home for that logic it either spreads into templates or gets copied into every script; the recurring decision is whether one page or form owns its request handling, or whether a central controller multiplexes all of them.
Server-side web presentation where URLs map one-to-one onto logical pages, forms or actions: CGI programs, servlets and JSP pages, controller actions, Razor Pages, route handlers in micro-frameworks. It fits sites whose pages share little behaviour, page-focused areas of larger applications, and frameworks whose native unit is a page; it stops fitting as soon as most pages need the same authentication, internationalisation, layout or tracing.
Small to medium websites where each page has its own URL, its own data and its own template (CMS front ends, marketing pages with forms, internal tools).
Form-heavy areas where one page owns one interaction end to end: show the form, validate the submission, run one workflow, render the result.
Prototypes and scripting-era deployments where one program, servlet or route function per page is the natural deployment unit.
Page-focused corners of a larger application (account settings, an admin console) whose pages genuinely differ from one another.
Frameworks whose canonical unit is the page itself: Razor Pages (PageModel = Page Controller), ASP.NET Web Forms code-behind, Java Struts Actions, Django FBV (Function-Based Views) mapped one-per-URL, Flask route functions, PHP single-file-per-page.
Per-page Ajax callbacks that are tightly coupled to a specific page's data and logic, where extracting them into a shared controller would create artificial coupling.
Situations where page-specific code is large enough to warrant a dedicated class but small enough that a full command-object framework is overkill.
ASP.NET Core Razor Pages: each PageModel owns the handlers and view data for one page, with OnGet/OnPost methods providing a concrete page-controller unit for page-specific forms. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/razor-pages/?view=aspnetcore-10.0
Django function-based views: URLconf maps a URL pattern to one Python view function that receives HttpRequest and returns the page response, making small page-specific interactions explicit. https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/6.1/topics/http/views/
Flask route functions: the route decorator binds a URL and HTTP methods to one view function, a lightweight Page Controller shape for independent pages and forms. https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/quickstart/

name: recursive-descent-parser
document:
recursive-descent-parser
recursive descent
recursive descent parsing
Parse a small grammar by translating every rule directly into a function that consumes the tokens the rule matches and calls the functions of the rules it references, so the parser's control flow is the grammar itself and stays readable, debuggable and free of a code-generation step.
A hand-written parser is the only option - no generator in the toolchain, or the grammar is a small DSL - yet the grammar is not a flat token sequence: alternatives must be chosen from lookahead, repetition must become a loop, and the natural grammar for expressions is left-recursive, which a top-down parser cannot translate directly. Without a disciplined mapping from rules to functions the parser degenerates into ad-hoc index arithmetic and exception-driven backtracking, and errors end up without positions.
Front ends for small languages, DSLs, query/filter/rule grammars, configuration and protocol formats, and the parsing layer of compilers and interpreters that want no code-generation step. It applies when a lexer or token stream already exists (or is cheap to write), the grammar is small to medium and reasonably LL-friendly or rewritable into LL form, and the team values readable, step-debuggable, position-precise parsing over generated tables.
Front ends for small languages, DSLs and configuration formats (filter expressions, rule engines, policy languages, template syntaxes) where a generator and its build integration would be overkill.
Expression and statement parsing in single-pass compilers and interpreters that emit bytecode or IR while parsing, as in Crafting Interpreters' Lox.
Tooling for a grammar you own - formatters, linters, syntax highlighters, language servers - where error tolerance, multiple diagnostics and exact positions matter more than raw throughput.
Protocol and wire-format decoding with a small fixed grammar, where errors must carry byte offsets and malformed input must be rejected deterministically.
Context-dependent or indentation-sensitive syntaxes (templates with interpolation, layout-based blocks, configuration with embedded expressions) that a generated lexer handles poorly.
Codebases that must not carry generated code: security-reviewed, vendored or cross-compiled projects where an ordinary source file beats a build-time generator.
Clang's C-family front end uses a unified hand-built recursive-descent parser for C, C++, Objective-C and Objective-C++, pairing rule-oriented control flow with production-quality diagnostics.
The Go standard library's go/parser is a production recursive-descent parser for Go source, with explicit parser state, nesting-depth guards and error recovery.
rustc_parse is the Rust compiler's recursive-descent parser module, showing how a hand-written parser can scale to macros, recovery modes and detailed token/state handling.
Lua's reference implementation compiles with lparser.c, a single-pass recursive-descent parser that emits bytecode opcodes while reducing expressions instead of building a syntax tree, with precedence handled by parsing levels.

name: event-message
document:
event-message
event notification
Announce that something has happened by publishing an immutable, self-describing event message - a past fact that expects no reply - on a channel, so that any number of interested receivers can react without the producer knowing who they are or what they do.
A component has completed a state change that other parts of the system care about, but it must not - and usually cannot - know which ones care. Calling each interested party directly couples the producer to every consumer, to their availability and to their processing order, and every new consumer (search index, audit, notification, analytics) forces a change and a redeploy in the producer. The trigger is open-ended interest: something changed, and the set of parties wanting to know is neither closed nor known at compile time.
Applies wherever a system reports occurrences instead of requesting work: integration between services over a broker or a log (Kafka, RabbitMQ, NATS, SNS/SQS/EventBridge), module boundaries inside one process (domain publishing to notification, search or reporting modules), and state propagation towards caches, read models or clients. It fits when the announcement matters more than any single response - audit trails, cache invalidation, read-model updates, downstream reactions - when consumers may be slow or temporarily offline, and when the producer's transaction boundary is the natural publication point.
Order placement in a service landscape: after the order transaction commits, OrderPlaced is published once and consumed independently by billing, warehouse, loyalty, search-index and notification services.
Cache and replica invalidation: CustomerAddressChanged tells every service holding a copy of the customer data to refresh or drop it, without the producing service knowing the replicas.
Audit and compliance: every state transition is emitted as an event to an append-only log, giving an ordered record of facts that a separate consumer turns into the audit trail.
Read-model / projection maintenance in CQRS: events from the write model update materialized views and search indexes asynchronously.
In-process module decoupling: a domain model publishes InvoiceIssued on an internal channel; e-mail, reporting and webhook modules subscribe without the domain importing them, keeping the dependency direction inward.
Platform-wide notifications: user lifecycle events (AccountCreated, PasswordResetRequested) fanned out to analytics, anti-fraud and e-mail consumers, each with its own retention and retry policy.
Financial trade confirmation: a matching engine emits TradeExecuted to a topic; clearing, risk management, position keeping and regulatory reporting services each consume the same event independently without the exchange knowing their identities or processing logic.
IoT telemetry ingestion: sensors publish DeviceReading events to a broker; stream-processing consumers compute rolling aggregates, rule engines evaluate thresholds, and archival systems persist the raw history — all decoupled from the sensor firmware.
Healthcare resource-change events: a FHIR-compliant system emits ObservationCreated, PatientUpdated and EncounterClosed events; downstream systems (clinical decision support, population health, billing) subscribe to precisely the event types they need without tight coupling to the EMR.
Apache Kafka event streams: producers append events (OrderPlaced, PaymentSettled) to a retained topic; consumer groups for billing, analytics and search indexing each read the same log at their own offsets, and a new consumer can replay from any point without the producer changing a line of code.
RabbitMQ fan-out notification: a producer publishes to a fanout exchange and the broker copies every event message to each bound queue - the official 'logs' tutorial has ephemeral subscribers joining and leaving while every bound consumer still receives every message.
GitHub webhooks: GitHub posts past-tense event messages (push, pull_request, release) with an event-type header, delivery GUID and HMAC signature to subscribed endpoints; integrations declare which event types they care about without ever modifying the producer.

name: test-data-builder
document:
test-data-builder
test builder
Give each domain type used in tests a builder that starts from valid, commonly used defaults, so a test states only the data its assertion depends on and everything else is supplied correctly without being mentioned.
Strict constructors and immutable value objects make test setup a chore: every test that needs an object must supply all constructor arguments, so tests fill up with values that have nothing to do with the behaviour under test, break whenever a constructor argument or the object's structure changes, and copy the same construction code from test to test. The ready-made fixtures of an object mother remove the repetition but not the variation - every slightly different case adds another factory method, and the mother degenerates into duplicated code or a swarm of methods holding a single new statement.
Applies to test suites over a domain model whose objects have many required fields or cross-field invariants, where each test varies only a small part of the data and a valid instance can be constructed without external systems. It is language-neutral but pays off most where the language lacks named/default arguments or copy-with-modification, and it belongs to the test sources: production code keeps its own constructors and must not depend on a builder whose defaults are chosen for tests.
Unit tests over domain types with many constructor parameters and cross-field invariants (invoices, users, policies) where each test cares about one or two values.
Mock-based interaction tests that must hand a valid collaborator object to the system under test with e.g. only its id varied to observe request routing.
Bug-reproduction tests: the builder encodes the standard valid case and the test states only the faulty value from the report.
Suites with many test classes over the same domain fixtures (payroll, insurance, orders) that need per-test variation rather than a handful of canned objects.
Table-driven or property-style tests over one dimension: build the valid base once and override that dimension for each case.
Integration tests that need a complete, plausible object graph (nested entities, collections, ids) deviating in a single field.
factory_bot (thoughtbot) for Ruby/Rails: one factory per class holding a minimal valid set of default attributes, with tests overriding only the fields under test at call time (build(:user, email: "bad@example.com")) - the builder shape generalized into a library.
factory_boy for Python: class-based factories declare the default keyword arguments for the target class' __init__ (Meta.model), and each test overrides just what it asserts (UserFactory.build(first_name="Joe")), with factory inheritance standing in for object-mother variants.
Instancio for Java implements the same contract generically: create(Person.class) populates every field, and .set(field(Person::getName), "Homer") overrides only the fields the test names - its user guide states the goal as populating everything you are not interested in.
