name: function-composition
document:
function-composition
compose
function pipeline
Combine a chain of small unary transformations into one reusable function by sequencing them with a composition combinator (compose/pipe), so the order of the steps is stated once, every step stays independently testable, and the chain itself becomes a value that can be named, passed and reassembled.
A transformation that is naturally a sequence of small pure steps gets written as nested calls or as repeated imperative assignment (`h(g(f(x)))`, or `y = f(x); y = g(y); ...; return y`) at every call site. The order is duplicated wherever the chain is used, the intermediate values need throwaway names, steps cannot be reused in a different order, and changing one stage means editing every copy.
Pure or nearly pure value transformations - parsing, normalisation, validation, formatting, pricing, AST rewriting - where each step is unary and the language treats functions as values. It pays off when the chain is reused or assembled from data (configuration, plugin lists, per-request policy), when steps must be unit-tested in isolation, and when the same steps must also run element-wise over a collection or lazily over a stream. It stops applying where steps need side effects or branching between stages: there the shell around the pure core owns control flow.
Input normalisation: trim, parse, canonicalise and validate a payload before it reaches domain logic, with the same chain reused by HTTP handlers and message consumers.
Pricing and rule chains: base price, discount, tax and rounding applied in a fixed, configurable order to an immutable value object.
Compiler and AST work: a pass list of rewrite functions composed once and applied over the tree, with passes added or reordered per optimisation level.
Serialisation and formatting: sanitise, format, encode and sign a document, where each step is tested separately and the composed chain is stored as a constant.
Data transformation over collections: the same pure steps composed into one function and passed to map/filter/stream operations, so element-wise processing reuses the chain.
Policy assembly at startup: the processing chain is built from configuration or plugin registrations and then applied per request without further branching.
Reactive stream processing: RxJS Observable.pipe chains the same logical steps across asynchronous event sequences, with operators composed once and reused across streams.
ETL and data pipeline transformation: extract-transform-load chains where each stage (parse, clean, enrich, aggregate, write) is a unary pure function composed into a reusable pipeline run over batches or streaming data.
HTTP request/response middleware: the middleware stack is a composed function chain where each layer (authenticate, authorise, rate-limit, deserialize, validate) is a unary handler; composition is resolved once at startup.
Matrix and vector transformations in numerical code: each linear algebra operation (scale, rotate, translate, project) is a unary function on a matrix type; composing them once builds the transformation pipeline that is applied to every vertex or pixel.
Ramda pipelines: R.pipe and R.compose assemble reusable data-last transformations from small functions, centralising the order while letting the same composed value run over many inputs.
Redux store setup: Redux's compose helper combines store enhancers right-to-left into one enhancer, so the enhancer order is defined once instead of reconstructed at each store boundary.
lodash/fp transformations: lodash/fp's auto-curried, data-last compose/flow helpers assemble immutable-friendly transformations from reusable steps that can be passed as values.

statement: Choose the ownership boundary for persisting an order and all of its dependent parts as one synchronized unit of work.
name: higher-order-component
document:
higher-order-component
HOC
component enhancer
Add cross-cutting behaviour to many components at once by wrapping them in an enhancer function that takes a component and returns a new, enhanced component, so no wrapped component knows about the concern or has to be edited.
The same cross-cutting logic - subscribing to a data source, checking a permission, firing analytics, injecting a theme, a translation or a feature flag - is needed by many components, and copying it into each one couples every component to the concern, re-couples them to every change of it, and leaves the behaviour to be remembered at each new call site. React tried mixins and inheritance first and removed them (implicit dependencies between mixin and component, name clashes, snowballing coupling), so the recurring decision is how to apply one behaviour to many components without editing them, while the components stay reusable and unaware of the enhancement.
Component-model UI code where components are values the framework mounts with a stable identity (React and its ecosystem first; the same shape recurs with Compose composables, SwiftUI views, Blazor components, Scala.js layers and handler-based Go/Java web UIs), where the concern is genuinely cross-cutting rather than local to one screen, where the enhancement can be expressed as a pure function from component to component and applied once at the definition or export site, and where the wrapped component's inputs form a prop-like contract that can be extended by injection without touching its internals.
Subscribing many components to an external data source — React documentation's withSubscription example, or Redux's connect: store state arrives as injected props with no component knowing about the store.
Apollo Client data injection: graphql(Query, { options, props }) HOC maps query results and loading state to props; multiple graphql HOCs composed with @compose; historically the standard before useQuery.
Authorization and feature gating at the boundary: withAuthorization(Component, { requiredRole }) or withFeatureFlag(...) decides rendering without editing the component; useful for route-level guards applied across many pages.
Analytics, telemetry and instrumentation applied at export sites (withAnalytics): tracking calls stay out of presentation code and can be added or removed at one location per module.
Injecting ambient context into components that take it as props — translations via withTranslation (react-i18next), routing via withRouter (React Router v5 and below), theming via withTheme (Material-UI v4) — enabling third-party and vendored components to participate without modification.
Error and loading boundaries as an enhancer (withErrorBoundary): the boundary exists as a component in the tree anyway; an enhancer consolidates the concern into one reusable definition rather than repeating the try/catch at each call site.
Sharing logic into class components and older codebases where hooks cannot be used: the HOC reaches class components and library component-shaped APIs that hooks cannot wrap.
Material-UI v4 theming: withStyles and withTheme HOCs inject classes and theme as props; compose chains combine styling with data (connect + withStyles + graphql on the same export).
Internationalization testing: export both wrapped and unwrapped components; tests use the raw component with a mock t function while integration tests use the full I18nextProvider setup.
Conditional prop injection: a data-enhancer that only injects props when a condition is met (e.g. user is authenticated) lets the wrapped component remain agnostic about the absence of that data.
React Compiler (React Forget) compatibility: heavy HOC layering reduces the compiler's static analysis surface and may cause it to bailout — test compiler output when adding HOCs to a compiled codebase; prefer hooks for new logic the compiler should see.
React Server Components boundary: a HOC that calls hooks or reads client-only context (useAuth, useTheme, useRouter) cannot execute during a server render; the wrapped component may receive undefined injected props on the server and flash-change on hydration. Pass server-fetched data as props through the HOC boundary from a server parent instead.
Streaming SSR and Suspense integration: a HOC that wraps a component behind a Suspense boundary adds a node that may delay streaming; if the HOC itself is async it must be carefully placed to avoid blocking the fallback from showing.
Partial hydration patterns: on islands architectures (Next.js App Router, Astro), a HOC that subscribes to client-side state forces the entire island to be hydrated even if the wrapped component has no server payload; prefer passing hydrated state as props from a server parent.
Recompose (acdlite): a 'lodash for React' utility belt built entirely from composable HOCs (withState, mapProps, pure, branch) piped through enhance/compose - the pattern industrialised; its October 2018 deprecation in favour of Hooks (bug-fix maintenance only) is the canonical case study of the pattern's cost when a runtime offers a cheaper reuse primitive.
MobX React binding: observer from mobx-react / mobx-react-lite is an official HOC that subscribes the wrapped component to every observable read during render, re-rendering it automatically; MobX guidance is to apply observer first (innermost) when composing it with other HOCs, and to wrap every component that reads observables.

name: coarse-grained-lock
document:
coarse-grained-lock
aggregate lock
cluster lock
Give a cluster of objects that must change together one shared lock — held on the cluster's root object, on a lock entry keyed by that root, or on a version token the root carries — so a caller locks one thing instead of discovering and locking every member.
Changing one object really means changing a cluster: an edit that touches any member (a line item, an address, a child entity) has to be atomic with respect to the others, but a separate lock per member forces every caller to find and lock the whole set, makes the amount of locking grow with the object graph, and produces deadlocks whenever two callers acquire member locks in different orders.
Domain layers whose natural unit of change spans several related objects (an aggregate root plus its members) and whose edit sessions outlive a single statement — multi-user applications, rich clients, batch jobs — on stores that offer row locks, lock tables or version columns and where the team must pick one lock granularity that matches the unit of change.
Editing an order together with its lines and delivery addresses in one user session: the order is locked or versioned once and every line edit is covered.
A customer with its addresses and contacts that must stay consistent, where leaving one member stale breaks a business rule.
Pessimistic offline edit sessions in a rich client that hold a lock for minutes without locking dozens of rows across several tables.
Optimistic commit of a whole aggregate: the root's version token detects that any member changed since load, so members need no version columns of their own.
Batch jobs that rewrite every member of a cluster: one lock or one version check for the batch instead of thousands of row locks.
Sharded or multi-tenant stores where the cluster root is also the shard key, so locking the root pins the partitions that the edit will touch.
DDD aggregates where an invariant spans multiple child entities (e.g., total order quantity must not exceed 10) — the coarse-grained lock on the aggregate root prevents parallel transactions from breaking the invariant at the per-line level.
Saga state machines where concurrent messages may touch the same saga instance — NHibernate pessimistic locking combined with forced version increment on child updates ensures the saga instance stays consistent.
Multi-granularity lock hierarchies in database systems: coarse area/file locks for large scans paired with fine row locks for point updates, using intention-lock protocols (IS/IX/SIX) to prevent deadlocks.
Kubernetes control plane: kube-scheduler and kube-controller-manager contend for a single coordination.k8s.io Lease object — one coarse lock covering a whole controller, renewed at about half the lease duration, with resourceVersion optimistic concurrency so only one candidate can hold it.
CockroachDB epoch-based node leases: one lease per node covers every Raft range that node holds instead of one lease per range, cutting lease-renewal traffic; bumping the node's liveness epoch revokes all of its range leases at once.
JPA/Hibernate applications locking an aggregate with a single LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE on the root row (SELECT … FOR UPDATE) and relying on the root's @Version column as the version token for the whole cluster.

name: pessimistic-offline-lock
document:
pessimistic-offline-lock
pessimistic lock
Prevent conflicts between concurrent business transactions by making each one acquire an explicit, persisted lock on the data before it starts to use it, so that once work begins it is almost certain to complete without a concurrency conflict.
A business transaction spans several system transactions (user think time, multiple requests), so the database cannot enforce isolation for its whole duration; where conflict between sessions is likely and a late failure is expensive, detecting conflicts only at commit makes users repeat minutes of work, while a single long-running system transaction is not an option.
Interactive, multi-session applications over shared persisted state: several users (or jobs) may edit the same record or aggregate, sessions last minutes to hours across requests, and the store can host a small, fast lock registry with owner, acquisition time and timeout. It is the deliberate alternative to Optimistic Offline Lock where conflicts are frequent, costly, or both.
Multi-step editing wizards over one record - insurance claim adjustment, order or invoice editing - where a session lasts minutes and a commit-time conflict would discard all of it.
Allocation against a scarce shared resource: inventory reservation, seat or capacity planning, where two planners must not promise the same units.
Periodic reconciliation work where a reviewer checks out an account, ledger or reporting period and the system must show others who is working on it.
Enterprise master-data maintenance over a shared database with low write volume but very expensive conflicts (pricing tables, contracts, configuration).
Long-running operational flows where an operator explicitly checks a configuration or document out of a repository and back in when finished.
Microsoft SharePoint document libraries with required check-out: one editor can check a document out, work offline, and check it back in; use this when exclusive ownership and visible stale-checkout recovery matter.
Redis distributed locks with a TTL (including the documented Redlock pattern): a service can claim a resource with a unique token, renew within the validity window, and let expiry recover abandoned ownership; use this only when its timing and availability assumptions fit the workload.
etcd's Lock service attached to a lease: a named lock is released by Unlock or automatically when the lease expires; use this for distributed resource ownership across nodes when automatic recovery matters, not as a substitute for database transaction isolation.

name: optimistic-offline-lock
document:
optimistic-offline-lock
optimistic locking
optimistic concurrency control
Let a business transaction span several system transactions without holding a database lock by validating at commit that the records it read are still unchanged - and aborting or retrying the business transaction when they are not.
A business transaction (an edit session) spans several system transactions, so the database's own locking cannot protect it: two sessions read the same record, both modify it, and the second commit silently overwrites the first (lost update); a reader can likewise see another session's half-finished edits. Holding a database lock for the whole session is not acceptable because the session lasts minutes or hours while a conflict is unlikely.
Editing shared persistent state where conflicts are rare, the edit session outlives a single database transaction, and every write path can be routed through the guarded statement - interactive forms, offline/mobile sync, batch jobs over shared records, and HTTP resource updates. The validation and the write must sit in one system transaction, so the mechanism is chosen together with the transaction boundary and the mapping.
Form-based editing of a shared record (product, customer, policy, invoice) where the user loads the values, thinks for minutes, then submits.
Offline or mobile clients that edit records locally and sync later: the version token travels in the sync payload and the server rejects a stale push.
Long-running batch jobs that re-read and update records other actors may touch, where holding row locks across the whole batch is unacceptable.
REST/HTTP resource updates with ETag and If-Match, so a stale representation cannot overwrite a newer one (412 Precondition Failed as the conflict signal).
Collaborative editing of case files, configuration or catalogue data where conflicts are rare but must never pass unnoticed.
Data-migration and repair scripts that must fail loudly rather than overwrite rows changed after they were read.
Jakarta Persistence entities annotated with @Version: the provider compares the stored revision and raises OptimisticLockException when a detached edit is stale.
EF Core entities configured with a concurrency token (SQL Server rowversion or an application-managed token): SaveChanges adds the token predicate and raises DbUpdateConcurrencyException when no row matches.
HTTP PUT, PATCH or DELETE guarded by a strong ETag in If-Match: the origin server rejects a stale representation with 412 Precondition Failed before applying the change.

name: implicit-lock
document:
implicit-lock
framework-managed locking
automatic locking
Make the framework or layer-supertype code that every business operation must pass through acquire and release the locks, so no application method can forget an acquisition and silently invalidate the concurrency policy.
A locking scheme has no gaps only if every path that touches a lockable item acquires its lock: one forgotten acquisition, one lock released too early or too late, makes the whole offline concurrency strategy useless. Because the error shows up only under concurrent conflicting sessions, it survives unit tests, code review and single-user manual testing.
Multi-user enterprise applications whose business transactions outlive a single database transaction - a user reads a record, thinks for minutes, then saves - so locks live in a lock table or in version columns rather than in the database transaction. Typically a Unit of Work, a layer supertype, a session facade or a declarative transaction layer already exists, giving the application a place that can own the locking protocol centrally.
Request-as-business-transaction: a web application where an ORM Unit of Work or declarative transaction (Spring @Transactional, .NET TransactionScope, Django ATOMIC_REQUESTS) acquires the row locks or version checks for every record the request reads and writes.
Offline edit sessions: a user edits a record for minutes, and the session facade or layer supertype acquires a pessimistic lock when the record enters the business transaction and releases it on commit or abort, so no controller can forget it.
Batch and import jobs that modify aggregates: each chunk runs inside the framework's transactional scope, so locking follows the changed aggregates automatically.
In-process shared state in a service or worker: a scope construct (RAII guard, with block, defer, using declaration, withLock closure) binds release to the lexical block so exceptions and early returns cannot leak the lock.
Multi-tier clients with a session facade: the lock must follow the business transaction rather than the HTTP request, so the facade — not the UI — owns acquisition and release.
Optimistic concurrency: the mapper compares and increments the version column inside the framework's update path, so a hand-written UPDATE statement cannot skip the check.
Microservices saga orchestrator: the orchestrator drives each step inside an implicit transaction scope; each participant's framework layer acquires the lock or version check locally so the saga can compensate without distributed deadlocks.
Event-sourcing projections: a projection handler reads an event stream and writes to a read-model; the handler runs inside an implicit transaction so concurrent projection rebuilds do not corrupt the read-model — the framework decides whether to use optimistic or pessimistic locking based on the change set.
CQRS read-model updates: commands update the write model under an implicit write lock; the read-model update is published as an async event; the projection runs under its own implicit scope with conflict detection (optimistic) rather than blocking (pessimistic).
Database advisory locks for cross-connection coordination: an application holds a PostgreSQL advisory lock across a multi-statement business transaction that is not itself a DB transaction (e.g., involves an external HTTP call in the middle); the lock is acquired via a thin wrapper so callers do not call pg_advisory_lock directly.
Container-managed persistence (EJB CMT, Spring @Transactional): the container acquires and releases locks as part of the transaction lifecycle; developers write business methods without explicit lock calls, relying on the container's implicit concurrency control.
Retry and compensation with implicit lock release: when a business transaction fails after the lock is acquired but before commit, the framework's rollback path releases the lock automatically so the compensating transaction can retry without manual unlock calls.
Spring Framework proxy-managed services: a proxied @Transactional service method is the business entry point; Spring starts or joins the transaction for external calls, so persistence work and its configured optimistic or pessimistic checks stay inside one framework-owned boundary.
Hibernate ORM persistence contexts: an EntityManager or Session transaction can apply @Version optimistic checks or an explicit PESSIMISTIC_WRITE LockMode at the framework boundary, keeping lock acquisition and stale-version detection out of business methods.
EF Core Unit of Work: SaveChanges compares configured concurrency tokens, including SQL Server rowversion, and raises DbUpdateConcurrencyException on a stale update, making the version check implicit in the framework's commit path rather than a hand-written UPDATE predicate.

name: characterization-test
document:
characterization-test
golden master
approval test
golden file test
snapshot test
golden session test
Pin the actual, currently deployed behaviour of existing code in committed reference artefacts (golden masters) so that a later edit can be distinguished from an accidental regression even when nobody can say what the code is supposed to do.
You must change code whose behaviour is undocumented, surprising or only known to production: there is no specification to test against, and tests written from intended behaviour would take too long and silently encode guesses as fact. The safety net therefore has to be built from observed behaviour: replay a corpus of real inputs through the untouched subject, capture everything observable, commit the result as the reference, and let every later run diff against it - pinning what the code does today before changing how it does it.
Applies whenever the subject already runs and can be exercised in a test process or from a test script: untested legacy modules, data transformations and report pipelines, serializers, parsers and code generators, CLI and protocol endpoints, rendering pipelines whose images can be diffed, and dependency or runtime upgrades where the old behaviour is the baseline. The precondition is determinism: volatile parts (timestamps, identifiers, paths, memory addresses, collection order, locale, floating-point formatting) must be normalized or redacted before capture, otherwise the comparison is noise. The pattern is a first move - build the net, then refactor under it - and pairs with a deliberate approval step, because a characterization test does not know which behaviour was intended.
Before refactoring an untested legacy module: capture outputs for a corpus of inputs, restructure the code, and require the reference artefacts to stay identical.
Data processing and batch jobs: pin how representative input files are transformed into output files or reports, so the nightly job can be changed safely.
Serializers, formatters and code generators: pin the emitted text or structured output for representative documents, with a redaction step for volatile values.
Rendering and UI pipelines: pin generated images (screenshot goldens) or rendered text output with an approval workflow and a visual diff tool.
CLI and protocol behaviour: pin stdout, stderr and exit codes, or request/response bytes, for a set of recorded invocations.
Dependency or runtime upgrades: pin behaviour before the upgrade and re-run afterwards, so only intended differences have to be reviewed.
Production defect triage: replay the failing production input into a new reference artefact, then fix the defect against that regression test.
AI/LLM output regression testing: pin model responses to a curated golden dataset; on model or prompt change, compare distributions, embedding similarity, or token-level diffs against the baseline rather than requiring exact matches (LLM eval pipelines, 2024-2026).
Generated code verification: pin the exact output of OpenAPI client generators, GraphQL type generators, SDK wrappers, or database migration previews so formatting and structural changes are caught.
Database schema migration testing: capture the before/after output of migration scripts for a set of schema variants, approving only intentional structural differences.
Computer vision pipeline regression: pin bounding-box distributions or classification confidence vectors from CV models across runs; statistical comparison prevents flaky failures from minor pixel noise.
Smart contract and blockchain output regression: pin deterministic contract outputs for a given input state; any divergence in on-chain behaviour is immediately visible (Nexlify case, 2025).
Database-engine regression suites: PostgreSQL's pg_regress replays each sql/*.sql script and diffs results/*.out against committed golden files in expected/*, with variant comparison files and a resultmap absorbing known platform differences (locale, float formatting, row ordering).
Compiler test corpora: LLVM's lit/FileCheck pins emitted IR and machine code by piping compiler output to FileCheck, which verifies CHECK directives committed inside each test file across the whole input corpus.
ORM query-change detection: ApprovalTests.Ruby's verify_sql approves the SQL an ActiveRecord call emits, so a gem or framework upgrade that silently rewrites generated queries fails the suite.

name: pattern-matching
document:
pattern-matching
structural pattern matching
case analysis
Eliminate a value drawn from a closed set of variants by matching its structure and binding the payload, so the compiler proves that every variant is handled before the program runs.
Code that inspects which variant of a tagged value it received - a result type, a domain event, an AST node, a protocol frame, a state - drifts into chains of type tests, casts and accessor calls, and nothing guarantees that a variant added later is handled: the missing branch is found in production rather than by the compiler.
Applies when a value's type is a closed sum - an enum with payloads, a sealed hierarchy, a discriminated union, a tagged union - and behaviour depends on which variant arrived. It needs a match construct (language syntax, a variant type with visitation, or a type-level bottom-type check) plus a compiler or checker able to see the set as closed: same-unit sealing, private constructors, or explicit non_exhaustive / @unknown markers where a set is published to other teams.
Interpreter and compiler front ends: expression and statement types are evaluated with one total match per operation, and a new node kind cannot be forgotten.
Protocol and RPC dispatch: a frame or command is one of a fixed set of shapes, and each shape is deconstructed into its fields instead of being cast.
Result and error mapping at boundaries: translating domain failures into transport errors, where every failure variant must be given a mapping.
State machines and workflow states: states carry state-specific data, and transitions are written as a total match over (state, event) pairs.
Domain-event handling in reducers and event-sourced aggregates, where every event type must be applied to rebuild state.
Command-line and query parsing: token or request shapes are matched structurally, including literals and sequence patterns, before validation logic runs.
OpenJDK Java 21 sealed hierarchies: pattern switches over AST or domain-event variants can enumerate permitted types without a default, using the compiler's exhaustiveness analysis.
rustc and Rust enum APIs: match expressions destructure enum variants and the compiler rejects non-exhaustive arms, making protocol and compiler AST dispatch explicit.
CPython 3.10+ match/case: parsers and protocol adapters can select class, sequence, mapping and literal shapes with ordered guards before constructing domain values.
Scala 3 sealed ADTs and union types: the Scala compiler checks exhaustiveness while case-class patterns bind payloads for interpreters, reducers and protocol decoders.

name: page-object
document:
page-object
page object model
window driver
Wrap each UI surface a test drives - a page or a significant component - in an object that exposes the services the surface offers and hides every locator, driver call and wait, so a UI change is absorbed by one class instead of by every test that touched the markup.
A UI test that drives the automation API directly - find an element, type, click, wait, read text - keeps the page's locators and interaction mechanics in the test body: the same selector is repeated across dozens of tests, a markup change breaks them all at once, and a reader must reconstruct the page's structure to understand what the test does. The catalog's trigger: a UI change should touch one class, not fifty assertions.
Automated tests that drive a user interface through a driver API - a browser (Selenium/WebDriver, Playwright, Cypress, WebdriverIO), a mobile app (Appium, Espresso, XCUITest) or a desktop window - where the same screens are exercised by many tests, where the UI changes independently of the tests, and where the suite is expected to survive redesigns. The pattern pays off when the interface can be named in the user's terms ('sign-in page', 'product row') and the driver offers stable element lookup; it is unnecessary for a single throwaway script or when the presentation logic has already been extracted behind a humble object.
A regression suite over a web application whose pages are exercised by dozens of tests: login, search, checkout and admin screens each get a class, and a redesign changes only those classes (the Selenium and Playwright POM guides' home scenario).
The same screens are driven by different kinds of test - functional, visual, accessibility, smoke - and the locator knowledge must live in one place that all of them import.
Mobile application suites (Appium, Espresso, XCUITest) where screens are widget hierarchies with platform-specific queries, and the page object is the only place that codifies the platform lookup.
BDD suites: Gherkin steps stay business-readable because step definitions delegate to page objects instead of calling the driver (Fowler's layering recommendation).
Suites migrating drivers or frameworks (Selenium to Playwright, a WebdriverIO restructure): the page API is kept while only its internals change.
A scripting interface over an application whose behaviour is stuck in the UI (Fowler's scripting use), or a legacy system that can only be exercised through its window.
Selenium's documented login flow: SignInPage.loginValidUser returns HomePage, so a regression suite can exercise authentication through services while locators and page-load checks stay in the page objects.
Playwright's official playwright.dev example: PlaywrightDevPage wraps a Page, owns locators for the getting-started flow and exposes goto, getStarted and pageObjectModel methods used by tests.
WebdriverIO's official The Internet login example: a getter-based LoginPage centralizes selectors and open/submit actions, letting login specs survive selector changes without duplicating driver calls.

name: spatial-partition
document:
spatial-partition
spatial index
bucket grid
Store every object in a structure indexed by its position so that neighbourhood queries visit only the objects near a point or region instead of scanning the whole population.
Queries that ask 'what is near this position?' - collision checks, proximity and aggro radii, culling, spatial analytics - repeatedly scan every object: each query is linear in the population and a whole simulation step becomes quadratic, even though every object interacts only with the few objects next to it.
Per-object runtime systems and simulations - game worlds, crowd and particle solvers, location services, robotics - where objects are mobile, spread over space, and the queries are local (radius, region, k-nearest). The pattern applies once the population is large enough that a full scan dominates the frame or the request budget, and it requires a position-to-cell mapping and an update discipline that match how the objects move.
Game worlds: collision, proximity and aggro checks between many moving entities each tick (bullets versus enemies, pickups, area effects).
Physics broadphase: pruning candidate pairs before narrow-phase tests where colliders move constantly.
Map and GIS services: 'all points within radius' and viewport queries over millions of features.
Crowd, flocking and particle simulations: neighbours within a radius for boids or social forces instead of all-pairs tests.
Spatial analytics and robotics: k-nearest or region queries over vehicles, sensors and delivery points, and occupancy grids for pathfinding.
Physics engines: Box2D's broadphase is a dynamic AABB tree (b2DynamicTree) whose fattened leaf boxes absorb small moves before reinsertion, and whose region queries and ray casts prune candidates before narrow-phase tests.
Location services: Redis geospatial indexes store members as 52-bit geohash scores in a sorted set (GEOADD) so GEOSEARCH answers circle and bounding-box proximity queries server-side instead of scanning members.
GIS and analytics databases: PostGIS prunes radius queries through a GiST spatial index (the index-aware ST_DWithin predicate checks bounding boxes before computing exact distances), and scikit-learn backs radius and k-nearest neighbour queries with KDTree and BallTree instead of all-pairs distances.

name: copy-on-write
document:
copy-on-write
lazy copy
clone-on-write
implicit sharing (Qt)
shadow paging
Let several handles of a value share one expensive body until the first write, which clones that body privately, so copying costs a pointer instead of a deep copy while every handle still behaves as an independent value.
A value with an expensive body (large buffer, collection, tree, document) is copied eagerly on assignment, argument passing and return even though most copies are never modified: time and memory are spent duplicating data that would have stayed identical. The naive fix - handing out one mutable object behind several handles - breaks the copy contract, and unrelated parts of the program then observe each other's writes.
Applies when copies of an expensive payload vastly outnumber modifications, when the payload is large enough that the copy dominates the cost of the handle (multi-kilobyte buffers, collection snapshots, editor or model state), and when the language offers a cheap way to know whether the body is still shared - a reference count, an explicit shared flag, or a uniqueness test. It is a single-threaded optimization first; sharing the count across threads turns it into the separate thread-safe copy-on-write concern.
Large buffers passed by value through API layers: strings, byte arrays and image/document payloads whose copies are usually read-only (Qt QString/QByteArray implicit sharing, ATL CString, pre-C++11 std::string).
Read-mostly collections whose traversals vastly outnumber mutations and must not block readers: listener and handler registries, routing tables, RuleEngine rule sets (CopyOnWriteArrayList/CopyOnWriteArraySet).
Configuration and state snapshots swapped atomically at the write boundary (feature flags, reloaded settings, event-sourced folds) so readers keep a consistent version without locking.
Persistent and functional data structures where an update returns a new version that structurally shares everything the change did not touch (Scala immutable collections, Immer drafts, persistent lists and maps).
Operating-system and memory-mapped sharing: fork and page-level copy-on-write share physical pages until a mapping is written, and file-backed buffers are shared until modified.
Columnar and data-frame workloads where slices are views and only the columns actually written are duplicated (pandas copy-on-write mode, Arrow buffers).
Fork-based process snapshots: Redis BGSAVE/BGREWRITEAOF forks a child to serialize memory to disk while the parent continues serving writes; only pages modified by the parent after fork are COW-copied, keeping the child's view consistent (vm.overcommit_memory=1 recommended).
COW filesystems for instant snapshots: ZFS and Btrfs never overwrite blocks in place; creating a snapshot is O(1) — save the root block pointer; reclaims O(1) more when the snapshot is deleted and no other reference remains. Enables self-healing via checksum propagation and efficient incremental replication via zfs send / btrfs send.
Database MVCC at row granularity: Postgres, LMDB, CockroachDB Pebble write new row versions on UPDATE/DELETE and reclaim old versions via VACUUM once no active transaction can see them; readers see consistent snapshots without read locks.
Container image layering: Docker/OCI images use layered COW where lower layers are read-only and the upper layer copies on write; base images are shared across many containers until a layer is actually modified.
APFS reflinks and XFS/ref ext4 ioctl(FICLONE): file-level COW that shares extents until either fork writes, enabling instant file clones (e.g., `cp --reflink=auto`) at near-zero cost.
LMDB's single-level store: a CoW B+tree using two fixed root pages (double buffering) where readers are fully latch-free and writers never block readers; no WAL needed because old trees remain intact until the new root is durably synced.
Swift standard library collections (Array, Dictionary, Set, String, Data) where isKnownUniquelyReferenced() checks the heap object's strong reference count at runtime to decide whether to mutate in-place or clone.
Qt QSharedData/QSharedDataPointer: implicit sharing for pimpl'd d-pointer classes where non-const operator-> triggers detach() automatically before any write access; QExplicitlySharedDataPointer suppresses automatic detach.
Rust std::borrow::Cow: a generic enum (Borrowed | Owned) that defers the clone until to_mut() is called, especially useful in APIs that accept both borrowed and owned data without multiple signatures.
PHP arrays and strings: reference-counted value types where assignment and argument passing share the zval and the first write 'separates' it (copy-on-write) when refcount > 1; taking a reference with & turns the sharing into an explicit alias set (php.net reference counting, php-src core docs).
pandas 3.0, where copy-on-write is the default and only mode: any DataFrame or Series derived by indexing behaves as an independent copy, chained assignment (df["foo"][mask] = v) silently doing nothing is eliminated - it raises ChainedAssignmentError - and every update must be a single .loc step (PDEP-7).
Linux kernel OverlayFS copy_up: a container write to a lowerdir file (open for write or metadata change) copies the file up into upperdir first; the metacopy feature delays the data copy until the first data write, and an fsync before the finalizing rename guards against zero-filled files after a crash (kernel overlayfs docs, Docker overlay2 driver).

name: model-view-intent
document:
model-view-intent
mvi
Structure one UI feature as a single loop in which every user interaction becomes an intent value, a pure reduce step derives the next immutable state from the previous state and that intent, and the view renders only that state - so the screen's behaviour is determined by data instead of by scattered event handlers.
Presentation state is spread across the view, its presenter and several observable channels: every handler sets its own field or widget directly, a loading flag, a data field and an error field can contradict each other, the view keeps state of its own that a configuration change or process death destroys, and no state transition can be exercised without instantiating the UI.
Interactive applications with a declarative view layer and some reactive runtime - Android/Compose with coroutines and Flow, SwiftUI, React, Scala.js, or a hand-rolled event loop - where one screen or app-level feature can own a single immutable state object, user events can be represented as data values, and the view can re-render from a new state value. It is applied per feature, not per widget, and it is independent of any particular framework.
A search or feed screen where loading, empty, error and result states are concurrent flags in the old design and must become one state value the view can render without contradictions.
Complex screen flows - checkout, wizards, media players, editors - whose transitions must be explicit and reviewable rather than emerging from scattered handler code.
Screens that must survive configuration changes or process death by restoring one serializable state object instead of replaying a history of view commands.
Crash reports and support cases that carry the current state plus the last intent, making reproduction and replay possible without reproducing the exact tap sequence.
Cross-platform features that share the reducer between platforms and swap only the view layer (Android and iOS, web and desktop).
Large applications where each feature module exposes an intent/state contract and different teams own the loop for their screens.
A Cycle.js component whose DOM and HTTP driver streams become intents, whose model derives state, and whose view renders that state is a direct stream-based MVI implementation.
A Kotlin Multiplatform feature built with Orbit MVI can share an OrbitContainer's intent, reduce, state, and side-effect flow across Android, iOS, and desktop.
An Android Jetpack Compose feature following Android's official unidirectional-data-flow guidance can use a ViewModel-owned immutable UiState, upward events, and downward rendering as a framework-native MVI realization.

name: messaging-gateway
document:
messaging-gateway
Encapsulate access to a messaging system behind an ordinary interface of domain methods, so calling application code makes method calls while a single component owns message construction, correlation, timeouts and error translation.
Application code that talks to a broker keeps importing messaging concepts: it builds the payload, picks the channel, attaches a reply address and a correlation id, parses the response and interprets broker errors. The trigger for this pattern is that callers should make a method call instead of writing messaging code - the messaging knowledge belongs in exactly one place that can change without touching business rules.
At the boundary between application logic and a messaging system (message broker, MQ, queue service or actor runtime): the other side is reached by messages, but the caller is ordinary domain code that should see typed parameters and typed results. Applies to one-way (fire and forget) and request-reply interactions alike, and to blocking as well as asynchronous call styles.
A domain service that must query another system (inventory, pricing, credit scoring) over a queue: the caller invokes checkStock(sku) and receives a typed answer.
An HTTP or API layer whose controller awaits a brokered round trip (Spring Integration gateway interface, NestJS ClientProxy, MassTransit request client).
Batch and background jobs that dispatch work through a typed job API instead of assembling payloads (ActiveJob perform_later, Celery delay).
Wrapping a legacy system's MQ interface once, so the rest of the codebase never learns its message format.
Test seams: unit tests substitute a fake gateway, integration tests run the same interface against a real broker.
Migration seam: keep the gateway contract stable while the transport moves from one broker to another.
Actor and streaming stacks where a facade wraps ask/request so callers never hold ActorRefs or inboxes.
Spring Integration's @MessagingGateway and GatewayProxyFactoryBean let application code inject a typed interface while the framework routes calls into channels and returns replies.
MassTransit's IRequestClient<T> and GetResponse<TResponse> provide a typed request-reply client over the bus, keeping request and response message contracts out of the calling service.
RabbitMQ's RPC tutorial demonstrates a gateway-like client that publishes to rpc_queue with reply_to and correlation_id, then resolves the matching callback response.

name: make-illegal-states-unrepresentable
document:
make-illegal-states-unrepresentable
make invalid states unrepresentable
Encode each domain rule in the shape of the data type so that values violating the rule cannot be constructed at all, replacing scattered run-time validation and defensive checks with a model in which only legal states exist.
Domain values are modelled as one record with independent fields - a status tag plus several nullable or optional attributes, or a handful of booleans - so the type admits every combination of those fields, including the ones the business rules forbid. Consumers cannot trust the type: each branch re-checks which fields are meaningful, the same guard is written in several places (and forgotten in one), and illegal states become runtime bugs that surface when a code path finally combines the wrong flags.
Applies when a value has a small, known set of mutually exclusive shapes whose payloads differ, when the same invalid combination keeps being defended against in several places, and when the language can close a set of variants (Rust/Swift enums, sealed hierarchies, discriminated unions) or at least hide constructors. It is equally a boundary discipline: untrusted input is parsed once into a type whose existence already proves it is valid, so no downstream code has to re-validate.
Lifecycle and state machines: orders, payments, subscriptions, bookings and connection states, one variant per state carrying exactly the data that exists in that state.
Client and API request state: a loading/success/error union instead of a data field, an error field and an isLoading flag that can contradict one another.
Message and protocol modelling: a closed set of commands, events or JSON payload shapes decoded once and dispatched with an exhaustive match (event sourcing, interpreters, RPC handlers).
Refined scalars that travel through the model: money with currency, email addresses, quantities with units and identifiers that are parsed once and never re-validated.
Configuration whose combinations are illegal: TLS settings that only apply when TLS is enabled, cursor-based versus offset pagination, mutually exclusive feature flags.
Import and deserialization boundaries: convert untrusted rows, CSV cells, query parameters or JSON into domain types with a failing factory, so invalid input cannot travel further.
Rust's standard `Option`/`Result` enums and exhaustive `match` make presence, absence, success and failure explicit cases that downstream code must handle at compile time (Rust Reference/Book).
Swift enums with associated values and exhaustive `switch` model state-specific payloads such as error cases without nullable companion fields (The Swift Programming Language).
Kotlin sealed classes and interfaces with exhaustive `when` expressions provide a closed hierarchy for finite state machines and error/result models, with the compiler checking that every known case is handled.

name: policy-guard
document:
policy-guard
policy pattern
policy decision point / policy enforcement point
Keep every authorisation decision out of the protected resource's code by moving the rules into a separate Policy component and letting a Guard - the enforcement point every access must pass through - obtain a decision from that policy before the operation is performed.
Access rules written inside the resource's own methods (checking roles or ownership inline) entangle business logic with security logic: the same rule is re-implemented at every call site, a forgotten check silently opens a bypass, and the rules cannot be reviewed, tested or changed without touching the resource's code.
Components that own protected resources or operations and must decide per access whether the authenticated subject - with its roles, attributes, tenant and request context - may perform the requested action. Typical at object, module or boundary scope: request handlers, domain services, document stores, message consumers and administrative tooling that all reach the same resources and should obey the same rules, especially when the rules change more often than the resource code.
HTTP and API request handling: authentication establishes the security context once, then every endpoint or method invocation is guarded by a policy decision (for example Spring Security's AuthorizationManager behind its AuthorizationFilter, or ASP.NET Core authorization middleware over registered policies).
Domain services that expose several operations on one aggregate: the guard checks the (subject, operation, resource) triple before each service method executes, instead of scattering role checks through the methods.
Multi-tenant backends where the decision must consider tenant, ownership and request attributes, not only roles; the guard resolves them from the security context and passes them to the policy.
Document or file stores: every read or write is wrapped by a guard that consults rules keyed by the document identifier and its classification.
Administrative and background code - CLI tools, batch jobs, message consumers - that must obey the same policy as the interactive API so that no side door exists.
Regulated environments where every access decision, including denials, must be logged consistently and the policy itself must be independently testable.
Spring Security request boundaries: AuthorizationFilter passes the current Authentication and HttpServletRequest to an AuthorizationManager and proceeds only after a grant; configure every protected route so an unlisted path cannot become a side door.
ASP.NET Core policy authorization: named policies combine requirements evaluated by IAuthorizationHandler implementations and attach with [Authorize(Policy = "...")] or RequireAuthorization; place UseAuthorization after authentication and before endpoints.
Open Policy Agent (OPA) deployments: AWS Prescriptive Guidance models a centralized or distributed Policy Decision Point with Policy Enforcement Points on APIs, allowing shared policy while using local sidecars when latency or availability requires it.

name: update-method
document:
update-method
per-frame update
tick method
Give every live object one self-contained per-frame step and let a single driver call each object's step every frame, so behaviour advances one frame at a time while input and rendering stay responsive.
A running world is full of objects that each have to keep doing their own thing - guards patrolling, statues charging, agents acting - and the recurring decision is where one object's per-frame behaviour lives and how all those behaviours get driven. Coding a behaviour as a loop that runs to completion blocks input and rendering (the skeleton walks, but nobody sees it); coding it inline in the game loop turns the loop into a switchboard over every kind of object, so every new behaviour edits central code; and there is no way for two actors to evolve independently and simultaneously.
Real-time software with many concurrent live objects whose behaviour is mostly independent and must be simulated over time: games, agent-based simulations, animation and particle systems, tick-based servers and live visualisations. It is the natural partner of a frame driver (Game Loop) - the loop supplies the cadence, Update Method supplies the per-object step - and it becomes the wrong shape in turn-based or purely event-driven domains where nothing changes between inputs.
Real-time games and simulations with many concurrent actors: patrolling guards, projectiles, particle effects and crowd agents each advance themselves once per frame while the driver walks the collection.
Component-based engines where the parts of one entity evolve independently - rendering, physics and AI components each implement their own step and the engine's registry dispatches per component (Unity, MonoGame, Bevy, GameplayKit, libGDX).
Per-frame animation and effect timelines outside games: tween/spring systems, sprite animation and UI transitions advanced from the browser's frame callback or a UI toolkit's animation timer.
Tick-based servers and headless simulations: game servers, digital twins and agent-based models where each agent's behaviour is a resumable step and the world advances in whole discrete frames.
Tools, editors and dashboards with continuously animating scenes, where many independent scene items (markers, live charts, gizmos) must advance on every repaint without a central per-item switch.
Porting straight-line behaviour into a frame loop: turning a scripted sequence (walk left, walk right) into a per-frame step, either by storing explicit state or by using coroutines/generators to keep the code linear.
Godot's SceneTree is the driver: a node opts into the walk with set_process(true) and its _process(delta) runs every render frame with the frame time passed in as an argument, while _physics_process(delta) is called at a fixed rate - so one object can implement two steps on two clocks and can leave the walk entirely (set_process(false)) instead of paying an enabled-flag check every frame.
Engines whose built-in driver leaves per-object order unspecified expose the order as configuration: Unity states you should not rely on the order of Update across GameObjects, so real projects fix dependencies through the Script Execution Order panel, a LateUpdate pass that runs after every Update, or the PlayerLoop API rather than through registration order.
Agent-based simulation models step whole populations in NetLogo: the go procedure runs ask turtles [ ... ] to give every agent its one turn and then tick advances the discrete clock - with documented semantics that agents take their turns in random order and only agents present when the ask began get to act.

name: authenticator
document:
authenticator
authentication provider
authentication service
Verify the identity a subject claims from mechanism-specific credentials and return one normalized principal or an explicit failure, so callers can select or replace password, certificate, token, Kerberos or passkey verification without coupling login, session, audit or authorization code to a credential format.
A request must decide whether presented evidence proves a subject's identity, but password, client-certificate, OIDC/JWT, Kerberos and passkey checks differ by deployment, tenant and channel. If one mechanism is hard-wired into the request path, every caller learns its credential format; adding OIDC, migrating from LDAP or accepting service tokens becomes a cross-cutting change, while comparison, retry/lockout and verifier-failure handling drift between endpoints.
Systems that verify identities at a trust boundary - HTTP APIs, message endpoints, CLIs or device onboarding - where more than one credential form is in use or expected, the mechanism is selectable per deployment, tenant or route, and downstream authorization, session and audit code needs a mechanism-independent principal. It is also the seam for composing MFA or step-up checks and for replacing an external identity provider in tests.
A web application that must accept password login, federated OIDC login and API bearer tokens, all producing the same session principal.
An enterprise service deployed at sites with different directories (LDAP/AD, Kerberos, local database) that selects its mechanism per deployment without a code fork.
A microservice that validates self-issued JWTs for normal traffic and falls back to token introspection at the corporate authorization server for opaque tokens.
A CLI or desktop agent with pluggable credential providers: OS keychain, smart card, TPM-backed passkey or an interactive password prompt.
Step-up authentication: a second authenticator (one-time code, WebAuthn assertion) chained behind the primary one for sensitive operations.
Test and simulation environments where a fake authenticator replaces the identity provider while the production authentication gate remains the exercised path.
A passkey Relying Party (RP) backend that implements WebAuthn registration and authentication ceremonies: generates session-bound challenges (CSPRNG, 16+ bytes, 60-120s TTL), verifies authenticator assertions (origin, challenge replay prevention via single-use challenge, UP/UV flags, signCount monotonicity, signature), and issues a normalized session principal.
Zero-trust microservice mesh: SPIFFE/SPIRE-issued short-lived X.509 SVIDs via mTLS, where each service presents a workload certificate encoded with its SPIFFE ID; the authenticator verifies the certificate chain and extracts the cryptographic workload identity as the principal.
Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) token storage: the BFF holds access/refresh tokens in server-side memory or encrypted httpOnly cookies, issuing scoped session cookies to the SPA; the authenticator seam is the BFF's token refresh logic, not the browser.
OAuth2 authorization code + PKCE public client: the authenticator validates the code, verifier and state on the backend, rotates refresh tokens on every use, and issues short-lived JWTs; the same interface normalizes this flow alongside password and passkey flows.
A Java service can keep application code independent of the mechanism by driving configured JAAS LoginModules through LoginContext, while Spring Security exposes the same seam through AuthenticationProvider and ProviderManager.
A Keycloak deployment can add a custom credential or challenge step by implementing the Authenticator and AuthenticatorFactory SPIs and placing that execution in an authentication flow.
A Node.js service can install Passport.js strategies such as passport-local or passport-openidconnect, register them with passport.use(), and normalize the verify callback's user into the application's principal.
A Django project extends authentication beyond its user database by listing custom backends in AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS; django.contrib.auth.authenticate() tries each backend's authenticate(request, **credentials) in order, first success wins, and the returned User is the normalized principal.
An ASP.NET Core app registers one named scheme per mechanism (AddJwtBearer, AddCookie, a custom AuthenticationHandler) and composes them with policy schemes (AddPolicyScheme, ForwardDefaultSelector) so one endpoint routes bearer and cookie requests to the right handler without branching in the controller.
The Kubernetes API server authenticates every request through a union of authenticators - front-proxy request-header (X-Remote-User / X-Remote-Group, trusted only after the proxy's client certificate validates against the configured CA), X.509 client certificates and TokenReview webhooks with cached decisions - and hands the resulting normalized user info to authorization.

name: recursive-descent-parser
document:
recursive-descent-parser
recursive descent
recursive descent parsing
Parse a small grammar by translating every rule directly into a function that consumes the tokens the rule matches and calls the functions of the rules it references, so the parser's control flow is the grammar itself and stays readable, debuggable and free of a code-generation step.
A hand-written parser is the only option - no generator in the toolchain, or the grammar is a small DSL - yet the grammar is not a flat token sequence: alternatives must be chosen from lookahead, repetition must become a loop, and the natural grammar for expressions is left-recursive, which a top-down parser cannot translate directly. Without a disciplined mapping from rules to functions the parser degenerates into ad-hoc index arithmetic and exception-driven backtracking, and errors end up without positions.
Front ends for small languages, DSLs, query/filter/rule grammars, configuration and protocol formats, and the parsing layer of compilers and interpreters that want no code-generation step. It applies when a lexer or token stream already exists (or is cheap to write), the grammar is small to medium and reasonably LL-friendly or rewritable into LL form, and the team values readable, step-debuggable, position-precise parsing over generated tables.
Front ends for small languages, DSLs and configuration formats (filter expressions, rule engines, policy languages, template syntaxes) where a generator and its build integration would be overkill.
Expression and statement parsing in single-pass compilers and interpreters that emit bytecode or IR while parsing, as in Crafting Interpreters' Lox.
Tooling for a grammar you own - formatters, linters, syntax highlighters, language servers - where error tolerance, multiple diagnostics and exact positions matter more than raw throughput.
Protocol and wire-format decoding with a small fixed grammar, where errors must carry byte offsets and malformed input must be rejected deterministically.
Context-dependent or indentation-sensitive syntaxes (templates with interpolation, layout-based blocks, configuration with embedded expressions) that a generated lexer handles poorly.
Codebases that must not carry generated code: security-reviewed, vendored or cross-compiled projects where an ordinary source file beats a build-time generator.
Clang's C-family front end uses a unified hand-built recursive-descent parser for C, C++, Objective-C and Objective-C++, pairing rule-oriented control flow with production-quality diagnostics.
The Go standard library's go/parser is a production recursive-descent parser for Go source, with explicit parser state, nesting-depth guards and error recovery.
rustc_parse is the Rust compiler's recursive-descent parser module, showing how a hand-written parser can scale to macros, recovery modes and detailed token/state handling.
Lua's reference implementation compiles with lparser.c, a single-pass recursive-descent parser that emits bytecode opcodes while reducing expressions instead of building a syntax tree, with precedence handled by parsing levels.

name: authentication-enforcer
document:
authentication-enforcer
authentication interceptor
authentication gateway
auth middleware
Put one request-boundary checkpoint in front of protected actions that decides whether authentication is required, delegates credential verification to a replaceable mechanism, and attaches the resulting subject to request-scoped context before dispatch, so coverage is uniform without making handlers understand credentials.
When each handler decides whether and how to authenticate, protection is duplicated or omitted on exceptional paths, credential formats and user stores leak into business code, and a mechanism or policy change requires editing every handler instead of one auditable boundary.
Server-side request processing — web APIs, web applications and service endpoints — where many handlers share one protection policy, credentials arrive through a uniform convention (Authorization header, cookie, session id), verification technology must be replaceable or differ per route, and the runtime provides a request-pipeline hook (servlet filter, middleware chain, framework guard). Applies to session-based and token-based authentication alike; permissions and roles are out of scope. Three implementation strategies exist: (1) Container-Managed Authentication — the runtime container owns the checkpoint and realm configuration; (2) Authentication Provider Strategy — a custom provider behind a narrow interface, swapped without touching handlers; (3) JAAS Login Module Strategy — pluggable via standard JAAS configuration, supporting multifactor authentication via smart cards, biometrics, or third-party IdPs. The pattern is equally applicable at the edge level (API gateway, ingress proxy) and the service level (in-process middleware).
Web APIs where every route except health and login requires a bearer token, and the checkpoint is mounted in front of the whole router.
Multi-tenant applications with mixed protection levels: public marketing pages, session-protected tenant UI and token-protected integration endpoints behind one enforcement layer.
Services that must accept several credential types at once — browser sessions, mobile JWTs, mutual TLS for service-to-service traffic — while keeping one uniform enforcement point.
Credential-technology migration (basic auth to OIDC, on-premises LDAP to SSO) where enforcement stays put while the mechanism behind it is swapped.
Regulated environments where every rejected authentication attempt has to be logged centrally and identically across all endpoints.
Legacy applications with authentication checks scattered through servlets or handlers that must be consolidated behind one intercepting layer before an audit.
Zero Trust microservices where every internal service verifies JWTs independently (per-service verification) while an ingress gateway provides the first checkpoint — the enforcer exists at both layers.
OIDC/OAuth2 migration where an existing session-based app adds bearer-token support; the mechanism adapts to both while the enforcement point remains unchanged.
Multi-tenant SaaS platforms where tenant isolation depends on the enforcer resolving a tenant identifier from the token before the handler processes any data.
Platform-as-a-Service with mounted sub-applications where a parent ASGI middleware dispatches per-path authentication requirements from a config registry, injecting identity into ASGI scope for all sub-apps.
Spring Security servlet applications that use a SecurityFilterChain with anyRequest().authenticated() and an AuthenticationManager/AuthenticationProvider chain, so controllers consume the SecurityContext rather than parse credentials.
ASP.NET Core APIs that register JWT or cookie schemes, call UseAuthentication before dependent middleware, and use a fallback authorization policy to make authenticated access the default.
An nginx ingress location using auth_request to delegate identity verification to a central authentication service, forwarding only after a 2xx result and propagating 401/403 failures while services still verify their own trust boundary.

name: separation-of-duties
document:
separation-of-duties
separation of privilege
four-eyes principle
Require two or more distinct principals or components to complete a sensitive operation, so that no single account, role or object can initiate and finish it alone.
A sensitive workflow is reachable end to end from one identity or one code path: the same operator creates and approves the payment, the same administrator changes the production configuration and signs it off, the same service account holds both the maker and the checker permission. The trigger is structural rather than accidental - all steps share one principal, one session, one process or one role, because splitting them costs a second pair of hands - and the failure surfaces only when an insider error or abuse is unremarkable in the audit trail: every step was authorized, because one principal held both halves of the duty.
Sensitive operations whose consequences must survive mistakes, coercion or misuse by authorized insiders: payments and disbursements, entitlement and permission changes, production configuration and deployment, key custody and signing, destructive data operations. It applies where identities can be kept distinct and authenticated (separate accounts, roles, services, processes), where the intermediate states of the operation can be persisted and observed, and where an enforcement point exists that can compare the acting principal with the recorded initiator - a policy engine, method security, an approval service, a separate process or account, a dual-control key ceremony. It is as much an organizational rule as a technical one: the split must follow the duties people actually hold, and recombination must be made awkward by design rather than merely discouraged.
Maker-checker payments: an operator above a threshold creates a disbursement and a second operator releases it; the ledger records both identities and refuses a release signed by the maker.
Change control and deployment: production IAM policy or infrastructure changes require a second administrator's approval, and the pipeline refuses to run a change approved by its own author (required reviewers / second signature).
Key custody and dual control: signing keys or root credentials are split so two authorized operators must each contribute a share (split knowledge, m-of-n threshold, dual-control key ceremony) and no single share can sign.
Access provisioning: the requester of an entitlement, its approver and the administrator who grants it are three distinct roles; the administrator cannot approve their own request, and access-control administrators do not administer the audit log.
Destructive data operations: schema migrations, production data edits and deletion jobs are prepared by one engineer and executed by a different operator account that cannot author the change.
Regulated back-office workflows: journal entries, refunds, credit adjustments and account closures are initiated by one clerk and posted by another, with the pairing recorded for audit.
GitHub protected branches: a pull request targeting a protected branch needs the configured number of approving reviews before it can merge, the platform refuses an approval from the PR author by design, and with dismiss-stale-review enabled a commit pushed after the review voids the approval - four-eyes enforced at the merge gate with the approval bound to the reviewed revision.
AWS Systems Manager Change Manager: a change request may run its Automation runbook only after approvals from named IAM users, groups or roles arrive across up to five approval levels, and a single rejection stops execution; because change templates list approvers separately from requesters, a request submitted under one IAM principal is released by another.
HashiCorp Vault key custody: vault operator init splits the root key with Shamir's Secret Sharing into key shares (default 5) under a threshold (default 3); unsealing or generating a root token needs a quorum of distinct share holders, and PGP-encrypting each share for a named operator makes dual control a property of the mechanism rather than of the procedure.

name: function-composition
document:
function-composition
compose
function pipeline
Combine a chain of small unary transformations into one reusable function by sequencing them with a composition combinator (compose/pipe), so the order of the steps is stated once, every step stays independently testable, and the chain itself becomes a value that can be named, passed and reassembled.
A transformation that is naturally a sequence of small pure steps gets written as nested calls or as repeated imperative assignment (`h(g(f(x)))`, or `y = f(x); y = g(y); ...; return y`) at every call site. The order is duplicated wherever the chain is used, the intermediate values need throwaway names, steps cannot be reused in a different order, and changing one stage means editing every copy.
Pure or nearly pure value transformations - parsing, normalisation, validation, formatting, pricing, AST rewriting - where each step is unary and the language treats functions as values. It pays off when the chain is reused or assembled from data (configuration, plugin lists, per-request policy), when steps must be unit-tested in isolation, and when the same steps must also run element-wise over a collection or lazily over a stream. It stops applying where steps need side effects or branching between stages: there the shell around the pure core owns control flow.
Input normalisation: trim, parse, canonicalise and validate a payload before it reaches domain logic, with the same chain reused by HTTP handlers and message consumers.
Pricing and rule chains: base price, discount, tax and rounding applied in a fixed, configurable order to an immutable value object.
Compiler and AST work: a pass list of rewrite functions composed once and applied over the tree, with passes added or reordered per optimisation level.
Serialisation and formatting: sanitise, format, encode and sign a document, where each step is tested separately and the composed chain is stored as a constant.
Data transformation over collections: the same pure steps composed into one function and passed to map/filter/stream operations, so element-wise processing reuses the chain.
Policy assembly at startup: the processing chain is built from configuration or plugin registrations and then applied per request without further branching.
Reactive stream processing: RxJS Observable.pipe chains the same logical steps across asynchronous event sequences, with operators composed once and reused across streams.
ETL and data pipeline transformation: extract-transform-load chains where each stage (parse, clean, enrich, aggregate, write) is a unary pure function composed into a reusable pipeline run over batches or streaming data.
HTTP request/response middleware: the middleware stack is a composed function chain where each layer (authenticate, authorise, rate-limit, deserialize, validate) is a unary handler; composition is resolved once at startup.
Matrix and vector transformations in numerical code: each linear algebra operation (scale, rotate, translate, project) is a unary function on a matrix type; composing them once builds the transformation pipeline that is applied to every vertex or pixel.
Ramda pipelines: R.pipe and R.compose assemble reusable data-last transformations from small functions, centralising the order while letting the same composed value run over many inputs.
Redux store setup: Redux's compose helper combines store enhancers right-to-left into one enhancer, so the enhancer order is defined once instead of reconstructed at each store boundary.
lodash/fp transformations: lodash/fp's auto-curried, data-last compose/flow helpers assemble immutable-friendly transformations from reusable steps that can be passed as values.

name: repository
document:
repository
collection-oriented repository
repository layer
Mediates between the domain model and the data mapping layer with a collection-like interface, so domain code adds, removes and finds persistent objects as if they lived in memory and never constructs queries or touches persistence APIs itself.
Persistence code spreads: every application service re-derives the same SQL or ORM queries, duplicate query logic drifts apart, table and column names leak into domain decisions, and testing domain rules without a database becomes impossible. Callers should be able to think in collections of domain objects instead of queries.
Applies to systems with a non-trivial domain model sitting on a data-mapping layer (Data Mapper, metadata mapping, or a hand-written mapper) where the same queries recur across application services; it becomes more valuable as domain classes and query volume grow. It is the standard persistence boundary of DDD aggregates (one repository per aggregate root) and presumes a unit of work or session that owns flush and commit. It is not a per-table data-access wrapper and not a replacement for transaction control.
DDD application services that must load an aggregate root, run domain logic on it and store it again without knowing the table layout.
Data-mapper backends where several application services and background jobs share recurring complex queries (overdue invoices, pending orders, open tickets).
Applications that must be unit-testable away from the database: repositories are the substitution point for in-memory doubles.
Systems that must support more than one store behind a stable domain interface — relational in production, in-memory in tests, a document store for a particular deployment.
Uniform cross-cutting access policy for an aggregate: caching, read-replica routing, audit logging or authorization applied as decorators around one interface.
Migration work where the persistence technology changes (ORM swap, schema split, service extraction) while the domain model and its tests stay untouched.
CQRS write-side aggregate loading where the aggregate must be reconstructed fully to apply business rules and enforce invariants.
Integration with heterogeneous data sources where one repository unifies access to a cache, primary database and a third-party API behind a domain interface.
Spring Data JPA applications can use Repository/CrudRepository for aggregate-typed CRUD, paging and derived queries, then add only domain-specific methods rather than wrapping every persistence operation.
The .NET eShopOnContainers ordering microservice uses an EF Core BuyerRepository over a shared scoped DbContext/unit of work, while CQRS/Dapper handles presentation reads.
Python applications using SQLAlchemy ORM can place an aggregate-facing repository over Session, whose identity map and unit-of-work flush semantics provide the mapper/session boundary.
