name: query-object
document:
query-object
Represent a database query as an ordinary object that composes through the language's own constructs and is translated into SQL by an interpreter, so that queries can be built, stored, passed and reused independently of the tables and columns behind them.
Fixed finder methods hide one statement each: an ad-hoc query with optional filters cannot be assembled without either duplicating finders combinatorially or concatenating SQL strings, which spreads schema knowledge, dialect quirks and injection risk across every call site and leaves the query itself un-cacheable, un-testable and impossible to hand to another layer.
Data-access code over relational stores where queries are assembled from optional, reusable criteria (search forms, tenant scopes, report filters) and must run against one or more SQL dialects; typically paired with mapping metadata - table descriptors or an entity metamodel - that lets the query name classes and fields instead of tables and columns, and with a mapper that turns result rows back into domain objects.
Search and report screens where status, date-range or tenant filters are added only when the request supplies them.
Repository or DAO internals that build the same logical query for different stores or dialects.
Caching compiled statements by query shape or identity instead of rendering SQL per call.
Stored, reusable queries: named fetch-request templates, named queries or serialised filter trees that can be re-run unchanged.
Passing a query between layers or processes (controller to service to repository, or to a worker) without passing SQL text.
Testing query logic without a database: compose and assert the object, then execute one rendering as a smoke test.
Django applications pass unevaluated QuerySet objects through service or repository layers, chaining filter(), Q() and order_by() before evaluation at the boundary.
SQLAlchemy Core and ORM code composes generative Select objects with where(), join() and subqueries, then executes them through a Connection or Session for the target dialect.
Jakarta Persistence repositories use CriteriaBuilder and CriteriaQuery to build type-safe predicates, joins, ordering and parameters from optional search criteria.

name: metadata-mapping
document:
metadata-mapping
declarative mapping
orm mapping metadata
Holds the correspondence between object fields and database columns in metadata - annotations, mapping files, table objects, struct tags or a schema definition - so that one generic mapping engine performs the reads, inserts and updates instead of hand-written per-class mapper code.
Every class that is persisted needs the same tedious, repetitive code: which field maps to which column, which key is generated, how nulls and types convert, what the table is called. Written per class it is duplicated everywhere and drifts from the schema; the catalogue's trigger is that the mapping knowledge belongs in metadata or configuration, duplicated in no class.
Object-relational (or object-document) mapping layers where classes and tables do not line up mechanically - renamed columns, generated keys, relationships, inheritance strategies - and where many classes share the same mapping shape. It applies when the mapping can be declared once in a form a machine can read (code annotations or attributes, external XML, code-first table objects, struct tags, a schema DSL) and when the schema can either be generated from that metadata or validated against it at startup.
A system with dozens of similarly shaped tables where hand-written data mappers would be repetitive: one mapping engine plus one metadata declaration per class.
Schema-first projects where the database already exists and the mapping should be derived from it by introspection or a code generator (EF Core reverse engineering, Rails schema introspection, SeaORM entity generation).
Framework and library builders who must let users map their own classes without shipping per-class code - an ORM, an object-document mapper or a serialization library.
Multi-database products in which only the dialect and type map of the metadata changes between targets while the domain classes stay identical.
Teams that want one declaration to drive several artifacts: DDL or migrations, typed query APIs, validation rules and documentation.
Hibernate ORM/Jakarta Persistence applications declare @Entity, @Table and @Column metadata; the provider builds a persistent metamodel and generic Session or EntityManager operations perform CRUD, so one declaration replaces per-entity mapper code.
EF Core applications combine conventions, data annotations and Fluent API configuration to build an entity model that drives LINQ translation and updates; explicit configuration pins renamed columns and relationships.
SQLAlchemy declarative mappings turn class attributes and mapped_column() declarations into Table and Mapper metadata; that metadata feeds SQL compilation and unit-of-work persistence, while imperative mapping keeps existing classes annotation-free.

name: lightweight-entity
document:
lightweight-entity
persistence-ignorant entity
pojo entity
Keep domain entity classes free of persistence logic - no queries, no save/delete, no table knowledge - so that all knowledge of how the object maps to the store lives in metadata (annotations, mapping files, tags, descriptor tables) that a generic mapper consumes.
When each entity class carries its own mapping code (table name, column list, SQL, load/save methods) the same schema knowledge is duplicated in every class, the domain model is welded to the store, and a schema change becomes an edit inside the model. Moving the mapping out then raises the reverse problem: the entities must be dumb enough for a generic mapper to drive them, i.e. they may carry state and domain behaviour but no persistence behaviour.
The persistence-state layer of an application whose domain objects outlive a single operation: entities are stored relationally or document-wise, their schema evolves independently of the model, and a mapper (Data Mapper/ORM/session) - not the object itself - must own reads, writes, identity and lazy loading. It applies where the language can carry mapping metadata outside the entity (annotations, XML/DSL mapping files, struct tags, descriptor tables, external schema files) and something can read that metadata generically.
Layered applications whose domain model is persisted through an ORM: JPA/Hibernate annotations or orm.xml, EF Core configuration, SQLAlchemy mappings, Diesel/SeaORM derives.
Products that map one domain model onto different schemas per customer or deployment through interchangeable metadata sets, without recompiling the model.
Legacy schemas with hostile column names and shapes that must not leak into the domain model: the mapping layer is the translation seam.
Systems that need entities testable in isolation without a database, while the mapping layer is exercised separately against a real database.
Schema-as-code workflows where the mapping metadata also drives migrations or DDL and generated query clients (Prisma, EF Core migrations, SQLAlchemy metadata.create_all).
CQRS read-side projections: lightweight entities serve as denormalized read models populated from the write side, with no behaviour beyond data access.
Event-sourcing snapshots: entities are rebuilt from an event stream and must carry state without invoking the event store.
API boundary DTOs that translate between the internal domain model and external representations, decoupling schema evolution from API contracts.
Distributed system message payloads: serialized lightweight entities travel across process boundaries (queues, event buses) where no persistence context exists.
Hibernate/JPA applications can keep POJO entities focused on domain state while annotations or XML mapping descriptors tell the ORM how to persist them through an EntityManager or Session.
EF Core applications can configure CLR entity-to-table and property-to-column metadata in OnModelCreating/Fluent API or data annotations, leaving persistence orchestration in the DbContext rather than entity methods.
SQLAlchemy applications can use registry-based declarative or imperative mappings to bind Python classes to tables while sessions, not entities, own database operations.

name: iterator
document:
iterator
cursor
enumerator
Provide a way to access the elements of an aggregate object sequentially without exposing its underlying representation, by moving traversal state and the traversal algorithm out of the aggregate into a separate iterator object.
Traversal leaks into every client: code that walks a collection has to know its storage layout (array indices, node links, hash buckets), the same loop is rewritten once per aggregate and once per client, and adding a new traversal order means changing the aggregate's interface — which is exactly what prevents algorithms from being written once and applied to any collection.
Applies wherever a collection with a non-trivial or changeable representation must be traversed by outsiders: collection libraries, trees and graphs with several traversal orders, lazy or unbounded sources, and streaming pipelines. It matters most when more than one traversal may be pending at the same time, when the storage must stay hidden for encapsulation or safety, or when traversal algorithms must be added without touching the aggregate; the toolchain only decides which realization is available (a language iteration protocol, generators, lazy sequences, or a hand-written cursor).
Collection libraries that must serve arrays, linked lists, trees, and hash tables through one protocol — e.g. std::begin/end in C++, java.util.Iterator, IEnumerable<T> in C#, Symbol.iterator in JavaScript, IntoIterator in Rust.
Tree and graph APIs exposing depth-first, breadth-first, in-order, or post-order traversal without publishing node links or parent pointers, enabling clients to walk composite structures without coupling to the storage representation.
Lazy or unbounded sources consumed one element at a time: file lines (BufferedReader.lines()), network socket streams, paginated API responses, sensor data, event streams, and generated sequences (random numbers, Fibonacci, permutations).
Streaming data pipelines (map/filter/reduce over any iterable) that stay O(1) in memory regardless of input size, implemented via itertools, Java Stream API, Kotlin Sequence, C++ ranges, Rust iterator adapters, or Go iter package.
Legacy or third-party aggregates whose internal layout must stay private behind a stable traversal interface, allowing the aggregate to refactor its storage without breaking existing clients.
Custom containers that must participate in the language's own for/foreach/for-in/for-await loop, spread operators, destructuring assignment, or list comprehensions.
Database result sets and ORM cursors where the full result set is never materialised in memory; the iterator fetches pages on demand.
Parser and lexer token streams where the input is consumed incrementally and the full source may not fit in memory.
Async I/O pipelines where the iteration protocol yields Promises (JavaScript async generators, C# IAsyncEnumerable<T>, Python async generators) enabling for-await iteration over network responses or file reads.
Multidimensional collection traversal (matrices, nested lists, spatial grids) via flattened iterators that expose a flat index space while hiding the multi-dimensional layout.
Paginated REST or GraphQL API clients where a client-side iterator transparently fetches successive pages as the consumer pulls elements, keeping memory constant regardless of result set size.
Kafka, log-processor, or ETL pipelines where each stage is a transforming iterator: parse → filter → enrich → validate → sink, with each stage evaluated lazily.
Event-driven systems using async iterators to consume WebSocket messages, SSE streams, or queue consumers through a uniform for-await-of interface.
Batch-processing jobs over large file sets (CSV, Parquet, NDJSON) where an iterator wraps a file reader and yields one record per next() call without loading the file into memory.
Cursor-based (keyset) pagination over large, live datasets where offset/limit pagination causes duplicates or missed rows when data is inserted or deleted mid-traversal; the iterator stores the last-seen key rather than a page offset, making traversal stable across concurrent modifications.
Iterator fusion in compilers and runtimes: adjacent map/filter/map chains fused into a single pass with zero intermediate allocation (Rust iterator adapters, Java Spliterators, Haskell stream fusion, C++ range views), giving lazy pipelines near-handwritten performance.
Parallel iterators for data-parallel workloads: Rust Rayon, Java parallel streams, and Kotlin asFlow().buffer() split the iterator across worker threads — identical interface to serial iteration, transparent parallel execution.
Reactive streams bridging pull and push: RxJava, RxJS, and Project Reactor implement backpressure (consumer signals demand, producer emits at requested rate), combining iterator's pull semantics with observer's push delivery.
LLM and streaming AI responses where the model yields tokens incrementally; an async iterator wraps the SSE/stream endpoint and the client consumes tokens one at a time via for-await-of, keeping first-token latency low and enabling progressive rendering.
Cursor-based database driver iterators (Node.js pg cursor, Python asyncpg, Go database/sql rows) where the driver streams rows from the server without loading the full result set, with configurable fetch size controlling server-side memory usage.
Java's Spliterator API exposes a cursor that can be advanced one element at a time or split into subranges for parallel streams; it demonstrates that an iterator contract can include explicit partitioning and size/order characteristics rather than only next().
.NET's IAsyncEnumerable<T> and IAsyncEnumerator<T> expose asynchronous pull iteration through await foreach; GetAsyncEnumerator(CancellationToken) makes cancellation part of the iterator boundary for network, file, and database streams.
WHATWG ReadableStream async iteration lets browser and server consumers use for-await-of over streamed chunks while the iterator locks a reader and defines whether early return() cancels or merely releases it.

newtype
strong typedef
opaque type
Give a single primitive its own distinct type so that values with different meanings cannot be substituted for one another, and the raw representation is reachable only through the wrapper's own construction and accessors.
Several domain concepts share one representation - customer id, order id and tenant id are all strings or UUIDs, width/height/offset are all numbers, milliseconds and seconds are both integers - and the API therefore accepts them interchangeably. A swapped argument, a mixed unit or a mistyped literal compiles (or runs) silently, and the defect surfaces late, as a wrong lookup or a cross-tenant bug rather than a type error.
Code in which two or more values with the same underlying representation flow through the same functions, collections or persistence mapping, and in which a single value owns a rule (identifier syntax, non-emptiness, numeric range, unit). Applies at the value level of one field; clusters of attributes that change together belong to Value Object, and closed constant sets to Type-Safe Enum.
Identifier families in one codebase: CustomerId, OrderId, TenantId and SessionId all string- or UUID-shaped and passed to the same repository, logger and cache.
Unit-carrying measurements: Milliseconds vs Seconds, Meters vs Feet, Radians vs Degrees, Cents vs Dollars, where arithmetic must stay inside one unit and conversion is explicit.
Validated single values: EmailAddress, PhoneNumber, Iban, Slug, Percentage (0-100), PortNumber, NonEmptyString - parsed once at the edge, trusted everywhere afterwards.
Security-adjacent tokens: API token vs session id vs tenant id, where a swap becomes a cross-tenant or privilege defect rather than a wrong lookup.
Geometry and graphics APIs where Width, Height, X, Y, Offset and Length are all numbers and transposition should be a compile error.
Pagination and buffer arithmetic: PageSize vs PageIndex vs ByteOffset vs Count, integers that are trivially transposable in a long argument list.
Rust's official newtype examples use Millimeters(u32) and Meters(u32) to keep units distinct, and use Wrapper(Vec<T>) to give a local wrapper its own trait implementations.
Scala 3 opaque types model values such as Logarithm over Double as distinct outside their defining scope, with controlled extension methods and no runtime boxing.
Kotlin @JvmInline value classes wrap one property into a non-interchangeable domain type such as Password while allowing unboxed representations in many uses.

name: update-method
document:
update-method
per-frame update
tick method
Give every live object one self-contained per-frame step and let a single driver call each object's step every frame, so behaviour advances one frame at a time while input and rendering stay responsive.
A running world is full of objects that each have to keep doing their own thing - guards patrolling, statues charging, agents acting - and the recurring decision is where one object's per-frame behaviour lives and how all those behaviours get driven. Coding a behaviour as a loop that runs to completion blocks input and rendering (the skeleton walks, but nobody sees it); coding it inline in the game loop turns the loop into a switchboard over every kind of object, so every new behaviour edits central code; and there is no way for two actors to evolve independently and simultaneously.
Real-time software with many concurrent live objects whose behaviour is mostly independent and must be simulated over time: games, agent-based simulations, animation and particle systems, tick-based servers and live visualisations. It is the natural partner of a frame driver (Game Loop) - the loop supplies the cadence, Update Method supplies the per-object step - and it becomes the wrong shape in turn-based or purely event-driven domains where nothing changes between inputs.
Real-time games and simulations with many concurrent actors: patrolling guards, projectiles, particle effects and crowd agents each advance themselves once per frame while the driver walks the collection.
Component-based engines where the parts of one entity evolve independently - rendering, physics and AI components each implement their own step and the engine's registry dispatches per component (Unity, MonoGame, Bevy, GameplayKit, libGDX).
Per-frame animation and effect timelines outside games: tween/spring systems, sprite animation and UI transitions advanced from the browser's frame callback or a UI toolkit's animation timer.
Tick-based servers and headless simulations: game servers, digital twins and agent-based models where each agent's behaviour is a resumable step and the world advances in whole discrete frames.
Tools, editors and dashboards with continuously animating scenes, where many independent scene items (markers, live charts, gizmos) must advance on every repaint without a central per-item switch.
Porting straight-line behaviour into a frame loop: turning a scripted sequence (walk left, walk right) into a per-frame step, either by storing explicit state or by using coroutines/generators to keep the code linear.
Godot's SceneTree is the driver: a node opts into the walk with set_process(true) and its _process(delta) runs every render frame with the frame time passed in as an argument, while _physics_process(delta) is called at a fixed rate - so one object can implement two steps on two clocks and can leave the walk entirely (set_process(false)) instead of paying an enabled-flag check every frame.
Engines whose built-in driver leaves per-object order unspecified expose the order as configuration: Unity states you should not rely on the order of Update across GameObjects, so real projects fix dependencies through the Script Execution Order panel, a LateUpdate pass that runs after every Update, or the PlayerLoop API rather than through registration order.
Agent-based simulation models step whole populations in NetLogo: the go procedure runs ask turtles [ ... ] to give every agent its one turn and then tick advances the discrete clock - with documented semantics that agents take their turns in random order and only agents present when the ask began get to act.

name: consumer-driven-contract-test
document:
consumer-driven-contract-test
consumer-driven contract
contract test
Capture, from each consumer's own tests, the concrete provider interactions that consumer depends on, and verify the provider against that contract inside the provider's own build, so consumer and provider can be released independently without a shared end-to-end environment.
Independently released consumers and providers must keep working together, yet the only reliable check is a shared end-to-end environment per pair - slow, brittle and usually out of date; at the same time the provider cannot see which parts of its API each consumer actually exercises, so every refactoring is a guess about who will break.
HTTP/request-reply, messaging and gRPC integrations where consumer and provider are owned by different teams on different release cadences and each consumer uses only a narrow slice of the provider's surface. It assumes the provider team is willing to run verification of consumer contracts in its own build; without that half, the consumer test is only a better mock.
Microservice landscapes where a front end, a mobile app or another service consumes an API released by a different team on its own schedule.
A provider team that must refactor or replace internals and needs to know, before merging, which consumer expectations it is about to break.
Mobile or desktop clients that cannot be deployed in lockstep with the backend, so each client's expectations must hold against every backend version.
Event- and message-based integrations (Kafka, SQS, SNS, RabbitMQ) where the consumer processes messages produced by another team; contracts pin the message body shape and metadata (topic, headers, content-type) while abstracting the transport.
Migration or strangler-fig work, where a replacement provider must be proven compatible with the existing consumers before traffic is moved.
Using the contract as the source of stubs for development and integration environments, so those environments no longer need the real provider.
BFF (Backend for Frontend) patterns where each frontend channel (web, mobile, third-party) has its own contract with a shared backend, allowing independent evolution of each BFF without cross-channel breakage.
Multi-team Kafka event streaming where consumers (downstream services) define which topics, partitions and message schemas they depend on, so producers can evolve events without silently breaking subscribers; Pact message pacts handle both JSON and Schema Registry messages (with magic bytes for Avro/Protobuf over Schema Registry).
gRPC service integrations where protocol buffer message shapes are exercised by the actual consumer client code, pinning the wire format, service method signatures and metadata the consumer actually calls; synchronous message pacts cover the request-response pairing.
Breaking up a monolith: individual microservices are extracted and their CDC contracts verify that the new service boundaries behave identically to the original module interfaces before traffic is migrated.
Schema Registry integrations (Confluent, AWS Glue) where consumers pin compatible message schemas and producers must not publish breaking schemas without migrating all dependent consumers first.
Third-party or vendor API integrations where the consumer team cannot rely on the provider to run verification: the consumer-side mock-only workflow with published contracts documents expectations even without provider participation.
Webhook and callback integrations where a provider calls a consumer-defined endpoint; CDC captures the consumer's expected payload shape, headers and authentication, and the provider verifies it can deliver to that shape.
Contract migration at scale: when a provider must migrate from v1 to v2 of an API, CDC with pending/wip pacts allows the provider to signal new expectations to consumers without blocking either side's pipeline while migration is in progress.
Spring Cloud Contract in JVM/Spring landscapes: the consumer's contract change lands in the producer's repository (or an external contract repo), the producer build generates verification tests from the contract DSL, and the consumer develops against StubRunner-served WireMock stubs pulled from an artifact repository (Nexus/Artifactory) - the contract is the single artifact both sides build from.
Nubank replaced its flaky shared-environment end-to-end suite with consumer-driven contract tests to regain deploy velocity - the public account of the pattern paying off as an e2e-substitute at a single organisation rather than as an addition to it.
Large polyglot estates such as JSTOR/ITHAKA (300+ microservices, 12+ teams, Pact) and M1 Finance (Pact plus PactFlow rolled out to 17 teams in under six months): the broker's compatibility matrix replaces per-pair end-to-end environments as the release gate.

name: double-checked-locking
document:
double-checked-locking
double-checked locking optimization
DCL
DCLP
Initialise a shared resource exactly once and lazily while keeping the steady-state read path free of lock acquisition - by testing a cheaply published state first and taking the lock only for the one-time construction, where the platform can publish the built object safely to every reader.
An expensive object - configuration, a connection pool, a compiled plan, a cache - must be created once and only when it is first needed, but its accessor is called from many threads. The naive check-then-act form lets two threads build it at the same time, and guarding every read with a lock serialises a path that almost never needs synchronisation. The tempting fix - test a flag cheaply, lock only for the initialisation, test again inside the lock - is sound only if the write that publishes the object is ordered with respect to the readers' loads, which is exactly the part the classic formulation leaves implicit and the reason the idiom is famous for rare, unreproducible failures.
Concurrent, shared-memory software in which one object or cell must be built once and read many times: process-wide singletons and registries, per-object caches inside an object shared between threads, lazily built statics in languages whose runtime also provides the once semantics. The pattern presupposes a memory model with a defined publication ordering (volatile, acquire/release, an initialisation lock, or a runtime once primitive) and a read path hot enough that the lock it removes is measurable. On single-threaded runtimes there is nothing to synchronise, and where a single-threaded composition root can initialise eagerly the pattern is unnecessary.
Process-wide singletons whose construction is expensive or configuration-dependent: configuration snapshot, metrics registry, logger, connection pool, feature-flag view.
Per-object caches inside an object shared by several threads - compiled regular expression or query plan, parsed schema, symbol table - where the build is expensive and the read is hot.
Lazily built statics in languages where the runtime owns the once semantics: C++ function-local static, Swift static let or global let, Kotlin by lazy, Scala lazy val, Go sync.Once, Rust OnceLock/LazyLock.
Compensating for the static-initialisation-order problem: an accessor that builds the global on first use instead of relying on cross-translation-unit initialisation order.
Avoiding lock overhead on a read-mostly, write-once hot path (memo tables, symbol caches, thread-safe lazy proxies) where a contended lock would show up in a profile.
Small or freestanding runtimes without a once primitive, where the first caller must build the cell and an eager initialiser is not available.
RWMutex-protected maps in Go where readers check a fast path before the slower write-locked re-check, as a safer alternative to sync.Map for workloads with known access patterns.
Per-connection or per-session lazy fields in object-pooled servers where the pool itself is the shared cell and each borrowed object gets a lazy-computed field.
Cross-language plugin or extension registries where one language's runtime initialises a global handle that other language shards read without repeated synchronisation.
Rate-limiter or circuit-breaker state that must be lazily built from configuration: building eagerly would couple the policy to startup time, but the read path must be lock-free under high throughput.
Lazy compilation or query-plan warming in database connection pools where the pool is shared but individual plans are built on first use by the owning thread.
Spring Framework's DefaultSingletonBeanRegistry.getSingleton: check the singletonObjects map lock-free, take the singletonLock only when the bean is absent, re-check inside - a production evolution of the idiom whose correctness was formally challenged (SPR-13463) and upheld because the concurrent-map read already carries the needed memory barrier.
Chromium's base::LazyInstance / GetOrCreateLazyPointer: an atomic state word with a 'creating' bit, acquire-load fast path and release-store publication - since deprecated in favour of function-local statics with base::NoDestructor, a signal of how far hardened platforms have moved from hand-rolled DCL.
ACE toolkit's ACE_Singleton<TYPE, ACE_LOCK>: the pattern's original industrial home (the 1997 paper was written alongside ACE) - the template still guards instance() with a double-checked ACE_LOCK acquire and recommends ACE_Recursive_Thread_Mutex for multi-threaded access.
Swift runtime: every global/static let is lowered to swift_once (dispatch_once on Darwin), so the double-checked once structure is the default initialisation mechanism for lazily computed immutable globals rather than hand-written code.

name: recursive-descent-parser
document:
recursive-descent-parser
recursive descent
recursive descent parsing
Parse a small grammar by translating every rule directly into a function that consumes the tokens the rule matches and calls the functions of the rules it references, so the parser's control flow is the grammar itself and stays readable, debuggable and free of a code-generation step.
A hand-written parser is the only option - no generator in the toolchain, or the grammar is a small DSL - yet the grammar is not a flat token sequence: alternatives must be chosen from lookahead, repetition must become a loop, and the natural grammar for expressions is left-recursive, which a top-down parser cannot translate directly. Without a disciplined mapping from rules to functions the parser degenerates into ad-hoc index arithmetic and exception-driven backtracking, and errors end up without positions.
Front ends for small languages, DSLs, query/filter/rule grammars, configuration and protocol formats, and the parsing layer of compilers and interpreters that want no code-generation step. It applies when a lexer or token stream already exists (or is cheap to write), the grammar is small to medium and reasonably LL-friendly or rewritable into LL form, and the team values readable, step-debuggable, position-precise parsing over generated tables.
Front ends for small languages, DSLs and configuration formats (filter expressions, rule engines, policy languages, template syntaxes) where a generator and its build integration would be overkill.
Expression and statement parsing in single-pass compilers and interpreters that emit bytecode or IR while parsing, as in Crafting Interpreters' Lox.
Tooling for a grammar you own - formatters, linters, syntax highlighters, language servers - where error tolerance, multiple diagnostics and exact positions matter more than raw throughput.
Protocol and wire-format decoding with a small fixed grammar, where errors must carry byte offsets and malformed input must be rejected deterministically.
Context-dependent or indentation-sensitive syntaxes (templates with interpolation, layout-based blocks, configuration with embedded expressions) that a generated lexer handles poorly.
Codebases that must not carry generated code: security-reviewed, vendored or cross-compiled projects where an ordinary source file beats a build-time generator.
Clang's C-family front end uses a unified hand-built recursive-descent parser for C, C++, Objective-C and Objective-C++, pairing rule-oriented control flow with production-quality diagnostics.
The Go standard library's go/parser is a production recursive-descent parser for Go source, with explicit parser state, nesting-depth guards and error recovery.
rustc_parse is the Rust compiler's recursive-descent parser module, showing how a hand-written parser can scale to macros, recovery modes and detailed token/state handling.
Lua's reference implementation compiles with lparser.c, a single-pass recursive-descent parser that emits bytecode opcodes while reducing expressions instead of building a syntax tree, with precedence handled by parsing levels.

name: adapter
document:
adapter
wrapper
adaptor
Present an existing component through the exact target contract its client already consumes, translating calls, results and boundary semantics without adding responsibilities or pretending a missing capability exists.
An existing or foreign component has useful behaviour but speaks a different protocol: method names and signatures, data shapes, units, lifecycle, error model or sync/async contract do not satisfy the target. If every caller performs ad hoc conversion, semantics drift, vendor types leak and provider replacement becomes a cross-cutting rewrite; changing the adaptee or target may be impossible or too disruptive.
Integration work where one side is outside your control: legacy modules, vendor SDKs, generated clients, foreign data formats or units, and the ports-and-adapters boundary of a hexagonal architecture. Applies in statically typed languages - where an adapter class is also the compile-time proof that the required interface is satisfied - and in structurally or dynamically typed ones, where a thin wrapper usually replaces a declared target interface.
Wrapping a third-party or vendor SDK behind your own interface so business code never imports vendor types.
Modernising a legacy module incrementally: new code talks to the target interface while the old component is adapted in place.
Supporting several interchangeable providers (payments, storage, messaging, analytics) through one internal contract, with one adapter each.
Adapting a callback- or error-first API to promises/async or to an observer-style interface.
Ports-and-adapters boundaries where one domain port is realized over different transports (HTTP, message queue, in-process fake).
Unifying differently shaped data sources (row sets, DTOs, XML or JSON payloads) into one model before they reach domain logic.
Test doubles: an in-memory adapter satisfies the target interface without the real infrastructure.
API wrapper libraries: normalising third-party REST/gRPC APIs (Stripe, Twilio, payment providers) into a stable internal contract so business logic never imports vendor SDK types.
Legacy system integration: wrapping SOAP, CORBA, or mainframe APIs behind a modern interface, enabling incremental migration without rewriting existing clients.
Cloud provider abstraction: a single internal storage or queue interface implemented by AWS, GCP, or Azure adapters, letting the application swap providers via configuration.
ETL pipelines: adapting heterogeneous source record schemas (CSV, JSON, XML, database rows) into one canonical domain record, isolating format changes from downstream consumers.
Event-stream and streaming adapters: translating WebSocket frames or server-sent events into domain events in real time.
Multi-cloud and provider-agnostic interfaces: storage adapters (S3, GCS, Azure Blob), queue adapters (SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka), and notification adapters that abstract away provider-specific SDKs.
Backend for Frontend (BFF): each front-end client (web, mobile, third-party) gets its own lightweight adapter that shapes internal service responses into the exact payload that client needs.
Java's java.io.InputStreamReader is a byte-to-character bridge: it presents an InputStream through the Reader contract while decoding with an explicit charset.
SLF4J uses providers such as slf4j-reload4j to bind one Logger API to different backends, while log4j-over-slf4j and jul-to-slf4j redirect legacy APIs at a migration boundary; Spring MVC's HandlerAdapter similarly lets DispatcherServlet handle heterogeneous handler types through one SPI.
Go's net/http.HandlerFunc gives an ordinary func(ResponseWriter, *Request) the http.Handler contract by attaching ServeHTTP, so routing and middleware can consume functions and handlers uniformly.

name: request-reply
document:
request-reply
request-response
request-response messaging
Let a sender obtain a result or a domain error from an asynchronous or remote receiver by pairing each request with a correlated reply, and give the missing reply a defined outcome: timeout, cancellation and disposal of late replies.
Messaging is one-way, but the sender frequently needs a return value or a domain error from the receiver before it can continue. Without an agreed reply destination, a way to match replies to requests, and a rule for what happens when no reply arrives, the caller either blocks forever, mis-associates the next reply with the wrong request, or accumulates pending state it never cleans up.
Asynchronous interaction across a process, thread or network boundary where the caller cannot continue without the receiver's result: HTTP/gRPC-style RPC, broker-based RPC over a queue, actor or thread mailboxes, and browser-to-server exchanges over a socket. It applies when the interaction is naturally one request and one reply, and each exchange has a bounded deadline.
Service-to-service RPC where the caller needs the result to continue (HTTP, gRPC, or a broker-based RPC queue such as the RabbitMQ tutorial's rpc_queue).
Command dispatch that must return a domain error - a validation failure or business rejection - rather than only an acknowledgement of receipt.
In-process actor or thread mailboxes: ask a worker for state with a deadline so the caller can never block forever.
Front-end over a WebSocket asking the server for a value correlated by message id or acknowledgement callback.
Talking to devices, sensors or legacy systems over a socket whose protocol is inherently one request and one response.
Querying a cache or index cluster from a client library where each call is a key lookup with a per-call deadline.
NATS request-reply service calls: a client publishes with a unique inbox as the reply subject and waits for a response under a per-request timeout.
RabbitMQ RPC over an rpc_queue: the client sends reply_to and a unique correlation_id, then matches the worker's response on its callback queue.
gRPC unary RPC: a generated client stub sends one request and receives one response under a propagated deadline, with cancellation available for abandoned work.

name: monitor-object
document:
monitor-object
thread-safe passive object
monitor
Serialise concurrent method invocations on a shared object by giving the object its own lock and condition variables, so that only one method executes inside it at a time and methods that cannot proceed wait cooperatively instead of polling.
Objects shared by several threads expose their state through ordinary methods, and nothing stops concurrent callers from interleaving inside those methods, corrupting the invariants they were written to maintain. The race is then papered over with ad-hoc locking, sleeps and busy-wait loops scattered through client code. The recurring decision is whether the object itself should own the serialisation (and the scheduling) of its methods instead of leaving that discipline to every caller.
Shared-memory concurrency, where the mutable state of an object is reached by more than one thread and its methods must be atomic with respect to one another. It matters most when some methods cannot run to completion until another method changes the state - a queue that is full or empty, a resource that is not yet available, a phase that has not been reached - because then a method must suspend and later resume, which requires releasing the lock while it waits.
Bounded buffers and work queues shared by producer and consumer threads, where producers wait while the queue is full and consumers wait while it is empty - the pattern's canonical example.
Session, connection or entity registries on a server, where lookups, insertion and eviction must be atomic and callers may have to wait for capacity or for an entry to reappear.
Caches with in-flight bookkeeping (single-flight computation), where a thread that requests an already-computed key waits for the first thread's result instead of recomputing it.
Shared configuration, counters or statistics objects read and updated by request threads, where each call must observe a consistent snapshot of the state.
State machines and simulators whose step methods block until another thread advances a transition, for example a test harness waiting for a worker to reach a known state.
In-process resource pools (connection, database or worker pools) where acquisition blocks until an entry is returned or a timeout expires.
Java's java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue is a fixed-capacity monitor-style bounded buffer: put blocks while full and take blocks while empty, making the producer-consumer coordination explicit.
.NET's System.Collections.Concurrent.BlockingCollection<T> supplies bounded Add/Take blocking, cancellation and completion semantics around a producer-consumer collection; use it instead of hand-rolling Monitor.Wait/Pulse.
Python's queue.Queue provides a thread-safe multi-producer/multi-consumer boundary with blocking put/get operations and optional timeouts, a standard monitor-style primitive for worker pools.

name: typestate
document:
typestate
type state
typestate programming
Encode an object's state in its type - a type parameter or a distinct state type - so that only the operations legal in the current state exist and every transition is a checked, type-changing step.
An object's methods are valid only in certain states (a closed file cannot be read, a client that has not connected cannot send), but the state lives in a runtime field: callers must remember the protocol, illegal calls still compile and fail at run time, and the legal sequences are documented rather than enforced.
Statically typed languages with generics or usable distinct-type support, where a small, fixed set of states and legal transitions is known at compile time: protocol handshakes, resource lifecycles (files, sockets, peripherals), staged builders and configuration objects, and single-owner workflows. It pays where a wrong sequence is expensive - hardware, protocols, money - and the state machine is stable.
Staged builders where build() must not compile before every required property is supplied (typed request builders, configuration objects).
Resource lifecycles: files, sockets and streams whose read/write/close operations are meaningful only after open and before close.
Protocol handshakes - connect, authenticate, exchange, disconnect - including TLS or HTTP session setup and stateful client APIs.
Embedded peripheral configuration: a GPIO pin or timer whose mode (input, output, alternate function) is a type parameter, so wrong-mode register access is a compile error.
Transaction and workflow objects: begin, mutate, commit or roll back, where committing twice or mutating after commit must not be expressible.
Iterators and streams with an exhausted state, where next() consumes the iterator until it yields the end state.
Hardware or network state machines where a wrong sequence causes a fault rather than a catchable error (bus faults, half-open connections).
Embedded HALs in the Rust ecosystem (embedded-hal and device crates such as stm32f4xx-hal) model a pin as Pin<M> with its mode as the type parameter: set_high() compiles only for an output-mode pin and into_input()/into_output() consume the old pin, as prescribed by the Embedded Rust Book's GPIO design chapter.
The Checker Framework for Java runs typestate analysis over unmodified code: its Called Methods and Resource Leak checkers track @MustCall obligations so an InputStream cannot be read before its required initialization methods ran and must be closed on every path - the state is inferred by a checker rather than written into the type.
TypeScript builder libraries such as ts-fluent-builder thread a phantom state type through the builder's generics so build() only compiles once every required property is present, turning missing-field errors from runtime throws into compile errors.

copy and swap idiom
create-temporary-and-swap
Implement assignment (and any in-place state replacement) so that a failure while producing the new state leaves the target untouched: build the complete replacement off to the side, commit it with operations that cannot fail, and let the temporary's destructor or the garbage collector release the old state.
A hand-written assignment has to tear down the old state and build a copy of the new one, but only the build can fail: destroying before allocating exposes a half-updated object when the allocation or the element copy throws, and the usual repair -- a self-assignment check plus manual rollback -- duplicates the per-member copying that already lives in the copy constructor. The trigger is an assignment (or, in a garbage-collected language, an in-place state replacement) that must satisfy the strong exception guarantee: either it completes, or the target still holds its previous value.
Types that own resources -- heap buffers, handles, file descriptors, trees, containers -- in a language where the programmer controls copy semantics: C++ special member functions, a C ADT with error codes, Rust with panic/abort failure modes. The same ordering also applies in garbage-collected languages whenever published state must never be mutated in place: building the complete replacement and publishing it once keeps readers consistent and moves the release of the old state to the collector. The precondition is a commit step that genuinely cannot fail -- a noexcept member swap, one reference or pointer store, or an atomic publish.
Container and buffer classes that own heap memory (dynamic array, string, matrix, tree) and must be assignable without leaking or leaving the target inconsistent when an allocation fails.
Handle/pimpl classes that keep their state behind a single pointer: the swap is a pointer exchange, so the commit is unconditionally non-throwing while the deep copy still happens in the copy constructor (Sutter's canonical Pimpl exception-safety transformation).
Pre-C++11 codebases where the same operator= must serve lvalues and rvalues and no move constructor exists, using the const-reference plus explicit-local-temporary form.
Value types stored inside standard containers: std::vector and friends need element assignment to be safe before they can offer their own strong guarantee on reallocation, and a noexcept swap participates in their internal move/swap dispatch.
Garbage-collected languages where shared state must be replaced rather than mutated: build a complete replacement value and publish it with one store (AtomicReference.updateAndGet, atomic.Pointer[T].Store, a record with-expression) so readers never observe a partially updated object.
In-place state replacement where identity must be preserved (a registry entry, a cached object with live references): copy into a scratch value, then commit with a member-wise exchange or a replace-style API instead of repointing the reference.
Concurrent programming with thread-safe local-then-publish: build the replacement in a local object (thread-private by definition), then publish atomically -- readers never see a partially updated state, and the previous value is released by the collector after the atomic write is visible.
Version-control-style update: check out a local copy, mutate freely, then commit or discard; copy-and-swap maps directly to this workflow and provides the same transactional semantics (Howard Hinnant's analogy from his C++ Con 2018 talk).
Compiler tooling treats the idiom as the canonical self-assignment-safe assignment: LLVM's clang-tidy bugprone-unhandled-self-assignment checker explicitly recognizes 'build a temporary in operator=, then swap it' as correct handling and matches extended (allocator-aware) constructors plus ADL swap forms so real copy-and-swap code is not flagged (llvm/llvm-project PR #147066).
Boost's move/assignment guidance converged on the single by-value form T operator=(T b) { swap(*this, b); return *this; } as the common way to get copy-, move-, and convertible-assignment from one operator, with dedicated macros (BOOST_COPYABLE_AND_MOVABLE_ALT) for classes that adopt it instead of separate overloads.
When a strong guarantee is needed on the standard containers, libc++ maintainers advise exactly this idiom at the call site -- 'construct a new vector and swap it with the one you want to assign to' (libc++ PR #117516 discussion) -- because the library's own copy assignment deliberately offers only the basic guarantee.

name: dependency-injection
document:
dependency-injection
di
constructor injection
setter injection
interface injection
ioc container
pure di
manual di
Supply an object with the collaborators it needs from the outside — through its constructor, its setters/properties, or a dedicated injection interface — so it never constructs or looks a dependency up itself and every wiring decision is made once, in a composition root or container.
An object that creates its own collaborators hard-wires a concrete class, a construction recipe and often a lifetime into itself: swapping the implementation for a test double, a second deployment or a new platform means editing the class, and the dependency graph stays invisible in the API. The recurring trigger is exactly the catalog's rule: an object should not create what it depends on — the caller, the framework or the composition root decides, and hands the dependency in.
Applies whenever a component's collaborators are chosen per deployment, per environment or per test, whenever constructing them is expensive or platform-specific, and whenever a framework owns object creation (request handlers, scheduled jobs, UI screens, message consumers). It matters most in large object graphs where one abstraction has several implementations and lifetimes must be managed (singleton, request-scoped, transient); it is unnecessary when the collaborators are pure values or when construction is a private detail nobody needs to vary.
Web and API backends whose handlers need repositories, clocks, mailers and caches that must be replaced by fakes in tests and by sandbox services in staging.
Hexagonal and clean architectures where the domain declares ports (interfaces) and the infrastructure layer supplies adapters at the composition root.
Frameworks that own object creation — request handlers, scheduled jobs, UI controllers, message consumers — where the framework's injector is the only practical wiring point.
Deployment variants (on-prem vs cloud, SQL vs in-memory, real vs stub payment gateway) selected per environment through binding configuration rather than conditional code.
Plugin and extension systems where the concrete implementation is chosen at start-up from a plugin registry, enabling third-party adapters without touching core code.
Expensive shared resources whose lifetime must be managed centrally (connection pools, HTTP clients, circuit breakers) while service classes stay stateless.
Unit tests that construct the class under test directly with test doubles, and integration tests that swap only the outer layer's bindings.
Microservices with sidecar containers: the sidecar provides logging, tracing and retry policies as injected collaborators, keeping the service logic untouched.
Cloud-native applications where the composition root is the only place that knows whether a dependency resolves locally, across a service mesh, or via a remote gRPC call.
Multi-tenant SaaS where tenant-specific adapters (tenant-scoped repositories, per-tenant feature flags) are bound at the composition root and switched by middleware.
Event-driven systems where message handlers receive their dependencies through injection, making the handler logic identical between in-process and distributed deployment.
AOT-compiled applications (Native AOT, Blazor WebAssembly, serverless) where runtime reflection is unavailable — dependencies are resolved via source generators or manually at the composition root.
Functional codebases using effect systems (ZIO, fp-ts, Reader monad) where the DI container is replaced by typed environments passed through function compositions.
Consumer-driven contract testing (Pact, OpenAPI pact) where DI swaps provider implementations with contract-mock stubs at the boundary, enabling parallel service development without shared integration environments.
Resilience and fault-injection testing: proxies or decorator-based fault injectors (e.g., Gremlin SDK, WireMock) are injected as collaborators to validate retry, timeout and circuit-breaker behaviour under simulated failure conditions.
Single-page application frameworks with DI built into the component tree: Angular resolves components, directives and services through hierarchical injectors, scoping providers to the application root, a component subtree or a route so features override implementations and lazy-load without global registration.
Android apps using Dagger (and Hilt over it) to build the object graph at compile time — generated, reflection-free code, bindings and cycles checked at build time, with field injection reserved for framework-created entry points like Activities and Fragments.
Python web APIs (FastAPI) where each path operation declares Depends(callable) parameters: the framework resolves nested dependency graphs with per-request caching and uses yield-based dependencies to open and close connections around each request.

name: event-aggregator
document:
event-aggregator
event bus
messenger
message bus
event hub
Funnel the events of many source objects into one hub that owns the subscription wiring, so that subscribers register once with the aggregator instead of tracking down and registering with every publisher.
Many components raise events and many components want to react: if every consumer registers directly with every producer, each consumer has to find the sources and subscribe to each event type separately, each producer accumulates knowledge of who listens, and both sides repeat the same registration and unsubscribe code at every pair. The trigger is a many-publisher / many-subscriber setting in which the wiring itself has become the maintenance problem.
In-process, event-driven software - a modular UI shell, a domain-event pipeline inside one bounded context, a plugin host, a simulation or instrumentation layer - where publishers and subscribers grow independently, both sides should stay unaware of each other, and registration plus lifetime management should live in one place. The aggregator is a component- or module-scope element of one process (one node); events that must cross a process boundary, survive a restart or be delivered reliably need a messaging channel instead.
Modular UI shells (WPF/MAUI, Android, SwiftUI) where view models living in separate modules must react to each other without holding references — the classic Prism and CommunityToolkit.Mvvm scenario.
Domain-event fan-out inside one bounded context: 'order placed' reaches billing, stock, notification and audit services that each subscribe to the hub instead of to the Order aggregate.
Plugin, extension or rule hosts where the listener set is only known at runtime and plugins are loaded and unloaded while the application runs.
Test and simulation harnesses: a test subscribes to the hub, drives one publisher and asserts on the published events without wiring up the real consumers.
Cross-cutting instrumentation and audit: metrics, tracing, logging and audit collectors receive events from many components through one hub rather than being called from each component.
Long-running services broadcasting rare state changes (configuration reload, presence change, feature-flag flip) to every interested subsystem exactly once per change.
Micro-frontend communication: independent web apps in one page communicating via a shared event bus with typed event maps and cross-tab synchronization (BroadcastChannel bridge).
IoT sensor aggregation: many sensor streams funnelled through one hub for filtering, transformation and fan-out to display or downstream processing services.
CQRS command/event pipeline: commands are dispatched to handlers that publish domain events through a bus; read-model projectors subscribe to build consistent query views.
Redux/Flux-style frontend state updates where UI components subscribe to dispatched actions rather than mutating shared state directly.
Event storm prevention harness: wrapping a batch save operation in a scoped subscriber-disable guard so that handlers triggered by the save do not re-publish events that would cascade back through the same handler.
Transactional outbox companion: publishing domain events through the hub after a transaction commits, ensuring that state changes and event emission are not separated by a process crash (in-process equivalent of the outbox pattern).
Java in-JVM decoupling with Guava EventBus: objects register via @Subscribe-annotated methods and publishers post typed events that the bus routes by parameter type (superclasses and interfaces included), with unmatched events wrapped as DeadEvent for a second-chance subscriber.
Spring application-context event pipeline: beans publish through ApplicationEventPublisher and react via @EventListener methods - in-process domain-event fan-out with the ApplicationEventMulticaster owning the registry, no message broker involved.
Vue 2 cross-component communication through a shared root instance used as a global bus ($on/$emit); Vue 3 removed that instance-emitter API, making external typed emitters like mitt, provide/inject, or a store (Pinia) the supported replacement - a cautionary real-world case for untyped global buses.

name: extensible-visitor
document:
extensible-visitor
extensible visitor pattern
extensible visitors with defaults
Keep the visitor open on both axes at once - new element kinds and new operations arrive without editing or recompiling any visitor that already exists - by giving every visitor a default method that catches element kinds it was not written for, introducing extended element kinds under an intermediate base whose accept hooks overload (not override) accept, and extending an operation by subclassing the existing concrete visitor so it inherits every case it already handled.
A classic Visitor is cheap in one direction only: a new operation is a new visitor, but a new element kind forces every visitor to grow one more method, so shipped visitors must be edited and redeployed. The trigger is an element hierarchy that is extended by parties who do not own the operations - language dialects, plugin node types, versioned grammars, third-party message formats - where the existing operations must keep working unchanged on the extended structure.
Recursively defined element hierarchies (abstract syntax trees, intermediate representations, document and message models) that grow over time, in a statically typed language whose visitors are concrete classes or interfaces with default bodies, and where the traversal logic itself lives inside the operations. It pays off when old operations must run against new element kinds and when element kinds are added by a different team than the operations; it assumes the visitor protocol can carry a default case and that a runtime type test is acceptable on the dispatch path.
A compiler front-end whose node kinds are extended by language dialects while every existing analysis pass keeps running unchanged (the extensible-compiler case the pattern was derived from).
An IDE or linter analysing a versioned language grammar: the version-1 analysis must not be recompiled when version 2 adds syntax nodes it does not understand.
Plugin systems where third-party modules contribute new node types (document formats, workflow elements, protocol messages) to a host that ships the operations.
Optimisation or lowering pipelines whose passes are shipped separately from the node hierarchy: the platform team adds representations, users add passes.
A published visitor API where other teams implement visitors and the element set grows every release, making 'which kinds does this visitor handle' an explicit, versioned contract.
Migration and validation tooling that must keep working on messages produced by newer producers than the tool itself.
Serialization and schema-generation frameworks such as Jackson's JsonFormatVisitor API, which uses a visitor to traverse Java type hierarchies for JSON/XML schema generation and allows third-party serializers to contribute handlers for new POJO shapes without modifying the core framework.
Query engines over tree-structured data (e.g. Apache Calcite's relational algebra, Rascal's AST analysis): new relational operators or AST node types are contributed by extension modules while existing optimisers and evaluators continue to function unchanged.
Static analysis and bug-finding tools (Coverity, CodeQL, ESLint plugin architectures): new checker plugins add new node-type coverage while the core traversal engine ships unchanged, and old checkers degrade gracefully over unknown node types.
Game engine entity-component systems: new component types are contributed at runtime while existing systems (physics, rendering, AI) continue to process entities; the visitor with default case handles component types added after a given system was written.
Python's ast.NodeVisitor: visit() dispatches to a visit_<Node> method and falls back to generic_visit as the built-in default case, so analysis tools written before newer node kinds existed (Match, TryStar, TypeAlias) keep traversing Python's evolving AST unchanged, exactly the degrade-don't-break contract of the pattern.
The JDK Compiler Tree API (com.sun.source.tree.TreeVisitor / SimpleTreeVisitor): every visit method defaults to visitOther/defaultAction as the catch-all, so javac-based tooling written against Java 8 trees keeps compiling and running as Java adds records, patterns and switch labels - old visitors land in visitOther instead of failing.
Roslyn's CSharpSyntaxVisitor / CSharpSyntaxWalker: the generated visitor carries one Visit method per syntax node kind plus DefaultVisit as the default case, and each C# language version extends the node hierarchy while existing analysers and the compiler's own passes keep working over the extended tree.

name: transaction-script
document:
transaction-script
service object
Organizes the business logic of a single request as one procedure - read the data it needs, validate and calculate, write the results and complete in one database transaction - trading object-model structure for a straight-line implementation that can be read top to bottom.
A request-scoped use case (book a room, place an order, recognize revenue, import a file) has to be implemented, and its logic mixes input validation, calculation and persistence. Modelling the domain as objects may be premature, or the team may not be ready for it, yet the implementation still needs each request's steps to stay visible and its transaction boundary to be explicit.
Applies where business logic is simple to moderately complex, where the system is naturally described as a series of transactions each driven by one request (HTTP handler, CLI command, queue message, batch job), and where a thin data-source gateway or the database itself is the persistence seam. Also the right starting point under delivery pressure or for a team new to domain modelling - provided the growth path to a Domain Model is watched deliberately.
Booking a hotel room: check availability, calculate the rate, insert the booking and confirm - one request, one transaction.
Revenue recognition (Fowler's example): given a contract and an as-of date, calculate the recognitions and persist them, or report the revenue already recognized.
CRUD write endpoints in a simple admin or back-office application where each screen maps to one operation.
Batch and integration jobs: import a file, validate rows, write the accepted rows and report the rejects in one transaction per batch.
Queue or message handlers that carry out one command (place order, cancel subscription, refund payment) and acknowledge only after commit.
Reporting and ETL steps that read a slice of data, transform it and write results, where the logic is genuinely a straight line of steps.
Django request-atomicity: with ATOMIC_REQUESTS enabled (or @transaction.atomic on the view), the whole view function is the script - Django begins the transaction at request start, commits on a successful response and rolls back on exception, exactly the one-script-one-transaction shape.
Laravel request handlers that wrap the validate-calculate-persist sequence in a DB::transaction closure: the closure commits when it returns and rolls back automatically if it throws, so the closure body is the script and its extent is the boundary.
Spring @Transactional service methods: an AOP proxy begins the transaction before the method and commits after it returns, making each annotated method a Transaction Script whose signature is the request and whose boundary is declarative.

statement: Decide where and how persistent entities retain their stable database identifier so repeated loads, references, cache entries, updates, and deletions resolve to the same stored record.
name: identity-field
document:
identity-field
primary key field
identity column
Store the relational primary key inside the object so that an in-memory instance and its database row are recognised as the same entity across sessions, caches and process restarts, instead of relying on object identity.
Mappers, identity maps and unit-of-work bookkeeping need a stable handle on every object: without a key carried by the object there is no way to tell whether two instances are the same row, which row an UPDATE or DELETE must touch, or what value a referring row should store - and loading the same row twice silently produces two divergent objects.
Applies wherever objects outlive a single operation and are mapped to key-addressed rows: entities behind a Data Mapper or Row Data Gateway, aggregates in a Repository, session caches keyed by table plus id, and object graphs whose children must refer to a parent that is not inserted yet. The key has to survive serialisation and cross-process calls, and for application-generated keys it must exist before the row does.
ORM entities in a session: load a row into an object, mutate business fields, then flush an UPDATE or DELETE targeted at the same identity.
API resources addressed by key: /orders/{id} endpoints that fetch, mutate and delete by identity, with links stored as keys instead of object references.
Session-scoped identity maps and second-level caches keyed by (table, key), which need the key before they can return an existing instance.
Object graphs with parent-child references: the child's foreign key needs the parent's identity, generated before the insert (UUID/sequence) or read back after it (RETURNING/getGeneratedKeys).
Audit, versioning and optimistic locking: change logs and Version Number checks identify the affected row by its key.
Distributed or sharded writes: client-generated keys let a router place the row and let a retry overwrite the same identity idempotently.
Event-sourced aggregates: the aggregate root's identity is the correlation ID carried in every command and event, allowing the event log to reconstruct state by replaying events keyed to that identity.
GraphQL Relay node identification: globally unique node IDs are built from the entity's identity (base64 type-prefixed id), enabling the standardised node query and cache reching defined in the Relay specification.
Multi-tenant SaaS with tenant-scoped identity: a composite key of (tenant_id, id) ensures a tenant can never address another tenant's rows, even if the local id numbers happen to collide.
Idempotent message processing: a command's correlation ID (the entity's identity) lets a handler detect a duplicate and skip reprocessing without a distributed lock.
Hibernate ORM entities with an @Id and Session persistence context: loading by identifier reuses the session's first-level identity, while the chosen generated-id strategy determines when the key becomes available.
PostgreSQL tables with GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY and INSERT ... RETURNING id: the database owns key generation, then the mapper reads the assigned identity back onto the object in the same write.
Relay GraphQL servers implementing the Node interface: expose a globally unique opaque id and refetch the same object through node(id), carrying entity identity across a client cache and API boundary.

statement: Decide where and how persistent entities retain their stable database identifier so repeated loads, references, cache entries, updates, and deletions resolve to the same stored record.
name: foreign-key-mapping
document:
foreign-key-mapping
foreign key association
Map an association between objects to a foreign key column in the referencing table: the mapper stores the referenced object's identity key on save and resolves that key back into an object reference (usually through an identity map) on load.
Domain objects refer to each other by reference, but the relational schema can only hold key values in columns: something must translate an object reference into the referenced row's key, decide on which side of the relationship the column lives, and turn the stored key back into an object when a row is read.
Object-relational persistence of a pointer-linked domain model: entities are spread over normalised tables with primary keys and referential constraints, mappers (hand-written or framework-provided) sit between the two worlds, and the association may be single-valued or a collection, optional or mandatory, unidirectional or bidirectional.
Orders and customers: Order holds a Customer reference persisted as customer_id, with a constraint that keeps orphan orders out of the orders table.
Self-referential trees: a page's parent reference stored as a nullable parent_id in the same table.
Bidirectional graphs where one side stores the key and the other side exposes a collection over the same column.
Partial loading: dashboards list rows while the referenced object is fetched only when a detail view touches the reference.
Hand-written persistence layers over SQL: C and C++ structs/classes carry the key, and a mapper resolves it explicitly.
Legacy or externally owned schemas where the key column is unconventionally named or unconstrained, so the mapping must configure column and reference names.
DDD cross-aggregate references: an Order aggregate holds a CustomerId value (not a Customer reference) and resolves it via repository lookup, keeping aggregate boundaries intact.
Hierarchical data with self-referential FKs: a tree node stores parent_id; the mapper resolves the parent via identity map and exposes children as a lazy collection.
Polymorphic association workaround: rather than one FK column pointing at multiple parent tables, use per-parent intersection tables with real FK constraints (the sanctioned pattern for 'one child belongs to one of several parents').
Soft-delete with FK constraints: a deleted-flag column on the parent combined with RESTRICT/NO ACTION prevents hard deletes until children are archived, while the ORM tracks the soft-delete state separately.
Read-replica routing: FK resolution through the identity map works identically against a read replica, since the key-based lookup hits the replica and the identity map avoids a join.
Bulk import with deferred constraint checking: insert all parent and child rows with NO ACTION constraints, then SET CONSTRAINTS ALL DEFERRED and commit — the transaction boundary defers FK checking to the end.
Django ORM: a ForeignKey field maps to a column named <field>_id holding the related row's primary key; code assigns and navigates model instances while Django's descriptors translate to the key column (db_column overrides the name on legacy schemas).
Rails Active Record: belongs_to places the key on the declaring table (books.author_id references authors.id); the sanctioned setup is a migration adding the column with t.belongs_to :author, foreign_key: true plus an index, and belongs_to's presence validation covers only writes that go through the model.
Prisma ORM: relation fields (author: User) have no database column at all — only the relation scalar field (authorId) declared in @relation(fields: [authorId], references: [id]) is the foreign key; relationMode=prisma drops the constraint entirely and emulates referential integrity in the client.

statement: Decide where and how persistent entities retain their stable database identifier so repeated loads, references, cache entries, updates, and deletions resolve to the same stored record.
name: embedded-value
document:
embedded-value
embedded value object
embedded value type
Map a value object into several columns of its owner's row instead of giving it a table of its own, so a small identity-less concept survives the relational round trip without a join, a key or a foreign key.
A value object - a currency-aware money amount, a date range, an address, a coordinate - has no identity and no lifecycle of its own, so storing it as a row forces an invented key, an extra table and a join on every read. At the same time the object must not be flattened into loose primitives on the domain side: the cluster of attributes has to stay one typed concept with its invariants, and the mapper still has to write and read each of its fields. The decision is therefore where the fields go, not whether the object exists.
Relational stores, wherever a mapper persists an entity that holds one or more value objects. Applies when the value's fields belong together in the same row as the owner - money in an order, a period in an employment, an address in a customer - when the value is never queried on its own and never referenced by another row, and when the same value type is reused across several owners so its column layout must be reusable. The decision is taken together with the key strategy: the value contributes columns, never a key.
Money amounts on orders, invoices and payments: amount plus currency stored as two columns on the order row, so Money stays a typed concept in the domain model and the currency constraint is a column-level CHECK rather than application logic.
Date ranges for employment periods, validity windows and booking intervals: a Period value object (start date, end date, possibly duration) embedded in the Employment or Booking entity, with database-level constraint that end ≥ start.
Postal addresses and contact details on customers, suppliers and shipments: multiple addresses per owner (billing, shipping, registered office) are each embedded with an explicit @AttributeOverride prefix, so all address fields coexist on the same row without collision.
Geographic coordinates, dimensions and physical measurements: a Measurement value object (numeric value, unit of measure, precision) embedded in a Product or Cargo entity, ensuring the unit travels with the value and is never accidentally omitted.
Insurance premiums, claim amounts and benefit calculations: a Money-equivalent with currency, amount and settlement-date fields embedded on the Policy or Claim entity, enabling column-level NOT NULL and CHECK constraints on the financial figures.
Patient vitals and clinical measurements in healthcare systems: a VitalReading value object (value, unit, capture-timestamp, device-id) embedded in an Encounter or Observation entity, with the unit of measure encoded alongside the value so no ambiguity exists across international deployments.
Order-line price breakdowns in e-commerce: unit price, tax amount, discount amount and currency each live as columns on the order-line row, keeping the pricing calculation auditable and queryable at the column level rather than hidden in a serialized payload.
Audit timestamps and changelog entries: an AuditRecord value object (who, when, which version) embedded in entities that need lightweight audit metadata without a separate audit-log table join.
Sensor readings with calibration metadata in IoT platforms: a CalibratedMeasurement value object (raw value, calibrated value, unit, calibration-date) embedded in a SensorReading entity, stored alongside the owning sensor's row for co-located access.
Reusable name, code and identifier value types shared across many entities: a natural-key identifier (scheme, value, label) embedded wherever it appears, with one declaration of the three-column layout that every owner reuses.
Legacy wide tables that must map onto a clean domain model: a denormalised legacy schema is wrapped with embeddables that restore the typed concept, allowing a clean object model without introducing new tables.
Doctrine ORM embeddables: a User entity embeds an Address value object whose street, postal code, city and country are inlined as user-table columns with a configurable prefix (address_ by default, customizable or disabled via columnPrefix), and DQL filters on u.address.city as if it were a native field.
EF Core 8+ complex types: an Address or Coordinate value object declared with ComplexProperty is stored inline in the owner's table via table splitting, or as a single JSON column, with copy-by-value semantics and full ExecuteUpdate support - the recommended successor to owned entities for identity-free value objects.
Jakarta Persistence 3.2 embeddables: a Java record annotated @Embeddable is stored as an intrinsic part of the owning entity and shares its identity, making immutable record-based value types first-class embedded values under the specification itself.
