name: consumer-driven-contract-test
document:
consumer-driven-contract-test
consumer-driven contract
contract test
Capture, from each consumer's own tests, the concrete provider interactions that consumer depends on, and verify the provider against that contract inside the provider's own build, so consumer and provider can be released independently without a shared end-to-end environment.
Independently released consumers and providers must keep working together, yet the only reliable check is a shared end-to-end environment per pair - slow, brittle and usually out of date; at the same time the provider cannot see which parts of its API each consumer actually exercises, so every refactoring is a guess about who will break.
HTTP/request-reply, messaging and gRPC integrations where consumer and provider are owned by different teams on different release cadences and each consumer uses only a narrow slice of the provider's surface. It assumes the provider team is willing to run verification of consumer contracts in its own build; without that half, the consumer test is only a better mock.
Microservice landscapes where a front end, a mobile app or another service consumes an API released by a different team on its own schedule.
A provider team that must refactor or replace internals and needs to know, before merging, which consumer expectations it is about to break.
Mobile or desktop clients that cannot be deployed in lockstep with the backend, so each client's expectations must hold against every backend version.
Event- and message-based integrations (Kafka, SQS, SNS, RabbitMQ) where the consumer processes messages produced by another team; contracts pin the message body shape and metadata (topic, headers, content-type) while abstracting the transport.
Migration or strangler-fig work, where a replacement provider must be proven compatible with the existing consumers before traffic is moved.
Using the contract as the source of stubs for development and integration environments, so those environments no longer need the real provider.
BFF (Backend for Frontend) patterns where each frontend channel (web, mobile, third-party) has its own contract with a shared backend, allowing independent evolution of each BFF without cross-channel breakage.
Multi-team Kafka event streaming where consumers (downstream services) define which topics, partitions and message schemas they depend on, so producers can evolve events without silently breaking subscribers; Pact message pacts handle both JSON and Schema Registry messages (with magic bytes for Avro/Protobuf over Schema Registry).
gRPC service integrations where protocol buffer message shapes are exercised by the actual consumer client code, pinning the wire format, service method signatures and metadata the consumer actually calls; synchronous message pacts cover the request-response pairing.
Breaking up a monolith: individual microservices are extracted and their CDC contracts verify that the new service boundaries behave identically to the original module interfaces before traffic is migrated.
Schema Registry integrations (Confluent, AWS Glue) where consumers pin compatible message schemas and producers must not publish breaking schemas without migrating all dependent consumers first.
Third-party or vendor API integrations where the consumer team cannot rely on the provider to run verification: the consumer-side mock-only workflow with published contracts documents expectations even without provider participation.
Webhook and callback integrations where a provider calls a consumer-defined endpoint; CDC captures the consumer's expected payload shape, headers and authentication, and the provider verifies it can deliver to that shape.
Contract migration at scale: when a provider must migrate from v1 to v2 of an API, CDC with pending/wip pacts allows the provider to signal new expectations to consumers without blocking either side's pipeline while migration is in progress.
Spring Cloud Contract in JVM/Spring landscapes: the consumer's contract change lands in the producer's repository (or an external contract repo), the producer build generates verification tests from the contract DSL, and the consumer develops against StubRunner-served WireMock stubs pulled from an artifact repository (Nexus/Artifactory) - the contract is the single artifact both sides build from.
Nubank replaced its flaky shared-environment end-to-end suite with consumer-driven contract tests to regain deploy velocity - the public account of the pattern paying off as an e2e-substitute at a single organisation rather than as an addition to it.
Large polyglot estates such as JSTOR/ITHAKA (300+ microservices, 12+ teams, Pact) and M1 Finance (Pact plus PactFlow rolled out to 17 teams in under six months): the broker's compatibility matrix replaces per-pair end-to-end environments as the release gate.

name: double-dispatch
document:
double-dispatch
multiple dispatch
multiple polymorphism
two-level dispatch
Select the operation to execute from the runtime types of two collaborating objects, so behaviour can vary along two independent type axes instead of being resolved by hand-written type tests in the caller.
Behaviour depends on the runtime type of *two* objects - element and visitor, shape and surface, left operand and right operand - but an ordinary call resolves on the receiver only (or, in dynamic languages, on no argument at all). Every operation then grows its own type-test ladder, knowledge of the concrete classes leaks into callers, and adding a class silently breaks the cases nobody remembered to extend.
Object models in which two type hierarchies interact: shape x medium, AST node x operation, operand x operand, entity x entity in a collision matrix. It applies when the pair-specific behaviour is a real matrix rather than a single special case, when each hierarchy evolves on its own schedule, and when the language's own dispatch resolves only one of the two runtime types (classic single-dispatch OO) or none of them (method overloading is bound statically).
Collision and interaction rules in games and simulations: every pair of entity types (bullet × wall, ship × asteroid) has its own outcome. Double dispatch cleanly selects the correct collision algorithm at runtime. Used in Unity, Unreal, and custom game engines via visitor-like hierarchies or type-indexed collision matrices. Spatial partitioning (quad-trees, oct-trees) is used alongside to reduce O(n²) pair checks. Examples: Unity physics collision callbacks, Unreal collision/overlap event system, Box2D physics engine, custom engines with AABB/Sphere/OBB hierarchies.
Geometry predicates between two shape hierarchies: intersect, contains, distance and other predicates where each pair (circle-circle, circle-rectangle, rectangle-rectangle) uses a different algorithm and pairs are not symmetric. Used in game physics engines, computer graphics rendering pipelines, and GIS systems. Examples: Box2D, Chipmunk, computer graphics rendering engines.
Numeric promotion and operator semantics between unrelated numeric types: Rational × Integer, Money × Currency, BigInt × Float — operations that must consult both operands' concrete types. Ruby's Numeric#coerce is the canonical language mechanism enabling this pattern. Examples: Ruby Numeric#coerce, Java BigDecimal arithmetic, C# decimal/float/double mixed arithmetic.
Document rendering and media output: shapes or widgets × output targets (screen, printer, PDF, HTML), where each combination emits different code. The medium axis and the shape type axis independently determine the rendering path. Examples: Qt/wxWidgets painting systems, Java AWT/Swing paint(Graphics) dispatch, WebKit/Blink layout engines.
AST traversal and transformations: one node hierarchy × many analyses (type check, pretty-print, evaluate, optimise) — the primary use case the Visitor pattern was designed for. Each (Operation × NodeType) pair is a separate handler. Examples: Babel/TypeScript compiler, LLVM compiler infrastructure, Roslyn C# compiler API.
Plugin and extension architectures: a host application defines an element hierarchy and a plugin defines a visitor; new plugins add operations without modifying element classes. Examples: Eclipse IDE plugin system, Visual Studio Analyzer/extension APIs, static analysis tools (linters, formatters).
Serialization and deserialization frameworks: Format (JSON, XML, binary, protobuf) × type — each combination may need different encoding rules. Examples: Jackson/Gson in Java, Python dataclasses serialization, Protocol Buffers schema evolution.
Protocol handling in parsers and state machines: handler depends on both message kind and connection/session kind — a state × event matrix. Used in network protocol stacks, parsers, and finite state machine implementations. Examples: HTTP server request routing, game AI state machines, telecom protocol state tables.
Event handling in GUI frameworks: a widget hierarchy × an event hierarchy (mouse, keyboard, focus) — each (Widget × Event) pair may require different handling logic. The classic AWT/Swing processEvent double-dispatch was the motivating example for several academic multi-dispatch papers. Examples: Java AWT event delegation, Qt event handling, Swing ActionMap/InputMap.
Message routing in game architectures: entity × message type routing where the correct handler depends on both the receiver entity's type and the message's payload type. Common in Entity-Component-System (ECS) patterns where components process messages differently. Examples: Unity MessageSystem, Amazon Lumberyard (component × message routing).
Numeric and array operators as native multiple dispatch: Julia makes the pair axis first-class - arithmetic and promotion operators are generic functions whose methods select on the runtime types of all arguments, and the compiler emits a specialised version per concrete combination (Int,Int vs Float64,Float64) instead of a hand-rolled accept/visit round-trip; promote_type absorbs cross-type cells. The canonical modern realisation of the pattern. Examples: Julia Base arithmetic, Julia promote_type/coercion, heterogeneous-array dispatch costs documented in the Julia performance guide.
Generic functions in CLOS and Dylan-family languages: method selection keyed by the classes or identities of every required argument, with method combination (call-next-method) resolving ambiguity - double dispatch without the intrusive accept method, and the benchmark every manual encoding is measured against. Examples: ANSI Common Lisp CLOS defgeneric/defmethod, Dylan generic functions.
Runtime binder dispatch on the CLR: the C# dynamic keyword defers overload resolution to the Dynamic Language Runtime, binding the call on the runtime types of receiver and arguments with call-site caching; CallSiteBinder.Bind is documented as runtime binding (double-dispatch). A missing pair surfaces as a runtime binder exception rather than a compile error, so it suits dynamic-language and COM interop boundaries more than closed business matrices. Examples: DLR call-site caching, IronPython/IronRuby interop, COM interop via the runtime binder.

name: abstract-factory
document:
abstract-factory
kit
factory of factories
Expose one creation contract for each product kind in a coherent family, letting clients switch the selected family at the composition root without naming concrete products or mixing incompatible variants.
A client must construct several related products that collaborate as a matched set, but direct construction spreads family keys and concrete class names through the code. Adding a family then becomes configuration branches plus constructor edits, while mixing products from different families can fail only after incompatible objects interact.
Use in object- or interface-based subsystems with two independent axes of change: product kinds (button, slider, connection, command) and product families or variants (dark/light, PostgreSQL/Oracle, AWS/GCP). The family is normally selected once at a composition root, products from one family are intended to collaborate, and clients must compile, test and ship without knowing concrete product types; if products are intentionally mixed or only one kind is created, use a smaller creator instead.
Cross-platform or themable UI toolkits: Qt's QStyleFactory resolves keys such as "windows" and "fusion" to built-in or plugin QStyle implementations that govern a coherent widget look-and-feel; a fuller abstract factory applies the same family key across several product interfaces.
Provider-independent database code: ADO.NET's DbProviderFactory/DbProviderFactories create a matched DbConnection, DbCommand, DbParameter and DbDataAdapter set for a selected provider such as SQL Server or OLE DB.
Parser-provider plugins: JAXP's DocumentBuilderFactory and SAXParserFactory hide implementation classes behind standard factory APIs, allowing the composition root to select a provider while client code uses parser abstractions.
Java's ServiceLoader documentation uses a CodecFactory service with getEncoder and getDecoder operations; the selected provider supplies a coherent codec family while clients depend only on the service interface.
Test infrastructure: an in-memory factory family whose products are fakes, injected in place of the production family so integration tests need no network.
Game and simulation engines: per-biome object families (terrain, props, audio) that must stay aesthetically consistent when a level is loaded.
SaaS multi-tenant applications: per-tenant theme factories so every rendered page uses the tenant's brand colours, fonts and spacing without per-request conditionals.
Document-format parsers: factory per format (PDF, HTML, EPUB) producing matched tokenizer, layout engine and renderer so a viewer can switch formats from a single configuration key.

name: recursive-descent-parser
document:
recursive-descent-parser
recursive descent
recursive descent parsing
Parse a small grammar by translating every rule directly into a function that consumes the tokens the rule matches and calls the functions of the rules it references, so the parser's control flow is the grammar itself and stays readable, debuggable and free of a code-generation step.
A hand-written parser is the only option - no generator in the toolchain, or the grammar is a small DSL - yet the grammar is not a flat token sequence: alternatives must be chosen from lookahead, repetition must become a loop, and the natural grammar for expressions is left-recursive, which a top-down parser cannot translate directly. Without a disciplined mapping from rules to functions the parser degenerates into ad-hoc index arithmetic and exception-driven backtracking, and errors end up without positions.
Front ends for small languages, DSLs, query/filter/rule grammars, configuration and protocol formats, and the parsing layer of compilers and interpreters that want no code-generation step. It applies when a lexer or token stream already exists (or is cheap to write), the grammar is small to medium and reasonably LL-friendly or rewritable into LL form, and the team values readable, step-debuggable, position-precise parsing over generated tables.
Front ends for small languages, DSLs and configuration formats (filter expressions, rule engines, policy languages, template syntaxes) where a generator and its build integration would be overkill.
Expression and statement parsing in single-pass compilers and interpreters that emit bytecode or IR while parsing, as in Crafting Interpreters' Lox.
Tooling for a grammar you own - formatters, linters, syntax highlighters, language servers - where error tolerance, multiple diagnostics and exact positions matter more than raw throughput.
Protocol and wire-format decoding with a small fixed grammar, where errors must carry byte offsets and malformed input must be rejected deterministically.
Context-dependent or indentation-sensitive syntaxes (templates with interpolation, layout-based blocks, configuration with embedded expressions) that a generated lexer handles poorly.
Codebases that must not carry generated code: security-reviewed, vendored or cross-compiled projects where an ordinary source file beats a build-time generator.
Clang's C-family front end uses a unified hand-built recursive-descent parser for C, C++, Objective-C and Objective-C++, pairing rule-oriented control flow with production-quality diagnostics.
The Go standard library's go/parser is a production recursive-descent parser for Go source, with explicit parser state, nesting-depth guards and error recovery.
rustc_parse is the Rust compiler's recursive-descent parser module, showing how a hand-written parser can scale to macros, recovery modes and detailed token/state handling.
Lua's reference implementation compiles with lparser.c, a single-pass recursive-descent parser that emits bytecode opcodes while reducing expressions instead of building a syntax tree, with precedence handled by parsing levels.

name: cursor-pagination
document:
cursor-pagination
keyset pagination
cursor-based pagination
Bound what a read boundary returns for a large or changing ordered collection by sending one page plus an opaque continuation token that pins the filter and ordering, so clients advance deterministically without offsets and without watching rows move under them.
A boundary must expose a collection that is too large to return at once and keeps changing while clients read it. Offset or page-number requests make the store count or scan everything up to the requested page, and concurrent inserts or deletes shift rows across page boundaries so consumers see duplicates or miss items; the server has no way to state where the sequence should resume.
Any read boundary - an HTTP or gRPC list operation, a GraphQL connection, a database-backed feed, a batch export job - over an ordered collection that is large, growing, or read under concurrent writes, where the server can identify a unique, immutable ordering key and wants to cap both response size and per-request query cost while letting clients iterate the whole sequence.
Public REST or gRPC list endpoints over unbounded, growing tables - messages, orders, audit events - where deep offsets are slow and responses must stay small.
Infinite-scroll or load-more feeds that keep returning newer items while a user scrolls, with the already-seen pages stable against inserts.
Whole-collection sync and export jobs (warehouse loads, backups, search reindexing) that must iterate every row exactly once while writers continue.
GraphQL Relay connections where first/after, edges and pageInfo carry the continuation contract in the schema instead of the URL.
Consumers of third-party list APIs (Stripe-style starting_after/has_more, Google page_token iterators) that keep parameters fixed across auto-paginated calls.
Administrative and operational tooling that streams very large tables for verification or cleanup with bounded memory and predictable server load.
Audit log and event stream retrieval where events are append-only and chronological, and clients stream continuously without needing to revisit earlier pages.
Real-time activity feeds (social media timelines, notification streams) where inserts at the head must not disturb pages the user has already loaded.
Database replication and change-data-capture (CDC) pipelines that must consume a changelog exactly once across restarts and failures.
Paginating over search results from a vector database or full-text index where OFFSET at depth is expensive and results may change between queries.
Bi-directional data synchronization (CDC pipelines, replica lag-catching) where a consumer must iterate forward and occasionally needs to resume from a previous position or re-sweep a window — requiring stable forward cursors plus a defined backward-resumption path.
Paginating a partitioned or sharded database table where each partition is queried independently and cursors carry both the partition hint and the per-partition keyset position.
Slack Web API collection methods (users.list, conversations.history) where response_metadata.next_cursor drives the loop, page limits are clamped per method, and expired or malformed tokens surface as invalid_cursor so the client restarts from the first page.
GitHub GraphQL-style cursor connections where first/last (bounded 1-100) and pageInfo.startCursor/endCursor carry the continuation position for after/before traversal.
Timeline-style feeds served by Django REST framework's CursorPagination, whose default -created ordering gives a consistent view that does not repeat items as new rows are inserted.

name: secure-logger
document:
secure-logger
tamper-evident logging
secure audit log
Record security-relevant events through a single logging chokepoint and chain every record's authenticator to its predecessor, so that altering, deleting, reordering or truncating the log is detectable by an independent verifier rather than merely inconvenient for the party being recorded.
The audit trail exists, but the party it records - a privileged operator, a compromised service, the application itself - can also rewrite it: files are appendable and rotatable by the same process that writes them, there is no gap detection when a record or a whole file disappears, and nobody can prove after the fact that a log line is the line that was written. The log answers questions only as long as everyone trusts the host that produced it.
Systems where a security-relevant event stream has evidentiary or compliance weight - privileged action and break-glass accounts, authentication and authorisation decisions, regulated transaction trails - and where an adversary on the recording host (or the recorded subject itself) is inside the threat model. It applies to a component boundary: the application writes through one logger, the store is append-only for that application, and verification happens elsewhere, so key custody and the trust anchor are part of the design rather than an afterthought.
Privileged and administrative activity: break-glass accounts, role and policy changes, configuration and key operations that must remain provable after the fact.
Regulated transaction audit trails (PCI DSS 10.x, HIPAA, SOX) where an independently verifiable sequence of attributable events is the compliance artefact.
Authentication and authorisation decision records: who was denied, by which rule, in which service - the evidence security operations triages incidents from.
Cloud and API activity logging built the CloudTrail way: per-file digests plus signed digest files that chain the previous digest, so a customer can verify what the provider delivered.
Edge and IoT devices that can be physically captured: the device keeps chaining into a remote anchor, so records written before an attack stay trustworthy after it.
systemd-journald Forward Secure Sealing: journalctl --setup-keys keeps a sealing key on the host that derives forward-securely per epoch while the verification key is stored externally; per-epoch SHA-256 HMAC tags seal the journal file, and journalctl --verify with the external key detects alteration, removal or reordering of records.
Certificate Transparency (RFC 6962) generalises the chain into an append-only Merkle tree: the log signs each tree head within the Maximum Merge Delay, and auditors verify with Merkle consistency proofs that newer heads preserve every earlier entry - the anchor is published and independently checked rather than merely kept.
Google Pixel Binary Transparency: factory images are leaves of a tile-based Merkle tree whose signed checkpoint roots are published, and witness monitors routinely verify consistency between checkpoints so a rolled-back or rewritten log is detected by third parties, not just the log operator.

name: newtype
document:
newtype
strong typedef
opaque type
Give a single primitive its own distinct type so that values with different meanings cannot be substituted for one another, and the raw representation is reachable only through the wrapper's own construction and accessors.
Several domain concepts share one representation - customer id, order id and tenant id are all strings or UUIDs, width/height/offset are all numbers, milliseconds and seconds are both integers - and the API therefore accepts them interchangeably. A swapped argument, a mixed unit or a mistyped literal compiles (or runs) silently, and the defect surfaces late, as a wrong lookup or a cross-tenant bug rather than a type error.
Code in which two or more values with the same underlying representation flow through the same functions, collections or persistence mapping, and in which a single value owns a rule (identifier syntax, non-emptiness, numeric range, unit). Applies at the value level of one field; clusters of attributes that change together belong to Value Object, and closed constant sets to Type-Safe Enum.
Identifier families in one codebase: CustomerId, OrderId, TenantId and SessionId all string- or UUID-shaped and passed to the same repository, logger and cache.
Unit-carrying measurements: Milliseconds vs Seconds, Meters vs Feet, Radians vs Degrees, Cents vs Dollars, where arithmetic must stay inside one unit and conversion is explicit.
Validated single values: EmailAddress, PhoneNumber, Iban, Slug, Percentage (0-100), PortNumber, NonEmptyString - parsed once at the edge, trusted everywhere afterwards.
Security-adjacent tokens: API token vs session id vs tenant id, where a swap becomes a cross-tenant or privilege defect rather than a wrong lookup.
Geometry and graphics APIs where Width, Height, X, Y, Offset and Length are all numbers and transposition should be a compile error.
Pagination and buffer arithmetic: PageSize vs PageIndex vs ByteOffset vs Count, integers that are trivially transposable in a long argument list.
Rust's official newtype examples use Millimeters(u32) and Meters(u32) to keep units distinct, and use Wrapper(Vec<T>) to give a local wrapper its own trait implementations.
Scala 3 opaque types model values such as Logarithm over Double as distinct outside their defining scope, with controlled extension methods and no runtime boxing.
Kotlin @JvmInline value classes wrap one property into a non-interchangeable domain type such as Password while allowing unboxed representations in many uses.

name: cancellation-token
document:
cancellation-token
cancellation signal
cooperative cancellation
Give a caller-owned operation tree a one-way request to stop: pass a read-only cancellation signal through every cancellable call, observe it at safe points, clean up what was acquired, and report a distinct cancelled outcome without pretending that cooperative cancellation is forced termination.
A request handler, background job or UI action starts work that fans out into nested calls, tasks or threads. When the caller disconnects, a deadline expires, the user presses stop or a sibling fails, merely abandoning the result leaves already-started work burning CPU, holding connections and calling dependencies. Force-killing a thread or process can interrupt a critical section and corrupt shared state, while a signal that is not propagated or observed cannot stop the call tree or make its cleanup visible to the joiner.
Use where work can outlive the caller's interest and the runtime exposes checkpoints, suspension points or interruptible waits: request-scoped servers, workers, UI tasks, stream pipelines and batch loops. The operation owns cleanup, cancellation may race any checkpoint, and the design must state what happens when a request arrives after an irreversible side effect or while a dependency ignores the signal.
Request-scoped server work: the handler gets a request signal that fires when the client disconnects or the deadline expires, cancelling in-flight database, queue and upstream calls instead of pinning worker threads and connections after the caller is gone.
UI and mobile tasks: navigating away, closing a window or pressing stop cancels the task tree that loads, renders or downloads for that view, and only that view's tokens are affected.
Graceful shutdown: a supervisor stops accepting work and cancels the token shared by worker loops; every worker stops at its next safe point, flushes and releases resources, and the process exits inside the shutdown budget.
Fan-out with short-circuit: as soon as one subtask fails, or as soon as any one result suffices (hedged or racing replicas), the scope cancels the siblings instead of waiting for all of them.
Batch and stream pipelines: a processor subscribes to the pipeline signal and stops consuming and producing when the pipeline is torn down, abandoning the current chunk when the job's deadline elapses.
Testing and tooling: inject an already-cancelled signal, or one cancelled after N iterations, to exercise the stop path without racing an actual shutdown.
HTTP client redirect and retry cancellation: when a request is redirected or a lower-level retry budget is exhausted, cancel the in-flight operation so the client can proceed with the next action without waiting for a result that is no longer relevant.
Health-check abortion: a liveness probe times out or a readiness check fails mid-flight; cancel the in-progress health metric collection so the pod can be restarted or pulled from service without waiting for a hung check.
GRPC deadline and cancellation propagation: a server receives a client deadline and cancellation token; both must be threaded through every async operation so that an expired deadline or a client disconnect promptly frees server resources.
LLM request fan-out: multiple model providers are queried in parallel; the first successful response wins and all pending requests are cancelled immediately, avoiding wasted compute on a result that will be discarded.
Database connection pool eviction: a query timeout or client disconnect cancels the in-flight query, releasing the connection back to the pool before the server's statement timeout fires; the pool's token is derived from the request context so pool eviction and request cancellation share the same stop signal.
Container orchestrator graceful shutdown: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM and waits the terminationGracePeriodSeconds; the application maps SIGTERM to a cancellation token that is shared by all in-flight request handlers, background workers and health-check loops, giving each the termination budget to drain cleanly.
Interactive search with typeahead: each keystroke cancels the previous search task and starts a new one; the token for the previous task is cancelled immediately on the next keystroke, preventing stale results from overwriting fresher ones.
File transfer with resume support: a large upload or download uses chunked transfers; cancelling the transfer sets a flag that causes the next resume attempt to verify which chunks were already received before retransmitting from scratch.
Event streaming with backpressure: a consumer reading from a message queue or Kafka partition uses the cancellation token to stop reading when the application is shutting down or the consumer group is rebalanced, committing its offset before exiting.
Machine learning inference pipeline: a batch inference job can be cancelled when a new model version is deployed or the job's priority drops; the cancellation token is checked between batches so that partial results are preserved and the job can resume without reprocessing completed chunks.
ASP.NET Core's HttpContext.RequestAborted token is passed into HttpClient, database and other long-running operations so a client disconnect or server abort releases work that can no longer contribute to the response.
Go net/http handlers propagate Request.Context through database/sql QueryContext and RPC calls; cancelling the request context closes the subtree's Done channel so backend goroutines can stop and return their resources.
Kotlin kotlinx.coroutines Job cancellation follows structured parent-child scopes, so a screen, request or worker scope can cancel its child coroutines while finally blocks release resources and CancellationException remains distinguishable from failure.
Node.js and browser fetch cancellation: AbortController.signal is passed as { signal } to fetch, EventTarget listeners and streams, so abort() tears down the socket and pending promises; AbortSignal.timeout and AbortSignal.any combine a deadline or several triggers into one signal without polling.
Database query abortion over a side channel: PostgreSQL's frontend/backend protocol sends a CancelRequest on a separate connection carrying the backend PID and secret key, letting a client that gave up - or an administrator via pg_cancel_backend - abort a running query without killing the session.
TPL/PLINQ cancellation acknowledgement: a delegate that throws OperationCanceledException carrying the supplied CancellationToken is treated by the Task Parallel Library as a cancellation acknowledgement rather than a fault, so joiners observe a cancelled task instead of an aggregated error.

name: option-maybe
document:
option-maybe
Option
Maybe
Make the possible absence of a result part of the value and of the signature, so every caller has to decide what happens when nothing is there instead of meeting a null, a sentinel or a silently defaulted value at run time.
A function has something to return for some inputs and nothing for others, but the signature does not say so: it returns a null reference, a sentinel (-1, empty string, NULL), an out-parameter, or a value that quietly means 'not found'. Callers forget the check, dereference the null or treat the sentinel as data, and the 'this case does not exist' path is discovered in production rather than at the call site.
Lookups, parsing, searches, optional configuration, nullable database columns and any API whose result may legitimately not exist - wherever the language can express absence as a type (Option/Maybe/Optional, a nullable type, a union with undefined) or a convention can carry it. It pays off at module and service boundaries, in chains of partial steps, and wherever 'absent' must stay distinguishable from a legitimate empty, zero or falsey value.
Lookups that can miss: configuration keys, cache entries, registry entries, map/dictionary access - either through the language's two-value form or an Optional-returning accessor.
Parsing and conversion (integers, dates, URLs, decimal numbers, external identifiers) where 'no valid value' is a legitimate answer rather than an error.
Searches over collections and structures (find, first, min/max, binary search, regex match, tree traversal) where a miss is part of the contract.
Genuinely optional data: middle names, second addresses, unset feature flags, optional protocol fields - as opposed to missing state, which is a domain error.
Chains of partial steps (look up user, then their company, then its billing address) where any hop may be absent and the whole chain should collapse to 'nothing'.
Boundaries from nullable interfaces: a database column admits NULL, a legacy or interop API returns null or -1, a deserialized document lacks a field - converted once at the adapter.
Container and stream operations that can be empty (head, pop, next, dequeue, min) and should report emptiness instead of throwing or returning a sentinel.
Rust's standard library uses std::option::Option<T> with Some(T) and None for optional values; its map and pattern-matching APIs let lookup or parsing pipelines stop at absence without a null pointer.
Java SE's java.util.Optional<T> is a production API for method results that may be absent: ofNullable converts a nullable boundary value, map/flatMap compose follow-up work, and orElse/orElseThrow make the exit policy explicit.
Scala's standard-library scala.Option[A] models Some/None and documents map, flatMap, and for-comprehensions for chained partial steps; its API also demonstrates wrapping a Java HashMap lookup so a missing key becomes None.

name: facade
document:
facade
façade
Provide one coarse-grained entry interface that hides a subsystem of many cooperating classes behind the few operations its clients actually need, so callers depend on a single stable API instead of orchestrating the subsystem themselves.
Every client of a complex subsystem must know which classes exist, in which order to call them, how to configure and dispose them and how to interpret their errors; that orchestration is then duplicated across the codebase, and any change inside the subsystem ripples through all callers.
Applies when a subsystem (a library, framework, legacy module, remote SDK, or a layer of your own system) is much broader than any single client needs, when its correct use is a recurring sequence of collaborations, and when client code should be insulated from its types and its evolution. Typical at module and system-boundary scope, where one entry point per layer or per external system is wanted.
Wrapping a third-party SDK, media framework or payment/HTTP client behind one class or module that exposes the application's own vocabulary (convert, charge, upload).
Application services that orchestrate repositories, gateways and domain services for one use case (checkout, report generation) and are the only seam controllers or jobs talk to.
Layered systems where every layer offers a facade as its entry point, so dependencies flow through coarse interfaces instead of reaching into a layer's internals.
Isolating a legacy subsystem while it is replaced incrementally: new code depends on the clean facade, and the migration swaps implementations behind it.
Remote and coarse-grained boundaries: a remote facade exposes a few chunky operations over a fine-grained object model to avoid chatty calls (see Remote Facade, Fowler's PEAA).
Startup/teardown sequences and device orchestration (the classic home-theatre example): clients need one 'watch movie' operation, not a dozen subsystem calls in the right order.
Service-container proxy facades (e.g. Laravel): a static-looking front-end that forwards calls to a resolved service instance, giving a terse API without sacrificing testability or DI flexibility.
JPA/service-layer facades: a single transactional entry point that receives DTOs, maps them to domain objects, orchestrates business logic, maps results back, and commits — one transaction per use case.
Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) in microservices: a thin per-client aggregation service (web, mobile, partner) that fans out to downstream microservices, reshapes responses for the client, and handles perimeter concerns. Each BFF is a specialized facade owned by the team that ships the corresponding client.
Anti-Corruption Layer (DDD): a facade placed between a bounded context and an external/legacy system to translate that system's model into domain concepts, preventing external concepts from polluting the internal domain model.
Event-driven/observable facades: a facade that exposes reactive streams (Observables, Promises, async generators) over the subsystem, buffering, batching or debouncing events for consumers that prefer push-based or streaming interfaces.
API gateway composition: an API gateway acts as a system-wide facade that unifies multiple backend services at the edge, handling auth, routing and cross-cutting concerns before delegating to more specific facades or services.
SDK wrapper facades: publishing a public-facing SDK over an internal microservice mesh; the facade shapes the external API surface, applies default configurations, and provides a stable consumer experience independent of internal service topology changes.
SLF4J (Simple Logging Facade for Java): slf4j-api is a minimal logging facade; applications code against Logger.debug()/info() once and bind the concrete framework (Logback, Log4j 2, java.util.logging) at deployment time by swapping the provider jar on the classpath — the textbook runtime-swappable facade.
Spring Framework JdbcClient / JdbcTemplate: a fluent facade over raw JDBC that owns connection and statement lifecycle, iterates ResultSets and translates SQLException into the DataAccessException hierarchy, so callers supply only SQL and result mapping instead of the full boilerplate workflow.
jQuery $.get/$.post/$.getJSON over $.ajax: a per-task facade layer that collapses cross-browser XMLHttpRequest differences, Deferred plumbing and HTTP defaults into one-line calls — the canonical JavaScript-library facade.

name: guarded-suspension
document:
guarded-suspension
conditional block
suspended execution
Suspend a state-dependent method call inside the object that owns the state until another thread makes its guard predicate true, so callers neither poll nor get refused while the object is temporarily not ready.
A method may only proceed while a precondition over shared state holds - a buffer is non-empty, a pool still has a free lease, a session is authenticated, a worker has a task - and that state is produced by another thread at an unknown time. The recurring decision is what the caller should do while the guard is false: refusing the request would drop work the application still needs, forcing the transition would break the object's invariants, and polling wastes a core and still races. Guarded suspension answers it by waiting on a condition the object itself owns, and by making that wait atomic with respect to the state change that ends it.
Concurrent objects whose methods are state-dependent and whose state changes arrive from other threads: bounded buffers and handoff queues, resource pools, server request/response handoffs, readiness and shutdown gates, worker idle loops. Applicable where the runtime can efficiently park or suspend a caller (OS threads, coroutines) and where the object already owns a lock or monitor, so no notification can be lost between the predicate check and the wait. Ill-suited to single-threaded event loops, to callers that must never be delayed, and to waits whose eventual completion cannot be guaranteed.
Actor mailbox handoff: an Akka/Orleans/Swift-Actor mailbox is a lock-free guarded queue; the actor suspends on an empty mailbox and resumes when a message arrives, which is the same monitor-wait pattern expressed at the language level.
Swift async / Structured Concurrency: a Task.sleep or async let that suspends until a condition is a coroutine-level guarded suspension; the suspension point is backed by a condition variable or event channel inside the runtime.
CompletableFuture / async result: a future's blocking get() is a timed guarded suspension on the thread that submitted the asynchronous operation; the completion path (complete()) is the notifier.
Pipeline stage coordination: in a multi-stage streaming pipeline each stage blocks on input while the upstream stage processes, synchronising via a bounded channel whose put/get implement the guard.
Bounded buffers and handoff queues: a consumer's take waits while the buffer is empty and a producer's put waits while it is full (producer-consumer).
Resource pools: acquire blocks until a lease is returned to a connection, thread or object pool instead of failing or spinning when the pool is exhausted.
Server-side handoff: an acceptor or reader thread publishes a request and the worker waits for work to appear; a caller waits for the response slot to be filled.
Readiness and start-up gates: components wait until a dependency reports connected, initialised or ready, and callers wait until a session, device or circuit is open.
Shutdown and flush coordination: a terminator waits until in-flight work has drained, and a flusher waits while the buffer still holds entries (two-phase termination).
Platform queue and channel APIs: BlockingQueue.take/put, Queue#pop, Channel.receive/for-await, condition-variable waits - the same guard hidden behind a library type.
Project Loom virtual threads (JEP 444): a virtual thread calling Object.wait() parks its Continuation; the carrier thread is released for other virtual threads, so the program continues throughput while one virtual thread waits. The guarded action still re-checks the predicate on wake, and the pattern's semantics are preserved — only the threading model changes.
Akka typed actor mailbox: each actor has a single-threaded mailbox; receive() suspends the actor's continuation when the mailbox is empty, resuming when a message is dispatched. This is language-level guarded suspension where the wait set is the mailbox queue and the guard is 'mailbox non-empty'.
Kotlin coroutines rendezvous channel: Channel() (unbuffered/rendezvous) suspends the sender until a receiver is ready, and vice versa — the same lock-free handoff as an unbuffered Go channel. The suspension is a coroutine-level guarded wait on rendezvous.
Python asyncio.Condition: an async context manager that wraps an asyncio.Lock; await cond.wait() releases the lock and suspends the task until notify() is called, making it an async guarded suspension where the runtime schedules other tasks during the wait.
Go unbuffered channel send/receive: goroutine G1 executing ch <- x on an unbuffered channel sleeps (gopark) until goroutine G2 executes <-ch, at which point the runtime directly transfers the value and stack copy (rendezvous handoff). This is the language-level form of guarded suspension: the guard is 'receiver present', the wait set is the sudog queue in hchan.
Erlang/OTP process mailbox: a gen_server receiving messages from its mailbox blocks (receive...end) until a matching message arrives — the OTP process is a state machine whose transitions are guarded by message arrival, making each receive a suspension point in the actor's event loop.
.NET TaskCompletionSource<T>: GetAwaiter().GetResult() on a not-yet-completed TCS is a synchronous guarded suspension; the async continuation (ConfigureAwait, await) is an asynchronous one. SetResult() is the notifier. TCS is a one-shot asymmetric guarded suspension where one side never waits (the completor) and one side always waits (the synchronously blocked caller).
JDK ArrayBlockingQueue: the queue is one ReentrantLock plus two Condition objects, notEmpty and notFull - take() awaits notEmpty while count == 0, put() awaits notFull while the buffer is full, and each signals the other condition only after mutating count and the circular buffer inside the same critical section. It is the reference production realisation of a two-predicate guarded suspension, including the fairness switch and the timed offer/poll variants.
Go standard library: database/sql guards queries against a concurrent Close with closingMutex, which parks readers and the closing writer on two sync.Cond values (read/write), and net/http's Server.Shutdown waits until in-flight requests have drained. Both are the case Go's own guidance reserves sync.Cond for - a predicate that changes back and forth over time rather than a one-shot handoff.
HikariCP connection pool: DataSource.getConnection() suspends the caller until a lease is returned while the pool already holds maximumPoolSize connections, bounded by connectionTimeout (default 30000 ms, minimum 250 ms), after which it throws SQLException rather than waiting on - a guarded suspension in which the deadline is a documented, first-class outcome instead of an accident.

name: table-module
document:
table-module
Organise the domain logic of a table or view as one module with a single instance whose operations act on whole sets of rows, so table-shaped rules are written once against tabular record sets instead of being scattered over per-row objects or per-request procedures.
The rules for a table are set-shaped - recalculating a column across all rows, validating an import batch, posting a period, aggregating or exporting a whole table - and the platform already speaks in tables and record sets (result sets, DataTables, grids, reports). A Domain Model would build one object per row and pay for identity, hydration and per-object behaviour the rules never use, while a Transaction Script repeats the same table-shaped logic in every use case that touches the table.
Data-centric enterprise applications with moderate, table-shaped logic: batch jobs, imports and reconciliation, reporting and export modules, and applications whose UI and data tooling is table-based (typed DataSets, data grids, report engines). It assumes that data access is already provided by a Table Data Gateway or equivalent, and that callers - typically a Service Layer - own the transaction boundary around the module's calls.
Periodic batch posting: recompute balances or fees for every row in a period in one set-oriented pass.
Import and reconciliation: validate, normalise and promote a staging table before its rows become live data, reporting row-level errors as a batch.
Reporting and export modules that fetch a record set for a grid, report engine or CSV/Excel export, where tabular output is the goal.
Bulk recalculation after a rule change: apply a corrected formula to all existing rows of a table without loading them into a model.
Small-to-medium applications where each table has a handful of well-defined operations and no rich invariants spanning rows or tables.
Cleansing and reconciliation jobs over an operational table where the database should do the heavy lifting (aggregate, update ... where) and the application only orchestrates.
.NET ADO.NET typed DataSet / typed DataTable modules: the generated table is the record set, business methods operate over all its rows and it binds directly to grids and report controls.
Ruby on Rails set-oriented surface: an ActiveRecord::Relation scoped to one table applies table-wide rules via update_all/delete_all as a single SQL statement without instantiating row models, whose official documentation warns that validations and callbacks are skipped so the statement must carry the rule.
Django set-wide recalculation: QuerySet.update() and bulk_update() write whole filtered sets with direct SQL that bypasses per-row save(), used exactly where per-object persistence would mean one round trip per row.

name: remote-facade
document:
remote-facade
coarse-grained facade
Provide a single coarse-grained facade over a web of fine-grained objects so that a remote client can complete a unit of work in one round trip, while the fine-grained objects keep their local-only interfaces and the facade stays free of domain logic.
An object model tuned for in-process use has small objects with small methods and heavy interaction. Across a process boundary every one of those interactions becomes a marshalling, security and routing event, so one user action turns into dozens of remote calls; the decision is whether, and at which seam, to replace that chatty protocol with a few coarse operations.
Applies at any distribution boundary - a network hop, a service-mesh sidecar or merely a second process on the same host - where a fine-grained object model or service layer must be made remotely usable. It matters most when the interaction pattern is chatty (many small reads and writes per use case), when the model must not be exposed to remote clients, and when the transport is expensive relative to the work being done.
Enterprise application whose rich domain model is consumed by a thick client, another service or a batch job: the service layer gets a coarse remote interface instead of exposing entities and value objects.
Microservice boundary where a use case (place an order, update a shipment) must be a single call while the fine-grained aggregates stay internal to the service.
Legacy integration: a coarse adapter facade over an old object model so that new clients never see the legacy structure and the old model can be refactored behind it.
Mobile or high-latency clients, where every avoided round trip directly improves perceived latency and battery cost.
Batch and offline clients that need bulk operations (fetch a set, submit a set) instead of per-item calls.
Security boundary: one authenticated, authorised and audited entry point in front of the model.
Salesforce Composite API and Composite Graph API: a client submits related record operations, reference IDs and explicit all-or-none/graph boundaries in one request instead of making a remote call per sObject.
Microsoft Graph JSON batching: a `$batch` request groups up to 20 Graph operations behind one HTTP boundary while dependencies and per-request failures remain visible to the caller.
gRPC services such as the official RouteGuide example: generated stubs expose typed unary or streaming RPCs as the remote contract while the server's fine-grained implementation stays local.

name: update-method
document:
update-method
per-frame update
tick method
Give every live object one self-contained per-frame step and let a single driver call each object's step every frame, so behaviour advances one frame at a time while input and rendering stay responsive.
A running world is full of objects that each have to keep doing their own thing - guards patrolling, statues charging, agents acting - and the recurring decision is where one object's per-frame behaviour lives and how all those behaviours get driven. Coding a behaviour as a loop that runs to completion blocks input and rendering (the skeleton walks, but nobody sees it); coding it inline in the game loop turns the loop into a switchboard over every kind of object, so every new behaviour edits central code; and there is no way for two actors to evolve independently and simultaneously.
Real-time software with many concurrent live objects whose behaviour is mostly independent and must be simulated over time: games, agent-based simulations, animation and particle systems, tick-based servers and live visualisations. It is the natural partner of a frame driver (Game Loop) - the loop supplies the cadence, Update Method supplies the per-object step - and it becomes the wrong shape in turn-based or purely event-driven domains where nothing changes between inputs.
Real-time games and simulations with many concurrent actors: patrolling guards, projectiles, particle effects and crowd agents each advance themselves once per frame while the driver walks the collection.
Component-based engines where the parts of one entity evolve independently - rendering, physics and AI components each implement their own step and the engine's registry dispatches per component (Unity, MonoGame, Bevy, GameplayKit, libGDX).
Per-frame animation and effect timelines outside games: tween/spring systems, sprite animation and UI transitions advanced from the browser's frame callback or a UI toolkit's animation timer.
Tick-based servers and headless simulations: game servers, digital twins and agent-based models where each agent's behaviour is a resumable step and the world advances in whole discrete frames.
Tools, editors and dashboards with continuously animating scenes, where many independent scene items (markers, live charts, gizmos) must advance on every repaint without a central per-item switch.
Porting straight-line behaviour into a frame loop: turning a scripted sequence (walk left, walk right) into a per-frame step, either by storing explicit state or by using coroutines/generators to keep the code linear.
Godot's SceneTree is the driver: a node opts into the walk with set_process(true) and its _process(delta) runs every render frame with the frame time passed in as an argument, while _physics_process(delta) is called at a fixed rate - so one object can implement two steps on two clocks and can leave the walk entirely (set_process(false)) instead of paying an enabled-flag check every frame.
Engines whose built-in driver leaves per-object order unspecified expose the order as configuration: Unity states you should not rely on the order of Update across GameObjects, so real projects fix dependencies through the Script Execution Order panel, a LateUpdate pass that runs after every Update, or the PlayerLoop API rather than through registration order.
Agent-based simulation models step whole populations in NetLogo: the go procedure runs ask turtles [ ... ] to give every agent its one turn and then tick advances the discrete clock - with documented semantics that agents take their turns in random order and only agents present when the ask began get to act.

name: intercepting-validator
document:
intercepting-validator
validation interceptor
Insert one interception layer on the ingress path that validates every inbound message before any handler runs, so that input checking is uniform, central and impossible to forget per endpoint.
Inbound data - HTTP requests, RPC messages, queue events, protocol frames - is validated inside each handler: every new endpoint re-implements parsing, range and encoding checks, rules drift between handlers, and some paths end up with no validation at all. The recurring decision is where to put validation so that all inbound data passes through it exactly once, before application logic.
Request- or message-driven systems with a well-defined ingress - HTTP APIs, RPC services, queue consumers, protocol front ends - where several handlers accept external data, where shared constraints (schema, ranges, encodings, size limits) can be expressed without loading domain state, and where the ingress pipeline (filter chain, middleware stack, plugin pipeline, responder chain) can be owned and configured by the team.
A public REST or GraphQL API where every request body and query parameter must pass schema, range and size validation before any controller is invoked.
A message-queue consumer that validates every inbound event against its schema and version before dispatching it to a handler.
A file or protocol ingest pipeline (CSV, XML, binary frames) that validates frames in one front layer before domain processing begins.
A multi-tenant service that enforces tenant-scoped constraints uniformly - allowed fields, payload caps, encoding policy - on all inbound requests.
An RPC or WebSocket gateway that rejects non-conforming request messages with one error format before they reach service handlers.
A GraphQL API gateway that validates incoming query operations for schema conformance, depth limits and argument types at the boundary before query execution begins.
A gRPC service fronted by a protobuf interceptor that enforces proto-schema type and structural constraints on all inbound RPC requests before they reach the service implementation.
A FastAPI service that attaches a shared Depends() dependency to an APIRouter and uses Pydantic request models so invalid requests are rejected before the path operation.
An ASP.NET Core application that places request validation in the middleware pipeline or a Minimal API endpoint filter, short-circuiting with a problem response before the endpoint delegate.
An Express application that mounts schema-validation middleware on a router before its routes, returning a 4xx response without calling next() when the request is invalid.

name: function-composition
document:
function-composition
compose
function pipeline
Combine a chain of small unary transformations into one reusable function by sequencing them with a composition combinator (compose/pipe), so the order of the steps is stated once, every step stays independently testable, and the chain itself becomes a value that can be named, passed and reassembled.
A transformation that is naturally a sequence of small pure steps gets written as nested calls or as repeated imperative assignment (`h(g(f(x)))`, or `y = f(x); y = g(y); ...; return y`) at every call site. The order is duplicated wherever the chain is used, the intermediate values need throwaway names, steps cannot be reused in a different order, and changing one stage means editing every copy.
Pure or nearly pure value transformations - parsing, normalisation, validation, formatting, pricing, AST rewriting - where each step is unary and the language treats functions as values. It pays off when the chain is reused or assembled from data (configuration, plugin lists, per-request policy), when steps must be unit-tested in isolation, and when the same steps must also run element-wise over a collection or lazily over a stream. It stops applying where steps need side effects or branching between stages: there the shell around the pure core owns control flow.
Input normalisation: trim, parse, canonicalise and validate a payload before it reaches domain logic, with the same chain reused by HTTP handlers and message consumers.
Pricing and rule chains: base price, discount, tax and rounding applied in a fixed, configurable order to an immutable value object.
Compiler and AST work: a pass list of rewrite functions composed once and applied over the tree, with passes added or reordered per optimisation level.
Serialisation and formatting: sanitise, format, encode and sign a document, where each step is tested separately and the composed chain is stored as a constant.
Data transformation over collections: the same pure steps composed into one function and passed to map/filter/stream operations, so element-wise processing reuses the chain.
Policy assembly at startup: the processing chain is built from configuration or plugin registrations and then applied per request without further branching.
Reactive stream processing: RxJS Observable.pipe chains the same logical steps across asynchronous event sequences, with operators composed once and reused across streams.
ETL and data pipeline transformation: extract-transform-load chains where each stage (parse, clean, enrich, aggregate, write) is a unary pure function composed into a reusable pipeline run over batches or streaming data.
HTTP request/response middleware: the middleware stack is a composed function chain where each layer (authenticate, authorise, rate-limit, deserialize, validate) is a unary handler; composition is resolved once at startup.
Matrix and vector transformations in numerical code: each linear algebra operation (scale, rotate, translate, project) is a unary function on a matrix type; composing them once builds the transformation pipeline that is applied to every vertex or pixel.
Ramda pipelines: R.pipe and R.compose assemble reusable data-last transformations from small functions, centralising the order while letting the same composed value run over many inputs.
Redux store setup: Redux's compose helper combines store enhancers right-to-left into one enhancer, so the enhancer order is defined once instead of reconstructed at each store boundary.
lodash/fp transformations: lodash/fp's auto-curried, data-last compose/flow helpers assemble immutable-friendly transformations from reusable steps that can be passed as values.

name: audit-interceptor
document:
audit-interceptor
audit trail interceptor
audit logging interceptor
Declare an audit policy at an invocation seam that records the actor, action, target, correlation id and both attempt and terminal outcome around a delegated operation, then sends the structured event to a dedicated integrity-protected sink, so security accountability is consistent without inline logging in every service.
Security-relevant operations (privileged actions, state changes and access to sensitive data) must be attributable, but inline logging misses denied and failed attempts, varies in schema, can leak raw arguments and disappears with a rolled-back transaction. Teams also need to cover components they cannot modify without pretending that a proxy sees calls that bypass it.
Business or service tiers whose sensitive operations pass through an interceptable seam: container-managed beans, proxied service objects, ORM entity lifecycles, message endpoints or an HTTP pipeline. Audit selection must be declarative and uniform, while the sink has its own integrity and retention requirements (Secure Logger); the design must make mediation gaps, redaction, transaction coupling, failure policy, clock source and correlation propagation explicit.
Business-tier auditing of money-moving or otherwise regulated operations (fund transfer, order placement, claim submission): who requested it, on which object, when, and whether it succeeded.
Privileged administration surfaces (role changes, key rotation, configuration changes) where every sensitive operation must leave a record naming the acting principal.
Authentication and authorization outcomes: successful and failed logins, access-denial decisions and lockouts routed into the same audit pipeline instead of ad-hoc log lines.
Access-to-sensitive-data events (who read which patient/customer record) recorded at the gateway or service boundary to satisfy data-protection obligations.
Retrofitting auditing onto legacy components whose code cannot be modified, by wrapping the service object or binding an interceptor to its interface.
Middleware-level auditing of message endpoints and database calls in a business tier, correlating the caller's subject with the operation performed.
Financial API request interception (Spring Boot global request interceptors) capturing who accessed which endpoint, with what payload, and what outcome — satisfying SOX financial reporting controls.
Entity-level change tracking via ORM subscribers (e.g., EF Core SaveChangesInterceptor, TypeORM subscribers): automatically diff old vs. new property values on create/update/delete and emit audit envelopes without manual logging calls.
API gateway-level audit logging: capture every external API call with timestamp, user identity, endpoint, method, and outcome, correlating across microservices via X-Request-ID / traceparent headers.
Compliance reporting automation: generate audit-ready reports for SOX (~7-year retention), HIPAA (~6-year retention), GDPR (data residency-aware), and PCI-DSS from structured interceptor events.
Zero-trust data access trails: record every read of sensitive fields (PHI, PII, financial data) so data-protection obligations (GDPR Article 5 data minimization, HIPAA access logging) are demonstrably met.
Hibernate Envers: @Audited entity lifecycle changes create per-entity _AUD revisions at transaction commit; a custom revision entity/listener can attach actor or request metadata.
Django admin: django.contrib.admin.models.LogEntry records action time, user, object, addition/change/deletion and change_message for ModelAdmin activity.
Rails Audited: the audited ActiveRecord extension creates audit rows for model create, update and destroy callbacks, including changed attributes and optional acting-user attribution.

statement: Choose where to enforce one consistent policy that captures attributable, outcome-aware security events around delegated payment operations without relying on each service to emit its own records.
name: secure-logger
document:
secure-logger
tamper-evident logging
secure audit log
Record security-relevant events through a single logging chokepoint and chain every record's authenticator to its predecessor, so that altering, deleting, reordering or truncating the log is detectable by an independent verifier rather than merely inconvenient for the party being recorded.
The audit trail exists, but the party it records - a privileged operator, a compromised service, the application itself - can also rewrite it: files are appendable and rotatable by the same process that writes them, there is no gap detection when a record or a whole file disappears, and nobody can prove after the fact that a log line is the line that was written. The log answers questions only as long as everyone trusts the host that produced it.
Systems where a security-relevant event stream has evidentiary or compliance weight - privileged action and break-glass accounts, authentication and authorisation decisions, regulated transaction trails - and where an adversary on the recording host (or the recorded subject itself) is inside the threat model. It applies to a component boundary: the application writes through one logger, the store is append-only for that application, and verification happens elsewhere, so key custody and the trust anchor are part of the design rather than an afterthought.
Privileged and administrative activity: break-glass accounts, role and policy changes, configuration and key operations that must remain provable after the fact.
Regulated transaction audit trails (PCI DSS 10.x, HIPAA, SOX) where an independently verifiable sequence of attributable events is the compliance artefact.
Authentication and authorisation decision records: who was denied, by which rule, in which service - the evidence security operations triages incidents from.
Cloud and API activity logging built the CloudTrail way: per-file digests plus signed digest files that chain the previous digest, so a customer can verify what the provider delivered.
Edge and IoT devices that can be physically captured: the device keeps chaining into a remote anchor, so records written before an attack stay trustworthy after it.
systemd-journald Forward Secure Sealing: journalctl --setup-keys keeps a sealing key on the host that derives forward-securely per epoch while the verification key is stored externally; per-epoch SHA-256 HMAC tags seal the journal file, and journalctl --verify with the external key detects alteration, removal or reordering of records.
Certificate Transparency (RFC 6962) generalises the chain into an append-only Merkle tree: the log signs each tree head within the Maximum Merge Delay, and auditors verify with Merkle consistency proofs that newer heads preserve every earlier entry - the anchor is published and independently checked rather than merely kept.
Google Pixel Binary Transparency: factory images are leaves of a tile-based Merkle tree whose signed checkpoint roots are published, and witness monitors routinely verify consistency between checkpoints so a rolled-back or rewritten log is detected by third parties, not just the log operator.

name: obfuscated-transfer-object
document:
obfuscated-transfer-object
obfuscated TO
Carry sensitive business data across components and tiers in a transfer object that protects its own designated elements, so the intermediaries, logs and audit trails it passes through never see those values in the clear.
Transfer objects are convenient carriers precisely because every component on the route can read them. When one of the carried fields is a credit-card number, a Social Security number or an account balance, each intermediate component - business services, presentation helpers, audit interceptors, debug output - can print it, log it or dump it, and preventing that would mean modifying and retesting every one of them. The recurring trigger: sensitive fields travel between layers and must not be readable to the components they merely pass through.
Layered or distributed applications whose transfer objects cross component and tier boundaries (in-process layers, remote calls, asynchronous messages), where some receiving components are not trusted with the sensitive fields or are simply unaware of them, and where logs, audit trails and debug output routinely render whole objects. It applies when producers and consumers can agree on which elements are protected and how they are recovered - a protected-name manifest inside a closed trust domain, or a shared symmetric key where intermediaries must be kept from the values altogether.
Customer or profile transfer objects carrying credit-card, SSN or account fields through presentation, business and integration layers, where many of those components log the object or write it into audit records - the motivating example in the source pattern.
Audit-heavy operations where an audit interceptor records arguments and results: masked or sealed fields keep the audit trail from becoming a concentration of the very data the system protects.
Asynchronous flows (queue/JMS payloads) whose message content is visible in broker consoles, dead-letter queues and consumer logs.
Partner or multi-party integration where an object must traverse middleware or a service owned by another team that is not allowed to read the protected fields.
Session and identity data carried between the web and business tiers, where session contents can end up in diagnostics and support dumps.
Compliance-driven designs (PCI DSS, data-protection rules) that must keep primary account numbers or personal identifiers out of logs and non-production stores while still moving them to the system that legitimately needs them.
Java applications can place a protected partition of a serializable transfer object in the JCE SealedObject API before it crosses an EJB, JMS or service boundary; only a consumer with the matching Cipher can recover it.
Apache Camel routes can marshal a protected message partition with the Crypto (JCE) Data Format and unmarshal it only at the intended consumer, keeping route intermediaries from reading the encrypted payload.

name: point-to-point-channel
document:
point-to-point-channel
point-to-point queue
p2p channel
Deliver each message on a channel to exactly one consumer, so senders never have to coordinate with receivers and no unit of work is handled twice.
A producer must hand work to exactly one handler while several receivers are running (or the intended handler is temporarily unavailable): broadcasting the message makes every receiver deduplicate, and addressing a specific consumer instance couples the sender to its identity, location and liveness.
Asynchronous messaging inside one process, between processes or across services, where each message is a unit of work (command, job, document, RPC request) and duplicate handling is as unacceptable as loss. Applies to in-process worker queues and to brokered channels (JMS queue, AMQP queue, Kafka partition, cloud queue) alike; the channel - not the consumer and not the sender - owns the routing decision.
Work queues: a web tier enqueues jobs and a pool of workers consumes them, with each job running exactly once.
Request-reply over messaging: the request goes to a queue, exactly one service instance answers it, and the reply returns on a reply queue identified by a correlation identifier.
Command dispatch in a service-oriented system: an order service appends commands that exactly one instance of the command processor executes.
Media or log processing pipelines where every stage pulls its input from a queue and each item is handled by one of the stage's replicas.
Legacy and batch integration: jobs handed to a single consumer daemon through a queue, with the channel providing the transactional hand-off.
Scaling an existing single-consumer endpoint by attaching additional instances (Competing Consumers) without changing producers or the message contract.
Apache Kafka consumer groups: records in each topic partition are assigned to one group member at a time, so a group scales work while separate group IDs retain independent pub-sub copies.
RabbitMQ Work Queues: a task queue distributes jobs among competing workers with round-robin or fair dispatch; manual acknowledgements allow unacknowledged work to be redelivered after a worker failure.
Amazon SQS Standard queues: distribute background jobs among consumers with visibility timeouts, while at-least-once delivery requires idempotent handlers because duplicate deliveries remain possible.

name: version-number
document:
version-number
rowversion
entity versioning
Store a version token alongside each persistent record and make every write assert the token it read, so a write computed from stale data fails as a detectable conflict instead of silently overwriting a newer value.
Two sessions read the same record, both edit it, and the later write wins: the earlier update vanishes without any error (the lost update). Once the read-modify-write spans more than one system transaction the database cannot tell 'this is the record I read' from 'this record changed under me', so no code path can notice in time - unless the record itself carries a per-row token that changes on every write and the write tests that token before committing.
Applies to records that outlive the transaction that read them: edits spanning user think time, a web form round-trip, an offline client, a batch worker holding aggregates, or any read-modify-write over data other writers touch in between. It needs a store that can test the token and change the record in one atomic step (a conditional UPDATE, a compare-and-swap, a document revision check) and a caller willing to act on the conflict - re-read, merge, retry, or report. It assumes conflicts are the exception; when they are the rule a pessimistic lock prevents the wasted work instead.
Web forms and editors: a record is loaded into a page, edited for minutes or hours, then saved - the token makes the stale save fail instead of clobbering the other editor's change.
Distributed workers applying commands to the same entity: the second worker's write is rejected so it can refresh and re-apply, giving first-writer-wins with no held lock.
Data mappers and units of work: every dirty entity flushed at commit carries the version it was loaded with, so the whole transaction aborts on the first stale row.
Document stores and revision-based APIs: Mongoose's __v with optimisticConcurrency, CouchDB-style revisions, or a REST ETag/If-Match precondition all expose the same per-document token.
Leases, leader election and configuration records: one row represents ownership or a monotonic generation, and a write must prove it still holds the revision it acted on.
Offline or mobile sync: clients push edits made against a snapshot taken days earlier, and the version check decides which edits apply directly and which must go through a merge.
Hibernate ORM / JPA @Version: the mapper owns an integer (or timestamp) version property, appends it to every UPDATE's WHERE clause, bumps it on flush and raises StaleObjectStateException / OptimisticLockException when zero rows match, so the application code never writes the predicate by hand.
DynamoDB conditional writes: each item carries a Version attribute; UpdateItem sends ConditionExpression 'Version = :read_value' and increments Version in the same request, and ConditionalCheckFailedException is the conflict signal that triggers a bounded re-read-and-retry — the same contract exposed as @DynamoDBVersionAttribute in the enhanced client.
Cassandra lightweight transactions: UPDATE ... SET col = ? WHERE id = ? IF col = ? is a Paxos-backed compare-and-set, giving the token test linearizable semantics across replicas — at a documented cost (roughly four extra round-trips per conditional write), so it is reserved for rows that genuinely need the guard.
