name: table-data-gateway
document:
table-data-gateway
table gateway
Confine every SQL statement that touches one table or view inside a single gateway object whose methods take and return plain record structures, so that no other code contains SQL for that table and rows cross the boundary as data rather than as domain objects.
Access to one table is spread across the codebase: SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE fragments are copied into every caller, nobody can say which queries a schema change will break, DBAs cannot find the SQL that needs tuning, and each caller has to know the dialect, the placeholders and the column order. The desired boundary is a single object that mediates all access to the whole table while the individual rows remain records (tuples, structs, hashes, DataRows) instead of becoming mapped objects.
Relational persistence where the database is a stable, schema-first integration point and SQL-level control matters (indexes, hints, bulk loads, vendor features), where the team deliberately does not want O/R mapping machinery in the domain layer, and where the domain logic is simple enough that rows may travel as records - CRUD and query services, reporting/read models, ETL writers, local SQLite stores, or a legacy database mediated for several applications. It is also the packaging decision for 'the SQL has to live somewhere well known' before a DAO, repository or query object is justified.
A service or CRUD application over a handful of tables where every screen maps to a few statements per table and an ORM would add more machinery than it removes.
Reporting and read models: read-only gateways over views or wide tables that return records directly to a formatter, export or BI job.
Legacy databases mediated for several applications: one gateway library per database becomes the documented API and the place where vendor quirks are hidden.
Embedded/local storage (SQLite, SQLCipher) in a desktop or mobile app, where one gateway per table keeps SQL out of the UI and can be tested with an in-memory database.
Batch and ETL writers that need explicit control over statement batching, cursors and transaction size - control that generated mappers hide.
Gradual refactoring of SQL scattered through transaction scripts: the first step is to move each table's statements into a gateway, after which a Data Mapper or repository can be introduced deliberately.
Test fixtures and seeders that must write through the same statements as production code rather than through a second, divergent SQL path.
Generated gateways in Go: sqlc compiles a schema plus a file of named queries into one struct per table and one type-safe method per SQL statement, with the caller holding the database handle and opening transactions - the gateway's invariants are then enforced by the generator and compiler rather than by convention.
Local SQLite storage on Android: each Room @Dao is a gateway over one table - the SQL lives in @Query-annotated methods validated at compile time, rows travel as plain entity data classes, and @Transaction or database-level transactions keep atomic multi-DAO boundaries in the caller.
Java teams that want the gateway structure without hand-writing it: jOOQ's code generator emits one DAO class per table or view (findAll, findById, generated fetchByColumn methods) that reads and writes Record/POJO rows and borrows the caller's Configuration, so the per-table SQL surface is regenerated when the schema changes.

name: stub
document:
stub
test stub
stub object
Replace a collaborator with a test-specific stand-in that returns canned answers, so the component under test can be driven down paths - success, empty, error, timeout - that the real collaborator cannot be made to produce on demand.
The component under test receives indirect inputs through a collaborator, and the branch that must be exercised is selected by what that collaborator returns. The real collaborator will not produce the needed value on request: it is slow, remote, licensed, non-deterministic, or simply never returns the rare case - the empty result, the declined payment, the timeout - that the test exists for. Without a controllable replacement the test either cannot reach the path at all or has to provoke it through the production system, which is exactly what unit testing was supposed to avoid.
Unit and component tests of a component whose collaborators are already, or can cheaply become, abstractions: the values and exceptions a collaborator returns are inputs to the component under test, and the test asserts what the component does with them rather than how the collaboration happened. Typical where the collaborator is remote or stateful (HTTP client, database, queue, clock, payment gateway) or where the branch under test is an edge case - empty page, declined payment, expired token, feature off. The pattern assumes a substitutable seam: a constructor parameter, an injected interface, a factory, a lookup, or a patchable module.
Exercising a rare branch of the component: an empty result set, a declined payment, a 429 from a gateway, a missing feature flag.
Testing error handling: programme the stub to raise the exception the real service would raise - timeout, connection reset, malformed payload - and assert that the SUT surfaces or recovers from it.
Unit-testing a component against a collaborator that is slow, paid, unavailable in CI or still being implemented; the stub encodes the agreed response while the real adapter is built.
Removing non-determinism from a path the real collaborator decides by clock, randomness or remote state (token expired, cache cold, retry budget exhausted), so one outcome can be asserted exactly.
View and presentation tests: a fixed dataset from the stub, so the assertion is about the rendering or the decision logic and nothing else.
Boundary values on contract edges - zero, maximum, empty string, unicode payloads - that the real system cannot be asked to return on demand.
Mockito (Java): when(warehouse.hasInventory(...)).thenReturn(false) programmes the declined-branch answer and thenThrow(SocketTimeoutException.class) injects the failure, and consecutive-value stubbing (thenReturn(v1, v2)) drives retry-then-succeed paths that the real warehouse would never produce on request.
Python unittest.mock (standard library): Mock(return_value=...) fixes the canned answer while side_effect set to an exception or an iterable raises or sequences answers per call - the library ships Responder and Saboteur behaviour as first-class configuration.
Moq (.NET): mock.Setup(x => x.HasInventory(...)).Returns(false) and .Throws<InvalidOperationException>() are the canned-answer primitives, so a C# test reaches the empty-inventory and fault branches of Order.Fill without touching a database.

name: configurable-test-double
document:
configurable-test-double
configurable test stub
configurable mock object
Configure one reusable Test Double per collaborator role during fixture setup - before the test installs it in the system under test - so the values it returns and the calls it expects are stated as configuration data in the test itself instead of being hard-coded into a purpose-built double class per scenario.
Several tests need the same collaborator role (clock, gateway, repository, notifier) to behave differently: some need canned successes, others exceptions, timeouts or specific call arguments. When every variation is its own hard-coded double class, the suite duplicates double code and the configured behaviour is buried inside the double rather than visible in the test, which is Meszaros' Test Code Duplication and Obscure Tests territory.
Unit tests that isolate a system under test by replacing a depended-on component, where the same collaborator role recurs across many tests with slightly different data or failure modes and a substitutable-dependency seam (constructor or parameter injection, factory, registry, subclass hook) exists to install the double. It covers both construction routes - a hand-built reusable double and a toolkit that statically or dynamically generates one - and both configuration styles, a test-only configuration interface or a record/playback configuration mode.
A collaborator role used by many tests with different canned answers - time provider, pricing or tax service, identifier generator, feature-flag client - where only the returned value varies between tests.
Injecting failures on demand: the double is configured per test to raise timeouts, throw exceptions or return error codes so the error-handling paths of the system under test are exercised without a second double class.
Verifying indirect outputs: expected arguments are configured on the same double and the test asserts afterwards that the right message was sent with the right payload.
A suite-wide fixture double for a slow, unavailable or side-effecting dependency, re-configured per test instead of re-implemented per test.
Generated doubles for collaborators with wide interfaces, where hand-writing a double class would be pure boilerplate and would have to be kept in step with the interface.
Cutting a deep chain of real collaborators during refactoring: one configured double stands in for the chain so fixture setup stops constructing and persisting a network of objects.
Contract testing with external services: configure a double to return contract-compliant responses that verify the system under test produces correctly-formatted requests (see Pact, consumer-driven contracts).
Testing async/await code paths: configure the double to return awaitable results or throw exceptions asynchronously, exercising the calling code's async error handling.
Performance boundary testing: configure a double with deliberate delays or throttling to verify timeout and retry logic behaves correctly under degraded conditions.
State machine testing across transitions: configure the double to return specific state-dependent responses as the system under test walks through a sequence of transitions.
Consumer-driven contract verification: use a mock server (e.g., Pact mock) to record expected interactions, generating a contract that the provider can verify independently.
Testing retry and circuit-breaker logic: configure the double to fail a configurable number of times before succeeding, exercising back-off and recovery paths.
Data-driven test scenarios: parameterize the double's configuration with external data (CSV, JSON) to cover many input combinations without duplicating test code.
Java suites configure one Mockito mock per collaborator interface - when(clock.now()).thenReturn(instant) for indirect inputs, verify(gateway).send(msg) for indirect outputs - replacing hand-built double classes.
Python tests install unittest.mock.patch(..., autospec=True) or create_autospec(...) doubles per test, configuring return_value/side_effect and asserting calls via assert_called_with, with signatures checked against the real object.
Go tests run mockgen (uber-go/mock) over the collaborator interface once and configure expectations during setup - mockFoo.EXPECT().Bar(gomock.Eq(99)).Return(101).Times(1) - since Go offers no runtime proxying.

name: cache-aside
document:
cache-aside
look-aside cache
lazy loading cache
Place the cache beside the authoritative store and make the application own the protocol: look up the cache first, load the entry from the store on a miss and populate it with a TTL, and invalidate the entry right after each write to the store - so repeated reads stay cheap while the store, never the cache, decides what is true.
A source of truth (relational database, downstream service, object store) is expensive or rate-limited for the read volume an application receives, while most reads repeat a small set of keys: without a cache every request pays the source-of-truth cost, and with an unmanaged cache the copies silently drift. The recurring decision is where the read path looks first, when a miss may populate the entry, and what a write must do so the cached copy stops lying.
Read-heavy paths in front of a slower or metered authoritative store, typically several application instances sharing a Redis or Memcached tier, or each holding an in-process cache, where a bounded amount of staleness is acceptable and every writer can be held to the same invalidation discipline. It applies when the read/write ratio is high, when the cache itself does not provide read-through or write-through, and when lost or evicted entries can always be recomputed from the store.
Read-heavy lookups by natural key (product catalogs, user profiles, article pages) in front of a relational database.
Several service instances sharing a Redis or Memcached tier where every instance must see the same cached copy and the same invalidation.
Reference data that changes slowly (currency rates, feature flags, configuration, price lists) refreshed by TTL with explicit invalidation when it is edited.
Expensive aggregate or derived results (dashboards, search pages, recommendations) recomputed into the cache per request key.
Per-instance in-process caches for hot, rarely changing values where a shared cache would add network latency without adding much.
Multi-level caching in Kubernetes: an in-process L1 (Caffeine) sidecar on each pod with an L2 Redis cluster, where the L1 is invalidated on each incoming request via a bloom filter or pub/sub.
CDN edge caching for static or semi-static API responses: the application server acts as the origin and issues cache-aside reads; CDN edges serve from their own look-aside cache with short TTLs and PURGE invalidation on writes.
RAG and vector cache in AI pipelines: embedding results cached by query hash so repeated semantically identical questions hit the vector store once and reuse cached results; TTL bounds staleness of the embedding index.
Django's low-level cache API (cache.get / cache.get_or_set with a per-key timeout, cache.delete on save) is cache-aside as a framework primitive; MediaWiki's WANObjectCache does the same at Wikipedia scale via getWithSet, invalidating page parses through cross-datacenter purges rather than direct writes.
Spring's cache abstraction applies the pattern declaratively: @Cacheable loads and populates on a miss, @CacheEvict removes the entry after the writer, with RedisCacheManager supplying the TTL - the application still owns both paths, the annotation only moves where.
Hibernate's second-level cache read-write concurrency strategy is a managed cache-aside: the updated entry is soft-locked around the transaction so concurrent readers miss to the database instead of repopulating the cache with the pre-commit value.

name: durable-subscriber
document:
durable-subscriber
durable subscription
durable consumer
Keep a publish-subscribe consumer's place while it is offline: the broker binds a stable subscription identity to retained messages or a committed position, then resumes delivery after reconnect until retention, expiry, or quota says the backlog is no longer available.
A subscriber on a publish-subscribe channel can be unavailable during redeployment, maintenance, device disconnects, or scheduled batch work. A non-durable subscription drops messages published during that gap, so the design must choose a stable identity and broker-side state, then make finite retention, replay pressure, and at-least-once redelivery explicit; durable state prevents a gap only while that state remains available.
Broker-mediated publish-subscribe messaging where consumers are intermittently offline but individual messages matter: JMS topics, MQTT sessions, Kafka consumer groups, NATS JetStream durable consumers, cloud topic subscriptions. It presumes the messaging system can store messages (or positions) durably, so it is as much a broker-configuration decision as a client one, and it presumes at-least-once delivery is acceptable once the consumer is idempotent. It does not apply to in-process notification or to broadcast where only the newest value counts.
A Kafka-backed order-processing service that is redeployed or scaled to zero while events keep arriving: the consumer group resumes from its committed offsets and replays what it missed.
An IoT or mobile client on an intermittent link: an MQTT persistent session holds QoS 1/2 publications for its client id and delivers them when the client reconnects.
A partner integration that receives published documents while the partner's system is down: an unshared JMS durable subscription, or a cloud topic subscription, is registered on their behalf and holds the backlog until they acknowledge it.
A nightly audit or analytics consumer that must see every published change: the day's backlog is drained in bounded batches and acknowledged as it is persisted.
A ledger or compliance consumer that must never silently skip events: retention and lag alarms are configured so an offline subscriber is noticed before its backlog expires.
A cloud event-driven architecture (SNS FIFO → SQS FIFO): SNS preserves ordering and deduplication while SQS queues hold messages for durable fan-out to Lambda or EC2 consumers, with DLQs capturing failed deliveries for replay.
An industrial SCADA/IoT sensor fleet where devices connect sporadically over unstable networks: MQTT persistent sessions with a long session expiry interval preserve every telemetry reading until each device reconnects, even after multi-day outages.
A financial audit trail that must immutably record every state-changing event: events are durably retained in Kafka or JetStream and consumed by a compliance subscriber that must not skip or duplicate entries; idempotent deduplication and offset commits after durable persistence enforce this.
A supply-chain or logistics event-sourcing system where downstream services reconstruct state by replaying events after a crash or deliberate seek: the durable consumer starts from the committed position and replays the missing event window atomically with the state reconstruction.
A cross-region disaster-recovery subscriber that mirrors events to a secondary site: the durable subscription in the secondary region receives every event from the primary's topic, with a DLQ holding any events that fail cross-region delivery for manual retry.
A JMS topic consumer that must receive publications made while it is offline: the client reconnects with the same client identifier and durable subscription name, and the provider retains messages until acknowledgement, expiry, or unsubscribe.
An MQTT 3.1.1 device gateway that reconnects with the same client identifier and CleanSession=0: the broker resumes the stored session and queues matching QoS 1/2 publications for delivery after the link returns.
A NATS JetStream billing worker that restarts after an outage: it binds to the same durable consumer name and explicit-acks each message, so the server resumes its acknowledgement floor and redelivers unacknowledged work.
An Azure Service Bus fan-out topology: topic subscriptions are durable by default and each subscription stores its own copy of matching messages, so a receiver that reconnects later still drains its backlog; client-affine durable subscriptions bind the durable state to a stable client id.
A high-throughput replay consumer on RabbitMQ Streams: the consumer attaches with a stable tracking reference (name) and periodically stores its offset server-side, so a restart resumes from the last stored offset instead of re-reading the whole stream.
An event-sourced system on Google Cloud Pub/Sub that must reprocess history after a bug fix: the subscription enables acknowledged-message retention (default window 7 days, up to 31) and is seeked back to a past timestamp or snapshot to replay already-acked messages.

name: recursive-descent-parser
document:
recursive-descent-parser
recursive descent
recursive descent parsing
Parse a small grammar by translating every rule directly into a function that consumes the tokens the rule matches and calls the functions of the rules it references, so the parser's control flow is the grammar itself and stays readable, debuggable and free of a code-generation step.
A hand-written parser is the only option - no generator in the toolchain, or the grammar is a small DSL - yet the grammar is not a flat token sequence: alternatives must be chosen from lookahead, repetition must become a loop, and the natural grammar for expressions is left-recursive, which a top-down parser cannot translate directly. Without a disciplined mapping from rules to functions the parser degenerates into ad-hoc index arithmetic and exception-driven backtracking, and errors end up without positions.
Front ends for small languages, DSLs, query/filter/rule grammars, configuration and protocol formats, and the parsing layer of compilers and interpreters that want no code-generation step. It applies when a lexer or token stream already exists (or is cheap to write), the grammar is small to medium and reasonably LL-friendly or rewritable into LL form, and the team values readable, step-debuggable, position-precise parsing over generated tables.
Front ends for small languages, DSLs and configuration formats (filter expressions, rule engines, policy languages, template syntaxes) where a generator and its build integration would be overkill.
Expression and statement parsing in single-pass compilers and interpreters that emit bytecode or IR while parsing, as in Crafting Interpreters' Lox.
Tooling for a grammar you own - formatters, linters, syntax highlighters, language servers - where error tolerance, multiple diagnostics and exact positions matter more than raw throughput.
Protocol and wire-format decoding with a small fixed grammar, where errors must carry byte offsets and malformed input must be rejected deterministically.
Context-dependent or indentation-sensitive syntaxes (templates with interpolation, layout-based blocks, configuration with embedded expressions) that a generated lexer handles poorly.
Codebases that must not carry generated code: security-reviewed, vendored or cross-compiled projects where an ordinary source file beats a build-time generator.
Clang's C-family front end uses a unified hand-built recursive-descent parser for C, C++, Objective-C and Objective-C++, pairing rule-oriented control flow with production-quality diagnostics.
The Go standard library's go/parser is a production recursive-descent parser for Go source, with explicit parser state, nesting-depth guards and error recovery.
rustc_parse is the Rust compiler's recursive-descent parser module, showing how a hand-written parser can scale to macros, recovery modes and detailed token/state handling.
Lua's reference implementation compiles with lparser.c, a single-pass recursive-descent parser that emits bytecode opcodes while reducing expressions instead of building a syntax tree, with precedence handled by parsing levels.

statement: Whether to replace the remote classifier with a test-specific responder that returns selected classifications and raises selected failures to drive each policy branch.
name: state-colocation
document:
state-colocation
colocated state
colocation
Keep each piece of presentation state in the component closest to where it is used — down to the single component that owns and reads it — instead of hoisting it to a common ancestor or a global store, so that a change touches only the smallest part of the view that can observe it.
State gets hoisted 'just in case': a value only one component reads is lifted to the screen or application root, or pushed into one global store, because someone may want it later. The consequences are components that receive props they never read, updates that invalidate far more of the UI than the value's actual consumers, an unclear owner for each value, and tests that must assemble the whole state container to exercise one field. The recurring decision is where a new piece of state should live: keep it at the smallest scope that actually needs it.
Declarative component UIs (React, Vue, Svelte, SwiftUI, Compose, Blazor, Qt Quick) and, in generalized form, any system where a mutable value is owned by one component-like unit: the consumers determine the state's scope, the framework invalidates only what the owner's subtree can observe, and components are composed, moved and deleted. Most compelling where over-lifted or global state has already become a performance and ownership problem.
A search or form input whose value is read only by the input, its own validation and its own preview: keep it in that component instead of the screen root (the canonical typing example where hoisting made every keystroke re-render the page).
Which panel of an accordion is open: leave it per panel while panels are independent, then lift exactly to the accordion once only one panel may be open at a time (the closest common parent).
Tooltip, hover, popover and dropdown state in a chart or table cell: own it in the cell component rather than in a global UI store.
Per-row edit or selection state in a data grid: the row component owns it; only cross-row operations need the grid to own it.
Dialog and modal open state in the button or list that opens it, until another surface must close or observe it.
Form draft state in the form component; lift it only when a sibling — summary panel, preview pane, wizard footer — genuinely must read it.
Extracting a self-contained widget for reuse or publication: keeping its state local makes the component portable and shrinks its API.
Per-cell expansion state in a tree view or file explorer: the tree node component owns whether it is expanded; the parent tree only coordinates multi-select or bulk-expand operations.
Media playback state for a single player (play/pause, current time, volume): colocate in the player component rather than a global audio store unless the same track plays in multiple places simultaneously.
Local filter/sort state for a data table or list: keep it in the list component until a URL parameter, shareable link, or sibling panel requires sharing it.
Vue: composable-local state (useSearch, useToggle) where each consumer needs its own independent instance of the same reactive logic pattern.
Angular Signals: feature-level signal stores scoped to a route or feature slice, not the entire application store, for UI state and feature-derived state.
SwiftUI: @State for view-local value types; @StateObject for view-owned reference types; keep @EnvironmentObject for genuinely cross-cutting state (auth session, theme) mounted as low in the hierarchy as consumers allow.
Svelte 5 runes: `let count = $state(0)` inside a component is per-component-instance reactive state — the component that declares it is its owner; Svelte's v5 migration explicitly replaced the pre-runes habit of reaching for a store whenever state sat at a component's top level, with $state plus $derived/$effect as the local cells, and module-level .svelte.js state only for deliberate sharing.
Jetpack Compose: the official hoisting guidance is this pattern's placement ladder — keep state as close as possible to where it is consumed, hoist only to the lowest common ancestor of all composables that read or write it, pass value down and onValueChange up, and make the ViewModel the owner only when business logic or lifecycle outlives the composition.
Blazor: component fields are the default owner for UI-local state; the official state-management guidance promotes to an in-memory state container service only when components must share non-persistent state, and to Protected Browser Storage only when the value must survive circuits or sessions — a three-rung ladder that mirrors local state, scoped provider, persistence.

name: repository
document:
repository
collection-oriented repository
repository layer
Mediates between the domain model and the data mapping layer with a collection-like interface, so domain code adds, removes and finds persistent objects as if they lived in memory and never constructs queries or touches persistence APIs itself.
Persistence code spreads: every application service re-derives the same SQL or ORM queries, duplicate query logic drifts apart, table and column names leak into domain decisions, and testing domain rules without a database becomes impossible. Callers should be able to think in collections of domain objects instead of queries.
Applies to systems with a non-trivial domain model sitting on a data-mapping layer (Data Mapper, metadata mapping, or a hand-written mapper) where the same queries recur across application services; it becomes more valuable as domain classes and query volume grow. It is the standard persistence boundary of DDD aggregates (one repository per aggregate root) and presumes a unit of work or session that owns flush and commit. It is not a per-table data-access wrapper and not a replacement for transaction control.
DDD application services that must load an aggregate root, run domain logic on it and store it again without knowing the table layout.
Data-mapper backends where several application services and background jobs share recurring complex queries (overdue invoices, pending orders, open tickets).
Applications that must be unit-testable away from the database: repositories are the substitution point for in-memory doubles.
Systems that must support more than one store behind a stable domain interface — relational in production, in-memory in tests, a document store for a particular deployment.
Uniform cross-cutting access policy for an aggregate: caching, read-replica routing, audit logging or authorization applied as decorators around one interface.
Migration work where the persistence technology changes (ORM swap, schema split, service extraction) while the domain model and its tests stay untouched.
CQRS write-side aggregate loading where the aggregate must be reconstructed fully to apply business rules and enforce invariants.
Integration with heterogeneous data sources where one repository unifies access to a cache, primary database and a third-party API behind a domain interface.
Spring Data JPA applications can use Repository/CrudRepository for aggregate-typed CRUD, paging and derived queries, then add only domain-specific methods rather than wrapping every persistence operation.
The .NET eShopOnContainers ordering microservice uses an EF Core BuyerRepository over a shared scoped DbContext/unit of work, while CQRS/Dapper handles presentation reads.
Python applications using SQLAlchemy ORM can place an aggregate-facing repository over Session, whose identity map and unit-of-work flush semantics provide the mapper/session boundary.

name: converter
document:
converter
translator
Give a pair of corresponding representations one owner that maps them into each other in both directions, so every caller converts through one place and neither representation has to import, know or be aware of the other.
The same information lives in two representations - domain object and DTO, in-memory value and wire or column format, internal model and third-party schema - and both directions are exercised in production. Hand-written field copying at each call site duplicates the mapping rules, drifts whenever either representation changes, and forces at least one side (or every caller) to import the other.
Component boundaries where an internal model meets an external representation: service or API layers exchanging DTOs, persistence layers mapping values to column formats, integration seams facing a third-party or legacy schema, and codec layers mapping typed values to a wire format. It applies whenever both directions are needed (read and write, decode and encode) and either side must stay independent of the other - different modules, teams, release cycles or libraries.
Domain object <-> DTO at a service or API boundary, where the transport shape must not leak into the model.
Value object <-> database column representation (JPA AttributeConverter, EF Core ValueConverter, Rails custom attribute type).
Third-party or legacy schema <-> internal model at an integration seam, including versioned wire formats.
Typed value <-> JSON, XML or protobuf payload with a custom codec when the default mapping is wrong (formats, units, enums).
Query rows or record sets <-> domain objects, where a full mapper framework would be oversized.
Single-value wrappers such as identifiers, money or unit-carrying quantities mapped to and from their primitive form.
Palindrome conversion chain (Entity -> DAO -> DTO -> Controller -> DTO -> DAO -> Entity) where each layer owns exactly one transformation direction, making the data flow explicit and each boundary independently testable.
Versioned API contracts: a DTO for API v1 and a separate DTO for API v2 coexist; a converter pair maps each version's DTO to the shared internal model, isolating API consumers from internal changes.
API gateway transformation: external third-party API payloads are normalized into an internal canonical format at the gateway, and outbound responses are converted back to the third-party schema; converters live at the seam.
Event-driven payload normalization: domain events carry one representation (e.g., enriched entity) while the event bus transports a flattened wire format (e.g., protobuf); converters at producer and consumer ends keep the two shapes in sync.
ORM entity vs. read-model DTO at the query boundary: a repository executes a query and the row-set converter maps each row to a read-model DTO, avoiding the entity in read-only paths entirely.
Anti-corruption layer at legacy integration seams: external system payloads are translated into the internal domain model at the boundary, and responses translated back; the converter owns the translation vocabulary, protecting the domain model from foreign concepts (Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design; Microsoft Azure Architecture Center; AWS Prescriptive Guidance).
Immutable value type <-> wire format for cryptographic or financial domains: the converter is a lawful isomorphism ensuring every wire value round-trips to an identical object (tested via property-based round-trip laws, as in the lawful-conversions Haskell library and Higher-Kinded-J Iso optics library).
Strangler-fig migration seam: new microservice functionality is accessed through an ACL that converts legacy system payloads to the new domain model and back, keeping the legacy interface unchanged while the new service evolves behind the seam.
Guava com.google.common.base.Converter<F, T>: an abstract bidirectional function with convert()/reverse(), automatic reverse() derivation for subclasses, mapAll() for whole iterables and Converter.normalize() to lift a converter into a function converter - the pattern as a shipped JDK-adjacent library type (Google Guava).
Go database/sql custom types: a type implementing both sql.Scanner (Scan(src any) error) and driver.Valuer (Value() (driver.Value, error)) owns the Go value <-> database column pair in both directions; the standard library's NullString, NullInt64 and NullTime are built-in pairs of exactly this shape.
Rails custom attribute types: subclass ActiveModel::Type::Value, override serialize (Ruby value -> database value) and deserialize (database value -> Ruby value) and bind with attribute :col, MyType.new - the converter pair at the ORM seam, with cast_value kept separate for user-input coercion.

name: producer-consumer
document:
producer-consumer
bounded buffer
consumer-producer
Insert a bounded buffer between producers and consumers of work items so the two sides run concurrently at their own rates, the buffer absorbs bursts and slack, and its bound turns overload into backpressure, queueing or an explicit drop policy instead of unbounded growth.
Production and consumption proceed at different rates: a fast producer outruns its consumer and either drops items or grows a backlog until memory runs out, a slow producer leaves consumers idle, and bursts arrive faster than they can be processed. Wiring the two sides together directly also couples their lifetimes and schedules - a synchronous hand-off makes the faster side wait for the slower - so neither side can be scaled, restarted or tested on its own.
Concurrent in-process software (threads, tasks, coroutines, event-loop callbacks) with one or more producers and one or more consumers that can run at the same time but not at the same average rate. The buffer is a component-level data structure owned by the application - a work queue for a thread pool, a pipeline hand-off, a logging or telemetry sink - not a durable broker, so the decisions are how to hand items over, how to bound the queue and how to end the arrangement cleanly.
Work queues behind thread or worker pools: request handlers enqueue tasks and a fixed set of workers consumes them, so pool size is independent of the arrival rate. Industry examples: Celery (Python), Sidekiq (Ruby), BullMQ (Node.js) all use this shape with Redis or a broker as the durable backing store.
Asynchronous logging and telemetry: hot paths enqueue records cheaply while a background writer drains, formats and writes them, keeping I/O latency off the request path. Structured log collectors (Fluent Bit, Vector) ingest from many sources into one consumer.
Multi-stage data pipelines (decode - transform - encode, extract - transform - load): bounded queues between stages give each stage its own workers and let a slow stage backpressure a fast one. Used in media transcoding, ETL workflows, and stream processors.
Ingestion buffers: a socket, file or broker reader produces records faster than the processing or indexing stage can absorb them, and the buffer smooths the mismatch without dropping data. Common in IoT telemetry ingestion, click-stream collection, and log aggregation.
UI/host integration: a background thread posts work or results to the main/event-loop thread's queue and vice versa, keeping the UI responsive without locks around application state. All major GUI frameworks (Qt, Swing, Flutter) use this internally.
Batch job scheduling: producers enqueue compute jobs (image resize, PDF generation, report creation) and a pool of consumers processes them. Systems like Celery, Hangfire, and AWS SQS follow this pattern, often with priority queues, delayed execution, and dead-letter routing.
Event streaming pre-processing: a Kafka, Pulsar, or NATS consumer-producer chain filters, transforms, and routes events through a series of bounded queues before landing in a data warehouse or search index.
Simulation and testing: a producer generates a deterministic stream of items while a consumer asserts on what it receives, with a sentinel marking the end of the stream. Property-based testing frameworks use this to drive scenario generation.
Print spooling and document processing: print jobs or document conversion tasks are queued and processed by a pool of workers, with bounded queues preventing runaway memory use even under burst load.
ML inference pipelines: a model-serving host receives requests via an API, enqueues them into a bounded queue, and a pool of worker coroutines or threads dequeues and runs inference. The queue decouples HTTP latency from inference latency and provides backpressure when the model GPU is saturated. Tools like Ray Serve, Triton Inference Server, and TorchServe use this shape.
Streaming audio/video processing: a media pipeline (capture - encode - mux - stream) uses bounded queues between stages; frames that arrive during a temporary encoding stall are buffered rather than dropped, and a full encoder output queue backpressures the camera capture stage to prevent unbounded memory growth from frame accumulation.
WebSocket connection management: a server's accept loop enqueues new connections into a bounded connection queue; a pool of handler coroutines or threads dequeues and upgrades them, preventing connection exhaustion under burst load while the handler pool limits concurrency independently of the arrival rate.
Financial order processing: high-frequency trading systems receive market data feeds (producer) and route orders through risk checks and execution engines (consumers), with bounded queues between stages preventing downstream latency from backpressuring the market data ingestion and applying backpressure to upstream feed handlers.
Go channel pipelines: a source goroutine produces values into a channel, transformation stages consume and emit through downstream channels, and a sink drains the final stage. Go's documented pipeline pattern makes channel closure and cancellation part of the producer-consumer lifecycle.
Python asyncio worker queues: an asyncio.Queue(maxsize=N) accepts work from coroutine producers while worker coroutines await get(), process items and call task_done(); finite maxsize suspends producers when consumers fall behind.
Java executor work queues: java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue coordinates multiple producer threads and consumer workers, with put()/take() waiting on full and empty capacity so an Executor-style worker pool can be bounded independently of arrival rate.

name: metadata-mapping
document:
metadata-mapping
declarative mapping
orm mapping metadata
Holds the correspondence between object fields and database columns in metadata - annotations, mapping files, table objects, struct tags or a schema definition - so that one generic mapping engine performs the reads, inserts and updates instead of hand-written per-class mapper code.
Every class that is persisted needs the same tedious, repetitive code: which field maps to which column, which key is generated, how nulls and types convert, what the table is called. Written per class it is duplicated everywhere and drifts from the schema; the catalogue's trigger is that the mapping knowledge belongs in metadata or configuration, duplicated in no class.
Object-relational (or object-document) mapping layers where classes and tables do not line up mechanically - renamed columns, generated keys, relationships, inheritance strategies - and where many classes share the same mapping shape. It applies when the mapping can be declared once in a form a machine can read (code annotations or attributes, external XML, code-first table objects, struct tags, a schema DSL) and when the schema can either be generated from that metadata or validated against it at startup.
A system with dozens of similarly shaped tables where hand-written data mappers would be repetitive: one mapping engine plus one metadata declaration per class.
Schema-first projects where the database already exists and the mapping should be derived from it by introspection or a code generator (EF Core reverse engineering, Rails schema introspection, SeaORM entity generation).
Framework and library builders who must let users map their own classes without shipping per-class code - an ORM, an object-document mapper or a serialization library.
Multi-database products in which only the dialect and type map of the metadata changes between targets while the domain classes stay identical.
Teams that want one declaration to drive several artifacts: DDL or migrations, typed query APIs, validation rules and documentation.
Hibernate ORM/Jakarta Persistence applications declare @Entity, @Table and @Column metadata; the provider builds a persistent metamodel and generic Session or EntityManager operations perform CRUD, so one declaration replaces per-entity mapper code.
EF Core applications combine conventions, data annotations and Fluent API configuration to build an entity model that drives LINQ translation and updates; explicit configuration pins renamed columns and relationships.
SQLAlchemy declarative mappings turn class attributes and mapped_column() declarations into Table and Mapper metadata; that metadata feeds SQL compilation and unit-of-work persistence, while imperative mapping keeps existing classes annotation-free.

name: range
document:
range
interval
Represent a span of values as a single interval value whose bound inclusivity and open ends are explicit, so containment and interval-to-interval comparisons live in one place instead of repeated ad-hoc endpoint tests.
Start and end travel together through the code but every caller re-derives what they mean: containment is written as scattered <= / < comparisons that drift apart, "unbounded" is smuggled in as a sentinel value (Long.MAX_VALUE, 9999-12-31), and interval-to-interval questions - do these two overlap, does one enclose the other, what is the gap between them - have no home at all.
Applies wherever a domain concept is a span rather than a point: validity and effectivity periods, booking and availability windows, quantity or price tiers, measurement buckets, version and address ranges, pagination windows, and query parameters such as a date range. It pays off when the same interval is compared repeatedly or crosses a boundary (persistence, API payloads, UI widgets), because the bound convention then has to be written once instead of re-decided per call site. For a single comparison between two local variables the type is pure overhead.
Validity and effectivity windows: a contract, price or membership is valid over [effectiveFrom, effectiveTo), and every check is a membership test against one interval.
Booking and availability: a room, seat or resource is reserved during an interval; overlap (not adjacency) decides whether a new booking is possible, and back-to-back bookings must be allowed deliberately.
Quantity and price tiers: the unit price depends on the quantity interval ([1,10), [10,50), [50, +inf)), so a container of intervals with containment lookup replaces a cascade of if-statements.
Temporal queries and reporting: "last 7 days", "this quarter", "since the migration" are half-open or open-ended intervals passed to repositories and rendered by date-range pickers.
Version, port and address ranges: a compatibility claim covers [1.2, 2.0) of a library, a firewall rule covers a port interval - containment answers "is this covered?" and intersection answers "do these rules conflict?".
Pagination and slicing windows: a page is an interval over a sequence, and half-open semantics make adjacency exact ([0,20) followed by [20,40)),
PostgreSQL range and multirange columns: PostgreSQL's daterange, tsrange and numeric range types make lower-inclusive/upper-exclusive bounds, overlap and containment operators, and indexed range queries part of the persistence contract; choose the bound convention before mapping domain intervals.
Guava Range: Java's Guava Range models convex bounded or unbounded intervals with nine open/closed forms, isConnected and intersection; use ContiguousSet only when a discrete domain really requires enumeration rather than treating the interval itself as a sequence.
Standard-library and container choices: Rust's std::ops::RangeBounds covers included, excluded and unbounded bounds when its range forms fit; for many intervals requiring join/split policies, Boost ICL's interval_set and interval_map supply the container semantics instead of overloading one Range value.

name: lazy-acquisition
document:
lazy-acquisition
lazy loading
deferred acquisition
Defer acquiring an expensive or scarce resource until it is first used, so the acquisition cost is paid only by the holders that actually use it, while clients keep seeing an ordinary interface.
A resource is costly to acquire, scarce, and on many execution paths never needed at all, yet the code that holds it acquires it during construction, at start-up or on a hot entry path: the process pays for resources it never dereferences, start-up time grows with every optional subsystem, and scarce capacity (descriptors, connections, licenses, memory) is consumed by holders that never use it.
Applies to long-lived holders - objects, modules, services, containers - that front an external resource such as a file, socket or database connection, license, thread pool, GPU context, translation catalog or large lookup table. It pays off when the acquisition cost is large relative to a use, when a significant fraction of holders never use the resource, and when the runtime offers a one-time guard (or the holder is provably single-threaded). It is the wrong tool when the resource must be validated at boot, when acquisition is cheap, or when first use sits on a latency-critical path.
A request-handling object that opens a file or blob stream only on the code paths that actually read it (report export, attachment download, audit sink).
A service holding connections to a rarely consulted downstream — archive store, fallback provider, secondary region — that most requests never call.
A large lookup table, model or translation catalog loaded on first use instead of at process start, keeping start-up and memory bounded for the sessions that never need it.
Optional subsystems in desktop and mobile apps (camera, location, payment SDK, plugins) initialized when the feature is opened rather than when the app launches.
Test fixtures and tooling: starting a container, browser or database only for the tests that need it, so the fast path stays fast.
Per-session state in a server — a scratch buffer, a decompressor, a TLS session or prepared statement — allocated on first use of the session rather than on accept.
Database connection pools: HikariCP and similar pools typically create connections lazily on the first checkout rather than at pool construction, to avoid pinninglicenses and consuming file descriptors before the application is fully started.
Dependency injection containers (Spring @Lazy, Dagger 2 Lazy<T>) defer the creation of bean instances until they are first injected, reducing start-up time and breaking circular dependency cycles during bootstrap.
Logging frameworks (SLF4J/Logback): Logger instances are static final but the actual appender (file, socket, console) is initialized when the first log event at that level is fired, so logging infrastructure does not block application start.
Configuration objects: large YAML or JSON config trees are parsed and validated lazily on first access rather than eagerly at start-up, keeping CLI tools fast for commands that do not need the full configuration.
GPU contexts in graphics applications (OpenGL, Vulkan, CUDA) are expensive to create and are deferred until the first draw call or compute kernel launch, allowing the application to start and display a window without claiming GPU memory.
HTTP/service clients (gRPC channels, REST clients): a channel is lazily opened on the first request, enabling the client to be instantiated at module load time while deferring the TCP handshake and TLS handshake to the first real call.
Spring Framework @Lazy bean definitions instantiate singleton beans when first requested rather than during ApplicationContext startup, making an optional integration genuinely demand-driven while retaining the container's proxy and lifecycle semantics.
Go's sync.Once lets a service wrap a one-time connection, parser or cache acquisition so concurrent first callers wait for one initializer and later callers reuse the published result.
.NET's System.Lazy<T> defers a factory until Value is first read and makes the thread-safety and exception-caching policy explicit through its constructors and LazyThreadSafetyMode.

name: compound-components
document:
compound-components
compound component
compound component pattern
Give a family of cooperating components one owner — the parent — that holds the shared state and publishes it implicitly to every child, so consumers compose the family declaratively while the parent alone enforces its invariants and behaviour.
A widget only works when a parent and its children agree on one piece of state (which option is selected, which panel is open, whether a field is invalid), but the call site is the only place that knows the children. Holding the state at the call site means threading the value and its update callbacks into every child (prop drilling), and holding it in the children means the parent cannot enforce the family's invariants — exclusivity, ordering, keyboard behaviour — nor react to a child's change in one place. The recurring decision is where the shared state lives and how children participate in it without the call site wiring them.
Component-tree UI code: design-system and widget libraries (select/option, tabs, menus, field groups) in frameworks that can inject state into descendants without passing it through props — React context or child cloning, Angular content projection plus DI, Vue provide/inject, Compose CompositionLocal and slot scopes, SwiftUI environment and preference keys, Blazor cascading values, WPF attached properties over the logical tree — and in widget toolkits whose group objects (Swing ButtonGroup, JavaFX ToggleGroup, Qt QButtonGroup, tkinter control variables) play the same role. It pays off where the public API must stay small and the children must stay replaceable; it does not apply in languages without a component tree or without an implicit-injection channel.
Custom select, combobox or autocomplete families built from Option children — the canonical example: the parent owns the selection, the highlight and the keyboard interaction while options only declare their value and label.
Tabs, accordions and menus where Tab/TabPanel/MenuItem children register their identity and the parent owns the active item, the ordering and the ARIA wiring.
Form-field families (Field + Label + Input + Error) that share one validation/invalid state and generated ids without the call site passing them around.
Data-group widgets: tables with Column definitions, list widgets with Item children, tree views with Node children, chart legends with Series children.
Design-system libraries that export one namespaced symbol whose parts must be used together — the context in which the pattern is most often documented and most valuable.
Collapsible panel families (Disclosure pattern) where a parent owns the open/closed state and Trigger/Content children read it — also known as the Disclosure pattern in ARIA authoring practices.
Stepper/wizard widgets where a parent owns current-step state and Step/StepIndicator children read it without the consumer threading step indices.
Popover/tooltip families where a trigger button and a content panel share open/close state through the parent without prop drilling.
Radix UI Primitives — Dialog.Root owns the open/close context and Trigger/Portal/Content/Title/Description consume it, while asChild (Slot) merges each part's props, refs and keyboard behaviour into the consumer's own button or link.
Ark UI headless components (built on Zag.js state machines) — Popover.Root/Trigger/Positioner/Content share state through the root, ids props compose aria bindings across two families, and the same compound anatomy works in React, Solid, Vue and Svelte.
Headless UI's Dialog family (Dialog, DialogBackdrop, DialogPanel, DialogTitle, Description) — the root enforces the dismiss contract (open prop, onClose callback, focus trap, aria-labelledby) and every part reads the shared open/closed state, exposed for styling as data-open/data-closed attributes.

name: single-table-inheritance
document:
single-table-inheritance
table per hierarchy
discriminator column mapping
Map an inheritance hierarchy of classes onto one shared table whose columns are the union of all classes' fields, using a type code (discriminator) column to decide which class each row instantiates, so polymorphic reads need no joins.
A class hierarchy must be persisted, the hierarchy is small and its classes share most fields, and cross-class queries or polymorphic loads are frequent: mapping each class to its own table would force a join per level on almost every read, while the subtypes differ by only a few columns.
Object-relational mapping of a small, shallow, stable class hierarchy whose subclasses are mostly variations on shared state - domain-model inheritance (Employee/Engineer/Manager), payment or content types - where the storage layer is chosen by the team and the persistence framework can be taught the type code (JPA/EF Core/ActiveRecord/SQLAlchemy/most ORMs make this their default strategy) or the mapping is written by hand over SQL.
Small stable hierarchies where subclasses share most state: Employee/Engineer/Manager, Payment/CardPayment/WirePayment, Notification/EmailNotification/PushNotification.
Content or asset models with a handful of similar types (Photo/Question/Post, Blog/RssBlog) distinguished by a type code, where cross-type queries and listings are the dominant read.
Legacy or third-party schemas that already hold a hierarchy in one table with a kind column and must be mapped onto domain classes without restructuring the database.
Reporting and analytics over a hierarchy where one wide table with a type column beats joining four tables for every subtype question.
ORM-default configurations: teams that pick the framework's default hierarchy mapping (JPA SINGLE_TABLE, EF Core TPH) because join avoidance and mapping simplicity outweigh column honesty for their hierarchy size.
Rails Active Record single-table inheritance: ActiveRecord::Inheritance stores the subclass name in the table's type column by default (Company/Firm/Client all live in companies with type = 'Firm'), so fetching via the base class returns correctly-typed objects - GitLab runs a production monolith on this mechanism and maintains a written policy on when STI must not be used.
EF Core's default table-per-hierarchy mapping: a Blog/RssBlog hierarchy shares one table, the discriminator's name, CLR type and per-class values are set with HasDiscriminator/HasValue, and EF Core automatically adds the discriminator predicate to derived-type queries (throwing on unmapped discriminator values).
SQLAlchemy declarative polymorphic mappers: the base class declares polymorphic_on = 'type' in __mapper_args__ and each subclass a unique polymorphic_identity, so one person table answers polymorphic queries for Person/Employee rows without joins.

name: entity
document:
entity
reference object
domain entity
Give a domain concept a stable identity that survives attribute changes, representation changes and time, and define its equality, lifecycle and lookup in terms of that identity instead of in terms of its attributes.
A model that compares objects by their attributes cannot answer whether two instances are the same thing: a customer whose e-mail and plan changed looks like a different customer, while two distinct people who share a name look like one. References held by other objects, caches and audit records break silently, and every state change forces callers to re-identify the object.
Rich domain models in which some concepts must be tracked through time: the object is created, changes state, is stored and reloaded, and may exist in several representations (in-memory instance, database row, message payload, UI snapshot) that all have to denote the same thing. It is the modelling decision that pairs with Value Object: attribute clusters become values, while the things whose history matters keep an identity.
Master data tracked for years — customers, accounts, contracts, products, patients — where attributes change but the business entity stays the same (e.g., a Customer who moves house is still the same Customer).
Documents with a lifecycle: orders, invoices, bookings and shipments that move through states (pending → paid → shipped → delivered) while remaining the same document with a stable order number.
Shopping cart to order transition: a ShoppingCart is reconstituted as an Order with the same customer identity but a new order identity, preserving the correlation to the customer while starting a new business process.
Correlating representations across layers: an entity persisted as database rows, published as domain events, and displayed in a UI must be recognisable as the same thing in all three — identity is the correlation key across representations.
In-memory session consistency: a unit of work or identity map ensures the same Customer loaded twice in one request is one object reference, preventing edits from silently diverging into two copies.
Referencing across bounded contexts: one microservice holds a CustomerId reference to another service's aggregate root, allowing independent deployment and loading without a direct object pointer.
Healthcare records: a Patient entity persists across multiple visits, lab results and prescriptions — the patient identity is the anchor for the entire medical history regardless of demographic changes.
Versioned documents: an InsurancePolicy entity may be replaced by a new version while the original policy number (identity) remains the correlation handle for auditors and legacy systems.
Hibernate/JPA: an @Entity class with an @Id is managed by the persistence context, which guarantees one in-memory instance per identity per session — loading the same row twice in a session returns the same object reference, an Identity Map built into the framework.
Entity Framework Core: identity resolution makes the DbContext track a single entity instance per primary key, so duplicate instances arriving in a deserialized graph are merged into the already-tracked entity instead of diverging into two tracked copies.
Drupal Entity API: nodes, users and taxonomy terms (content entities) and roles or image styles (configuration entities) are identity-bearing objects with typed storage handlers, revisions and field bundles behind one CRUD and validation API.

name: page-controller
document:
page-controller
model-1
Give each logical page or form its own input controller that handles the requests addressed to it — reading the request, invoking domain logic and choosing the view — instead of routing every request through one shared handler.
Dynamic pages repeat the same request handling: parse and validate the incoming request, call domain logic, pick a view, report errors. Without a per-page home for that logic it either spreads into templates or gets copied into every script; the recurring decision is whether one page or form owns its request handling, or whether a central controller multiplexes all of them.
Server-side web presentation where URLs map one-to-one onto logical pages, forms or actions: CGI programs, servlets and JSP pages, controller actions, Razor Pages, route handlers in micro-frameworks. It fits sites whose pages share little behaviour, page-focused areas of larger applications, and frameworks whose native unit is a page; it stops fitting as soon as most pages need the same authentication, internationalisation, layout or tracing.
Small to medium websites where each page has its own URL, its own data and its own template (CMS front ends, marketing pages with forms, internal tools).
Form-heavy areas where one page owns one interaction end to end: show the form, validate the submission, run one workflow, render the result.
Prototypes and scripting-era deployments where one program, servlet or route function per page is the natural deployment unit.
Page-focused corners of a larger application (account settings, an admin console) whose pages genuinely differ from one another.
Frameworks whose canonical unit is the page itself: Razor Pages (PageModel = Page Controller), ASP.NET Web Forms code-behind, Java Struts Actions, Django FBV (Function-Based Views) mapped one-per-URL, Flask route functions, PHP single-file-per-page.
Per-page Ajax callbacks that are tightly coupled to a specific page's data and logic, where extracting them into a shared controller would create artificial coupling.
Situations where page-specific code is large enough to warrant a dedicated class but small enough that a full command-object framework is overkill.
ASP.NET Core Razor Pages: each PageModel owns the handlers and view data for one page, with OnGet/OnPost methods providing a concrete page-controller unit for page-specific forms. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/razor-pages/?view=aspnetcore-10.0
Django function-based views: URLconf maps a URL pattern to one Python view function that receives HttpRequest and returns the page response, making small page-specific interactions explicit. https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/6.1/topics/http/views/
Flask route functions: the route decorator binds a URL and HTTP methods to one view function, a lightweight Page Controller shape for independent pages and forms. https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/quickstart/

name: monitor-object
document:
monitor-object
thread-safe passive object
monitor
Serialise concurrent method invocations on a shared object by giving the object its own lock and condition variables, so that only one method executes inside it at a time and methods that cannot proceed wait cooperatively instead of polling.
Objects shared by several threads expose their state through ordinary methods, and nothing stops concurrent callers from interleaving inside those methods, corrupting the invariants they were written to maintain. The race is then papered over with ad-hoc locking, sleeps and busy-wait loops scattered through client code. The recurring decision is whether the object itself should own the serialisation (and the scheduling) of its methods instead of leaving that discipline to every caller.
Shared-memory concurrency, where the mutable state of an object is reached by more than one thread and its methods must be atomic with respect to one another. It matters most when some methods cannot run to completion until another method changes the state - a queue that is full or empty, a resource that is not yet available, a phase that has not been reached - because then a method must suspend and later resume, which requires releasing the lock while it waits.
Bounded buffers and work queues shared by producer and consumer threads, where producers wait while the queue is full and consumers wait while it is empty - the pattern's canonical example.
Session, connection or entity registries on a server, where lookups, insertion and eviction must be atomic and callers may have to wait for capacity or for an entry to reappear.
Caches with in-flight bookkeeping (single-flight computation), where a thread that requests an already-computed key waits for the first thread's result instead of recomputing it.
Shared configuration, counters or statistics objects read and updated by request threads, where each call must observe a consistent snapshot of the state.
State machines and simulators whose step methods block until another thread advances a transition, for example a test harness waiting for a worker to reach a known state.
In-process resource pools (connection, database or worker pools) where acquisition blocks until an entry is returned or a timeout expires.
Java's java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue is a fixed-capacity monitor-style bounded buffer: put blocks while full and take blocks while empty, making the producer-consumer coordination explicit.
.NET's System.Collections.Concurrent.BlockingCollection<T> supplies bounded Add/Take blocking, cancellation and completion semantics around a producer-consumer collection; use it instead of hand-rolling Monitor.Wait/Pulse.
Python's queue.Queue provides a thread-safe multi-producer/multi-consumer boundary with blocking put/get operations and optional timeouts, a standard monitor-style primitive for worker pools.

name: model-view-intent
document:
model-view-intent
mvi
Structure one UI feature as a single loop in which every user interaction becomes an intent value, a pure reduce step derives the next immutable state from the previous state and that intent, and the view renders only that state - so the screen's behaviour is determined by data instead of by scattered event handlers.
Presentation state is spread across the view, its presenter and several observable channels: every handler sets its own field or widget directly, a loading flag, a data field and an error field can contradict each other, the view keeps state of its own that a configuration change or process death destroys, and no state transition can be exercised without instantiating the UI.
Interactive applications with a declarative view layer and some reactive runtime - Android/Compose with coroutines and Flow, SwiftUI, React, Scala.js, or a hand-rolled event loop - where one screen or app-level feature can own a single immutable state object, user events can be represented as data values, and the view can re-render from a new state value. It is applied per feature, not per widget, and it is independent of any particular framework.
A search or feed screen where loading, empty, error and result states are concurrent flags in the old design and must become one state value the view can render without contradictions.
Complex screen flows - checkout, wizards, media players, editors - whose transitions must be explicit and reviewable rather than emerging from scattered handler code.
Screens that must survive configuration changes or process death by restoring one serializable state object instead of replaying a history of view commands.
Crash reports and support cases that carry the current state plus the last intent, making reproduction and replay possible without reproducing the exact tap sequence.
Cross-platform features that share the reducer between platforms and swap only the view layer (Android and iOS, web and desktop).
Large applications where each feature module exposes an intent/state contract and different teams own the loop for their screens.
A Cycle.js component whose DOM and HTTP driver streams become intents, whose model derives state, and whose view renders that state is a direct stream-based MVI implementation.
A Kotlin Multiplatform feature built with Orbit MVI can share an OrbitContainer's intent, reduce, state, and side-effect flow across Android, iOS, and desktop.
An Android Jetpack Compose feature following Android's official unidirectional-data-flow guidance can use a ViewModel-owned immutable UiState, upward events, and downward rendering as a framework-native MVI realization.

name: side-effect-free-function
document:
side-effect-free-function
pure function
Put the model's logic into operations that compute a result from their inputs alone, so that a caller - and a test - can predict the result without knowing any state the operation might secretly touch.
Reasoning about a design becomes guesswork when operations do more than return a result: the caller must read the implementation and every delegation to know which state a call changes, and no result can be reproduced in a test without recreating the state around it. As rules compose, the number of hidden interactions grows faster than the behaviour being built, so the model stops being safely predictable.
Applies inside the model layer of any codebase whose rules are combined and composed - pricing, eligibility, allocation, validation - and where a computation must be exercised in tests without a database, clock or message broker in the loop. It matters most where several rules interact (composition multiplies hidden coupling) and in languages whose defaults are mutable objects, because there the discipline has to be stated rather than assumed.
Pricing and discount rules: unit prices, tax and rebates computed from immutable inputs, so the same basket always prices the same way.
Eligibility and specification checks: a rule expressed as a predicate over a value and reused in validation, selection and tests.
Money and quantity arithmetic: scaling, adding and rounding return new values instead of adjusting a running total in place.
Deriving test data and expected values from the same pure functions the model uses, instead of hand-copied golden values.
Query-side report assembly: projections, summaries and totals built by composing pure functions over already-loaded immutable data.
Memoizing an expensive domain computation, which is sound exactly because the function is referentially transparent.
Redux reducers: the store computes the next state by calling (previousState, action) => newState with no mutation, no clock, no randomness, so DevTools can replay a recorded action log and reproduce the exact state and useSelector can detect changes by reference comparison alone.
React function components: the official contract is that rendering must be a pure function of props, state and context, so React can cache components whose inputs are unchanged, abandon an outdated render mid-flight, and call each component twice in Strict Mode to expose impurity.
Haskell: ordinary functions are pure by default and effects are confined to IO-typed values, so the type signature itself states whether a computation touches the world and the compiler, not review, enforces the query half of the split.

name: test-data-builder
document:
test-data-builder
test builder
Give each domain type used in tests a builder that starts from valid, commonly used defaults, so a test states only the data its assertion depends on and everything else is supplied correctly without being mentioned.
Strict constructors and immutable value objects make test setup a chore: every test that needs an object must supply all constructor arguments, so tests fill up with values that have nothing to do with the behaviour under test, break whenever a constructor argument or the object's structure changes, and copy the same construction code from test to test. The ready-made fixtures of an object mother remove the repetition but not the variation - every slightly different case adds another factory method, and the mother degenerates into duplicated code or a swarm of methods holding a single new statement.
Applies to test suites over a domain model whose objects have many required fields or cross-field invariants, where each test varies only a small part of the data and a valid instance can be constructed without external systems. It is language-neutral but pays off most where the language lacks named/default arguments or copy-with-modification, and it belongs to the test sources: production code keeps its own constructors and must not depend on a builder whose defaults are chosen for tests.
Unit tests over domain types with many constructor parameters and cross-field invariants (invoices, users, policies) where each test cares about one or two values.
Mock-based interaction tests that must hand a valid collaborator object to the system under test with e.g. only its id varied to observe request routing.
Bug-reproduction tests: the builder encodes the standard valid case and the test states only the faulty value from the report.
Suites with many test classes over the same domain fixtures (payroll, insurance, orders) that need per-test variation rather than a handful of canned objects.
Table-driven or property-style tests over one dimension: build the valid base once and override that dimension for each case.
Integration tests that need a complete, plausible object graph (nested entities, collections, ids) deviating in a single field.
factory_bot (thoughtbot) for Ruby/Rails: one factory per class holding a minimal valid set of default attributes, with tests overriding only the fields under test at call time (build(:user, email: "bad@example.com")) - the builder shape generalized into a library.
factory_boy for Python: class-based factories declare the default keyword arguments for the target class' __init__ (Meta.model), and each test overrides just what it asserts (UserFactory.build(first_name="Joe")), with factory inheritance standing in for object-mother variants.
Instancio for Java implements the same contract generically: create(Person.class) populates every field, and .set(field(Person::getName), "Homer") overrides only the fields the test names - its user guide states the goal as populating everything you are not interested in.

name: object-mother
document:
object-mother
test object mother
Centralise the creation of ready-made, valid domain objects in one factory so that every test across the suite starts from the same named, well-understood fixtures instead of rebuilding object graphs by hand.
Tests throughout a codebase need valid instances of the same domain objects, and constructing them by hand - wiring value objects, dependent entities, identities and required collections - is verbose and duplicated in every test class. The copies drift apart, churn whenever a constructor or validation rule changes, and let a test fail for accidental setup reasons rather than the behaviour under test; a per-class setUp/BeforeEach method cannot be shared between test classes.
Applies to test suites over a domain model with real invariants: entities and aggregates with many required fields, value objects, dependent objects and identity rules, where a handful of named business scenarios (an employee hired last week, an overdue invoice, a VIP customer) can be reused across many test classes. The mother belongs to test sources and is meaningless in production code; where every test needs unique data rather than a shared canonical example, a Test Data Builder fits better.
Domain aggregates with many required fields and cross-field invariants are needed in dozens of test classes (an employee with marital status, dependents and payroll history).
Persistence or ORM tests need valid saved entities with stable identities and the related rows the schema requires.
The suite must exercise named business scenarios (VIP customer, trial account, overdue invoice) that should mean the same thing everywhere.
A regression suite wants the same fixture data as before a refactor, so behaviour changes show up instead of being masked by rewritten setup.
Contract or integration tests across services need the same canonical examples in several codebases, behind one mother per language.
Microsoft's EF4/EF6 testability guidance uses EmployeeObjectMother.CreateEmployees() to supply shared employees across MVC controller test fixtures.
The Python object-mother-pattern package provides reusable mother classes for valid and invalid values plus composed collections, giving Python suites a concrete implementation of the pattern.
Java's Matriarch library exposes a Mother factory with JUnit integration and field overrides; it is an Object Mother-style option when canonical fixtures need controlled variation.
