name: strategy
document:
strategy
policy
Define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one behind a common operation, and make them interchangeable, so the algorithm a context executes can vary independently of the context and its clients - including at run time.
One class supports several variants of the same computation - sort orders, pricing or tax rules, routing and backoff policies, compression codecs - and the variant has to be selected at run time. Hard-wiring the variants into the class (or into one subclass per variant) mixes algorithm detail with the class's own logic, forces recompilation for every new variant, and turns selection into a growing conditional that runs on every call.
Applies when one context object owns the data but delegates one algorithm (or a small set of related algorithms) to a pluggable implementation, when the implementations share a stable operation signature, and when the choice is made at run time - from user input, configuration, request data or deployment - or from a closed family of variants that already differ in space/time or accuracy trade-offs. Typical homes: pricing, discount and tax calculation; sorting and comparison orders; routing, load-balancing, retry/backoff and rate-limiting policies; compression, serialization and encoding codecs; validation and normalization rules; numerical solvers chosen per problem.
Pricing, discount and tax calculation where the rule set is selected per customer, region or campaign and changes independently of the checkout or invoicing flow.
Sorting and comparison orders chosen by context - a UI column, a request parameter, a locale - which is how the JDK uses the pattern for Comparator in Collections.sort/List.sort and how C uses it for qsort's comparison function.
Routing and policy selection: path finding, load balancing, retry/backoff and rate-limiting algorithms chosen from configuration without editing the caller.
Compression, serialization and encoding codecs (gzip/deflate/zstd, JSON/Protobuf, character encodings) selected per stream, per record or per request.
Validation and normalization rule sets for pluggable document or form types, where each variant knows its own schema quirks and error format.
Numerical and scientific kernels: integration, interpolation or solver algorithms chosen per problem with different accuracy/performance trade-offs.
Pluggable authentication/authorization or hashing policies chosen per tenant, where the same code path must run different algorithms behind one signature.
E-commerce shipping provider selection (UPS, FedEx, DHL) where each carrier implements a different rate-calculation algorithm, and the shipping calculator is decoupled from the carrier specifics.
Payment processing gateways (credit card, virtual account, wallet) where each method has distinct validation, fee calculation and settlement rules, but the checkout flow is uniform.
Data retrieval at runtime: selecting between an API client, a web scraper, a database query or a cache-first lookup depending on availability, cost or latency requirements.
ML inference: choosing between ONNX, TensorRT, CPU or GPU backends for model execution, each with different latency/throughput trade-offs, selected per request or per deployment environment.
Travel and navigation: routing algorithms (walking, cycling, driving, public transit) with distinct distance/time/transfer calculations, chosen by user preference or real-time conditions.
Hybrid AI systems: combining symbolic decision logic with sub-symbolic ML model inference behind a uniform interface, enabling runtime selection of the reasoning strategy.
Log routing: dispatching log events to different backends (file, console, cloud observability platforms) selected by deployment environment or tenant configuration.
Encryption and cipher suites: selecting TLS cipher suites, password hashing algorithms (bcrypt, argon2), or encoding schemes based on security policy and compliance requirements.
File format processing: parsing and rendering strategies for documents, images, or data files where each format requires different handling but the pipeline remains uniform.
Game AI: selecting enemy behavior algorithms (aggressive, defensive, evasive, patrol) per entity type or difficulty level, enabling runtime personality changes.
Apache Kafka producers select or replace the partition-selection algorithm through the org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.Partitioner interface (default sticky/key-hash, RoundRobinPartitioner for even distribution), configured per producer via partitioner.class.
Envoy proxy chooses one load balancing algorithm per upstream cluster from the envoy.load_balancing_policies extension category (ROUND_ROBIN, LEAST_REQUEST and third-party policies), each implementing one host-selection operation behind the cluster's router call path.
scikit-learn estimators expose interchangeable optimization algorithms behind one fit/predict API via the solver parameter (LogisticRegression: lbfgs, liblinear, saga, newton-cg, newton-cholesky), documented as a choice driven by dataset size and penalty rather than by a different client interface.

statement: Choose where recurring actor-specific behavior resides and define the uniform contract by which the frame driver advances every live participant exactly once.
name: bulkhead
document:
bulkhead
bulkhead isolation
cell-based architecture
Partition finite shared capacity at the failure domain (dependency, tenant, priority class, or cell) into independently bounded pools or permits, with an explicit queue and saturation policy, so one slow, saturated, or failing participant cannot consume capacity reserved for others.
Several dependencies or tenants share thread, connection, worker, or permit pools. When one becomes slow, leaky, or overloaded, its calls hold shared slots and fill shared queues, so unrelated work queues and fails behind it; the design needs a boundary that contains resource exhaustion without pretending to isolate CPU, network, or server-side limits that remain shared.
Any component whose concurrency is a finite resource: a service calling multiple downstream APIs, a multi-tenant workload, a job runner mixing interactive and batch work, or an inference and gateway tier with per-deployment quotas. The failure mode to contain is degradation and overload (slow dependency, connection leak, traffic spike), not only hard failure, and the isolation boundary must be chosen at the failure domain - instance, dependency, tenant or priority class.
A service that calls several downstream APIs through one shared HTTP client: give each downstream its own connection and thread budget so one hanging endpoint cannot block the others.
Multi-tenant SaaS where one tenant's workload must not consume the concurrency available to other tenants (per-tenant pools).
Interactive request traffic sharing a database with batch or report jobs: separate pools per workload class keep the database from serialising everything behind the batch.
An API gateway or backend-for-frontend routing to many backends with per-route concurrency caps, so a slow backend does not consume the proxy's shared capacity.
Job workers that mix latency-critical and background queues: per-queue worker pools prevent a backlog of background jobs from starving urgent work.
Inference and AI serving where each model deployment has its own concurrency quota and a saturated model must not consume the shared request capacity.
Cell-based architectures: each cell (complete, independent service instance) is a bulkhead partition; load grows by adding cells, and a failure is contained to the single cell — used at AWS, Google, and Netflix scale.
Shuffle sharding: Amazon Route 53-style virtual shard assignment where each tenant is assigned to a random shard of two or more cells; with eight cells and two-per-shard there are 28 unique shards, so a problem affects only 1/28th of tenants — far better than regular per-cell partitioning.
AI and inference workloads: per-deployment or per-tenant Azure OpenAI or LLM deployment quotas prevent one saturated model from consuming the shared request capacity across the platform.
Database RU isolation: Azure Cosmos DB request-unit throughput assigned per container acts as a storage-layer bulkhead; one noisy container cannot exhaust the RU budget of others.
Resilience4j's SemaphoreBulkhead and FixedThreadPoolBulkhead give a JVM service per-dependency permits versus a bounded queue and worker pool; choose based on whether caller threads may be occupied.
Netflix Hystrix's per-command thread pools or semaphore isolation reject work and route it to fallback, containing a slow downstream to its command boundary (historical and deprecated).
.NET services use Polly's BulkheadPolicy/AsyncBulkheadPolicy (maxParallelization plus maxQueuingActions, rejecting with BulkheadRejectedException when both are full); Polly v8 replaced it with ConcurrencyLimiter over System.Threading.RateLimiting, whose partitioned per-key limiters give per-tenant bulkheads.
Service meshes enforce bulkheads at the platform layer: an Istio DestinationRule's trafficPolicy.connectionPool caps tcp.maxConnections, http.http1MaxPendingRequests and http.http2MaxRequests per upstream host, enforced by Envoy alongside its circuit-breaking limits.
Netflix's concurrency-limits library replaces hand-tuned static partitions with per-dependency adaptive limits (Vegas and Gradient algorithms modelled on TCP congestion control) that shrink the concurrency budget automatically as downstream latency rises, e.g. separating live from batch traffic on one gRPC server.
Envoy maintains per-upstream-cluster connection pools and circuit-breaking limits, while Kubernetes ResourceQuota caps aggregate namespace CPU, memory, or object use; both are platform-level capacity partitions rather than application call-site wrappers.

statement: Choose where recurring actor-specific behavior resides and define the uniform contract by which the frame driver advances every live participant exactly once.
name: abstract-factory
document:
abstract-factory
kit
factory of factories
Expose one creation contract for each product kind in a coherent family, letting clients switch the selected family at the composition root without naming concrete products or mixing incompatible variants.
A client must construct several related products that collaborate as a matched set, but direct construction spreads family keys and concrete class names through the code. Adding a family then becomes configuration branches plus constructor edits, while mixing products from different families can fail only after incompatible objects interact.
Use in object- or interface-based subsystems with two independent axes of change: product kinds (button, slider, connection, command) and product families or variants (dark/light, PostgreSQL/Oracle, AWS/GCP). The family is normally selected once at a composition root, products from one family are intended to collaborate, and clients must compile, test and ship without knowing concrete product types; if products are intentionally mixed or only one kind is created, use a smaller creator instead.
Cross-platform or themable UI toolkits: Qt's QStyleFactory resolves keys such as "windows" and "fusion" to built-in or plugin QStyle implementations that govern a coherent widget look-and-feel; a fuller abstract factory applies the same family key across several product interfaces.
Provider-independent database code: ADO.NET's DbProviderFactory/DbProviderFactories create a matched DbConnection, DbCommand, DbParameter and DbDataAdapter set for a selected provider such as SQL Server or OLE DB.
Parser-provider plugins: JAXP's DocumentBuilderFactory and SAXParserFactory hide implementation classes behind standard factory APIs, allowing the composition root to select a provider while client code uses parser abstractions.
Java's ServiceLoader documentation uses a CodecFactory service with getEncoder and getDecoder operations; the selected provider supplies a coherent codec family while clients depend only on the service interface.
Test infrastructure: an in-memory factory family whose products are fakes, injected in place of the production family so integration tests need no network.
Game and simulation engines: per-biome object families (terrain, props, audio) that must stay aesthetically consistent when a level is loaded.
SaaS multi-tenant applications: per-tenant theme factories so every rendered page uses the tenant's brand colours, fonts and spacing without per-request conditionals.
Document-format parsers: factory per format (PDF, HTML, EPUB) producing matched tokenizer, layout engine and renderer so a viewer can switch formats from a single configuration key.

statement: Choose where recurring actor-specific behavior resides and define the uniform contract by which the frame driver advances every live participant exactly once.
name: messaging-gateway
document:
messaging-gateway
Encapsulate access to a messaging system behind an ordinary interface of domain methods, so calling application code makes method calls while a single component owns message construction, correlation, timeouts and error translation.
Application code that talks to a broker keeps importing messaging concepts: it builds the payload, picks the channel, attaches a reply address and a correlation id, parses the response and interprets broker errors. The trigger for this pattern is that callers should make a method call instead of writing messaging code - the messaging knowledge belongs in exactly one place that can change without touching business rules.
At the boundary between application logic and a messaging system (message broker, MQ, queue service or actor runtime): the other side is reached by messages, but the caller is ordinary domain code that should see typed parameters and typed results. Applies to one-way (fire and forget) and request-reply interactions alike, and to blocking as well as asynchronous call styles.
A domain service that must query another system (inventory, pricing, credit scoring) over a queue: the caller invokes checkStock(sku) and receives a typed answer.
An HTTP or API layer whose controller awaits a brokered round trip (Spring Integration gateway interface, NestJS ClientProxy, MassTransit request client).
Batch and background jobs that dispatch work through a typed job API instead of assembling payloads (ActiveJob perform_later, Celery delay).
Wrapping a legacy system's MQ interface once, so the rest of the codebase never learns its message format.
Test seams: unit tests substitute a fake gateway, integration tests run the same interface against a real broker.
Migration seam: keep the gateway contract stable while the transport moves from one broker to another.
Actor and streaming stacks where a facade wraps ask/request so callers never hold ActorRefs or inboxes.
Spring Integration's @MessagingGateway and GatewayProxyFactoryBean let application code inject a typed interface while the framework routes calls into channels and returns replies.
MassTransit's IRequestClient<T> and GetResponse<TResponse> provide a typed request-reply client over the bus, keeping request and response message contracts out of the calling service.
RabbitMQ's RPC tutorial demonstrates a gateway-like client that publishes to rpc_queue with reply_to and correlation_id, then resolves the matching callback response.

name: pipeline
document:
pipeline
assembly line
processing pipeline
Decompose a transformation into an ordered sequence of named stages that each consume the previous stage's output and produce the next stage's input, so the workflow reads top to bottom and every step can be tested, instrumented, reordered or replaced on its own.
A multi-step transformation is written as one long function or a tangle of nested calls: the steps are unnamed, their order is implicit in statement order, intermediate values need throwaway names, there is no seam at which a single step can be logged, tested or replaced, and the same sequence is retyped at every call site that needs it.
Processing that naturally decomposes into successive transformations of the same payload - request handling, ETL, compiler passes, message enrichment, image or byte-stream processing - whether the payload is a single value or a stream. It fits in-process, staged execution where one driver owns ordering, error handling and cancellation; distributing the stages across processes, transports and independently deployed filters is the architectural pipe-and-filter pattern instead.
Request handling: deserialise, authenticate, validate, enrich, persist and render a request, with each step named so a failing stage is attributable and testable in isolation.
ETL and data import: extract, clean, transform, validate and load large files as a stream, so no intermediate collection is materialised and memory stays bounded.
Compiler and interpreter passes: source, tokens, AST, resolution, optimisation and code emission, where each pass is an independent stage over the intermediate representation and the pass list is the pipeline.
Message enrichment in an integration flow: unwrap, translate, enrich and route a message, one stage per concern, with per-channel ordering; the cross-process version stays pipe-and-filter.
Image or byte-stream processing: decode, crop or resize, watermark and encode, lazily per frame or chunk, optionally overlapping stages across cores.
Configuration-driven data cleaning: the stage list is assembled from configuration or a plugin registry so different tenants get different ordered steps without changing the stages themselves.
TensorFlow tf.data input pipelines: tf.data.Dataset pipelines that chain map, prefetch, parallel_interleave and shuffle stages to feed a training loop efficiently, with each stage independently configurable and the whole pipeline testable in isolation.
LLM token streaming: HTTP server-sent event streams where an LLM produces tokens at inference speed while clients consume at variable network speed; stream.pipeline() prevents the inference server from buffering unbounded tokens in memory when a slow client disconnects (Node.js stream backpressure case study).
Observability telemetry pipelines: OpenTelemetry Collector chains receivers, processors (memory_limiter, batch, filter, transform, tail_sampling) and exporters for traces, metrics and logs, with connectors (e.g., spanmetrics) bridging signal types and memory_limiter placed first to prevent OOM before filtering.
Typed TypeScript pipeline with schema validation: Zod or io-ts schemas define the stage contract at each boundary, catching schema violations at the exact stage that produced bad data rather than at a distant consumer.
Async generator pipelines in Python: asyncio queues with bounded capacity connect async generator stages, propagating backpressure by pausing producers when the queue is full; the FinStream analytics case study showed 82% memory reduction and 99.7% latency reduction versus unbounded buffering.
Event-streaming pipelines with Kafka and Flink: producers, topic partitions, Flink consumers and checkpointing form a distributed pipeline where backpressure cascades across every boundary; the Kafka max.block.ms and Flink backpressure.sample.interval settings interact under partition saturation and must be tested together under load.
Dynamic pipeline parallelism: construct-and-run pipelines (MapReduce, Spark) fix stage count at construction, while on-the-fly pipelines (Cilk-P Piper algorithm) allow the structure to emerge at runtime, varying per iteration and supporting data-dependent branching; on-the-fly enables pipelines like x264 that cannot be expressed with a fixed static structure.
LLVM compiler pass pipelines: PassBuilder assembles ModulePassManager, CGSCCPassManager, FunctionPassManager and LoopPassManager across the IR hierarchy (Module → CGSCC → Function → Loop), with registered callbacks injecting passes at named extension points (pipeline-start, vectorizer-start, optimizer-last); incorrect PreservedAnalyses declarations invalidate all downstream analyses.
Continuous data pipelines at scale (Google model): periodic pipelines run on cron and suffer from depth growth and resource exhaustion as organic load increases; continuous pipelines (master-slave or event-triggered) replace idle-waiting with always-on processing, eliminating the 'pipeline vs cron' discontinuity at the cost of operational complexity.
ML pipeline orchestration (Airflow, Kubeflow, Prefect, Dagster): each orchestrator applies the pipeline pattern at the workflow level - Airflow's DAG-of-tasks, Kubeflow's per-container-step pipelines with GPU scheduling, Prefect's monoflow/subflow/orchestrator pattern, and Dagster's software-defined assets where asset dependencies imply the pipeline; the pipeline is the scheduler's unit of execution, not an implementation detail.
Apache Beam: PCollections flow through composable PTransforms (ParDo, Combine and GroupByKey) in a pipeline graph, making each transform boundary explicit while the runner handles execution.
Node.js stream.pipeline(): Readable, Transform and Writable stages compose with built-in backpressure, error propagation and AbortSignal cancellation; this is a concrete streaming realization, not a durable workflow engine.

name: lazy-acquisition
document:
lazy-acquisition
lazy loading
deferred acquisition
Defer acquiring an expensive or scarce resource until it is first used, so the acquisition cost is paid only by the holders that actually use it, while clients keep seeing an ordinary interface.
A resource is costly to acquire, scarce, and on many execution paths never needed at all, yet the code that holds it acquires it during construction, at start-up or on a hot entry path: the process pays for resources it never dereferences, start-up time grows with every optional subsystem, and scarce capacity (descriptors, connections, licenses, memory) is consumed by holders that never use it.
Applies to long-lived holders - objects, modules, services, containers - that front an external resource such as a file, socket or database connection, license, thread pool, GPU context, translation catalog or large lookup table. It pays off when the acquisition cost is large relative to a use, when a significant fraction of holders never use the resource, and when the runtime offers a one-time guard (or the holder is provably single-threaded). It is the wrong tool when the resource must be validated at boot, when acquisition is cheap, or when first use sits on a latency-critical path.
A request-handling object that opens a file or blob stream only on the code paths that actually read it (report export, attachment download, audit sink).
A service holding connections to a rarely consulted downstream — archive store, fallback provider, secondary region — that most requests never call.
A large lookup table, model or translation catalog loaded on first use instead of at process start, keeping start-up and memory bounded for the sessions that never need it.
Optional subsystems in desktop and mobile apps (camera, location, payment SDK, plugins) initialized when the feature is opened rather than when the app launches.
Test fixtures and tooling: starting a container, browser or database only for the tests that need it, so the fast path stays fast.
Per-session state in a server — a scratch buffer, a decompressor, a TLS session or prepared statement — allocated on first use of the session rather than on accept.
Database connection pools: HikariCP and similar pools typically create connections lazily on the first checkout rather than at pool construction, to avoid pinninglicenses and consuming file descriptors before the application is fully started.
Dependency injection containers (Spring @Lazy, Dagger 2 Lazy<T>) defer the creation of bean instances until they are first injected, reducing start-up time and breaking circular dependency cycles during bootstrap.
Logging frameworks (SLF4J/Logback): Logger instances are static final but the actual appender (file, socket, console) is initialized when the first log event at that level is fired, so logging infrastructure does not block application start.
Configuration objects: large YAML or JSON config trees are parsed and validated lazily on first access rather than eagerly at start-up, keeping CLI tools fast for commands that do not need the full configuration.
GPU contexts in graphics applications (OpenGL, Vulkan, CUDA) are expensive to create and are deferred until the first draw call or compute kernel launch, allowing the application to start and display a window without claiming GPU memory.
HTTP/service clients (gRPC channels, REST clients): a channel is lazily opened on the first request, enabling the client to be instantiated at module load time while deferring the TCP handshake and TLS handshake to the first real call.
Spring Framework @Lazy bean definitions instantiate singleton beans when first requested rather than during ApplicationContext startup, making an optional integration genuinely demand-driven while retaining the container's proxy and lifecycle semantics.
Go's sync.Once lets a service wrap a one-time connection, parser or cache acquisition so concurrent first callers wait for one initializer and later callers reuse the published result.
.NET's System.Lazy<T> defers a factory until Value is first read and makes the thread-safety and exception-caching policy explicit through its constructors and LazyThreadSafetyMode.

name: poison-pill
document:
poison-pill
sentinel message
end-of-stream marker
Terminate queue consumers cooperatively by sending a reserved sentinel message that each consumer recognises as "no more work", so consumers drain the backlog and exit without a separate control channel or forced cancellation.
A producer-consumer system must shut down, but its consumers block on an empty queue and the queue has no built-in "no more items" signal: callers either kill the workers mid-work and drop buffered items, or leave them blocked forever. Production has ended - how do the consumers learn that while still processing everything already queued?
In-process or broker-mediated producer-consumer systems with a FIFO work queue, a fixed set of long-lived consumers (threads, coroutines, actors) that block when the queue is empty, and a shutdown requirement that work already accepted by the queue be drained before the consumers exit - typically deployment, signal handling or test teardown.
Signal-driven shutdown of an in-process worker pool: the SIGTERM handler stops accepting work, then enqueues one pill per worker so the backlog is processed before the process exits.
Batch importers and ETL stages whose consumers block on a work queue and must finish the current batch before a run is considered complete.
Test harnesses and simulations: an explicit stop message makes thread-based systems deterministic to shut down, without sleeps or guessed timeouts.
Actor systems: a reserved stop message (for example Akka PoisonPill) terminates an actor after the messages already queued for it have been handled.
Log and event writers where the last records must reach the sink before consumers release their buffers and files.
Bounded-queue stages in a pipeline: pills travel the same backpressured channel as work, so upstream cannot keep producing after the stop decision.
Kubernetes pod shutdown: containers receive SIGTERM, workers stop pulling from the job queue, drain in-flight tasks, then exit within the terminationGracePeriodSeconds window.
Redis/Bull queue workers: a shutdown signal pushes a sentinel via BLPOP so workers exit cleanly without losing the right to process pending tasks.
Akka Streams and similar streaming frameworks: the GraphStage signals completion via onPull/downstream cancellation, which is the materialised equivalent of a poison pill.
Redis Streams consumer groups: XREADGROUP with block timeout naturally returns when the stream is empty; a special ID (e.g. ">") polling loop plus a shared shutdown flag replaces the in-process sentinel.
Broker-level poison message isolation: in Kafka, RabbitMQ, or Azure Service Bus, a permanently failing message (deserialisation error, validation failure) blocks a partition/consumer indefinitely; DLQ-based routing (publish to dead-letter topic after N retries, then commit offset and continue) is the broker-level analogue that prevents one poison message from halting the entire pipeline.
Kubernetes preStop hooks + pill drain: a container's lifecycle preStop hook can enqueue a sentinel into an in-process work queue while the orchestrator grants terminationGracePeriodSeconds for the drain to complete, ensuring zero work-drop during rolling updates.
Azure Service Bus competing-consumers workers: when a worker receives a shutdown notification it completes its current PeekLock message, then calls Abandon on any held locks before unregistering; Azure Service Bus dead-letter queues handle the poison-message variant when a message exceeds MaxDeliveryCount and cannot be delivered.
Akka hierarchical actor trees: sending PoisonPill to a parent actor stops it after all queued messages ahead of the pill are processed, and automatically sends stop messages to all children in bottom-up order; this is the idiomatic way to orchestrate ordered multi-actor shutdown.
Non-blocking retry architectures (RabbitMQ): rather than local Thread.sleep retries that block the consumer thread, use server-side TTL queues with Dead Letter Exchange routing to implement exponential backoff, keeping the consumer responsive to new messages and to shutdown pills.
Java's JDK BlockingQueue worker pools: because BlockingQueue has no built-in close, producers can enqueue a unique end-of-stream object after all work; each consumer takes until that sentinel and then the coordinator joins workers.
Python multiprocessing worker pools: multiprocessing.Queue/JoinableQueue supports FIFO task delivery with sentinel values and join-based drain tracking; send one sentinel per worker and join them after the queue is exhausted.
Akka Classic actors: PoisonPill is enqueued in the mailbox and processed after already queued messages, while Akka Typed requires an explicit Stop/Shutdown protocol; choose the API that matches the actor model.

name: function-composition
document:
function-composition
compose
function pipeline
Combine a chain of small unary transformations into one reusable function by sequencing them with a composition combinator (compose/pipe), so the order of the steps is stated once, every step stays independently testable, and the chain itself becomes a value that can be named, passed and reassembled.
A transformation that is naturally a sequence of small pure steps gets written as nested calls or as repeated imperative assignment (`h(g(f(x)))`, or `y = f(x); y = g(y); ...; return y`) at every call site. The order is duplicated wherever the chain is used, the intermediate values need throwaway names, steps cannot be reused in a different order, and changing one stage means editing every copy.
Pure or nearly pure value transformations - parsing, normalisation, validation, formatting, pricing, AST rewriting - where each step is unary and the language treats functions as values. It pays off when the chain is reused or assembled from data (configuration, plugin lists, per-request policy), when steps must be unit-tested in isolation, and when the same steps must also run element-wise over a collection or lazily over a stream. It stops applying where steps need side effects or branching between stages: there the shell around the pure core owns control flow.
Input normalisation: trim, parse, canonicalise and validate a payload before it reaches domain logic, with the same chain reused by HTTP handlers and message consumers.
Pricing and rule chains: base price, discount, tax and rounding applied in a fixed, configurable order to an immutable value object.
Compiler and AST work: a pass list of rewrite functions composed once and applied over the tree, with passes added or reordered per optimisation level.
Serialisation and formatting: sanitise, format, encode and sign a document, where each step is tested separately and the composed chain is stored as a constant.
Data transformation over collections: the same pure steps composed into one function and passed to map/filter/stream operations, so element-wise processing reuses the chain.
Policy assembly at startup: the processing chain is built from configuration or plugin registrations and then applied per request without further branching.
Reactive stream processing: RxJS Observable.pipe chains the same logical steps across asynchronous event sequences, with operators composed once and reused across streams.
ETL and data pipeline transformation: extract-transform-load chains where each stage (parse, clean, enrich, aggregate, write) is a unary pure function composed into a reusable pipeline run over batches or streaming data.
HTTP request/response middleware: the middleware stack is a composed function chain where each layer (authenticate, authorise, rate-limit, deserialize, validate) is a unary handler; composition is resolved once at startup.
Matrix and vector transformations in numerical code: each linear algebra operation (scale, rotate, translate, project) is a unary function on a matrix type; composing them once builds the transformation pipeline that is applied to every vertex or pixel.
Ramda pipelines: R.pipe and R.compose assemble reusable data-last transformations from small functions, centralising the order while letting the same composed value run over many inputs.
Redux store setup: Redux's compose helper combines store enhancers right-to-left into one enhancer, so the enhancer order is defined once instead of reconstructed at each store boundary.
lodash/fp transformations: lodash/fp's auto-curried, data-last compose/flow helpers assemble immutable-friendly transformations from reusable steps that can be passed as values.

name: inversion-of-control
document:
inversion-of-control
Hollywood Principle
IoC
Invert the direction of control between a reusable framework and application code: the framework owns the call flow and invokes the application's hooks at its extension points, so the generic sequence is reused while application code supplies only behaviour.
A reusable component - framework, container, UI toolkit, event loop, test runner - must own the sequence of calls (main loop, request dispatch, component lifecycle), while the behaviour at each step is application-specific; if application code had to call the framework's steps itself, the generic flow could neither be reused as a whole nor be extended without modifying it.
Applies wherever generic flow logic has to be specialised by application code: UI toolkits and event loops that decide when handlers fire, server containers and engines that own request dispatch and component lifecycle, test runners that own fixture and test sequencing, plugin hosts, and effect runtimes that own program entry. It is the defining characteristic of a framework as opposed to a library (a library is called by your code; a framework calls your code), and it usually arrives bundled with a container, dispatcher or engine - what remains to design is where the boundary sits and how much lifecycle you hand over.
GUI and event-driven applications: the windowing system or runtime owns the event loop and calls your event handlers, app delegate or declarative view body.
Server-side request handling: the container, engine or router owns listen-accept-dispatch and invokes the servlets, handlers, routes or middleware you registered.
Test frameworks: the runner owns discovery, fixture setup and teardown and calls your test methods and lifecycle hooks (JUnit, pytest, xUnit).
Container-managed components: EJB, Spring, Angular or Nest components whose construction, wiring and lifecycle callbacks are driven by the container that also owns the entry point.
Plugin and extension architectures: a host defines extension points and third-party plugins implement them, with the host deciding when each plugin is consulted (IDEs, browsers, build tools, game engines).
Inverted program entry: effect runtimes and app frameworks where the runtime's main calls the run value or app structure you provide instead of you orchestrating from main.
Callback-based C APIs: a library call such as qsort or a GLib main loop calls your function pointer per element or event - a small-scale realization of the same inversion.
Cloud Functions-as-a-Service: AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, and Google Cloud Functions own the request dispatch and cold-start lifecycle; your handler is a hook called by the platform, making serverless a live deployment of the Hollywood principle.
Reactive streams and event-driven pipelines: frameworks like Reactor, RxJava, or Node.js EventEmitter own the subscription and back-pressure loop; operators and subscribers are hooks that the runtime calls on data availability.
Microservices sidecar and service mesh: an Envoy or Linkerd proxy sidecar owns the connection lifecycle and calls application code through a defined protocol; the application registers health checks and request handlers as IoC hooks.
Orleans virtual actor model: the Orleans runtime owns the grain lifecycle, activation and deactivation, and calls grain methods as directed by the scheduler; grain code is a hook implementation invoked by the framework.
ASP.NET Core middleware: the host builds the request pipeline and invokes each registered RequestDelegate in order; middleware can run before and after the next delegate or short-circuit, so the application supplies components while the server owns request dispatch.
JUnit Jupiter extension model: the JUnit engine discovers tests and invokes registered Before*/After* lifecycle callbacks around user test methods; extensions customize execution without owning when tests run.
Kubernetes controllers: the controller manager owns reconciliation loops that watch API state and repeatedly invokes controller reconciliation logic to converge current state on desired state; controllers supply behavior while Kubernetes schedules dispatch.

name: repository
document:
repository
collection-oriented repository
repository layer
Mediates between the domain model and the data mapping layer with a collection-like interface, so domain code adds, removes and finds persistent objects as if they lived in memory and never constructs queries or touches persistence APIs itself.
Persistence code spreads: every application service re-derives the same SQL or ORM queries, duplicate query logic drifts apart, table and column names leak into domain decisions, and testing domain rules without a database becomes impossible. Callers should be able to think in collections of domain objects instead of queries.
Applies to systems with a non-trivial domain model sitting on a data-mapping layer (Data Mapper, metadata mapping, or a hand-written mapper) where the same queries recur across application services; it becomes more valuable as domain classes and query volume grow. It is the standard persistence boundary of DDD aggregates (one repository per aggregate root) and presumes a unit of work or session that owns flush and commit. It is not a per-table data-access wrapper and not a replacement for transaction control.
DDD application services that must load an aggregate root, run domain logic on it and store it again without knowing the table layout.
Data-mapper backends where several application services and background jobs share recurring complex queries (overdue invoices, pending orders, open tickets).
Applications that must be unit-testable away from the database: repositories are the substitution point for in-memory doubles.
Systems that must support more than one store behind a stable domain interface — relational in production, in-memory in tests, a document store for a particular deployment.
Uniform cross-cutting access policy for an aggregate: caching, read-replica routing, audit logging or authorization applied as decorators around one interface.
Migration work where the persistence technology changes (ORM swap, schema split, service extraction) while the domain model and its tests stay untouched.
CQRS write-side aggregate loading where the aggregate must be reconstructed fully to apply business rules and enforce invariants.
Integration with heterogeneous data sources where one repository unifies access to a cache, primary database and a third-party API behind a domain interface.
Spring Data JPA applications can use Repository/CrudRepository for aggregate-typed CRUD, paging and derived queries, then add only domain-specific methods rather than wrapping every persistence operation.
The .NET eShopOnContainers ordering microservice uses an EF Core BuyerRepository over a shared scoped DbContext/unit of work, while CQRS/Dapper handles presentation reads.
Python applications using SQLAlchemy ORM can place an aggregate-facing repository over Session, whose identity map and unit-of-work flush semantics provide the mapper/session boundary.

name: protected-system
document:
protected-system
protection proxy
Give a resource exactly one owning object whose published operations are the only way to touch it, so that every access is decided by an authorization check before the resource is used.
A resource - a credential store, a file tree, a socket, a connection pool, a device handle - is referenced from many places. When each use site performs its own permission check, the checks drift, new code paths forget them, and the resource remains reachable as a raw handle, so a missing check cannot even be detected. The recurring trigger: one object can own the resource and clients can be made to hold only that object, so ownership itself can carry the enforcement.
Applies where ownership is expressible in the language or runtime (private field, unexported type, opaque handle, module boundary) and an authorization policy - identity, role, permission, capability - can be evaluated at each public operation. The guard may sit in-process (object or module scope) or at a process/kernel boundary, where the same pattern becomes a real reference monitor; the assurance the implementation can claim depends on which side of that line it lives.
Credential and key stores: an in-process vault owns the keys and exposes only operations (sign, decrypt, rotate), so callers never receive the secret material.
Storage gateways: a library owns the directory handle or object-store client and applies path and tenant rules on every operation instead of handing out a raw client.
Pools: the pool owns its connections and leases checked-out views, so a caller cannot keep, share or resurrect a connection the pool must reclaim.
Multi-tenant data access: a tenant-scoped repository wrapper pins the tenant filter and refuses operations that would query outside it.
Device and driver access: a supervisor object owns the device handle and validates commands, or a privileged daemon owns the socket and checks each request from an unprivileged client.
Module-level boundaries: a package exports only the guard type and keeps the resource unexported, so code outside the package cannot even name the protected representation.
Linux Landlock: a kernel-enforced ruleset restricts a process and its future children to explicitly allowed filesystem or network rights, placing mediation below application code.
Kubernetes RBAC: the API server evaluates Roles and bindings for each API request, mediating verbs and resources instead of exposing the cluster's backing store to clients.
HashiCorp Vault policies: authenticated tokens are checked against path and capability rules before secret operations, while the storage backend remains behind the Vault service.

name: composite-entity
document:
composite-entity
coarse-grained-entity
Represent a cluster of related, dependent objects through one coarse-grained entity that owns them and persists and synchronises the whole graph as a single unit of work, so clients never reference, sequence, or save the parts themselves. Coined for coarse-grained EJB business objects; its modern form is the aggregate root with cascading or owned mappings.
A business concept clients treat as one thing (an order with its lines, a customer with addresses) is really a cluster of dependent objects, and persisting each part separately forces callers to know the parts, save them in the right order in the right transaction, delete the ones that left the relationship, and absorb a leaking physical schema. The catalog trigger: a cluster of related objects must persist and synchronise as one unit.
Relational or document stores where a coarse-grained business object is composed of finer-grained dependent objects whose lifecycle is bound to it. Applies when clients - especially remote ones - should exchange one coarse-grained structure instead of the parts, when the persist/synchronise boundary must coincide with one transaction, and when each dependent can still own its own mapping. Modern form: an aggregate root mapped with cascading associations or with components stored in the root's own row.
Order with line items, shipment addresses and payment allocations that must be written and deleted as one business unit.
Customer or account aggregate holding addresses, contact methods and preferences that are edited in one form and saved once.
Document-style clusters (invoice with revisions, article with embedded sections) where the parts only exist inside the root.
Legacy-style coarse-grained entity beans that wrap fine-grained POJOs so that clients exchange one composite transfer object instead of many fine-grained ones.
Mobile or remote clients that must send one coarse-grained payload per edit instead of a sequence of dependent calls.
Batch imports where a cluster is validated and written transactionally, so a partially imported entity never exists.
DDD Bounded Contexts where one aggregate encapsulates a complete business invariant enforced across multiple related entities — e.g., a Rental aggregate containing a rental agreement, reserved vehicle, and driver assignment that must all be created or fail together.
CQRS write models where the aggregate is the sole write target and all state changes flow through the root's command methods, ensuring every mutation is a coherent cluster-level operation.
Event sourcing snapshots where the aggregate root serialises its entire graph so that snapshot restore reconstructs the full composite in one operation rather than re-playing individual dependent events.
Legacy system facades that wrap a network of fine-grained remote beans behind a single coarse-grained composite interface, collapsing many remote calls into one round-trip for external clients.
SQLAlchemy parent-child clusters mapped with cascade='all, delete-orphan' on relationship(): disassociating a child deletes the row, so the Session flushes the cluster as one unit without per-child Session.delete() calls.
EF Core owned types: dependent types stored in the owner's table (or as owned navigations) share the aggregate root's identity and save with a single context.SaveChanges().
Mongoose subdocument arrays: embedded parts are saved, validated and removed through the top-level document, so the cluster's lifecycle is bound to the root document's save.

name: watchman
document:
watchman
dead man's switch
heartbeat monitor
Detect that a message flow has gone silent - not that a message failed - and tell a responsible person or system within a bounded time by comparing each flow's arrivals against the cadence its business deadline implies.
Message systems fail silently in the one way no error handler observes: nothing arrives. A producer stops emitting, a consumer stops draining, a scheduled job never fires, a credential expires, a partition goes offline - and because no failing code path is ever entered, error dashboards stay green while downstream data quietly goes stale. The recurring trigger: a flow whose absence is business-visible (a nightly feed, an order stream, a partner interface) has no owner-facing signal for 'no messages', so the gap is discovered late - by a customer or a downstream job - instead of by the team that can fix it.
Applies wherever messages are expected on a knowable cadence (event streams, queues, batch hand-offs, partner interfaces, device check-ins) and their absence is a business-visible failure: the flow has an owner, the expected period and grace window can be derived from a downstream deadline, and either the transport can be observed passively (queue counters, a wire tap) or the producers can emit out-of-band heartbeats. The watchman sits at message-flow or boundary scope - an in-process watcher beside the consumer, a periodic sweep over persisted last-seen state, or a rule in the monitoring stack fed by metrics - and it must itself be watched, because a silent watchman is exactly the failure it exists to catch.
Nightly batch or ETL feed: page the integration owner when the 02:00 import has produced no messages by its deadline, instead of noticing an empty report at the morning stand-up.
Business-critical event stream (orders, payments, telemetry): alarm when the produce rate stays at zero through business hours, which separates a healthy quiet topic from a stopped producer.
External partner interface: notify when no messages have arrived from a B2B partner within the agreed window, turning a looming SLA breach into an early, actionable alert.
Long-running workflow stage: require a heartbeat from each process-manager step so a stuck instance is noticed before the surrounding batch closes or a compensation becomes necessary.
Retry or dead-letter pump: verify that the pump still drains failed messages - silence means the pump died, not that the backlog is empty.
Fleet check-ins (edge devices, agents, cron jobs on many hosts): raise a per-device or per-site alarm when scheduled check-ins stop arriving.
The alerting pipeline itself: an always-firing watchdog alert routed to an external service, so a broken alert path is discovered by its silence.
Cron and scheduled-job fleet via Healthchecks.io: each job pings a unique URL, the service holds the Period and Grace Time, flips the check Late then Down when no ping arrives by period + grace, and notifies integrations.
Dashboard alert rules in Grafana: an alert rule whose query returns no series enters the No Data state and can raise a DatasourceNoData alert - the platform form of deciding what silence means (No Data, Alerting, Normal or Keep last state).
Apache Burrow for Kafka (LinkedIn): committed offsets are evaluated per partition over a sliding window and a consumer is classified STALLED when its offset is frozen with non-zero lag, or STOPPED when no new commits arrive - consumer-silence detection without fixed lag thresholds.

name: version-number
document:
version-number
rowversion
entity versioning
Store a version token alongside each persistent record and make every write assert the token it read, so a write computed from stale data fails as a detectable conflict instead of silently overwriting a newer value.
Two sessions read the same record, both edit it, and the later write wins: the earlier update vanishes without any error (the lost update). Once the read-modify-write spans more than one system transaction the database cannot tell 'this is the record I read' from 'this record changed under me', so no code path can notice in time - unless the record itself carries a per-row token that changes on every write and the write tests that token before committing.
Applies to records that outlive the transaction that read them: edits spanning user think time, a web form round-trip, an offline client, a batch worker holding aggregates, or any read-modify-write over data other writers touch in between. It needs a store that can test the token and change the record in one atomic step (a conditional UPDATE, a compare-and-swap, a document revision check) and a caller willing to act on the conflict - re-read, merge, retry, or report. It assumes conflicts are the exception; when they are the rule a pessimistic lock prevents the wasted work instead.
Web forms and editors: a record is loaded into a page, edited for minutes or hours, then saved - the token makes the stale save fail instead of clobbering the other editor's change.
Distributed workers applying commands to the same entity: the second worker's write is rejected so it can refresh and re-apply, giving first-writer-wins with no held lock.
Data mappers and units of work: every dirty entity flushed at commit carries the version it was loaded with, so the whole transaction aborts on the first stale row.
Document stores and revision-based APIs: Mongoose's __v with optimisticConcurrency, CouchDB-style revisions, or a REST ETag/If-Match precondition all expose the same per-document token.
Leases, leader election and configuration records: one row represents ownership or a monotonic generation, and a write must prove it still holds the revision it acted on.
Offline or mobile sync: clients push edits made against a snapshot taken days earlier, and the version check decides which edits apply directly and which must go through a merge.
Hibernate ORM / JPA @Version: the mapper owns an integer (or timestamp) version property, appends it to every UPDATE's WHERE clause, bumps it on flush and raises StaleObjectStateException / OptimisticLockException when zero rows match, so the application code never writes the predicate by hand.
DynamoDB conditional writes: each item carries a Version attribute; UpdateItem sends ConditionExpression 'Version = :read_value' and increments Version in the same request, and ConditionalCheckFailedException is the conflict signal that triggers a bounded re-read-and-retry — the same contract exposed as @DynamoDBVersionAttribute in the enhanced client.
Cassandra lightweight transactions: UPDATE ... SET col = ? WHERE id = ? IF col = ? is a Paxos-backed compare-and-set, giving the token test linearizable semantics across replicas — at a documented cost (roughly four extra round-trips per conditional write), so it is reserved for rows that genuinely need the guard.

statement: Choose where recurring actor-specific behavior resides and define the uniform contract by which the frame driver advances every live participant exactly once.
name: newtype
document:
newtype
strong typedef
opaque type
Give a single primitive its own distinct type so that values with different meanings cannot be substituted for one another, and the raw representation is reachable only through the wrapper's own construction and accessors.
Several domain concepts share one representation - customer id, order id and tenant id are all strings or UUIDs, width/height/offset are all numbers, milliseconds and seconds are both integers - and the API therefore accepts them interchangeably. A swapped argument, a mixed unit or a mistyped literal compiles (or runs) silently, and the defect surfaces late, as a wrong lookup or a cross-tenant bug rather than a type error.
Code in which two or more values with the same underlying representation flow through the same functions, collections or persistence mapping, and in which a single value owns a rule (identifier syntax, non-emptiness, numeric range, unit). Applies at the value level of one field; clusters of attributes that change together belong to Value Object, and closed constant sets to Type-Safe Enum.
Identifier families in one codebase: CustomerId, OrderId, TenantId and SessionId all string- or UUID-shaped and passed to the same repository, logger and cache.
Unit-carrying measurements: Milliseconds vs Seconds, Meters vs Feet, Radians vs Degrees, Cents vs Dollars, where arithmetic must stay inside one unit and conversion is explicit.
Validated single values: EmailAddress, PhoneNumber, Iban, Slug, Percentage (0-100), PortNumber, NonEmptyString - parsed once at the edge, trusted everywhere afterwards.
Security-adjacent tokens: API token vs session id vs tenant id, where a swap becomes a cross-tenant or privilege defect rather than a wrong lookup.
Geometry and graphics APIs where Width, Height, X, Y, Offset and Length are all numbers and transposition should be a compile error.
Pagination and buffer arithmetic: PageSize vs PageIndex vs ByteOffset vs Count, integers that are trivially transposable in a long argument list.
Rust's official newtype examples use Millimeters(u32) and Meters(u32) to keep units distinct, and use Wrapper(Vec<T>) to give a local wrapper its own trait implementations.
Scala 3 opaque types model values such as Logarithm over Double as distinct outside their defining scope, with controlled extension methods and no runtime boxing.
Kotlin @JvmInline value classes wrap one property into a non-interchangeable domain type such as Password while allowing unboxed representations in many uses.

name: state-colocation
document:
state-colocation
colocated state
colocation
Keep each piece of presentation state in the component closest to where it is used — down to the single component that owns and reads it — instead of hoisting it to a common ancestor or a global store, so that a change touches only the smallest part of the view that can observe it.
State gets hoisted 'just in case': a value only one component reads is lifted to the screen or application root, or pushed into one global store, because someone may want it later. The consequences are components that receive props they never read, updates that invalidate far more of the UI than the value's actual consumers, an unclear owner for each value, and tests that must assemble the whole state container to exercise one field. The recurring decision is where a new piece of state should live: keep it at the smallest scope that actually needs it.
Declarative component UIs (React, Vue, Svelte, SwiftUI, Compose, Blazor, Qt Quick) and, in generalized form, any system where a mutable value is owned by one component-like unit: the consumers determine the state's scope, the framework invalidates only what the owner's subtree can observe, and components are composed, moved and deleted. Most compelling where over-lifted or global state has already become a performance and ownership problem.
A search or form input whose value is read only by the input, its own validation and its own preview: keep it in that component instead of the screen root (the canonical typing example where hoisting made every keystroke re-render the page).
Which panel of an accordion is open: leave it per panel while panels are independent, then lift exactly to the accordion once only one panel may be open at a time (the closest common parent).
Tooltip, hover, popover and dropdown state in a chart or table cell: own it in the cell component rather than in a global UI store.
Per-row edit or selection state in a data grid: the row component owns it; only cross-row operations need the grid to own it.
Dialog and modal open state in the button or list that opens it, until another surface must close or observe it.
Form draft state in the form component; lift it only when a sibling — summary panel, preview pane, wizard footer — genuinely must read it.
Extracting a self-contained widget for reuse or publication: keeping its state local makes the component portable and shrinks its API.
Per-cell expansion state in a tree view or file explorer: the tree node component owns whether it is expanded; the parent tree only coordinates multi-select or bulk-expand operations.
Media playback state for a single player (play/pause, current time, volume): colocate in the player component rather than a global audio store unless the same track plays in multiple places simultaneously.
Local filter/sort state for a data table or list: keep it in the list component until a URL parameter, shareable link, or sibling panel requires sharing it.
Vue: composable-local state (useSearch, useToggle) where each consumer needs its own independent instance of the same reactive logic pattern.
Angular Signals: feature-level signal stores scoped to a route or feature slice, not the entire application store, for UI state and feature-derived state.
SwiftUI: @State for view-local value types; @StateObject for view-owned reference types; keep @EnvironmentObject for genuinely cross-cutting state (auth session, theme) mounted as low in the hierarchy as consumers allow.
Svelte 5 runes: `let count = $state(0)` inside a component is per-component-instance reactive state — the component that declares it is its owner; Svelte's v5 migration explicitly replaced the pre-runes habit of reaching for a store whenever state sat at a component's top level, with $state plus $derived/$effect as the local cells, and module-level .svelte.js state only for deliberate sharing.
Jetpack Compose: the official hoisting guidance is this pattern's placement ladder — keep state as close as possible to where it is consumed, hoist only to the lowest common ancestor of all composables that read or write it, pass value down and onValueChange up, and make the ViewModel the owner only when business logic or lifecycle outlives the composition.
Blazor: component fields are the default owner for UI-local state; the official state-management guidance promotes to an in-memory state container service only when components must share non-persistent state, and to Protected Browser Storage only when the value must survive circuits or sessions — a three-rung ladder that mirrors local state, scoped provider, persistence.

name: container-component
document:
container-component
smart component
connected component
stateful wrapper
Keep presentation state and its access to a data source in an outer wrapper component, so that the components rendering the markup stay stateless functions of the data they are handed.
The same state, or the same data source, is needed by several components below a point in the tree: state ends up duplicated in siblings, intermediate components forward props they never use, and every new field forces edits through components that do not care about it.
Declarative component frameworks with props/state and a re-render step - web UI frameworks, mobile declarative toolkits, server-rendered view hierarchies and data-app frameworks with a session cursor. It applies when a subtree needs a shared state owner or a data-fetching wrapper, when children must stay reusable and renderable from plain data, and when the source (store, API, session, fixture) should be swappable without touching the markup.
A screen where several widgets need the same live data: one container owns the subscription and renders every widget from the fetched snapshot.
A reusable list, table or form that must render identically from a live store, a server payload and a literal fixture in tests.
A route or page entry that owns navigation parameters and data fetching while its children stay presentation-only.
A form whose draft state and validation live in a wrapper while the fields are stateless inputs driven by value plus change handlers.
A data or terminal application page where session-scoped state drives plain render helper functions.
A legacy or framework-agnostic subtree whose markup is reused by two different data sources (desktop shell and web shell).
A real-time dashboard where a container subscribes to a WebSocket or streaming endpoint and fans the resulting data out to multiple visualization widgets.
A multi-tenant application where the container injects tenant context (ID, permissions, theme) from a session or JWT into a reusable child tree.
A/B or feature-flag experiments where the container resolves the active variant and passes it as a prop to the same stateless content.
A Redux screen where connect() wraps a view component: the wrapper subscribes to the store via mapStateToProps and passes bound action creators as props, so the wrapped component never imports the store.
A Relay page where each subtree declares its data needs with createFragmentContainer and one QueryRenderer at the root fetches the composed query, so children render guaranteed fragment data without fetching anything.
An Angular app using NgRx where smart components inject the Store and pipe selector observables into presentational children, with NgRx ComponentStore owning feature-local state that cleans up on component destroy.

name: context-provider
document:
context-provider
context api
provider pattern
provide/inject
environment values
CompositionLocal
InheritedWidget
Publish a value once at an outer scope so that any descendant subtree can read the nearest published value without every intermediate layer declaring and forwarding it.
Cross-cutting props - theme, locale, current user, feature flags, request/trace context - are owned at an outer node but needed by a sparse set of descendants far below it. Threading them through every intermediate layer produces prop drilling: signatures carry data the component never uses, unrelated layers become coupled to the value, and every new reader forces an edit along the whole path.
Tree- or scope-structured programs where an outer node owns a value that a few descendants need and that intermediate nodes must not know about: component trees (React, Compose, SwiftUI, Blazor, Vue), and dynamic scopes such as request contexts, coroutine/task scopes and async-local storage. The value is either read-mostly (theme, locale, session) or scoped to a short-lived execution unit (one request, one task), and the platform or framework is expected to deliver it and to notify or reset readers when the scope ends.
Theming and appearance: colour scheme, density and elevation tokens published at the app root and read by leaf components (MaterialTheme's CompositionLocals, SwiftUI environment values, ThemeContext provider in React, Vuetify's theme injection).
Identity and session: the currently authenticated user or tenant, with nested providers for 'act as another user' or multi-account surfaces.
Localisation and formatting: locale, time zone and number/date formatters, so leaves format without receiving the locale as a parameter.
Feature flags and experiment variants: a variant assigned once at the edge changes the behaviour of an entire subtree without threading the flag through it.
Request- and task-scoped diagnostics: correlation ids, transaction context and tenant data delivered to every function in a request or task via contextvars (Python), AsyncLocal<T> (.NET), or JavaScript's AsyncContext (proposal).
Component-library configuration: a compound component (select/option, tabs, form fields) publishes its internal parts so children coordinate implicitly instead of receiving coordinated props or cloned elements (Flutter's InheritedModel is purpose-built for this).
Svelte cross-component reactive state: sibling or unrelated components share behaviour through a module-level writable store or context API without a common parent.
Coroutine/task-local resource management: database connections, tracing spans, and feature flags that must follow the async execution flow rather than the call stack.
Cascading values in Blazor: a CascadingValue<T> component wraps a subtree and descendants receive it via [CascadingParameter] matched by type (plus optional Name), so a parent such as a TabSet can cascade itself to its Tab children and coordinate rendering with zero per-child parameter bindings.
Request-scoped execution context in Node.js: AsyncLocalStorage.run(store, callback) binds a request or trace store for one logical operation and getStore() resolves it inside every callback, timer and promise chain the operation spawns - the substrate most Node APM/logging layers use for transaction context.
Provider-scoped services in Angular: a service listed in a component's providers or a route's config creates one instance per subtree, injected by token in descendants; resolution climbs ElementInjectors before falling back to the EnvironmentInjector, giving lazy features and reusable components isolated state per scope.

name: model-view-viewmodel
document:
model-view-viewmodel
mvvm
model-view-binder
Separate a screen's presentation state and behaviour from the markup that renders it: the view-model exposes view-shaped observable properties and commands, the view binds to them declaratively through the platform's binding engine, and neither side needs a reference to the other.
Presentation logic gets tangled into the view: event handlers and widget objects hold screen state, the same value is duplicated across controls, validation and enablement live in code-behind, and neither the screen's behaviour (untestable without the UI) nor its markup (unchangeable without touching logic) can evolve independently.
Markup- or component-driven UI stacks that ship a binding engine - XAML/WPF/MAUI/WinUI, JavaFX/FXML, QML, SwiftUI, Compose, Android Views/LiveData, Vue/Angular - and screens whose state is long-lived enough to own a view-model: forms, editors, dashboards, list/detail navigation, and any screen that must survive a redesign or be tested without launching a UI.
Data-entry and line-of-business screens (WPF/MAUI/WinUI, JavaFX, Android) where fields validate, depend on each other and must be tested without launching the UI.
Mobile screens that must survive configuration changes or process re-creation: Android ViewModel + StateFlow/LiveData, SwiftUI @Observable models.
Desktop applications with designer-authored markup (QML, FXML, XAML) that must be restyled or re-themed without touching behaviour.
Web and multi-platform SPAs whose screen state must be observable, typed and testable (Vue ref/reactive, Angular signals, MobX observable view-models).
Dashboards and editors where the same state feeds several views or widgets and updates arrive from streams or background work.
Applications ported across platforms while keeping one presentation logic layer (shared view-models over per-platform views).
Cross-platform XAML screens in .NET MAUI: bind XAML controls to a BindingContext view-model with one-way/two-way properties and ICommand actions, so interaction logic stays testable outside the page.
Android Jetpack Compose screens: a screen-level ViewModel exposes one immutable UI state as StateFlow, and composables collect it lifecycle-aware while sending user events back as methods.
SwiftUI screens on Apple platforms: an @Observable model is the source of truth, @State owns its lifetime, and views read tracked properties or create Bindable two-way editors.

name: repository
document:
repository
collection-oriented repository
repository layer
Mediates between the domain model and the data mapping layer with a collection-like interface, so domain code adds, removes and finds persistent objects as if they lived in memory and never constructs queries or touches persistence APIs itself.
Persistence code spreads: every application service re-derives the same SQL or ORM queries, duplicate query logic drifts apart, table and column names leak into domain decisions, and testing domain rules without a database becomes impossible. Callers should be able to think in collections of domain objects instead of queries.
Applies to systems with a non-trivial domain model sitting on a data-mapping layer (Data Mapper, metadata mapping, or a hand-written mapper) where the same queries recur across application services; it becomes more valuable as domain classes and query volume grow. It is the standard persistence boundary of DDD aggregates (one repository per aggregate root) and presumes a unit of work or session that owns flush and commit. It is not a per-table data-access wrapper and not a replacement for transaction control.
DDD application services that must load an aggregate root, run domain logic on it and store it again without knowing the table layout.
Data-mapper backends where several application services and background jobs share recurring complex queries (overdue invoices, pending orders, open tickets).
Applications that must be unit-testable away from the database: repositories are the substitution point for in-memory doubles.
Systems that must support more than one store behind a stable domain interface — relational in production, in-memory in tests, a document store for a particular deployment.
Uniform cross-cutting access policy for an aggregate: caching, read-replica routing, audit logging or authorization applied as decorators around one interface.
Migration work where the persistence technology changes (ORM swap, schema split, service extraction) while the domain model and its tests stay untouched.
CQRS write-side aggregate loading where the aggregate must be reconstructed fully to apply business rules and enforce invariants.
Integration with heterogeneous data sources where one repository unifies access to a cache, primary database and a third-party API behind a domain interface.
Spring Data JPA applications can use Repository/CrudRepository for aggregate-typed CRUD, paging and derived queries, then add only domain-specific methods rather than wrapping every persistence operation.
The .NET eShopOnContainers ordering microservice uses an EF Core BuyerRepository over a shared scoped DbContext/unit of work, while CQRS/Dapper handles presentation reads.
Python applications using SQLAlchemy ORM can place an aggregate-facing repository over Session, whose identity map and unit-of-work flush semantics provide the mapper/session boundary.

name: cursor-pagination
document:
cursor-pagination
keyset pagination
cursor-based pagination
Bound what a read boundary returns for a large or changing ordered collection by sending one page plus an opaque continuation token that pins the filter and ordering, so clients advance deterministically without offsets and without watching rows move under them.
A boundary must expose a collection that is too large to return at once and keeps changing while clients read it. Offset or page-number requests make the store count or scan everything up to the requested page, and concurrent inserts or deletes shift rows across page boundaries so consumers see duplicates or miss items; the server has no way to state where the sequence should resume.
Any read boundary - an HTTP or gRPC list operation, a GraphQL connection, a database-backed feed, a batch export job - over an ordered collection that is large, growing, or read under concurrent writes, where the server can identify a unique, immutable ordering key and wants to cap both response size and per-request query cost while letting clients iterate the whole sequence.
Public REST or gRPC list endpoints over unbounded, growing tables - messages, orders, audit events - where deep offsets are slow and responses must stay small.
Infinite-scroll or load-more feeds that keep returning newer items while a user scrolls, with the already-seen pages stable against inserts.
Whole-collection sync and export jobs (warehouse loads, backups, search reindexing) that must iterate every row exactly once while writers continue.
GraphQL Relay connections where first/after, edges and pageInfo carry the continuation contract in the schema instead of the URL.
Consumers of third-party list APIs (Stripe-style starting_after/has_more, Google page_token iterators) that keep parameters fixed across auto-paginated calls.
Administrative and operational tooling that streams very large tables for verification or cleanup with bounded memory and predictable server load.
Audit log and event stream retrieval where events are append-only and chronological, and clients stream continuously without needing to revisit earlier pages.
Real-time activity feeds (social media timelines, notification streams) where inserts at the head must not disturb pages the user has already loaded.
Database replication and change-data-capture (CDC) pipelines that must consume a changelog exactly once across restarts and failures.
Paginating over search results from a vector database or full-text index where OFFSET at depth is expensive and results may change between queries.
Bi-directional data synchronization (CDC pipelines, replica lag-catching) where a consumer must iterate forward and occasionally needs to resume from a previous position or re-sweep a window — requiring stable forward cursors plus a defined backward-resumption path.
Paginating a partitioned or sharded database table where each partition is queried independently and cursors carry both the partition hint and the per-partition keyset position.
Slack Web API collection methods (users.list, conversations.history) where response_metadata.next_cursor drives the loop, page limits are clamped per method, and expired or malformed tokens surface as invalid_cursor so the client restarts from the first page.
GitHub GraphQL-style cursor connections where first/last (bounded 1-100) and pageInfo.startCursor/endCursor carry the continuation position for after/before traversal.
Timeline-style feeds served by Django REST framework's CursorPagination, whose default -created ordering gives a consistent view that does not repeat items as new rows are inserted.
