Front ends for small languages, DSLs and configuration formats (filter expressions, rule engines, policy languages, template syntaxes) where a generator and its build integration would be overkill.
Expression and statement parsing in single-pass compilers and interpreters that emit bytecode or IR while parsing, as in Crafting Interpreters' Lox.
Tooling for a grammar you own - formatters, linters, syntax highlighters, language servers - where error tolerance, multiple diagnostics and exact positions matter more than raw throughput.
Protocol and wire-format decoding with a small fixed grammar, where errors must carry byte offsets and malformed input must be rejected deterministically.
Context-dependent or indentation-sensitive syntaxes (templates with interpolation, layout-based blocks, configuration with embedded expressions) that a generated lexer handles poorly.
Codebases that must not carry generated code: security-reviewed, vendored or cross-compiled projects where an ordinary source file beats a build-time generator.
Clang's C-family front end uses a unified hand-built recursive-descent parser for C, C++, Objective-C and Objective-C++, pairing rule-oriented control flow with production-quality diagnostics.
The Go standard library's go/parser is a production recursive-descent parser for Go source, with explicit parser state, nesting-depth guards and error recovery.
rustc_parse is the Rust compiler's recursive-descent parser module, showing how a hand-written parser can scale to macros, recovery modes and detailed token/state handling.
Lua's reference implementation compiles with lparser.c, a single-pass recursive-descent parser that emits bytecode opcodes while reducing expressions instead of building a syntax tree, with precedence handled by parsing levels.

statement: Choose the request-processing location and component boundary that verify credentials for every protected route and populate request-scoped identity before controller dispatch, while preserving explicit public-route exceptions.
name: deadline-propagation
document:
deadline-propagation
timeout propagation
Bound the total time and work of a logical request by carrying one deadline through its whole call tree: every hop forwards the remaining budget and the cancellation signal instead of inventing a fresh timeout, so work that can no longer succeed is abandoned at every level.
A request fans out into a chain or tree of downstream calls and each hop applies its own timeout: the end-to-end latency budget becomes the sum of N independent timeouts, servers keep working after the originating client has given up, and cancellation never reaches the deeper work - resources are consumed producing answers nobody will read.
Networked request handling with multi-hop calls: RPC and HTTP chains, service meshes, gateways, fan-out and hedged requests. It applies when one latency budget is meaningful for the whole logical request (an SLO or a user-facing timeout), when the hops are under your control and can carry request-scoped state (context, token, signal, call option or header), and when downstream work is cancellable or can be interrupted at checkpoints.
Microservice request chains (gateway -> frontend service -> several backends) under one user-facing latency SLO, where each hop converts the inbound deadline into its own outgoing calls.
gRPC services whose clients set a deadline and whose servers propagate it as a remaining timeout to downstream calls while cancelling server-side work once the deadline passes.
Fan-out and aggregation endpoints calling several backends in parallel: every sub-call shares the parent budget, and sub-calls still running when it expires are cancelled instead of awaited.
Hedged requests: the first replica to answer wins, and the duplicate requests are cancelled through the same carrier so their downstream work is stopped too.
Streaming and long-poll endpoints that must stop processing when the client disconnects or the connection times out, propagating that stop to services and storage.
Batch or pipeline steps with a per-request time budget that must check the remaining time before each stage and abandon a request that can no longer be finished in time.
ROS 2 / DDS-based robotics pipelines: autonomous vehicle perception pipelines where sensor data must traverse a chain of processing nodes (detect -> classify -> plan -> act) and missed deadlines invalidate downstream results entirely.
Distributed real-time databases with multi-hop queries (gateway -> shard router -> storage node -> index node) where each hop's latency budget is derived from a user-facing SLA.
Service mesh sidecar configurations (Istio/Linkerd/Envoy) where per-route timeout policies propagate deadline context to application code via headers like grpc-timeout or custom X-Request-Deadline headers.
Industrial IoT and edge computing pipelines (edge gateway -> fieldbus bridge -> PLC -> sensor) where end-to-end control loop deadlines must be enforced across heterogeneous network boundaries.
GraphQL federation: a federated query hitting multiple subgraphs in parallel must bound the total resolution time and cancel subgraph requests whose partial results can no longer affect the final response.
Go services on the standard library context package: context.WithDeadline and WithTimeout derive a child whose Done channel closes at the earliest of its own deadline, an explicit cancel, or the parent's cancellation, so cancelling the root request context tears down the whole goroutine tree, and WithDeadlineCause/WithTimeoutCause attach an explicit cause for attribution.
Envoy router filter in service meshes: Envoy sets x-envoy-expected-rq-timeout-ms on internal requests - derived from x-envoy-upstream-rq-timeout-ms or the route timeout - so upstream services can read the expected total completion time and exit early instead of finishing work the proxy has already timed out.
ASP.NET Core gRPC services map the inbound call's deadline onto the handler's CancellationToken; passing that token to database queries, HttpClient calls and Task.Delay stops server-side work the moment the client's deadline expires.

statement: Should a wire above the threshold require approval and release by different treasury specialists before any funds can be sent?
name: newtype
document:
newtype
strong typedef
opaque type
Give a single primitive its own distinct type so that values with different meanings cannot be substituted for one another, and the raw representation is reachable only through the wrapper's own construction and accessors.
Several domain concepts share one representation - customer id, order id and tenant id are all strings or UUIDs, width/height/offset are all numbers, milliseconds and seconds are both integers - and the API therefore accepts them interchangeably. A swapped argument, a mixed unit or a mistyped literal compiles (or runs) silently, and the defect surfaces late, as a wrong lookup or a cross-tenant bug rather than a type error.
Code in which two or more values with the same underlying representation flow through the same functions, collections or persistence mapping, and in which a single value owns a rule (identifier syntax, non-emptiness, numeric range, unit). Applies at the value level of one field; clusters of attributes that change together belong to Value Object, and closed constant sets to Type-Safe Enum.
Identifier families in one codebase: CustomerId, OrderId, TenantId and SessionId all string- or UUID-shaped and passed to the same repository, logger and cache.
Unit-carrying measurements: Milliseconds vs Seconds, Meters vs Feet, Radians vs Degrees, Cents vs Dollars, where arithmetic must stay inside one unit and conversion is explicit.
Validated single values: EmailAddress, PhoneNumber, Iban, Slug, Percentage (0-100), PortNumber, NonEmptyString - parsed once at the edge, trusted everywhere afterwards.
Security-adjacent tokens: API token vs session id vs tenant id, where a swap becomes a cross-tenant or privilege defect rather than a wrong lookup.
Geometry and graphics APIs where Width, Height, X, Y, Offset and Length are all numbers and transposition should be a compile error.
Pagination and buffer arithmetic: PageSize vs PageIndex vs ByteOffset vs Count, integers that are trivially transposable in a long argument list.
Rust's official newtype examples use Millimeters(u32) and Meters(u32) to keep units distinct, and use Wrapper(Vec<T>) to give a local wrapper its own trait implementations.
Scala 3 opaque types model values such as Logarithm over Double as distinct outside their defining scope, with controlled extension methods and no runtime boxing.
Kotlin @JvmInline value classes wrap one property into a non-interchangeable domain type such as Password while allowing unboxed representations in many uses.

statement: Whether to use an in-test device implementation that enforces the required command sequence, argument, and cardinality as the client performs them.
name: dynamic-router
document:
dynamic-router
dynamic routing
rules-based routing
Route each message to a destination chosen from a rule base that can be changed while the system runs, so the router never depends on - or is redeployed for - the set of destinations it serves.
Routing logic hard-coded into the router (switch chains, static filter tables, deployment-time route configuration) couples it to every destination: adding, moving, throttling or retiring a destination needs a code change, a review and a restart, and each topology change forces the router back through the release process instead of being an operational edit.
Message-based integration where the destination set or the routing policy changes faster than the router's release cycle: rules are owned by operations, destinations announce themselves, scale out, or go down for maintenance, or one router instance serves several tenants or environments. Applies when the route can be expressed as rules over message content, headers or context evaluated per message, and the platform offers a usable control channel (config watch, control bus, admin endpoint, hot-reloadable table) to publish rule changes.
Multi-tenant integration hub: each tenant has its own routing table, loaded and swapped per tenant instead of one deployed router per tenant.
Event distribution where downstream teams add or retire consumers by publishing routing conditions rather than requesting a router release.
Canary and blue/green rollouts: send a slice of traffic to a new destination by editing a rule, and roll back by restoring the previous rule set.
Maintenance windows: reroute a destination's traffic to a standby, drain the destination, then restore the rule when it returns.
Regional or sharded routing where the region-to-destination mapping is maintained by operations and changes with capacity, not with code.
Rule-driven enterprise integration in the classic EIP sense, where a rule base is consulted per message and recipients announce themselves on a control channel.
Kubernetes Gateway API traffic splitting: use HTTPRoute weighted backends to shift a configurable percentage of traffic between versions without redeploying the router.
Service mesh canary deployments: an Istio VirtualService or Linkerd ServiceProfile acts as the rule base; routing rules are edited at runtime to steer canary traffic, then promoted or rolled back.
Multi-tenant SaaS routing: Spring Cloud Gateway or Envoy.DynamicRouter loads per-tenant routing rules from a registry, injecting tenant-specific headers or rewrites so one router instance serves hundreds of isolated tenants.
API version routing and A/B testing: route by Accept header, API version path prefix, or experimentCohort header to different backend versions, controlled by rules updated without a release.
Database or cache sharding: route a tenant or user ID hash to the correct shard's endpoint via a rule table that is repointed during resharding without touching application code.
BGP route-server testing: use a chaos-testing framework against a route server to validate that policy changes converge correctly and do not produce route leaks before production deployment.
Traefik dynamic configuration: Traefik builds its routing table at runtime from providers (Docker labels, Kubernetes IngressRoute, Consul/etcd KV stores), so services announce their own routes and rule changes hot-swap without restarting the proxy.
HAProxy Runtime API: add server and set server state/weight over the runtime socket repoint and drain backends without a reload; the Data Plane API layers persistence and validation on top of these runtime changes.
Kong Gateway admin API: Routes - including the expressions DSL when router_flavor is set to expressions - are created and updated at runtime via POST /routes and take effect on the next matching request, with priority-ordered rule evaluation replacing a redeployed config.

statement: Choose whether to isolate console locators and interactions behind screen-specific test wrappers instead of embedding them in security regression tests.
name: assertion
document:
assertion
design by contract
Express a model object's preconditions, postconditions and class invariants as executable, side-effect-free predicates at the operations that must uphold them, so a broken contract fails at its boundary instead of remaining a comment or surfacing later as corrupt state. This pattern is for design-by-contract correctness checks, not routine validation of untrusted input or test-only assertions.
Model rules - a balance never below its floor, a period whose end follows its start, a status that cannot move backwards - are left in comments, documents and team memory while constructors and mutators check nothing. A caller can violate a precondition or an operation can break an invariant, allowing invalid state to propagate until an unrelated reader fails; if the assertion is elided by the build, the shipped program may enforce a different contract from the one tested.
Objects with genuine invariants - entities, value objects and aggregate roots - whose state changes through several operations or paths, in a language with an assertion facility, contract syntax or an exception mechanism. The invariant must be expressible as a deterministic, side-effect-free predicate over observable state. Use assertions for programmer/model defects; use always-on validation or typed errors for expected input failures, and decide explicitly whether a release build may elide the check.
Entities and value objects with cross-field rules: an amount that always carries its currency and scale, a date range whose end follows its start, an order whose total equals the sum of its lines.
Aggregate roots that enforce consistency across a cluster of objects: the root asserts its invariant before accepting a change and after applying it.
Domain services and application services checking the preconditions of a use-case operation, so a mis-wired caller fails on the spot instead of writing corrupt state.
Library and framework code that must state its contract: precondition checks on public constructors and methods that clients cannot legitimately violate.
Legacy models under refactoring: assertions turn implicit rules into explicit ones, and where the language strips assertions the same predicates are pasted into the test suite (Evans's fallback).
Reconstitution code that rebuilds objects from stored data, asserting that persisted state still satisfies the model's invariants before the object is used.
Event-sourced aggregates: each state-transition command asserts the preconditions before applying the event, and the event handler asserts the invariant after the state is reconstituted from the event stream.
CQRS write models: the command handler asserts that the incoming command is valid for the current aggregate state before persisting, catching mis-wired or concurrent commands at the write edge.
Microservice boundary contracts: the inbound adapter asserts the precondition of the domain operation before dispatching, preventing malformed commands from entering the domain core regardless of which transport delivered them (HTTP, queue, gRPC).
Money and quantity types: value objects that wrap a numeric amount and a currency/unit, asserting that amounts are non-negative and operations preserve currency matching, preventing silent unit-mixing bugs.
Workflow or saga state machines: assertions on transition preconditions (this status can only advance to that one) prevent illegal state progression from corrupted or out-of-order events.
Property-based test oracle: postconditions double as generative test properties - for all inputs satisfying preconditions, the postcondition holds - turning the same predicate into a specification that a property-based testing library (e.g. Eris for PHP, Hypothesis for Python, fast-check for TypeScript) can falsify.
EiffelBase container classes such as LINKED_LIST and HASH_TABLE: EiffelStudio contract monitoring checks exported-routine preconditions/postconditions and class invariants while the containers preserve their representation rules.
AutoProof-verified Eiffel classes: executable assertions also serve as formal specifications that the verifier can discharge or flag, pairing runtime diagnostics with static proof where available.

statement: Decide how tests can control the internally invoked clock when production code cannot be altered to expose an injection point.
name: cancellation-token
document:
cancellation-token
cancellation signal
cooperative cancellation
Give a caller-owned operation tree a one-way request to stop: pass a read-only cancellation signal through every cancellable call, observe it at safe points, clean up what was acquired, and report a distinct cancelled outcome without pretending that cooperative cancellation is forced termination.
A request handler, background job or UI action starts work that fans out into nested calls, tasks or threads. When the caller disconnects, a deadline expires, the user presses stop or a sibling fails, merely abandoning the result leaves already-started work burning CPU, holding connections and calling dependencies. Force-killing a thread or process can interrupt a critical section and corrupt shared state, while a signal that is not propagated or observed cannot stop the call tree or make its cleanup visible to the joiner.
Use where work can outlive the caller's interest and the runtime exposes checkpoints, suspension points or interruptible waits: request-scoped servers, workers, UI tasks, stream pipelines and batch loops. The operation owns cleanup, cancellation may race any checkpoint, and the design must state what happens when a request arrives after an irreversible side effect or while a dependency ignores the signal.
Request-scoped server work: the handler gets a request signal that fires when the client disconnects or the deadline expires, cancelling in-flight database, queue and upstream calls instead of pinning worker threads and connections after the caller is gone.
UI and mobile tasks: navigating away, closing a window or pressing stop cancels the task tree that loads, renders or downloads for that view, and only that view's tokens are affected.
Graceful shutdown: a supervisor stops accepting work and cancels the token shared by worker loops; every worker stops at its next safe point, flushes and releases resources, and the process exits inside the shutdown budget.
Fan-out with short-circuit: as soon as one subtask fails, or as soon as any one result suffices (hedged or racing replicas), the scope cancels the siblings instead of waiting for all of them.
Batch and stream pipelines: a processor subscribes to the pipeline signal and stops consuming and producing when the pipeline is torn down, abandoning the current chunk when the job's deadline elapses.
Testing and tooling: inject an already-cancelled signal, or one cancelled after N iterations, to exercise the stop path without racing an actual shutdown.
HTTP client redirect and retry cancellation: when a request is redirected or a lower-level retry budget is exhausted, cancel the in-flight operation so the client can proceed with the next action without waiting for a result that is no longer relevant.
Health-check abortion: a liveness probe times out or a readiness check fails mid-flight; cancel the in-progress health metric collection so the pod can be restarted or pulled from service without waiting for a hung check.
GRPC deadline and cancellation propagation: a server receives a client deadline and cancellation token; both must be threaded through every async operation so that an expired deadline or a client disconnect promptly frees server resources.
LLM request fan-out: multiple model providers are queried in parallel; the first successful response wins and all pending requests are cancelled immediately, avoiding wasted compute on a result that will be discarded.
Database connection pool eviction: a query timeout or client disconnect cancels the in-flight query, releasing the connection back to the pool before the server's statement timeout fires; the pool's token is derived from the request context so pool eviction and request cancellation share the same stop signal.
Container orchestrator graceful shutdown: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM and waits the terminationGracePeriodSeconds; the application maps SIGTERM to a cancellation token that is shared by all in-flight request handlers, background workers and health-check loops, giving each the termination budget to drain cleanly.
Interactive search with typeahead: each keystroke cancels the previous search task and starts a new one; the token for the previous task is cancelled immediately on the next keystroke, preventing stale results from overwriting fresher ones.
File transfer with resume support: a large upload or download uses chunked transfers; cancelling the transfer sets a flag that causes the next resume attempt to verify which chunks were already received before retransmitting from scratch.
Event streaming with backpressure: a consumer reading from a message queue or Kafka partition uses the cancellation token to stop reading when the application is shutting down or the consumer group is rebalanced, committing its offset before exiting.
Machine learning inference pipeline: a batch inference job can be cancelled when a new model version is deployed or the job's priority drops; the cancellation token is checked between batches so that partial results are preserved and the job can resume without reprocessing completed chunks.
ASP.NET Core's HttpContext.RequestAborted token is passed into HttpClient, database and other long-running operations so a client disconnect or server abort releases work that can no longer contribute to the response.
Go net/http handlers propagate Request.Context through database/sql QueryContext and RPC calls; cancelling the request context closes the subtree's Done channel so backend goroutines can stop and return their resources.
Kotlin kotlinx.coroutines Job cancellation follows structured parent-child scopes, so a screen, request or worker scope can cancel its child coroutines while finally blocks release resources and CancellationException remains distinguishable from failure.
Node.js and browser fetch cancellation: AbortController.signal is passed as { signal } to fetch, EventTarget listeners and streams, so abort() tears down the socket and pending promises; AbortSignal.timeout and AbortSignal.any combine a deadline or several triggers into one signal without polling.
Database query abortion over a side channel: PostgreSQL's frontend/backend protocol sends a CancelRequest on a separate connection carrying the backend PID and secret key, letting a client that gave up - or an administrator via pg_cancel_backend - abort a running query without killing the session.
TPL/PLINQ cancellation acknowledgement: a delegate that throws OperationCanceledException carrying the supplied CancellationToken is treated by the Task Parallel Library as a cancellation acknowledgement rather than a fault, so joiners observe a cancelled task instead of an aggregated error.

statement: Choose how each expected payment rejection is represented and propagated so its category and field survive the full parsing, validation, and reservation flow.
name: request-reply
document:
request-reply
request-response
request-response messaging
Let a sender obtain a result or a domain error from an asynchronous or remote receiver by pairing each request with a correlated reply, and give the missing reply a defined outcome: timeout, cancellation and disposal of late replies.
Messaging is one-way, but the sender frequently needs a return value or a domain error from the receiver before it can continue. Without an agreed reply destination, a way to match replies to requests, and a rule for what happens when no reply arrives, the caller either blocks forever, mis-associates the next reply with the wrong request, or accumulates pending state it never cleans up.
Asynchronous interaction across a process, thread or network boundary where the caller cannot continue without the receiver's result: HTTP/gRPC-style RPC, broker-based RPC over a queue, actor or thread mailboxes, and browser-to-server exchanges over a socket. It applies when the interaction is naturally one request and one reply, and each exchange has a bounded deadline.
Service-to-service RPC where the caller needs the result to continue (HTTP, gRPC, or a broker-based RPC queue such as the RabbitMQ tutorial's rpc_queue).
Command dispatch that must return a domain error - a validation failure or business rejection - rather than only an acknowledgement of receipt.
In-process actor or thread mailboxes: ask a worker for state with a deadline so the caller can never block forever.
Front-end over a WebSocket asking the server for a value correlated by message id or acknowledgement callback.
Talking to devices, sensors or legacy systems over a socket whose protocol is inherently one request and one response.
Querying a cache or index cluster from a client library where each call is a key lookup with a per-call deadline.
NATS request-reply service calls: a client publishes with a unique inbox as the reply subject and waits for a response under a per-request timeout.
RabbitMQ RPC over an rpc_queue: the client sends reply_to and a unique correlation_id, then matches the worker's response on its callback queue.
gRPC unary RPC: a generated client stub sends one request and receives one response under a propagated deadline, with cancellation available for abandoned work.

statement: Choose how WorkspaceTabs, TabTrigger, and TabPanel share and enforce one active-tab state while allowing consumers to declare the family in ordered JSX.
name: range
document:
range
interval
Represent a span of values as a single interval value whose bound inclusivity and open ends are explicit, so containment and interval-to-interval comparisons live in one place instead of repeated ad-hoc endpoint tests.
Start and end travel together through the code but every caller re-derives what they mean: containment is written as scattered <= / < comparisons that drift apart, "unbounded" is smuggled in as a sentinel value (Long.MAX_VALUE, 9999-12-31), and interval-to-interval questions - do these two overlap, does one enclose the other, what is the gap between them - have no home at all.
Applies wherever a domain concept is a span rather than a point: validity and effectivity periods, booking and availability windows, quantity or price tiers, measurement buckets, version and address ranges, pagination windows, and query parameters such as a date range. It pays off when the same interval is compared repeatedly or crosses a boundary (persistence, API payloads, UI widgets), because the bound convention then has to be written once instead of re-decided per call site. For a single comparison between two local variables the type is pure overhead.
Validity and effectivity windows: a contract, price or membership is valid over [effectiveFrom, effectiveTo), and every check is a membership test against one interval.
Booking and availability: a room, seat or resource is reserved during an interval; overlap (not adjacency) decides whether a new booking is possible, and back-to-back bookings must be allowed deliberately.
Quantity and price tiers: the unit price depends on the quantity interval ([1,10), [10,50), [50, +inf)), so a container of intervals with containment lookup replaces a cascade of if-statements.
Temporal queries and reporting: "last 7 days", "this quarter", "since the migration" are half-open or open-ended intervals passed to repositories and rendered by date-range pickers.
Version, port and address ranges: a compatibility claim covers [1.2, 2.0) of a library, a firewall rule covers a port interval - containment answers "is this covered?" and intersection answers "do these rules conflict?".
Pagination and slicing windows: a page is an interval over a sequence, and half-open semantics make adjacency exact ([0,20) followed by [20,40)),
PostgreSQL range and multirange columns: PostgreSQL's daterange, tsrange and numeric range types make lower-inclusive/upper-exclusive bounds, overlap and containment operators, and indexed range queries part of the persistence contract; choose the bound convention before mapping domain intervals.
Guava Range: Java's Guava Range models convex bounded or unbounded intervals with nine open/closed forms, isConnected and intersection; use ContiguousSet only when a discrete domain really requires enumeration rather than treating the interval itself as a sequence.
Standard-library and container choices: Rust's std::ops::RangeBounds covers included, excluded and unbounded bounds when its range forms fit; for many intervals requiring join/split policies, Boost ICL's interval_set and interval_map supply the container semantics instead of overloading one Range value.

statement: Choose how to encode precedence, association, and operand handling for a growing set of prefix, infix, postfix, and mixfix expression operators.
name: strategy
document:
strategy
policy
Define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one behind a common operation, and make them interchangeable, so the algorithm a context executes can vary independently of the context and its clients - including at run time.
One class supports several variants of the same computation - sort orders, pricing or tax rules, routing and backoff policies, compression codecs - and the variant has to be selected at run time. Hard-wiring the variants into the class (or into one subclass per variant) mixes algorithm detail with the class's own logic, forces recompilation for every new variant, and turns selection into a growing conditional that runs on every call.
Applies when one context object owns the data but delegates one algorithm (or a small set of related algorithms) to a pluggable implementation, when the implementations share a stable operation signature, and when the choice is made at run time - from user input, configuration, request data or deployment - or from a closed family of variants that already differ in space/time or accuracy trade-offs. Typical homes: pricing, discount and tax calculation; sorting and comparison orders; routing, load-balancing, retry/backoff and rate-limiting policies; compression, serialization and encoding codecs; validation and normalization rules; numerical solvers chosen per problem.
Pricing, discount and tax calculation where the rule set is selected per customer, region or campaign and changes independently of the checkout or invoicing flow.
Sorting and comparison orders chosen by context - a UI column, a request parameter, a locale - which is how the JDK uses the pattern for Comparator in Collections.sort/List.sort and how C uses it for qsort's comparison function.
Routing and policy selection: path finding, load balancing, retry/backoff and rate-limiting algorithms chosen from configuration without editing the caller.
Compression, serialization and encoding codecs (gzip/deflate/zstd, JSON/Protobuf, character encodings) selected per stream, per record or per request.
Validation and normalization rule sets for pluggable document or form types, where each variant knows its own schema quirks and error format.
Numerical and scientific kernels: integration, interpolation or solver algorithms chosen per problem with different accuracy/performance trade-offs.
Pluggable authentication/authorization or hashing policies chosen per tenant, where the same code path must run different algorithms behind one signature.
E-commerce shipping provider selection (UPS, FedEx, DHL) where each carrier implements a different rate-calculation algorithm, and the shipping calculator is decoupled from the carrier specifics.
Payment processing gateways (credit card, virtual account, wallet) where each method has distinct validation, fee calculation and settlement rules, but the checkout flow is uniform.
Data retrieval at runtime: selecting between an API client, a web scraper, a database query or a cache-first lookup depending on availability, cost or latency requirements.
ML inference: choosing between ONNX, TensorRT, CPU or GPU backends for model execution, each with different latency/throughput trade-offs, selected per request or per deployment environment.
Travel and navigation: routing algorithms (walking, cycling, driving, public transit) with distinct distance/time/transfer calculations, chosen by user preference or real-time conditions.
Hybrid AI systems: combining symbolic decision logic with sub-symbolic ML model inference behind a uniform interface, enabling runtime selection of the reasoning strategy.
Log routing: dispatching log events to different backends (file, console, cloud observability platforms) selected by deployment environment or tenant configuration.
Encryption and cipher suites: selecting TLS cipher suites, password hashing algorithms (bcrypt, argon2), or encoding schemes based on security policy and compliance requirements.
File format processing: parsing and rendering strategies for documents, images, or data files where each format requires different handling but the pipeline remains uniform.
Game AI: selecting enemy behavior algorithms (aggressive, defensive, evasive, patrol) per entity type or difficulty level, enabling runtime personality changes.
Apache Kafka producers select or replace the partition-selection algorithm through the org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.Partitioner interface (default sticky/key-hash, RoundRobinPartitioner for even distribution), configured per producer via partitioner.class.
Envoy proxy chooses one load balancing algorithm per upstream cluster from the envoy.load_balancing_policies extension category (ROUND_ROBIN, LEAST_REQUEST and third-party policies), each implementing one host-selection operation behind the cluster's router call path.
scikit-learn estimators expose interchangeable optimization algorithms behind one fit/predict API via the solver parameter (LogisticRegression: lbfgs, liblinear, saga, newton-cg, newton-cholesky), documented as a choice driven by dataset size and penalty rather than by a different client interface.

statement: Choose the data organization and maintenance strategy for participants that makes position-based neighborhood queries efficient despite frequent movement.
name: subject-descriptor
document:
subject-descriptor
principal
subject
Give every part of a system one credential-independent representation of the entity on whose behalf an operation is performed, so authorization, audit and domain code can ask who is acting and read that subject's security-relevant attributes without knowing which credential format proved it.
Authentication arrives in many formats - password plus session cookie, OIDC/JWT, mTLS certificate, API key, Kerberos ticket, signed assertion - while every decision downstream only needs the same few facts: a stable identifier for the acting subject and its roles or attributes. Without a common representation each consumer parses the credential itself, or a raw token or user-record type is threaded through the layers: consumers are coupled to one mechanism, two layers can disagree about who the caller is, attributes are re-derived per component, and values that were never verified get treated as authenticated.
Systems that establish identity once at a trust boundary and consume it in many places afterwards, and that have (or expect to have) more than one authentication mechanism feeding the same authorization and domain logic: server-side request processing (filters, middleware, interceptors, handlers), enterprise applications in front of JAAS, an STS or an identity provider, and service meshes where mTLS, bearer tokens and session cookies meet.
A web API reached by several mechanisms at once - session cookie for the browser app, bearer token for mobile clients, mTLS for service-to-service calls - where every path ends in the same descriptor and controllers and policies are written once.
An enterprise application behind a JAAS login module, an STS or an identity provider: the validated authentication result is converted into the descriptor, which carries subject id, roles and tenant for downstream authorization and audit.
A multi-tenant SaaS where tenant membership and subject identity travel together, so repository-level guards enforce isolation by reading one attribute instead of trusting a request parameter.
Support and impersonation workflows: the descriptor records acting subject and impersonated subject separately, so audit names both while authorization evaluates the acting one.
An authorization engine or policy decision point that expects subject attributes as input: the descriptor is serialized into the policy request instead of the raw token.
Migrating off a legacy identity stack (JAAS, Windows identities, a homegrown user table) to OIDC: consumers are switched to the descriptor first, and the mechanism behind it is replaced second.
Java SE with JAAS: login modules of any type assemble one javax.security.auth.Subject holding the caller's Principals plus public/private credential sets, and application code running inside Subject.doAs authorizes from the principals without ever touching the ticket that logged the subject in.
An ASP.NET Core app with cookie, JWT-bearer and certificate handlers registered as separate authentication schemes: each handler turns its verified credential into the same ClaimsPrincipal on HttpContext.User, so [Authorize] and authorization policies inspect claims whichever scheme authenticated the request.
A Spring Security application combining form login, OAuth2/OIDC login and mTLS: every AuthenticationProvider emits the same authenticated Authentication object inside a SecurityContext held by the SecurityContextHolder, so @PreAuthorize rules and domain services read one subject shape for all mechanisms.

statement: Choose how the checkout screen will represent all user interactions and derive one consistent, immutable screen snapshot through testable transitions.
name: make-illegal-states-unrepresentable
document:
make-illegal-states-unrepresentable
make invalid states unrepresentable
Encode each domain rule in the shape of the data type so that values violating the rule cannot be constructed at all, replacing scattered run-time validation and defensive checks with a model in which only legal states exist.
Domain values are modelled as one record with independent fields - a status tag plus several nullable or optional attributes, or a handful of booleans - so the type admits every combination of those fields, including the ones the business rules forbid. Consumers cannot trust the type: each branch re-checks which fields are meaningful, the same guard is written in several places (and forgotten in one), and illegal states become runtime bugs that surface when a code path finally combines the wrong flags.
Applies when a value has a small, known set of mutually exclusive shapes whose payloads differ, when the same invalid combination keeps being defended against in several places, and when the language can close a set of variants (Rust/Swift enums, sealed hierarchies, discriminated unions) or at least hide constructors. It is equally a boundary discipline: untrusted input is parsed once into a type whose existence already proves it is valid, so no downstream code has to re-validate.
Lifecycle and state machines: orders, payments, subscriptions, bookings and connection states, one variant per state carrying exactly the data that exists in that state.
Client and API request state: a loading/success/error union instead of a data field, an error field and an isLoading flag that can contradict one another.
Message and protocol modelling: a closed set of commands, events or JSON payload shapes decoded once and dispatched with an exhaustive match (event sourcing, interpreters, RPC handlers).
Refined scalars that travel through the model: money with currency, email addresses, quantities with units and identifiers that are parsed once and never re-validated.
Configuration whose combinations are illegal: TLS settings that only apply when TLS is enabled, cursor-based versus offset pagination, mutually exclusive feature flags.
Import and deserialization boundaries: convert untrusted rows, CSV cells, query parameters or JSON into domain types with a failing factory, so invalid input cannot travel further.
Rust's standard `Option`/`Result` enums and exhaustive `match` make presence, absence, success and failure explicit cases that downstream code must handle at compile time (Rust Reference/Book).
Swift enums with associated values and exhaustive `switch` model state-specific payloads such as error cases without nullable companion fields (The Swift Programming Language).
Kotlin sealed classes and interfaces with exhaustive `when` expressions provide a closed hierarchy for finite state machines and error/result models, with the compiler checking that every known case is handled.

statement: Choose how notifications from multiple changing sources reach multiple independently deployed consumers without duplicating pairwise registration and cleanup.
name: facade
document:
facade
façade
Provide one coarse-grained entry interface that hides a subsystem of many cooperating classes behind the few operations its clients actually need, so callers depend on a single stable API instead of orchestrating the subsystem themselves.
Every client of a complex subsystem must know which classes exist, in which order to call them, how to configure and dispose them and how to interpret their errors; that orchestration is then duplicated across the codebase, and any change inside the subsystem ripples through all callers.
Applies when a subsystem (a library, framework, legacy module, remote SDK, or a layer of your own system) is much broader than any single client needs, when its correct use is a recurring sequence of collaborations, and when client code should be insulated from its types and its evolution. Typical at module and system-boundary scope, where one entry point per layer or per external system is wanted.
Wrapping a third-party SDK, media framework or payment/HTTP client behind one class or module that exposes the application's own vocabulary (convert, charge, upload).
Application services that orchestrate repositories, gateways and domain services for one use case (checkout, report generation) and are the only seam controllers or jobs talk to.
Layered systems where every layer offers a facade as its entry point, so dependencies flow through coarse interfaces instead of reaching into a layer's internals.
Isolating a legacy subsystem while it is replaced incrementally: new code depends on the clean facade, and the migration swaps implementations behind it.
Remote and coarse-grained boundaries: a remote facade exposes a few chunky operations over a fine-grained object model to avoid chatty calls (see Remote Facade, Fowler's PEAA).
Startup/teardown sequences and device orchestration (the classic home-theatre example): clients need one 'watch movie' operation, not a dozen subsystem calls in the right order.
Service-container proxy facades (e.g. Laravel): a static-looking front-end that forwards calls to a resolved service instance, giving a terse API without sacrificing testability or DI flexibility.
JPA/service-layer facades: a single transactional entry point that receives DTOs, maps them to domain objects, orchestrates business logic, maps results back, and commits — one transaction per use case.
Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) in microservices: a thin per-client aggregation service (web, mobile, partner) that fans out to downstream microservices, reshapes responses for the client, and handles perimeter concerns. Each BFF is a specialized facade owned by the team that ships the corresponding client.
Anti-Corruption Layer (DDD): a facade placed between a bounded context and an external/legacy system to translate that system's model into domain concepts, preventing external concepts from polluting the internal domain model.
Event-driven/observable facades: a facade that exposes reactive streams (Observables, Promises, async generators) over the subsystem, buffering, batching or debouncing events for consumers that prefer push-based or streaming interfaces.
API gateway composition: an API gateway acts as a system-wide facade that unifies multiple backend services at the edge, handling auth, routing and cross-cutting concerns before delegating to more specific facades or services.
SDK wrapper facades: publishing a public-facing SDK over an internal microservice mesh; the facade shapes the external API surface, applies default configurations, and provides a stable consumer experience independent of internal service topology changes.
SLF4J (Simple Logging Facade for Java): slf4j-api is a minimal logging facade; applications code against Logger.debug()/info() once and bind the concrete framework (Logback, Log4j 2, java.util.logging) at deployment time by swapping the provider jar on the classpath — the textbook runtime-swappable facade.
Spring Framework JdbcClient / JdbcTemplate: a fluent facade over raw JDBC that owns connection and statement lifecycle, iterates ResultSets and translates SQLException into the DataAccessException hierarchy, so callers supply only SQL and result mapping instead of the full boilerplate workflow.
jQuery $.get/$.post/$.getJSON over $.ajax: a per-task facade layer that collapses cross-browser XMLHttpRequest differences, Deferred plumbing and HTTP defaults into one-line calls — the canonical JavaScript-library facade.

statement: Whether the inventory snapshot flow should have a deadline-based absence check that alerts on silence even though all processes remain healthy.
name: durable-subscriber
document:
durable-subscriber
durable subscription
durable consumer
Keep a publish-subscribe consumer's place while it is offline: the broker binds a stable subscription identity to retained messages or a committed position, then resumes delivery after reconnect until retention, expiry, or quota says the backlog is no longer available.
A subscriber on a publish-subscribe channel can be unavailable during redeployment, maintenance, device disconnects, or scheduled batch work. A non-durable subscription drops messages published during that gap, so the design must choose a stable identity and broker-side state, then make finite retention, replay pressure, and at-least-once redelivery explicit; durable state prevents a gap only while that state remains available.
Broker-mediated publish-subscribe messaging where consumers are intermittently offline but individual messages matter: JMS topics, MQTT sessions, Kafka consumer groups, NATS JetStream durable consumers, cloud topic subscriptions. It presumes the messaging system can store messages (or positions) durably, so it is as much a broker-configuration decision as a client one, and it presumes at-least-once delivery is acceptable once the consumer is idempotent. It does not apply to in-process notification or to broadcast where only the newest value counts.
A Kafka-backed order-processing service that is redeployed or scaled to zero while events keep arriving: the consumer group resumes from its committed offsets and replays what it missed.
An IoT or mobile client on an intermittent link: an MQTT persistent session holds QoS 1/2 publications for its client id and delivers them when the client reconnects.
A partner integration that receives published documents while the partner's system is down: an unshared JMS durable subscription, or a cloud topic subscription, is registered on their behalf and holds the backlog until they acknowledge it.
A nightly audit or analytics consumer that must see every published change: the day's backlog is drained in bounded batches and acknowledged as it is persisted.
A ledger or compliance consumer that must never silently skip events: retention and lag alarms are configured so an offline subscriber is noticed before its backlog expires.
A cloud event-driven architecture (SNS FIFO → SQS FIFO): SNS preserves ordering and deduplication while SQS queues hold messages for durable fan-out to Lambda or EC2 consumers, with DLQs capturing failed deliveries for replay.
An industrial SCADA/IoT sensor fleet where devices connect sporadically over unstable networks: MQTT persistent sessions with a long session expiry interval preserve every telemetry reading until each device reconnects, even after multi-day outages.
A financial audit trail that must immutably record every state-changing event: events are durably retained in Kafka or JetStream and consumed by a compliance subscriber that must not skip or duplicate entries; idempotent deduplication and offset commits after durable persistence enforce this.
A supply-chain or logistics event-sourcing system where downstream services reconstruct state by replaying events after a crash or deliberate seek: the durable consumer starts from the committed position and replays the missing event window atomically with the state reconstruction.
A cross-region disaster-recovery subscriber that mirrors events to a secondary site: the durable subscription in the secondary region receives every event from the primary's topic, with a DLQ holding any events that fail cross-region delivery for manual retry.
A JMS topic consumer that must receive publications made while it is offline: the client reconnects with the same client identifier and durable subscription name, and the provider retains messages until acknowledgement, expiry, or unsubscribe.
An MQTT 3.1.1 device gateway that reconnects with the same client identifier and CleanSession=0: the broker resumes the stored session and queues matching QoS 1/2 publications for delivery after the link returns.
A NATS JetStream billing worker that restarts after an outage: it binds to the same durable consumer name and explicit-acks each message, so the server resumes its acknowledgement floor and redelivers unacknowledged work.
An Azure Service Bus fan-out topology: topic subscriptions are durable by default and each subscription stores its own copy of matching messages, so a receiver that reconnects later still drains its backlog; client-affine durable subscriptions bind the durable state to a stable client id.
A high-throughput replay consumer on RabbitMQ Streams: the consumer attaches with a stable tracking reference (name) and periodically stores its offset server-side, so a restart resumes from the last stored offset instead of re-reading the whole stream.
An event-sourced system on Google Cloud Pub/Sub that must reprocess history after a bug fix: the subscription enables acknowledged-message retention (default window 7 days, up to 31) and is seeked back to a past timestamp or snapshot to replay already-acked messages.

statement: Choose how each order command reaches exactly one processing worker while multiple interchangeable workers can scale horizontally and recover unfinished work after failures.
name: pratt-parser
document:
pratt-parser
top-down operator precedence
tdop
Parse expressions with many prefix, infix and postfix operators by associating a binding power and a handler with each token type, so precedence and associativity live in one rule table instead of one parsing function per precedence level.
Operator precedence turns expression parsing into a ladder of near-identical functions - one per level - each of which must re-implement associativity, delegate to the next level for its operands, and be edited whenever an operator is added or moves. Grammars with prefix, infix, postfix and mixfix operators (ternary conditionals, assignment, calls, indexing, user-registered operators) make that ladder long, make associativity easy to get subtly wrong, and scatter the grammar across the parser so it cannot be read in one place.
Hand-written parsers for an expression-bearing language, DSL, query or configuration syntax: a token stream is already available (or is cheap to lex), the operator set is large or expected to grow, and the team wants the grammar visible as data. It is typically the expression layer under an ordinary recursive-descent parser for statements and declarations - interpreters, calculators, filter and rule engines, formula tools - and it is unnecessary when a parser generator already declares precedence for the grammar.
Expression evaluators and calculators whose operator set is expected to grow (arithmetic, units, comparisons, percentages, function calls, user-defined functions).
Query, filter and rule languages - search filters, feature-flag conditions, access-policy conditions, spreadsheet formulas - with many comparison, logical and string operators.
Front ends for small languages and DSLs that parse statements and declarations with recursive descent and need real precedence handling for the expression layer.
Single-pass compilers and interpreters that emit bytecode or IR while parsing, where each handler is also the point that emits the operator's instruction.
Template and configuration expression languages that must attach exact source positions and precise errors to every operator.
Host-language extension points that let plugins or users register additional operators at runtime, because registration is just a table entry.
Rust PEG grammars that use pest::pratt_parser::PrattParser to map prefix, postfix and infix operator pairs into calculator or DSL ASTs.
Rust parser-combinator expression grammars built with chumsky's pratt combinator, where atom parsers and prefix, postfix and infix operators declare precedence and associativity.
JavaScript expression-only tooling built on JSEP, where a compact Pratt-style parser produces ASTs and allows custom unary and binary operators with explicit precedence.

statement: Maintain routing rules in reloadable configuration so destinations and traffic allocations can change while the running gateway continues processing messages.
name: dependency-injection
document:
dependency-injection
di
constructor injection
setter injection
interface injection
ioc container
pure di
manual di
Supply an object with the collaborators it needs from the outside — through its constructor, its setters/properties, or a dedicated injection interface — so it never constructs or looks a dependency up itself and every wiring decision is made once, in a composition root or container.
An object that creates its own collaborators hard-wires a concrete class, a construction recipe and often a lifetime into itself: swapping the implementation for a test double, a second deployment or a new platform means editing the class, and the dependency graph stays invisible in the API. The recurring trigger is exactly the catalog's rule: an object should not create what it depends on — the caller, the framework or the composition root decides, and hands the dependency in.
Applies whenever a component's collaborators are chosen per deployment, per environment or per test, whenever constructing them is expensive or platform-specific, and whenever a framework owns object creation (request handlers, scheduled jobs, UI screens, message consumers). It matters most in large object graphs where one abstraction has several implementations and lifetimes must be managed (singleton, request-scoped, transient); it is unnecessary when the collaborators are pure values or when construction is a private detail nobody needs to vary.
Web and API backends whose handlers need repositories, clocks, mailers and caches that must be replaced by fakes in tests and by sandbox services in staging.
Hexagonal and clean architectures where the domain declares ports (interfaces) and the infrastructure layer supplies adapters at the composition root.
Frameworks that own object creation — request handlers, scheduled jobs, UI controllers, message consumers — where the framework's injector is the only practical wiring point.
Deployment variants (on-prem vs cloud, SQL vs in-memory, real vs stub payment gateway) selected per environment through binding configuration rather than conditional code.
Plugin and extension systems where the concrete implementation is chosen at start-up from a plugin registry, enabling third-party adapters without touching core code.
Expensive shared resources whose lifetime must be managed centrally (connection pools, HTTP clients, circuit breakers) while service classes stay stateless.
Unit tests that construct the class under test directly with test doubles, and integration tests that swap only the outer layer's bindings.
Microservices with sidecar containers: the sidecar provides logging, tracing and retry policies as injected collaborators, keeping the service logic untouched.
Cloud-native applications where the composition root is the only place that knows whether a dependency resolves locally, across a service mesh, or via a remote gRPC call.
Multi-tenant SaaS where tenant-specific adapters (tenant-scoped repositories, per-tenant feature flags) are bound at the composition root and switched by middleware.
Event-driven systems where message handlers receive their dependencies through injection, making the handler logic identical between in-process and distributed deployment.
AOT-compiled applications (Native AOT, Blazor WebAssembly, serverless) where runtime reflection is unavailable — dependencies are resolved via source generators or manually at the composition root.
Functional codebases using effect systems (ZIO, fp-ts, Reader monad) where the DI container is replaced by typed environments passed through function compositions.
Consumer-driven contract testing (Pact, OpenAPI pact) where DI swaps provider implementations with contract-mock stubs at the boundary, enabling parallel service development without shared integration environments.
Resilience and fault-injection testing: proxies or decorator-based fault injectors (e.g., Gremlin SDK, WireMock) are injected as collaborators to validate retry, timeout and circuit-breaker behaviour under simulated failure conditions.
Single-page application frameworks with DI built into the component tree: Angular resolves components, directives and services through hierarchical injectors, scoping providers to the application root, a component subtree or a route so features override implementations and lazy-load without global registration.
Android apps using Dagger (and Hilt over it) to build the object graph at compile time — generated, reflection-free code, bindings and cycles checked at build time, with field injection reserved for framework-created entry points like Activities and Fragments.
Python web APIs (FastAPI) where each path operation declares Depends(callable) parameters: the framework resolves nested dependency graphs with per-request caching and uses yield-based dependencies to open and close connections around each request.

statement: Choose a traversal architecture that hides route storage details, preserves independent traversal state, and permits the requested traversal order to be selected per request.
name: double-checked-locking
document:
double-checked-locking
double-checked locking optimization
DCL
DCLP
Initialise a shared resource exactly once and lazily while keeping the steady-state read path free of lock acquisition - by testing a cheaply published state first and taking the lock only for the one-time construction, where the platform can publish the built object safely to every reader.
An expensive object - configuration, a connection pool, a compiled plan, a cache - must be created once and only when it is first needed, but its accessor is called from many threads. The naive check-then-act form lets two threads build it at the same time, and guarding every read with a lock serialises a path that almost never needs synchronisation. The tempting fix - test a flag cheaply, lock only for the initialisation, test again inside the lock - is sound only if the write that publishes the object is ordered with respect to the readers' loads, which is exactly the part the classic formulation leaves implicit and the reason the idiom is famous for rare, unreproducible failures.
Concurrent, shared-memory software in which one object or cell must be built once and read many times: process-wide singletons and registries, per-object caches inside an object shared between threads, lazily built statics in languages whose runtime also provides the once semantics. The pattern presupposes a memory model with a defined publication ordering (volatile, acquire/release, an initialisation lock, or a runtime once primitive) and a read path hot enough that the lock it removes is measurable. On single-threaded runtimes there is nothing to synchronise, and where a single-threaded composition root can initialise eagerly the pattern is unnecessary.
Process-wide singletons whose construction is expensive or configuration-dependent: configuration snapshot, metrics registry, logger, connection pool, feature-flag view.
Per-object caches inside an object shared by several threads - compiled regular expression or query plan, parsed schema, symbol table - where the build is expensive and the read is hot.
Lazily built statics in languages where the runtime owns the once semantics: C++ function-local static, Swift static let or global let, Kotlin by lazy, Scala lazy val, Go sync.Once, Rust OnceLock/LazyLock.
Compensating for the static-initialisation-order problem: an accessor that builds the global on first use instead of relying on cross-translation-unit initialisation order.
Avoiding lock overhead on a read-mostly, write-once hot path (memo tables, symbol caches, thread-safe lazy proxies) where a contended lock would show up in a profile.
Small or freestanding runtimes without a once primitive, where the first caller must build the cell and an eager initialiser is not available.
RWMutex-protected maps in Go where readers check a fast path before the slower write-locked re-check, as a safer alternative to sync.Map for workloads with known access patterns.
Per-connection or per-session lazy fields in object-pooled servers where the pool itself is the shared cell and each borrowed object gets a lazy-computed field.
Cross-language plugin or extension registries where one language's runtime initialises a global handle that other language shards read without repeated synchronisation.
Rate-limiter or circuit-breaker state that must be lazily built from configuration: building eagerly would couple the policy to startup time, but the read path must be lock-free under high throughput.
Lazy compilation or query-plan warming in database connection pools where the pool is shared but individual plans are built on first use by the owning thread.
Spring Framework's DefaultSingletonBeanRegistry.getSingleton: check the singletonObjects map lock-free, take the singletonLock only when the bean is absent, re-check inside - a production evolution of the idiom whose correctness was formally challenged (SPR-13463) and upheld because the concurrent-map read already carries the needed memory barrier.
Chromium's base::LazyInstance / GetOrCreateLazyPointer: an atomic state word with a 'creating' bit, acquire-load fast path and release-store publication - since deprecated in favour of function-local statics with base::NoDestructor, a signal of how far hardened platforms have moved from hand-rolled DCL.
ACE toolkit's ACE_Singleton<TYPE, ACE_LOCK>: the pattern's original industrial home (the 1997 paper was written alongside ACE) - the template still guards instance() with a double-checked ACE_LOCK acquire and recommends ACE_Recursive_Thread_Mutex for multi-threaded access.
Swift runtime: every global/static let is lowered to swift_once (dispatch_once on Darwin), so the double-checked once structure is the default initialisation mechanism for lazily computed immutable globals rather than hand-written code.

statement: Whether to replace the closed two-way contract with an extension mechanism that lets new node kinds and new operations arrive independently while preserving existing packages.
name: consumer-driven-contract-test
document:
consumer-driven-contract-test
consumer-driven contract
contract test
Capture, from each consumer's own tests, the concrete provider interactions that consumer depends on, and verify the provider against that contract inside the provider's own build, so consumer and provider can be released independently without a shared end-to-end environment.
Independently released consumers and providers must keep working together, yet the only reliable check is a shared end-to-end environment per pair - slow, brittle and usually out of date; at the same time the provider cannot see which parts of its API each consumer actually exercises, so every refactoring is a guess about who will break.
HTTP/request-reply, messaging and gRPC integrations where consumer and provider are owned by different teams on different release cadences and each consumer uses only a narrow slice of the provider's surface. It assumes the provider team is willing to run verification of consumer contracts in its own build; without that half, the consumer test is only a better mock.
Microservice landscapes where a front end, a mobile app or another service consumes an API released by a different team on its own schedule.
A provider team that must refactor or replace internals and needs to know, before merging, which consumer expectations it is about to break.
Mobile or desktop clients that cannot be deployed in lockstep with the backend, so each client's expectations must hold against every backend version.
Event- and message-based integrations (Kafka, SQS, SNS, RabbitMQ) where the consumer processes messages produced by another team; contracts pin the message body shape and metadata (topic, headers, content-type) while abstracting the transport.
Migration or strangler-fig work, where a replacement provider must be proven compatible with the existing consumers before traffic is moved.
Using the contract as the source of stubs for development and integration environments, so those environments no longer need the real provider.
BFF (Backend for Frontend) patterns where each frontend channel (web, mobile, third-party) has its own contract with a shared backend, allowing independent evolution of each BFF without cross-channel breakage.
Multi-team Kafka event streaming where consumers (downstream services) define which topics, partitions and message schemas they depend on, so producers can evolve events without silently breaking subscribers; Pact message pacts handle both JSON and Schema Registry messages (with magic bytes for Avro/Protobuf over Schema Registry).
gRPC service integrations where protocol buffer message shapes are exercised by the actual consumer client code, pinning the wire format, service method signatures and metadata the consumer actually calls; synchronous message pacts cover the request-response pairing.
Breaking up a monolith: individual microservices are extracted and their CDC contracts verify that the new service boundaries behave identically to the original module interfaces before traffic is migrated.
Schema Registry integrations (Confluent, AWS Glue) where consumers pin compatible message schemas and producers must not publish breaking schemas without migrating all dependent consumers first.
Third-party or vendor API integrations where the consumer team cannot rely on the provider to run verification: the consumer-side mock-only workflow with published contracts documents expectations even without provider participation.
Webhook and callback integrations where a provider calls a consumer-defined endpoint; CDC captures the consumer's expected payload shape, headers and authentication, and the provider verifies it can deliver to that shape.
Contract migration at scale: when a provider must migrate from v1 to v2 of an API, CDC with pending/wip pacts allows the provider to signal new expectations to consumers without blocking either side's pipeline while migration is in progress.
Spring Cloud Contract in JVM/Spring landscapes: the consumer's contract change lands in the producer's repository (or an external contract repo), the producer build generates verification tests from the contract DSL, and the consumer develops against StubRunner-served WireMock stubs pulled from an artifact repository (Nexus/Artifactory) - the contract is the single artifact both sides build from.
Nubank replaced its flaky shared-environment end-to-end suite with consumer-driven contract tests to regain deploy velocity - the public account of the pattern paying off as an e2e-substitute at a single organisation rather than as an addition to it.
Large polyglot estates such as JSTOR/ITHAKA (300+ microservices, 12+ teams, Pact) and M1 Finance (Pact plus PactFlow rolled out to 17 teams in under six months): the broker's compatibility matrix replaces per-pair end-to-end environments as the release gate.

statement: Decide whether Fleet Server should acquire tracing backends from separately packaged modules discovered at start-up, rather than compiling every backend into the server.
name: watchman
document:
watchman
dead man's switch
heartbeat monitor
Detect that a message flow has gone silent - not that a message failed - and tell a responsible person or system within a bounded time by comparing each flow's arrivals against the cadence its business deadline implies.
Message systems fail silently in the one way no error handler observes: nothing arrives. A producer stops emitting, a consumer stops draining, a scheduled job never fires, a credential expires, a partition goes offline - and because no failing code path is ever entered, error dashboards stay green while downstream data quietly goes stale. The recurring trigger: a flow whose absence is business-visible (a nightly feed, an order stream, a partner interface) has no owner-facing signal for 'no messages', so the gap is discovered late - by a customer or a downstream job - instead of by the team that can fix it.
Applies wherever messages are expected on a knowable cadence (event streams, queues, batch hand-offs, partner interfaces, device check-ins) and their absence is a business-visible failure: the flow has an owner, the expected period and grace window can be derived from a downstream deadline, and either the transport can be observed passively (queue counters, a wire tap) or the producers can emit out-of-band heartbeats. The watchman sits at message-flow or boundary scope - an in-process watcher beside the consumer, a periodic sweep over persisted last-seen state, or a rule in the monitoring stack fed by metrics - and it must itself be watched, because a silent watchman is exactly the failure it exists to catch.
Nightly batch or ETL feed: page the integration owner when the 02:00 import has produced no messages by its deadline, instead of noticing an empty report at the morning stand-up.
Business-critical event stream (orders, payments, telemetry): alarm when the produce rate stays at zero through business hours, which separates a healthy quiet topic from a stopped producer.
External partner interface: notify when no messages have arrived from a B2B partner within the agreed window, turning a looming SLA breach into an early, actionable alert.
Long-running workflow stage: require a heartbeat from each process-manager step so a stuck instance is noticed before the surrounding batch closes or a compensation becomes necessary.
Retry or dead-letter pump: verify that the pump still drains failed messages - silence means the pump died, not that the backlog is empty.
Fleet check-ins (edge devices, agents, cron jobs on many hosts): raise a per-device or per-site alarm when scheduled check-ins stop arriving.
The alerting pipeline itself: an always-firing watchdog alert routed to an external service, so a broken alert path is discovered by its silence.
Cron and scheduled-job fleet via Healthchecks.io: each job pings a unique URL, the service holds the Period and Grace Time, flips the check Late then Down when no ping arrives by period + grace, and notifies integrations.
Dashboard alert rules in Grafana: an alert rule whose query returns no series enters the No Data state and can raise a DatasourceNoData alert - the platform form of deciding what silence means (No Data, Alerting, Normal or Keep last state).
Apache Burrow for Kafka (LinkedIn): committed offsets are evaluated per partition over a sliding window and a consumer is classified STALLED when its offset is frozen with non-zero lag, or STOPPED when no new commits arrive - consumer-silence detection without fixed lag thresholds.

statement: Decide how to compose a sequence whose next action depends on the prior result while absence, failure, and asynchronous completion are propagated uniformly.
name: copy-and-swap
document:
copy-and-swap
copy and swap idiom
create-temporary-and-swap
Implement assignment (and any in-place state replacement) so that a failure while producing the new state leaves the target untouched: build the complete replacement off to the side, commit it with operations that cannot fail, and let the temporary's destructor or the garbage collector release the old state.
A hand-written assignment has to tear down the old state and build a copy of the new one, but only the build can fail: destroying before allocating exposes a half-updated object when the allocation or the element copy throws, and the usual repair -- a self-assignment check plus manual rollback -- duplicates the per-member copying that already lives in the copy constructor. The trigger is an assignment (or, in a garbage-collected language, an in-place state replacement) that must satisfy the strong exception guarantee: either it completes, or the target still holds its previous value.
Types that own resources -- heap buffers, handles, file descriptors, trees, containers -- in a language where the programmer controls copy semantics: C++ special member functions, a C ADT with error codes, Rust with panic/abort failure modes. The same ordering also applies in garbage-collected languages whenever published state must never be mutated in place: building the complete replacement and publishing it once keeps readers consistent and moves the release of the old state to the collector. The precondition is a commit step that genuinely cannot fail -- a noexcept member swap, one reference or pointer store, or an atomic publish.
Container and buffer classes that own heap memory (dynamic array, string, matrix, tree) and must be assignable without leaking or leaving the target inconsistent when an allocation fails.
Handle/pimpl classes that keep their state behind a single pointer: the swap is a pointer exchange, so the commit is unconditionally non-throwing while the deep copy still happens in the copy constructor (Sutter's canonical Pimpl exception-safety transformation).
Pre-C++11 codebases where the same operator= must serve lvalues and rvalues and no move constructor exists, using the const-reference plus explicit-local-temporary form.
Value types stored inside standard containers: std::vector and friends need element assignment to be safe before they can offer their own strong guarantee on reallocation, and a noexcept swap participates in their internal move/swap dispatch.
Garbage-collected languages where shared state must be replaced rather than mutated: build a complete replacement value and publish it with one store (AtomicReference.updateAndGet, atomic.Pointer[T].Store, a record with-expression) so readers never observe a partially updated object.
In-place state replacement where identity must be preserved (a registry entry, a cached object with live references): copy into a scratch value, then commit with a member-wise exchange or a replace-style API instead of repointing the reference.
Concurrent programming with thread-safe local-then-publish: build the replacement in a local object (thread-private by definition), then publish atomically -- readers never see a partially updated state, and the previous value is released by the collector after the atomic write is visible.
Version-control-style update: check out a local copy, mutate freely, then commit or discard; copy-and-swap maps directly to this workflow and provides the same transactional semantics (Howard Hinnant's analogy from his C++ Con 2018 talk).
Compiler tooling treats the idiom as the canonical self-assignment-safe assignment: LLVM's clang-tidy bugprone-unhandled-self-assignment checker explicitly recognizes 'build a temporary in operator=, then swap it' as correct handling and matches extended (allocator-aware) constructors plus ADL swap forms so real copy-and-swap code is not flagged (llvm/llvm-project PR #147066).
Boost's move/assignment guidance converged on the single by-value form T operator=(T b) { swap(*this, b); return *this; } as the common way to get copy-, move-, and convertible-assignment from one operator, with dedicated macros (BOOST_COPYABLE_AND_MOVABLE_ALT) for classes that adopt it instead of separate overloads.
When a strong guarantee is needed on the standard containers, libc++ maintainers advise exactly this idiom at the call site -- 'construct a new vector and swap it with the one you want to assign to' (libc++ PR #117516 discussion) -- because the library's own copy assignment deliberately offers only the basic guarantee.
