name: separation-of-duties
document:
separation-of-duties
separation of privilege
four-eyes principle
Require two or more distinct principals or components to complete a sensitive operation, so that no single account, role or object can initiate and finish it alone.
A sensitive workflow is reachable end to end from one identity or one code path: the same operator creates and approves the payment, the same administrator changes the production configuration and signs it off, the same service account holds both the maker and the checker permission. The trigger is structural rather than accidental - all steps share one principal, one session, one process or one role, because splitting them costs a second pair of hands - and the failure surfaces only when an insider error or abuse is unremarkable in the audit trail: every step was authorized, because one principal held both halves of the duty.
Sensitive operations whose consequences must survive mistakes, coercion or misuse by authorized insiders: payments and disbursements, entitlement and permission changes, production configuration and deployment, key custody and signing, destructive data operations. It applies where identities can be kept distinct and authenticated (separate accounts, roles, services, processes), where the intermediate states of the operation can be persisted and observed, and where an enforcement point exists that can compare the acting principal with the recorded initiator - a policy engine, method security, an approval service, a separate process or account, a dual-control key ceremony. It is as much an organizational rule as a technical one: the split must follow the duties people actually hold, and recombination must be made awkward by design rather than merely discouraged.
Maker-checker payments: an operator above a threshold creates a disbursement and a second operator releases it; the ledger records both identities and refuses a release signed by the maker.
Change control and deployment: production IAM policy or infrastructure changes require a second administrator's approval, and the pipeline refuses to run a change approved by its own author (required reviewers / second signature).
Key custody and dual control: signing keys or root credentials are split so two authorized operators must each contribute a share (split knowledge, m-of-n threshold, dual-control key ceremony) and no single share can sign.
Access provisioning: the requester of an entitlement, its approver and the administrator who grants it are three distinct roles; the administrator cannot approve their own request, and access-control administrators do not administer the audit log.
Destructive data operations: schema migrations, production data edits and deletion jobs are prepared by one engineer and executed by a different operator account that cannot author the change.
Regulated back-office workflows: journal entries, refunds, credit adjustments and account closures are initiated by one clerk and posted by another, with the pairing recorded for audit.
GitHub protected branches: a pull request targeting a protected branch needs the configured number of approving reviews before it can merge, the platform refuses an approval from the PR author by design, and with dismiss-stale-review enabled a commit pushed after the review voids the approval - four-eyes enforced at the merge gate with the approval bound to the reviewed revision.
AWS Systems Manager Change Manager: a change request may run its Automation runbook only after approvals from named IAM users, groups or roles arrive across up to five approval levels, and a single rejection stops execution; because change templates list approvers separately from requesters, a request submitted under one IAM principal is released by another.
HashiCorp Vault key custody: vault operator init splits the root key with Shamir's Secret Sharing into key shares (default 5) under a threshold (default 3); unsealing or generating a root token needs a quorum of distinct share holders, and PGP-encrypting each share for a named operator makes dual control a property of the mechanism rather than of the procedure.

statement: Should all SQL for each database table be confined to one component whose methods exchange plain record structures, rather than leaving statements in transaction scripts?
name: spatial-partition
document:
spatial-partition
spatial index
bucket grid
Store every object in a structure indexed by its position so that neighbourhood queries visit only the objects near a point or region instead of scanning the whole population.
Queries that ask 'what is near this position?' - collision checks, proximity and aggro radii, culling, spatial analytics - repeatedly scan every object: each query is linear in the population and a whole simulation step becomes quadratic, even though every object interacts only with the few objects next to it.
Per-object runtime systems and simulations - game worlds, crowd and particle solvers, location services, robotics - where objects are mobile, spread over space, and the queries are local (radius, region, k-nearest). The pattern applies once the population is large enough that a full scan dominates the frame or the request budget, and it requires a position-to-cell mapping and an update discipline that match how the objects move.
Game worlds: collision, proximity and aggro checks between many moving entities each tick (bullets versus enemies, pickups, area effects).
Physics broadphase: pruning candidate pairs before narrow-phase tests where colliders move constantly.
Map and GIS services: 'all points within radius' and viewport queries over millions of features.
Crowd, flocking and particle simulations: neighbours within a radius for boids or social forces instead of all-pairs tests.
Spatial analytics and robotics: k-nearest or region queries over vehicles, sensors and delivery points, and occupancy grids for pathfinding.
Physics engines: Box2D's broadphase is a dynamic AABB tree (b2DynamicTree) whose fattened leaf boxes absorb small moves before reinsertion, and whose region queries and ray casts prune candidates before narrow-phase tests.
Location services: Redis geospatial indexes store members as 52-bit geohash scores in a sorted set (GEOADD) so GEOSEARCH answers circle and bounding-box proximity queries server-side instead of scanning members.
GIS and analytics databases: PostGIS prunes radius queries through a GiST spatial index (the index-aware ST_DWithin predicate checks bounding boxes before computing exact distances), and scikit-learn backs radius and k-nearest neighbour queries with KDTree and BallTree instead of all-pairs distances.

statement: Choose the ownership boundary for persisting an order and all of its dependent parts as one synchronized unit of work.
name: audit-interceptor
document:
audit-interceptor
audit trail interceptor
audit logging interceptor
Declare an audit policy at an invocation seam that records the actor, action, target, correlation id and both attempt and terminal outcome around a delegated operation, then sends the structured event to a dedicated integrity-protected sink, so security accountability is consistent without inline logging in every service.
Security-relevant operations (privileged actions, state changes and access to sensitive data) must be attributable, but inline logging misses denied and failed attempts, varies in schema, can leak raw arguments and disappears with a rolled-back transaction. Teams also need to cover components they cannot modify without pretending that a proxy sees calls that bypass it.
Business or service tiers whose sensitive operations pass through an interceptable seam: container-managed beans, proxied service objects, ORM entity lifecycles, message endpoints or an HTTP pipeline. Audit selection must be declarative and uniform, while the sink has its own integrity and retention requirements (Secure Logger); the design must make mediation gaps, redaction, transaction coupling, failure policy, clock source and correlation propagation explicit.
Business-tier auditing of money-moving or otherwise regulated operations (fund transfer, order placement, claim submission): who requested it, on which object, when, and whether it succeeded.
Privileged administration surfaces (role changes, key rotation, configuration changes) where every sensitive operation must leave a record naming the acting principal.
Authentication and authorization outcomes: successful and failed logins, access-denial decisions and lockouts routed into the same audit pipeline instead of ad-hoc log lines.
Access-to-sensitive-data events (who read which patient/customer record) recorded at the gateway or service boundary to satisfy data-protection obligations.
Retrofitting auditing onto legacy components whose code cannot be modified, by wrapping the service object or binding an interceptor to its interface.
Middleware-level auditing of message endpoints and database calls in a business tier, correlating the caller's subject with the operation performed.
Financial API request interception (Spring Boot global request interceptors) capturing who accessed which endpoint, with what payload, and what outcome — satisfying SOX financial reporting controls.
Entity-level change tracking via ORM subscribers (e.g., EF Core SaveChangesInterceptor, TypeORM subscribers): automatically diff old vs. new property values on create/update/delete and emit audit envelopes without manual logging calls.
API gateway-level audit logging: capture every external API call with timestamp, user identity, endpoint, method, and outcome, correlating across microservices via X-Request-ID / traceparent headers.
Compliance reporting automation: generate audit-ready reports for SOX (~7-year retention), HIPAA (~6-year retention), GDPR (data residency-aware), and PCI-DSS from structured interceptor events.
Zero-trust data access trails: record every read of sensitive fields (PHI, PII, financial data) so data-protection obligations (GDPR Article 5 data minimization, HIPAA access logging) are demonstrably met.
Hibernate Envers: @Audited entity lifecycle changes create per-entity _AUD revisions at transaction commit; a custom revision entity/listener can attach actor or request metadata.
Django admin: django.contrib.admin.models.LogEntry records action time, user, object, addition/change/deletion and change_message for ModelAdmin activity.
Rails Audited: the audited ActiveRecord extension creates audit rows for model create, update and destroy callbacks, including changed attributes and optional acting-user attribution.

statement: Choose one shared concurrency guard for the order header and every line, discount, and address it contains, rather than requiring callers to coordinate each child separately.
name: mock
document:
mock
mock object
Replace a collaborator of the system under test with a test-specific object that is programmed with the expected calls and verifies them as they happen, so the interaction itself - not the resulting state - is what the test asserts.
The expected interaction sequence is the behaviour under test: the outcome of the exercised method is not visible in the system under test's own state, and no observation point exposes the indirect outputs (the messages sent to collaborators) that the requirement is about. State-based assertions cannot reach them, so the test either reaches into the collaborator's internals - duplicating the collaboration logic - or asserts nothing at all.
Unit and component tests of an object whose collaboration protocol is the specification: exact calls, arguments, cardinality or order matter (handshakes, publish-once, audit logging, cache invalidation) and the collaborator is slow, unavailable, non-deterministic or side-effecting. It requires a substitutable dependency (dependency injection or lookup) and, for framework-based realizations, an interception mechanism - dynamic proxy, bytecode agent, generated code or macro. Typical in mockist, interaction-first TDD and in need-driven development.
Verifying that a component emits exactly the expected messages to a collaborator whose effects are otherwise invisible: an audit logger, notifier, event publisher or payment gateway.
Pinning an interaction protocol whose ordering and cardinality are the requirement - open before send, publish exactly once, flush before close - in tests of clients and adapters.
Simulating failure paths of a remote collaborator (timeout, exception, malformed response) to assert that the SUT surfaces or recovers from them deterministically.
Unit-testing a domain service against repository, clock, or gateway interfaces when the real implementations are slow, licensed or unavailable in the development environment.
Driving interface design from the outside in: write the expectation for the call the SUT should make, then let the implementation satisfy it (mockist TDD).
Verifying that a main operation triggers its side effects - cache invalidation, metrics emission, compensating call - with the required arguments.
In C++ tests built with GoogleTest gMock, using EXPECT_CALL matchers, Times cardinalities and InSequence ordering verifies an outbound collaborator protocol before the SUT runs.
In Java tests using Mockito, verify and InOrder assert required interactions with a dependency while keeping the interaction contract separate from the dependency's implementation.
In Python's unittest.mock, assert_called_once_with and assert_has_calls verify argument, cardinality and sequence requirements for calls made through a replaceable collaborator.

name: policy-based-design
document:
policy-based-design
policy-based class design
policy-based programming
Assemble a class's behaviour, structure and defaults from small interchangeable policy units bound when the host type is instantiated, so that each orthogonal design decision can be varied independently instead of being frozen in the class's code.
A reusable class hard-codes several independent design decisions - allocation, ownership, storage, threading, validation, error handling - inside its implementation, so a different combination is only reachable by editing or copying the class, while the runtime Strategy alternative costs a virtual call per use and gives up the guarantee that the choice is fixed, inlineable and checked before the program runs.
Generic library and framework code in languages whose type system can bind behaviour to types - C++ templates and concepts, Rust trait bounds, Scala contextual abstractions, and to a lesser degree C#, Kotlin, Swift and TypeScript generics: several orthogonal axes vary independently, the variant is known when the host type is instantiated, and the component is a widely reused primitive or a hot path where a virtual call, an allocation, or a per-instance configuration flag is undesirable.
Library primitives with several orthogonal decisions: smart pointers (ownership, checking, conversion, storage), object pools and allocators (allocation, threading), hash containers (hasher, equality, allocator) - a few policy classes covering an exponential family of types.
Numerical and algorithmic kernels that must run checked (assertions, bounds checks) in debug builds and unchecked in release builds without maintaining two parallel class hierarchies.
Object factories and registries whose creation method is the axis (new, clone/prototype, arena, pooled) while the lookup algorithm stays fixed - Alexandrescu's Creator/PrototypeCreator example.
Reusable components whose logging, locking or serialization strategy must be chosen per product configuration: no-op versus real logger, single-threaded versus thread-safe, compact versus verbose encoding.
Framework and standard-library style extension points: a component that must accept a user-written hash, comparison or allocation policy without being modified and without a class hierarchy.
Compile-time configuration of a data structure's shape (node layout, cache size, index arithmetic) where the decision is a type-level or constant policy rather than a value passed at run time.
Rust's std::collections::HashMap<K, V, S> makes hashing a type-bound policy: S implements BuildHasher and defaults to RandomState, while with_hasher selects a custom builder for specialized maps.
C++'s std::unordered_map<Key, T, Hash, KeyEqual, Allocator> exposes hashing, equality, and allocation as independent template policy parameters with standard defaults.
.NET 7 generic math uses C# static abstract interface members (for example INumber<TSelf>) so generic algorithms bind arithmetic behavior through a constrained type parameter instead of a runtime strategy.

statement: Decide where and how persistent entities retain their stable database identifier so repeated loads, references, cache entries, updates, and deletions resolve to the same stored record.
name: range
document:
range
interval
Represent a span of values as a single interval value whose bound inclusivity and open ends are explicit, so containment and interval-to-interval comparisons live in one place instead of repeated ad-hoc endpoint tests.
Start and end travel together through the code but every caller re-derives what they mean: containment is written as scattered <= / < comparisons that drift apart, "unbounded" is smuggled in as a sentinel value (Long.MAX_VALUE, 9999-12-31), and interval-to-interval questions - do these two overlap, does one enclose the other, what is the gap between them - have no home at all.
Applies wherever a domain concept is a span rather than a point: validity and effectivity periods, booking and availability windows, quantity or price tiers, measurement buckets, version and address ranges, pagination windows, and query parameters such as a date range. It pays off when the same interval is compared repeatedly or crosses a boundary (persistence, API payloads, UI widgets), because the bound convention then has to be written once instead of re-decided per call site. For a single comparison between two local variables the type is pure overhead.
Validity and effectivity windows: a contract, price or membership is valid over [effectiveFrom, effectiveTo), and every check is a membership test against one interval.
Booking and availability: a room, seat or resource is reserved during an interval; overlap (not adjacency) decides whether a new booking is possible, and back-to-back bookings must be allowed deliberately.
Quantity and price tiers: the unit price depends on the quantity interval ([1,10), [10,50), [50, +inf)), so a container of intervals with containment lookup replaces a cascade of if-statements.
Temporal queries and reporting: "last 7 days", "this quarter", "since the migration" are half-open or open-ended intervals passed to repositories and rendered by date-range pickers.
Version, port and address ranges: a compatibility claim covers [1.2, 2.0) of a library, a firewall rule covers a port interval - containment answers "is this covered?" and intersection answers "do these rules conflict?".
Pagination and slicing windows: a page is an interval over a sequence, and half-open semantics make adjacency exact ([0,20) followed by [20,40)),
PostgreSQL range and multirange columns: PostgreSQL's daterange, tsrange and numeric range types make lower-inclusive/upper-exclusive bounds, overlap and containment operators, and indexed range queries part of the persistence contract; choose the bound convention before mapping domain intervals.
Guava Range: Java's Guava Range models convex bounded or unbounded intervals with nine open/closed forms, isConnected and intersection; use ContiguousSet only when a discrete domain really requires enumeration rather than treating the interval itself as a sequence.
Standard-library and container choices: Rust's std::ops::RangeBounds covers included, excluded and unbounded bounds when its range forms fit; for many intervals requiring join/split policies, Boost ICL's interval_set and interval_map supply the container semantics instead of overloading one Range value.

name: point-to-point-channel
document:
point-to-point-channel
point-to-point queue
p2p channel
Deliver each message on a channel to exactly one consumer, so senders never have to coordinate with receivers and no unit of work is handled twice.
A producer must hand work to exactly one handler while several receivers are running (or the intended handler is temporarily unavailable): broadcasting the message makes every receiver deduplicate, and addressing a specific consumer instance couples the sender to its identity, location and liveness.
Asynchronous messaging inside one process, between processes or across services, where each message is a unit of work (command, job, document, RPC request) and duplicate handling is as unacceptable as loss. Applies to in-process worker queues and to brokered channels (JMS queue, AMQP queue, Kafka partition, cloud queue) alike; the channel - not the consumer and not the sender - owns the routing decision.
Work queues: a web tier enqueues jobs and a pool of workers consumes them, with each job running exactly once.
Request-reply over messaging: the request goes to a queue, exactly one service instance answers it, and the reply returns on a reply queue identified by a correlation identifier.
Command dispatch in a service-oriented system: an order service appends commands that exactly one instance of the command processor executes.
Media or log processing pipelines where every stage pulls its input from a queue and each item is handled by one of the stage's replicas.
Legacy and batch integration: jobs handed to a single consumer daemon through a queue, with the channel providing the transactional hand-off.
Scaling an existing single-consumer endpoint by attaching additional instances (Competing Consumers) without changing producers or the message contract.
Apache Kafka consumer groups: records in each topic partition are assigned to one group member at a time, so a group scales work while separate group IDs retain independent pub-sub copies.
RabbitMQ Work Queues: a task queue distributes jobs among competing workers with round-robin or fair dispatch; manual acknowledgements allow unacknowledged work to be redelivered after a worker failure.
Amazon SQS Standard queues: distribute background jobs among consumers with visibility timeouts, while at-least-once delivery requires idempotent handlers because duplicate deliveries remain possible.

statement: Choose where to enforce one consistent policy that captures attributable, outcome-aware security events around delegated payment operations without relying on each service to emit its own records.
name: bulkhead
document:
bulkhead
bulkhead isolation
cell-based architecture
Partition finite shared capacity at the failure domain (dependency, tenant, priority class, or cell) into independently bounded pools or permits, with an explicit queue and saturation policy, so one slow, saturated, or failing participant cannot consume capacity reserved for others.
Several dependencies or tenants share thread, connection, worker, or permit pools. When one becomes slow, leaky, or overloaded, its calls hold shared slots and fill shared queues, so unrelated work queues and fails behind it; the design needs a boundary that contains resource exhaustion without pretending to isolate CPU, network, or server-side limits that remain shared.
Any component whose concurrency is a finite resource: a service calling multiple downstream APIs, a multi-tenant workload, a job runner mixing interactive and batch work, or an inference and gateway tier with per-deployment quotas. The failure mode to contain is degradation and overload (slow dependency, connection leak, traffic spike), not only hard failure, and the isolation boundary must be chosen at the failure domain - instance, dependency, tenant or priority class.
A service that calls several downstream APIs through one shared HTTP client: give each downstream its own connection and thread budget so one hanging endpoint cannot block the others.
Multi-tenant SaaS where one tenant's workload must not consume the concurrency available to other tenants (per-tenant pools).
Interactive request traffic sharing a database with batch or report jobs: separate pools per workload class keep the database from serialising everything behind the batch.
An API gateway or backend-for-frontend routing to many backends with per-route concurrency caps, so a slow backend does not consume the proxy's shared capacity.
Job workers that mix latency-critical and background queues: per-queue worker pools prevent a backlog of background jobs from starving urgent work.
Inference and AI serving where each model deployment has its own concurrency quota and a saturated model must not consume the shared request capacity.
Cell-based architectures: each cell (complete, independent service instance) is a bulkhead partition; load grows by adding cells, and a failure is contained to the single cell — used at AWS, Google, and Netflix scale.
Shuffle sharding: Amazon Route 53-style virtual shard assignment where each tenant is assigned to a random shard of two or more cells; with eight cells and two-per-shard there are 28 unique shards, so a problem affects only 1/28th of tenants — far better than regular per-cell partitioning.
AI and inference workloads: per-deployment or per-tenant Azure OpenAI or LLM deployment quotas prevent one saturated model from consuming the shared request capacity across the platform.
Database RU isolation: Azure Cosmos DB request-unit throughput assigned per container acts as a storage-layer bulkhead; one noisy container cannot exhaust the RU budget of others.
Resilience4j's SemaphoreBulkhead and FixedThreadPoolBulkhead give a JVM service per-dependency permits versus a bounded queue and worker pool; choose based on whether caller threads may be occupied.
Netflix Hystrix's per-command thread pools or semaphore isolation reject work and route it to fallback, containing a slow downstream to its command boundary (historical and deprecated).
.NET services use Polly's BulkheadPolicy/AsyncBulkheadPolicy (maxParallelization plus maxQueuingActions, rejecting with BulkheadRejectedException when both are full); Polly v8 replaced it with ConcurrencyLimiter over System.Threading.RateLimiting, whose partitioned per-key limiters give per-tenant bulkheads.
Service meshes enforce bulkheads at the platform layer: an Istio DestinationRule's trafficPolicy.connectionPool caps tcp.maxConnections, http.http1MaxPendingRequests and http.http2MaxRequests per upstream host, enforced by Envoy alongside its circuit-breaking limits.
Netflix's concurrency-limits library replaces hand-tuned static partitions with per-dependency adaptive limits (Vegas and Gradient algorithms modelled on TCP congestion control) that shrink the concurrency budget automatically as downstream latency rises, e.g. separating live from batch traffic on one gRPC server.
Envoy maintains per-upstream-cluster connection pools and circuit-breaking limits, while Kubernetes ResourceQuota caps aggregate namespace CPU, memory, or object use; both are platform-level capacity partitions rather than application call-site wrappers.

statement: Select the approach that lets an independent control service invalidate future session use after logout without destroying the account or requiring the handler's cooperation.
name: identity-field
document:
identity-field
primary key field
identity column
Store the relational primary key inside the object so that an in-memory instance and its database row are recognised as the same entity across sessions, caches and process restarts, instead of relying on object identity.
Mappers, identity maps and unit-of-work bookkeeping need a stable handle on every object: without a key carried by the object there is no way to tell whether two instances are the same row, which row an UPDATE or DELETE must touch, or what value a referring row should store - and loading the same row twice silently produces two divergent objects.
Applies wherever objects outlive a single operation and are mapped to key-addressed rows: entities behind a Data Mapper or Row Data Gateway, aggregates in a Repository, session caches keyed by table plus id, and object graphs whose children must refer to a parent that is not inserted yet. The key has to survive serialisation and cross-process calls, and for application-generated keys it must exist before the row does.
ORM entities in a session: load a row into an object, mutate business fields, then flush an UPDATE or DELETE targeted at the same identity.
API resources addressed by key: /orders/{id} endpoints that fetch, mutate and delete by identity, with links stored as keys instead of object references.
Session-scoped identity maps and second-level caches keyed by (table, key), which need the key before they can return an existing instance.
Object graphs with parent-child references: the child's foreign key needs the parent's identity, generated before the insert (UUID/sequence) or read back after it (RETURNING/getGeneratedKeys).
Audit, versioning and optimistic locking: change logs and Version Number checks identify the affected row by its key.
Distributed or sharded writes: client-generated keys let a router place the row and let a retry overwrite the same identity idempotently.
Event-sourced aggregates: the aggregate root's identity is the correlation ID carried in every command and event, allowing the event log to reconstruct state by replaying events keyed to that identity.
GraphQL Relay node identification: globally unique node IDs are built from the entity's identity (base64 type-prefixed id), enabling the standardised node query and cache reching defined in the Relay specification.
Multi-tenant SaaS with tenant-scoped identity: a composite key of (tenant_id, id) ensures a tenant can never address another tenant's rows, even if the local id numbers happen to collide.
Idempotent message processing: a command's correlation ID (the entity's identity) lets a handler detect a duplicate and skip reprocessing without a distributed lock.
Hibernate ORM entities with an @Id and Session persistence context: loading by identifier reuses the session's first-level identity, while the chosen generated-id strategy determines when the key becomes available.
PostgreSQL tables with GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY and INSERT ... RETURNING id: the database owns key generation, then the mapper reads the assigned identity back onto the object in the same write.
Relay GraphQL servers implementing the Node interface: expose a globally unique opaque id and refetch the same object through node(id), carrying entity identity across a client cache and API boundary.

statement: Choose how to give the iterator adapter compile-time access to the custom iterator's core hooks without exposing its storage or unrelated private operations.
name: iterator
document:
iterator
cursor
enumerator
Provide a way to access the elements of an aggregate object sequentially without exposing its underlying representation, by moving traversal state and the traversal algorithm out of the aggregate into a separate iterator object.
Traversal leaks into every client: code that walks a collection has to know its storage layout (array indices, node links, hash buckets), the same loop is rewritten once per aggregate and once per client, and adding a new traversal order means changing the aggregate's interface — which is exactly what prevents algorithms from being written once and applied to any collection.
Applies wherever a collection with a non-trivial or changeable representation must be traversed by outsiders: collection libraries, trees and graphs with several traversal orders, lazy or unbounded sources, and streaming pipelines. It matters most when more than one traversal may be pending at the same time, when the storage must stay hidden for encapsulation or safety, or when traversal algorithms must be added without touching the aggregate; the toolchain only decides which realization is available (a language iteration protocol, generators, lazy sequences, or a hand-written cursor).
Collection libraries that must serve arrays, linked lists, trees, and hash tables through one protocol — e.g. std::begin/end in C++, java.util.Iterator, IEnumerable<T> in C#, Symbol.iterator in JavaScript, IntoIterator in Rust.
Tree and graph APIs exposing depth-first, breadth-first, in-order, or post-order traversal without publishing node links or parent pointers, enabling clients to walk composite structures without coupling to the storage representation.
Lazy or unbounded sources consumed one element at a time: file lines (BufferedReader.lines()), network socket streams, paginated API responses, sensor data, event streams, and generated sequences (random numbers, Fibonacci, permutations).
Streaming data pipelines (map/filter/reduce over any iterable) that stay O(1) in memory regardless of input size, implemented via itertools, Java Stream API, Kotlin Sequence, C++ ranges, Rust iterator adapters, or Go iter package.
Legacy or third-party aggregates whose internal layout must stay private behind a stable traversal interface, allowing the aggregate to refactor its storage without breaking existing clients.
Custom containers that must participate in the language's own for/foreach/for-in/for-await loop, spread operators, destructuring assignment, or list comprehensions.
Database result sets and ORM cursors where the full result set is never materialised in memory; the iterator fetches pages on demand.
Parser and lexer token streams where the input is consumed incrementally and the full source may not fit in memory.
Async I/O pipelines where the iteration protocol yields Promises (JavaScript async generators, C# IAsyncEnumerable<T>, Python async generators) enabling for-await iteration over network responses or file reads.
Multidimensional collection traversal (matrices, nested lists, spatial grids) via flattened iterators that expose a flat index space while hiding the multi-dimensional layout.
Paginated REST or GraphQL API clients where a client-side iterator transparently fetches successive pages as the consumer pulls elements, keeping memory constant regardless of result set size.
Kafka, log-processor, or ETL pipelines where each stage is a transforming iterator: parse → filter → enrich → validate → sink, with each stage evaluated lazily.
Event-driven systems using async iterators to consume WebSocket messages, SSE streams, or queue consumers through a uniform for-await-of interface.
Batch-processing jobs over large file sets (CSV, Parquet, NDJSON) where an iterator wraps a file reader and yields one record per next() call without loading the file into memory.
Cursor-based (keyset) pagination over large, live datasets where offset/limit pagination causes duplicates or missed rows when data is inserted or deleted mid-traversal; the iterator stores the last-seen key rather than a page offset, making traversal stable across concurrent modifications.
Iterator fusion in compilers and runtimes: adjacent map/filter/map chains fused into a single pass with zero intermediate allocation (Rust iterator adapters, Java Spliterators, Haskell stream fusion, C++ range views), giving lazy pipelines near-handwritten performance.
Parallel iterators for data-parallel workloads: Rust Rayon, Java parallel streams, and Kotlin asFlow().buffer() split the iterator across worker threads — identical interface to serial iteration, transparent parallel execution.
Reactive streams bridging pull and push: RxJava, RxJS, and Project Reactor implement backpressure (consumer signals demand, producer emits at requested rate), combining iterator's pull semantics with observer's push delivery.
LLM and streaming AI responses where the model yields tokens incrementally; an async iterator wraps the SSE/stream endpoint and the client consumes tokens one at a time via for-await-of, keeping first-token latency low and enabling progressive rendering.
Cursor-based database driver iterators (Node.js pg cursor, Python asyncpg, Go database/sql rows) where the driver streams rows from the server without loading the full result set, with configurable fetch size controlling server-side memory usage.
Java's Spliterator API exposes a cursor that can be advanced one element at a time or split into subranges for parallel streams; it demonstrates that an iterator contract can include explicit partitioning and size/order characteristics rather than only next().
.NET's IAsyncEnumerable<T> and IAsyncEnumerator<T> expose asynchronous pull iteration through await foreach; GetAsyncEnumerator(CancellationToken) makes cancellation part of the iterator boundary for network, file, and database streams.
WHATWG ReadableStream async iteration lets browser and server consumers use for-await-of over streamed chunks while the iterator locks a reader and defines whether early return() cancels or merely releases it.

name: strategy
document:
strategy
policy
Define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one behind a common operation, and make them interchangeable, so the algorithm a context executes can vary independently of the context and its clients - including at run time.
One class supports several variants of the same computation - sort orders, pricing or tax rules, routing and backoff policies, compression codecs - and the variant has to be selected at run time. Hard-wiring the variants into the class (or into one subclass per variant) mixes algorithm detail with the class's own logic, forces recompilation for every new variant, and turns selection into a growing conditional that runs on every call.
Applies when one context object owns the data but delegates one algorithm (or a small set of related algorithms) to a pluggable implementation, when the implementations share a stable operation signature, and when the choice is made at run time - from user input, configuration, request data or deployment - or from a closed family of variants that already differ in space/time or accuracy trade-offs. Typical homes: pricing, discount and tax calculation; sorting and comparison orders; routing, load-balancing, retry/backoff and rate-limiting policies; compression, serialization and encoding codecs; validation and normalization rules; numerical solvers chosen per problem.
Pricing, discount and tax calculation where the rule set is selected per customer, region or campaign and changes independently of the checkout or invoicing flow.
Sorting and comparison orders chosen by context - a UI column, a request parameter, a locale - which is how the JDK uses the pattern for Comparator in Collections.sort/List.sort and how C uses it for qsort's comparison function.
Routing and policy selection: path finding, load balancing, retry/backoff and rate-limiting algorithms chosen from configuration without editing the caller.
Compression, serialization and encoding codecs (gzip/deflate/zstd, JSON/Protobuf, character encodings) selected per stream, per record or per request.
Validation and normalization rule sets for pluggable document or form types, where each variant knows its own schema quirks and error format.
Numerical and scientific kernels: integration, interpolation or solver algorithms chosen per problem with different accuracy/performance trade-offs.
Pluggable authentication/authorization or hashing policies chosen per tenant, where the same code path must run different algorithms behind one signature.
E-commerce shipping provider selection (UPS, FedEx, DHL) where each carrier implements a different rate-calculation algorithm, and the shipping calculator is decoupled from the carrier specifics.
Payment processing gateways (credit card, virtual account, wallet) where each method has distinct validation, fee calculation and settlement rules, but the checkout flow is uniform.
Data retrieval at runtime: selecting between an API client, a web scraper, a database query or a cache-first lookup depending on availability, cost or latency requirements.
ML inference: choosing between ONNX, TensorRT, CPU or GPU backends for model execution, each with different latency/throughput trade-offs, selected per request or per deployment environment.
Travel and navigation: routing algorithms (walking, cycling, driving, public transit) with distinct distance/time/transfer calculations, chosen by user preference or real-time conditions.
Hybrid AI systems: combining symbolic decision logic with sub-symbolic ML model inference behind a uniform interface, enabling runtime selection of the reasoning strategy.
Log routing: dispatching log events to different backends (file, console, cloud observability platforms) selected by deployment environment or tenant configuration.
Encryption and cipher suites: selecting TLS cipher suites, password hashing algorithms (bcrypt, argon2), or encoding schemes based on security policy and compliance requirements.
File format processing: parsing and rendering strategies for documents, images, or data files where each format requires different handling but the pipeline remains uniform.
Game AI: selecting enemy behavior algorithms (aggressive, defensive, evasive, patrol) per entity type or difficulty level, enabling runtime personality changes.
Apache Kafka producers select or replace the partition-selection algorithm through the org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.Partitioner interface (default sticky/key-hash, RoundRobinPartitioner for even distribution), configured per producer via partitioner.class.
Envoy proxy chooses one load balancing algorithm per upstream cluster from the envoy.load_balancing_policies extension category (ROUND_ROBIN, LEAST_REQUEST and third-party policies), each implementing one host-selection operation behind the cluster's router call path.
scikit-learn estimators expose interchangeable optimization algorithms behind one fit/predict API via the solver parameter (LogisticRegression: lbfgs, liblinear, saga, newton-cg, newton-cholesky), documented as a choice driven by dataset size and penalty rather than by a different client interface.

name: abstract-factory
document:
abstract-factory
kit
factory of factories
Expose one creation contract for each product kind in a coherent family, letting clients switch the selected family at the composition root without naming concrete products or mixing incompatible variants.
A client must construct several related products that collaborate as a matched set, but direct construction spreads family keys and concrete class names through the code. Adding a family then becomes configuration branches plus constructor edits, while mixing products from different families can fail only after incompatible objects interact.
Use in object- or interface-based subsystems with two independent axes of change: product kinds (button, slider, connection, command) and product families or variants (dark/light, PostgreSQL/Oracle, AWS/GCP). The family is normally selected once at a composition root, products from one family are intended to collaborate, and clients must compile, test and ship without knowing concrete product types; if products are intentionally mixed or only one kind is created, use a smaller creator instead.
Cross-platform or themable UI toolkits: Qt's QStyleFactory resolves keys such as "windows" and "fusion" to built-in or plugin QStyle implementations that govern a coherent widget look-and-feel; a fuller abstract factory applies the same family key across several product interfaces.
Provider-independent database code: ADO.NET's DbProviderFactory/DbProviderFactories create a matched DbConnection, DbCommand, DbParameter and DbDataAdapter set for a selected provider such as SQL Server or OLE DB.
Parser-provider plugins: JAXP's DocumentBuilderFactory and SAXParserFactory hide implementation classes behind standard factory APIs, allowing the composition root to select a provider while client code uses parser abstractions.
Java's ServiceLoader documentation uses a CodecFactory service with getEncoder and getDecoder operations; the selected provider supplies a coherent codec family while clients depend only on the service interface.
Test infrastructure: an in-memory factory family whose products are fakes, injected in place of the production family so integration tests need no network.
Game and simulation engines: per-biome object families (terrain, props, audio) that must stay aesthetically consistent when a level is loaded.
SaaS multi-tenant applications: per-tenant theme factories so every rendered page uses the tenant's brand colours, fonts and spacing without per-request conditionals.
Document-format parsers: factory per format (PDF, HTML, EPUB) producing matched tokenizer, layout engine and renderer so a viewer can switch formats from a single configuration key.

name: bulkhead
document:
bulkhead
bulkhead isolation
cell-based architecture
Partition finite shared capacity at the failure domain (dependency, tenant, priority class, or cell) into independently bounded pools or permits, with an explicit queue and saturation policy, so one slow, saturated, or failing participant cannot consume capacity reserved for others.
Several dependencies or tenants share thread, connection, worker, or permit pools. When one becomes slow, leaky, or overloaded, its calls hold shared slots and fill shared queues, so unrelated work queues and fails behind it; the design needs a boundary that contains resource exhaustion without pretending to isolate CPU, network, or server-side limits that remain shared.
Any component whose concurrency is a finite resource: a service calling multiple downstream APIs, a multi-tenant workload, a job runner mixing interactive and batch work, or an inference and gateway tier with per-deployment quotas. The failure mode to contain is degradation and overload (slow dependency, connection leak, traffic spike), not only hard failure, and the isolation boundary must be chosen at the failure domain - instance, dependency, tenant or priority class.
A service that calls several downstream APIs through one shared HTTP client: give each downstream its own connection and thread budget so one hanging endpoint cannot block the others.
Multi-tenant SaaS where one tenant's workload must not consume the concurrency available to other tenants (per-tenant pools).
Interactive request traffic sharing a database with batch or report jobs: separate pools per workload class keep the database from serialising everything behind the batch.
An API gateway or backend-for-frontend routing to many backends with per-route concurrency caps, so a slow backend does not consume the proxy's shared capacity.
Job workers that mix latency-critical and background queues: per-queue worker pools prevent a backlog of background jobs from starving urgent work.
Inference and AI serving where each model deployment has its own concurrency quota and a saturated model must not consume the shared request capacity.
Cell-based architectures: each cell (complete, independent service instance) is a bulkhead partition; load grows by adding cells, and a failure is contained to the single cell — used at AWS, Google, and Netflix scale.
Shuffle sharding: Amazon Route 53-style virtual shard assignment where each tenant is assigned to a random shard of two or more cells; with eight cells and two-per-shard there are 28 unique shards, so a problem affects only 1/28th of tenants — far better than regular per-cell partitioning.
AI and inference workloads: per-deployment or per-tenant Azure OpenAI or LLM deployment quotas prevent one saturated model from consuming the shared request capacity across the platform.
Database RU isolation: Azure Cosmos DB request-unit throughput assigned per container acts as a storage-layer bulkhead; one noisy container cannot exhaust the RU budget of others.
Resilience4j's SemaphoreBulkhead and FixedThreadPoolBulkhead give a JVM service per-dependency permits versus a bounded queue and worker pool; choose based on whether caller threads may be occupied.
Netflix Hystrix's per-command thread pools or semaphore isolation reject work and route it to fallback, containing a slow downstream to its command boundary (historical and deprecated).
.NET services use Polly's BulkheadPolicy/AsyncBulkheadPolicy (maxParallelization plus maxQueuingActions, rejecting with BulkheadRejectedException when both are full); Polly v8 replaced it with ConcurrencyLimiter over System.Threading.RateLimiting, whose partitioned per-key limiters give per-tenant bulkheads.
Service meshes enforce bulkheads at the platform layer: an Istio DestinationRule's trafficPolicy.connectionPool caps tcp.maxConnections, http.http1MaxPendingRequests and http.http2MaxRequests per upstream host, enforced by Envoy alongside its circuit-breaking limits.
Netflix's concurrency-limits library replaces hand-tuned static partitions with per-dependency adaptive limits (Vegas and Gradient algorithms modelled on TCP congestion control) that shrink the concurrency budget automatically as downstream latency rises, e.g. separating live from batch traffic on one gRPC server.
Envoy maintains per-upstream-cluster connection pools and circuit-breaking limits, while Kubernetes ResourceQuota caps aggregate namespace CPU, memory, or object use; both are platform-level capacity partitions rather than application call-site wrappers.

statement: Choose where every inbound queue message receives schema, size, encoding, and range validation so malformed events cannot reach any business handler.
name: policy-based-design
document:
policy-based-design
policy-based class design
policy-based programming
Assemble a class's behaviour, structure and defaults from small interchangeable policy units bound when the host type is instantiated, so that each orthogonal design decision can be varied independently instead of being frozen in the class's code.
A reusable class hard-codes several independent design decisions - allocation, ownership, storage, threading, validation, error handling - inside its implementation, so a different combination is only reachable by editing or copying the class, while the runtime Strategy alternative costs a virtual call per use and gives up the guarantee that the choice is fixed, inlineable and checked before the program runs.
Generic library and framework code in languages whose type system can bind behaviour to types - C++ templates and concepts, Rust trait bounds, Scala contextual abstractions, and to a lesser degree C#, Kotlin, Swift and TypeScript generics: several orthogonal axes vary independently, the variant is known when the host type is instantiated, and the component is a widely reused primitive or a hot path where a virtual call, an allocation, or a per-instance configuration flag is undesirable.
Library primitives with several orthogonal decisions: smart pointers (ownership, checking, conversion, storage), object pools and allocators (allocation, threading), hash containers (hasher, equality, allocator) - a few policy classes covering an exponential family of types.
Numerical and algorithmic kernels that must run checked (assertions, bounds checks) in debug builds and unchecked in release builds without maintaining two parallel class hierarchies.
Object factories and registries whose creation method is the axis (new, clone/prototype, arena, pooled) while the lookup algorithm stays fixed - Alexandrescu's Creator/PrototypeCreator example.
Reusable components whose logging, locking or serialization strategy must be chosen per product configuration: no-op versus real logger, single-threaded versus thread-safe, compact versus verbose encoding.
Framework and standard-library style extension points: a component that must accept a user-written hash, comparison or allocation policy without being modified and without a class hierarchy.
Compile-time configuration of a data structure's shape (node layout, cache size, index arithmetic) where the decision is a type-level or constant policy rather than a value passed at run time.
Rust's std::collections::HashMap<K, V, S> makes hashing a type-bound policy: S implements BuildHasher and defaults to RandomState, while with_hasher selects a custom builder for specialized maps.
C++'s std::unordered_map<Key, T, Hash, KeyEqual, Allocator> exposes hashing, equality, and allocation as independent template policy parameters with standard defaults.
.NET 7 generic math uses C# static abstract interface members (for example INumber<TSelf>) so generic algorithms bind arithmetic behavior through a constrained type parameter instead of a runtime strategy.

name: identity-map
document:
identity-map
first-level cache
session cache
Guarantee that within one session every database row is represented by exactly one in-memory object, by keeping a keyed registry of loaded objects that every load consults before hitting the database.
Two code paths in the same session load the same row into two different objects: updates through one are invisible to the other, the last flush silently wins, and every load pays the remote-call cost again. The catalog states the invariant as: the same row must never be two different in-memory objects in one session.
Object-oriented persistence (data mappers, repositories, unit of work) where entities carry a stable database identity (an Identity Field) and several parts of one business transaction or request refer to the same rows. Applies whenever duplicate in-memory instances would break graph consistency or lose updates - typically inside an ORM session or a hand-written persistence context whose lifetime bounds staleness.
ORM sessions in web request handling (JPA EntityManager, EF Core DbContext, SQLAlchemy Session, MikroORM EntityManager) where several services touch the same entities in one request.
Batch import and synchronisation jobs that re-read the same rows repeatedly inside one transaction and must not operate on divergent copies.
Object graph reconstruction in data mappers, where cycles and shared references need one in-memory instance per row.
Desktop and document applications with a context-scoped object space (Core Data contexts) where objects are edited, undone and saved as one unit.
Hand-written persistence layers over plain SQL where two repositories serve the same table and must agree on identity.
CQRS command handlers where the same aggregate is loaded multiple times within one command execution — the identity map prevents duplicate instances from forming across repository calls within the same session.
Event-sourced aggregate reconstruction: replaying events to rebuild aggregate state requires the same aggregate instance to accumulate state across multiple event applications; identity map guarantees a single instance per aggregate ID per reconstruction session.
Microservices saga and choreography: within one service's unit-of-work, multiple steps may load the same entity; identity map ensures all steps operate on the same instance even when the entity is referenced across different event handlers.
DDD bounded-context integration: when one bounded context holds a reference to an entity from another context (by ID), that entity is resolved through the local identity map — multiple resolution paths must all consult the same map to stay consistent.
Testing scenarios where the same entity is accessed via multiple repository paths: identity map guarantees test assertions see the same instance regardless of which repository method returned it, enabling meaningful state verification.
Multi-tenant applications where each tenant request gets its own session/identity-map scope, preventing cross-tenant data leakage by construction — a shared/global map would allow one tenant's rows to shadow another's.
SQLAlchemy Session.get in a unit of work: repeated primary-key loads return the same Python object from the Session identity map, while the Session is deliberately not a cross-session query cache.
EF Core tracked queries and AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution: the DbContext keeps one entity instance per key for tracked results, while no-tracking identity resolution is opt-in for read models.
Hibernate Session persistence contexts: repeated loads of the same entity type and identifier resolve to the one managed instance per Session, so entity graphs and dirty checking share state.

name: dynamic-router
document:
dynamic-router
dynamic routing
rules-based routing
Route each message to a destination chosen from a rule base that can be changed while the system runs, so the router never depends on - or is redeployed for - the set of destinations it serves.
Routing logic hard-coded into the router (switch chains, static filter tables, deployment-time route configuration) couples it to every destination: adding, moving, throttling or retiring a destination needs a code change, a review and a restart, and each topology change forces the router back through the release process instead of being an operational edit.
Message-based integration where the destination set or the routing policy changes faster than the router's release cycle: rules are owned by operations, destinations announce themselves, scale out, or go down for maintenance, or one router instance serves several tenants or environments. Applies when the route can be expressed as rules over message content, headers or context evaluated per message, and the platform offers a usable control channel (config watch, control bus, admin endpoint, hot-reloadable table) to publish rule changes.
Multi-tenant integration hub: each tenant has its own routing table, loaded and swapped per tenant instead of one deployed router per tenant.
Event distribution where downstream teams add or retire consumers by publishing routing conditions rather than requesting a router release.
Canary and blue/green rollouts: send a slice of traffic to a new destination by editing a rule, and roll back by restoring the previous rule set.
Maintenance windows: reroute a destination's traffic to a standby, drain the destination, then restore the rule when it returns.
Regional or sharded routing where the region-to-destination mapping is maintained by operations and changes with capacity, not with code.
Rule-driven enterprise integration in the classic EIP sense, where a rule base is consulted per message and recipients announce themselves on a control channel.
Kubernetes Gateway API traffic splitting: use HTTPRoute weighted backends to shift a configurable percentage of traffic between versions without redeploying the router.
Service mesh canary deployments: an Istio VirtualService or Linkerd ServiceProfile acts as the rule base; routing rules are edited at runtime to steer canary traffic, then promoted or rolled back.
Multi-tenant SaaS routing: Spring Cloud Gateway or Envoy.DynamicRouter loads per-tenant routing rules from a registry, injecting tenant-specific headers or rewrites so one router instance serves hundreds of isolated tenants.
API version routing and A/B testing: route by Accept header, API version path prefix, or experimentCohort header to different backend versions, controlled by rules updated without a release.
Database or cache sharding: route a tenant or user ID hash to the correct shard's endpoint via a rule table that is repointed during resharding without touching application code.
BGP route-server testing: use a chaos-testing framework against a route server to validate that policy changes converge correctly and do not produce route leaks before production deployment.
Traefik dynamic configuration: Traefik builds its routing table at runtime from providers (Docker labels, Kubernetes IngressRoute, Consul/etcd KV stores), so services announce their own routes and rule changes hot-swap without restarting the proxy.
HAProxy Runtime API: add server and set server state/weight over the runtime socket repoint and drain backends without a reload; the Data Plane API layers persistence and validation on top of these runtime changes.
Kong Gateway admin API: Routes - including the expressions DSL when router_flavor is set to expressions - are created and updated at runtime via POST /routes and take effect on the next matching request, with priority-ordered rule evaluation replacing a redeployed config.

statement: Choose a type-specific test setup API that supplies valid account defaults while each lockout test states only the security condition it verifies.
name: adapter
document:
adapter
wrapper
adaptor
Present an existing component through the exact target contract its client already consumes, translating calls, results and boundary semantics without adding responsibilities or pretending a missing capability exists.
An existing or foreign component has useful behaviour but speaks a different protocol: method names and signatures, data shapes, units, lifecycle, error model or sync/async contract do not satisfy the target. If every caller performs ad hoc conversion, semantics drift, vendor types leak and provider replacement becomes a cross-cutting rewrite; changing the adaptee or target may be impossible or too disruptive.
Integration work where one side is outside your control: legacy modules, vendor SDKs, generated clients, foreign data formats or units, and the ports-and-adapters boundary of a hexagonal architecture. Applies in statically typed languages - where an adapter class is also the compile-time proof that the required interface is satisfied - and in structurally or dynamically typed ones, where a thin wrapper usually replaces a declared target interface.
Wrapping a third-party or vendor SDK behind your own interface so business code never imports vendor types.
Modernising a legacy module incrementally: new code talks to the target interface while the old component is adapted in place.
Supporting several interchangeable providers (payments, storage, messaging, analytics) through one internal contract, with one adapter each.
Adapting a callback- or error-first API to promises/async or to an observer-style interface.
Ports-and-adapters boundaries where one domain port is realized over different transports (HTTP, message queue, in-process fake).
Unifying differently shaped data sources (row sets, DTOs, XML or JSON payloads) into one model before they reach domain logic.
Test doubles: an in-memory adapter satisfies the target interface without the real infrastructure.
API wrapper libraries: normalising third-party REST/gRPC APIs (Stripe, Twilio, payment providers) into a stable internal contract so business logic never imports vendor SDK types.
Legacy system integration: wrapping SOAP, CORBA, or mainframe APIs behind a modern interface, enabling incremental migration without rewriting existing clients.
Cloud provider abstraction: a single internal storage or queue interface implemented by AWS, GCP, or Azure adapters, letting the application swap providers via configuration.
ETL pipelines: adapting heterogeneous source record schemas (CSV, JSON, XML, database rows) into one canonical domain record, isolating format changes from downstream consumers.
Event-stream and streaming adapters: translating WebSocket frames or server-sent events into domain events in real time.
Multi-cloud and provider-agnostic interfaces: storage adapters (S3, GCS, Azure Blob), queue adapters (SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka), and notification adapters that abstract away provider-specific SDKs.
Backend for Frontend (BFF): each front-end client (web, mobile, third-party) gets its own lightweight adapter that shapes internal service responses into the exact payload that client needs.
Java's java.io.InputStreamReader is a byte-to-character bridge: it presents an InputStream through the Reader contract while decoding with an explicit charset.
SLF4J uses providers such as slf4j-reload4j to bind one Logger API to different backends, while log4j-over-slf4j and jul-to-slf4j redirect legacy APIs at a migration boundary; Spring MVC's HandlerAdapter similarly lets DispatcherServlet handle heterogeneous handler types through one SPI.
Go's net/http.HandlerFunc gives an ordinary func(ResponseWriter, *Request) the http.Handler contract by attaching ServeHTTP, so routing and middleware can consume functions and handlers uniformly.

statement: Decide where the payment validation and navigation rules should live so they can be verified synchronously outside the framework-controlled screen.
name: table-module
document:
table-module
Organise the domain logic of a table or view as one module with a single instance whose operations act on whole sets of rows, so table-shaped rules are written once against tabular record sets instead of being scattered over per-row objects or per-request procedures.
The rules for a table are set-shaped - recalculating a column across all rows, validating an import batch, posting a period, aggregating or exporting a whole table - and the platform already speaks in tables and record sets (result sets, DataTables, grids, reports). A Domain Model would build one object per row and pay for identity, hydration and per-object behaviour the rules never use, while a Transaction Script repeats the same table-shaped logic in every use case that touches the table.
Data-centric enterprise applications with moderate, table-shaped logic: batch jobs, imports and reconciliation, reporting and export modules, and applications whose UI and data tooling is table-based (typed DataSets, data grids, report engines). It assumes that data access is already provided by a Table Data Gateway or equivalent, and that callers - typically a Service Layer - own the transaction boundary around the module's calls.
Periodic batch posting: recompute balances or fees for every row in a period in one set-oriented pass.
Import and reconciliation: validate, normalise and promote a staging table before its rows become live data, reporting row-level errors as a batch.
Reporting and export modules that fetch a record set for a grid, report engine or CSV/Excel export, where tabular output is the goal.
Bulk recalculation after a rule change: apply a corrected formula to all existing rows of a table without loading them into a model.
Small-to-medium applications where each table has a handful of well-defined operations and no rich invariants spanning rows or tables.
Cleansing and reconciliation jobs over an operational table where the database should do the heavy lifting (aggregate, update ... where) and the application only orchestrates.
.NET ADO.NET typed DataSet / typed DataTable modules: the generated table is the record set, business methods operate over all its rows and it binds directly to grids and report controls.
Ruby on Rails set-oriented surface: an ActiveRecord::Relation scoped to one table applies table-wide rules via update_all/delete_all as a single SQL statement without instantiating row models, whose official documentation warns that validations and callbacks are skipped so the statement must carry the rule.
Django set-wide recalculation: QuerySet.update() and bulk_update() write whole filtered sets with direct SQL that bypasses per-row save(), used exactly where per-object persistence would mean one round trip per row.

statement: Choose the contract for a registry miss so callers must recognize ordinary absence without discarding or confusing actionable lookup failures.
name: durable-subscriber
document:
durable-subscriber
durable subscription
durable consumer
Keep a publish-subscribe consumer's place while it is offline: the broker binds a stable subscription identity to retained messages or a committed position, then resumes delivery after reconnect until retention, expiry, or quota says the backlog is no longer available.
A subscriber on a publish-subscribe channel can be unavailable during redeployment, maintenance, device disconnects, or scheduled batch work. A non-durable subscription drops messages published during that gap, so the design must choose a stable identity and broker-side state, then make finite retention, replay pressure, and at-least-once redelivery explicit; durable state prevents a gap only while that state remains available.
Broker-mediated publish-subscribe messaging where consumers are intermittently offline but individual messages matter: JMS topics, MQTT sessions, Kafka consumer groups, NATS JetStream durable consumers, cloud topic subscriptions. It presumes the messaging system can store messages (or positions) durably, so it is as much a broker-configuration decision as a client one, and it presumes at-least-once delivery is acceptable once the consumer is idempotent. It does not apply to in-process notification or to broadcast where only the newest value counts.
A Kafka-backed order-processing service that is redeployed or scaled to zero while events keep arriving: the consumer group resumes from its committed offsets and replays what it missed.
An IoT or mobile client on an intermittent link: an MQTT persistent session holds QoS 1/2 publications for its client id and delivers them when the client reconnects.
A partner integration that receives published documents while the partner's system is down: an unshared JMS durable subscription, or a cloud topic subscription, is registered on their behalf and holds the backlog until they acknowledge it.
A nightly audit or analytics consumer that must see every published change: the day's backlog is drained in bounded batches and acknowledged as it is persisted.
A ledger or compliance consumer that must never silently skip events: retention and lag alarms are configured so an offline subscriber is noticed before its backlog expires.
A cloud event-driven architecture (SNS FIFO → SQS FIFO): SNS preserves ordering and deduplication while SQS queues hold messages for durable fan-out to Lambda or EC2 consumers, with DLQs capturing failed deliveries for replay.
An industrial SCADA/IoT sensor fleet where devices connect sporadically over unstable networks: MQTT persistent sessions with a long session expiry interval preserve every telemetry reading until each device reconnects, even after multi-day outages.
A financial audit trail that must immutably record every state-changing event: events are durably retained in Kafka or JetStream and consumed by a compliance subscriber that must not skip or duplicate entries; idempotent deduplication and offset commits after durable persistence enforce this.
A supply-chain or logistics event-sourcing system where downstream services reconstruct state by replaying events after a crash or deliberate seek: the durable consumer starts from the committed position and replays the missing event window atomically with the state reconstruction.
A cross-region disaster-recovery subscriber that mirrors events to a secondary site: the durable subscription in the secondary region receives every event from the primary's topic, with a DLQ holding any events that fail cross-region delivery for manual retry.
A JMS topic consumer that must receive publications made while it is offline: the client reconnects with the same client identifier and durable subscription name, and the provider retains messages until acknowledgement, expiry, or unsubscribe.
An MQTT 3.1.1 device gateway that reconnects with the same client identifier and CleanSession=0: the broker resumes the stored session and queues matching QoS 1/2 publications for delivery after the link returns.
A NATS JetStream billing worker that restarts after an outage: it binds to the same durable consumer name and explicit-acks each message, so the server resumes its acknowledgement floor and redelivers unacknowledged work.
An Azure Service Bus fan-out topology: topic subscriptions are durable by default and each subscription stores its own copy of matching messages, so a receiver that reconnects later still drains its backlog; client-affine durable subscriptions bind the durable state to a stable client id.
A high-throughput replay consumer on RabbitMQ Streams: the consumer attaches with a stable tracking reference (name) and periodically stores its offset server-side, so a restart resumes from the last stored offset instead of re-reading the whole stream.
An event-sourced system on Google Cloud Pub/Sub that must reprocess history after a bug fix: the subscription enables acknowledged-message retention (default window 7 days, up to 31) and is seeked back to a past timestamp or snapshot to replay already-acked messages.

A subscriber on a publish-subscribe channel can be unavailable during redeployment, maintenance, device disconnects, or scheduled batch work. A non-durable subscription drops messages published during that gap, so the design must choose a stable identity and broker-side state, then make finite retention, replay pressure, and at-least-once redelivery explicit; durable state prevents a gap only while that state remains available.
Broker-mediated publish-subscribe messaging where consumers are intermittently offline but individual messages matter: JMS topics, MQTT sessions, Kafka consumer groups, NATS JetStream durable consumers, cloud topic subscriptions. It presumes the messaging system can store messages (or positions) durably, so it is as much a broker-configuration decision as a client one, and it presumes at-least-once delivery is acceptable once the consumer is idempotent. It does not apply to in-process notification or to broadcast where only the newest value counts.
A Kafka-backed order-processing service that is redeployed or scaled to zero while events keep arriving: the consumer group resumes from its committed offsets and replays what it missed.
An IoT or mobile client on an intermittent link: an MQTT persistent session holds QoS 1/2 publications for its client id and delivers them when the client reconnects.
A partner integration that receives published documents while the partner's system is down: an unshared JMS durable subscription, or a cloud topic subscription, is registered on their behalf and holds the backlog until they acknowledge it.
A nightly audit or analytics consumer that must see every published change: the day's backlog is drained in bounded batches and acknowledged as it is persisted.
A ledger or compliance consumer that must never silently skip events: retention and lag alarms are configured so an offline subscriber is noticed before its backlog expires.
A cloud event-driven architecture (SNS FIFO → SQS FIFO): SNS preserves ordering and deduplication while SQS queues hold messages for durable fan-out to Lambda or EC2 consumers, with DLQs capturing failed deliveries for replay.
An industrial SCADA/IoT sensor fleet where devices connect sporadically over unstable networks: MQTT persistent sessions with a long session expiry interval preserve every telemetry reading until each device reconnects, even after multi-day outages.
A financial audit trail that must immutably record every state-changing event: events are durably retained in Kafka or JetStream and consumed by a compliance subscriber that must not skip or duplicate entries; idempotent deduplication and offset commits after durable persistence enforce this.
A supply-chain or logistics event-sourcing system where downstream services reconstruct state by replaying events after a crash or deliberate seek: the durable consumer starts from the committed position and replays the missing event window atomically with the state reconstruction.
A cross-region disaster-recovery subscriber that mirrors events to a secondary site: the durable subscription in the secondary region receives every event from the primary's topic, with a DLQ holding any events that fail cross-region delivery for manual retry.
A JMS topic consumer that must receive publications made while it is offline: the client reconnects with the same client identifier and durable subscription name, and the provider retains messages until acknowledgement, expiry, or unsubscribe.
An MQTT 3.1.1 device gateway that reconnects with the same client identifier and CleanSession=0: the broker resumes the stored session and queues matching QoS 1/2 publications for delivery after the link returns.
A NATS JetStream billing worker that restarts after an outage: it binds to the same durable consumer name and explicit-acks each message, so the server resumes its acknowledgement floor and redelivers unacknowledged work.
An Azure Service Bus fan-out topology: topic subscriptions are durable by default and each subscription stores its own copy of matching messages, so a receiver that reconnects later still drains its backlog; client-affine durable subscriptions bind the durable state to a stable client id.
A high-throughput replay consumer on RabbitMQ Streams: the consumer attaches with a stable tracking reference (name) and periodically stores its offset server-side, so a restart resumes from the last stored offset instead of re-reading the whole stream.
An event-sourced system on Google Cloud Pub/Sub that must reprocess history after a bug fix: the subscription enables acknowledged-message retention (default window 7 days, up to 31) and is seeked back to a past timestamp or snapshot to replay already-acked messages.
